units.la: REFERT Xenophon (Illustris & Generose Domine Baro) Socratem πάντων ἀνθρώπων σοφώτατον Phœbi ex adytis habitum, quod Philosophiam, queis destinata primum foret, usibus accommodarit humanis. Nam cum ThaleThaletem, Anaximandrum, cæterósque priscorum Coryphæos philosophantium, cœli fiderúmque speculationi tantum intentos, nihílque ne sibi quidem sæpenumero, ne dum aliis aut Reipublicæ prodesse videret: relicta hac inani contemplatione, quâ peritiores non meliores indies fieri poterant homines, ad Philosophiam Practicam, quæ ad bene honesteque vivendum instruit, hortari cunctos serió cœpit: Unde Philosophiam è cœlo primus devocasse dictus erat. Socratis innixus vestigiis Plato, quæ moralem spectant Philosophiam passim ferè scriptis suis infspergit tanta famæ nominisque celebritate sui, ut non Athenis modo, sed & in tota Græcia, nec in Græcia tantum, sed in remotissimis orbis terrarū regionibus Philosophus audiret plane nè divinus. Successit his Ariftoteles, cujus ut in omni doctrinæ genere plurima & præclariffima summo cum judicio artificioq; mirabili exstant scripta, ita hic unus omnibus præmiu palmamq; præripuisse videtur: Namque Socrates & Plato per πώμας aut Dialogos laxè prolixéque protulissent, ille in brevis facilisq; disciplinæ modum & Methodum eleganter & succinctè concinnavit, adeo ut quod quis jure hic desideret, nihil jam fit reliquum.
units.tr: Xenophon tells us, Illustrious and Noble Lord Baron, that Socrates, judged by the oracle of Phoebus [πάντων ἀνθρώπων σοφώτατον] to be the wisest of all men, was the first to bring philosophy, which had been designed for contemplation, down to the uses of human life. For when he saw that Thales, Anaximander and the other chief philosophers of the ancients were intent only on the study of heaven and the stars, and that this was of little use to themselves, or indeed to anyone else or to the commonwealth, he set aside this empty speculation, by which men could not become any better though they became more learned every day, and began earnestly to urge everyone towards practical philosophy, which instructs us how to live well and honourably. For this reason he was said to have first called philosophy down from heaven. Following in the footsteps of Socrates, Plato scattered through his writings much of the moral philosophy, and gained such fame and renown that he was heard as a philosopher, and indeed as a truly divine one, not only at Athens and throughout Greece, but in the most distant regions of the world. After these came Aristotle. Although he left very many excellent writings in every branch of learning, written with great judgement and marvellous skill, he alone seems to have snatched the prize and palm from all the rest. For while Socrates and Plato had set forth their teaching loosely and at length in [πώμας] or dialogues, he arranged the discipline of philosophy elegantly and concisely into a brief and easy method, so that nothing further remains for anyone who rightly seeks it here.

units.la: Verùm ut solis splendorem crasse obscurant nubes, ut mellificis apibus vespæ & fuci crebrò molesti esse solent, sic importuni quidam homines Practicæ Philosophiæ, prout à Stagirita traditur, quantum possunt detrahere conantur, partim ipsius odio Philosophi, ut Ramus, Patricius, cæterìque Philosophiæ veteris hostes hærchæretici, partim etiam rerum, quæ tractantur præjudicio, ut Vives & Talæus, qui sibi persuaderi non patiuntur, quin felicitas & virtutes Ethicæ beatitudini & virtutibus profsus repugnent Theologicis, cum potius subordinentur, & quousque humanæ per se vires naturæ ductu & rationis luce progredi possint, liquidò demonstrent: multos etiam à Philophi lectione deterruit Interpretum incogitantia, dum quidam Spinosè nimis per curiosarum quarundam salebras quæstionum singula tractant, ut Scholastici; quidam se Criticos præbent, & aut diversas in textu requirunt lectiones, aut Grammaticas gerras; quidam pro vera Philosophi mente spurias nugas suíque suppo- nunt figmenta cerebri: paucos reperire licet, qui vel scopum verum primoribus moribus, quod dicitur digitis intentendant, ufumq; in Republica verum & genuinum proponant. Quod me primum impulit, ut cum Philosophiam in Gymnasio Dantiscano interpretandam non ita pridem suscepissem, hic pro virili ingeniiq; modulo operam impenderem: Quid praestiterim, si quis legere dignetur, facile deprehendet, & opus malo opificem, quam opifex suum opus commendet. Cur vero Generositati Vestrę tenuiculas hasce, quales a me proficisci poterant, lucubrationes inscripserim, causae sunt non leves: Prima summus & plane Heroicus in omnes literatos & Philosophię inprimis cultores (quorum unus fautor auctorque nunc audis) amor. Eruditio dein singularis, quâ summopere excellis; judiciû etiam acre, quo singula nõ examinare minare modo, sed recte ritéque cen- sere, & justâ trutinæ libra pensitare vales, hoc jure suo exigunt. Accedit etiam serium piumque in fovendis ac promovendis studium literatis, quod me licet nullum, cuiq; à primo statim limine Musas salutare nondum contigit, huc propulit audaciæ, ut cum quo Generositati Tuæ pro votis (pro meritis enim cum opis non sit meæ, non licet) colerem non haberem, hoc levidense saltem munusculum, quo Generositatis Tuæ nomen exteris posterisque meritissimo commendetur, & semper recens viva per ora virûm, ut ait Ennius, vigeat, grati symbolum animi gratus humilisque nuncuparem. Quod si quâ exhibitum mente accipias, si quo debito animi se tibi debentis cultu delatum admittas, ad majus meliusque que ingenii ferant modo vires mei, etiam ut supra vires audeam, excitabit animúmque addet, si conatus hic Vestræ Generositati arridet uni, nihil Zoilos aut Momos (quibus nemo unquam facere potuit satis) latrantes aut frementes morabor. Sic Te Deus Ter-Optimus Maximus Regi, cui propter summas ingenii dotes merito charus, Patriæ, cui Tu auspicatissimè natus, Reipublicæ, cui dexteritate animi, rerum cata celeritate singularique experientia gerendarum dileCtissimus, literis deniq; & literatis omnibus, quibus Tu unus in-star omnium Mecœnas unicè faves & foves, quam diutissimè sospitet. Vale & diu feliciter vive præsidium & dulce decus meum. Heidelberga 1614.
units.tr: But just as clouds grossly obscure the light of the sun, and as wasps and drones are often troublesome to honey-making bees, so certain unwelcome men try as hard as they can to detract from practical philosophy as it is handed down by the Stagirite. Some do so from hatred of the philosopher himself, such as Ramus, Patricius, and the other enemies of ancient philosophy, who are heretics. Others do so from prejudice about the subject matter, such as Vives and Talaeus, who will not allow themselves to be persuaded that the happiness and virtues of ethics are wholly opposed to the blessedness and theological virtues, although they are rather subordinate to them; and they clearly demonstrate how far human natural powers can advance by the guidance of nature and the light of reason. Many too have been put off reading the philosopher by the thoughtlessness of his interpreters. Some treat each point too thornily, through the brambles of certain over-curious questions, like the Scholastics. Some set themselves up as critics and either seek out various readings in the text or make grammatical quarrels. Some, in place of the true mind of the philosopher, put forward spurious trifles and figments of their own brains. There are few to be found who point at the true goal with the very tips of their fingers, as they say, and set forth its true and genuine use in the commonwealth. This is what first prompted me, when not long ago I undertook to expound philosophy in the Gymnasium at [Dantiscano] Danzig, to devote my efforts there to the best of my powers and ability. Anyone who deigns to read the work will easily discover what I have achieved; and the work should commend its maker rather than the maker his work. Why I have dedicated these slender efforts, such as they could come from me, to your Nobility, is for no slight reasons. The first is your supreme and truly heroic love for all men of letters, and especially for the cultivators of philosophy (of whom you now hear that you are both a patron and an author). Next comes your singular learning, in which you greatly excel; and also your keen judgement, by which you are able not merely to examine each thing but to assess it rightly and properly, and to weigh it on the just balance of the scales; these qualities demand this of me. Moreover, there is your earnest and pious zeal in cherishing and promoting learning. This, though I am nobody, and though I have not yet been granted the favour of greeting the Muses from the very first threshold, has driven me to such boldness that, since I had no other way to honour your Nobility as I wished (for I cannot repay your merits with any help of my own), I have dared to offer this small and humble gift, so that your name may be most deservedly commended to foreigners and to posterity, and may always flourish fresh and alive on the lips of men, as Ennius says. I hope that, if you receive it in the spirit in which it is offered, and accept it as a token of the devoted respect of a mind that owes you everything, my efforts, if they please your Nobility alone, will encourage me to attempt greater and better things, even beyond my powers; and I shall not be hindered by the barking or growling of Zoilus or Momus, whom no one has ever been able to satisfy. So may God, Best and Greatest, keep you safe for as long as possible: dear to the King, deservedly so for your outstanding gifts of mind; dear to your country, under whose auspices you were most happily born; most beloved by the commonwealth for the skill of your mind, your quickness in dealing with affairs, and your singular experience in conducting them; and finally dear to letters and to all men of learning, for whom you alone, as a patron to them all, favour and foster them with unique devotion. Farewell, and live long and happily, my protection and sweet glory. Heidelberg, 1614.

units.la: Illustri Generositati Tuæ devotissimus, debitissimus ANDREAS AIDIUS.
units.tr: Most devoted and most indebted to your Illustrious Nobility, ANDREAS AIDY.

units.la: LECTORI CANDIDO S.
units.tr: To the Candid Reader, greetings

units.la: NÆ ego audax, Lector, qui post tot & tam varias variorum lucubrationes doctorum, quibus forte nihil addi demive possit, manum Aristotelis Ethicæ admoverim, dubio procul a-ctum hic agere aut ut proverbio dicitur, Iliadam post Homerum scribere dicar. Sed candide ego apud te candidum (neque enim nisi candidis & ingenuis hæc dicta sint) instituti proferam rationes mei. Cum non infimæ quamplures notæ Græcos, Latinos, Veteres, Recentiores hic desudasse vidissem, & quos videre contigit, evolvissem, mentem Philosophi ad omnium captum & intellectum non reserasse satis videbantur. Nam quod pace eorum modo vere dictum sit, stricte Ele aut laxè aut remissè nimis pleraque tra-ctant, & quæ accuratiore imprimis explica-tione egent, prætereunt, aut leviori saltem, quam ut legenti satisfiat brachio perstrin-gunt, & Philosophum mutilationis aut ob-scuritatis reum sæpe relinquunt: ut huic ma-lo, quantum per ingenii ⁊vires licet, quo-dammodo mederer, ex immensis istarum O-ceanis commentationum tenues mearum deducere rivulos lucubrationum coepi, ut sic arescentis Ethicæ flores irrigarem & in ⁊vi-tam pro ⁊vera Philosophi mente, & in usum pro præsentis sæculi statu revocarem. Quid hic laboris suscepering, si queis inquirendi fuerit animus, judicandum relinquo: men-tem Philosophi partim ex textu, partim ex ex scopo quam brevissimè fieri potuit, eruo, singula capita in suas partes seorsim explicatas distinguo, axiomata, quæ fundamen-torum loco sint (quod à nullo hactenus fa-ctum reor) seligo, dubia, si quæ latent aut le-gentem gentem remorari possunt, discutio, exemplis classicorum, sicubi opus sit, omnia illustro, ac ut dilucide omnia explicentur Aristotelem ex ipso Aristotele editionis Pacianæ, quâ hic usus sum, ubique interpretor. Verùm plerosque obiecturos scio, tot recentiorum præ manibus teri, ut vulgò vocantur Systemata, quæ plenius & accuratius ista, si credere fas sit, tractant. Fieri potest, sed hic primi fontes, hic scaturigo latet. Si tantum ex recentioribus hisce percipere licet commodi, cur universus doctorum per omnes Europæ Academias unanimi consensu Senatus uni tantum tribuunt Aristoteli, ut illum solum, qui in omnibus publicè legatur Scholis, dignum putent: Nunquam hoc profecto facerent, nisi scientiarum & artium bases hinc depromendas ducerent. Imò Neoterici hisce hoc fuisse consilii, testantur ipsi, ut per ista tanquam per rivulos liquidiores ad limpidas ipsorum fontium scaturigines deducerentur
units.tr: Perhaps, reader, I may be thought rash for putting my hand to Aristotle's Ethics after so many and such varied labours of learned men, to which perhaps nothing can be added or taken away, and so doing, undoubtedly, something already done, or, as the proverb says, writing an Iliad after Homer. But I will set out my reasons for this undertaking candidly before you, who are candid (for these things are said only to the candid and ingenuous). When I saw that not a few well-known Greeks, Latins, ancients and moderns had toiled over this, and I read those I had the chance to read, they did not seem to have unlocked the mind of the Philosopher to the grasp and understanding of all. For, with all respect to them, it may truly be said that they treat most things either strictly, or loosely, or too carelessly, and pass over those that especially need a more exact explanation, or touch on them too lightly to satisfy the reader, and often leave the Philosopher guilty of mutilation or obscurity. So that I might in some measure remedy this evil, as far as my ability allows, I began to draw from the vast oceans of those commentaries small streams of my own studies, so as to water the withering flowers of the Ethics and restore them, according to the true mind of the Philosopher, to use in the present age. What labour I have undertaken I leave to be judged by those who wish to inquire. I bring out the mind of the Philosopher partly from the text and partly from its aim, as briefly as possible; I divide each chapter into its parts, explained separately; I select axioms which serve as foundations (which I think no one has done hitherto); I discuss doubts, if any lie hidden or may delay the reader; I illustrate everything, where needed, with examples from the classics; and so that everything may be clearly explained, I interpret Aristotle throughout from Aristotle himself, in the edition of Pacius which I use here. But I know that many will object that the so-called Systems of many recent writers are in everyone's hands, and that these, if one may believe it, treat these matters more fully and accurately. This may be so, but here lie the first sources, here the spring is hidden. If so much advantage can be gained from these recent writers, why do the learned men of all the academies of Europe, by the unanimous consent of their senates, assign to Aristotle alone, thinking him alone worthy to be publicly read in all the schools? They would never do this unless they drew from him the foundations of the sciences and arts. Indeed the moderns themselves testify that their intention was that, through these as through clearer streams, one might be led to the clear springs of the sources themselves.

units.la: Ϲηλοπαθεῖς. Quærat aliquis ex istis recentioribus unde sua habeant, si invenisse se dicant, omnis contra testabitur vetustas: sin à veteribus desumpserint, cur idem nobis hoc seculo non liceat. Ut navis licet maria omnia circumvagetur, à polo in polum per Æquatorem transcurrat, à Solis cunis ad cubile & retrò cursum dirigat, nunquam suum subibit portum, nisi littus tutum certumque legat, ubi fidæ stationis suæ anchoram jaciat. Sic legat quis, quantum volet, & in evolvendis recentiorum scriptis defatiget se quàtum libet, currat, discurrat, recurrat, semper dubius ancepsq; fluctuabit, nulla insciētiis metā percipiendis deprehendet solidam, nisi priscorum monumenta adeat, & ex eorum adytis veluti primo ab ovo primam cognitionis suæ certitudinem accersat. Nam quæ veteres statuerunt principia, & rationibus stabilierunt firmis & longa nunc temporis experientia pro veris & immotis haberi voluit.
units.tr: Ϲηλοπαθεῖς. Let someone ask some of these recent writers where they got their material; if they say they found it themselves, all antiquity will testify against them; but if they took it from the ancients, why should it not be allowed to us in this age as well? As a ship, however much it wanders over all the seas, runs from pole to pole across the equator, and directs its course from the cradle of the sun to its bed and back again, it will never reach its harbour unless it finds a safe and certain shore where it may cast its anchor in a faithful station. So let someone read as much as he likes, and wear himself out unrolling the writings of the moderns; let him run, rush about, and rush back, he will always wander doubtful and wavering, and will find no solid goal in the things to be known, unless he goes to the monuments of the ancients and draws from their sanctuaries, as it were from the egg at the beginning, the first certainty of his knowledge. For the principles which the ancients laid down and established with firm reasons, long experience has wished to be held as true and immovable.

units.la: Ϲηλοπαθεῖς. voluit. Verùm ne impotenti nimis φιλαρχαίας affectu rapi me putes, hic sisto, teque si quando vacet ad horum lectionem amicè & ingenuè invito, ubi legeris, si quid novisti rectius istis, candidus imperti, si non his, utere mecum, libet modo, sin minus, tuo hic tuum ad palatum fruere judicio, & Vale.
units.tr: Ϲηλοπαθεῖς. voluit. But lest you think I am carried away by an unrestrained affection for antiquity, I stop here, and I invite you kindly, when you have leisure, to read these, and when you have read them, if you know anything more correct than these, impart it candidly; if not, use these with me, if you like; otherwise, enjoy your own judgment here to your own taste. Farewell.

units.la: TERENTIANUS MAURUS: Pro captu lectoris habent sua fata libelli.
units.tr: TERENTIANUS MAURUS: Books have their own fates according to the capacity of the reader.

units.la: PROLEGOMENA QVÆDAM IN ARISTOTELIS LIBROS AD NICOMACHVM.
units.tr: Certain Prolegomena to the Books of Aristotle to Nicomachus.

units.la: SOLENT Interpretes, qui autorem aliquem sibi explicandum & Commentariis illustrandum proponunt, initio statim multa præfari, ut si Philosophum explicare velint, (qualis in omnibusferè jam Scholis tantum Philosophiæ Coryphæus explicatur Aristoteles) de Philosophiæ definitione, divisione, & variis proprietatibus fusè agant, sin de Philosophiæ instrumentis sermonem instituant, de iis, quatenus instituti requirit ratio, prolixè tractant. Nos, Deo dante, Aristotelis libros de Moribus ad Nicomachum explicaturi, omissis iis, quæ passim & ubique habentur, hæc novem breviter tantum attingemus:
units.tr: Interpreters who propose to explain and illustrate some author with commentary usually begin by saying many things in advance. If they wish to explain a philosopher (such as Aristotle, who is now taught in almost all schools as the leader of philosophy alone), they treat at length the definition, division and various properties of philosophy; if they discuss the instruments of philosophy, they treat those at length insofar as the purpose of their undertaking requires. We, God willing, are about to explain Aristotle's books On Morals, to Nicomachus, and, leaving aside those things which are found everywhere, we will touch briefly on only the following nine points:

units.la: 1. De Autore ipso, quem pra manibus habemus.
units.tr: 1. The author himself, whom we have before us.

units.la: 2. De materia quam tractat.
units.tr: 2. The matter which he treats.

units.la: 3. De nomine, quo vocetur haec Philosophiae pars, quam vulgo vocant Moralem, & an uno eodemq; semper insignia-tur nomine.
units.tr: 3. The name by which this part of philosophy, which is commonly called Moral, is designated, and whether it is always marked by one and the same name.

units.la: 4. De utilitate, & quid commodi hac Philosophiae pars vitae adferat communi.
units.tr: 4. The usefulness, and what advantage this part of philosophy brings to common life.

units.la: 5. De scopo autoris, quem in ista materia sibi propositum habet, ubi tres etiam adjiciemus quaestiones.
units.tr: 5. The author's aim, which he has set before himself in this subject, where we will also add three questions.

units.la: 6. De modo pralibabimus docendi, & quomodo apud tum veteres tum recentiores doceri soleat haec Philosophia moralis.
units.tr: 6. We will first touch on the method of teaching, and how this moral philosophy has customarily been taught both by the ancients and by the more recent writers.

units.la: 7. De methodo, quautitur in hac materia tractanda.
units.tr: 7. On the method used in treating this subject.

units.la: 8. De argumento sive de summa rerum, quae in hoc opere continentur.
units.tr: 8. On the argument, or the sum of the things contained in this work.

units.la: 9. & ultimo: De titulo, & cur sic ad Nicomachum inscribantur isti libri, nam accurationem praemittere explicationem non puto esse huius loci, cum, ut testatur Averroes super 1. Phys. commen. 12. ad Logicam spectet, generalia, quae omnibus disciplinis inserviunt tractare, & qui velit accuratiorem de Philosophia in genere tractationem habere, consulat Zabarellam lib. 1. de nat. Logic. Fortunatum Crellium in praefamio ad Phys. Acroal. Aristot. Pererium lib. 1 Peripatet. quaest. c. 9. aliosque; quamplures, qui ex professo haec tractarunt. Et Aristoteles ipse dicit lib. 1. Metaph. cap. 3. communia omnibus scientiis tractanda esse in Metaphysica. Nos igitur, quo ordine & qua serie singula proposuimus, hic breviter & succincte, priusquam ipsum aggrediamur textum, attingere statuimus.
units.tr: 9. And last: On the title, and why these books are inscribed to Nicomachus. For I do not think that a precise explanation belongs in this place, since, as Averroes testifies on the first book of the Physics, comment. 12, it pertains to logic and treats general matters which serve all disciplines; and whoever wishes a more exact treatment of philosophy in general should consult Zabarella, book 1 of On the Nature of Logic; Fortunatus Crellius in the preface to the Physics, Acroasis of Aristotle; Pereira, book 1 of the Peripatetic questions, chapter 9; and others, very many, who have treated these matters professedly. And Aristotle himself says, in book 1 of the Metaphysics, chapter 3, that matters common to all sciences are to be treated in Metaphysics. We have therefore decided to touch on these things briefly and succinctly here, in the order and sequence in which we have set out each, before we approach the text itself.

units.la: I. DE AVTORE.
units.tr: I. ABOUT THE AUTHOR.

units.la: Autor horum librorum, quos habemus prae manibus, est Aristoteles: natus olympiade 99. anno mundi 3596. ante Christum 379. patriam habuit Stagyram obscuram & ignobilem alioquin civitatem, sed quam claram & nobilem reddiderit tantus civis, patre natus erat Nicomacho in re medica peritissimo, & ob hoc ipsum Amyntæ Alexandri Magni avo Macedoniæ Regi charissimo. Matre etiam Æstide, & utrumque genus duxit ab Æsculapio, ut testatur Epigramma illud Græcum, quod citat Ammonius:
units.tr: The author of these books that we have at hand is Aristotle, born in the 99th Olympiad, in the year of the world 3596, 379 years before Christ. His homeland was Stagira, a city otherwise obscure and undistinguished, but made famous and noble by so great a citizen. He was born to a father, Nicomachus, very skilled in medicine, and for this reason was dear to Amyntas, king of Macedonia and grandfather of Alexander the Great. His mother was Aestis, and he traced both lines back to Aesculapius, as the Greek epigram cited by Ammonius attests:

units.la: Φαίσιδ͂ ... Τῶν Ασκληπιαδῶν ... Αεσκυπίλης.
units.tr: Phaestis ... of the Asclepiadae ... Aesculapius. [Φαίσιδ ... Τῶν Ασκληπιαδῶν ... Αεσκυπίλης]

units.la: Decimoseptimo ætatis anno Athenas studiorum gratia venit, ubi triennium totum Socratem audivit: Socrate demum sublato, Platoni totos 20. annos adhæsit, tanto ingenii acumine famaque tanta, ut illum solum filio suo Alexandro, quem præficeret Philippus Macedoniæ Rex, dignum putarit. Solitus est Alexander dicere: Plus se Aristoteli Præceptori debere, quàm Philippo Patri, quod is esse tantum, ille vero bene esse dedisset. Ideoque Stagyram in Præceptoris sui gratiam à patre Philippo jam dirutam restauravit, & in meliorem quàm ante unquam Reip. formam redegit. Scripsit Aristot. plurima volumina: nam Diog. Laërt. lib. 5. de vit. Philos. in Aristotele testatur, illum ad quater centies quadragies quinquies millia, trecenta triginta volumina scripsisse, quorum pleraque partim temporis injuria, partim hominum incuria, partim etiam scriptorum inopia aut negligentia perierunt, itaut vix jam centum triginta duo superstint. Sectam instituit Peripateticorum, qui hoc nominis sortiti sunt, quod inambulantes non in cathedris aut pulpitis sedentes docerent. Hæc secta reliquis omnibus penè deletis in hodiernum usque tempus durat, tum quia minus errorum quam reliquę habet, tum quia quicquid fundaméti loco substernit, rationib. certis & evidentib. stabilire conatur: q plura de Arist. legere velit, cósulat Ammō. in proœm. Phys. Arist. Diog. Laërt. l. 5. de vit. Philos. Dion. Hal. l. 3 Strab. l. 13. Suid. in voce Arist. & Plut. in vit. Syll.
units.tr: At the age of seventeen he came to Athens for the sake of study, where he heard Socrates for a full three years. After Socrates was taken away, he attached himself to Plato for a full twenty years, with such keenness of mind and such renown that Philip, king of Macedonia, thought him alone worthy to be set over his son Alexander. Alexander used to say that he owed more to Aristotle, his teacher, than to Philip, his father, since the one had given him merely life, but the other a good life. And so, in gratitude to his teacher, he restored Stagira, which his father Philip had already razed, and brought it back to a better constitution than the state had ever had before. Aristotle wrote very many volumes: Diogenes Laertius, in book 5 of the Lives of the Philosophers, testifies that he wrote four hundred and forty-five thousand three hundred and thirty volumes, most of which have perished, partly through the injury of time, partly through human carelessness, and partly through the scarcity or negligence of copyists, so that barely one hundred and thirty-two now survive. He founded the school of the Peripatetics, who got their name from the fact that they taught while walking about, not sitting in chairs or on pulpits. This school, with nearly all the others destroyed, has lasted to the present day, both because it contains fewer errors than the rest and because it tries to establish by certain and evident reasons whatever it lays down as its foundation. Whoever wishes to read more about Aristotle should consult Ammonius, in the preface to Aristotle's Physics; Diogenes Laertius, book 5 of the Lives of the Philosophers; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 3; Strabo, book 13; Suidas, under the word Aristotle; and Plutarch in the Life of Sulla.

units.la: II. DE MATERIA.
units.tr: II. ON THE SUBJECT MATTER.

units.la: AGIT Aristotele sin libris de Moribus de Philosophia morali in communi, & instituit hominem communibus principiis, quibus ad determinatum & certum aliquot vitæ genus aut Oeconomicum aut Politicum applicare se possit. Constat enim totam Philosophiā proprie dictam dividi in Contemplativam & Actīvam, cujus rationem, cum veteres sic distinxerint, & hodie etiam eam sic distinguant, duplicem affert Ammonius in proœm. super Phys. Acroas.
units.tr: In the books on Morals, Aristotle treats moral philosophy in general and equips a man with common principles, by which he may apply himself to some determinate and certain way of life, whether domestic or political. For it is agreed that philosophy properly so called is divided into Contemplative and Active. Ammonius gives a twofold reason for this division, which the ancients drew and which people still draw today, in his preface to the Physics lectures.

units.la: 1. Ratio est; Quia cum Philosophia sit similitudo ad Deum, prout homini possibile seu quatenus homini licet, sicut Plato in Gorgia docet; Et cum omnis Dei actio proprie consistat in duobus, in cognitione, qua cuncta cognoscit & contemplatur, & in prudentia, qua cuncta se inferiora regit & moderatur. Jure igitur Philosophia ratione finis in Actīvam & Contemplativam est divisa: Nam contemplationis opere cuncta, quæ sunt, etsi in nostra potestate non sint, ut fiant, vel non fiant, cognoscimus, & naturam eorum contemplamur: per actionem vero cuncta nobis inferiora, & quæ in nostra sunt potestate, moderamur & disponimus, unde nos similes Deo efficimur. 2. Ratio est ducta a materia circa quam Philosophia versatur. Nam cum geminæ sint animi functiones, aliæ cognoscibiles, quæ cognoscendi vim habét, habêt, ut sunt, Ratio, Sensus, Opinio, Phantasia: alii sunt Vitales, quæ in appetitu versantur, ut sunt, Voluntas, Electio, Ira, Libido. Cum igitur Philosophus omnes animi functiones, adeoque nos totos perfectos reddere cupit per cognitionem illam animi partem aut functionem perficit, quæ cognoscibilis dicitur, per actionem vero illam, quæ actualis dicitur, unde Ammonius in Activam & Speculativam distinctam esse Philosophiam ait. Tertiam rationem addit discertiorem a forma sumtam, Plutarchus lib. 1. de placitis Philosophorum, Aristoteles, inquit, Theophrastus, & alii jure Philosophiam partiti sunt in Activam & Contemplativam: necesse est enim virum absolutum & perfectum, & eorum, quæ sunt, quæque a Deo & natura producuntur esse contemplatorem, & eorum, quæ desunt, quæque vitæ bene beateque transigendæ inserviunt esse actorem.
units.tr: (1) The first reason is this: since philosophy is a likeness to God, so far as it is possible for man, or so far as it is permitted to man, as Plato teaches in the Gorgias; and since every action of God consists properly in two things, in knowledge, by which he knows and contemplates all things, and in prudence, by which he rules and governs all things beneath him. Philosophy is therefore rightly divided, by reason of its end, into Active and Contemplative. For by the work of contemplation we know all the things that exist, and we contemplate their nature, even though they are not in our power to make or not make; but by action we govern and dispose all the things beneath us that are in our power, and so we become like God. (2) The second reason is drawn from the matter with which philosophy is concerned. For since the functions of the soul are twofold, some knowable, which have the power of knowing, namely Reason, Sense, Opinion and Imagination; and others vital, which belong to appetite, namely Will, Choice, Anger and Lust. Since the philosopher wishes to make us wholly perfect, he perfects by knowledge that part or function of the soul which is called knowable, and by that action which is called actual he perfects the other. Hence Ammonius says that philosophy is distinguished into Active and Speculative. (3) A third reason, more distinct and taken from form, is added by Plutarch in book 1 of On the Opinions of the Philosophers: Aristotle, he says, Theophrastus and others have rightly divided philosophy into Active and Contemplative. For it is necessary that a complete and perfect man should be a contemplator of the things that exist, and of those that are produced by God and nature, and an actor of the things that are lacking, and that serve to lead life well and happily.

units.la: III. DE NOMINE.
units.tr: III. ON THE NAME.

units.la: Licet Philosophus hîc in his libris de Philosophia agat Morali, non uno tamen eodemque nomine apud autores insignitur, & cum nomina sint rerum symbola rebus denotandis imposita, ut præclarè Philosophus 1. Peri herm. c. 1. Ideo operæ preciuм erit, de Nomine pauca dicere. Vocatur primò Philosophia practica, vel quod finis ipsius non sit γνῶσις, ἀλλὰ πρᾶξις, vel quod versetur περὶ τὰ πράξεις seu actiones humanas, quas secundum honesti & decori normam informat. 2. Vocatur καθ' ἐξοχὴν Philosophia, quod hæc illius pars tam eximia & nobilis sit, ut merito nomen totius sibi vendicet præter cæteras. teras. Sic apud Cic.2.de nat.Deor. Philosophia vocatur magistra morum, virtutum indagatrix, vitiorum expultrix. Item cum apud Senecam dicitur: Natura dat vivere, Philosophia dat recte vivere: quae omnia Philosophiae morali tantum competunt, propterea quod omnes vitae actiones regat & dirigat non secus ac in mari navem gubernator. 3. Vocatur Philosophia moralis, quod modum informandi mores vitamque moratam instituendi tractet. 4. Politica seu scientia Civilis, vel quia hominem, qui a Philosopho 1. Nicom. c. 7. vocatur, honestis & civilibus informat moribus, vel quia omnia sua praecepta eo dirigit, ut tandem homo in societate civili quam rectissime vivat, totaque civitas & Respubl. cujus membra sunt singuli homines, & ex his constitutae familiae, sit florens & felix. 5. Etiam dicitur, Ratio bene vivendi, quia scilicet modum bene, hoc est, probe, honesteque vivendi explicat. 6. & ult. Vocatur Ethica ἀπὸ τῆς ἤθος, a more, quod totam hominis vitam moribus rectissime informet, & sola sit ea Philosophiae pars, quae honestatem & civilitatem morum praescribat. Unde vulgo definiri solet; Ars seu scientia bene honesteque vivendi. Timpler.1.Eth.c.3.
units.tr: Although the Philosopher in these books on Philosophy treats of Moral philosophy, he is not designated by one and the same name among authors. Since names are symbols imposed on things to denote them, as the Philosopher well says in Peri hermeneias, ch. 1, it will be worth saying a few things about the Name. First, it is called practical philosophy, either because its end is not knowledge [γνῶσις] but action [πρᾶξις], or because it is concerned with human actions [περὶ τὰ πράξεις], which it shapes according to the norm of what is honourable and fitting. 2. It is called philosophy above all [καθ' ἐξοχὴν], because this part of it is so outstanding and noble that it rightly claims the name of the whole for itself, above the others. So Cicero, in De natura deorum, 2, calls philosophy the teacher of morals, the seeker out of virtues, the expeller of vices. Likewise when Seneca says: Nature gives us life, philosophy teaches us to live well. All these things belong only to moral philosophy, because it governs and directs all the actions of life, as a helmsman steers a ship at sea. 3. It is called moral philosophy because it treats of the method of shaping manners and of establishing a morally upright life. 4. It is called political or civil science, either because it shapes man, who is called by the Philosopher Nic. 1, ch. 7, with honourable and civic manners, or because it directs all its precepts to this end, that at last man may live as rightly as possible in civil society, and the whole state and commonwealth, of which individual men are the members and the families made up of them, may flourish and be happy. 5. It is also called the reason of living well, because it sets out the way of living well, that is, uprightly and honourably. 6. And lastly, it is called ethics [Ethica], from ἦθος, custom, because it shapes the whole life of man most rightly in manners, and it is the only part of philosophy that prescribes the honourableness and civility of manners. Hence it is commonly defined thus: the art or science of living well and honourably. Timpler, Eth. 1, ch. 3.

units.la: IV. DE UTILITATE.
units.tr: IV. On Usefulness.

units.la: DE Utilitate hoc satis sit dicere, eam ex disciplinis omnibus praecipuam & civitates omnes constituisse & conservare, omnibus deniq; artibus & disciplinis, maxime tamen Theologiae, Jurisprudentiae & Historiarum cognitioni prodesse. Recte igitur & argute Stoici trium Philosophiae partium {ut} ut illi quidem trifariam dividebant Philosophiam) Logicam sepimento, Physicam arboribus, fructibus Ethicam similem iudicarunt; comparata universa Philosophia horto seu agro, ut sicut sepimentum ponitur propter arbores, arbores vero foventur propter fructum, quia ex fructu dependet totius horti utilitas, sic totius etiam Philosophiae commoditas ab Ethica.
units.tr: Concerning usefulness, it is enough to say that it is the most important of all the disciplines, that it has founded and preserves all states, and that, in short, it benefits all the arts and disciplines, and above all the knowledge of Theology, Jurisprudence and History. The Stoics therefore rightly and shrewdly compared the parts of philosophy. Though they divided philosophy threefold, they likened Logic to the hedge, Physics to the trees, and Ethics to the fruit. They compared all of philosophy to a garden or field: as the hedge is put in place for the sake of the trees, and the trees are cherished for the sake of their fruit, because the usefulness of the whole garden depends on the fruit, so too the value of all philosophy comes from Ethics.

units.la: Alii Philosophiam ovo comparant, ita ut testae seu putamini assimiletur Logica, albumini Physica, sed vitello Ethica, & omnium elegantissime Posidonius teste Sexto Empirico lib. adverf. scientias, animanti assimilavit Philosophiam, ossibus quidem & nervis Logicam, carni & sanguini Physicam, animae denique Ethicam, propterea quod sit vitae humanae velut anima. Rationes etiam ad hanc probandam utilitatem non paucae vulgo afferri solent, numero undecim. 1. Quod rationem praescribat in omni vita & vocatione probe honesteque vivendi. 2. Quia virtutes omnes morales earumque naturas & proprietates, causas etiam & subiecta & species explicat, & quanta sit vitiorum deformitas, demonstrat. 3. Quia omnes actiones humanas a libera voluntate pendentes informat, ut cum lege naturae & recta ratione congruant. 4. Quia media ostendit regendi & domandi omnes appetitus & affectus illicitos, eosque rectae rationis imperio subjicit, unde non immerito medicina animi dicitur. 5. Quia format non tantum virum bonum in genere, sed etiam bonum patremfamilias & civem bonum, & sic efficit, ut homo tum sibi & suae familiae, tum aliis & Reip. consuconsulere possit. 6. Quia est invétrix & procreatrix omnium legum politivarum, ut vocantur à JCtis, in quolibet vitæ genere ab homine observandarum.
units.tr: Others compare philosophy to an egg, so that Logic corresponds to the shell or husk, Physics to the white, and Ethics to the yolk. Most elegantly of all, Posidonius, according to Sextus Empiricus in his book against the scientists, likened philosophy to a living creature: Logic to the bones and sinews, Physics to the flesh and blood, and Ethics to the soul, because it is, as it were, the soul of human life. Many reasons are commonly offered to prove this usefulness, eleven in number: (1) because it prescribes reason for living uprightly and honourably in every stage and calling of life; (2) because it explains all the moral virtues, their natures and properties, and also their causes, subjects and kinds, and shows how great the ugliness of the vices is; (3) because it shapes all human actions, which depend on the free will, so that they agree with the law of nature and right reason; (4) because it shows the means of governing and taming all unlawful appetites and passions, and brings them under the command of right reason, whence it is not without reason called the medicine of the soul; (5) because it forms not only a good man in general but also a good head of a household and a good citizen, and so enables a person to look after both himself and his family and also others and the commonwealth; (6) because it is the discoverer and mother of all the positive laws, as the jurists call them, which a person must observe in every kind of life.

units.la: 7. Quia viam nobis planam & compendiariam aperit & sternit, ad consequêdum in hac vita summum bonum, hoc est, felicitatem terrenâ ac corporalem.
units.tr: (7) Because it opens and lays out for us a plain and short way to attain in this life the highest good, that is, earthly and bodily happiness.

units.la: 8. Quia sine hujus præceptis nulla societas humana neque privata, neque domestica, neque civilis conservari potest. Hinc etiam Cic. 1. offic. ait; Nulla vita pars neque publica, neq; privata, neq; forensibus, neq; domesticis in rebus, neque si tecum aliquid agas, neque si cum altero contrahas, vacare officio potest. 9. Quia sine hujus cognitione nemo feliciter & cum fructu vel in Historiarum cognitione, vel in Oratoria facultate, vel in Jurisprudentia, vel in Theologia, vel in ulla deniq; alia disciplina versari potest. 10. Quia Philosophia practica hominem præparat ad studium verae pietatis, unde etiam à quodam vocatur Padagogia ad Christianam Religionem, docet enim quousque homo per lucem naturæ & suis viribus assurgere possit. 11. & alt. Quia omnium prudentium & sapientum virorum elogiis commendatur velut vitæ inprimis humanæ utilis. Hinc Cic. 5 Tusc. quæst. exclamat: O vita Philosophia dux, ô virtutis indagatrix, expultrixq; vitiorum, quid non modo nos, sed omnis vita hominum sine te esse potuisset! tu urbes peperisti, tu dissipatos homines in societatem vita convocasti, tu eos inter se primo domicilii, deinde conjugii, tum literarum & vocum communione junxisti, tu inventrix legum, tu magistra morum & disciplina fuisti. Hinc Aristoteles interrogatus, quid ex Philosophia lucratus esset? Hoc, inquit, ut injussus faciam, quaplerique legum legum metu faciunt. Et Dionysius junior Syracusarum tyrannus postquam fuisset regno expulsus, cuidam dicenti, quid tibi profuit Philosophia? Respondit, ut tantam fortunae mutationem facilius feram. Quod vero quidam objiciunt, Practicam inprimis Ethicam generalem repugnare Theologiae sacrae & a verae pietatis studio homines abducere, id omnino falsum & erroneum est. Sicut enim proba & honesta vita non repugnat vitae piae & sanctae, neque probitas morum pietati Christianae; sed potius illa ad hanc praeparator: ab hac perficitur: ita neque Philosophia practica repugnat Theologiae sacrae, sed potius hominem ad hanc discendam & melius percipiendam instruit.
units.tr: (8) Because without its precepts no human society, whether private, domestic or civil, can be preserved. Hence Cicero also says in the first book of Duties: No part of life, whether public or private, whether in forensic or domestic affairs, whether you are doing something by yourself or dealing with another, can be free of duty. (9) Because without knowledge of this no one can live happily and profitably in the study of History, or in the art of oratory, or in Jurisprudence, or in Theology, or indeed in any other discipline. (10) Because practical philosophy prepares a person for the pursuit of true godliness; for this reason someone has even called it a pedagogy to the Christian Religion, since it teaches how far a person can rise by the light of nature and by his own powers. (11) And others. Because it is commended by the praises of all prudent and wise men as especially useful for human life. Hence Cicero in the fifth book of the Tusculan Disputations exclaims: O life, Philosophy, guide, searcher out of virtue, and expeller of vices, what could not only we, but all human life have been without you! You have founded cities; you have gathered scattered men into the fellowship of life; you have joined them together first by a home, then by marriage, then by the sharing of letters and speech; you have been the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and the mistress of discipline. Hence when Aristotle was asked what he had gained from philosophy, he answered: This, that I do without being ordered what most men do out of fear of the laws. And Dionysius the Younger, tyrant of Syracuse, after he had been driven from his kingdom, when someone said to him what has philosophy profited you?, replied: that I may bear so great a change of fortune more easily. But as for what some object, that practical and especially general Ethics is opposed to sacred Theology and draws people away from the pursuit of true godliness, this is wholly false and mistaken. For just as an upright and honourable life is not opposed to a pious and holy life, nor integrity of morals to Christian godliness, but rather the former prepares the way for the latter and is completed by it, so practical philosophy is not opposed to sacred Theology, but rather instructs a person to learn it and to understand it better.

units.la: V. DE MODO DOCENDI.
units.tr: V. ON THE METHOD OF TEACHING

units.la: MODUS docendi Ethicam triplex esse solet, alius Gnomologicus, quando breves & argutae sententiae proponuntur ad mores informandos & accommodatos ad vitam bene instituendam. Harum sententiarum facilis est intelligentia, utpote quae sensu & experientia constat, diuturna etiam memoria, quia grata sunt & delectant, & quia magnum usum in vita humana habent, & saepe recurrunt, maximam afferunt utilitatem, quoniam vitae humanae breves quasdam regulas proponunt, ut sunt, Parentes ama: Deum cole: Nosce teipsum: Ne quid nimis, &c.
units.tr: There are usually three methods of teaching ethics. The first is the Gnomologic, when brief and pointed maxims are set forth to form morals and to suit a well-ordered life. These maxims are easy to understand, since they rest on common sense and experience, and they are long remembered because they are pleasing and delightful, because they have great use in human life and are often recalled, and because they offer the greatest benefit by proposing short rules for living, such as Honour your parents: Worship God: Know yourself: Nothing in excess, and so on.

units.la: Secundus modus dicitur Paradeigmaticus seu Exemplaris, quia virtutum & vitiorum exempla illarum quidem ad imitandum, horum vero ad fugiendum ob oculos nobis proponit. Tales sunt historiae, apologi Aesopici, & aliorum, Comoediae item & Tragoediae: & li quae alia alia utilitatis gratia à viris prudentibus confin-gantur.
units.tr: The second method is called Paradigmatic or Exemplary, because it places before our eyes examples of virtues to be imitated and of vices to be avoided. Such are histories, the fables of Aesop and of others, comedies likewise and tragedies, and whatever else wise men have devised for various useful purposes.

units.la: Tertius modus est Apodeicticus seu Demonstrativus, quando virtutum & actionum humanarum causæ, effecta, definitiones, divisiones, & cæteræ omnes affectiones proponuntur, & nihil prætermittitur, quod ad accuratam rei explicationem facere videtur, quales sunt, plerique Platonis dialogi, Annulus Epicteti, Stoici, Aristotelis libri de moribus ad Nicomach. Magna moralia, & ad Eudemum, in quibus omnibus Philosophiam moralem Aristoteles perspicuo & perfecto plane modo tractat; nam non tantum argumenta Logica adhibet, quibus præcepta morum demonstrantur, sed etiam ea omnia accommodat, quibus animi auditorum conciliantur, & ad Ethicæ studium inflammantur.
units.tr: The third method is the Apodeictic or Demonstrative, when the causes, effects, definitions, divisions and all the other properties of the virtues and of human actions are set out, and nothing is omitted that seems to contribute to an exact explanation of the matter. Such are most of Plato's dialogues, the Handbook of Epictetus, the Stoics, Aristotle's books on morals to Nicomachus, the Magna Moralia, and the Eudemian Ethics. In all of these Aristotle treats moral philosophy in a clear and thoroughly complete manner. For he not only employs logical arguments by which the precepts of morals are demonstrated, but also adapts everything that wins the minds of his hearers and kindles their zeal for the study of ethics.

units.la: VI. DE SCOPO.
units.tr: VI. ON THE AIM

units.la: Scopus autoris est tradere finem actionum humanarum, & media, quibus ad istum finem pervenitur, seu qua ratione modum & regulam bene beateque vivendi unusquisque sibi comparare possit. Unde non male duæ statuuntur partes Ethicæ; Eudæmonologia, quæ de ipsa felicitate agit, & Aretologia, quæ ipsas virtutes, tanquam certa media ad felicitatem comparandam tractat. Sed de his suo loco. Nunc has tres quæstiones breviter attingemus.
units.tr: The aim of the author is to set out the end of human actions and the means by which that end is reached, that is, by what method each person may acquire for himself the rule and manner of living well and happily. Hence it is not wrongly held that ethics has two parts: Eudaemonology, which deals with happiness itself, and Aretology, which treats the virtues themselves as the sure means of attaining happiness. But these matters belong in their proper place. Now we shall briefly touch on three questions.

units.la: 1. Unde originem traxerit Ethica?
units.tr: 1. Whence did ethics take its origin?

units.la: 2. Qui inventores fuerint?
units.tr: 2. Who were its inventors?

units.la: 3. An liceat homini Christiano ex Ethnicorum scriptis Philosophorum Philosophiam addiscere moralem?
units.tr: 3. May a Christian man learn moral philosophy from the writings of the heathen philosophers?

units.la: DE PRIMA QVÆSTIONE.
units.tr: ON THE FIRST QUESTION.

units.la: ORiginem traxit Ethica sicut cæteræ omnes disciplinæ & scientiæ ab his tribus: nempe à principiis nobiscum natis, ab experientia, & à ratiocinatione. Principia nobiscum nata sunt illæ communes notiones, quæ generalia de virtutum officiis præcepta tradunt, & earum prima fundamenta ponunt, quibus postmodum speciala exstruere licet, qualia sunt: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris: Honestum sequendum: Turpe fugiendum: Neminem lædendum, &c. 2. Experientia virtutum, vitiorum, & eventuum, quæ sequuntur exempla, colligit & inductione facta eorum, quæ certa esse probavit, pro certis habet, ut cum multos per virtutem ad dignitatem, ad honorem, ad opes pervenisse, vitiis vero infames in ultimam esse prolapsos miseriam. 3. Ratiocinatio, quæ natura & sensu cognita sunt, partim per demonstrationes, partim per alias rationes colligit & concludit, quæ sunt præcepta morum & virtutum regulæ, verbi gratia, Æqualitas est servanda, at ubi pœna respondet delicto, æqualitas servatur, Aristot. 5. Nicom. 7. Cic. pro Mil. sic etiam Vim vi repellere licet, at ubi aliquis in furem aut latronem incidet, se defendendo vim vi repellit.
units.tr: Ethics, like all other disciplines and sciences, takes its origin from three sources: from principles innate in us, from experience, and from reasoning. Innate principles are those common notions which deliver general precepts about the duties of the virtues and lay down their first foundations, on which more specific rules may afterwards be built. Examples are: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another; the honourable is to be pursued; the shameful is to be avoided; no one is to be harmed, and so on. 2. Experience of virtues, vices and the outcomes that follow gathers examples, and by induction it holds as certain those things it has shown to be certain: for instance, that many who have advanced through virtue to dignity, honour and wealth, and those notorious for vice have fallen into the greatest misery. 3. Reasoning, starting from what is known by nature and by the senses, partly through demonstrations and partly through other arguments, infers and concludes the precepts of conduct and the rules of the virtues. For example: equality must be preserved; and where the punishment answers to the offence, equality is preserved (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 5.7; Cicero, Pro Milone). Likewise: it is lawful to repel force with force; and when someone falls upon a thief or a robber, he repels force with force in self-defence.

units.la: DE SECUNDA.
units.tr: ON THE SECOND.

units.la: AUtorem habet Ethica seu moralis Philosophia 1. Deum ipsum, qui homini primum ad imaginem suam condito discrimen honesti & turpis indidit, secundo voce sua ipse promulgavit, in qua tanquam quam in speculo vitæ transigendæ rationem cernere licet, tertiò & magnos & præclaros viros peculiari quodam afflatu excitavit, qui pulcherrimas & utilissimas vitæ rationes tradiderunt, & plurima virtutum exempla in illustri loco sita post se reliquerunt. 2. Habet Ethica autores viros prudentes & præclaros, qui traditiones majorum sequuti, & criteriis rectæ rationis & experientiæ instructi, leges utilissimas condiderunt, & præclara in vita instituenda & moribus formandis præcepta descripserunt, quales fuerunt Pythagoras, qui aurea illa carmina, ut vocantur, descripsit, & septem Graciæ Sapientes, sed quæ illi tradiderunt, erant tantum breves & illustres sententiæ, in quibus nihil absoluti aut perfecti continebatur. Post hæc Socrates demum Philosophiam exercuit moralem, ut testatur Laërtius in vita ipsius, & Cic. 1. Acad. & 5. Tusc. quaest. & Pol. Virgil. lib. 1. de invent. rer. c. 16. Unde Philosophiam cælo deduci credebatur. Illi successit Plato, qui multa & varia tradidit de Philosophia morali, ut videre licet in variis Dialogis, in Politicis, & libris de legib. Aristoteles vero ista vaga & dispersa ad modum & methodum revocavit, & omnes Philosophiæ moralis partes accuratissimè pertractavit. Objeci. Chaldæorum Astrologi, Ægyptiorum Sacerdotes, Persarum Magi, Indorum Gymnosophistæ isti multo priores fuerunt, & præcepta moralia tradiderunt, ut ex Xenoph. παιδείας constat. Ergo male isti supra nominati Ethices inventores dicuntur. Resp. Philosophiæ naturalis potius & Mathematicos studiosi fuerunt, quàm moralis, ut ex Beroso & Mercurio Trismegisto liquet.
units.tr: Ethics, or moral philosophy, has as its author, first, God himself, who, when he created man in his own image, implanted in him the distinction between the honourable and the shameful; second, he himself promulgated it by his own voice, in which one may discern the rule of living as in a mirror; third, he stirred up, by a peculiar inspiration, wise and excellent men, great and distinguished, who handed down the most beautiful and most useful rules of life and left behind them many examples of virtue set in a famous place. 2. Ethics has as authors prudent and distinguished men, who, following the traditions of their elders and instructed by the standards of right reason and experience, framed most useful laws and set down excellent precepts for ordering life and forming character. Such were Pythagoras, who wrote those so-called Golden Verses, and the Seven Sages of Greece; but what they taught were only brief and famous maxims, containing nothing complete or perfect. After these, Socrates at last practised moral philosophy, as Laertius attests in his life of him, and Cicero in Academica 1 and Tusculanae Disputationes 5, and Polydore Vergil, book 1, On the Discovery of Things, chapter 16. Hence philosophy was believed to have been brought down from heaven. Plato succeeded him, who handed down many and varied teachings on moral philosophy, as may be seen in his various Dialogues, in the Politics, and in the books on the Laws. Aristotle indeed reduced these scattered and loose teachings to order and method, and treated all parts of moral philosophy most accurately. Objection: the Chaldean astrologers, the Egyptian priests, the Persian magi and the Indian gymnosophists were much earlier than these, and handed down moral precepts, as is clear from Xenophon's Education of Cyrus. Therefore those named above are wrongly called the inventors of ethics. Reply: they were students of natural philosophy and mathematics rather than of moral philosophy, as is clear from Berossus and Hermes Trismegistus.

units.la: DE TERTIA.
units.tr: On the Third [Objection]

units.la: RESpondetur breviter, licere propter has rationes: 1. Quia Philosophia est donum Dei etiam in homines Ethnicos collatum, neq; enim homines Ethnici per se illa scripserunt qua Ethnici, sed qua luce naturæ imbuti, & liberali disciplina instructi. Deus vero naturalia non tollit, neq; iis contrariatur, utpote quorum ipse autor est, ut acute disserit Scaliger exerc.278. 2. Deus principia ista communia hominum mentibus indidit, ex quibus postea artes & scientiæ prodierunt. At si artes & scientiæ Deo aut divinæ ordinationi essent contrariæ, Deum non haberent primâ causam, cum nihil sit causa sui contrarii, ut idem disserit Scalig. exerc.11 sect.1. 3. Eadem res tractatur in Ethica & Theologia licet diverso respectu, & licet sint diversa principia, diversæ proprietates unius rei, ut verbi gratia, idem est homo, qui est Christianus & Practicus; sed diversa sunt agendi principia, nam homo Christianus, quæ agit, impulsu Spiritus sancti agit, ut testatur Apostolus Rom.8. v.4. Quicunque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei; quæ vero agit homo Practicus juxta præcepta Ethica ductu rectæ rationis ea agit, & quæ recta ratio indicat esse honestum vel turpe, illa agit, quæ rectæ rationi consentanea videntur. Vide Martyrem p.8. ad Nicomach. Aristot. 4. Præcepta ista Ethica Theologiæ etiam inserviunt, nempe si cum recto judicio adhibeatur in explicatione secundæ tabulæ, & ubi agitur de consensu legis naturæ & legis divinæ; tum etiâ eæ virtutum moraliū definitiones & proprietates multum lucis afferunt rebus Theologicis, ostendunt enim quousque vires humanæ naturæ luce & instinctu illustratæ pertingere possint.
units.tr: It is answered briefly that it is permitted, for these reasons: (1) Philosophy is a gift of God, bestowed even on heathen men. For the heathen did not write those things as heathen, but as men imbued with the light of nature and instructed in the liberal arts. God does not take away natural things, nor is He opposed to them, since He is their author, as Scaliger argues acutely in Exercitationes 278. (2) God implanted these common principles in the minds of men, and from them the arts and sciences later arose. But if the arts and sciences were contrary to God or to the divine ordinance, they would not have God as their first cause, since nothing is the cause of its own contrary, as the same Scaliger argues in Exercitationes 11, section 1. (3) The same matter is treated in Ethics and in Theology, though under a different aspect, and though the principles are different. Different properties of one thing are possible: for example, the same man is both a Christian and a practical man. But the principles of acting are different. For the Christian man acts under the impulse of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle testifies in Romans 8:4: "Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God." But the practical man, who acts according to the precepts of Ethics, acts under the guidance of right reason, and he does those things which right reason shows to be honourable or base, and which seem consonant with right reason. See Martyr on the Nicomachean Ethics of Aristotle, p. 8. (4) These ethical precepts also serve Theology: namely, when they are applied with sound judgment in the explanation of the second table of the Law, and where the agreement of the law of nature with the divine law is discussed. Moreover, those definitions and properties of the moral virtues throw much light on theological matters, for they show how far the powers of human nature, illumined by light and instinct, are able to reach.

units.la: Sunt tamen, qui nefas esse putant Ethnicorum scripta attingere propter has rationes: 1. Decalogus perfectè docet, quicquid ad Philosophiam moralem pertinet. Ergo nihil prosunt Ethnicorum scripta. Resp. Verum est perfectè docere Decalogum, quicquid ad Philosophiam moralem spectat, non tamen sequitur, nihil opus esse hæc ex Ethnicorum scriptis depromere; nam illa ostendit, quousque vires naturæ humanæ instinctu & lumine illustratæ pervenire possunt, & cū homo Christianus videt, quousq; pertingat, tunc diffisus suis viribus ad perfectionē illam legis, quatenus per fidem inchoata, magis excitatur.
units.tr: Yet there are some who think it wrong to touch the writings of the heathen, for these reasons: (1) The Decalogue teaches perfectly whatever pertains to moral philosophy. Therefore the writings of the heathen are of no use. Answer: It is true that the Decalogue teaches perfectly whatever concerns moral philosophy; but it does not follow that there is no need to draw these things from the writings of the heathen. For those writings show how far the powers of human nature, illumined by instinct and light, can reach; and when a Christian sees how far they reach, then, distrustful of his own powers, he is more stirred up toward that perfection of the law, which is begun through faith.

units.la: 2. Paulus Apostolus Rom 14. dicit: Quicquid fit absq; fide, peccatū est. Ergo cum illa dicta Ethnicorū, quod ex fide non proveniunt, peccatum gignant, ideo non sunt attingenda. Resp. ad antecedens, duplicia esse opera hominis, alia voeari opera ex complacito, alia ex congruo, quicquid igitur fit tanquam opus ex complacito seu condigno absq; fide in spiritualibus, est peccatum, propterea quod actiones hominis spirituales fidem tanquam fundamentum suum requirunt, ut fiant secundum præscriptum legis divinæ. At verò, quod fit tanquam opus ex congruo, etsi ex fide, quæ in homine Christiano requiritur, non fiat, non dicitur esse peccatum, si modo fiat secundum præscriptum legis naturæ. Et hoc Paulus Apostolus ipse declarat 2.Rom.v.14. Ipsa enim gentes, cum non habent legem, naturaliter, quæ legis sunt, faciunt, ejusmodi legem (scilicet spiritus) non habentes, sibi ipsi sunt lex. 3. Apostolus ad Coloss 2. v. 8. inquit, Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam &c. Ergo nec ex Ethnicorum scriptis aliquid discere licet. Resp. Posteriora verba priora exponere, & ideo illum de abusu, non vero de usu Philosophiae loqui certum est, cum addit inanem fallaciam.
units.tr: (2) The Apostle Paul says in Romans 14: "Whatever is done without faith is sin." Therefore, since those sayings of the heathen, which do not proceed from faith, beget sin, they are not to be touched. Answer to the antecedent: there are two kinds of human works, one called works of agreement [ex complacito], the other works of congruity [ex congruo]. Whatever is done as a work of agreement, or of merit, without faith in spiritual matters, is sin, because the spiritual actions of man require faith as their foundation, in order to be done according to the prescription of the divine law. But what is done as a work of congruity, even if it is not done from the faith required in a Christian man, is not called sin, provided it is done according to the prescription of the law of nature. The Apostle Paul himself declares this in Romans 2:14: "For the Gentiles, who have not the law, by nature do the things of the law"; not having such a law (namely, of the Spirit), they are a law to themselves. (3) The Apostle in Colossians 2:8 says: "Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy, etc." Therefore it is not lawful to learn anything from the writings of the heathen. Answer: The latter words explain the former, and it is certain that he speaks of the abuse, not the proper use, of philosophy, since he adds "empty deceit."

units.la: VII. DE METHODO.
units.tr: VII. ON METHOD.

units.la: QVOD vero ad Methodum, qua Aristoteles utitur, certum est uti methodo Analytica, nam ut ipse ait cap. 13. lib. 7. Polit. duo sunt, in quibus omnis perfectio consistit in hujusmodi disciplinis. Unum est finem & scopum ponere actionum rectarum; alterum vero actiones ducentes ad finem seu media invenire; nam cum ratio Methodi analyticae postulat, ut vel ab effectis ad causas, quod fit interdum in disciplinis Theoreticis nostrę commoditatis gratia, vel a fine ad principia progrediamur. Sic Aristoteles in hac disciplina morali a beatitudine tanquam a fine rerum humanarum exorsus est, deinde ad principia & media virtutis, nempe voluptatem & amicitiam, quae sunt virtutum adjumenta, progreditur. Causae vero, cur a fine primo incipiat, non sunt leves, nam quia Ethica versatur circa τὰ πράκτα, & homines natura sua ad vitia sunt proclives, ideo necesse fuit finem primo ponere, ut hoc propositio magis ad virtutem inclinarent homines, & a vitiis abhorrerent. 2. Quia finis est mensura & regula actionum humanarum propter quem omnes actiones eduntur, & in quo tanquam operationis suae ultimo termino acquiescunt. 3. Sicut sagittarii non prius spicula aut sagittas in scopum dirigunt, quàm scopum sibi propositum videant; sic etiam homines ad virtutes non prius accenduntur, quàm scopum tanquam præmium propositum videant. 4. Demum, vt addit Eustathius, adipisci est laboriosissimum, ideo operæ precium est in principio laboris & molestiæ premium ob oculos proponere, vt homines hoc incitati minori cum anxietate ad finem contendant.
units.tr: As to the method which Aristotle uses, it is certain that he uses the analytic method. For, as he himself says in book 7, chapter 13 of the Politics, there are two things in which all perfection consists in disciplines of this kind. The first is to set down the end and goal of right actions; the second is to discover the actions and means which lead to the end. For the rule of the analytic method requires that we proceed either from effects to causes, which is sometimes done in theoretical disciplines for the sake of our convenience, or from the end to the principles. Thus Aristotle in this moral discipline began from happiness as the end of human affairs, and then proceeds to the principles and means of virtue, namely pleasure and friendship, which are aids to the virtues. The reasons why he begins from the first end are not slight. (1) Because Ethics is concerned with things to be done [τὰ πράκτα], and men by nature are prone to vices, it was necessary to set the end first, so that by this proposition men might be more inclined to virtue and abhor vices. (2) Because the end is the measure and rule of human actions, the sake for which all actions are performed, and in which, as in the ultimate term of their operation, they come to rest. (3) Just as archers do not aim their darts or arrows at the target before they see the target set before them, so men are not kindled to the virtues before they see the goal set before them as a reward. (4) Lastly, as Eustathius adds, to attain the end is the most laborious thing; therefore it is worth while to place before the eyes, at the beginning of labour and toil, the reward, so that men, spurred on by this, may strive toward the end with less anxiety.

units.la: VIII. DE ARGVMENTO.
units.tr: VIII. ON THE ARGUMENT.

units.la: SVMMA totius operis, quod continetur his libris, breviter hæc est: Primò agitur de fine actionum humanarum, & is definitur, & à variis códitionibus & proprietatibus, quibus dignosci possit, explicatur libro primo. Postea illa adjumenta aggreditur, quibus finem assequimur, quorum princeps est Virtus, ideo naturam explicat, non quatenus ad mentem & judicium pertinet, sed quatenus ad affectus moderandos spectat; & definitur habitus inter excessum & defectum libro secundo. Tertio libro agit de principiis virtutum, voluntario, involuntario, & de electione & consultatione, & cap. 8. orditur specialem tractatum virtutum singularum, & primò incipit à Fortitudine, quam explicat reliquo libro 3 una cum Temperantia. Libro quarto de Liberalitate & Magnificentia & cæteris agit, ubi etiam quasdam quæstiones interserit de Magnanimitate. Libro quinto toto agit de Iustitia, & illam accuratissimè tractat. Libro sexto agit de virtutibus illis, quæ vulgò vocantur Intellectuales, vt sunt, Intellectus, Scientia, Sapientia, Prudentia & Ars, & subtilissimè omnium tractat Prudentiam, tum quia est veluti norma virtutum moralium, tum quia circa actiones humanas sicut virtutes morales versatur. Libro septimo in initio agit de praecipua virtute nempe heroica, postea de Continentia, Incontinentia, Tolerantia & Intolerantia & hujusmodi virtutum affectionibus: ultimis quatuor capitibus de Voluptate & Dolore, Virtutis objecto, quaestiones variae spargit. Libro octavo & nono de Amicitia agit, tum quia est maximum virtutis adjumetum, tum quia sine ea vitam bene agere aut felicitatem consequi nemo potest: cum unio omnium aut saltem plurium inter se virtutum haec esse videatur Libro octavo Amicitiam definit, & naturā ipsius variis modis explicat, nec immerito Cic. praeclare in Lal. Quiamicitia e societate hominum tollunt, Solem e mundo tollere videntur. Libro nono quaestiones nobiliores undecim tractat. Decimo demum & ultimo libro tria agit: 1. Voluptatis naturam investigat, & accurate explicat 4. primis capitibus. 2. Membro (ut totius operis connexio & ordo in serie volvatur, & in idem desinat, unde inceperat) felicitatem breviter explicat, & duas ejus partes esse Theoreticam nempe & Practicam declarat. 3. Est Epilogus totius operis, ostenditque, quaenam sit conexio horum librorum Ethicorum cum libris Politicis, & quam necessario isti libri sint Politicis adjungendi.
units.tr: The SUMMARY of the whole work, which is contained in these books, is briefly this. First, the end of human actions is treated: it is defined and explained, by means of its various conditions and properties by which it may be recognised, in book one. Next, he takes up those aids by which we attain the end, the chief of which is Virtue; so he explains its nature, not as it pertains to the mind and judgement, but as it bears on moderating the passions, and defines it as a disposition lying between excess and deficiency, in book two. In the third book he treats of the principles of the virtues, the voluntary and the involuntary, and of choice and deliberation; and at chapter 8 he begins a special treatment of the individual virtues, starting with Courage, which he explains in the rest of book 3 together with Temperance. In book four he deals with Liberality and Magnificence and the others, where he also inserts some questions about Magnanimity. In book five he deals throughout with Justice, and treats it most thoroughly. Book six deals with those virtues commonly called Intellectual, namely Understanding, Knowledge, Wisdom, Prudence and Art, and of all of them he treats Prudence most subtly, both because it is as it were the rule of the moral virtues and because it is concerned with human actions just as the moral virtues are. Book seven at the beginning deals with the chief virtue, namely the heroic, then with Continence, Incontinence, Endurance and Intolerance and the affections of such virtues; in the last four chapters he scatters various questions about Pleasure and Pain and the object of virtue. Books eight and nine deal with Friendship, both because it is the greatest help to virtue and because no one can live well or attain happiness without it, since the union of all virtues, or at least of several of them among themselves, seems to be this. In book eight he defines Friendship and explains its nature in various ways, and not undeservedly Cicero nobly says in the Laelius: For those who take friendship away from the society of men seem to take the sun out of the world. Book nine treats eleven more noteworthy questions. Finally, the tenth and last book treats three things: (1) it investigates the nature of Pleasure and explains it carefully in the first four chapters; (2) Next (so that the connection and order of the whole work may turn in a series and end where it began) it briefly explains happiness, and declares that its two parts are the Theoretical and the Practical; (3) it is the Epilogue of the whole work, and shows what the connection of these Ethical books is with the Politics, and how necessarily these books must be joined to the Politics.

units.la: IX. DE TITVLO.
units.tr: IX. CONCERNING THE TITLE.

units.la: INSCRIBUNTUR isti libri Nicomachia, quia ad Nicomachum filium suum istos Aristot. & illius erudiendi ergo scripsit. Sunt tamen viri magni, qui hoc titulo falsi putant istos libros non ab Arist. sed a filio Nicomacho scriptos, quorum e numero est Cicero cero lib.5.de sin.statim initio sic scribit: Quare intelliga-mus Aristot.& filium ejus Nicomachum, cujus eruditi extat de moribus libri, dicitur illi quidem Aristotelis, sed non video, cur non potuerit patri similis esse filius. Idem testatur etiam Diog.Laërt.lib.8.de vit. Philos.in vita Eudoxi. Et Suidas testatur Nicomachum scripsisse 10. libros de morib. Idem etiam ex Neotericis testatur Francif. Patricius lib.4. tom.1.discurs.Perip. Quare operæ precium erit osten-dere genuinum esse opus Aristotelis, alioquin fru-stra pro Aristotelico opere obtruderetur. Esse verò ipsius Arist.hæc rationes evincunt: 1. In libris Polit. qui ab omnibus Arist. tribuuntur, horum facit mentio-nem,ut lib.2.c.2.lib 3 c.13.lib.1.Metaph c.1. 2. Ethica & Politica ita inter se conexa sunt (ut ex epilogo horum librorum cōstat) ut qui unius fuerit autor, etiam alte-rius sit necesse est. 3. Stylus & loquendi Phrasis ea-dem est in libris his atq; in aliis, ut ex collatione faci-le patet. 4. Ætas filii immatura (nam adolescens ad-modum obiit, ut testatur Suidas) hoc tam præcla-rum opus non fert, nam lectione plurimorum auto-rum, Poëtarum & Philosophorū excellu sse constat autorem huius operis, tum etiam experietiam & ju-dicium huiusmodi operis collectio requirit, quæ in adolescente nunquam reperiuntur. 5. Ubi autor lib.1. c.4. disputat contra Plat. de Idæis, ibi Platonem vocat amicum suum, quod nō conveniret Nicomacho, nam antequam ille nasceretur, Plato e vivis excesserat. 6. Testimonia gravissimorum autorū, ut Alex. Aphro-disi antiquissimi Aristot. interpretis, tum etiam Plu-tarchi & aliorū, ut Them.st., Ammonii, &c. hoc ipsum evincunt, nam illi omnes uno ore hoc opus Aristo-teli attribuunt.
units.tr: These books are entitled Nicomachia, because Aristotle wrote them to his son Nicomachus, for the sake of instructing him. Yet there are great men who, on the strength of this title, think that these books were written not by Aristotle but by his son Nicomachus. Among them is Cicero, who at the very beginning of lib. 5. de fin. writes: Wherefore let us understand Aristotle and his son Nicomachus, whose learned books on morals survive. They are indeed said to be Aristotle's, but I do not see why a son could not have been like his father. The same is attested by Diogenes Laertius, lib.8.de vit. Philos.in vita Eudoxi. Suidas also attests that Nicomachus wrote ten books on morals. Among the moderns, Francesco Patrizi likewise attests this, lib.4. tom.1.discurs.Perip. It is therefore worth the effort to show that this is a genuine work of Aristotle; otherwise it would be pushed upon us in vain as an Aristotelian work. That these books are truly Aristotle's is proved by the following arguments: (1) In the Politics, which all attribute to Aristotle, he makes mention of these books, as in lib.2.c.2., lib.3 c.13., lib.1.Metaph c.1. (2) Ethics and Politics are so connected with each other (as is clear from the epilogue of these books) that whoever was the author of one must necessarily be the author of the other. (3) The style and manner of expression are the same in these books as in the others, as is easily seen from comparison. (4) The son's age was immature (for he died quite young, as Suidas attests), and such an immature man could not produce a work so distinguished. It is clear from the reading of very many authors, poets and philosophers, that the author of this work excelled in learning, and such a collection of experience and judgment as this work requires is never found in a young man. (5) Where the author, lib.1. c.4., disputes against Plato about the Ideas, he calls Plato his friend, which would not suit Nicomachus, for Plato had departed this life before Nicomachus was born. (6) The testimonies of most weighty authors prove this very point: Alexander of Aphrodisias, the most ancient interpreter of Aristotle, and also Plutarch and others such as Themistius, Ammonius, etc., for all of them with one voice attribute this work to Aristotle.

units.la: DE LIBRO PRIMO, & ad CAPUT I.
units.tr: Book One, and on Chapter 1

units.la: PRimus Liber, qui ex præscripto Methodi Analyticæ de Summmo Bono agit, tanquam fine actionum humanarum duobus constat membris: Proœmio & ipsa Tractatione. Proœmium continet apparatum ad futuram disputationem. Tractatio variorum opiniones varias, & propriam Aristotelis de Summo Bono habet, quod reliquo postea libro fusè explicat.
units.tr: The first book, which by the rule of the Analytic Method treats of the Chief Good as the end of human actions, consists of two parts: the Proem and the Treatment itself. The Proem contains the preparation for the discussion to come. The Treatment sets out the various opinions and Aristotle's own account of the Chief Good, which he later explains at length in the remaining book.

units.la: Proœmium, quod primo hoc capite absolvitur, quatuor constat partibus. 1. Quærit; An aliquis sit finis actionum humanarum, & ostendit esse, primis statim verbis. 2. Cujus sit scientia seu disciplina de hoc fine agere, & respondet Politicæ seu Architectonicæ. 3. Quibus rationibus sit utendum circa finem & medium, quæ tendunt ad finem, & respondet probabilibus non demonstrativis. 4. Quis sit idoneus auditor Ethices, & respondet illum esse, qui non solum præcepta Ethica in usum suum adhibere possit, sed qui affectus regere & iis moderari queat.
units.tr: The Proem, which is completed in this first chapter, consists of four parts. (1) It asks whether there is any end of human actions, and shows at once, in its opening words, that there is. (2) It asks whose science or discipline it is to treat of this end, and answers that it belongs to Politics or Architectonics. (3) It asks what kinds of reasoning are to be used concerning the end and the means that lead to the end, and answers that probable, not demonstrative, reasoning is to be used. (4) It asks who is a fit hearer of Ethics, and answers that it is one who can not only apply the ethical precepts to his own use, but who can also govern his passions and moderate them.

units.la: Esse finem probat hoc modo, quia omnis methodus, omnis actio & electio bonum aliquod appetunt, tunt sua propensione & natura, & hoc bonum, quod appetunt, finis rationem obtinet, & ideo cum omnis ars, &c etiam humana omnia finem sibi praescriptum habeant necesse erit, dicit bonum aliquod appetere, quia boni & finis rationes sunt propinquissimae, nam omnis finis appetitur sub specie boni sive revera sive apparentis, & ideo finis intenditur, quia bonum esse judicatur, & quia hoc bonum est commune omnium moventium bonum, in quo agentia omnia motionis suae terminum & quietem habent, finis dicitur. Sed cum variae finium sint differentiae, alius enim finis dicitur actio, ubi post operationem agentis nihil remanet, ut, verbi gratia, musicae finis est cantus, & est mera tantum actio; alius finis dicitur opus, quod insequitur actionem ipsam, ut in arte frenaria, frenum est finis artis & opus, quod post operationem agentis relinquitur, & in his artibus, in quibus post operationem relinquitur opus ipsum, opus est praestantius actione, ut frenum in arte frenaria est praestantius quid, actione mallei & caeterorum instrumentorum per quae producitur, quod intelligendum est in una eademque arte, ubi opus insequitur actionem, at nihil vetat, quo minus in diversis artibus & disciplinis actio sit praestantior opere, ut cantus in Musica est quid praestatius quam frenum in arte frenaria, quia nobiliorum artium fines sunt nobiliores, minus nobilium artium finibus. Hoc ideo per parenthesin inseruit Aristoteles, quod licet felicitas sit actio, non opus, est praestantissimus & nobilissimus tamen rerum humanarum finis.
