At vero etiamsi omnis ars, &c. finem appetat, non est unus tamen & singularis aliquis finis omnium artium & scientiarum, sed unicuique scientiæ & arti suus peculiaris destinatus est finis, ut Medicæ artis finis est sanitas, nauticæ navis, ita tamen ut inferiorum artium fines referantur ad fines superiorum & principalium artium fines, tanquam ad ultimum suum scopum, ita superiorum & principaliorum artium fines sunt nobiliores iis quę subjacent, sive sint actiones sive opera, sed cum certus sit omnium agendorum finis, qui per seipsum expetitur, & propter ipsum cætera omnia, ideo iste finis erit ultimus actionum humanarum finis: & proprium hominis bonū, qui nisi daretur, frustra esset appetitus noster, vanum omne desiderium, si in infinitum excurreret, esset enim si in infinitū, ideo impossibile, si impossibile, ergo frustra, si frustra, ergo Deus & natura frustra aliquid faciunt, nempe appetitum, quod est absurdissimum: ideo cum cognitio hujus finis magnopere conferat ad vitæ totius cursum instituendum, sicut sagittarii scopum intuentes facilius spicula dirigunt, ideo facilior finis adsequendi erit facultas, proposito summo bono tanquam fine actionum humanarum. Hactenus finem esse & ultimum quidem, in quo appetitus motionem aut operationem suam sistat, demonstravit Philosophus: Jam in secunda parte quærit, cujus sit disciplina, & respondet, cum sit ultimus finis actionum humanarum, ad quem omnes alii fines referuntur, ideo est nobilissimus, & nobilissimæ disciplinæ debetur, talis vero est Politica seu moralis Philosophia. Politicam vero ideo nobilissimam dominam vocat scientiarum, quod constituat & ordinet, quæ disciplinæ in Rep. tradendæ sint, quæ utiles, & quæ inutiles, & quantum cuique disciplinæ temporis & operis sit impendendum, ut sic commune civitatis bonum plantari primum in Repub l. secundò diuturnum esse possit. Hinc docet se tradere commune civitatis bonum, quod universo generi hominum inservit, & ideo est præstantissimum, nam bonum, quo communius, eò est melius. Notandum vero Politicam hic dici non unam Philosophiæ moralis partem, sed totam & integram Philosophiam moralem, & ideo καὶ ἐξοχὴν nomine Politices insigniri, non tantum hic, sed ubique apud Aristotelem, propterea quodcunque homines agunt ad finem Politices, tanquam ultimum referri debeat. Vocat vero Architectonicam similitudine ducta ab ædificiis exstruendis. Sicut enim architecto inserviunt fabri lignarii, ferrarii, cæmentarii, sic & Politicæ reliquæ omnes artes inferiores.
units.tr: He proves that there is an end in this way. Every method, every action and every choice aims at some good, by its own inclination and nature, and this good which they aim at holds the nature of an end. Therefore, since every art and all human activities have some end set before them, it must be that they aim at some good. He says "good" because the notions of good and of end are very closely related: every end is sought under the aspect of good, whether it truly is good or only seems so. An end is pursued because it is judged to be good, and because this good is the common object of everything that desires good, in which all agents find the term and rest of their motion, it is called an end. But since there are various kinds of ends, one end is an action, where nothing remains after the agent's operation; for example, the end of music is the song, which is a mere action. Another end is a work, which follows the action itself; thus in the art of bridling, the bridle is both the end and the work of the art, which remains after the agent's operation. In those arts where the work remains after the operation, the work is more excellent than the action. Thus in the art of bridling the bridle is more excellent than the action of the hammer and the other instruments by which it is produced. This must be understood within one and the same art, where the work follows the action. Nothing, however, prevents an action in one art from being more excellent than a work in a different art or discipline: the song in music is something more excellent than the bridle in the art of bridling, because the ends of the more noble arts are more noble than the ends of the less noble arts. Aristotle inserted this in parentheses, because although happiness is an action and not a work, it is nonetheless the most excellent and noblest of human ends. Moreover, even if every art, and so on, aims at an end, there is not one single end for all arts and sciences. Each science and art has its own proper end: the end of the medical art is health, and the end of shipbuilding is the ship. Yet the ends of the lower arts are referred to the ends of the higher and principal arts, as to their ultimate goal. In this way the ends of the higher and principal arts are more noble than those subordinate to them, whether they are actions or works. But since there is a certain end of all things to be done, which is sought for its own sake and for the sake of which all other things are sought, this end will be the ultimate end of human actions, and the proper good of man. If it were not given, our appetite would be in vain, and all desire would be empty, running on to infinity. For if it ran on to infinity, it would be impossible; and if impossible, then in vain; and if in vain, then God and nature would do something in vain, namely, give us appetite, which is most absurd. Therefore, since the knowledge of this end contributes greatly to directing the whole course of life, just as archers who keep their eye on the target aim their arrows more easily, the ability to attain the end will be easier if the highest good is set before us as the end of human actions. Thus the Philosopher has shown that there is an end, and indeed an ultimate one, in which appetite comes to rest in its motion or operation. In the second part he asks whose discipline it is, and answers that, since it is the ultimate end of human actions, to which all other ends are referred, it is most noble and is owed to the most noble discipline. Such a discipline is Politics, or moral philosophy. He calls Politics the most noble mistress of the sciences because it establishes and orders which disciplines are to be taught in the commonwealth, which are useful and which useless, and how much time and labour is to be given to each discipline, so that the common good of the state may first be planted in the commonwealth and secondly may be able to endure. Hence he teaches that he is delivering the common good of the state, which serves the whole human race, and is therefore the most excellent, for the good that is more common is the better. It must be noted that Politics here is not taken as one part of moral philosophy, but as the whole and complete moral philosophy. It is therefore designated by the name of Politics par excellence [καὶ ἐξοχὴν], not only here but everywhere in Aristotle, because whatever men do ought to be referred to the end of Politics as their ultimate end. He calls it Architectonic by an analogy drawn from the construction of buildings. For just as carpenters, smiths and masons serve the architect, so all the other lower arts serve Politics.

units.la: In tertia parte probabilibus tantum non necessariis rationibus utendum in Ethica docet, propterea quod materia circa quam Ethica versatur, non natura constet, sed usu & consuetudine, & ideo est contingens, quæ pro ratione temporis, loci & personarum subinde mutari potest, & ideo in Ethica necessariæ & exactæ demonstrationes sicut in Mathematicis non sunt quærendæ, sed sufficit si probabiles adhibeantur, quæ materiæ subjectæ illustrandæ inserviunt: nam unumquodque est tractandum, prout natura ejus fert, natura vero rerum Ethicarum est inconstans, nam est magna morum dissimilitudo apud varias gentes, est magna etiam rerum multitudo & crebra legum mutatio & incertus rerum moralium eventus, & ob hanc causam exacte demonstrare nequeunt, neque hoc tantum in morali Philosophia fieri solet. Philosophus, sed etiam in artibus tam liberalibus quam mechanicis, quae circa ejusmodi res versantur, quae in sola hominum sunt potestate. In quarta demum part a ostendit: Quisnam sit idoneus auditor huius disciplinae, & excludit juvenem, quo nomine intelligit omnem hominem, qui seipsum vincere & affectibus moderari nequit, nam sicut juvenis peritia rerum destituitur propter aetatem immaturam, & ideo recte de rebus judicium ferre nequit, ita etiam quicunque est incontinens, & fluxu ac refluxu affectuum laborat, praecepta Ethica in usum suum adhibere nequit, & ideo ea frustra audiret, at vero qui affectibus rectae rationi subjugatis moderari potest, ille maximam inprimis utilitatem ex hac disciplina percipiet, ideo verus & genuinus auditor est, lib. etiam 10. cap. 9. cur juvenem excludat, hanc rationem affert, quia inquit, alii boni viri dicuntur natura, alii educatione, alii doctrina; At vero cum sint pauci, qui ex natura affectibus moderari possunt, etsi sit indoles quaedam multis ingenita, ut melius & facilius multo quam alii sibi ipsis moderari possint. Educatione vero & doctrina pauci imo nulli virtuti studebunt, nisi praeceptis Ethicis ad recte agendum imbuantur.
units.tr: In the third part he teaches that only probable, not necessary, reasons are to be used in Ethics. The reason is that the matter with which Ethics is concerned rests not on nature but on use and custom, and is therefore contingent, and can be changed from time to time according to the circumstances of time, place and persons. Hence in Ethics strict and necessary demonstrations, such as are sought in mathematics, are not to be looked for; it is enough if probable ones are employed, which serve to illustrate the subject matter. For each thing is to be treated as its nature requires, and the nature of ethical things is inconstant. For there is great diversity of manners among different peoples, great variety of affairs, frequent changes of law, and an uncertain outcome of moral matters, and for this reason they cannot be demonstrated exactly. This is not usually the case only in moral philosophy, Philosopher, but also in the liberal and mechanical arts, which deal with such things as lie solely within the power of men. Finally, in the fourth part he shows who is a fit hearer of this discipline, and he excludes the young man, by which name he understands every man who cannot master himself and moderate his passions. For just as the young man lacks experience of affairs because of his immature age, and therefore cannot rightly judge of things, so also whoever is incontinent, and labours under the ebb and flow of his passions, cannot apply the ethical precepts to his own use, and so would hear them in vain. But he who can moderate his passions, which are subjected to right reason, will above all derive the greatest benefit from this discipline. Therefore he is the true and genuine hearer. In book 10 chapter 9, he gives this reason why he excludes the young: for, he says, some good men are called good by nature, others by upbringing, others by teaching. But since only a few can moderate their passions by nature, though there is a certain disposition, innate in many, by which they can govern themselves much better and more easily than others, yet by upbringing and teaching only a few, or indeed none, will apply themselves to virtue unless they are imbued with the ethical precepts for acting rightly.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Omnia, quae fiunt, finis alicujus gratia fiunt.
units.tr: 1. Everything that is done is done for the sake of some end.

units.la: 2. Omnis finis aut est opus, aut operatio, quae cuilibet competit actioni.
units.tr: 2. Every end is either a work or an operation, which belongs to some action.

units.la: 3. Appetitus non frustra appetit, quae appetitionis sua finem, in quo consistat, habet.
units.tr: 3. Appetite does not desire in vain: whatever has an end to its desire, in which it may rest.

units.la: 4. Nobilißima disciplina nobilissimum est finis.
units.tr: 4. A most noble discipline has a most noble end.

units.la: 5. Bonum quo communius, eo melius & praestantius.
units.tr: 5. The more widely a good is shared, the better and more excellent it is.

units.la: 6. Unumquodque rei tractatio fieri debet, quantum natura rei patitur.
units.tr: 6. The treatment of each thing ought to be carried out as far as the nature of the thing allows.

units.la: 7. Unusquisque in sua arte est optimus judex.
units.tr: 7. Everyone is the best judge in his own art.

units.la: 8. Ethica finis est actio, non cognitio.
units.tr: 8. The end of ethics is action, not knowledge.

units.la: 9. Juvenis est aliquo aetate, aliquo moribus, ille digne audit hic non.
units.tr: 9. One young man is suited to one thing by age and another by character; the one listens profitably, the other does not.

units.la: Quaeritur I. An omnia bonum appetant, nam malum mali appetunt, & sciunt se appetere malum, ut fur appetit furtum, latro homicidium, &c. Boni etiam ex duobus malis minus eligunt, ideo non videtur vero consentaneum omnia bona appetere. Resp. Ex distinctione facile diluitur, nam cum bonum aliud sit verum, aliud apparens, teste ipso Arist. in procem. Polit. ideo nihil est, quod non appetat alterutrum, unde statim primis verbis Philosophus subjicit, bonum appetere videtur, quod appetitus non semper feratur in verum bonum.
units.tr: I. Whether all things seek the good. For bad men seek evil, and know that they seek evil, as the thief seeks theft, the robber murder, and so on. Also, of two evils men choose the lesser, so it does not seem true that all things seek good. Answer: The objection is easily resolved by a distinction. For since the good is one thing in truth and another in appearance (as Aristotle himself says in the preface to the Politics), there is nothing that does not seek one or the other. Hence the Philosopher at once adds in his opening words that the good seems to be what all things seek, because appetite does not always tend toward the true good.

units.la: II. An hoc sit verum, opus esse praestantius ipsa actione, nam charitas, qua vis alium cibare, vestire, sanare, est actio, & fit ista actio propter opus, nempe vestitum, cibationem; at ipsa charitas est longe praestantior opere ullo, cum sit virtutum Theologicarum praestantissima, quod diserte testatur Apostolus 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: II. Whether it is true that the work is more excellent than the action itself. For charity, by which one wishes to feed, clothe, and heal another, is an action, and this action is performed for the sake of a work, namely clothing and feeding. Yet charity itself is far more excellent than any work, since it is the most excellent of the theological virtues, as the Apostle plainly testifies in 1 Cor. 13.

units.la: Resp. Cum Aristoteles dicit opus esse praestantius quid actione, intelligit eju dem artis & disciplinae actionem & opus, at cum charitas & vestitus non sint ejusdem artis, nam illa pertinet ad Theologiam, haec vero ad sartoriam, ideo nihil facit contra opinionem Aristotelis. 2. Politice loquendo melius est membrum aliquod Reip. conservare, ne fame pereat & morbo, quam istam actionem per quam servatur edere.
units.tr: Answer: When Aristotle says that the work is more excellent than the action, he means the action and the work of the same art and discipline. But charity and clothing do not belong to the same art, for the one pertains to theology and the other to tailoring; so the objection does nothing against Aristotle's opinion. (2) Speaking politically, it is better to preserve some member of the commonwealth so that he does not perish of hunger or disease than to perform that action by which he is preserved.

units.la: III. Cum Aristoteles in textu dicat Imperatoriae artis finem esse victoriam, Medicinae sanitatem, Oeconomiae divitias, an isti sint vere fines humanarum scientiarum, nam Medicina verus finis videtur esse bene mederi, Oeconomia familiam bene administrare. Resp. In exemplis adferendis non semper solicitum esse Aristotelem, ut ad amussim veritatis semper congruant, sed accommodare se ad vulgi captum & opinionem, ut hoc modo doctrinam suam ipsorum animis magis accommodet, & quanquam isti non sunt vere fines, tamen a nullo negari potest, quin ista primum respiciant hae facultates, & pro viribus nitantur ea consequi, ut tandem ad verum & propositum finem perveniant.
units.tr: III. Since Aristotle in the text says that the end of the art of the general is victory, of medicine health, and of household management wealth, are these truly the ends of the human sciences? For medicine seems to have as its true end the good healing of the sick, and household management the good governing of the family. Answer: Aristotle was not always concerned, in the examples he brings forward, that they should agree exactly with the strict standard of truth. Instead he adapted himself to the grasp and opinion of the common people, so that in this way he might fit his teaching more readily to their minds. And although these are not truly ends, yet no one can deny that these faculties first aim at them and strive by their powers to attain them, so that at last they may reach the true and intended end.

units.la: IV. An Ethica fit rejicienda, quod non utatur veris demonstrationibus.
units.tr: IV. Whether ethics should be rejected because it does not use true demonstrations.

units.la: Resp. Minime; nam uniuscujusque rei tractatio debet provenire ab ipsa rei natura, & 2. Nobilissimae hae disciplinae Medicina, Rhetorica, Dialectica, &c. rejici etiam deberent, quod non utantur exquisitis demonstrationibus, sed probabilibus tantum materiae subjectae convenientibus. 3. Etsi Ethica versetur circa res contingentes, & ideo res varientur pro variis objectis, tamen praecepta collecta ex his rebus sunt certa, firma & veluti demonstrativa.
units.tr: Answer: Not at all. For the treatment of each thing ought to arise from the very nature of the thing. Moreover, (2) these most noble disciplines, medicine, rhetoric, dialectic, and so on, would also have to be rejected, since they do not use exact demonstrations but only probable arguments suited to their subject matter. (3) Although ethics is concerned with contingent things, and therefore its matters vary according to the various objects, yet the precepts gathered from these things are certain, firm, and, as it were, demonstrative.

units.la: V. An Ethica fit plane supervacanea, quia mali & incontinentes arcentur ab Aristotele tanquam minus idonei auditores Ethicae, boni vero ea opus non habent, quia recte per se vivunt, & secundum virtutem agunt.
units.tr: V. Whether ethics is altogether superfluous, since Aristotle excludes the wicked and the incontinent as unfit hearers of ethics, while good men have no need of it, because they live rightly of themselves and act according to virtue.

units.la: Resp. Non esse supervacaneam, nam utrisque prodest tam malis quam bonis, nam etii mali ad omnia vitia sint proclives, tamen a vitiis ad virtutem per praecepta Ethica revocari possunt, & indies meliorſ fieri, quod Polemoni accidisse testatur Diogenes Laërt. lib. 4. de vita Philos. in vita ejus: Hic enim cum audisset Xeno-cratem disserentem de Temperantia, ita a nequam & improbo mutatus est, ut dignißimus omnium haberetur, qui Xenocrati propter vitæ candorem in schola succederet. Bonis vero prodest Ethica, ut ex bonis meliores fiant, & actiones suas recte diri-gant: nam sicut se habet Medicina ad corpus, ita E-thica ad animum hominis, & veluti Medicina sani-tatem corpori restituit, si absit; si adsit, confervat in tenore suo & regit: ita etiam Ethica animum homi-nis, si virtus absit, virtute imbuit, & si adsit, regit ac dirigit, nam etsi voluntas hominis boni sit prona ad virtutem, tamē potest ignorare quem unem sibi ha-beat virtus, & quibus circumstantiis sit exercenda, nisi præcepta Ethica accedant, quæ viam demonstrent.
units.tr: Answer: It is not superfluous, for it benefits both: it benefits the wicked as well as the good. For although the wicked are prone to all vices, yet they can be called back from vice to virtue through ethical precepts, and daily become better. This happened to Polemo, as Diogenes Laertius testifies in book 4 of the Lives of the Philosophers, in his life: for when he heard Xenocrates discoursing on temperance, he was so changed from a worthless and wicked man that he came to be thought the most worthy of all to succeed Xenocrates in the school, on account of the purity of his life. Ethics benefits good men too, so that from good men they may become better and direct their actions rightly. For as medicine stands to the body, so ethics stands to the soul of man. Medicine restores health to the body if it is absent; if it is present, medicine preserves it in its tone and governs it. So ethics also imbues the soul of man with virtue if virtue is absent, and if it is present, governs and directs it. For although the will of a good man is inclined to virtue, yet he may fail to know which virtue he ought to have and in what circumstances it is to be exercised, unless the ethical precepts come in to show the way.

units.la: VI. Cur Aristoteles non annumerarit juvenibus, qui minus possunt moderari affectibus & incontinentibus, etiam illos qui tam desperato sunt ingenio, ut vix ac ne vix quidem corrigi possint.
units.tr: VI. Why Aristotle did not count among the young those who are less able to govern their passions and are incontinent, including even those of so hopeless a disposition that they can hardly, or scarcely at all, be corrected.

units.la: Nam Galenus in lib. qui inscribitur: Quod Mores animi sequantur Temperamentum corporis, tria enumerat hominum genera. 1. Eorum, qui per naturam ad virtutem & bonos mores sunt apti. 2. Eorum, qui tantum ad vitia & libidines sunt proni, nec corrigi volunt, nec in melius se recipere. 3. Qui nec plane sunt ad virtutem proclives, nec plane etiam ad vitia, ideo possunt in utramque se vergere partem, prout incideriteducatio. Causa vero cur Aristoteles hos non annumerarit hæc est, quia etsi prodeamus omnes in lucem igniculis vitiorum & pec-deamus cati infecti, ad turpitudines & flagitia proclives, tam nihil horum tam altas egit in nobis radices, quin per exercitium virtutis aut plane tolli aut saltem corrigi possit, quod de Socrate & Stilpone Megarensi refert Cic. 4. Tuscul. quaest. sub sin. Ideo hoc secundum genus hominum Aristoteles plane non videtur admittere. Nam;
units.tr: For Galen, in the book entitled That the Morals of the Soul Follow the Temperament of the Body, lists three kinds of men. (1) Those who are by nature apt for virtue and good morals. (2) Those who are prone only to vices and lusts, and who neither wish to be corrected nor to reform themselves for the better. (3) Those who are neither plainly inclined to virtue nor plainly to vice, and who therefore can turn to either side, according as education falls upon them. The reason why Aristotle did not count these among the young is this: although we all come into the light with the sparks of vices, and are infected with sin and prone to baseness and shameful deeds, yet none of these has struck such deep roots in us that it cannot either be wholly removed or at least corrected through the exercise of virtue. Cicero, in the end of book 4 of the Tusculan Disputations, reports this of Socrates and of Stilpo of Megara. So Aristotle does not seem to admit this second kind of men at all. For:

units.la: Nemo adeo ferus est, qui non mitescere possit,Si modo cultura patientem accommodet aurem.
units.tr: No one is so wild that he cannot be softened, if only culture fits a patient ear.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: HActenus Proemium, sequitur ipsa Tractatio de Summo Bono. Tractatio absolvitur quinque partibus. In prima aliorum opiniones adducit de Summo Bono. In secunda aliorum opiniones allatas refellit, tanquam minus vero consentaneas. In tertia peculiari quodam tractatu Platonem refellit, qui in Idaea summum bonum collocavit. In quarta suam opinionem profert, & summum bonum ex sua sententia definit & explicat. In quinta quasdam aliorum opiniones cum sua sententia reconciliare nititur, ubi etiam hanc quaestionem inducit, an felicitas homini in hac vita, an vero in futura contingat. In prima igitur parte dicit, quo ad nomen summi boni, omnes inter se convenire tam doctos quam indoctos; at vero quid hoc nomine significetur, & quid sit, quod essentiam & naturam summi boni explicet, non inter se convenire, sed hoc dubiae esse assertionis, ideo in hoc secundo capite duo facit. In prima parte aliorum opiniones adducit: In secunda per digressionem quandam ostendit, qua methodo sit utendum in hac disciplina, & a quibus incipiendum. In prima igitur parte ostendit vulgus differre a Sapientibus, nam vulgus putat id esse summum bonum, quod in sen-sus incurrit, cujusmodi sunt divitiæ, voluptas, honor, &c & multitudo hominum inter se dissentiens pro ratione temporis & status opinionem etiam mutat: nam æger putat valetudinem esse summum bonum, pauper vero divitias. Sapientiores vero non putant esse aliquid, quod sensibus pateat, sed animo tantum perceptibile est, & quod cæteris bonis non modo est præferendum, sed illis omnibus bonitatis usum & perfectionem præbet: At vero omnes omnium opiniones recensere majoris esset molestiæ quam utilitatis, ideo sufficit, si eas opiniones enumeret, quæ facile nobis imponere possunt propter aliquam cognationem, quam habet cum ipso summo bono, ut facilius eruatur ipsum revera summum bonum. Nam sicut aliquis visa columba statim putat esse columbam, at vero si aquilam conspiciat, minime putat esse columbam: Sic quædam sunt opiniones de summo bono, ut nullis aut paucis imponere possint, quædam vero adeo præsefterunt summum bonum, ut multis prima statim facie imponant. Nam ut ex M. Varrone refert Augustinus lib. 19 de civit. Dei, c. 1, ducentæ octoginta octo erant variæ opiniones de summo bono. In secunda parte capitu paucis agit de Methodo propter Platonem, qui dubitabat, qua esset methodo utendum in morali disciplina & cum duplex sit Methodus, una à principiis ad finem quam vocant Compositivam, altera à fine ad principia quam vocant Resolutivam. Quod Aristoteles elegante similitudine illustrat: Sicut in stadio bipartitus erat cursus, unus à carceribus ad calcem seu metam, alius reflexus à meta ad carceres, docet à nobis notiore esse incipiendum, seu quod idem est, Methodo Analytica utendum. Hinc oportet eum, qui cum fructu disciplinam moralem audire velit, moribus recte instructum & dispositum esse, seu cupiditate quadam indolis suae ad virtutes ferri. Sic enim cognoscet operationem virtutum, quae est ipsa Felicitas, & si cognoscat, quid sit ipsa felicitas, habebit, quod ejus instituto sufficiat, etsi ultra non quaerat propter quid seu causas principiorum, ideo apparet illum in summam bonorum possessionem pervenisse, qui non solum recte agit, sed etiam novit se recte agere, & causas exquirit actionum bene aut male gestarum. 2. Illum esse bonum Ethicum ait, licet non cum priore conferendum, qui causas actionum exquirit, qui recte suo munere fungitur, etsi rationes & singulares rerum circumstantias ignoret. At vero qui nihil horum facit, audiat Hesiodum Poetam, qui illum infrugi, inutilem & nauci hominem pronuntiat.
units.tr: Hitherto the Proem; there follows the Treatise on the Highest Good itself. The Treatise is completed in five parts. In the first he brings forward the opinions of others about the Highest Good. In the second he refutes the opinions brought forward, as less consistent with the truth. In the third, in a particular treatise, he refutes Plato, who placed the Highest Good in the Idea. In the fourth he sets out his own opinion, and defines and explains the Highest Good according to his own judgment. In the fifth he tries to reconcile certain opinions of others with his own, where he also raises this question: whether happiness happens to a man in this life, or rather in the future. In the first part, then, he says that as to the name of the Highest Good, all agree among themselves, both learned and unlearned; but what is signified by this name, and what it is, which explains the essence and nature of the Highest Good, is not agreed among them, but is a doubtful assertion. Therefore in this second chapter he does two things. In the first part he brings forward the opinions of others; in the second, by a certain digression, he shows what method is to be used in this discipline, and from what things one must begin. In the first part, then, he shows that the common people differ from the wise. For the common people think that to be the highest good which falls under the senses, such as riches, pleasure, honour, and so on; and the multitude of men, disagreeing among themselves, change their opinion according to the circumstances of time and condition: the sick man thinks health is the highest good, the poor man riches. The wiser, however, do not think there is anything which lies open to the senses, but only what is perceptible to the mind, and which is to be preferred not only to other goods, but also gives to all of them their usefulness and perfection. But to review the opinions of everyone would be more troublesome than useful; therefore it is enough if he enumerates those opinions which can easily deceive us because of some kinship they have with the Highest Good itself, so that the true Highest Good may more easily be drawn out. For just as someone, on seeing a dove, at once thinks it is a dove, but if he sees an eagle, does not at all think it is a dove: so there are certain opinions about the Highest Good which can deceive none or few, while others present the Highest Good so closely that they deceive many at first sight. For, as Augustine relates from M. Varro, book 19 of The City of God, ch. 1, there were two hundred and eighty-eight different opinions about the Highest Good. In the second part of the chapter he treats briefly of Method, on account of Plato, who doubted what method was to be used in moral discipline; and since there is a twofold method, one from principles to the end, which they call Compositive, the other from the end to principles, which they call Resolutive. Aristotle illustrates this with an elegant comparison: just as in the stadium the course was in two parts, one from the starting gates to the goal or turning-post, and the other back again from the turning-post to the gates, he teaches that we must begin from what is better known to us, or, what is the same, that the Analytic method must be used. Hence one who wishes to hear moral discipline with profit must be well instructed and disposed in morals, that is, borne by a certain inclination of his nature towards the virtues. For thus he will know the operation of the virtues, which is happiness itself; and if he knows what happiness itself is, he will have what suffices for his purpose, even if he does not seek further the reason why, or the causes of the principles. Therefore it is evident that he has come into possession of the highest goods who not only acts rightly but also knows that he acts rightly, and seeks the causes of actions well or badly performed. 2. He says that one is an ethical good man, though not to be compared with the former, if he seeks the causes of actions and performs his duty rightly, even if he does not know the reasons and particular circumstances of things. But whoever does none of these things, let him hear the poet Hesiod, who pronounces him a worthless, useless and good-for-nothing man.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Ignorantia rerum parit admirationem.
units.tr: 1. Ignorance of things gives rise to wonder.

units.la: 2. Docti & indocti diversimode de rebus judicant.
units.tr: 2. Learned and unlearned judge things in different ways.

units.la: 3. Notiora sunt duplicia, natura & nobis.
units.tr: 3. Things are better known in two ways, by nature and to us.

units.la: 4. A notioribus nobis in Ethica incipiendum.
units.tr: 4. In Ethics one must begin from what is better known to us.

units.la: Quaeritur I. Cur tot & varie opiniones exstiterint de summo bono, ita ferme ut quot fuerint Philosophi, tot etiam effent discrepantes sententiae de summo bono. Resp. Quia homines non semper deliberant cum intellectu tanquam cum meliore animae suae parte, sed affectus etiam consultores adhibent, & cum affectus sint inconstan-
units.tr: Question I. Why have so many and such varied opinions arisen about the Highest Good, so that there are almost as many differing opinions about the Highest Good as there have been philosophers? Answer: Because men do not always deliberate with the intellect, as with the better part of their soul, but also bring in the affections as advisers; and since the affections are inconstant and varied, they have also produced varied opinions in men's minds, which they have held as the end and highest good of their actions, as may be seen in love, ambition, and other such affections.

units.la: [catchword] constanconstantes & varii, varias etiam genuerunt opiniones in hominum animis, quas illi pro fine & summo bono actionum suarum habuerunt, ut in amore & ambitione, & aliis ejusmodi affectibus cernere licet.
units.tr: [catchword] constant and varied, they have also produced various opinions in men's minds, which they held as the end and highest good of their actions, as may be seen in love, ambition, and other such affections.

units.la: II. Cum Aristoteles dicat sanè esse nosse, quod est principii, non verò inquirendum esse propter quid seu causas hujus principii accuratas, quid intelligat nomine principii; Si verò ipsam felicitatem, videtur hoc habere pro absurdo, nam felicitas est finis, finis verò & principium longè inter se differunt. Resp. Duplex esse principium aliud componens & illud à fine æquè longè ut causa ab effectu differt; Aliud est principium dirigens, quod non ita distat à fine, verbi gratia, Felicitas quatenus animum agentis impellit ad aliquid producendum, potest principium dici; quatenus verò causa efficiens felicitatem assequitur, & dum adipiscitur, in ea tanquam motionis suæ perfectione conquiescit, jam finis dicitur, & ideo Aristot. felicitate vocavit principium, quod etsi sit exsecutione ultimum & finis, tamè intentione & directione est primum, à quo efficiens incipit.
units.tr: II. Since Aristotle says that it is indeed enough to know what belongs to the principle, and that one should not inquire exactly into the reason why, or the causes of this principle; what does he mean by the name of principle? But if it is happiness itself, he seems to hold this to be absurd, for happiness is the end, and end and principle differ greatly from one another. Answer: The principle is twofold. One is a constituent principle, which differs from the end as far as cause differs from effect. Another is a directing principle, which is not so far from the end. For example, happiness, insofar as it impels the mind of the agent to produce something, can be called a principle; but insofar as the efficient cause attains happiness, and when it has attained it rests in it as the perfection of its motion, it is now called the end. Therefore Aristotle called happiness a principle, which, though it is last in execution and is the end, is first in intention and direction, and from which the efficient cause begins.

units.la: III. An Aristoteles πωλολογίαν commiserit, cum hic dicat non esse accuratius inquirendum de causis principii, cum etiam juperius in proœmio monuerit, non esse utendum expeditis rationibus & demonstrationibus in morali Philosophia sicut in Mathematicis. Resp. Minimè: nam in proœmio generaliter egit de omnibus rationibus, quibuscunque rationibus utendum esset in morali disciplina; hic specialiter accommodat ad ipsam naturam felicitatis, & ideo nulla committitur inanis repetitio.
units.tr: III. Did Aristotle commit a tautology, when he says here that one should not inquire more exactly into the causes of the principle, since he had also warned earlier in the proem that one should not use hasty reasonings and demonstrations in moral philosophy as in mathematics? Answer: By no means. For in the proem he dealt generally with all the kinds of reasoning that were to be used in moral discipline; here he applies this specially to the very nature of happiness, and so no vain repetition is committed.

units.la: IV. An liceat Poëtarum testimonia adhibere ad aliquid in in Philosophia probandum, quod hic fecit Philosophus, dum citat Hesiodum. Resp. Maximè: nam sicut vox emissa per canalem aut fistulam suavius sensus afficit, quàm quæ ipso ore profertur: sic etiam Poëtarum carmina magis afficiunt animos suavitate sua, & diutius memoriæ inhærét, quàm quæ soluta oratione dicuntur. 2. Ea etiam continentur apud Poëtas & brevius quidem quàm apud Philosophos. 3. Ab exemplo Aristotelis Philosophorum Principis, qui variis in locis multa spargit ex Poëtis. Idem etiam fecit Plato: idem Plutarchus, Cicero & alii. 4. D. Paulus Apostolus gentium testimonia Poëtarum in rebus divinis adhibuit, ut Act. 17. locum ex Arato Poëta citat, 1. Cor. 15. ex Menandro, ad Tit. c. 1. ex Epimenide.
units.tr: IV. Is it lawful to use the testimonies of poets to prove something in philosophy, as the philosopher did here when he cites Hesiod? Answer: Most certainly. For just as a voice sent through a tube or pipe affects the senses more sweetly than what is uttered by the mouth itself, so too the songs of the poets affect minds more by their sweetness, and cling longer to the memory, than what is said in prose. 2. Those things are also contained in the poets, and indeed more briefly than among the philosophers. 3. There is the example of Aristotle, the prince of philosophers, who in various places scatters much from the poets. Plato did the same, and Plutarch, Cicero and others. 4. The apostle Paul used the testimonies of the heathen poets in divine matters: thus in Act. 17. he cites a passage from the poet Aratus, in 1. Cor. 15. from Menander, and in ad Tit. c. 1. from Epimenides.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: INstitutam de Felicitate doctrinam persequitur hoc capite tertio, ubi aliorum opiniones maximè excellentes refellit. Partes igitur capitis sunt duæ: In prima ostendit, homines plerunque accommodare opiniones suas de summo bono ad ea vitæ genera, quibus ii maximè delectantur, & cum vulgò sint quatuor vitæ genera, nempe Voluptuarium, Politicum, Contemplativum & Quæstuosum, opiniones trium vitæ generum adducit, reiecto quarto vitæ genere nempe Contemplativo suo loco. In secunda parte has breviter refellit, qui igitur Voluptuario vitæ genere delectantur in voluptate summum bonum ponunt, quos sic refellit, quod voluptas nobis nempe sit communis cum belluis, & ideo detestatur vulgus autorem hujus opinionis, qui propterea, quod viderent, derent Magnates & Principes in eminentia constitutos, hoc vitæ genere maximè delectari, ideo summum bonum in ea collocabant. At Politici in honore aut virtute collocant, sed non esse in honore probat, quod honor sit in honorate potius, quàm in honorato, ut cap.8. lib.4. hujus operis fusè declaratur. At summum bonum proprium ejus est, cujus est summum bonum, & ideo in honore non consistit, qui penes alium nempe honorantem manet, & qui honorem appetunt, ideo appetunt, ut boni videantur. Ergo bonitatem habent tanquam ulteriorem finem sibi propositum. Nec in virtute consistit, propterea quod virtus sit imperfectum quid, & medium tendens ad summum bonum, & secundo virtus poterit esse, in dormiente aut nihil agente per totam vitam. Felicitas autem esse non potest, propterea quod ejus natura in actione consistat. Qui quæstuoso vitæ genere capiuntur, divitias pro summo bono habent, quas non esse sic probat. 1. Quia sunt violentæ, seu vi plerunque acquiruntur, aut quod idem est, contra naturam: Nam ut ipse egregiè disserit lib.7. Pol. c.6. est contra naturam, ut nummus nummum pariat, aut pecunia pecuniam, cum hoc non possit fieri absque damno alterius. Quod verò est contra naturam, idem quoque est violentum, ut ipse testatur lib.1. de cælo, t.10. Secunda ratio est, quia divitiæ alterius gratia acquiruntur, & sunt utiles. Quod verò est utile, non est absolutum, sed ad aliud refertur, nempe ad id, cujus est utile. Ideo ex his rationibus concludere licet, neq; in voluptate, neq; in honore, neq; in virtute, neq; in divitiis, situm esse summum bonum.
units.tr: In this third chapter he pursues the doctrine of happiness that he has set out, and there he refutes the most prominent opinions of others. The chapter therefore has two parts. In the first, he shows that people generally fit their opinions about the highest good to the ways of life that they enjoy most. Since there are commonly four ways of life, namely the pleasure-seeking, the political, the contemplative and the money-making, he cites the opinions of three of them, leaving the fourth, the contemplative, to its own place. In the second part he briefly refutes these. Those who delight in the pleasure-seeking way of life place the highest good in pleasure, and he refutes them as follows: pleasure is common to us and the beasts, and so the common people denounce the author of this opinion. They placed the highest good in pleasure because they saw that magnates and princes, who are set on high, delight most in this way of life. The political men place it in honour or in virtue. He proves that it does not lie in honour, because honour resides in the one who honours rather than in the one who is honoured, as is fully explained in chapter 8 of book 4 of this work. The highest good, however, belongs properly to the one whose highest good it is, and so it does not consist in honour, which remains with another, namely the one who honours. Those who seek honour seek it so that they may appear good, so they hold goodness as a further end set before themselves. Nor does it consist in virtue, because virtue is something imperfect and tends towards the highest good as a means. Moreover, virtue could exist in a person who is asleep or who does nothing through his whole life, whereas happiness cannot exist in such a person, because its nature consists in activity. Those who are captured by the money-making way of life hold riches to be the highest good, and he proves that they are not so: (1) because they are violent, that is, they are for the most part acquired by force, or what is the same, against nature. For, as he discusses excellently in book 1 of the Politics, chapter 6, it is against nature for money to breed money, since this cannot happen without loss to another. What is against nature is also violent, as he himself testifies in book 1 of On the Heavens, text 10. (2) The second reason is that riches are acquired for the sake of something else, and they are useful. What is useful, however, is not absolute but is related to something else, namely to that for which it is useful. Therefore from these reasons we may conclude that the highest good lies neither in pleasure, nor in honour, nor in virtue, nor in riches.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Summum bonum est proprium illius, cujus est summum bonum.
units.tr: 1. The highest good belongs to that of which it is the highest good.

units.la: 2. Honor cum sit in honorante potius quam in honorato, non erit summum bonum.
units.tr: 2. Since honour lies in the one who honours rather than in the one who is honoured, it will not be the highest good.

units.la: Quæritur 1. Cur Aristoteles istam opinionem de voluptate affinxerit vulgo seu multitudini, cum habuerit patronum satis celebrem nempe Epicurum, qui primus sectam Epicureorum instituit. Resp. Hoc ideo fecisse Aristotelem, quia fuit ætate major ipso Epicuro, & cum ista scriberet, nondum florere cœperat Epicurus. Et quanquam Aristippus Aulicus Philosophus hanc ipsam opinionem tueretur, (qui Platoni coætaneus fuit) noluisse tamen istam opinionem attingere, quod putaret indignum Philosopho tam beluinam opinionem habere.
units.tr: Question 1. Why did Aristotle attribute this opinion about pleasure to the common people or the multitude, when he had a fairly famous champion of it, namely Epicurus, who first founded the sect of the Epicureans? Answer. Aristotle did this because he was older than Epicurus himself, and Epicurus had not yet begun to flourish when Aristotle was writing these things. And although Aristippus, the court philosopher, defended this very opinion (he was a contemporary of Plato), Aristotle nevertheless did not wish to touch on it, because he thought it unworthy of a philosopher to hold so beastly an opinion.

units.la: II. Cur Aristoteles dicat in textu, honorem esse finem Politices, cum sit bonum tantum secundarium tendens ad finem, & præmium virtutis. Resp. Hoc non ex sua opinione, sed aliorum facere & hac de causa præsertim, quod Athenis nihil esset communius, quàm honoris gratia omnia præclara esse facienda, & ideo ut honoris fructum carperent, naves exædificabant, muros extruebat, milites multis suis privatis stipendiis alebant. Et Achilles apud Hom. I. Iliad. optat sibi potius vitam brevem cum honore splendidam, quam longam absq; honore obscuram.
units.tr: II. Why does Aristotle say in the text that honour is the end of politics, since it is only a secondary good, tending towards the end, and the reward of virtue? Answer. He does this not on his own view but on the view of others, and especially for this reason: at Athens nothing was more common than doing all noble things for the sake of honour. Therefore, in order to gather the fruit of honour, men built ships, raised walls, and supported soldiers at their own private expense. And Achilles, in Homer, Iliad 1, wishes for himself rather a short life brilliant with honour than a long life obscure without honour.

units.la: III. Quæritur à Stoicis & maximè à Seneca Epistola 79. ad Lucil. An Aristoteles rectè fecerit, qui virtutem, summum bonum esse negarit, propterea quod se plerunque non exerat ad externas actiones, cum hoc sit proprium virtutis in animo
units.tr: III. The Stoics, and above all Seneca in Epistle 79 to Lucilius, ask whether Aristotle was right to deny that virtue is the highest good, on the ground that it does not for the most part stretch out to external actions, since this is the peculiar nature of virtue, to reside in the mind

units.la: C animo tantum desidere? Resp. In virtute duo consideran-tur, habitus & actio virtutis: habitus quidem in animo residere potest, per quem tamen eorum bonorum, quæ in vita aguntur, non possumus esse participes, & ideo neque felices. At per actionem virtutis sumus participes eorum, quæ in vita aguntur, & ideo non immerito virtutis habitum in animo residente felicitatem afferre negavit Aristoteles, quod elegantissimæ similitudine cap. 9. hujus libri illustrat; sicut, inquit, in ludis olympicis non, qui spectarent, etsi essent pulcherrimi & robustissimi, coronabantur, sed qui certarent, ita in actione non in nudo habitu virtutis consistit felicitas.
units.tr: C in the mind alone? Answer. Two things are to be considered in virtue: the habit and the action of virtue. The habit can indeed reside in the mind, but through it we cannot be partakers of those goods which are pursued in life, and so we cannot be happy either. But through the action of virtue we are partakers of those things which take place in life, and so Aristotle was not unreasonably denying that the habit of virtue residing in the mind brings happiness. He illustrates this by a most elegant similitude in chap. 9 of this book: just as, he says, at the Olympic games the spectators, however handsome and robust, were not crowned, but those who competed, so happiness consists in action, not in the bare habit of virtue.

units.la: IV. An hoc veritati consentaneum sit, posse aliquem virtutem habere & dormire, ideo neque felicem esse posse, & ideo videtur removere felicitatem a dormiente, aut virtutis actiones intermittente? Resp. Ipse in textu mentem suam explicat, nam cum dicit, virtutem habentem dormire, statim subjicit, aut in vita nihil agere, quo intelligit ad bene beateq; vivendum virtutis habitum nihil prodesse, nisi accedat actio virtutis, in qua consistit ipsa felicitas.
units.tr: IV. Is it consistent with the truth that someone may have virtue and yet sleep, and therefore cannot be happy either, and so it seems that happiness is removed from one who is asleep, or who interrupts the actions of virtue? Answer. He himself explains his meaning in the text. For when he says that one who has virtue may sleep, he immediately adds, or do nothing in life, by which he means that the habit of virtue is of no benefit for living well and blessedly, unless the action of virtue is added, in which happiness itself consists.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: SEquitur tertia pars Tractationis, in qua Platonis Idæam, in qua posito dicebat esse summum bonum Plato, re futurat. Quatuor sunt partes hujus cap. 4. In prima proponit sibi disputandum de idea, ubi modesta quadam excusatione utitur, ut deceum servet in libro de moribus: In secunda parte Platonis opinionem nionem in Idæa summum bonum statuentis quatuor rationibus refellit: In tertia dubium quoddam Platonicum proponit & soluit: In quarta ostendit Idæas non pertinere ad præsens institutum, utut concedantur dari Idæas, propterea quod summum bonum ab homine possit separari, Idæam minimè possit. In prima parte proponit dicendum de Idæa, & dicit non esse præsentis instituti, propterea quod quæ hic tractantur, ad actionem spectent, Idæa vero ad contemplationem. Addit, cur sit alienum ab Ethica, quia de virtute & felicitate per virtutem comparanda hic agitur: Etiam à virtute abhorrere videtur, & contra bonos mores amicis contradicere, sed hoc ideo se facere dicit, quod sit Philos. cui veritas amicis omnibus charior esse debet, & cujus gratia non aliorum opiniones, sed & suas, si veritati repugnent, Philosophus tollere debet. In secunda parte Platonem refellit his quatuor rationibus. 1. In quibus est prius & posterius, in iis nulla est Idea. At in bono est prius & posterius. Ergo boni nulla est Idea. Major est concessa ab ipso Platone & ejus sectatoribus, qui ideo nullam numerorum Idæam statuebant, propterea quod manifestè viderent in numeris esse prius & posterius, ut, v.g. binarius est prior, ternarius posterior, & sic de reliquis. Minorem sic probat, bonum est & substantia & accidens, at substantia est prior natura accidente, quod probat eleganti similitudine: sicut in arbore, inquit, ipsa arbor est natura prior suis stolonibus & ramusculis inde ena centibus 2. Quorum non est una categoria eorum non est una Idea. At boni non est una categoria. Ergo neque una Idea. Majorem tanquam manifestam praetermittit, nam quę natura nullū habent commune, etiam neq; Idæam possunt habere communem. Minorem sic probat, quia Ens est transcendens quid, & cernitur in omnibus categoriis, etiam & bonum: quia Ens & bonum convertuntur. 3. Quorum non est scientia una, eorum non est una Idea: At boni non est una scientia. Ergo; minore probata minore ad majus. Etiam boni in eadē Categoria non est una scientia: Ergo neq; multo magis in diversis, v.g. inquit, occasionis quæ est in Categoria Quando, non est una scientia: Nam in bello occasionis scientia est ars militaris, in morbo est medicina. Utraq; rectè occasionem rei bene agendæ maximè spectat, & ideo vocat tempóris occasiones. Sic etiam mediocritatis, quæ est in Categoria Quando, non est una scientia, nam in cibo aut dicta est medicina, in exercitiis gymnastica. Medicina enim præscribit mediocritate dietæ, quantum sufficit ægroto: sic exercitatoria ars, quantum firmo athletæ satis sit. 4. Utut esset Idæa sicut Plato vult, tamen est supervacanea, cum idem sit revera cum eare, cujus est idæa, quod hoc modo probat: Quorum una est definitio, ea sunt eadem. at boni & Idea boni est una definitio. Ergo sunt eadem. Ut argumentum melius intelligatur, iciendum Platonem in Alcib. & in epist. 7. ad socios Dionis, in rebus singulis statuisse duo, æternum scilicet, quod vocabat αὐτὸ ἕκαστον seu ipsum individuum, & caducum quod vocabat ἕκαστον, & pro hoc nihil aliud intelligebat, quam ipsam rei quidditatem & formam. At vero forma rei a re ipsa non differt, cum per formam rei res fit id quod est, ideo superfluum erat Idæam seu formam rei & rem ipsam tanquam diversa in singulis constituere, cum frustra fiant per plura, quæ fieri possunt per pauciora, ut vulgo dicitur. Proinde Pythagoreos magis laudat, quod, etsi omnia ad unum revocarent, hoc unum tamen à seipso distinxerint, nec ad huiusmodi unum revocarunt, quod esset à rebus ipsis avulsum aut separatum. Pythagoreis etiam astipulatur è Platonicis Speusippus Platonis ex sorore nepos, illi in Academia successor, quem ideo libentius adduxit testem Aristoteles, ut æquiores haberet contra Præceptorem insurgendi rationes. Quomodo Pythagoræi omnia ad unum revocarint, ostendit ex ipsorum bipartita serie. Nam seriem rerum constituebant duplicem, in quarum una statuebant 10. bonorum rationem habentia, in altera 10 mala. Series bonorum ex Aristot. 1. Metaph. c. 5. hæc fuit, Finitum Impar, Unum, Mas, Dextrum, Rectum, Lux, Quadratum, Quies, Bonum. In serie malorum erant hæc itidem 10. Infinitum, Par, Multitudo, Fœmina, Lævum, Currum, Tenebræ, Altera parte longius, motus, malum. Hujus etiam seriei meminit infra lib. 2. c. 5. lib. 9 c. 8. & 14 metaph. c. ult. In tertia parte capitis occurrit objectioni Platonicorum. Platonici enim sic dicebant, Platonem per Idæam non intellexisse omnium bonorum Idæam, sed cum bonorum alia sint per se & propter se, alia propter aliud, intellexisse tantum Idæam bonorum propter se. At contra asserit Aristoteles neq; boni propter se est una Idæa, quia non est una communis definitio, in qua, ut diximus, illi Idæam statuebant. Quod probat inductione trium exemexemplorum,Prudentia,voluptatis & honestas,quorum non est communis definitio etiam in eo, quod bona sint,neq; etiam ὁμωνύμως dici possunt bona,quia cum omnia homonyma sint vel fortunæ vel consilii, non possunt illa dici per homonymiam bona, quia talia dicuntur fortuito homonyma, quæ habent commune nomen,sed certa ratio hujus nominis non potest reddi, ut v. g. cum aliquis vocetur Johannes hic & in Hispania. Neque etiam ex consilio dici possunt homonyma, quia non natura sua sunt ejusdem nominis. Et probat in textu exinductione omnium specierum homonymias ex consilio, videlicet,quod alia dicantur homonyma ab uno, alia ad unum, alia secundum analogiam, sed mox horum explicationem rejicit ad alium locum, nempe ad lib. 4. metaph. sicut etiam sufiorem explicationem Idearum ad lib. 11. metaph. c. 12. & 13. ejusdem libri. In quarta parte capitis ostendit,utut daretur Idea,quod volebat Plato, tamen non posse dici bonum Politicum, propterea quod ab homine acquiri & possideri nequeat: neque valet illud, quod Platoes fert 6. de Repub. Etsi per se non sit summum bonum Politicum, ad cognitionem tamen summi boni plurimum affert, veluti exemplar quoddam in mente hominis, neque esse Ideam veluti exemplar in mente hominis, secundum quod actiones suas dirigat, probat hoc modo, quia artifices nullam habent ejusmodi Ideam, cum opus aliquod producunt, quod probat exemplo quatuor artium, Textoria, Fabrilis, Medica & Imperatoria. Artifices,inquit,in omnibus hisce artibus sicut & in aliis faciunt, quae artis suae propria sunt absque Idaeae hujus cognitione, & si his tanquam inferioribus nihil prodest Idaea, etiam Politicae Ethicae & Architectonicae non proderit.
units.tr: There follows the third part of the Treatise, in which Aristotle refutes Plato's Idea, in which Plato said the highest good was posited. This chapter has four parts. In the first he proposes to discuss the Idea, and uses a modest excuse for doing so, so as to keep decorum in his book on morals. In the second part he refutes Plato's opinion, which places the highest good in the Idea, by four arguments. In the third he proposes and resolves a certain Platonic doubt. In the fourth he shows that the Ideas do not belong to the present undertaking: even if Ideas are granted to exist, the highest good can be separated from the human being, but the Idea cannot be separated at all. In the first part he proposes to speak about the Idea, and says it is not part of the present undertaking, because the matters treated here concern action, whereas the Idea concerns contemplation. He adds why it is foreign to Ethics: here we deal with virtue and with happiness to be obtained through virtue. He also seems to shrink from opposing virtue and good morals in contradicting his friends. But he says he does this because he is a philosopher, and truth ought to be dearer to a philosopher than all his friends, and for whose sake the philosopher ought to set aside not only the opinions of others but also his own, if they stand against the truth. In the second part he refutes Plato with these four arguments. 1. In things where there is a prior and a posterior, there is no Idea. But in the good there is a prior and a posterior. Therefore there is no Idea of the good. The major premise is granted by Plato himself and his followers, who for this reason posited no Idea of numbers, because they plainly saw that in numbers there is a prior and a posterior: for example, the binary is prior, the ternary posterior, and so on for the rest. He proves the minor thus: the good is both substance and accident, and substance is prior in nature to accident. He proves this with an elegant comparison: as in a tree, he says, the tree itself is prior in nature to its shoots and twigs that spring from it. 2. Of things that do not fall under one category, there is not one Idea. But the good does not fall under one category. Therefore neither is there one Idea. He passes over the major as self-evident, for things that have nothing in common in nature cannot have a common Idea either. He proves the minor thus: Being is a transcendental, and is found in all the categories, and so is the good, because Being and the good are convertible. 3. Of things that do not have one science, there is not one Idea. But there is not one science of the good. Therefore, the minor having been proved, the argument passes from the lesser to the greater: even within the same category there is not one science of the good; therefore much less is there one across different categories. For example, he says, there is no one science of the opportune, which is in the category When: in war the science of the opportune is the military art, in sickness it is medicine. Both of these are chiefly concerned with the opportunity for doing a thing well, and for this reason he calls them the opportunities of time. Likewise there is no one science of the mean, which is also in the category When: in food the science is medicine, in exercises it is gymnastics. For medicine prescribes the measure of diet, as much as suffices for the sick man; so the art of training prescribes as much as suffices for the strong athlete. 4. Even if there were an Idea, as Plato wishes, it would still be superfluous, since it is in fact the same thing as that of which it is the Idea. He proves this as follows: Things of which there is one definition are the same. But the good and the Idea of the good have one definition. Therefore they are the same. To understand the argument better, it must be noted that in the Alcibiades and in Epistle 7 to the associates of Dion, Plato posited two things in individual things: the eternal, which he called the very individual itself [αὐτὸ ἕκαστον], and the perishable, which he called the individual [ἕκαστον]. By the latter he understood nothing other than the very quiddity and form of the thing. But the form of a thing does not differ from the thing itself, since through its form the thing is what it is. Therefore it was superfluous to posit in individuals an Idea or form of the thing and the thing itself as different things, since what can be done by fewer things is done in vain by more, as the common saying goes. Accordingly he praises the Pythagoreans more, because although they reduced all things to one, they nevertheless distinguished this one from itself, and did not reduce things to such a one as would be torn away from the things themselves or separated from them. Among the Platonists, Speusippus, Plato's nephew through his sister, who succeeded him in the Academy, also supports the Pythagoreans. Aristotle cited him as a witness all the more willingly, so that he would have fairer grounds for rising up against his teacher. He shows how the Pythagoreans reduced all things to one from their twofold series. For they constituted a double series of things: in one they placed ten things that have the character of good, in the other ten that have the character of evil. The series of goods, from Aristotle's Metaphysics 1, chapter 5, was this: Finite, Odd, One, Male, Right, Light, Square, Rest, Good. In the series of evils there were likewise ten: Infinite, Even, Multitude, Female, Left, Curved, Darkness, Extended in one direction, Motion, Evil. He also mentions this series below in Book 2, chapter 5, Book 9, chapter 8, and in the Metaphysics Book 14, the last chapter. In the third part of the chapter he meets an objection of the Platonists. For the Platonists used to say that Plato did not mean by the Idea the Idea of all goods, but, since some goods are good in themselves and for their own sake, and others for the sake of something else, he meant only the Idea of goods that are good for their own sake. But Aristotle maintains against this that there is no one Idea even of goods that are good for their own sake, because there is no one common definition, in which, as we have said, they posited the Idea. He proves this by induction from three examples: prudence, pleasure, and honour, of which there is no common definition even in respect of their being goods. Nor can they be called good homonymously [ὁμωνύμως], because although all homonyms are either by chance or by design, they cannot be called good by homonymy, since things are called homonyms by chance when they have a common name but no certain account of the name can be given, as when someone is called John both here and in Spain. Nor can they be called homonyms by design, since they are not of the same name by their own nature. And he proves in the text by induction over all the species of homonymy by design, namely, that some are called homonyms from one thing, others with reference to one thing, others according to analogy. But he soon refers the explanation of these to another place, namely to the Metaphysics Book 4, just as he also refers the fuller explanation of the Ideas to the Metaphysics Book 11, chapters 12 and 13 of that same book. In the fourth part of the chapter he shows that, even if an Idea were given, as Plato wished, it could not be called the political good, because it cannot be acquired and possessed by a human being. Nor is what Plato says in the Republic Book 6 valid, that although the political good is not in itself the highest good, it nevertheless contributes greatly to knowledge of the highest good, as a kind of pattern in the mind of a human being, and that there is an Idea, as a pattern in the mind of a human being, according to which he directs his actions. He proves this as follows: craftsmen have no such Idea when they produce some work. He shows this by the example of four arts: weaving, metalworking, medicine and generalship. The craftsmen, he says, in all these arts, as in the others, do what belongs to their art without knowledge of this Idea. And if the Idea is of no use to these lesser arts, it will be of no use to politics, ethics, or architectonic science either.

units.la: Axiomata.
units.tr: Axioms.

units.la: 1. Veritas est praeferenda autoritati & amicitiae.
units.tr: 1. Truth is to be preferred to authority and friendship.

units.la: 2. Veritatis gratia non tantum alienas, sed suas etiam opiniones revocare debet Philosophus.
units.tr: 2. For the sake of truth, the philosopher must retract not only others' opinions but also his own.

units.la: 3. Substantia est prior natura accidente.
units.tr: 3. Substance is prior in nature to accident.

units.la: 4. Quorum una est definitio, ea sunt una inter se.
units.tr: 4. Things of which there is one definition are one among themselves.

units.la: 5. Bonorum alia expetuntur propter se, alia propter aliud.
units.tr: 5. Some goods are desired for their own sake, others for the sake of something else.

units.la: 6. Summum bonum potest acquiri & possideri ab homine, cujus est summum bonum.
units.tr: 6. The highest good can be acquired and possessed by the man whose highest good it is.

units.la: Quaeritur I. An veritas sit praeferenda amicitiae, cum veritas odium pariat, ut habet commune proverbium, amicitia vero amorem & animorum consensum? Resp. Veritatem esse praeferendam amicitiae, quia fundatur in rebus ipsis, amicitia vulgaris vero in hominum opinione, idem sententium, idemque volentium, ut ait Cic. At veritas per se non odium parit, sed propter depravationem humanae naturae, cujus ulcera plerunque acerbius attingi solent veritati scalpro.
units.tr: Question I. Is truth to be preferred to friendship, since truth begets hatred, as the common proverb has it, whereas friendship begets love and agreement of minds? Answer: Truth is to be preferred to friendship, because truth is grounded in the things themselves, whereas ordinary friendship rests on the opinion of men, on agreeing in what one thinks and in what one wills, as Cicero says. But truth does not beget hatred of itself; it does so because of the corruption of human nature, whose sores are usually touched more painfully by the scalpel of truth.

units.la: II. An Aristoteles recte fecerit, quod impugnarit Idaeam Platonis, cum Plato per Ideam intellexerit plerunque Deum ipsum. Deus vero est summum bonum, quod etiam ratio ipsa docet, & Aristoteles ipse fatetur lib. 1. de caelo, c. 9. & 11. Metaph. c. 3. Resp. Non ideo Aristoteles culpavit Platonem, quod Idaeam summum bonum statuerit, sed quod pro bono Politico obtruserit, neque etiam secunda Idaea cum rebus conjuncta posse dici Politicum bonum, propterea cum sit forma rei, & ideo à Deo & natura producatur, non possit humanis actionibus acquiri.
units.tr: II. Did Aristotle act rightly in attacking Plato's Idea, since Plato by "Idea" generally understood God himself? God is the highest good, which reason itself teaches, and Aristotle himself confesses this in On the Heavens, book 1, chapter 9, and in the Metaphysics, chapter 3 of book 11. Answer: Aristotle did not blame Plato for positing the Idea of the highest good, but for thrusting it forward as a political good. Nor can the second Idea, joined to things, be called a political good, since it is the form of a thing and is therefore produced by God and nature, and so cannot be acquired by human actions.

units.la: III. Cur Deus ponatur ab Aristotele in Categoria Substantia, nam superat omnes regulas humanæ sapientia?
units.tr: III. Why does Aristotle place God in the category of Substance, when he surpasses all the rules of human wisdom?

units.la: Resp. Proprie quidem in nulla Categoria est Deus, cum non sit proprie Ens, sed principium & causa Entis, reductivè tamen potest referri ad Categoriam Substantiæ, cum consideretur ut Substantia aliqua simplicissima, & illud meminisse oportet, quod superius monuimus, Aristotelem in exemplis afferendis non omnia ad accuratam veritatis amussim exigere. Sed consuetudini receptæ pro omnium captu se accommodare.
units.tr: Answer: Strictly speaking, God is in no category, since he is not properly a being but the principle and cause of being. Nevertheless, he may be referred by reduction to the category of Substance, when he is considered as some most simple substance. We must remember what we pointed out above, that Aristotle, in the examples he brings forward, does not hold everything to the exact measure of truth, but adapts himself to the accepted usage and to the capacity of all.

units.la: IV. Cur Aristoteles dicat sub finem capitis, Medicinam & alias partes esse rerum singularium, seu versari circa singularia, cum artium præcepta sint universalia, quæ de universalibus tractant, tum etiam finis artium est universalis?
units.tr: IV. Why does Aristotle say at the end of the chapter that medicine and the other arts are parts of singular things, or deal with singulars, when the precepts of the arts are universal, treat of universals, and the end of the arts is also universal?

units.la: Resp. Artes considerari dupliciter vel in habitu vel in usu. In habitu versantur circa universalia & sic dantur in iis præcepta. In usu vero quatenus rebus applicantur, versantur circa singularia, & sic Aristoteles consideravit Medicinam, quatenus in usu est posita, non ut in habitu & mente existit, ut melius intelligatur hæc Aristotelis cum Platone disputatio, notandum Ideæ nomen apud Platonem triplicitep usurpari. Primò pro eminentia dum Deus dicitur Idæa omnium, ut enim unitas virtute includit omnes numeros, ita Deus, qui est ipsum unum eminentia & virtute includit oēs Idæas, quasi rerum numerus & præsertim unius boni & pulchri quæ cæterarum
units.tr: Answer: Arts may be considered in two ways, either in their habit or in their use. In their habit they deal with universals, and in this respect precepts are given in them. In their use, insofar as they are applied to things, they deal with singulars, and in this way Aristotle considered medicine, as it is put to use, not as it exists in habit and in the mind. So that this disputation of Aristotle with Plato may be better understood, it should be noted that the name Idea is used by Plato in three ways. First, for eminence, when God is called the Idea of all things; for just as unity contains all numbers in its power, so God, who is himself the One, contains by eminence and power all Ideas, as the number of things, and especially of the one good and beautiful, which are the origins of the other things

units.la: ruin rum rerum sunt origines. Secundò, Idæa sumitur pro forma dum consideratur in mente, pro ut una res contra distinguitur ab altera. Tertiò, Idæa pro similitudine usurpatur, dum omne quod universè concipitur animo, Idæa nuncupatur, qua significatione Plato in Philebo dixit, duas esse in unoquoque nostrum Idæas, innatam scilicet voluptatum cupiditatem, & acquisitam opinionem, per quam optimum quodque expetimus. Sicut præclarè etiam docetur in Phædro: sumitur quoque Idæa, vel pro externo objecto in quod omnes res ultimò feruntur, etsic dicitur Idæa eminentiæ aut Deus ipse. E quo sensu Plato de Idæa agit lib. 7. de Rep. sub finem vel sumitur secundo pro interna perfectione quadam, quæ perficit & terminat omnes actiones nostras, proin si in secunda significatione sumatur Idæa pro ut usurpari debet, & quo sensu agit de summo bono Philosophus, toto hoc lib. 1. non erit magna dissensio, cum illam Idæam boni dicat Plato in Philebo esse in sapientia positam, quâ comitatur prudentia & sequitur actio ex quibus duabus summum exsurgit gaudium. Arist. tamen Idæas nullas concedet ad mentem pertinentes nec putavit animam interventu mentis ac operationis & Idearum elevari ad summum bonum & cum ea connecti, quod Plato & omnes illius Sectatores statuunt, propterea quod in externis actionibus hominem intrinsecus perficientibus, ex quibus primò virtutum habitus ex illis deinde universalis vitæ actio, quæ dicitur felicitas, oritur, sicut esse putaret summum hominis bonum, consentiunt tamen in hic Plato & Aristot. quod summum bonum tanquam bonarum actionum finis, & quæ à virtute proveniat, & ad quam summa ope cuncti q; nitendum facultatibus, v. de Picol. gradu nono capp. 24.25.26 per totum.
units.tr: of things. Secondly, Idea is taken for form, insofar as it is considered in the mind, as one thing is distinguished from another. Thirdly, Idea is used for likeness, when whatever is conceived universally in the mind is called an Idea. In this sense Plato said in Philebus that there are two Ideas in each one of us, namely an innate desire for pleasures and an acquired opinion by which we pursue whatever is best. This is also taught excellently in Phaedrus. Idea is also taken either for the external object towards which all things are ultimately directed, and in this sense it is called the Idea of eminence or God himself, in which sense Plato treats of the Idea in book 7 of the Republic, near the end; or it is taken secondly for a certain internal perfection which perfects and terminates all our actions. Therefore, if Idea is taken in this second sense, as it ought to be used, and in which sense the Philosopher treats of the highest good throughout this first book, there will not be great disagreement, since Plato in Philebus says that this Idea of the good consists in wisdom, which is accompanied by prudence, and from which action follows; from these two arises the highest joy. Yet Aristotle will concede no Ideas pertaining to the mind, nor did he think that the soul is raised to the highest good, and joined with it, by the intervention of mind, operation and Ideas, as Plato and all his followers hold. He thought the highest good of man lies in external actions that perfect the man inwardly, from which first arise the habits of the virtues and then the action of the whole life, which is called happiness. Nevertheless, Plato and Aristotle agree in this, that the highest good is the end of good actions, which comes from virtue, and that everyone must strive for it with all their powers: see Piccolomini, ninth grade, chapters 24, 25 and 26 throughout.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: REfutatis aliorum opinionibus incipit agere de Felicitate ex opinione sua, & priusquam Felicitatem ex sua opinione definiat, præmittit quasdam proprietates, quæ descriptionem quandam istius felicitatis continent. Proprietates sunt numero tres: nempe: Quod summum bonum sit optimum. 2. Sit perfectum. 3. Sit per se sufficiens. Optimum esse probat, quod cum omnia agens, finis alicujus gratia agat, & ille finis obtineat ratione boni, & finis inferiorum artium & disciplinarum referantur ad bonum Politicum, tanquam ad summum & optimum, ideo est optimum bonum. 2. Esse perfectum hoc modo, quia propter se expetitur, nunquam propter aliud, alia vero omnia propter seipsum, quod probat exemplis Honoris, Voluptatis, Mentis & Virtutis. 3. Summum bonum est per se sufficiens, propterea quod reddat vitam nullius rei indigam, & hac sufficientia, non tantum ipsum bonum possessorem spectat, sed etiam se extendit ad parentes, cognatos & amicos, & ratio est, quia homo natura est animal politicum natum, qui in societate degat, & ut bene vivat, omnibus benefacere studeat, ne tamen putemus, cum summum bonum sit finitum, extendere se in infinitum, servandum esse modum docet Aristoteles, ut eousque se extendat, quo facultatum nostrarum vires & fortuna permittunt. Axio-
units.tr: Having refuted the opinions of others, he begins to treat of Happiness according to his own opinion. Before he defines Happiness according to his own view, he sets down certain properties which contain a kind of description of this happiness. There are three properties: namely, (1) that the highest good is the best; (2) that it is perfect; (3) that it is sufficient in itself. That it is the best he proves as follows: since every agent acts for the sake of some end, and that end is attained by reason of the good, and the ends of the lesser arts and disciplines are referred to the political good as to the highest and best, therefore it is the best good. (2) That it is perfect he shows in this way: because it is desired for its own sake and never for the sake of something else, whereas all other things are desired for its sake; he proves this by the examples of honour, pleasure, mind and virtue. (3) The highest good is sufficient in itself, because it makes life lacking in nothing; and this sufficiency concerns not only the one who possesses the good but also extends to parents, relatives and friends. The reason is that man is by nature a political animal, born to live in society, and in order to live well he strives to do good to all. Lest we think, however, that since the highest good is finite it extends itself to infinity, Aristotle teaches that a measure must be kept, so that it extends only as far as the powers of our faculties and our fortune allow. Axio-

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Quod per se expetitur, est optabilius eo, quod propter aliud.
units.tr: 1. That which is desired for its own sake is more desirable than that which is desired for the sake of something else.

units.la: 2. Summum bonum facit vitam nullius rei indigam, sed αὐτάρκειαν in se habet.
units.tr: 2. The highest good makes a life lacking nothing, and has self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] in itself.

units.la: 3. Homo est natura animal Politicum.
units.tr: 3. Man is by nature a political animal.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: Quæritur: I. Cur Aristoteles dicat in textu, mentem felicitatis gratia expeti: cum potius propter mentem expetatur felicitas, utpote quæ sit mentis actio, quæ à mente profluit? Resp. Ideo Aristotelem dicere mentem felicitatis gratia expeti, quod mens virtute exculta secundum virtutem agat, & inde felix evadat, vel quia etiam addit postea nomen virtutis, per mentem intelligit virtutes mentales, quales sunt scientia, sapientia, &c. quæ nisi eo tendant ut per eas homo felicitatem assequatur, frustra virtutes mentis dicerentur, ut plaeclarè docet Philosophus lib. 10. c. 7.
units.tr: The question is raised: I. Why does Aristotle say in the text that mind is sought for the sake of happiness, when rather happiness is sought for the sake of mind, since happiness is an action of the mind that flows from the mind? Answer: Aristotle says that mind is sought for the sake of happiness because a mind cultivated by virtue acts according to virtue and so becomes happy. Or, because he adds the name of virtue afterwards, by "mind" he means the intellectual virtues, such as knowledge, wisdom and so on. Unless these tend to this end, that through them a person attains happiness, they would be called virtues of the mind in vain, as the Philosopher teaches admirably in book 10, chapter 7.

units.la: II. Cur Aristoteles dixerit summum bonum esse optimum & perfectum, quasi essent duo diversa in summo bono, cum tamen sint unum & idem, ut ipse aperte testatur lib. 1. Mag. Mor. c. 2? Resp. Quod ideo distinxerit, quod summum bonum dicatur perfectum ratione sui, quatenus in se spectatur omnib. numeris absolutū, dicitur per se sufficiens ratione subjecti, in quo inest, quod subjectum omnium bonorum caput esset.
units.tr: II. Why did Aristotle call the highest good best and perfect, as if there were two different things in the highest good, when they are in fact one and the same, as he himself plainly testifies in book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter 2? Answer: He distinguished them because the highest good is called perfect by reason of itself, insofar as it is viewed in itself as complete in every respect. It is called self-sufficient by reason of the subject in which it inheres, since that subject would be the head of all goods.

units.la: III. An hoc cum veritate constet, quod summum bonum dicatur per se expeti, & non propter aliud cum tamen ipse lib. 10 cap. 7. dicat, summum bonum expeti propter animam? Resp. Expeti quidè summum bonū propter animā, non tanquam propter finem ulteriorem, sed propter sedem suam, in qua tanquam proprietas in subjecto insit.
units.tr: III. Does it agree with the truth that the highest good is said to be desired in itself and not for the sake of something else, when yet he himself says in book 10, chapter 7, that the highest good is desired for the sake of the soul?
