Answer: The highest good is indeed desired for the sake of the soul, not as for a further end, but on account of its seat, in which it inheres as a property in a subject.

units.la: IV. Cur Aristoteles dicat summum bonum, aliis bonis externis adnumeratum, expetibilium esse cum deo videretur in se imperfectum, quod non a seipso habeat, ut maxime omnium expetatur? Resp. In se quidem seu in essentia sua per se maxime omnium expetit, at in sua existentia quatenus respicit subjectam, aliis bonis adnumeratum magis expetitur & hoc secundo modo intellexit Philosophus in textu. Et Alexan: ad 3. Top. c. 4. Et Arist. ipse explicat lib. 1. Mag. Mor. c. 2. Caeterum an summum bonum possit crescere ex opinione Stoicorum, videatur Cic. 3. & 4. de Finibus.
units.tr: IV. Why does Aristotle say that the highest good, though numbered among other external goods, is among the things to be desired, when it seems imperfect in itself, since it does not have from itself that it is desired above all else? Answer: In itself, that is in its essence, it is desired above all things through itself. But in its existence, insofar as it relates to the subject, and numbered among other goods, it is desired more, and in this second sense the Philosopher understood it in the text. See also Alexander on the Topics, book 3, chapter 4. Aristotle himself explains the matter in Magna Moralia, book 1, chapter 2. As to whether the highest good can increase according to the opinion of the Stoics, see Cicero, De Finibus, books 3 and 4.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HOc capite definitionem felicitatis ex sua sententia proponit, partes cap. sunt dua. In prima investigat genus felicitatis, & ostendit actionem ejus esse genus. In secunda agit de differentia nempe quod sit actio secundum virtutem in vita perfecta. Notandum tamen ista fere quae afferuntur ab Arist. mutuata esse a Platone lib. 1. de Repub. qua de re agit Alexander Aphr. lib. 4. quaest. c. 4.
units.tr: In this chapter he sets out the definition of happiness according to his own view. The chapter has two parts. In the first he investigates the genus of happiness and shows that it is an action. In the second he deals with the difference, namely that it is action in accordance with virtue in a complete life. It should be noted, however, that most of what Aristotle here presents was borrowed from Plato, Republic, book 1. Alexander of Aphrodisias discusses this matter in Questions, book 4, ch. 4.

units.la: In prima igitur parte hic genus investigat, 1. inquirit, an sit, quod a similitudine demonstrat, in Tibicine, inquit, in statuario, in omni denique opificio est opus aliquod tanquam finis, ergo hominis in genere actio, aut operatio tanquam finis statuenda erit, utitur vero similitudine ab artibus mechanicis & vulgaribus, quae passim occurrunt ducta, tanquam evidenevidente, propterea quod utante dixeratcap. 2. Sicut à notioribus nobis est progrediendum, ita etiam argumentandum, notiora vero nobis sunt, quae in sensus incurrunt. 2. Ostendit esse actionem hominis, quia oculi, manus & caetera membra corporis habent suas operationes, absurdum igitur statuere hominem totum esse otiosum, cum singulas partes operari pro confesso sit, sic jam ostendit dari actionem, postea qualis sit, docet: tota, inquit, anima hominis est vegetans, sentiens & rationalis, ista actio est neque vegetantis, neque sentientis, quia illa nobis cum plantis haec cum bestiis communis est. Ergo haec actio, quae est genus felicitatis, est actio animae rationalis. Sed in anima rationali una est pars, quae ratione utitur, aut in se habet rationem, altera quae rationi paret, ut est pars animae irascibilis & concupiscibilis, & ab utraque hac parte finis ista actio, quae dicitur felicitas. At vero cum duplices sunt actiones animae rationalis, aliae enim sunt imperfectae, quae non limato & maturo satis judicio proveniunt, ut sunt actiones puerorum, aliae quae non a libero homine proveniunt, ut sunt actiones servorum & aliae, quae ab impetu naturali fluunt, qualis fuit Fortitudo in Achille. 2. Alia actiones sunt perfectae, quae ex deliberata mente proveniunt, & talis actio est genus felicitatis. Hanc distinctionem actionis in perfectam & in imperfectam illustrat a simili in citharaedo, qui quando quocunque modo pulsat citharam, agit quidem, sed non perfecte agit, donec bene pullet citharam.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he investigates the genus. (1) He asks whether there is some work that is an end. He demonstrates this by an analogy: in the flute player, he says, in the sculptor, and in every craft, there is some work as an end. Therefore an action or operation must be posited as the end of man in general. He uses an analogy drawn from the mechanical and common crafts, which occur everywhere, as something evident, because he had said in chapter 2 that just as we must proceed from what is better known to us, so we must also argue from it, and what is better known to us is what falls under the senses. (2) He shows that there is an action of man, because the eyes, hands and other members of the body have their own operations. It would be absurd, therefore, to hold that the whole man is idle, since it is admitted that each part operates. Thus he has already shown that there is an action, and next he teaches what sort it is: the whole soul of man, he says, is nutritive, sensitive and rational. That action belongs neither to the nutritive nor to the sensitive part, since the former we share with plants, the latter with beasts. Therefore this action, which is the genus of happiness, is the action of the rational soul. But in the rational soul there is one part which makes use of reason, or has reason in itself, and another which obeys reason, as the irascible and concupiscible part of the soul does. From both of these parts this action, called happiness, flows. Now since the actions of the rational soul are of two kinds, some are imperfect, which do not proceed from a judgment sufficiently ripe and mature, as the actions of children; others do not proceed from a free man, as the actions of slaves; and others flow from natural impulse, such as the courage of Achilles. (3) Other actions are perfect, which proceed from a deliberate mind, and such an action is the genus of happiness. He illustrates this distinction of action into perfect and imperfect by a comparison with the harpist, who, when he plucks the lyre in any way at all, does act, but not perfectly, until he plays the lyre well.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de differentiis, nempe quod haec actio, quae constituit felicitatem, sit actio secunsecundum virtutem & in vita perfecta, cujus posteriorem partem illustrata duplici similitudine, sicut nec una hirundo facit ver, nec unus serenus dies vere serenitatem, sic nec una actio etsi perfecta sit, sed plures actiones in aggregatu aut simul aggregatae.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the differences, namely that this action which constitutes happiness is action in accordance with virtue and in a complete life. He illustrates the latter part by a double comparison: as one swallow does not make a spring, nor one clear day clear weather, so neither does one action, even if it is perfect, but many actions taken together or in sum.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Anima humana una pars ratione utitur, altera paret.
units.tr: 1. The human soul has one part which makes use of reason, and another which obeys it.

units.la: 2. Unum quodque a propria sua virtute perficitur.
units.tr: 2. Each thing is perfected by its own proper virtue.

units.la: 3. Felicitas est actio animae rationalis secundum virtutem in vita perfecta
units.tr: 3. Happiness is the action of the rational soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life.

units.la: 4. Sicut una hirundo ver non facit, sic nec una virtutis actio felicitatem parit.
units.tr: 4. As one swallow does not make a spring, so one act of virtue does not produce happiness.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: Quaeritur. I. Cur Aristoteles vocet felicitatem modo opus, modo operationem, cum ista duo inter se differant, ut domus & aedificatio, domus ut ipse c. 1. huius libri dixit, opus esse aliquid praestantius operatione, unde sequeretur felicitatem esse seipsa praestantiorem? Resp. 1. Hoc solenne esse Aristotelis, ut raro utatur vocabulis in stricta significatione sumtis, nisi ubi de industria agit de aliqua re, &c. 2. Vocatur felicitas operatio sed diverso respectu, Opus, quatenus ex multis actionibus particularibus aggregatur tanquam universalis actio, quae sit particularium veluti quoddam opus: Dicitur operatio quatenus bene agendo perpetuo continuatur.
units.tr: Question I. Why does Aristotle call happiness now a work, now an operation, when these two differ from each other as a house and the building of a house? For a house, as he said in chapter 1 of this book, is something more excellent than the operation, whence it would follow that happiness is more excellent than itself. Answer: (1) It is a habit of Aristotle's to use words only rarely in their strict sense, except where he is deliberately treating of some matter. (2) Happiness is called an operation, but in a different respect. It is called a work insofar as it is compounded of many particular actions as a general action, which is as it were a certain work of the particular actions. It is called an operation insofar as it is continued perpetually by acting well.

units.la: II. Quomodo Aristoteles vocet felicitatem vitam quandam hominis & cum sit accidens tantum vita, sed non ipsa vita? Resp. Per vitam intelligit actionem animae rationalis, ut ipse explicat sequentibus statim verbis, DeinDeinde vocatur vita, quia in felicitate moralis homi- nis politici vita vere consistit.
units.tr: II. How does Aristotle call happiness a certain life of man, when it is only an accident and not life itself? Answer: By life he understands the action of the rational soul, as he explains himself in the words that immediately follow: Then it is called life, because the life of the morally happy man who lives in a state truly consists in it.

units.la: I. Cur homo constet anima & corpore & felicitas dicatur proprium hominis, cur vocarit felicitatem actionem animae tantum, & non animae & corporis simul? Resp. Quia felicitas est res perfectissima, & animae tanquam perfectissimae parti hominis debetur &c. 2. quia anima est Principium omnis actionis, quia ab ipsa fluit omnis motus. Teste Philosopho lib. 2. de anima C. 2.
units.tr: III. Why does man consist of soul and body, and yet happiness is said to belong to man, and why does he call happiness the action of the soul only, and not of soul and body together? Answer: (1) Because happiness is the most perfect thing, and is owed to the soul as the most perfect part of man, etc. (2) Because the soul is the principle of every action, since every motion flows from it. On the testimony of the Philosopher, On the Soul, book 2, ch. 2.

units.la: IV. Cur adjecerit in definitione, in vita perfecta, &c? Resp. quia abliq; temporis longinquitate actiones virtutis perfecti & absolvi nequeunt, utpote quae ab usu & exercitio proveniunt. 2. Quia in tempore excrescit numerus actionum, & ita felicitas subinde gradus acquirit. 3. Quia ad felicitatem requiruntur bona externa. Inter bona externa non minimum obtinet locum vita prolixa, utpote quae ex crebris actionibus plures & perfectiores acquirit habitus, & per istos habitus plures & perfectiores gradus felicitatis. 4. Quia longinquitas temporis aeternitatem imitatur: aeternitas vero divinitati, ut res convenient. Illa debetur, & cum felicitas divinitatem imitatur, teste Philosopho cap. 12 huius libri, ideo divinitatis durationem, aeternitatem nempe ut imitetur necesse est.
units.tr: IV. Why did he add in the definition "in a complete life," etc.? Answer: (1) Because the actions of virtue cannot be performed and completed without a lapse of long time, since they arise from habit and exercise. (2) Because the number of actions increases with time, and so happiness gradually acquires degrees. (3) Because external goods are required for happiness. Among external goods a long life holds no small place, since by frequent actions it acquires more and more perfect habits, and through these habits more and more perfect degrees of happiness. (4) Because length of time imitates eternity, and eternity belongs to divinity, as things agree. Since happiness imitates divinity, on the testimony of the Philosopher, ch. 12 of this book, it is necessary that it imitate the duration of divinity, namely eternity.

units.la: De fine actionum humanarum haec septem breviter observanda veniunt. 1. Quid sit. 2. Quotuplex sit. 3. Quibus nominibus insigniatur. 4. De variis opinionibus circa summum bonum. 5. Quid sit. 6. Proprietates & effecta. 7. Quae illum praecedere & comitari dicantur.
units.tr: Concerning the end of human actions, these seven things are to be briefly observed. (1) What it is. (2) How many kinds there are. (3) By what names it is designated. (4) The various opinions concerning the highest good. (5) What it is. (6) Its properties and effects. (7) What are said to precede and accompany it.

units.la: Quod ad primam quaestionem, nempe quis sit finis Ethicae, dicet. dicemus esse bonum τὸ ἀγαθόν; hoc vero cum omnia appetant, teste ratione & Philosopho 1.huius libri, sive illud sit revera & natura sua bonum, sive apparenter tantum & apparens bonum, huius enim gratia omnia faciunt omnes. Sic enim ait Philosophus 1.Polit. ștatim in proœm. causa huius rei est, quia cum bonum sit finis, & finis sit uniuscujusq; perfectio, unumquodque ad finem, tanquam ad perfectionem suam fertur.
units.tr: As to the first question, namely what is the end of Ethics, we shall say it is the good [τὸ ἀγαθόν]. Since all things desire this, as reason and the Philosopher, book 1 of this work, testify, whether it is really and by its nature good, or only apparently and an apparent good, for everyone does everything for its sake. For so the Philosopher says at the very beginning of Politics, book 1: the cause of this is that since the good is the end, and the end is the perfection of each thing, each thing tends to its end as to its own perfection.

units.la: 11. Cæterum cum omnia appetant bonum, tamen diversarum rerum diversi sunt fines, & fines omnes boni nomine veniunt, teste Aristotele 3.Met. t.3. nam quod est bonum sua natura, finis est: Et Averr. ibid.comment .8. qui destruit finem, destruit etiam bonum, ideo multiplex erit bonum, respectu rerum ex quibus comparatur, aliud enim spectatur in artibus mechanicis, & aliud dicitur bonum operativum, quod nimirum operando acquiritur, verbigratia: Cum artifex aliquis perfecit, quod artis suæ proprium est, dicitur bonum assecutus operativum. 2. Consideratur bonum in liberalibus artibus, & illud dicitur bonum respectu artium instrumentalium, instrumentale, quod nimirum instrumentum sit ad reliquas disciplinas percipiendas idoneum, cujusmodi est illud bonum, quod quis assequitur ex Grammatica, Logica, Rhetorica. Et utrumque hoc bonum tam Instrumentale, quam Operativum poterit dici minus præcipuum aut inferius bonum, propterea quod superior, nempe politico inserviat, omnes enim artes tam mechanicæ quam liberales, hunc habere debent scopum, ut ad utilutilitatem Keiptb. referantur. Bonum magis praecipuum vel superius est duplex, intellectuale vel morale. Supremum maximè bonum dicitur spirituale & uno nomine vocatur Beatitudo. Quae definitur fruitio Dei tanquam summi boni. Hoc bonum supremum, quia per exercitia pietatis & virtutum spiritualium inchoatur in hac vita, & in sequenti perficitur ad Theologiam proprie spectat: bonum verò intellectuale dicitur Sapientia, quae scientiam cum intellectu conjungit & proprie pertinet ad disciplinas Theoreticas, quae in contemplatione veri versantur, & quarum finis est cognitio certa, seu recta de rebus judicium. Secunda species boni superioris est bonum morale, quod uno plerumque nomine vocatur felicitas, quae exercitium virtutum moralium & honestatis acquirendae proponit, & de hoc bono nobis hic sermo erit, tum quia est finis Ethicae, tum quia per ipsum à reliquis scientiis & disciplinis plerumque distinguitur Ethica.
units.tr: II. Moreover, although all things desire the good, the ends of different things are different, and all ends come under the name of good, as Aristotle testifies in Metaphysics, book 3, text 3, for what is good by its nature is an end. And Averroes, ibid., commentary 8, says that whoever destroys the end also destroys the good. Therefore the good will be manifold with respect to the things from which it is obtained. For one good is looked for in the mechanical arts and another is called the operative good, which is acquired by operating: for example, when a craftsman has accomplished what is proper to his art, he is said to have attained the operative good. (2) The good is considered in the liberal arts, and that is called the instrumental good with respect to the instrumental arts, namely because it is a fit instrument for grasping the remaining disciplines, of which kind is the good that one obtains from grammar, logic and rhetoric. Both these goods, the instrumental and the operative, may be called a less principal or inferior good, because they serve the superior good, namely the political; for all arts, both mechanical and liberal, ought to have this aim, that they be referred to utility. The more principal or superior good is twofold, intellectual or moral. The supreme good is said to be most spiritual and is called by one name Beatitude, which is defined as the enjoyment of God as the highest good. This supreme good, because it is begun in this life through the exercises of piety and spiritual virtues and is perfected in the life to come, properly belongs to Theology. The intellectual good is called Wisdom, which joins knowledge with understanding and properly pertains to the theoretical disciplines, which are occupied with the contemplation of truth, and whose end is certain knowledge, or right judgment about things. The second species of the superior good is the moral good, which is commonly called by one name happiness, and which sets before us the exercise of the moral virtues and the acquiring of honesty; and it is of this good that our discussion will be here, both because it is the end of Ethics and because Ethics is for the most part distinguished from the other sciences and disciplines by it.

units.la: III. De nominibus 1. vocatur bonum, de quo supra, & de quo inter omnes ferè tam Philosophos quam plebejos convenit, teste Philosopho 1. Nic. 3. 1. dicitur εὐδαιμονία, non tantum, quia prudentia ducens ad summum bonum, est unicuique bonus Daemon, sed quia conditio illa eminentior quam ad divina elevatur mens humana, dicitur propter perfectionem & εὐδαιμονία ex sententia Platonis, quo- niam viri felices optimo Daemone regi & duci æstimantur. Saepius enim apud Plat. de Deniouis hominem ea genius fit mentio, 3. vocatur μακαρισμός beatitudo, quia maximè beatos ejus possessores reddit.
units.tr: III. On the names. 1. It is called bonum, the good, which we discussed above and on which nearly all people agree, philosophers and common folk alike, as the Philosopher testifies in Nic. 1.3. 1. It is called εὐδαιμονία [eudaimonia], happiness. This is not merely because prudence, leading us to the highest good, is each person's good spirit (daemon), but because the human mind, raised to a condition more eminent than the merely human, is called eudaimonia on account of its perfection. This is according to Plato's opinion, since happy men are thought to be ruled and guided by the best spirit. Plato often mentions in his work On Spirits that the genius is associated with man. 3. It is called μακαρισμός [makarismos], blessedness, because it makes its possessors most blessed.

units.la: 1. Nic. 3. 1. dict: prisci enim μαχάεσθαι ... ἀπὸ τῆς μάλιστα χαίρειν, id est, à maximè gaudendo derivabant, ut 10. Nic. 10. asserit Philosophus, nam qui hoc bono præditi sunt, summum verum q; mentis gaudium, ut postea patebit, habent. Cæterum hoc nomen hominibus tantum proprie, qui divina æmulantur, & supra humanam sorrem sunt, maximè convenit, ut testatur Philosophus cap. 12. Nic. ideo proprie pro fine Theologiæ, non Ethicæ usurpatur. 4. Dicitur εὐτυχία ab Arist. 1. Phys. Tex. 58. ubi dicit esse vel ipsam felicitatem, vel felicitate proximam & ratio hujus ex Arist. reliis sententia est, vel quia homo non potest esse felix sine bonis fortunæ tanquam instrumentis, quibus utatur ad ipsam felicitatem comparandam, vel quia nulla prosperior dari potest fortuna, quam hoc bono frui. 5. Vocatur εὐπραξία ut 2. Phys. 58. testatur Philosophus, ratio, quia in actionis probitate collocatum, est summum bonum, ut 1. Nic. 6. sentit Aristoteles. 6. εὐζωία, quasi vitæ rectitudo & vita bene acta, actio enim proba, est vita hominis optima, unde Plotinus Ennead. 4. lib. 3. cap. 4. colligit ex eo, quod soli homini inter mortalia integra & completa vita conveniat, illi etiam soli competere felicitatem. Hæc de Nominibus: plura qui volet de iis legere, consulat Pic. gradu 9. cap. 2.
units.tr: In Nic. 1.3. 1. the saying is: the ancients derived the word μακαρίζεσθαι [makarizesthai] from ἀπὸ τοῦ μάλιστα χαίρειν [apo tou malista chairein], that is, from rejoicing most, as the Philosopher asserts in Nic. 10.10, for those endowed with this good have the highest and truest joy of mind, as will be shown later. Moreover, this name properly belongs only to those who imitate the divine and stand above human condition, as the Philosopher attests in Nic. chapter 12. Hence it is properly used for the end of Theology, not of Ethics. 4. It is called εὐτυχία [eutychia], good fortune, by Aristotle in Phys. 1, text 58, where he says it is either happiness itself or close to happiness. The reason, according to Aristotle's other opinion, is either that a man cannot be happy without the goods of fortune as instruments by which he obtains happiness, or that no more prosperous fortune can be given than to enjoy this good. 5. It is called εὐπραξία [eupraxia], good action, as the Philosopher testifies in Phys. 2, text 58. The reason is that since it consists in the uprightness of action, it is the highest good, as Aristotle thinks in Nic. 1.6. 6. It is called εὐζωία [eudzōia], a good life, as if it were the rectitude of life and a life well lived, for a righteous action is the best life of man. Hence Plotinus, Ennead 4, book 3, chapter 4, infers from the fact that a whole and complete life belongs to man alone among mortal creatures, that happiness also belongs to him alone. So much for the names. Whoever wishes to read more about them may consult Pic., grade 9, chapter 2.

units.la: IV. De opinionibus variis
units.tr: IV. On various opinions

units.la: consulatur M. Varro, qui suo ævo 288. opiniones varias inter Philosophos de summo bono fuisse refert, sed tamen ad 4. præcipuas referri possunt, de quibus Pic. cap. 10. gradu 9. Prima Socratis & Platonis, qui statuebant, summum bonum esse situm in contemplatione Idææ summi buni boni: quod fi intellexerunt per Idaeam summi boni ipsum Deum, non prorsus improbari possunt, cum ille sit finis ultimus omnium, quae facta sunt, omnia enim propter se ipsum condidit, sicut Scriptura loquitur, Proverb. 16. v. 4. sed hoc bonum a morali Philosophia videtur alienum, cum proprie ad Theologiam spectet, & dein, cum in contemplatione situm esse dixerunt, ab Ethica semovendum judicabant, utpote cujus finis est praxis, non Theoria. Secunda opinio est Epicuraeorum, cujus sententiae fuit Eudoxus, qui in voluptate summum bonum statuebant, at si in voluptate animi vera, quae est gaudium mentis, ob recte cogitata & dicta vel facta, (sicut Diog. Laert. in vita Epicuri lib. 10. Seneca epistola 119. Erasm. in epistolis interpretatur) non est damnanda plane ipsius sententia, nisi quod summum bonum non discernat ab effectu suo, nam voluptas non est ipsum summum bonum, sed effectus mediate inde promanans, & sic definitur a D. Thoma: Voluptas est quietatio mentis in ultimo suo fine, id est, gaudium illud mentis, quo ex vita bene actu fruitur homo, at si voluptatem eam, quae cum bestiis communis est, statuit summum bonum, sicut plerique de ipso autumant, ut Cic. f. Tusc. qu. & Horat. in epistolis, nempe eam voluptatem, quae ex cibo, potu & Venere oritur, non hominis sed pecudis fuit haec opinio, & contra quam disputare nefas, cum homine contra bestias rationibus uti sit absonum: Ideo cum Sardanapalus sepulchro suo inscribi jussisset: Ede, bibe, dormi post mortem nulla voluptas:
units.tr: Consult M. Varro, who reports that in his age there were 288 different opinions among the philosophers about the highest good. Yet they can be referred to four principal ones, concerning which see Pic., chapter 10, grade 9. The first is the opinion of Socrates and Plato, who held that the highest good lies in the contemplation of the Idea of the highest good. If by the Idea of the highest good they understood God himself, it cannot altogether be condemned, since he is the ultimate end of all things that have been made, for he made all things for himself, as Scripture says in Prov. 16.4. But this good seems foreign to moral philosophy, since it properly belongs to Theology. Further, since they said it lies in contemplation, they judged it must be removed from Ethics, whose end is practice, not theory. The second opinion is that of the Epicureans, whose view was held by Eudoxus, who placed the highest good in pleasure. But if the pleasure meant is the true pleasure of the mind, which is the joy of the mind arising from rightly thought, said, or done actions (as Diogenes Laertius in the life of Epicurus, book 10, Seneca, letter 119, and Erasmus in his letters explain), then the opinion is not to be condemned outright, except that it does not distinguish the highest good from its effect. For pleasure is not itself the highest good, but an effect flowing from it indirectly. Thus Thomas defines it: Pleasure is the quieting of the mind in its ultimate end, that is, that joy of the mind by which a man enjoys a life well lived. But if he sets as the highest good that pleasure which is shared with beasts, as many, such as Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations and Horace in his letters, think of Epicurus, namely the pleasure arising from food, drink and sex, this opinion belongs to a beast, not a man, and it is impious to dispute against it, since it is absurd to use reason against beasts. Therefore, when Sardanapalus ordered this inscription on his tomb: "Eat, drink, sleep; after death there is no pleasure,"

units.la: dixit Aristoteles, teste Laert. in ipsius vita: Bovis illud potius, quam hominis sepulchro inscribi potuisse. Tertia est opinio Stoicorum, de quibus Pic. gradu 3. cap. 11. Qui summum bonum dixerunt interdum esse virtutem, interdum dixerunt esse habitum virtutis, contra quos disputat Aristoteles, quod medium tendens ad finem, non sit ipse finis: nam per virtutem, tanquam per medium tendimus ad finem ipsum, ut patet ex definitione felicitatis cap. 6. 1. Nic. Secundo, summum bonum est sua gratia expetibile bonum ex se contentum, ut 7. 1. Nic. docet Philosophus, at virtus non est talis, ut ratio docet. Interdum dixerunt esse conguentiam cum natura, in qua opinione fuit etiam Diog. Cynicus: test Laert. lib. 6. In vita ipsius, quod hoc modo refutari poterit, quia summum bonum non se actionibus naturę accommodat, sed a consuetudine & usu provenit, ut variis in locis docet Philosophus, praesertim cap. 1. Nic. 2. In virtute positum esse summum bonum, sic contendunt Stoici 1. illud quod natum est acquiri ab homine, nec aliquo externo indiget, est summum bonum. At virtus est ejusmodi, nam cum habitus sit ab homine comparatus, ideo etiam acquiri poterit, & cum sibi ipsi sit sufficiens, nulla re externa eget. Summum bonum debet esse tale, quod reddit hominem, qui est μιχρόχοσμος similem illi, quod est μεγαλόχοσμος, nempe perfectionem totius universi, at virtus est talis: Sed ad utrumque per infociationem minoris respondetur. Nam quod ad primum, plura requiruntur in felicitate, quam ut possit acquiri ab homine: Quod ad secundum, non virtus aliqua singularis hoc facit, sed virtus collective sumta, aut ejus actio universalis, quae nihil aliud est quam ipsa felicitas, ideo dicendum cum Alexan. Aphrod. 2. de anima cap.14. Si virtus esset summum bonum, vel ideo quia virtus producit vitam felicem, vel quia ipsa esset felicitatis essentia non prius, tunc enim virtus à felicitate distingueretur, ut causa ab effectu, nil enim se ipsam efficere valet, non secundum, quia sic non liceret homini eligere mortem, nam sic distingueret habitum virtutis, & simul etiam essentiam felicitatis, & sic non maneret ultra felicitas. At dicunt Stoici licere interdum mortem eligere, quanquam hoc revera de morte eligenda probari non debeat contra Stoicos: tamen hoc differentiis valere possit. Interdum dixerunt esse congruentiam cum Deo aut ἰσοθεΐαν, quod bonum non ad Philosophiam moralem pertinet, neq; in hac vita plane acquiri potest, sed in sequenti tantum: de horum opinionibus plura vide apud Lips. in manuductione ad Philosophiam Stoicam cap. 13. Quarta opinio est peripatheticorum, quorum Princeps est Aristoteles, illi statuerunt summum bonum in exercitio animae rationalis secundum virtutem, quam opinionem utpote naturae rei & rationi maximè consentaneam, omnes hodie tuentur.
units.tr: Aristotle said, as Laertius reports in his life, that it would have been more fitting to inscribe this on the tomb of an ox than of a man. The third opinion is that of the Stoics, concerning whom see Pic., grade 3, chapter 11. Some who called the highest good sometimes virtue and sometimes the habit of virtue, against whom Aristotle disputes, because what tends toward an end as a means is not itself the end. For we tend to the end itself through virtue as a means, as is clear from the definition of happiness in Nic. 1.6, chapter 6, where the highest good is a good desirable for its own sake and self-sufficient, as the Philosopher teaches in Nic. 1.7, and virtue is not such, as reason shows. Some said it is agreement with nature, which was also the opinion of Diogenes the Cynic, as Laertius reports in book 6, in his life, which can be refuted in this way: the highest good does not adapt itself to the actions of nature but arises from custom and practice, as the Philosopher teaches in many places, especially Nic. 1.2, chapter 1. The Stoics contend that the highest good lies in virtue, arguing thus: that which is by nature capable of being acquired by man, and needs nothing external, is the highest good. But virtue is of this kind, for since a habit is acquired by man, it can therefore also be acquired, and since it is sufficient for itself, it needs no external thing. The highest good must be such that it makes man, who is a microcosm [μικρόκοσμος], similar to that which is a macrocosm [μεγάλοκοσμος], namely the perfection of the whole universe; but virtue is such. But both arguments are answered by denying the minor premise. As to the first, more is required for happiness than that it can be acquired by man. As to the second, it is not any single virtue that does this, but virtue taken collectively, or its universal activity, which is nothing other than happiness itself. Therefore we must say, with Alexander of Aphrodisias, in his book On the Soul, chapter 14: if virtue were the highest good, it would be either because virtue produces a happy life, or because it would be the very essence of happiness. Not the former, for then virtue would be distinguished from happiness as cause from effect, since nothing can produce itself. Not the latter, for then it would not be lawful for a man to choose death, since that would separate the habit of virtue from the essence of happiness, and happiness would not remain. But the Stoics say it is sometimes permissible to choose death, although in truth this should not be approved concerning the choice of death, against the Stoics; yet this difference may still hold. Some said it is agreement with God or isotheia [ἰσοθεΐα], which good does not belong to moral philosophy, nor can it be fully acquired in this life, but only in the next. More on these opinions may be seen in Lipsius, Manuductio ad Philosophiam Stoicam, chapter 13. The fourth opinion is that of the Peripatetics, whose prince is Aristotle. They held that the highest good consists in the exercise of the rational soul according to virtue, an opinion which, as most fitting to the nature of the thing and to reason, all today uphold.

units.la: V. Quaestio. Definitur vero à Philosopho 6.1.Nic. ψυχῆς λογικῆς ἐνέργεια κατ' ἀρετὴν ἐν βίῳ τελείῳ: In qua definitione duo observanda veniunt. 1. Definitum, felicitas de qua supra in quaest. 3. 2. Definitio, quae constat 1. forma, 2. efficiente, 3. fine seu cui, non seu cujus gratia, quia summum bonum sui ipsius gratia appetitur, non vero alterius. Forma est actio illa non singularis, sed universalis, quae nos intrin-secu secus perficit contra distincta ab habitu virtutis, nam consumatio & perfectio virtutis, quae dicitur felicitas, non est in habitu virtutis, sed in operatione & exercitio, ut praeclare inquit, Cic. Virtutis omnis laus in actione consistit, & per actionem etiam distinguitur ab otio, quae tamen actio relata ad summum bonum futurae vitae non tam perfectio, quam praeparatio solum aestimatur, & haec actio non est transiens aliqua, sed immanens in subjecto, cujus est actio, propterea quod subjectum perficiat.
units.tr: Fifth question. The Philosopher defines it in Nicomachean Ethics 6.1 as "the activity of the rational soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life" [ψυχῆς λογικῆς ἐνέργεια κατ' ἀρετὴν ἐν βίῳ τελείῳ]. Two things must be noted in this definition. (1) The thing defined: happiness, discussed above in question 3. (2) The definition itself, which consists of (1) a form, (2) an efficient cause, and (3) an end, or that for which, not that of which, since the highest good is sought for its own sake and not for the sake of something else. The form is that universal activity, not a single act, which perfects us from within and is distinguished from the habit of virtue. For the completion and perfection of virtue, which is called happiness, lies not in the habit of virtue but in its operation and exercise, as Cicero rightly says: all the praise of virtue consists in action. It is also distinguished from idleness by being an activity. Yet this activity, when related to the highest good of the future life, is esteemed not so much as perfection as merely as preparation. And this activity is not transient but remains within the subject whose activity it is, since it perfects that subject.

units.la: Causa efficiens est Triplex, 1. Principalis nempe & remota. 2. Propinqua. 3. Instrumentalis. Efficiens principalis in hac definitione est anima rationalis, quia oportet felicitatem esse proprium hominis, atque adeo perficia forma hominis, ut omnia propria essentialia solent, & hac particula excluduntur actiones corporis & bestiarum. Actiones corporis, quia corpus per se nihil agit, nisi dirigente & ducente anima: Bestiarum etiam actiones felices proprie dici non possunt, cum careant anima rationali, a qua ipsa felicitas promanat: Causa efficiens propinqua, est virtus optima & perfectissima, nam quia felicitas est optima & perfectissima actio, ideo oportet eam habere medium conveniens, videlicet habitum virtutis perfectum, qui habitus duo ista requirit. 1. Ut sit perfectus omnibus partibus, atque adeo in se contineat omnes virtutum species, si enim vel unica deest virtus, felicitas plene possideri non poterit, propterea quod virtutes omnes arctissima inter se connexione & vinculo compingantur. 2. Periftum habitum seu causam propinqua, nempe virtutem denotatut perseperfectionis gradu, quod ad felicitatem requiratur, non levis aliquis dispositio, sed constans & longo rerum usu confirmatus habitus. Causa efficiens Instrumentalis est vita perfecta, per quam intelligitur. 1. Instrumentum naturale, nempe aetas matura & bene educata, ut praeclare docet Philosophus 2. 1. Nic. 2. Intelliguntur instrumenta artificialia, quae non oriuntur immediate a natura, sed aliunde comparantur, usu nempe, praxi & consuetudine, quae comitantur felicitatem, & licet essentiam non mutent, existentiam tamen illustrant.
units.tr: The efficient cause is threefold: (1) principal, that is, remote; (2) proximate; (3) instrumental. The principal efficient cause in this definition is the rational soul, because happiness must be proper to man and so a perfection of man's form, as all proper essential attributes are. By this particle the actions of the body and of beasts are excluded. The actions of the body are excluded because the body does nothing of itself, unless the soul directs and leads it. The actions of beasts also cannot properly be called happy, since they lack the rational soul from which happiness itself proceeds. The proximate efficient cause is the best and most perfect virtue. For since happiness is the best and most perfect activity, it must have a suitable means, namely a perfect habit of virtue, and this habit requires two things. (1) That it be perfect in all its parts, and so contain in itself all the species of virtues. For if even a single virtue is lacking, happiness cannot be fully possessed, since all the virtues are bound together by the closest connection and bond. (2) That the habit, or proximate cause, namely virtue, has reached the degree of perfection required for happiness. It is not some slight disposition but a settled habit, confirmed by long practice. The instrumental efficient cause is the complete life, which is understood as follows. (1) A natural instrument, namely a mature age, well educated, as the Philosopher teaches clearly in Nicomachean Ethics 1.2. Artificial instruments are also understood, which do not arise immediately from nature but are acquired from elsewhere, namely through use, practice and custom. These accompany happiness and, although they do not change its essence, they illuminate its existence.

units.la: Finis denique, in hac definitione, cui est ipse homo, qui animatur, cum additur, anima rationalis: Et etsi non expresse, implicite tamen continetur in ipsa definitione, nam actiones hujus, qui requiritur ad felicitatem triplex est: 1. Causa efficiens. Animus principium principale agendi. 2. Virtus principium instrumentale & ipsa ratio principium rectitudinis per quam actio dicitur recta, quae omnia innuuntur ab Arist. cum dicit κατ' ἀρετήν, quae additur, ut contra distinguatur ab actionibus vel vitio, vel sine habitu virtutis elaboratis. 3. Principium est homo virtute praeditus, qui principium est integrum, completum, & adaequatum, adeoque felicitatem tanquam bonum sibi proprium vindicat.
units.tr: Lastly, the end in this definition is man himself, who is animated when rational soul is added. Although it is not stated expressly, it is implicitly contained in the definition itself. For the actions of this man, which are required for happiness, are threefold: (1) The efficient cause: the mind, the principal source of acting. (2) Virtue, the instrumental source; and reason itself, the source of rectitude, through which an action is called right. All these are indicated by Aristotle when he says according to virtue [κατ' ἀρετήν], which is added in order to distinguish happiness from actions performed through vice or without the habit of virtue. (3) The principle is man endowed with virtue, who is a whole, complete and adequate principle, and therefore claims happiness as a good proper to himself.

units.la: Explicata jam definitione, dubia quaedam exoriuntur, ac 1. hoc; summum bonum est quod permanens, quod nos comitari quotidie debet: ut hujusmodi non est felicitas hic descripta, quia hic describitur ut actio, actio vero facile perit, nisi agens continuo agat, siquidem ex mutua relatorum natura, una sublata alterum facile tollitur? Resp. Verum esse de actione aliqua singulari & transeunte, non vero de actione uniuersali & immanente, siquidem singularis, nisi dato tali obiecto non producitur, universalis vero, quamdiu super est, humanum genus perire non potest.
units.tr: With the definition now explained, certain doubts arise. First: the highest good is that which is lasting and which ought to accompany us every day; happiness as described here is not of this kind, because it is described as an activity, and an activity easily perishes unless the agent acts continuously, since, from the mutual nature of correlatives, when one is removed the other is easily removed too? Answer: this is true of a single and transitory activity, but not of a universal and abiding activity. For a single act is not produced unless such an object is given, whereas the universal activity, as long as it exists, cannot perish from the human race.

units.la: II. Si in actione collocaretur summum bonum, jure homini egenti, & per naturam corruptam, insalubres possunt conferre culpam sua miseria in naturam & in parentes, quatenus eorum culpa non possunt assequi summum bonum, cum iis careant instrumentis, quibus ad ipsum pervenitur nempe sanitate & divitiis? Resp. Si haereditario jure ac opera naturae acquireretur felicitas, sequeretur Argumentum, at cum consuetudine ac usu acquiratur nihil probat hoc argumentum, nam sanitas & divitiae, non tam culpa naturae & parentum, quam proprio cujusq; vitio & intemperantia vivendi multi insunt.
units.tr: Second: if the highest good were placed in activity, then the unhealthy and needy man, who is corrupted by nature, could justly blame his misery on nature and on his parents, since through their fault he cannot attain the highest good, lacking the instruments by which it is reached, namely health and riches? Answer: if happiness were acquired by hereditary right and by the work of nature, the argument would follow. But since it is acquired by practice and use, this argument proves nothing. For health and riches depend less on the fault of nature and of parents than on each man's own vice and the intemperance of his way of living.

units.la: III. Si in actione collocatum esset summum bonum, tum felix Chamaeleontis instar variis mutationibus subjiceretur, modo ex otio in negotium, ex somno in vigiliam & vice versa transfiret, & propterea modo felix, modo infelix esset, felix quoties ageret, infelix quoties otiaretur, aut nihil secundum virtutem ageret? Resp. Actiones quidem naturales interrumpere actiones particulares hominis felicis, sed ipsam universalitatem seu perfectionem actionis, quae fit secundum virtutem, non magis interrumpi ab his, quam homine edenti ipsam essentiam rationis, aut tacente facultatem perfectam sermonis.
units.tr: Third: if the highest good were placed in activity, then the happy man would be subject to various changes like the chameleon, passing now from leisure to business, now from sleep to waking and back again, and so would be now happy, now unhappy: happy whenever he acted, unhappy whenever he was idle, or did nothing according to virtue? Answer: natural actions do interrupt the particular actions of the happy man, but the universality or perfection of the activity, which is done according to virtue, is no more interrupted by these than a man who eats loses the essence of reason, or a man who is silent loses his perfect faculty of speech.

units.la: IV. Si sit in actione collocatum vel est positum in actione omnium virtutum simul, vel modo uniuus, modo alterius, non omnium simul, quia non valet homo simul omnium virtutum tutum munere fungi, si modo unius, modo alterius, nunquam frueretur universo & consimili conjunctim bono, sed modo una parte, modo alia? Resp. Distinguendum esse inter particularem agendi modum, & universalem perfectionem agentis, nam etsi ille, qui habetur felix, agat in particulari secundum hanc vel illam virtutem, si tamen sciat in communi omnibus uti, perfecte dicitur possidere illam felicitatem, quae in actione secundum virtutem perfectissima & optima versatur, nam teste Arist. 10. Nic. c. 9. ipsa perfectio consistit in praelectione interna, non in externo opere aut modo agendi.
units.tr: Fourth: if the highest good is placed in the activity of all the virtues together, then it is either in the activity of all of them at once, or in the activity of one at one time and another at another; but not of all together, because a man cannot perform the duties of all the virtues at once; and if he performs the duties of one at one time and of another at another, he will never enjoy the whole and combined good together, but only one part at a time and then another? Answer: a distinction must be made between the particular mode of acting and the universal perfection of the agent. For although the one who is counted happy acts in particular according to this or that virtue, if he knows how to use all of them in common, he is said to possess perfectly that happiness which consists in the most perfect and best activity according to virtue. For, as Aristotle testifies in Nicomachean Ethics 10.9, perfection itself consists in inner delight, not in an outward work or mode of acting.

units.la: Post dubia hujus definitionis enodata, duae occurrunt quaestiones pulcherrimae. 1. In quo praedicamento sit haec actio, quae dicitur felicitas. Johan. Duns. Scotus in 4. Sententiarum, distinctione 49. quaest. 2. Non esse in praedicamento actionis, hoc modo probat. Perfectio actionis non est in Categoria actionis. At haec est talis, quia actionis perfectio est aggregatum quid ex multis actionibus, quae constituunt habitum: habitus vero est in Categoria Qualitatis ut illi contrariatur Aristoteles c. 2. lib. 10. Nic. cum dicit, ἐδὲ γὰρ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐνέργεια ποιότης εἶναι ἡ εὐδαιμονία. unde liquido apparet esse in Categoria Actionis, si secundum perfectionem agentis a quo ut actus secundus, promanat, consideretur. At vero, si ita rationis suae respectu quatenus crebro agendo continuatur, potest etiam ad Categoriam Qualitatis & primam ejus speciem referri & sic reconciliatur Scotus Aristoteli.
units.tr: After the doubts of this definition have been explained, two most beautiful questions arise. (1) In what category this activity, which is called happiness, lies. John Duns Scotus, in Sentences 4, distinction 49, question 2, argues that it is not in the category of action, and proves this as follows. The perfection of an action is not in the category of action. But happiness is such, because the perfection of an action is something aggregated from many actions which constitute a habit. A habit, however, is in the category of quality, as Aristotle opposes it in Nicomachean Ethics 10.2 when he says: οὐδὲ γὰρ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐνέργεια ποιότης εἶναι ἡ εὐδαιμονία [for happiness is not a quality but an activity of virtue]. Whence it clearly appears that happiness lies in the category of action, if it is considered according to the perfection of the agent from which it proceeds as second act. But if it is considered in respect of its own nature, insofar as it is continued by frequent acting, it can also be referred to the category of quality and to its first species, and thus Scotus is reconciled with Aristotle.

units.la: Secunda quaestio. Cujus sit disciplina de ipsa agere: utrum
units.tr: The second question: to which discipline does it belong to treat of the highest good, whether

units.la: trum Ethica in specie, an Politica cum Arist. 1. Nic. 1. Politica esse de eo agere dicat? Resp. Philosophū loco citato nomine Politices intelligere Practicam Philosophiam in genere, cuius est, primar o agere de summo bono tanquā fine suo ultimo, secūdario etiam agit Ethica in specie de summo bono, sed indeterminatè, quatenus media ad nullum certum vitæ genus determinata prescribit, agit de eo etiā Politica, sed quatenus summū respicit civitatis totius, finem ultimum: hæc de quinta quæstione.
units.tr: whether Ethics in particular, or Politics, as Aristotle says in Nic. 1. 1. that Politics treats of it? Answer: By "Politics" the Philosopher, in the passage cited, means practical philosophy in general. Its primary task is to treat of the highest good as its ultimate end. Secondarily, Ethics in particular also treats of the highest good, but indefinitely, insofar as it prescribes means not determined to any one certain kind of life. Politics also treats of it, but insofar as it regards the highest end of the whole state. This is on the fifth question.

units.la: Sexta est de proprietatibus summi boni, tum etiam de effectu qui insequitur ipsum, proprietates vulgò numerantur octo: quarum prima est, quod super se optabile non alterius cuius quam gratia, & quod vitæ totius norma quædam & scopus fit; quam intuentes virtutem appetimus, & à recto facile abertare non possumus, hoc docet Philosophus, 1. Nic. 1. & 1. Rhet. 6. 7. & 8. Nic. Sed contra hanc propriem occurrit dubium quoddam. 1. Quod summum bonum alterius gratia non sui ipsius petatur, nempe boni illius, quod in futura vita acquiritur? Resp. Bonum morale considerari duobus modis. 1. Respectu humanarum actionum in hac vita, quæ per virtutem acquiruntur, & sic dicitur per se optabile non propter aliud, vel respectu hominis cuius est summum bonum, & quæ præparat ad vitam futuram & sic dicitur optabile propter aliud, nempe beatitudinem. Consideratur ergo, vel perfectivè in hac vita vel præparativè ad alteram vitam, ut loquuntur Scholastici.
units.tr: The sixth question concerns the properties of the highest good, and also the effect that follows from it. The properties are commonly counted as eight. The first is that it is desirable in itself and not for the sake of anything else, and that it is a certain rule and goal of the whole of life; looking to it we desire virtue, and we cannot easily turn aside from what is right. The Philosopher teaches this in Nic. 1, Rhet. 1, and Nic. 6, 7, and 8. But against this property a certain doubt arises. 1. Since the highest good is not sought for the sake of another but for itself, does this not hold for that good which is acquired in the future life? Answer: moral good may be considered in two ways. 1. With respect to human actions in this life, which are acquired through virtue; and so it is said to be desirable in itself and not on account of another. Or with respect to the man whose highest good it is, and which prepares him for the future life; and so it is said to be desirable on account of another, namely blessedness. It is therefore considered either perfectively, in this life, or preparatively, for the other life, as the Scholastics put it.

units.la: Secunda proprietas, quod felicitas sit divinum quiddam, tum imitatione & exemplo, quatenus scil. divinaeactionis quoddam exemplar est, ut docet Philosophus 10. Nic. c.8. tum etiam, quia divino quodam instinctu opus est ei, qui felicitatem sequi vult, ut ibidem docet Philos. c.10. no enim, inquit, ut homo vivet, sed ut divinum quid in ipso existit. Sed hic dubium oriri videtur, an possit dici divinum quid, cum hoc proprium sit beatitudinis Theologicae? Resp. Divinum sumi duobus modis, 1. Ut ab instinctu S. Spiritus aliquid fit, & sic competit soli beatitudini. 2. Ut a ductu rectae rationis & legis naturae aliquid convenienter fit, ut cum homo quatenus potest divinas imitetur actiones, & sic Morale bonum poterit dici divinum quid, quatenus scilicet, ut ait Seneca, Deo similiorem, quam homini hominem reddat.
units.tr: The second property is that happiness is something divine, both by imitation and example, insofar as it is a certain pattern of divine action, as the Philosopher teaches in Nic. 10, c. 8; and also because a divine impulse is needed by one who wishes to pursue happiness, as the Philosopher teaches in the same place, c. 10: "For," he says, "we live not as men, but as something divine exists in us." But here a doubt seems to arise: can it be called something divine, since this is proper to theological blessedness? Answer: "divine" is taken in two ways. 1. As something is done from the impulse of the Holy Spirit; and so it belongs only to blessedness. 2. As something is done fittingly from the guidance of right reason and the law of nature, as when a man, so far as he can, imitates divine actions; and so moral good can be called something divine, insofar as, as Seneca says, it makes a man more like God than like a man.

units.la: Tertia proprietas, quod omnem superet laudem, de hac proprietate agit Philosophus 12. 1. Nic. & ratio est quod laus tantum sit earum rerum, cui aliquid addi potest ad perfectionem assequendam, at felicitati cum sit actionum humanarum ultima perfectio, laus enim, ut ait Philosophus, loco citato est bonorum intermediorum tantum, virtutum scilicet quae ducunt ad summum bonum. At hic obiicitur: Imo Deum laudare solemnis qui est omnium bonorum maximum & ipsissimum bonum, ut variis in locis Scriptura, & praesertim in Psalmis manifesto docet. Ergo multo magis felicitatem, quae est inferius bonum? Resp. Laudem sumi tribus modis. 1. Pro enumeratione effectorum alicujus rei, & sic Deo competit. 2. Pro enumeratione Qualitatum perfecte in existentium quae ulterius perfectionem suam extendere nequeunt. Et sic competit felicitati. 3. Pro praedicatione eorum quæ insunt sed non in summa perfectione & sic proprie virtuti competit. Obtinuit namque consuetudo ut propter virtutes tantum laudentur homines, sicut propter vitia vituperantur.
units.tr: The third property is that it surpasses all praise. The Philosopher treats of this property in Nic. 1, c. 12, and the reason is that praise belongs only to those things to which something can be added toward attaining perfection. But happiness is the ultimate perfection of human actions; for praise, as the Philosopher says in the passage cited, belongs only to intermediate goods, namely the virtues which lead to the highest good. But here the objection is raised: "Indeed, to praise God is a solemn duty, since he is the greatest of all goods and the very best good, as Scripture plainly teaches in various places, and especially in the Psalms. Therefore much more is happiness to be praised, since it is a lesser good?" Answer: praise is taken in three ways. 1. For the enumeration of the effects of something; and so it belongs to God. 2. For the enumeration of qualities perfectly existing in things which cannot extend their perfection any further; and so it belongs to happiness. 3. For the predication of those things which inhere but not in the highest perfection; and so it properly belongs to virtue. For custom has prevailed that men are praised only on account of virtues, just as they are blamed on account of vices.

units.la: Quarta, quod sit perpauc orum hominum, nempe, quod perpauci sunt, qui ad ipsum pervenire possunt, hoc docet Philosophus, 7. Polit. 8. pauci enim, quos Æquus amavit Jupiter, &c. Virg. 6. Æneid. & Rari quippe boni, ut ait Juven. Satyra 4.
units.tr: The fourth property is that it belongs to few men: that is, few are those who can attain to it. The Philosopher teaches this in Polit. 7, c. 8. "For few," as Virgil says, "are those whom impartial Jupiter has loved," Aen. 6; and "good men are indeed rare," as Juvenal says in Sat. 4.

units.la: Quinta, est quod non indivisibile veluti punctum, sed habeat suos gradus & quanquam summum & perfectissimum gradum raro aut nunquam quis attingere possit, primum tamen & secundum gradum pervenient, id quod innuit Philosophus loco modo citato, contingit scilicet ut aliqui possint illius esse participes sed in gradibus quibusdam, ita ut quicunque ex virtute agunt & honestatem exercent, possunt dici, quodam modo felices, etsi non habeant perfectum usum & omnibus numeris absolutum exercitium virtutis. Sed hic occurrit quæstio: an ista variatio summi boni per gradus fit de materia finis, an de forma, si de materia, sequitur materiam posse existere secundum formam, quod est absurdum & experientiæ repugnat. Si de forma, tum forma recipit magis & minus contra Porph. 1. de differentiis, & Aristotelem 7. Metaph. T. 2. & in lib. Categor. c. de substantia? Resp. Bonum cum sit accidens neque materiam, neque formam habere proprie dictam & proinde istos gradus non venire ab alterutra secundum, sed a natura subjecti, quia cum in se sit perfectissimum quid, hominis tamen respectu, cui inest per gradus, perfectionem suam acquirit.
units.tr: The fifth property is that it is not indivisible, like a point, but has its degrees. Although hardly anyone, or no one, can attain the highest and most perfect degree, yet some reach the first and second degrees, as the Philosopher hints in the passage just cited: it happens that some can be partakers of it, but in certain degrees, so that whoever acts from virtue and practises honour can in a certain way be called happy, even if they do not have perfect use and an exercise of virtue that is complete in every respect. But here the question arises: is this variation of the highest good by degrees in respect of the matter of the end, or of its form? If of matter, it follows that matter can exist according to form, which is absurd and contrary to experience. If of form, then form admits of more and less, contrary to Porphyry, On Differences 1, and Aristotle, Metaph. 7, T. 2, and in the Categories, the chapter on substance? Answer: since good is an accident, it has neither matter nor form properly so called. Therefore these degrees do not arise from either of the two, but from the nature of the subject; for although good is in itself something most perfect, in relation to man, in whom it inheres by degrees, it acquires its perfection by degrees.

units.la: Sexta
units.tr: Sixth

units.la: Sexta, quod sit constantissimum, tum quia continuatur perpetua virtutis actione, tum quia qui semel hoc bonum adeptus sit, non facile ab ejus possessione dejici potest, hoc additur à Philosopho, 1. Nic. 10. Etenim cum virtus propterea quod sit habitus, non possit facile amitti, sed sit constans quiddam & firmum. Ergo multo minus ipsa felicitas, quae est perfectio omnium virtutum. At huic opinioni de Constantia summi boni refragare videtur Aristoteles c. 9. 1. Nic. dicit enim, tales qui in Priami calamitates inciderit, aut misere ex hac vita discesserit, non possunt dici felices? Resp. Summum bonum consideratur duobus modis, primario vel secundario, secundum essentiam vel existentiam. Si prima non secundam essentiam consideretur, quatenus scilicet bona animi tantum in se complectitur poterit aliquis esse felix & si in miserias inciderit, sicut de Priamo referunt poetae & de M. Attilio Regulo Historiae Rom. at si secundario & secundum existentiam, quatenus scilicet aggregationem omnium bonorum, animi, corporis, & fortunae in se complectitur, tunc non poterit talis dici felix, qui inciderit in Priami calamitates, dicitur vero bonum constantissimum, propterea quod nihil humana opera aut industria acquiri possit, quod diutius permaneat aut difficilius permutetur, hinc Philosophus 1. Nic. 10. inquit, in nulla re humana tanta inest firmitas & constantia, quantum virtutum actionibus, id est, in ipsa felicitate, quae omnes actiones insequitur.
units.tr: Sixth, that it is most constant, both because it is sustained by a perpetual exercise of virtue, and because one who has once attained this good cannot easily be dispossessed of it. The Philosopher adds this in Nic. 1.10: since virtue, precisely because it is a habit, cannot easily be lost but is something constant and firm, much less can happiness itself be lost, since it is the perfection of all the virtues. Yet Aristotle seems to oppose this view of the constancy of the highest good in Nic. 1.9, for he says: those who have fallen into the calamities of Priam, or have died wretchedly from this life, cannot be called happy? Answer: the highest good is considered in two ways, primarily or secondarily, according to its essence or its existence. If it is considered primarily, according to its essence, insofar as it comprises only the goods of the soul, then a man may be happy even if he falls into misfortunes, as the poets report of Priam and the Roman histories of M. Atilius Regulus. But if it is considered secondarily and according to its existence, insofar as it comprises the aggregate of all goods, of soul, body and fortune, then one who falls into the calamities of Priam cannot be called happy. It is called the most constant good because nothing can be acquired by human effort or industry that lasts longer or is more difficult to change. Hence the Philosopher says in Nic. 1.10: in no human thing is there so much firmness and constancy as in the actions of virtue, that is, in happiness itself, which follows all actions.

units.la: Septima, quod requirat omnium virtutum copulam simul, nam etsi quis virtutem aliquam possidet & & non omnes simul, beatus dici nequit, sicut docet Philosophus [?]7. Pol. 1. & ratio hujus est, quod sicut diximus in explicatione definitionis summi boni, omnes virtutes inter se vinculo quodam connectantur & ipsa felicitas requirat perfectionem partium, ut omnes virtutes concurrant, nec qui secundum eas agit contrariis vitiorum actionibus se polluere debet, sic enim felicitatem amittere potest, cum contraria contrariis tollantur.
units.tr: Seventh, that it requires all the virtues together at once. For even if someone possesses some one virtue and not all together, he cannot be called blessed, as the Philosopher teaches in Pol. 1 [?7]. The reason is that, as we said in explaining the definition of the highest good, all the virtues are linked together by a certain bond, and happiness itself requires the perfection of the parts, so that all the virtues concur, and one who acts according to them must not defile himself with the contrary actions of vices; for in this way he can lose happiness, since contraries are destroyed by contraries.

units.la: Octava, quod sit αὐτάρκης, id est, sibi ipsi sufficiens, sicut docet Philosophus, 1. Nic. 5. & 10. 6. 6. & ratio est, quod cum felicitas, sit ultimus rerum humanarum finis, ideo omnium media includit ea quae praesupponit, quod autem omnia media praesupponit, id sibi ipsi sufficiens est, nam Instrumenta aut Media amplius non quaerit ad sui existentiam constituendam, illud autem vocatur insufficiens, quod nondum habet omnia media necessaria suae perfectioni adhibenda.
units.tr: Eighth, that it is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης], that is, sufficient to itself, as the Philosopher teaches in Nic. 1.5 and 10, and 6.6. The reason is that, since happiness is the ultimate end of human affairs, it therefore includes all the means which it presupposes. But whatever presupposes all means is sufficient to itself, for it no longer seeks instruments or means to constitute its own existence. That is called insufficient which does not yet have all the means necessary to be applied to its perfection.

units.la: Septima quaestio est de effectu summi boni.
units.tr: The seventh question concerns the effect of the highest good.

units.la: Effectus vero est voluptas, sed cum voluptas sit multiplex, alia corporis, alia animi, hic de voluptate tanquam effectu summi boni, mentali agitur, quae ex actione animi proficiscitur, est animi laetitia & gaudium, quod conscientiam recte factorum sequitur, & de hac voluptate agit Philosophus 10 Nicomach. c. 4. f. Sed haec voluptas rursus duplex est, una intellectualis, quae in rerum contemplatione versatur, cujusmodi colligitur ex disciplinis theoreticis, alia est voluntatis seu voluntaris, quae per praeelectionem & consultationem agit, & de hac hoc loco sermo erit. Quae definitur tranquillitas illa mentis, qua homo suaviter acquiescit
units.tr: The effect is pleasure. But since pleasure is manifold, some of the body and some of the soul, here we are speaking of pleasure as the effect of the highest good, the mental kind, which arises from an action of the soul. It is a joy and gladness of the mind that follows the consciousness of right deeds, and the Philosopher treats of this pleasure in Nic. 10, c. 4, at the end. But this pleasure is again twofold: one is intellectual, which is concerned with the contemplation of things, the kind gathered from theoretical disciplines; the other is that of the will, or voluntary, which acts through prior choice and deliberation, and it is of this that we shall speak here. It is defined as that tranquillity of mind by which a man quietly rests

units.la: in exercitio virtutum, & de hac dicit Philosloc.supra cit. quod consequens sit & effectus perfectæ operationis secundùm virtute, nam id hominum animis Deus indidit, ut ex vita bene & honestè acta internam lætitiam concipiat, sicut de Socrate, Miltiade, Camillo & aliis etiam Ethnicis legimus, nam mes practica cum in seipsum reflectitur, tum oritur ex hac reflexione lætitia in corde ex recordatione rerum bene gestarum, & hæc dicitur voluptas, & producit in homine 1. Conscientiam pacatam ob recte facta. 2. Tranquillitatem & quietè voluntatis & affectuum omnium, & 3. Lætitiam & gaudium quo quis exultat, & gratulatur sibi de recte honesteq; d ctis & factis. Unde Thom. inquit, Voluptas est quietatio mentis in ultimo suo fine, & Plutarch. de amore divit. Virtus gaudium parit, sive aliquis videat, sive omnes lateat. Cæterum voluptate non esse de essentia summi boni, quod vult D. Thom. (cui contrariatur Scotus, probat aperte Philos. 7.10. Nic. Inquiens, putamus voluptate commiscerī tantum felicitati, quod si copuletur aut commiscetur tantum, non est ipsum summum bonum, sed quia necessario sequitur, est affectio ipsius, & metem suam declarat illustri similitudine c. 4. ejusd. libri, ubi comparat voluptatem pulchritudini, quæ ex congruete partium corporis mensura & dispositione exsurgit, at ut pulchritudo non est optima corporis dispositio, sed ipsam sequitur tanquam comes & affectio, ita voluptas non erit summi animi bonum, sed affectio ipsius, hoc tamen posset dici, quamvis de summi boni essentia non sit, tamen summum bonum immediatè & individuè sequitur, non secus ac lumen sequitur. quitur lucem. Obiect. 1. Thomæ ex 7. Polit. c. 1. Aristotelis, Philosophus, ration. quibus voluptas summum bonum esse probatur, dicit: Beatam vitam in voluptate efsepositam. Ergo voluptas est summum bonum? Resp. Nihil inde concludi, nam Aristoteles non decisive loquitur, sed dubitative, inquiens, sive posita sit in gaudio ἐν τῷ χαίρειν ἐπὶ ἀρετῇ, &c. ibi enim tractans obiter hinc quæstionem, an felicitas consistat in bonis externis, nempe corporis & fortunæ, an in bonis internis animi, inquit, sive in voluptate propter Epicurum, qui ut supra diximus, summum bonum in voluptate statuebat, sive in virtute propter Stoicos, sive in utroque ex vulgari opinione, quia virtus est quasi materiale felicitatis, voluptas effectus est ipsam consequens.
units.tr: in the exercise of the virtues. Of this the Philosopher says, in the passage cited above, that it is the consequence and effect of a perfect operation according to virtue. For God has implanted this in human minds, so that from a life well and honourably lived one conceives inner gladness. We read the same of Socrates, Miltiades, Camillus and other pagans as well. For the practical mind, when it is reflected upon itself, then from this reflection arises joy in the heart, from the recollection of things well done, and this is called pleasure. It produces in a man: 1. a conscience at peace because of right deeds; 2. tranquillity and quiet of the will and of all the affections; and 3. gladness and joy, by which one exults and congratulates himself on rightly and honourably done words and deeds. Hence Thomas says: Pleasure is the quieting of the mind in its ultimate end, and Plutarch, On Love of Riches: Virtue begets joy, whether someone sees it or all remain hidden. Moreover, that pleasure is not of the essence of the highest good, which Thomas holds (Scotus contradicts him), the Philosopher clearly proves in Nic. 7.10 [sic], saying: we think pleasure is only mingled with happiness; but if it is merely joined or mixed with it, it is not the highest good itself, but because it necessarily follows, it is an affection of it. He declares his opinion by a striking comparison in c. 4 of the same book, where he compares pleasure to beauty, which arises from the suitable measure and arrangement of the parts of the body. But as beauty is not the best disposition of the body, but follows it as a companion and affection, so pleasure will not be the good of the soul, but its affection. This could nevertheless be said: although it is not of the essence of the highest good, it nonetheless follows the highest good immediately and inseparably, just as light follows the sun. Objection 1, from Thomas, from Aristotle's Pol. 7 c. 1, where the Philosopher, giving the reasons by which pleasure is proved to be the highest good, says: a blessed life is placed in pleasure. Therefore pleasure is the highest good? Answer: nothing follows from this, for Aristotle does not speak decisively but dubitatively, saying: whether it is placed in joy in rejoicing at virtue [ἐν τῷ χαίρειν ἐπὶ ἀρετῇ], etc. For there, treating in passing the question whether happiness consists in external goods, namely of body and fortune, or in internal goods of the soul, he says: whether in pleasure, as Epicurus held, who, as we said above, placed the highest good in pleasure; or in virtue, as the Stoics held; or in both, according to common opinion, because virtue is as it were the material of happiness, and pleasure is the effect following it.

units.la: Secundum argumentum, quod per internam naturæ commotionem ab omnibus animalibus maximè expetitur, est summum bonum. At voluptas, &c. Ratio major hæc est, quia bonum est id, quod omnia appetant. Quare voluptas censeri debet summum bonum, quia ab omnibus appetitur? Resp. Duplicem esse voluptatem, unam ex sensu & appetitu ortam, quæ dicitur externa, aliam ex intellectu & voluntate, quæ dicitur interna, quare cum major intelligat illam externam, quæ nobis cum belluis communis est, falsa erit major.
units.tr: The second argument: what is most desired by all animals through an inner movement of nature is the highest good. But pleasure, etc. The major premise is this: because the good is that which all things desire. Therefore pleasure should be deemed the highest good, because it is desired by all? Answer: there are two kinds of pleasure, one arising from sense and appetite, which is called external, and another from the intellect and will, which is called internal. Therefore, since the major premise understands that external pleasure, which is common to us and the beasts, the major is false.

units.la: Tertium: Quod omnia bona augget eaq; perficit, tanquam finis ultimus, est aut ipsum bonum aut de essentia summi boni. At voluptas, &c. Major inde patet, quia per voluptatem res videntur suam habere perfectionem, si quidem nullam gignunt voluptatem res, nisi perfectionem suam consequantur? Resp. Plato in Philebo, ideo colligit voluptatem non esse summum bonum, quod cum sit de natura summi boni esse perfectum quid, & per se optabile, non alterius gratia, ipsa sapientia addita voluptati sit optabilior, at illa de voluptate intellectuali intelligitur, non vero de Practica, de qua hic agitur, sed verior responsio est, falsam esse majorem superioris argumenti, nam voluptas nō perficit summum bonum, sed facit actus ridendi ostendit inesse facultatem ridendi, sic voluptas tanquam affectus summi boni ostendit inesse felicitatem, unde Aphr. 4. nat. quaest. cap.16. inquit, non honestum in gratiam voluptatis, sed voluptatem in gratiam honesti esse optandam, & ab honesto voluptatem recipere perfectionem & conditionem boni, non vice versa. Dein etiam ut detur, voluptatem perficere summum bonum, non perficit, ut habitus aliquis constituens, sed ut accedens aliquid ad summum bonum, sicut docet Philosophus lib.10 c.4. Nicom. & Plot. Ennead.6. lib.7. c.17. asserit, voluptatem comitari adeptionem summi boni. Bonum vero per se & absque voluptate esse eligendum. Caeterum voluptatem non esse de essentia summi boni, hae rationes probant, quia summum bonum est objectum voluptatis, sicut verum est objectum intellectus, at voluptas non est objectum, sed affectus animi. 2. A voluptate nemo bonus aut felix dicitur, sicut a summo bono. 3. Summum bonum est honore dignum, sicut Nic.1. cap.12. dicitur, at voluptas non est per se honore digna. 4. Id quod causa est, ut alterum sit bonum, id est, maxime bonum, at felicitas est causa, ut voluptas laudetur & aestimetur, ut bona. Ergo. 5. Evertit conditionem
units.tr: Third: that which, as ultimate end, augments and perfects all goods, is either the good itself or of the essence of the highest good. But pleasure, etc. The major is clear from this, because through pleasure things seem to have their perfection, if indeed things beget no pleasure unless they attain their perfection? Answer: Plato in the Philebus therefore concludes that pleasure is not the highest good, because it is of the nature of the highest good to be something perfect and desirable in itself, not for the sake of another; and wisdom itself, added to pleasure, is more desirable. But this is understood of intellectual pleasure, not of the practical, which is what is treated here. The truer answer is that the major of the preceding argument is false, for pleasure does not perfect the highest good, but as laughter shows that the faculty of laughing is present, so pleasure, as an affection of the highest good, shows that happiness is present. Hence Aphrodisias, Nat. Quest. 4 c. 16, says that the honourable is to be desired not for the sake of pleasure, but pleasure for the sake of the honourable, and that pleasure receives its perfection and character of good from the honourable, not the reverse. Further, even granting that pleasure perfects the highest good, it does not perfect it as a constituting habit, but as something accessory to the highest good, as the Philosopher teaches in Nic. 10, c. 4, and Plotinus, Ennead 6, lib. 7, c. 17, asserts that pleasure accompanies the attainment of the highest good, while the good itself is to be chosen per se and apart from pleasure. Moreover, that pleasure is not of the essence of the highest good is proved by these reasons: (1) because the highest good is the object of pleasure, as truth is the object of the intellect, but pleasure is not an object, it is an affection of the soul; (2) no one is called good or happy from pleasure, as from the highest good; (3) the highest good is worthy of honour, as is said in Nic. 1, c. 12, but pleasure is not in itself worthy of honour; (4) that which is the cause of something else being good, that is, most good, is the cause of pleasure being praised and esteemed as good, but happiness is the cause of this, therefore...; (5) it overturns the condition and nature of pleasure if it is said to be the highest good, for pleasure affects a man through some good, and the better the good, the greater the pleasure it brings; hence it is necessary that the highest good be one thing and the joy arising from the highest good another…

units.la: E & naturam voluptatis, esse dect sententia summi boni, nam voluptas per se afficit hominem, sed per aliquod bonum, & bonum quanto melius, tanto majore voluptate afficit, unde necesse est, ut aliud sit summum bonum, aliud lætitia ex summo bono proveniens, sicut super 4 sentent. quaest. 7. docet Scotus, & Aristoteles 10. Nicom. ubi dicit, sine actione non fit voluptas, nam illam perficit, & paulo post addit, differunt vero actiones mentis & sensuum, & ipsæ inter se specie, & voluptas, quæ ipsas perficit, & 3. Nicom. 10. multi inde falluntur propter voluptatem γίνεσθαι τῆς ἐοκ ἀγαθὴν φαίνεται, plura vide apud Picol. grad. 9. c. 16. & seq. aliquot. Hactenus de septima quaest.
units.tr: And as for the nature of pleasure, the opinion that it is the highest good is mistaken. Pleasure affects a person only through some good, and the better the good, the greater the pleasure it brings. Therefore the highest good must be one thing, and the joy that arises from the highest good must be another, as Scotus teaches on the fourth book of the Sentences, question 7, and as Aristotle says in the tenth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, where he states that pleasure does not arise without activity, since it perfects the activity. A little later he adds that the activities of the mind and of the senses differ, and also differ in kind from each other, and so does the pleasure which perfects them. In the third book, chapter 10, he says that many are deceived about pleasure because it seems to be good [γίνεσθαι τῆς ἐοκ ἀγαθὴν φαίνεται]. More on this may be seen in Piccolomini, Grade 9, chapter 16 and following, in several places. So much for the seventh question.

units.la: Sequitur octava, de iis nempe, quæ præcedunt, quæque sequuntur summum bonum, & vocantur bona secundaria, quæ quidem etsi summum bonum per se non constituant, nec ad ejus essentiam requiruntur, ad assecutionem tamen & existentiam summè necessaria videntur, & sunt 4. Libertas, sanitas, divitiæ, honor, & horum aliæ considerantur in ipso homine, ut libertas & sanitas: aliæ extra hominem, ut divitiæ, quæ sunt bona possessionis & honor, qui dicitur bonum dignitatis & merita. Primum igitur bonum secundarium, quod consideratur in homine, est libertas, quæ est vel absoluta vel respectiva, aut prima vel a prima orta. Absoluta libertas dicitur, quæ Deo soli competit, & dicitur libertas ex beneplacito, quia quicquid vult Deus, & quando vult ex beneplacito suo facit. Respectiva libertas est illa, quæ creaturis competit, & quamquam respectu principii, a quo manat, libertatis nomen sibi vendicet, secundum vim directricem, tamen legi divinæ subjicitur, & ideò dicitur libertas respectiva, respectu nempe Dei, quia non liberè, quicquid libet, creatura agit, sed vi divina dirigēte & ducēte, & ista libertas est multiplex, respectu multiplicis subjecti, cui inest, nam alia est libertas ad bonum in bonis Angelis, quæ dicitur libertas ex gratia, alia est libertas ad malū in malis, & dicitur libertas expermissu, quia nihil nisi permissu divino agere possunt mali angeli, alia est libertas hominis in naturalibus, in quib. licet ad tempus actiones suas suspendat, tamen penitus non posset suspendere, & ideo dicitur libertas ex tempore à Scholasticis, alia est in spiritualib. & dicitur à Theologis libertas Christiana, qua homines Christiani per fidem in Christum non tenētur sub lege, sed liberantur ex gratia, unde Paul. ad Rom. 6. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur, non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia, de qua vide Calvin. lib. 3. Inst. c. 9. per tot. alia est in moralib. actionibus, quæ proprie dicitur libertas hominis, quippe in his actionibus homo posset agere vel non agere, suspendere vel non suspendere intentionem agendi pro libitu suo, quia nempe in ejus potestate sunt positę ejusmodi actiones, & hæc libertas consideratur, vel ratione principii interni, unde fluit, nempe voluntatis, & dicitur libertas voluntatis, quia libera declarat voluntatem ad quamlibet actionem producendam vel non producendam, sed de hac posthac lib. 3. infr. vel ratione actionum internarum, quæ à voluntate agitantur, ut sunt cogitationes, consultationes, deliberationes, & hæc definitur facultas libera & expedita agendi, nulla vi exteriore impedita, seu jus ac potestas qua facilè & expeditè actiones virtutis omni loco & tempore, in omne obiectum exerceri possunt. Haec libertas consideratur in homine, vel respectu animi vel corporis, respectu animi dicitur facultas, qua homo, quicquid intendit, saltem in iis, quae ab ipso produci potest, liberè agit, quam his rationibus hominI inesse probat Aristot. 4 f. 3. Nicomach. quia electio & consultatio fiunt voluntariò, & à voluntate liberè proficiscuntur. 2. Quia agere & non agere in nobis sunt posita tanquam liberum quid & spontaneum. 3.
