Otiosè & frustra monita & consilia ad virtutem amplectendam, & vitium fugiendum adhiberentur, nisi libertas esset quaedam animi, qua hanc appetere & prosequi illud declinare & effugere possimus, & haec non potest cogi legibus humanis, ut testatur ipsae leges ff. de Pæn. l. 17.
units.tr: Next comes the eighth question, concerning those things which precede and follow the highest good and are called secondary goods. Although these do not constitute the highest good in themselves, and are not required for its essence, they seem to be very necessary for attaining it and for its existence. There are four: liberty, health, riches, and honour. Some of these are considered in the man himself, such as liberty and health; others outside him, such as riches, which are goods of possession, and honour, which is called the good of dignity and of merit. The first secondary good considered in man is therefore liberty, which is either absolute or relative, and either first or derived from the first. Absolute liberty is that which belongs to God alone, and it is called liberty of good pleasure, because whatever God wills, and whenever he wills, he does according to his own good pleasure. Relative liberty is that which belongs to creatures. Although, with respect to the principle from which it flows, it claims the name of liberty, nevertheless it is subject to the divine law as to its directing power; and so it is called relative liberty, namely relative to God, because the creature does not act freely whatever it pleases, but under the directing and guiding power of God. This liberty is manifold, according to the many subjects in which it inheres. For there is liberty to good in the good angels, which is called liberty from grace; there is liberty to evil in the evil angels, which is called liberty by permission, because evil angels can do nothing except by divine permission; there is the liberty of man in natural matters, in which, although he may for a time suspend his actions, he could not altogether suspend them, and so the Schoolmen call it liberty from time; there is liberty in spiritual matters, which the theologians call Christian liberty, by which Christian men through faith in Christ are not bound under the law but are set free by grace. Hence Paul, Romans 6: Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under grace. On this see Calvin, Institutes, book 3, chapter 9, throughout. There is also liberty in moral actions, which is properly called the liberty of man, since in these actions a man can act or not act, suspend or not suspend the intention to act at his pleasure, because such actions are placed in his power. This liberty is considered either with respect to its internal principle, from which it flows, namely the will, and is called liberty of the will, because the free will determines itself to produce or not to produce any action; of this more will be said later, in book 3 below; or with respect to the internal actions which are moved by the will, such as thoughts, considerations, and deliberations. And this is defined as the free and unhindered faculty of acting, not impeded by any external force, or the right and power by which the actions of virtue can be exercised easily and readily in every place and time, upon every object. This liberty is considered in man either with respect to the mind or to the body. With respect to the mind, it is the faculty by which a man acts freely in whatever he intends, at least in those things which he can produce himself. Aristotle proves that man has this liberty in the third book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, for the following reasons: (1) because choice and deliberation are voluntary and proceed freely from the will; (2) because to act and not to act lie in us as something free and spontaneous; (3) because admonitions and counsels to embrace virtue and shun vice would be given in vain, unless there were in the mind a certain liberty by which we could seek the one and avoid the other. And this cannot be compelled by human laws, as the laws themselves testify, Digest, On Punishments, law 17.

units.la: Scilicet quoad internum agendi modum, quàquam ratione actionum externarum, quae prodeunt, restringi possint, sed lege divina, quoad intra restringi etiam possint secundum vim directricem, scilicet non coactivam (nam lex divina duo haec in se habet, vim scilicet directivam & coactivam) quia quicunque virtute praeditus est, sponte sua & non coacte fertur ad recte agendum, unde Aristoteles interroganti, quid ei Philosophia prodesset, ut sponte, inquit, faciam, quod alii coacte, sicetiam illud Poëta: Oderunt peccare boni virtutis amore.
units.tr: Namely, with respect to the internal mode of acting, although external actions which proceed from it may be restrained, it can be restrained by divine law, even within, according to the directing power, though not the coercive power (for divine law contains both in itself, a directing power and a coercive power). For whoever is endowed with virtue is moved of his own accord, and not by compulsion, to act rightly. Hence Aristotle, when someone asked him what good philosophy did him, answered: that I may do willingly what others do under compulsion. So also the poet: Good men hate to sin, out of love of virtue.

units.la: Sed de hac libertate infra fusius agetur lib. 3.
units.tr: But this liberty will be treated more fully below, in book 3.

units.la: Libertas corporis est facultas obeundi virtutis actiones ab animo, & praesertim à voluntate injunctas, in omne externum virtutis obiectum, & haec libertas restringi potest & legibus divinis & consuetudine quadam, quæ inter Ethnicos etiamnum durat, ut inter Turcas, Persas, Tartaros & inter Judæos locum habuit, ut videre licet ex legibus Judaicis: Inter Christianos etiam ad tempus Justiniani Imperatoris viguit, sed illE edicto cavit, ne quis è Christianis servituti subjiceretur. Indignum enim existimabat, qui pretioso Christi sanguine redemti essent, hominum arbitrio absolutè subjici, & contra jus naturæ est, qui neminem servum facit, sed omnibus liberam nascendi conditionem concessit, unde tit. 5. lib. 1. Institutionum Justin. §. 2. servitus definitur, confiitutio juris gentium, quâ quis alieno arbitrio contra naturam subjicitur. Hæc verò libertas nisi adsit, felicitatem nemo plenè & planè assequi poterit, cum captivitate aut servitute à libero agendi modo (qui ad felicitatem assequendam tanquam bonum secundarium requiritur) prohibeatur. Sed objicitur etiam, absque libertate corporis posse aliquem dici felicem, verbi gratia, Æsopum illum fabulatorem, qui serviit 1. Mercatori. 2. Zantho Philosopho, sicut Maximus Planudes in vita ipsius testatur, nam & virtute præditus fuit, & secundum virtutem agebat, ut testantur isti Apologi, quibus homines ad amorem virtutum & odium vitiorum exemplo à brutis ratione carentibus ducto utebantur, & Julius Cæsar cum in Piratarum manus incidisset, erat non minus heros & fortis, quam ante fuit. Resp. Felicitatem considerari duobus modis, primario & secundario: Primario isti fuisse felices, secundario minimè. 2. Etsi secundum felicitatis essentiam felices dici potuerint, secundum existentiam, cum bonis istis secundariis caruerint, dici non potuerunt.
units.tr: Liberty of the body is the faculty of carrying out the actions of virtue, especially those enjoined by the mind and above all by the will, upon every external object of virtue. This liberty can be restrained both by divine laws and by a certain custom which still persists among the heathen, as among the Turks, Persians, and Tartars, and which had a place among the Jews, as may be seen from the Jewish laws. Among Christians also it prevailed until the time of the Emperor Justinian, but he by an edict provided that no one of the Christians should be subjected to slavery. For he judged it unworthy that those who had been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ should be subjected absolutely to the will of men. And it is contrary to the law of nature, which makes no one a slave but granted to all a free condition at birth. Hence in Justinian's Institutes, book 1, title 5, §2, slavery is defined as an institution of the law of nations, by which someone is subjected against nature to the will of another. Now if this liberty were absent, no one could fully and plainly attain happiness, since he would be prevented by captivity or slavery from the free manner of acting, which is required for attaining happiness as a secondary good. But it is also objected that someone may be called happy without liberty of the body, for example that fabulist Aesop, who served first a merchant and then the philosopher Xanthus, as Maximus Planudes testifies in his life. For he was endowed with virtue and acted according to virtue, as those Fables testify, by which he led men to the love of virtues and the hatred of vices, using as examples animals lacking reason. And Julius Caesar, when he fell into the hands of pirates, was no less a hero and brave than he had been before. I answer: happiness may be considered in two ways, primarily and secondarily. In the primary sense these men were happy; in the secondary sense, by no means. Second, although they could be called happy according to the essence of happiness, they could not be called happy according to its existence, since they lacked those secondary goods.

units.la: Quæri potest, num isti aulici, qui Principibus & Magnatibus serviunt, frui dicantur recte ista corporis libertate, cum toti a dominorum suorum nutu pendeant, neque agere quicquam, imo ne loqui quidem audeant, nisi quod domini suis placuerit, secus si fecerint, odium sæpe, sæpe amissionem honoris & dignitatis, sæpe etiam periculum vitæ incidunt? Resp. Si domini ipsi sint virtute præditi, tunc iis non restringitur ista corporis libertas, modo secundum virtutem agant, sin minus, felicitatis minus capaces dici possunt ejusmodi homines, unde præclarè Sophocl. Quisquis Tyranni ad tecta demigraverit, fit servus illi, liber etsi venerit. Cæterum cum hæc libertas sit in actionibus humanis, quæ a humana voluntate pendent, & ideo sunt rerum contingentium, quæ possunt fieri vel non fieri pro libitu hominis, in cujus potestate sunt omnes actiones morales, ideo locum non habet contra hominis libertatem, illud Stoicorum fatum: Omnia in causarum serie Necessitati attribuentium, cum dicunt: Omnia fiunt necessariò, quia a causarum serie pendent, quibus in actu positis res aliter se habere nequeunt. 2. Neque Astronomorum fatum, omnia in syderibus, eorumque cursu posita esse dicentium, ut ab iis necessariò dependeant. 3. Neque illud Metaphys. qui dicunt rerum causam & primum omnium rerum principium necessariò (quod tamen falsum est) operari. Ergo & quæ ab eo dependent, operandi necessitate sunt prædita, conditio enim eorum, quæ fiunt, imitantur conditionem sui principii, modumq; operandi ejus, nam quod ait Averrhoës super 2. Phys. quod pendet ex eo, quod causa factum est, ut etiam causa fiat necesse est, quare longè magis pendentia ex principio necessario erunt, necessaria? Resp. Ad haec omnia, quia ista sunt de rebus necessariis, circa quae nihil versatur libertas hominis, sicut praeclarè docet Philosophus lib. 3. Nicomach. cap. 5. ideo non impugnant hominis libertatem in moralibus. 2. Cum Medici dicunt, Mores animi sequi temperamentum corporis, ideo non potest homo liberè agere, sed ex temperatura tantum, ideo neque libertatem habet homo, verum hoc esse falsum, ratio & experientia docet. 2. Temperamentum esse formam hominis, quod illi volunt, quis concedet, quàquam Galenus in libello, quem inscribit: Mores animi sequuntur temperamentum corporis, hoc affirmet. Cum sic sequeretur animam esse mortalem, tot esset distinctas specie formas, quot sunt complexiones aut constitutiones hominum, Pico. gradu 1. cap. 29.
units.tr: It may be asked whether those courtiers who serve princes and great lords can rightly be said to enjoy this liberty of the body, since they wholly depend on the nod of their masters, and dare to do nothing, nay not even to speak, except what has pleased their masters; if they do otherwise, they often incur hatred, often the loss of honour and office, often even danger to life? I answer: if the masters themselves are endowed with virtue, then this liberty of the body is not restrained for them, provided they act according to virtue; but if not, such men can be said to be less capable of happiness. Hence the excellent saying of Sophocles: Whoever has gone over to the house of a tyrant becomes his slave, even if he came free. Moreover, since this liberty lies in human actions, which depend on the human will, and so belong to contingent things, which can be done or not done at a person's pleasure, and since all moral actions are in his power, the Stoic doctrine of fate does not apply against human liberty. That doctrine says that all things in the chain of causes are subject to necessity, when they say: All things happen necessarily, because they depend on a chain of causes, which, once they are set in act, cannot be otherwise. Nor does the doctrine of the astrologers apply, who say that all things are placed in the stars and their course, so that they depend necessarily upon them. Nor does that saying of the metaphysicians apply, who say that the cause of things and the first principle of all things acts necessarily (which is nonetheless false). Therefore those things which depend on him are endowed with the necessity of acting, for the condition of what is made imitates the condition of its principle and its manner of acting. For what Averroes says on the second book of the Physics, that whatever depends on something that was made a cause must itself necessarily become a cause, so that things depending on a necessary principle must be all the more necessary? I answer to all these points: they concern necessary things, with which human liberty has nothing to do, as the Philosopher teaches well in the third book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 5. Therefore they do not oppose human liberty in moral matters. Second, when physicians say that the habits of the mind follow the temperament of the body, therefore man cannot act freely but only according to his temperament, and so man has no liberty; but reason and experience teach that this is false. Third, that temperament is the form of man, which they wish, who would grant it, although Galen in the little book which he entitles The habits of the mind follow the temperament of the body does affirm this. For thus it would follow that the soul is mortal, and there would be as many distinct species of forms as there are complexions or constitutions of men. See Pico, Grade 1, chapter 29.

units.la: Tertiò, cum dicunt Philosophi hominem civilem esse obnoxium legibus civilibus & naturae firmul, non tollunt hominis libertatem, nam si sit virtute praeditus, sponte pareret, si vitiis coactè, ita tamen ut possit parere, vel non parere pro libitu, nam civilibus legibus non obligatur, neque naturalibus etiam absolutè, multos enim videre licet, qui ex depravata sua natura, ipsius naturae legibus refragantur, quod eleganti similitudine alt. cap. 1. Nicom. docet Philosophus.
units.tr: Thirdly, when the philosophers say that civil man is bound at once by civil laws and by the laws of nature, they do not take away man's liberty. For if he is endowed with virtue, he obeys willingly; if he is held by vices, he obeys under compulsion, yet in such a way that he can obey or not obey as he pleases, since he is not bound by civil laws, nor indeed absolutely by natural ones. For we may see many who, because of their depraved nature, resist the very laws of nature, as the Philosopher teaches with an elegant comparison alt. cap. 1. Nicom.

units.la: Quartò, cum Logici hoc sophismate tollunt libertatem hominis, quod Alexander Aphrod. affert 2. Moral. quaest. 4. cum homo liberè operatur, vel habet hanc libertatem antequam operetur, vel dum operatur,non ante quæ tunc non operatur,ergo nō liberè,quia quod nondum est, non habet ulla accidentia,neque ullos etiam effectus,nondum operatur, quia tunc necesse est, ut operetur, omne, quod est, quando est, necesse est, ut operetur. Resp. Est captio à figura dictionis, nam à facultate agendi ad ipsum actum, aut ad rem agentem non valet consequentia, & secundo falsum est utrumq; membrum disjunctionis, nam homo antequam operatur, valet liberè, quam velit partem eligere, ut agat, vel non agat, & dum operatur, ei competit quoque, ut liberè id agat, quod intendit, & ab ipso pendet tota agendi ratio, neq; etiam valet illud Theologorum, Homo libertum arbitrium non habet ad bonum, ut Scriptura variis in locis docet, præsertim 1.Cor.4. vers.7. Quid habes,quod non accepisti,&c. Resp. Discrimen est inter libertatem voluntaris, & liberum arbitrium, quia libertas voluntatis tendit ad omnes actiones, quæ ab homine produci possunt; liberum verò arbitrium, sicut vulgò à Theologis accipitur, spectat eas actiones, quæ ad bene beate q ie vivendum conducunt,&c ideo tantum ad spiritualem hominis statum tendunt, plura vide de his apud Pic.gradu 1.de principiis virtutum, à cap. 30. usque ad finem.
units.tr: Fourthly, the logicians take away man's liberty by this sophism, which Alexander of Aphrodisias gives in 2. Moral. quaest. 4.: When man acts freely, he has this liberty either before he acts or while he acts, not before, since then he is not acting; therefore not freely, because what does not yet exist has no accidents and no effects. He does not yet act, because then it is necessary that he act; whatever is, when it is, necessarily acts. Answer: This is a fallacy of figure of speech. The inference from the faculty of acting to the act itself, or to the agent, does not hold. Secondly, both members of the disjunction are false. For before a man acts, he is free to choose which part he will take, to act or not to act; and while he acts, it also belongs to him to do freely what he intends, and the whole manner of acting depends on him. Nor does that saying of the theologians hold, Man has no free will for good, as Scripture teaches in various places, especially 1 Cor. 4, vers. 7: What hast thou that thou didst not receive? etc. Answer: There is a distinction between freedom of the will and free choice (liberum arbitrium). For freedom of the will extends to all the actions that can be produced by man. Free choice, as theologians commonly take it, looks only to those actions which conduce to living well and blessedly, and therefore pertains only to the spiritual state of man. More on these matters may be found in Pic. gradu 1, de principiis virtutum, from ch. 30 to the end.

units.la: Hæc de libertate hominis: Secundum bonum, quod in ipso spectatur, est Sanitas, quæ hominis constitutionem attinet, & definitur, recta animi corporiq; in sua integritate & incolumitate dispositio. Ex ista namque dispositione consurgit facilitas ad recipiendos virtutum habitus, & probas actiones edendas, & ista partim respicitur vel in legitima commensuratione calidi & humidi, & immunitate à doloribus, verbi gratia, à vulnenbus, morbis, & hujusmodi casibus, item ne sit claudum aut mutilum corpus, aut cœcum, quæ oriri possit ex dissolutione continui, & dicitur corporis sanitas, vel in recta membrorum confirmatione & dispositione, sic enim corpus redditur aptum ad functiones suas obeundas, & ut animo rité pareat: vel respicitur sanitas in integra dispositione facultatum animæ sive superiorum, ut intellectus voluntatis, sive inferiorum, ut phantasia & memoria, &c, utut enim ipsa animi substantia lædi non possit, turbatione tamen cerebri & variis casibus ita perturbari possit, ut homines satis sanæ mentis sæpe non dicantur, sicut experientia docet. Et sanitas ista animi requirit in homine Moralis boni studiosò, inclinationem quandam morum & ingenii indolem ad virtutem, & qui voluntatem depravatam ligare, affectibus & cupiditatibus moderari queat, & qui tales non sunt, Philosophus I.Nicom. cap. 1. ab Ethicis studio excludit, nam ad habitum necessaria acquirendam tria requiruntur. 1. Φύσις (seu pravia natura mulimatio. 2. Præcepta seu regula, quibus informetur animus ad actiones recte & rite edendas. 3. Exercitium sine quo nullus acquiri poterit habitus, multi sunt ingenio excellenti & doctibus excellentissimis præditi, moribus tamen desperatissimis, & animo tam ad vitia propenso, ut nihil in vita recte & secundum virtutem agere velint, & tales sunt maxime excellentissimis muniis præditi, quibus tamen ad libidinem suam, non ad bonitatis legem attributur, ut omnis tempotis & nostra etiam doctrina experientia, & hic maximaximè locum habere puto illud Galeni: Moresani-mi sequuntur temperamentum corporis, nempe in ægris & male affectis, quod testatur Philosophus lib. 1. Physiognomias,statim ab initio, ubi dicit quod animi sequantur corpora, & non sint impatibiles,manf stum sit in ebrietatibus & agritudinibus, multum enim mutata videntur a corporis passionibus, sed quæri posset, an ista [anitas sit necessaria ad felicitatem,cum a natura fluat, & felicitas ipsa ab actionibus, quæ visu & consuetudine fiunt, proveniat?
units.tr: These things concerning man's liberty. The second good observed in him is health (Sanitas), which concerns the constitution of man, and is defined as the right disposition of soul and body in their integrity and soundness. For from this disposition arises facility in receiving habits of virtue and in performing good actions. This health is regarded partly in the due proportion of hot and moist, and in freedom from pains, for example from wounds, diseases and such accidents; likewise in the body not being lame, maimed or blind, which may come from a break in continuity. This is called bodily health. Or it is regarded in the right strengthening and arrangement of the limbs, for thus the body is made fit to perform its functions and to obey the mind properly. Or health is regarded in the integral disposition of the faculties of the soul, both the higher, such as intellect and will, and the lower, such as imagination and memory. For although the substance of the soul itself cannot be harmed, yet through disturbance of the brain and various accidents it can be so disordered that men are often not called of sound mind, as experience teaches. And this health of soul requires in the man who is zealous for moral good a certain inclination of character and a disposition of nature towards virtue, and one who can restrain a depraved will and moderate affections and desires. Those who are not such the Philosopher excludes from the study of ethics, Nicom. I, ch. 1, for three things are required for acquiring the necessary habit: (1) nature, or a prior natural disposition; (2) precepts or rules by which the mind is formed to perform actions rightly and properly; (3) exercise, without which no habit can be acquired. Many men are endowed with excellent talent and most excellent learning, yet have most desperate morals and a mind so prone to vices that they will do nothing in life rightly or according to virtue. Such men are especially endowed with the most excellent gifts, which nevertheless are devoted to their lust rather than to the law of goodness, as all time and our own teaching and experience show. And I think that saying of Galen applies most of all here: Morals follow the temperament of the body, namely in the sick and ill-disposed. The Philosopher bears witness to this in Physiognomics, book 1, at the very beginning, where he says that souls follow bodies and are not unaffected by them; it is plain in drunkenness and sickness, for souls seem much changed by bodily affections. But it may be asked whether this health is necessary for happiness, since it flows from nature, and happiness itself arises from actions which are performed by practice and habit?

units.la: Resp. Etsi felicitas sic acquiratur,eget tamen inst umentis istis naturalibus,ut libertate, quæ conditionem suam a natura sortitur, & sanitate, quæ a recta & sana corporis & animi dispositione fluit,& quanquam a natura procedat, usu tamen & consuetudine in suo statu & vigore conservari possit.
units.tr: Answer: Although happiness is acquired in this way, it still needs those natural instruments, such as liberty, which receives its condition from nature, and health, which flows from the right and sound disposition of body and soul. And although it proceeds from nature, it can nevertheless be preserved in its state and vigour by use and custom.

units.la: Quæritur 11. An,qui ægrotet, sit recta felicitate praditus, cum non possit agere secundum virtutem ex defectu isti:us boni secundarii,nempe sanitatis,quam divitiis prefert Aristoteles, quod cum majorem animi contentationem pariat, sit optabilior? Resp. Ab ægritudine quidem brevi non tolli,sed intermitti,a longiori ita languescere,ut vix unus & alter gradus felicitatis appareat, nam, ut ait Aristoteles 7. Polit. cap. 13. posset quidem vir bonus recte uti paupertate & morbis & aliis infortuniis, sed in contrariis constat felicitas. Ad felicitatem etiam tanquam appendix sanitatis requiritur pulchritudo, quæ in duobus consistit. 1. In justa statura seu proportione totius corporis & singulorum membrorum ejusdem. 2. In coloris suavitate & amabilitate, unde & Augustinus lib. 2. de civit.Dei, cap.19. inquit, pulchritudo est partium congruentia cum corpora suavitate, quæ videtur desumta sumta ex Cic.2.offic.&3.Tufculquaeft.& ex Scalig.exer-cit.307.fect.5. & 27.&lib.4 de re Poetica, cap.1. definitur varietas conflata ex temperatura qualitatum & ex partium situ & convenientia, de quibus vide Pic. gradu 8.deinstrumentis virtutum,cap.36. Sed jure quaeri potest, an ista pulchritudo sit necessaria ad felicitatem asse-quendam? Resp. Duplicem esse pulchritudinem, unam animi, alteram corporis, illam animi esse summe ne-cessariam, quae nihil aliud est, teste Socrate, quam virtus in animo, nam quatenus actiones per virtute perficiunt animum, & maxime voluntatem dicuntur boni, quatenus delectant voluntatem & appetitum, dicuntur pulchrae, ipsarumque perfectio est bonitas & delectatio, ex quibus duobus oritur illa voluptas practica seu conscientia recta ex recte cogitatis dictis & factis. At pulchritudinem corporis non esse ex bonis illis secundariis, quae ad felicitatem assequendam sunt necessaria, hinc patet. 1. quia cum felicitas moralis sit actio animae rationalis, & iis indigeat maxime instrumentis, quae rationi parent, quaeque a recta ratione reguntur, sequitur pulchritudinem corporis non esse ejusmodi instrumentum, quia non unu acquiritur, cum a naturali dispositione corporis seu a complexione procedat, nec ratione regitur, quia non est instrumentum corporis, sed qualitas inhaerens instrumentis corporeis, ut ex definitione patet. 2. Aristoteles enumeratis proprietatibus & partibus felicitatis 1 Rhet. 5. nihil pene omiserit, quod ad felicitatem necessarium sit, nullam tamen facit pulchritudinis corporeae mentionem.
units.tr: Question 11: Is one who is sick endowed with true happiness, since he cannot act according to virtue for lack of that secondary good, namely health, which Aristotle prefers to riches, and which, because it brings a greater contentment of mind, is more desirable? Answer: A short sickness does not take away happiness but interrupts it; a longer one makes it so languish that scarcely one or another degree of happiness appears. For as Aristotle says in 7 Polit. ch. 13, a good man could indeed use poverty, diseases and other misfortunes well, but happiness consists in the contrary. Beauty also is required for happiness, as an appendix of health, and consists in two things: (1) in the proper stature, or proportion, of the whole body and of its individual members; (2) in the sweetness and loveliness of colour. Whence also Augustine, book 2 de civitate Dei, ch. 19, says that beauty is the harmony of parts together with sweetness of colour. This seems taken from Cicero, 2 Offic. and 3 Tusc. Quaest., and from Scaliger, Exercitationes 307, sect. 5 and 27, and book 4 de re Poetica, ch. 1, where it is defined as a variety compounded from the tempering of qualities and from the position and agreement of parts. On this see Pic. gradu 8, de instrumentis virtutum, ch. 36. But it may rightly be asked whether this beauty is necessary for attaining happiness. Answer: There are two kinds of beauty, one of the soul and the other of the body. The beauty of the soul is highly necessary, and it is nothing other, as Socrates testifies, than virtue in the soul. For insofar as actions perfected through virtue perfect the soul, and especially the will, they are called good; insofar as they delight the will and the appetite, they are called beautiful. Their perfection is goodness and delight, and from these two arises that practical pleasure, or right conscience, from rightly thought words and deeds. But that bodily beauty is not among those secondary goods which are necessary for attaining happiness is plain from this: (1) since moral happiness is an action of the rational soul, and it especially needs those instruments which obey reason and are governed by right reason, it follows that bodily beauty is not such an instrument. It is not acquired by will, since it proceeds from the natural disposition of the body or complexion, and it is not governed by reason, since it is not an instrument of the body but a quality inhering in bodily instruments, as is clear from its definition. (2) Aristotle, having enumerated the properties and parts of happiness in 1 Rhet. 5., omitted almost nothing necessary to happiness, yet makes no mention of bodily beauty.

units.la: §. Si esset necessarium instrumentum, tunc sic essent capaciores felicitatis ipsis viris, illæ enim for- ma exteriore viris longè excellunt, ut constat, & tamen Aristoteles II.3. Pol. negat habere libertatem in actionibus suis, propterea quod viris subjectæ sint. 4. Experientia docet, eos, qui hac forma exteriore præditi sunt, maximè vitiis esse deditos, ut in Absolomo & Paride historiæ docent, adeo ut Seneca Tragicus exclamet in Hippolito: O vita fallax abditos sensus geris animoq; pulchram turpibus faciem induis. Contra Herculi & aliis heroibus corporis elegantiam non ascribunt Poetæ, imò nec ipsi virtuti formam istam externam concedunt, sed manus callosas, corpus strigosum, curis & macie confectum, quibus significant, ad virtutem assiduo labore & cura pervenien- dum esse. 5. Si coloris suavitas esset necessaria ad felicitatem, tunc alia esset ratio apud Æthiopas, quibus niger perplacet color, alia apud Indos, quibus subcinericius, alia apud Ægyptiós, quib. subfuscus, alia apud Eropos, quibus albus rubro permixtus inprimis gratus esse solet; at verò si de tali pulchritudine intelligatur, qualem innuit Aristot. I.Rhetor. 5. nempe corporis in omni ætate, juvenili, senili, vigorem & promtitudinem ad res bene gerendas, talem puto esse necessariam, secus verò illam, quę in linearum dispositione & coloris suavitate consistit, minimè. At objicitur ex Plat. in Menone: Pulchritudinem nos reddere conformes Deo, quippe in Deo sunt bonitas & pulchritudo, ita ut una sine altera esse non possit, & bonitas, ut inquit idem, est origo, quæ omnia dulcissimè nectat tanquam essentia & finis ex sententia Platonis, quæ omnia procreat & perficit: Pulchritudo tanquam splendor refulgens, admiadmirationem, amorem & desiderium excitat, & Socrates, ut est apud Laërt. lib. 2. in vita ipsius, non nisi pulcherrimos ad Philosophiæ studium admittebat, & Theologi quidam consideratā corporis humani fabrica dixerunt, secundario Dei imaginem latere in pulchritudine corporis humani, unde necessaria videtur ista corporis pulchritudo ad felicitatem, utpote sine qua ad bonum spirituale ascendere nequimus? Respon. Si de pulchritudine quidem corporis ille locus Platonis intelligeretur, sequeretur Deum habere corpus, quod vero ad illud Socratis de sola animi forma intelligendum erit, at illis Theologis opponimus D. Paulum, qui ad Eph. 4. v. 24. imaginem Dei longè aliter exponit. 2. Cum objicitur à Jurecon-sultis, deformitatem corporis, quæ opponitur pulchritudini, declarare animi deformitatem, hoc falsum esse vel experientia docet, & exempla veterum Aesopi, Ulyssis, de quo Poëta sic canit:
units.tr: §. If it were a necessary instrument, then women would be more capable of happiness than men, since they far surpass men in outward form, as is plain. Yet Aristotle (Pol. 2.3) denies that women have freedom in their actions, because they are subject to men. 4. Experience teaches that those who are endowed with this outward form are most given over to vices, as the histories of Absalom and Paris show, so that Seneca the Tragedian exclaims in the Hippolytus: O deceitful life, you hide your thoughts and clothe a fair face over a foul mind. On the contrary, the poets do not ascribe bodily elegance to Hercules and the other heroes. Indeed they do not even grant this outward form to virtue itself, but give them calloused hands and a lean body, worn down by cares and hardship, by which they signify that virtue is to be reached through constant labour and care. 5. If sweetness of colour were necessary to happiness, there would be one reckoning among the Ethiopians, to whom black is most pleasing; another among the Indians, to whom ash-grey is pleasing; another among the Egyptians, to whom dusky is pleasing; and another among the Europeans, to whom white mixed with red is especially agreeable. But if it is understood of such beauty as Aristotle hints at in Rhet. 1.5, namely the body's vigour and readiness for doing things well at every age, whether youthful or aged, I think that is necessary; but the beauty that consists in the arrangement of lines and sweetness of colour is by no means necessary. But it is objected from Plato in the Meno: that beauty makes us conformed to God, since in God there are goodness and beauty, so that the one cannot exist without the other; and goodness, as the same author says, is the origin which most sweetly binds all things together, as essence and end, according to Plato's view, which produces and perfects all things; beauty, like a shining splendour, excites admiration, love and desire. Socrates too, as is reported in Laertius, book 2, in his life, admitted to the study of philosophy only the most beautiful. And certain theologians, considering the structure of the human body, have said that the image of God lies secondarily in the beauty of the human body; whence this bodily beauty seems necessary to happiness, since without it we cannot ascend to spiritual good? Answer: If that passage of Plato were understood of bodily beauty, it would follow that God has a body. The saying of Socrates must be understood of the beauty of the soul alone. Against those theologians we set St Paul, who in Eph. 4:24 explains the image of God quite differently. 2. When the jurists object that bodily deformity, which is opposed to beauty, declares deformity of the soul, experience itself teaches that this is false; and so do the examples of the ancients, such as Aesop and Ulysses, of whom the poet sings thus:

units.la: Non formosus erat, sed erat facundus Ulysses, nam ut pulcherrime Seneca epistola 82. ait, Pulchritudine animi corpus ornatur. & Bernhard. sermone 25. Est quaedam corporis nigredo felix, quae conjunctum habet animi candorem.
units.tr: Ulysses was not handsome, but he was eloquent, for, as Seneca says most beautifully in epistle 82, the body is adorned by the beauty of the soul. And Bernard in sermon 25: There is a certain happy blackness of body which has joined with it the whiteness of the soul.

units.la: Sequuntur jam externa bona, quæ ad felicitatem necessario requiruntur, cujusmodi sunt divitiæ, quæ vocantur bona possessionis, & honor, qui dicitur bonum dignitatis & meriti. De divitiis primò agendum erit, quæ iis tanquam mediis necessariis utuntur homines, tam ad honorem, quam ad felicitatem assequendam, esse vero divitias ad felicitatem necessarias hinc patet, quia, ut ait Alexand. Aphrod. lib. 1. de anima, virtus sit tanquam opifex felicitatis, & quia omnia
units.tr: There follow now the external goods which are necessarily required for happiness, such as riches, which are called goods of possession, and honour, which is called the good of dignity and merit. We must treat of riches first, since men use them as necessary means both to attain honour and to attain happiness. That riches are necessary to happiness is clear from this: as Alexander of Aphrodisias says in book 1 of On the Soul, virtue is as it were the craftsman of happiness, and because all

units.la: omnis opifex necessario eget instrumentis, nec sibi est satis, sic felicitas quoque suis egebit instrumentis, & Philosophus 1. Nicom. 9. inquit, impossibile est aut non facile honeste agere, cui opes desunt. Multa enim fiunt tanquam per instrumenta, & constat liberalitatem & munificentiam absque his bonis, quæ vocantur divitiæ exercere non posse. Quis enim felicem putabit tenm, qui semper necessarius indigeat, naturam non matrem, sed novercam habeat, & fortunam tam aduersam, ut nullam probam & præclaram actionem edere possit, & nunquam secum aut cum aliis ad votum vixerit, nam cum homo vivat vitam animo & corpori communem & ratione corporis actionumque animi multis egeat, ut optime se habeat, & ad felicitatem contendat, necesse est, ut felici conspiratione in eo omnia connectantur, quæ splendori & perfectioni vitæ conducere valent, & præclare Philosophus 7. Pol. cap. 1. cum tria sint bonorum genera, nempe externa, corporis, & animi, sta omnia ad felicitatem requiruntur. Cæterum cum ex his patet, necessarias opes esse ad felicitatis assecutionem, quærendum erit, in quibus verus divitiarum modus consistat. Aristoteles 1. Rhetor. c. 1. enumeratis divitiarum partibus, tandem concludit elegantèr, omnino divitiarum modus in usu, non in possessione consistit. Iuxta illud Pt ætæ:
units.tr: every craftsman necessarily needs instruments and is not sufficient unto himself, so happiness too will need its instruments. The Philosopher says in Nic. 1.9: It is impossible, or at least not easy, to act honourably when resources are lacking. For many things are done as if through instruments, and it is plain that liberality and munificence cannot be exercised without those goods which are called riches. For who would think him happy who always lacks necessities, who has nature as a stepmother rather than a mother, and fortune so adverse that he can produce no upright and excellent action, and who has never lived according to his wish, either with himself or with others? Since a man lives a life shared by soul and body, and needs many things for the body's good condition and for the actions of the soul, if he is to be in the best state and strive towards happiness, it is necessary that all the things which can contribute to the brilliance and perfection of life be joined in him in happy harmony. The Philosopher says admirably in Pol. 7.1 that since there are three kinds of goods, namely external, of the body, and of the soul, all of these are required for happiness. Moreover, since it is clear from this that wealth is necessary for attaining happiness, we must inquire in what the true measure of riches consists. Aristotle, Rhet. 1.1, after enumerating the parts of riches, finally concludes elegantly that the measure of riches consists entirely in use, not in possession. To this accords the verse of a poet:

units.la: Quo mihi fortuna si non conceditur uti.
units.tr: What is fortune to me, if I am not allowed to use it?

units.la: Quo innuitur divitias per se non esse ad felicitatem necessarias, nisi in usum deducantur, & actus sint instrumenta virtutis, & Cic. lib. 1. Acad. quæst. scribit, hanc fuisse Academicorum sententiam, quod in sola virtute virtute posita esset beatitudo, sed non esset perfecta, nisi corporis & externa accedant bona & cætera ad virtutis usum pertinentia. quod vero Aristoteles 1. Nicomach. 1. Oeconomiæ finem ponat divitias, quia ista divitiarum partes sunt instrumenta œconomiæ necessaria, ut sine iis externus ille finis haberi non possit, quippe quod singula familiæ membra, ut aptiora sint Reipubl. efficiant. Vide plura ad cap. 1. Cæterum hic oritur gravis controversia inter Stoicos & Peripateticos de qua Pic. gradu 10. Stoici sic impugnant Peripateticorum opinionem, divitias ad felicitatem necessarias esse, distantium hoc modo; Summum bonum, ut describitur a Peripatetica, est firmum & stabile quid. Ergo cum rebus mutationi & inconstantiæ obnoxiis necessitudinis vinculo connecti non poterit. Divitiæ enim cum sint munera fortunæ, sunt fluxa & fragiles: nam ut Pasibus ambiguis fortuna volubilis errat, sic illæ etiam, cujus sunt munera? Resp. Felicitatem duobus modis considerari, primario & sic non eget, secundario & sic eget, vel etiam ratione sui & ratione subjecti cui inest. 2. Objectio, cum homo præelectionis & virtutis sua munere sit faber sua fortunæ, & cum libere feratur ad suum illud bonum, quod appetit, necessaria non sunt, quæ in ejus manibus non sunt posita, cujusmodi sunt natura & fortunæ munera? Resp. Hoc falsum esse experientia docet. 3. Si felicitas actio sit proba, ut sensit Aristot. secundum virtutem, quæ melior actio moralis censeri potest, quæ mentem supra corpus elevare, munera naturæ & fortunæ conculcare? Resp. Negligere ea media, quæ virtuti inserviunt in externum objectum exercendæ nullo modo actio Mor. proba censeri potest. 4. lib. Plotin. Ennead. lib. 4. cap. 7. cap.7. adversus Aristotelem, inquit, dicit Aristoteles adversitates non quaslibet, sed magnas mutare felicitatem, ut de Priamo lib.1. refert cap.10. at quidnam erit in rebus humanis adeo magnum, quod ab eo despici non queat, qui ad altiora omnia se extendit, nempe ad summam actionum, quae ab homine fieri possunt, perfectionem, idem quoq; Plato in Menaxano repetit, & ex illo Ciceronis 5.Tuscul. quaest. quod confirmatur exemplo Socratis, qui morti adjudicatus veneno hilariter, quasi per jocum sumto, meditabatur fabulas, & amicis id agre ferentibus amice insultabat? Resp. Graves ejusmodi casus non mutare naturam felicitatis, sed statum subjectum, ut qui jam exercere virtutem vellet, ita ac vellet, posset. 7. Divitiarum contemtus commendat, nam Seneca epistola 63. ad Lucil. inquit, Brevissima ad divitias per contemtum divitiarum est via, & Crates Thebanus laudatur, quod Athenas ad Philosophiam discendam profecturus, magnam auri vim abjecerit, existimans se non posse aurum, & virtutes simul posse dere, & Diogenes vocat paupertatem αὐτοδίδακτον ἐπιτήδευμα πρὸς τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, id est, sponte doctum studium ad Philosophiam, sed contra esse medium necessarium experientia docet, verum enim illud Poetae: Haud facile emergunt, quorum virtutibus obstat, Res angusta domi.
units.tr: By this it is implied that riches are not in themselves necessary to happiness, unless they are brought into use and their actions become the instruments of virtue. Cicero, in book 1 of the Academic Questions, writes that this was the opinion of the Academics: that happiness lay in virtue alone, but it would not be perfect unless bodily and external goods and the rest pertaining to the use of virtue were added. As for Aristotle, Nic. 1.1, who sets riches as the end of household management, this is because those parts of riches are necessary instruments of household management, so that without them that external end cannot be had, since each member of the household is made more fit for the commonwealth. See more at chapter 1. Moreover, a grave controversy arises here between the Stoics and the Peripatetics, on which see Pic. gradu 10. The Stoics attack the Peripatetic opinion that riches are necessary to happiness in this way: The highest good, as the Peripatetics describe it, is something firm and stable. Therefore it cannot be bound by the chain of connection to things subject to change and inconstancy. For riches, since they are gifts of fortune, are fleeting and fragile; for as fortune, wandering on uncertain steps, is fickle, so those things too, of which she is the giver? Answer: Happiness may be considered in two ways: primarily, and thus it does not need riches; secondarily, and thus it does need them, either by reason of itself or by reason of the subject in which it inheres. 2. Objection: since man, by his choice and virtue, is the maker of his own fortune, and since he is freely borne towards the good that he desires, those things are not necessary which are not placed in his hands, such as nature and the gifts of fortune? Answer: Experience teaches that this is false. 3. If happiness is a proper action according to virtue, as Aristotle thought, what better moral action can be deemed one that lifts the mind above the body and tramples under foot the gifts of nature and fortune? Answer: To neglect those means which serve virtue, when virtue is to be exercised upon an external object, can in no way be deemed a proper moral action. 4. Plotinus, Ennead 4, book 7, against Aristotle, says: Aristotle holds that not just any adversities, but great ones, change happiness, as he reports of Priam in book 1, ch. 10. But what in human affairs will be so great that it cannot be despised by one who extends himself to higher things, namely to the highest perfection of the actions that man can perform? Plato repeats the same in the Menexenus, and from that of Cicero in Tusculan Questions 5, which is confirmed by the example of Socrates, who, condemned to death, drank the poison cheerfully, as if taken in jest, and meditated fables, and mockingly insulted his friends who took it hard? Answer: Such grave cases do not change the nature of happiness, but only the subject's state; so that one who wished to exercise virtue could do so as he wished. 7. The contempt of riches is commended. For Seneca, in epistle 63 to Lucilius, says: The shortest way to riches is through contempt of riches. And Crates the Theban is praised because, setting out for Athens to learn philosophy, he cast away a great quantity of gold, thinking that he could not possess gold and virtues at the same time. Diogenes calls poverty an autodidacton epitedeuma pros ten philosophian [αὐτοδίδακτον ἐπιτήδευμα πρὸς τὴν φιλοσοφίαν], that is, a self-taught pursuit for philosophy. But experience teaches that, on the contrary, it is a necessary means, for that saying of the poet is true: Those whose virtues are hindered by a narrow household seldom rise.

units.la: Nam contemtus divitiarum & paupertas per accidens tantum non per se sunt causa boni, divitias vero esse bonas hinc patet, quia sunt dona Dei, Prover. 10. v.22. Benedictio Domini divites facit: & plane exempla piorum in Scriptura, ut Abrahami, Jacobi, Salomonis, & aliorum id evincunt. Hacte-
units.tr: For contempt of riches and poverty are only incidental, not in themselves, causes of good. That riches are good is clear from this, that they are gifts of God: Prov. 10. v.22. The blessing of the Lord maketh rich, and the examples of pious people in Scripture, such as Abraham, Jacob, Solomon, and others, plainly prove it. So far-

units.la: Hactenus de bonis fortuna & natura, sequuntur bona dignitatis, quæ ideò ultimo loco rejiciuntur, propterea quod à virtute fluant, & sicut actiones virtutis absque bonis naturæ & fortunæ, exerceri nequeunt, sic neq; bona ista dignitatis, quæ à virtute proveniunt, & quia inter ista bona dignitatis præcipuam locum sibi vendicat Honor, ideò sub vulgata loquendi consuetudine sub nomine honoris comprehenduntur, adeò, ut ab Arist.4.Nicomach.c.7. honor vocetur bonorum externorum maximum quid. Unde honoris vocabulum sumitur interdum generaliter, interdum specialiter. Generaliter pro qualibet dignitate personæ ex virtute proveniente, quam Scalig. exerc. 317.sect.3. vocat conditionem virtutis in persona, & sic honor comprehedit sub se honorem proprie dictum, auctoritatem, gloriam, laudem, & bonam famam. Specialiter vel stricte pro gradu eminenti in virtute qualibet, vel in gradu excellenti in virtute Theologica aut bellica, & sic vocatur Nobilitas. Honor prout stricte sumitur in gradu eminente virtutis, duobus modis consideratur, vel pro merito & effectu virtutis, quo virtus per se honore digna censetur, etsi nemo illi istum honorem tribuat, imò etsi ignominia notetur, & hic honor vocatur internus seu honor meriti profluens ab æstimatione ipsius rei. 2. Sumitur pro signo externo, quo aliquis propter virtutem honore dignus censetur aut honoratur. Prior ista honoris significatio, quia à virtute immediate profluit, non pertinet ad hunc locum, sed tunc innotescit, cum virtutes ipsæ declarantur. At verò in posteriore significatione hic à nobis sumi-tur, tur, quatenus dicitur bonum necessarium, quod excitet homines ad virtutem & actiones probas tanquam externum signum impellens. Ex ista honoris distinctione facile intelligitur illud axioma Arist. 1. Nic. c. 4. Honor est magis in honorante quam in honorato. Quod verum est, si de honore signi hic sumatur, non vero de honore meriti, nam honor meriti est in ipso honorato, honor signi in honorante, qui externum illud signum exhibet. Definitur honor, signum, quo testamur affectum nostrum in aliquem propter virtutem, ubi consideranda veniunt haec tria, Efficiens, finalis, & impellens. Efficiens est ille, qui externum hoc signum exhibet seu vultu seu gestu aliquo externo. Finalis causa, cui, est homo aliquis virtute praeditus: Impellens vero est ipsa virtus, quae hoc habet proprium, quae admirationem, amorem & desiderium sui hominum animis injiciat, unde & vultum & externam istam reverentiam excitat. Cum teste Aristot. 2 mag moral. tria sint honorabilia, nimirum Deus (scil. numen) tanquam principium, animus tanquam optimum quid in homine, & demum virtus per quam homo probus efficitur, quod & totidem fere verbis refert Plato 5. de leg. primum honor debetur Deo, secundum animae, tertius virtuti, unde virtuti aut ipsi homini propter virtutem deferendum esse constat. Caeterum hic quaeri potest, cui virtuti honor hic debeatur, virtuti in genere, an alicui tantum speciali? Arist. quidem cap. 9. lib. 8. de moribus sensit honore tantum esse deferendum iis, qui meritis in Remp. clare cunt. Et 1. Rhet. c. 5. definit honorem signum beneficae opinionis, quia eiusmodi homines, qui beneficia in Remp. conferunt, praeclaram ram virtutis suæ apud homines æstimationem concitat, & paulò post addit Philosoph. Honoramus verò maximè qui vel benefecerunt, vel benefacere possunt, quales sunt magnatum filii, qui spem virtutum patriarum omnibus injiciunt. Et si verò virtutes publicæ, quæ studio iuvandæ Remp. fiunt, honore primario dignæ sint, secundario tamen etiam honor defertur hominibus privatam vitam agentibus, qui imitatione & exemplo ad effectum & reverentiam sui invitant.
units.tr: So far of the goods of fortune and nature. There follow the goods of dignity, which are placed last for this reason: they flow from virtue, and just as the actions of virtue cannot be exercised without the goods of nature and fortune, so neither can these goods of dignity, which proceed from virtue. Because Honour claims the chief place among these goods of dignity, they are commonly comprised under the name of honour, so much so that Aristotle (Nic. 4, c. 7) calls honour the greatest of external goods. Hence the word honour is sometimes taken generally, sometimes specially. Generally, it means any dignity of a person arising from virtue, which Scaliger (Exerc. 317, sect. 3) calls the condition of virtue in a person; and in this sense honour comprises under itself honour properly so called, authority, glory, praise, and good name. Specially, or strictly, it means an eminent degree in any virtue, or an excellent degree in theological or military virtue, and in this sense it is called Nobility. Honour, as taken strictly for an eminent degree of virtue, is considered in two ways: either as the merit and effect of virtue, by which virtue is judged worthy of honour in itself, even if no one bestows that honour on it, and even if it is marked with disgrace; and this honour is called internal, or the honour of merit, flowing from the esteem of the thing itself. Second, it is taken for the external sign by which someone is judged, or is honoured, as worthy of honour on account of virtue. The former meaning of honour, since it flows immediately from virtue, does not belong to this place, but becomes known when the virtues themselves are declared. In the latter sense, however, it is taken here by us, insofar as it is called a necessary good, which stirs men to virtue and to upright actions, impelling them like an external sign. From this distinction of honour is easily understood that axiom of Aristotle (Nic. 1, c. 4): Honour is more in the one who honours than in the one honoured. This is true if honour is taken here as the honour of the sign, not the honour of merit; for the honour of merit is in the one honoured, the honour of the sign in the one who honours and displays that external sign. Honour is defined as a sign by which we testify our affection toward someone on account of virtue, where three things must be considered: Efficient, final, and impelling. Efficient is the one who displays this external sign, by countenance or some external gesture. The final cause is the person endowed with virtue. The impelling cause is virtue itself, which has this peculiar property, that it instils admiration, love, and desire of itself into men's minds, and so also excites that countenance and that outward reverence. Since, as Aristotle testifies (Mag. Moral. 2), there are three things worthy of honour, namely God (the deity) as the principle, the soul as the best thing in man, and finally virtue, through which a man becomes upright, and Plato (De leg. 5) reports almost the same in nearly the same words: honour is first due to God, second to the soul, third to virtue; hence it is clear that honour must be paid to virtue, or to the man himself on account of virtue. Moreover, here one may ask: to which virtue is this honour due, virtue in general, or only some special virtue? Aristotle indeed (De mor. 8, c. 9) thought that honour is to be paid only to those who shine in the commonwealth by their merits. And in Rhet. 1, c. 5 he defines honour as a sign of beneficent opinion, because men who confer benefits on the commonwealth win for their virtue a distinguished esteem among men; and a little later the Philosopher adds: We honour most those who have either done good or are able to do good, such as the sons of great men, who give everyone hope of their fathers' virtues. And if public virtues, which are practised for the sake of helping the commonwealth, are worthy of honour in the first place, nevertheless honour is also paid in a secondary way to men who lead a private life, who by imitation and example invite others to effort and reverence.

units.la: Quæritur & hoc, an honorans sit præstantior honorato? Baptista Possivinus in lib. de honore c. 7. dicit, honorantem planè esse præstantiorem honorato, tum quia agens est præstantior patiente, tum quia maiore voluptate fruitur in ista actione honorans, quam honoratus. Repugnat illi Gualandus, & contrariam tuetur sententiam lib. 12 c. 14. in methodo societatis civilis, & 1. respondet ad illud: Agens est præstantior honorante, hoc tantum esse verum, quæ actionis suæ causam non habet impellente à patiente; at hic contrarium est. 2. Quod dicatur honorante maiore frui voluptate, hoc falsum esse & potius competere honorato, qui benefecerit, & cum actiones suas rectè successisse, & in bonam partem acceptas esse videt, hinc summopere gaudet: quemadmodum creditor debito persoluto à debitore maiori fruitur gaudio, quod jam sit ditior, & tantum addiderit bonis suis. Honoratus verò est veluti creditor, qui ab honorante propter virtutem sibi inexistentem honorem istum veluti debitum jure suo exigit, unde quod honoratus & causam honorandi in se habeat, & honoranti eam concedat, præstantiorem esse honoratum honorante concludit. Honor in latitudine sua recipit gradus, qui partim dependent à diversitate præmiorum, quæ virtutem insequuntur, partim à diversa conditione eorum, quibus honos tribuitur, ut alius tribuitur Regibus, Magnatibus, alius inferioris conditionis hominibus, partim à diversa qualitate & quantitate eorum, quæ honoris loco tribuuntur, cuiusmodi sunt, munera, statuæ, monumenta, sepulturæ & eiusmodi multa, de quibus Philos. 1. Rhet. c 5. Si honor consideretur in gradu virtutis eminente, potestate, & potentia armata, dicitur Auctoritas, quæ nihil aliud est quàm dignitas quædam cum reverentia & affectu conjuncta, promptitudinem & lubentiâ exigens parendi & præstandi, quod persona armata hac auctoritate placet. Nam cum virtus hoc habeat, ut ad reverentiam sui homines excitet, occasionem etiam præbet, ut homini virtute insigni præditio potestatem & jus quoddam deferant, quo summæ rerum recte præesse possit. Unde auctoritas maximè ii competit, qui eminentia virtutis cum potestate præditi sunt, ut sunt, qui Magistratu aut munere aliquo in Repub. funguntur. Cæterum dubitari hic potest, an tantum auctoritas ii competat, qui munere publico funguntur, nam Arist. 7. de moribus dicit: Auctoritate instructum esse patrem in liberos, & totam familiam, & ratio hoc ipsum comprobat, cum tamen publico nullo munere fungatur? Et Resp. Patrem eadem auctoritate frui in liberos & totam familiam, qua Magistratus in populum aut Rempub. non tantum ista auctoritas procedit à virtute patris, quæ usu & consuetudine acquiritur, sed ab institu&tu quodam naturali. Nam jus naturæ, ut parentes docuit liberos educare & conseruare, sic etiam liberis hoc indidit, ut pro istis meritis jus omne & obsequium parentibus præbeant.2. Objicitur à JCtis auctoritatem competere cuilibet, cujuscunq; conditionis sit etiã nulla virtute prædito? Et Resp. Nomen auctoritatis esse multiplex, interdum enim sumitur pro sententia aut dicto alicujus viri clari, ut autoritas Aristotelis, &c. interdum pro potestate & jure, quod quis habet in bona sua propria, ut ff. de verb. fig. l. 9. Titius auctoritatem in fundum suum habet & jus & potestatem: interdum pro periculi præstatione & evictione ut apud Paulum 2. sent. l. 17. Si venditor eius rei, quam vendidit, dominus non sit precio accepto, auctoritatis manet obnoxius, 1. evictionis. Et istæ sunt latissimæ significationes auctoritatis: proprie tamen iis competit, ut diximus, qui in gradu virtutis eminenti potentia armati sunt. Honor etiam in virtute excellenti consideratur, ut ad rerum gestarum magnitudinem referatur, & sic à multis alicui tribuitur, & proprio nomine vocatur Gloria, quam Aristot. 1. Rhet. c. 5. sic definit: Gloria est, quæ ab omnibus bonis existimatur habere tale aliquid, quod expetunt aut omnes, aut multi, aut prudentes. Et Cic. 3. Tusc. ad eundem fere modum describit: Gloria est consentiens laus bonorum aut eorum unio de virtute recte judicantium. Ab honore proprie sic dicto differt, quod honor absq; signo esse nequeat, gloria vero potest. 2. Gloria cuilibet virtuti competit excellenti seu præteritæ, seu futuræ seu etiam præsenti, honor tantum præsenti: & 3. ab aliquo singulari honor deferri potest, gloria vero non, nisi
units.tr: This too is asked: is the one who honours more excellent than the one honoured? Battista Possevino (in the book On Honour, c. 7) says that the one who honours is plainly more excellent than the one honoured, both because the agent is more excellent than the patient, and because the one who honours enjoys greater pleasure in that action than the one honoured. Gualandi opposes him and defends the contrary opinion (Book 12, c. 14, in the Method of Civil Society), and first answers that the saying, the agent is more excellent than the one who honours, is true only where the cause of his action does not come from the one who is affected; but here it is the contrary. Second, as to the claim that the one who honours enjoys greater pleasure, this is false, and it rather belongs to the one honoured, who has done good, and who sees that his actions have turned out rightly and been taken in good part, and therefore rejoices greatly; just as a creditor, once the debt has been paid by the debtor, enjoys greater joy because he is now richer and has added to his goods. The one honoured, however, is like a creditor who, on account of virtue that inheres in him, demands that honour from the one who honours as a debt due by his right; hence, since the one honoured both has the cause of being honoured in himself and grants it to the one who honours, Gualandi concludes that the one honoured is more excellent than the one who honours. Honour, in its breadth, admits of degrees, which depend partly on the diversity of the rewards that follow virtue, partly on the diverse condition of those to whom honour is paid (honour is paid one way to kings and magnates, another to men of lower condition), and partly on the diverse quality and quantity of those things which are given in place of honour, such as gifts, statues, monuments, burials, and many things of this kind, on which the Philosopher (Rhet. 1, c. 5) speaks. If honour is considered in the eminent degree of virtue, joined with power and armed might, it is called Authority, which is nothing other than a certain dignity joined with reverence and affection, demanding a readiness and willingness to obey and to perform what is commanded, because a person armed with this authority pleases. For since virtue has this property, that it stirs men to reverence for itself, it also gives occasion for men to confer on a man distinguished by virtue a certain power and right by which he may rightly preside over the highest affairs. Hence authority belongs most of all to those who are endowed with power together with the eminence of virtue, such as those who discharge a magistracy or some office in the commonwealth. Yet here it may be doubted whether authority belongs only to those who discharge a public office, for Aristotle (De mor. 7) says: A father is invested with authority over his children and his whole household, and reason itself proves this, although he holds no public office. And the answer is that a father enjoys the same authority over his children and his whole household as the magistrate has over the people or the commonwealth; and this authority does not proceed merely from the father's virtue, which is acquired by use and custom, but from a certain natural institution. For the law of nature, as it taught parents to bring up and preserve their children, so it also implanted in children this, that for such services they should show all right and obedience to their parents. Second, the jurists object that authority belongs to anyone whatsoever of whatever condition, even one endowed with no virtue? And the answer is that the name of authority is manifold: sometimes it is taken for the opinion or saying of some famous man, as the authority of Aristotle, etc.; sometimes for the power and right which someone has over his own goods, as in the Digest, de verb. sig., law 9: Titius has authority and right and power over his own estate; sometimes for the guarantee of danger and eviction, as in Paul, Sent. 2, law 17: if the seller of a thing he has sold is not its owner, having received the price, he remains liable to eviction (1. evictionis). And these are the widest senses of authority; properly, however, as we have said, it belongs to those who, in an eminent degree of virtue, are armed with power. Honour is also considered in excellent virtue, as it is related to the greatness of deeds done, and thus is given to someone by many, and is called by its proper name Glory, which Aristotle (Rhet. 1, c. 5) defines thus: Glory is what is judged by all good men to have some such quality as all, or many, or the wise, desire. And Cicero (Tusc. 3) describes it in nearly the same way: Glory is the agreeing praise of good men, or of those who judge rightly about virtue. It differs from honour properly so called in that honour cannot exist without a sign, but glory can. Second, glory belongs to any virtue that is excellent, whether past, future, or even present; honour only to the present. And third, honour can be paid by a single person, but glory cannot, unless it comes from the consent of many good men, as Seneca testifies (Epist. 103).

units.la: F à consensu multorum & bonorum, teste Seneca Epist. 103. Etsi vero gloria propriè Deo competat, tribuitur etiam modo quodam hominibus, si duae iltæ insint conditiones: nempè ut persona sit virtute excellenti praedita, & 2. benefica facultate seu studio juvandi genus humanum: unde raris & perpaucis tantum competit. Ad honorem generaliter considerantur referuntur etiā laus & bona fama, quæ à Francisco Petr. vocantur ala virtutis, quod sicut volucres alarum remigio in sublime feruntur, sic etiam homines laudis & bonæ famæ stimulis ad virtutem exercendam feruntur, & ad actiones probas ulterius edendas. Dicitur laus ἔπαινος τῶν λαῶν, à populis, quod sit populi consensus de aliquo rectè loquentis & tribuitur homini propter virtutem quamlibet, quia ut ait Poeta:
units.tr: It arises from the consent of many good people, as Seneca, Epist. 103 says. Although glory belongs properly to God, it is also given to human beings in a certain way, if these two conditions are present: namely, that the person is endowed with excellent virtue, and, second, has the beneficial ability or zeal to help the human race. For this reason it belongs only to rare and very few people. Under honour in general are also included praise and good reputation, which Francis Petrarch calls the wings of virtue, because just as birds are carried aloft by the beating of their wings, so people are carried by the spurs of praise and good reputation to practise virtue and to perform further upright deeds. Praise is called epainos tōn laōn [ἔπαινος τῶν λαῶν] from the peoples, because it is the agreement of the people speaking rightly about someone, and it is given to a person for any virtue whatever, since, as the poet says:

units.la: Virtus laudata crescit.
units.tr: Praised virtue grows.

units.la: Et sit veluti calcar quoddam, qua excitantur homines ad virtutem. Definitur verò Laus ab Aristot. oratio ostendens magnitudinem virtutis cap. 9. 1. Rhet. In qua definitione latius sumpitur nomen laudis, quàm nunc usurpatur, quatenus nimirum non inferiori tantum, sed cuilibet etiam in quocunque gradu aut genere competit. Nam cum esse Philos. 12. 1. Nic. laus sit propriè virtutum, tanquam mediorum ducentium ad finem, ideò omni virtuti competere necesse est. Improbatur tamen ista definitio à Gualando cap. ult. lib. 13. de societ. civil. tribus his rationibus. 1. Si laus esset oratio, tot essent partes laudis, quot orationis. 2. Oratio recipit magis & minus, si igitur laus esset oratio, sequeretur laudem interdum esse majorem, interdum minorem. 3. Cum virtus sit habitus animi, quo aliquis bene operatur, si ita definiretur laus, nempe oratio ostendens magnitudinem virtutis, sequeretur laudem esse proprium hominis, cujus est proprie virtus; at vero homini non tantum competit laus, sed etiam aliis rebus, quibuscunque insunt qualitates bonae. Ideo ex opinione Gualand: haec erit vera definitio boni, quod est in re qualibet verbis expressa significatio? Sed resp. ad priora duo argumenta, cum laus sit proprie virtutis ore expressa significatio, quot modis institui possit oratio de qualitatibus virtutum, aut qualitate, tot etiam dici possunt partes laudis, tot etiam gradus reciperet. Ad ultimum vero argumentum respon. Laudem tantum proprie tribui hominibus, qui proprie possunt excitari laudis stimulis ad exercitium virtutis & ad perfectionem aliquam virtutis quaerendam: alias vero res omnes improprie laudari cum nihil sua opera addere possint iis qualitatibus, quae inesse praedicantur. Bona fama vero est etiam instrumentum necessarium ad felicitatem, quia, ut inquit Augustinus, lib.1.conf. c.1 ut bene vivas, duo haec sunt necessaria. Conscientia & bona fama. Conscientia propter te & Deum, bona fama propter proximum est necessaria. Sic Bernhardus serm. 17. super Cant. bona fama reddit virtutem illustriorem, & si non vel majorem. Modum acquirendi bonam famam describit Epictetus in suo annulo: Si vis bene audire, bene loqui disce, si bene loqui didicerit, disce etiam bene facere, sic enim bonam famam auro & gemmis preciosiorem acquires.
units.tr: And it is like a sort of spur by which people are roused to virtue. Aristotle defines praise as a speech showing the greatness of virtue, in chapter 9 of the first book of the Rhetoric. In this definition the word praise is taken more broadly than it is now used, since it belongs not only to a superior person but to anyone at any level or kind whatever. For since, according to Aristotle in the twelfth chapter of the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics, praise belongs properly to virtues as means leading to the end, it must belong to every virtue. Yet this definition is rejected by Gualandus in the last chapter of book 13, On Civil Society, on three grounds: (1) if praise were a speech, there would be as many parts of praise as of speech; (2) a speech admits of more and less, so if praise were a speech, it would follow that praise is sometimes greater and sometimes less; (3) since virtue is a habit of the mind by which someone acts well, if praise were defined thus, namely as a speech showing the greatness of virtue, it would follow that praise belongs only to the human being whose proper quality virtue is; but praise belongs not only to a human being but also to other things in which good qualities are present. Hence, on Gualandus's view, this would be the true definition of good: a verbal expression of the significance of any thing whatever? But I reply to the first two arguments: since praise is properly the verbal expression of the significance of virtue, in as many ways as a speech can be framed about the qualities or the quality of virtues, so many parts of praise can be named, and it would admit of as many degrees. To the last argument I reply: praise belongs properly only to human beings, who can properly be stirred by the spurs of praise to the exercise of virtue and to seeking some perfection of virtue; otherwise all things are praised improperly, since they can add nothing by their own work to those qualities which are said to be in them. Good reputation is also a necessary instrument for happiness, because, as Augustine says, Confessions, book 1, chapter 1: "For you to live well, two things are necessary: conscience and good reputation. Conscience is necessary for your own sake and for God's, good reputation for your neighbour's." So Bernard, sermon 17 on the Song of Songs: "A good reputation makes virtue more illustrious, if it does not make it greater." Epictetus in his handbook describes the way of acquiring good reputation: "If you wish to be well spoken of, learn to speak well; if you have learned to speak well, learn also to act well; for thus you will acquire a good reputation, more precious than gold and gems."

units.la: Hactenus de honore generaliter consideravit, sequitur honor consideratus in gradu eminenti virtutis eximiae praesertim bellicae, & dicitur proprie hominis Nobilitas. Nobilitas vero dicitur, quasi Noscibilitas, quod nomen possessoris dignum reddat, ut innotescat. Sumitur tam in malam, quam in bonam partem. Cum in bonam partem, tunc refertur ad splendorem generis, ut in illo Sallust. Catilina nobili genere natus. In malam partem apud Livium, de Cannensi vico Apulia: Nobilis ille clade Rom. locus 1. insigni strage edita ab Hannibale caesis 60. Rom. militibus. De nobilitate ista pauca observabimus, unde promanarit, utrum ex iure gentium, an ex iure civili. 2. quid sit. 3. quotuplex sit. 4. qua vera nobilitas sit. Nam dubitare, an sit, ut quidam faciunt, est non modo animi ignobilis, sed etiam naturae fere coercentis: natura enim quae rerum parens est, ita in rebus lusit, ut alii aliis nobiliore gradu praestent, ut inter quadrupedia leonem nobilitate animae & generositate quadam prae ceteris animalibus finxit: in metallis etiam dignitatem & praestantiam auro & argento super caetera quandam concessit, quae non tantum opinione hominum vana, ut Thomas Morus inquit, sed re ipsa sunt res praestantes. Nam & puritatem & perfectionem affectant, & rubiginem nullam contrahunt. Sic etiam inter pisces Delphinus primas tenet, & inplantis aliae aliis sunt nobilitate superiores, ut experientia ipsa docet, cur igitur hoc humano generi cum homo sit nobilissima creatura, denegari debeat, ratio certa reddi nequit. 2. Dubitant Politici, utrum promanet Nobilitas ejure gentium, an ejure civili, & suas singuli afferunt rationes. Qui enim e jure gengentium promanare dicunt, hanc afferunt rationem: Quod ratio constituit inter omnes gentes tanquam commune illis omnibus, id est de jure gentium: Ratio constituit, &c. Ergo. Maior patet, est enim definitio Jurisgentium, tit.2. lib.1. Instit. Juris §. 5. Alii vero etiam a definitione juris civilis argumentantes, statuunt esse de jure civili hoc modo: Jus civile est, quod quisque, sibi populus constituit, tit.2. ff.3. At quisque populus constituit servandam esse differentiam inter virtute claros & non claros. At reconciliari possunt hac ratione. Si enim Nobilitas consideretur in genere pro existimatione virtutis insignis, tunc est de jure gentium: at si in specie pro existimatione hujus vel illius virtutis, tunc est de iure civili, exempli gratia, Violare legatos, est contra jus gentium, quatenus nimirum legati sacri sunt propter personam domini sui, quam praese ferunt, qui est aut caput Reipubl. aut aliquis excellenti virtute praeditus, quibus propter virtutem in genere honorem omnes gentes tribuunt. At vero, si consideretur virtus hujus vel illius legati, qua posset prodesse vel obesse, si jam violetur ab hoste vel inimico vitae suae, hoc dicitur esse de iure civili.
units.tr: So far he has considered honour in general. There follows honour considered at the eminent level of outstanding virtue, especially military virtue, and this is properly called nobility of a person. Nobility, Nobilitas, is so called as if it were noscibilitas, that is, a quality that makes the possessor worthy of being known. The word is taken in both a bad and a good sense. In a good sense it refers to the splendour of a family, as in Sallust: Catiline, born of noble stock. In a bad sense, in Livy, on the town of Cannae in Apulia: "That noble place, the scene of the Roman disaster, where a great slaughter was made by Hannibal of 60 Roman soldiers." On this nobility we shall make a few observations: (1) whence it arises, whether from the law of nations or from the civil law; (2) what it is; (3) how many kinds there are; (4) what true nobility is. For to doubt whether it exists at all, as some do, is not only the mark of an ignoble mind but also almost of a nature that restrains itself; for nature, the parent of all things, has so arranged things that some excel others in a higher rank: thus among the four-footed animals she has made the lion more noble than the others in spirit and a certain generosity; among metals she has granted gold and silver a certain dignity and pre-eminence over the rest, which are not merely vain in human opinion, as Thomas More says, but are in fact excellent things; for they both aim at purity and perfection and contract no rust. So too among fishes the dolphin holds the first place, and among plants some are more noble than others, as experience itself teaches. Why then should this be denied to the human race, since man is the most noble creature, cannot be given a certain reason. (2) The politicians dispute whether nobility arises from the law of nations or from the civil law, and each advances his own reasons. Those who say it arises from the law of nations give this reason: what reason has established among all nations as common to them all is the law of nations. Reason has established, etc. Therefore. The major premise is plain, for it is the definition of the law of nations, title 2, book 1 of the Institutes, §5. Others, however, reasoning also from the definition of civil law, hold that it belongs to the civil law in this way: civil law is what the people has established for itself, title 2, Digest 3. And each people has established that a distinction be kept between the illustrious in virtue and the non-illustrious. These can be reconciled as follows. If nobility is considered in general, as the esteem of outstanding virtue, then it belongs to the law of nations; but if it is considered in particular, as the esteem of this or that virtue, then it belongs to the civil law. For example, to violate envoys is against the law of nations, insofar as envoys are sacred on account of the person of their lord whom they represent, who is either the head of the commonwealth or someone endowed with excellent virtue, and to such persons all nations give honour in general on account of virtue. But if one considers the virtue of this or that envoy, by which he could benefit or harm, and if he is then violated by an enemy or foe of his life, this is said to belong to the civil law.

units.la: Definitur Nobilitas a variis varie Arist. in lib. de nobilitate citante Stobaeo serm. 84. definit nobilitatem hoc modo: Quod sit facultas alicujus familiae procreandi viros ingenuos ad virtutem faciles, multorum aut ad minimum trium successione confirmata. Recepta tamen definitio haec est: Nobilitas sive dignitas quaedam, quam quis virtute propria & majorum beneficio Principis acquisivit. Ex qua definitione facile elicere est, unde originem riginem traxerit Nobilitas, nempe exvirtute, & saepe virtus consideratur ratione Nobilitatis duobus modis ut fundamentum seu causa efficiens, Fundamentum est tam generale quam speciale. Generale est virtus eximia, quae praeclaris in Rempubl. meritis fulget, aut in totam Rempubl. aut in Reipubl. caput (scilicet Principem), aut in totum populum. Speciale fundamentum est virtus bellica, & praesertim aliquod magnum & memorabile facinus. Est virtus etiam causa nobilitatis efficiens, sed remotior, quia ab ipsa primo constituitur & dicitur nobilitas praesertim a virtute bellica, cui inter omnes actiones humanas summam dignitatem & praestantiam tribuit Arist. 7. Polit. c. 14. & Alciat. de singulari certamine, cap. 30. quod ficeit intelligendum, tum demum interactiones virtutis primas obtinere virtutem bellicam si efferat se per praeclarum aliquod facinus, quod Reip. & hominum societati conducat. Causa efficiens proxima est privilegium & jus a Principe concessum alicui propter virtutem singularem; nam cum Princeps ut pater Reipubl. ita summae rerum praeest, ut totam Rempubl. conservent praemia & poenas, ideo jure quodam auctoritatis suae nobilitatem tanquam virtutis singulare praemium alicui de Repubi. bene merito pro plenitudine auctoritatis suae conferre potest, quod apud diversas gentes diversimode conferebatur, ut videre est ex insignibus & clypeis nobilium familiarum, & apud Romanos quicunque nobilitate donabatur, illi licebat imaginem suam in privatis aedibus servare, teste Sigonio de antiquo jure Romano. Unde quot quis posset numerare imagines, tot habebat maiores nobiles, hinc illud Cicer. Nulla sunt maiorum imagines, quæme vobis commendent. Dividitur Nobilitas in Theologicam, Naturalem, & Politicam. Sed quia Theologica ad actiones pertinet spirituales, & non à virtute humana provenit; & quia Naturalis profluit ab hominis temperie proprie dictæ nobilitatis nomen non merentur. Politica est ea, quam supra definivimus, quæ rursum est triplex: vel propria, quæ à virtute cujusq; propria est, vel est nobilitas maiorum, quæ à longa serie maiorum deducta est, tertia est nobilitas mixta, quæ partim propria virtute, partim maiorum nititur, & hæc dicitur proprie vera Nobilitas, de qua Philosophus f. Polit. cap. 1. Hujusmodi igitur Nobilitas, quæ generis splendore & virtute constat, paucis competit.
