Nobiles enim & bonos vix centum reperias, id est, tales, qui sua virtute & maiorum excellant simul. Et de hac nobilitate Solon referente Stobæo: Pulchrius multo est parari nobilem, quàm creari, sed longè est pulcherrimum & parari & creari nobilem simul. Siquidem nascendi conditioni præclarè faciendi additur corona, plura vide apud Mag. Ang. in tract. de Nobilitate.
units.tr: Nobility is defined variously by various writers. Aristotle, in the book On Nobility, as cited by Stobaeus, sermon 84, defines nobility thus: the capacity of a family to produce men of free birth, apt for virtue, confirmed by the succession of many, or at least three, generations. The accepted definition, however, is this: Nobility, or a certain dignity, which a person has acquired by his own virtue and by the benefit of his ancestors through the prince's favour. From this definition it is easy to infer whence nobility has drawn its origin, namely from virtue, and virtue is often considered, with respect to nobility, in two ways, as foundation or as efficient cause. The foundation is both general and special. The general is outstanding virtue, which shines by distinguished services to the commonwealth, either to the whole commonwealth, or to its head (namely the prince), or to the whole people. The special foundation is military virtue, and especially some great and memorable deed. Virtue is also the efficient cause of nobility, but a more remote one, because nobility is first established by virtue itself, and especially by military virtue, to which Aristotle, in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 14, and Alciato, On Single Combat, chapter 30, assign the highest dignity and pre-eminence among all human actions; this must be understood to mean that military virtue holds the first place among the virtues only when it manifests itself through some distinguished deed that serves the commonwealth and the society of men. The proximate efficient cause is a privilege and right conferred by the prince on someone because of singular virtue; for since the prince, as father of the commonwealth, presides over the highest affairs so that the rewards and punishments preserve the whole commonwealth, therefore by a certain right of his authority he can, as the single reward of virtue, confer nobility on someone who has deserved well of the commonwealth, in the fullness of his authority. This was conferred in different ways among different nations, as can be seen from the insignia and shields of noble families; and among the Romans whoever was granted nobility was allowed to keep his own image in his private house, as Sigonius testifies in On Ancient Roman Law. Hence as many noble ancestors as one could count images, so many nobles he had; hence Cicero's saying: There are no images of ancestors that commend you to me. Nobility is divided into theological, natural, and political. But since theological nobility pertains to spiritual actions and does not arise from human virtue, and since natural nobility flows from a person's temperament, they do not deserve the name of nobility properly so called. Political nobility is that which we defined above, and it is in turn threefold: either proper, which belongs to each person by his own virtue; or the nobility of ancestors, which is derived from a long line of ancestors; or third, mixed nobility, which rests partly on one's own virtue and partly on that of ancestors, and this is properly called true nobility, of which the Philosopher speaks in the Politics, book 4, chapter 1. Such nobility, which consists of the splendour of birth together with virtue, belongs to few. For you would scarcely find a hundred noble and good men, that is, such as excel at once through their own virtue and that of their ancestors. And of this nobility Solon, as reported by Stobaeus, says: It is far finer to be made noble than to be born so, but by far the finest thing is to be both made and born noble. For a crown is added to the condition of birth when one acts nobly. More on this may be seen in Magister Angelus, in his treatise On Nobility.

units.la: De objecto Felicitatis.
units.tr: On the Object of Happiness.

units.la: In omni disciplina operativa, sicut etiam in practica hæc ratio methodi servatur, ut à fine progrediamur ad media, quibus finis præfigitur, & cum membra tria sint præcipua finis, de quo hactenus, objectum, cui finis applicari debet, media per quæ finis objecto applicatur. De medijs posteaagemus ex instituto Philosophi, hic tantum pauca de objecto explicabimus, sequuti rationem Aristotelis, qui, ubi eg ... lib. 1. Eth. de fine, statim ubi præstruit struit viam ad obiectum. Obiectum igitur Ethices consideratur vel indeterminatè vel determinatè. Indeterminatum obiectum est homo agens hanc vitā civilem, qui etsi proprie subiectum sit Ethices, tamen possit diverso respectu dici etiam obiectum. Obiectum vero quatenus præceptis Ethicis excolitur & informatur, ut bene beateque vivat, quatenus vero recipit in se habitam prudentiæ, ut bene vivat, hinc poterit dici subiectum Ethices. Obiectum vero determinatum est duplex: internum, nempe voluntas, quæ dicitur obiectum primarium, quo etiam referri possunt appetitus & locomotiva. Externum obiectum Ethices sunt omnia ea, quæ circa virtutū actiones exercentur & sicut virtutū actiones sunt variæ & multiplices: sic etiā obiectū externū est tale iis competes. Voluntas ergo est primarium obiectum internum, quæ quatenus est proprietas animæ & facultas rationalis quæ res ab intellectu apprehensas & diiudicatas deligit vel avertitur, eatenus spectat ad considerationē Physicam, & de ea agit Arist. l. 3. de anima, c. 10. quatenus verò præceptis moralibus excolitur, & circa eam regendam & gubernandam Ethica versatur, est considerationis Ethicæ. In Ethica traduntur media, quibus voluntas informari & gubernari potest, & quibus bonum morale sibi possit applicare. Etsi verò voluntas primariò fertur ad summum & perfectissimum bonum, nempe divinum, ita ut ad nihil creatū se extendere tantum possit, quippe in quo nemo acquiescit, tamē propter hujus vitæ cōditiones, quam homo agit, dirigitur proximè ad bonum morale quærendum, tum quia ejusmodi mediis acquiritur, ritur, quæ à consuetudine & usu dependent, & proinde à libera voluntate procedunt, tum etiam quia bonum morale excedit voluntatem hominis ad ultimam bonum quærendum. Cæterum cum bonum sit duplex: aliud revera & sua natura bonum, aliud apparens tantum, quod voluntati humanæ male affectæ & dispositæ sub specie boni se offert: ideo duplex erit objectum voluntatis, in quod fertur bonum revera, & bonum apparens, sed bonum revera appetit voluntas & per se & sua natura, 1.2. Polit. Arist. bonum apparens per accidens propter dispositionem male affectam in homine, & hæc opinio comprobatur ab Aristotele lib.3. Eth. cap.4. ubi consilium à voluntate distinguit. At oritur controversia inter Arist. & Platonem, nam Plato (cui adstipulatur etiam inter Latinos Boëtius de consolat. Philos. lib.2. c.7.) dicit, voluntatem vergere tantum per se ad bonum sua natura; nam lib.9. de legib. dicit, tyrannos & improbos non fieri ad malum voluntate sua, cum voluntas sit tantum bonum per se, sed ex opinione quadam prava, quæ repugnat voluntati. Et ratio hujus rei affertur talis, quia voluntas proprie fertur ad id, in quo acquiescit: ut in nullo malo aut in apparenti bono, quod non sit revera bonum, acquiescit, tum quia malum est infinitum, tum quia etiam parit tristitiam & dolorem. Et respond. Voluntatem quidem per se ferri tantum ad bonum & revera bonum, per accidens vero ad malum. Quod vero Plato dicit, tyrannos non ex voluntate male facere, id falsum esse libertas voluntatis convincit, quæ pro suo libitu in quodlibet objectu fertur. At voluntas fertur per se sua natura ad malum. Ergo non tantum per acci- dens. Probatur antecedens experientia quotidia- na, quæ plane ostendit hominem plerunque ad ma- lum ferri, idque suopte ingenio. Et respond. Hoc non esse de natura voluntatis, quà voluntas in se consideratur, sed provenire à depravatione volun- tatis vel universali, quam contraxit ex lapsu primo- rum parentum, vel particulari ex male disposita af- sectione ingenii & voluntatis in subjecto, ut in ava- ro & prodigo contingit. Hactenus de objecto volun- tatis, sequuntur modi seu proprietates quædam, per quas vires & conditionem suam exserit. 1. Conditio voluntatis consistit in voluntaris libertate, qua fertur ad quodlibet objectum pro libitu suo, ut possit dili- gere, si velit, & prosequi aut fugere, si nolit. Ad libertatem conditionis duas conditiones requirit Philosophus. 1. Ut habeat principium internum, seu inclinationem per quam fertur ad subjectum appe- tendum. 2. Ut sit voluntas communis à vi & coactione externa, & ita possit agere, ut nullo objecto impedimento possit ferri ad suum objectum spontaneo & motu libero, nam voluntas, quà voluntas, cogi non potest. Quod quidem verum est ratione primæ voluntatis, aut ratione primi principii, ut loquuntur, etsi cogi possit vi externa, tamen quoad interiorem suum motum vi externe aut coactioni non subjicitur, licet quoad vim directivam voluntati divinæ se subjicere & conformare teneatur. Et hoc est illud, quod Jurisconsulti dicunt, etiam voluntas coacta, est vera voluntas, hoc est, ratione principii interni, quod in ipso subjecto est, ubi est voluntas, licet totus homo possit cogi, ut aliter atq; aliter agat, quàm velit, tamen voluntas hominis istam vim quoad intra non admittit. Notandum tamen, non idem esse libertatem voluntatis & liberum arbitrium, nam liberum arbitrium proprie est motus & inclinatio voluntatis ad bonum, quod est sua natura bonum & sic sumitur à Theol. ubi de libero arbitrio agunt. At hic oritur dubium: Quomodo voluntas feratur motu suo ad bonum, cum omnes cogitationes humanæ sint ita corruptæ, ut nihil in se boni habeant, Gen. 5. v. 6. & Psal. 51. v. 6? Et resp. Obiectum voluntatis nempe bonum esse varium & multiplex, aut pro diversarum rerum qualitatibus diversimodè consideratur. Nam aliud est bonum naturale, aliud spirituale, aliud morale: Etsi voluntas proprie non refertur ad bonum spirituale per se, propter depravatam naturam voluntatis in homine: ad naturale tamen & morale fertur inclinatione sua, propter scintillas & vires quasdam reliquas in animo à lapsu, & liberum habere arbitrium in actionibus naturalibus & moralibus, quæ sunt bonæ, testantur Theologi, vide Perkinsum in Catal. reform. cap. 1. Libertas verò voluntatis ultra se extendit, & ad quodcunque obiectum sive sit bonum revera, sive apparens bonum & recipiendum & applicandum sibi ad imperandum affectibus & cupiditatibus. Et licet feratur sua natura ad bonum revera amplectendum, tamen ex libertate sua ad quodlibet bonum fertur. At verò etsi reliquiæ hominum animis insitæ & à lapsu primorum parentum superstites doceant notitiam generalem, qua voluntas posse discernere honestum à turpi, tamen quia ista notitia est generalis ralis & indeterminata,ideo erit generalis tantum & indeterminatus impetus voluntatis, ut ferarur ad bonum appetendum. Determinata vero notitia & distinctum judicium honesti & turpis, tum etiam singularum virtutum a vitiis petenda est, non ex luce naturae,sed ex disciplinis maxime practicis & bonae educationis,quae est ipsa pars œconomicae. Atq; huic opinioni refragari videtur Aristoteles, qui c. 1. Nicom. cap. 1. Polit. 1. & alibi vocat hominem animal natura πολιτικὸν, & cap. ult. 6. Nicom. dicit, virtutes esse nobis a natura insitas. Ergo notitia haec non promanat ex lucena-tura, non ex disciplinis practicis aut bona educatione. Et respond. Hominem quidem esse a natura animal πολιτικὸν, quod notitiam generalem, quam habet in rebus divinis a luce naturae, etiam virtutes esse nobis insitas, quoad inclinationem & impetum naturalem, quo ferimur ad virtutes amplectendas, vide 6. Nicom. cap. ult. At vero homo non est animal a natura politicum, quoad notitiam specialem seu distinctam, quam solam debet disciplinis practicis, & quae solae ostendunt rationem specialem & distinctam, qua virtutes consuetudine & usu acquirant, & non a natura proveniant.
units.tr: In every practical discipline, and in this practical one too, the order of method is kept: we proceed from the end to the means by which the end is set. There are three principal members: the end, which we have discussed so far; the object, to which the end must be applied; and the means by which the end is applied to the object. We shall deal with the means afterwards, following the Philosopher's plan, and here we shall explain only a few things about the object, following the reasoning of Aristotle, who, in Eth. 1, on the end, straightaway where he prepares the way to the object ... The object of Ethics is therefore considered either indeterminately or determinately. The indeterminate object is man living this civil life. Although he is properly the subject of Ethics, he can in a different respect also be called the object. The object, insofar as it is cultivated and shaped by ethical precepts so that it may live well and happily, and insofar as it receives in itself the habit of prudence so that it may live well, may for this reason be called the subject of Ethics. The determinate object is twofold: internal, namely the will, which is called the primary object, and to which the appetites and the locomotive faculty may also be referred. The external object of Ethics is all those things that are involved in the actions of the virtues; and just as the actions of the virtues are various and manifold, so the external object is of a corresponding kind. The will, then, is the primary internal object. Insofar as it is a property of the soul and a rational faculty that chooses or rejects things apprehended and judged by the intellect, it belongs to physical consideration, and Aristotle treats of it in De anima 3, c. 10. But insofar as it is cultivated by moral precepts, and Ethics is concerned with governing and directing it, it belongs to ethical consideration. Ethics hands down the means by which the will can be shaped and governed, and by which it can apply the moral good to itself. Although the will is primarily directed to the highest and most perfect good, namely the divine, so that it can extend itself to no created thing, since no one rests in such things, nevertheless, because of the conditions of this life which man lives, it is directed most immediately to seeking the moral good. This is so both because the moral good is acquired by means that depend on custom and practice, and therefore proceed from free will, and also because the moral good leads the will of man on toward seeking the ultimate good. Moreover, since good is twofold: one is good in truth and by its own nature, the other is good only in appearance, which presents itself under the guise of good to a human will that is badly affected and disposed. Therefore the object of the will is twofold, the good that is in truth and the apparent good. But the will desires true good both by itself and by its nature, as Aristotle says in Polit. 1.2, while it desires apparent good only accidentally, because of the badly affected disposition in man. This opinion is confirmed by Aristotle in Eth. 3, c. 4, where he distinguishes counsel from the will. But a controversy arises between Aristotle and Plato, for Plato (whom Boethius among the Latins also supports, De consolatione philosophiae 2, c. 7) says that the will tends by itself, by its nature, only to the good. For in De legibus 9 he says that tyrants and wicked men do not become evil by their own will, since the will is only good in itself, but through some wicked opinion which is opposed to the will. The reason given for this is that the will properly tends to that in which it rests; it rests in nothing evil, nor in an apparent good that is not truly good, both because evil is infinite and because it also brings forth sadness and pain. The reply is that the will indeed tends by itself only to the good and to what is truly good, but accidentally to evil. As for Plato's statement that tyrants do not do evil from their will, the freedom of the will proves the contrary, since it is borne toward any object at its own pleasure. But the will tends by its own nature to evil, and therefore not only accidentally. The antecedent is proved by daily experience, which plainly shows that man for the most part tends to evil, and that by his own disposition. The reply is that this does not belong to the nature of the will as it is considered in itself, but arises from a depravity of the will, either universal, which it contracted from the fall of our first parents, or particular, from the ill-disposed affection of the mind and will in the subject, as happens in the greedy and the prodigal. So far concerning the object of the will. There follow certain modes or properties by which it exercises its powers and condition. (1) The condition of the will consists in the liberty of the will, by which it is borne toward any object at its pleasure, so that it may love if it wills, and pursue or flee if it does not will. For the freedom of this condition the Philosopher requires two conditions: (1) that it have an internal principle, or inclination, by which it is borne toward the object to be desired; (2) that the will be free from force and external coercion, so that it can act, and be borne toward its object by a spontaneous and free motion without any impediment, for the will, as will, cannot be compelled. This is indeed true with respect to the first will, or the first principle, as they say, even though it can be compelled by external force; nevertheless, as to its inner motion, it is not subject to external force or coercion, although it is bound to submit and conform itself to the directive power of the divine will. This is what the jurists mean when they say, even a coerced will is a true will, that is, by reason of the internal principle which is in the subject itself, where the will is. Although the whole man may be compelled to act one way or another than he wishes, nevertheless the will of man does not admit such force as far as its inner part is concerned. It must be noted, however, that freedom of the will and free choice are not the same. For free choice properly is the motion and inclination of the will toward the good, which is good by its nature, and it is taken in this sense by the theologians, who treat of free choice. But here a doubt arises: how can the will be borne by its motion toward the good, since all human thoughts are so corrupt that they have nothing good in them, Gen. 5.6 and Ps. 51.6? The answer is that the object of the will, namely the good, is various and manifold, or is considered in different ways according to the qualities of different things. For one good is natural, another spiritual, another moral. Although the will is not properly directed to spiritual good by itself, because of the depraved nature of the will in man, nevertheless it is borne by its inclination toward natural and moral good, because of the sparks and certain remaining powers in the mind after the fall. The theologians testify that man has free choice in natural and moral actions, which are good; see Perkins, in Catalogus reformatorum 1. But the freedom of the will extends further than this, and it can receive and apply to itself any object, whether it be good in truth or apparent good, so as to command the affections and desires. And although by its nature it is borne toward embracing the good in truth, nevertheless by its freedom it is borne toward any good whatsoever. Yet although the remnants of humanity implanted in men's minds, surviving from the fall of our first parents, teach a general knowledge by which the will can distinguish the honourable from the base, nevertheless, because this knowledge is general and indeterminate, the impulse of the will toward seeking the good is also only general and indeterminate. A determinate knowledge and a distinct judgment of the honourable and the base, and likewise of the individual virtues and vices, is to be sought not from the light of nature but from the most practical disciplines and from good education, which is itself a part of domestic economy. Aristotle seems to oppose this opinion, for in Nicomachean Ethics 1, c. 1, Politics 1, and elsewhere, he calls man a political animal by nature, and in Nicomachean Ethics 6, the last chapter, he says that the virtues are implanted in us by nature. Therefore this knowledge does not come from the light of nature, nor from practical disciplines or good education. The answer is that man is indeed a political animal by nature, in that the general knowledge he has of divine things comes from the light of nature; and that the virtues are implanted in us, as to the natural inclination and impulse by which we are borne toward embracing the virtues; see Nicomachean Ethics 6, last chapter. But man is not a political animal by nature as regards special or distinct knowledge, which he owes only to practical disciplines, and which alone show the special and distinct reason by which the virtues are acquired by custom and practice, and do not arise from nature.

units.la: Secundus modus voluntatis est in regimine & imperio, quod supra inferiores facultates obtinet, nempe affectus, cupiditates, & locomotivam: sic enim vires & potentiam suam maxime exercet voluntas, nam cum homo sit animal rationale, non tamen habet animae rationalis proprietates, nempe intellectum & voluntatem, sed habet etiam facultates inferiores, quae vulgo vocantur animales, eique cum brutis communes, in quas voluntas domina ratio-nis imperium tenet, & ad cujus libitum & nutum regun-tur & diriguntur. Agunt quidem istæ facul-tates in homine, sed ductu & auspiciis voluntatis, nam cum voluntas sit perfectissimum quid, quod & à natura ipsa promanat, & sua natura fertur in bo-num, ideo jure illi imperium in istas facultates de-betur, ut nihil nisi rationi consentaneum agant, & bonum appetant. At hîc movetur quæstio ab Ale-xandro Aphrod. lib. 4. natur quast. cap. 11. An ista facul-tates p sint vere dici anima facultates, cum facultates ani-ma sint libera anime functiones, quibus vires suas exerant: At si iste facultates non libere sungantur imperio animi, sed ad nutum & ductum voluntatis, non erunt vera anima fa-cultates? Respondetur, alias esse animæ facultates principales, alias minus principales. Principales qui-dem libere animi vires exprimere & in actum pro-ducere sua vi & non alieno libitu, at hoc vere dici non posse de minus principalibus, quippe, ut ait Pla-to lib. 3. de leg. sic se habent facultates animi in homine, sic-ut magistratus & populus in Republ. Facultates vero minores sunt, ut diximus, affectus, qui varie hominem af-ficiunt, pro varia ratione objecti & variis circumstan-tiis, ut amor, odium, ira, dolor, &c. cupiditates ab appe-titu proveniunt, & quia natura innatæ videntur, ho-minem varie exagitant, ut sunt sitis, fames, libido.
units.tr: The second mode of the will lies in the governance and command that it exercises over the lower faculties, namely the affections, the appetites, and the locomotive faculty. For it is in this that the will chiefly exercises its powers and authority. Man is a rational animal, but he does not possess only the properties of the rational soul, namely intellect and will. He also has lower faculties, commonly called animal, which he shares with the brutes. Over these the will holds dominion as the mistress of reason, and they are governed and directed at its pleasure and command. These faculties do act in man, but under the guidance and auspices of the will. For the will is the most perfect thing, which also proceeds from nature itself and by its nature is carried towards the good. Therefore it is rightly owed authority over these faculties, so that they do nothing but what agrees with reason and seek the good. Here, however, Alexander of Aphrodisias raises a question (Nat. Quaest. bk. 4, ch. 11): Can these faculties really be called faculties of the soul, since the faculties of the soul are the free functions of the soul by which it exerts its powers? But if these faculties do not act freely at the command of the mind, but at the nod and guidance of the will, will they not be true faculties of the soul? The answer is that some faculties of the soul are principal and others less principal. The principal faculties freely express the powers of the soul and bring them into act by their own force and not at another's pleasure. This cannot truly be said of the less principal faculties. Just as Plato says (Laws, bk. 3), the faculties of the soul stand in man as the magistrate and the people stand in a commonwealth. The lesser faculties, as we have said, are the affections, which variously stir man according to the various nature of the object and various circumstances, such as love, hatred, anger, grief, etc. The appetites arise from the appetite, and because they seem to be innate by nature, they variously harass man, as thirst, hunger, and lust do.

units.la: Locomotiva est motus externorum membrorum, ut internis animi facultatibus morem gerat, ut cum pedes incedunt, manus aliquid operantur, quia sic voluntas jubet, & cujus nutu facultas loco motiva regitur, & per quam voluntas actiones suas externas exserit. At vero etsi istæ facultates nobis cum brutis communes sunt, tamen quia à ratione non proficiscuntur, nec voluntatem propriè dictam habent bruta, ideo affectibus & istis facultatibus moderari nequeunt, sed inordinato impetu feruntur pro varia conditione ejus subjecti, in quo insunt. Imperium, quod voluntas obtinet, in inferiores facultates est duplex, elicitum & imperatum. Imperium elicitum est, cum statim facultates istæ inferiores, ratione imperante sine impedimento voluntati se subjiciunt, & sine mora & reluctatione se obsequentes præbent, ut si voluntas virtuti operam dandam velit, affectus statim assentiuntur, cupiditates sequuntur, locomotiva in actionem externam producit hoc ipsum, quod voluntas jubet. Imperatum regimen est, cum facultates istæ non statim se subjiciunt voluntati, sed quantum possunt, reluctantur, & impedimenta objiciunt, quod in subjectis male affectis & dispositis plerunque evenit, ut bonum animi & vitia inter se pugnant, quod de se testatur Medea apud Poetam 7. Metamor. ubi affectus amoris in Jasonem jubet prodere mysteria patriæ & parentum, & relinquere parentes, ratio contrarium suadet; sic enim inquit: Me trahit invitam nova vis, aliudque Cupido, Mens aliud suadet; video meliora probóque, Deteriora sequor.
units.tr: The locomotive faculty is the motion of the external members, so that they obey the internal faculties of the soul: for instance, when the feet walk or the hands do something, because the will so commands. At its nod the locomotive faculty is governed, and through it the will puts forth its external actions. Yet although these faculties are common to us and the brutes, still, because they do not proceed from reason, and brutes do not have the will properly so called, they cannot be moderated by the affections and these faculties, but are carried by an unordered impulse according to the varying condition of the subject in which they inhere. The command that the will holds over the lower faculties is twofold, elicited and commanded. Elicited command is when these lower faculties, with reason commanding, at once submit to the will without hindrance and, without delay or reluctance, yield obedience. For example, if the will wishes to devote itself to virtue, the affections at once assent, the appetites follow, and the locomotive faculty carries out in external action exactly what the will commands. Commanded government is when these faculties do not submit to the will at once, but resist as far as they can and put up obstacles. This happens for the most part in subjects that are ill affected and disposed, where the good of the mind and vices fight against each other. Medea bears witness to this of herself in the poet, Metamorphoses bk. 7, where the affection of love for Jason bids her betray the mysteries of her country and forsake her parents, while reason urges the contrary. She says: A strange force drags me, though I am unwilling, and a different desire; my mind urges another course. I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse.

units.la: Id in ista lucta facultatum inferiorum cum voluntate plerunque evenire solet, vel ex ignorantia rerum, quod iis accidit, qui disciplinis probis & virtutum actionibus se non exercent, vel qui nimium sensibus tribuunt, iisque tantum inhærent, nihil ultra tra quæretentes, sublimia non ascendentes. At hujusmodi errores etiam in corda hominum propellit, vel flexibilitas in malum carnis, vel pravitas temperamenti, vel prava sodalitia, vel pravæ ejusmodi illecebræ. Cæterum quia diximus voluntatem obtinere imperium in affectibus, quæri potest, An in homine possit moderari affectibus? Nam ut voluntas secundum rectam rationem affectus imperare videatur, ideo voluntas posset moderari affectibus. Contrarium quidam adstruere videntur quidā his præcipuè rationib. 1. Quod est naturale, scil. à natura insitum, id non est in hominis potestate, ut ei homo pro libitu suo moderari possit: Affectus sunt ejusmodi. Ergo. Major inde patet, quia quæ à natura fiunt, semper eodem modo finem suum appetunt, nec impediri possunt, nisi à potentia superiore, v delicet ipsa natura. Minor etiam clara est, nam affectus sunt proprie motus formæ ejus subjecti, cui insunt, forma verò est natura ipsa, & maximè natura, quod probat variis argumentis Aristoteles lib. 2. natural. auscult. cap. 1. Resp. distinguendum esse inter naturale absolutè, & naturale quodammodo. Si major accipiatur simpliciter seu omni modo, tunc minor erit falsa, quod affectus sint planè naturales, nam affectus sunt quodammodo naturales, quodammodo voluntarii. Sunt naturales ratione originis, quatenus à causa efficiente naturali promanant, sunt voluntariæ, quatenus ex libitu voluntatis per προαίρεσιν sive electionem ad bonum vel malum determinantur. 2. Si affectus possunt moderari aut regi, tunc essent voluntarii. At non sunt voluntarii, invitum enim hominem, quo velint, rapiunt, rapiunt,ut in ira,odio,amore videre licet? Resp. In subjecto bene affecto & dispositο sunt plane voluntarii, & voluntati subjiciuntur, at in male dispositο subjecto invitum subjectum rapiunt non sua natura, sed per pravitatem subjecti. Ideo facile erit respondere ad illud tertium, quod affertur, nempe quod rationi repugnat, id ne voluntati quidem subjici potest, & ideo non est in hominis potestate, ut id possit regere pro libitu. Ataff &tus rationi semper repugnant, quod probat Philos. ult. cap. 1. Nicom. cum inquit, videtur esse in bis, scilicet affectibus aliquid contra rationem naturā insitum, repugnant enim & resistunt semper rationi? Et Respon. etsi ad tempus repugnare videantur, tamen facile rationi subjici possunt, sicut equus indomitus, nec frenos admittit, nec sessorem, donec dometur, sic aff&tus etsi rationi repugnant, possunt tamen intra gyrum rectae rationis deduci, ubi subjectum est bene affectum, & animus ad se redit. Atque haec de primariis motibus voluntatis, quibus voluntas vires & conditionem suam maxime exerit. Sequuntur modi secundarii, qui maxime considerantur in appetitione objecti, quod voluntas appetit. Nam quia voluntas libere agit, etiam libere objectum suum appetit, etsi libere appetat, etiam el gere possit modum, quo appetat, & si eligere possit modum, etiam actionem suā suspendere possit in modo appetendi, & si suspendere possit, possit etiam exequi, pro libitu suo, unde oriuntur modi voluntatis circa objectum appetendum tres, nempe electio, suspensio & executio. Voluntas igitur, ut subjectum suum melius appetat, electiolectione uritur, sciendum tamen hominem aliquid velle duobus modis, vel simpliciter vel comparatè. Simpliciter cum recta propendet ad unam rem, nec aliam appetit, sed eam ipsam amplectitur: & in ea sibi acquiescendum ducit. Comparatè ut cum inter duo vel plura obiecta mens humana deliberat, utrum deligat, & adsumat, utrum negligat, & repudiet, & tandem cum mens deliberavit pro variis circumstantiis, temporis, loci & rei, tandem intellectus movet voluntatem, ut illud ex his, quae conferuntur, adsumat, quod ad finem suum & propositum maximè facere videtur, unde ista oritur in rebus electio, & sic definiri possit electio actus voluntatis, quo voluntas è duobus vel pluribus obiectis sive bonis, sive malis illud adsumit, quod ad finem suum maximè videtur facere, ex duobus quidè bonis aut pluribus maximum & perfectissimum aut revera, aut judicio eligentis, ex malis illud, quod minus est, nam minus malū respectu majoris, quodammodo bonum dici potest, & ideo nullum locū habet illud Buridani, electionem non proprie esse actionem voluntatis, propterea quod voluntas feratur sua natura in bonum, electio verò tàm ad bonum, quàm ad malum: nam etsi ad malum feratur, nó ad malum promanat, sed sub aliqua specie boni. Cæterum, in quibus rebus consistat electio, & quo modo à voluntate superetur, tractat Philos. 3. Nic. cap. 5. & ex illo Keckermannus, ubi hoc maximum discrimé ab electione voluntatis ponitur, quod scil. voluntas tantum respiciat ad finem, electio verò sit mediorum ad finem ostensio, quae sententia Philosophi in dubium vocatur, quod voluntas non tantum circa finem versetur, sed etiam circa media ad finem spectantia ut ex vulgari illo axiomate patet: Qui vult finem, vult etiam media destinata ad finem? Et Respon. voluntaris vocabulum duobus modis sumi, late & stricte: late pro qualibet appetitione rationali, sive ea appetitio versetur circa finem, sive circa media ducentia ad finem, & sic in hac significatione verum est illud, qui vult finem, vult etiam media destinata ad finem. Stricte sumitur pro appetitione perfecta, quae, ut est ipsa perfectum quid, sic finem tanquam perfectionem suam proprie appetit, & in hac secunda significatione voluntatis vocabulum sumsit Aristoteles, cum eam destinxit ab electione.
units.tr: This usually happens in such a struggle of the lower faculties against the will, either from ignorance of things, which befalls those who do not exercise themselves in sound disciplines and in virtuous actions, or who give too much to the senses, cling only to them, seek nothing beyond, and do not rise to lofty things. But such errors also drive their way into men's hearts, whether from the proneness of the flesh to evil, or the depravity of temperament, or wicked companionships, or such wicked allurements. But since we have said that the will holds command over the affections, it may be asked: Can a man moderate his affections? For if the will is to seem to command the affections according to right reason, then the will would be able to moderate the affections. Some seem to maintain the contrary, chiefly on these grounds. (1) What is natural, that is, implanted by nature, is not in man's power, so that he can moderate it at his pleasure. The affections are of this kind. Therefore (the conclusion follows). The major premise is plain, because things that are done by nature always seek their end in the same way, and cannot be hindered except by a superior power, namely nature itself. The minor premise is also clear, for the affections are properly motions of the form of the subject in which they inhere, and the form is nature itself, and especially nature, as Aristotle proves by various arguments (Physics, bk. 2, ch. 1). The answer is that one must distinguish between what is natural absolutely and what is natural in a certain respect. If the major premise is taken simply, that is, in every way, then the minor premise is false, because the affections are not wholly natural; they are natural in a certain respect and voluntary in a certain respect. They are natural by reason of their origin, insofar as they proceed from a natural efficient cause; they are voluntary insofar as they are determined by the pleasure of the will, through prohairesis [προαίρεσιν], or choice, towards good or evil. (2) If the affections can be moderated or governed, then they would be voluntary. But they are not voluntary, for they carry an unwilling man wherever they please, as can be seen in anger, hatred, and love. The answer is that in a subject well affected and disposed they are entirely voluntary and submit to the will. But in an ill-disposed subject they carry the unwilling subject away, not by their nature, but through the depravity of the subject. Therefore it will be easy to answer the third objection, which is put forward: that what is opposed to reason cannot even be subject to the will, and so it is not in man's power to govern it at his pleasure. The affections are always opposed to reason, which the Philosopher proves (Nicomachean Ethics, bk. 7, ch. 1), when he says: There seems to be in these, namely the affections, something against reason implanted by nature, for they always resist and oppose reason. The answer is that although they may seem for a time to resist, they can nevertheless easily be subjected to reason. Just as an unbroken horse accepts neither bridle nor rider until it is tamed, so the affections, although they resist reason, can nevertheless be brought within the circle of right reason, where the subject is well affected and the mind comes back to itself. So much for the primary motions of the will, by which the will chiefly exerts its powers and its condition. There follow the secondary modes, which are chiefly considered in the appetite for the object that the will desires. For because the will acts freely, it also desires its object freely. And although it desires freely, it can also choose the mode in which it desires; and if it can choose the mode, it can also suspend its action in the mode of desiring; and if it can suspend it, it can also carry it out at its pleasure. Hence arise the three modes of the will with regard to the object to be desired: choice, suspension, and execution. So, in order to desire its object better, the will is exercised by choice. It must be noted, however, that a man wills something in two ways, either simply or comparatively. Simply, when the right inclination tends to one thing, and does not desire another, but embraces that very thing, and considers itself at rest in it. Comparatively, as when the human mind deliberates between two or more objects, whether to choose and take up one, or to neglect and reject the others; and finally, when the mind has deliberated, according to the various circumstances of time, place and matter, the intellect at last moves the will to take up, from those that are compared, that which seems to contribute most to its end and purpose. Hence this kind of choice in things arises, and thus choice may be defined as the act of the will by which, from two or more objects, whether good or evil, it takes up that which seems most to serve its end: from two goods, the greatest and most perfect, either in reality or in the judgment of the one choosing; from evils, that which is less, for a lesser evil compared with a greater can in some sense be called good. Therefore that saying of Buridan, that choice is not properly an act of the will because the will is by its nature carried towards the good, whereas choice is directed to evil as well as to good, has no place here. For although the will is carried towards evil, it does not proceed to evil except under some appearance of good. Moreover, in what things choice consists, and how it is surpassed by the will, Aristotle treats (Nicomachean Ethics, bk. 3, ch. 5), and following him Keckermann, where this greatest difference between the will and choice is laid down: that the will regards only the end, whereas choice is the pointing out of the means to the end. But this opinion of the Philosopher is called in question, since the will is concerned not only with the end but also with the means that bear on the end, as is clear from that common axiom: Whoever wills the end, also wills the means destined for the end. The answer is that the word voluntas is taken in two ways, broadly and strictly. Broadly it means any rational desire, whether that desire is concerned with the end or with the means leading to the end; and in this sense it is true that whoever wills the end also wills the means destined for the end. Strictly it is taken for the perfect desire, which, as it is itself something perfect, properly desires the end as its own perfection. It is in this second sense that Aristotle took the word will when he distinguished it from choice.

units.la: Cum electio versetur circa duo vel plura objecta, ut quod optimum videtur pro fine consequendo assumat, & reliqua negligat, necessario praesupponit in rebus consultationem, scilicet deliberationem, quae est actio voluntatis circa bonum aliquot de quo dubitatur, sine ampletendum, necne? Causa vero hujus dubitationis, quae proprie parit consultationem, consistit in duobus nempe in ignorantia mediorum, cum ignorat voluntas, quibus potissimum mediis utiliceat ad finem asequendum, & secundo, in dubitatione de medio, cum dubitat voluntas, quae sint potiora media & amplectenda, quae vero relinquenda: Nam ubi certa & nota sunt media, homo non consultat, sed operam dat, ut ista media finem suum assequantur, sed quoniam voluntas variis perturbationibus obnoxia est, ideo statim non percipit notitiam & certitudinem rerum, sed tam diu in hanc vel illam partem exagitatur, donec certò & verè exploraverit, quibus rationibus ad finem, quem intenderat, pervenire possit. Aut si homo ipse per impertitiam aut imprudentiam in rebus agendis rationem expeditam in mediis explorandis invenire nequeat, tum prudentiores adire suadet Philosophus, ut certum in rebus capiant consilium, sicuti enim cap.5.3 Nicom. habetur, ad res magnas gerendas adhibere solemus consiliarios, quasi diffidentes nobis ipsis, & quia non satis sumus idonei ad res cognoscendas, ut electio scilicet consultatio est rerum conjunctarum, quæ inter se conferuntur, quæ est propriè in his rebus, quæ possunt aliter atque aliter fieri, & in hujusmodi quidem rebus, quæ ad nos spectant, & in nostra facultate sunt, ut fiant, vel non fiant, & ideò quia perfectionem suam non assequuntur, ita mediorum tantum est consultatio. Unde definitur vulgo investigatio mediorum latentium quæ ad nos spectant, & in nostra facultate sunt, ut pociora inveniamus, pro fine consequendo.
units.tr: Since choice is concerned with two or more objects, so that it takes up what seems best for attaining the end and neglects the rest, it necessarily presupposes in things deliberation, that is, consultation, which is an act of the will concerning some good about which there is doubt whether it is to be embraced or not. The cause of this doubt, which properly gives rise to consultation, consists in two things: first, in ignorance of the means, since the will does not know by which means especially it may be useful for attaining the end; and second, in doubt about the means, since the will is uncertain which means are better and to be embraced, and which are to be left aside. For where the means are certain and known, a person does not consult but labours to bring those means to their end; but because the will is subject to various disturbances, it does not at once perceive the knowledge and certainty of things, but is tossed back and forth to this side or that until it has clearly and truly explored by what reasons it can reach the end it had intended. Or if a person, through inexperience or imprudence in dealing with affairs, cannot find a ready method of exploring the means, then the Philosopher advises him to approach the more prudent, so that they may take a sure counsel in the matter. For, as is said in Nicomachean Ethics 3.5, in undertaking great affairs we are accustomed to employ counsellors, as if distrusting ourselves, and because we are not sufficiently fit to know things. Thus choice is a consultation about things joined together which are weighed against one another; and this properly applies to those things which can be done in one way or another, and to such things as concern us and lie within our power to do or not to do. And because they do not attain their perfection, consultation is only about means. Hence it is commonly defined as the investigation of hidden means which concern us and lie within our power, so that we may find the better ones for attaining the end.

units.la: Notandum tamen consultationem propriè non habere locum in Ethica, propriè sic dicta, nisi quatenus in genere consideratur, tanquam principium actionum moralium, propriè quidem refertur consultatio, sic etiam electio ad Oeconomicam & Politicam, ubi res considerantur in specie & alicui materiæ applicatæ. Sic de electione & consultatione, quæ eam præcedit necessariò, propterea quod vires & modum secundum naturam agendi electioni consultatio suppetit, sequitur suspensio voluntaris, qua maximè indicatur liber agendi modus in volunvoluntate, nam etsi voluntas natura sua feratur ad objectum suum tanquam ad finem, tamen pro variis circumstantiis differre & suspendere actionem suam potest in aliud atque aliud tempus, & hoc est proprium omnium liberè agentium, ut possint deproperare ad finem suum, vel possunt inhibere & differre, si ratio & consultatio sic suadeant. Et hinc apparet discrimen evidens inter naturalia agentia & libere agentia. Naturalia enim semper eodem modo agunt, nec actionem suam suspendere possunt, ut, verbi gratia, hic ignis urit, & semper urit aptam materiam, quae urere potest, sive sit tempus utendi sive non, quia hoc habet sibi a natura inditum, ut agat in objectam materiam, necactionem suam ad minimum tempus suspendere potest. Voluntarie vero agentia etsi etiam natura sua feratur ad finem, tamen eadem natura libertatem agendi indidit, ut possint differre actionem suam in aliud atque aliud tempus, pro libitu suo. Notandum tamen iam suspensionem habere locum in mediis ejusmodi, quae nondum sub consultationem venerunt, at ubi de iis in consultatione actum est, tunc voluntas non suspendit actionem suam, sed ultro ad finem fertur, nisi noluit, & ex impedimento quaedam remora injiciatur, quo minus in appetendo fine pergat. Et ut consultatio est de fine, sic etiam est suspensio ex natura voluntatis, quae naturali impetu ad finem fertur, ut nullam de fine moram sibi injici patiatur, ut, verbi gratia, voluntas non differt appetitionem suam, quia fertur in felicitatem, quia felicitatem pro fine habet, in qua tanquam perfectione actioactionem moralium sibi acquiescendum putat. Catertam sunt, qui putant non minus voluntatem suspendere actionem suam circa appetitionem finis, quàm circa mediorum appetitionem hac ratione: Voluntas etsi statim appetat finem, non statim tamen fertur ad finem, quia varia sunt rationes & circumstantia, in quibus voluntas interdum haeret, interdum pergit, & ideo suspendit appetitionem suam circa finem. Et respond. Aliud esse assecutionem finis, aliud appetitionem, in appetitione dari varias circumstantias & rationes, cur voluntas id, quod intenderat, non statim assequatur, quae potius pertinent ad media, quam ad finem, vel ubi media vel dubia sunt vel non satis cognita voluntati, tum haeret voluntas, at ubi inclinaverint media, tum sine impedimento ad assecutionem finis pergit: at vero ratione appetitionis semper voluntas eodem modo in actione sua progreditur. Ultimus modus de voluntate secundarius est assecutio, scilicet determinatio voluntatis circa appetitionem objecti, cum voluntas non tantum ad assequendam fertur, quod intenderat, sed etiam assequitur & determinat, quod duobus etiam modis fieri Philosophus ostendit, cap. 5. lib. 3. Nicomach. mediatè vel immediatè. Mediatè, cum media ad consultationem veniunt, & ideo tempus & modum requirunt. Immediatè, cum statim cogniti & exploratis mediis voluntas finem sibi propositum assequitur. Etsi vero voluntas actionem suam circa objectum determinet, tamen no uno eodemque modo ad eam determinationem fertur, nam voluntas, quod agit, plenè & plane cum toto naturae suae impetu fertur ad id consequendum, quod intendintenderat, ita ut adjunctam addat laetitiam & lu-bentiam in appetenda & consequenda re, quae duo voluntatem liberè agere declarant, interdum verò vultaliud non plenè, sed ex parte tantum, ita ut imperfectam & semiplenam habeat prudentiam; interdum vero voluntas aliquid determinat, ad quod nullo suo impetu fertur, sed appetitu quodam tristi & aegro, & ut loquimur invito, & sic triplices oriuntur actiones ex illa triplici affectu voluntatis, nempe spontaneae, invitae & mixtae, de quibus Philosophus lib.3. Nicomach. c.1.2.3. Caeterum istam divisionem actionum humanarum & a ratione ipsa, & ab Aristotele probata, improbant nonnulli his rationibus: Omnes actiones sunt voluntariae. Ergo male feruntur quaedam actiones mixtae & invitae. Antecedens probatur, quia omnes actiones morales habent principium in ipso agente, cujus sunt actiones morales, & tales actiones omnes spontaneas vocat Aristoteles lib.3. Nicomach. primis statim verbis, ut etiam cap.3. ejusdem libri. 2. Nihil laudem vel vituperium meretur, nisi idem sit spontaneum. Nam cum omnes actiones hominis sint vel bonae vel malae, & ideo vel laudem vel vituperium meretur, sequitur omnes esse spontaneas, nisi iis laudem & vituperium detrahere velimus. 3. Omnis actio hominis aut precedit habitum tanquam causa, aut sequitur tanquam effectus. Si praecedit tanquam causa efficiens, tunc iponte agit, quia causa efficiens vi sua producit effectum, si sequitur tanquam effectus, siquidem causa fuit libera, est spontanea, a qua promanavit effectus, sic etiam effectus erit spontaneus. 4. Cum omne id, quod homo agit, fit sit vel bonum vel malum, id omne sponte agit, non invite. Et ratio est, quia nemo, nisi sponte fit probus vel improbus. Sed respond. ad priores tres rationes, committi elenchum, a dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter, nam quod competit proprie actioni spontaneae, scilicet voluntariae, id tribuitur omni actioni qualicunque etiam, & ideo sequeretur omnes actiones esse spontaneas. Ad quartam vero rationem dicimus in ea committi fallaciam a consequente; nam etsi hoc verum sit, nemo nisi sponte fit probus vel improbus, non tamen convertendo sequitur, omne, quod homo agit, sive probum sit, sive improbum, necessario competit. Alii volunt, omnes actiones hominis esse aut spontaneas aut invitas, propterea quod duplex sit tantum principium, internum & externum nempe, & omne, quod homo agit, vel secundum naturalem propensionem & voluntatem agit, & sic sponte agit; vel contra naturalem propensionem principio externo nolente, & sic invite agit. Sed tamen sunt quaedam actiones, quae neque plane secundum voluntatem vel naturalem propensionem fiunt, neque plane contra sunt: sed sunt mediae cujusdam naturae, & negatione extremorum exprimuntur, & vocantur mixtae scil. mediae, quod partim fiant ab externo, partim ab interno principio, & vocantur idcirco heterogeneae, quod non sint ejusdem naturae, sed diversae, actiones vero tam spontaneae, quam invitae dicuntur homogeneae, quod ejusdem naturae semper sint. Definitur actio spontanea, cujus principium est in ipso agente sciente singulas actionum circumstantias, ab ipso Philosopho lib. 3. Nicomach. cap. 3. & ideo requirit duas conditiones, principium nempe internum & notitiam singularum circumstantiarum circa objecta. Etsi vero actiones spontaneæ fluant à voluntate & eatenus hîc de iis agendum esset, tamen quia sunt principia virtutis, ideo cum de virtute agetur, de iis fusius agemus. Quæ itaque potest, an actiones spontaneæ soli homini competant, an etiam brutis, & rationem carentibus? Quod soli homini competant, ista sunt rationes: Quia omnis actio spontanea differt à voluntate, & ideo habet electionem sibi adjunctam, ista vero fluunt à ratione. 2. Philosopho teste statim initio 3. Nicomach. Omnes actiones spontaneæ merentur laudem vel vituperium, quæ proprie competunt hominī. Pro contraria parte sunt, quod etiam brutis competant. 1. Communis consuetudo loquendi. Sic etiam equus sponte dicitur currere, nempe cum freno soluti usi liberè pro suo affectu fertur, quocunque velit. 2. Cui competunt invitæ actiones, eidem competunt etiam spontaneæ; At etiam brutis competunt invitæ actiones, & ratio est, quando equus flagello cædítur, vel calcaribus adigitur à suo sessore, dicitur invitè currere, quia non naturali impetu ad cursum fertur, sed vi externa cogente, qua coactus. 3. Philosophus 3. Nicomach. c. 3. dicit, absurdum est negare pueros & bruta sponte agere. Resp. Spontanea actio sumitur duobus modis, vel pro modo agendi liberè, contra distinctò à vi externa, sive iste agendi modus sit conjunctus cum cognitione sive non, & sic brutis competit sponte agere, quatenus nimirum liberè remota vi externa impetu suo feruntur. 2. Sponte agere sumitur strictè pro modo agendi cum voluntate & cognitione conjuncto, & sic soli homini competit, & hoc modo Philosophus de actionibus spontaneis agens, quatenus opponitur invitæ, scil. involuntariæ agitcap. 3. 3. Nicomach. Involuntaria actio seu invita ab Aristotele definitur, quæ per vim aut per ignorantiam fit, unde duplicem esse actionem invitam constat, aliam ex coactione, quando agens vi externa ad agendum impellitur, aliam ex ignorantia, quando agens singulas circumstantias actionis producendæ plane ignorat. Ut raque actio provenit ex voluntatis rectitudine, quando voluntas ad objectum contrarium est potius affecta & quando se non regit, sed ab alio regitur, quod tamen non tam de ipsa voluntate intelligendum, quæ proprie sua natura cogi non potest, ut albo, quam inrenderat, feratur, quam de ipso homine, in quo inest voluntas, qui quidem tanquam agens contra naturalem propensionem & voluntarem suam impelli & cogi potest, ut aliud atque aliud agat. Ad invitam seu violentam actionem producendam duo requirit Philosophus cap. 1. 3. Nicom. 1. Ut principium sit externum, quod ad violentam actionem impellit. 2. Ut nihil opis & auxilii conferat agens ad actionem producendam, sed quatenus in se est, reluctatur principio externo. 3. Conditio etiam potest tradi, nempe ut illud principium externum sit satis validum ad agentem cogendum, secus enim non sequeretur violenta actio, nisi vis externa satis valida ad eam impelleret. Exemplum exstat 2. Maccab. cap. 3. de Antiocho tyranno, qui Judæos ad sacrificia Bacchi compellebat hedera coronatos.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that deliberation strictly speaking has no place in Ethics, properly so called, except insofar as it is considered in general, as the principle of moral actions. Deliberation is properly referred to in this way, and so is choice, in Economics and Politics, where things are considered in particular and applied to some matter. So choice and the deliberation that necessarily precedes it, since deliberation supplies the powers and the manner of acting that choice depends on, are followed by voluntary suspension. This is the strongest sign of the free manner of acting in the will. For although the will by its nature tends toward its object as toward an end, it can, according to varying circumstances, put off and suspend its action to one time or another. This belongs to all freely acting beings: they can hasten toward their end, or they can hold back and defer, if reason and deliberation so advise. From this the clear difference between natural agents and free agents appears. For natural agents always act in the same way and cannot suspend their action. For example, this fire burns, and it always burns suitable material that can be burned, whether or not it is the time for using it, because it has been given by nature to act upon the material it is set to. It cannot suspend its action even for the shortest time. Voluntary agents, however, although their nature also tends toward the end, have been given by that same nature the freedom to act, so that they can defer their action to one time or another, as they please. It should be noted, though, that suspension has a place in those means that have not yet come under deliberation. But when they have been deliberated on, the will does not suspend its action; it moves toward the end of its own accord, unless it is unwilling, or unless some hindrance is thrown in as a delay, so that it does not proceed in pursuing the end. And just as deliberation concerns the end, so there is also suspension arising from the nature of the will, which tends toward the end by a natural impulse, so that it does not allow any delay to be put in its way regarding the end. For example, the will does not defer its desire because it tends toward happiness, since it holds happiness as its end, in which, as in perfection, it thinks it should rest its moral actions. There are some, however, who think that the will suspends its action regarding the desire for the end no less than regarding the desire for the means, for this reason: the will, although it desires the end at once, does not at once move toward the end, because there are various reasons and circumstances in which the will sometimes stops and sometimes proceeds, and so it suspends its desire regarding the end. And the reply is: attaining the end is one thing, desiring it another. In the desire there are various circumstances and reasons why the will does not at once attain what it intended. These pertain rather to the means than to the end: where the means are doubtful or not well enough known to the will, then the will stops. But when the means have become clear, then the will proceeds without hindrance to attaining the end. Yet regarding the desire, the will always advances in its action in the same way. The last, secondary mode of the will is attainment, namely the determination of the will regarding the desire of the object, when the will not only moves toward attaining what it intended but also attains and determines it. The Philosopher shows that this happens in two ways, in book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 5, either mediately or immediately. Mediately, when means come under deliberation, and therefore require time and a manner. Immediately, when, the means having been at once known and examined, the will attains the end it has set before itself. Although the will determines its action regarding the object, it does not move toward that determination in one and the same way. For the will, in what it does, moves fully and plainly with the whole impulse of its nature to obtain what it intended, so that it adds joy and delight in desiring and obtaining the thing, and these two things show that the will acts freely. Sometimes, however, it moves toward something not fully but only in part, so that its prudence is imperfect and half-complete. Sometimes the will determines something toward which it moves not by its own impulse but by a certain sad and sick desire, and, as we say, unwillingly. Thus three kinds of action arise from this threefold disposition of the will: voluntary, unwilling, and mixed, concerning which the Philosopher speaks in book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapters 1, 2, and 3. Moreover, some reject this division of human actions, which is approved both by reason itself and by Aristotle, for these reasons: All actions are voluntary. Therefore certain mixed and unwilling actions are wrongly so described. The premise is proved because all moral actions have their principle in the agent whose moral actions they are, and Aristotle calls all such actions voluntary in book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, in its very first words, and also in chapter 3 of the same book. 2. Nothing deserves praise or blame unless it is voluntary. For since all human actions are either good or bad, and so deserve either praise or blame, it follows that all are voluntary, unless we wish to take praise and blame away from them. 3. Every human action either precedes a habit as its cause or follows it as its effect. If it precedes as an efficient cause, then it acts of its own accord, because an efficient cause by its power produces its effect. If it follows as an effect, then, provided the cause was free, it is voluntary, since the effect proceeds from it, and so the effect will also be voluntary. 4. Since everything that a human does is either good or bad, everything of this kind is done voluntarily, not unwillingly. The reason is that no one becomes upright or wicked except voluntarily. But the reply to the first three arguments is that they commit the fallacy from a statement qualified to a statement unqualified. For what properly belongs to a voluntary action, namely one done by choice, is here ascribed to every action of whatever kind, and so it would follow that all actions are voluntary. To the fourth argument we say that it commits the fallacy of the consequent. For although it is true that no one becomes upright or wicked except voluntarily, it does not follow by conversion that whatever a human does, whether upright or wicked, necessarily belongs to the voluntary. Others maintain that all human actions are either voluntary or unwilling, because there are only two principles, namely internal and external. Everything a human does either proceeds from natural inclination and will, and so is done voluntarily, or else it proceeds against natural inclination, through an external principle that he does not will, and so he acts unwillingly. But there are some actions that are neither wholly according to will or natural inclination nor wholly contrary to them. They are of an intermediate kind, and are expressed by denying the extremes. They are called mixed, that is, intermediate, because they partly proceed from an external principle and partly from an internal one. And for this reason they are called heterogeneous, because they are not of the same nature but of different natures. Actions that are either voluntary or unwilling are called homogeneous, because they are always of the same nature. A voluntary action is defined, by the Philosopher himself in book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, as one whose principle lies in the agent himself, who knows the particular circumstances of the actions. Therefore it requires two conditions: an internal principle, and knowledge of the individual circumstances concerning the objects. Although voluntary actions do flow from the will, and so this would be the place to treat them, yet because they are principles of virtue, we will treat them more fully when we come to virtue. So the question is: do voluntary actions belong only to man, or also to brute beasts, which lack reason? That they belong only to man, these are the reasons: because every voluntary action differs from the will, and so has choice joined to it, and this choice flows from reason. 2. As the Philosopher testifies at the very beginning of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, all voluntary actions deserve praise or blame, and these properly belong to man. On the other side, that they belong also to brutes: 1. Common usage of speech: so a horse is said to run voluntarily, namely when, loosed from the bridle, it moves freely, wherever it wishes, according to its own inclination. 2. Whatever kind of action can be unwilling can also be voluntary. But unwilling actions also belong to brutes. The reason is that when a horse is beaten with a whip or spurred on by its rider, it is said to run unwillingly, because it is not moved to running by its natural impulse but is compelled by external force. 3. The Philosopher, in book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, says: it is absurd to deny that children and brutes act voluntarily. Reply: a voluntary action is taken in two ways. Either it means acting freely, in contrast with external force, and whether or not this manner of acting is joined with knowledge; and in this sense it belongs to brutes to act voluntarily, insofar as, external force being removed, they move freely by their own impulse. Or, second, acting voluntarily is taken strictly for a manner of acting joined with will and knowledge, and in this sense it belongs only to man. The Philosopher, treating voluntary actions in this way, sets them against the unwilling, that is, involuntary, action. In book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, an unwilling or involuntary action is defined by Aristotle as one that happens through force or through ignorance. From this it is plain that there are two kinds of unwilling action: one from compulsion, when the agent is driven to act by external force, and another from ignorance, when the agent is entirely ignorant of the individual circumstances of the action to be performed. Each kind arises from a defect of the will, when the will is more inclined toward the contrary object, and when it does not govern itself but is governed by another. This, however, must be understood not so much of the will itself, which by its nature cannot be forced to move toward something other than what it intended, as of the man in whom the will resides. He, as an agent, can be impelled and compelled against his natural inclination and will, so as to act otherwise. To produce an unwilling or violent action, the Philosopher requires two things in chapters 1 and 3 of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics: first, that the principle be external, impelling him to violent action; second, that the agent contribute nothing of help or aid to the action, but resists the external principle as far as he is able. A third condition can also be given: that the external principle be strong enough to compel the agent. Otherwise the violent action would not follow, unless the external force were strong enough to drive him to it. An example is found in 2 Maccabees, chapter 3, concerning the tyrant Antiochus, who compelled the Jews, crowned with ivy, to the sacrifices of Bacchus.

units.la: Hedera coronatos. natos. Actio invita fit etiam per ignorantiam, quando ab ignorantia tanquam causa principali ipsa provenit, monet tamen Philosophus cap. 2. 3. Nicom. diligenter distinguendum esse inter ista duo, nempe ex ignorantia agere, & ignoranter agere; nam ignoranter agere, est ita agere, ut quicquid agas, tunc temporis ignores, quando agis, ita tamen, ut ignorantia non sit causa istius pravae actionis, sed aliud aliquod vitium, quod ad istam actionem induxit, ut cum ex vehemente animi perturbatione, ita nempe, aut ebrietate, aut huiusmodi vitioso affectu aliquis facinus aliquot parrat, ut cum in ebrietate aliquis hominem occidit, igne tanter quidem agit, quatenus isti vitiosi affectus animi acient mentis pervertunt & obscurant, non tamen ex ignorantia agit, poterat enim facti circumstantias scivisse, & ideo nec veniam nec excusationem meretur. Ex ignorantia verò agere, est ita agere, ut ista ignorantia sit causa pravae actionis, adeo ut agens facti circumstantias scire non potuerit, nec sibi istam ignorantiam accersivit: Exemplum habet luculentum Philosophus in Aeschylo Poeta Tragico, qui Tragoediam scripsit, quam vocat Mysteria Cereris, cum vero in theatro ageretur, tumultu exorto in populo, quod mysteria Cereris divulgasset, ad Bachiaden confugit, sed inde abreptus, & tractus est ad judicium Areopagitarum, apud quos se excusavit, nescivisse se ista mysteria plane fuisse mysteria, & ideo non divulganda, & ideo judicio Areopagitarum absolutus est, quod nec dedita opera hoc fecisset, nec facti circumstantias scivisset. Caeterum quia dicit Philosophus actionem ex ignorantia mereri veniam, propropterea quod fit plane invita, quaedam potest: An homine actio ex ignorantia, post dicti invita? Et Respond. aliam esse ignorantiam universalem seu ignorantiam juris universalis, aliam particularem, quae dicitur ignorantia aut juris particularis aut facti. Ignorantia juris universalis non potest dici invita, sed potius affecta et voluntaria, et ideo non meretur veniam. Quilibet enim rationis recte compos, tenetur scire praecepta communia de honesto et turpi, justo et injusto, et ejusmodi universalia principia, secundum quae omnes vitae actiones recte instituere et formare possit: At vero ignorantia juris particularis vel facti potest dici invita, et ideo mereri veniam, si modo poenitentiam et tristitiam cum facto adjunctam habeat, secus vero si poenitentia nulla sequatur, factum non possit dici invita actio, sed potius mixta quaedam ex spontanea et invita, nam ratione voluntatis praecedentis actionem, quatenus facti circumstantias scivit, potest dici invita: at vero ratione voluntatis subsequentis, quae nullum poenitentiae aut moeroris indicium praefert, potest dici spontanea. Hinc non omnes, qui ex ignorantia juris particularis peccant, veniam promerentur, sed quos post factum errore deprehenso, serio facti poeniter, et hoc illud est, quod vult Philosophus 2. cap. 3. Nicom. cum dicit, aliam esse ignorantiam singularium, quae dolorifica appellatur, quae dolorem et poenitentiam conjunctam habet, aliam doloris et poenitentiae expertem, quae ostendit voluntatem agentis a facto penitus non abhorruisse, sed suo potius consensu approbasse. Voluntas cum non plene, sed ex parte fertur ad objectum, proproducit actiones, quæ vulgò vocantur mixtæ,quæ ratione principii interni, unde fluunt, possunt dici spontaneæ, ratione verò causæ impellentis, quæ extrinsecus est principium ad agendum, possunt dici invitæ, & quia non plane sunt spontaneæ nec invitæ,dicuntur ex reversione extremorum mixtæ: at si cum externis conferantur magis accedunt ad naturam spontaneæ actionis, quam invitæ propter has rationes. 1. respectu finis, quia omnis finis est boni alicujus sive revera sive apparentis, & ideo finem tanquam aliquod bonum sponte assequitur. 2. ratione principii unde fluunt, nam in ejusmodi actionibus mixtis præcedit consultatio & præelectio rectæ rationi consentanea, verbi gratia, inquit Philosoph. 3. Nicom. cap. 1. si parentes aut liberi alicujus viri boni penes crudelem tyrannum sint, nisi ipse vir bonus aliquid contra decorum faciat, ut tyranno morem gerat, mortem & interitum tyrannus iis, qui in sua potestate sunt, minatur, tum vir bonus maturam consultationem adhibet, & cum consuluerit quo facto opus sit, tunc sibi eligit, quod sibi optime videtur, non tamen plane sponte nec plane invite, magis tamen sponte quàm invitè consultat & præeligit. 3. ratione mediorum & instrumentorum, per quæ ad finem collimant istæ actiones mixtæ, nam ista media sunt plane in agentis potestate, etsi ratione finis vis externa sit adhibita, ita ut necessario agens cogatur aut hunc aut illum finem saltem appetere, mediis tamen ad istum finem ducentibus liberè pro libitu suo uti poterit, ut sint in ejus potestate, verbi gratia, si quis in latronum manus incideri[t]. aerit, & vitæ retinendæ gratia velit pecuniæ summam enumerare, nisi de se ipso actum esse velit. Hic etsi finis sit plane ex coactione, nempe aut numerare pecuniæ summam, aut interire, tamen poterit præbere jugulum potius, quam hoc facere, & ideo liberum est ei, quem velit finem eligere. 4. demum quia violentia abest respectu objecti, quod appetunt, & ignorantia circumstantiarum, quæ rem producendam spectant, quæ quidem conditiones cum competant actionibus spontaneis, ut ex definitione patet, ideo mixtæ actiones inclinant potius ad naturam spontaneæ actionis quam invitæ. Cæterum quia diximus, aliud esse per ignorantiam agere, aliud ignoranter agere, quæri potest, an ignoranter agere sit sponte agere, aut etiam mixte agere? 1. nec plane spontè, nec invitè. Et de hac opinione sunt differentes Platonis & Aristotelis sententiæ. Plato enim dialog. 9. de leg. hujusmodi actiones ad mixtas refert. Aristoteles vero lib. 3. Nicom. cap. 1. sub finem, istas actiones ab ira vel cupiditate promanantes sponte fieri contendit. Et rationes suas addit Aristoteles: Plato vero asserit ideo istas actiones esse mixtas. 1. quia primæ animi perturbationes non sunt in nostra potestate, utpote quæ sunt naturales & non prohibitu nostro feruntur, sed ad præscriptum & legem naturæ, & quia non sunt in nostra potestate, ideo quæ ab iis fiunt, non plane à voluntate nostra pendent, ideo etiam, quæ dependent ab iis, non sponte à nobis fieri dicuntur, nam quale est principium, talis est actio promanans ex isto principio. 2. Si quæ per ignorantiam facti fiant, & veritate perspecta dolor & pœnitentia non sequatur factum, non dicantur neque invitè fieri neque etiam sponte, sed media inter sponte & invitè facta, ideo etiam, quæ ab ira aut cupiditate, vel animi perturbatione vehementi fiunt, medio modo fieri dicuntur, nempe mentis perturbatione, quæ judicium mentis omne pervertit, ut homo nesciat, quid agat, & ideo ex ignorantia agat, & similiter, quæ per ignorantiā facti fiunt, si sequatur pœnitentia, vel dolor, invitè fieri dicuntur, & etiā quæ ex ira aut cupiditate, &c. si pœnitentia facti sequatur, dicuntur etiam invitè fieri. 3. Quæ veniunt ab ira & cupiditate veniam merentur, si modo agens pœnitentiam agat, culpam deprecetur & peccasse se ingenuè profiteatur. Ergò quæ fiunt ab his affectibus, non fiunt sponte. Aristoteles econtra sponte fieri ista contendit his rationibus. 1. Quæ à natura fieri dicuntur, sponte fieri dicuntur, etsi cum cognitione iste appetitus non sit conjunctus. Ergò multò magis quæ ab homine fieri dicuntur, in quo est cognitio & appetitus rationalis. 2. Honesta, quæ fiunt ab ira aut cupiditate, sponte fieri dicuntur, propterea quod fluant à principio rectæ rationi consentaneo. Ergò etiam turpia, quia contrariorum eadem est ratio. Cum igitur, quæ fiunt ab ira, cupiditate, &c. sint vel honesta vel turpia, est, ista omnia sponte fiant, ergò omnes istæ actiones ab ira & cupiditate profluentes erunt spontaneæ. 3. Illa dicuntur sponte fieri, quæ fluunt à principio interno, & quæ habent jucunditatem quandam in actione adjunctam, ut patet ex definitione spontaneæ actionis. Ergò quæcunque fiunt ab ira & cupiditate aut alia animi perturbatio-ne sponte fieri dicentur, propterea quod fluant à principio interno,cap.3 lib.3.Nic. verbi gratia, qui ex ira aliquid facit, id facit ex principio interno & ebul-litione sanguinis circa cor scilicet & in actione habet conjunctam jucunditatem, toto enim impetu ad istam actionem fertur. 4. Quia quae fiunt ex ira & cupiditate neque per violentiam fiunt neque per ignorantiam. Ergo sponte fieri dicuntur, nam uno contrariorum remoto, alterum ponitur. Pro decisione huius quaestionis propositae, non ada sunt quaedam theoremata. 1. Aliud esse hominem iratum aliquid agere, & aliud hominem per iram aliquid agere. Prius enim latius patet quam posterius, sicut & ignoranter agere & per ignorantiam agere, nam omnis, qui per iram agit, iratus agit, sed non e contra. Per iram dicitur aliquis agere, quando ira est principalis causa ejus actionis, & nisi ira adesset, quae ad hanc actionem impellit, non ageret, iratus vero dicitur aliquid agere, quando ira non est principalis causa actionis, & sic iratus saepenumero multa consentanea rectae rationi facit, ut verbi gratia, cum aliquis iratus suis vitiis abstinet, & in contrarias virtutes fertur, quae actio procedit à recta dispositione seu generatione animi licet irati. 2. Notandum est spontaneum aliter ab Aristotele dici, aliter à Platone. Spontaneum ab Aristotele dicitur, quod habet principium internum & neque à coactione neque ab ignorantia facti poenitentis provenit, quatenus scilicet opponitur invita, quod per violentiam & ignorantiam fit. Spontaneum à Platone dicitur non tantum quod habet principium internum, sed etiam quàdo principium illud est obscuratum & perturbatum. Igitur neq; recta ratione recte non utatur, sicut nec illi qui per iram aliquid faciunt. Et negat Plato spontaneum posse plane dici, quod nō à ratione sincera & omni perturbatione libera proveniit, sicut inquit, neq; bestiæ, neque pueri sponte agunt, propterea quod illæ bestiæ ratione plane careant, istam rationem sinceram ac confirmatam adhuc non habeant.3. Verior est sententia Aristot. propterea quod quæ fiunt ab ira, cupiditate, &c. fiant à principio interno, neq; etiam à coactione aut ab ignorantia, sed notitia circumstantiarum ejus actionis, quam intedit agens, & si ex ira agat, unde ex definitione spontaneæ actionis, quæ ei competit, quæ ab ira vel cupiditate, &c. fiunt. Spontaneæ ergo illæ plane esse cum Arist. concludimus. 1. Atque hæc de voluntate actionis, triplici affectu voluntatis quatenus scil. naturæ voluntatis explicandę inserviunt in appetitione objecti sui. Cœterum cum voluntas fertur ad obiectum suum externum, interdum gignit in appetitu & sensu jucunditatem quandam & suavem commotionem si ad perfectionem operationis suæ nullo impedimento injecto feratur, & hæc commotio dicitur voluptas ex appetitu & sensu. At si in appetitione obiecti impedimentum aliquod injiciatur sive ex parte sui sive ex parte medio-rum, gignit tristitiam & mœrorem quendam in appetitu & sensu, inde oritur ex actionibus voluptatis dolor, & circa hæc duo nempe voluptatem & dolorem tanquam obiectum aliquod secundarium versari dicit Philosophus virtutes morales c. 3. 1. Nicom. Cæterum cum voluptas & duplex, alia interra ani-mi. mi, quae ex actionibus praeclare gestis & ipsa animi tranquillitate oritur, de ista interna tanquam obiecto non agit Philosophus, propterea quod ista sit appendix ipsius felicitatis, & ipsam felicitatem necessario sequitur: alia est externa, quae ex appetitu & sensu oritur in actionibus, & de ista tanquam obiecto, sicut de eius oppositio dolore, nempe agendi esse in Ethicis, probat Philosophus loco citato, variis rationibus, ut ibidem videre licet. Notandum tamen, etsi maxime virtutes morales versentur circa dolorem & voluptatem, quae ex sensu & appetitu oriuntur, versari etiam circa voluptatem animi internam quatenus scilicet virtutes animi moderatione indigent maxime, ubi voluptas & dolor accedunt. 2. Notandum, etsi circa dolorem sicut & circa voluptatem versentur virtutes morales, magis tamen circa voluptatem, quam dolorem, tum quia voluptas est communis nobis cum bestiis, tum quia est assidua comes rerum eligendarum, tum quia nobiscum educata est, & vitam continuo insequitur, quod scilicet reddat vitam gratiorem, tum quia difficilius est voluptari, quam dolori moderari, nam ubi voluptas fertur in aliquod obiectum, ut effrenis quaedam bestia inordinato impetu fertur, & ideo est omnium vehementissima passionum, a qua homines saepe moriuntur, cum a nulla alia passione hoc eveniat. Caeterum potest dubitare hic aliquis, an verum sit voluptatem esse omnium passionum vehementissimam & fortissimam, nam ita videtur ex effectu multo vehementior, sola enim est ministra rationis, sola arma ministrat, sola hominem ad vindictam impellit, sola hominem alterat & permutat,ut experientia docet. Resp. Iram quidem quoad effecta externa,quae operatur extra subjectum suum esse multo vehementiorem passione quam sit voluptas: non vero quoad effecta interna ejus subjecti,cui inest, nam non deprehensum estiram enecasse hominem,in quo inesset: voluptas vero saepe hoc effecit, quod variae testantur historiae. Nam Philon Lacedaemonius, cum filium Olympiacoronatu amplexus est, prae nimia voluptate, qua assi-ciebatur, statim exspiravit, teste Laertio lib. 1. in vita Philof. Hoc etiam de Sophocle in Dionysio majore Siciliae Tyranno refert, Plin.nat.hist.l.7.c.7. & ejusmodi exempla multa refert Valerius Maximus,lib.3.c.f. de morte non vulgari: & Cicero de Timagio quodam Rhodio lib.1.Tusc.quaest.& Gellius lib 3 cap.16.
units.tr: Crowned with ivy. natos. An action is also done unwillingly through ignorance, when it arises from ignorance as its principal cause. Yet the Philosopher, cap. 2. 3. Nicom., warns that we must carefully distinguish between two things: acting from ignorance and acting ignorantly. To act ignorantly is to act in such a way that you do not know, at the time you act, whatever you are doing. But ignorance is not the cause of that wrong action. Some other vice has led to the action, as when someone commits a crime under the influence of a violent disturbance of mind, or of drunkenness or some similar sinful passion.
