For example, when someone kills a man while drunk, he acts ignorantly, in so far as those sinful passions cloud and darken his mind. Yet he does not act from ignorance, for he could have known the circumstances of the deed, and so he deserves neither pardon nor excuse. To act from ignorance, on the other hand, is to act in such a way that the ignorance is the cause of the wrong action, so that the agent could not have known the circumstances of the deed and did not bring this ignorance upon himself. The Philosopher gives a clear example in Aeschylus, the tragic poet, who wrote a tragedy he called The Mysteries of Ceres. When it was performed in the theatre, a tumult arose among the people because he had divulged the mysteries of Ceres. He fled to Bachiades, but was dragged from there and brought before the court of the Areopagites. There he defended himself by saying that he had not known that these things were plainly mysteries, and so they should not be divulged, and so he was acquitted by the judgment of the Areopagites, since he had neither done this deliberately nor known the circumstances of the deed. Moreover, because the Philosopher says that an action done from ignorance deserves pardon, since it is wholly unwilling, someone may ask: Is an action done from ignorance, after all, unwilling? The answer is that there is one universal ignorance, or ignorance of universal law, and another particular ignorance, which is called ignorance either of particular law or of fact. Universal ignorance of law cannot be called unwilling, but rather deliberate and voluntary, and so it does not deserve pardon. For every person who is rightly in possession of reason is bound to know the common precepts about what is honourable and shameful, just and unjust, and universal principles of this kind, by which he can rightly arrange and shape all the actions of his life. But ignorance of particular law or of fact can be called unwilling, and so deserve pardon, provided that repentance and sorrow for the deed follow it. Otherwise, if no repentance follows, the action cannot be called unwilling, but rather a mixed action, partly voluntary and partly unwilling. For by reason of the prior will, in so far as he knew the circumstances of the deed, it can be called unwilling; but by reason of the subsequent will, which shows no sign of repentance or grief, it can be called voluntary. Hence not all who sin through ignorance of particular law merit pardon, but only those who, after the error has been discovered, sincerely repent of the deed. This is what the Philosopher means in 2. cap. 3. Nicom., when he says that there is one kind of ignorance of particulars which is called painful, since it has grief and repentance joined to it, and another kind which is free of grief and repentance, and which shows that the will of the agent did not wholly shrink from the deed, but rather approved it with his consent. Since the will is carried towards its object not fully but partly, it produces actions which are commonly called mixed. By reason of the internal principle from which they flow, they can be called voluntary; but by reason of the compelling cause, which is an external principle of action, they can be called unwilling. Because they are neither plainly voluntary nor plainly unwilling, they are called mixed, from the reciprocal relation of the extremes. Yet if they are compared with the external causes, they come closer to the nature of a voluntary action than of an unwilling one, for these reasons: (1) with respect to the end, since every end is of some good, whether real or apparent, and so the agent voluntarily pursues the end as some good; (2) by reason of the principle from which they flow, for in such mixed actions there comes first deliberation and prior choice in agreement with right reason. For example, the Philosopher says, 3. Nicom. cap. 1., that if the parents or children of a good man are in the power of a cruel tyrant, and the tyrant threatens death and destruction to those in his power unless the good man does something shameful to please him, then the good man takes careful counsel. When he has considered what must be done, he then chooses what seems best to him, yet not wholly voluntarily nor wholly unwillingly, but more voluntarily than unwillingly does he deliberate and prefer; (3) by reason of the means and instruments through which these mixed actions aim at their end. For these means are wholly within the agent's power, even though external force has been applied with respect to the end, so that the agent is necessarily compelled to desire at least this end or that one. Yet he can freely use the means that lead to that end as he pleases, so that they are within his power. For example, if someone falls into the hands of robbers, and to keep his life wishes to count out a sum of money, unless he wants to be done away with. Here, although the end is wholly forced, namely either to count out the sum of money or to perish, he may still prefer to offer his throat rather than do this, and so it is up to him which end he chooses; (4) finally, because there is no violence with respect to the object they seek, and the ignorance concerns the circumstances bearing on the thing to be done. These conditions belong to voluntary actions, as is clear from the definition, and so mixed actions incline more to the nature of a voluntary action than of an unwilling one. Moreover, since we have said that to act through ignorance is one thing and to act ignorantly is another, the question may be asked: Is acting ignorantly to act voluntarily, or to act mixedly? (1) Not plainly voluntarily, nor unwillingly. Here the opinions of Plato and Aristotle differ. For Plato, Dialogue 9 of the Laws, refers such actions to the mixed kind. But Aristotle, Book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, ch. 1, near the end, insists that actions proceeding from anger or desire are done voluntarily. Aristotle adds his own reasons, and Plato asserts that these actions are mixed for the following reasons. (1) The first disturbances of the mind are not in our power, since they are natural and are not carried on by our decision, but according to the rule and law of nature. And since they are not in our power, the actions done by them do not depend wholly on our will. Therefore, those actions which depend on them are not said to be done by us voluntarily, for the action is of the same kind as its principle. (2) If things done through ignorance of fact, when the truth is seen, are followed by no grief or repentance, they are said to be done neither unwillingly nor voluntarily, but as something between the two. So too, actions done from anger or desire or some violent disturbance of mind are said to be done in an intermediate way, namely through a disturbance of mind which overturns all the judgment of the mind, so that the man does not know what he is doing and acts from ignorance. Likewise, things done through ignorance of fact are said to be done unwillingly if repentance or grief follows, and so too for things done from anger or desire, etc.; if repentance for the deed follows, they are said to be done unwillingly. (3) Those things which come from anger and desire deserve pardon, provided that the agent repents, asks forgiveness for his fault, and frankly confesses that he has sinned. Therefore, the things done from these passions are not done voluntarily. Aristotle, on the contrary, insists by these reasons that they are done voluntarily. (1) Things said to be done by nature are said to be done voluntarily, even though this appetite is not joined with knowledge. Much more, then, things said to be done by a human being, in whom there is knowledge and rational appetite. (2) Honourable deeds done from anger or desire are said to be done voluntarily, because they flow from a principle in agreement with right reason. Therefore shameful deeds too, since the reason for contraries is the same. Since, then, the things done from anger, desire, etc. are either honourable or shameful, all these things are done voluntarily; therefore all actions flowing from anger and desire will be voluntary. (3) Those things are said to be done voluntarily which flow from an internal principle, and which have a certain pleasure joined to the action, as is clear from the definition of a voluntary action. Therefore whatever is done from anger, desire, or another disturbance of mind will be said to be done voluntarily, because it flows from an internal principle. Ch. 3, Book 3 Nic. For example, whoever does something from anger does it from an internal principle, namely the boiling of the blood about the heart, and in the action there is joined a certain pleasure, for he is carried to that action with his whole impetus. (4) Because things done from anger and desire are done neither through violence nor through ignorance, they are said to be done voluntarily; for when one of two contraries is removed, the other is posited. To decide the question proposed, the following propositions may be added. (1) It is one thing for a man to do something while angry, and another for a man to do something through anger. The former has a wider scope than the latter, just as acting ignorantly and acting through ignorance differ, for everyone who acts through anger acts while angry, but not the reverse. A person is said to act through anger when anger is the principal cause of that action, and if the anger which drives him to this action were not present, he would not act. But a man is said to do something while angry when anger is not the principal cause of the action. So an angry man often does many things in agreement with right reason, as when, being angry, he abstains from his vices and is carried towards contrary virtues, an action which proceeds from a right disposition or generation of the mind, even though he is angry. (2) It must be noted that Aristotle and Plato use the word voluntary in different ways. For Aristotle, the voluntary is what has an internal principle and does not arise from compulsion or from ignorance of the facts that the agent repents of, that is, what is opposed to the unwilling, which is done through violence and ignorance. For Plato, the voluntary is called not only what has an internal principle, but also what proceeds when that principle is darkened and disturbed. Therefore those who do something through anger do not use right reason rightly. Plato also denies that what does not proceed from sincere reason, free of all disturbance, can be called voluntary in the full sense. He says that neither beasts nor children act voluntarily, because beasts wholly lack reason and do not yet have that sincere and confirmed reason. (3) Aristotle's opinion is more true, because things done from anger, desire, etc. come from an internal principle, and not from compulsion or ignorance, but from knowledge of the circumstances of the action which the agent understands. If he acts from anger, this agrees with the definition of a voluntary action, which fits those things done from anger or desire, etc. So we conclude with Aristotle that these are plainly voluntary. (1) Thus far concerning the will in action, which serves to explain the nature of the will as it is threefold in its desire for its object. But when the will is carried towards its external object, it sometimes produces in appetite and sense a certain pleasure and a sweet emotion, if it is carried towards the perfection of its operation without any impediment. This emotion is called pleasure of appetite and sense. But if some impediment is placed in the pursuit of the object, whether on the part of the object or on the part of the means, it produces a certain sadness and grief in appetite and sense, and from the actions of pleasure there arises pain. The Philosopher says that the moral virtues are concerned with these two, namely pleasure and pain, as with a certain secondary object, Nic. Ethics 1, ch. 3. But since pleasure is twofold, one kind internal to the mind, which arises from actions well performed and from the tranquillity of the mind itself, the Philosopher does not treat of this internal pleasure as an object, because it is an appendage of happiness itself and necessarily follows happiness. The other kind is external, which arises in actions from appetite and sense, and it is of this, as an object, and of its opposite pain, that the Philosopher, in the passage cited, proves by various arguments that one must treat in ethics, as may be seen there. It must be noted, however, that although the moral virtues are chiefly concerned with pain and pleasure arising from sense and appetite, they are also concerned with the internal pleasure of the mind, in so far as the virtues especially need moderation of the mind when pleasure and pain come upon it. (2) It must be noted that although the moral virtues are concerned with pain as well as with pleasure, they are more concerned with pleasure than with pain, for several reasons: because pleasure is common to us and to the beasts; because it is the constant companion of things to be chosen; because it is raised along with us and continually follows life, so that it makes life more pleasant; and because it is more difficult to moderate pleasure than to moderate pain. For when pleasure is carried towards some object, it is carried with an impetus, like an unbridled beast, and so it is the most vehement of all passions, by which men often die, which happens from no other passion. Here someone might doubt whether it is true that pleasure is the most vehement and strongest of all passions, for it seems so from its effects, since it alone is the servant of reason, it alone supplies arms, it alone drives a man to revenge, and it alone alters and transforms a man, as experience teaches. The answer is that anger, indeed, with respect to its external effects, which it works outside its subject, is much more vehement than pleasure. But it is not so with respect to the internal effects on the subject in which it is present, for it has not been found that anger has killed the man in whom it resides. Pleasure, however, has often done this, as various histories testify. For Philon the Lacedaemonian, when he embraced his son crowned at Olympia, immediately expired because of the excess of pleasure with which he was affected, as Laertius reports, Book 1, in the life of Philo. Pliny, Natural History, Book 7, ch. 7, reports the same of Sophocles in the time of Dionysius the Elder, tyrant of Sicily. Valerius Maximus, Book 3, ch. last, on an uncommon death, reports many such examples; and Cicero concerning a certain Timagenes of Rhodes, Tusculan Disputations Book 1, and Gellius, Book 3, ch. 16.

units.la: Quaeritur,an voluptas actione iam expedita & perfecta maneat,an simul etiam cum actione evanescat? Et respondetur, tam diu durare voluptatem, quamdiu potentia operandi in objecto manet,ut ex ista operatione laetitia aliqua gignatur, propter perfectionem operationis instantem. At ubi cessit potentia operandi in objectum, tum etiam cessit voluptas aut saltem fit debilior, propterea quod objecti potentia vilescat. Ratio est,quia nulla hujusmodi voluptas perpetua esse potest, quod nulla functio sensus, & appetitus durare perpetuo possit, ideo neq; voluptas, quae oritur ex ista functione. Haec sic breviter de Felicitate in genero dicta sint, jam ad textum Aristotelis.
units.tr: The question is raised: does pleasure remain once the action is already carried out and complete, or does it vanish together with the action? The answer is that pleasure lasts as long as the power of acting remains directed at the object, so that some joy arises from that activity on account of the perfection of the operation which is at hand. But when the power of acting has ceased to be directed at the object, then the pleasure also ceases, or at least becomes weaker, because the object's power to please diminishes. The reason is that no pleasure of this kind can be perpetual, since no function of the senses or of the appetite can continue for ever, and therefore neither can the pleasure which arises from that function. These points have been stated briefly concerning happiness in general; now let us turn to the text of Aristotle.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: TRaditam jam definitione Felicitatis ex sua opinione fusius explicare nititur Philosophus trib. bifce capitibus proxime sequentib. ut sic suam definitionem veram esse confirmet, & veteres aliter de summo bono sentientes taxet: In hoc capite praestruit viam quandam ad singulas definitionis partes latius explicandas. Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima ostendit artium & scientiarum explicationes ab initio breves & rudes fuisse, postmodum vero temporis progressu prolixiores & magis expeditas factas esse. In secunda parte ostendit, non in omnibus artibus eandem quaerendam esse subtilitatem, aut accuratum tractandi modum, sed pro materiae diversitate, nunc majorem nunc minorem adhibendam esse utilitatem, quod exemplo illustrat, Geometra & faber versantur circa considerationem anguli, sed faber non accurate inquirit de natura anguli, sed sufficit illi, si operi producendo inserviat angulus. Geometra vero & naturam anguli explorat, & causas, cur hoc vel illo modo construatur, inquirit: Ideo & si circa eandem materiam versentur diversae disciplinae, tamen subtilitas non est transferenda ex una in aliam, sed modus tractandi proprius cuique disciplinae servari debet. In tertia parte capitis excusat se, quod singularum partium in definitione felicitatis causas non adduxerit, propterea quod in principiis, cujusmodi est ipsa felicitas, ut supra c.2. dixerat, non requiritur cognitio a causis: nam non habet causas se priores, quia principiis nihil est prius, ideo probantur vel in-duductione & sensu, ut principia Mathematica, & plê raque Physica universalia, vel usu & experientia, ut principia Ethica & Medica, vel mens statim amplecitur tanquam vera & infallibilia, cujusmodi sunt illa principia, quæ vocantur communes notiones seu principia nobiscum nata.
units.tr: Having set out the definition of happiness as it stands, the Philosopher undertakes to explain it more fully according to his own view in the three following chapters. His aim is to confirm that his definition is true and to censure the ancients, who thought differently about the highest good. In this chapter he prepares a path for explaining each part of the definition more broadly. The chapter has three parts. In the first he shows that the explanations of the arts and sciences were at first brief and crude, and that later, as time went on, they became fuller and more efficient. In the second part he shows that the same precision or exact method is not to be sought in every art, but that, according to the diversity of the subject matter, a greater or lesser degree of exactness is to be applied. He illustrates this with an example: the geometer and the craftsman both deal with the consideration of an angle, but the craftsman does not inquire exactly into the nature of the angle; it is enough for him if the angle serves the work he is producing. The geometer, however, examines the nature of the angle and inquires into the causes of why it is constructed in this or that way. So, although different disciplines may deal with the same matter, precision is not to be carried over from one into another; each discipline must keep its own method of treatment. In the third part of the chapter he excuses himself for not having given the causes of each part of the definition of happiness, because, as he had said above, chapter 2, knowledge of causes is not required in first principles, such as happiness itself. For first principles have no prior causes, since nothing is prior to a first principle. Therefore they are proved either by induction and sense, like the principles of mathematics and most universal principles of physics, or by use and experience, like the principles of ethics and medicine, or the mind embraces them at once as true and infallible, as are those principles called common notions or innate principles.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Facile est inventis addere, sed non æque facile invenire, cum illud ingenium solers, hoc tantum sequax & sedulum requirere videatur.
units.tr: 1. It is easy to add to discoveries, but not equally easy to make them, since the one seems to require a clever wit, while the other requires only a diligent and compliant one.

units.la: 2. Principia a prioribus non possunt probari, cum nihil se prius, quia talia habeant.
units.tr: 2. First principles cannot be proved from earlier ones, since nothing is prior to them, if they have such things.

units.la: 3. Principia aut sensu aut inductione, aut ipsa ratione probantur, hic vide 2. posteriorum analyt. cap. ult.
units.tr: 3. First principles are proved either by sense, or by induction, or by reason itself; see here Posterior Analytics 2, last chapter.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DIFFICULTIES.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Cur in textu Aristoteles dicat tempus esse inventorem & adjutorem artium, cum tempus per se nihil agat? Resp. Proprie quidem & sua natura tempus nihil agere, sed quia quamplura eveniunt temporis progressu, quæ occasionem præbent artes melius & accuratius explicandi, ideo tempus vocat inventorem & adjutorem artium.
units.tr: I. Question: Why does Aristotle in the text say that time is the discoverer and helper of the arts, when time by itself does nothing? Answer: Strictly speaking, and by its nature, time does nothing. But because many things happen as time goes on that offer occasion for explaining the arts better and more accurately, for this reason he calls time the discoverer and helper of the arts.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Cur sub finem capitis dicat, principium esse plus dimidio totius, & quomodo hoc fit intelligendum? Resp. Ideo dici, quia principia virtute continent in se totum, utpote ex quibus totum pervenit, nam a principiis totum dependet, ut effectus a causis, & ideo Plato in Cratil. & 1. de legib. monet, unicuique laborandum esse, ut principia tanquam fundamenta prudenter statuat, & 7. de legib. hoc argumento usus, hoc ipso proverbio Politicum monet, ut diligenter curam adhibeat in pueris recte instituedis, tanquam totius Reipub. seminariis: nam cum principium sit plus de medio totius, si recte primo instituatur pueri, utiles per totam vitam futuri sunt Reipub. Sic & Aristoteles lib. 5. Polit. cap. 4. monet hoc ipso, initia seditionum in Republ. esse cavenda, ne parvum, inquit, error in principio fiat, major in progressu, & maximus in excessu.
units.tr: II. Question: Why does he say at the end of the chapter that the beginning is more than half of the whole, and how is this to be understood? Answer: It is said because the principles contain the whole within themselves in power, since the whole comes forth from them; for the whole depends on its principles as an effect depends on its causes. Therefore Plato, in the Cratylus and in Laws 1, warns that each person must labour to lay down principles prudently as foundations. And in Laws 7, using this same argument and this very proverb, he warns the statesman to take diligent care in properly educating children, as the seedbeds of the whole commonwealth: for since the beginning is more than half of the whole, if children are rightly trained from the start, they will be useful to the commonwealth throughout their whole lives. Thus also Aristotle, Politics 5, chapter 4, warns by this same saying that the beginnings of sedition in a commonwealth must be guarded against: "lest a small error at the beginning becomes greater in its progress and greatest in its outcome."

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: POstquam praestruxit sibi viam ad singulas definitionis partes accurate explicandas, jam ipsas partes à consensu veterum singulatim comprobat. Partes huius capitis sunt duae: In prima ostendit res controversas, cujusmodi est felicitas, non argumentis tantum evidentibus & certis rationibus esse stabiliendas, sed etiam auctoritatibus & testimoniis virorum insignium, maxime vero Philosophorum, & hoc comprobat à communi axiomate, quia verum cum vero consentit, à falso vero dissentit, quae igitur veteres vera dixere, cum nostra definitione tanquam vera consentient, quae vero falsa, dissentient. Et sic, ut vulgo dicitur, contraria juxta seposita maxime elucescunt. In secunda parte capitis genus felicitatis, nempe actionem recte à se assignatam comprobat à consensu veterum tribus hisce argumentis: Triplicia sunt hominis bona, alia animi, alia corporis, alia externa, quae divisio admittetur tanquam vera ab omnibus aut saltem plerisque veterum. 1. A Socrate, ut est apud Plat. lib. 5. de legib. & 9. in Phaedone Philos. à Stoicis omnibus, ut testis est Cicero 1. Acad. quaest. & 5. Tusc. Cum igitur inter haec bona præstantissima judicarunt bona animi, & ideo in bonis animi posuerunt felicitatem, idem quod nos, dixerunt, nam nos ponimus esse actionem animi. 2. Et hoc convenit inter nos vernaculam cujusquerei actionem seu peculiarem esse ejus rei finem, nam & nos dicimus felicitatem esse propriam hominis actionem & ultimum ejus finem. 3. Dixerunt veteres idem esse feliciter vivere, quod bene vivere & bene agere. Ergo pro certo statuerunt actionem genus ejus legitimum.
units.tr: Having paved his way to explaining each part of the definition precisely, he now confirms each of its parts by the agreement of the ancients. The parts of this chapter are two. In the first, he shows that controverted matters, such as happiness, must be established not only by clear arguments and certain reasons but also by the authorities and testimonies of distinguished men, and above all of the philosophers. He proves this from the common axiom, that truth agrees with truth and dissents from falsehood. So whatever the ancients said that was true will agree with our definition as true, and whatever they said that was false will disagree with it. And so, as the common saying goes, opposites are most clearly brought out when set side by side. In the second part of the chapter, he confirms the genus of happiness, namely that it is an activity, the one he has assigned, by the agreement of the ancients, using these three arguments: There are three kinds of human good, some of the mind, some of the body, and some external. This division will be admitted as true by all of the ancients, or at least by most of them. (1) From Socrates, as found in Plato, Laws, book 5, and Philebus, in the Phaedo; from all the Stoics, as Cicero is a witness in Academica, book 1, and Tusculanae, book 5. Since they judged that the goods of the mind were the most excellent of these goods, and therefore placed happiness among the goods of the mind, they said the same as we do, for we hold that happiness is an activity of the mind. (2) It is agreed between us that the proper activity of each thing is its peculiar end, for we too say that happiness is the proper activity of man and his ultimate end. (3) The ancients said that to live happily is the same as to live well and to act well. Therefore they rightly established that activity is its proper genus.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Res controversæ non rationibus tantum, sed autoritatibus etiam virorum insignium comprobanda sunt.
units.tr: 1. Controverted matters must be proved not only by reasons but also by the authorities of distinguished men.

units.la: 2. Cum verum vero consentit, à falso dissentit.
units.tr: 2. When truth agrees with truth, it dissents from falsehood.

units.la: 3. Triplex est hominis bonum, animi, corporis, & fortuna.
units.tr: 3. There is a threefold good of man: of the mind, of the body, and of fortune.

units.la: DUBIUM.
units.tr: DOUBT.

units.la: Quæritur: Cur Aristoteles approbarit veterum opinionem dicentium, actionem rei esse finem, cum actio tantum sit motio ad finem, & ubi sit, ibi cum definit actio? Resp. Distinguendum esse inter actionem universalem (cujusmodi est felicitas ipsa, & ad quam omnes & singulares actiones tanquam ad finem referuntur) & inter particularem, nam particularis actio est motio, propter finem, & de hac universali locutus est Philosophus, cum dixit actionem esse finem, & ideo de hac particulari valet argumentum Baridani tantum.
units.tr: The question is asked: why did Aristotle approve the opinion of the ancients who said that the activity of a thing is its end, since an activity is only a motion towards an end, and it ceases when the end is reached? The answer: one must distinguish between universal activity (of which happiness itself is an example, and to which all single activities are referred as to their end) and particular activity, for a particular activity is a motion for the sake of an end. The Philosopher spoke of the universal activity when he said that activity is the end, and therefore the argument of Buridan applies only to the particular activity.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Postquam Genus Definitionis comprobarit à consensu veterum, etiam ulu comprobat ipsam Differentiam. Partes capitis sunt duae: In prima annumerat opiniones insigniores veterum, & ostendit, in quibus consentiant, & quibus dissentiant. In secunda parte ostendit bona externa esse necessaria ad felicitatem tanquam instrumenta. In prima igitur quinque opiniones maxime celebres enumerat, alii enim, inquit, sunt, qui felicitatem statuunt esse in virtute, ut Stoici, alii in prudentia, ut Socrates, vel te Platone in Phaed. alii in sapientia, ut Anaxagoras, de quibus Aristoteles lib. 1. ad End. cap. 5. alii in virtute cum voluptate, ut Plato, alii denique in virtute cum bonis externis conjuncta, ut Zenocrates Aristotelis discipulus, & ante illum Bryson. Harum quinque opinionum duas celebriores eligit, nempe Stoicorum & Platonis, ostendens, in quibus cum definitione data consentiant, & in quibus dissentiant, qui igitur in virtute collocarunt summum bonum, idem fere quod nos dicebant, nam nos statuimus esse actionem secundum virtutem: Dissentiunt vero, quod nos in actione & usu virtutis collocamus, illi vero in habitu & possessione, cujus absurditatem rationibus quibusdam demonstrat, de quibus supra cap. 3. Plato vero, qui in virtute cum voluptate conjuncta statuebat summum bonum aliquid dicebat, nam nos statuimus ex actione virtutis oriri voluptatem, dissentit vero Plato cum suis a vero, quod virtutem & voluptatem, tanquam duo diversa a diversis principiis orta statueret; nam & voluptas & virtus oriuntur ex actione viri boni, tanquam uno eodemque principio. Ex actione enim secundum virtutem gignitur in animo laetitia seu pura voluntas, vide supra ad sin. cap. 6. de qua quaestione ne fufius agit Aristot. lib.10. c.3.4.5.&c. nos ubi egimus de 5.quaest.supra loco citato. Quod vero ab actione viri boni oriatur & virtus & voluptas, probat in textu inductione exemplorum, verbi gratia, qui juste agit, gaudet se juste agere. Ergo ex actione iusta oritur & justitia, & voluptas, unde reprehendit illud Epigramma a Theognide appensum in Templo Apollinis Delphici, quod Justitia tribuerit honestatem, sanitati utilitatem, adeptioni rerum voluptatem quasi ista tria inter se essent diversa, & non ab eodem principio, nempe ab actione bona proficiscerentur. In secunda parte capitis ostendit, quantum Zenocratis opinio cum vero consentiat. Dicebat Zenocrates felicitatem consistere in virtute, cum bonis externis conjuncta, nos etiam dicimus bona externa esse necessaria ad felicitatem, non tamen absolute, sed tanquam instrumenta, quod probat duabus rationibus. 1. Quia si bona externa absint, impediunt actionem felicitatis, verbi gratia liberalitatis, justitiae, &c. nam quod vulgo dicitur.
units.tr: Having established the genus of the definition from the agreement of the ancients, he now confirms the difference by their practice as well. The chapter has two parts. In the first he lists the more notable opinions of the ancients and shows where they agree and where they disagree. In the second he shows that external goods are necessary to happiness as instruments. In the first part, then, he enumerates five very famous opinions. Some, he says, hold that happiness lies in virtue, as the Stoics; others in prudence, as Socrates, or, according to Plato in the Phaedo; others in wisdom, as Anaxagoras, about whom Aristotle speaks in Book 1 of the Ethics, chapter 5; others in virtue together with pleasure, as Plato; and finally others in virtue joined with external goods, as Xenocrates, a pupil of Aristotle, and before him Bryson. Of these five opinions he selects the two more celebrated, namely those of the Stoics and of Plato, and shows where they agree with the definition given and where they disagree. Those who placed the chief good in virtue were saying nearly the same thing as we do, for we hold that it is an activity according to virtue. They differ, however, in that we place it in the activity and exercise of virtue, whereas they place it in the habit and possession of it. He demonstrates the absurdity of this by certain arguments, which are discussed above in chapter 3. Plato, who held that the chief good was virtue joined with pleasure, was saying something true, for we hold that pleasure arises from the activity of virtue. But Plato and his followers depart from the truth in that they hold virtue and pleasure to be two different things arising from different principles. For both pleasure and virtue arise from the action of the good man, as from one and the same principle. For from activity according to virtue there is produced in the mind joy, or pure will; see above, at the end of chapter 6. Aristotle treats this question more fully in Book 10, chapters 3, 4, 5, and so on; we have treated it ourselves in the 5th question above, in the place cited. That both virtue and pleasure arise from the action of the good man he proves in the text by an induction of examples: for instance, he who acts justly rejoices that he acts justly; therefore from just action both justice and pleasure arise. Hence he rebukes that epigram attributed to Theognis and hung in the temple of Apollo at Delphi, which says that justice bestows honour, health bestows usefulness, and the attainment of things bestows pleasure, as if these three were different from one another and did not proceed from the same principle, namely good action. In the second part of the chapter he shows how far the opinion of Xenocrates agrees with the truth. Xenocrates said that happiness consists in virtue joined with external goods. We too say that external goods are necessary to happiness, yet not absolutely, but as instruments. He proves this by two arguments. (1) If external goods are absent, they impede the activity of happiness, for example of liberality, justice, and so on; for what is commonly said is: Those whose virtues are hindered by a narrow household seldom emerge.

units.la: Haud facile emerguut, quorum virtutibus obstat Res angusta domi.
units.tr: Seldom do those rise up whose virtues are held back by a narrow fortune at home.

units.la: 2. Si quis premitur bonis externis, dolore afficitur, &c. & ideo abstrahitur saepe a virtutis actione, ex qua oritur ipsa felicitas, fusius de hac quaestione agit lib. 7. Pol. c.13.
units.tr: (2) If someone is oppressed by lack of external goods, he is afflicted with pain, and so is often drawn away from the activity of virtue, from which happiness itself arises. He treats this question more fully in Book 7 of the Politics, chapter 13.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Quo quis maxime delectatur, ad id maxime fertur.
units.tr: 1. That to which someone is most attracted, to that he is most inclined.

units.la: 2. Voluptas alia est naturalis, alia contra naturam.
units.tr: 2. Pleasure is of two kinds: natural, and contrary to nature.

units.la: 3. Actio proba voluptatem semper habet comitem.
units.tr: 3. An upright action always has pleasure as its companion.

units.la: 4. Bona externa non sunt simpliciter necessaria ad felicitatem, sed tanquam Instrumenta. DUBIUM.
units.tr: 4. External goods are not simply necessary to happiness, but as instruments. A DOUBT.

units.la: Quaeritur: Cur Aristoteles inter bona necessaria ad felicitatem pulchritudinem numerarit, cum id non vere consentaneum videatur, ut variis rationibus probari poterit? Resp. Non requirit Aristoteles pulchritudinem, quae in lineamentis corporis & coloris suavitate constitit, ut ipse seipsum explicat, ne quis sit omnino deformis, nam distortum vultum sequitur distorsio morum plerumque, neque addit necessarium esse ad felicitatem, sed sine hac forma, aliquem non posse esse felicem omnino, quia deformitas externa multum de ornatu & splendore externo felicitatis detrahere videtur, sicut de Aesopo fabulatore Phrygio legimus, vide cap. 6. ubi de sanitate.
units.tr: It is asked: Why does Aristotle count beauty among the goods necessary to happiness, when this does not seem truly consistent, as can be proved by various arguments? Answer: Aristotle does not require that beauty which consists in the features of the body and the pleasantness of colour, as he himself explains, lest anyone be altogether misshapen, for a distorted face usually goes with distorted morals. Nor does he add that it is necessary to happiness in the sense that without this form a person cannot be altogether happy; rather, external deformity seems greatly to diminish the adornment and external splendour of happiness, just as we read of Aesop the Phrygian fabulist. See chapter 6, where he speaks of health.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Postquam partes definitionis quam de Felicitate tradiderat fuse explicasset, posteà captata occasione è superioribus, quod bona externa dixerit necessaria tanquam instrumenta ad felicitatem assequendam sub finem superioris capitis: Hic ne quis putet felicitatem dependere a bonis externis, tanquam a causa, inquirit de causis felicitatis seu quibus mediis perveniatur ad felicitatem. Partes capitis sunt tres. In prima varias opiniones refert de causis felicitatis. In 2. ostendit a Socrate virtute provenire aliquot rationibus. In 3. de iis, qui sunt felicitatis capaces, agit. In prima igitur parte ad imitationem Platonis, quia Men. & Protag. hanc ipsam quæstionem pluri- bus agitat, recenset quinq; opiniones, quæ omnes vulgò æstimantur causæ felicitatis. Dubitatur enim, inquit, an à doctrina, an à consuetudine, an à virtute, an à Deo, an à fortuna proveniat. Quarum priores tres pos- sunt dici internæ causæ, quia ab ipso homine proue- niunt, nempe doctrina, consuetudo, virtus. Aliæ duæ externæ, quia extrinsecus homini adveniunt, nempe Deus & fortuna. In secunda parte capitis agit de his opinionibus, & primò incipit agere de eorū opinione, qui putant à Deo tanquam à prima causa provenire felicitatem, & ait: Si quod fit bonum, quod à Deo provenit, de quo non est dubitandum, certè felicitas tan- quam bonorum maximum provenit. Cæterum leviter & parcè attingit hanc quæstionem, propterea quod Politica agit de rebus humanis non divinis, & adeò relegat ad aliam disciplinam, nempe ad Metaphys. Provenire autem à virtute tanquam à sola causa tri- bus rationibus probat. 1. Etsi felicitas non sit plane di- vinum quid, utpote quod non immediatè à Deo proficiscatur, sed ab usu & exercitio virtutis, cum sit virtutis finis & præmium, ideo est præstantissima, perinde non debet asscribi, fortunæ, causæ tam i- gnobili, nam cum naturalia causam habeant natu- ram, & artificialia causam habeant habitum, & ideo utraq; habeant causam optimam, ridiculum est fe- licitati rerum humanarū summo bono, adscribere fortunam, causam tam ignobilem. 2. Ratio petitur à definitione felicitatis. Felicitas definita est actio se- cundum virtutem, ideo à virtute provenit, & cum animus humanus nihil fortuito agat, sed consultò & deliberatò, ideo felicitas felicitas, cum fit actio animæ rationalis, fortuitò accidere hominι nequit. 3. Quia felicitas est bonum optimum, & finis Politicæ. Politica verò hoc agit, ut cives perfectos & bonos reddat. Ergo felicitatem ejus finem à virtute provenire, & non aliunde necesse est. In tertia parte capitis ostendit, qui sint felicitatis capaces & qui non, cum à virtute proveniat felicitas, ideo bruta ratione carentia provenire ad felicitatem non possunt, neque etiam pueri, quia etsi ratione non destituantur ut bruta, tamen non est firma in iis voluntas & constans electio, nam & per ætatem tenerâm immaturo sunt judicio, nec experientia etiam valent, & ratio redditur ex definitione felicitatis: Felicitas enim requirit virtutem perfectam & vitam perfectam, quæ in pueris reperiri non possunt. Hinc viam sibi sternit ad ea, quæ dictarus est capite sequenti, & an pueri non sunt felicitatis capaces, & multæ accidunt in vita etiam confirmata mutationes, & variæ subinde fortunæ procellæ, vita hominum etiam perfecta jactetur, inquirit, an ille, qui in Priami calamitates & infortunia inciderit, possit dici felix.
units.tr: Having fully explained the parts of the definition he had given of Happiness, he then seized an occasion from the preceding chapter, where at the end he had called external goods necessary as instruments for attaining happiness. Here, lest anyone think happiness depends on external goods as on a cause, he inquires into the causes of happiness, or by what means one arrives at happiness. The chapter has three parts. In the first he reports various opinions about the causes of happiness. In the second he shows, for several reasons, that happiness comes from virtue, as Socrates held. In the third he treats of those who are capable of happiness. In the first part, then, following Plato, who discusses this same question at length in the Meno and Protagoras, he lists five opinions, all of which are commonly regarded as causes of happiness. For it is disputed, he says, whether it comes from teaching, from habit, from virtue, from God, or from fortune. The first three of these can be called internal causes, because they arise from the man himself: teaching, habit, and virtue. The other two are external, because they come to a man from outside: God and fortune. In the second part of the chapter he treats these opinions, and first begins with the view of those who think happiness comes from God as from the first cause, and says: If there is some good that comes from God, about which there is no doubt, then surely happiness, as the greatest of goods, comes from him. But he touches on this question only lightly and sparingly, because Politics deals with human, not divine, matters, and so he refers it to another discipline, namely Metaphysics. That happiness comes from virtue alone, he proves by three reasons: (1) Even though happiness is not strictly something divine, since it does not proceed immediately from God but from the use and exercise of virtue, and since it is the end and reward of virtue, and therefore most excellent, it should not be ascribed to fortune, so ignoble a cause. For natural things have a nature as their cause, and artificial things have a habit as their cause; so both have a best cause. It is absurd to ascribe to fortune, so ignoble a cause, the highest good of human affairs, which is happiness. (2) The reason is drawn from the definition of happiness. Happiness is defined as activity in accordance with virtue; therefore it comes from virtue. And since the human mind does nothing by chance but acts deliberately and with reflection, happiness, since it is an activity of the rational soul, cannot happen to a man by chance. (3) Because happiness is the highest good and the end of Politics. Politics, however, aims at making citizens perfect and good. Therefore it is necessary that its end, happiness, comes from virtue and from nowhere else. In the third part of the chapter he shows who are capable of happiness and who are not. Since happiness comes from virtue, brute animals, lacking reason, cannot attain happiness, and neither can children; for although they are not destitute of reason as brutes are, their will is not firm in them, nor is their choice constant. They are immature in judgment because of their tender age, and they lack experience as well. The reason is given from the definition of happiness: for happiness requires perfect virtue and a perfect life, which cannot be found in children. From this he paves the way for what he will say in the following chapter, whether children are not capable of happiness, and whether many changes occur even in a confirmed life, and various storms of fortune at times, and whether even a perfect human life can be shaken. He inquires whether a man who has fallen into the calamities and misfortunes of Priam can be called happy.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Felicitas est maximum Dei donum, inter morali scilicet, cum sit finis & perfectio.
units.tr: 1. Happiness is the greatest gift of God, among moral goods, since it is both end and perfection.

units.la: 2. Felicitas est finis & præmium virtutis.
units.tr: 2. Happiness is the end and reward of virtue.

units.la: 3. Politicæ finis est, cives bonos & perfectos reddere.
units.tr: 3. The end of Politics is to make citizens good and perfect.

units.la: 4. Pueri non re, sed spe felices dicuntur.
units.tr: 4. Children are called happy not in reality but in hope.

units.la: 5. Bruta, cum ratione destituantur felicia dici nequeunt.
units.tr: 5. Brutes, since they lack reason, cannot be called happy.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: 1. Quæritur, cur Aristoteles felicitatem vocet aliquid dividivinum, cum sit plane humanum quid, & ab actionibus humanis tota proveniat? Respond. Duabus de causis dicitur divinum aliquid. 1. Quia à Deo tanquam rerum omnium prima causa provenit. 2. Quia per felicitatem Deo assimulantur homines, & actiones imitantur, ut paulò infra docet cap. 12.
units.tr: 1. It is asked: why does Aristotle call happiness something divine, when it is plainly something human, and wholly comes from human actions? Answer: Something is called divine for two reasons. 1. Because it comes from God as the first cause of all things. 2. Because through happiness men are made like God and imitate his actions, as he teaches a little later in chapter 12.

units.la: II. Quaeritur, cur neget Aristoteles felicitatem esse quid fortuitum, aut provenire à fortuna, quia ab agente, ut finis certus, cum raro contingat hominibus & extrinsecus proveniat homini, utpote quae ab actionibus in externum objectu editis proficiscatur, at talia sunt fortuita, ut patet 2. Phys. textu 48. Respond. Etsi felicitas raro homini contingat, & extrinsecus accedat, tamen non provenit a fortuna, quia ab agente, ut finis certus & determinatus intenditur, at fortuita non intenduntur ab operante, sed praeter scopum & intentionem adveniunt, verbi gratia. Fodiens terram incidit in serpentem & laeditur, scopus erat terram fodere, & non incidere in serpentem & laedi.
units.tr: II. It is asked: why does Aristotle deny that happiness is something fortuitous, or that it comes from fortune, since an agent aims at a certain end, and since happiness rarely befalls men and comes to them from outside, as it arises from actions directed at an external object; but such things are fortuitous, as is clear in Physics 2, text 48? Answer: Although happiness rarely befalls a man and comes to him from outside, it does not come from fortune, because it is aimed at by the agent as a certain and determined end. Fortuitous things, however, are not intended by the one acting, but come beside the goal and intention. For example: a man digging the ground falls upon a serpent and is injured. His aim was to dig the ground, not to fall upon a serpent and be hurt.

units.la: III. Quaeritur, cur mutilis & mancis deneget felicitatem, cum mutilatio sit vitium corporis, at felicitas sit actio animi, & ideo etsi corpus mutilatur, animus manet integer? Respond. Per mutilos intelligit prava indole praeditos, qui plane in vitia proclives sunt. 2. Quia locomotiva utitur animo ad actiones suas obeundas, si quae pars corporis sit mutila seu manca, actionem facultate corporis ei parti debitam in externum objectum animus edere non potest, & proinde sive ista mutilatio referatur ad animum sive ad corpus, hominem minus aptum reddit, ad virtutis actiones quae obeundas.
units.tr: III. It is asked: why does he deny happiness to the maimed and crippled, since mutilation is a defect of the body, whereas happiness is an activity of the mind, and so even if the body is mutilated, the mind remains whole? Answer: By the maimed he means those endowed with a wicked disposition, who are wholly prone to vices. 2. Because the mind uses the body's locomotion to carry out its actions; if any part of the body is maimed or crippled, the mind cannot direct the faculty of that part, which is due to it, toward an external object so as to perform the action. Therefore, whether this mutilation is referred to the mind or to the body, it makes a man less fit for performing actions of virtue.

units.la: IV. Quæritur, cur negetpueri felicitatem, cumpue-ri non minus sint felicitatis capaces, quam sint ætate perfecta viri,nam talium est Regnum cœlorum,inquit,Christus Mat. 19. & Luc.18. Tales vero esse felices, probatur ex Apoc.c.19. Beati, qui ad cœnam agni nuptiarum vocati sunt, ut tales sunt, quorum est regnum cœlorum? Resp. Spiritualiter sunt felices,non moraliter propter rationes supra al-latas.
units.tr: IV. It is asked: why does he deny happiness to children, since children are no less capable of happiness than grown men? For "of such is the kingdom of heaven," says Christ, Matt. 19 and Luke 18. That such are happy is proved from Rev. 19: "Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb"; as those are whose is the kingdom of heaven? Answer: They are happy spiritually, not morally, for the reasons given above.

units.la: V. Quæritur, an illi, qui incidunt in Priami calamitates & summas hujus vitæ miserias,an non possunt dici felices,quod innuere videtur in text.Philosophus? Resp.Competere iis felicitatem, quoad essentiam non quoad existentiam, manent enim felices, si res adversas fortiter ferant, si affectibus non cedant, si clypeum patientiæ non abjecerint. De qua quæst. fusius capite sequenti agit Philosophus.
units.tr: V. It is asked: whether those who fall into the calamities of Priam and the greatest miseries of this life cannot be called happy, which the Philosopher seems to suggest in the text? Answer: Happiness belongs to them in essence, not in existence. For they remain happy if they bear adverse things bravely, if they do not yield to their passions, and if they do not cast away the shield of patience. The Philosopher treats this question more fully in the following chapter.

units.la: VI. Quæritur, an Aristoteles sibi non sit contrarius, qui enim in hoc capite statuit inquirendum de causis felicitatis, & cap.2. hujus lib. negat inquirendum de causis principiorum,at felicitas est maximum principium Ethices? Respon. Minimè, nam cap. 2. dixit non inquirendum esse de hoc principio, propter quid, aut cur sit principium, seu demonstrationes exactas non esse adhibendas, ut huic principio credamus: Hic vero non inquirit, cur sit principium,sed quia non est proprie dictum principium , nempe componens, sed dirigens & intensive, ut loquuntur, principium inquirit de causis,à quibus proficiscatur,cum igitur supra de causis probationis,ut loquuntur,hic vero de causis emanationis, unde scilicet provenit felicitas, agit. Ergo non est sibi ipsi contrarius. I
units.tr: VI. It is asked: whether Aristotle does not contradict himself, since in this chapter he lays down that the causes of happiness must be inquired into, and in chapter 2 of this book he denies that the causes of principles are to be inquired into, yet happiness is the greatest principle of Ethics? Answer: Not at all. For in chapter 2 he said that one should not inquire about this principle, why or how it is a principle, or that exact demonstrations need not be applied so that we may believe this principle. Here, however, he does not inquire why it is a principle, but because it is not properly speaking a principle in the sense of constituting, but a principle that directs and, as they say, intensively, he inquires into the causes from which it proceeds. Thus above he treated the causes of proof, as they say, but here the causes of emanation, namely whence happiness comes. Therefore he is not contrary to himself.

units.la: Poterit & hoc etiam (propter magnam, quam cum iis, quæ hoc traduntur capite, affinitatem habet) quæri, num minus malum sit, semper prosperā caruiſse fortuna, quam semel expertum fuisse & ab ea totum deflitui & relinqui? Refpon. Communi quidem consensu primum asseritur, minus esse malum, ideo Seneca lib. de tranquillit. anima, latiores, inquit, reliquit fortuna quos nunquam respexit, quàm quos deseruit, & Boëtius de consol. lib. 2. ait, in omni adversitate, fortuna infelicissimum genus fortuna est fuisse felicem, nec sine ratione quidem, possessio enim parit exactiorem cognitionem boni, quod autem exactius cognoscimus, id magis appetimus, quod autem magis appetimus, id non adepti magis dolemus. Et 1. ratio poterit hæc esse, quia unū oppositū alterius cognitione juvat, itaque ut myrrha post saccarū assumpta longè videtur amarior, sic quæ fortuna secundam excipiunt, calamitates longè putantur acerbiores, ideo Cæsar 1. comment. de bello Gallico, confuefse Deos, inquit, quo gravius homines ex commutatione rerum doleant, quos pro scelere eorum ulcisci velint, his secundiores interdum res concedere: Hæc tamen sententia admodum dubia videtur. Cum enim munera fortunæ bona sint, si privari bono sit malum, privari eo diutius erit deterius malum. Quare privari per totam vitam censeri debet deterrimum. 2. Si melius sit nunquam possedisse opes, quam semel possessas iterū amittere, pariterquoque melius esset numquam fuisse quā esse, cum hac conditione & lege ut moriaris, melius esset per omne vitam oculorum lumine captū fuisse, quàā natiuitate incorruptāobtinuisse oculorū acie & postea progressu tēporis ea orbari. At quis nō mamavult, ad tępus licet illud perbreve fit, esse, quàm plane non esse? Quis non paucarum horarum visione frui mavult, quàm plane videndi munere destitui? hac sanè parte longè beatiores sunt, qui oculorum sensu à natura præditi, eum postea casu aliquo amiserunt, quàm qui cæci nati sunt, quod illi sciunt, quid sit videre & scientiam de coloribus habeant per phantasmata servatam, qua hi desti-tuuntur, adeò ut ea communis sententia si non plane falsa, saltem apprime, dubia videri possit. Pro determinatione hujus quæstionis sciendum aliquid posse esse minus malum vel absolutè vel certi temporis respectu. Absolutè minus mala est privatio in parte quàm in toto, quia privatio boni mala est, possessio verò boni est bona, quare absolutè loquendo privatio, quo est diuturnior & major, eò deterior. Verùm eo tempore, quo homo privatus est bonis externis, ea privatio per se est molestior, quia magis nos afficit, nam major cognitio & assuetudo majorè parit appetitionē & tali est privatio in parte temporis, quo illud pertinet commune adagium: Ab assuetis non fit passio.
units.tr: This question may also be raised (because it has a close affinity with the matters treated in this chapter): is it a lesser evil never to have enjoyed good fortune, or to have experienced it once and then been wholly forsaken and abandoned by it? The answer: by general consent it is first asserted that it is the lesser evil. So Seneca, in On the Tranquillity of the Soul, says: Fortune has left more gently those whom she never regarded than those whom she has deserted; and Boethius in On the Consolation of Philosophy, book 2, says: In every misfortune, the most unhappy kind of fortune is to have been happy. Nor is this without reason. For possession produces a more exact knowledge of the good, and the more exactly we know a thing, the more we desire it, and the more we desire it, the more we grieve when we fail to obtain it. And a first reason may be this: one opposite is helped by the knowledge of the other. Thus myrrh taken after sugar seems far more bitter, and so the calamities that follow good fortune are thought far more grievous. Hence Caesar, in the first book of his Commentaries on the Gallic War, says: The gods have been accustomed, so that men may grieve more heavily at the change of their circumstances, to grant more favourable conditions at times to those whom they wish to punish for their crimes. Yet this opinion seems quite doubtful. For since the gifts of fortune are goods, if to be deprived of a good is an evil, then to be deprived of it for longer will be a greater evil. Therefore to be deprived of it for one's whole life must be judged the greatest evil. (2) If it is better never to have possessed riches than to have possessed them once and then lost them again, then by the same reasoning it would be better never to have existed than to exist on the condition and law that you must die. It would be better to have been blind from birth all one's life than to have obtained the sight of one's eyes uncorrupted from birth and afterwards to be deprived of them as time went on. But who does not prefer to exist for a time, however brief it may be, than not to exist at all? Who does not prefer to enjoy the sight of a few hours rather than to be wholly deprived of the gift of seeing? In this respect, indeed, those who were endowed by nature with the sense of sight and afterwards lost it through some accident are far happier than those who were born blind, because the former know what seeing is and possess a knowledge of colours preserved through images, which the latter lack. So that this common opinion, if not plainly false, may at least seem very doubtful. To determine this question, it must be understood that something may be a lesser evil either absolutely or with respect to a certain period of time. Absolutely, the deprivation of a part is a lesser evil than the deprivation of the whole, since the privation of a good is an evil, while the possession of a good is a good. Hence, speaking absolutely, the longer and greater the privation, the worse it is. But at the time when a man is deprived of external goods, that privation is in itself more troublesome, because it affects us more; for greater knowledge and familiarity produce greater desire, and such is the privation within a part of time, to which the common saying applies: Suffering does not arise from things we are accustomed to.

units.la: CAPUT XI
units.tr: Chapter XI

units.la: QUia sub finem capitis decimi dixerat, eum, qui in Priami calamitates incideret, & in summis miseriis moreretur, non posse dici felicem, hinc quæstionem hanc infert, an aliquis in hac vita possit dici felix nec ne, & ostendit posse felicem dici variis rationibus, reprehensa etiam Solonis sententia. Partes cap. sunt duæ. In 1. refellit Solonem, qui negabat ante mortem posse quenquam dici felicem. In 2. tractat
units.tr: Because near the end of the tenth chapter he had said that a man who fell into the calamities of Priam and died in the greatest miseries could not be called happy, he now raises the question whether anyone in this life can be called happy or not, and shows by various arguments that a man can be called happy, also refuting the opinion of Solon. The chapter has two parts. In the first he refutes Solon, who denied that anyone could be called happy before death. In the second he treats the question whether a man in distress or misery can be called happy, and whether adverse circumstances can cast someone down from the level of happiness.

units.la: istam quæstionem, an aliquis in angustiis aut miseriis possit dici felix, & an res adversæ possint e felicitatis gradu aliquem deturbare. Solonis sententia prolata fuit apud Crœsum Lydorum regem, ut refert Herodotus lib. 1. & Plutarch. in vita Solonis: Nec solus in hac opinione fuit Solon, sed Euripides Poëta Tragicus in Andromache, & Plinius lib. 7. Naturalis historiæ c. 40. Ovid. 3. Metam. Fab. 2. Plato etiam ipse in Epinomide nullum, dicit, posse in hac vita felice dici, nisi solum sapientem, posthanc vitam alios quoque posse felices dici, maximè tamen sapientes pro Aristotelis sententia, contra stant omnes Stoici, teste Cic. lib. 3. sin. tum etiam ipse Cic. lib. 2. Finibus. In prima igitur parte Solonis sententiam tribus rationibus oppugnat, vel enim Solon dicebat felicitatem competere demum mortuo, aut hominem tum demum pronunciandum esse felicem, cum è vivis excessisset, propterea quod extra omnes hujus vitæ ærumnas & pericula esset: at neutra sententia est vera, quod sic probat, nam felicitas definitur actio secundum virtutem, mortui nulla est actio secundum virtutem, ideo felicitas non competit mortuo; cum cui non competat definitio, nec ei comperat definitum, & propterea prior sententia vera esse nequit. Posterior etiam sic impugnatur tribus rationibus, nam cum Solon diceret, hominem post hanc vitam felicem pronunciari debere, quod esset extra hujus vitæ pericula & mala omnia: Hoc falsum esse ostendit. 1. Si viventi & non sentienti & absenti contingere possunt bona & mala, etiam & mortuo contingere possunt; at prius esse verum experientia docet: Non sensentienti enim aut absenti contingere possunt dignitates, opes, honores, &c. quæ sunt bona, possunt etiam in fortunia accidere, verbi gratia, fieri potest, ut ignominiâ notetur, pœnâ aut exilio multetur, depereant amici & cognati. Quare cum in hac vita non sit tutum vocare aliquem felicem propter multas & varias Fortunæ vicissitudines, etiam neque post hanc vitam aliquem felicem vocare possumus, fieri enim potest, ut in varias anxietates incidat, ex rebus posterorum male gestis: Hoc argumentum cum levius videtur, quam ut Solonem premat, hic non ultro urget, sed postea fusius explicat, ubi illam quæstionem tractat: An res posterorum secundæ vel adversæ ad defunctos pertineant. 1 Postea incipit Aristoteles urgere Solonem ab absurdo, nam q; absurdum est, tribuere aliquid alicui non cum habeat, sed propterea tribuere, quod aliquando habuerit, & tamen cum haberet, illi plane negabatur, hoc Solon facit, qui dicit mortuum ideo esse felicem, non quod jam sit in morte felix, sed quod aliquando in vita fuerit felix, & tamen cum in vita esset, negabat illi omnem felicitatem Solon, quod absurdum est: nam nihil poterit dici aliquando fuisse, quod non poterit etiam aliquando dici esse, & si verum sit, fuisse hominem aliquando felicem, etiam verum poterit dici, aliquando esse felicem.3 Si à fortuna dependeret felicitas, sequeretur, quod vult Solon, nempe hominem in hac vita, propter varias & crebras fortunæ mutationes, non posse dici felicem, sed cum à fortuna non dependeat, ut capite superiori probarat, ideo poterit aliquis in hac vita esse felix: Nisi a fortuna penderet felicitas, tunc homo esset instar Camaeleontis, qui ut refert Plin. lib.8.Natur.hist. cap.13. mutat colorem suum pro colore objecti, & potest se transformare in quemlibet colorem, praeter album, sic etiam homo pro vario fortunae statu, nunc felix nunc miser & e contra esset, sed cum felicitas dependeat a virtute, ut ex definitione patet, tum etiam ex capite superiore: & cum virtus sit stabilis & firma, felicitatem ipsam stabilem esse oportet, & perinde felicitas non est obnoxia fortunae mutationib. Virtutem vero esse stabilem probat ex actionibus virtutis, quae sunt multo stabiliores & constantiores theoreticis actionibus, propterea quod actionum virtutis usus in vita longe lateque patet, & earum exercitium est multo crebrius quam theoreticarum actionum, unde cum crebrius obversentur homini, firmius etiam inhaerent. In secunda parte capitis ostendit felicem non posse dici miserum, quod ut melius demonstret, inducit tripartitam divisionem eorum, quae homini accidere possunt, vel enim quae homini accidunt sunt prospera vel adversa, & utraque demum sunt vel magna vel parva, prospera & magna non mutant felicem, sed potius felicitatem beatiorem & ornatiorem reddunt, quoad externum splendorem, adversa etiam magna non mutant felicitatem, si quis ea fortiter ferat prout virum bonum decet: nam in rebus adversis maxime exercentur actiones virtutis, in quibus consistit ista felicitas, si vero rebus adversis succumbat mollitie quadam animi, ut Cic. accusatus a Clodio, tunc non felix, sed miser dicendus dus est, propterea quod virtutis actionibus excide rit, quod si vero quis in hujus mundi calamitates inciderit, ut virtutis actiones exercere nequeat, ut de Priamo, Niobe & Croeso legitur, si constans tamen manserit, felix nihilominus dicetur intrinsecus. Quod si vero tandem priftinū vitæ statum recuperaverit, tunc multo magis felicitas in ipso splendebit, quod de Jobo testantur sacræ literæ. Parva vero adversa vel prospera nullo modo virum bonum concutiunt, sed immotum reddunt,
units.tr: Solon's opinion was stated before Croesus, king of the Lydians, as Herodotus reports in book 1 and Plutarch in the Life of Solon. Nor was Solon alone in this view: the tragic poet Euripides in Andromache held it, and so did Pliny Natural History, book 7, ch. 40, and Ovid, Metamorphoses 3, fable 2. Plato himself, in the Epinomis, says that no one can be called happy in this life except the wise man alone, but that after this life others too can be called happy, and most of all the wise, in line with the opinion of Aristotle. All the Stoics, on the testimony of Cicero, book 3 of the Tusculans, stand against this, and Cicero himself, book 2 of De Finibus. In the first part, then, he attacks Solon's opinion with three arguments. For Solon either said that happiness belongs only to the dead, or that a man must be pronounced happy only when he has departed from the living, because he is then beyond all the troubles and dangers of this life. But neither view is true, and he proves this as follows. Happiness is defined as activity in accordance with virtue. The dead have no activity in accordance with virtue. Therefore happiness does not belong to the dead. What the definition does not fit, the thing defined does not fit either, and so the former opinion cannot be true. The latter opinion is also attacked by three arguments. Solon said that a man should be pronounced happy after this life, because he is then beyond this life's dangers and all its evils. He shows this to be false: (1) If goods and evils can befall a man who is living but unaware of them and absent from them, they can also befall a dead man. But experience teaches that the former is true. For honours, wealth, dignities and so on, which are goods, can befall one who is unaware of them and absent. Accidents of fortune can also happen to him: for example, he may be branded with disgrace, fined or exiled, and his friends and kinsmen may perish. Therefore, since in this life it is not safe to call anyone happy on account of the many and varied changes of fortune, neither can we call anyone happy after this life; for it may happen that he falls into various anxieties over the ill conduct of his descendants. This argument seems too weak to press Solon, so Aristotle does not push it further here, but explains it at greater length later, where he treats the question whether the prosperity or adversity of one's descendants affects the dead. (2) Next Aristotle presses Solon with an absurdity. It is absurd to attribute something to a person who does not have it, on the ground that he once had it, while denying it to him when he did have it. Solon does this: he says the dead man is happy not because he is now happy in death but because he was once happy in life, and yet while he was alive Solon denied him all happiness. This is absurd, for nothing can be said to have once been the case that cannot also be said to be the case at some time; and if it is true that a man was once happy, it can also be truly said that he is happy at some time. (3) If happiness depended on fortune, then what Solon wants would follow, namely that a man in this life, because of the various and frequent changes of fortune, could not be called happy. But since happiness does not depend on fortune, as he proved in the previous chapter, a man can be happy in this life. Were happiness dependent on fortune, a man would be like the chameleon, which, as Pliny reports in book 8 of the Natural History, ch. 13, changes its colour to match the colour of whatever it is near and can turn into any colour except white. So too man, according to the varying state of his fortune, would now be happy, now wretched, and the reverse. But since happiness depends on virtue, as is clear from the definition and from the previous chapter, and since virtue is stable and firm, happiness itself must be stable, and so happiness is not subject to changes of fortune. He proves that virtue is stable from the activities of virtue, which are much more stable and constant than theoretical activities, because the exercise of virtue extends far and wide over life and is far more frequent than theoretical activity; and since these activities occur more often to a man, they also cling to him more firmly. In the second part of the chapter he shows that a happy man cannot be called miserable. To demonstrate this better, he introduces a threefold division of the things that can happen to a man. What happens to a man is either prosperous or adverse, and each of these is either great or small. Prosperous things, if great, do not change a happy man, but rather make his happiness more blessed and more adorned in its outward splendour. Great adversities also do not change happiness, if a man bears them bravely, as a good man should; for it is in adversity that the activities of virtue are most exercised, and this happiness consists in them. But if he yields to adversity through some softness of spirit, as Cicero did when accused by Clodius, then he must be called not happy but miserable, because he has fallen from the activities of virtue. And if a man falls into the calamities of this world so that he cannot exercise the activities of virtue, as is read of Priam, Niobe and Croesus, yet if he remains steadfast, he will nonetheless be called happy within himself. And if he at last recovers his former state of life, then his happiness shines all the more brightly, as the Holy Scriptures testify of Job. Small adversities or prosperities, however, do not shake a good man at all, but leave him unmoved,

units.la: Ac fi dura silex, aut stet marpesia cautes.
units.tr: As if a hard flint, or the Marpesian crag, stood fast.

units.la: Felix igitur dicetur is, qui quocunque modo secundum virtutem egerit, & si bonis externis non sit satis instructus, proinde in definitione nostra non erat addendum, quod Solon voluit, non solum ut quisque secundum virtutem agat in vita perfecta, sed ut sic moriatur, nam cum futura sint incerta, felicitas vero certa & cognita, istæ definitioni ejus non sunt addenda.
units.tr: He therefore will be called happy who acts in accordance with virtue in whatever way, even if he is not fully furnished with external goods. So in our definition it was not necessary to add what Solon wanted, namely that a man should not only act in accordance with virtue throughout a complete life, but also die in that way. For since the future is uncertain, while happiness is certain and known, these things are not to be added to the definition.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Non sentienti etiam absenti accidere possunt bona & mala. (ciesse.
units.tr: 1. Good and evil things can happen even to a person who does not perceive them and is absent.

units.la: 2. Nihil poterit dici fuisse, quod non poterat aliquando di-
units.tr: 2. Nothing can be said to have been that could not at some time have been ...

units.la: 3. Bona externa felicitatem ipsam non perficiunt, sed humana vitæ necessaria sunt.
units.tr: 3. External goods do not perfect happiness itself, but are necessary for human life.

units.la: 4. Virtutum actiones quoad usum & frequens exercitium sunt theoreticæ actionibus multo constantiores.
units.tr: 4. In practice and frequent exercise, the actions of the virtues are far more constant than theoretical actions.

units.la: 5. Felix fortuna procellis premitur, sed non opprimitur.
units.tr: 5. Good fortune is pressed down by storms, but it is not overwhelmed.

units.la: 6. Ut strenuus & fortis Imperator cum quovis milite fortiter dimicat, sic vir bonus in quovis vita statu secundum virtutem agit.
units.tr: 6. As a vigorous and brave general fights bravely with any soldier, so a good man acts in accordance with virtue in any condition of life.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Aristoteles Solonis sententiam jure taxarit, cum certum sit, neminem in hac vita posse felicem dici, nam ille tantum dicendus est felix, qui continuò secundum virtutem agit, at nemo continuè agit, nec agere potest, ut manifestè probavit Aristoteles, cap. 3. hujus lib. & 8.
units.tr: I. Question: Did Aristotle rightly criticise the saying of Solon, since it is certain that no one in this life can be called happy? For only one who continually acts in accordance with virtue is to be called happy, and no one acts continually, nor can he, as Aristotle clearly proved in chapter 3 and chapter 8 of this book.

units.la: Respon. Non ideo negandum est, felicitatem non competere homini in hac vita, quod non continuò singulares virtutum actiones edat, si modo ita agat, prout tempus postulat & res, nam virtus interdum quiescit, non ocii aut desidii causa, sed ut majori cum alacritate ad officium suum redeat, Quemadmodum enim longius prosiliunt illi, qui paulatim regressi spiritus recolligunt: sic homines ad virtutum actiones ferventiores videri solent, si quiescere nonnunquam liceat.
units.tr: Answer. It must not be denied that happiness belongs to a man in this life merely because he does not produce single actions of virtue without interruption, provided that he acts as time and circumstances require. For virtue sometimes rests, not from idleness or sloth, but so that it may return to its duty with greater readiness. Just as those who draw back a little and gather their breath leap farther, so people are wont to appear more eager for the actions of virtue if they are allowed to rest now and then.

units.la: Instantia. Homines in hac vita, à via virtutis sæpe deflectunt, & in errorem sapius labuntur. Ergo, neque felicitas in hac vita competere potest, Resp. Non sequi. Nam vita beata dici poterit, ubi virtus rerum potitur, denominatio enim à meliore parte sumenda est, nam etsi vita hominis cum erroribus conflictetur, tamen si hoc præcipuè respiciat, ut secundum virtutem agat, felix dici poterit, quemadmodum seges uberibus spicis, læta & optima dicuntur bona, etsi sterilis avena alicubi conspiciatur, sic etiam & vita hominis & si in quosdam errores incidant, modo virtutem non commaculent, aut virtutis actionib. sint impedimenta, vide Pic. c. 6. gradu 8.
units.tr: Objection: People in this life often turn aside from the path of virtue and fall into error more often. Therefore happiness cannot belong to this life. Answer: It does not follow. For a life may be called blessed when virtue holds sway, since the name is to be taken from the better part. For although a human life is beset with errors, yet if its chief aim is to act in accordance with virtue, it can be called happy, just as a crop is called joyful and excellent for its rich ears, even though a barren oat may be seen here and there. So also human life, even if people fall into certain errors, can be called happy, provided they do not stain their virtue or hinder its actions. See Pico, chapter 6, degree 8.

units.la: II. Quæritur, Cur Aristoteles hac similitudine utatur, ut dicat idem posse contingere mortuo, quod vivo, absenti, & non non sentienti, cum dissimillima sit ratio vivi licet absentis & mortui : nam vivus licet sit absens, adesse tamen poterit & particeps fieri eorum, quae illi accidunt: at mortui neque sentire neque adesse possunt, cum a morte non detur reditus? Respond. Aristoteles ex communi & recepta opinione argumentatur, nam nihil erit communius etiam inter praecipuos Philosophos, quam homines post hanc vitam, si bene & sapienter vixissent, Deorum consilius adesse, & quid ibi gereretur, observare, unde cum saepius de rebus humanis deliberantes audirent, possunt inde percipere, quid boni aut mali in hac vita fieret. In hac opinione fuit etiam Socrates, ut ex Epitaphio patet apud Plat. tum etiam ipse Plato in epistola quadam ad Dionysi Syracusarum Tyrannum, Aristoteles tamen non plane videtur approbare hanc opinionem, ut infra patebit lib. 3. c. 9. ubi nihil amplius homini restare post hanc vitam neque boni, neque mali dicit.
units.tr: II. Question: Why does Aristotle use this comparison, saying that the same can happen to a dead man as to a living one, to an absent man, and to one who does not perceive it, when the case of a living man, though absent, is very unlike that of a dead man? For a living man, though absent, can still be present and share in what happens to him, but the dead can neither perceive nor be present, since there is no return from death? Answer: Aristotle argues from common and accepted opinion. For nothing is more common, even among the leading philosophers, than the view that men after this life, if they have lived well and wisely, are present at the counsels of the gods and observe what is done there; and so, when they hear men deliberating about human affairs more often, they can perceive what good or evil is happening in this life. Socrates also held this opinion, as is clear from the Epitaph in Plato; and Plato himself in a certain letter to Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse. Aristotle, however, does not seem fully to approve this opinion, as will appear below in book 3, chapter 9, where he says that nothing good or evil remains for man after this life.

units.la: III. Quaeritur, quomodo dicat virtutum actiones esse multo constantiores theoreticis actionibus, cum theoretica actiones sint circa res necessarias, & ideo non possunt se aliter habere, & proinde sunt constantissima, actiones virtutum vero sunt circa res contingentes, quia sunt in hominis potestate, ut fiant vel non fiant?
units.tr: III. Question: How does he say that the actions of the virtues are much more constant than theoretical actions, since theoretical actions concern necessary things, and therefore cannot be otherwise and are most constant, while the actions of virtue concern contingent things, because they are in man's power to be done or not done?

units.la: Respond. Hoc dici propter usum & frequens exercitium actionum virtutis, nam in omni vita opus est, ut secundam virtutem agatur, in qualibet actione opus est prudentia. In periculis opus est fortitudine, in commerciis opus est justitia, in victu opus est temperantia, proinde cum semper occurrant virtutis actiones, dicuntur constantiores theoreticis, propterea quod earum oblivio livio in hominem facile non possit cadere, at vero theoreticarum oblivio facile in hominem cadit, propter quod etiam rerum a sensibus remotarum, tum etiam earum usus exiguus, aut nullus in vita communi est.
units.tr: Answer: This is said on account of the practice and frequent exercise of the actions of virtue. For in every life it is necessary to act in accordance with virtue; in every action prudence is needed. In dangers fortitude is needed, in dealings justice is needed, in food temperance is needed. Therefore, since the actions of virtue always occur, they are called more constant than theoretical actions, because the forgetting of them cannot easily fall upon a man. But the forgetting of theoretical things easily falls upon a man, for they are removed from the senses, and their use in common life is small or nil.
