units.la: IV. Quæritur: quomodo dicat illum non posse dici mi- serum, qui incidit in Priami calamitates, qui exuitur bonis omnibus, divitiis & possessionibus, cum tales miseros dici experientia probet? Respond. Nomen miseri sumitur, 3. modis 1. dicitur miser, qui pecunia aut rebus hisce externis indiget, & sic secundum vulgi consuetudinem felix privatus bonis externis potest dici miser. 2. Sumitur miser, pro vilis & abjecti animi homine, & sic felix non potest dici miser, quamdiu res adversas fortiter fert. 3. Pro homine sceleri & flagitiis mancipato aut addicto, & sic nullo modo felix miser dici potest.
units.tr: IV. Question: How does he say that the man who falls into the calamities of Priam, who is stripped of all goods, riches and possessions, cannot be called wretched, when experience shows that such men are called wretched? Answer: The name "wretched" is taken in three ways. (1) A man is called wretched who lacks money or other external things; and in this sense, according to common usage, a happy man deprived of external goods can be called wretched. (2) "Wretched" is taken for a man of base and abject spirit; and in this sense a man cannot be called wretched so long as he bears adverse things bravely. (3) It is taken for a man given over and enslaved to crime and vice; and in this sense the happy man can by no means be called wretched.

units.la: V. Quæritur: quomodo dicat in textu felicem non esse felicem, si incidat in Priami calamitates, cum hac duo implicent contradictionem? Respond. Felix dicitur non felix, cum incidit in magnas calamitates, non quod revera jam non sit felix, sed quod sic videatur sublatis rebus secundis.
units.tr: V. Question: How does he say in the text that a happy man is not happy if he falls into the calamities of Priam, since these two statements imply a contradiction? Answer: The happy man is said to be not happy when he falls into great calamities, not because he is in truth no longer happy, but because he seems so once his prosperous circumstances are removed.

units.la: VI. Quæritur, Quomodo dicat aliquem privatum rebus externis, exiguo tempore non posse ad felicitatem redire, seu felicem fieri quoad externum ornatum intra breve tempus, cum historia multa testentur, multos reges folio suo detrusos, ad infimam paupertatem & miseriam redactos, exiguo tempore regna, possessiones, & pristinam vita conditionem recuperasse? Resp. Cum Aristoteles dicat, neminem exiguo tempore ad felicitatem posse redire, intelintelligit per se & propriis suis viribus. Quod vero ad illos Reges & Magnates, qui recuperarunt illico pristinum vitæ splendorem, id factum est alienis viribus & auxiliis, ut variæ subinde historiæ testantur.
units.tr: VI. Question: How does he say that a man deprived of external things cannot return to happiness in a short time, or become happy as regards outward adornment within a brief period, since many histories testify that many kings, thrown from their throne and reduced to the lowest poverty and misery, have in a short time recovered their kingdoms, possessions and former condition of life? Answer: When Aristotle says that no one can return to happiness in a short time, he means by himself and by his own powers. As for those kings and great men who at once recovered their former splendour of life, this happened through the help and aid of others, as various histories from time to time attest.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: EXplicata jam præcipua quæstione, an aliquis in hac vita sit dicendus felix, aliam ex ea ortam hoc capite subjungit, nempe an posterorum res adversæ vel secundæ ad defunctos pertineant. Partes capitis sunt 2. In prima rationibus probat ad defunctos pertinere res posterorum. In 2. ex sua opinione quæst. solvit. Rationes breviter sunt hæ duæ. 1. Videtur alienum ab amicitia, mortuos nullam habere curam eorum, quæ in hac vita geruntur, nam cum amicitia sit animæ non corporis & anima non intereat neque etiam ista animæ affectio interibit. 2. Ratio ducitur à communi hominum opinione, omnes enim pro certo credunt defunctos hac vita, aliquam habere notitiam aut intelligentiam eorum, quæ in hac vita geruntur, unde notæ sunt illæ Poëtarum Fabulæ de cura & solicitudine, quam animæ defunctæ pro vivis maximè cognatis & amicis habent. Sic Hom. 11. Odyss. inducit matrem Vlyssis multo ante jam tempore vita defunctam, filium suum solicitè monentem, ut sibi prospiciat & domum redeat ad extrudendos Penelopis procos: Sic Virg. 6. Æneid. inducit Anchisen apud inferos filium monentem de rebus futuris in Italia.
units.tr: Having explained the main question, whether anyone in this life can be called happy, he adds another that arises from it in this chapter: whether the affairs of the living concern the dead. The chapter has two parts. In the first he proves by arguments that the affairs of the living do concern the dead. In the second he resolves the question according to his own opinion. The arguments, briefly, are these two. (1) It seems foreign to friendship for the dead to have no concern for what goes on in this life, for since friendship belongs to the soul and not the body, and the soul does not perish, that affection of the soul will not perish either. (2) The argument is drawn from the common opinion of humankind, for everyone firmly believes that the dead have some knowledge or awareness of what happens in this life. Hence the familiar stories of the poets about the care and anxiety that departed souls feel for the living, especially their closest kin and friends. Thus Hom. 11. Odyss. introduces the mother of Ulysses, who had died long before, anxiously warning her son to look after himself and return home to drive out Penelope's suitors. Thus Virg. 6. Æneid. introduces Anchises in the underworld warning his son about future events in Italy.

units.la: In 2. parte capitis priusquam ad quæstionem responspondeat fundamenti loco duplicem distinctionem ponit. 1. Distinctio sumitur ab eventis, quae homini accidere solent, 2. Distinctio sumitur ab iis, quibus ista eventa accidunt. Quod ad primam dictum erat superius eventorum alia esse magna & gravia, alia parva & exigua, & parva nulla habere vim ad felicitatem interturbandam, magna vero habere: sic se habet in eventis, quae defunctis accidunt. Si quae sint eventa, quae ad defunctos pertineant, aut comovere aliquo modo possunt, ea sunt gravia, non exigua aut levia. Secunda distinctio quae ibi sumitur, quibus ista evenia accidunt, hunc habet sensum, casus accidunt tam mortuis quam vivis, magis tamen afficiunt vivos quam mortuos, quia vivi sentiunt & subeunt calamitates, mortui vero non, quae coram sentimus, multo nos magis commovent, quam quae longo post tempore percipimur. Quod illustrat a simili a Tragoediis sumato, nam sicut in Tragoediis, caedes, exitia, interitus Regum & Magnatum exhibentur, & ita quidem ut interdum ad vivum oculis spectatorum exhibeantur, interdum vero tanquam acta in scena referantur, & quae ad vivum exhibentur, magis afficiunt spectatorum animos, quam quae gesta tantum referuntur. Sic se habet in iis casibus, quae vivis ad oculos quasi exhibentur, & mortuis tanquam acta referuntur, accidunt. Tandem vero sic quaestionem solvit, ut dicat respondentes ad defunctos pertinere, ita tamen ut nec statum meliorem vel deteriorem efficere possint. Haec est Aristotelis sententia. In contrarium sunt variae rationes. 1. Sacra scriptura, Esa. 63. Abraham nefinescivit nos, Israel gnoravit nos. Tu Domine Pater es redemptor noster in saecula. Sic etiam, 2. Reg. 18 Dicit Joías Regi Dominus, Colligam te ad Patres tuos, ne videant oculi tui omnia mala, quae inducturus sum super locum istum.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter, before he answers the question, he lays down as a foundation a twofold distinction. (1) The first distinction is taken from the events that usually befall a person. (2) The second is taken from those to whom these events happen. As to the first, it was said above that events are of two kinds, some great and serious, others small and trifling, and that small ones have no power to disturb happiness, while great ones do. So it is with the events that befall the dead. If there are any events that concern the dead, or can in any way move them, these are serious, not slight or trivial. The second distinction, drawn here according to whom these events happen, has this sense: calamities happen both to the dead and to the living, but they affect the living more than the dead, because the living feel and undergo misfortunes, whereas the dead do not. What we see before our eyes moves us far more than what we learn of long after. He illustrates this by a comparison with tragedies. In tragedies, slaughters, deaths and the downfall of kings and great men are presented, sometimes openly before the eyes of the spectators, and sometimes related as things done offstage. What is presented openly moves the minds of the spectators more than what is only reported as done. So it is with those misfortunes that happen to the living as if before their eyes, and to the dead as things related as past. Finally he resolves the question by saying that these events do concern the dead, yet in such a way that they cannot make their condition either better or worse. This is Aristotle's opinion. On the other side there are various arguments. (1) Holy Scripture, Isa. 63: Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O Lord, are our Father and our Redeemer from everlasting. Likewise, 2 Kings 18: The Lord says to King Josiah, "I will gather you to your fathers, that your eyes may not see all the evil that I am about to bring upon this place."

units.la: 2. Communis sensus Orthodoxae Ecclesiae, quae ex hoc fundamento, quod Sanctis non sit perspectum aut cognitu, quid in hac vita geratur, tollunt invocationem Sanctorum. 3. Authoritas Patrum quorundam, qui dicunt piorum mentes posthanc vitam, tanta caelestis gaudii copia repletas, ut omnium penitus, quae hic gerantur, oblivionem contrahant.
units.tr: (2) The common sense of the Orthodox Church, which, on the ground that the saints do not perceive or know what goes on in this life, rejects the invocation of the saints. (3) The authority of certain Fathers, who say that the minds of the pious, after this life, are so filled with the abundance of heavenly joy that they utterly forget everything that happens here.

units.la: 4. Si res posteorum pertinerent ad defunctos, interturbarent ac labefactarent felicitatem.
units.tr: (4) If the affairs of the living concerned the dead, they would disturb and weaken their happiness.

units.la: Pro decisione notandum est, etsi Argumenta ab Aristotele allata, utut non sint tanti ponderis, ut quaestionem solvant, tamen non male esse solutam a Philosopho. Nam aliquam noticiam pertinere ad defunctos, nec beatitudinem illam coelestem obliterare istam noticiam, hinc patet cap. 6. Apoc. Martyres in coelis sic clamant ad DEUM. Ulciscere Domine sanguinem nostrum super inimicos nostros. Quod si expetat vindictam contra inimicos, & amicorum etiam recordabuntur. Nec hoc tantum beatis accidit, sed & damnatis: Sic Luc. 16. Damnatus Epulo fratrum suorum recordatur, qui adhuc in vivis essent, quod vero ista notitia nullo modo labefactet felicitatem defunctorum, praeter Aristotelis sententiam, hinc patet, quia piorum voluntas per omnia est conformis voluntati divinae, & cum divina voluntas sit immutabilis, sic & piorum erit voluntas. 2. Affectus carnales hujus praesentis vitae non amplius regnabunt, bunt, sed cognitio justitiae Dei omnes affectus naturales superabit, qui plura velit de hac re videre, consulat Zwingerum in praefatione supra Ethicam Aristotelis, nam aperte dicit, res posterorum ita ad defunctos pertinere, ut statum nullo modo mortuorum mutent. 1. Frustra igitur solennes Missae pro defunctis animabus celebrantur. 2. Frustra etiam πανὰ-γιον seu omnium Sanctorum festum a Pontificibus ideo institutum. 3. Frustra etiam purgatorium a Pontificiis fuit aedificatum, cum ex Aristotelis sententia nihil in hac vita fieri possit, quod mortuorum statum vel minimum immutet.
units.tr: For the decision, it should be noted that although the arguments brought forward by Aristotle, however weighty they are not, do not settle the question, yet the Philosopher has not resolved it badly. That the dead have some awareness, and that this awareness does not blot out that heavenly blessedness, is plain from Rev. 6: the martyrs in heaven cry out to God, "O Lord, avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth". If they seek vengeance on their enemies, they also remember their friends. And this happens not only to the blessed but also to the damned. Thus in Luke 16 the damned Dives remembers his brothers, who were still alive. That this knowledge in no way weakens the happiness of the dead, contrary to Aristotle's opinion, is plain for this reason: the will of the pious is wholly conformed to the will of God, and since the divine will is unchangeable, so the will of the pious will be unchangeable. (2) The carnal affections of this present life will no longer reign, but the knowledge of the justice of God will overcome all natural affections. Whoever wishes to see more on this matter, let him consult Zwinger in the preface to his edition of Aristotle's Ethics, for he plainly says that the affairs of the living concern the dead in such a way that they in no way alter the condition of the dead. (1) In vain, therefore, are solemn Masses celebrated for the souls of the dead. (2) In vain also has the feast of all the saints [πανάγιον], or All Saints' Day, been instituted by the Papists for this reason. (3) In vain also has purgatory been built by the Papists, since on Aristotle's view nothing that can be done in this life changes the state of the dead even in the least.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Dicere respositorum non pertinere ad defunctos, est alienum ab amicitia, & communi hominum opinioni contrarium.
units.tr: 1. To say that the affairs of the living do not pertain to the dead is foreign to friendship and contrary to common human opinion.

units.la: 2. Pertinent respositorum ad defunctos, ita ut defunctorum statum neque meliorem neque deteriorem reddant.
units.tr: 2. The affairs of the living do pertain to the dead, so that they make the state of the dead neither better nor worse.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat dubitandum esse, animas defunctorum sint participes boni aut mali, nam hinc statuere videtur animas esse mortales, & nihil iis post hanc vitam esse reliquum, quod sapere videtur Epicurum, idem quoq; c.9.l.7. statuit. Resp. Non dubitat Aristot. de immortalitate animae, sed hanc movet quaestionem, an animae sint participes bonorum aut malorum, quae in hac vita geruntur, & respondet ita quidem esse participes, sed ita tamen, ut si antea beatae non fuerint animae, non possunt mala vel bona hujus vitae reddere beatas, quod si antea beatae fuerint, non possunt eripere beatitudinem, aut in deteriorem redigere statum. Ca-
units.tr: I. The question is how he can say that we should doubt whether the souls of the dead partake of good or evil, for from this he seems to establish that souls are mortal and that nothing remains for them after this life, which seems to savour of Epicurus, who also held this c.9.l.7. Answer: Aristotle does not doubt the immortality of the soul. He raises this question: whether souls partake of the good or evil things done in this life. He replies that they do partake, but in such a way that if the souls were not blessed before, the evils or goods of this life cannot make them blessed; and if they were blessed before, these things cannot take away their blessedness or reduce them to a worse state. Ca-

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: EXplicata definitione Felicitatis, & quando homini contingat, progreditur Philosophus ad aliam quæstionem, de dignitate felicitatis, an nempe felicitas sit de genere bonorum laudabilium, an vero honoratorum, quæ quæstio ut melius intelligatur sciendum est ut ex Aristotele ipso liquet lib.1. Mag. Mor. capit. 3. In Rhetorica, capit. 26. Ex lib. 4. Cic. de finib. Ex lib. 4. quæst. naturalium Alexandri Aphrod. cap.17. & in 4. Top. c. 9. Tripartitam fuisse bonorum divisionem, ut alia bona vocarentur facultates, ut sunt bona corporis & fortunæ, quæ per se neq; laudem neque honorem merentur, sed quatenus homines iis bene vel male utuntur, nam facultates propriè sunt promiscua & indifferentia bona, Teste Alex. Aphrod. ad cap. 11. lib. 1. Top. Aristot. Alia vocantur laudabilia, & sunt virtutes & facta honesta, quæ laudem merentur propter utilitatem, quam habent ad aliud majus bonum comparandum. Alia vocantur bona honorabilia, quæ sunt summa & præstantissima inter bona, ut sunt Deus, Mens, Antiquitas, Felicitas, Principia rerum & origines.
units.tr: Having explained the definition of happiness and when it falls to a human being, the Philosopher goes on to another question, concerning the dignity of happiness: namely, whether happiness belongs to the class of praiseworthy goods or of honourable ones. To understand this question better, one should know what is clear from Aristotle himself, Magna Moralia, book 1, chapter 3; in the Rhetoric, chapter 26; from Cicero, De finibus, book 4; from Alexander of Aphrodisias, Quaestiones naturales, book 4, chapter 17; and in the Topics, book 4, chapter 9. The division of goods was threefold: some goods are called faculties, such as the goods of body and fortune, which deserve neither praise nor honour in themselves, but only insofar as people use them well or badly. For faculties are strictly speaking goods common to good and bad and indifferent, as Alexander of Aphrodisias testifies in his commentary on Topics, book 1, chapter 11. Others are called praiseworthy: these are the virtues and honourable deeds, which merit praise because of their usefulness in securing some greater good. Others are called honourable goods: these are the highest and most excellent among goods, such as God, Mind, Antiquity, Happiness, the principles and origins of things.

units.la: Partes capitis sunt duæ: In prima proponit hanc quæstionem: An felicitas sit laudabile; an honorabile quid? In secunda tribus rationibus probat esse quid honorabile. In prima igitur propositâ quæstione objectioni statim occurrit; poterat enim objici, non sufficienter enumerata esse ab Aristotele omnia bonorum genera, cum bona non tantum sint honorabilia & laudabilia, sed sit tertium quoddam genus, nemnempe facultates. Ad hoc respondet, pro confesso esse apud omnes, felicitatem inter bona animi esse numerandam, & ideo de facultatibus agere non esse praesentis instituti, quod & cap. 8. supra probavit à consensu veterum: nam cum veteres dividerent bona in bona animi, corporis, & fortunae, tantum inter bona animi numerarunt Felicitatem. In secunda parte capitis ostendit, felicitatem esse à genere bonorum non laudabilium, sed honorabilium tribus rationibus: 1. Laudabilia sunt ejusmodi, quae ad aliud referuntur, veluti ad virtutis habitum, vel ad actionem virtutis; Felicitas ad aliud non refertur, quia est bonorum omnium ultimum, & sui tantum gratia expetitur. Ergo non est laudabile. Minorem confirmat exemplis virtutum, veluti Justitia, Fortitudinis, &c. quae non propter se expetuntur, sed propter aliud quid perfectius, & e contrario ostendit, Deos non posse laudari, propterea quod sint in se perfecti, absurdum est enim Deos veluti homines laudare, utpote quod juste aut temperanter egerint.
units.tr: The chapter has two parts. In the first he puts forward the question: is happiness something praiseworthy or something honourable? In the second he proves by three arguments that it is something honourable. In the first part, then, having put forward the question, he at once meets an objection. For it could be objected that Aristotle had not listed all the kinds of goods sufficiently, since goods are not only honourable and praiseworthy, but there is also a third kind, namely faculties. To this he replies that it is accepted by all that happiness must be counted among the goods of the soul, and therefore it is not the business of the present undertaking to treat of faculties. He had also proved this in chapter 8 above from the agreement of the ancients: for when the ancients divided goods into goods of the soul, of the body, and of fortune, they counted happiness only among the goods of the soul. In the second part of the chapter he shows, by three arguments, that happiness belongs to the class not of praiseworthy goods but of honourable ones. (1) Praiseworthy things are of such a kind that they are referred to something else, as to a habit of virtue or to an act of virtue. Happiness is not referred to something else, because it is the last of all goods and is desired only for its own sake. Therefore it is not praiseworthy. He confirms the minor premise by examples of the virtues, such as justice, fortitude, and so on, which are not desired for their own sake but for something more perfect. On the other hand, he shows that the gods cannot be praised, because they are perfect in themselves; for it would be absurd to praise the gods as we praise human beings, on the ground that they have acted justly or temperately.

units.la: Secunda ratio petitur à communi loquendi consuetudine, quod res optimas nemo laudaret, sed lentas praedicaret & honore coleret, quod confirmat tum exemplo Deorum, quos omnes felices & beatos praedicant, non vero proprie laudant. Et confirmat secundo, exemplo Eudoxi Philosophi, qui summum bonum in voluptate statuebat, & cum nemo hanc opinionem laudaret, adeo dicebat voluptatem esse summum bonum, quod nemo inter bona laudabilia numerarer. Etsi Aristoteles non comprobet opinionem Eudoxi, in voluptate summum bonum statuentis, hoc tamen in ipso comprobat, quod summum bonum aliquid laude majus diceret esse, inde distinguit inter laudem & encomium, quod laus sit proprie propter habitum virtutis. Encomium propter actionem aliquam singularem, verbi gratia, si quis velit laudare Ciceronem a Consulatu quem gessit, proprie dicitur illum encomiare; si vero ab habitu reliquarum virtutum, dicitur illum proprie laudare. De laudis & encomii discrimine fusius agit Aristoteles lib. 1. Rhetor. & Keckerman problem. 21. fyst. Ethic.
units.tr: The second argument is taken from common usage of speech: no one praises the best things, but calls them blessed and honours them with reverence. He confirms this first by the example of the gods, whom everyone calls happy and blessed but does not properly praise. Secondly, he confirms it by the example of the philosopher Eudoxus, who held that the highest good lies in pleasure. Since no one praised this opinion, he said that pleasure is the highest good, so that no one would count it among praiseworthy goods. Although Aristotle does not approve of Eudoxus's opinion that the highest good lies in pleasure, he does approve of this in it: that he called the highest good something greater than praise. From this he distinguishes between praise and encomium: praise properly belongs to a habit of virtue, encomium to some single action. For example, if someone wished to praise Cicero for the consulship he held, it would properly be called an encomium of him; but if he were praised for the habit of his other virtues, it would properly be called praise of him. Aristotle treats the distinction between praise and encomium more fully in Rhetoric, book 1, and Keckermann in Systema Ethicae, problem 21.

units.la: Tertia ratio, quia principia non laudantur, sed honore & cultu digna aestimantur, at felicitas est principium saltem dirigens, sic supra cap. 2. dixerat, tum quia impellit ad actiones virtutis, & ejus genera omnia facimus, cur vero principia non laudentur proprie, rationem hanc reddit Alexand. Aphrod. ad cap. 6. lib. 3. Topic. Aristot. quia principia sunt antiquissima, & propter antiquitatem honoranda, tum etiam sunt fontes, unde omnia promanant reliqua & descendunt. Vide cap. 6. huius libri.
units.tr: The third argument: principles are not praised but are esteemed as worthy of honour and reverence. But happiness is a principle, at least a directing one, as he had said above in chapter 2, both because it impels us to acts of virtue, and because we do all the kinds of virtue for its sake. Why principles are not properly praised, Alexander of Aphrodisias gives as the reason in his commentary on Topics, book 3, chapter 6: because principles are most ancient, and are to be honoured on account of their antiquity; and also because they are the sources from which all the rest proceed and descend. See chapter 6 of this book.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Laus est eorum, quae ad aliud referuntur, cum locatum respiciat.
units.tr: 1. Praise is of those things which are referred to something else, since it regards the thing placed in a certain position.

units.la: 2. Virtus praecipue non honoratur, sed laudatur.
units.tr: 2. Virtue is chiefly not honoured but praised.

units.la: 3. Deos non laudamus, sed praedicamus beatos, & honore colimus.
units.tr: 3. We do not praise God, but call Him blessed and honour Him with reverence.

units.la: 4. Felicitas non est bonum laudabile, sed honorabile.
units.tr: 4. Happiness is not a praiseworthy but an honourable good.

units.la: 5. Felicitas est causa & principium, cuius gratia omnia alia facimus.
units.tr: 5. Happiness is the cause and principle for the sake of which we do all other things.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: Doubts.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Cur neget Aristot. felicitatem sit bonum laudabile, cum sit bonum honorabile, cum omne honorabile sit laudabile, propterea quod honor, ut majus bonum contineat in se laudem tanquam minus bonum? Resp. Cum Aristot. vocat honorabile, non excludit etiam laudem, sed negat proprie esse laudabile, propterea quod non ad aliud referatur, cujusmodi sunt omnia ea, quæ proprie laudem merentur dicuntur.
units.tr: I. Question: Why does Aristotle deny that happiness is a praiseworthy good, when it is an honourable good, and every honourable thing is praiseworthy, because honour contains praise within itself as a lesser good within a greater? Answer: When Aristotle calls happiness honourable, he does not exclude praise. He denies that it is properly praiseworthy, because it is not referred to anything else, which is the case with all those things that are said to deserve praise in the strict sense.

units.la: II. Quæritur: quomodo vocet felicitatem honorabile quid, cum ipse lib. 4. cap. 10. hujus tractatus dicit honorem competere modesto, propterea quod modestia circa honorem tanquam objectum suum versetur & cum modestia sit una quædam virtus, ideo affectio unius virtutis non est attribuenda toti felicitati, quæ est collectio omnium virtutum? Resp. Honorem esse duplicem, alium internum, alium externum, cum dicit infra lib. 4. modestiam versari circa honorem, non dicit versari circa omne honorem, sed circa externum & modicum non magnum, propterea quod modestia versetur circa res humiles & exiles, quæ non magnum sed exilem merentur honorem, at vero honor internus non uni competit virtuti proprie sed omnibus simul, & ideo felicitati tanquam perfectiori scopo omnium virtutum proprie attribuitur.
units.tr: II. Question: How does he call happiness something honourable, when in book 4, chapter 10 of this treatise he says that honour belongs to the modest person, since modesty is concerned with honour as its object, and since modesty is one particular virtue, the affection of one virtue should not be attributed to the whole of happiness, which is the collection of all the virtues? Answer: Honour is twofold, internal and external. When he says later in book 4 that modesty is concerned with honour, he does not mean every kind of honour, but external honour, and that only a modest and not great amount. Modesty concerns humble and slight things, which deserve a small rather than a great honour. Internal honour, however, does not belong properly to any one virtue but to all of them together, and so it is properly attributed to happiness, as the more perfect goal of all the virtues.

units.la: Instantia. Magnanimitas est singularis quædam virtus tantum, at versatur circa magnum honorem, sicut diserte, cap. 6. 7. 8. 9. lib. 4. hujus operis docet Philosophus, proinde non soli felicitati competit magnus honos, ergo neque felicitatis proprietas duci poterit, quod bonum sit summè honoratum? ratum? Respond. Negatur sequi, nam Magnanimitas versatur circa magnum honorem tanquam objectum suum, non vero tanquam proprietatem affectionem, neque circa omnem honorem in summo gradu consideratum, sed circa illum honorem, qui proprie viris Politicis in dignitate & eminentia constitutis competit, sicut docet cap. 7. 4. Nic. Aristoteles: Aliud ergo est honorem considerare pro felicitatis ornamento, aliud pro Magnanimitatis objecto.
units.tr: Objection: Magnanimity is a single special virtue, and it is concerned with great honour, as the Philosopher clearly teaches in chapters 6 to 9 of book 4 of this work. Therefore great honour does not belong to happiness alone, and so the property of happiness cannot be drawn from this, that it is the good most highly honoured. Answer: It does not follow. For magnanimity is concerned with great honour as its object, not as a property or affection of itself. Nor is it concerned with every honour considered at its highest degree, but with that honour which properly belongs to men placed in political dignity and eminence, as Aristotle teaches in chapter 7 of book 4. It is one thing, then, to consider honour as an ornament of happiness, and another to consider it as the object of magnanimity.

units.la: III. Quaeritur: Cur neget virtuti honorem hoc loco cum tamen sub finem cap. 7 lib. 4. dicat, integra & absoluta virtutis nullus tribui dignus honor potest, ergo virtus non minus bonum erit honorabile, quam ipsa felicitas? Resp. Honor trib. sumitur modis ut habetur loco citato. 1. Pro eo, quod Diis attribuitur, aut rebus divinis & sic beatitudini sequentis vitae, & felicitati hujus vitae competit, quo sensu dicitur divinum quid, hoc ipso c. 1. 2. Sumitur honor pro eo, quod defertur Politicis, sic competit Magnanimitati. 3. Pro praemio virtutis, & sic etiam competit virtuti in genere. IV. Quaeritur: An felicitati competat honor tanquam proprietas, cum tamen consuetudo & experientia doceat, Regi, Magistratui, Patri, & caeteris ejusmodi, honorem quoque esse tribuendum? Respon. In genere duplicem esse honorem, divinum & humanum: divinus Deo soli debetur: de quo supra; humanus distinguitur vel in servilem, qui debetur Domino a servo propter metum. 2. Naturalem, qui patri debetur propter naturae instinctum 3. Civilem qui debetur Regi propter justum imperium. Felicitati vero comcompetit honor tanquam omnis virtutis cumulatæ præmium.
units.tr: III. Question: Why does he deny honour to virtue in this place, when at the end of chapter 7 of book 4 he says that no honour worthy of it can be given to complete and perfect virtue? Therefore virtue will be no less an honourable good than happiness itself. Answer: Honour is taken in several senses, as is stated in the passage cited: (1) for what is given to God, or for divine things, and in this sense it belongs to the blessedness of the life to come and to the happiness of this life, which is why it is called something divine, as in the same chapter, lines 1 and 2; (2) honour taken as what is paid to men in political life, and in this sense it belongs to magnanimity; (3) honour taken as the reward of virtue, and in this sense it belongs to virtue in general. IV. Question: Does honour belong to happiness as a property, when custom and experience teach that honour is also to be paid to the king, the magistrate, the father, and others of that kind? Answer: In general honour is twofold, divine and human. Divine honour is due to God alone, as discussed above. Human honour is divided into (1) servile honour, which a servant owes to his master out of fear; (2) natural honour, which is owed to a father by natural instinct; and (3) civil honour, which is owed to a king on account of his just rule. Honour belongs to happiness, however, as the reward of all accumulated virtue.

units.la: Commodè moveri poterit & hæc quæstio, an cum felicitas bonum dicatur honorabile, ideoque, qui felicitate præditi sunt, honorari debent, an etiam qui ex hac vita excesserunt, propter beatitudinem tanquam summum & perfectissimum bonum honorari debeant? Respon. Diversas esse de hac re opiniones, nam non tantum inter Philosophos, sed etiam Theologos, agitata & disceptata fuit hæc quæstio; Utrum mortui sint honorandi? Fuerunt enim nonnulli præsertim ex Ethnicis, Religione Christiana non imbutis, qui nullum plane honorem, ne sepulturæ quidem mortuis tribuendum esse censuerunt, unde illud Æneid. 10. Facilis jactura sepulchri.
units.tr: This question may also be fairly raised: since happiness is called an honourable good, and so those who are endowed with happiness ought to be honoured, ought those also who have departed this life to be honoured on account of their blessedness, as the highest and most perfect good? The answer is that opinions on this matter differ. The question Are the dead to be honoured? has been debated and disputed not only among the philosophers but also among the theologians. For there were some, chiefly among the Gentiles, who were not imbued with the Christian religion, and who judged that no honour at all, not even burial, is to be paid to the dead. Hence that line of the Aeneid, 10: The loss of a tomb is an easy one.

units.la: Et dictum [Theodorici Philosophi, parum interest, humine an sublime putrescas, exististimabant namque mortem extremam esse rerum lineam, nihilque post mortem boni superesse, (ut videre est apud Philosophū cap. 9. lib. 3. Nicom.) cujus gratia defuncti sint honorandi, & cum ipsi quoq; omni sensu tam boni quam mali careant, quippe, qui sunt quasi non entia, rem vanam & inanem esse de iis honorandis, ullam curam & cogitationem suscipere. 1. Alii vero fuerunt & nunc etiam sunt, etiam ex iis, qui nomen suum inter Christianos profitentur, ut sunt Pontificii, qui superiorem hanc opinionem tanquam impiam & profanam detestantur, sed tamen in mortuis honorandis nimis sunt superstitiosi, eoq; audaciæ & temeritatis, ne dicam impietatis, progrediuntur, ut eos etiam, qui cum in vivis essent aliqua insigni five veræ
units.tr: There is also the saying of the philosopher Theodoric: It makes little difference whether you rot on the ground or in the air. For they thought that death is the final line of things, and that nothing good remains after death (as may be seen in the philosopher, Nicom. book 3, chapter 9). They held that the dead, for whose sake they should be honoured, have no sensation of good or evil, since they are as it were non-beings, so that it is a vain and empty thing to take any care or thought about honouring them. 1. But there have been others, and there still are, even among those who profess the Christian name, such as the Papists. They detest the former opinion as impious and profane, yet they are so superstitious in honouring the dead that they proceed with such audacity and rashness (not to say impiety) that they judge even those who, while alive, were famous for some notable reputation of holiness, whether true or false, to be worthy of religious worship, and invoke them as special patrons of men before God. Hence that invocation of the saints has burst forth, which detracts from the merit of Christ the Mediator. So the former opinion errs by defect, and this one by excess.

units.la: vere sive falsò sanctimonię opinione claruerunt, dignos judicent, quibus religiosus aliquis cultus exhibeatur, quiq; ut singulares hominū apud Deum patroni invocentur. Hinc illa Invocatio Sanctorum erupit, quæ Christi Mediatoris merito derogat, utergò prior opinio in defectu, ita hæc in excessu peccat: At verò cum in omnibus rebus medium sit optimum & tutissimum, videtur certè probanda esse eorum sententia, qui in mortuis honorandis, neque ad parum, neque ad nimium deflectunt, sed mediam & quasi regiam tenent viam; illi enim duplicem inprimis honorem esse statuunt, qui cum aliis pie defunctis, tum præcipuè viris bonis, de Ecclesia & Republica bene meritis, etiam post obitum præstari possit & debeat, unum honestam sepulturam, alterum, honorificam eorundem recordationem & commendationem, rationes afferunt inprimis tres: 1. Quia cum certò credamus, omnes eos qui pie in Domino moriuntur, esse viva veræ Ecclesiæ catholicæ membra, nostri id debet esse officii, ad profitendam fraternitatem Christianam & testificandam communionem illam spiritualem, quæ nobis cum iis intercedit, ut honestè non tantum eorum funera deducamus, sed pro loco, tempore & persona convenienti etiam honore sepulchri, prosequamur. 2. Quia ipsa justitia, quæ suum cuique tribuit, postulat ut ob virtutes insignes, quæ in defunctis eluxerunt, præclaras-que actiones, quibus de Ecclesia & Repub. optimè meruerunt, honorificam semper eorum usurpemus mentionem & in aliorum præsentia dignis eos celebremus laudibus. 3. Quia licet ipsi mortui honorem norem ejusmodi non desiderent, cum rebus humanis exempti simul etiam omnium bonorum externorum curam abjecerint, tamen æquum & pium est, ut præclara Dei dona, quibus ornati fuerunt in iis suspiciamus & commendemus, imo ad communem societatis humanæ utilitatem plurimum conferre extare tam privatim, quam publice aliorum de pietate & virtutibus defunctorum testimonia, propter duas causas: 1. Ut alia ad ipsorum imitationem invitentur & inflammentur. 2. Ut inimicis & malevolis hominibus, qui ejusmodi honorem morrum invident, os obstruatur, omnis calumniandi & obtrectandi aula præcidatur.
units.tr: But since in all things the mean is best and safest, the view of those seems certainly to be commended who, in honouring the dead, incline neither too little nor too much, but keep to the middle and, as it were, royal way. For they hold that a twofold honour is to be paid, and may rightly be paid, even after death, both to other godly departed persons and especially to good men who have deserved well of the Church and the commonwealth: one is an honourable burial, the other an honourable remembrance and commendation of them. They offer chiefly three reasons: (1) Since we firmly believe that all who die piously in the Lord are living members of the true catholic Church, it is our duty, in order to profess Christian brotherhood and to bear witness to that spiritual communion which exists between us and them, not only to escort their funerals honourably but also, according to place, time and person, to honour them with a fitting sepulchral honour. (2) Since justice itself, which gives to each his due, requires that, on account of the notable virtues which shone forth in the departed and their distinguished actions, by which they deserved well of the Church and commonwealth, we should always make honourable mention of them and in the presence of others celebrate them with fitting praises. (3) Although the dead themselves do not desire honour of this kind, since, having been released from human affairs, they have also cast off all care for external goods, nevertheless it is fair and pious that we should admire and commend the excellent gifts of God with which they were adorned. Indeed, the testimonies of others concerning the piety and virtues of the departed, both private and public, contribute greatly to the common benefit of human society, for two reasons: (1) so that others may be invited and inflamed to imitate them; (2) so that the mouths of enemies and malicious men, who envy such honour to the dead, may be stopped, and every opportunity for slander and detraction may be cut off.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: EXplicata jam felicitatis natura, de qua agendum tanquam fine & scopo & omnium humanarum institutorum, incipit de virtute agere tanquam medio, per quod felicitatem ipsam aflequimur sub finem hujus libri, nam solenne est Aristotelis in uno eodemque opere res cum rebus connectere & librum cum libro, & quoniam de virtute sibi agendum propositum libro sequenti, hic ejus mentionem injicit, sub calcem hujus libri. Partes capitis tres sunt. In prima, de virtute agendum proponit, ut definitio felicitatis melius intelligatur. In secunda, animam secundum partes seu facultates dividit, ut a qua parte animæ virtus proveniat tanquam a principio facilius cognoscatur. In tertia, secundum animæ facultates virtutes etiam dividit.
units.tr: Having now explained the nature of happiness, which must be treated as the end and goal of all human institutions, he begins to treat of virtue as the means by which we attain happiness itself, to be dealt with at the end of this book. It is Aristotle's custom to connect matters with matters and book with book within one and the same work. Since he has proposed to treat of virtue in the following book, he mentions it here, near the end of this one. The chapter has three parts. In the first, he proposes to treat of virtue, so that the definition of happiness may be better understood. In the second, he divides the soul according to its parts or faculties, so that the part of the soul from which virtue proceeds may be more easily known as its source. In the third, he also divides the virtues according to the faculties of the soul.

units.la: In prima igitur parte, duabus rationibus ostendit de virtute agendum esse, 1. quia iuvat ad felicitatis cognitionem: nam felicitas definitur per virtutem, veluti per medium, cuius ope felicitate ipsam assequimur, ut ex capite 6 huius libri constat. 2. Ratio sumitur ab exemplo Politicorum, qui de virtute in Politicis agunt, Ergo, & nos Politicam explicantes, de virtute agere debemus. Politicos agere de virtute inde probat, quia in hoc maxime incumbunt, ut cives bonos & legibus obedientes per veritatem reddant, quod probat exemplo Cretensium & Lacedaemoniorum, quia tunc temporis in illis Politica maxime florebant, (vide cap. 6. lib. 3. Politic.) sed quanquam de virtute agat, non tamen de omni virtute nam nomen virtutis est multiplex, quia alia est virtus divina, alia humana, & de humana tantum agere instituit, propterea quod bonum humanum, quod viribus humanis acquiritur, antea tractavit, & rursus virtus humana est alia corporis, ut sensuum perspicacitas, corporis proceritas, robur, &c. alia est virtus animi, virtutem corporis idcirco reicit, quod sit communis nobis plerumque cum beluis & de virtute tantum animi acturum se pollicetur, propterea quod ea sola sit hominis propria, per quam felicitatem acquirit.
units.tr: In the first part, he shows by two reasons that virtue must be treated: (1) because it helps us to know happiness, for happiness is defined through virtue as through a means, by whose help we attain happiness itself, as is clear from chapter 6 of this book; (2) the reason is taken from the example of the Politics writers, who treat of virtue in their Politics. Therefore we too, in explaining Politics, ought to treat of virtue. He proves that the political writers treat of virtue because they especially labour to make citizens good and obedient to the laws through virtue. He shows this by the example of the Cretans and Lacedaemonians, because at that time Politics flourished most among them (see book 3 of the Politics, chapter 6). But although he treats of virtue, he does not treat of every virtue, for the word "virtue" has many senses. There is divine virtue and human virtue, and he intends to treat only of human virtue, because he has already dealt with the human good, which is acquired by human powers. Again, human virtue is of two kinds: virtue of the body, such as keenness of the senses, bodily stature, strength, and so on; and virtue of the mind. He therefore sets aside bodily virtue, because it is for the most part common to us and the beasts, and he promises to treat only of virtue of the mind, because this alone is proper to man, and through it he acquires happiness.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis, ostendit de anima agendum esse, ut melius sciamus a quo principio fluat virtus: Probat de anima agendum esse argumento a minori ad majus hoc modo: Si Medicus, ut curator corporis in corpore cognoscendo diligenter laborat, ut videre est in Anatomicis, Ergo, multo magis Politicus, qui est medicus & curator animae, in anima cognoscenda laborare debet, sed quia de anima hic non ex professo agit, sed eatenus tantum, quatenus virtutis cognoscendæ explicationi inservit, ideo accuratam magis de anima deque ejus natura explicationem ad Phys. relegat. Deinde animam secundum suas facultates dividere incipit, sicut antea fecerat, capite 6, hujus libri, cum felicitatis definitionem investigaret; Dividit vero animam hoc modo, ut alia pars animæ sit irrationalis merè, alia sit merè rationalis. Alia sit media, quæ participat de natura utriusque. Primam animæ partem merè irrationalem vocat Vegetativam; secundam merè rationalem vocat Logisticam; tertiam mediam, vocat Orecticam seu appetitivam.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter, he shows that the soul must be treated, so that we may better know from what principle virtue flows. He proves that the soul must be treated by an argument from the less to the greater, in this way: If the physician, as the healer of the body, diligently labours to know the body, as can be seen in the anatomists, then much more the political philosopher, who is the physician and healer of the soul, ought to labour to know the soul. But because he does not treat of the soul here professedly, but only so far as it serves the explanation of the virtue to be known, he refers the more accurate account of the soul and its nature to the Physics. Then he begins to divide the soul according to its faculties, as he had done before, in chapter 6 of this book, when he was investigating the definition of happiness. He divides the soul in this way: one part of the soul is purely irrational, another is purely rational, and a third is intermediate, sharing in the nature of both. He calls the first part, which is purely irrational, the vegetative; the second, purely rational, he calls the logistic; the third, intermediate, he calls the appetitive or orectic.

units.la: Primam illam partem nempe vegetativam ab hac consideratione reijcit duabus de causis. 1. quia nobis communis est cum plantis & belu̇is. 2. Quia anima hominis propria insomnis quiescit, at vero ista vegetativa, & ejus rursus partes altrix nempe & augens in somnis non quiescunt, sed maximè tunc exserunt vires suas, nam ex cibo per somnum concosto & in sanguinem converso alunt & augent corpus, quod vero anima hominis propria in somnis quiescat, probat, 1. à communi proverbio; Fortunatos & miseros dimidiato vitæ tempore, nihil inter se differre, propterea quod anima utriusq; in somnis nihil agat, & perinde in actionibus somni, nihil differant. Secundò confirmat à vi & natura somni, nam somni vis & natura, hæc est, teste Aristotele lib. de somno & vigil. cap. 3. ut sensus consopiat, & vires animæ quiescere faciat, animæ saltem appetiti-væ væ qua boni aut mali dicimur. At nequis putet Aristotelem, sic statuere quasi anima nihil in somnis agat, dicit agere per insomnia, ita tamen ut in bonis somnia sint meliora & honestiora, in malis deteriora & turpiora: nam bonorum somnia malorum insomniis sunt meliora, propter has rationes: 1. Propter altam impressionem bonorum objectorum sensibus externis, qualia sunt simulachra virtutum, ob oculos veluti obversantia, & verba sapientum in auribus quasi sonantia. 2. Propter continuam actionem bonorum operum, qualia sunt inopes sublevare, ignorantes consilio juvare. 3. propter summam meditationem optimarum virtutum, quæ sic animum informant, ut ne in somnis quidem a studio & contemplatione virtutis abstinere boni velint. De quibus rationibus eleganter disserit Plato lib. 4. de Rep. sub sin. & Cic. lib. 1. de divin. ex Plat. ad verbum, & Plut. in lib. qui inscribitur Quomodo quis seipsum percipiat.
units.tr: He sets aside that first part, namely the vegetative, from this consideration for two reasons: (1) because it is common to us with plants and beasts; (2) because the proper soul of man rests in sleep, whereas that vegetative part, and its parts, the nutritive and the augmentative, do not rest in sleep, but then especially exert their powers, for they nourish and enlarge the body from food digested during sleep and turned into blood. That the proper soul of man rests in sleep he proves: (1) from a common proverb, that the fortunate and the wretched differ nothing in the half of their lifetime, because the soul of each does nothing in sleep, and so in the actions of sleep they do not differ. Secondly, he confirms it from the power and nature of sleep. The power and nature of sleep, according to Aristotle, in the book on sleep and waking, chapter 3, is to lull the senses and cause the powers of the soul to rest, at least the appetitive power by which we are called good or bad. But lest anyone think that Aristotle holds that the soul does nothing in sleep, he says that it acts through dreams, yet in such a way that in good men the dreams are better and more honourable, and in bad men worse and more base. For the dreams of good men are better than the dreams of bad men, for these reasons: (1) because of the deep impression of good objects on the external senses, such as the images of the virtues hovering before the eyes and the words of the wise as if sounding in the ears; (2) because of the continual performance of good works, such as relieving the needy and helping the ignorant with counsel; (3) because of the constant meditation on the best virtues, which so form the mind that good men do not wish to refrain even in sleep from the pursuit and contemplation of virtue. Plato in book 4 of the Republic, near the end, and Cicero in book 1 of On Divination, drawing word for word from Plato, discuss these reasons elegantly, and so does Plutarch in the book entitled How one may perceive oneself.

units.la: Deinde accedit illam animæ partem, quæ partim participat de natura rationis, partim vero non: vulgò dicitur ἀλογον. Non participare de ratione probat argumento ducto à continente & in incontinente. Nam in continente & in incontinente anima varie distrahitur, & propter contrarios affectus pugna excitatur, ubi vero est pugna, ibi sunt adversarii, & si in anima sint adversarii, alterum adversarium oportet esse rationem ipsam, quæ ad res optimas hortatur & affectibus moderari conatur. Alter vero adversarius qui rationi repugnat, a ratione alienum esse eum necesse est, quod probat à simili in corpore dissoluto, ubi omnia membra dissoluta soluta & laxata sunt, nam sicut ibi, quæ pars debet tendere ad dextram, tendit ad sinistram & econtra. Sic illi animæ impetus, qui cum ratione aliquid agere debent, cum rationi repugnant, aliquid agere contra rationem certum est, & proinde hujusmodi animæ impetus seu facultates sunt irrationales. De pugna vero affectuum, in anima latius agit Philosophus infra l.7 cap. 6. Et Plato lib. 4. de Repubt. Et Cic. lib.1. Tusc. quaest. Et Ovid. 7. Metam. fab.1. At vero participare de natura rationis, & proinde rationale esse probat ex eo, quod rationi pareat, ut exemplis & similibus illustrat, nam fieri fortes, & fieri prudentes, affectus sunt rationales, quia rationi se subijciunt, & a ratione regi se patiuntur. Simile vero est hoc: Sicut parentibus & amicis dicuntur dicto obedientes, rationem ipsorum habent, & econtra, qui rationem ipsorum habent, dicuntur ipsis dicto obedientes, ita illa pars animæ humanæ, quæ dicitur Appetitiva, cum rationi morem gerit, dicitur rationem habere, & proinde esse rationalis. Tandem accedit ad tertiam animæ partem, quæ dicitur λογιστικὴ, & hac dicit esse mere rationalem, quia vere in se rationem habet, tum etiam, quia rationi paret, ut supra c.6. hujus lib. dixerat.
units.tr: Next he comes to that part of the soul which partly shares in the nature of reason and partly does not; it is commonly called irrational [ἄλογον]. He proves that it does not share in reason by an argument drawn from the continent and the incontinent. For in the continent and the incontinent the soul is variously pulled apart, and a struggle arises from contrary affections. Where there is a struggle, there are adversaries; and if there are adversaries in the soul, one of the adversaries must be reason itself, which urges toward the best things and tries to moderate the affections. The other adversary, which resists reason, must be alien to reason. He proves this by a likeness to a body that is dissolved, where all the limbs are loosed and slackened: as there the part that ought to tend to the right tends to the left, and conversely, so those impulses of the soul which ought to act together with reason, when they resist reason, certainly act against reason; and therefore such impulses or faculties of the soul are irrational. On the struggle of the affections in the soul, the Philosopher treats more fully below, book 7, chapter 6; so also Plato in book 4 of the Republic, Cicero in book 1 of the Tusculan Disputations, and Ovid in book 7 of the Metamorphoses, fable 1. But that the appetitive part shares in the nature of reason, and is therefore rational, he proves from the fact that it obeys reason, as he illustrates by examples and comparisons. For to become brave and to become prudent are affections that are rational, because they submit themselves to reason and suffer themselves to be ruled by reason. The comparison is this: just as those who are obedient to parents and friends are said to heed their word, and so are said to have their reason, and conversely, those who have their reason are said to be obedient to them, so that part of the human soul which is called appetitive, when it complies with reason, is said to have reason, and therefore to be rational. Finally, he comes to the third part of the soul, which is called [λογιστικὴ], and says that this is purely rational, because it truly has reason in itself, and also because it obeys reason, as he had said above, in chapter 6 of this book.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis, pro duplici animæ facultate, nempe appetitiva & λογιστικὴ bifariam partitur virtutes, ut aliæ sunt virtutes mentales, quæ à λογιστικὴ fluunt immediate, quales sunt scientia, intellectus, ars, Sapientia, Prudentia, de quibus agit lib. 6. hujus operis. Al æ vero sunt Morales, quæ ab orectica animæ facultate fluunt, de quibus statim in principio agit lib.2. & reliquis etiam libris omnibus excepto 6. & ult.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter, he divides the virtues in two ways, according to the twofold faculty of the soul, the appetitive and the logistic [λογιστικὴ]. Some are mental virtues, which flow immediately from the logistic faculty, such as science, understanding, art, wisdom and prudence, which he treats of in book 6 of this work. The others are moral virtues, which flow from the orectic faculty of the soul. He treats of these at once, at the beginning of book 2, and in all the remaining books except 6 and the last.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Veri Politici in hoc maxime incumbunt, ut cives bonos & legibus obedientes reddant.
units.tr: 1. True politicians devote themselves chiefly to this, that they make citizens good and obedient to the laws.

units.la: 2. Virtus alia est divina, alia humana, alia corporis, alia animi.
units.tr: 2. Virtue is one kind divine and another human; one kind belongs to the body and another to the mind.

units.la: 3. Ut Medicus curat corpus, sic Politicus curat animam, & quanto est anima praestantior corpore, tanto est Politica praestantior Medicina.
units.tr: 3. As the physician cures the body, so the politician cures the soul; and as the soul is more excellent than the body, so political science is more excellent than medicine.

units.la: 4. Fortunatus a misero dimidiato vitae tempore nihil differt.
units.tr: 4. A fortunate man differs in no way from a wretched man in half of his lifetime.

units.la: 5. Bonorum somnia sunt meliora & honestiora, malorum vero nequiora & turpiora.
units.tr: 5. The dreams of good men are better and more honourable, while those of bad men are worse and more base.

units.la: 6. Ubi anima appetitiva facultas rationi repugnat, in irrationalem degenerat.
units.tr: 6. Where the appetitive faculty of the soul resists reason, it degenerates into the irrational.

units.la: 7. Viri prudentis & viri fortis actiones plerumque ex ratione & virtute fluunt.
units.tr: 7. The actions of the prudent man and of the brave man generally flow from reason and virtue.

units.la: 8. Animam appetitivam recte rationi parere, docent admonitiones, adhortationes, increpationes, quas a recta ratione patitur, & quarum consilium sequitur.
units.tr: 8. The admonitions, exhortations and rebukes which the appetitive soul undergoes from right reason, and whose counsel it follows, teach that it obeys right reason.

units.la: 9. Ex duplici anima facultate Logistica & appetitiva duplices fluunt virtutes, mentales & morales.
units.tr: 9. From the twofold faculty of the soul, the logistic and the appetitive, flow twofold virtues, mental and moral.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quid Aristoteles intelligat per vere Politicos; nam omnes homines videntur veri Politici, propterea quod homo fit natura animal Politicum, ut supra c.7. offenderat? Resp. Hoc ideo agit, quia ejus tempore multi erant, qui se jactabant esse Politicos & revera non erant, quales erat Sophistae, qui virtutis tantum umbram praese ferebant, virtutem ipsam minime curabant, ut ipse testatur lib.2.cap.3. Vocat hic vere Politicos, ticos, qui virtuti bene student, cujusmodi apud Lacedæmonios erat Lycurgus, apud Cretenses Minos. Quod vero ad illud homo est natura animal politicum, etsi aptitudo quædam sit hominibus innata secundum virtutem agendi, tamen ex virtute agere non possunt, nisi ab usu & consuetudine sibi habitum acquirant.
units.tr: I. Question: What does Aristotle mean by "truly political"? For all men seem to be truly political, since man is by nature a political animal, as he stated above in chapter 7? Answer: He does this because in his time there were many who boasted that they were political and were not really so, such as the Sophists, who displayed only the shadow of virtue and did not care at all for virtue itself, as he himself testifies in book 2, chapter 3. Here he calls "truly political" those who take pains to be good, such as Lycurgus among the Spartans and Minos among the Cretans. As for the claim that man is by nature a political animal: although a certain aptitude for acting virtuously is innate in men, they cannot act from virtue unless they acquire the habit through practice and custom.

units.la: II. Quæritur : Cur excludat à consideratione Ethica virtutes corporis, cum sint necessaria ad bonas actiones edendas, & per consequens sint media ad felicitatem ipsam assequendam? Resp. Ideo excludere, quod non ab usu & consuetudine proveniant (cujusmodi sunt illæ virtutes animæ, quæ sunt vera media ad felicitatem assequendam) sed à natura, quia nobiscum nascuntur, deinde nobis non sunt propriæ, quia nobis cum belluis plerunque sunt communes.
units.tr: II. Question: Why does he exclude the virtues of the body from ethical consideration, since they are necessary for performing good actions and consequently are means to attaining happiness itself? Answer: He excludes them because they do not arise from practice and custom (as do those virtues of the soul which are the true means to attaining happiness) but from nature, since they are born with us; and further, they are not properly our own, since for the most part they are common to us and the beasts.

units.la: III. Quæritur : Quomodo dicat superficiem concavam & convexam non differre reipsa, sed ratione quadam, cum sensus plerunque doceat loco & subjecto differre, ideo & reipsa, verbi gratia, concava superficies orbis lunæ attingit elementum ignis. Convexa verò attingit orbem Mercurii, unde cum tanta inter se distantia differant, quanta est latitudo orbis lunæ, reipsa differre, non ratione tantum convexam & concavam superficiem constat? Resp. Superficiem considerari dupliciter, vel in figura vel in corpore solido. Superficies in figura tam concava quam convexa non differunt reipsa, sed ratione quadam, quia sunt in una eademque linea, quæ tantum longitudinem habet & non latitudinem, & hoc modo Aristoteles intellexit, cum dixerit ratione tantum & non re differre. At verò si consideretur superficies des concava & convexa in corpore solido re ipsa non ratione tantum differunt, ut exemplo supra alias lito liquet.
units.tr: III. Question: How can he say that a concave and a convex surface differ not in reality but by a certain reason, when sense generally shows that they differ in place and in subject, and therefore in reality? For example, the concave surface of the lunar sphere touches the element of fire, while the convex surface touches the sphere of Mercury. Since they differ by as great a distance as the breadth of the lunar sphere, does it not follow that the convex and concave surfaces differ in reality, and not merely by reason? Answer: A surface can be considered in two ways: either in its figure or in a solid body. A surface considered in figure, whether concave or convex, does not differ in reality but by a certain reason, because both lie in one and the same line, which has length but no breadth. It is in this way that Aristotle understood it, when he said that they differ by reason only and not in reality. But if the concave and convex surfaces are considered in a solid body, they differ in reality and not merely by reason, as is clear from the example given above elsewhere.

units.la: IV. Quæritur: An hæc ratio sit firma, quam affert Aristoteles, nempe quod anima hominis propria in somnis quiescat, & nihil agat. nam si anima nihil agat, nihil omnino erit, quia per actum definitur 2. de anima, cap. 2. Unde ubi agere definit & anima definit? Resp. Aristotelem non statuere animam in somnis nihil omnino agere, sed nihil secundum virtutem agere, quod inde probatur, quia dicit, fortunatu à misero dimidiato vitæ tempore nihil differre, qui scil. somnus aut actio somni naturaliter omnibus competat; deinde cum somnia objiciat phantasiæ, aliquid agere perspicuè docet.
units.tr: IV. Question: Is the argument that Aristotle brings forward firm, namely that man's proper soul rests in sleep and does nothing? For if the soul does nothing, it will be nothing at all, since it is defined by its action, On the Soul 2, chapter 2. Hence where it ceases to act, there the soul ceases too? Answer: Aristotle does not hold that the soul does absolutely nothing in sleep, but that it does nothing according to virtue. This is proved by the fact that he says the fortunate man differs in nothing from the wretched man in half of life's time, since sleep, or the activity of sleep, naturally belongs to all. Further, since he attributes dreams to the imagination, he clearly teaches that the soul does something.

units.la: V. Quæritur: Annon hæc duo contradictionem includant, animam hominis propriam in somnis quiescere, & proinde bonum à malo per somnum non differre, & tamen somnia bonorum esse bona, malorum vero mala, unde per somnum differunt, & non differunt, quæ includunt contradictionem? Resp. Somnus consideratur duobus modis, naturaliter vel moraliter. Naturaliter per somnum non differt bonus à malo, & hoc modo Philosophus intellexit: In priori membro Moraliter tamen bonus à malo per somnum differt, propterea quod ex qualitate personarum meliora vel deteriora somnia phantasiæ objiciantur, & hoc modo posterius membrum intellexit.
units.tr: V. Question: Do not these two statements include a contradiction: that man's proper soul rests in sleep, and therefore good does not differ from evil through sleep; and yet the dreams of good men are good and those of bad men are bad, whence they both differ and do not differ through sleep, which includes a contradiction? Answer: Sleep is considered in two ways, naturally or morally. Naturally, through sleep the good does not differ from the bad, and it is in this way that the Philosopher understood the first member. Morally, however, the good does differ from the bad through sleep, because better or worse dreams are presented to the imagination according to the quality of the persons; and it is in this way that he understood the latter member.

units.la: VI. Quæritur: Quomodo anima appetitiva inesse possunt virtutes morales, cum appetitus, ex quo constituitur, illa facultas appetitiva accidens & virtus etiam fit accidens. At accidens accidenti inesse non potest. Appetitum esse accidens probatur,quia est potentia naturalis in secunda specie qualitatis. Virtus enim est accidens in prima specie, nempe habitu, accidens accidenti inesse non potest, ut constat ex Aristotele 2. Top. 3. Resp. Appetitum considerari duplicitér, vel pro potentia naturali aliquid appetendi, & sic est accidens; vel pro facultate animæ, & sic est substantia, à qua fluunt virtutes morales, vel dicendum est subjectum esse duplex quod & quo. Subjectum quod immediatè accidens recipit; Quo, per quod accidens recipitur, nam ut per superficiem recipitur in subjectum color, ita per appetitum recipitur in voluntatem virtus.
units.tr: VI. Question: How can the moral virtues inhere in the appetitive soul, since the appetitive faculty, from which it is constituted, is an accident, and virtue too becomes an accident? But an accident cannot inhere in an accident. That appetite is an accident is proved because it is a natural power in the second species of quality. For virtue is an accident in the first species, namely habit, and an accident cannot inhere in an accident, as is clear from Aristotle, Topics 2, chapter 3. Answer: Appetite may be considered in two ways: either as a natural power of desiring something, and so it is an accident; or as a faculty of the soul, and so it is a substance from which the moral virtues flow. Or it must be said that the subject is twofold: that which and that by which. The subject that immediately receives the accident; that by which is the means through which the accident is received. For as colour is received into a body through the surface, so virtue is received into the will through appetite.

units.la: Notandum est, cum Aristoteles dicit ab anima appetitiva provenire virtutes morales, animam appetitivam esse duplicem: nam una est in sensu occupata, quæ proprie dicitur appetitus, altera rationi se subjiciens, quæ dicitur voluntas. In voluntate igitur proprie sedem habent virtutes morales, non tamen sensus appetitivus à virtute prorsus excluditur; nam in eo est proprie ira & concupiscentia, sed quia virtutes initium faciunt in sensu appetitivo, incrementum verò & perfectionem in intellectu practico seu in voluntate.
units.tr: It should be noted that when Aristotle says the moral virtues come from the appetitive soul, the appetitive soul is twofold. For one is occupied with sense and is properly called appetite; the other, subjecting itself to reason, is called will. The moral virtues therefore have their proper seat in the will. Yet the sensitive appetite is not wholly excluded from virtue, for in it properly lie anger and concupiscence; but the virtues take their beginning in the sensitive appetite, and their growth and perfection in the practical intellect, or in the will.

units.la: His jam dictis corollarii loco adjiciemus hanc quæstionem: An virtus moralis sit præstantior virtute intellectuali, necne, cum intellectuali fluat, ut dictum est, à facultate animæ logistica. Moralis verò ab appetitiva? Resp. Moralem esse præstantiorem propter has rationes: 1. Virtus moralis reddit virum probum & bonum; Intellectualis verò non. 2. Virtus moralis est per se laudabilis; Intellectualis verò non, nisi cum morali conconjuncta. 3. Virtus moralis est principium actionum honestarum, quae ad honeste agendum impellit; Intellectualis vero non. 4. Virtute morali nemo abuti potest ad libidinem; Intellectuali vero quis potest. 5. Durabilior est virtus moralis intellectuali, nam frequentior ejus exercendae in hominum societate usus occurrit, neque per oblivionem deleri potest, ut praeclare supra disseruit Philosophus cap. 11. hujus libri. 6. Virtus intellectualis tam malis quam bonis communis est; Moralis vero solis bonis competit.
units.tr: Having said these things, we will add, by way of a corollary, this question: Is moral virtue more excellent than intellectual virtue or not, since intellectual virtue flows, as has been said, from the logistic faculty of the soul, and moral virtue from the appetitive? Answer: Moral virtue is more excellent for these reasons: (1) moral virtue makes a man upright and good, but intellectual virtue does not; (2) moral virtue is praiseworthy in itself, but intellectual virtue is not, unless it is conjoined with moral virtue; (3) moral virtue is the principle of honourable actions and impels one to act honourably, but intellectual virtue does not; (4) no one can abuse moral virtue for the sake of lust, but one can abuse intellectual virtue; (5) moral virtue is more durable than intellectual, for its exercise in human society occurs more often, and it cannot be destroyed by forgetting, as the Philosopher excellently argued above in chapter 11 of this book; (6) intellectual virtue is common to the bad as well as the good, but moral virtue belongs only to the good.

units.la: Secundo & haec quaestio non incommode moveri poterit: An virtus scilicet moralis, prout in Ethica tractatur, essentialiter differat a virtute Christiana, quam Theologia considerat; sunt enim nonnulli, qui in hac quaestione thesin affirmantem defendunt, rationes ipsorum sunt quinque?
units.tr: Secondly, this question may also fairly be raised: Does moral virtue, as it is treated in Ethics, differ in essence from Christian virtue, as Theology considers it? For some hold the affirmative in this question, and their arguments are five.

units.la: 1. Quia virtus moralis cadit etiam in homines Ethnicos & verae religionis ignaros. Christiana autem virtus non, nisi in pios & vere regeneratos. 2. Quia virtus moralis tantum informat mores externos hominis, quibus in civili hominum societate opus habet. Christiana autem virtus informat etiam mores internos hominis ad verum Dei cultum maxime requisitos. 3. Quia virtus moralis Deo non est grata, praesertim, si infit homini non renato, sine fide enim impossibile est placere Deo, sicut dicitur ad Hebr. 11. v. 6. Christiana vero virtus Deo est grata & accepta. 4. Quia virtus moralis, nisi ad Deum referatur, non est virtus, teste Augustino lib. 15. de civit. Dei, cap 25. & ut Hieronymus ait, sine Christo omnis virtus vitium est. 5. Quia virtus moralis ab homine assuetudine acquiritur. Christiana vero virtus a Deo infunditur, esse-
units.tr: 1. Moral virtue belongs even to heathen men who are ignorant of the true religion, whereas Christian virtue belongs only to the godly and truly regenerate. 2. Moral virtue shapes only the external conduct of a man, which he needs in civil society, whereas Christian virtue shapes also the inward conduct of a man, which is especially required for the true worship of God. 3. Moral virtue is not pleasing to God, especially when it is found in an unregenerate man, for without faith it is impossible to please God, as is said in Hebrews 11:6. Christian virtue, however, is pleasing and acceptable to God. 4. Moral virtue, unless it is referred to God, is not virtue, according to Augustine in On the City of God, book 15, chapter 25, and, as Jerome says, without Christ every virtue is a vice. 5. Moral virtue is acquired by a man through habit, whereas Christian virtue is infused by God and is effected by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: ctumőtumque est Spiritus sanđti. Verum hæc opinio non omnibus placet, & sunt, quæ statuunt virtutem moralem à Christiana tantum gradibus perfectionis differre, non secus ac lucem matutinam à luce meridiana, aut teporem à feruore, & in hac secunda opinione sunt viri celebres Dan.lib.1.Ethic.Christiana,c.1. Timpler.system.Ethic.probl.21. Keckerm.probl.9.10. Et respondent ad argumenta allata superius. Nam primo licet virtus moralis cadat etiam in hominem Ethnicum & verę religionis ignarum; inde tamen non sequitur illam à Christiana virtute essentialiter differre, sed tantum hoc sequitur, illam non ita perfectam esse ac hanc, quia virtus moralis est tantum gradus ad Christianam, & illa ab hac complementum capit. Ad secundum argumentum respondendum erit per negationem, nam virtus moralis non tantum informat mores externos hominis, sed etiam internos, licet non eo gradu perfectionis quo Christiana. Ad tertium quoque per inficiationem responderi poterit, nam virtus moralis per se grata & accepta est Deo suo modo, quia est res bona, honesta & laudabilis, licet in homine non renato reperiatur, nam quod dicitur: sine fide impossibile, &c. id non de qualibet placentia, sed de ea, quæ ad salutem æternam dirigitur, est accipiendum. 4. Dura admodum videntur esse dicta Augustini & Hieronymi: licet enim virtus moralis sine Christo & relatione ad Deum non sit virtus. Christiana tamen est vera virtus, non secus ac lux matutina est vera lux, tametsi non sit meridiana, & tepor est verus calor, tametsi non sit feruor. s. Virtus Christiana à Deo infundi-turtur interdum immediatè sine ullis mediis, interdum mediatè, intervenientibus nempe causis secundis, cujusmodi sunt pia precatio, diligens meditatio verbi divini, feria coverfio hominis ad Deum, exercitatio assidua & pia in actionibus sanctis, & per has causas Spiritus sanctus dicitur ordinariè in homine renato virtutè producere Christianam. Pro decisione quæstionis notandū, virtutè considerari duobus modis, vel respectu sui, vel respectu subjecti cui inest. Respectu subjecti duob. modis considerari potest, vel respectu subjecti nō renati, nempe Ethnici, & hoc respectu virtus moralis distinguitur, etiam essentialiter à Christiana, cum habeat suam definitionem veram & legitimam, quæ constituit veram cujusque rei essentiam, habet etiam suum verum finem, qui proprie ipsum spectat: at vero respectu subjecti renati hominis Christiani virtus moralis tendit, velut gradus quidam ad virtutem Christianam. Respectu sui etiam virtus poterit considerari tanquam genus imperfectum, ut habeat istas duas species Christianam & Moralem, & sic non differunt reali essentia, sed gradibus quibusdam, sicut amicitia utilis ab honesta, ideo non valet, si quis objiciat virtutem moralem, si non per se, saltem per accidens degenerare in vitiū, nempe respectu subjecti mali, cui inest, ideoque esse damnandam. Virtus autem moralis, si modo vera sit, perficit subjectū, cui inest, ideo ei, quatenus est malum, inesse non potest, neque valet similitudo, quæ affertur vini & vasis impuri, quia longè alia est ratio vini boni in vas impurum infusi, utrumque enim corpus est capax mutuæ commixtionis & infectionis. Vir-
units.tr: Yet this opinion does not please everyone, and there are those who maintain that moral virtue differs from Christian virtue only in degrees of perfection, just as morning light differs from midday light, or lukewarmth from heat. Among the famous men who hold this second opinion are Dan., Ethics, Christian book 1, chapter 1; Timpler, System of Ethics, problem 21; Keckermann, problems 9 and 10. And they answer the arguments adduced above. For, to the first: although moral virtue also falls upon a heathen man ignorant of the true religion, it does not follow from this that it differs in essence from Christian virtue; it follows only that it is not as perfect as the latter, since moral virtue is merely a step towards Christian virtue, and receives its completion from it. To the second argument the answer must be given by denial, for moral virtue shapes not only the external conduct of a man but also his internal conduct, though not to the same degree of perfection as Christian virtue. To the third also it may be answered by denial, for moral virtue is in its own way pleasing and acceptable to God, since it is a good, honourable and praiseworthy thing, even though it is found in an unregenerate man; for what is said, without faith it is impossible, &c., must be understood not of any pleasing whatever, but of that which is directed towards eternal salvation. To the fourth: the words of Augustine and Jerome seem very harsh. For although moral virtue without Christ and without reference to God is not virtue, Christian virtue is nevertheless true virtue, just as morning light is true light even though it is not midday light, and lukewarmth is true warmth even though it is not heat. To the fifth: Christian virtue is infused by God sometimes immediately, without any means, and sometimes mediately, namely through intervening second causes, such as devout prayer, diligent meditation on the divine Word, a serious turning of man to God, and constant and pious exercise in holy actions; and through these causes the Holy Spirit is said ordinarily to produce Christian virtue in a regenerate man. To settle the question, it must be noted that virtue may be considered in two ways, either with respect to itself or with respect to the subject in which it inheres. With respect to the subject, it may be considered in two ways: either with respect to a subject that is not regenerate, namely a heathen, and in this respect moral virtue is also distinguished in essence from Christian virtue, since it has its own true and lawful definition, which constitutes the true essence of each thing, and it also has its own true end, which properly belongs to it; but with respect to a regenerate subject, a Christian man, moral virtue tends as a certain step towards Christian virtue. With respect to itself, virtue may also be considered as an imperfect genus, so that it has these two species, Christian and moral; and thus they do not differ in real essence but in certain degrees, just as useful friendship differs from honourable friendship. Therefore the objection is not valid, if someone objects that moral virtue, if not per se, at least per accidens, degenerates into vice, namely with respect to the evil subject in which it inheres, and that it is therefore to be condemned. Moral virtue, however, if it is indeed true, perfects the subject in which it inheres, and therefore it cannot inhere in him as he is evil; nor does the comparison hold that is brought forward of wine and an impure vessel, for the case of good wine poured into an impure vessel is quite different, since both substances are capable of mutual mixing and contamination. Virtue

units.la: L tus autem & homo non renatus non ita inter se commiscceri possunt, ut illa ab hac vitiositatem verè contrahat, tametsi impei fectior merito statuaturin homine non renato, quàm renato.
units.tr: and an unregenerate man, however, cannot so mix with each other that the former truly contracts vice from the latter, although the unregenerate man is rightly judged to be more imperfect than the regenerate.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CAPUT I.

units.la: VIA in toto hoc opere methodo utitur Analytica Philos. Ideo incipit à Felicitate tàquàm fine, & eam explicat toto libro 1. Et quia in definitione felicitatis virtutem accipit loco differentiæ, ideo de virtute agit in genere toto hoc libro secundo, ut melius & commodius cognoscatur, quid sit ipsa felicitas, tum quia felicitas est effectus virtutis, tum quia virtus medium est, per quod assequimur felicitatem. Partes hujus libri sunt tres; In prima agit de causis virtutum, seu unde oriantur virtutes. In secunda virtutis naturam per definitionem investigat, ut intelligatur, quid sit virtus.
