In tertia dividit virtutem in suas species, de quibus reliquo libro acturus est. Primæ rursus partis membra sunt quatuor: In primo ostendit, à quo proveniat virtus. In secundo, quales sint operationes, ex quibus oritur virtus. In tertio, circa quid versetur virtus, seu quod sit objectum virtutis. In quarto, quomodo ex bonis actionibus signatur virtus.
units.tr: In this whole work the author uses the analytic method of Philosophy. Therefore he begins from happiness as the end, and explains it throughout the first book. And because in the definition of happiness he takes virtue in the place of the differentia, he treats of virtue in general throughout this second book, so that what happiness itself is may be better and more conveniently known, both because happiness is the effect of virtue, and because virtue is the means through which we attain happiness. The parts of this book are three. In the first he treats of the causes of the virtues, or whence virtues arise. In the second he investigates the nature of virtue through definition, so that it may be understood what virtue is. In the third he divides virtue into its species, which he will treat of in the rest of the book. The members of the first part are four. In the first he shows from what virtue arises. In the second, what kinds of operations give rise to virtue. In the third, what virtue is concerned with, or what is the object of virtue. In the fourth, how virtue is marked by good actions.

units.la: Primi hujus capitis, in quo continetur primum membrum, partes sunt tres: In prima repetitur divisio virtutis in Intellectualem & Moralem allata sub fi- nem superioris libri. In secunda ostendit virtutem provenire à consuetudine & usu, non à natura & hoc demonstrat, 4. rationibus. In tertia, docet educatio- ni magnam adhibendam esse diligentiam, ut quisq; prudens consideret, quibusnam actionibus assue- scat, quia ex qualitate actionum oriuntur boni vel mali habitus.
units.tr: The first chapter, which contains the first member, has three parts: In the first the division of virtue into intellectual and moral, given at the end of the previous book, is repeated. In the second he shows that virtue comes from custom and practice, not from nature, and he demonstrates this by four reasons. In the third he teaches that great diligence must be applied to upbringing, so that every prudent person considers with which actions he is accustomed, because good or bad habits arise from the quality of actions.

units.la: In prima igitur parte capitis resumit divisionem su- pra datam, & affert differentiam inter Moralem & Intellectualem virtutem, non à subjecto, ut supe- rius, cum pro facultatibus animæ diviserit virtutem, sed à causa efficiente, qua differentia allata praetermittit virtutem intellectualem, de qua postea lib. 6. est acturus, & persequitur tractatione virtutis moralis libri hu proxime sequentibus. Differentia igitur à causa est, quod virtus intellectualis ortum & incrementum habeat à doctrina, & ut recte acquiratur, experientia & tempore indiget, unde Gal. lib. 1. de Method. dicit, virtutes rationales seu intellectuales, duobus insistere cruribus, doctrina & experientia. Virtus verò Moralis non à doctrina ortum trahit, sed à consuetudine & more, unde & Moralis dicta est, nam multi nulla instructi doctrina eam habent, ut inter Turcas & Tartaros multi sunt virtute, sed nulla doctrina instructi.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter, then, he takes up the division given above and states the difference between moral and intellectual virtue. He draws it not from the subject, as above, when he divided virtue according to the faculties of the soul, but from the efficient cause. By this difference he sets aside intellectual virtue, which he will treat of later in book 6, and pursues the treatment of moral virtue in the books immediately following. The difference from the cause, therefore, is this: intellectual virtue has its origin and growth from teaching, and to be acquired rightly it needs experience and time. Hence Galen, in book 1 of De Methodo, says that rational or intellectual virtues rest on two legs, teaching and experience. Moral virtue, however, does not draw its origin from teaching but from custom and habit, and for this reason it is also called moral. For many have it without any instruction, as among the Turks and Tartars there are many who are virtuous but have no instruction.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit virtutem Moralem non provenire à natura, sed ab usu & assuefactione 4. rationibus. 1. Quæ à natura proveniunt aliter assuefieri nequeunt, at virtus aliter assuefieri potest. Ergo non est à natura. Major probatur exemplis Lapi enim quocunque modo assuefiat, ut ascendat, nunquam tamen natura sua ascendet, sed descendet propter gravitatem, sic ignis etiam nunquam sua natura descendet propter levitatem, at virtus assuefactione aliter se habere potest, nam ex bonis actionibus conservatur, ex pravis vero corrumpitur & tollitur, ut intra patebit. Et hoc est, quod Plato dicit in Protag. quod virtus malis actionibus & prava institutione tolli & adimi possit, natura vero non possit, unde recte Poëta:
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he shows that moral virtue does not arise from nature but from practice and habituation, by four reasons. (1) What arises from nature cannot be brought about in another way, but virtue can be brought about in another way. Therefore it is not from nature. The major premise is proved by examples. A stone, however it is accustomed to be made to rise, will never by its nature rise but will fall because of its weight; so fire will never by its nature sink because of its lightness. But virtue can be otherwise disposed by habituation, for it is preserved by good actions, and it is corrupted and destroyed by bad ones, as will be shown below. And this is what Plato says in the Protagoras: that virtue can be destroyed and taken away by bad actions and bad training, but nature cannot. Hence the poet rightly says:

units.la: Naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurret.
units.tr: You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will keep coming back.

units.la: Hinc corollarii loco respondet cuidam objectioni, quam afferebat Socrates, virtutes si non sunt a natura, sunt contra naturam aut praeter naturam, & respondet non esse praeter aut contra naturam, quia potentiam naturalem, habemus & aptitudinem ad illas suscipiendas. Virtutes vero sunt in Anima tanquam in subjecto. Deus vero animā creavit cum tali aptitudine, ut possit in se recipere virtutes, tanquam formam in materia, virtutes igitur etsi a consuetudine proveniant, non tamen sunt nobis praeter naturam, quia habemus potentiam naturalem ad eas suscipiendas, quae si inesset, tunc viderentur esse praeter aut contra naturam, & observandum est non competere hoc tantum virtuti morali, de qua in praesentia agit, sed etiam intellectuali, & propter istam potentiam seu aptitudinem quā a natura habemus ad recipiendas virtutes Aristotel. alibi vocat virtutes naturales ut infra lib. 6. cap. ultim. lib. 10. cap. 9. lib. 7. Polit. cap. 6. videre licet.
units.tr: By way of corollary he answers an objection which Socrates raised: if virtues are not from nature, they are contrary to nature or beyond nature. He replies that they are neither beyond nor contrary to nature, because we have a natural power and aptitude for receiving them. Virtues are in the soul as in a subject, and God created the soul with such an aptitude that it can receive virtues in itself as form in matter. Therefore virtues, even if they come from custom, are not beyond nature for us, because we have a natural power to receive them. If that power were not present, they would seem to be beyond or contrary to nature. It should be observed that this applies not only to moral virtue, which he is treating at present, but also to intellectual virtue, and on account of this power or aptitude which we have from nature for receiving virtues, Aristotle elsewhere calls them natural virtues, as may be seen below in book 6, last chapter; book 10, chapter 9; book 7 of the Politics, chapter 6.

units.la: Secunda ratio in naturalibus sic proceditur, ut poten-
units.tr: The second reason proceeds as follows. In natural things the

units.la: potentia seu facultas praecedat actum: In virtute vero è contra actus praecedit facultatem, ergo virtus non est a natura, quod in naturalibus procedatur a facultate ad actum, probatur exemplis, verbi gratia. In visu prius habemus facultatem videndi, & postea videmus, & sic de aliis: In virtute vero ab actione procedimus: nam prius agimus, & ex crebris actionibus acquirimus habitum, ex habitu acquirimus facultatem bene & cum facultate agendi, quod exemplis etiam probat in artibus, semper ab actu procedimus ad habitum, ab habitu ad facultatem seu facilitatem bene operandi secundum artem.
units.tr: power or faculty comes before the act. In virtue, on the contrary, the act comes before the faculty. Therefore virtue is not from nature. That in natural things one proceeds from faculty to act is proved by examples. For instance, in sight we first have the faculty of seeing and afterwards we see, and so with other things. In virtue, however, we proceed from action: for we act first, and from frequent actions we acquire a habit, and from the habit we acquire the faculty of acting well and readily. He proves this also by examples from the arts: we always proceed from act to habit, and from habit to faculty, or facility of working well according to the art.

units.la: Tertia ratio, quod virtus non proveniat a natura, sed a consuetudine, ducitur a testimonio & auctoritate Legumlatorum: nam illi non natura sed moribus & cufu leges instillari existimar, qui enim leges ferunt & cupiunt cives bonos fieri, hoc non naturae committunt, sed ideo leges condunt, ut bonis premium, malis poenam statuant, atque adeo ut cives bonis operationibus se exerceant, ut inde bonos habitus id est. Virtutes sibi comparet, & nisi hoc sit propositum & scopus Legumlatorum, errant: In quacunque enim Repub. leges non conduntur, ut cives bene agendo bene vivant, ea Resp. non est bona, quod etiam Plato in Protag. fusissime tractat.
units.tr: The third reason, that virtue does not come from nature but from custom, is drawn from the testimony and authority of lawgivers. For they think that laws are instilled not by nature but by morals and custom. Those who enact laws and wish their citizens to become good do not entrust this to nature; they therefore make laws so that they may set a reward for good men and a penalty for bad, and so that citizens may exercise themselves in good operations, and thereby acquire for themselves good habits, that is, virtues. If this is not the purpose and aim of lawgivers, they are mistaken. For in any commonwealth in which laws are not made so that the citizens may live well by acting well, that commonwealth is not good. Plato also treats this very fully in the Protagoras.

units.la: Quarta ratio est ejusmodi si virtus iisdem actionibus diversimode se habentibus acquiritur & corrumpitur, non est a natura, connexum probatur, quia operatio naturae non est ad oppositum, sed uniformiter semper agit, ut gravia semper tendunt deorsum, levia sursum. Aliunde probatur a simili
units.tr: The fourth reason is of this kind: if virtue is acquired and corrupted by the same actions when these are variously disposed, it is not from nature. The connection is proved because the operation of nature is not towards the opposite, but always acts uniformly, as heavy things always tend downwards and light things upwards. It is proved also by a comparison

units.la: L in artibus. Nam pulsatio cytharae est eadem actio genere, sed poterit diversimode se habere. Mala pulsatio cytharae destruit artem cytharisticam, bona vero acquirit & conservat, sic etiam in aliis artibus, & si artifex a natura esset, nihil opus esset doctore, & tamen contrarium experientia ipsa docet, sicse habet in virtutibus, per bonas actiones comparantur virtutes & conservantur, per malas vero corrumpuntur, quod probat exemplis Justitiae, Fortitudinis, & Temperantiae, trium praecipuarum virtutum.
units.tr: in the arts. For the striking of a lyre is the same kind of action, yet it can be done in different ways. A bad striking of the lyre destroys the art of lyre-playing, but a good striking acquires and preserves it. So also in the other arts. And if the craftsman were from nature, there would be no need of a teacher; yet experience itself teaches the contrary. It is the same with the virtues: they are acquired and preserved by good actions and corrupted by bad ones. He proves this by examples of justice, fortitude and temperance, the three chief virtues.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis jubet diligenter considerare, quibusnam actionibus assuescamus, nam operationibus similes nascuntur habitus, ex bonis operationibus nascuntur boni habitus & econtra, unde non parum, imo plurimum refert quomodo educentur adolescentes: nam si bene agere assueverunt, virtuti studebunt & habitus virtutis sibi acquirent. Si male vero, viriis laborabunt, quod & Plato in Alcib. & Lycurgus Lacedaemoniorum legislator exemplo duorum canum luculenter demonstravit.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he bids us diligently consider with which actions we are accustomed, for habits are born from like operations: good habits arise from good operations and bad from bad, and conversely. Hence it matters not a little, indeed very much, how young people are brought up. For if they have been accustomed to act well, they will strive for virtue and acquire the habits of virtue for themselves. But if they have been accustomed to act badly, they will labour under vices. This Plato in the Alcibiades and Lycurgus, the lawgiver of the Lacedaemonians, clearly demonstrated by the example of two dogs.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Virtus intellectualis doctrina & experientia comparatur, moralis vero consuetudine & usu.
units.tr: 1. Intellectual virtue is acquired by teaching and experience; moral virtue, however, by habit and practice.

units.la: 2. Virtus est non infit nobis a natura, neque prater naturam inest, quia potentiam & aptitudinem eam assequendi a natura habemus.
units.tr: 2. Virtue is not innate in us from nature, nor is it present in us contrary to nature, because we have from nature the capacity and aptitude to attain it.

units.la: 3. In naturalibus facultas praecedit actum, in virtute vero actus praecedit facultatem.
units.tr: 3. In natural things the capacity comes before the act; in virtue, however, the act comes before the capacity.

units.la: 4. Virtus iisdem actionibus genere comparatur & corrumpitur.
units.tr: 4. Virtue is acquired and destroyed by the same kinds of actions.

units.la: Quales sunt operationes precedentes habitum, talis ex iis nascitur habitus.
units.tr: Whatever kind of operations precede a habit, that kind of habit arises from them.

units.la: Plurimum refert quibus rationibus juventus educetur, nam ex educatione tota vita ratio dependet.
units.tr: It matters greatly by what principles young people are brought up, for the whole course of life depends on their upbringing.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An recte assignarit differentiam inter virtutem intellectualem & moralem, cum intellectualis comparetur experientia, moralis consuetudine: nam non minus intellectualis consuetudine constat, dum enim quis rebus cognoscendis assuescit, scientiam in rebus acquirit, sic etiam moralis experientia comparatur, verbi gratia: Quicunque pericula experitur, & fortiter in iis se gerit, dicitur jam fortis experientia, & sic in aliis? Respond. Aristotelem posuisse discrimen inter intellectualem & moralem ex causis per se, non vero per accidens, intellectualis quidem consuetudine comparatur, sed non tanquam a causa per se, sed tantum per accidens, quatenus cum usu & experientia est conjuncta, dum aliquis experientia aliquid discit, per accidens se assuescit isti rei discendæ: Sic etiam moralis experientia interdum constat, sed non proprie & per se, sed tantum per accidens. Differunt vero experientia & consuetudo hoc modo. Quod consuetudo fit in nobis ipsis, experientia vero extra nos. Non enim possumus aliquid consuetudine comparare, nisi nosmetipsos exercemus & rebus agendis nos assuescamus: Experientia potest haberi & si nihil in nobis ipsis experiamur, ut verbi gratia: in arte Medica aliquis discit per experientiam rhebarbarum purgare choleram, quia in pluribus hoc innotuit, etsi in se ipso nunquam quis expertus sit.
units.tr: I. The question is: Did he rightly assign the difference between intellectual and moral virtue, since intellectual virtue is acquired by experience and moral virtue by habit? For intellectual virtue also consists in habit: when someone becomes accustomed to knowing things, he acquires knowledge of them; so too moral experience is acquired, for example: whoever experiences dangers and acts bravely in them is already said to be brave by experience, and so on in other cases? Answer: Aristotle laid down the distinction between intellectual and moral virtue according to their causes per se, not per accidens. Intellectual virtue is indeed acquired by habit, but not as from a cause per se, only per accidens, insofar as habit is joined with practice and experience: when someone learns something by experience, he accustoms himself to that thing to be learned, per accidens. So too moral experience sometimes exists, but not properly and per se, only per accidens. Experience and habit differ in this way: habit arises in ourselves, but experience outside us. For we cannot acquire anything by habit unless we exercise ourselves and accustom ourselves to doing things. Experience can be had even if we undergo nothing in ourselves: for example, in the medical art someone learns through experience that rhubarb purges bile, because this has become known in many cases, even though he himself has never tried it on his own body.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: An recte Aristoteles neget virtutem provenire a natura, cum ipse fateatur in textu, nos habere potentiam naturalem eam acquirendi, ut verum sit illud axioma Physicum: Qui dat causam rei, dat etiam medium ejusdem rei producenda, ut ipse Aristoteles docet lib. 2. Naturalis auscultat, cap. 9. Et notum illud logicum: Qui dat finem, dat etiam media ad producendum finem: Ergo cum potentia naturalis sit causa acquirenda virtutis, necessario proveniet virtus a natura? Respond. Virtutem moralem provenire a potentia naturali, tanquam a causa remota, non vero tanquam causa proxima, & proinde illud axioma Physicum: Qui dat causam rei, dat etiam medium ejusdem rei producendae, intelligendum est de causa proxima, ut ipse luculenter docet loco citato. Caeterum cum consuetudo & assuefactio sit causa proxima virtutis moralis, erit etiam medium per quod producitur.
units.tr: II. The question is: Did Aristotle rightly deny that virtue comes from nature, when he himself admits in the text that we have a natural capacity to acquire it? For the physical axiom is true: whoever gives the cause of a thing also gives the means of producing that thing, as Aristotle himself teaches in book 2 of the Physics, chapter 9. And the familiar logical maxim: whoever gives the end also gives the means of producing the end. Therefore, since natural capacity is the cause of acquiring virtue, virtue must necessarily come from nature? Answer: Moral virtue comes from natural capacity as from a remote cause, not as from a proximate cause. Therefore the physical axiom, whoever gives the cause of a thing also gives the means of producing that thing, must be understood of the proximate cause, as he himself clearly teaches in the passage cited. Moreover, since habit and custom are the proximate cause of moral virtue, habit is also the means by which it is produced.

units.la: III. Quaeritur: Quomodo sic distinguat virtutem intellectualem a morali, quod intellectualis proveniat a doctrina, moralis vero a consuetudine & usu, cum ipse ex communi Philosophorum consensu dicat, lib. 7. Polit. cap. 3. lib. 3. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 12. ad omnem habitum comparandum tria esse requirenda, naturam, doctrinam, & usum sive exercitationem. Nam ut ait Plutarchus lib. 1. de educatione puerorum, natura absque doctrina est caeca, doctrina absque natura est manca, exercitatio vero absque utraque est imperfecta, cum igitur virtus moralis sit habitus necesse est, ut a doctrina etiam proveniat? Respond. Virtutem quidem moralem provenire a natura, doctrina etiam sicut & ab usu, sed a natura tanquam causa remota, quae est aptitudo quaedam exorta ab anima rationali. nali, & à temperamento corporis & vulgò dicitur seminarium naturæ, instinctus naturæ, igniculus naturæ quo excitamur ad aliquid agendū. A doctrina verò proficiscitur virtus moralis, non tanquam à causa per se, sed per accidens, quia per doctrinam hausimus aliquam notitiam honesti & turpis, & cognitionem aliquam legum, secundum quas est agendum & vivendum: Sed à consuetudine & exercitatione oritur virtus moralis tanquam à causa per se, & sic Philosophus, cum distingueret ab intellectuali dixit provenire à consuetudine, qua intelligebat causam per se.
units.tr: III. The question is: How does he distinguish intellectual from moral virtue by saying that the former comes from teaching, the latter from habit and practice, when he himself, by the common consent of the philosophers, says in Politics book 7, chapter 3, and in Rhetoric book 3, addressed to Theodectes, chapter 12, that three things are required for acquiring any habit: nature, teaching, and practice or exercise? For, as Plutarch says in his book on the education of children, nature without teaching is blind, teaching without nature is lame, and exercise without either is imperfect. Since, then, moral virtue is a habit, must it not also come from teaching? Answer: Moral virtue indeed comes from nature, and from teaching as well as from practice; but from nature as a remote cause, which is a certain aptitude arising from the rational soul and from the temperament of the body, and is commonly called the seed of nature, the instinct of nature, the little spark of nature by which we are stirred to act. Moral virtue comes from teaching not as from a cause per se but per accidens, because through teaching we have drawn some notion of honourable and base, and some knowledge of the laws according to which one must act and live. But moral virtue arises from habit and exercise as from a cause per se, and so the Philosopher, when he distinguished it from intellectual virtue, said that it comes from habit, meaning by this the cause per se.

units.la: IV. Queritur: Quomodo dicat in secunda ratione in naturalibus facultatem precedere ipsam actionem, in virtute morali facultatem subsequi ipsam actionem & proinde virtutem moralem non esse à natura, cum ipse fateatur in textu, aptitudinem quandam naturalem seu facultatem precedere etiam actiones virtutis, unde videretur hic nulla differentia aut distinctio?
units.tr: IV. The question is: How does he say, in the second principle, that in natural things the capacity precedes the action itself, while in moral virtue the capacity follows the action itself, and therefore that moral virtue is not from nature, when he himself admits in the text that a certain natural aptitude or capacity also precedes the actions of virtue? Hence there seems to be no difference or distinction here.

units.la: Respond. Duplex est facultas virtutis, alia est remota, quæ non tam instruit ad actiones virtutis, quam ad quaslibet actiones promiscuè, & istaprææcedit actiones virtutis, alia est proxima, quæ instruit ad bene agendum & perfectè quæ insequitur actiones virtutis, aut ipsos habitus & nihil est aliud quam facultas, promptitudo & perfectio secundum virtutem agendi, & de hac facultate proprie hic intelligit Aristoteles.
units.tr: Answer: The capacity for virtue is twofold. One is remote, which does not so much prepare for the actions of virtue as for any actions whatever, and this precedes the actions of virtue. The other is proximate, which prepares one to act well and perfectly, and which follows the actions of virtue, or the habits themselves; and it is nothing other than the capacity, readiness and perfection of acting in accordance with virtue. It is of this capacity that Aristotle properly speaks here.

units.la: V. Queritur: Quomodo dicat in quarta ratione. Ex actionibus oriri virtutes, cū verum sit illud: nihil perfectum ab imperfecto oriri & produci potest, virtus vero est perfectū quid, actiones verò sunt imperfectæ, quæ propter virtutem tanquam propter finem perfectu fiunt: nam quod nihil perse-ctum ab imperfecto tanquam a causa produci possit, hinc pro-batur, quia omne quod oritur ab aliquo, vel est aequalei, a quo oritur, vel est minus perfectum eo a quo oritur, unde se-quitur ab actionibus oriri non posse virtutem? Resp. Actiones considerari duobus modis, vel singulatim, & sic fit minus perfecta, quam est ipsa virtus, vel collective, & sic sunt tam perfectae, quam est ipsa virtus, deinde quod ad illud Axioma: Nihil magis perfectum a minus perfecto oriri potest, poterit sic intelligi, ut non possit oriri a minus perfecto, tanquam a causa totali, sed poterit oriri tanquam a causa socia, ficatio non est causa totalis producendae virtutis, sed etiam accedit recta ratio, quae affectibus moderatur & mediocritatem ponit in rebus ipsis, unde infra in definitione virtutis hanc particulam ponit Philosophus, habitus ratione definitus quia etiam ratio accedit ad actiones bonas produ-cendas.
units.tr: V. The question is: How does he say, in the fourth principle, that virtues arise from actions, when it is true that nothing perfect can arise or be produced from what is imperfect, while virtue is something perfect and actions are imperfect, and they are done for the sake of virtue as for a perfect end: for that nothing perfect can be produced from the imperfect as from a cause is proved thus, because everything that arises from something is either equal to that from which it arises or less perfect than it; hence it follows that virtue cannot arise from actions? Answer: Actions may be considered in two ways. Taken singly, they are less perfect than virtue itself; taken collectively, they are as perfect as virtue itself. As for the axiom, nothing more perfect can arise from what is less perfect, it may be understood in this way: it cannot arise from what is less perfect as from a total cause, but it can arise as from a contributing cause. ... [the appetite/affection] is not the whole cause of producing virtue, but right reason also contributes, which moderates the affections and establishes the mean in the things themselves. Hence below, in the definition of virtue, the Philosopher adds this phrase, "a habit defined by reason," because reason too contributes to producing good actions.

units.la: VI. Quaeritur: Cum duplices sint actiones hominis externa & interna, a quibus proficiscatur virtus Moralis? Resp. Ab utrisque, sed ab internis primario, quia actiones internae reddunt appetitum rectae rationi obedientem. Ab externis vero secundario, quatenus indicant ipsam virtutem, & impulsu internarum actionum edunt in externum aliquod objectum.
units.tr: VI. The question is: Since human actions are twofold, external and internal, from which of them does moral virtue arise? Answer: From both, but from the internal primarily, because internal actions make the appetite obedient to right reason. From the external, however, secondarily, insofar as they manifest virtue itself and, driven by the internal actions, produce some external object.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Continetur hoc capite, Secundum membrum primi tractatus huius libri, nam ubi egisset, c. 1. de causis virtutum, seu unde proveniret virtus.
units.tr: This chapter contains the second part of the first treatise of this book. In chapter 1 the author dealt with the causes of the virtues, that is, with where virtue comes from.

units.la: Hoc capite ostendit, quales sint actiones, ex quibus generatur virtus. Partes capitis sunt quatuor. In primo ostendit cur de operationibus, seu actionib. ex quibus virtus nascitur agat. In secundo docet quomodo agat de his actionibus. In tertio, quales actiones virtutem efficiant & conservent, quales destruant. In quarto, cujusmodi actiones partos jam habitus consequantur.
units.tr: In this chapter he shows what kind of actions produce virtue. The chapter has four parts. In the first he shows why he treats of the operations, or actions, from which virtue arises. In the second he teaches how he treats of these actions. In the third, he shows which actions produce and preserve virtue, and which destroy it. In the fourth, he shows what kinds of actions follow once the habits have been acquired.

units.la: In prima igitur parte capitis, duabus rationibus ostendit, cur de actionibus hisce agat. 1. est a causa finali, quia Ethicae finis non est cognitio sed actio, & omnia ejus praecepta huc tendunt, ut cives boni & beati reddantur, sicut lib. superiori cap. 1. 11. 12. demonstrarat. Ergo de actionibus tractare debet. Secunda ratio ducitur a causa efficiente, quia actiones sunt causae virtutum, & ut supra dixerat, cap. 11. lib. 1. actiones sunt vitae dominae, quae si bonae fuerint, vitam bonam & virtuosam reddunt, si malae vero, vitiosam.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter, he gives two reasons why he treats of these actions. The first is from the final cause: the end of ethics is not knowledge but action, and all its precepts aim at making citizens good and happy, as he demonstrated in the previous book, chapters 1, 11 and 12. Therefore he must treat of actions. The second reason is drawn from the efficient cause: actions are the causes of the virtues, and as he had said above, in chapter 11 of book 1, actions are the mistresses of life; if they are good they make life good and virtuous, but if they are bad, they make it vicious.

units.la: Allatis jam rationibus ostendit, quales debent fieri actiones in genere, ex quibus nascitur virtus, debet, inquit, fieri secundum rectam rationem, id est, prudentia, & non ultra prosequitur hac rem, sed relinquit tractandam infra lib. 6. ubi de prudentia, (quaespectat ad rectam rationem) agit, & vocat prudentiam condimentum omnium virtutum & quasi necessarium, sine quibus nihil omnino sapiant caeterae virtutes. Haec tamen ratio potest reddi, ex 2. lib. Eud. c. 5. quia virtus est optimum quid, optima vero omnia a recta ratione debent perfici, ideo virtus eadem ratione perfici debet: perfici vero non potest nisi actiones illae ex quibus nascitur secundum rectam ratio-
units.tr: Having given these reasons, he shows what kind of actions in general produce virtue. They must, he says, be performed according to right reason, that is, prudence. He does not pursue the matter further here but leaves it to be treated in book 6, where he deals with prudence (which concerns right reason). He calls prudence the seasoning of all the virtues, and as it were necessary, without which the other virtues have no savour at all. This reasoning can also be put this way, from book 2 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 5: virtue is something best, and all the best things must be perfected by right reason; therefore virtue must be perfected in the same way. But it cannot be perfected unless the actions from which it arises are performed according to right reason.

units.la: rationem fiant. Unde pulchrè Plato in Men. ait. Omnia nostra studia, voluntates & consilia prælucente ratione vitæ beatæ efficiendæ esse utilia, secus verò contra.
units.tr: Hence Plato rightly says in the Meno: All our pursuits, wills and plans are useful for achieving the happy life when reason goes before them, but otherwise they are not.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis, agit de modo, quo fieri debent actiones istæ ex quibus nascitur virtus, & ostendit modum non debere fieri exquisitum aut exactum, sed communem tantum aut popularem, sicut in Proœmio, lib.1. docuerat in rebus Ethicis non esse quærendam exactam demonstrationem, sed vulgarem tantum, & argumentatur à majori ad minus. Si tractatio de universalibus est incerta, seu instabilis ideo et exquisita esse nõ potest, multo magis tractatio de singularibus, quales sunt actiones producentes virtutem & quæ præceptis contineri nequeunt, erit instabilis & minimè exquisita. Singularia enim variant pro ratione temporis, loci, personarum, ætatum, voluntatis, dignitatis, aut status, ut probat in exemplo: nam effectiva sanitatis, quia sunt singularia subinde variant pro ratione ætatis & diversarum complexionum in homine.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter, he treats of the manner in which those actions from which virtue arises ought to be performed. He shows that the manner should not be exact or precise, but only common or popular, as he taught in the Preface to book 1: in ethical matters one should not seek exact demonstration, but only ordinary demonstration. He argues from the greater to the less. If the treatment of universals is uncertain and unstable, and so cannot be exact, much more will the treatment of particulars be unstable and by no means exact. Such particulars are the actions that produce virtue, and these cannot be contained in precepts. For particulars vary according to time, place, persons, ages, will, dignity or station. He proves this by an example: the things that produce health, since they are particulars, vary from time to time according to age and the different constitutions of people.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis ostendit quales actiones efficiant virtutem & quales destruant, & dicit actiones, quæ sunt in medio, efficere virtutem & conservare, quæ sunt in extremis in excessu aut defectu corrumpere aut destruere virtutem. Argumentatur hoc modo. Quæ ab extremis corrumpuntur & destruuntur, à medio constituuntur & conservantur. At virtutes ab extremis, ab excessu & defectu corrumpuntur & destruuntur. Ergo. Major probatur exemplo virium & sanitatis. Vires enim iis exercitiis, quæ in medio consistunt, aut moderatis gignuntur & conservantur. Immoderatis vero, quae sunt in excessu & defectu, destruuntur, de quibus pulcherrime disputat Aristoteles, l. 8. Polit. cap. 5. Uti reprehendit Lacedaemonios, quod immoderatis nimis uterentur exercitiis, quia de re Galenus ait, in libro de Sanitate tuenda. Minor argumenti probatur exemplo fortitudinis & temperantiae, ut patet in textu. Hoc argumentum fusius etiam tractat. lib. 2. Eadem. cap. 1. quod totum sumptum ex Platonis Dialogo de amore. Causa vero cur extrema i.e. excessus & defectus destruant virtutem aut corrumpant sunt variae, praecipuae vero hae. 1. propter declinationem a medio. Nam dum homines a medio declinant, in alterutram partem virtutem negligunt & ubi virtutis actio negligitur, ibi virtus ipsa corrumpitur. 2. propter delectationem in ipso vitio cujus dulcedine pelleti impellimur ad peccandum. Nam natura hominis corrupta, sponte sua delabitur in vitia, ad virtutes vero non nisi invite & coacte descendit. 3. propter obcaecationem animi in bono, sit enim pene numero, ut animus caecutiat in iis, quae vere bona sunt. 4. propter obduirationem in malo, quo animus desperare cogitur, dum nihil per se boni posse intendere, propter habitum vitiorum contractu, & ut uno verbo dica, declinates a medio, dulci quodam vitii veneno capimur, capti obcaecamur, obcaecati obduriscimus, obdurati desperamus.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he shows which actions produce virtue and which destroy it. He says that actions that lie in the mean produce and preserve virtue, while those that lie at the extremes, in excess or deficiency, corrupt and destroy it. He argues in this way: What is corrupted and destroyed by the extremes is constituted and preserved by the mean. But virtues are corrupted and destroyed by the extremes, by excess and deficiency. Therefore (the conclusion follows). The major premise is proved by the example of strength and health. For strength is generated and preserved by exercises that lie in the mean, or are moderate; but it is destroyed by immoderate exercises, which are in excess or deficiency. On this Aristotle disputes most admirably in book 8 of the Politics, chapter 5, where he reproves the Spartans for using exercises that were too immoderate. Galen says much the same on this subject in his book On Preserving Health. The minor premise is proved by the example of courage and temperance, as appears in the text. He also treats this argument more fully in book 2 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 1, which is taken entirely from Plato's dialogue on love. The reasons why the extremes, that is, excess and deficiency, destroy or corrupt virtue are various, but the chief ones are these: (1) Because of the departure from the mean. For when men depart from the mean, toward one or the other extreme, they neglect virtue; and where the practice of virtue is neglected, there virtue itself is corrupted. (2) Because of the delight in the vice itself, by whose sweetness we are driven to sin. For corrupt human nature slides of its own accord into vices, but it descends to the virtues only unwillingly and by compulsion. (3) Because of the blinding of the mind with regard to the good; for it happens almost always that the mind grows blind in those things that are truly good. (4) Because of the hardening in evil, by which the mind is compelled to despair, since it cannot aim at anything good in itself, owing to the habit of vices it has contracted. And, to say it in one word: those who depart from the mean are caught by the sweet poison of vice; having been caught, they are blinded; having been blinded, they grow hard; having grown hard, they despair.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis agit de iis actionibus, quae consequuntur partes jam habitus virtutis, & dicit easdem esse actiones specie quae consequuntur habitum, cum iis quae praecedunt, nam ut bonis actioni-bus bus acquiritur virtutis habitus, sic iildem etiam in suo tenore servatur, quod probat simili adducto à viribus corporis, ut sic per notiora & sensibilia minus nota & à sensibus remotiora stabilire possit, ut enim cibo & exercitio moderato acquiritur robur corporis, & qui jam robusti sunt, seu qui jam acquisiverunt robur corporis, facile possunt omnes molestias & labores subire, sic se habet in virtute, verbi gratia, qui abstinet voluptatib.non concessis aut immoderatis, ille temperantiâ sibi acquirit, & qui jam temperans est, facile abstinet voluptatib. illicitis, quæ temperatiæ ipsi contrariatur. Sic etiâ qui graves casus & pericula fortiter subit, acquirit fortitudinem, & qui jam fortis est, facile & frequeter durissima quæq; subire potest. Differunt tamen actiones, quæ præcedunt virtutis habitum ab iis quæ sequuntur, quod quæ præcedant, difficulter fiant, quæ vero sequuntur, cum facilitate & nullo quasi labore, unde Aristoteles, sub 1.cap. hujus libri, in secunda ratione dixit, facilitatem in virtute sequi habitum: & lib.3.de anima 13. dicit, nos ex habitu quando velimus & cum facilitate operari posse.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he treats of those actions that follow once the habit of virtue is already possessed. He says that the actions which follow the habit are of the same kind as those which precede it. For just as the habit of virtue is acquired by good actions, so it is also preserved in its course by the same actions. He proves this by an analogy with the powers of the body, so that by means of things better known and perceptible he may establish things less known and more remote from the senses. For just as strength of body is acquired by food and moderate exercise, and those who are already strong, or who have already acquired bodily strength, can easily undergo all hardships and labours, so it is in virtue. For example, whoever abstains from pleasures that are not permitted or are immoderate acquires temperance for himself; and whoever is already temperate easily abstains from illicit pleasures, which are contrary to temperance. So too, whoever bravely undergoes grave misfortunes and dangers acquires courage; and whoever is already brave can easily and frequently undergo the hardest things. Nevertheless, the actions that precede the habit of virtue differ from those that follow it, in that the former are done with difficulty, while the latter are done with ease and almost without effort. Hence Aristotle, under the first chapter of this book, in the second argument, said that ease in virtue follows from the habit; and in book 3 of On the Soul, chapter 13, he says that we can act from habit whenever we wish, and with ease.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Virtutis actio, non cognitio magnam adfert vitæ utilitatem.
units.tr: 1. The action of virtue, not knowledge of it, brings great benefit to life.

units.la: 2. Actiones hominis tum demum rectæ fiunt, cum secundum rectam rationem fiunt.
units.tr: 2. Human actions become right only when they are done in accordance with right reason.

units.la: 3. Singularia præceptis & arte non continentur, cum sint infinita.
units.tr: 3. Particulars are not contained in precepts and art, since they are infinite.

units.la: 4. Virtutis actiones ut à medio conservantur, sic ab extremis corrumpuntur. 5. Ob-
units.tr: 4. The actions of virtue are preserved by the mean, just as they are corrupted by the extremes. 5. Ob-

units.la: 5. Obscura probanda per spicua sunt adhibenda testimonia, ne petatur principium.
units.tr: 5. Unclear matters must be proved by clear testimonies, which must be brought in, lest the principle be begged.

units.la: 6. Actiones quae praecedunt habitum, sunt eadem cum iis, quae sequuntur, sed specie tantum eadem.
units.tr: 6. The actions that precede a habit are the same as those that follow it, but the same only in species.

units.la: 7. Actiones praecedentes habitum, fiunt cum difficultate, quae subsequuntur cum facilitate.
units.tr: 7. Actions that precede a habit are performed with difficulty; those that follow it are performed with ease.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat in textu, cognitionem virtutis nullam adferre vitae utilitatem, cum hoc modo omnis ista cura quam adhibet Philosophus in Ethicis tractandis foret inutilis. Traduntur enim praecepta Ethica, ut cognoscamus, quae sit finis ultimus actionum humanarum, tum per quae media ipsum assequamur? Resp. Duplex est cognitio, alia est cognitio per se & propter se, & haec cognitio nullam affert vitae utilitatem, de qua intelligit Philosophus in textu; alia est cognitio non propter se, sed propter aliud, & sic ista cognitio virtutum, quae traditur per praecepta Ethica, eo tendit, ut tandem in praxin relegatur, & sic plurimum vitae prodest modum scire, quo secundum virtutem agere quis debeat.
units.tr: I. It is asked: how does he say in the text that knowledge of virtue brings no benefit to life, when on this view all the care the Philosopher takes in treating ethics would be useless? For the precepts of Ethics are handed down so that we may know what the ultimate end of human actions is, and by what means we may attain it? Answer: knowledge is twofold. One kind is knowledge through itself and for its own sake, and this kind brings no benefit to life; it is this that the Philosopher means in the text. The other kind is knowledge not for its own sake but for the sake of something else. The knowledge of the virtues that is delivered through the ethical precepts belongs to this second kind, and it aims at being finally applied in practice. Thus it is very useful for life to know the manner in which one ought to act according to virtue.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: Quomodo hic dicat, artes non versari circa singularia, aut singularia non contineri arte & praecepto, cum tamen lib. 1. c. 4. sub finem dicat, artes versari circa singularia, verbi gratia, Medicina circa curam huius vel illius hominis, unde videtur sibi & experientiae contrarius Aristoteles? Resp. Artes consideran-tur, ut ibi diximus, vel in habitu vel in actu. Artes in habitu versantur tantum circa universalia, ut eo loco ostendimus, dein aliud est versari circa singularia, aliud singulariaria ria contineri præceptis & arte, & sic sibi ipsi non contradicit.
units.tr: II. It is asked: how does he say here that arts are not concerned with singulars, or that singulars are not contained in art and precept, when yet in book 1, chapter 4, near the end, he says that arts are concerned with singulars, for example medicine with the care of this or that man? Whence Aristotle seems to contradict both himself and experience. Answer: arts are considered, as we said there, either in habit or in act. Arts in habit are concerned only with universals, as we showed in that place. It is one thing to be concerned with singulars, and another for singulars to be contained in precepts and art. So he does not contradict himself.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat hic omnem declinationem à medio in alterutrum extremorum corrumpere virtutem, & tamen cap. 9. hujus lib. dicit, non omnem declinationem à medio, aut non omnem excessum & defectum corrumpere aut destruere virtutem? Resp. Duplex est declinatio à medio: alia est major, alia minor. Major omnis declinatio corrumpit virtutem, quia jam est in ipsis extremis ista declinatio. Minor non ita corrumpit, quia tantum est in via ad extrema, modo ita parva sit, ut non statim appareat, aut ab animi malitia non proficiscatur; nam declinatio à medio fit variis modis, aut per infirmitatem quandam cum animi lapsu, aut naturæ depravatæ quis peccat, aut per violentiam affectuum, cum affectus irregulares animi partem meliorem transversam rapiunt, aut per ignorantiam cum errore quis labitur, aut per malitiā cum furore quodam animi aliquid enorme committitur, quæ igitur declinatio non provenit à malitia & parva fit, ut diximus, non plane corrumpit virtutem, & sic locus ille cap. 9. est intelligendus. At verò quia omnis declinatio à medio est in vitio, dicitur hic corrumpere virtutem, propterea quod quicquid ad vitium tendat, contrariatur virtuti, & sic hoc loco intelligit Aristoteles.
units.tr: III. It is asked: how does he say here that every deviation from the mean toward either extreme corrupts virtue, and yet in chapter 9 of this book he says that not every deviation from the mean, or not every excess and defect, corrupts or destroys virtue? Answer: deviation from the mean is twofold: one kind is greater, another smaller. Every greater deviation corrupts virtue, because such deviation already lies in the extremes themselves. The smaller does not corrupt in the same way, since it is only on the way toward the extremes, provided it is so slight that it does not appear at once, or does not arise from malice of mind. For deviation from the mean happens in various ways. It may happen through a certain weakness with a slip of the mind, when someone sins from a depraved nature; or through the violence of the passions, when irregular affections drag the better part of the soul awry; or through ignorance, when someone falls into error; or through malice, when something monstrous is committed in a kind of frenzy of mind. The deviation that does not arise from malice and is slight, as we said, does not wholly corrupt virtue, and so that passage of chapter 9 is to be understood in this way. But because every deviation from the mean lies in vice, it is said here to corrupt virtue, since whatever tends toward vice is opposed to virtue; and in this sense Aristotle understands it in this place.

units.la: IV. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat easdem esse actiones, quæ consequuntur partes jam habitus, cum iis, quæ precedunt habitum, cum omne idem sit vel genere vel specie, vel numero idem, ut præclarè docet Aristoteles lib. 1. Topic. cap. 9. si dicantur eadem genere, tunc non magis convenient quam bona & & mala actiones, qua genere sunt eadem, neque numero sunt eadem, quia non simul exiſunt, nec uno eodemq; temporis momento producuntur, neq; etiam ſpecie poſſunt eſſe eadem, quia proveniunt a diverſis principiis. Nam qua præcedunt virtutis habitum, proveniunt a voluntate ſecundum rectam rationem conformata, qua vero ſubſequuntur, proveniunt ab ipſo virtutis habitu? Resp. Esse ſpecie eaidem, etsi a diversis proveniant principiis; nam non prohibet hoc esse eadem ſpecie, quæ a diversis producuntur principiis, verbi gratia, in Physicis animalia imperfecta, ut sunt inſecta, quæ proveniunt ex putri materia, producantur non tantum ex ſqualore innato huic putri materiæ, ſed etiam a calore cœli & Solis, ut recte Averroës contra Avicennam disputat. Dein ipse etiam Aristoteles lib.6. Metaphyſ.text.23. dicit, eadem fieri ex arte & non ex arte, vel poterit breviuſ sic responderi: ſi actiones considėrentur ex parte ſui, ſunt eædem ſpecie, licet illæ, quæ præcedunt habitum, ſint imperfectæ, quæ ſubſequuntur, ſunt perfectæ; majus vero & minus non mutant ſpeciem in gradibus accidentium. At vero ſi conſiderentur ex parte agentis, poſſunt dici diverſæ ſpecie, quia aliud eſt agens ante virtutis habitum, nempe imperfectus & nondum virtuoſus, alius poſt virtutis habitum, nempe perfectus & ipſa virtute præditus.
units.tr: IV. It is asked: how does he say that the actions which follow the parts of an already formed habit are the same as those which precede the habit, since whatever is the same is either the same in genus, or in species, or in number, as Aristotle teaches admirably in Topics book 1, chapter 9? If they are said to be the same in genus, then they agree no more than good and bad actions, which are the same in genus but not the same in number, since they do not exist together and are not produced in one and the same moment of time; nor can they be the same in species, since they proceed from different principles. For those that precede the habit of virtue proceed from the will conformed to right reason, whereas those that follow proceed from the habit of virtue itself? Answer: they are the same in species, even though they proceed from different principles. For it does not prevent things from being the same in species that are produced from different principles. For example, in physics, imperfect animals such as insects, which arise from putrid matter, are produced not only from the innate filth of that putrid matter but also from the heat of heaven and sun, as Averroes rightly argues against Avicenna. Then Aristotle himself, Metaphysics book 6, text 23, says that the same things come about from art and not from art. Or it may be answered more briefly thus: if actions are considered in themselves, they are the same in species, although those that precede the habit are imperfect and those that follow are perfect; a greater or lesser degree does not change the species within the degrees of accidents. But if they are considered in respect of the agent, they can be called different in species, because the agent before the habit of virtue is one thing, namely imperfect and not yet virtuous, and the agent after the habit of virtue is another, namely perfect and endowed with virtue itself.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Continet hoc caput tertium membrum primi tractatus hujus libri, nempe circa quid versetur virtus moralis. Partes capitis sunt dua: In prima ostendit, quomodo quis sciat virtutis habitum se acquisisse, visse, si nempe actiones inter agendum, voluptatem agendi pariant, & nullam molestiam in agendo sen- tiat agens. In secunda parte circa voluptatem & do- lorem verisi virtutem moralem octo rationibus de- monstrat.
units.tr: This chapter contains the third member of the first treatise of this book, namely what moral virtue is concerned with. The chapter has two parts. In the first part he shows how someone may know that he has acquired the habit of virtue, namely if his actions, while he performs them, bring pleasure in doing them and the agent feels no distress in doing them. In the second part he proves, by eight reasons, that moral virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain.

units.la: In prima igitur parte cum plures & frequentes a- ctiones requiratur ad virtutis habitum contrahen- dum, commodum erit demonstrare, quot actiones sint producendæ, ut habitum acquiramus, sed cum numerus actionum certus & determinatus haberi nequeat, ut tot actiones dicantur habitum acquisi- visse; nam variæ sunt hominum dispositiones ad vir- tutem consequendam, alii enim sunt promtiores, alii tardiores, alii magis, alii minus ad hanc vel illam virtutem idonei. Ideo cum variæ se habeant actio- nes pro variis hominum dispositionibus, ideo si- gnum & indicium erit quærendum, ut sciatur habi- tum esse acquisitum, vel non acquisitum. Signum vero tale affert hoc capite, si voluptas comitetur ac- tiones & operationes, signum est habitum jam esse acquisitum, quod nempe actiones cum volu- ptate & lubentia producantur. At vero si molestia vel dolor comitetur actiones, hoc ipso, quod præ- stetur, agens perturbetur, aut molestia afficiatur, o- stenditur habitum nondum esse acquisitum. Declara- rat hoc Philosophus exemplo Temperantia & Fortitu- dinis: Nam si quisà voluptatibus oblatis facilè absti- net, jam temperàs est, & si cum voluptate & lubentia abstinet, jam habitum temperantiæ sibi acquisi- vit, sin verò molestiam pariat ista abstinentia, non- dum temperans est, & sic de Fortitudine & aliis virtutibus est intelligendum, plura vide apud Kecker. probl. 8o. 81. fyflem. Ethic.
units.tr: In the first part, since many and frequent actions are required to acquire the habit of virtue, it will be useful to show how many actions must be performed before we acquire the habit. But no certain and fixed number can be given, so that one could say that so many actions yield an acquired habit. For people's dispositions towards attaining virtue vary: some are quicker, others slower, some are more and others less fit for this or that virtue. Therefore, since actions vary with the variety of human dispositions, a sign and indication must be sought by which one may know whether the habit has been acquired or not. The sign that this chapter gives is this: if pleasure accompanies the actions and operations, it is a sign that the habit has already been acquired, namely that the actions are performed with pleasure and delight. But if distress or pain accompanies the actions, so that the agent is disturbed or afflicted by distress in doing what is required, this shows that the habit has not yet been acquired. The Philosopher explains this by the example of temperance and fortitude: for if someone abstains easily from the pleasures offered, he is already temperate; and if he abstains with pleasure and delight, he has already acquired for himself the habit of temperance; but if that abstinence causes him distress, he is not yet temperate. The same is to be understood of fortitude and the other virtues. For more on this, see Kecker, Problems 8o. 81, System of Ethics.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit circa voluptatem & dolorem versari virtutem moralem octo rationibus, quia voluptas & dolor sunt perturbationum genera. Perturbationes vero & affectus sunt in ea parte animae, quae ratione vacat, nempe in appetitiva, a qua etiam profluit virtus moralis, ut sup. cap. ult. lib. 1. diximus. Virtus vero intellectualis est in animae parte rationali, & ideo perturbationibus vacat, propterea recte addidit virtutem moralem versari circa voluptatem & dolorem, ut distingueret ab intellectuali. Harum octo rationum, quatuor priores sumuntur ex parte ipsius voluptatis & doloris; quatuor posteriores ex parte ipsius hominis, in quo generatur virtus.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he shows, by eight reasons, that moral virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain, because pleasure and pain are kinds of disturbances. Disturbances and affections lie in that part of the soul which lacks reason, namely the appetitive part, from which moral virtue also flows, as we said in the last chapter of the first book. Intellectual virtue, however, lies in the rational part of the soul and so is free of disturbances. Therefore he rightly added that moral virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain, in order to distinguish it from intellectual virtue. Of these eight reasons, the first four are drawn from the nature of pleasure and pain themselves; the last four from the person in whom virtue is generated.

units.la: 1. Ratio est, quia ob voluptatem multa agimus mala, constat enim, quanta saepe excitent mala voluptates cibi, potus, Veneris, & ludorum intemperantium (sed tamen voluptas non est per se causa mali, sed per accidens, quatenus nimirum a sensu & appetitu subiecti male dispositi & affecti oritur) saepe quoque patriae, parentum, amicorum, & innocentium defensio amittitur, ne molestiae & dolores effenr subeundi. Ob dolorem vero ab honestis saepe abstinemus, quatenus nimirum honesta interdum cum difficultate conjuncta sunt, & ideo metuentes, ne ex praepedita actione, quam dirigente voluntate appetimus, aut sensus exterior intenderat, tristitia & dolore afficiamur, quae nos ab appetitione honesti saepenumero deterrent. 2. Qua necesse est, nos, ut ait Plato 2. de legib. & 4. de Repub. a pueris quodammodo educatos
units.tr: 1. The first reason is this: we do many evil things because of pleasure. It is well known how often the pleasures of food, drink, sex, and intemperate games provoke great evils (yet pleasure is not in itself the cause of evil, but incidentally, insofar as it arises from the sense and appetite of a badly disposed and affected subject). Often too the defence of one's country, parents, friends, and the innocent is abandoned, lest one undergo troubles and pains. And because of pain we often abstain from honourable things, insofar as honourable things are sometimes joined with difficulty; and so, fearing that from an impeded action, which the will directs us to desire or the outer sense has aimed at, we may be affected by sadness and pain, which often deter us from pursuing what is honourable. 2. The second reason: as Plato says in the second book of the Laws and the fourth book of the Republic, we must be brought up from boyhood to be, in a manner, trained and instructed to rejoice and grieve at the proper things. For this is right education: to know in what things and in what way we ought to conduct ourselves.

units.la: educatos & institutos esse, ut quibus rebus oportet, latemur & doleamus. Hæc enim est recta institutio, Scire quibus rebus & qua ratione nos gerere debeamus. 3. Omnis virtus moralis versatur circa actiones & affectus; omnem autem actionem & affectum sequitur voluptas aut dolor, quod patet inductione. Omnis enim affectus vel lætitia afficit subjectum, si bene successat, ut amor, ambitio, & sic voluptatem generat, si male procedat, tunc mœrorem generat, ut odium & invidia & amor infortunatus. 4. Quia propterea supplicia in maleficos statuuntur, ut doloris perpessione à voluptatibus abstrahantur, & pœnis inflictis, quæ dolorem habent conjunctum, à vitiis deterreantur, qua de re Plato in Gorg. & 1. de leg. b. ubi usum & finem ostendit pœnarum. Sunt enim supplicia veluti curationes per contraria.
units.tr: 3. Every moral virtue is concerned with actions and affections; but every action and affection is followed by pleasure or pain, as induction makes plain. For every affection either delights the subject, if it succeeds well, as love and ambition do, and so produces pleasure; or, if it turns out badly, it produces sorrow, as hatred, envy and unhappy love do. 4. For this reason punishments are imposed on wrongdoers, so that by enduring pain they may be drawn away from pleasures, and by the infliction of penalties, which carry pain with them, they may be deterred from vices. Plato discusses this in the Gorgias and the first book of the Laws, where he shows the use and purpose of punishments. For punishments are like cures by contraries.

units.la: Quinta: Propter voluptates aut dolores omnis animi habitus fit deterior aut melior, dum illas consequimur & hos fugimus, non quando aut quomodo decet, aut econtra, nam habitus animi fit melior, dum ex actione non præpedita, gignitur in appetitu & sensu voluptas, quæ ab iis paulatim ad ipsum animum promanat, fit vero deterior habitus animi, cum actionem intendit, vel quando non decet intendere, vel quia eo modo intendit, quo non dolet, atque ita dolore afficitur, & inde habitus fit aliquo modo deterior. Cæterum sub finem hujus rationis dicit Philosophos fuisse quosdam, quorum meminit Cic. lib. 1. de sin. qui definiebant virtutes, tranquillitates & indolentias (non enim de Stoicis intelligit hic Philosophus, quia illi erant posteriores, & non-dum dum erant hujus opinionis.) Non recte illos fecisse contendit Aristoteles, quia simpliciter aufer ebant affectus, cum potius debuissent secundū quid tollere, nempe secundum summum & intensum gradum, nam virtus non tollit omnes affectus in homine, sed potius reprimit, & rectæ rationi subjicit. Est autem hæc magna disputatio: An vir bonus ab omni vacuus perturbatione esse debeat: Improbat hoc Plato multis in locis & Aristoteles hoc loco, & Plutarch. in libello de virtute morali, ubi Stoicos acutissimè refellit, & sunt hujus etiam opinionis, recentiores etiam Theolog. ut Phil. Mel. in Epit. Moral. Philosophiæ sub principio, & Petrus Martyr hoc ipso loco: contra probant hanc opinionem, nempe quod vir bonus omni affectu vacuus esse debet, Cic. lib. 3. 4. Tusc. quæst. ubi Arist. diligentissimè refellit, aliquipulantur Cic. veteres quidam Theol. Nazian. Basil. Augustinus & inter recentiores Politicos Justus Lipsius lib. 1. de Constantia cap. 6. Rationes Stoicorum pro hac opinione sunt præcipuè tres. 1. Quanto virtus est perfectior tanto magis affectum & appetitum superat, ergo perfectissima & in summo gradu virtus ita superabit, ut nullo modo sentiatur affectus ab eo, qui virtutem habet in summo gradu. 2. Contrariorum ea est natura, ut cum unum subjecto adsit, alterum absit, sed virtus & appetitus vel affectus secundum Stoicos sunt contraria: Ergo cum unum, id est, virtus adest perfectissima, alterum, id est, affectus absit, necesse erit: Non enim in eodem subjecto simul consistunt. 3. Definitur Felicitas cap. 6. lib. 1. operatio secundum virtutem perfectam, sed virtus perfecta est sedatio & purgatio animi, ex quo sequitur animū virtutib. prædicturn, in tranquillitate & quiete summa esse. Ad primum respondetur per negationem consequentiæ; non enim prorsus extinguunt affectus,sed potius ad mediocritatem rationis revocant. Ad 2. virtus & appetitus regularis inter se non contrariantur,ideo simul inesse possunt eidem subjecto. Ad 3. Etsi felicitas sit operatio secundum virtutem perfectam,hæc virtus perfecta non purgat animum ab omni motu,sed tantum ab immoderato.
units.tr: Fifth: on account of pleasures or pains, every habit of the mind becomes worse or better, according as we pursue the former and flee the latter, not when or how we ought, or the reverse. For the habit of the mind becomes better when, from an unimpeded action, pleasure arises in the appetite and sense, which then gradually passes up into the mind itself. But the habit of the mind becomes worse when it pursues an action either when it ought not to, or in a manner in which it does not rejoice, and so is afflicted by pain, and from this the habit becomes in some way worse. Moreover, at the end of this reason he says that there were certain philosophers, whom Cicero, in the first book of De finibus, mentions, who defined the virtues as tranquillities and freedoms from feeling; (the Philosopher here does not mean the Stoics, since they came later and were not yet of this opinion). Aristotle contends that they were wrong, because they simply removed the affections, whereas they ought rather to have removed them in a certain respect, namely to the highest and most intense degree; for virtue does not remove all affections from a man, but rather restrains them and subjects them to right reason. This, however, is a great debate: whether a good man ought to be free of all disturbance. Plato rejects this in many places, and Aristotle in this passage, and Plutarch in his little book On Moral Virtue, where he very acutely refutes the Stoics. Those of the same opinion include more recent theologians as well, such as Philip Melanchthon in the beginning of his Epitome of Moral Philosophy, and Peter Martyr in this very passage. On the other side, Cicero, in the third and fourth books of the Tusculan Disputations, where Aristotle is most carefully refuted, supports the opinion that a good man must be free of every affection; and certain ancient theologians, Nazianzen, Basil and Augustine, do the same, and among more recent political writers Justus Lipsius, On Constancy, book 1, chapter 6. The Stoics' reasons for this opinion are chiefly three. 1. The more perfect a virtue is, the more it overcomes affection and appetite; therefore the most perfect virtue, in its highest degree, will so overcome that the affection is in no way felt by one who has virtue in its highest degree. 2. Contraries are of such a nature that when one is present in a subject the other is absent; but, according to the Stoics, virtue and appetite or affection are contraries. Therefore, when one, namely virtue, is present in its most perfect form, the other, namely affection, must be absent, for they cannot stay together in the same subject. 3. Happiness is defined, Book 1, chapter 6, as an operation according to perfect virtue; but perfect virtue is a calming and purging of the mind; from which it follows that the mind endowed with virtue is in the highest tranquillity and quiet. To the first, it is answered by denying the consequence: for virtue does not utterly extinguish the affections, but rather recalls them to the moderation of reason. To the second: virtue and a well-regulated appetite are not contrary to each other, and so they can be present together in the same subject. To the third: although happiness is an operation according to perfect virtue, this perfect virtue does not purge the mind of every movement, but only of the immoderate one.

units.la: Sexta ratio est: Virtus moralis circa res expetendas versatur,cujusmodi sunt ista tria : honestum, utile, jucundum, vel circa res fugiendas, nempe turpe, injucundum molestum, his autem omnibus communes sunt voluptas & dolor.
units.tr: Sixth reason: Moral virtue is concerned with things to be pursued, of which there are three: the honourable, the useful, the pleasant; or with things to be avoided, namely the shameful, the useful-less, the painful. Pleasure and pain are common to all of these.

units.la: Septima: Quia voluptatis & doloris regula, metiri & dirigere solemus omnes actiones nostras, alii magis alii minus, ideoque omnis virtutis tractatio circa hæc duo versatur, non enim parum momenti ad actionem affert recte aut perperam dolere aut lætari, quod latius confirmat Plato 2. de legib. & 4. de Republica.
units.tr: Seventh: Because we ordinarily measure and direct all our actions by the rule of pleasure and pain, some more and some less, every treatment of virtue is concerned with these two. For to feel pain or joy rightly or wrongly makes no small difference to action, as Plato confirms at length in the second book of the Laws and the fourth of the Republic.

units.la: Octava ratio est hæc: Quia difficilius est ex opinione Heraclidi voluptati resistere quam iræ, at virtus sicut & ars versatur circa difficilima & si virtus versatur circa iram, quia mitigat talem in homine affectum & difficilius sit voluptati resistere, quam iræ. Et si virtus versetur circa iram, versabitur etiam circa voluptatem, antecedens probatur auctoritate Heraclidi cujus opinionē latius refert Philosophus lib. 5. Polit. cap. 10. Et de hac etiam quæstione agit Plato in Dialo Dialogo de amore, & Stobaeus in sermone de ira, & Plutarcho in vita Caesaris Cariolani: ratio vero cur difficilius sit voluptati resistere, quam irae, varia reddi potest. 1. quia voluptas est nobiscum nata & nutrita, ira vero non. 2. quia voluptas est diuturnior, ira enim est furor brevis, ut ait Poeta, voluptas dicitur diuturnior, quia fovet interiores animi actiones, & exteriores sensuum & corporis. 3. quia voluptas est amoena, est enim passio amica & congrua naturae, ira vero est molesta. 4. voluptas latius patet, nam diffundit se per totum hominem, ira vero est tantum ebullitio sanguinis circa cor, 5. voluptas est fraudulenta & insidiosa, blanditur enim appetitui & sensibus, & ipsi deniq; animo insidiatur, ira vero est aperta & omnibus patet.
units.tr: The eighth reason is this: According to the opinion of Heraclides, it is harder to resist pleasure than anger. But virtue, like art, is concerned with the most difficult things. If virtue is concerned with anger, because it tempers that passion in a person, and it is harder to resist pleasure than anger, then virtue will be concerned with pleasure too. The premise is proved by the authority of Heraclides, whose opinion the Philosopher reports at greater length in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 10. This question is also treated by Plato in the dialogue on love, by Stobaeus in his discourse on anger, and by Plutarch in the life of Caesar Coriolanus. The reasons why it is harder to resist pleasure than anger can be given in various ways: (1) pleasure is born and reared along with us, but anger is not; (2) pleasure is more lasting, for anger is a brief madness, as the poet says, whereas pleasure lasts longer because it nourishes the inner activities of the mind and the outer activities of the senses and body; (3) pleasure is agreeable, for it is a passion friendly and congenial to nature, whereas anger is unpleasant; (4) pleasure extends more widely, for it spreads through the whole person, whereas anger is merely a boiling of the blood around the heart; (5) pleasure is deceitful and insidious, for it flatters the appetite and the senses and at last lays a trap for the mind itself, whereas anger is open and visible to all.

units.la: Poterit & haec 9. ratio adhiberi, qui bene voluptatibus & doloribus utitur, est vir bonus, qui male improbus, eandem sententiam repetit autor Magnor. Mor. lib.1.cap.6. ubi hanc rationem addit, quia absque dolore & voluptate non licet virtutem cognoscere, idem etiam habetur, lib.2. Eud. cap.2. 7. Item, lib. 7. Phys. Acr. cap. 3. Agit vero de voluptate Philosophus lib.7. hujus operis a cap.11. ad finem libri, & lib.10. ab initio ad c. 5. Notandum vero virtutes Mor. non tantum versari circa voluptates & dolores corporis, sed etiam animi, quatenus illae scilicet rationis moderamine egent 2. virtutem moral. magis versari circa voluptatem, quam dolorem, tum quia voluptas omnibus animalib. est communis, tum quia educata & nata est nobiscum, totamque vitam nostram comitatur, tum quia virtus circa difficilius verversatur, est autem difficilius resistere voluptati, quam dolori, est enim voluptas veluti effrenis quaedam bestia ubi ad malum tendit, adeo ut vehementissima omnium sit passio, nam sola voluptate multos perire constat, alia vero animi passione non. Plura vide apud Pic. gradu 1. c. 39.
units.tr: This ninth reason may also be applied: he who uses pleasures and pains well is a good man, and he who uses them badly is wicked. The author of the Magna Moralia, book 1, chapter 6, repeats this same opinion, and adds this reason: without pain and pleasure it is not possible to recognise virtue. The same is found in Eudemian Ethics, book 2, chapter 2. Likewise, Physics book 7, chapter 3 (as printed, Phys. Acr.). The Philosopher treats of pleasure in book 7 of this work from chapter 11 to the end of the book, and in book 10 from the beginning to chapter 5. It should be noted that the moral virtues are concerned not only with bodily pleasures and pains but also with those of the mind, insofar as these need the governance of reason. (2) Moral virtue is concerned more with pleasure than with pain, both because pleasure is common to all animals, and because it is bred and born with us and accompanies our whole life, and because virtue is concerned with what is more difficult; and it is harder to resist pleasure than pain. For pleasure is like an unbridled beast, when it strains toward evil, so that it is the most vehement of all passions; for it is well known that many have perished by pleasure alone, but not by any other passion of the mind. More on this may be seen in Pico, Gradus 1, chapter 39.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Voluptas & dolor actiones hominum comitantes, habitum acquisitum, vel non acquisitum significant.
units.tr: 1. Pleasure and pain, which accompany human actions, indicate an acquired or unacquired habit.

units.la: 2. Circa voluptatem & dolorem versatur omnis virtus moralis.
units.tr: 2. All moral virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain.

units.la: 3. Latar & dolere quando & sicut decet, ea demum recta institutio est.
units.tr: 3. To rejoice and to grieve when and as is fitting: that alone is right training.

units.la: 4. Contraria contrariis curantur, nam cum se invicem non frangant, se mutuo expellunt.
units.tr: 4. Contraries are cured by contraries; for since they do not break one another, they drive one another out.

units.la: 5. Tria sunt hominis appetenda, honestum, utile, jucundum. Tria etiam fugienda, turpe, inutile, injucundum, circa quae omnia bonus bene se habet, malus vero male.
units.tr: 5. Three things are to be sought by a human being: the honourable, the useful, the pleasant. Three things are also to be avoided: the base, the useless, the unpleasant. In all of these a good man fares well, but a bad man fares badly.

units.la: 6. Voluptas quia nobis cum natura nascitur, difficilius extirpatur, adeo contra naturam lia non facile pugnatur.
units.tr: 6. Because pleasure is born with us by nature, it is more difficult to root out; so it is not easy to fight against what is contrary to nature.

units.la: 7. Difficilius est voluptati resistere, quam ira.
units.tr: 7. It is more difficult to resist pleasure than anger.

units.la: 8. Virtus sicut & Ars versantur circa difficillima.
units.tr: 8. Virtue, like art, is concerned with the most difficult things.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat in textu, circa voluptatem & dolorem versari omnem virtutem moralem, cum ipse ingenii fateatur, lib. 3. huius operis cap. 10. voluptatem & dolorem esse obiecta unius temperantia, obiectum vero temperantiae, quae est una species virtutis moralis, non poterit esse obiectum virtutis moralis in genere? Resp. Voluptatem & dolorem sumi bifariam late vel stricte. Stricte pro hisce affectibus, qui circa appetitum & sensum versantur. fantur, sive pro ejusmodi passionibus, quæ in sensu & appetitu, aliquid naturæ amicum vel inimicum gignunt, & sic sunt objecta solius temperantiæ. Latè vero pro quibusvis perturbationibus, tam in sensu & appetitu ortis, quam in ipsa anima rationali, & sic sunt objecta virtutis moralis in genere.
units.tr: I. Question: How does he say in the text that every moral virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain, when in book 3, chapter 10, of this work he himself admits that pleasure and pain are the objects of temperance alone, and the object of temperance, which is one species of moral virtue, cannot be the object of moral virtue in general? Answer: Pleasure and pain may be taken in two senses, narrowly or broadly. Narrowly, they are the affections that concern appetite and sense, or those passions which, in sense and appetite, produce something agreeable or hostile to nature; and in this sense they are the objects of temperance alone. Broadly, they are any disturbances, whether arising in sense and appetite or in the rational soul itself; and in this sense they are the objects of moral virtue in general.

units.la: 11. Quæritur: Quomodo dicatur in quarta ratione: contraria contrariis curari, cum saepenumero similia similibus curentur, verbi gratia: Loco igne adusto, adhibere solent ignem, ut ardor ille prior excolatur, Ergo, non videtur omnino verum, quod dixit Philosophus? Respond. Nihil aliud vult dum dicit, curationes per contraria fieri, quam qui voluptatis gratia aut delectationes aliquid enorme comiserunt, contraria dolorum perpessione eam voluptatem luunt, ut ipsa ratio aperte indicat, cum dicit, propterea supplicia statui in fontes, ut si quid delectationis male agendo perceperint, eam ipsam male patiendo luant. Quod vero curationes fiant per contraria, ratio ipsa & experientia docet, nam cum omnis morbus sit declinatio à mediocritate, in qua consistit sanitas ad alterutrum extremorum, non potest revocari ab isto extremo, nisi adhibito contrario, ut horum duorum pugnæ medium aliquod, in quo consistit ipsa sanitas, producatur, ut in febri patet. Quod vero ad illam instantiam, de igne curante ignem, etsi ignis ratione substantiæ, sibi non contrarietur, ratione virium tamen poterit esse aliqua contrarietas, vel quia major vis expellit minorem, vel quia vis ignis adhibita secundo, priorem sua vi destruat, aut ex loco affecto ad se propter naturæ similitudinem alliciat.
units.tr: 11. Question: How is it said in the fourth reason that contraries are cured by contraries, when very often like is cured by like? For example, when something has been burnt by fire, people are accustomed to apply fire so that the earlier burning is drawn out. Therefore what the Philosopher said does not seem to be wholly true? Answer: When he says that cures are effected by contraries, Aristotle means nothing other than this: those who have committed something wicked for the sake of pleasure or delight atone for that pleasure by suffering the contrary pains. This is clear from his own reasoning, when he says that punishments are established for this reason, namely, that whoever has taken some delight in doing wrong may atone for that very delight by suffering wrongly. That cures are effected by contraries, reason itself and experience teach. For since every disease is a departure from the mean in which health consists towards one of the extremes, it cannot be recalled from that extreme unless a contrary is applied, so that some middle state, in which health itself consists, is produced from the conflict of these two; as is evident in fever. As for that instance of fire curing fire: although fire is not contrary to fire in respect of its substance, there may nevertheless be some contrariety in respect of its powers, either because a greater power drives out a lesser, or because the fire applied a second time destroys the force of the first, or because it draws the affected part towards itself on account of the similarity of nature.

units.la: III. Quæritur: an juste taxarit Stoicos Aristoteles, quod definirent virtutes quietes animi, seu tranquillitates ab omni affectu, cum ipse Aristoteles c.ult. lib.1. hujus operis dicat, sic se habere Ethicam ad animam, sicut se habet Medicina ad corpus, & perconsequens sicut se habet sanitas ad corpus, ita se virtus habet ad animam, at ubi sanitas adfuerit corpori, tunc abeunt omnes morbi, ne recta operationes tenor impediatur, & ubi virtus adfuerit anima, omnia impedimenta tolluntur, qua cursum virtutis inhibere possunt affectus vero omnes sunt veluti impedimenta in anima, sicut morbi sunt impedimenta corporis, & proinde non male definierunt Stoici virtutem, quod redderet animam tranquillam ab omni affectu? Respond. Affectus in anima esse duplices, alios immoderatos & irregulares, & illi sunt impedimenta animæ, qui per virtutem tolluntur, quia virtus docet moderari affectibus: alios esse regulares & moderatos, & illi non sunt impedimenta animæ, sed potius adjumenta, quia ministros & rectæ rationi obedientes se præbent.
