units.tr: III. Question: Did Aristotle rightly censure the Stoics for defining virtues as a quietness of soul, or a tranquillity free from every affection? For Aristotle himself, at the end of book 1 of this work, says that ethics stands to the soul as medicine stands to the body, and consequently that virtue stands to the soul as health stands to the body; and just as, when health is present in the body, all diseases depart so that the course of right action is not impeded, so, when virtue is present in the soul, all hindrances are removed, which could inhibit the course of virtue; but all affections are like impediments in the soul, just as diseases are impediments of the body. Therefore the Stoics did not define virtue badly, as that which makes the soul tranquil from every affection? Answer: There are two kinds of affections in the soul: some are immoderate and irregular, and these are impediments of the soul, and they are removed through virtue, because virtue teaches us to moderate the affections. Others are regular and moderate, and these are not impediments of the soul but rather aids, since they present themselves as servants obedient to right reason.

units.la: IIII. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat in ultima ratione, ideo virtutem versari circa voluptatem, quia voluptas est difficilimum quid, cum tamen non sit difficilimum, nam ut ipse docet Philosophus cap.12. lib.3. hujus operis, difficilius est circa res molestas, periculorumque plenas versari, quæ ab iis, quæ voluptatem adferunt, abstinere? Resp. Aliquid dicitur difficilius duobus modis, vel respectu naturæ nostræ, vel respectu objecti præsentis, cap.12 lib.3. dicit, difficilius esse circa res molestas versari, quia fortitudo, quando habet mortem pro objecto circa difficillima versatur, nam & mors respectu naturæ nostræ abhorrentis mortem, propterea quod mors imporimportet solutionem animae a corpore, est aliquid difficilius, quam abstinere ab iis, quae voluptatem adferunt: At vero respectu objecti praesentis, difficilius est multo voluptati resistere quam periculo irruenti, propterea quod saepe numero in nostra potestate non sit affectibus moderari, quia a voluptate plerumque ducuntur.
units.tr: IV. Question: How does he say in the last reason that virtue is concerned with pleasure because pleasure is something difficult, when it is not difficult? For, as the Philosopher himself teaches in book 3, chapter 12, of this work, it is more difficult to be concerned with unpleasant things full of dangers than to abstain from those things which bring pleasure? Answer: Something is said to be more difficult in two ways: either with respect to our nature or with respect to the present object. In book 3, chapter 12, he says that it is more difficult to be concerned with unpleasant things, because courage, when it has death for its object, is concerned with the most difficult things. For death, with respect to our nature, which shrinks from death because death requires the separation of the soul from the body, is something more difficult than abstaining from those things which bring pleasure. But with respect to the present object, it is much more difficult to resist pleasure than to face a danger that rushes upon us, because it is often not in our power to moderate the affections, since they are for the most part led by pleasure.

units.la: V. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat artem versari circa difficillima, cum ars versetur circa res quotidianas & obvias, quilibet dicitur, sua arte peritus, at quod omnibus patet non est difficile? Respon. Quoad perfectionem & excellentiam artes dicuntur versari circa difficillima, nam in communibus & vulgaribus non admiramur artificium, sed in arduis & magnis, & ideo etsi multi sint artifices, pauci tamen sunt perfecti, & in excellenti gradu artifices, exempli gratia: Etsi multi essent tempore Alexandri Magni pictores, ab uno tamen Apelle se depingi tantum volebat, quia ille solus erat perfectus artifex.
units.tr: V. Question: How does he say that an art is concerned with the most difficult things, when an art is concerned with everyday and common matters? Anyone is said to be skilled in his own art, yet what is plain to everyone is not difficult? Answer: With regard to perfection and excellence, the arts are said to be concerned with the most difficult things. For we do not admire craftsmanship in common and ordinary things, but in arduous and great ones; and therefore, although there may be many craftsmen, few are perfect, and only a few are craftsmen of the highest rank. For example: Although in the time of Alexander the Great there were many painters, he nevertheless wished to be painted by Apelles alone, because he alone was a perfect artist.

units.la: VI. Quaeritur: An vera sit illa opinio Heraclīti, quam probat Aristoteles, nempe, difficilius esse, voluptati resistere, quam irae, quia in ira ipsius rationis tollitur, ut infra docet ipse lib. 3. huius operis, cap. 4. At in voluptate ipsius rationis non tollitur, ut & idem docet, lib. 7. cap. 2. huius operis, verbi gratia: Incontinentes saepe meliora vident, quam agunt, quia ipsius rationis in iis non tollitur. Ergo, difficilius irae, tanquam irrationali bestiae resistere, quam voluptati in qua ipsius rationis manet? Respon. In neutra cernitur usus rationis vere, nisi illicite si modum excedunt, nam si incontinens, meliora videat, ex parte intellectus, non tamen videt meliora, ex parte appetitus. In incontinente usus rationis non tollitur, si naturam ipsam humanam consideres, at si actum rationis consideres, tollitur, propterea quod incontinens secundum rectam rationem non agat, cum igitur voluptas actum rationis magis obtundat, quam ira, ideo vere dicitur: difficilius esse voluptati resistere quam irae.
units.tr: VI. Question: Is that opinion of Heraclitus true, which Aristotle approves, namely, that it is more difficult to resist pleasure than anger, because in anger the very use of reason is taken away, as he teaches later in book 3, chapter 4, of this work; whereas in pleasure the use of reason is not taken away, as the same Aristotle teaches in book 7, chapter 2, of this work? For example, the incontinent often see better things than they do, because the use of reason is not removed in them. Therefore it is more difficult to resist anger, as the irrational beast, than pleasure, in which the use of reason remains? Answer: In neither is the use of reason truly seen, unless it is in some way exceeded in measure. For if the incontinent man sees better things on the side of the intellect, he nevertheless does not see them on the side of the appetite. In the incontinent man the use of reason is not taken away if you consider human nature itself; but if you consider the act of reason, it is taken away, because the incontinent man does not act according to right reason. Therefore, since pleasure more thoroughly blunts the act of reason than anger does, it is rightly said that it is more difficult to resist pleasure than anger.

units.la: VII. Quaeritur: & ulc. An recte Aristoteles fecerit, quod circa dolorem & voluptatem dixerit vagari omnem virtutem moralem, cum si hoc verum esset, sequeretur, vel virtutes inter se non distingui, nam ab objecto, ut cognoscitur sic distinguitur una virtus ab alia. 2. Etiam ipse Philosophus in progressu, nempe, lib. 3. 4. 5. huius operis, unicuique virtuti suum proprium assignat objectum. Ergo, male facisse videtur? Respond. Objectum considerari duobus modis, generaliter & specialiter: in genere omnes virtutes versantur circa dolorem & voluptatem tanquam affectus, qui comitantur singulas ipsarum actiones, In specie sua habent propria objecta, quibus a se invicem distinguuntur, ita tamen ut in modo, quo versantur circa hoc objectum ad producendam aliquam actionem semper adsit voluptas aut dolor. Caeterum quia variis rationibus circa voluptatem & dolorem virtutem versari probavit Philosophus, cumque omnis voluptas & dolor sint affectus, aut affectuum saltem comites, hic quaeri poterit de illa controversia inter Stoicos & Peripateticos: Utrum scilicet affectus omnes sint sua natura pravi & vitiosi. Affirmativam tuentur Stoici hisce rationibus 1. quia affectus sunt motiones a recta ratione contra naturam averse, adeoque aegritudines quasdam animi virtute curandae. 2. quia humanam tranquillitatem perturbant &c & evertunt. Unde etiam à Latinis vulgò dicuntur perturbationes. 3. quia ex falso depravatoque rationis judicio oriuntur. Nisi enim judicium à rectæ rationis scopo interdum aberraret, nullum in mente humana affectibus locum relinqueret. 4. Quia corrumpunt rectum de rebus judicium. Non enim patiuntur judicium suo se modulo metiri, sed transversum pro suo libitu rapiunt. 5. Quia homines incitant ad omnis generis peccata & vitia. Unde non male calcaria ad vitia & irritamenta peccatorum dicuntur. 6. Quia affectus omnes sunt voluptate & dolore permixti, qui, ut ait Plato, lib. 1. de leg. sunt consiliarii amentes ac insipientes. Quis enim horum ducti, quod verum hominem decet præstitisse, visufuit. 7. Quia à veræ felicitatis via hominem abducunt, & in miseriæ barathrum præcipitant. 8. Quia cum virtutibus moralibus consistere non possunt, cum illæ animum tranquillum & quietum reddant, hæ vero perturbent. 9. Demum quia digni sunt, ut eliminentur, ac procul à sapientis animo arceantur, cum rationem ipsam non turbent modo, sed ita interdum transversum rapiant, ut nihil ne homine quidem dignum, nedum sapiente sapiens efficere possit.
units.tr: VII. Question: and so on. Did Aristotle act rightly in saying that every moral virtue wanders about pleasure and pain? For if this were true, it would follow either that the virtues are not distinguished from one another, since one virtue is distinguished from another by its object as it is known; or else that the Philosopher himself, in the course of books 3, 4 and 5 of this work, assigns to each virtue its own proper object. Therefore he seems to have done wrong? Answer: An object may be considered in two ways, generally and specifically. In general, all the virtues are concerned with pain and pleasure as affections which accompany each of their actions. In their own species they have proper objects, by which they are distinguished from one another; yet in such a way that, in the manner in which they are concerned with this object so as to produce some action, pleasure or pain is always present. Moreover, since the Philosopher has proved in various ways that virtue is concerned with pleasure and pain, and since every pleasure and pain is an affection, or at least a companion of affections, a question may be raised here about that controversy between the Stoics and the Peripatetics: Whether all affections are by their nature depraved and vicious. The Stoics defend the affirmative on these grounds: (1) because affections are movements turned away from right reason, contrary to nature, and so are certain sicknesses of the soul to be cured by virtue; (2) because they disturb and overturn human tranquillity, whence they are also commonly called perturbationes by the Latins; (3) because they arise from a false and corrupted judgment of reason, for unless judgment sometimes strayed from the aim of right reason, affections would have no place in the human mind; (4) because they corrupt the right judgment about things, for they do not allow judgment to measure itself by its own standard, but seize it crooked as they please; (5) because they incite men to every kind of sin and vice, whence they are not badly called the spurs and incitements of sins; (6) because all affections are mixed with pleasure and pain, which, as Plato says in book 1 of the Laws, are mad and foolish counsellors; for no one who is led by them has been seen to do what befits a true man; (7) because they lead man away from the way of true happiness and hurl him into the abyss of misery; (8) because they cannot exist together with the moral virtues, since the virtues render the soul tranquil and quiet, whereas the affections disturb it; (9) finally, because they deserve to be eliminated and kept far from the mind of the wise man, since they not only disturb reason but so violently carry it off crooked that they can make the wise man do nothing even worthy of a man, much less of a wise man.

units.la: Negativam tuentur Peripatetici, à quorum partibus rationes stant longè firmiores hæ: 1. Quia affectus sunt motus naturales, quibus homo incitatur ad persequendum bonum & fugiendum malum. 2. Quia à Deo ejusque famula Natura indita est homini facultas ciendi & recipiendi in se affectus, quod non fieret, si omnes sua natura vitiosi essent. Sic enim Deus & natura mali auctores statuerentur, quod non absurdum modò, sed & blasphemum. 3. Quia sunt virtutum stimuli & calcaria adeoque instrumenta, quorum beneficio potentius in optatum finem homo fertur, cumulatius illum assequitur, jucundiusque eo fruitur, dum scilicet amanda amat, odiosa odit, speranda sperat, metuenda metuit, denique dum irascitur malefacientibus, & favet benefacientibus, adeoque laetatur in bonis, tristatur in malis. 4. Quia sine affectibus homo lentus & ignavus solet esse ad agendum, non secus ac navis ventis destituta tardè & difficulter provehitur, imò vix unquam loco se movet. 5. Quia voluptas & dolor, qui sunt praecipui inter affectus & perpetui omnium affectuum comites, sunt duo fontes, ex quibus, qui haurit quando & quantum oportet, felix habetur. Nam & actionibus bene moderatur suis, & in finem ultimum ipsque destinatum dirigit. 6. Quia ex horum coetu arcendus est, qui quę debet, non amat, non odit, non sperat, non metuit, non miseretur, neque quando & quantum debet, quia ut eleganter ait Poeta:
units.tr: The Peripatetics defend the negative position, and their arguments are far stronger: (1) affections are natural motions by which a man is stirred to pursue the good and shun evil; (2) from God, and through Nature his handmaid, man has been given the faculty of stirring up affections and receiving them within himself. This would not be so if all affections were evil by nature. In that case God and nature would be made the authors of evil, which is not only absurd but blasphemous; (3) affections are the spurs and goads of the virtues, and so instruments by whose help a man is carried more forcefully towards the desired end, attains it more fully, and enjoys it more sweetly. Namely, he loves what is to be loved, hates what is hateful, hopes for what is to be hoped for, fears what is to be feared, and finally, he is angry at wrongdoers and favours those who do good, and so rejoices in good things and grieves at evil ones; (4) without affections a man tends to be sluggish and idle in acting, just as a ship without wind is moved slowly and with difficulty, or rather hardly ever moves from its place; (5) pleasure and pain, which are the chief of the affections and the constant companions of all the affections, are two fountains from which the man who draws when and as much as he ought is counted happy. For he both governs his actions well and directs them to the final end appointed for him; (6) the man who does not love what he ought, nor hate, hope, fear or pity, nor when and as much as he ought, must be excluded from this company. As the poet elegantly says:

units.la: Crimen ob ipsumTimon Palladis olim lapidatus Athenis.
units.tr: Timon was once stoned at Athens for that very crime.

units.la: 7. Quia affectus moderati, sunt velut equi currum vitae nostrae vehentes in metam rectae rationis, adeoque sunt honesti & laudabiles. 8. Denique quia affectibus utendum non tanquam ducibus, qui ducunt, aut consiliariis, qui dirigant, sed tanquam auxiliariis ad explenda majore cum lubentia & appetitu rationis dominae mandata. Hisce
units.tr: (7) Moderate affections are like horses drawing the chariot of our life towards the goal of right reason, and so they are honourable and praiseworthy; (8) finally, affections are to be used not as leaders who guide, nor as counsellors who direct, but as helpers to carry out with greater willingness and eagerness the commands of reason, their mistress. To these

units.la: Peripateticorum rationibus addi possunt quatuor hæ Theologicæ. 1. Quia affectus etiam Deo & beatis mentibus, in sacra Scriptura tribuuntur: malum vero, iis nec tribui debet, nec potest. 2. Quia affectus à Deo sunt mandati, dum jubemur Deum & proximum nostrum diligere. Hic charitas, quæ implet legem, ut inquit Apostolus, præcipitur. 3. Quia ipse Christus, qui boni viri perfectissimum exemplar se exhibuit, affectibus fuit præditus, cum in terris versaretur, nam nobis per omnia similiſ factus fuit, excepto peccato, & etiamnum illos habet. Nam, ut alibi ait Apostolus, compatitur nobis. 4. Quia vita æterna sine affectibus, sed ardebunt beati amore Dei & lætitia ineffabili orta ex plena Dei agnitione fruentur. Cæterum ut veritas huius quæstionis innotescat, distinguendum erit inter affectus, quatenus sunt naturales aut etiam moderati & moraliter boni, & quatenus sunt immoderati & moraliter mali. De priori genere vera est sententia Peripateticorum, de posteriori vero Stoicorum. Et nisi Stoicorum sententia ad immoderatos restringatur affectus, omnino fatua erit & naturæ ipsi adversa adeoque virtuti, & communi hominum societati noxia, & proinde reijcienda & damnanda, cum ex illa sequatur ἀπάθεια, vacuitas affectuum. Ex Peripateticorum vero sententia μετριοπάθεια affectuum moderamen. Hinc etiam jure quæri potest, an in potestate hominis sit, moderari affectus? Disceptatur vero in utramq; partem. Nam pro affirmativa faciunt hæc argumenta. 1. Quia in potestate hominis est sibi virtutem moralem acquirere & acquisitam exercere, re, illud autem fieri non potest nisi in ejusdem potestate sit moderari affectus. 2. Quia homo liberè determinare potest affectus suos naturales ad bonum morale, eos qui recte rationis imperio subjicere. 3. Quia vana esset omnis puerorum institutio, quâ homo ab incunte aetate assuefit, ut discat delectari & dolere iis rebus, quibus, quando & quantum decet, nisi in potestate hominis esset moderari affectus. 4. Quia vanae essent omnes leges & praeceptiones de sedandis & moderandis affectibus, iisque si modum excedant fugiendis, nisi homo pro suo arbitrio frenum laxare aut coarctare posset. 5. Quia nullus homo jure posset vituperari & punire ob immoderationem, nisi in ejusdem potestate esset moderari affectus. At in contrariam partem objici potest, quod affectus sint naturales homini à natura insiti & proinde illis moderari non esse in hominis potestate. 2. Quodcunque moderari homo potest, id debet esse voluntarium. Affectus vero cum voluntati hominis imperare videantur, & quocunque velint, transversum rapiant, voluntarii non sunt. 3. Quodcunque rectae rationis imperium detrectat, id homo moderari non potest. Affectus vero hoc faciunt, quod non tantum communis probat experientia, sed etiam Aristoteles 1. N. com. cap. ult. cum ait, rationem semper ad optima hominem hortari, sed appetitum sensitivum (seu quod idem sonat ipsos affectus) rationi repugnare ac reluctari, similemque esse membro paralytico, quod cum dextrorsum moveri debet, sinistrorsum perperam fertur. Verum responderi solet ad primum argumentum, propositione esse veram de eo, quod simsimpliciter naturale dicitur, falsum autem de eo, quod secundum quid, cujusmodi sunt affectus. Illi autem sunt naturales, quatenus à causa efficiente naturali primam suam trahunt originem. Et rursus sunt voluntarii, quatenus per proæresin vel ad bonum vel ad malum morale liberè ab homine determinantur. Secundi argumenti assumptio non est simpliciter vera. Licet enim affectus quatenus sunt naturales, sæpe hominem invitum rapiant, sunt tamen voluntarii, quatenus ab homine approbantur vel improbantur. Nec propositio tertiæ rationis ut simpliciter vera haberi debet. Nam sicut equus qui alias frenos detrectat, tandem domari potest & infesforis imperio subjici, ita & affectus, qui aliquando detrectat imperium rectæ rationis, tandem in gyrum rectæ rationis per judicii sanitatem reduci possunt.
units.tr: To the Peripatetic arguments may be added these four theological ones: (1) affections are attributed in Holy Scripture even to God and to the blessed minds, but evil cannot and must not be attributed to them; (2) affections are commanded by God, since we are ordered to love God and our neighbour, and here the charity which fulfils the law, as the Apostle says, is enjoined; (3) Christ himself, who showed himself the most perfect exemplar of a good man, was endowed with affections while he dwelt on earth, for he was made like us in all things except sin, and still has them, for, as the Apostle says elsewhere, he suffers with us; (4) eternal life is not without affections, but the blessed will burn with love of God and enjoy an unspeakable joy arising from full knowledge of God. Moreover, that the truth of this question may become known, one must distinguish between affections as they are natural, or even moderate and morally good, and as they are immoderate and morally evil. The view of the Peripatetics is true of the former kind, and the view of the Stoics of the latter. Unless the Stoic view is restricted to immoderate affections, it will be altogether foolish and contrary to nature, and so to virtue, and harmful to human society, and therefore to be rejected and condemned, since from it follows apatheia [ἀπάθεια], freedom from affections. From the Peripatetic view, however, comes metriopatheia [μετριοπάθεια], the moderation of affections. Hence one may rightly ask whether it is within man's power to moderate the affections? It is disputed on both sides. For the affirmative, these arguments hold: (1) it is in man's power to acquire moral virtue for himself and to exercise it once acquired, and this cannot happen unless it is in his power to moderate the affections; (2) man can freely determine his natural affections towards moral good, bringing them under the command of right reason; (3) all the training of children, by which from earliest age a man is accustomed to learn to take delight and grief in those things in which, when and as much as is fitting, would be pointless unless it were in man's power to moderate the affections; (4) all laws and precepts about calming and moderating the affections, and about avoiding them if they exceed due measure, would be vain unless a man could loosen or tighten the rein at his own discretion; (5) no man could rightly be blamed or punished for immoderation unless it were in his power to moderate the affections. On the other side, it may be objected: (1) affections are natural, implanted in man by nature, and therefore it is not in man's power to moderate them; (2) whatever man can moderate must be voluntary, but affections seem to command the will of man and, wherever they wish, carry it off by force, so they are not voluntary; (3) whatever defies the command of right reason, man cannot moderate. Yet affections do this, as not only common experience proves but also Aristotle, in Nicomachean Ethics 1, last chapter, where he says that reason always urges man towards the best things, but the sensitive appetite (or what is the same thing, the affections themselves) resists and struggles against reason, and is like a paralysed limb which, when it ought to be moved to the right, is carried wrongly to the left. But it is usually replied to the first argument that the proposition is true of what is called natural simply, but false of what is natural in a certain respect, such as affections. These are natural insofar as they derive their first origin from a natural efficient cause; and again they are voluntary insofar as they are freely determined by man, by deliberate choice [προαίρεσις], towards either moral good or moral evil. The assumption of the second argument is not simply true: for although affections, insofar as they are natural, often carry off man against his will, nevertheless they are voluntary insofar as they are approved or disapproved by man. Nor should the proposition of the third argument be held as simply true, for just as a horse which at first refuses the bit can in the end be tamed and made subject to the rider's command, so affections, which sometimes defy the command of right reason, can in the end be brought back into the circle of right reason through soundness of judgement.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: COntinet hoc caput quartum membrum primi tractatus hujus libri, nempe quomodo ex actionibus studiosis sive ex bonis generetur virtus, sed priusquam ipsam quæstionem accedat, dubitationem quandam solvit, quæ ex iis oriri poterat, quæ cap. 1. huius libri dicta sunt. Dixerat enim non à natura, sed à consuetudine & assuefactione oriri virtutem, & sicut fabricando fabri fimus, & cytharam pulsando cytharœdi, sic juste agendo nos justos fieri. Hinc dubitare aliquis poterit, an hoc verum sit: Multi enim multa juste faciunt, qui tamen ipsi justi non sunt, quod de Tyrannis patet. Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima parte N hanc dubitationem proponit & soluit. In secunda adfert suam opinionem, quomodo quis juste agendo, justus fiat, & sic quomodo ex actionibus bonis generetur virtus. In tertia parte removet sinistram eorum opinionem, qui putant ad virtutem consequendam satis esse scire, quid sit ipsa virtus.
units.tr: This fourth chapter takes up the fourth section of the first treatise of this book, namely how virtue is generated from studious actions, that is, from good actions. Before coming to that question, however, it resolves a certain difficulty which could arise from what was said in chapter 1 of this book. There he had said that virtue arises not from nature but from custom and habituation, and that just as we become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre, so we become just by acting justly. From this, someone may doubt whether this is true, for many do many just things who are nevertheless not themselves just, as is plain in the case of tyrants. The chapter has three parts. In the first part he proposes and resolves this difficulty. In the second he brings forward his own opinion, how someone becomes just by acting justly, and thus how virtue is generated from good actions. In the third part he removes the mistaken opinion of those who think it is enough to know what virtue is in order to attain it.

units.la: In prima igitur parte dicit Philosophus, dubitaverit aliquis, an justus putetur, qui justa egerit, & temperans qui temperiter: nam si justi sint, cur amplius justitiam quaerunt, cum eam jam habeant, hoc illustrata similitudine artium. Nam sicut ars videtur primo in animo haberi, quam artificium, aut artis opus producatur, sic de virtutibus est statuendum (quia artis & virtutis magna est convenientia; nam utraque non a natura, sed a consuetudine & usu proveniunt prius ipsae virtutes sint in animo, quam earum actiones aut operationes prodeant, adfert exempla Justitiae & Temperantiae, quia justitia & temperantia virtutes maxime sunt illustres, & in omni vita maxime vulgares: Argumentum sic formatur; Sicut se habent operationes artis, ita se habent operationes virtutis: at operationes artis ars ipsa producit. Ergo & virtutis operationes ipsa virtus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, the Philosopher says that someone may doubt whether he is thought just who has done just things, and temperate who has acted temperately. For if they are just, why do they seek justice any further, since they already have it? He illustrates this by a comparison with the arts. Just as an art seems first to be held in the mind before the work of the craft is produced, so it must be determined about the virtues. There is a great likeness between art and virtue, for both arise not from nature but from custom and practice. The virtues themselves must be in the mind before their actions or operations come forth. He gives the examples of justice and temperance, because justice and temperance are the most conspicuous virtues and the most common in all of life. The argument is formed thus: Just as the operations of an art stand, so the operations of virtue stand; but the operations of an art are produced by the art itself. Therefore the operations of virtue are produced by virtue itself.

units.la: Ad hanc dubitationem dupliciter respondet: 1. Per negationem, quod scilicet non omne, quod arti consentaneum videtur, producatur ab ipsa arte, aut putandum illos, qui aliquid arti consentaneum agunt, omnes artis habitu esse praeditos: Et instantiam dat (quia universali propositioni destruendae sufficit particularis quaelibet instantia) Instantia vero est haec, fieri potest, ut aliquid cadat fortuito, ut in cane Protoginis refert Plinius lib. 35. natural. hist. cap.10. & Plutarch. in lib. de extrema fortuna, vel alterius ope & adminiculo non proprio Marte aliquid arti consentaneum quis proferat, qui non sit arte praeditus, verbi gratia: potest aliquis sententiam Grammaticam proferre, quae revera sit Grammatica, cum tamen ipse Grammatica arte non sit praeditus, nec possit ullam rationem hujus suae loquelae reddere ex regulis Grammaticis, quod non est ex arte agere, aut artis habitu instructum esse. Secundo negat similitudinem, quae proposita erat, nam etsi ars & virtus ratione originis non a natura, sed ab usu & consuetudine proveniat, & ideo quandam convenientiam inter se habeat, est magna tamen in iis dissimilitudo, nam in artium operibus ipsa laus & praestantia, quae ab arte petitur, posita est, & non consideratur, quis ea fecerit, sitne probus vel improbus, verbi gratia: in tabula depicta quaeritur, an eleganter, an scienter sit depicta, non vero consideratur pictor, sitne probus vel improbus, nam in artificibus scientia quaeritur non mores; at in virtutibus longe alia est ratio, nam considerantur & ipsa facta, & autor: Facta an sint verae virtuti consentanea; In autore tria ista requiruntur, scientia, judicium, constantia, & ut scienter cum judicio & constanter agat. Ut scienter agat, non casu aut ignorantia, quanquam scientia per se parum aut nihil ad virtutem consequendam prodest, quia virtus non cognitionis, sed actionis gratia requiritur, ut supra dictum erat lib. 1. cap. 1. & cap. 2. hujus lib. sed ut modum & circumstantias agendi noscat, reliqua vero duo sunt magis ad virtutis actionem ctionem producendam necessaria, nam judicium seu electio aut voluntas (ista enim pro eodem hic sumuntur) est verissima nota virtutum omnium seu morum, ut infra cap. 4. lib. 3. hujus operis probabit. Constantia requiritur etiam, nam hoc est proprium virtutis, ut quis in recte factis perseveret, & cum ita, ut inquit Plato, ad umbras descendat: Unde Stoici vocarunt virtutem vita constantiam, quia vitæ usus in omnes virtutes maxime confirmatur, ut inquit Cicero 1. Tuscul. quast. & ut uno verbo dicam, agenti ad actionem virtutis producendam necessaria est voluntas, quæ incipit actionem; Scientia, quæ dirigit, aut modum agendi præscribit; Constantia quæ perficit, & perseverationem addit. Causa vero curandæ operationes artium sola requiratur scientia, ad operationes vero virtutis requiratur etiam electio & constantia, hæc est, quia ars est in ea animæ parte, quæ veræ rationis est particeps, seu in intellectu, cujus propria est scientia, unde 2. lib. 6. hujus operis ars inter virtutes intellectuales numeratur. Virtus vero est in ea animæ parte, quæ ratione per se vacat, nempe in appetitiva, ut supra dictum erat cap. ult. lib. 1. Electio vero quia dux est omnium actionum, quæ ab anima appetitiva proficiscuntur, ideo est necessaria ad virtutis actionem. Constantia etiam, quia, ut jam diximus, necessarium omnino est, ut quis in recte factis perseveret, tum etiam, quia virtus est habitus multo stabilior & firmior arte, ut patet ex cap. 11. lib. 1. Notandum etiam istas tres conditiones, quæ requiruntur ad actionem virtutis, pertinere ad ista tria, nempe ad Intellectum, Appetitum & Habitum. Ad Intellectum pertinet ScienScientia, cujus proprium est scire. Ad Appetitum pertinet Electio, ut quis cum imperio rectæ rationis & cōsultatione rectè agat, ut infra patebit lib.3. cap.f. hujus operis. Constantia verò seu agere cum immobili judicio pertinet ad Habitum. Est enim Habitus difficulter mobilis, ut dicitur in Logicis cap.de Qualitate.
units.tr: He answers this doubt in two ways. (1) By denial: not everything that seems consistent with an art is produced by the art itself, nor should we suppose that all who do something consistent with an art possess the habit of that art. He gives a counterexample, since a particular instance is enough to destroy a universal proposition. The instance is this: something can happen by chance, as Pliny reports of Protogenes' dog (Natural History book 35, chapter 10), and as Plutarch reports in his book On Extreme Fortune. Or someone, by the help and aid of another rather than by his own power, may bring forth something consistent with an art although he is not himself endowed with it. For example, someone may utter a grammatical sentence which is truly grammatical, although he is not himself skilled in grammar and cannot give any reason for his speech from the rules of grammar. This is not to act from art, nor to be furnished with the habit of an art. (2) Second, he denies the likeness that had been put forward. For although art and virtue, as to their origin, come not from nature but from practice and custom, and so have a certain likeness to each other, there is nevertheless great dissimilarity between them. In the works of the arts, the praise and excellence sought lies in the work itself, and it is not considered who made it, or whether he is upright or wicked. For example, in a painted picture one asks whether it is elegantly and skilfully painted; the painter is not considered, whether he is honest or dishonest, for in artists skill is sought, not morals. But in virtues the case is quite different, for both the deeds themselves and their author are considered. As to the deeds, one asks whether they are consistent with true virtue. In the author three things are required: knowledge, judgement and constancy, so that he acts knowingly, with judgement, and constantly. He must act knowingly, not by chance or ignorance. Knowledge by itself contributes little or nothing to attaining virtue, because virtue is sought for the sake of action, not of knowledge, as was said above in book 1, chapter 1 and chapter 2 of this book; but knowledge is needed so that he may know the manner and circumstances of acting. The other two are more necessary for producing the action of virtue. For judgement, or choice, or will (for these are taken here as the same) is the most true mark of all virtues or morals, as he will prove below in book 3, chapter 4 of this work. Constancy is also required, for this is the proper mark of virtue, that one persist in right actions, and when one does so, as Plato says, one descends to the shadows. Hence the Stoics called virtue the constancy of life, because the practice of life is most strongly confirmed in all the virtues, as Cicero says in Tusculan Disputations book 1. In a word: for the agent to produce the action of virtue, there is needed will, which begins the action; knowledge, which directs it and prescribes the manner of acting; and constancy, which perfects it and adds perseverance. For the operations of the arts, knowledge alone is required; but for the operations of virtue, choice and constancy are also required. The reason is that art is in that part of the soul which shares in true reason, namely the intellect, whose proper function is knowledge; hence in book 6 of this work art is numbered among the intellectual virtues. Virtue, however, is in that part of the soul which by itself lacks reason, namely the appetitive part, as was said above at the end of book 1. Choice, since it is the leader of all actions that proceed from the appetitive soul, is therefore necessary for the action of virtue. Constancy too is necessary, because, as we have already said, it is absolutely required that one persist in right actions; and also because virtue is a habit far more stable and firm than art, as is clear from book 1, chapter 11. It should also be noted that these three conditions required for the action of virtue pertain to these three things: the intellect, the appetite and the habit. To the intellect belongs knowledge, whose proper function is to know. To the appetite belongs choice, so that one acts rightly with the command of right reason and with deliberation, as will be shown below in book 3, last chapter of this work. But constancy, that is, acting with an unmoved judgement, belongs to the habit. For a habit is with difficulty moved, as is said in the Logic, in the chapter on Quality.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis soluta jam dubitatione dicit suam sententiam fuisse veram, quam attulerat supra cap. 1. nempe juste agendo aliquem justum fieri, si nempe quæ juste facti sunt, aut quæcunq; alio modo bene fiunt, sint prædita illis tribus qualitatibus, de quibus modo diximus, seu fiant secundum habitum, qui est in agente, virtute autem præditos non statim esse, qui aliqua facta virtutis producunt, nisi ea facta ab habitu virtutis proficiscantur. Si igitur quæratur: Quomodo ex bonis actionibus generetur ipsa virtus? Resp. Si actiones istæ sint veræ virtuti consentaneæ, & ipse agens sit scientia, judicio & constantia prædituss.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter, the difficulty having now been resolved, he says that his opinion, which he had stated above in chapter 1, was true. That opinion is that by acting justly someone becomes just, if indeed the things done justly, or those done well in any other way, are endowed with those three qualities of which we have just spoken, that is, are done in accordance with the habit which is in the agent. Those who perform some deeds of virtue are not at once possessed of virtue, unless those deeds proceed from a habit of virtue. If therefore it is asked, How is virtue itself generated from good actions? the answer is: if those actions are truly consistent with virtue, and the agent himself is endowed with knowledge, judgement and constancy.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis removet eorum opinionem, qui sola scientia, non factis virtutem comparari æstimant, & quia in omni vita non re & facto, sed verbis tantum philosophantur, de quibus etiam Plato in orat. contra Sophistas, multa disserit, & Cic. 1. Tusc. quaest. dicit igitur Philosophus hujusmodi homines, qui in sola cognitione virtutem positam esse existimant, non absimiles esse ægrotis, qui præcepta medicorum diligenter audiunt, sed ea postea minimè observant: Sicisti de virtute multa verba faciunt, sed secundum virtutem non agunt & sunt ægroti, non possunt sani fieri, & si millies præcepta Medicorum corum audierint, nisi postea in praxin redigant, sic isti non possunt in virtuosos seu virtute praeditos evadere, nisi istam virtutis cognitionem in praxin & vitae communem usum transferant.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he removes the opinion of those who think virtue is acquired by knowledge alone, not by deeds. Because in all of life they philosophise not by deed and fact but only in words (about which Plato too discourses at length in his oration against the Sophists, and Cicero in Tusculan Disputations book 1), the Philosopher says that men of this kind, who think virtue lies in knowledge alone, are not unlike the sick who diligently listen to the precepts of physicians but afterwards do not observe them at all. So these men talk much about virtue but do not act according to virtue, and they remain sick; they cannot become well, and even if they have heard the physicians' precepts a thousand times, unless they afterwards put them into practice. In the same way, these men cannot become virtuous, or endowed with virtue, unless they transfer this knowledge of virtue into practice and the common use of life.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Artificium tum recte fit, cum ab artis habitu proficiscitur.
units.tr: 1. A work of art is then done rightly when it proceeds from the habit of the art.

units.la: 2. In artibus sola requiritur scientia, at in virtutibus requiritur, cum scientia, voluntas & constantia agendi, cum judicio conjuncta.
units.tr: 2. In the arts knowledge alone is required, but in the virtues there is required, along with knowledge, the will and steadfastness of acting, joined with judgment.

units.la: 3. Scientia per se parum aut nihil ad virtutem prodest.
units.tr: 3. Knowledge in itself does little or nothing for virtue.

units.la: 4. Juste agendo fit aliquis justus cum ex habitu justitiae juste agit.
units.tr: 4. By acting justly someone becomes just when he acts justly from a habit of justice.

units.la: 5. Qui virtutem in sola cognitione positam esse putant, similes sunt agrotis, qui praecepta Medicorum audiunt, sed iis non obtemperant.
units.tr: 5. Those who think that virtue consists in knowledge alone are like sick people who listen to the physicians' instructions but do not obey them.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat initio hujus capitis, dubitaverit aliquis an juste agendo, fiat justus, nam quicunque juste agit, est justus, quia juste agere & justum esse, sunt conjugata, ut ipse lib. 2. Top. cap. 4. sub finem dicit, si unum conjugatorum inest, inest & alterum? Resp. Juste & justus sunt conjugata, si in se considerentur, aut secundum naturam suam, at non statim ratione subjecti, cui insunt, dicuntur conjugata, nam poterit aliquid esse justum quoad factum, quod non est statim justum, quoad personam, verbi gratia: Potest Tyrannus justitiam administrare, (quod de Cambyse legimus, qui iniquo judici cutem detraxit,) qui non statim fit justus, quia multa alia flagitia justitiae repugnantia patrarit.
units.tr: I. The question is: How does he say at the beginning of this chapter that someone may doubt whether, by acting justly, he becomes just? For whoever acts justly is just, since to act justly and to be just are conjugates, as he himself says at the end of Topics book 2, chapter 4: if one of the conjugates is present, the other is present too? Answer: Just and justly are conjugates when they are considered in themselves, or according to their own nature; but they are not called conjugates immediately with respect to the subject in which they inhere. For something can be just with respect to the deed without being just at once with respect to the person. For example, a tyrant may administer justice (as we read of Cambyses, who flayed an unjust judge), and yet he does not at once become just, because he has committed many other crimes that are contrary to justice.

units.la: Quod igitur ad illud Axioma Topicum. Si unum conjugatorum inest, inest & alterum, intelligendū est de eodem modo inexiftendi, verbi gratia: Si unum conjugatorum infit secundum dispositionem, & alterum inerit secundum dispositionem, & si quis juste egeritio uno facto, justus erit in uno facto, sed non statim erit justus simpliciter, aut secundum habitum, & sic illud Axioma exponit Alexand. Aphrod. super 2. Top. cap. 4.
units.tr: Therefore, as for that topical axiom, "If one of the conjugates is present, the other is present too," it must be understood in the same mode of inherence. For example: if one of the conjugates inheres according to a disposition, and the other inheres according to a disposition, then if someone acts justly in a single deed, he is just in that single deed, but he is not at once just simply, or according to habit. This is how Alexander of Aphrodisias, on Topics book 2, chapter 4, explains that axiom.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo voluntas requiratur ad actionem virtutis producendam, cum si sic esset, sequeretur voluntatem moveri & impelli ab ipsis actionibus virtutis, at voluntas ipsa non movetur, ergo neq; ad virtutis actionem necessario requiritur. Consequentia probatur, quia sicut mens non nisi apprehensam objecto intelligit, sic voluntas nisi impellitur ab objecto, non valet agere, ut diserte testatur Philosophus lib. 3. de anima, cap. 4. Assumptum verò quod voluntas non sit mobilis, probatur ex Philosopho lib. 3. cap. 4. hujus operis & 3 de Anima 3. quia voluntas est ipsum principium movens à quo proficiuntur omnes actiones? Resp. Voluntatem considerari bifariam, vel absolutè in sua essentia, & sic est principium movens à quo fluunt actiones & hoc modo non dicitur mobilis, 2. comparatè in sua existentia quatenus ab objecto impellitur, ad aliquid volendum & agendum & sic potest dici mobilis, quatenus scilicet primo intentionis suo motum ab objecto sumit.
units.tr: II. The question is: How is the will required to bring about the action of virtue? For if it were so, it would follow that the will is moved and driven by the very actions of virtue; but the will itself is not moved; therefore it is not necessarily required for the action of virtue. The consequence is proved, because just as the mind understands only what is apprehended by its object, so the will cannot act unless it is driven by the object, as the Philosopher clearly testifies in On the Soul book 3, chapter 4. The assumption, that the will is not mobile, is proved from the Philosopher in book 3, chapter 4 of this work and in On the Soul book 3, because the will is the moving principle itself from which all actions proceed. Answer: The will may be considered in two ways. Either absolutely, in its essence, and so it is the moving principle from which actions flow, and in this way it is not called mobile. Or comparatively, in its existence, insofar as it is driven by the object to will and to act something; and in this way it can be called mobile, insofar as, at its first intention, it receives its motion from the object.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo dicatur in textu scientiam parum aut nihil prodesse ad virtutem, cum certum sit nos absque cognitione modi, secundum quem agere debemus, nihil recte posse agere, & ideo scientia plurimum ad virtutem consequendam prodest? Respond. Scientiam esse duplicem, aliam, quae per fe expetitur, quae in sola rerum contemplatione existit, & de ista scientia dicit, parum aut nihil prodesse ad virtutem, Alia est quae no per fe, sed propter aliud expetitur, qualis est cognitio circumstantiarum, temporis, personae & loci, & ista est ad virtutem maxime necessaria.
units.tr: III. The question is: How is it said in the text that knowledge contributes little or nothing to virtue, when it is certain that without knowledge of the manner in which we ought to act we can act rightly in nothing, and therefore knowledge contributes very much to attaining virtue? Answer: Knowledge is twofold. One kind is desired for its own sake, and exists in the mere contemplation of things; and it is of this knowledge that he says it contributes little or nothing to virtue. The other kind is desired not for its own sake but for the sake of something else, such as the knowledge of circumstances: of time, person and place; and this is most necessary for virtue.

units.la: IV. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat necessariam esse constantiam ad actiones virtutum producendas, cum tamen lib. 1. cap. 1. negarit, ullam esse in rebus Ethicis Constantiam, & proinde non dari demonstrationes & cap. 2. huius lib. argumentatur a majori adminu, si nulla sit constantia aut firmitas in universalibus, multo minus erit in singularibus, unde videtur non necessario requirenda constantia ad actiones virtutum producendas, cum nulla sit in iis constantia? Resp. Actiones considerantur duobus modis, vel in se ipsis vel secundum modum, quo ex iis producitur habitus. Si in seipsis consideretur, nulla est in iis constantia neque firmitas, quia sunt in agentis potestate, ut fiant, vel non fiant, & sic sumenda sunt illa loca citata ex Aristotele. At vero secundum modum, quo ex iis producitur habitus, necessario requiritur, firmum propositum, constans agendi voluntas, & immobile judicium, & sic Aristoteles hoc loco debet intelligi.
units.tr: IV. The question is: How does he say that steadfastness is necessary for producing the actions of virtues, when yet in book 1, chapter 1, he denied that there is any steadfastness in ethical matters, and therefore that there are no demonstrations; and in chapter 2 of this book he argues from the greater to the less: if there is no constancy or firmness in universals, much less will there be in particulars? Hence it seems that steadfastness is not necessarily required for producing the actions of virtues, since there is no steadfastness in them? Answer: Actions are considered in two ways: either in themselves, or according to the manner in which a habit is produced from them. If they are considered in themselves, there is in them neither steadfastness nor firmness, because it lies in the power of the agent whether they are done or not done, and so those passages cited from Aristotle must be taken in that sense. But according to the manner in which a habit is produced from them, a firm purpose, a constant will to act, and an unchanging judgment are necessarily required; and it is in this sense that Aristotle must be understood in this place.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Sic fuit primus Tract hujus libri, nempe de principiis virtutum, sequitur secundus de natura virtutis per definitionem explicanda, quae quidem definitio non tantum naturam virtutis declarat, sed etiam naturam felicitatis illustriorem reddit, quia in definitione felicitatis ponebatur virtus, ut patet, ex cap. 6. lib. superioris. Membra huius tractatus sunt duo, in primo genus virtutis investigat. In secundo differentiam generi adjungit, & ut sic ex genere & differentia completa habeatur definitio, & integre explicetur natura virtutis. Partes huius capitis sunt duae. In prima scopum suum proponit. In secunda genus virtutis per divisionem investigat.
units.tr: So the first tract of this book, on the principles of the virtues, is complete. The second follows, which is to explain the nature of virtue by definition. This definition not only declares the nature of virtue but also makes the nature of happiness clearer, because virtue was placed in the definition of happiness, as is evident from chapter 6 of the previous book. This tract has two parts. In the first, he looks for the genus of virtue. In the second, he adds the differentia of the genus, so that a complete definition is obtained from genus and differentia and the nature of virtue is fully explained. This chapter has two parts. In the first he sets out his aim. In the second he investigates the genus of virtue by division.

units.la: In prima igitur parte, brevissimo transitu dicit, post haec videndum est, quid sit virtus, id est, postquam de principiis virtutum egerimus, explicanda est natura virtutis, & sic elegante Methodo utitur Aristoteles, ut prius de virtute inquirat an sit, quam ad naturam ejus explicandam & quaerendam quid sit, se accingat.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he says in a very brief transition: "After this we must consider what virtue is." That is, after we have discussed the principles of the virtues, the nature of virtue must be explained. Aristotle uses this elegant method: he first inquires whether virtue exists, before he sets himself to explain and inquire what its nature is.

units.la: In secunda parte genus virtutis per divisionem investigat hoc modo: quicquid est in animo, est aut potentia, aut affectus, aut habitus. Sed virtus non est affectus neq; potentia. Ergo est habitus. Quod virtus sit in animo pro confesso sumit, quia supra cap. ult. lib. 1. probarat virtutem esse in ea animae parte, quae dicitur appetitiva, at vero curtia tantum dicatur esse in animo, affectum nempe, potentiam & habitum, id explicatione indigere videtur. Ut hoc melius intelligatur, sciendum est numerari vulgo 4. species qualitatis. Habitum, potentiam, passionem seu affectum, & formam seu figuram externam: Quod vero ad formam externam, cum non fluat ab animo, neq; pertineat ad ea, quae sunt in animo, nullum hic habet locum, reliqui sunt tantum tres, Affectus, Potentia
units.tr: In the second part he investigates the genus of virtue by division, in this way: whatever is in the soul is either a power, an affection, or a habit. But virtue is neither an affection nor a power. Therefore it is a habit. He takes for granted that virtue is in the soul, because above, at the end of book 1, chapter he proved that virtue is in that part of the soul which is called appetitive. But since only affection, power and habit seem to be said to be in the soul, this seems to need explanation. To understand this better, it must be known that four species of quality are commonly counted: habit, power, passion or affection, and external form or figure. As for external form, since it does not flow from the soul nor belong to those things which are in the soul, it has no place here. Only three remain: affection, power and habit.

units.la: tentia sentia & Habitus, & cum virtus ut supra dictum est, sit in anima appetitiva, appetitum sequitur motus seu passio ad rem appetitam consequendam necessaria est potentia, quæ affectum seu passionem ad rem consequendam possit producere. Hinc tandé ex assiduo usu nascitur habitus virtutis aut vitii. Cum igitur constet virtutem moralem esse in animo & esse qualitatem, recte igitur dicit Aristoteles: tria tantum esse in animo: Affectus, Potentia & Habitus. Assumtum probatur per partes, virtutem scilicet neque esse affectum neq; potentiam. Non esse affectum probat 4. rationibus. Non esse potentiam vero seu facultatem. 3. Quod virtus non sit affectus sic probatur.
units.tr: Since virtue, as was said above, is in the appetitive soul, a motion or passion follows the appetite, and for attaining the desired thing a power is necessary, one which can produce the affection or passion for attaining the thing. Hence finally a habit of virtue or vice arises from constant practice. Since it is established that moral virtue is in the soul and is a quality, Aristotle rightly says that only three things are in the soul: affection, power and habit. The assumption is proved part by part: namely, that virtue is neither an affection nor a power. That it is not an affection he proves by four reasons. That it is not a power or faculty he proves by three reasons. That virtue is not an affection is proved as follows.

units.la: Primò: Quia ab effectibus nemo dicitur bonus aut malus, sicut a virtutibus dicitur aliquis bonus. Ab effectibus nemine m dici bonum aut malum paret, nam si quis irascit aut miseratur, nō adhibita distinctione, nō dicitur ab ira aut misericordia bonus, at si modum in ira servet & moderatè irascatur, ut virum fortem & magnanimum decet, & misereatur ut decet virum vere justum, tum ira & misericordia non sunt amplius affectus, sed quia cum mediocritate sunt conjunctæ virtutis speciem induunt.
units.tr: First: because no one is called good or bad from the affections, as someone is called good from the virtues. That no one is called good or bad from the affections is evident: for if someone becomes angry or feels pity without any distinction, he is not called good from anger or from pity. But if he keeps due measure in anger and is moderately angry, as befits a brave and magnanimous man, and feels pity as befits a truly just man, then anger and pity are no longer mere affections, but because they are joined with moderation they take on the species of virtue.

units.la: Secundò, Quod virtus non sit affectus, ducitur a consequentibus, quia ab affectibus nemo laudatur vel vituperatur, quæ ratio est intelligenda, ut superior adhibita scilicet distinctione, at a virtutibus homines laudantur.
units.tr: Second, that virtue is not an affection is drawn from the consequences: because no one is praised or blamed for the affections. This reason must be understood with the distinction mentioned above. But men are praised for the virtues.

units.la: Tertiò, Ducitur a causis, quia in affectibus nullam ernitur consilium, utpote qui temeritate ac fervo- requodam animi concitentur: Nam ut ait Seneca, Affectus sunt subditi animi motus, qui frequentes & crebri fuere morbum, sicut distillatio levior facit tussim, gravior vero phthisin, at in virtutibus semper cernitur consilium, quia rectricem habent prudentiam, cujus propriu est consilia examinare, nec facili credulitate in falsa prolabi, nec cito desinere, sed suspensam diu sententiam tenere, ut præclarè Seneca lib.4. de virtutibus, & sysms ipse Philosophus lib.3. hujus operis cap. 7. docet.
units.tr: Third, it is drawn from the causes: because in the affections no counsel is discerned, since they are stirred up by a certain rashness and heat of mind. For, as Seneca says, "Affections are motions of a mind subject to them, which when frequent and repeated become a disease, as a light catarrh produces a cough, but a heavier one produces consumption." But in the virtues counsel is always discerned, because they have prudence as their guide, whose proper task is to examine counsels, neither to fall into falsehoods through easy credulity nor to abandon them quickly, but to keep judgment suspended for a long time. Seneca teaches this admirably in book 4 of On Virtues, and the Philosopher himself teaches it in book 3 of this work, chapter 7.

units.la: Quarta ratio ducitur ab effectis, quia ab affectibus moveri dicimur, à virtutibus vero non, sed afficitantum, nam est Actus sunt animi motus & impulsus, à quibus mutari & alterari dicimur, nō moveri, quia illis inclinamur tantum & propensi reddimur ad bene agendum, non autem impellimur.
units.tr: The fourth reason is drawn from the effects: because we are said to be moved by the affections, but not by the virtues; rather, we are only affected by them. For the affections are motions and impulses of the mind, by which we are said to be changed and altered, not moved, since we are only inclined by them and made prone to act well, but are not impelled.

units.la: Notandum omnes affectus provenire ab anima appetitiva, & esse vel in parte concupiscibili, aut irascibili. In parte concupiscibili, aut respectu inclinationis ad bonum, unde oritur amor; cui opponitur odium, aut respectu progressionis, & motus ad bonum unde dimanat desiderium, cui opponitur fuga, aut respectu perfectionis & quies in bono unde oritur delectatio aut voluptas, cui opponitur dolor, sub quo continentur, invidia, ζηλοτυπία, misericordia. In parte irascibili, aut respectu boni difficilis, unde oritur spes, cui opponitur desperatio; Aut respectu mali difficilis, unde oritur timor, cui opponitur audacia, aut respectu molesti repugnantis naturae, unde ira, furor, excandescentia, cui opponitur clementia naturae.
units.tr: It should be noted that all the affections arise from the appetitive soul, and are either in the concupiscible part or in the irascible part. In the concupiscible part, they arise with respect to the inclination toward good, whence love arises, to which hatred is opposed; or with respect to the progression and movement toward good, whence desire flows, to which flight is opposed; or with respect to perfection and rest in good, whence delight or pleasure arises, to which pain is opposed, under which are included envy, jealousy (zēlotypia) and pity. In the irascible part, they arise either with respect to a difficult good, whence hope arises, to which despair is opposed; or with respect to a difficult evil, whence fear arises, to which boldness is opposed; or with respect to what is troublesome and opposed to nature, whence anger, fury and rage arise, to which gentleness of nature is opposed.

units.la: Probat verò non esse potentiam 3. rationibus, quorum duæ priores sunt communes cum iis, qui-bus probavit virtutem non esse affectum, tertium est propria, id est, quia est potentia seu ex eo, quod quis potest bene vel malè agere, nemo dicitur bo-nus vel malus. 2. Quia à potentia nemo laudatur aut vituperatur, nam quia potentia inest nobis à na-tura, ideo ejus laus & vituperium non nobis adscri-bitur, cum nostra cura vel incuria non fiat. 3. Ratio est hæc: Quia potentia est à natura, virtus verò non est à natu a sed usu & consuetudine comparatur, ut supra probatum erat cap. 1. quod verò potentia fit à natura, hoc patet ex eodem cap. 1. ubi Philoso-phus dicit, etsi virtus non fit à natura, tamen non est contra naturam, sed habemus potentiam quan-dam naturalem, per quam ad virtutem capescen-dam sumus apti. Tandem verò concludit virtutem esse habitum, cum priorum nihil sit, ut jam pro-bavit, in qua opinione est etiam Plato, nam in Men. variis rationib.id probat & fere omnes Philosophi, unde Aristoteles ipse lib. 6. cap. ult. dicit, omnes qui virtutem definierunt, eam habitum esse dixerunt, habitum verò secundum rectam rationem.
units.tr: He proves that virtue is not a power by three reasons, of which the first two are common with those by which he proved that virtue is not an affection, while the third is proper. The third is this: because one who is able to act well or badly is not called good or bad from that power. The second: because no one is praised or blamed for a power, since we have the power from nature, and so its praise or blame is not ascribed to us, since it does not come about by our care or carelessness. The third reason is this: because a power is from nature, but virtue is not from nature; it is acquired by use and custom, as was proved above in chapter 1. That a power comes from nature is evident from the same chapter 1, where the Philosopher says that although virtue does not come from nature, yet it is not contrary to nature, but we have a certain natural capacity by which we are apt to receive virtue. Finally he concludes that virtue is a habit, since none of the former is so, as he has now proved. Plato also holds this opinion; he proves it by various arguments in the Meno, and almost all philosophers agree. Hence Aristotle himself says in book 6, last chapter, that all who have defined virtue have said that it is a habit, and a habit according to right reason.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Ab affectibus qua tales, nemo dicitur bonus aut malus, nemo etiam laudatur vel vituperatur.
units.tr: 1. No one is called good or bad from the affections as such, and no one is praised or blamed for them.

units.la: 2. Non omnis ira est vitium, sed qua verum modum ad nimium vel parum excedit.
units.tr: 2. Not every anger is a vice, but only that which exceeds or falls short of the true measure.

units.la: 3. Ab affectibus moveri & impelli dicimur, à virtutibus affici tantum & disponi.
units.tr: 3. We are said to be moved and impelled by the affections, but to be only affected and disposed by the virtues.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: 1. Quæritur: Quomodo tria tantum numeret Philosophus in animo, affectum nempe, potentiam & habitum, cum sint longè plura in animo, veluti species rerum intelligibilium, id est, rerum notitiæ, operationes humanæ & hujusmodi, quæ non possunt referri ad tria memorata ab Aristotele, unde non videtur sufficiens enumeratio eorum, quæ sunt in anima? Respon. Cum virtus sit in ea parte animæ, quæ dicitur appetitiva, ideo recensere voluit Aristoteles eas quatuor, quæ fluerent ab anima appetitiva, & ideo rectè dixit tria esse in anima, nempe in anima appetitiva. Species verò intelligibilium, &c. sunt in anima quidem, sed non in appetitiva animæ parte, sed in intellectuali. Operationes verò humanæ, quæ sunt communes, utrique animæ parti hic non attingit, sed tantum ea, quæ sunt propria animæ appetitivæ.
units.tr: 1. Question: How does the Philosopher count only three things in the soul, namely affection, power and habit, when the soul contains far more, such as the species of intelligible things (that is, the knowledge of things), human operations and the like, which cannot be referred to the three named by Aristotle? So his enumeration of what is in the soul does not seem sufficient. Answer: Since virtue is in that part of the soul which is called appetitive, Aristotle chose to list those four things which flow from the appetitive soul. So he rightly said that there are three things in the soul, namely in the appetitive soul. The species of intelligible things, and so on, are indeed in the soul, but not in its appetitive part; they are in its intellectual part. Human operations, which are common to both parts of the soul, he does not touch on here, but only those which belong to the appetitive soul alone.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat tria tantum esse principia agendi, affectum, potentiam, habitum, quæ concurrunt ad actionem virtutis producendam, cum cap. 6. lib. 6. hujus operis alia etiam numeret principia, quæ concurrunt ad actiones virtutis, sensum nempe, appetitum & intellectum. Ergo aut sunt plura principia, aut Aristoteles est sibi contrarius? Resp. Diverso respectu ista dicuntur, nam hic enumerat tantum tria principia agendi, affectum, potentiam, habitum, quia agit de virtute morali, illic etiam loco citato alia tria enumerat, sensum, appetitum, intellectum, quia agit toto eo libro de virtute intellectuali, ut hic sunt tria principia, quæ respiciunt bonum, sic illic sunt tria, quæ respiciunt verum, illic est sensus unde Mechanici & operatio, ratio, hic appetitus unde Politici & actio, intellectus unde Theorici & contemplatio, hic est potentia, quæ inchoat, affectus, qui excitat & acuit habitus, qui perficit.
units.tr: II. Question: How does he say there are only three principles of acting, affection, power and habit, which combine to produce an action of virtue, when in chapter 6 of Book 6 of this work he also enumerates other principles which combine in the actions of virtue, namely sense, appetite and intellect? So either there are more principles, or Aristotle contradicts himself. Answer: These are said with different respects. Here he lists only three principles of acting, affection, power and habit, because he is treating of moral virtue. In the passage cited he lists three others, sense, appetite and intellect, because in that whole book he is treating of intellectual virtue. As here there are three principles which relate to the good, so there are three there which relate to the true. There is sense, whence come the craftsmen and their operation; reason, whence come the politicians and action; intellect, whence come the theorists and contemplation. Here there is power, which initiates; affection, which stirs and sharpens; and habit, which perfects.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo dicatur in secunda ratione, ubi probat virtutem non esse affectum, propter affectum nec minem laudari vel vituperari, cum tamen invidia sit affectus, & ut patet sub finem c. 7. huius libri, propter invidiam vituperamur. Ergo minus firma videtur illa ratio? Resp. Alii sunt affectus animæ bene dispositæ & propter illos affectus, qui sunt tales, nemo laudatur vel vituperatur, nisi adhibita distinctione: nam si accedat moderatio virtutis, tunc propter istam moderationem laudantur, si vero econtra vitium accedat, vituperantur. Alii sunt affectus animi male dispositi & ægri, qui potius sunt mera vitia quam affectus, & sic invidia cum sit vitium, dicitur simpliciter vituperabilis. IV. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat simpliciter iracin on esse vitium, sed quodammodo, nam iracin ut decet, est virtus, seu mediocriter iracin, cum potius videatur affectus, quam virtus, nam mediocriter irascentes alteramur, at secundum nullam virtutem alteramur, teste ipso Philosopho? Resp. Non dicit Philosophus mediocriter iracin esse plane virtutem, sed mediocriter irascentes esse bene affectos, quia modum prescribunt irae: nam omnis affectus moderationem virtutis laudatur, & speciem virtutis induit, ut verecundia in juvene, misericordia in judice. V. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat virtutem esse habitum, cum quae ipse requirit ad constituendum habitum nullibi in rerum
units.tr: III. Question: How is it said, in the second argument, where he proves that virtue is not an affection, because no one is praised or blamed for affections, when yet envy is an affection, and as is clear near the end of chapter 7 of this book, we are blamed for envy? So that argument seems less firm? Answer: Some affections belong to a well-disposed soul, and no one is praised or blamed for such affections unless a distinction is made. For if the moderation of virtue is added, they are praised on account of that moderation; but if vice is added on the contrary, they are blamed. Other affections belong to a badly disposed and sick mind, and these are rather mere vices than affections. Thus envy, since it is a vice, is simply blameworthy. IV. Question: How does he say that anger is not simply a vice, but in a certain way, for anger as it ought to be is virtue, or moderate anger; when it seems rather to be an affection than a virtue, for those who are moderately angry are moved, whereas we are moved by no virtue, as the Philosopher himself testifies? Answer: The Philosopher does not say that moderate anger is plainly virtue, but that those who are moderately angry are well affected, because they prescribe a measure for anger. For every affection that observes the moderation of virtue is praised and takes on the appearance of virtue, as modesty in a young man and mercy in a judge. V. Question: How does he say that virtue is a habit, when the things he requires for the constitution of a habit are found nowhere

units.la: rerum natura reperiantur, nullum enim reperitur, qui vera sit scientia, firme iudicio & constantia semper praeditus, nam ut dicit Scriptura, iustus cadit septies in die. & Hierax Philosophus apud Stobaeum, id est, oratione de iustitia dubitare se dicit, an debeat vocare iustitiam habitum ex communi opinione, an habitum tantum, an aliquod factum pro libitu huius vel illius productum, ut apud Tribal los, ut testatur Aristoteles lib. 5. Topic. cap. 1. Iustitia erat occidere patres senio confectos, ne senio languescerent, & sic & sibi & aliis molestiam parerent, & sic de aliis enormibus factis, quatamen pro summa iustitia, apud varias gentes habebantur? Resp. Virtutem omnino esse habitum, nam si quis secundum circumstantias, loci, temporis, personarum agat, jam est scientia praeditus, si quis non aberret a modo aut a medio, sed intra limites rectae rationis se contineat, est firmo judicio praeditus, si quis etiam sic bene agat, ut nunquam ad contraria vitia deflectat, erit constantia praeditus, & sic illis tribus conditionibus, quas ad habitum virtutis requirit Aristoteles, instructus erit. Quod vero ad locum illum scripturae, intelligendum est, in actionibus divinis non politicis: nam ut air Iobus, non est mundities in Angelis, si scilicet conferantur cum ea munditia & puritate, quae est in Deo, quia finiti ad infinitum non est proportio. Quod vero ad illud dictum Philosophi, quia non tantum communi hominum opinioni repugnat, sed & rectae rationi & legibus naturae, meram esse opinionem, non dictum Philosopho dignum esse dicimus.
units.tr: in nature. For no one is found who is possessed of true science, firm judgement and constancy at all times. As Scripture says, the just man falls seven times a day. And Hierax the philosopher, in Stobaeus, that is, in his speech on justice, says that he doubts whether justice should be called a habit according to common opinion, or only a habit, or some deed done at the pleasure of this or that person; as among the Triballi, as Aristotle testifies in Topics Book 5, chapter 1: it was justice to kill aged fathers, lest they grow feeble with old age and so cause trouble both to themselves and to others; and so with other outrageous deeds which among various peoples were held to be the height of justice? Answer: Virtue is altogether a habit. For if anyone acts according to the circumstances of place, time and persons, he is possessed of science; if anyone does not stray from measure or mean, but keeps himself within the limits of right reason, he is possessed of firm judgement; if anyone so acts well that he never turns aside to the contrary vices, he will be possessed of constancy. And so he will be furnished with those three conditions which Aristotle requires for the habit of virtue. As for that passage of Scripture, it must be understood of divine actions, not political ones: for as Job says, there is no purity in the angels, namely if they are compared with that cleanness and purity which is in God, since there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. As for that saying of the Philosopher, that it is mere opinion because it contradicts not only common human opinion but also right reason and the laws of nature, we say it is not a saying worthy of the Philosopher.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: POstquâ inuestigavit Philosophus genus virtutis & ostendit esse habitum, jam quaerit differentias in hoc capite. Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima praemittit conditionem quandam virtutis seu nominalem definitionem. In 2. explicat accuratius medium ut melius intelligatur, circa quod medium versetur virtus. In 3. virtutem circa medium seu mediocritatem versari aliquot rationibus ostendit.
units.tr: After investigating the genus of virtue and showing that it is a habit, the Philosopher now asks about its differences in this chapter. The chapter has three parts. In the first he sets out a certain condition of virtue, or a nominal definition. In the second he explains more precisely the mean, so that it may be better understood what the mean is about which virtue is conversant. In the third he shows, by several reasons, that virtue is conversant about the mean, or mediocrity.

units.la: In prima igitur praemittit definitionem nominalem virtutis, quod virtus sit id, quo quis f- optimè habet, & munus suum exsequitur, & licet iam definit lib. 7. naturalis auscult. cap. 2. Metopus vel ò Pythagoreus in orat. 1. de virtute, apud Stobaeum & Alex. Aphrod. sup. 3. lib. Top. Aristotelis, cap. 2. & Cic. lib. 1. de legibus, virtutem nihil aliud esse dicunt, quam cujusque rei vim ac perfectionem insitam, ut velocitas equi, est virtus equi. Caeterum virtutis nomen variè accipitur. 1. Pro omni eo, quod rem quamlibet bene affectam & dispositam reddit, ut apud Aristotelem hoc loco, & sic denotat, omnem facultatem sive omnem rei perfectionem tam hyperphysicam quam physicam, tam innatam quam accessoriam, quo sensu virtutes Dei, Angelorum, animae rationalis, virtutes coeli, elementorum, &c. quamrumcunq; denique rerum dicere solemus. 2. Sumitur pro corporis habitu, sic vires, sanitas, pulchritudo, &c. virtutes appellari solent. 3. Virtutes animi sunt potentia & facultates aliquid exsequendi, idq; non uno modo, nam & vegetativa anima suas virtutes, nutriendi conconcoquendi & expellendi habet, sensitiva sentiendi, rationalis ratiocinandi, &c. 4. Sumitur pro solis habitibus bonis introductis, idque non uno modo, nam competit tam habitibus infusis, quam acquisitis, quomodo etiam Theologicae virtutes in numerum virtutum veniunt, sed hae non proprie spectant ad Ethicam. Interdum etiam virtus sumitur pro dispositione naturali, quae est causa virtutis proprie dictae, ut supra asserunt Philosophus cap. 1. hujus libri, & quomodo etiam sumitur virtus, cap. ult. lib. 6. hujus operis, ubi dicit: nos per naturam possidere virtutem, & a natura esse temperantes & fortes. Ultimo & propriissime accipitur virtus pro habitu mentis, frequenti usu & exercitatione comparato, & sic est duplex, intellectualis & moralis, de qua divisione egit ibid. ult. lib. 1. De morali autem, quae perficit hominis voluntatem & appetitu, in Ethicis tantum agitur: De intellectualibus vero non item propter 3. causas. 1. Quia finé habent diversum ab Ethica doctrina. 2. Quia circa aliud objectum versantur. 3. Quia praecepta virtutum intellectualium, magna ex parte pertinent ad Philosophiam theoreticam, quod vero Philosophus in 6. lib. hujus operis, de virtutibus intellectualibus agat, id ideo fit, ut per illam comparationem virtutum intellectualium, doctrina moralium magis illucescat. Dicitur vero virtus Graecis ἀρετή vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρεως, id est, à Marte, quod in bello praecipue virtus se exerat, ibi-que illius vis conspiciatur, unde per excellentiam sola fortitudo dici solet virtus, vel dicitur ἀρετή quasi ἀϊρετή, id est, eligenda, quia virtus maxime est eligenda
units.tr: In the first part, then, he sets out the nominal definition of virtue: that virtue is that by which someone is best disposed and performs his task. He has already defined it in Book 7 of the Physics, chapter 2. Metopus, or a Pythagorean, in the first oration on virtue, reported by Stobaeus and by Alexander of Aphrodisias on the third book of Aristotle's Topics, chapter 2, and Cicero in the first book of the Laws, say that virtue is nothing other than the innate force and perfection of each thing, as the swiftness of a horse is the virtue of a horse. Moreover, the name of virtue is taken in various ways. (1) It is used for everything that makes any thing well disposed and well arranged, as Aristotle uses it in this place. In this sense it denotes every faculty, or every perfection of a thing, both hyperphysical and physical, both innate and acquired; in this sense we are accustomed to speak of the virtues of God, of angels, of the rational soul, the virtues of the heavens, of the elements, and so on, of whatever things at all. (2) It is taken for the condition of the body; thus strength, health, beauty and the like are commonly called virtues. (3) The virtues of the soul are powers and faculties for doing something, and this not in one way only, for the vegetative soul has its virtues of nourishing, digesting and expelling, the sensitive soul has the virtue of sensing, the rational soul of reasoning, and so on. (4) It is taken for good habits alone that have been introduced, and this again not in one way only, for it applies both to infused and to acquired habits. In this way the theological virtues too come into the number of virtues, but these do not properly belong to Ethics. Sometimes virtue is also taken for the natural disposition which is the cause of virtue properly so called, as the Philosopher asserts above in chapter 1 of this book, and in the same way virtue is taken in the last chapter of Book 6 of this work, where he says that we possess virtue by nature, and that we are temperate and brave by nature. Lastly, and most properly, virtue is taken for a habit of the mind, acquired by frequent use and exercise; and so it is twofold, intellectual and moral. He treated this division in the last chapter of Book 1 of the same work. But moral virtue, which perfects the will and the appetite of man, is treated only in the Ethics; intellectual virtues are not treated in the same way, for three reasons. (1) Because they have an end different from that of ethical teaching. (2) Because they are conversant about a different object. (3) Because the precepts of the intellectual virtues for the most part belong to theoretical philosophy. That the Philosopher, however, treats of the intellectual virtues in the sixth book of this work, is done so that by that comparison of the intellectual virtues the teaching of moral matters may shine more clearly. The Greeks call virtue ἀρετή [arete], either from Ares [ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρεως], that is, from Mars, because virtue shows itself especially in war, and there its force is seen; whence by excellence courage alone is usually called virtue; or ἀρετή is said as it were ἀϊρετή [aireté], that is, what is to be chosen, because virtue is above all to be chosen,

units.la: appetenda, vel quia nulla est virtus nisi ex certo animi judicio & proaresi, vel etiam dicitur ξουν τὸ αἱρέσθαι, id est, ab attollêdo, quia animum ad summa & praeclarissima quaeque elevat & attollit. Latinè dicitur virtus, quasi à viro, sic Cic. 2. Tusc. quaest. appellata fuit ex viro virtus, viri enim propriè maxima est fortitudo, cujus munera duo maximè sunt, Mortis doloris contemtio.
