Credum est igitur his, si virtutis compotes, vel potius si viri volumus esse, quoniam à viris virtus nomen est mutuata. Alii virtutem derivant à vi, quia vis sit virtus quaedam animi, in rerum arduarum aggressione & adversarum perpessione, & placitarum abstinentia. Nonnulli Ethici alliso-ne quadam virtutem dictam volunt, quasi viri statum vel etiam, quod virtus sit quasi viriartus. Haec de ratione nominis, jam de re ipsa. Quod virtus sit id, secundum quod aliquid munus suum exsequitur, probat inductione exemplorum Philosophus, ut virtus equi, virtus oculi, sunt perfectiones oculi & equi, & quidem secundum quas oculus & equus, munus suum bene exsequuntur, & si in aliis rebus sic se habet, multo magis in homine se habebit, ut virtus hominis sit illa hominis perfectio, secundum quam bene possit agere.
units.tr: to be desired; or because there is no virtue except from a certain judgment of the mind and deliberate choice (proairesis); or it is also said from ξουν τὸ αἱρέσθαι [raising up], that is, from lifting up, because it raises and lifts the mind to the highest and most distinguished things. In Latin it is called virtus, as if from vir (man). So Cicero in the second book of the Tusculan Disputations: "virtus was named from vir, for the greatest thing in a man is courage, whose two chief duties are the contempt of death and of pain. We must believe, then, that we are possessed of virtue, or rather that we wish to be men, since virtue has borrowed its name from men." Others derive virtue from vis (force), because virtue is a certain strength of the mind in undertaking difficult things, in enduring adversities, and in abstaining from pleasant things. Some ethicists want virtue to be named by a certain play on words, as if it were the state of a vir, or even that virtue is as it were viriarte. These are concerning the reason of the name; now concerning the thing itself. That virtue is that by which something performs its task, the Philosopher proves by induction of examples: the virtue of the eye and the virtue of the horse are the perfections of the eye and of the horse, namely those by which the eye and the horse perform their task well. And if it is so in other things, much more will it be so in man, so that the virtue of man is that perfection of man by which he is able to act well.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis de medio agit, ut quia in definitione virtutis adhibitur sit medium, intelligatur, per quod medium definiatur virtus, sic igitur à simili incipit, ut in omni re continua & divisibili & majus & minus & aequale in partibus (nam quicquid potest dividi, habet etiam partes majores, minores & medias, seu aequales,) sic etiam in actionibus bus hominū, circa quas versatur virtus, licet magis, minus, vel mediocriter agere, æquale vero & medium æquivalent, teste Platone in Parm. qui æquale definit medii inter majus & minus: nam cum medium seu mediocritas (nam ista pro eodem sumuntur) sit duplex, aliud medium rei, aliud rationis seu quoad nos. Medium rei est, quod æqualiter distat ab utroque extremorum. Medium vero rationis definitur, quod neq; redundat, neq; deficit plus quam oportet. Medium vero rei est unum idemque apud omnes, quia nostra intelligentia seu ratio rem ipsam non mutat, nam quocunq; rem referas, est una ubique & eadem, & ideo hoc medium rei vocatur medium Arithmeticum, seu secundum proportionem arithmeticā, quia numerus, qui est subjectū arithmeticæ est invariabilis, nec unquam pro circūstantiis varias mutat naturam & definitionem suam. Exemplum medii rei in numeris adfert Philosophus, ut in denario est majus & minus, verbi gratia, decem & duo, medium vero inter decem & duo sunt sex, quæ dicuntur medium rei, quæ æqualiter distant ab utroq; extremo, quia sicut sex superat binarium quaternario numero, sic superantur à denario numero quaternario. Et hæc proportio dicitur Arithmetica, quæ non variatur: nam in æternum sic se habebit, ut sex, inter duo & decem sint medium, & æqualiter superent, & superentur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he treats of the mean, so that, because the mean is used in the definition of virtue, it may be understood by what mean virtue is defined. He therefore begins from a likeness: in every continuous and divisible thing there is the greater, the less, and the equal among its parts (for whatever can be divided has also larger, smaller and middle, or equal, parts). So also in human actions, about which virtue is conversant, one may act more, less, or moderately; and the equal and the mean are equivalent, as Plato testifies in the Parmenides, who defines the equal as the mean between greater and less. For since the mean, or mediocrity (for these are taken as the same), is twofold, one is the mean of the thing, the other the mean of reason or relative to us. The mean of the thing is that which is equally distant from each of the extremes. The mean of reason is defined as that which neither exceeds nor falls short more than it ought. The mean of the thing is one and the same for all, because our understanding or reason does not change the thing itself; for wherever you refer the thing, it is one and the same everywhere; and therefore this mean of the thing is called the arithmetical mean, or according to arithmetical proportion, because number, which is the subject of arithmetic, is unchangeable, and never changes its nature and definition according to circumstances. The Philosopher gives an example of the mean of the thing in numbers: in ten there is the greater and the less, for instance ten and two; the mean between ten and two is six, which is called the mean of the thing, since it is equally distant from each extreme: for just as six exceeds two by four, so six is exceeded by ten by four. And this proportion is called arithmetical, and it does not vary; for to eternity it will be so, that six is the mean between two and ten, and exceeds and is exceeded equally.

units.la: Medium vero rationis respectu nostri, non sic se habet, necest unum idemque apud omnes, & vulgò vocatur medium Geometricum, verbi gratia, sicut se habent quatuor ad sex, sic se habent sex ad no-vem vem. Sex vero inter quatuor & novem, non sunt medium rei ipsius nec aequaliter differunt a quatuor ad novem, sed medium rationis nostrae, ut sicut se habent sex ad quatuor, ita novem ad sex se habeant. Sed sex continent quatuor semel cum dimidio & sic continentur a novem semel cum dimidio. Hic vero excessus & defectus non sunt referendi ad medium aliquod, quod constituit medium rei, quia nullum hic tale est, quod aequaliter superet & superetur, sed ad medium rationis nostrae, ut ubique sit proportio sesquialtera. Sic etiam sicut se habent tria ad sex, ita se habent quatuor ad octo, nam utrobique est proportio dupla, quia sicut ternarius continetur bis a senario, sic & quaternarius continetur bis ab octonario: Exemplum adferrur a Philosopho in textu valde accommodatum huic medio applicando: Nam si duas libras panis omnibus athletis, qui in Palestra se exercent comedere parum sit, decem vero nimium, non statim erit conveniens, unicuique sex libras panis dare, quod est medium inter decem & duo, medium inquam rei: Sed conveniens erit dare medium respectu nostri, quantum cujusque complexio aut constitutio fert, ut aliis erit satis tres libras panis comedere, aliis quinque, & in hoc medio respectu nostri res ipsa non sunt terminni, sed nos ad quos respicere oportet, si tale medium in venire velimus, quod sit secundum proportionem Geometricam, verbi gratia, quanto Tyronis & primo se in palestra exercentis robur superatur a Milone veterano Athleta (de quo multa historia & Aelianus) etiam tanto plus cibi debet dari Miloni. At robur MiloMilonis superat Tyronis robur duplo aut triplo, Ergo duplo aut triplo plus cibi dari debet.
units.tr: But the mean of reason with respect to us is not so; it is not one and the same for all, and is commonly called the geometrical mean. For example, just as four is to six, so six is to nine. Six, between four and nine, is not the mean of the thing itself, nor does it differ equally from four and from nine; but it is the mean of our reason, so that just as six is to four, so nine is to six. But six contains four once and a half, and so it is contained by nine once and a half. Here the excess and the defect are not to be referred to some mean which constitutes the mean of the thing, because there is no such mean here which exceeds and is exceeded equally; they are referred to the mean of our reason, so that everywhere there is a sesquialternate proportion. Likewise, just as three is to six, so four is to eight, for in both there is a double proportion, because just as three is contained twice in six, so four is contained twice in eight. The Philosopher, in the text, adduces an example very well suited to applying this mean: for if two pounds of bread is too little for all the athletes who train in the palaestra to eat, and ten pounds is too much, it will not at once be fitting to give each one six pounds of bread, which is the mean between ten and two, I mean the mean of the thing. But it will be fitting to give the mean relative to us, as much as each one's constitution or build bears; so that for some three pounds of bread will be enough to eat, for others five. And in this mean relative to us, the things themselves are not the terms, but we to whom one must have regard, if we wish to find such a mean as is according to geometrical proportion. For example, in proportion as the strength of a novice who is just beginning to train in the palaestra is surpassed by that of Milo the veteran athlete (of whom there is much history, and Aelian), so much more food must be given to Milo. But Milo's strength surpasses the strength of the novice by double or triple; therefore double or triple more food must be given to him.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis: Virtutem versari circa mediocritatem duabus rationibus ostendit, 1. est, a minori ad majus. Sic, artes omnes, qui opus suum ad perfectionem producere volunt, medium aliquod quaerunt. Ergo, multo magis ars, quae est praestantior, medium aliquod quaerit, non vero medium rei sed medium rationis seu respectu nostri. Antecedens probatur communi proverbio, quod illa dicantur demum perfecta & bona, quib. nihil addi nec adimi potest, verbi gratia: In arte sutoria ea calceamenta sunt optima, quae ad pedem sunt accommodatissima, ut neque sint latiora vel arctiora, quam pro pede cui convenire debent, sic in pictura, ea pictura dicitur perfecta, cui nulla linea potest ad perfectionem confituendam, nihil etiam adimi potest, quin aliquid de perfectione detractur, proinde ista perfectio versatur circa medium seu mediocritatem quia respuit majus & minus, seu excessum & defectum. At virtus est praestantior arte & ratio quatruplex reddi potest. 1. Quia in artibus sola requiritur scientia, in virtutum actionibus requiritur etiam electio & constantia, ut supra cap. 4. dictum erat 2. quia artes tam ad bonum quam ad malum est apta, nam multi pravi viri optimas artes optime callent, nec tamen ideo sunt boni, virtus vero ad solum bonum tendit nec in malis habere locum potest. 3. Ars licet perficiat artificem, ista tamen perfectio magis respicit res artE constantes quam ipsos artifices. Virtus vero perficit cum solum in quo inest tanquam ejus perfectio
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter: He shows that virtue is concerned with the mean by two arguments. The first is from the less to the greater. All arts that wish to bring their work to perfection seek some mean. Therefore, much more so the art that is more excellent, namely virtue, seeks some mean, but not the mean of the thing, rather the mean of reason, or relative to us. The antecedent is proved by the common proverb that those things are called perfect and good to which nothing can be added or taken away. For example, in the shoemaker's art, the best shoes are those that fit the foot most exactly, neither wider nor tighter than the foot for which they must be suited. Likewise in painting, a picture is called perfect when no line can be added to complete its perfection, and nothing can be taken away without detracting from its perfection. Therefore this perfection is concerned with the middle, or mean, because it rejects the greater and the less, that is, excess and deficiency. But virtue is more excellent than art, and this can be shown in four ways. (1) In the arts knowledge alone is required, but in the actions of the virtues choice and constancy are also required, as was said above in chapter 4. (2) Arts are suited both to good and to evil, for many wicked men are very skilled in the best arts, and yet they are not therefore good. Virtue, however, aims only at the good and cannot have a place in evil. (3) Art, although it perfects the artist, nevertheless this perfection regards the things that are constant in art more than the artists themselves. Virtue, however, perfects the very one in whom it inheres, as its perfection.

units.la: 4. Artes omnes virtuti inserviunt, verbi gratia: Sartoria ars vestes præbet, quibus modeste & decore vestiamur: Ars coquinaria cibos parat, quibus temperanter vescamur, omnia denique opera & commercia materia sunt justitiæ, proinde cum artes sint ancillæ virtutis, virtutem arte longè præstantiorem esse constat.
units.tr: (4) All the arts serve virtue. For example, the tailor's art provides clothing with which we dress modestly and becomingly; the art of cookery prepares food with which we eat temperately. In short, all works and dealings are the matter of justice. Therefore, since the arts are the handmaids of virtue, it is clear that virtue is far more excellent than art.

units.la: Sed ne quis putet Philosophum aliam hic intelligere virtutem, quam moralem addit: dico autem moralem virtutem, nam virtus moralis versatur circa affectus & actiones hominis, ut supra cap. 3. dictum erat. In affectibus vero & actionibus liceet reperire majus, minus, & mediocre, verbi gratia: in affectibus poterit aliquis timere majus aut minus, quam oportet, poterit etiam quando & quantum oportet, & sic mediocriter in isto timore afficietur. In actionibus etiam poterit aliquid dari majus aut minus, poterit etiam mediocritas dari: at vero virtus intellectualis quales sunt illæ: Intellectus, Scientia, Sapientia, maximè non tam circa mediocritatem, quo ad nos versantur, quam circa medium rei, quia sunt ipsæ retu perfectiones in summo gradu, & quia res Theoricæ, circa quas virtus intellectualis versatur, nullam admittunt mediocritatem, ideo nec ipsa intellectualis virtus: nam quo quis accuratius & diligentius circa has res elaboraverit, tanto erit præstantior, verbi gratia: in Mathematicis nullum reperire licet modum subtilitatis ultimum, sic & in Physicis & Metaphysicis.
units.tr: But lest anyone think that the Philosopher here understands a virtue other than moral virtue, he adds: I mean moral virtue. For moral virtue is concerned with the affections and actions of man, as was said above in chapter 3. In affections and actions one can find the greater, the less, and the mean. For example, in the affections a person may fear more than he ought, or less, but he may also fear when and as much as he ought, and so he will be moderately affected in that fear. In actions too something may be done more or less, and the mean may be found. But the intellectual virtues, such as understanding, knowledge and wisdom, are not chiefly concerned with the mean relative to us, but with the mean of the thing, because they are themselves perfections of things at the highest degree, and because the theoretical subjects with which the intellectual virtue is concerned admit no mean; therefore the intellectual virtue itself admits none either. For the more accurately and diligently a man has worked on these subjects, the more excellent he will be. For example, in mathematics one cannot find any ultimate limit of subtlety; so too in physics and metaphysics.

units.la: Secunda ratio, qua probatur virtutem versari circa mediocritatem, est hæc, quod medium sit unum, extrema vero multa: Nam si virtus ponere ut retur in extremis, multis modis extaret seu recede-ret à sua perfectione, quod probatur autoritate Py-thagoricorum, qui dicebant, bonum esse finitum, malum vero infinitum, de quo supra lib. 1. c. 4. egimus, nam bonum & medium uno tantum fiunt modo, malum vero multis modis fit, quoties scilic. recedKitur à medio versus extrema. Idque illustrat similitudine sagittarum, qui multis modis possunt aberrare à scopo, uno tantum modo & recto attingere scopū, tandem concludit virtutem versari circa mediocritatem; vitium vero circa extrema. Divus Thomas circa hunc locum adfert tria argumenta, quod probet virtutem versari circa mediocritatem, nempe quod facta, ex quibus generatur virtus, & per quę conservatur, sint mediocria, ergo & ipsam versari circa mediocritatē necesse est, facta vero ex quibus constat, & quibus conservatur virtus, constat ex c. 2. huius lib.
units.tr: The second argument by which it is proved that virtue is concerned with the mean is this: the mean is one, but the extremes are many. For if virtue were to lie in the extremes, it would be in many ways outside its perfection, or would recede from it. This is proved by the authority of the Pythagoreans, who said that the good is finite but evil is infinite, which we discussed above in book 1, chapter 4. For the good and the mean are made in only one way, but evil is made in many ways, namely whenever one recedes from the mean towards the extremes. He illustrates this by the similarity of arrows: they can miss the target in many ways, but hit it straight in only one way. Finally he concludes that virtue is concerned with the mean, but vice with the extremes. St Thomas, on this passage, brings three arguments to prove that virtue is concerned with the mean: that the acts from which virtue is generated, and by which it is preserved, are moderate; therefore virtue itself must necessarily be concerned with the mean. The acts of which virtue consists, and by which it is preserved, are set out in the second chapter of this book.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Virtus id ipsum, cuius est virtus, bene affectum reddit, & praeparat ad omne bonum.
units.tr: 1. Virtue makes that very thing of which it is the virtue well disposed, and prepares it for every good.

units.la: 2. A virtute homo dicitur bonus, & secundum ea recte agit.
units.tr: 2. A man is called good from virtue, and acts rightly according to it.

units.la: 3. In omni re divisibili est major & minor & aequale.
units.tr: 3. In every divisible thing there is a greater, a lesser, and an equal.

units.la: 4. Aequale est medium inter excessum & defectum, tanquam sua extrema.
units.tr: 4. The equal is the mean between excess and deficiency, as their extremes.

units.la: 5. Omne medium est vel medium rei, vel medium rationis seu quo ad nos.
units.tr: 5. Every mean is either the mean of the thing, or the mean of reason, or relative to us.

units.la: 6. Medium rei est, quod aequaliter distat ab utroque extremorum, & est unum idemque apud omnes.
units.tr: 6. The mean of the thing is that which is equally distant from either of the extremes, and is one and the same for all.

units.la: 7. Medium rationis est quod neque deficit, neque abundat plus, quam oportet, & non est unum idemque apud omnes.
units.tr: 7. The mean of reason is that which neither falls short nor exceeds more than it ought, and is not one and the same for all.

units.la: 8. Medium rei vulgò dicitur Arithmeticum, medium rationis dicitur Geometricum.
units.tr: 8. The mean of the thing is commonly called arithmetical; the mean of reason is called geometrical.

units.la: 9. Rebus perfectis nihil adimi nec addi potest, alias enim aut superflua aut imperfecta essent.
units.tr: 9. Nothing can be taken away from or added to perfect things, for otherwise they would be superfluous or imperfect.

units.la: 10. Virtus omnis est praestantior arte, cum hominem bonum, quod ars non facit, reddat.
units.tr: 10. Every virtue is more excellent than art, since it makes a man good, which art does not do.

units.la: 11. Errare licet multis modis, recte vero agere uno tantum modo.
units.tr: 11. One may err in many ways, but act rightly in only one way.

units.la: 12. Virtutis est mediocritas, vitii vero extremitas.
units.tr: 12. Mediocrity belongs to virtue, but extremity to vice.

units.la: 13. Recte agere difficile est; errare vero cuivis facile.
units.tr: 13. To act rightly is difficult; to err is easy for anyone.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur, sicut in omni re divisibili est majus, minus, & aequale, sic etiam in actibus & affectibus, qui sunt objecta virtutis, est majus, minus, & medium, cum omnis divisio pertineat ad Categoriam Quantitatis: Virtus vero & ea, circa quae virtus versatur, pertinet ad Categoriam Qualitatis, ideo nisi detur transitus de genere in genus, non possunt objecta virtutis dividi secundum majus, minus & aequale? Resp. Ex ipso Aristotele lib.2. Eud. cap.3. res sic dijudicari potest. Constat ex Physicis omnem motum esse in tempore. Constat itidem ex Logicis, tempus esse in Categoria Quantitatis. Ergo in quibus est motus, in iis etiam tempus, & proinde possunt dividi, si non ratione motus, ratione tamen temporis in quo est motus. Objecta vero virtutis esse motus hic constat: nam affectus sunt motus & impulsus animi, sicut supra c.5 probatum erat, actus etiam esse motus agentis civis facile patet.
units.tr: Question: How can it be said that, just as in every divisible thing there is a greater, a less and an equal, so too in acts and affections, which are the objects of virtue, there is a greater, a less and a mean? For all division belongs to the category of Quantity, whereas virtue, and what virtue is concerned with, belongs to the category of Quality. Unless there is a transition from one genus to another, the objects of virtue cannot be divided according to greater, less and equal. Answer: The matter can be settled from Aristotle himself, Eudemian Ethics book 2, chapter 3. It is established from the Physics that every motion is in time, and it is established from the Logic that time is in the category of Quantity. Therefore in those things in which there is motion, there is also time, and so they can be divided, if not by reason of the motion, then at least by reason of the time in which the motion occurs. That the objects of virtue are motions here is clear, for affections are motions and impulses of the soul, as was proved above in chapter 5. That acts too are motions of the agent is easily seen.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur ars versari circa medium, cum omnis ars versetur potius circa extremum: nam
units.tr: II. Question: How can it be said that art is concerned with the mean, when every art is rather concerned with the extreme, for

units.la: tum tam demum dicitur perfectus artifex, quando artis suae ultimum & perfectissimum gradum assecutus est? Resp. Ars versatur circa medium & extremum diversorespecta; versatur circa extremum perfectionis, versatur vero circa medium deviationis, & vulgo dicitur cum neque artifex, neque minus facit, quam artis suae praecepta requirunt. Sic enim arte factum non habet suam perfectionem, utpote cui aliquid potest addi, neque plus facit, sic enim artis suae perfectionem destruit, quia sic aliquid potest adimi.
units.tr: a craftsman is then said to be perfect only when he has attained the final and most perfect degree of his art? Answer: Art is concerned with the mean and with the extreme in different respects. It is concerned with the extreme of perfection, but it is concerned with the mean of deviation, and it is commonly said that the craftsman neither does more nor does less than his art's precepts require. For a thing made by art does not have its perfection if something can be added to it, nor if it does more, for in that way it destroys the perfection of its art, since something can then be taken away from it.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: POstquam investigavit genus virtutis & ex distinctione medii, ostendit virtutem in mediocritate versari, adfert hoc capite integram & completam definitionem virtutis. Partes capitis sunt duae: In prima definitionem ipsam affert. In secunda quosdam esse affectus & actus, in quibus nullam licet reperire mediocritatem, ostendit.
units.tr: Having investigated the genus of virtue, and having shown from the distinction of the mean that virtue lies in a mean, he now gives in this chapter a complete and full definition of virtue. The chapter has two parts. In the first he gives the definition itself. In the second he shows that there are certain affections and actions in which no mean can be found.

units.la: In prima igitur talem virtutis definitionem adfert. Virtus est habitus electivus in mediocritate consistens, quo ad nos, ratione definitus & sicut prudens definiret. Partes definitionis sunt genus & differentia, cujus singulae particulae sunt breviter sic explicandae. Dicitur in prima habitus, ut excludantur affectus & potentiae naturales, quae non sunt virtutes, cum a natura ingenerentur, ut supra cap. 5. ostensum erat, & de quibus lib. 6. cap. ult. fuius agit. Additur Electivus ad excludendas artes & scientias, in quibus non est proprie electio, sed ipsa potius ratio: nam sunt in ea anima parte, quae ratione praedita est, quia sunt virtutes. tutes intellectuales,utsupra cap.ult.lib. 1. ostensum erat. Electio vero est in appetitiva parte animæ,quæ per fe non est ratione prædita,ut in fra lib. 3.cap.4.ma-gis patebit. Excluduntur etiam,quæcunque temerè vel prave, non ex deliberato fiunt, in quibus nulla est electio. In mediocritate, additur hæc particula, ut excludatur vitia,quæ sunt habitus, & habitus etiam cum consilio & electione,sed tamen in extremis, id est,in excessu & defectu,non in medio posita. Additur,quo ad nos,ad tollendam ambiguitatem medii, quod supra distinxerat in medium rei, & medium quo ad nos.Definitus ratione,hæc particula mediocritatis definiendæ modum ostendit, nam tum demum habitus dicitur esse perfectus fecundum virtutem,cum in recta & bene affecta ratione fe prodit ille habitus. Et sicut prudens definiret, quia ratio est multiplex,hic ostendit,qualis nam ratio fit necessaria ad virtutem moralem producendam,nó illa quæ versatur in contemplatione, qualis est Mathematica aut Physica,in quibus etiam est ratio,sed longè alia& diversa ab hac,quæ requiritur ad moralem virtutem,nempe ratio viri prudentis: Nam prudentia per quam vir dicitur prudens, est sal & condimentum virtutum moralium,ut infra patebit lib.6.cap.pe-nult. hujus operis.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he gives this definition of virtue: Virtue is an elective habit, lying in a mean relative to us, defined by reason, and as the prudent man would define it. The parts of the definition are the genus and the differentia, and each of its particles should be briefly explained as follows. It says habit first, so as to exclude the natural affections and powers, which are not virtues because they are produced in us by nature, as was shown above in chapter 5, and of which he treats in the last chapter of Book 6. Elective is added to exclude the arts and sciences, in which there is strictly no choice but rather reason itself: for these lie in the part of the soul endowed with reason, since they are intellectual virtues, as was shown above in the last chapter of Book 1. Choice, however, lies in the appetitive part of the soul, which in itself is not endowed with reason, as will become clearer below in Book 3, chapter 4. Also excluded are all those things done rashly or wickedly, not from deliberation, in which there is no choice. In a mean is added so as to exclude vices, which are habits, and also habits formed with counsel and choice but placed at the extremes, that is, in excess or defect, and not in the mean. Relative to us is added to remove the ambiguity of the mean, which he had earlier distinguished into the mean of the thing and the mean relative to us. Defined by reason shows the manner in which the mean is to be defined: for a habit is then said to be perfect in respect of virtue only when that habit shows itself in a right and well-disposed reason. And as the prudent man would define it shows, since reason is of many kinds, what sort of reason is necessary for producing moral virtue: not that which is occupied with contemplation, such as mathematical or physical reason, in which there is also reason, but one very different from this, which is required for moral virtue, namely the reason of the prudent man. For prudence, through which a man is called prudent, is the salt and seasoning of the moral virtues, as will be shown below in Book 6, near the end of this work.

units.la: Allata jam definitione ostendit, inter quæ virtus fit mediocritas, nempe inter duo vitia, quorum alterum fit excessus,alterum defectus, & non est mediocritas inter actus & affectus, in quibus alter fit excessus, alter defectus, sed virtus versatur circa actus & affectus, in quibus vitia excedunt & deficiunt: ciunt: virtus vero in iis medium eligit & tenet. At objici poterat, Virtutem non esse in mediocritate sicut definitur, sed esse potius extremum quid: nam virtus est cujusque rei perfectio, & ea est virtutis vis & efficacia, ut secundum eam unumquodque munus suum recte exsequatur, ut supra ostensum erat initio cap. 6. Resp. Esse mediocritatem & esse extremum, sed dissimili ratione. Nam est mediocritas, si secundum naturam & definitionem spectetur. Est vero extremum, si secundum bonitatem consideretur: Nam ut virtus consideratur tanquam bonum quid, opponitur vitio seu malo, & sic dicitur extremum. Plutarchus vero in lib. de virtute morali paulo aliter solvit: Virtus, inquit, ratione quantitatis est mediocritas, nempe inter nimium & parum, ratione qualitatis, est extremitas, quia tunc ejus bonitas spectatur, & sic Theages Pythagoreus apud Stobaeum orat. 1. de virtute, hanc dubitationem quoque solvit, vide infra idem dubium.
units.tr: Having now given the definition, he shows between what a virtue becomes a mean, namely between two vices, one of which is excess and the other defect. And there is no mean between actions and affections in which one is excess and the other defect; rather, virtue is concerned with actions and affections in which vices exceed and fall short, and virtue chooses and holds the mean among them. But it could be objected: Virtue is not in a mean as it is defined, but is rather some kind of extreme. For virtue is the perfection of each thing, and it is the power and efficacy of virtue that each thing performs its function rightly according to it, as was shown at the beginning of chapter 6. Answer: it is both a mean and an extreme, but for different reasons. It is a mean if it is considered according to its nature and definition. It is an extreme if it is considered according to its goodness: for insofar as virtue is considered as some kind of good, it is opposed to vice or evil, and so it is called an extreme. Plutarch, however, in his book On Moral Virtue, solves the difficulty somewhat differently: virtue, he says, is a mean in respect of quantity, namely between too much and too little, but in respect of quality it is an extreme, because then its goodness is considered. Theages the Pythagorean, in Stobaeus, Oration 1, On Virtue, also solves this doubt in the same way; see below on the same question.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit, quosdam esse actus & affectus, qui nullam admittant mediocritatem: Nam etsi circa actus & affectus versetur virtus tanquam circa objectum suum, ut saepius diximus, frustra tamen in omnibus actibus & affectibus quaerit aliquis mediocritatem aut virtutem: & id probat tribus rationibus: 1. Ratio est haec, quia quidam sunt actus & affectus, qui simulac nominantur, cum vitio statim conjuncti sunt, & quia natura sunt pravi, & apud omnes pro malis habentur, ut sunt affectus ejusmodi, malevolentia, imprudentia: Actus ut furtum, stuprum, quia natura sua sunt pravi, in quibus semper delinquitur, nec quocunq; modo in iis egeris, reperire licet mediocritatem.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he shows that there are certain actions and affections which admit no mean. For although virtue is concerned with actions and affections as its object, as we have often said, nevertheless one seeks a mean or virtue in all actions and affections in vain. He proves this by three reasons: 1. The reason is this: there are certain actions and affections which, as soon as they are named, are at once joined with vice, and which, because they are wicked by nature and are regarded as bad by all, are of this kind: malevolence, shamelessness; actions such as theft and adultery, which are wicked in their nature, and in which one always does wrong, and in no way in which one may act in them can a mean be found.

units.la: Secunda ratio, qua idem probat, est hæc, sicut in excessibus & defectibus, qui sunt vitiosi habitus, non licet reperire mediocritatem, quia sunt ipsa extrema, sic etiam in quibusdam affectibus & actibus, nullam quoque reperire licet mediocritatem. Assumptum probatur inductione exemplorum, ut sunt injuria, timiditas, luxuria, quæ sunt oppositæ Justitiæ, Fortitudinis, Temperantiæ: In his nullam reperire licet mediocritatem, non quod virtus, quæ est media inter hæc vitia, non consistat in mediocritate, sed quia hæc extrema, quæ sunt in excessu & defectu, nullum admittere possunt medium: sic enim sequeretur hoc absurdum, nempe dari progressum in infinitum: nam illius excessus & defectus, in quo esset mediocritas, daretur alius excessus & defectus & illius alius, & sic usque in infinitum.
units.tr: The second reason, by which he proves the same thing, is this: just as in excesses and defects, which are vicious habits, no mean can be found, because they are themselves the extremes, so also in certain affections and actions no mean can be found. The assumption is proved by induction from examples, such as injustice, cowardice, and intemperance, which are opposed to justice, fortitude, and temperance. In these no mean can be found, not because the virtue which lies between these vices does not consist in a mean, but because these extremes, which are in excess and defect, can admit no mean between them. For otherwise this absurdity would follow, namely that there would be a progress to infinity: for there would be some excess and defect in which there would be a mean, and there would be another excess and defect of that, and another of that, and so on to infinity.

units.la: Tertia ratio, qua probat, in affectibus non dari mediocritatem, est hæc. Sicut in virtutib. non est excessus & defectus. Sic in quibusdam affectib. & actibus non est mediocritas, nam etsi virtus sit media inter excessum & defectum, nullum recipit tamen in se excessum & defectum, hic enim virtus amplius non esset virtus. At vero affectus sunt quidā, ut & actus ejusmodi sunt illi, quos supra nominavimus, in prima ratione, qui sunt natura adeo pravi, ut nullā recipere possint mediocritatem, quocunque se modo quis in iis gesserit. Quare ut excessus & defectus non recipiunt mediocritatem, sic neque mediocritas admittit excessum & defectum.
units.tr: The third reason, by which he proves that there is no mean in affections, is this. Just as there is no excess and defect in virtues, so in certain affections and actions there is no mean. For although virtue is a mean between excess and defect, it nevertheless admits no excess or defect in itself, for then it would no longer be virtue. But there are certain affections, and such actions too, which we named above in the first reason, which are so wicked by nature that they can admit no mean, however a man may conduct himself in them. Therefore, just as excess and defect do not admit a mean, so a mean does not admit excess and defect.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Virtus est habitus electivus in mediocritate consistens, quoad quoad nos, ratione definitum, & sicut prudens definiret,
units.tr: 1. Virtue is an elective habit consisting in a mean relative to us, defined by reason, and as the prudent man would define it.

units.la: 2. In affectibus & actibus circa quos virtus versatur tanquam objectum suum, virtus medium invenit & elegit.
units.tr: 2. In the affections and actions with which virtue is concerned as its object, virtue finds and chooses the mean.

units.la: 3. Virtus quoad naturam & essentiam suam est mediocritas, quoad perfectionem & excellentiam est extremitas.
units.tr: 3. Virtue, in its nature and essence, is a mean; in its perfection and excellence, it is an extreme.

units.la: 4. Quidam sunt affectus & actus adeo natura pravi, ut nullam admittant mediocritatem.
units.tr: 4. There are certain affections and actions so evil by nature that they admit of no mean.

units.la: 5. Sicut excessu & defectu daretur mediocritas, daretur progressus in infinitum.
units.tr: 5. If there were a mean by way of excess and defect, there would be a progress to infinity.

units.la: 6. Ut excessus & defectus non recipiunt mediocritatem, sic mediocritas non admittit excessum & defectum.
units.tr: 6. Just as excess and defect do not admit of a mean, so a mean does not admit of excess and defect.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur virtus, Habitus electivus, cum electio competat pueris & natura servis, teste ipso Aristotele. 1. Politic. cap. 3. At virtus iis non competit: Pueri enim per aetatem secundum virtutem agere non possunt: servi etiam, ea ratione, qua requiritur in prudente viro deliberantur? Resp. Duplicem esse electionem, alia est imperfecta & naturalis, quae competit servis & pueris, & de ea electione loquitur ibi Aristoteles loco citato: Alia est electio perfecta & moralis, per quam hic definitur virtus: Dein' non est absurdum, genus latius patere suo definito, nam hic virtus definitur per habitum electivum, tanquam genus, quod competit viciosis etiam habitibus, proinde non sequitur: cuicunque competit electio, eidem etiam competit virtus moralis.
units.tr: I. It is asked: How can virtue be called an elective habit, since election belongs to children and, by nature, to slaves, as Aristotle himself testifies, Politics book 1, chapter 3? For virtue does not belong to them: children, because of their age, cannot act according to virtue, and slaves, in the way required of a prudent man, do not deliberate. Answer: election is of two kinds. One is imperfect and natural, which belongs to slaves and children, and it is of this election that Aristotle speaks in the place cited. The other is perfect and moral, and it is by this that virtue is defined here. Next, it is not absurd for a genus to extend more widely than its defined species: for here virtue is defined through an elective habit as its genus, and this genus also belongs to vicious habits. Therefore it does not follow that whatever has election also has moral virtue.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo dicatur virtus habitus in mediocritate,cum virtus sit media inter vitia, ut habetur in textu,at nullum medium in vitiis dari potest,nam vitia sunt infinita, ut suprapatuit ex sententia Pythagoraorum subfi-nem cap. 6. hujus libri. In infinitis non poteris certum sta-tuere medium, quia nescis, ubi sit finis, proinde virtus non poterit esse habitus in mediocritate? Resp. Media esse duorum generum, alia sunt media per participationem extremorum & in ejusmodi mediis si extrema sint infinita, difficile est medium aliquod certum statuere. 2. Alia sunt media per abnegationem extremorum, & sic virtus est media inter duo vitia per abnegationem,non per participationem: nam sive vitia sint finita vel infinita, medium invenire poteris recedendo & abnegando ista vitia tanquam extrema.
units.tr: II. It is asked: How can virtue be called a habit consisting in a mean, since virtue is a mean between vices, as stated in the text, when no mean can be found among vices, for vices are infinite, as was shown above from the opinion of the Pythagoreans near the end of chapter 6 of this book? In infinites you cannot fix a definite mean, because you do not know where the end is; therefore virtue cannot be a habit in a mean. Answer: there are two kinds of mean. Some are means by participation in the extremes, and in such means, if the extremes are infinite, it is difficult to fix any definite mean. Others are means by abnegation of the extremes, and in this way virtue is a mean between two vices by abnegation, not by participation. For whether the vices are finite or infinite, you can find the mean by withdrawing from those vices as extremes and denying them.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo definiatur virtus habitus in mediocritate consistens,quoad nos, cum hoc modo justitia commutativa non esset virtus, non enim ei definitio virtutis competeret: nam non consistit in mediocritate quoad nos,sed in medio rei, teste ipso Aristotele lib. 5. cap. 4. hujus operis? Resp. In justitia commutativa duo considerari. Primo: Rem circa quam versatur (nam in rerum commutatione & in venditione & emptione & cæteris versatur) & sic dicitur versari circa medium rei, ratione objecti sui scilicet. Secundo: Commensurationem rei, quæ dependet non à natura rei ipsius, sed ab opinione & judicio hominum, & sic justitia commutativa non minus dicitur versari in mediocritate quoad nos, quam reliquæ virtutes: nam versatur circa rem ipsam,tanquam objectum,circa quod agit, git, sed non in natura rei suam naturam & essentiam habet; Sed in commensuratione rei, quae dependet à judicio hominum.
units.tr: III. It is asked: How is virtue defined as a habit consisting in a mean relative to us, when in this way commutative justice would not be a virtue, since the definition of virtue would not fit it: for it does not consist in a mean relative to us, but in the mean of the thing, as Aristotle himself testifies in book 5, chapter 4 of this work? Answer: two things must be considered in commutative justice. First, the thing with which it is concerned (for it is concerned with the exchange of goods, with selling and buying and the like), and in this sense it is said to be concerned with the mean of the thing, namely by reason of its object. Second, the commensuration of the thing, which depends not on the nature of the thing itself but on the opinion and judgment of men; and in this sense commutative justice is no less said to be concerned with a mean relative to us than the other virtues are. For it is concerned with the thing itself as its object, about which it acts, but the thing does not have its nature and essence in the commensuration, which depends on the judgment of men.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: SEquitur tertius tractatus huius libri, in quo, postquam ostendit originem virtutis, & naturam per definitionem explicavit, dividit virtutem in varias species & unicuique nomen assignat: Hujus tertii tractatus membra sunt tria: In primo dividit virtutem, tanquam genus in suas species, In secundo ostendit oppositionem inter virtutem & vitia, & vitiorum inter se. In tertio, modos nonnullos & regulas proponit, quibus possimus virtutem acquirere aut invenire. Primum membrum continetur hoc capite cujus tres sunt partes. In prima proponit intentionem suam, quod nimirum actarus sit de virtutibus singulatim. In secunda brevem ac rudem catalogum virtutum affert, ut postea fusius & expeditius de singulis agere possit, & iste catalogus continet divisionem virtutis in suas species. In tertia in affectibus quibusdam dari mediocritatem & extrema, ostendit.
units.tr: Here follows the third treatise of this book. Having shown the origin of virtue and explained its nature by definition, Aristotle now divides virtue into its various species and assigns a name to each. This third treatise has three parts. In the first he divides virtue, as a genus, into its species. In the second he shows the opposition between virtue and vice, and among the vices themselves. In the third he sets out some modes and rules by which we may acquire or find virtue. The first part is contained in this chapter, which has three sections. In the first he states his purpose, namely that he will treat of the virtues one by one. In the second he gives a brief and rough catalogue of the virtues, so that he may later deal with each more fully and efficiently; this catalogue contains the division of virtue into its species. In the third he shows that in certain affections there is a mean and extremes.

units.la: In prima igitur dicit non satis esse assignare definitionem virtutis in genere, sed opus est descendere ad singulas virtutes in specie, verbi gratia: Si declarabitur temperantiam esse virtutem in mediocritate consistentem, & fortitudinem & justitiam & liberalitatem, hinc merito colligetur, omnem virtutem consistere in mediocritate, & rationem affert, cur de singulis virtutibus agere debeat, quia universalium tractatio est minus certa: nā est remotior à sensib. speciali ū vero tractatio est magis certa, quia incurrit in sensus, & hominibus, qui ex actionib. singularib. virtutes cognoscere solent, magis satisfacit.
units.tr: In the first section he says it is not enough to give a definition of virtue in general; we must descend to the individual virtues in particular. For example, if it is declared that temperance, courage, justice and liberality are each a virtue consisting in a mean, it will rightly be concluded that every virtue consists in a mean. He gives the reason why he must treat of each virtue separately: the treatment of universals is less certain, since they are more remote from the senses, whereas the treatment of particulars is more certain, because it falls under the senses and better satisfies people, who usually recognise virtues from particular actions.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis, Catalogum adfert singularem virtutum, & cum singulis virtutibus affert etiam extrema inter quae versatur. Virtutes hae triplicem dividi possunt, vel enim versantur circa affectus internos, vel circa res externas, vel circa actus externos, & primo affert eas virtutes cum suis extremis, quae versantur circa affectus. Primo loco occurrit Fortitudo, quae versatur circa timorem & audaciam: Ipsa Fortitudo est mediocritas, extrema in excessu sunt intimiditas & audacia, in defectu est ignavia. Secundo loco est Temperantia, quae versatur circa voluptatem & dolorem, sed magis circa voluptatem, quam dolorem. Ipsa Temperantia est virtus, quae consistit in mediocritate, extremum in excessu dicitur Intemperantia. In defectu extremum proprio carer nomine, sed tamen vulgo vocatur insensibilitas. Tertio occurrit quaedam virtus, quae versatur circa iram, mediocritas dicitur mansuetudo, extremum in excessu dicitur iracundia: In defectu iniracundia. Secundo loco tradun-tur illae virtutes, quae versantur circa res externas, ut circa pecunias dandas accipiendasque, horum duo adfert exempla, Liberalitatem & Magnificentiam, liberalitatis extremum, in excessu est prodigalitas, in defectu avaritia. Magnificentia versatur circa res dandas accipiendasque, sed magnos sumptus requirit, & differt ab ipsa liberalitate, quod sit summus & excellentissimus quasi gradus in rebus dandis & accipienpiendis. Ipsa virtus dicitur Magnificentia, extremum in excessu sordiditas aut luxus circa decorem, in defectu Modicitas. Tertio loco adfert eas virtutes, quæ versantur circa actus externos, & primò occurrunt Magnanimitas, quæ versatur circa honores magnos, extremum in excessu dicitur Elatio aut inflatio, in defectu Pusillanimitas. Circa honores mediocres, qui privatis etiam hominibus contingere possunt, versatur quædam virtus, sed proprio caret nomine, extremum in excessu dicitur Ambitio in secularibus: In Ecclesiasticis dicitur Simonia. Extremum in defectu suo quoque caret nomine, sed qui est in defectu, dicitur vacuus ambitione, aut simonia: Medium quia proprio nomine destituitur, appellatur interdum nominibus extremorum. Postea adfert Philosophus tres virtutes, quæ in hoc conveniunt omnes, quod circa communionem verborum & actuum versentur, differunt tamen ratione certæ materiæ quam tractant: Prima est in verbis, quæ seriò dicuntur, & dicitur Veritas in verbis. Extrema possunt uno nomine appellari, fictio, sed extremum in excessu dicitur Arrogantia, in defectu dissimulatio. Secunda virtus versatur circa jocundum in verbis, quibus in jocunda conversatione uti solemus, sed circa jocundum minus artificiosum ipsa virtus dicitur comitas: Extremum in excessu dicitur scurrilitas, in defectu rusticitas. Tertia etiam virtus versatur circa jocundum, sed magis artificiosum. Ipsa virtus dicitur Amicitia, non quod sit proprie dicta amicitia, sed quia proprio nomine destituitur, poterit tamen amicitia vocari, quasi apta & jocunda aptabilitas ad
units.tr: In the second section of the chapter he gives a particular catalogue of the virtues, and with each virtue he also gives the extremes between which it lies. These virtues may be divided into three kinds: they are concerned either with inner affections, or with external things, or with external actions. He first gives those virtues that concern the affections, together with their extremes. In the first place comes courage, which concerns fear and boldness. Courage itself is the mean; the extreme in excess is rashness and recklessness, and the extreme in defect is cowardice. In the second place is temperance, which concerns pleasure and pain, but more pleasure than pain. Temperance itself is a virtue that consists in a mean; the extreme in excess is called intemperance. The extreme in defect has no proper name of its own, but is commonly called insensibility. Third, there is a certain virtue which concerns anger; the mean is called mildness, the extreme in excess is called irascibility, and in defect unirascibility. In the second group are those virtues that concern external things, such as giving and receiving money. He gives two examples of these: liberality and magnificence. The extreme of liberality in excess is prodigality, and in defect avarice. Magnificence concerns the giving and receiving of things, but it requires great expense, and it differs from liberality in that it is a kind of highest and most excellent degree in giving and receiving. The virtue itself is called magnificence; the extreme in excess is vulgarity or luxury with regard to display, and in defect meanness. Third, he gives those virtues that concern external actions. First come magnanimity, which concerns great honours; its extreme in excess is called vainglory or conceit, and in defect pusillanimity. Concerning ordinary honours, which can also fall to private persons, there is a certain virtue which has no proper name of its own; its extreme in excess is called ambition in secular matters, and simony in ecclesiastical ones. Its extreme in defect also lacks a name, but the person who is deficient is called one free of ambition or of simony. Since the mean lacks a proper name, it is sometimes called by the names of the extremes. Afterwards the Philosopher gives three virtues, which all agree in this, that they concern the communication of words and deeds, yet differ in terms of the particular matter they treat. The first is in words that are spoken seriously, and it is called truthfulness in words. Its extremes may be called by one name, pretence; but the extreme in excess is called boastfulness, and in defect dissimulation. The second virtue concerns playfulness in words, such as we are accustomed to use in pleasant conversation; but the virtue concerning playfulness that is less artful is called good humour. Its extreme in excess is called buffoonery, and in defect boorishness. The third virtue also concerns playfulness, but of a more artful kind. The virtue itself is called friendliness; not that it is friendship properly so called, but because it lacks a proper name of its own, it may nevertheless be called friendship, as a fitting and pleasant aptness for winning people over.

units.la: P demulcendos homines extrema in excessu sunt assentatio & adulatio, quæ hoc modo differunt, quod assentatio sit nullius emolumenti gratia, adulatio vero si alicujus commodi gratia aut publici aut privati. Extremum in defectu dicitur morositas.
units.tr: To win people over, the extremes in excess are obsequiousness and flattery. These differ in this way: obsequiousness is practised for no advantage, whereas flattery is practised for some benefit, either public or private. The extreme in defect is called surliness.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis, postquam recensuit plurimarum virtutum cum suis extremis catalogum, ostendit in quibusdam aliis dari mediocritatem, quod ideo affert, non quod aliis sint virtutes aut habitus, ut supra probatum est, cap. 5. sed ut ostendat in omnibus rebus laudandam esse mediocritatem, extrema vero esse vituperanda, exempla 2. adfert 1. verecundia est affectus, qui consistit in mediocritate, extremum ejus in excessu est impaviditas, in defectu est impudentia. Sic indignatio est affectus & versatur circa voluptatem & dolorem ex iis rebus perceptum, quæ indigne fiunt: est mediocritas etiam inter duo extrema: Extremum ejus in excessu est invidentia, quæ est ægritudo concepta ex alienis rebus secundis, sive digne fiant sive indigne. Extremum in defectu est malevolentia, quæ est voluptas concepta ex malo alterius. Tandem excusat se quod de justitia non egerit in hoc catalogo, sicut etiam de virtutibus intellectualibus, nam quia justitia est duplex, alia est distributiva alia commutativa, & quia alia erat ratio medii, alia extremorum in commutativa alia in distributiva, ideo commode hic agere non poterat de justitia, sed infra fuse & accurate aget, toto lib. 5 de virtutib. vero intellectualibus lib. 6.
units.tr: In the third section of the chapter, after reviewing the catalogue of very many virtues with their extremes, he shows that in certain other matters there is also a mean. He offers this not because these are virtues or habits, as has been proved above, ch. 5., but to show that a mean is to be praised in all things, while the extremes are to be blamed. He gives two examples. The first: shame is an affection that consists in a mean; its extreme in excess is shamelessness of the wrong sort, and in defect impudence. Likewise indignation is an affection that concerns the pleasure and pain conceived from those things that are done undeservedly; it too is a mean between two extremes. Its extreme in excess is envy, which is grief conceived at the good fortune of others, whether they deserve it or not. The extreme in defect is malevolence, which is pleasure conceived at another's misfortune. Finally, he excuses himself for not treating justice in this catalogue, as also for not treating the intellectual virtues. For justice is twofold: one kind is distributive, the other commutative; and since the principle of the mean is one in commutative justice and another in distributive, it was not convenient to deal with justice here. He will treat it fully and accurately below, in the whole of the fifth book; the intellectual virtues he will treat in the sixth book.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Res practicæ versantur circa singularia, in actu scilicet, non in habitu. 2.
units.tr: 1. Practical matters are concerned with singulars, namely in act, not in habit.

units.la: 2. Quia non sunt tot nomina, quot sunt res, perspicuitatis gratia licet nomen affingere.
units.tr: 2. Because there are not as many names as there are things, a name may be added for the sake of clarity.

units.la: 3. Mediocritas in rebus omnibus est laudanda, extrema vero vituperanda.
units.tr: 3. Moderation is to be praised in all things, but the extremes are to be blamed.

units.la: 4. Qui dolorem concipit ex alieno rebus secundis, invidus est, qui vero voluptatem ex malo alterius, malevolus est.
units.tr: 4. He who feels pain at the good fortune of another is envious; but he who takes pleasure in another's misfortune is malevolent.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Quomodo hic dicatur initio capitis; singularia esse certiora & majorem habere certitudinem ipsis universalibus, cum tamen cap. 2. hujus libri contrarium asseruerit: Dixit enim si in universalibus nulla sit certitudo, multo minus quærenda erit certitudo in singularibus? Respond. Universalia considerantur duobus modis, vel respectu naturæ suæ vel respectu subjecti in quo insunt. Universalia respectu naturæ suæ majorem habent certitudinem singularibus, quia habent naturam certam & determinatam, qua possunt definiri, at vero respectu subjecti cui insunt nullam habent certitudinem nisi à suis singularibus, verbi gratia: Universales actiones practicæ, quæ insunt homini tanquam subjecto suo, tum demum virtutem & certitudinem habere dicuntur, cum homo in singularibus (quæ sensibus subjiciuntur, propter circumstantias loci, temporis & personarum) & certo evenire probat. De universalibus in sua natura loquitur Philosophus, supra cap. 2. hic de universalibus cum respectu ad subjectum, & sic nulla est contradictio.
units.tr: I. It is asked: how can it be said at the beginning of this chapter that singulars are more certain and have greater certainty than the universals themselves, when in chapter 2 of this book the opposite is asserted, for it says: "if there is no certainty in universals, much less is certainty to be sought in singulars"? Answer: Universals may be considered in two ways, either with respect to their own nature or with respect to the subject in which they inhere. Universals with respect to their own nature have greater certainty than singulars, because they have a fixed and determinate nature by which they can be defined. With respect to the subject in which they inhere, however, they have no certainty except from their singulars. For example, universal practical actions, which inhere in man as their subject, are said to have virtue and certainty only when man proves that they occur with certainty in singulars, which fall under the senses and are determined by the circumstances of place, time and persons. The Philosopher speaks of universals in their nature in chapter 2 above; here he speaks of universals with respect to their subject, and so there is no contradiction.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat in affectibus reperiri mediocritatem & extrema; & proinde vel laudari vel vituperari perari affectus cum supra cap. 5 strenue laudarit? Resp. Affectus quidem perse nullam habent mediocritatē, neque extrema, & proinde neque laudantur vel vituperantur, & sic de iis egit supra cap. 5. At vero si consiederentur affectus cum modo vel extra modū, tunc propter modum erunt laudabiles, quia diriguntur secundum rectam rationem, & proinde consistunt in mediocritate: At vero si considerentur extra modum, quatenus repugnant rectæ rationi, dicuntur jam vituperabiles & esse in extremis.
units.tr: II. It is asked: how does he say that mediocrity and extremes are found in the affections, and that the affections are therefore praised or blamed, when above in chapter 5 he vigorously praised them? Answer: Affections in themselves have neither mediocrity nor extremes, and therefore are neither praised nor blamed, and this is how he treated them above in chapter 5. But if the affections are considered with measure or beyond measure, then on account of the measure they are praiseworthy, because they are directed according to right reason and therefore consist in mediocrity. If, however, they are considered beyond measure, insofar as they conflict with right reason, they are now blameworthy and are in the extremes.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: SEquitur secundum membrum hujus tractatus, in quo Philosophus ostendit oppositionem inter virtutem & extrema, tum etiam extremorum inter se. Partes hujus capitis sunt tres. In prima ostendit virtutem tanquam mediocritatem opponi duobus extremis. In secunda extrema magis inter se contrariari, quam ipsi virtuti. In tertia virtutem magis contrariari uni extremorum quam alteri.
units.tr: Follows the second member of this treatise, in which the Philosopher shows the opposition between virtue and the extremes, and also of the extremes among themselves. The parts of this chapter are three. In the first he shows that virtue, as a mean, is opposed to the two extremes. In the second the extremes are more contrary to one another than to virtue itself. In the third virtue is more contrary to one of the extremes than to the other.

units.la: In prima igitur parte docet virtutem opponi extremis diverso respectu, quod probat à simili, nam sicut æquale est magis, si conferatur cum minus æquali, sed minus est, si conferatur cum magis æquali. Sic virtus, si conferatur cum defectu, contrariatur ei, ut excessus, si veó conferatur cum excessu, contrariatur ei, ut defectus, quod illustrat duobus exemplis: nam fortis si conferatur cum timido, est audax, si vero cum audaci, est timidus. Sic temperans collatus cum stupido videtur intemperans, at collatus cum intemperanti videtur contra stupidus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he teaches that virtue is opposed to the extremes in different respects. He proves this from a like case: just as the equal is greater when compared with the lesser, but lesser when compared with the greater, so virtue, when compared with the deficiency, is contrary to it as the excess is, and when compared with the excess, is contrary to it as the deficiency is. He illustrates this with two examples: the brave man, compared with the coward, is rash, but compared with the rash man, is cowardly. So the temperate man, compared with the insensible man, seems intemperate, but compared with the intemperate man, seems insensible.

units.la: Notandum verò virtutem considerari duobus modis. 1. Ut est mediocritas, alio modo, ut est bonum quid. Ut est mediocritas, opponitur duobus extremis, quorum unum est in excessu, alterum in defectu. Ut virtus est bonum quid, opponitur duobus illis extremis simul sumtis sub nomine mali, & sic opponitur ut bonum malo. Hic cum dicitur virtutem opponi duobus extremis, consideratur ut mediocritas, sic etiam cum extrema dicuntur inter se contrariari, non contrariantur, qua sunt vitia aut mala, sed qua sunt excessus & defectus.
units.tr: It must be noted that virtue is considered in two ways. (1) As a mean, and in another way, as some good. As a mean, it is opposed to the two extremes, one of which lies in excess and the other in deficiency. As virtue is a good, it is opposed to those two extremes taken together under the name of evil, and so it is opposed as good to evil. When it is said here that virtue is opposed to the two extremes, it is considered as a mean; likewise, when the extremes are said to be contrary to one another, they are not contrary as vices or evils, but as excess and deficiency.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit, extrema magis inter se contrariari quam ipsi virtuti duabus de causis: 1. Propter distantiam extremorum inter se: Nam extrema inter se longius distant, quam ab ipso medio, quod probat a simili, sicut magnum & parvum longius inter se distant, quam medium utriusque, sic etiam extrema inter se, & proinde sunt maxime inter se contraria, & ratio est, quia contraria definiuntur, quae sub eodem genere posita, maxime inter se distant. Secunda ratio, quia major est dissimilitudo extremorum inter se, quam cum ipso medio; nam medium quandam habet similitudinem cum extremis: nam interdum participat de natura defectus, & interdum de natura excessus, ut infra patebit, & citius pervenient ad medium ab alterutro extremorum, quam ab uno extremorum ad alterum.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he shows that the extremes are more contrary to one another than to virtue itself, for two reasons. (1) On account of the distance between the extremes themselves. For the extremes are farther apart from each other than from the mean itself. He proves this by a like case: just as the great and the small are farther apart than the mean between them, so too the extremes are farthest apart from one another, and therefore are most contrary. The reason is that contraries are defined as those which, placed under the same genus, are farthest apart. The second reason is that the dissimilarity of the extremes to each other is greater than their dissimilarity to the mean itself. For the mean has some likeness to the extremes: at times it shares in the nature of the deficiency, and at times in the nature of the excess, as will appear below. Also, one arrives at the mean from either extreme more quickly than one passes from one extreme to the other.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis ostendit virtutem uni extremorum magis contrariari, quam alteri, nam interdum excessus magis contrariatur medio, quam defectus, verbi gratia: Intemperantia magis contrariatur riatur temperantiæ quam stupiditas, interdum vero defectus magis contrariatur medio, quam excessus. Ut avaritia magis contrariatur liberalitati quam profusio, & id evenire decet, propter duas rationes, quarum 1. sumitur ex parte rei, altera ex parte nostri. Ex parte rei, quod est dissimilimum medio, id est, magis est contrarium medio, verbi gratia: Avaritia est dissimilior liberalitati, quam prodigalitas aut profusio, nam prodigalitas sicut & liberalitas consistit maximè in dando, avaritia verò maximè in retinendo & parcendo, sic etiam stupiditas, quoad rem est similior temperantiæ, quam intemperantiæ: Nam stupiditas sicut temperantia consistit in abstinenda, intemperantia verò in fruendo & percipienda voluptate. Secunda ratio, quæ ducitur ex parte nostri, est ad quod natura sumus proclivիores, id est maximè contrarium medio, verbi gratia: Quia natura trahimur ad voluptatem, incontinentia est magis contraria continentiæ, quia est cum voluptate conjuncta, in quam sumus natura proclives, quam est ipsa stupiditas. Notandum verò per naturam hic intelligere Philosophum naturam appetitus sensitivi, nam appetitus sensitivus est sua natura irrationalis, & nutu suo ad id semper fertur, quod rationi repugnat, nempe ad voluptatem illicitam, & id quod est sensui jucundum: At verò virtus quæ consistit in medio, est semper cum recta ratione conjuncta: Proinde ad quod natura magis impellimur, natura inquam appetitus sensitivi, id est virtuti maximè contrarium.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he shows that virtue is more contrary to one extreme than to the other. For at times the excess is more contrary to the mean than the deficiency is; for example, intemperance is more contrary to temperance than insensibility is. At other times the deficiency is more contrary to the mean than the excess is; for example, avarice is more contrary to liberality than prodigality is. And it is fitting that this should happen, for two reasons, of which the first is taken from the side of the thing and the second from our side. On the side of the thing: what is most unlike the mean is most contrary to it. For example, avarice is more unlike liberality than prodigality or profusion is, since prodigality, like liberality, consists chiefly in giving, whereas avarice consists chiefly in keeping back and sparing. So too insensibility, as far as the thing itself goes, is more like temperance than intemperance is: for insensibility, like temperance, consists in abstaining, whereas intemperance consists in enjoying and taking in pleasure. The second reason, which is drawn from our side, is that to which we are more naturally inclined is most contrary to the mean. For example, since we are drawn by nature to pleasure, incontinence is more contrary to continence than insensibility itself is, because incontinence is joined with pleasure, toward which we are naturally inclined. It must be noted that by "nature" here the Philosopher understands the nature of the sensitive appetite. For the sensitive appetite is by its nature irrational, and by its own impulse is always carried toward what opposes reason, namely unlawful pleasure and what is agreeable to the senses. But virtue, which consists in the mean, is always joined with right reason. Therefore, that to which we are more strongly impelled by nature, namely by the nature of the sensitive appetite, is most contrary to virtue.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Virtus opponitur suis extremis, & extrema sibi invicem.
units.tr: 1. Virtue is opposed to its extremes, and the extremes to one another.

units.la: 2. Vitia
units.tr: 2. Vices

units.la: 2. Virtus ratione defectus, videtur excessus, ratione excessus, videtur defectus.
units.tr: 2. Virtue, by reason of deficiency, seems to be excess; by reason of excess, seems to be deficiency.

units.la: 3. Extrema quae sunt excessus & defectus, sibi invicem contrariantur magis quam ipsi virtuti.
units.tr: 3. The extremes, which are excess and deficiency, are contrary to one another more than they are to virtue itself.

units.la: 4. Virtus uni extremorum magis contrariatur quam alteri, propter naturam extremorum longe dissitam.
units.tr: 4. Virtue is more contrary to one extreme than to the other, on account of the nature of the extremes, which lie far apart.

units.la: 5. Quod est dissimilius medio & ad quod natura magis impellimur, id est medio maxime contrarium.
units.tr: 5. That which is more unlike the mean, and to which nature impels us more, is most contrary to the mean.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: Difficulties.

units.la: 1. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur virtutem contrariari duobus extremis, cum, ut ex Topicis patet, unum uni tantum contrarietur: nam cum contraria sint causa sibi invicem corruptionis, natura saepe fecit, ut unum tantum uni contrarietur, quo magis unumquodque conservaretur? Resp. Verum illud est unum uni tantum contrariari proprie, virtus enim, non proprie contrariatur duobus extremis, sed dum contrariatur ut medio oritur, naturam plane obtinet diversam a suis extremis, unde quodammodo dicitur illis contrariari: At vero si consideratur ut bonum quid, iis contrariatur (scilicet extremis) proprie, quatenus nimirum extrema considerantur sub natura unius mali, & alterum alteri contrariatur, ut malum bono.
units.tr: 1. The question is asked: How can virtue be said to be contrary to both extremes, when, as is clear from the Topics, one thing is contrary to only one other? For since contraries are the cause of each other's destruction, has not nature often arranged that one thing is contrary to only one other, so that each may be better preserved? Answer: It is true that properly one thing is contrary to only one other. Virtue, then, is not properly contrary to both extremes. But insofar as it is contrary to them as the mean, it arises from them and takes on a nature plainly different from theirs, and so in a certain way it is said to be contrary to them. Yet if virtue is considered as a certain good, it is properly contrary to the extremes (namely, to them), in so far as the extremes are considered under the nature of a single evil, and the one is contrary to the other as evil is to good.

units.la: 11. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur extrema magis interse contrariari, quam ipsi virtuti, nam cum extrema sint vitia, inter se non contrariantur, quia in hoc conveniunt, quod sint mala? Resp. Extrema quae sunt vitia, inter se non contrariantur, sed sub uno nomine mali ipsi virtuti opponuntur: At vero ratione distantiae, tum etiam dissimidissimilitudinis: nam inter se longissime distant, & sunt inter se difficillima, propterea inter se contrariantur, & magis quidem quam ipsi virtuti: nam nec tantum a virtute distant, quantum a se invicem, nec sunt tam dissimilia virtuti, quam sunt excessus & defectus, quam sunt sibi invicem.
units.tr: II. The question is asked: How can the extremes be said to be more contrary to each other than they are to virtue itself? For since the extremes are vices, they are not contrary to each other, because they agree in this, that they are evils? Answer: The extremes, which are vices, are not contrary to each other, but they are opposed to virtue under the one name of evil. Yet they are contrary to each other by reason of distance, and also of dissimilarity: for they are very far apart from each other and are most unlike each other. Therefore they are contrary to each other, and indeed more so than they are to virtue itself. For they are not as far from virtue as they are from each other, nor are they as unlike virtue as excess and defect are unlike each other.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo dicatur virtus uni extremorum magis contrariari, quam alteri: nam virtus est medium, medium vero, cum medio se modo habeat inter sua extrema, non potest uni magis esse contrarium, quam alteri? Resp. Medium esse duplex ut supra patet, aliud rei, quod medio se modo habet in sua extrema, aliud rationis medium, quod etsi medium dicatur inter duo extrema, tamen non æqualiter ab iis distat, sed subinde variatur pro ratione viri prudentis. Proinde argumentum procedere de medio rei, non vero de medio rationis, in quo consistit virtus, diximus.
units.tr: III. The question is asked: How can virtue be said to be more contrary to one of the extremes than to the other? For virtue is the mean, and the mean, since it stands between its extremes, cannot be more contrary to one than to the other? Answer: The mean is of two kinds, as stated above: one is the mean of a thing, which stands between its extremes in the way described; the other is the mean of reason, which, although it is called a mean between two extremes, is not equally distant from them, but varies from time to time according to the judgment of the prudent person. Therefore, as we have said, the argument proceeds from the mean of the thing, not from the mean of reason, in which virtue consists.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: SEquitur tertium & ultimum membrum hujus ultimi tractatus, in quo Philosophus modes nonnullos ostendit ad regulas, quibus possimus nobis medium acquirere. Partes hujus capitis sunt tres. In prima ostendit virtutem esse acquisitu difficilem. In secunda tres modos proponit, quibus possimus ipsum medium invenire. In tertia ad difficultatem virtutis acquirendæ redit, & medium ipsum, quo fieri potest, secundum subjectam materiam determinat.
units.tr: There follows the third and last part of this final treatise, in which the Philosopher sets out some methods, by rules, through which we may acquire the mean for ourselves. This chapter has three parts. In the first he shows that virtue is difficult to acquire. In the second he proposes three methods by which we may find the mean itself. In the third he returns to the difficulty of acquiring virtue and determines, as far as it can be done, the mean itself according to the subject matter.

units.la: In prima igitur: Virtutem acquisitu difficilem esse ostendit, quod & præclare explicat Plato lib. 5. de Republ. & quo etiam pertinet Litera Pythagora bifor-mis, mis, in qua humanæ vitæ speciem præfigurabat. Rationem verò, cur virtus sit acquisitu difficilis, Plato hanc adfert lib.12. sub sin. de legib. quia virtus est scopus ad quem collimare debemus. Scopum verò attingere difficile admodum est, aberrare verò facile, ut supra cap. 6. huius libri, ostensum erat. Est & alia ratio nobis Christianis notior, quia animirum lapsus nostri vitio proniores sumus ad vitia & mala, quam ad virtutes. Ratio Aristotelis, quod virtus sit acquisitu difficilis, est hæc, quia virtus est medium, & medium invenire difficile est, quod probat à simili, nam sicut in circulo medium invenire non est facile cuivis, sed tantum perito & scienti Mathematico, sic etiam neq; medium, in quo consistit virtus, invenire facile est: nam si medium rei, quod est unum & idem apud omnes, invenire sit difficile, multò difficilius erit invenire medium rationis seu quoad nos, quod subinde pro variis circumstantiis variatur, & hoc illustrat exemplis, nam irasci & pecuniam expendere facile est cuivis, at verò irasci, & pecuniam expendere, quando & sicut oportet, servatis nempe circumstantiis, non est cuivis facile, sed difficile.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he shows that virtue is difficult to acquire, which Plato also explains admirably in book 5 of the Republic. To this belongs the Pythagorean letter, two-formed, in which he prefigured the shape of human life. Plato gives the reason why virtue is difficult to acquire in lib. 12. sub fin. de legib., namely that virtue is the goal at which we ought to aim. Now it is very difficult to hit the goal, and easy to miss it, as was shown above in chapter 6 of this book. There is also another reason better known to us Christians: because of our fall we are more inclined to vices and evils than to virtues. Aristotle's reason why virtue is difficult to acquire is this: virtue is a mean, and it is difficult to find the mean. He proves this from a likeness: just as finding the centre of a circle is not easy for just anyone, but only for one skilled and learned in mathematics, so neither is it easy to find the mean in which virtue consists. For if it is difficult to find the mean of a thing, which is one and the same for all, it will be far more difficult to find the mean relative to us, which varies from time to time according to varying circumstances. He illustrates this with examples: to become angry or to spend money is easy for anyone, but to be angry, or to spend money, when and as one ought, with the circumstances duly observed, is not easy for anyone but is difficult.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis adfert tres modos seu tres rationes, quibus possimus medium acquirere: 1. Modus, quoniam dictum erat in cap. superiori, virtutem uni extremorum magis contrariari quam alteri, ut ab eo extremo maximè caveamus, quod medio maximè opponitur, & hoc probat ex versu quodam Homerico: nam apud Homerum lib.12. Odyss. Circe ut ystis in patriam redituro suadet, ut à fumo atque undis navem removeat, id nimirum inter duos scopos. periculosissimos Scyllam nempe & Charybdim navigaturus, navem diverter versus medium ab extremis scopulis, ne si propius accedat, fumo & undis ex æstu ab ipsis scopulis ejecto orientibus aberret, & cæcus in ipsos scopulos impingat. Quod si verò medium ipsum non possimus attingere, ex duobus malis minus eligendum est, & secunda quandoque navigatione utendum est, ut proverbio dicitur, id est, ut eo modo, quo melius possimus, agamus, si eo modo, quo volumus, agere non licet. Secunda regula inveniendi medium est, ut ab iis vitiis abstineamus maximè, in quæ sumus natura proniores, & in contrarium nitamur: & signum dat, quo possumus cognoscere, in quæ sumus vitia natura procliviores, cognoscemus namque ex voluptate & dolore, quæ proveniunt ex ipsis actionibus, verbi gratia: si quis delectetur luxuria, signum est, pronum esse in prodigalitatem seu profusionem, & si dolet sublata luxuriâ ad facultate, debet ab ipsa prodigalitate, in quâ est natura proclivior, recedere, & niti quantum potest in contrarium vitium, nempe in avaritiam, hoc enim facto in contrarium trahendo & nitendo, incidit in medium, quia ab uno extremorum in alterum non datur progressus, nisi per medium, quemadmodum qui ligna curva recta efficere conantur, in contrariam quasi curvitatem inflectunt, ut rectitudinem induant. Cavendum tamen, nedum ab uno extremorum in alterum contrarium nitimur, in contrarium nimium nitamur. Sic enim quadrat in nostrum illud Poëtæ;
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he gives three methods, or three reasons, by which we may acquire the mean. (1) The first method: since it was said in the previous chapter that virtue is more opposed to one extreme than to the other, we should above all guard against that extreme which is most opposed to the mean.
