He proves this from a certain verse of Homer, for in Homer, Odyssey book 12, Circe advises Ulysses, who is about to return to his homeland, to steer the ship away from the smoke and the waves, namely between two most dangerous rocks, Scylla and Charybdis. Since he is about to sail between them, he should turn the ship towards the middle, away from the rocks at the extremes, lest, if he came nearer, he should be led astray by the smoke and waves rising from the surge thrown up by the rocks themselves, and blindly strike against the rocks. But if we cannot reach the mean itself, one should choose the lesser of two evils, and sometimes make use of a second-best course, as the proverb says, that is, we should act in the way that is best open to us, if we are not permitted to act in the way we would wish. Second rule for finding the mean: we should above all abstain from those vices towards which we are naturally more inclined, and strive against them. And he gives a sign by which we may recognise which vices we are naturally more inclined to: for we will know this from the pleasure and pain that arise from the actions themselves. For example, if someone takes delight in luxury, this is a sign that he is inclined to prodigality or extravagance; and if he is grieved when luxury is taken away from his means, he must withdraw from prodigality itself, to which he is more naturally inclined, and strive as hard as he can towards the opposite vice, namely avarice. For by pulling and straining in the opposite direction in this way, he falls upon the mean, since there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through the mean. It is like those who try to make crooked wood straight: they bend it into a contrary crookedness, so that it may take on straightness. Yet we must take care that, while we strive away from one extreme towards the opposite, we do not strive too much towards the opposite. For this fits that saying of the poet:

units.la: Dum vitant stulti vitium, in contraria currunt.
units.tr: While fools avoid one vice, they run into its opposites.

units.la: Tertia regula est, ut à voluptate nobis maximè cavea-mus: mus: nam est in sita nobis ab ipsis cunabulis, ut supra dixerat cap.3. & licet videatur amica naturæ, decipit tamen nos, & prius nos occupat & corrumpit, quam animadvertamus, proinde à voluptate nobis insita fugere maximè debemus, ut medium verum inveniamus, quod illustrat elegantî similitudine. Nam sicut seniores Trojani apud Homerum in duello Menelai & Paridis, cum in turri quadam stantem vidisset Helenam, & pugnantes prospicientem, laudata primum ejus forma, tanquam admirabili & pene divina, tandem dixerunt; etsi pulchra sit, & digna pro qua bellum gerant juvenes, discedat tamen ad naves, & redeat ad patriam, ne nobis, liberis nostris, & patriæ nostræ certum afferat exitium.
units.tr: Third rule is that we should above all guard ourselves against pleasure. For it is implanted in us from our very cradle, as he said above in chapter 3. And although it seems friendly to nature, it deceives us, and it seizes and corrupts us before we notice. Therefore we must above all flee the pleasure implanted in us, if we are to find the true mean. He illustrates this with an elegant comparison. Homer tells how the elders of Troy, when they saw Helen standing on a certain tower and looking down at the men fighting in the duel between Menelaus and Paris, first praised her beauty as wonderful and almost divine, and at last said: Though she is beautiful, and worthy of the young men fighting for her, let her nonetheless depart to the ships and return to her homeland, lest she bring certain destruction upon us, our children, and our country.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis redit ad difficultatem virtutis acquirendæ ostendendam, & dicit non tantum difficile esse medium invenire, in quo consistit ipsa virtus, sed etiam determinare aut definire, quando sit medium, & ratio est, quia actiones practicæ versantur circa singularia, singularia vero non tam cadunt sub ipsam rationem & judicium intellectus, quam sub sensum, & tantam habet varietatem, ut nullam certam de iis statuere quis possit regulam, propter varias circumstantias, quibus subinde mutantur. Ita ut difficile sit scire, quid in unaquaque sit agendum, quod illustrat exemplo iræ: Nam medium in ira, sicut oportet, & sicut decet, invenire & determinare, est difficillimum: Tandem vero concludit, cum medium ubique laudetur, necesse est declinare quandoque ad excessum, quandoque ad defectum, ut medium assequamur, aut si non possumus vere assequi. sequi, saltem ut appropinquemus, quod fieri li-cet.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he returns to showing the difficulty of acquiring virtue, and says that it is not only difficult to find the mean in which virtue itself consists, but also to determine or define when something is the mean. The reason is that practical actions are concerned with particulars, and particulars fall not so much under reason and the judgement of the intellect as under the senses. They have such variety that no one can lay down any fixed rule about them, because of the various circumstances by which they are continually changed. So it is hard to know what must be done in each case. He illustrates this with the example of anger: to find and determine the mean in anger, as one ought and as is fitting, is extremely difficult. Finally he concludes that, since the mean is always praised, it is necessary at times to incline towards excess and at other times towards deficiency, so that we may attain the mean, or, if we cannot truly attain it, at least come near to it, which is permitted.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Medium in omni re invenire est difficile.
units.tr: 1. To find the mean in every matter is difficult.

units.la: 2. Agere in quavis re est facile, bene vero agere est difficile.
units.tr: 2. To act in any matter is easy, but to act well is difficult.

units.la: 3. Recedere debemus ab uno extremorum ad alterum, ut medium interjectum inveniamus.
units.tr: 3. We ought to withdraw from one of the extremes to the other, so that we may find the mean lying between them.

units.la: 4. Ex duobus malis eligendum est minus, si necessitas urgeat, ut alterum amplectamur.
units.tr: 4. Of two evils the lesser is to be chosen, if necessity presses, so that we embrace the one.

units.la: 5. In qua vitia summa natura proniores, ab iis recedere debemus, ut medium virtutis assequamur.
units.tr: 5. In those vices to which our nature is most prone, we ought to withdraw from them, so that we may attain the mean of virtue.

units.la: 6. In singularibus, qua pro varia circumstantiis subinde mutantur, ne dum invenire & determinare est difficile.
units.tr: 6. In particulars, which are changed from time to time according to varying circumstances, it is not only difficult to find the mean but also to determine it.

units.la: 7. Singularia non sub intellectum, sed sub sensum cadunt proprie.
units.tr: 7. Particulars fall properly under sense, not under the intellect.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo ad hoc probandum, virtutem nempe esse acquisitu difficilem, adferat medium circuli. Medium vero circuli est medium rei, & medium rei male accommodatur ad medium rationis probandum: Nam medium rei, & medium rationis natura & proprietatibus differunt, ut supra cap. 6. ostendit? Resp. Argumentatur Philosophus a majori ad minus. Nam si medium rei, quod non variatur, sit inventu difficile, multo magis erit medium rationis, seu quo ad nos, quod pro hominum arbitrio subinde mutatur: Proinde non male accommodavit medium circuli ad probandum medium rationis.
units.tr: I. How does he use the figure of the circle to prove that virtue is difficult to acquire? The figure of the circle is the mean of the thing itself, and the mean of the thing is badly suited to proving the mean of reason, for the mean of the thing and the mean of reason differ in nature and properties, as he showed above in chapter 6. Answer: The Philosopher argues from the greater to the lesser. For if the mean of the thing, which does not vary, is hard to find, the mean of reason, or the mean relative to us, which changes at people's discretion from time to time, will be much harder to find. So he was not wrong to use the figure of the circle to prove the mean of reason.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat in prima regula, quam tratradit de inveniendo medio, recedendum esse ab eo extremo, quod est ipsi medio maxime contrarium, & in secunda regula jubet recedere ab eo extremo, in quod sumus natura proclivores, & haec videntur inter se oppositta, verbi gratia: Prima regula jubet, ut ab avaritia magis recedam, quam a prodigalitate, quia avaritia magis contrariatur liberalitati, quam prodigalitas. Secunda regula econtra jubet magis recedere a prodigalitate, quam ab avaritia, quia in prodigalitatem sumus natura proniores. Unde ista duae regulae videntur sibi contradicere? Resp. Diverso respectu ista dici, & proinde non inter se opponi. Nam prima regula respicit extremum & medium in sua natura, proinde jubet, ut ad naturam medii inveniendam maxime recedatur ab eo extremo, quod sua natura medii naturae contrariatur maxime. Secunda regula respicit ipsum subjectum, in quo insunt media, extrema, non vero naturam ipsam medii & extremorum, proinde istae duae regulae non sibi contradicunt.
units.tr: II. How can he say in the first rule, which he gives for finding the mean, that we must withdraw from the extreme that is most opposed to the mean, and in the second rule bid us withdraw from the extreme to which we are more naturally inclined? These seem to contradict each other. For example: the first rule bids me withdraw from avarice rather than from prodigality, because avarice is more opposed to liberality than prodigality is. The second rule, on the contrary, bids me withdraw from prodigality rather than from avarice, because we are by nature more prone to prodigality. So how do these two rules not contradict each other? Answer: They are said with different respects, and so they are not opposed to each other. The first rule looks at the extreme and the mean in their own nature, and so it bids us, in order to discover the nature of the mean, to withdraw most from that extreme whose nature is most opposed to the nature of the mean. The second rule looks at the subject in which the means and extremes inhere, not at the nature of the mean and the extremes themselves. So these two rules do not contradict each other.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat ultimus verbis capitis, medium invenire esse facile, cum tamen nihil aliud hoc capite probarit, quam medium inventu esse difficillimum? Resp. Non simpliciter dici medium invenu esse facile, sed declinantes interdum ad excessum, interdum ad defectum, facilius nos in medium incidere possumus; cognita enim natura extremorum, facilius pervenimus ad naturam medii, quod est inter utrumque.
units.tr: How can he say at the end of this chapter that it is easy to find the mean, when in this chapter he has proved nothing except that the mean is most difficult to find? Answer: It is not said simply that the mean is easy to find, but that, since we sometimes deviate toward excess and sometimes toward defect, we can more easily fall upon the mean. For once the nature of the extremes is known, we more easily arrive at the nature of the mean, which lies between them.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat non omnem declinationem esse vituperandam, cum omnis declinatio sit vitium; omne vero vitium sit vituperandum: quia contrariatur virtuti. Omnem declinationem esse vitium hinc constat, quia omnis mnis declinatio est aut excessus aut defectus, proinde omnis declinatio à medio vituperanda videtur, secus quam statuit hic Aristoteles? Resp. Omnem declinationem perse quidem esse vituperandam, propterea quod sit recessus à medio, & solum medium, in quo consistit virtus, est laudabile. Hic vero Aristotelem dicere declinationem, quæ sit leviör & minus manifesta, non esse plane vituperandam: Nam cum medium inventu non modo sit difficile, sed etiam nequefacile determinari possit, adeo ut si quis non verum attingat medium, dicit non statim esse culpandum. De hac re vide plura ad cap. 2. huius lib.
units.tr: How can he say that not every deviation is to be blamed, when every deviation is a vice, and every vice is to be blamed because it is contrary to virtue? That every deviation is a vice follows from this: every deviation is either an excess or a defect, so every deviation from the mean seems to be blameworthy, contrary to what Aristotle here lays down? Answer: In itself every deviation is indeed to be blamed, because it is a departure from the mean, and only the mean, in which virtue consists, is praiseworthy. But here Aristotle is saying that a deviation which is slighter and less obvious is not altogether to be blamed. For since the mean is not only hard to find but also cannot easily be determined exactly, so that if someone does not hit the true mean, he is not to be blamed at once. On this matter see more at chapter 2 of this book.

units.la: Coronidis loco adjiciemus hanc quæstionem: An, quia recta ratio statuitur causa exemplaris virtutis, sola etiam sit causa exemplaris virtutis: 1. De hac re discrepantes sunt sententiæ, alii enim statuunt solam Scripturam esse causam exemplarem virtutis moralis propter has rationes: 1. Quia sola Scriptura continet præcepta piè sanctéque vivendi, cuius præcepta omnia sunt verissima, quia sunt à Deo profecta. 2. Quia quicunque vitam suam instituit secundum præcepta in sacra Scriptura proposita, ille vere probus est & moralis virtutis particeps. 3. Quia sacra Scriptura continet varia exempla virtutum imitandarum, & vitiorum fugiendorum. At sunt, qui contrarium statuunt, nam etsi sacra Scriptura sit causa exemplaris virtutis moralis, quatenus virtus moralis consideratur à Theologo in perfectissimo suo gradu, tamen ut consideratur à Philosopho luce naturæ instructo, causa ejus exemplaris erit recta ratio, & exemplar virtutis in aliis nobis propositum. Per rectam rationem, nihil aliud intelligitur, quam rectum hominis judicium de honesto & turpi, tum etiam principia practica, quae ex luce naturae, tanquam rivulus ex fonte derivantur.
units.tr: By way of a crown to this discussion we will add this question: whether, because right reason is established as the exemplary cause of virtue, it is also the sole exemplary cause of virtue. 1. On this matter opinions differ. For some hold that Scripture alone is the exemplary cause of moral virtue, for these reasons: (1) because Scripture alone contains the precepts of living piously and holily, and all its precepts are most true, since they proceed from God; (2) because whoever shapes his life according to the precepts set forth in holy Scripture is truly upright and partakes of moral virtue; (3) because holy Scripture contains various examples of virtues to be imitated and vices to be shunned. But others hold the contrary. For although holy Scripture is the exemplary cause of moral virtue, insofar as moral virtue is considered by the theologian in its most perfect degree, yet insofar as it is considered by the philosopher, who is instructed by the light of nature, its exemplary cause will be right reason, and the example of virtue proposed to us in others. By right reason nothing else is understood than the correct human judgment about what is honourable and shameful, and also the practical principles which flow from the light of nature as a stream flows from its spring.

units.la: 11. Quaeritur: An quia catalogum virtutum moralium cap. 8. huius lib. descripserit Philosophus, certus dari possit numerus virtutum moralium? Resp. Cum actiones hominum non sint infinitae, etiam neque habitus, qui ex iis nascuntur, sed de numero virtutum inter se differunt Philosophi: Alii enim quatuor tantum statuunt, quas vocant Cardinales, Justitiam, Fortitudinem, Prudentiam & Temperantiam. Alii his quatuor addunt Sanctitatem, ut Plato. Alii φιλαυτίαν, sapientiam, prudentiam, pietatem, parsimoniam, benevolentiam, obedientiam, hospitalitatem, amicitiam, gratitudinem, verecundiam, taciturnitatem, civilitatem, humilitatem, gravitatem, misericordiam, spem, & id genus alias. Aristoteles vero undecim tantum constituit, de quibus his libris agit, cujusmodi sunt: Fortitudo, temperantia, liberalitas, magnificentia, magnanimitas, modestia, mansuetudo, affabilitas, urbanitas, veracitas, & justitia, de quibus sigillatim cum Philosopho posthac agemus.
units.tr: 11. Since the Philosopher described a catalogue of moral virtues in chapter 8 of this book, can a certain number of moral virtues be given? Answer: Since the actions of men are not infinite, neither are the habits which arise from them, but philosophers differ among themselves about the number of virtues. Some hold only four, which they call cardinal: justice, fortitude, prudence and temperance. Others add holiness to these four, as Plato does. Others add self-love [φιλαυτίαν], wisdom, prudence, piety, thrift, benevolence, obedience, hospitality, friendship, gratitude, modesty, taciturnity, courtesy, humility, gravity, mercy, hope, and other such kinds. Aristotle, however, lays down only eleven, with which he deals in these books, namely: fortitude, temperance, liberality, magnificence, magnanimity, modesty, gentleness, affability, wittiness, truthfulness, and justice, about which we shall speak in detail with the Philosopher hereafter.

units.la: Caeterum non incommode moveri poterit & haec quaestio: An virtutes morales ita inter se sint connexae, ut una sine altera consistere non possit? Resp. Diversas esse de hac quaestione opiniones, quidam enim statuunt, quidam contra: pro priore parte sunt haec argumenta; 1. Quia sicut vitia summopere inter se dissident, & cum virtutem, tum seipsam destruunt, ita ex adverso summa est consensio & harmonia inter ter virtutes morales, qua sibi mutuò respondent, seque mutuò perficiunt. 1. Quia omnes virtutes morales pendent à prudentia tanquam duce & moderatrice. 2. Quia dirigunt omnes ad honestum tanquam ad communem finem. 4. Quia non tantum honestum constanter amant & expetunt omnes, sed etiam seipsas mutuò diligunt, cum unaquæque in sit honesta. 5. Quia virtutis universalis ambitu omnes comprehenduntur, quod non fieret, nisi inter se forent connexæ. 6. Quia actiones à virtutibus moralibus prodeuntes, ita inter se conspirant, & sunt colligatæ, ut una sine altera perfectè exerceri non possit. 7. Quia à qualibet virtute morali homo absolutè probus denominatur, non secus ac à quolibet vitio dicitur absolutè improbus: Nemo autem dicitur absolutè probus, nisi qui omnibus virtutibus simul est præditus, nisi velimus aliquem statuere absolutè simul probum & improbum dici posse. 8. Quia omnes virtutes morales pendentà proærefi recta: Proærefis autem recta sequitur rectam consultationem; Recta consultatio sequitur rectam finis expetitionem; at cui recta proærefis, consultatio, finisque expetitio competunt, ei necesse est omnes virtutes competere. 9. Quia omnes particulares virtutes morales constituunt unam virtutem universalem, tanquam membra suum integrum. Integrum autem est, quod omnibus suis membris constat. 10. Quia nulla virtus moralis omnibus suis numeris est absoluta, nisi cum cæteris sit juncta, siquidem sese mutuò perficiunt, augent, sibiq; opem ferunt. 11. Quia per cujusl bet virtu-tis tis actiones recte paramur erga communem finem, nec perfecte exercemur pro una, quin exerceamur pro aliis. 12. Hoc idem testatur Aristoteles lib. 6. Nicom. cap. 13. cum inquit, in virtutibus naturalibus fieri posse, utinter se separentur: In virtutibus autem moralibus, secundum quas homo absolute dicitur probus non posse.
units.tr: Besides this, the following question may also be raised not unfittingly: Are the moral virtues so connected with one another that one cannot exist without the others? Answer: Opinions on this question are divided, for some hold one thing and some the contrary. For the first view the following arguments are offered: (1) just as vices are wholly at odds with one another, and destroy both virtue and themselves, so on the other hand there is the greatest agreement and harmony among the moral virtues, which correspond to one another and mutually perfect one another; (2) all moral virtues depend on prudence as on their guide and moderator; (3) they all direct us to the honourable as to a common end; (4) all of them not only steadfastly love and seek the honourable, but also love one another, since each is honourable; (5) all are comprehended within the scope of universal virtue, which would not be so unless they were connected with one another; (6) the actions which proceed from the moral virtues so agree and are so bound together that one cannot be perfectly exercised without another; (7) a man is called absolutely upright from any one moral virtue, just as he is called absolutely wicked from any one vice; but no one is called absolutely upright unless he is endowed with all the virtues at once, unless we wish to say that someone may be called absolutely upright and wicked at the same time; (8) all moral virtues depend on right choice (proairesis); right choice follows right deliberation; right deliberation follows the right pursuit of the end; and whoever has right choice, deliberation and the pursuit of the end must necessarily have all the virtues; (9) all the particular moral virtues constitute one universal virtue, as the members constitute a whole. Now a whole is that which consists of all its members; (10) no moral virtue is complete in all its parts unless it is joined with the others, since they mutually perfect, increase and help one another; (11) by the actions of any one virtue we are rightly directed toward the common end, nor are we perfectly exercised in one without being exercised in the others; (12) Aristotle himself bears witness to the same thing in book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 13, when he says that natural virtues can be separated from one another, but moral virtues, according to which a man is called absolutely upright, cannot.

units.la: Pro contraria sententia sunt haec argumenta: 1. Quia communis experientia testatur in uno homine hanc, in alio aliam virtutem moralem reperiri, & propterea etiam Protagoras apud Plat. asserit, multos extitisse viros fortes, qui neque fuerint temperantes, neque justi, & rursus multos extitisse temperantes & justos, qui non fuerint fortes. 2. Quia si virtutum moralium una sine altera consistere nequit, sequitur neminem esse virtute morali praeditum, cum nemo reperiatur, in quo omnes virtutes morales simul refulgeat nihilque desideretur. 3. Quia virtutes nonnullae inter se pugnare videntur, ita ut una alteram repellat, ut verbi gratia: Liberalitas magnificentiam, modestia magnanimitatem. 4. Quia conditiones quorundam hominum pugnare videntur cum conditionibus quorundam virtutum, siquidem viri pauperes & obscuri non possunt esse magnifici & magnanimi. 5. Quia virtutes morales assuetudine honestarumque actionum iteratione acquiruntur, ac saepe contingit, ut aliquis in actionibus hujus virtutis magis quam alterius versetur, magisque ad unum quam ad alterum actionum genus sit facilis, magisque abundet instrumentis & opportunitatibus pro una, quam pro altera virtutis actione, & quoniam homoactionibus temperantiæ non evadit fortis, neq; actionibus fortitudinis temperans, ideo potest homo unam virtutem moralem acquirere sine aliis. 6. Quia connexio virtutum moralium neque est de essentia illarum, neq; essentiam necessario consequitur, sed tantum contingenter. 7. Quia una virtus non potest esse sine altera, sequeretur inde. 1. Unam esse causam procreantem alterius. 2. Unam non prius nobis quam alteram generari. 3. Una in homine posita omnes poni, & una destructa omnes destrui, quæ absurda videntur. Pro enodatione hujus quæstionis Pic. gradu 4 cap 41. & sequent. distinguit inter virtutes morales, quatenus sunt inchoatæ & imperfectæ, & quatenus sunt perfectæ, omnibusque numeris absolutæ, priori modo concedit virtutes morales, non esse necessario inter se connexas, sed ut plurimum sejunctas, posteriori autem modo negat, deinde distinguit inter attributa virtutum moralium interna, necessaria & essentialia, cujusmodi sunt prudentia, præelectio, honestum desiderium, constantia & inter attributa externa contingentia & separabilia, cujusmodi sunt, quod homo per naturam ad unum potius, quam aliud actionis genus est facilior, quod magis abundet instrumentis unius quam alterius virtutis, quod magis per varias occasiones versetur in uno, quam alio actionis genere, quod in uno eodemque homine, modo una modo alia virtus refulgeat, ob externas circumstantias, respectu priorum attributorum. Aut virtutes morales perfectas esse inter se necessario connexas, non autem respectu posteriorum. rum. Verum sententia Pic. gravibus urgetur difficultatibus. Nam 1. Virtus moralis, aut nunquam aut rarissime invenitur in homine omnibus numeris perfecta & absoluta, sed plerumque imperfecta, & hoc indicare voluit Diog. cum in meridie accensa lucerna hominem exactè probum quaereret, & nullum se invenire posse affirmaret. 2. Etiamsi fieri posset, ut virtus aliqua moralis in homine esset perfecta: non tamen ulla firma & solida ratio proferri poterit, cur necesse sit, cum ea caeteras omnes necessario esse connexas. 3. Quia unaquaeque virtus non tantum habet sua communia attributa, sed etiam suam propriam essentiam, suas proprias causas, sua propria obiecta & adjuncta. Videtur ideo una absque altera, in uno & eodem homine existere posse, & hoc etiam ipse Pic. quasi sui oblitus fatetur sub finem cap. 2. gradu 4. quando ait, virtutes cum Scoto, ut imperfectas, & quoad ea, quae sunt propria singularum, & quoad extrinsecus concurrentia, non esse necessario complicatas. Proinde concludendum erit, virtutes morales esse quidem inter se necessario connexas, ratione communium attributorum, quibus inter se consentiunt & conveniunt, non autem ratione propriorum attributorum, & sic unam absque altera in homine existere posse. Restat igitur, ut ad argumenta pro thesi affirmante allata breviter respondeamus. 1. Concedimus summam esse harmoniam inter virtutes morales, qua sibi mutuo respondent, seque mutuo perficiunt, nempe accidentaliter, sed inde non sequi, illas ita inter se esse connexas, ut una absque altera in homine consistere non possit. In 1.3.4.5. argumento exprimuntur communia
units.tr: The following arguments support the opposing view: (1) Common experience shows that one man has this moral virtue and another has a different one. This is why Protagoras in Plato says that there have been many brave men who were neither temperate nor just, and again many temperate and just men who were not brave. (2) If one moral virtue cannot exist without another, it follows that no one has any moral virtue, since no one is found in whom all the moral virtues shine together and nothing is lacking. (3) Some virtues seem to fight with one another, so that one drives out the other: for example, liberality and magnificence, or modesty and magnanimity. (4) The circumstances of certain people seem to conflict with the conditions of certain virtues, since poor and obscure men cannot be magnificent or magnanimous. (5) Moral virtues are acquired by habit and by repeated honourable actions. Often it happens that someone is more occupied with the actions of one virtue than of another, is more inclined to one kind of action than to another, and has more tools and opportunities for one virtue's actions than for another's. Since a man who practises temperance does not become brave, nor one who practises courage become temperate, a man can acquire one moral virtue without the others. (6) The connection of the moral virtues is neither part of their essence nor a necessary consequence of it, but only contingent. (7) If one virtue could not exist without another, the following would follow: (a) one would be the cause producing the other; (b) one would not be generated in us before the other; (c) when one is present in a man all are present, and when one is destroyed all are destroyed. These seem absurd. To explain this question, Pico (degree 4, chapter 41 and following) distinguishes between moral virtues as they are incipient and imperfect, and as they are perfect and absolute in every respect. In the first sense he grants that the moral virtues are not necessarily connected with one another but for the most part separated; in the second sense he denies it. Then he distinguishes between the internal attributes of the moral virtues, which are necessary and essential, such as prudence, choice, honest desire and constancy, and the external attributes, which are contingent and separable, such as: that by nature a man is more inclined to one kind of action than another; that he has more tools for one virtue than another; that he is more occupied with one kind of action than another because of various occasions; and that in one and the same man now one virtue and now another shines forth because of external circumstances. Compared with the former attributes, the latter are of this kind. So either the perfect moral virtues are necessarily connected with one another, but not with respect to the latter attributes. But Pico's opinion is pressed by serious difficulties. For (1) a moral virtue is either never or very rarely found in a man perfect and absolute in every respect, but usually imperfect; and Diogenes meant this when, seeking an exactly upright man with a lamp lit at noon, he declared that he could find none. (2) Even if it were possible for some moral virtue to be perfect in a man, no firm and solid reason could be offered why it must necessarily be connected with all the others. (3) Each virtue has not only its common attributes but also its own essence, its own causes, its own objects and its own adjuncts. It seems therefore that one virtue can exist in one and the same man without another. Pico himself confesses this, as though forgetful of himself, near the end of chapter 2, degree 4, when he says that the virtues, with Scotus, are not necessarily interlinked as imperfect things, either with regard to what is proper to each or with regard to what concurs from outside. Accordingly we must conclude that the moral virtues are indeed necessarily connected with one another in respect of their common attributes, in which they agree and harmonise, but not in respect of their proper attributes; and so one can exist in a man without another. It remains, then, to answer briefly the arguments brought for the affirmative thesis. 1. We grant that there is great harmony among the moral virtues, by which they correspond to one another and mutually perfect one another, namely accidentally; but it does not follow from this that they are so connected that one cannot exist in a man without another. In arguments 1, 3, 4 and 5 only the common attributes of the moral virtues are expressed.

units.la: {§} Vide superius. munia duntaxat attributa virtutum moralium quorum respectu concedimus illas inter se esse cónexas, sed inde non concluditur, quod ratione propriorū attributorum inter se non sint sejunctæ, i relíquis argumentis omnibus petitur principium, falsum enim est. 1. Omnium virtutum actiones ita inter se esse colligatas, ut una sine altera perfecte exerceri non possit. 2. A qualibet virtute morali hominem absolutè dici probum, cum tantum dicatur probus secundum quid. 3. Falsum quoque ei, cui competit recta proærefis, consulatio, & expetitio honesti, in genere competere omnes virtutes morales, cum una quæque virtus à propria proærefi & expetitione honesti pendeat. 4. Virtutem universalem habere se ad particulares virtutes tanquam integrum ad sua membra, cum habeat se tanquam genus ad suas species. 5. Falsum & illud, nullam virtutem moralem omnibus suis numeris posse esse absolutam, nisi cum cæteris sit conjuncta. 6. Nos perfecte exerceri non posse pro una virtute, quin exerceamur pro aliis. Sed de his satis, nunc ad sequentia pergamus.
units.tr: {§} See above. Only the common attributes of the moral virtues are at issue, and in respect of these we grant that they are connected with one another; but it is not concluded from this that they are not separated in respect of their proper attributes. All the other arguments take as their principle what is false. For: (1) the actions of all the virtues are so bound together that one cannot be exercised perfectly without another; (2) a man is called upright absolutely by any moral virtue, when he is called upright only in a certain respect; (3) it is also false that what belongs to one who has right choice, deliberation and desire for the honourable belongs to all the moral virtues in general, since each virtue depends on its own choice and desire for the honourable; (4) a universal virtue relates to the particular virtues as a whole to its parts, when it relates to them as a genus to its species; (5) it is also false that no moral virtue can be absolute in all its respects unless it is joined with the others; (6) we cannot be exercised perfectly in one virtue without being exercised in the others. But enough of these; let us now proceed to what follows.

units.la: LIBER TERTIUS.
units.tr: Book Three.

units.la: IN secundo libro docuit Philosophus de virtute in genere, de cujus ortu, definitione, divisione in species, deq; aliis ad virtutem pertinentibus, ut de inventione medii, in quo consistit virtus, fusius egit: Consequens videbatur, batur, ut sigillatim de una quaque virtute tractaret hoc libro tertio, & sic plena & perfecta habeatur virtutis cognitio, sed quia virtus ex actionibus seu operationibus nostris oritur, ut supra cap. 1. 2. lib. 2. probatum est: Videndum etiam erit, à quibus principiis oriantur actiones nostrae. Principia vero ex quibus oriuntur actiones nostrae sunt spontaneum & invitum, seu voluntarium & involuntarium, ut vulgò dicuntur: Electio, consultatio, voluntas & similia, de quibus sibi agendum proponit Philosophus, antequam singulas virtutes in specie tractandas aggredi atur. Dividitur hic liber in tres tractatus: In primo agit de hisce principiis, à quibus promanant operationes naturae virtutem constituentes, & sub finem primi tractatus accuratissime disputat contra Plat. qui negat facta tam bona quam mala nostri esse arbitrii, & hoc facit ab initio libri usque ad cap. 8. In secundo tractatu agit de Fortitudine, in quibus rebus versetur, & quae sint ejus extrema. Postremò ostendit, etsi Fortitudo in rebus gravibus & tristioribus versetur, voluptatem tamen in actionibus suis conjunctam habere à cap. 8. usque 13. In tertio tractatu agit de Temperantia, quibus in rebus seu voluptatibus fit sita, & confert eam cum suis extremis, allata divisione voluptatum seu cupiditatum: tandem sub finem libri instituit comparationem inter ignaviam & intemperantiam, utra sit magis voluntaria, seu facilius suscipiatur, & in utra magis peccetur. Primi tractatus membra sunt quinque: In primo ostendit, quid sponte, quid invitè fiat. In secundo agit de electione. In tertio de consultatione. In quarto de voluntate. In quinto accommodat hæc principia virtutibus & viciis, & redarguit opinionem Platonis.
units.tr: In the second book the Philosopher taught about virtue in general, and treated at length its origin, its definition, its division into species, and other matters pertaining to virtue, such as the finding of the mean in which virtue consists. It seemed the logical next step to treat each virtue individually in this third book, so that a full and perfect knowledge of virtue might be had. But since virtue arises from our actions or operations, as was proved above in chapters 1 and 2 of the second book, we must also consider from what principles our actions arise. The principles from which our actions arise are the voluntary and the involuntary, or, as they are commonly called, the spontaneous and the unwilling; also choice, deliberation, the will and similar things. The Philosopher proposes to deal with these before he sets out to treat the individual virtues in particular. This book is divided into three treatises. In the first he deals with these principles, from which the operations that constitute virtue proceed, and near the end of this first treatise he disputes most carefully against Plato, who denies that good and bad deeds alike are within our power; he does this from the beginning of the book to chapter 8. In the second treatise he deals with Courage: in what things it is concerned, and what its extremes are. Finally he shows that, although courage is concerned with serious and more painful things, it nonetheless has pleasure joined with its actions; this is from chapter 8 to chapter 13. In the third treatise he deals with Temperance: in what things or pleasures it is set, and he compares it with its extremes, after setting out a division of pleasures or desires. Lastly, at the end of the book he institutes a comparison between cowardice and intemperance, asking which is more voluntary, or more easily undertaken, and in which we sin more. The first treatise has five parts: (1) in the first he shows what is done willingly and what is done unwillingly; (2) in the second he deals with choice; (3) in the third, with deliberation; (4) in the fourth, with the will; (5) in the fifth he applies these principles to virtues and vices, and refutes the opinion of Plato.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: PRimum membrum continetur tribus primis capitibus. Primi cap. partes quatuor sunt: In prima duplex ratio reddитur, cur tractatio de voluntariis & involuntariis, pertineat ad moralem Philosophiam. In secunda, voluntarium definit & dividit. In tertia, quia invitū est duplex, sit enim aut per vim, aut per ignorā iam, disputat, utrum quæ metu majoris mali, aut boni alicujus assequendi gratia fiunt, voluntariis, an involuntariis actionibus sint annumerandæ. In quarta parte refellit opinionem eorum, qui tertium genus invitarum actionum statuebant.
units.tr: The first part of the book is contained in the first three chapters. The four parts of the first chapter are these: in the first, a twofold reason is given why the treatment of voluntary and involuntary actions belongs to moral philosophy; in the second, he defines and divides the voluntary; in the third, since the involuntary is of two kinds (for it happens either through force or through ignorance), he discusses whether things done out of fear of a greater evil, or for the sake of obtaining some good, are to be counted among voluntary or involuntary actions; in the fourth part he refutes the opinion of those who posited a third kind of involuntary actions.

units.la: In prima igitur parte, duas adfert rationes, cur de spontaneis & invitis actionibus in Ethicis tractetur. Prima ratio est: Quia in actionibus (ex quibus virtutem oriri constat) quæ laude digna sunt, aut vituperio, quę venia & commiseratione digna sunt, cernitur exeo, an actiones sint spontaneæ, an invitæ: Et si actiones virtutem efficientes pertinent ad moralem philosophiam, etiam & ipsa principia pertinebunt. Secunda ratio ducitur ab auctoritate legum latorum: nam legumlatores actiones voluntarias, honoribus & præmio, pœna item & vituperio afficere solent, alias vero actiones non, quæ vero legumlatoribus conside randa venit, huc etiam spectant: nam legumlatores versantur circa res politicas, quæ fundamentum suum ex morali Philosophia habent. Addi potest & tertia ratio, quia supra lib. 2. definiit virtusvirtutem, per habitum proæreticum seu electivum ideo, ad melius cognoscendam naturam virtutis, explicandum est, quid sit electio. Et 5. explicandum, quid sit electio, tum etiam voluntarium erit explicandum, quia est electionis genus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he gives two reasons why spontaneous and involuntary actions are treated in the Ethics. The first reason is this: in those actions from which virtue is known to arise, which are worthy of praise or blame, or of pardon and pity, it is seen from this whether the actions are spontaneous or involuntary. And if the actions that produce virtue belong to moral philosophy, the principles of those actions belong to it too. The second reason is drawn from the authority of lawgivers: for lawgivers are accustomed to bestow honours and rewards on voluntary actions, and likewise punishment and blame, but not on other actions. What is to be considered by lawgivers also belongs here, for lawgivers are concerned with political affairs, which have their foundation in moral philosophy. A third reason may also be added: since in book 2 he defined virtue as a habit of choice, or elective habit, therefore, to understand the nature of virtue better, it must be explained what choice is. And since choice is to be explained, the voluntary too must be explained, because it is a kind of choice.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis incipit agere, de invito seu involuntario, de quo primo loco agit, quia maior cernitur varietas in actionibus invitis, quam in spontaneis. 1. Quia invitae actiones magis incurrunt in sensus: nam, quae aliis cogentibus, aut vi extrinsecus impellente fiunt, videre licet, aut aliquo saltem sensu percipere. Invitum primo definit, cujus principium est externum, & cui nihil adjumenti adfert, qui illam actionem producere debet, postea dividit in invitum per vim & per ignorantiam. Definit vero invitum per vim, cujus principium est externum, & ille, qui agit aut patitur, nihil adjumenti adferat ad actionem producendam, in qua definitione tres requiruntur conditiones. 1. Ut principium sit externum; principium autem hoc loco, ut & alias idem valet, quod causa, quare Aristoteles, 1. Mag. Mor. c. 15. definit invitum per causam, sed cum multa sint causarum genera, ut patet ex logicis, non hic de aliis causis, nisi de efficiente agitur, causa vero efficiens virtutum & actionum humanarum omnium septuplex enumeratur ab Aristotele. 1. Rhet. quae ad duo genera revocari debent, ut aliae causae sint externae & adventitiae, nempe necessitas, fortuna, ratio quoque, sed externa seu ars & quaecunque extrinsecus adhibentur. Interiores sunt tres: Natura, voluntas, & ratio ipsa, interna ait igitur Philosophus, vi factum esse, cujus causa sit externa, seu quod suopte motu non agat, naturalia ergo omnia propria vi facta dici non possunt, & cum addit externa, excludit vi facta a naturalibus iisque omnibus, quae vi sua agunt. 2. Conditio definitionis est, ut illud principium externum sit satis validum, ad hanc compulsionem & vim inferendam, sed non satis hoc est, ut principium sit externum & validum satis, verbi gratia: Si quis ab aliquo volens deportetur, externum quidem est principium, nam deportatur ab alio, sed factum non est vi factum. Rursus opificum opera fiunt quidem omnia principio externo (cista, verbi gratia: non fit sua vi, sed manu opificis) quae tamen vi fieri dici non possunt: Ideo adjicit tertiam conditionem, nempe ut nihil agens vel patiens adjumenti conferat: Dicitur agens vel patiens diverso respectu, nam ea ratione, qua suscipit in se vim, dicitur pati, ea vero ratione, qua compulsus aliud aliud agit, dicitur agens. Deinde definitionem duobus exemplis illustrat, quorum alterum est de rebus inanimatis, ut de vento, qui aliquem vi deportat, alterum est de rebus animatis, ut cum ab hominibus vis aliqua nobis infertur, ut in libris Machabaeor. Antiochus Tyrannus, per lictores suos haedera coronat pios Judaeos, & pertrahit ad Sacrificia Bacchi. Sed de his pluribus sub finem cap. 6. ubi de potestate voluntatis.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he begins to treat of the involuntary, or non-voluntary, which he discusses first because greater variety is seen in involuntary actions than in spontaneous ones. 1. Because involuntary actions fall more under the senses: for whatever is done by others compelling, or by force driving from outside, can be seen, or at least perceived by some sense. He first defines the involuntary as that whose principle is external, and to which the agent or patient contributes nothing toward producing that action; afterwards he divides it into the involuntary through force and through ignorance. He defines the involuntary through force as that whose principle is external, and to which the one who acts or suffers contributes nothing toward producing the action. In this definition three conditions are required. 1. That the principle be external. The word "principle" here, as elsewhere, means the same as cause. Aristotle, in 1 Magna Moralia, ch. 15, defines the involuntary by its cause. But since there are many kinds of cause, as is clear from the logicians, only the efficient cause is meant here. Aristotle lists seven efficient causes of virtues and of all human actions in 1 Rhetoric, which must be reduced to two kinds, so that some causes are external and adventitious, namely necessity, fortune, and also reason, but external reason, or art, and whatever is applied from outside. There are three internal causes: nature, will, and reason itself. The Philosopher therefore says that what is done by force has an external cause, or that it does not act of its own motion. Naturally, then, things done by their own force cannot all be said to be done by force. And when he adds "external," he excludes from the forced those natural things and all those that act by their own power. 2. A condition of the definition is that the external principle be strong enough to bring about this compulsion and to inflict force. But it is not enough that the principle be external and strong enough. For example: if someone is carried by another with his consent, the principle is indeed external, for he is carried by another, but the thing is not done by force. Again, the works of craftsmen are all done by an external principle (a chest, for example, is not made by its own power but by the craftsman's hand), yet these cannot be said to be done by force. Therefore he adds a third condition, namely that the agent or patient contributes nothing. One is said to be agent or patient in different respects: by the same reasoning by which one takes force upon oneself, one is said to suffer, but by the reasoning by which one, when compelled, does something else, one is said to act. Then he illustrates the definition with two examples: one about inanimate things, such as the wind which carries someone by force; the other about animate things, as when some violence is done to us by men, as in the Books of the Maccabees, where the tyrant Antiochus, through his lictors, crowns the pious Jews with ivy and drags them to the sacrifices of Bacchus. But of these more is said near the end of chapter 6, where he treats of the power of the will.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis, quia invitum est duplex, vel purum, de quo supra, vel mixtum, quando scilicet vel metu evitandi alicujus mali, vel spe consequendi alicujus boni, vel alia aliqua necessitate non simplici pliciter quidem violenta, sed valde tamen urgente movemur, ad suspiciendum & agendum aliquid, quod nunquam ageremus, nisi necessitas illa ad-sfet, verbi gratia : quando mercator oborta gravi tempestate, ut suam & aliorum vitam redimat, & naufragium evitet, merces pretiosas in mare ejicit, aut quando viator a latronibus petitus, pollicetur magnam pecuniæ summam, pro redimenda vita, aut si quis proditionem committat, ut amicis gratificari possit, utrum istæ actiones sint voluntariis actionibus, an invitis accensendæ, & ostendit esse mixtas, quæ partim participant de natura invita & actionum, partim spontanearum, sed potius tamen spontaneas seu voluntarias esse dicendas propter tres rationes. 1. Ducitur a tempore, in quo fiunt, quia respectu temporis sunt in arbitrio agentis, ut possint fieri, vel praetermitti, potest enim aliquis in mari merces ejicere, aut non ejicere, proinde hujusmodi actiones sunt voluntariæ. 2. Ducitur a principio, in quo fiunt, nam principium & causa harum actionum sunt in ipso agente non extra agentem.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter: since the involuntary is twofold, either pure, of which we have spoken above, or mixed, namely when we are moved, through fear of avoiding some evil, or hope of obtaining some good, or some other necessity, not simply violent but very urgent, to undertake and do something which we would never do unless that necessity were present. For example: when a merchant, a violent storm having arisen, throws precious goods into the sea to redeem his own life and the lives of others and to avoid shipwreck; or when a traveller, attacked by robbers, promises a large sum of money to ransom his life; or if someone commits betrayal in order to be able to oblige his friends. He asks whether such actions are to be counted among voluntary actions or among involuntary ones. He shows that they are mixed, partly sharing in the nature of the involuntary and partly in that of the spontaneous, but that they are rather to be called spontaneous or voluntary, for three reasons. 1. It is drawn from the time at which they are done: with respect to time they are in the agent's power, so that they may either be done or left undone. For a man can throw goods into the sea or not throw them; therefore actions of this kind are voluntary. 2. It is drawn from the principle from which they are done: for the principle and cause of these actions lie in the agent himself, not outside him.

units.la: 3. Quia ab hujusmodi actionibus provenit laus & vituperium, proinde sunt voluntariæ magis quam invitæ: quod proveniat laus & vituperium ab hisce actionibus, inde patet, quia, ut supra probatum est, cap.4.lib.2. virtus circa difficilia versatur, & si quis in difficilibus bene gerat, laudem meretur, si vero e contra a virtute ad vitium deflectat, meretur vituperium. Ut hæc 3. ratio melius intelligatur, adfert 4. generas actionum mixtarum, (nam & si sing ulares actiones propter varias & infinitas penè circumstantias tias videantur infinitæ, ad quatuor tamen actionum genera reducit) 1. Genus est earum actionum, quæ laudem merentur, quales sunt actiones eorum, qui ob res præclarè gestas, damna, exilia, ignominiam, supplicium & quævis indigna perperi non recusant, qualis fuit Marcus Atilius Regulus qui, ut bene de patria mereret, gravissimos cruciatus apud Pœnos pertulit, testeCic. 1. lib. 1. offic. Talis etiam fuit Ulysses, qui plurima indigna passus est à procis uxoris suæ Penelopes, ut refert Hom. lib. 13. Odyss. Tales etiam fuerunt omnes S. Dei Martyres.
units.tr: 3. Because praise and blame arise from actions of this kind; therefore they are voluntary rather than involuntary. That praise and blame arise from these actions is plain, because, as has been proved above, chapter 4 of book 2, virtue is concerned with difficult things, and if someone acts well in difficult circumstances he deserves praise, but if, on the contrary, he turns aside from virtue to vice, he deserves blame. To make this third reason better understood, he sets out four kinds of mixed actions (for although individual actions seem almost infinite on account of the various and countless circumstances, he reduces them to four kinds). 1. The first kind is of those actions that deserve praise, such as the actions of those who, for the sake of notable achievements, do not refuse losses, exile, disgrace, punishment, or any unworthy suffering. Such was Marcus Atilius Regulus, who, to deserve well of his country, endured the most severe torments among the Carthaginians, as Cicero attests in 1 De Officiis, book 1. Such also was Ulysses, who suffered many indignities from the suitors of his wife Penelope, as Homer relates in Odyssey, book 13. Such too were all the holy martyrs of God.

units.la: Secundum genus actionum est earum, quæ vituperium merentur, quales sunt eorum actiones, qui lucri causa turpe aliquid committunt, verbi gratia: Si quis propter pecuniam sibi legatam in testamento, in foro falsaret, aut si quis, ut vitæ suæ parceret, aut potius ut ocio consuleret, insaniam simularet, quod de Ulysse refert Cic. 3. offic. ille enim, ne cum reliquis Græcorum Ducibus ad bellum Trojanum ire cogeretur, insaniam simulavit.
units.tr: The second kind of action is of those that deserve blame, such as the actions of those who, for the sake of gain, commit some shameful deed; for example, if someone, for money left to him in a will, were to forge documents in the courts, or if someone, to spare his life, or rather to secure his leisure, were to feign madness. This Cicero relates of Ulysses in 3 De Officiis: for he feigned madness so that he would not be compelled to go to the Trojan War with the other Greek leaders.

units.la: Tertium genus actionum est earum, quæ nec laudem, nec vituperium per se proprie merentur, sed veniam & commiserationem, tales sunt actiones eorum, qui propter gravissimos cruciatus & tormenta, aut etiam necessitates, quibus ferendis humana conditio non est par, aliquid grave contra naturam & voluntatem committunt, ut si quis ab hoste compulsus, ad iniquissimas conditiones descendert, quales fuerunt Capitolinites qui occisione & angustiis ab Hannibale inclusi, lora & pelles scutis detractas madere sunt coacti, ut refert Livius dec. 3. lib. 3.
units.tr: The third kind of action is that which deserves neither praise nor blame in itself, but pardon and pity. Such are the actions of those who, under the most severe torments and pains, or even under necessities which human nature is not equal to bearing, commit something grave against their nature and will. For example, if someone, compelled by an enemy, agrees to the most unjust terms, as the men of the Capitol did when they were shut in by Hannibal, reduced to famine and distress, and were forced to boil straps and hides stripped from their shields, as Livy relates dec. 3. lib. 3.

units.la: Quartum genus est earum actionum, quae nec veniam quidem merentur, quales sunt omnes illae actiones, quae sua natura sunt turpes & inhonestae, ut si quis Tyranni alicujus interficiendi gratia, cum uxore ejus consuescat, ut sicaditum sibi patefaciat ad Tyrannum interficiendum. Sic etiam si quis fidem, religionem, patriam aut parentes prodere velit, nullam, inquit Philosophus, meretur veniam.
units.tr: The fourth kind is that of actions which do not even deserve pardon: all those actions which are by their nature base and dishonourable. For example, if someone, in order to kill a tyrant, sleeps with the tyrant's wife so as to open a secret way for himself to the tyrant. Likewise, if someone is willing to betray faith, religion, country or parents, the Philosopher says that such a person deserves no pardon at all.

units.la: Notandum tamen ex his 4. actionum generibus secundum, quod vituperium meretur, & quartum, quod nullum meretur veniam, concedere, & prouno genere actionum vulgo usurpari, & cum sint prave hujusmodi actiones, ideo traduntur, ut ex earum natura cognita, cognoscatur melius natura bonarum actionum, quae virtutem constituunt, cujusmodi sunt illae actiones, quae laudem, veniam & commiserationem merentur.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that of these four kinds of actions the second, which deserves blame, and the fourth, which deserves no pardon, are to be admitted, and are commonly used as one kind of action. Since such actions are wicked, they are handed down so that, once their nature is known, the nature of good actions, which constitute virtue, may be better understood. Such are the actions which deserve praise, pardon and pity.

units.la: Allatis jam 4. generibus actionum mixtarum, duas adserit difficultates, quae in hujusmodi actionibus occurrere solent. 1. Difficultas est in electione: Difficillimum est enim videre, quae sint eligenda, aut fugienda, cum alio vocat honestas aut utilitas, alio tormenta, alio damna. 2. Difficultas est in perseveratione, non enim est levis momenti scire, an debeas progredi an subsistere, propter difficultatem adjunctam hisce actionibus: Sic Cicero saepius & anxie quidem secum & cum Attico amico suo disputat, an in bello civili sequi debeat partes Caesaris, quod videretur utilius, an vero partes Pompeji, quod videretur honestius, & magi e Repub.
units.tr: Having now set out the four kinds of mixed actions, he asserts two difficulties which usually arise in actions of this sort. (1) The first difficulty lies in choice: it is very hard to see what is to be chosen or avoided when honour or advantage calls one way, torments another, and losses another. (2) The second difficulty lies in perseverance: it is of no slight importance to know whether one ought to press on or stand still, because of the difficulty attached to these actions. Thus Cicero often and anxiously debates with himself and with his friend Atticus whether, in the civil war, he ought to follow the party of Caesar, which seemed more useful, or rather that of Pompey, which seemed more honourable, and more so in the interests of the Republic.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis refellit Philosophus opinionem
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter the Philosopher refutes the opinion

units.la: nemi illorum (quos interpretes quidam Cyrenaicos esse putant) qui tertium genus invitarum actionum statuebant, nempe pravas actiones à voluptate & utilitate profectas, hos refellit tribus rationibus; 1. est, fiactiones pravae, quae ob voluptatem & utilitatem fiunt essent invitae, tu omnes nostrae actiones essent invitae, quicquid enim agimus propter voluptatem & utilitatem agimus. 2. Quia omne violentum aut invitum est cum tristitia & maerore conjunctum, at qui ob voluptatem & utilitatem agunt, laetè agunt, proinde apparet tales actiones non esse invitas. 3. Quia sic omnis pravus excusaret pravas suas actiones, culpam in causas externas conjiciens, nempe in utilia & jucunda, à quibus se coactum diceret, quod est ridiculum & nulla excusatione dignum.
units.tr: He refutes, with three arguments, those of them (whom some interpreters think to be the Cyrenaics) who posited a third kind of unwilling actions, namely wicked actions proceeding from pleasure and advantage. (1) If wicked actions done for the sake of pleasure and advantage were unwilling, then all our actions would be unwilling, for whatever we do, we do for the sake of pleasure and advantage. (2) Because everything violent or unwilling is joined with sadness and grief, but those who act for the sake of pleasure or advantage act with joy; so it is clear that such actions are not unwilling. (3) Because in that case every wicked man would excuse his wicked actions by throwing the blame on external causes, namely on what is useful and pleasant, by which he would say he had been compelled, which is ridiculous and deserves no excuse at all.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Actiones spontanea merentur interdum laudem, interdum vituperium, invita interdum veniam, interdum commiseratio nem.
units.tr: 1. Spontaneous actions sometimes deserve praise, sometimes blame; unwilling actions sometimes deserve pardon, sometimes pity.

units.la: 2. Omnis invita actio fit, aut per vim, aut per ignorantiam.
units.tr: 2. Every unwilling action happens either by force or through ignorance.

units.la: 3. Actio, quae fit per vim habet principium externum, & ille, qui cogitat, nihil adjumenti adfert ad actionem producendam.
units.tr: 3. An action which happens by force has an external principle, and the one who is compelled contributes nothing to bringing the action about.

units.la: 4. Quae metu majoris mali fiunt, aut boni alicuius asse-quendi gratia, sunt magis spontanea actiones quam invita.
units.tr: 4. Those things done through fear of a greater evil, or for the sake of obtaining some good, are more spontaneous actions than unwilling ones.

units.la: 5. Turpia perpetrare levis lucelli gratia, summa est amentia.
units.tr: 5. To commit base deeds for the sake of a small gain is the height of madness.

units.la: 6. Quaedam sunt actiones mixta, quae nullam omnino merentur veniam. 7. Qua
units.tr: 6. Some actions are mixed, and deserve no pardon at all. 7. Which

units.la: 7. Quæ à voluptate aut utilitate proficiscuntur actiones, non sunt invitæ.
units.tr: 7. Actions which proceed from pleasure or advantage are not unwilling.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: Doubts.

units.la: I. Quæritur: cur Philosophus diviserit omnes actiones invitas, in actiones quæ fiunt per vim aut per ignorantiam, & non in plures species? Resp. Hoc ideo fit, quia omnis actio, quæ virtutem vel constituit vel destruit, est motus quidam animæ appetitivæ: nam ab appetitu tanquam principio proficiscitur, ut ideo aliquid sponte fiat, duo hæc requiruntur principia, appetitus nempe & cognitio: Nam ad id, quod sponte fieri debet, oportet appetitum fieri, & cognitionem præcedere appetitum. Unde Poëta dixit:
units.tr: I. Question: Why did the Philosopher divide all involuntary actions into those that happen through force or through ignorance, and not into more kinds? Answer: This is done because every action that either establishes or destroys virtue is a certain movement of the appetitive soul, for it proceeds from appetite as from its principle. So that something may be done willingly, two principles are required, namely appetite and knowledge. For what ought to be done willingly must be desired, and knowledge must precede the desire. Hence the poet said:

units.la: Ignoti nulla Cupido.
units.tr: No desire for the unknown.

units.la: Qui nisi cognitio animi præcedit, appetitus nullam actionem intendit: quando igitur vel impeditur appetitus, quod vi fit, vel abest cognitio, ǫ per ignorantiam fit. Omnis actio, quæ ab appetitu profluit impedito vel nesciente, fit vel per vim vel per ignorantiam, proinde non immerito divisit actiones invitas in eas, quæ fiunt per vim & per ignorantiam.
units.tr: Unless knowledge of the mind comes first, appetite aims at no action. So when appetite is either hindered, which happens by force, or knowledge is absent, which happens through ignorance. Every action that flows from appetite that is either hindered or unaware happens either by force or through ignorance. Therefore he not unreasonably divided involuntary actions into those done by force and those done through ignorance.

units.la: II. Quæritur: An jure diviserit actiones omnes in Voluntarias & Mixtas, cum nulla actiones videntur esse voluntaria, quia si quæ esset actio voluntaria, esset actio mali, sed actio mali non est voluntaria. Ergo nulla. Major probatur ex lib. 3. hujus operis, cap. 8. ubi dicit Philosophus, actiones pravæ sunt maximè voluntariæ, & rationem addit, quia natura sumus proniores in malum quam in bonum. Minor probatur ex cap. 2. hujus lib. ubi dicit Philosophus, actiones improborum non esse voluntarias, & ratio est, quia per ignorantiam, inquit, fiunt, & addit paulò post, ignorant omnes improimprobi, quasint sequenda, quæ fugienda? Resp. Igno-rantia est duplex; alia pura negationis, alia prauæ dispositionis. Ignorantia pura negationis facit actionem inuitam seu inuoluntariam: agens enim inscius & ignorans ruit in malum. At ignorantia prauæ dispositionis facit actionem voluntariam, quia agens prauæ actioni præbet assensum. Cum igitur dicit Philosophus, ignorant improbi, quid fit faciendum, intelligit ignorantiam illam crassam prauæ dispositionis, qua fascinati homines, contumaciter volunt in ignorantiæ tenebris versari.
units.tr: II. Question: Whether he rightly divided all actions into voluntary and mixed, since no action seems to be voluntary. For if some action were voluntary, it would be an action of evil, but an action of evil is not voluntary; therefore none is. The major premise is proved from book 3 of this work, chapter 8, where the Philosopher says that wicked actions are most voluntary, and he gives the reason: we are by nature more prone to evil than to good. The minor premise is proved from chapter 2 of this book, where the Philosopher says that the actions of the wicked are not voluntary, and the reason is, he says, that they are done through ignorance; and he adds shortly after, all the wicked are ignorant what things are to be pursued and what avoided? Answer: Ignorance is twofold: one is of pure negation, the other of a depraved disposition. Ignorance of pure negation makes an action involuntary or unwilling, for the agent, unaware and ignorant, rushes into evil. But ignorance of depraved disposition makes an action voluntary, because the agent gives assent to the depraved action. Therefore when the Philosopher says the wicked are ignorant what must be done, he means that gross ignorance of depraved disposition, by which men, bewitched, obstinately choose to dwell in the darkness of ignorance.

units.la: III. Quæritur: An, quæ metu maioris malifiunt, ut cum tempestate oborta ejiciuntur merces, sint voluntaria actionibus annumeranda, quod vult Philosophus, an potius inuitæ actiones sint dicenda, & posterius probatur hac ratione, in quibus non est promta ac parata voluntas, ea actiones non sunt voluntaria dicenda; at in iis, quæ metu fiunt, non est promta & parata voluntas, remoto enim metu non fierent omnino, proinde videntur inuitæ magis quam voluntariæ?
units.tr: III. Question: Whether those actions done through fear of a greater evil, as when wares are thrown overboard because a storm has arisen, should be counted among voluntary actions, as the Philosopher wills, or should rather be called involuntary. The latter is proved by this reasoning: actions in which the will is not ready and prepared are not to be called voluntary; but in those done through fear the will is not ready and prepared, for if the fear were removed they would not be done at all; therefore they seem more involuntary than voluntary?

units.la: Resp. A Philosopho vocantur ejusmodi actiones mixtæ, quæ ratione principii externi impellentis videntur inuitæ, nam nisi necessitas aliqua externa urgeret, appetitus ad hanc actionem producendam non impelleretur; at verò ratione principii interni proximi voluntatis nempe, sunt voluntariæ, quia voluntas, qua voluntas, non potest cogi. Proinde illa major non valet, in quibus non est promta & parata voluntas, ea fiunt inuitæ, nam voluntas, quo ad intra, semper est promta & parata, licet quo ad extra necessitatem quandam impellentem videatur habere adjunctam. Ut melius intelligantur na-tura tura actionis invitæ, solet vulgò distingui in violentam & imprudentem. Violenta dicitur, quæ vi aliqua sit, vim generaliter hîc accipe, ut cujus necessitati urgenti competat, & duplex constituitur, vel absolutè violenta vel mixta. Absolutè violenta dicitur actio, cujus principium extrinsecus hujusmodi adhibetur, ad quam actionem nihil adjuméti adferet is, qui agit aut patitur, ut in textu hîc dicitur. Actio mixta definitur, cujus principium, cum in nostra sit potestate, & res per se mala videatur, ideoq; nec eligenda, respectu verò circumstantiarum bona & eligenda censetur. Actiones has mixtas in quatuor genera dividit Aristoteles, ut in textu videre licet. Verùm hîc tria ista disquirenda veniunt, cum Philosophus actiones partim ex proprietatibus, partim ex principiis, à quibus fluunt, varie dividat, & actiones quidem invitas in invitas, per vim & per ignorantiam quæri possunt ista tria: 1. An bona intentio reddat actionem bonam? 2. An actio, quæ absolutè & per se mala est, pro ratione circumstantiarum possit fieri & censeri bona? Et 3. An ex duobus malis minus sit eligendum? Quod ad primam attinet quæstionem, disceptatur in utramque partem. Nam pro thesi negante faciunt hæ rationes: 1. Quia experientia testatur, finem posse esse bonum, cum tamen actio in se sit mala, ut si quis eleemosynæ dandæ gratia aliis sua bona sive clam sive vi eripiat. 2. Quia bonitas actionis æstimatur potius ex bonitate σκοπῶν, quam ex bonitate finis, quia vulgò examinari solent actiones ex animo agentis. At pro thesi affirmante plures adduci solent rationes: 1. Quia actiones vulgò finis respectu inter ter se distingui solent. 2. Quia finis dicitur bonitatem conciliare mediis, ut lib. 2. Metaph. c. 2 docetur. Nam media ex suo fine naturam & mensuram accipiunt. 3. Quia qui in constituendo fine errat, etiam in mediis ad finem ordinatis errat. 4. Quia intentio mala semper reddit actionem malam. Ergo ex vi contrariorum intentio bona actionem reddet bonam. Pro huius determinatione quaestionis sciendum, etsi bona intentio non semper reddat actionem bonam vere, apparenter tamen bonam reddere solet. Proin ad argumenta in utramque partem allata sic responderi potest: 1. Actionem in se malam dici posse apparenter bonam, respectu finis boni. 2. Bonitatem actionis aliam esse absolutam, aliam respectivam, eamque vel veram vel apparentem. Licet igitur respectiva & apparens bonitas actionis ex bonitate finis aestimetur, de absoluta tamen non semper est verum. 3. Actiones sine quidem discernuntur, sed non semper secundum qualitatem moralem, ita ut illae sint judicandae bonae, quae finem sibi bonum habent propositum. 4. Finem conciliare mediis bonitatem, si non absolutam & veram, saltem respectivam & apparentem. 5. Rectam finis constitutionem non semper recte formare media, nisi illa constitutio a virtute proficiscatur, quod 5. cap. huius lib. praeclare testatur. 6. Non esse parem rationem intentionis malae & bonae, respectu mediorum. Illa enim semper facit media mala, haec vero non semper facit media bona, cum non tantum per honesta & licita, sed etiam per turpia & illicita media quis ad bonum finem tendere possit. Secunda quæstio etiam disceptatur pro & contra. Pro thesi affirmante afferuntur rationes: 1. In modum exemp-li. Projectio mercium in mare coorta gravi & periculosa tempestate absolute & per se est mala, & tamen à mercatore sæpe tanquam bonum medium eligitur ad vitandum naufragium & conservandam vitam. 2. Sectio & combustio alicujus membri, licet per se sit mala, ab ægroto tamen interdum eligere ad curandum morbum & recipiendam sanitatem. Et ratio hinc pendet, quia minus malum comparatum cum majori malo, obtinet rationem boni. Pro negativa parte objicitur regula Philosophorum, quæ statuit, aliquid quod per se est tale, nec per se, nec per accidens posse reddi non tale, seu oppositam obtinere conditionem & naturam. Quæstio hæc deciditur, hoc modo, nempe affirmativam partem esse veram de illo genere mali, quod noxium dicitur & molestum, non autem de eo, quod turpe existit ac inhonestum, præsertim si ut tale consideretur. Quod igitur ad rationem pro negativa parte allatam respondetur: quæ absolute sunt mala, (scilicet in genere noxiorum & molestorum) semper esse mala in suo definito gradu, & nunquam ratione sui esse absolute eligenda, tamen comparata cum aliis, minus mala & sic bona dici posse. Philosophorum vero regula prius allata de absolutis consideran debet, non vero de his, quæ in relatione & comparatione sunt posita. Hæc enim per varias comparationes variis modis judicari possunt, cum tamen absolute semper mala sint, siquidem absolute malum & alicui bonum, inter se non pugnant. At tertiam quæstionem rerespondetur per distinctionem. Nam licet habeatur hoc apud Philosophum 5. Nicom.cap.7. non simpliciter iumi debet, sed tantum secundū quid, nempe de malis noxiis & molestiis, quorum electio liberae esse solet, nec honestati repugnat. Inter duo enim mala turpia seu inhonesta neutrum est eligendum, nec minus, nec minus, quod praeclarè docet hoc ipso cap. 1. Philosophus. Simile inter duo mala poenae, quorum optio innocenti offertur neutrum est eligendum, si um conscientia & honestate pugnant, & divinis legibus adversentur, vel etiam ne in criminis suspicionem veniamus. Hinc princeps Condaeus cum ei à Carolo IX. Galliarum Rege optio daretur, utrum Missam eligere, aut morte aut carcerem perpetuum, prudenter respondit: Primum Deo juvante, nunquam eligam, duo reliqua Regis arbitrio permitto, sic tamen ut bene sperem, Deum hac quoque suaa paterna providentia gubernaturum. Sciebat enim malum turpe & impium simpliciter esse repudiandum. Ex malis autem poenae sibi innocenti neutrum eligendum, ne sceleris aut criminis suspicione se onerarec.
units.tr: Answer: The Philosopher calls such actions mixed; by reason of an external impelling principle they seem involuntary, for unless some external necessity pressed, appetite would not be driven to produce this action. But by reason of the internal and proximate principle, namely the will, they are voluntary, because the will, as will, cannot be compelled. Therefore that major premise does not hold: actions in which the will is not ready and prepared are not done unwillingly, for the will, as regards what is within, is always ready and prepared, even though as regards what is outside it may seem to have some pressing necessity attached to it. To understand the nature of involuntary action better, it is commonly distinguished into violent and imprudent. An action is called violent if it is done by some force (here take "force" in a general sense, as that to which urgent necessity belongs), and violence is of two kinds: either absolutely violent or mixed. An action is called absolutely violent when its principle is applied from outside in such a way that the agent or the one suffering adds nothing to it, as is said here in the text. A mixed action is defined as one whose principle, since it lies within our power, and the thing itself seems evil and therefore not to be chosen, is nevertheless judged good and to be chosen with respect to the circumstances. Aristotle divides these mixed actions into four kinds, as may be seen in the text. But here three questions come up for inquiry, since the Philosopher divides actions in various ways, partly according to their properties and partly according to the principles from which they flow, and since involuntary actions can be sorted into those done by force and those done through ignorance. These three questions are: 1. Does a good intention make an action good? 2. Can an action that is absolutely and in itself evil be done and judged good, according to the circumstances? 3. Of two evils, is the lesser to be chosen? As to the first question, it is disputed on both sides. For the thesis that denies it, these arguments are offered: 1. Experience shows that an end can be good while the action itself is evil, as when someone seizes another's goods, secretly or by force, for the sake of giving alms. 2. The goodness of an action is judged rather by the goodness of its aim (skopos) than by the goodness of its end, since actions are usually examined by the mind of the agent. But for the affirmative thesis several arguments are usually brought forward: 1. Actions are commonly distinguished among themselves by their relation to their end. 2. The end is said to lend goodness to the means, as is taught in book 2 of the Metaphysics, chapter 2, for means take their nature and measure from their end. 3. Whoever errs in setting the end also errs in the means ordered to that end. 4. A bad intention always makes an action bad; therefore, by the force of contraries, a good intention will make an action good. To determine this question, it should be understood that although a good intention does not always make an action truly good, it usually makes it apparently good. Accordingly, the arguments on both sides may be answered thus: 1. An action evil in itself may be apparently good with respect to a good end. 2. The goodness of an action is of two kinds: absolute and relative, and the relative is either true or apparent. Although relative and apparent goodness of an action is judged by the goodness of the end, this is not always true of absolute goodness. 3. Actions are indeed distinguished by their ends, but not always according to moral quality, so that those are to be judged good which have a good end in view. 4. The end lends goodness to the means, if not absolute and true goodness, at least relative and apparent goodness. 5. A right constitution of the end does not always rightly shape the means, unless that constitution proceeds from virtue, as the fifth chapter of this book bears splendid witness. 6. The case of an evil intention and that of a good intention are not on a par with respect to means. The former always makes the means evil, but the latter does not always make them good, since one may aim at a good end not only through honourable and lawful means but also through shameful and unlawful ones. The second question too is disputed for and against. For the affirmative thesis these reasons are given: 1. By way of example: the throwing of wares into the sea when a grave and dangerous storm has arisen is absolutely and in itself evil, and yet the merchant often chooses it as a good means of avoiding shipwreck and preserving his life. 2. The cutting off and cauterising of a limb, although evil in itself, is sometimes chosen by a sick man to cure his illness and recover his health. And the reason depends on this: a lesser evil, compared with a greater evil, takes on the character of a good. Against the negative side the rule of the philosophers is objected, which lays down that what is by itself such a thing cannot by itself or by accident be made not such, or obtain the opposite condition and nature. This question is decided as follows: the affirmative side is true of that kind of evil which is called harmful and troublesome, but not of that which is base and dishonourable, especially when it is considered as such. Therefore, as to the reason brought for the negative side: things that are absolutely evil (namely in the class of harmful and troublesome things) are always evil at their own defined degree and are never by their nature to be chosen absolutely; yet, compared with others, they can be called less evil and so good. But the rule of the philosophers mentioned earlier must be understood of absolute things, not of those which are placed in relation and comparison. For these can be judged in various ways by various comparisons, although they are always absolutely evil, since what is absolutely evil and good to someone are not mutually opposed. The third question is answered by a distinction. For although it is held by the Philosopher in book 5 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 7, that this must not be taken simply, but only in a certain respect, namely of harmful and troublesome evils, whose choice is usually free and does not conflict with honour. Between two base or dishonourable evils neither is to be chosen, nor is one less so than the other, as the Philosopher teaches admirably in chapter 1 of this same book. Similarly, between two penalties offered to an innocent man as an option, neither is to be chosen if they conflict with conscience and honour and oppose the divine laws, or even to avoid falling under suspicion of crime. Hence when the prince Condé was offered by Charles IX, King of France, the choice of either attending Mass, or death, or perpetual imprisonment, he prudently replied: The first I will never choose, by God's help; the other two I leave to the King's decision, yet in such a way that I hope well that God will govern these too by his fatherly providence. For he knew that what is base and impious is to be rejected outright. But among penalties, an innocent man should choose neither, lest he burden himself with the suspicion of wickedness or crime.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: EGit in primo capite, de primo membro, invitae actionis, nempe de invito per vim, secundo hoc capite agit de invito per ignorantiam. Partes capitis sunt tres. In prima ostendit non omne, quod fit per ignorantiam facere actionem invitam. In secunda parte distinguit inter agere per ignorantiam & agere ignoranter. In tertia distinguit ignorantiam, in universalem lem & particularem,& ostendit,quæ ignorantia faciat actionem invitam,& quæ non.
