units.tr: In the first chapter he dealt with the first kind of involuntary action, namely involuntary action through force. In this second chapter he deals with involuntary action through ignorance. The chapter has three parts. In the first he shows that not everything done through ignorance is an involuntary action. In the second part he distinguishes between acting through ignorance and acting in ignorance. In the third he distinguishes ignorance into universal and particular, and shows which ignorance makes an action involuntary and which does not.

units.la: In prima igitur parte capitis dicit, non omnis ignorantia facit actionem invitam, quia est quædam ignorantia, quam sequitur pœnitentia & dolor,& ista facit actionem invitam,qualis fuit actio Laconis cujusdam, de quo Herodotus lib. 1. Qui Cræsi Lydorum Regis filium pro apro in venatione interfecit. Quædam etiam est ignorantia,quam non sequitur dolor & pœnitentia, & talis actio dicitur non volens aut non voluntaria: qualis fuit Mutii Scevolæ actio, qui scribam Porcennæ, Regis Hetruscorum pro Rege interfecit, per ignorantiam quidem,sed tamen istam ignorantiam non est secutus dolor,nec impœnitentia, teste Liv. lib.2.Dec. 1. plura vide apud Keckerm. in præcognitis Ethicis pag. 51. Sciendum est ignorantiam vulgò distingui in ignorantiam juris & facti, ignorantia juris dicitur quando ignoratur aliquid recte- ne sive juste an injuste fiat,& hæc rursus dividitur in ignorantiam juris universalis vel particularis. Ignorantia juris universalis est, qua ignorantur præcepta communia justi & injusti,atque adeo quæ omnes homines scire poterant & debebant, & hæc ignorantia non excusat factum agentis, cum hujus cognitio omnibus naturali instinctu & quotidiana praxi inesse debeat. Ignorantia juris particularis, est qua ignoratur speciale aliquod, & extraordinarium edictum aut mandatum promulgatum, qui leges condendi potestatem habent,& hæc ignorantia excusat ad tempus,non vero semper ac perpetuo. Plerique Ethici nimis generaliter de ignorantia juris loquuntur, & absolutam hanc sententiam imponunt, quod ignorantia juris non excuser, cum tamen necessario distinguendum sit inter ignorantiam juris universalis, & juris particularis, de qua distinctione monet Martyr ad cap. 13 lib. 1. Samuelis ubi disputat, an Jonathan filius Saulis excusandus fuerit, dum comedit mel eo die, quo Rex pater ejus, praeceperat publico edicto, ab omni cibo & potu esse abstinendum. Et concludit Jonathanem esse excusandum duplici ratione. 1. Quia valde fessus & famelicus impellebatur ad capiendum aliquid cibi necessitate naturae, & deinde, quia ignorantia ista Jonathae contigit, ut mel gustaret, non fuit ignorantia juris universalis, sed particularis tantum. Ideo addit Martyr scribitur in Autenticis, quaedam decreta ante certum tempus vim suam non obtinere, & paulo post, ignorantia autem juris communis, etsi non excuset in totum, excusat tamen ex parte. Ignorantia fit dicitur, quando non ignoramus, an honeste vel inhoneste aliquid fiat, sed ignoramus facti circumstantias. Addit vero Philosophus rationem hic, quare hae circumstantiae reddant factum invitum, quia voluntas agentis per harum ignorantiam impeditur, aliud enim agere volebat quam egit.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter he says that not all ignorance makes an action involuntary. There is a kind of ignorance that is followed by regret and sorrow, and this kind does make an action involuntary, as was the action of a certain Spartan, of whom Herodotus writes in book 1, who killed Croesus's son, king of the Lydians, while hunting, thinking him a boar. There is also a kind of ignorance that is not followed by sorrow or repentance, and an action of this kind is called non-willing or non-voluntary. Such was the action of Mucius Scaevola, who killed the secretary of Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, instead of the king. He did this through ignorance, but this ignorance was not followed by sorrow or remorse, as Livy, book 2, Decade 1 attests. See more in Keckermann, Praecognita Ethica, p. 51. It should be noted that ignorance is commonly divided into ignorance of law and ignorance of fact. Ignorance of law is when one does not know whether something is done rightly or justly or unjustly, and this in turn is divided into universal and particular ignorance of law. Universal ignorance of law is ignorance of the common precepts of just and unjust, which all men could and ought to know. This ignorance does not excuse the agent's deed, since knowledge of these precepts should be present in everyone by natural instinct and daily practice. Particular ignorance of law is ignorance of some special and extraordinary edict or command that has been promulgated by those who have the power to make laws. This ignorance excuses for a time, but not always and permanently. Most ethicists speak of ignorance of law too generally, and they lay down this absolute rule, that ignorance of law does not excuse. Yet it is necessary to distinguish between universal and particular ignorance of law, as Martyr reminds us on chapter 13 of 1 Samuel, where he discusses whether Jonathan, son of Saul, should be excused for eating honey on that day when his father the king had commanded by public edict that all food and drink be abstained from. He concludes that Jonathan should be excused for two reasons. 1. Because, being very weary and hungry, he was driven by the necessity of nature to take some food. 2. Because Jonathan's ignorance, which led him to taste the honey, was not universal ignorance of law but only particular. Martyr therefore adds that it is written in the Authentics that certain decrees do not take effect until a certain time; and shortly after, that ignorance of common law, although it does not excuse altogether, excuses in part. Ignorance of fact is said to be when we do not doubt whether something is done honourably or dishonourably, but do not know the circumstances of the deed. The Philosopher gives the reason here why these circumstances make the deed involuntary: the agent's will is hindered by ignorance of them, for he was wishing to do one thing other than what he did.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis distinguit inter agere per ignorantiam & agere ignoranter; agere per ignorantiam est ita agere, ut ignorantia sit sola causa istius malae actionis: nam si notitia adfuisset, talem actionem omnem non produxisset agens, exemplum e multis poterit esse in Jacobo Patriarcha, qui pro Rachele duxit Leam in uxorem, deceptus a socero suo Genesis. nef.19. Ignoranter ag t, qui etiam fi in actione producenda ignarus sit, tamen ignorantia non est causa istius pravae actionis, sed aliquid al ud quod istam ignorantiam induxit, ut si quis per ebrietatem aut periram vel proximu vel seipsum interficiat, quod de Leomade Lacedaemonio refert Aristoteles in problem. sect 31 qui per ebrietatem sibi ipsi manus intulit, ignorantia non fuit causa istius malae actionis, sed ebrietas, quae istam ignorantiam induxit, & ideo Pittacus, ex septem Graeciae sapientibus unus, legem tulit sapientem, ut qui ebrii peccassent, majori poena afficerentur, quam si sobrii fuissent, teste Aristotele lib.2. Polit.cap.10. sic si quis periram aliquem interficiat, quod de Alexandro Magno, Clitum interficiente refert Q. Curtius lib. 8. de rebus gestis Alexandri Magni, ignorantia non est causa istius caedis, sed ira, quae istam ignorantiam induxit.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he distinguishes between acting through ignorance and acting in ignorance. To act through ignorance is to act in such a way that ignorance is the sole cause of that bad action. For if knowledge had been present, the agent would not have produced such an action at all. An example out of many may be Jacob the Patriarch, who took Leah as wife in place of Rachel, having been deceived by his father-in-law, Genesis 29. He acts in ignorance who, although he is ignorant while producing the action, nevertheless is not moved to that wicked action by ignorance, but by something else which brought about that ignorance. For example, if someone through drunkenness or anger kills either a neighbour or himself. Aristotle reports this of Leomas the Spartan, in Problems, section 31, who laid violent hands on himself through drunkenness. Ignorance was not the cause of that evil action, but drunkenness, which brought about that ignorance. For this reason Pittacus, one of the seven wise men of Greece, passed a wise law that those who sinned while drunk should be punished more severely than if they had been sober, as Aristotle attests in Politics, book 2, chapter 10. Likewise, if someone kills another through anger, as Quintus Curtius reports of Alexander the Great, who killed Clitus, in book 8 of his History of Alexander the Great, then ignorance is not the cause of that killing, but anger, which brought about that ignorance.

units.la: Cur vero distinguat inter ignoranter agere & per ignorantiam duas adfert rationes. 1. Quia ebrius & iratus agunt non per ignorantiam, sed per iram & ebrietatem: At ebrius & iratus agunt ignoranter, ira enim & ebrietate impediti ignorant, quid agant: ergo non omnis, qui agit, ignoranter agit per ignorantiam. 2. Quia non omnis malus qui malum agit, agit per ignorantiam. Sic enim mereret veniam & commiserationem, cujus contrarium supra ostendit. Attamen omnis malus, qui malum agit, ignorans agit, ignorat enim verum finem propter quem debeat agere, quia corruptum est judicium intellectus ipsius.
units.tr: He gives two reasons why he distinguishes between acting in ignorance and acting through ignorance. 1. Because a drunk man and an angry man act not through ignorance but through anger and drunkenness. But a drunk man and an angry man act in ignorance, for, hindered by anger and drunkenness, they do not know what they are doing. Therefore not everyone who acts in ignorance acts through ignorance. 2. Because not everyone who does evil acts through ignorance. For if that were so, he would deserve pardon and pity, the opposite of which he has shown above. Yet every wicked man who does evil acts in ignorance, for he does not know the true end for which he ought to act, because the judgment of his intellect is corrupted.

units.la: In tertia parte capituli distinguit ignorantiam, in universalem & particularem, & dicit craflam seu supi-nam illam ignorantiam, quę diciturnuiversalis non facere actionem invitā, sed potius esse causam malitiæ: nam ignorantia non tam est in causa, quā perversa voluntas agentis, quia agens universalia principia de honesto & turpi, de justo & injusto scire poterat & debebat si voluisset, nisi istam ignorantiam de industria affectasset: nam si ignorantia universalis faceret actionem invitam, nullus malus posset puniri, quia prætenderet istam ignorantiam, & tamen contrarium ratio & experientia docet. Ista ignorantia universalis aggravat factum seu peccatum, quia provenit vel ex socordia, ut in otiosis, vel ex φιλαυτία, ut in superbis, vel ex malitia, ut in desperatis. At verò ignorantia particularis, sive facti facit actionem invitam, & proinde meretur veniam, quia est ignorantia particularium circumstantiarum: nam accidere possunt casus hujusmodi, ut quis omnes circumstantias particulares, quæ ad actionem aliquam producendam requiruntur, scire non posset, & quia istæ circumstantiæ sunt maximi momenti, ideo illas recensset Aristoteles, ut melius cognitæ & explicatæ habeantur: Circumstantiæ hæ sunt septem, quæ vulgari hoc versiculo continentur: Quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quomodo, quando.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he distinguishes ignorance into universal and particular, and says that that gross or supine ignorance, which is called universal, does not make an action involuntary but rather is the cause of wickedness. For the ignorance is not so much the cause as the perverse will of the agent, since the agent could and should have known the universal principles of the honourable and the shameful, and of the just and the unjust, had he wished, unless he had deliberately aimed at that ignorance. For if universal ignorance made an action involuntary, no wicked man could be punished, since he would plead this ignorance; yet reason and experience teach the contrary. This universal ignorance aggravates the deed or sin, because it arises either from carelessness, as in idle people, or from self-love [φιλαυτία], as in the proud, or from malice, as in the desperate. But particular ignorance, that is, ignorance of fact, makes an action involuntary, and therefore deserves pardon, because it is ignorance of particular circumstances. For cases of this kind can occur, so that someone could not know all the particular circumstances that are required for producing a given action. And because these circumstances are of the greatest importance, Aristotle lists them, so that they may be better known and explained. These circumstances are seven, contained in this common little verse: Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when.

units.la: Nisi quod omiserit unam, nempe circa quid. Ratio harum circumstantiarum hæc reddi poterit. In omni actione vel quærimus de causis actionis, vel de natura ipsius actionis. Si causas respicimus, tunc quæritur de causa principali efficiente, & sic occurrit circumstantia Quis, vel de instrumentali causa, dicitur, quo instrumento, quibus auxilio, vel de materali causa, & dicitur, circa quid, vel de finali, & dicitur, cuius gratia, seu cur; vel respicimus naturam ipsius actionis, & tunc dicitur, quid, vel attendimus ad mensuram actionis, & tunc quaeritur de loco & tempore in quo actio fit, vel de mensura modi, & tunc quaeritur, quomodo fiat, sensim, an vehementer, parum, an nimium, quam oportet fit? Alii recentiores octo circumstantias particularium actionum, quarum quatuor priores vocant magis principales, ut sunt: Finis, objectum, agens & actio, alias quatuor minus principales, ut sunt locus, tempus, instrumentum & modus, de quibus ut Keckermann pag. 50 sqq. Ethic. Sed hic cum Philosopho conveniunt.
units.tr: Except that he has omitted one, namely "about what." The reason for these circumstances can be stated thus. In every action we ask either about the causes of the action or about the nature of the action itself. If we look to causes, then we ask about the principal efficient cause, and so the circumstance "who" arises; or about the instrumental cause, which is called "by what instrument, by what aid"; or about the material cause, which is called "about what"; or about the final cause, which is called "for whose sake," or "why." Or we look to the nature of the action itself, and then it is called "what." Or we attend to the measure of the action, and then we ask about the place and time in which the action is done; or about the measure of manner, and then we ask how it is done: gently or vehemently, little or much, or as it ought to be done. Other more recent writers count eight circumstances of particular actions, of which the first four they call more principal, namely: end, object, agent and act; and four less principal, namely place, time, instrument and manner. On these see Keckermann, Ethics, pp. 50ff. But here they agree with the Philosopher.

units.la: Has omnes circumstantias particulares colligi(?) sive sumitas, etsi aliquas ignorare quis possit: distributive sumitas, nemo sane nentis, inquit Philosophus, ignorabit. Nam utut quisque alias omnes circumstantias ignoraverit, seipsum tamen ignorare non poterit, quia agens est. Exempla harum circumstantiarum varia adfert Philosophus: & 1. de ci cumstantia quid seu de facto, ut de Æschylo Tragico Poeta, qui in Tragoedia quadam, quam vocavit Orgia, evulgavit mysteria Cereris, quae nefas erat enunciare, & quia ignoravit haec esse mysteria, veniam facti ab Areopagitis meruit. De circumstantia causae finalis, seu cujus gratia tale adfert exemplum, si quis sanitatis tuendae gratia, venam incidat, aut pharmacum sumat, & contrarius sequatur effectus, nempe morbus, aut mors. De objecto aut de circumstantia circa quid, exemplum est de Merope, Polybii Corinthiorum Regis uxore, quæ filium suum interficere voluit, hostem aut sicarium esse rata. Sic etiam de circumstantia, quo instrumento, si quis ferire alium velit hasta, quam putabat esse obtusam, cum tamen sit acuta & ferrea cuspide, aut si quis lapide alterum interficiat, ratus esse pumicem, & sic de aliis. Tandem vero concludit, si quis unam aliquam ex supra dictis circumstantiis ignoraverit, maximè vero circumstantiam, circa quid, seu objectum & finem, seu cujus gratia, si iltam ignorantiam sequatur pœnitentia & dolor, actionem ab ejusmodi ignorantia profectam esse invitam, & proinde merere veniam, cum histamen duabus conditionibus, ut ignorantia ista circumstantiarum fraude careat & dolo, & secundo ne sit accersita, aut affectata, sic enim in eandem pœnam agens incurrit, in quam incurrere solent peccantes per ignorantiam universalem.
units.tr: These particular circumstances, whether they are all collected or taken together, though someone may be ignorant of some of them. Taken distributively, says the Philosopher, no one of sound mind will be ignorant of them all. For however much a person may be ignorant of all the other circumstances, he cannot be ignorant of himself, because he is the agent. The Philosopher gives various examples of these circumstances. As to the first, what, or the fact, he gives Aeschylus the tragic poet, who in a certain tragedy, which he called Orgia, made public the mysteries of Ceres, which it was unlawful to disclose. Because he did not know these were mysteries, he obtained pardon for the deed from the Areopagites. As to the circumstance of the final cause, or for the sake of which, he gives this example: if someone opens a vein or takes a medicine to preserve his health, and the opposite effect follows, namely sickness or death. As to the object, or the circumstance concerning what, the example is Merope, the wife of Polybus, king of the Corinthians, who wanted to kill her own son, supposing him to be an enemy or an assassin. Likewise as to the circumstance of the instrument by which, if someone wishes to strike another with a spear that he thinks is blunt, though it is sharp and has an iron point; or if someone kills another with a stone, supposing it to be pumice, and so on for the others. Finally he concludes that if someone is ignorant of any one of the circumstances mentioned above, and especially the circumstance concerning what, that is, the object and the end, or for the sake of which, and if this ignorance is followed by repentance and grief, then the action arising from such ignorance is involuntary, and therefore deserves pardon. Yet this holds on two conditions: first, that the ignorance of the circumstances be free of deceit and trickery; and secondly, that it not be sought out or feigned. For in that case the agent incurs the same punishment that those who sin through universal ignorance usually incur.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Non omnis ignorantia facit actionem invitam, sed quam sequitur pœnitentia & dolor.
units.tr: 1. Not every ignorance makes an action involuntary, but only that which is followed by repentance and grief.

units.la: 2. Aliud est per ignorantiam agere, aliud ignoranter.
units.tr: 2. It is one thing to act through ignorance, another to act in ignorance.

units.la: 3. Eorius sicut & ratus non agit per ignorantiam, ignoranstamen agit.
units.tr: 3. The one who errs, like the one who is mistaken, does not act through ignorance, yet he does act in ignorance.

units.la: 4. Ignorantia universalis, quia est cum proaresi conjuncta, non meretur veniam.
units.tr: 4. Universal ignorance, because it is joined with deliberate choice, does not merit pardon.

units.la: 5. Particularis autem, quia est ignorantia quarundam circumstantiarum, veniam meretur.
units.tr: 5. Particular ignorance, however, because it is ignorance of certain circumstances, merits pardon.

units.la: 6. Fieri non potest, ut quis omnes circumstantias, quæ ad actionem producendam concurrunt, ignoret.
units.tr: 6. It cannot happen that someone is ignorant of all the circumstances that concur in producing an action.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: 1. Quæritur: An verum sit, quod dicit Philosophus, ignorangnorantiam universalem non mereri veniam, cum tamen sit ignorantia quaedam universalis, qua meretur veniam, verbi gratia: Si quis peccet contra leges universales alicujus Regni aut Provinciae, si probet, se non de industria, sed ignorantia quadam peccasse, meretur interdum veniam. Talefuit actum Jonathanis filii Saulis. 1. Sam. 14. Qui cum Rex Saulis leges de jejunio praescripsisset toti populo, jejunium tamen violavit & veniam promeruit? Resp. Aliud esse universale simpliciter, aliud secundum quid, cum dicit Aristoteles ignorantiam universalem non excusare. Intelligit ignorantiam illam simpliciter universalem, quae est fundata super leges naturae & gentium. Ignorantia universalis, secundum quid, dicitur ea, quae etsi sit universalis respectu alicujus regni aut regionis, tamen se non extendit ad omnia, & ejusmodi ignorantia consideratur, vel ante intimationem legum, ut loquuntur JCti, vel post intimationem. Haec ignorantia ante intimationem meretur quidem veniam: at vero post intimationem nullam meretur. Proinde illa ignorantia Jonathanis, quia erat ante intimationem factam universis & singulis, jure debebat promerere veniam, maxime vero cum nullum detrimentum attulisset Reipub.
units.tr: 1. The question is: whether it is true, as the Philosopher says, that universal ignorance does not merit pardon, when there is nonetheless a certain universal ignorance that does merit pardon. For example, if someone sins against the universal laws of some kingdom or province, and proves that he sinned not from deliberate purpose but from a certain ignorance, he sometimes merits pardon. Such was the deed of Jonathan, son of Saul. 1. Sam. 14. Although King Saul had prescribed the fast for the whole people, Jonathan nonetheless broke the fast and obtained pardon. Answer: The universal is one thing absolutely, another in a qualified sense, and when Aristotle says that universal ignorance does not excuse, he means ignorance that is universal absolutely, which is founded on the laws of nature and of nations. Ignorance that is universal in a qualified sense is that which, although it is universal with respect to some kingdom or region, does not extend to everything; and such ignorance is considered either before the promulgation of the laws, as the jurists say, or after the promulgation. Ignorance before promulgation indeed merits pardon, but ignorance after promulgation merits none. Therefore the ignorance of Jonathan, since it occurred before the law was made known to all and each, rightly deserved pardon, especially since it had caused no harm to the commonwealth.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Egit Philosophus de invito per vim & per ignorantiam, declarat hoc cap quid sit spontaneum, sed brevissime, propterea quod uno contrario cognito, cognoscatur & alterum. Partes capitis sunt duae. In prima tradit definitionem spontanei. In secunda ostendit, quae ita aut cupiditate geri non, fieri invitè.
units.tr: The Philosopher has treated of the involuntary, which is caused by force and by ignorance. This chapter defines the voluntary, but very briefly, because once one contrary is known the other is known too. The chapter has two parts. In the first he gives the definition of the voluntary. In the second he shows which things done in anger or desire are not done unwillingly.

units.la: In prima igitur, hanc definitionem spontanei tra-dit. Spontaneum est, cujus principium est in ipso a-gente & sciente singulas actionum circumstantias. Ut igitur actio dicatur spontanea, duæ requiruntur conditiones. 1. Ut principium sit internum, qua particula opponitur invito per vim, seu actioni vio-lentæ. 2. est, Ut agens sciat singulas actionum circumstantias, quia particula opponitur invito per i-gnorantiam.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he gives this definition of the voluntary: the voluntary is that whose principle lies in the agent himself, who knows the individual circumstances of the action. So for an action to be called voluntary, two conditions are required. (1) The principle must be internal, a clause set against what is involuntary through force, that is, against a violent action. (2) The agent must know the individual circumstances of the action, a clause set against what is involuntary through ignorance.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit, quæ ira aut cupi-ditate fiunt, non fieri invitè, quod ideo facit, pro-pterea quod Plato, 9. de legibus, sicut ipse Aristoteles exponit. lib.2 Eud. cap.8 in fine dicit ret actiones ejus-modi esse plane invitas, vel saltem mediare inter a-ctiones spontaneas & invitas, & proinde esse mixtas. Hanc opinionem refutat Aristoteles, 6. rationibus.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he shows that things done in anger or desire are not done unwillingly. He does this because Plato, in the ninth book of the Laws, as Aristotle himself expounds in the Eudemian Ethics, book 2, chapter 8, at the end, says that actions of this kind are plainly involuntary, or at least intermediate between voluntary and involuntary actions, and therefore mixed. Aristotle refutes this opinion with six arguments.

units.la: 1. Si quæ ira aut cupiditate geruntur, fiunt invitè, tum quæcunque animantes & pueri agunt, invitè agunt, ratio consequentiæ est, quia cæteræ animan-tes præter hominem, cum ratione destituantur, sola cupiditate feruntur in obj-ectam, quod & parti-cularium inductione potest probari: Pueri etiam non tam ratione, quam sola cupiditate, quæ agunt, agere videntur. Ut melius intelligatur hæc ratio, scien-dum est, appetitum esse duplicem, unum rationis participem, alterum sensitivum: in pueris est appe-titus rationalis, sed imperfectè, propter immaturā ætatem & judicium longo rerum usu & experien-tia nondum confirmatum, est in pueris etiam appe-titus sensitivus, sed perfectiore quodam modo. Nam obje-cta movent sensus, & sensus moti appeti-tum tum excitant, ut cupiditate quadam ferantur in sua objecta, in brutis non est appetitus rationalis, sed tantum sensitivus, quo naturali quodam impetu feruntur in suum objectum. 2. Honesta, quae fiunt, non invite, sed sponte fiunt, nam fluunt a principio interno rectae rationi consentaneo. Ergo & turpia, quae fiunt ab ira & cupiditate, sponte fiunt, est enim eadem utriusque causa. 3. Si, quae cupiditate fiunt, invite fiunt, tum quaecunque appetimus, invite appetimus, verbi gratia: cum appetimus scientiam, sanitatem & caetera animi corporisque; At bona absurdum est dicere, ista a nobis invitis appeti oportere: nam pleno appetitu & desiderio animi ad ista appetenda ferimur. 4. Quae invite fiunt, habent tristitiam & moerorem conjunctum: at quae per iram & cupiditatem fiunt, habent voluptatem sibi adjunctam: nam cupiditas excitatur, propter voluptatem, & iratus exerit suas actiones propter voluptatem, quam ex iis percipit. 5. Quae per rationem deviantem peccantur, & quae per iram & cupiditate male fiunt, sunt in nostra potestate, & possunt fieri, vel non fieri, possumus enim ea agere vel omittere, cum principium a quo fluunt, sit in nobis situm, proinde non invite fiunt. 6. Ira & cupiditas, sunt proprie hominis affectiones. Ergo & actiones ab iis manantes, etsi sint hominis cujusque propriae, sponte non invite fiunt propter consensum voluntatis, quia affectus moventur a voluntate precedente, tum etiam propter appetitum delectationis, cum voluntas a voluptate vincitur, & ei propter delectationem cedit,
units.tr: (1) If things done in anger or desire are done unwillingly, then whatever animals and children do is done unwillingly. The inference holds because the other animals, lacking reason, are carried only by desire towards their object, which can also be proved by induction from particular cases. Children too seem to act less from reason than from desire alone. To understand this argument better, we must recognise that appetite is twofold: one sharing in reason, the other sensitive. In children there is a rational appetite, but imperfect, because of their immature age and a judgement not yet confirmed by long experience of things. In children there is also a sensitive appetite, and in a more perfect form. For objects move the senses, and moved senses in turn stir up the appetite, so that it is carried by a certain desire towards its objects. In brutes there is no rational appetite, only the sensitive, by which they are carried by a natural impulse towards their object. (2) Honourable deeds are not done unwillingly but voluntarily, for they flow from an internal principle agreeing with right reason. Therefore shameful deeds done from anger and desire are also done voluntarily, for the cause of both is the same. (3) If things done from desire are done unwillingly, then whatever we desire we desire unwillingly. For example, when we desire knowledge, health and other goods of soul and body. But it is absurd to say that we ought to desire these things against our will, for we are carried to desire them with full appetite and longing of the mind. (4) Things done unwillingly have sadness and grief joined to them, but things done through anger and desire have pleasure attached to them, for desire is stirred up on account of pleasure, and the angry man puts forth his actions on account of the pleasure he perceives from them. (5) Things sinned through a deviating reason, and things done badly through anger and desire, are in our power, and can be done or not done, for we can perform or omit them, since the principle from which they flow lies in us; therefore they are not done unwillingly. (6) Anger and desire are properly affections of man. Therefore the actions that flow from them, although they are peculiar to each man, are done voluntarily and not unwillingly, on account of the consent of the will, since the affections are moved by a preceding will, and also on account of the appetite for pleasure, when the will is overcome by pleasure and yields to it on account of delight.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Spontaneum est, cuius principium est in ipso agente, sciente singulas actionum circumstantias.
units.tr: 1. The voluntary is that whose principle lies in the agent himself, who knows the individual circumstances of the action.

units.la: 2. Qua ab ira & cupiditate fiunt, sponte & non invite fiunt.
units.tr: 2. Things done from anger and desire are done voluntarily and not unwillingly.

units.la: 3. Ridiculum est dicere, honesta fieri sponte, turpia vero invite, cum eadem sit utriusque causa, quia quacunque appetimus, sponte & non invite agimus.
units.tr: 3. It is ridiculous to say that honourable deeds are done voluntarily but shameful deeds unwillingly, since the cause of both is the same, because whatever we desire we do voluntarily and not unwillingly.

units.la: 4. Ratio, qua ratio, nunquam errat, sed qua devians, interdum peccat.
units.tr: 4. Reason, as reason, never errs, but reason that deviates sometimes sins.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Annon, qua ira & cupiditate fiunt, non etiam invite fiant, cum primae animi perturbationes seu affectus, cujusmodi sunt ira & cupiditas non sint in nostra potestate. Ergo neque actiones, qua ab iis manant, erunt in nostra potestate: nam quale est principium tale est actio fluens a principio, & cum non sint in nostra potestate, sequetur invite fieri? Resp. Primae animi perturbationes seu effectus non sunt in nostra potestate, quatenus sunt naturales, & a natura fluunt, sunt tamen in nostra potestate, quatenus sunt moderandae, & ad bonum vel malum morale determinandae.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Are not things done from anger and desire also done unwillingly, since the first perturbations or affections of the mind, such as anger and desire, are not in our power? Therefore neither will the actions that flow from them be in our power, for such as the principle is, such is the action flowing from the principle; and since they are not in our power, it will follow that they are done unwillingly? Answer: the first perturbations or affections are not in our power insofar as they are natural and flow from nature; yet they are in our power insofar as they are to be moderated and directed towards moral good or evil.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: Quomodo conveniat sexta ratio cum prima, prima tribuit cupiditatem & iram caeteris animantibus, non tamen homini; sexta dicit esse proprias hominis affectiones. Ergo videntur sibi contrariae? Resp. Proprium in Logicis sumitur quatuor modis: 1. quod soli & non omni. 2. quod omni etsi non soli. 3. quod omni soli & non semper. 4. quod omni soli & semper, hic intelligitur proprium in secundo modo, quod omni homini solo & ficira & cupiditas sunt propriæ hominis affectiones: nam vulgò hominis anima ab Epicuræis dividi solet in rationem, iram & cupiditatem, tanquam proprias suas facultates.
units.tr: II. It is asked: How does the sixth argument agree with the first? The first attributes anger and desire to the other animals, but not to man; the sixth says they are proper affections of man. Therefore they seem to be contrary to each other? Answer: in the logicians "proper" is taken in four ways: (1) what belongs to one alone and not to all; (2) what belongs to all, though not to one alone; (3) what belongs to one alone and to all, but not always; (4) what belongs to all and to one alone, and always. Here "proper" is to be understood in the second way, namely, that anger and desire are proper affections of man, because they belong to every man and to him alone; for commonly the soul of man is divided by the Epicureans into reason, anger and desire, as its own proper faculties.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: HActenus de primo membro primi tractatus, sequitur secundum de Proæresi: (quod vocabulum varie redditur ab interpretibus, vulgò dicitur electio, à Jureconsultis vocatur animi propositum, à Plauto, Terentio & Cicerone consilium, institutum, nos vocabulum Græcum ut significatissimum retinemus) Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima ostendit tractationem de proæresi pertinere ad moralem Philosophiam. In secunda ostendit, quid non sit. In tertia, quid sit, & quæ ejus natura sit. In prima igitur parte duas adferunt rationes, cur proæresis ad Ethicam pertinear: 1. Quia est virtuti maxime cognata, nam ut ex c.4 lib.2. supra patet, ad actionem virtutis tria requiruntur, Scientia, Constantia, Proæresis, quarum virtuti proprissima est proæresis, propterea quod reliquis duabus in aliis rebus, puta in artibus, uti licet absque virtute; proæresi vero non licet, nisi in sola virtutis actione. 2. Ratio, quia de moribus magis licet capere judicium proæresi, quia ex ipsis factis, unde Philosophus lib.1.Magn.Mor.cap.ult. inquit, ex proæresi possumus scire, qualis quisque sit, id est, quo consilio, quo instituto quis quid agat.
units.tr: So far we have dealt with the first part of the first treatise. Next comes the second, on proairesis (the word is rendered variously by the translators: commonly election, by the jurists settled purpose of mind, and by Plautus, Terence and Cicero counsel and resolve. I keep the Greek word, as the most expressive.) This chapter has three parts. In the first, he shows that the discussion of proairesis belongs to moral philosophy. In the second, he shows what it is not. In the third, what it is and what its nature is. In the first part he gives two reasons why proairesis belongs to Ethics. (1) Because it is most closely akin to virtue. For, as is plain from Book 2, chapter 4 above, three things are required for virtuous action: knowledge, constancy and proairesis. Of these, proairesis is the most proper to virtue, because the other two may be used apart from virtue in other matters, such as the arts, but proairesis may be used only in the exercise of virtue. (2) Because we can form a judgment of morals more readily from proairesis, since it is drawn from the deeds themselves. Hence the Philosopher says in Book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter last: from proairesis we can know what kind of person each is, that is, with what counsel and with what settled purpose someone acts.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ostendit quid non sit proæresis (nam hoc est Aristoteli familiare de parte negativa primo agere) & adfert quinque, puta spontaneum, iram, cupiditatem, voluntatem seu volitionem, & opinionem, nem, à quibus omnibus removet ἀπροαίρετον, & primò à spontaneo: nam licet omne illud (sic spontaneum, quod fit ex proæresi, spontaneum tamen latius patet quod duabus ostendit rationibus. 1. Quia animantes cæteræ præter hominem & pueri sponte agunt, non tamen ex proæresi agunt, nam proæresis non est absque ratonis agitatione & disputatione, ratione carent bruta, rationis agitatione carent pueri. 2. Quia quæcunque repente fiunt, ut sunt repentini animæ motus, quæ ab ira aut alia animi perturbatione proveniunt sponte fiunt, non tamen ex proæresi fiunt, quia proæresis tempus ad deliberandum postulat. Ut hæc ratio melius intelligatur, sciendum est, tria esse quæ proæresi destituuntur. 1. Bruta, quod non sint rationis capacia. 2. Pueri, quod etsi sint ratione præditi, ea per ætatem uti non possunt. 3. Repentini animæ motus, qui hominib. accidunt, nam etsi homines ratione polleant & ætate valeant, quia tamen tempus & spacium deliberandi non adhibent, cum aliquid alicujus impetu affectus agunt, dicuntur non ex proæresi seu non ex consilio & instituto egisse.
units.tr: In the second part he shows what proairesis is not (for it is characteristic of Aristotle to proceed first by the negative part), and he names five things: the spontaneous, anger, desire, will or volition, and opinion. From all of these he removes proairesis [ἀπροαίρετον, involuntary], and first from the spontaneous. For although everything that is done from proairesis is spontaneous, the spontaneous has a wider range, which he shows by two reasons. (1) Because the other animals, apart from man, and children act spontaneously, yet they do not act from proairesis. For proairesis cannot exist without the exercise and discussion of reason; brute beasts lack reason, and children lack the exercise of reason. (2) Because whatever happens suddenly, such as sudden movements of the soul that arise from anger or some other disturbance of the mind, is done spontaneously but not from proairesis, since proairesis requires time for deliberation. To understand this reasoning better, we should note that there are three things lacking proairesis. (1) Brute beasts, which are not capable of reason. (2) Children, who, although endowed with reason, cannot use it because of their age. (3) Sudden movements of the soul, which happen to men. For although men have reason and are of mature age, yet when they act under the impulse of some passion, without taking time and room for deliberation, they are said not to have acted from proairesis, that is, not from counsel and settled purpose.

units.la: Secundò probat, non esse iram aut cupiditatem quatuor rationibus, quarum 1. 2. & 4. sunt communes irę cum cupiditate, 3. propria est cupiditati. Prima igitur ratio est, quia ira & cupiditas competunt brutis & pueris, ut supra probavit cap. 3. proæresis non item. 2. Quia incontinens cupiditate agit, non ex proæresi: nam cupiditatibus abripitur, quibus paret rejecta ratione rejectoq; consilio, ut infra explicat lib. 7. cap. 2. sic etiam iratus ex ira agit, non ex proæresi.
units.tr: Second, he proves by four reasons that it is not anger or desire. Of these, the first, second and fourth are common to anger and desire, and the third is peculiar to desire. The first reason is that anger and desire belong to brute beasts and children, as he proved above in chapter 3, but proairesis does not. (2) Because the incontinent man acts from desire, not from proairesis. For he is carried away by his desires, obeying them, with reason cast off and counsel rejected, as he explains below in Book 7, chapter 2. So too the angry man acts from anger, not from proairesis.

units.la: 3. Ratio, quæ est cupiditati propria, est, quod cupiditas cupiditati non adversetur: nam cum appetimus diviti s, non appetimus pauperta em, & cum appetimus honores, non appetimus dedecus. Sed quod cupiditas contrarietur proæreti, hinc pater, proæresis est cum rectà ratione continuò conjuncta; cupiditas vero non. 4. Qua cupiditas, sicut & ira, versatur circa jucundum & molestum, nam cum aliquid appetimus, si adest, est jucundum, si abest, est molestum, at proæresis versatur in iis rebus, de quibus deliberamus, deliberamus verò de honesto & utili, ut infra cap 5. patebit. Nam etsi utilia & honesta sint jucunda, etiam præcipuum tantum caput deliberationis solet esse de honesto & utili; secundarò tantum de jucundo, seu per consequentias, ut loquuntur Jurisconsulti.
units.tr: (3) The reason peculiar to desire is that desire is not opposed to desire. For when we desire riches, we do not desire poverty, and when we desire honours, we do not desire disgrace. But that desire is opposed to proairesis is plain from this: proairesis is always joined with right reason, but desire is not. (4) Desire, like anger, is concerned with the pleasant and the painful. For when we desire something, if it is present it is pleasant, if absent it is painful. But proairesis is concerned with those things about which we deliberate, and we deliberate about the honourable and the useful, as will become plain below in chapter 5. For although useful and honourable things are also pleasant, the chief head of deliberation is usually the honourable and the useful, and only secondarily the pleasant, or by consequence, as the jurists say.

units.la: Tertio loco removet proæresin à voluntate, seu volitione: nam etsi proæresis sit valdè affinis voluntati, voluntas tamen latius patet, quod 3. ostendit rationibus. 1. (Quæ & sic continetur & lib. 1. Mag. mor. cap. 18. Et l. b. 2. Eud. cap. 10.) quod voluntas sit impossibilium & earum rerum, quæ nullo fieri modo à nobis possunt; proæresis non, item quod ostendit exemplo immortalitatis: Volumus, inquit, immortalitatem, seu non cupimus mori, at de ea re deliberare, cum naturaliter fieri non possit, ut quis non moriatur videtur ridiculum. Et ratio est, cur voluntas sit impossibilium. Proæresis verò rerum, quæ à nobis fieri possunt, quia voluntas absolutè & per se bonum spectat, proinde illud quod est optimum, sive sit possibile sive non appetit: proæresis verò nostra tantantum respicit mysteria, ad ea semper se accommodans, quæ nobis usui esse possunt, quæque quocunque modo in nostra sunt potestate. Secunda ratio est, quia voluntas ad aliena se extendit, & ad ea, quæ nos non spectant: Proœresis ea tantum respicit, quæ nos spectant, & quæ à nobis fieri possunt, & ab aliis nostro jussu geri. Exemplum adfert tale, solent spectatores in theatro vel palæstra, huic vel illi Athletæ vel pugili magis velle, quam alteri, & cupere ut hic potius vincat, quam ille, cum tamen nihil horum ad ipsos spectet, at vero deliberare, quomodo hic vel ille vincat, ridiculum videtur, qua de re fusius agetur infra cap. 5. 3. Quia voluntas est finis ipsius proprie: nam cum bonum per se respiciat, & finis omnis sub nomine boni veniat, ideo proprie respicit finem. Proœresis vero media respicit, per quæ putamus nos finem assecuturos: nam quia media sunt varia, per quæ finem assequimur, de iis deliberare solemus, quæ bona sint & quæ mala, ut melius & commodius ipsum finem assequamur.
units.tr: (3) In the third place he removes proairesis from the will, or volition. For although proairesis is very closely related to the will, the will has a wider range, which he shows by three reasons. (1) (This is also contained in Book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter 18, and in Book 2 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 10.) The will is of impossible things, and of those things which in no way can be done by us; proairesis* is not. He shows this also by the example of immortality: "We wish," he says, "for immortality, or we do not want to die; but to deliberate about it, since it cannot naturally happen that someone should not die, seems ridiculous." And this is the reason why the will extends to impossible things. But proairesis concerns only things that can be done by us. For the will regards the good absolutely and in itself, and therefore desires what is best, whether it is possible or not; but our proairesis looks only to means, always adapting itself to those things which can be of use to us, and which are in our power in any way. (2) The second reason is that the will extends to things that belong to others, and to things that do not concern us. Proairesis regards only those things that concern us, that can be done by us, and that can be done by others at our bidding. He gives this example: spectators in a theatre or a wrestling ground are accustomed to wish more for this or that athlete or boxer than for another, and to desire that this one rather than that one should win, although none of these things concerns them at all. But to deliberate about how this man or that one may win seems ridiculous. This will be discussed more fully below, in chapter 5, section 3. (3) Because the will is the end properly so called. For since it regards the good in itself, and every end comes under the name of good, it therefore properly regards the end. But proairesis regards the means by which we think we shall attain the end. For since the means by which we attain the end are various, we are accustomed to deliberate about which of them are good and which bad, so that we may attain the end itself better and more conveniently.

units.la: Quarto loco removet opinionem a proœresi, & quia opinio est duplex, alia communis, alia singularis: Probat primo non esse opinionem communem duabus rationibus. 1. Non esse singularem quinque rationibus (quæ omnes repetuntur etiam lib. 2. Eud. cap. 10.) 1. Ratio, quod proœresis non sit opinio communis, quia opinio versatur in rebus omnibus, tam in rebus æternis seu universalibus, & quæ nullo modo sunt in nostra potestate, quam in iis rebus, quæ nostri sint arbitrii. Proœresis vero tantum in iis rebus versatur, quæ in nostra sunt potestate, quod opinio versetur in rebus omnibus, probatur exemplo: videmus enim homines multa opinari de Deo, de mundo, de astris etiā absurda multa, ut Chimeram, & infinitos mundos, ut Democritus, & ratio hçcest, quia opinio pertinet ad partē animi cognoscētem, ratio vero & cognitio vagantur & discurūt per omnia, & in omnibus verum quærunt, quæ non patent sensui. 2. Ratio est, quia opinio solet dividi vero & falso. Proærcesis vero malo & bono distinguitur: Nam de opinione non quæritur proprie, sitne bona an mala, sed an sit vera an falsa, & ratio hæc est, quia opinio pertinet ad theoriam seu contemplationem, cui opposita est veritas. De proæresi vero quæritur, sitne bona vel mala, versetūrne circa utile & honestum, an circa turpe & pravum, quia pertinet ad appetitum & praxin, cui propositum est bonum. Secundo loco probat non esse opinionem singularem quinque rationibus: Prima est, ab opinione non dicimur quales, sed à proæresi, nam quod quis opinetur bonum esse aut malum, non statim sequitur illud esse bonum aut malum, at vero si quid homines eligant boni aut mali, dici solent boni aut mali, inde exemplum adfert de incontinente, nam quod incontinens opinerur se esse bonum, non statim sequitur eum esse bonum, quia cupiditatibus suis pravis abripitur ad malum. sed quia ex proæresi agit malū, dicitur malus. Secunda ratio est, quia proæreseos est appetere & persequi, aut aspernari aliquid, opinionis vero munera sunt quærere, quid sit hoc aut illud, cui rei sit utile, quatenus eo sit utendum, verbigratia: Opinio quærit quid sit virtus; an dulcia nutriant; an de-
units.tr: Fourth, he removes opinion from proairesis. Since opinion is twofold, one common, the other singular, he first proves that it is not common opinion, by two reasons, and then that it is not singular opinion, by five reasons (all of which are also repeated in Book 2 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 10). (1) The first reason, that proairesis is not common opinion, is that opinion is concerned with all things, both eternal or universal things, which in no way are in our power, and things which are within our choice. But proairesis is concerned only with those things which are in our power. That opinion is concerned with all things is proved by example: we see men holding many opinions about God, the world, and the stars, even many absurd ones, such as the Chimera and infinite worlds, as Democritus held. The reason is that opinion belongs to the knowing part of the soul, while reason and knowledge wander and range through all things, and seek the truth in all things that do not lie open to the senses. (2) The second reason is that opinion is usually divided into true and false, but proairesis is distinguished as bad and good. For concerning opinion we do not properly ask whether it is good or bad, but whether it is true or false, and the reason is that opinion belongs to theory or contemplation, to which truth is opposed. But concerning proairesis we ask whether it is good or bad, whether it is concerned with the useful and honourable or with the base and wicked, because it belongs to appetite and practice, to which the good is the object. (Secondly) he proves that it is not singular opinion by five reasons. The first is that we are not called such as we are by opinion, but by proairesis. For that someone holds a thing to be good or bad does not at once mean that it is good or bad; but if men choose something as good or bad, they are usually called good or bad by it. He gives the example of the incontinent man: that the incontinent man thinks himself good does not at once mean that he is good, because he is carried away by his wicked desires into evil; but because he does evil from proairesis, he is called wicked. The second reason is that it belongs to proairesis to seek after, pursue, or reject something, but the office of opinion is to inquire what this or that is, and to what thing it is useful, and in what way it is to be used. For example, opinion asks what virtue is, whether sweet things nourish, whether a walk after dinner is useful or not; but proairesis does not ask what remains, but whether we ought to seek that thing or not. (3) Because proairesis is praised for being right, and blamed for not being right or being wrong…

units.la: S ambuambulatio à cœna sit utilis nec ne, at vero proœrefis non exquirit quid restat, sed an debeamus rem illam appetere nec ne. 3. Quia proœresis ex eo quod sit recta, laudatur, ex eo quod non sit recta vel prava vituperatur, opinio vero, si sit vera, laudatur, si falsa, vituperatur, & ratio differentiæ est, quia opinio pertinet ad contemplationem, cui proposita est veritas, proœresis facta ipsa respicit, de quibus non quæritur, an sint vera vel falsa, sed an sint recta vel prava.
units.tr: Opinion asks whether a walk after dinner is useful or not, but choice (proairesis) does not ask what remains to be done; it asks whether we ought to desire that thing or not. 3. Because choice is praised for what is right and blamed for what is not right or is wrong, while opinion is praised if it is true and blamed if it is false, the reason for the difference is that opinion belongs to contemplation, which has truth as its aim, whereas choice looks to the deeds themselves. About these we do not ask whether they are true or false, but whether they are right or wrong.

units.la: 4. Proœresis est in iis rebus, quas scimus & quas jam exploratas habemus, opinio vero plerumque in rebus incertis versatur: nam opinio est esse incertam quandam in rebus assensionem, constat, at vero proœresis uti in rebus incertis, de quibus non constat, sint nec ne, an sint in nostra potestate necne, est ridiculum.
units.tr: 4. Choice concerns those things which we know and have already examined, whereas opinion is for the most part occupied with uncertain matters, for opinion is, as is agreed, a certain assent to uncertain things. But to make use of choice in uncertain matters, about which it is not established whether they are so or not, or whether they are within our power or not, is absurd.

units.la: 5. Si opinio & proœresis essent unum tunc quæcunque opinarentur homines ea etiam sequerentur ac non sequuntur: nam multos videre est, qui id, quod melius est, opinantur, sequuntur tamen id, quod est deterius, vel cupiditatibus abreptos vel animi vitio vel perturbatione, quod in Medea expressit Ovid.
units.tr: 5. If opinion and choice were the same, then men would follow whatever they opined. But we see many who opine what is better and yet follow what is worse, carried off either by their lusts, or by a fault of mind, or by passion. Ovid expressed this in the case of Medea.

units.la: Metam. 7. Video meliora probóque, Deteriora sequor.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7: "I see and approve the better course, but follow the worse."

units.la: Et Lipsius lib. 1. de Constantia cap. 7. ut oculus qui per nebulam aut aquam res inspicit, falso metitur modo, sic animus quiper opinionis nubem, hæc homini malorum mater, hæc autor in nobis confusæ & perturbatæ vitæ.
units.tr: And Lipsius, On Constancy, book 1, chapter 7: just as an eye that looks at things through mist or water measures them falsely, so the mind that does so through the cloud of opinion (this is the mother of all evils for man, the author of a confused and disturbed life within us).

units.la: Tandem subjicit quæstionem Philosophus, an proœresis præcedat proœresin, an vero ubsequatur, quæ breviter hic dissolvitur, præcedit & subsequitur sed diverso respectu: nam quia opinio pertinet ad partem animi cognoscentem, proaeresis vero ad appetitum & appetitus non solet excitari, nisi a praecedente cognitione; nam nisi cognitio impellat, appetitus ad aliquod objectum non fertur, juxta illud: Ignoti nulla Cupido. Subsequitur vero Proaeresin opinio cum aliquid intervenit, quod priorem sententiam mutare facit, quod plerumque; in iis evenit, qui non probant judicant, amant, sed probant amant, judicant, verbi gratia: Si quis propter amicum sententiam mutet & plus amico quam veritati tribuat, & ideo haec opinio, quae subsequitur proaeresin in levioribus, non in viris constantibus reperiri solet.
units.tr: Lastly, the Philosopher raises the question whether opinion precedes choice or follows it. It is briefly resolved here: it both precedes and follows, but in different respects. For since opinion belongs to the knowing part of the soul, and choice to the appetite, and the appetite is not usually stirred except by a preceding cognition (for unless cognition impels it, the appetite is not carried toward any object, according to the saying: There is no desire for the unknown.), opinion precedes choice. But opinion follows choice when something intervenes which causes us to change our earlier judgment. This happens mostly with those who do not judge what they approve and love, but approve and love first and then judge. For example, if someone changes his view for the sake of a friend and gives more weight to his friend than to the truth. Thus this kind of opinion, which follows choice, is usually found in the lighter sort of people, not in steadfast men.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis ostendit, quid sit proaeresis, & dicit esse spontaneum quod, sed non omne, sed id tantum quod fit praecedente consultatione aut deliberatione, & hoc duabus rationibus breviter ostendit. 1. Quia proaeresis non fit absque ratione & discursu, & absque discursu non fit consultatio. 2. Sum tur a nomine proaireseos, quod proaeresis sive electio sit unius prae alio quasi lectio, cum ex duobus vel pluribus propositis unum ante aliud sumitur vel eligitur.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he shows what choice is, and says it is a voluntary act, but not every voluntary act, only that which is done after prior consultation or deliberation. He shows this briefly by two reasons: (1) because choice is not made without reason and reasoning, and without reasoning there is no consultation; (2) it is taken from the name of proairesis, that choice or election is the taking of one thing before another, as if by reading, since from two or more options one is taken or chosen before the others.

units.la: Notandum proaeresin sive electionem vulgo esse duplicem, unam divinam, aliam creaturarum, divina illa est, qua Deus nos in se ante mundi fundamenta in filios adoptavit, Ephes. 1. vers. 4. Electio creaturarum est rursus duplex, inchoata & perfecta, inchoata quae brutis etiam competit, cum impetu quodam materiae objectae, id quod melius videtur, eligunt; & quae etiam pueris competit, qui nondum maturo judicio & perfecta ratione uti possunt: Electio oper- perfecta secta est, quæ hominibus matura ætate, judicio & perfecta ratione prædicti competit, & requirit hæc quatuor, intellectum ut principium, voluntatem ut subjectum, rationem seu discursum ut medium, finem actionis ut solidum & constans, non fragile fortunæ bonum.
units.tr: It should be noted that choice, or election, is commonly twofold: one divine, the other of creatures. The divine choice is that by which God adopted us as sons in himself before the foundation of the world, Ephesians 1:4. The election of creatures is again twofold: incipient and perfect. The incipient election belongs even to brutes, who by a certain impulse toward the matter before them choose what seems better; and it belongs also to children, who cannot yet use mature judgment and perfect reason. The perfect election belongs to men of mature age endowed with judgment and perfect reason, and it requires these four things: the intellect as its principle, the will as its subject, reason or reasoning as its means, and the end of the action as its solid and constant object, not the fragile good of fortune.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Certius de moribus sumitur iudicium ex proæresi, quam ex factis ipsis.
units.tr: 1. A surer judgment about morals is drawn from choice than from the deeds themselves.

units.la: 2. Quod subito & repente fit, non fit ex proæresi, cum tempus deliberationi non habeat.
units.tr: 2. What is done suddenly and at once is not done from choice, since it has no time for deliberation.

units.la: 3. Cupiditas cupiditati non semper adversatur, adversatur tamen semper proæresi.
units.tr: 3. Desire does not always oppose desire, but it always opposes choice.

units.la: 4. Proæresis non est rerum impossibilium, sicut voluntas, neque est finis proprie, sed mediorum tantum, quæ ad finem tendunt.
units.tr: 4. Choice is not of impossible things, as the will is, nor is it properly of the end, but only of the means that tend toward the end.

units.la: 5. Proæresis proprie dicitur bona vel mala, opinio vero vera aut falsa.
units.tr: 5. Choice is properly called good or evil, but opinion true or false.

units.la: 6. Ab opinione sola nemo dicitur bonus, sicut a proæresi.
units.tr: 6. No one is called good from opinion alone, as he is from choice.

units.la: 7. Multi opinantur id, quod est optimum, sequuntur tamen ex proæresi determinatum.
units.tr: 7. Many opine what is best, yet from a settled choice they follow what is worse.

units.la: 8. Opinio præcedit & subsequitur proæresin, sed diverso respectu.
units.tr: 8. Opinion both precedes and follows choice, but in different respects.

units.la: 9. Proæresis dicitur spontaneum quid, cum precedente deliberatione.
units.tr: 9. Choice is said to be something voluntary, with prior deliberation.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat in secunda ratione, quā probat proæresin pertinere ad moralem Philosophiam certius ex proæresi, de moribus sumi judicium, quam ex factis ipsis, cum tamen lib. 1. Magnor. Moral. cap. 20 contrarium affirmat, solere nempe homines ex facto, non ex proæresi de morimoribus judicare & in Jure civili non ex proæresi seu intentione judicantur homines, sed ex ipsis factis l.cogitationes, ff. de pœnis? Resp. Aliud est vulgò aliquid fieri, aliud secundum rei veritatem. Cum dicit Philosophus loco citato, solere homines judicare ex factis, non ex proæresi, affert vulgarem opinionem, nam solet vulgò sic judicare homines, propterea quod inquit Philosophus, animus & proæresis non cadant sub sensus, facta vero sub sensus cadant & oculis, quasi cernantur: At verò, qui secundum rei veritatem dijudicare aliquid vult, non tam in factis, quam in animum & proæresin inspicere dicitur, quo quis animo & intentione quid fecerit, ut ipse Aristoteles præclarè testatur, cap. ult. lib. 1. Mag. Mor. Quod verò ad locum illum è jure civili citatum, hoc tantum vult, leges humanas differre à divinis, quod leges divinæ & facta, & intentiones simul respiciant, leges verò humanæ factum tantum, cogitat ores verò minimè, nisi educantur in actum, ut eadem illa lex citata præclarè asserit: Cogitationes hominum non puniuntur legibus, nisi facta sequantur cogitationes.
units.tr: I. It is asked how he can say, in the second reason by which he proves that moral philosophy deals with choice (proairesis), that a judgment about morals is drawn more surely from choice than from the deeds themselves. In Magna Moralia 1, chapter 20, he asserts the contrary: people usually judge from the deed and not from choice, and in civil law men are judged not by their choice or intention but by the deeds themselves (l. cogitationes, ff. de poenis). Answer: it is one thing for something to be done as commonly supposed, and another thing according to the truth of the matter. When the Philosopher says in the passage cited that people usually judge from deeds and not from choice, he is giving the common opinion, for people commonly do judge in this way, because, as the Philosopher says, the mind and choice do not fall under the senses, whereas deeds do fall under the senses and eyes, as if they could be seen. But whoever wishes to judge something according to the truth of the matter is said to look not so much at deeds as at the mind and choice, that is, with what mind and intention someone has done something, as Aristotle himself clearly testifies in the last chapter of Magna Moralia 1. As for that passage from civil law which is cited, it means only this: human laws differ from divine laws in that divine laws look at both the deeds and the intentions together, whereas human laws look only at the deed and not at thoughts, unless these are brought forth into action, as that same cited law clearly asserts: The thoughts of men are not punished by laws unless deeds follow the thoughts.

units.la: 11. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus in prima ratione, ubi distinguit proæresin à spontaneo, proæresin non competere brutis, sicut spontaneum, cum tamen in brutis fit certa quadam electio, nam eligunt, quod in profesto est, & id prosequuntur pleno impetu, & vitant, quod iis nocet, proinde & proæresis iis competit? Resp. Ex superioribus proæresin esse duplicem, aliam imperfectam seu inchoatam, quæ ab impetu naturæ fluit, & hæc brutis competit, aliam perfectam, quæ tantum hominibus recta ratione, matura ætate & judicio competit,
units.tr: II. It is asked how the Philosopher can say, in the first reason, where he distinguishes choice from the voluntary, that choice does not belong to brutes, as the voluntary does, when in brutes there is indeed a certain kind of choice: for they choose what is pleasant, pursue it with full impulse, and avoid what harms them; therefore choice also belongs to them. Answer: from what has been said above, choice is of two kinds. One is imperfect or incipient, which flows from the impulse of nature, and this belongs to brutes. The other is perfect, which belongs only to human beings, who have right reason, mature age and judgment.

units.la: de hac loquitur hic Aristoteles, quam vere negat brutis inesse.
units.tr: It is of this latter that Aristotle speaks here, and he rightly denies that it is found in brutes.

units.la: III. Quaeritur: An cum veritate constet quod dicit Philosophus, cupiditas cupiditati non adversatur seu contrariatur, cum tamen ratio contrarium dictitet, verbi gratia: Avaritia contrariatur prodigalitati, & Cic. lib. 1. officiorum inquit, Ambitiosi saepe sunt avari, ac ambitiosus, ut possit pervenire ad honores nullo parcit sumtibus, avaro vero omnibus, & Augustus Caesar, ut est apud Dionem Cassium lib. 58. cupiebat non dominari populo Romano, & tamen imperio se abdicare nolebat? Resp. Non hoc vult Philosophus nullam omnino cupiditatem nulli cupiditati contrariari, sed in uno eodemque homine, uno eodemque tempore simul & semel, cupiditatem cupiditati non avare licet succedive contrarientur sibi invicem, etiam in eodem subjecto, at cupiditas avaritiae semper proxime est, quia proxime est conjuncta cum recta ratione, cupiditas vero, raro aut nunquam sit subjecta rectae rationi.
units.tr: III. It is asked whether what the Philosopher says is true, namely that desire does not oppose desire, when reason seems to say the contrary. For example: avarice is contrary to prodigality; and Cicero, in On Duties, book 1, says: "Ambitious men are often avaricious, and the ambitious man spares no expense in order to reach honours, while the avaricious man spares none in anything." And Augustus Caesar, as Dio Cassius reports in book 58, desired not to rule the Roman people, and yet was unwilling to give up the empire. Answer: the Philosopher does not mean that no desire at all is opposed to any desire, but that in one and the same man, at one and the same time, simultaneously, desires are not opposed to one another. They may indeed be contrary to each other in succession, even in the same subject. But the desire of avarice is always close at hand, because it is closely joined with right reason, whereas desire is seldom or never subject to right reason.

units.la: IV. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat voluntatem esse finis, proxime vero mediorum tantum, quae ad finem conducunt, cum tamen lib. 1. c. 7 huius op. dicat, alios esse fines, qui expetatur propter se, alios qui expetatur propter aliud, quod fieri non potest, si finis non sub proxime caderet, nam quomodo possumus unum fine ab alio distinguere, unum pro alio eligere, aut expetere nisi proxime ad finem pertineret ad finem? Resp. Proxime sumitur duobus modis, vel late vel stricte: late pro quolibet actu voluntatis, ind. Sic spectat ad finem, vel stricte pro actu voluntatis tendentis per media certa ad finem. Auteriam commodius sponderi potest, finis esse duplices, ultimos & subordinatos.
units.tr: IV. Question: How can he say that the will is the end, but that it is properly only of the means that lead to the end? Yet in book 1, chapter 7 of this work he says that there are some ends which are desired for their own sake and others which are desired for the sake of something else. This could not be so unless the end fell under the proximate, for how could we distinguish one end from another, choose one in preference to another, or desire one unless it pertained proximately to the end? Answer: "Proximate" is taken in two ways, either broadly or strictly. Broadly, it means any act of the will, and in this sense it concerns the end. Strictly, it means an act of the will tending through certain means to the end. It can be answered more conveniently in another way: that there are two kinds of ends, ultimate and subordinate.

units.la: ardi. ordinator, proæresin esse finem subordinatorum, non qua sunt fines, sed qua sunt media tendentia ad ultimum finem, nunquam vero esse proæresin finis ultimi sed certam & determinatam voluntatem.
units.tr: It can be said more fittingly that proairesis is of subordinate ends, not inasmuch as they are ends, but inasmuch as they are means tending toward the ultimate end; and that proairesis is never of the ultimate end, but is a certain and determinate will.

units.la: V Quæritur: Quomodo dicat opinionem non dici bonam aut malam, sed tantum veram aut falsam, cum hoc consuetudini vulgari repugnet, nam qui aliquid consentaneum rectæ rationi opinatur, dicitur habere bonam opinionem, qui vero contra, malam? Resp. Opinio per se tantum dicitur vera aut falsa, abusive & per aliud bona aut mala. Propter commoditatem scilicet, aut incommoditatem, quæ inde ad vitam communem redundat, at vero, si opinio sit rectæ rationi consentanea, non tam dicitur bona opinio, quam recta ratio, at si dissentiat à recta ratione, & incerta vagetur, tum proprie dicitur opinio, quasi aberratio à recta ratione & excursus liberi ab æquo.
units.tr: V. Question: How can he say that an opinion is not called good or bad, but only true or false, when this contradicts common usage? For whoever holds an opinion agreeing with right reason is said to have a good opinion, and whoever holds the contrary, a bad one? Answer: An opinion is called true or false in itself alone; it is called good or bad improperly, and by reference to something else, namely on account of the advantage or disadvantage which thence flows into common life. But if an opinion agrees with right reason, it is called not so much a good opinion as right reason itself; whereas if it dissents from right reason and wanders uncertainly, then it is properly called opinion, as a straying from right reason and a free deviation from what is fair.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: SEquitur hoc c. 3. membrum hujus tractatus primi, nempe de consultatione: nam quia finis superioris capitis definita erat proæresis spontaneum quid, cum præcedente consultatione, ideo hoc capite statim de consultatione agit, ut sic progressos naturam melius innotescat. Partes capitis sunt tres. In prima ostendit, quæ res sub consultationem cadat. In secunda, de objecto, modo & consultationis fine agit, nam duæ sunt res maxime consideranda in omni consultatione. Objectum nempe, seu materia circa quam, aut de qua deliberatur, & modus quatenus ratione ad affectionem rei deveniatur. In tertia tertia parte consultationem cum proæresi comparat & inter se distinguit.
units.tr: This is followed by the third chapter, the fifth member of this first treatise, namely on deliberation. Because the end of the preceding chapter defined proairesis as a voluntary act together with prior deliberation, this chapter treats of deliberation at once, so that, having advanced, its nature may be better known. The chapter has three parts. In the first he shows what things fall under deliberation. In the second he treats of the object, the mode and the end of deliberation, for there are two things chiefly to be considered in every deliberation: the object, that is, the matter about which one deliberates, and the mode, insofar as by reason one arrives at a decision about the thing. In the third part he compares deliberation with proairesis and distinguishes the two from each other.

units.la: In prima igitur parte ostendit, quæ res sub consultationem cadant, & dicit non de omnibus fieri consultationem, sed de quibus homo sanæ mentis consultaret, ut hoc melius ostendat, afferrt rerum distinctionem a quadruplici causa efficiente. Nam res omnes vel proveniunt a causa necessaria, quæ semper sic se habet, cujusmodi sunt mundus & res in mundo contentæ, seu res illæ, quæ a Deo & natura proveniunt vel fiunt, ab ejusmodi causa necessaria quæ aliter se habere nequit, ut sunt res Mathematicæ, verbi gratia: Diametrum non esse commensurabilem lateri. 2. Res quæ vel proveniunt a motu, quæ non semper fiunt sed subinde eveniunt, ut sunt siccitates & grandines. 3. Res eveniunt a fortuna, ut est inventio thesauri & cætera, quæ casu & temere fiunt. 4. Res proveniunt a mente nostra, quæ sunt in nostra potestate ut fiant vel non fiant, sed nihil priorum trium cadit sub consultationem, non enim a nobis fiunt, nec sunt in nostra potestate, ergo relinquitur, ut res illæ, quæ fiunt a nobis sub consultationem cadant, nec tamen omnes res, quæ fiunt a mente nostra, in consultationem veniunt: nam eæ res, quæ ad nos nō spectant, de iis non deliberamus, verbi gratia: Nemo Lacedæmoniorum deliberat de iis, quæ spectant ad Rempub. Scytarum. Deinde quædam sunt res, quæ a mente nostra proveniunt, tam certe, ut nullam disputationem admittant, seu agitationem in utramque partem, cujusmodi sunt principia scientiarum & artium exquisitarum, magis tamen artes, sub consultationem veniunt quam scientiæ, quia artes sunt plerumque de rebus incertis aut saltem contingentibus, quæ sunt in nostra potestate ut possint fieri vel non fieri pro libitu nostro. Scientiæ vero sunt de rebus certis & necessariis, quæ à nobis fieri non possunt. In summa sub consultationem cadunt non res quæ à necessaria causa pendent, sive ea causa semper sic se habeat, sive nō semper, ut fit in iis rebus, quæ plerumque eveniunt, cujusmodi sunt Meteora Physica, non etiam res fortuitæ, non etiam eæ res, quæ à nobis effici non possunt, ut nec principia scientiarum & artium exquisitarum, & inter artes conjecturales, aliæ magis, aliæ minus sub consultationem cadunt, ut quæ certioribus nituntur principiis, de iis minus deliberatur, quæ minus certis, de iis magis, verbi gratia: De Medica practica & Nautica magis consultatur, quam de Gymnastica. Sub deliberationem vero cadunt res, quæ à nobis effici possunt, quarum principium est in nobis positum, quæ plerumque evenient, & quarum exitus est incertus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he shows what things fall under deliberation. He says that deliberation is not made about all things, but about those a sane person would deliberate about. To make this clearer, he gives a distinction of things according to a fourfold efficient cause. All things either come from a necessary cause, which always acts in the same way, as the world and the things contained in it, that is, those things which come from or are made by God and nature; or from a cause which cannot act otherwise, as the things of mathematics, for example that the diagonal is not commensurable with the side; (2) things which come from motion, which do not always happen but occur from time to time, such as droughts and hailstorms; (3) things which come from chance, such as the finding of a treasure and other things that happen by accident or at random; (4) things which come from our own mind, and which are in our power to make or not to make. None of the first three falls under deliberation, for they are not made by us and are not in our power. It follows, then, that those things which are made by us fall under deliberation; yet not all things made by our mind come into deliberation, for we do not deliberate about those things that do not concern us. For example, no Lacedaemonian deliberates about the affairs of the state of the Scythians. Further, some things come from our mind so certainly that they admit no dispute or debate on either side, such as the principles of the sciences and of the more refined arts. Yet the arts come under deliberation more than the sciences do, because the arts are mostly concerned with things uncertain, or at least contingent, which are in our power so that they may be done or not done at our pleasure. The sciences, on the other hand, are concerned with certain and necessary things, which cannot be done by us. In sum, not those things which depend on a necessary cause fall under deliberation, whether that cause always acts in the same way or not always, as happens with things that for the most part come to pass, such as physical meteors; nor do chance events, nor those things which cannot be made by us, such as the principles of the sciences and of the more refined arts. Among the conjectural arts, some fall under deliberation more and some less: those which rest on more certain principles are deliberated about less, and those which rest on less certain principles are deliberated about more. For example, practical medicine and navigation are deliberated about more than gymnastics. Indeed, those things fall under deliberation which can be made by us, whose principle lies within us, which for the most part come to pass, and whose outcome is uncertain.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de modo & termino consultationis, & dicit in omni consultatione præsupponendum esse finem: nam si de fine esset consultatio, daretur progressus in infinitum, quod probat exemplo Medici & aliorum, qui semper statuunt finem certum: Dein exquirunt media, quibus istum finem assequantur: nam ut ipse Philosophus dicit lib. 7. Polit. cap. 13. In omni re beneinstituenda duo consideranda veniunt, finis & media, quæ ducunt ad finem. Præsupposito igitur fine, consultatio tatur de mediis an sint plura, an unū tātū; & si plura sint media, tunc deliberatur, quib. mediis melius, commodus & facilius ad finē pervenia ur, si ve ō unum sit medium, quomodo hoc uno ad finē devenīatur, nam si à fine sit, progrediendū erit ut ab una causa in aliam, donec ad primā totius consultationis causam perveniatur, & procedamus, verbi gratia: exemp ū sit de plutib. mediis, an bellū gerēdum sit equitatu, an peditatu; an pugnā navali, an terrestri victoria acquiri possit, an in urbe aliqua oppugnāda, scalis statim urbē aggredi debeant, an corona cingere, an cuniculis effossis, an torn ēts, an simul omnib. De uno medio ad finem tendēte consultatur, v.g. an bellum geri debeat solo equitatu, postea consultatur, quomodo hic equitatus acquiri possit, & cognito, eū pecunia comparari, inquirūntur causæ invenientę pecuniæ, & certissima reperitur tributi ind ctio, hic finis hic est bellī gerere, de quo non consultatur, medium est equitatus, per quod geratur. & de eo consultatur, quomodo possit cōparari, & sic ab una causa in aliam devenitur ad primum totius cōsultationis caput, verbi gratia: in hoc exēplo sit tributi ind ctio.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he treats of the mode and limit of deliberation. He says that in every deliberation the end must be presupposed. For if the end itself were the subject of deliberation, there would be an infinite progression, which he proves by the example of the physician and others, who always fix a definite end. Then they seek the means by which they may attain that end. For, as the Philosopher himself says (Polit. 7, ch. 13): in every matter to be rightly ordered two things must be considered, the end and the means that lead to the end. Therefore, with the end presupposed, deliberation concerns the means: whether there are several or only one. If there are several means, one deliberates which of them leads to the end more advantageously, conveniently and easily; if there is only one means, one deliberates how the end is reached by this one means. For if one proceeds from the end, one must go on from one cause to another, as from one cause to the next, until one arrives at the first cause of the whole deliberation. Let us proceed by example. Suppose the question is about several means: whether war should be waged with cavalry or with infantry; whether victory can be won by a naval battle or a land battle; whether, in attacking some city, they should at once assault it with ladders, or surround it with a siege, or use dug mines, or towers, or all of these at once. One deliberates about the one means which tends to the end: for example, whether war ought to be waged with cavalry alone. Afterwards one deliberates how this cavalry may be acquired; and once that is known, that it must be obtained with money, the sources of money are sought, and the most certain is found: the levying of a tax. Here the end is to wage war, and that is not deliberated about; the means is the cavalry, by which the war is waged, and about this one deliberates how it may be procured.
