And so one proceeds from one cause to another, until one reaches the first head of the whole deliberation. In this example, that is the levying of a tax.

units.la: Ne tamen quis putet, idem esse investigationem seu inquisitionem terum per media, quod consultationem, discrimen ponit inter inquisitionem & consultationem: nam inquisitio est in rebus omnibus tam certis quam incertis, & habet pro fine cognitionem. Consultatio verò est de rebus plerunq; in certis, & habet pro fine actionem; proinde neque sensibus sub consultationem cadunt, nam quæ sensibus patent, sunt plerunq; certa, verbi gratia: nemo conconsultat de pane, an hoc vel illo modo fit subactus, sed de modo acquirendi panem saepe consultatur, quia modus iste saepius intellectui aut menti quam sensibus patet. Effectus tandem consultationis est rei exsecutio, de qua deliberatur: solent enim consultantes, si res commodè fieri posset, eam exsequi, si vero fieri non posset, neque per se, neque per amicos, ab incerta consultatione desisterc.
units.tr: Lest anyone think that the investigation or inquiry into ends through means is the same as deliberation, he draws a distinction between inquiry and deliberation. Inquiry concerns all things, both certain and uncertain, and has knowledge as its aim. Deliberation, however, concerns things that are mostly uncertain, and has action as its aim. Accordingly, things that are evident to the senses do not fall under deliberation, for what is open to the senses is mostly certain. For example, no one deliberates about bread, whether it has been kneaded in this way or that; but one often deliberates about the way of acquiring bread, because that way is more often open to the intellect or mind than to the senses. Finally, the effect of deliberation is the carrying out of the thing deliberated about. For those who deliberate are accustomed, if the thing could be done conveniently, to carry it out; but if it could not be done, neither by themselves nor through friends, to desist from uncertain deliberation.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis comparationem instituit inter consultationem & electionem, nam quia electio definitur per consultationem, ut ex fine superioris capitis patet, ideo istam consultationis tractationem adduxit, ut melius innotesceret natura electionis, comparat igitur sic, ut ostendat, in quo conveniant, & in quod screpent. Conveniunt in objecto, nam idem est consultabile, quod est eligibile, & e contra; ratione tamen differunt, (nam etsi objectum sit idem re, ratione tamen est diversum) nam id, quod est eligibile, praecedit seipsum, in quantum est consultabile, seu consultatio semper praecedit electionem, verbi gratia: quando deliberatur, an bellum debeat geri nec ne, iam est consultabile; at cum est decretum bellum esse gerendum, iam est eligibile, aut sub electionem venit. In summa, quod in consultatione determinatum aut statutum est, id dicitur eligibile, quod duabus rationibus probat Philosophus: 1. est, quia tum demum deliberare desinimus, cum ad illud principium agendi, a quo primò incipiendum est, devenimus, seu tum demum est consultationis finis, cum res sub electionem cadit, ut possimus, quam velimus partem appetere vel adversus. versari. 2. Ducitur ab instituto veterum Rerumpubl.Græciæ,nam,ut refert Homer.lib.2 iliad. Agamemnon Græcorum Dux cum prioribus Græciæ consultare solebat, de rebus dubiis & magnis, & cum demum elegisset, quod facto optimum esset, tum populo proponebat, ut id populus executioni mandaret, quod ille communi in proceribus convocatis ex longa deliberatione elegisset. Sic etiam apud Romanos Regibus statim ex actis solebant senatores agitare in senatu, quæ e Republ. essent, & demum decreta aut Senatusconsulta facta ad concionem referre, teste Dion.Halycarnassæo lib 7. Tandem electionis definitionem perfectam affert, ut electio sit appetitio earum rerum, quæ sunt in nostra potestate, & quatum exitus est incertus à consultatione proveniens.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he institutes a comparison between deliberation and choice. For since choice is defined through deliberation, as is clear from the end of the preceding chapter, he has therefore brought in this treatment of deliberation so that the nature of choice might be better known. He compares them so as to show where they agree and where they differ. They agree in their object, for the same thing is deliberable as is eligible, and conversely. Yet they differ in reason (for although the object is the same in reality, it is diverse in concept). For that which is eligible precedes itself insofar as it is deliberable; that is, deliberation always precedes choice. For example, when one deliberates whether war ought to be waged or not, the matter is already deliberable; but when it has been decided that war is to be waged, it is now eligible, or has come under choice. In sum, what has been determined or settled in deliberation is called eligible. The Philosopher proves this by two reasons: (1) we cease to deliberate only when we have arrived at that principle of action from which we must begin; that is, deliberation comes to an end only when the matter falls under choice, so that we may seek whichever part we wish, or turn against it. (2) The point is drawn from the custom of the ancient commonwealths of Greece. For, as Homer reports (Iliad 2), Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks, used to deliberate with the elders of Greece about doubtful and important matters; and when he had at last chosen what seemed best, he then proposed it to the people, so that the people might carry out what he had chosen in common with the chiefs convened after long deliberation. So too among the Romans, the senators were accustomed, from the acts of the kings onward, to debate in the senate what was for the good of the republic; and finally the decrees, or senatus-consulta, that were made were referred to the assembly, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports (Book 7). Finally, he gives the complete definition of choice: choice is the appetite for those things which are in our power, whose outcome is uncertain, and which arise from deliberation.

units.la: Notandum consultationem duobus modis sumi; Primò communiter pro quavis indagatione rerum futurarum, & sic Astrologi in divinationibus & profigiis suis consultare dicuntur. Secundò, proprie pro iagaci meditatione, de rebus futuris in nostra potestate sitis, & sic hoc loco sumitur, Fit verò consultatio, inquit Philosophus, vel per compositionem, vel per resolutionem. Per compositionem, cum à causis veris & germanis, vel etiam communibus procedituradeff indagranda, & talis consultatio raro fit. 2. Per resolutionem, cum ab effectis ad causas veras, vel genuinas, vel etiam communes procedit, & talis consultatio in communi hominum vita plerumque incidit.
units.tr: It should be noted that consultation (consultatio) is taken in two ways. First, commonly, for any inquiry into future things; and so astrologers, in their divinations and prodigies, are said to consult. Second, properly, for a shrewd deliberation about future things that lie within our power; and it is in this sense that it is taken here. The Philosopher says that consultation takes place either by composition or by resolution. By composition, when one proceeds from true and genuine causes, or even common ones, to be investigated; and such a consultation rarely happens. By resolution, when one proceeds from effects to true or genuine causes, or even common ones; and such consultation usually occurs in the common life of men.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Consultatio sit non de rebus ridiculis, de quibus fatuus consultaret, sed de quibus vir sanae mentis deliberaret.
units.tr: 1. Deliberation is not about ridiculous things, the kind a fool might deliberate about, but about those a man of sound mind would deliberate upon.

units.la: 2. Non de omnibus rebus est consultatio, ut de rebus a Deo & natura productis, aut necessariis aut forte uitu, aut rebus certis, aut de iis quae neque ad nos spectant, neque per nos effici possunt.
units.tr: 2. Deliberation is not about all things, such as things produced by God and nature, which are either necessary or happen by chance, or things that are certain, or those that neither concern us nor can be brought about by us.

units.la: 3. In artibus consultatione magis opus est, quam in scientiis, idque objectorum respectu.
units.tr: 3. There is more need of deliberation in the arts than in the sciences, and this in respect of their objects.

units.la: 4. De fine nulla est consultatio, sed de mediis tantum ad finem ducentibus.
units.tr: 4. There is no deliberation about the end, but only about the means that lead to the end.

units.la: 5. Consultores adhibere solemus, cum de rebus dubiis & magnis, quas per nos ipsos expedire non possumus, deliberamus.
units.tr: 5. We are accustomed to call in advisers when we deliberate about doubtful and important matters, which we cannot settle by ourselves.

units.la: 6. Quod per amicos nostro iussu fit, id etiam per nos fieri debet.
units.tr: 6. What is done through friends at our bidding must also be done by ourselves.

units.la: 7. Si de rebus omnibus esset consultatio, daretur progressus in infinitum,
units.tr: 7. If there were deliberation about all things, there would be progress to infinity.

units.la: 8. Omnem electionem semper aliqua praecedit consultatio aut longa, aut brevis,
units.tr: 8. Every choice is always preceded by some deliberation, either long or short.

units.la: 9. Electio perfecte definitur appetitio a consultatione proveniens, earum rerum, quae in nostra sunt potestate, & quorum exitus est incertus.
units.tr: 9. Choice is perfectly defined as an appetite arising from deliberation, of those things which are in our power and whose outcome is uncertain.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus consultationem tantum fieri de iis rebus, quae ad nos spectent, cum tamen experientia testetur contrarium, nam consiliarii Principum & Magnatum deliberant de iis rebus, quae ad ipsos non spectant, verbi gratia: An leges sint condenda, an tales leges sint salutares Reipub. futura nec ne, nec tamen ista spectant ad ad ipsos, nec sunt in eorum potestate, sed in potestate Principum ac Dominorum suorum: Sic etiam parentes deliberant de rebus liberorum suorum, & amici de rebus amicorum suorum, quae tamen ad illos proprie non spectant? Resp. Vera est sententia Philosophi consultationem tantum instituì debere de rebus ad nos spectantibus, nam per particulam Nos non tantum intelligendi sunt nos in individuo, ut loquitur, sed etiam omnes illi, qui nos spectant vel cognationis, vel amicitiae, vel officii ratione, & sic consiliarii Principum dicuntur consultare de rebus ad se pertinentibus, cum consultant de rebus Principum suorum, nam iis res ad ipsos spectant officii ratione, & quoties aliquis deliberat de rebus ad se non pertinentibus, ut res eas melius cognoscat, & prudentior evadat, cum hac conditione consulitat, si eas ad me spectarent, his utendum putarem medius.
units.tr: I. Question: How can the Philosopher say that deliberation is only about things that concern us, when experience shows the opposite? For the counsellors of princes and magnates deliberate about things that do not concern them: for example, whether laws ought to be enacted, and whether such laws will or will not be wholesome for the commonwealth. Yet these matters do not concern the counsellors, nor are they in their power, but in the power of the princes and their lords. Likewise parents deliberate about the affairs of their children, and friends about the affairs of their friends, which nonetheless do not properly concern them? Answer: The Philosopher's view is true, that deliberation should be undertaken only about things that concern us. For by the word us we must understand not only ourselves as individuals, as he puts it, but also all those who concern us by reason of kinship, friendship or duty. So counsellors of princes are said to deliberate about matters that pertain to themselves when they deliberate about the affairs of their princes, since those affairs concern them by reason of their office. And whenever someone deliberates about things that do not pertain to him, in order to know those things better and become more prudent, he deliberates on this condition: if these things did concern me, I would think these means should be used.

units.la: 11. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus, de fine nullam esse consultationem, sed tantum de mediis ad finem ducentibus, cum tamen experientia testetur, homines saepe numero deliberare, utrum nimirum hoc vel illud vitae genus sequi velint, an hoc vel illi arti vel opificio operam dare debeant, & tamen hac consultat o est de ipso fine, quia hoc aut illud vitae genus est finis quem quisque sibi propositum tanquam scopum ad quem collimat? Resp. Finem esse dupicem, ultimum qui per se est notus & expetendus, & de quo nulla incidit consultatio, & subordinatum, qui relatus ad ultimum finem suspicit rationem medii, quo finis ultimus acquiri & effici possit, & sic consultatio de hoc aut illo vitae genere sequendo, est de fine subordinato, non quatenus est finis propriè prie,sed quatenus medium ducens ad ulteriorem finem, nempe ut vita bene honesteque transigatur. Ubi etiam notandum, aliud esse consultare pro fine, aliud de fine, nam de fine ipso proprie consulare nemo dicitur.
units.tr: 11. Question: How can the Philosopher say that there is no deliberation about the end, but only about the means that lead to the end, when experience shows that men often deliberate whether they wish to follow this or that way of life, or whether they ought to devote themselves to this or that art or trade? Yet such deliberation is surely about the end itself, since this or that way of life is the end which each person sets before himself as the goal at which he aims? Answer: The end is twofold: the ultimate end, which is known and desired in itself, and about which no deliberation arises; and the subordinate end, which, related to the ultimate end, takes on the character of a means by which the ultimate end can be obtained and achieved. So deliberation about following this or that way of life is about a subordinate end, not insofar as it is an end properly speaking, but insofar as it is a means leading to a further end, namely that life may be spent well and honourably. Here it should also be noted that to deliberate for an end is one thing, and to deliberate about an end is another, for no one is said to deliberate about the end itself in the proper sense.

units.la: III. Quaeritur: Quomodo neget Philosophus artes cadere sub consultationem, non tantum hic loco, sed etiam 2. Phys. 6. cum tamen in instituendis artium praeceptis maxime soleat fieri consultatio, & quot sint homines, to fere sensus aut opiniones, etiam in artibus mechanicis tanta est varietas ut pauci sint artifices qui inter se de opere producendo consentiant? Resp. Artes sunt duplices liberales & mechanicae. In liberalibus nullam esse consultationem, non tantum de fine, qui certus est & determinatus, sed etiam de praeceptis, consultationem vero incidere non in ipsa praecepta, sed in hominum opiniones varias, de praeceptis recte & rite confirmandis, in artibus vero mechanicis (quas Philosophus hic vocat conjecturales) magnam incidere consultationem, propterea quod versentur circa res externas, ut circa corpus hominis, variae & diversae sint regiones, diversi hominum mores, diversa populorum ingenia, etsi finis statuatur in iis certus, propter has tamen causas magna est varietas in praeceptis, quibus tanquam mediis acquiritur ipse finis.
units.tr: III. Question: How does the Philosopher deny that the arts fall under deliberation, not only here but also in 2. Phys. 6., when in setting out the precepts of the arts there is usually a great deal of deliberation? Moreover, as many men, so nearly as many opinions, and even among the mechanical arts there is such variety that few craftsmen agree with one another about how a work is to be produced? Answer: The arts are of two kinds, liberal and mechanical. In the liberal arts there is no deliberation, not only about the end, which is certain and fixed, but also about the precepts; deliberation arises not over the precepts themselves but over the varying opinions of men about how the precepts are to be rightly and properly established. In the mechanical arts (which the Philosopher here calls conjectural) there arises a great deal of deliberation, because they are concerned with external things, such as the human body. The regions are various and different, the customs of men diverse, and the natures of peoples differ. Although the end in these arts is fixed, for these reasons there is great variety in the precepts by which the end itself is attained as a means.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: QUartum membrum primi tractatus continetur hoc capite, nempe de voluntate, quae est actus internus, ex quo fluunt operationes externae. Partes capitis sunt duae. In prima refellit quorundam opinionem de objecto voluntatis. In secunda suam sententiam de objecto voluntatis adfert & rationibus confirmat.
units.tr: The fourth member of the first treatise is contained in this chapter, namely on the will, which is an internal act from which external operations flow. The chapter has two parts. In the first he refutes the opinion of certain people about the object of the will. In the second he sets out his own view of the object of the will and confirms it with reasons.

units.la: In prima igitur parte refertur opinionem Platonis, qui dicebat voluntatis objectum esse simpliciter bonum, & Pyrrhonis Philosophi, qui dicebat objectum voluntatis esse tantum apparens bonum. Primo igitur Platonis opinionem refellit, nam Plato lib. 9. de legib. dicit flagitiosos homines & Tyrannos non facere, quae velint, sed stimulo tantum percitos violento, perturbatione & poenitentia in idipsum redundare. Hoc etiam reperit in Gorgia. Et inter Latinos B. Ejus lib. 2. de consolatione Philosophiae prosa 7. illud ipsum approbat. Hanc opinionem refutat Aristoteles argumento ducto ab absurdo. Nam si tantum revera bonum esset objectum voluntatis, sequeretur id, quod quis pravus malevelit non esse objectum voluntatis, at hoc est absurdum, cum sit contra naturam conjugatorum, ut quod quis velit, illud ipsum non sit objectum voluntatis, & si illud sit objectum voluntatis, quoque sequeretur apparens bonum esse revera bonum, cum quod quis malus malevelit, illud non sit natura sua bonum, sed tantum apparens, id potius est natura sua malum, unde malum revera, esset bonum revera, quod est absurdum: Absurdum igitur dicere, tantum revera bonum, esse objectum voluntatis.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he reports the opinion of Plato, who said that the object of the will is simply the good, and that of the philosopher Pyrrho, who said that the object of the will is only the apparent good. First, then, he refutes Plato's opinion. For Plato, in book 9 of the Laws, says that wicked men and tyrants do not do what they wish, but are driven only by a violent goad, and that this ends in the same place as disturbance and repentance. He also finds this in the Gorgias. And among the Latins, Boethius, in book 2 of the Consolation of Philosophy, prose 7, approves the same thing. Aristotle refutes this opinion by an argument from absurdity. For if only the good in truth were the object of the will, it would follow that what a wicked man wills in his wickedness is not an object of the will. But this is absurd, since it is contrary to the nature of correlatives that what someone wills should not be the object of his will. And if that were the object of the will, it would also follow that the apparent good is in truth good, since what a bad man wills in his wickedness is not good by its own nature but only apparently good; rather, it is by its nature evil. Hence evil in truth would be good in truth, which is also absurd. It is absurd, therefore, to say that only the good in truth is the object of the will.

units.la: Secundam quoque opinionem, quae adscribitur Pyrrhoni Philosopho, nam ut testis est Lae. t. lib. 9. de vitis Philosophorum, postquam cum Magis Persarum, & cum Indorum Gymnosophistis perlustratis domum redijsset, nihil plane discernebat, sed omnia in dubium vocabat, & qualitates has boni aut mali pro hominum opinione inesse dicebat, quod & Protagoras Philosophus etiam asserit, refellit etiam Philosophus ratione ducta ab absurdo, quia si tantum apparens bonum esset obiectum voluntatis, sequeretur nihil per se bonum esse obiectum voluntatis, aut si aliquid per se bonum esset obiectum voluntatis, tum id, quod est per se bonum, esset tantum apparens bonum. Apparens vero bonum non est sua natura bonum, sed malum tantum: unde sequeretur, bonum revera esse malum revera, quod etiam est absurdum.
units.tr: He also refutes the second opinion, which is ascribed to the philosopher Pyrrho. For, as Laertius witnesses in book 9 of the Lives of the Philosophers, after travelling through the territory of the Magi of Persia and the Gymnosophists of India and returning home, Pyrrho discerned nothing at all but called everything into doubt, and said that these qualities of good or evil are present in things only according to human opinion. The philosopher Protagoras also asserts this. Aristotle refutes it too by reasoning from absurdity: if only the apparent good were the object of the will, it would follow either that nothing good in itself is the object of the will, or, if something good in itself were the object of the will, that what is good in itself would be only apparently good. But the apparent good is not good by its nature but only evil. Hence it would follow that good in truth is evil in truth, which is also absurd.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis suam opinionem quasi medium inter utramque adfert, & dicit voluntatem considerari duobus modis, vel absolutè & per se, & sic ejus subjectum est revera bonum, vel comparatè, quatenus est hoc vel illo modo affecta, & sic ejus objectum est apparens bonum, seu id, quod habet speciem boni, hanc suam assertionem probat duabus rationibus: 1. A similitudine corporum: nam sicut in corporibus sanis & bene affectis, quae vere sunt salubria, sic videntur & judicantur. In morbus vero contra: Sic etiam voluntas bene affecta & disposita appetit id, quod vere tantum est bonum, male vero affecta id, quod ei videtur bonum. 2. Ratio, quia qui bene affectus de omnibus rebus bene judicat, est enim norma & mensura rerum bene gerendarum: male vero affectus propter animi depravationem male de rebus sentit, & ideo id saepe mero eligit, quod non debet. Tandem sub finem capitis respondit, unde
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he offers his own opinion, as a kind of middle way between the two, and says that the will may be considered in two ways, either absolutely and in itself, and so its subject is good in truth, or comparatively, insofar as it is disposed in this or that way, and so its object is the apparent good, that is, what has the appearance of good. He proves this assertion by two reasons: (1) from the likeness of bodies. For just as in healthy and well-disposed bodies, things that are truly wholesome appear and are judged to be so, while in sick bodies it is otherwise, so too a well-disposed and well-ordered will desires what is truly good, while a badly disposed will desires what seems good to it. (2) The reason is that a man who is well disposed judges all things rightly, for he is the rule and measure of things to be done well. But a man who is badly disposed, because of the corruption of his mind, judges badly of things, and so he often chooses purely what he ought not to choose. Finally, near the end of the chapter, he answers the question of whence

units.la: Hatus natus sit iste error de objecto voluntatis, propterea quod homines voluptatis illecebris capti, raro sanum, sicut debent, de rebus ferant judicium, quod vero cum tristitia est conjunctum, ut malum fugiunt, cum tamen non ab his exrernis qualitatibus, sed a natura rerum sumere debeat judicium rerum.
units.tr: this error about the object of the will arises: men, captivated by the allurements of pleasure, seldom form a sound judgement of things as they ought to, and they flee as evil what is joined with sadness. Yet they ought to take their judgement of things not from these external qualities but from the nature of things.

units.la: Notandum voluntatem duobus modis vulgo accipi: 1. Naturaliter pro vi quadam animae rationatricis, qua propter semina virtutum & vitiorum in se posita homo liberè appetere potest, aut bonum reveraaut apparens bonum. 2. Moraliter & sic rursus est duplex, aut rationi rectae subjectae, & sic secundum naturam & essentiam suam appetit tantum revera bonum, vel affectibus obruta, & sic appetit tantum apparens & fucatum bonum.
units.tr: It should be noted that the will is commonly understood in two ways: (1) naturally, as a certain power of the rational soul, by which a man, having the seeds of virtues and vices placed within him, can freely desire either the good in truth or the apparent good. (2) Morally, and in this sense it is again twofold: either it is subject to right reason, and so by its nature and essence desires only the good in truth, or it is overwhelmed by the affections, and so desires only the apparent and counterfeit good.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Voluntatis objectum non est tantum revera bonum, quod volebat Plato, nec tantum apparens bonum, quod volebat Pyrrho, sed utrumque est ejus objectum, diverso respectu.
units.tr: 1. The object of the will is not only the good in truth, as Plato wished, nor only the apparent good, as Pyrrho wished, but both are its object, in different respects.

units.la: 2. Vir bene affectus de rebus omnibus bene judicat, & quod bonum est, eligit.
units.tr: 2. A man who is well disposed judges all things rightly, and chooses what is good.

units.la: 3. Vir bonus est regula & mensura rerum practicarum, quippe qui ex virtute agit.
units.tr: 3. A good man is the rule and measure of practical things, since he acts from virtue.

units.la: 4. Vulgus hominum quod cum voluptate conjunctum est, ut bonum appetunt, quod vero est cum tristitia conjunctum, ut malum fugiunt.
units.tr: 4. The common run of men desire what is joined with pleasure as good, and flee what is joined with sadness as evil.

units.la: DUBIUM.
units.tr: DOUBT.

units.la: Quaeritur: An tantum voluntatis objectum sit revera bonum aut apparens, seu id, quod induit speciem boni, cum tamen men malum qua malum, fit interdum objectum voluntatis: nam voluntas sic res appetit, sicut ab intellectu ei offeruntur, teste Philosopho lib. 3. de anima, cap. 4. At res ab intellectu offeruntur voluntati sapientumero, ut sunt mala, quia cum intellectus res dijudicat & ponderat, qua sunt natura sua mala, ut mala etiam voluntati appetenda objicit? Resp. Nihil quidem obiicitur voluntati ab intellectu, quod intellectus ante non bene discussit, sed si voluntas sit bene affecta, quod malum est, avertatur, si male affecta, id appetit sub specie boni.
units.tr: The question is: is the object of the will truly only the good, or the apparent good, that is, that which wears the appearance of good? Yet evil as evil sometimes becomes the object of the will. For the will desires things just as the intellect presents them to it, as the Philosopher teaches in De Anima, book 3, chapter 4. But are things often presented to the will by the intellect as they are evil, since when the intellect judges and weighs things, it presents to the will evils, which are evil by their own nature, as things to be desired even as evil? Answer: Indeed, nothing is presented to the will by the intellect that the intellect has not first discussed carefully. But if the will is well disposed, it turns away from what is evil; if it is badly disposed, it desires it under the appearance of good.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: REstat 5. & ultimum membrum huius primi tractatus, hoc capite explicandum, nam postquam Philosophus egit, de quatuor principiis actionum humanarum, de spontaneo, electione, consultatione & de voluntate, quae sunt actus interni, a quibus profluunt operationes externae, & ipsi virtutum habitus: Hoc capite accommodat ista principia virtutibus & vitiis. Partes capitis sunt quatuor. In prima ostendit virtutes & vitia esse in nostra potestate. In secunda opinionem eorum adducit, qui dicunt virtutes esse in nostra potestate, vitia vero minime. In tertia duo fundamenta istius opinionis affert, & solidis rationibus refellit. In quarta epilogat omnia, quae de virtute in genere dicta sunt.
units.tr: It remains to explain here the fifth and last part of this first treatise. After the Philosopher has treated the four principles of human actions (the voluntary, choice, deliberation and will), which are internal acts from which external operations and the habits of the virtues themselves flow, in this chapter he applies these principles to virtues and vices. The chapter has four parts. In the first he shows that virtues and vices are in our power. In the second he sets out the opinion of those who say that virtues are in our power but vices are not. In the third he brings forward two foundations of that opinion and refutes them with solid reasons. In the fourth he sums up everything that has been said about virtue in general.

units.la: In prima igitur ostendit non tantum virtutes, quod pleriq; concedunt, sed etiam vitia esse in nostra potestate: nam Plato lib. 9. de legibus multis demonstrare nititur, neminem sponte sua esse improbum, proinde vitia hominum no esse in hominum potestate, quæ opinio Poëtis vulgi magistris, tum etiam ipsi multitudini inprimis attribuit, quæ hac specie & hac similitudine peccata sua elevare & excusare consuevit, idipsam asserit Socrates in Protag. apud Plat. At vero Aristoteles, hac ratione probat, tam vitia, quam virtutes esse in nostra potestate, seu utiplæloquitur, in nobis sita, quia honesta & turpia facere vel non facere est in nostra potestate, nam ex mutua contrariorum lege si unum contrariorum sit in nobis situm, situm erit & alterum, & cum I lato cum suis confiteatur, honesta facere est in nostra potestate, ergo & turpia facere, cum sint contraria quod ex Logicis patet.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he shows that not only virtues, as most people concede, but also vices are in our power. For Plato, in the ninth book of the Laws, tries to demonstrate by many arguments that no one is wicked of his own accord, and so the vices of men are not in their power. This opinion is ascribed to the poets, the teachers of the common people, and above all to the crowd itself, which is accustomed to lessen and excuse its sins in this way and by this kind of comparison. Socrates in the Protagoras of Plato asserts the same thing. Aristotle, however, proves by this argument that vices as well as virtues are in our power, or, as he puts it, lie within us. For to do honourable deeds or not to do them is in our power; for by the mutual law of contraries, if one of two contraries lies within us, the other will lie within us too. And since he and all his followers grant that to do honourable deeds is in our power, so too is it to do shameful deeds, since they are contraries, as is clear from the logicians.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis opinionem Platonis adfert ex versu Epicharmi Pœtæ, neminem scilicet sponte sua esse malum, & neminem invitum esse beatū. Posteriorem partem tanquam veram, scilicet neminem invitum esse beatum, approbat Philosophus, quia sponte nostra bene agimus, & bene agentes, gradatim ad fœlicitatem pervenimus, sed priorem partem, neminem scilicet sponte sua esse malum, tanquam falsam rejicit propter has rationes. Prima. Quia sic nemo pravus esset principium actionum suarum, & omnia quæ de principiis actionum humanarum, sive eæ actiones sint bonæ sive malæ à pleno appetitu profluebus traditæ sunt, essent frustranea. Nam non minus videtur pravus principiū actionum suarum, imo eitieveia, quam pater principium suorum liberorum, quos sponte generat & non invitus. Secunda ratio. Actiones tam pravas quam bonas esse in nostra potestate, ostendunt fa-cta &c Legum latorum, qui bonis actionibus proemia statuunt, malis vero poenam, quod non facerent, nisi pravae actiones essent in voluntate agentium, & ipse Plato, lib. 12. de legibus, & in Gorgia inquit, Vitia hominum atque fraudes, damnis, ignominiis, vinculis, verberibus, exilio, morte punire solent homines. Et Ulpian. Jurisconsultus, l. 1. ff. de justitia & jure, hoc ipsum asserit, & rationem reddit, quia justitia suum cuique tribuit. Tertia ratio ducitur ab experientia quotidiana, nam videmus, non tantum illos, qui aliquid scienter peccarunt, puniri legibus, sed etiam, qui per imprudentiam aut ignorantiam aliquid fecerint, si modo hujus ignorantiae ipsi sunt autores & causae. Puta qui per brevitatem, iram, aut amorem, aut fraudem aliquam commiserint, quia sunt arum affectionum in ipsis agentibus est causa, & possunt sibi imperare ut caveant sibi ab ejusmodi actionibus, sequeque abstineant, proinde magnopere laudat hoc loco &c cap. 10. 1. Pittacum qui Mitelenae legem tulit, ut duplici poena animadverteretur in ebrios, una propter ebrietatem, quam sponte sua contraxissent, altera propter delictum, si quod committerent ex ebrietate, sed de hac ratione uberius egit supra cap. 2. hujus libri.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he cites the opinion of Plato from a verse of the poet Epicharmus: that no one is wicked of his own accord, and no one is happy against his will. The Philosopher approves the latter part as true, namely that no one is happy against his will, because we act well by our own choice, and in acting well we reach happiness step by step. But the former part, that no one is wicked of his own accord, he rejects as false, for the following reasons. First. If this were so, no one would be the origin of his own wicked actions, and everything that has been taught about the principles of human actions, whether those actions are good or bad, proceeding from full appetite, would be pointless. For a wicked man seems to be the principle of his own actions no less than a father is the principle of the children he begets willingly and not against his will. Second reason. That both wicked and good actions are in our power is shown by the deeds of lawgivers, who set rewards for good actions and punishments for bad ones. They would not do this unless wicked actions lay in the will of those who perform them. Plato himself, in the twelfth book of the Laws and in the Gorgias, says: men are accustomed to punish the vices and frauds of men with losses, disgrace, chains, lashes, exile and death. The jurist Ulpian, in the first law of the Digest, de justitia et jure, asserts the same thing and gives the reason, because justice gives to each what is his due. Third reason is drawn from daily experience. For we see that not only those who have sinned knowingly are punished by the laws, but also those who have done something through carelessness or ignorance, provided that they themselves are the authors and causes of that ignorance. For example, those who have committed a wrong through haste, anger, love or some fraud, because the cause lies in these affections within the agents themselves, and they are able to command themselves to take care against such actions and to abstain from them. Therefore, in this passage and in chapter 10 he greatly praises Pittacus, who enacted the law at Mytilene that drunkards should be punished twice: once for the drunkenness itself, which they had brought on of their own accord, and again for any offence they committed while drunk. But he treated this reasoning more fully above, in chapter 2 of this book.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis, duo fundamenta illorum, qui dicunt vitia non esse in nostra potestate sicut virtutes. 1. Fundamentum est, multi sunt imbecilles & ineptii propter constitutionem corporis, quasi naturaliter propter talem complexionem, quae nollent, facere cogantur: Proinde vitia provenire a prava constitutione aut complexione corporis dicant, cunt, non ab habitu animi hoc fundamentum tanquam absurdum & velamen nequitiæ 4. rationibus refellit Philosophus, 1. Quorum causæ effectivæ seu causæ proximæ sunt in nostra potestate, & ipsi actus seu operationes sunt in nostra potestate, at causæ & effectivæ vitiosorum habituum, verbi gratia: Operationes pravæ sunt in nostra potestate, fluunt enim a voluntate, tanquam a principio interno, & possunt a nobis fieri vel non fieri prolibitu nostro. 2. ratio est. Qui vult causam alicujus effectus, vult etiam ipsum effectum, verbi gratia: Qui vult operationem injustam, quæ est causa injustitiæ, vult etiam ipsum habitum injustitiæ, & qui vult operationem aliquam pravam, tanquam causam alicujus vitii, vult etiam vitiosum habitum, & ratio quia tam causæ vitiorum, quam ipsa vitia fluunt a voluntate non coacta sed libera. 3. Dato & non concesso vitiosos habitus non esse in nostra potestate, postquam tales habitus acquisiti fuerint, tamen erit in nostra potestate non acquirere tales habitus, quod probat a simili, sicut morbis corporis evenire solet, ut multi sibi sponte sua morbos accersant, dum Medicorum præceptis non parent, aut etiam ab iis non abstinent, quæ morbos inducere solent, sed postquam jam contraxerint morbum, non facile possunt depellere, sed tamen erat in ipsorum potestate, non incidere in istos morbos, sic fit in vitiis animi, quæ plane sunt in nostra potestate priusquam contrahantur: nam possumus ea fugere vel non fugere: at postquam contracti fuerint, & habitum induerint, no facile possunt depelli. 4. Nisi vitia tam animi quam corporis essent
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter, the two foundations of those who say that vices are not in our power as virtues are. (1) The first foundation is this: many men are weak and unskilled because of the constitution of their bodies, as if by nature, on account of such a temperament, they are forced to do things they would not wish to do. Therefore they say that vices arise from a bad constitution or temperament of the body, not from a habit of the mind. The Philosopher refutes this foundation, as absurd and a veil for wickedness, with four arguments. (1) The efficient causes, or proximate causes, of things are in our power, and the actions or operations themselves are in our power. But the causes and efficient causes of vicious habits, for example bad operations, are in our power, for they flow from the will as from an inner principle, and they can be done or not done by us at our pleasure. (2) The second argument is this: whoever wills the cause of an effect also wills the effect itself. For example, whoever wills an unjust operation, which is the cause of injustice, also wills the habit of injustice itself; and whoever wills some wicked operation as the cause of a vice also wills the vicious habit. The reason is that both the causes of vices and the vices themselves flow from a will that is not compelled but free. (3) Granted, though it is not conceded, that vicious habits are not in our power once they have been acquired, it will still be in our power not to acquire such habits. He proves this by analogy: just as it often happens to bodies that many men bring diseases on themselves of their own accord, when they do not obey the precepts of physicians, or do not abstain from those things that are accustomed to cause disease. But once they have contracted the disease, they cannot easily drive it away; yet it was in their power not to fall into those diseases. So it is with the vices of the mind, which are clearly in our power before they are contracted, for we can flee from them or not flee from them; but once they have been contracted and have taken hold as a habit, they cannot easily be cast out. (4) Unless vices of the mind as well as of the body in our power, these men would be blamed in vain for such vices. For things that come from nature are not usually reproached. For example, no one blames natural blindness, but everyone is accustomed to blame blindness brought on by drunkenness or excessive drinking, because a blind man could easily have guarded himself against that vice. So too no one is accustomed to blame ignorance in one who is not fully in possession of his mind, but everyone is accustomed to blame ignorance in a healthy man of sound mind, because the man has contracted that ignorance through his own carelessness and negligence. Therefore that foundation is erroneous, the one which holds that vices are not in our power because men are by nature compelled, through a bad temperament, to do what they would not wish. For they can resist a bad temperament and strive against it, through good upbringing and the cultivation of morals, as Laertius reports of Socrates in the second book of Lives of the Philosophers.

units.la: s feh in nostra potestate, frustra vituperarentur isti homines ob ejusmodi vitia,nam quæ à natura sunt, non solent vitio verti, verbi gratia: Cæcitatem naturalem nemo vituperat,at vero cæcitatem ebrietate aut nimio potu inductam, omnes vituperare solent, propterea quod cæcus facilè potuerit ab ejusmodi vitio sibi cavere: Sic ignorantiam in eo,qui mentis non est satis compos,nemo vituperare solet, sed ignorantiam in homine sano & mentis compote,propterea quod sua incuria & negligentia homo istam ignorantiam contraxerit, vituperare omnes solent. Proinde erroneum est iHud fundamentum, quod vitia ideo non sint in nostra potestate,quia ob pravam complexionem homines naturaliter quæ nollent, facere cogantur: Possunt enim pravæ complexioni resistere, & in contrarium niti, honesta educatione & cultura morum, quod de Socrate refert Laërtius lib.2. de vitis Philosophorum.
units.tr: The second foundation, by which they try to prove that vices are not within our choice, is this: everyone desires what seems good to him. But the appearance, or what seems, is not under our control; it is nature itself that forms such an imagination in a man, so that some desire what is truly good and others only what seems good. He refutes this foundation with two arguments. (1) The nature of this appearance is not the cause; the cause is the disposition and affection of the agent. For whatever sort of person each is, that is the end he desires. For example, if someone is endowed with true virtue, he desires what is truly good; but if on the contrary he is given over to vices, he desires what only seems good.

units.la: Secundum fundamentum,quo probare nituntur, vitia non esse nostri arbitrii, est hoc, unusquisque id appetit, quod sibi videtur bonum, apparentiæ seu ejus,quod videtur,non semus Domini, sed natura ipsa, quæ talem in homine phantasiam efformat, ut quidam appetant id, quod revera est bonum, quidam vero quod tantum videtur bonum, hoc fundamentum duabus rationibus refellit. 1. Quia non est in causa hujus apparentiæ natura, sed affectio & dispositio agentis, nam qualis quisque est, talem appetit finem, veluti gratia: Si quis sit vera virtute præditus, id appetit quod revera est bonum, sin è contrario vitiis sit deditus, id quod tantum videtur bonum.
units.tr: For the nature of the thing does not determine it. Therefore nature is not the sole cause of why men desire what seems good to them. Rather, the disposition and affection of the one who desires is the cause, for operations flow from the will, habits emerge from operations, and finally the choice of an end comes from the habits. (2) The second reason is: if…

units.la: nam num appetit. Proinde non tantum natura est causa, cur id appetant homines, quod iis videtur, quam dispositio & affectio appetentis: nam à voluntate profluunt operationes, ab operationibus proman- nant habitus, ab habitibus demum electio finis. 2. ratio est: Si idem natura effectum in causa, cur magis eligeremus hoc bonum vel illud, quia gignit in nobis phantasiam, non magis virtutes efficiunt in nostra potestate quam vitia, eadem enim est utriusque ratio. & fluunt ab iisdem principiis, nam etsi natura primam affectionem aut appetitionem finis in uno quoq; homine producat, proximam tamen appetitionem producit voluntas hoc vel illo modo disposita.
units.tr: For [the wicked] does not desire [what is good in itself]. Therefore nature is not so much the cause of why people desire what seems good to them as the disposition and affection of the one who desires. For actions flow from the will, habits flow from actions, and finally the choice of the end flows from habits. The second reason is this: if nature were the cause of why we choose this good rather than that, because it produces an appearance in us, then virtues would be no more within our power than vices, for the reason is the same for both, and they spring from the same principles. For although nature produces in every person the first affection or appetite for an end, it is the will, disposed in this way or that, that produces the immediate appetite.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis concludit ea omnia, quae de virtute in genere dicta sunt lib. 2. tum etiam, quae de principiis actionum humanarum, à quibus promanant virtutes, allata sunt: Hoc lib. 3. demum ostendit ipsas operationes seu actus esse magis in nostra potestate, quia immediate profluunt ab ipsa hominis voluntate, quam sunt habitus, qui mediate & per operationes proveniunt à voluntate. Proinde magis cavendum est à pravis actionibus, quam ab ipsis habitibus, quia actiones pravae sunt principia habituum viciosorum, & quia sunt in nostra potestate, scilicet ceri possunt pro nostro libitu, at vitiosos habitus ex actio ibus pravis contractos removere summa est difficultas.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he sums up everything said about virtue in general in book 2, and also what was said about the principles of human actions, from which virtues arise. In book 3 he finally shows that the operations or acts themselves are more within our power than habits are, because they flow immediately from the human will itself, whereas habits come only mediately, through operations, from the will. Therefore we must guard against wicked actions more than against the habits themselves, because wicked actions are the principles of vicious habits, and because they are in our power, that is, they can be avoided at our pleasure. But to remove vicious habits contracted from wicked actions is a very great difficulty.

units.la: Notandum hanc disputationem institutam contra Platonem de voluntatis libertate, innixi quatuor hic erationibus. 1. Quia agere vel non agere in nobis est situm liberum & spontaneum. 2. Voluntas est proximum principium actionum humanarum, à qua fluunt omnes omnino actiones hominum, sive bonæ sint sive malæ. 3. Nisi tam mala quam bona essent in nostra potestate, frustra præmium bonis, & pœna malis in Rebuspub. proponeretur. 4. Otiosè omnia monita & consilia adhiberentur ad virtutem amplectendam, vitium fugiendum.
units.tr: It should be noted that this disputation against Plato about the freedom of the will rests on four arguments: (1) to act or not to act lies within us, freely and spontaneously; (2) the will is the proximate principle of human actions, from which all human actions flow, whether good or bad; (3) unless bad things as well as good were in our power, rewards would be offered to good men and punishments to bad men in commonwealths in vain; (4) all warnings and counsels to embrace virtue and shun vice would be applied to no purpose.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Bene vel male agere, turpiter vel honestè facere, est in nobis situm. Proinde & virtutes & vitia sunt in nostra potestate.
units.tr: 1. To act well or badly, to act basely or honourably, lies within us. Therefore both virtues and vices are in our power.

units.la: 2. Legumlatores præmium bonis, pœnam malis statuere solent.
units.tr: 2. Lawgivers are accustomed to set rewards for the good and punishments for the bad.

units.la: 3. Puniri solent commissa per ignorantiam accersita, vide cap. 2.
units.tr: 3. Things committed through ignorance that was itself brought on are usually punished; see chapter 2.

units.la: 4. Laudabile est illud institutum Pittaci, qui duplici pœna animadvertendam statuit in ebrios.
units.tr: 4. That institution of Pittacus is praiseworthy, who decreed a double penalty for drunkards.

units.la: 5. Ridiculum est dicere, nos ex dispositione corporis & naturaliter male agere,
units.tr: 5. It is ridiculous to say that we act badly because of the disposition of the body and by nature.

units.la: 6. Ut quivis potest facilè morbum accersere, non facilè depellere, sic nemo non poterit incidere in vitium, sed non facilè inde eluctari.
units.tr: 6. As anyone can easily bring on a disease but not easily drive it away, so anyone can fall into vice, but cannot easily struggle out of it.

units.la: 7. Nemo vitium à natura contractum, sicut nostra culpa & negligentia accersitum, vituperare debet.
units.tr: 7. No one ought to blame a vice contracted from nature in the same way as one brought on by our own fault and negligence.

units.la: 8. Non natura, sed nos ipsi causa sumus nostrorum habituum bonorum aut malorum.
units.tr: 8. Not nature, but we ourselves, are the cause of our good or bad habits.

units.la: 9. Actiones sunt magis in nostra potestate, quia immediatè fluunt à voluntate, quam habitus, qui per actiones à voluntate proveniunt.
units.tr: 9. Actions are more within our power than habits, because actions flow immediately from the will, whereas habits come from the will through actions.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An jure Aristoteles taxarit Platonem, quod negarit vitia esse in nostra potestate, cum nemo sit tam mentis impos, ut malum appetat, cum omne malum destruat naturam boni. 1. Etsi quis generaliter sciat malum no esse faciendum, tamen particulariter nescit hoc, quod ipse facit esse malum, alioquin non faceret? Resp. Verum est quidem, nemo appetere malum, qua malu, sed tamen ex depravato apperitu multi appetunt, quod est natura sua malum, sub specie boni, & quatenus iis bonum videtur. 2. Ridiculum illud videtur, aliquem scire aliquid generaliter seu in genere, & nescire hoc ipsum speciali-er seu in specie, cum haec sit ignorantia plane accersita, cum non tam ipsa ignorantia sit in causa, quam depravata agentis voluntas, ut supra eleganter cap. 1. disseruit Philosophus. Proinde & si quis dicat, se nescire hoc esse malum, quod facit, tamen est in ejus potestate scire, hoc esse malum, nam communia principia de honesto & turpi, quivis ex lege naturae & rationis scire tenetur.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Did Aristotle rightly rebuke Plato for denying that vices are in our power, since no one is so deprived of reason as to desire evil, given that every evil destroys the nature of good? 1. Even if someone knows in general that evil is not to be done, does he not in particular fail to know that what he himself does is evil? Otherwise he would not do it? Answer: It is indeed true that no one desires evil as evil, but nevertheless, from a depraved appetite, many desire what is evil by its very nature, under the appearance of good and insofar as it seems good to them. 2. That seems ridiculous: that someone should know something in general, or in its genus, and yet not know this same thing specifically, or in particular. This is plainly ignorance brought on by oneself, since it is not so much the ignorance itself that is the cause as the depraved will of the agent, as the Philosopher elegantly argued above in chapter 1. Therefore, even if someone says he does not know that what he does is evil, it is still in his power to know that it is evil, for everyone is bound by the law of nature and reason to know the common principles of the honourable and the shameful.

units.la: II. Quaeritur: An jure dicantur vitia esse in nostra potestate, cum tamen ipse fateatur Philosophus, nos non posse magis a viris declinare, cum velimus, quam agrotantes possunt convalescere cum velint, idem etiam probatur alio simili: sicut nemo poterit lapidem projectum revocare, etsi maxime velit, sic neque ex vitio emergere, proinde his similibus probare videtur Philosophus, vitia non esse in nostra potestate? Resp. Per haec similia nihil aliud intelligit Aristoteles, quam difficultatem emergedi ex vitiorum habitibus semel contractis: nam sicut aegrotantes non possunt facile evadere ex morbo, sed summa cum difficultate, sic, qui semel habitum vitiorum contraxerit, non facile potest eum amittere, etsi maxime velvellet, nec qui flagitium aliquod commisit, non potest id infectū reddere, quantumvis maxime vellet.
units.tr: II. It is asked: Are vices rightly said to be in our power, when the Philosopher himself admits that we cannot turn away from vices when we wish, any more than the sick can recover when they wish? He also proves the same by another similar example: just as no one can recall a stone once thrown, however much he wants to, so neither can one rise out of vice. Does the Philosopher, by such comparisons, seem to prove that vices are not in our power? Answer: By these comparisons Aristotle means nothing other than the difficulty of emerging from vicious habits once they have been contracted. For just as the sick cannot easily escape from disease but only with great difficulty, so one who has once contracted a habit of vice cannot easily shed it, even if he very much wished to. Nor can one who has committed some shameful deed undo it, however much he might wish to.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: Chapter 9

units.la: SEquitur secundus tractatus huius libri, in quo de singulis virtutibus in specie agit, & 1. de Fortitudine, cuius rei ratio haec reddi poterit, quia naturae humanae, hic ordo virtutum, quem observavit Aristoteles, est accommodatissimus: nam in pueris statim elucent fortitudinis vestigia, pueris & adolescentibus maxime congruunt vires & fortitudo, tum etiam temperatia, ut bene & modeste se gerant. Qua de re eleganter disserit Philosophus 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 7. provectiorem aetatem, & maturum judicium, cum ratione paratis postulant liberalitas & justitia. Extremae aetati convenit prudentia, tanquam omnium virtutum corona & compendium: licet vero, temperantia naturae ordinem (cum in omnibus ab incunte aetate insit) praecedere videatur, praestantiae tamen ordine praecedere debet fortitudo, cum publice magis, quam privatim haec prosit, temperantia e contra privatim maxime, ut posthac cap. 11. huius libri, patebit. Recte igitur Philosophus de fortitudine primo egit, & postea de temperantia hoc lib. 3. De liberalitate lib. 4. De justitia lib. 5. & demum de prudentia lib. 6. Contra ac Cic. qui dignitatis & praestantiae habita ratione in Officiis primo agit de Prudentia. 2. de Justitia. 3. de Liberalitate. 4. de Fortitudine, & Temperantia. In secundo igitur hoc tractatu agit de Fortitudine. Membra huius tractatus sunt quatuor. Primo, de objecto seu materia circa quam.
units.tr: There follows the second treatise of this book, in which he deals with the individual virtues one by one, and first with fortitude, and the reason for this order can be given: the order of the virtues that Aristotle observed is most suited to human nature. For the traces of fortitude already shine forth in boys, and strength and courage especially suit boys and young men, and temperance too, so that they conduct themselves well and modestly. On this matter the Philosopher discusses elegantly in the first book of the Rhetoric to Theodectes, chapter 7: liberality and justice require a more advanced age and mature judgment, prepared by reason. Prudence suits the last age, as the crown and summary of all the virtues. Although temperance seems to precede fortitude in the order of nature (since it is present in all from earliest age), fortitude ought nevertheless to precede in the order of excellence, since it benefits the public more than the private person, whereas temperance benefits the private person most, as will become clear later in chapter 11 of this book. Therefore the Philosopher rightly treats fortitude first, and afterwards temperance in book 3 of this work, liberality in book 4, justice in book 5, and at last prudence in book 6. Cicero acts otherwise: in the Offices, taking account of dignity and excellence, he treats prudence first, then justice, then liberality, and then fortitude and temperance. In this second treatise, then, he deals with fortitude. The parts of this treatise are four. First, he deals with the object or matter with which it is concerned.

units.la: Ioan. 3. quam versatur fortitudo, agit. In secundo de operationibus fortitudinis, tum etiam vitiorum illi opposito uni seu de exc\u0304[?] & defectu fortitudinis In tertio, Fo titudinis non veræ quinq; species enumerat. In quarto, varias proprietates explicat, ut fortitudinis natura magis innotescat.
units.tr: John 3. The matter with which fortitude is concerned. In the second part he treats of the operations of fortitude, and also of the vice opposed to it, namely the excess and the defect of fortitude. In the third he lists five species of false fortitude. In the fourth he explains various properties, so that the nature of fortitude may become better known.

units.la: Primum membrum continetur hoc capite. Cujus partes sunt tres: In prima agit de materia circa quam versatur fortitudo, (nam omnis habitus habet suum objectum, per quod ejus actio dignoscitur, ex actione cognoscitur potentia, ex potentia essentia, & sic a notioribus nobis procedimus ad ea, quæ nobis sunt minus nota, ut præclarè docet Philosophus 2. de Anima cap. 7.) In secunda parte removet ea, quæ non sunt vera objecta fortitudinis. In tertia determinat ipsum fortitudinis objectum in specie.
units.tr: The first part is contained in this chapter. Its parts are three. In the first he deals with the matter with which fortitude is concerned (for every habit has its object, by which its act is recognised; from the act we know the power, from the power the essence, and so we proceed from what is better known to us to what is less known to us, as the Philosopher teaches admirably in book 2 of the On the Soul, chapter 7). In the second part he removes those things that are not the true objects of fortitude. In the third he determines the proper object of fortitude itself.

units.la: In prima igitur agit de materia circa quam versatur fortitudo, & dicit versari circa fiduciam & metū, seu circa res formidolosas, nam magis versatur circa metū, quam circa fiduciam; sicut temperantia in doloribus & voluptatibus moderandis versatur, magis tamen circa voluptates, quam dolores, & declarat, quæ sint eæ res, quæ vulgò vocantur formidolosæ, uno, inquit, verbo, vocantur mala, hoc probat à communi definitione metus, nam omnes sic metum definiunt: metus est exspectatio mali, & sic Plato in Protag. & Lachete, & Cicer. 2. Tusc. sub sin. Si spes, inquit, est exspectatio boni, tum metum exspectationem mali esse necesse est, hac etiam definitione usi sunt Stoici, teste Laër. lib 9. de vita Philosophorum. Notandum malum consideraři duobus momodis: uno modo, ut est vitium animi & operatio vitiosa, & quia hoc malum est in nostra potestate, non est objectum fortitudinis, sed omnes promiscuè virtutes malo animi mederi dicuntur. Secundò sumitur malum pro laesione quadam, quæ extrinsecus accidit, ut sunt paupertas, ignominia, exilium, mors, & quia hoc malum non est in nostra potestate, hoc dicitur objectum fortitudinis, & metus ille circa quem versatur fortitudo, dicitur expectatio hujus mali, quod extrinsecus accidit.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he deals with the matter with which fortitude is concerned, and says that it is concerned with confidence and fear, or with frightening things. For it is concerned more with fear than with confidence, just as temperance is concerned with moderating pains and pleasures, yet more with pleasures than with pains. He declares what those things are that are commonly called frightening: in one word, he says, they are called evils. He proves this from the common definition of fear, for everyone defines fear thus: fear is the expectation of evil. So Plato in the Protagoras and Laches, and Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations book 2 at the end. If hope, he says, is the expectation of good, then fear must be the expectation of evil. The Stoics also used this definition, as Laertius testifies in book 9 of the Lives of the Philosophers. It must be noted that evil is considered in two ways. In one way, as a vice of the soul and a vicious action; and since this evil is within our power, it is not the object of fortitude, but all the virtues are said to heal the evil of the soul in common. Secondly, evil is taken as a certain injury that happens to us from outside, such as poverty, disgrace, exile, death; and since this evil is not within our power, this is called the object of fortitude, and that fear with which fortitude is concerned is called the expectation of this evil, which happens from outside.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis distinguit res formidolosas, ut inveniat, in quibus vere posita sit fortitudo; distinguit vero in tria genera: Nam alia res sunt formidolosæ, quas metuere est honestum; non vero metuere, in honestum & turpe, ut sunt ignominia, dedecus, convitia, belli famosi, &c. Sed in his non est posita fortitudo, quia ut fortis proprie non metuit, ab his tamen rebus metuere unusquisque debet et fortis: nam qui ab his sibi non metuit, cum honestati repugnent, & famã laedant, non fortis, sed imprudens dici debet.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he distinguishes frightening things, in order to find those in which fortitude truly consists. He distinguishes them into three kinds. For some things are frightening, and it is honourable to fear them, but not honourable to fear them in an unseemly and shameful way, such as ignominy, dishonour, reproaches, infamous war, and so on. But fortitude does not consist in these, because the brave man properly does not fear them, yet everyone, even the brave man, ought to fear these things: for the one who does not fear them, since they are opposed to honour and harm one's reputation, should be called not brave but imprudent.

units.la: 2. Alia sunt res, quæ quidem videntur formidolosæ, sed proprie non sunt, ut paupertas, dolor morbi, dejectio à Magistratu aut ab aliqua dignitate, invidia, &c. tum etiam omnia ea, quæ non per nos fiunt, sed extrinsecus accidunt, ut sunt debilitas, cæcitas, mors liberorum & amicorum, & ratio est, quia vitari non possunt, frustra igitur ab iis caveamus, quæ vitari nequeunt, frustra igitur & metuamus.
units.tr: 2. Other things are those which indeed seem frightening, but properly are not, such as poverty, the pain of sickness, removal from office or from some dignity, envy, and so on; also all those things that do not come about through us but happen from outside, such as weakness, blindness, the death of children and friends. The reason is that they cannot be avoided; therefore it is in vain that we guard against what cannot be avoided, and so it is in vain that we fear them.

units.la: 3. Denique quædam sunt res maximè formidolosæ, sed in iis aliæ sunt acerbiores, aliæ minus acerbæ, sed in acerbissimis, maximeque formidolosis posita est vera fortitudo.
units.tr: 3. Finally, some things are most frightening, but among them some are more bitter and some less bitter; true fortitude is placed in the most bitter and most frightening things.

units.la: In tertia parte cap. determinat ipsum fortitudinis objectum in specie, & ostendit mortem esse objectum circa quod versatur, & ratio redditur, quia mors fit maxime formidabilis: nam cum fortitudo versetur circa res maxime formidolosas, & ut inter omnes constat, nemo constantius & patientius res acerbas & formidolosas perferre potest viro forti, nihil vero morte est formidabilius; nam est rerum omnium ultimum, ut ait Philosophus, & vitae huius omnia commoda, & lucis huius usuram eripit, & iis hominibus tanto magis timenda videbatur, propterea quod Ethnici homines, de meliori post hanc vitam conditione, nihil certum & exploratum habebant, ut videre est apud Cic. lib. 2, Tuscul. Sed quia mors est varia, alia enim est mors in bello & acie, alia in morbo, alia in mari, alia in supplicio, inquirit, in quo genere mortis posita sit vera fortitudo, & dicit uno verbo positam esse in morte bellica, & ratio est, quia est omnium pulcherrima, unde Virg. 2. Aen. Pulchramque petunt per vulnera mortem, nam pro rebus pulcherrimis, oppetere solent haec mors, puta pro patria, liberorum, amicorum, libertatis, & religionis defensione, & honestatis & decoris gratia, omnes hanc mortem maxime appetunt. At vero non versatur fortitudo circa mortem in mari, aut in morbo, quia mors in mari provenit a causa fortuita, puta a tempestate, aut alia aliqua causa externa, mors e morbo debetur materiae, quae in homine est corruptibilis, nec perpetuo durare potest, si fortitudo versaretur circa mortem naturalem, tum omnes, qui naturaliter diem suum obirent, etsi nunquam in via virtutem coluissent, vere fortes essent, quod est absurdum. Probat mortem bellicam esse pulcherrimam a signo quodam ab honoribus, nempe a praemiis, quibus insigniter affici solent, qui mortem opperiuntur pro Republ. in Regnis aut in Rebuspublicis afficiuntur, puta statuis, immunitatibus, libero victu, tum etiam divinis honoribus, ut testatur Philosophus lib. 1. Rhet. cap. 9. hinc tot militum commoda & priv. leg. a. Unde Imperator Justinianus per gloriam, inquit, vivunt, qui in praelio pro patria occubuerunt lib. 1. Institut. tit. 25. §. 1. De excusationibus tutorum idem etiam habetur lib. 1. ff. bello am. si. At vero veram fortitudinem non veritati ca mortem in mari, probat duabus rationibus: 1. Quia fortis dolet in hujusmodi morte. At vero longissime omnis dolor abesse debet a vera fortitudine, hinc Ulysses lib. 5. Odyss. apud Hom. & Ajax Oileus apud Sophoclem, & Aeneas apud Virg. gravissime conqueruntur se ingloriam mortem in mari opperire, & non in acie, ubi possent Patriae & Reipub. prodesse. 2. Quia vero fortis in iis cernitur, in quibus possit viriliter agere, & verae fortitudinis signa ostendere, quod in mari fieri vix possit. Poterit tamen aliqua fortitudo in morte marina apparere, si quis intrepido & infracto animo ad hanc mortem subeundam, quam evitare nequit, se pararet, sicut de Arione citharaedo Gellius refert.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he determines the proper object of fortitude itself, and shows that death is the object with which fortitude is concerned, and the reason is given that death becomes most formidable. For since fortitude is concerned with the most frightening things, and as everyone agrees, no one can bear bitter and frightening things more steadfastly and patiently than the brave man; and nothing is more formidable than death. For it is the last of all things, as the Philosopher says, and it snatches away all the goods of this life and the use of this light; and it seemed the more to be feared by men, because the heathen had nothing certain and proven about a better condition after this life, as can be seen in Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 2. But since death is of various kinds — for one death is in war and battle, another in sickness, another at sea, another by execution — he inquires in which kind of death true fortitude is placed, and he says in one word that it is placed in death in battle. The reason is that this is the most beautiful of all; hence Virgil in the Aeneid book 2: They seek a glorious death through wounds. For men are accustomed to meet this death for the most noble causes, namely in defence of country, children, friends, liberty and religion, and for the sake of honour and dignity; all seek this death most eagerly. But fortitude is not truly concerned with death at sea or in sickness, because death at sea comes from a chance cause, namely a storm or some other external cause; death from sickness is owed to the matter that is corruptible in man, and cannot last forever. If fortitude were concerned with natural death, then all who died naturally, even though they had never practised virtue on the way, would be truly brave, which is absurd. He proves that death in battle is the most beautiful by a sign drawn from honours, namely from the rewards with which those who meet death for the commonwealth are usually signally honoured in kingdoms or republics: statues, exemptions, free food, and even divine honours, as the Philosopher attests in book 1 of the Rhetoric, chapter 9. Hence the many advantages and privileges of soldiers. Whence the Emperor Justinian says: those who have fallen in battle for their country live through glory, in book 1 of the Institutes, title 25, §1, on the excuses of guardians; the same is also found in book 1 of the Digest, on the military ... . But he proves that true fortitude is not concerned with death at sea by two reasons: 1. Because the brave man grieves in such a death. Yet all grief ought to be far from true fortitude. Hence Ulysses in book 5 of the Odyssey among Homer, and Ajax son of Oileus in Sophocles, and Aeneas in Virgil, lament most grievously that they await an inglorious death at sea and not in battle, where they could be of service to country and commonwealth. 2. Because fortitude is seen in those circumstances in which a man can act manfully and show the signs of true fortitude, which can hardly happen at sea. Yet some fortitude may appear in death at sea, if someone prepares himself to undergo this death, which he cannot avoid, with a fearless and unbroken spirit, as Gellius relates of the lyre-player Arion.

units.la: Notandum Fortitudinis vocabulum trifariam vulgo accipi: Pro robore corporis, cum artubus validis, firmioribus musculis & membris quispiam praevalet, exempla extant apud Plin. lib. 7. naturalis hist. cap. 20. & 18. Talis fuit Hercules, talis etiam Milo CrotoCrotoniates, cujus memi nit Gellius lib. 15. Noctium Attic. cap 16. Talis etiam Cacus, cujus meminit Virgil. 8. Æneid. & Ovid. 1. Fast. & hoc sensu Dion dixit, Fortitudine, dum juvenes sumus utimur, prudentia senescentes & consilio valemus, teste Lært. lib. 4. de vit. Philos. in Dion. 2. Similitudo Fortitudo pro omni susceptione periculorum, maxime vero belli-corum, sicut recta ratio & lex jubet, teste Philosopho lib. 1. Rhet. cap. 9. & hoc loco. Ex his quæ supra dicta sunt, talis definitio fortitudinis elici potest. Fortitudo est virtus, quæ metum & fiduciam in periculis honestatis gratia subeundi & ferendis, maximeque vero in morte bellica adferre solet. Constat definitio tribus partibus. Genere, fine & objecto. Genus est virtus, de qua toto lib. superiore, 2. actum est; Finis, ut pericula decoris & honesti gratia suscipiantur. Objectum est duplex, commune & proprium. Commune est omne formidolosum, quod vires humanas non superat, & quicquid fiduciam aut metum in periculis adferre solet. Proprium est mors bellica, quæ ideo dicitur fortitudinis proprium objectum: 1. Quia est difficillima per certamen. 2. Est pulcherrima propter decorum. 3. Est honestissima propter causam. 4. Est celeberrima propter famam, quæ viros bellicosos comitari solet.
units.tr: It should be noted that the word fortitude is commonly taken in three ways. First, for bodily strength, when someone excels with sturdy limbs, firmer muscles and robust members. Examples occur in Pliny, Natural History, book 7, chapters 20 and 18. Such was Hercules, and such also was Milo of Croton, whom Gellius mentions in book 15 of the Attic Nights, chapter 16. Such too was Cacus, whom Virgil mentions in Aeneid 8 and Ovid in Fasti 1. In this sense Dion said, "We use fortitude while we are young, but as we grow old we are strong in prudence and counsel," as Laertius reports in book 4 of his Lives of the Philosophers, in the life of Dion. Second, fortitude is taken for the enduring of every kind of danger, and especially of war, as right reason and law require, according to the Philosopher in Rhetoric book 1, chapter 9, and in this place. From what has been said above, the following definition of fortitude can be drawn: fortitude is the virtue which usually brings about fear and confidence in undertaking and bearing dangers for the sake of honour, and especially in death in battle. The definition consists of three parts: genus, end and object. The genus is virtue, of which the whole of the previous book (2.) has treated. The end is that dangers are undertaken for the sake of what is seemly and honourable. The object is twofold, common and proper. The common object is everything frightening that does not exceed human strength, and whatever is wont to bring confidence or fear in dangers. The proper object is death in battle, which is called the proper object of fortitude for these reasons: (1) because it is the most difficult to face in combat; (2) it is the most beautiful because of its seemliness; (3) it is the most honourable because of its cause; (4) it is the most celebrated because of the fame that usually accompanies warlike men.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Fortitudo est virtus circa fiduciam & metum.
units.tr: 1. Fortitude is a virtue concerned with confidence and fear.

units.la: 2. Metus est expectatio mali, ut spes dicitur expectatio boni.
units.tr: 2. Fear is the expectation of evil, as hope is called the expectation of good.

units.la: 3. Quædam sunt, quæ metuere honestum est, verbi gratia: infamiam, dedecus, contemtum non metuere, turpe.
units.tr: 3. There are some things which it is honourable to fear; for example, not to fear infamy, dishonour or contempt is shameful.

units.la: 4. Ab omni metu longè abesse debet verè fortis, cum metuere sibi vitium sit.
units.tr: 4. The truly brave person ought to be far removed from all fear, since to fear for oneself is a vice.

units.la: 5. Quae nostra culpa non accidunt, ea vir fortis metuere non debet.
units.tr: 5. The brave person ought not to fear those things that do not happen through our own fault.

units.la: 6. Non circa omne formidolosum versatur propriè fortitudo, sed circa mortem tantum bellicam.
units.tr: 6. Fortitude properly is not concerned with every thing that is frightening, but only with death in battle.

units.la: 7. Neque poterit fortitudo dici, quae versatur circa mortem in morbo aut in mari.
units.tr: 7. Nor can that be called fortitude which is concerned with death from sickness or at sea.

units.la: 8. In quocunque demum periculo fortitudinis signa ostendere, & pulchrè mori non licet, ubi fortitudo propriè non versatur.
units.tr: 8. In whatever danger it is not permitted to show the signs of fortitude or to die nobly, where fortitude is not properly exercised.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: 1. Quaeritur: An fortitudo possit recte dici virtus, cum omnis virtus sit medium inter duo extrema vitia, at fortitudo non est medium inter duo vitia, nam dicitur in textu, virtus circa fiduciam & metum. Fiducia verò & metus non sunt vitia animi, sed affectus naturales, qui à natura provenient? Resp. Metus & fiducia considerantur duobus modis. 1. Naturaliter, quatenus scilicet ieguuntur talem vel talem corporis constitutionem, & sic inter fiduciam & metum non collocatur fortitudo tanquam extrema. 2. Considerantur moraliter, quatenus scilicet ex habitu agendi tales acquiruntur in homine, & sic potius sunt vitia animi, quam affectus naturales, & hoc modo inter fiduciam & metum moraliter consideratos, versatur fortitudo.
units.tr: 1. Question: Can courage rightly be called a virtue, since every virtue is a mean between two extreme vices, yet courage is not a mean between two vices? The text says that virtue is concerned with confidence and fear, but confidence and fear are not vices of the mind; they are natural affections that arise from nature. Answer: Fear and confidence can be considered in two ways. (1) Naturally, that is, insofar as they follow from this or that bodily constitution; in this sense courage is not placed between confidence and fear as their extremes. (2) Morally, that is, insofar as they are acquired in a person through habits of acting; in this sense they are vices of the mind rather than natural affections, and it is between confidence and fear considered morally that courage lies.

units.la: 11. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat paupertatem & morbum non esse timendum, & quacunque nostra culpa non fiunt, non esse timenda, cum paupertas inducat contemptum & rerum omnium necessitatem, morbus debilitatem & dolorem sape etiam mortem, ideo paupertas & morbus maxime timeri debent? Resp. Paupertas sicut & morbus consideratur duobus modis: nam interdum paupertas nostra culpa fit, verbi gratia: Prodigus nimia profusione, accersit sibi paupertatem, sic etiam incontinens, qui intemperanter vivit, accersit sibi morbum. & haec esse timenda docet Aristoteles, quia vitiis onerant animum: nam quae nostra culpa contrahuntur, gignunt in nobis vitiosum habitum.
units.tr: 11. Question: How can he say that poverty and sickness are not to be feared, and that whatever happens without our fault is not to be feared, since poverty brings contempt and want of everything, and sickness brings weakness and pain, often even death, so that poverty and sickness ought above all to be feared? Answer: Poverty, like sickness, can be considered in two ways. Sometimes poverty comes about through our own fault: for example, the spendthrift brings poverty upon himself by excessive extravagance, and likewise the intemperate man, who lives without restraint, brings sickness upon himself. Aristotle teaches that these are to be feared, because they burden the mind with vices; for what we contract through our own fault produces a vicious habit in us.

units.la: 2. Paupertas & morbus consideratur, quatenus non nostra culpa, sed ex causa alia extrena proveniunt, & secundo modo considerATOS, non esse timendos constat, sed qui fortiter & intrepido animo se in iis gerit, vere fortis dici debet, ut Stilpho ille Thebanus apud Senecam Epistola 6. qui Thebis direptis nihil se amisisse dicebat: & Posidonius Stoicus apud Cic. 2. Tusc. Podagra laborans, exclamat, nihil agis dolor, quamvis sis molestus, nunquam dicam te esse malum.
units.tr: 2. Poverty and sickness, considered as not coming through our fault but arising from some other external cause, are clearly not to be feared. Whoever bears himself bravely and with an undaunted mind in them ought truly to be called brave. So it was with that Stilpo of Thebes in Seneca, Letter 6, who, when Thebes had been plundered, said that he had lost nothing. So too Posidonius the Stoic, in Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 2, while suffering from gout, cries out: "You do nothing, pain; though you are troublesome, I will never say that you are evil."

units.la: III. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicatur fortitudo versari circa mortem bellicam, tanquam proprium suum objectum, propterhanc rationem, quia mortem bellicam praclare opperiri est difficillimum, at difficilius est furentes animi impetus cohibere, & incompositis animi affectibus moderari: proinde si ideo mors bellica dicatur proprium objectum fortitudinis, quod sit difficillima & ideo magis deberet esse eius objectum proprium, irregulares animi affectus, quae moderari sit difficillimum?
units.tr: III. Question: How is courage said to be concerned with death in war as its proper object, for this reason, that it is most difficult to meet death in war nobly, whereas it is more difficult to restrain the furious impulses of the mind and to moderate disordered affections?
