Therefore, if death in war is called the proper object of courage because it is most difficult, then the irregular affections of the mind, which are most difficult to moderate, ought rather to be its proper object.

units.la: Resp. Objectū fortitudinis est duplex. Internum & externum: Interni sunt furentes animi impetus, sed hoc est objectum commune fortitudini, cum aliis virtutibus, nam omnes virtute dig debent moderari animi affectibus quibuscunque. Externum sunt omnia ea pericula, quae metum aut homini fiduciam afferre possunt, inter quae nihil difficilius, quam praeclare mortem oppetere in bel-lo, ut supra diximus.
units.tr: Answer: The object of courage is twofold, internal and external. The internal object is the furious impulses of the mind, but this is an object common to courage along with the other virtues, for all who are virtuous ought to moderate the affections of the mind, whatever they may be. The external object is all those dangers which can bring fear or confidence to a person, among which nothing is more difficult than to meet death nobly in war, as we said above.

units.la: IV. Quaeritur: An fortitudo circa mortem bellicam, poterit dici virtus, cum omnis virtus sit habitus: Habitus vero crebris actionibus comparetur, at fortitudo, quae versatur circa mortem bellicam, non comparatur crebris actionib. nam vel una actione morte scilicet cadit vir fortis, & sic non poterit dici comparasse iflum habitum fortitudinis crebris actionibus. Ergo aut fortitudo non erit virtus, aut non versabitur circa mortem bellicam, tanquam proprium objectum? Resp. Minor non est vera, nam omnes graves & molestae afflictiones, quas justa adhibita consideratione fortis sustinet, pericula circa mortem dici possunt, perinde non ipsa actio, qua fortis morte cadit, dicitur tantum objectum fortitudinis, sed omnia ea, quae mortem in bello adferre possunt.
units.tr: IV. Question: Can courage concerned with death in war be called a virtue, since every virtue is a habit, and a habit is acquired through frequent actions, whereas courage concerned with death in war is not acquired through frequent actions? For by a single action, namely dying, the brave man falls, and so it cannot be said that he acquired this habit of courage through frequent actions. Therefore either courage will not be a virtue, or it will not be concerned with death in war as its proper object? Answer: The minor premise is not true. For all the grave and troublesome afflictions which the brave man endures, when rightly considered, can be called dangers concerning death. Thus it is not the very act by which the brave man falls in death that is called the object of courage, but all those things which can bring death in war.

units.la: V. Quaeritur: An si fortitudo versatur circa mortem bellicam tanquam proprium objectum, sequetur esse virtutem specialem Politicam, non Ethicam in genere consideratam. Ergo aut male hic tractatur, aut objectum ejus non erit mors bellica, ratio consequentia est, quia ad politica spectat agere de bello, & iis, quae ad bellum spectant? Resp. Non sequitur, nam mors bellica consideratur bifariam vel determinate ad aliquod subjectum & membrum Reipubl. puta Principem vel subditum, & sic spectat ad Politicam. 2. Indeterminate & late, quatenus quemvis in genere hominem virtutis capacem spectat, quae sicut objectum fortitudinis in Ethica hic consideratur.
units.tr: V. Question: If courage is concerned with death in war as its proper object, it will follow that it is a special political virtue, not an ethical one considered in general. Therefore either it is wrongly treated here, or its object will not be death in war. The consequence is clear, since it belongs to politics to treat of war and of the things that pertain to war. Answer: It does not follow, for death in war can be considered in two ways. (1) Determinately, with reference to some subject and member of the commonwealth, say the prince or the subject, and in this sense it belongs to Politics. (2) Indeterminately and broadly, insofar as it concerns any man in general who is capable of virtue; and in this sense, as the object of courage, it is considered here in Ethics.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: SEquitur secundum membrum secundi tractatus in quo Philosophus ostedit operationes fortitudinis & extremorum ipsius, id est, excessus & defectus. Partes capitis sunt tres. In prima: nova distinctione distinguit formidabilia aut terribilia, circa quæ versatur fortitudo. In secunda: agit de extremis oppositis ipsi fortitudini. In tertia adfert hanc quæstionem, An ille fortis dici debeat, qui sibi ipsi violentas manus adfert.
units.tr: The second part of the second treatise follows, in which the Philosopher shows the operations of fortitude and its extremes, that is, excess and defect. The chapter has three parts. In the first, by a new distinction he separates the frightening or terrible things with which fortitude is concerned. In the second, he treats of the extremes opposed to fortitude itself. In the third he raises this question, whether he should be called brave who lays violent hands on himself.

units.la: In prima igitur dividit terribilia in duo genera, nam alia sunt supra hominem seu supra humanam conditionem, & vires humanas, quæ nimirum sunt majora, quam aut possunt aut debent, ab homine sana mente prædito contemni, cujusmodi sunt omnia ea portenta, & extraordinaria prodigia, quæ manifesta Dei iram denunciant, veluti sunt exundationes extraordinariæ, magnæ & concitatæ tempestates, fulmina horrenda, terræ motus, &c. qui ab his sibi non metuit, aut despicit aut fatuus est. Tales fuerunt Psilli, (Thraciæ populus est) quos refert Herodot. lib. 4. in Euterpe, contra Austrum & ventum illis nimis infestum armata manu profectos, sed arena omnes obruros, stultitiæ mercedem retulisse: Tales etiam fuerunt Celtæ, quos Ælianus lib. 12. varia historia, cap. 13. contra exundationem marinam pugnasse refert, sed fluctibus adversis omnes ad unum periisse. In his fortitudo locum proprie non habet, nam cum fortitudo sit virtus humana, circa res humanes, quæ ab hominibus produci possunt, versari debet. Secundo cundò alia sunt terribilia, secundum hominē, quæ ab homine sustineri possunt, & non superat metam conditionis humanæ, & hæc sunt bipartita, aut enim sunt ejusmodi, quæ certi quidam homines metuunt, nempe ignari, & hæc sunt levissima quæque, & in his non versatur fortitudo: Aut sunt ea, quæ omnes plerumque homines sana mente præditi metuunt, ut sunt gravissima pericula, vulnera, mors, &c. & in his proprie versatur fortitudo, & ab his metuit sibi fortis, sine reprehensione tamen, id est, sicut recta præscribit & dictat ratio, nā quoquo modo ista fortis metuat, honestatis tamen gratia facile tolerabit, quod probat duabus rationibus: 1. est, qui confidit sic, sicut præscribit ratio, ille vere dicetur fortis, etsi in aliquo casu metuere dicatur: nam regula & mensura virtutum omnium est recta ratio, sicut patet ex definitione virtutis supra tradita lib. 2. cap. 7. Secunda ratio est, qui secundum finem fortitudinis agit, & qui subit ea, quæ oportet, & quando oportet gratia honestatis, ille vere est fortis.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he divides terrible things into two kinds. Some lie above man, that is, above the human condition and human powers, being greater than man, of a sound mind, can or ought to despise. Such are all those portents and extraordinary prodigies that announce God's anger: extraordinary floods, great and violent storms, dreadful lightning, earthquakes, and so on. Whoever is not afraid of these is either contemptuous or foolish. Such were the Psylli (a people of Thrace), whom Herodotus, book 4, in Euterpe, reports to have set out against the south wind and a wind that was too hostile to them, with armed men, and who, being buried by the sand, all paid the price of their folly. Such too were the Celts, whom Aelian, Varia Historia, book 12, chapter 13, reports to have fought against a sea flood, and who all perished to a man in the hostile waves. In such matters fortitude properly has no place, for since fortitude is a human virtue, it ought to be concerned with human affairs, which can be produced by human beings. Secondly, other things are terrible in relation to man: those which man can bear and which do not exceed the limit of the human condition. These are of two kinds. Some are feared by certain particular men, namely the ignorant; these are the slightest things, and fortitude is not concerned with them. Others are those which most men of sound mind generally fear, such as the gravest dangers, wounds, death, and so on; fortitude is properly concerned with these, and the brave man fears them, yet without blame, that is, as right reason prescribes and dictates. For however the brave man may fear them, for the sake of honour he will readily endure them. He proves this by two arguments. (1) He who acts with confidence as reason prescribes is truly called brave, even if he is said to fear in some case; for the rule and measure of all the virtues is right reason, as is clear from the definition of virtue given above, book 2, chapter 7. (2) He who acts according to the end of fortitude, and who undergoes what he ought, and when he ought, for the sake of honour, is truly brave.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis: adfert extrema fortitudini oppositá, & confert ea cum ipsa fortitudine, & 1. Adfert extrema in excessu, quia majorem habent cognationem cum fortitudine, Extrema in excessu duo, quorum alterum nomine vacat, & ratio est, quia raro tales reperiuntur, qui non timeant timenda, aut absque omni ratione ruunt in pericula, quales fuerunt Psilli & Celtæ, de quibus supra. Poterit tamen hoc extremum vocari ἀσωτία. Latinè temeritas: Alterum extremum dicitur audacia, cujus hanc notam adfert Philosophus, quod nempe sit gloriosa & imitatrix veræ fortitudinis, hinc plærumque fit, ut audaces sæpè dicantur & habeantur fortes, qua de re eleganter Plato lib. 8. de legib. & Cic. in Partition. nam ut verè fortis intrepidò solet subire pericula animo, sic etiam & audax, extremum in defectu dicitur ignavia, cujus itidem duo sunt peccata, 1. quod ignavus omnia metuat, 2. quod nihil omnino confidat, magis tamen ex eo dicitur ignavus, quod omnia pericula metuat, omnesque labores & dolores detrectet, quam quod nihil omnino confidat: Unde ut duo erant extrema in excessu, temeritas & audacia, sic duo possunt dici in defectu, ignavia & diffidentia. Tandem confert fortem, audacem & timidum inter se, & primò fortem cum timido; nam licet, inquit, fortitudo & ejus extrema versentur circa unum idemque objectum, tamen diversò modo versantur. Nam fortis, quia confidit, benè quoq; sperat, gnavus vero ò seu timidus, quia omnia metuit, nihil confidit, sed semper malè sperat.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he sets out the extremes opposed to fortitude and compares them with fortitude itself. First, he sets out the extremes in excess, since they have greater kinship with fortitude. There are two extremes in excess, one of which has no name. The reason is that such men are rarely found who do not fear what is to be feared, or who rush into dangers without any reason, such as the Psylli and Celts mentioned above. This extreme, however, may be called asotia [ἀσωτία], in Latin temeritas (rashness). The other extreme is called audacity. The Philosopher gives this mark of it: that it is glorious and imitates true fortitude. Hence it often happens that the audacious are often called and considered brave, a point which Plato, De legibus, book 8, and Cicero, Partitiones, make elegantly. For just as the truly brave man is accustomed to face dangers with an intrepid spirit, so too the audacious man does. The extreme in defect is called cowardice. It likewise has two faults: (1) that the coward fears everything; (2) that he has no confidence at all. Yet he is called a coward more because he fears all dangers and shrinks from all labours and pains, than because he has no confidence at all. Hence, as there were two extremes in excess, rashness and audacity, so two can be named in defect, cowardice and diffidence. Finally, he compares the brave man, the audacious man, and the timid man with one another, and first the brave man with the timid man. For although, he says, fortitude and its extremes are concerned with one and the same object, they are concerned in different ways. For the brave man, because he is confident, also hopes well; but the coward, or timid man, because he fears everything and has no confidence, always hopes badly.

units.la: Notandum timidum dici dupliciter. 1. A natura cujusmodi sunt omnes Melancholici, qui propter frigiditatem sanguinis natura timidiores sunt. 2. Ab usu, quales sunt, qui omnia pericula refugiunt, & nullum omnino subire audent, & talis timiditas opponitur fortitudini. Secundò confert fortem cum audaci, nam etsi circa eandem naturam, inquit, versentur, diferunt tamen inter se quatuor modis: 1. Audax imprudenter & sine ratione pericula adit, fortis contra. 2. Audax est arrogans & minax ante periculum, in periculo verò remissior & timidior. Fortis contra ante periculum sedato & tranquillo est animo mo, in ipso periculo cum acrimonia & absque omni metu se gerit. Exempla sunt de Aristogetone Athenienji, qui ut refert Ælianus lib. 3. varia historia cap 5. per multos dies de sua animi promtitudine & bello animose gerendo disputavit, cum bellum indicendum esset, crure obligato morbum simulavit, sic etiam Livius lib. 3 dec. 2. refert Dictatorem in milites quosdam haec verba protulisse in castris, inquit, feroces sunt Leones, in pugna timidi lepores: Et pulcherrimus extat locus apud Appianum de bello civili, cum bellum commemorat inter consules, Priscum & Pansam & M. Antonium, in quo milites veteranos summo cum silentio & acrimonia pugnasse refert. Tyrones vero magno strepitu & confusis clamoribus. 3. Differt fortis ab audace, quod audax subeat quidem pericula ardua, sed non constanter sustineat, sed ubi res in arduum venit, fugam arripit: Fortis contra inter stanter pericula subit, sed constanter perfert, & quia honestatem respicit, fugam sibi colere in honestum & turpe putat, & fortissime se in summo vitae discrimine gerit, talem describit Livius Fabium Maximum, qui cognomento Dictator dictus erat. 4. Audaces sunt maledici & dicaces, fortes contra, unde Virg. 10 Æneidos.
units.tr: It should be noted that timid is said in two ways. (1) By nature, as are all melancholics, who are more timid by nature on account of the coldness of their blood. (2) By habit, as are those who flee all dangers and dare to undergo none at all; and this timidity is opposed to fortitude. Secondly, he compares the brave man with the audacious man. For although they are concerned with the same matter, he says, they differ from one another in four ways. (1) The audacious man rushes into dangers imprudently and without reason; the brave man does the opposite. (2) The audacious man is arrogant and threatening before danger, but in danger he is more relaxed and timid. The brave man, by contrast, before danger is of a calm and tranquil spirit, and in danger itself he conducts himself with keenness and without any fear. Examples are Aristogeiton of Athens, who, as Aelian reports, Varia Historia, book 3, chapter 5, for many days disputed about his own readiness of mind and about waging war boldly, and when war was to be declared, pretended illness with a bound leg. So too Livy, book 3, decade 2, reports that a dictator spoke these words to certain soldiers in camp: "The lions are fierce in the camp, but the hares are timid in battle." And there is a most beautiful passage in Appian, On the Civil War, where he recounts the battle between the consuls Priscus and Pansa and Mark Antony, in which he reports that the veteran soldiers fought with the greatest silence and keenness, while the raw recruits fought with great noise and confused shouting. (3) The brave man differs from the audacious man in that the audacious man indeed undertakes arduous dangers, but does not endure them steadily; when the matter becomes difficult, he takes to flight. The brave man, by contrast, undertakes dangers steadily and bears them steadily, and because he regards honour, he thinks flight to be base and shameful, and he conducts himself most bravely at the highest peril of life. Livy describes such a man in Fabius Maximus, who was called Dictator by surname. (4) The audacious are slanderers and railers, the brave are not. Hence Virgil, Aeneid book 10:

units.la: Vesano talia late
units.tr: Such mad words fly widely

units.la: Dicta volant Lygeri, sed non & Trojae Heros
units.tr: From Lygerus, but the hero of Troy

units.la: Dicta parat contra, Jaculum nam torquet in hostem:
units.tr: Does not prepare words in reply; for he hurls his javelin at the enemy.

units.la: Notandum quoque & audacem dici simpliciter vel perse, qui sine omni consideratione circumstantiarum, ferarum more in pericula fertur, & talis dicitur proprie temerarius & insanus, vel composite, qui praeter ter temeritatem adeundi pericula, superbus & glo- riosus existit.
units.tr: It should also be noted that the audacious man is called audacious simply or per se, who without any consideration of circumstances rushes into dangers like wild beasts; such a man is properly called rash and mad. Or he is called audacious compositely, who, besides the rashness of facing dangers, is also proud and boastful.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis proponit hanc quæstionem; an ille fortis dicendus fit, qui sibi ipsi manus violentas adfert, negat duabus præcipue rationibus. 1. Quia mollis & fracti animi est, gravia pericula, dolores & incommoda non perferre, quam animi vera fortitudine præditi, cum vitæ fortis propria sit patientia, omnino hæc sunt semper in ore verba:
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he proposes this question: whether he should be called brave who lays violent hands on himself. He denies it, chiefly for two reasons. (1) Because it is the mark of a weak and broken spirit not to endure grave dangers, pains and troubles, whereas those endowed with true fortitude of spirit do endure them; since patience is the proper virtue of the brave life. Accordingly these words are always on the lips of the brave:

units.la: Tu ne cede malis, sed contra audacior ito.
units.tr: Do not yield to misfortunes, but go on the more boldly against them.

units.la: Hac etiam ratione utitur D. Aug. lib. 1. de civ. Dei, c. 21.
units.tr: Augustine also uses this argument, City of God, book 1, chapter 21.

units.la: 2. Ratio est: Quia non decoris & honestatis causa, sed mali fuga & molestiæ vitandæ causa, homines desperati sibi manus inferunt, cum contra vir fortis honestatis gratia omnia agat, ut ex definitione fortitudinis patet.
units.tr: 2. The reason is: because men in despair lay violent hands on themselves not for the sake of decency and honour but to flee evil and avoid distress, whereas the brave man does everything for the sake of honour, as is clear from the definition of courage.

units.la: Possunt & hæ addi rationes tres. 3. Quia tales sunt pusillanimes: nam cupiunt formidabilia declinare, quæ vir fortis maxime appetit, & in quibus se vere fortem ostendit, at illi in formidando modum excedunt, & in confidendo omnino deficiunt,
units.tr: Three further reasons may also be added. 3. Such men are faint-hearted. They wish to avoid frightening things, which the brave man especially seeks and in which he shows himself truly brave, but they exceed the proper measure in fearing and altogether fail in confidence.

units.la: 4. Vir fortis semper bene sperat, nec spes illum unquam deserit, hinc Seneca: unica veræ fortitudinis anchora est spes, quà sola in omnibus vitæ tempestatibus firmum & immotum vir fortis se præbet: At qui sibi manus inferunt, spem omnem prorsus abjecerunt.
units.tr: 4. The brave man always hopes well, and hope never deserts him. Hence Seneca: "The only anchor of true courage is hope, by which alone the brave man shows himself firm and unmoved in all the storms of life." But those who lay hands on themselves have utterly cast off all hope.

units.la: 5. Vir fortis nihil contra justitiam & rectæ rationis normam agit, at isti contra, cum se ipsos læduunt, quod ratio vetat, & justitia prohibet.
units.tr: 5. The brave man does nothing against justice or the rule of right reason. These men do, when they harm themselves, which reason forbids and justice prohibits.

units.la: 6. Vir fortis mortem moderatè metuit: nam ut supra dictum est, metuit sicut rectæ ratio præscribit, & vitam longiorem captat, ut possit sua virtute, & sibi & aliis prodesse, isti contra, vitae pertaesi mortem exoptant, ut per eam a malis praesentibus, quae tolerare nolunt, eripiantur.
units.tr: 6. The brave man fears death moderately, for, as said above, he fears as right reason prescribes, and he seeks a longer life so that by his virtue he may benefit both himself and others. These men, weary of life, desire death so that by it they may be snatched from present evils which they refuse to endure.

units.la: Possunt addi & hae rationes Theologicae: 1. Ab imagine Dei, ad quam homo conditus est, & quam neque in aliis neque in se ipso homo destruere debet. 2. A charitate Christiana, nam sicut non laedere debemus proximum, ita neque nos ipsos, nam nemo carnem suam odio habere debet, inquit Apostolus. 3. A magnitudine pretii, quo Christus nos redemit, quia hoc est Christi mortem contemnere, gratiam oblatam respuere, unde Martyr. in 1. Sam. cap. ult. In summa nemo sibi manus violentas adferre debet, propter has quatuor rationes. 1. est. Quia mortem sibiipsi conscire, est contra naturam, quae omnibus certam vitae periodum, usumque dedit, & quae jubet omnia potius mala, & omnem poenam tolerare, quam mortem subire voluntariam, quia mors est omnium malorum naturae quid infensissimum: nam destruit ipsam naturam. 2. est: contra leges civitatis, quae idipsum prohibent, quaeque semper ignominiam suiipsorum homicidis constituunt. Hinc apud Thebanos, teste Plutarcho; si quis sibi mortem conscivisset, velut immanis belua, & suiipsius carnifex habebatur: Et apud Athenienses, alterutram manum corpore abscindebant, tanquam facinorosam, & seorsim a cadavere inhumatam relinquebant. Et Plato lib. 6. & 9. de leg. statuit horum corpora perpetua ignominia esse afficienda, & sepultura honore privanda: Et jus civile statuit. si quis sibi manus inferat, ut dextera cadaveri abscindatur & patibulo publico affigatur, corpus vero canibus & volucribus cæli objiciatur, lib. si quis, ff. de pœnis. 3. ratio est: Contrarectam rationem, nam desperationem rectæ rationi infensissimam importat: nam isti, qui sibi manus inferunt, abjectâ spe rectæ rationi repugnant. 4. Est contra Majestatem divinam: nam tales divino auxilio per desperationem facinorosè diffidunt, & potentiæ divinæ quantum in ipsis est, detrahunt, & Deum ad iram concitant, unde Plato in Phædone: Nemo, inquit, sibi mortem consciscere debet, quia injussu magistratus nemo e statione sua sibi assignata discedere debet, homo autem in custodia corporis à Deo collocatus est, à qua, nisi Deo jubente, recedere non debet. Secundo Dei mancipia omnes sumus, nec aliter irascitur Deus, si quis sibi manus intulerit, quam Dominus aliquis, si aliquod mancipiorum (mancipia enim non sunt sui juris, sed absolutum jus vitæ & necis habet proprie Dominus) se ipsum occiderit, plura vide de hac quæst. apud Augustinum lib. 1. de civ. Dei, à cap. 20. nsq; ad 24. Apud Josephum lib. 3. excidii Hierosolymitani, apud Plutarchum in vita Cleomenis, & apud Picolomineum gradu 9. cap. 16. 17. & 21.
units.tr: These theological reasons may also be added: (1) from the image of God, after which man was made, and which man ought neither to destroy in others nor in himself; (2) from Christian charity, for as we ought not to harm our neighbour, so neither should we harm ourselves, since no one ought to hate his own flesh, as the Apostle says; (3) from the greatness of the price by which Christ redeemed us, for to do this is to despise Christ's death and to spurn the grace offered, whence the Martyr on 1 Sam. last chapter. In sum, no one ought to lay violent hands on himself, for four reasons. (1) It is contrary to nature, which has given all men a certain period and course of life, and which bids them endure all evils and every punishment rather than undergo a voluntary death, because death is the most hostile of all evils to nature, for it destroys nature itself. (2) It is contrary to the laws of the state, which forbid this very thing and which have always fixed infamy on self-slayers. Hence among the Thebans, as Plutarch testifies, anyone who had brought death on himself was regarded as a savage beast and his own executioner; and among the Athenians they cut off one hand from the body, as that of a criminal, and left the corpse unburied apart. Plato, in books 6 and 9 of the Laws, decreed that their bodies should be subjected to perpetual disgrace and deprived of the honour of burial; and the civil law decrees: "if anyone lays hands on himself, let the right hand be cut off from the corpse and fastened to the public gibbet, but the body be thrown to dogs and the birds of the sky," lib. si quis, ff. de poenis. (3) It is contrary to right reason, for it implies despair, which is most hostile to right reason; for those who lay hands on themselves, having cast off hope, oppose right reason. (4) It is contrary to the majesty of God. Such people, through despair, wickedly distrust divine help, and as far as in them lies they detract from the power of God and stir up God to anger. Hence Plato in the Phaedo: "No one, he says, ought to bring death on himself, because just as no one ought to leave his assigned post without the magistrate's order, so man has been placed by God in the guard of the body, from which he ought not to depart unless God commands. Secondly, we are all God's slaves, and God is angered if anyone lays hands on himself no differently than a master would be if one of his slaves killed himself (for slaves are not their own masters, but the master alone has the absolute right of life and death). See more on this question in Augustine, book 1 of The City of God, from chapter 20 to 24; in Josephus, book 3 of the Destruction of Jerusalem; in Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes; and in Piccolomini, grade 9, chapters 16, 17 and 21.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Quædam sunt terribilia, quæ superant vires humanas, & ab hac nemo sibi non metuit, nisi idem sit amens.
units.tr: 1. Some things are terrible and exceed human strength, and no one who is not out of his mind fears them not at all.

units.la: 2. Quædam sunt, quæ non nocent, & in his timere debet vir fortis, sicut recta ratio præscribit.
units.tr: 2. Some things do not harm, and in these the brave man ought to fear as right reason prescribes.

units.la: 3. Finis actionis singularis est ipsi habitus, si non proximus, sed ultimus. 4. Vir fortis honestatis & decoris gratia agit, & perfert omnia.
units.tr: 3. The end of a single action is the habit itself, if not proximate then ultimate. 4. The brave man acts and endures everything for the sake of honour and decency.

units.la: 5. Fortitudini opponitur in excessu temeritas & audacia, in defectu timiditas & ignavia.
units.tr: 5. Opposed to courage are rashness and boldness in excess, and timidity and cowardice in deficiency.

units.la: 6. Audax & arrogans est & vera fortitudinis affectator, sed non actor.
units.tr: 6. The bold and arrogant man is a pursuer of true courage, but not its practitioner.

units.la: 7. Vir fortis semper sperat: ignavus vero nihil confidit, nihil sperat.
units.tr: 7. The brave man always hopes; the coward trusts in nothing and hopes for nothing.

units.la: 8. Audaces ante periculum sunt arrogantes & minaces, in ipso periculo leves & inconstantes.
units.tr: 8. Bold men are arrogant and threatening before danger, and fickle and inconstant in danger itself.

units.la: 9. Vir fortis ante periculum lenis & mitis est, in ipso periculo acris & constans.
units.tr: 9. The brave man is gentle and mild before danger, and keen and steadfast in danger itself.

units.la: 10. Circa unum idemque obiectum versatur audacia, fortitudo & timiditas, sed diverso longe respectu.
units.tr: 10. Boldness, courage and timidity are concerned with one and the same object, but with very different respects.

units.la: 11. Qui ob paupertatem & amorem, aut aliquod hujusmodi malum sibi mortem conscivit, non fortis, sed timidus & ignavus dici debet.
units.tr: 11. He who has brought death on himself because of poverty, love, or some such evil ought not be called brave, but timid and cowardly.

units.la: 12. Qui non honestatis gratia, sed fuga mali mortem subit, ignavi & imbelles est animi.
units.tr: 12. He who undergoes death not for the sake of honour but to flee evil is of a cowardly and unwarlike spirit.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: Doubtful Questions

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus, audaciam in periculo timere, ideoque sibi fuga saepe consulere, cum ista implicent contradictionem: nam audere & timere sunt contradictoria? Respon. In audaci considerantur duo: 1. Coeca quaedam temeritas, quae pellit in periculum, & secundum istam temeritatem dicitur audax & arrogans. 2. Consideratur natura infirmitas, non respondens animo, & secundum istam infirmitatem timere dicitur, & fugam arripere contra naturam arrogantiae.
units.tr: I. It is asked: how can the Philosopher say that the bold man fears in danger, and therefore often takes flight for his own good, when these statements involve a contradiction? For to dare and to fear are contradictory. Answer: two things are to be considered in the bold man: (1) a certain blind rashness, which drives him into danger, and by this rashness he is called bold and reckless; (2) a natural weakness, which does not match his spirit, and by this weakness he is said to fear and to seize flight, contrary to the nature of arrogance.

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo improbet ipsos, qui sibi manus violentas afferunt, cum tamen historia tam sacra, quam profana tanquam bene factum in multis laudent, ex sacris sunt exempla: 1. De Samsone, Judicum 16. quite cum Philistinis interemit; & apud Apostolum 11. Hebr. verf. 32. numeratur in catalogo fidelium Sanctorum. & recte, ut ait Augustin. nam typus fuit Christi: sic etiam exemplum est de Razia 2. Maccab. c. 12. Sic etiam in profanis pro infinitis exemplis unum sufficiat de Catone, qui mirifice laudatur ab Appiano lib. 1 de bello civili? Resp. Non exemplis, sed legibus esse vivendum. 2. Multa exempla proponuntur in Scripturis non tam ad imitandum, quam ad vitandum, ut ebrietas Noë, incestus Lothi. Ad Samsonem quod attinet, respondet Augustinus lib. 1. de civit. Dei, cap. 21. Samson excusatur, inquit, quod se una cum hostibus ruina domus oppresserit, quia Spiritus hoc latenter jubebat, qui per illum mirabilia faciebat. Ad Raziam quod attinet, autor illorum librorum satis gentiliter illum laudat. Nam verf. 41. dicit illum generose & fortiter fecisse, quod se gladio trajecerit, ne in hostium potestatem veniret. At Augustin. loco citato, Solent, inquit, gentes & historiæ gentium sic suos viros fortes laudare, non vero Ecclesia Dei, sic Martyres Christi: Deinde liberiste est Apocryphus, proinde nullum certum testimonium ex eo desumi debet, ad probandam aliquam Christianæ religionis regulam, ut recte Augustin. lib. 1. contra Gaudent. cap. 24. disserit. Ad Catonem etiam quod attinet, sic respondet idem Augustinus lib. 19. de civit. Dei, cap. 4. utrum, obsecro, Cato ille patientia, an impatientia se interemit, non enim se perimisset,
units.tr: II. It is asked: how does he condemn those who lay violent hands on themselves, when sacred and profane history alike praise many such deeds as well done? From sacred history there are examples: (1) Samson, in Judges 16, who died together with the Philistines; and in the Apostle, Hebrews 11, verse 32, he is counted among the catalogue of the faithful saints. And rightly so, as Augustine says, for he was a type of Christ. Likewise there is the example of Razis in 2 Maccabees, chapter 12. Likewise in profane history, out of countless examples let one suffice, that of Cato, who is wonderfully praised by Appian, book 1 of the Civil Wars? Answer: we must live not by examples but by laws. (2) Many examples in Scripture are set forth to be avoided rather than imitated, such as Noah's drunkenness and Lot's incest. As for Samson, Augustine answers in book 1 of The City of God, chapter 21: Samson is excused, he says, because he brought the house down on himself together with his enemies, since the Spirit, which worked wonders through him, secretly commanded it. As for Razis, the author of those books praises him in a rather pagan manner. For in verse 41 he says that he acted nobly and bravely in running himself through with his sword so that he would not fall into the enemy's power. But Augustine, in the place cited, says: nations and the histories of nations are accustomed to praise their brave men in this way, but the Church of God does not praise its martyrs of Christ thus. Besides, that book is apocryphal, and therefore no certain testimony should be drawn from it to prove any rule of the Christian religion, as Augustine rightly argues in book 1 against Gaudentius, chapter 24. As for Cato too, the same Augustine answers in book 19 of The City of God, chapter 4: I beg you, did that Cato kill himself in patience or in impatience? For he would not have killed himself,

units.la: perimisset, missel, nisi Cæsaris victoriam impatienter tulisset: ubi illa est Catonis fortitudo, nempe cessit, nempe succubuit, atque adeo frustrata jacet, ut vitam beatam relinqueret, fugeret, deserteret, &c.
units.tr: would not have killed himself, unless he had borne Caesar's victory impatiently. Where then is Cato's fortitude? Namely, he yielded, namely he succumbed, and so he lies there defeated, in that he abandoned, fled from and deserted a blessed life, and so on.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Annon liceat sibi manus inferre, cum Philosophus ipse testetur lib. 5. cap. 9. hujus operis, tales sibi ipsis injuriam non facere? Resp. Philosophi plerique concedebant mortem voluntariam, si non esset metu gravioris supplicii, aut ab avaritia, aut a simili quadam animi imbecillitate profecta, reliquas causas justas esse putabant; ut videre est apud Cic. lib. 1. offic. & multo clarius lib 2. Tusc. quaest. Et Stoici plerunque hoc concedebant, ut videre est apud Diogen. Laert. in vita Zenonis. Aristoteles tamen hoc omnino hic improbat, & nulla de causa mortem voluntariam concedit. Quod ad locum illum citatum ex libro 5. hoc tantum vult, cum scilicet qui metu gravioris supplicii, aut majoris mali vitandi gratia, etsi sibi injuriam non facere videatur, civitati tamen toti facere, quippe qui hac violenta morte civitatem aut Rempubl. membro uno privat.
units.tr: III. It is asked: is it not lawful to lay hands on oneself, since the Philosopher himself testifies in book 5, chapter 9 of this work that such people do no wrong to themselves? Answer: most philosophers granted voluntary death if it was not done from fear of a heavier punishment, or arose from avarice or some similar weakness of spirit; they thought the other causes were just, as may be seen in Cicero, On Duties, book 1, and much more clearly in Tusculan Disputations, book 2. And the Stoics for the most part granted this too, as may be seen in Diogenes Laertius, in the life of Zeno. Aristotle, however, here wholly disapproves of this and grants voluntary death for no cause. As for that passage cited from book 5, he means only this: a person who, from fear of a greater punishment, or to avoid a greater evil, even though he seems to do no wrong to himself, nevertheless does wrong to the whole state, since by this violent death he deprives the city or commonwealth of one of its members.

units.la: IV. Quæritur: An liceat omnino se occidere, ne cogatur peccare, verbi gratia: Spartana virgines so cum ad Mysseniorum urbem pervenissent, sibi ipsis manus violentas attulerunt, ne a juventute stolida vim impudicam paterentur, ut auctor est Plutarch. Apolonia etiam virgo in ignem se sponte conjecit, ne cogeretur idola adorare, ut testis est Ruffin. Scribit etiam Augustin. mulieres quasdam se in fluvium praecipites dedisse, ne a persecutoribus suis impiis & nefariis hominibus violarentur: Quaeritur, an hoc sit recte factum nec ne, cum ex duobus malis semper minus sit eligendum, & minus sit sit malum mortem eligere, quam in horrenda ejusmodi peccata incidere? Resp. Nec licet omnino fe occidere, nec hoc recte factum habetur propter has rationes: 1. Haberi debet ratio sexti Praecepti: Non occides, cum constanti proposito, quod vel decies millies satius sit, mortem aliena manu oppetere, quam sibi mortem consciscere, aut etiam impiae coacti oni consentire. 2. Bona sunt bene agenda, ut inquiunt Jurisconsulti, Nam non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniat inde bonum, & si finis bonus sit, debent & media esse bona, siquidem a fine mesuram & rationem sui accipiunt media. 3. Qua, ut ait Augustinus cap. 23. lib. 1. de civit. Dei, si haec esset justa causa in ignem se conjicere, ne cogantur idola adorare, tum nihil esset melius aut beatius, quam statim fe post Baptismum occidere, ne semel per fidem Christo insiti ad peccata relabantur. 4. Recte etiam Antimus Nicodemiensis Ecclesiae Antistes a virgine quadam Euphrasia nomine, interrogatus, utrum ex duobus deberet eligere, an mortem sibi consciscere, an persecutoribus suis se violandam praebere? Respondet: Filia Euphrasia, pulcherrimum quidem est castissimae virginitatis donum, sed majus constantiusque est fidei praeceptum, si utrumque conservare non licet, animam saltem puram conserves, & hoc faciendum tibi duco, ut mente ipsa per fidem in Christo confirmata carnem improborum contumeliis & injuriis objicias: Nicephorus lib. 7. Ecclesiasticae historiae, cap. 17. §. Vim pati sine consensu, non est actio, sed passio, proinde veniam & commiserationem meretur non poenam, unde de Lucretia Romana, quae ob stuprum prum à Tarquinio juniore manus violentas intulit, egregiè cecinit Theod. Beza hoc Epigrammate:
units.tr: IV. It is asked whether it is ever lawful to kill oneself so as not to be compelled to sin. For example: when the Spartan virgins had reached the city of Messene, they laid violent hands on themselves so as not to suffer shameful violence from the foolish youth, as Plutarch reports. Apollonia the virgin also threw herself willingly into the fire so as not to be compelled to adore idols, as Rufinus bears witness. Augustine also writes that certain women threw themselves headlong into a river so as not to be violated by their impious and wicked persecutors. The question is whether this was rightly done or not, since of two evils one should always choose the lesser, and it is a lesser evil to choose death than to fall into such horrible sins? Answer: it is not lawful at all to kill oneself, nor is this considered rightly done, for these reasons: (1) The sixth commandment must be taken into account: You shall not kill; with a steadfast resolve, which would be a thousand times better, to meet death at another's hand rather than to bring death upon oneself, or even to consent to impious compulsion. (2) Good things are to be done well, as the jurists say: for evil things are not to be done so that good may come of them; and if the end is good, the means must also be good, since the means receive their measure and rule from the end. (3) As Augustine says in chapter 23 of book 1 of The City of God: if this were a just cause for throwing oneself into the fire so as not to be compelled to adore idols, then nothing would be better or more blessed than to kill oneself at once after baptism, so as not to fall back into sins once grafted into Christ through faith. (4) Antimus, bishop of the Church at Nicomedia, also rightly answered a certain virgin named Euphrasia, who asked him whether, of two things, she ought to choose either to kill herself or to offer herself to be violated by her persecutors. He replied: Daughter Euphrasia, virginity most chaste is indeed a most beautiful gift, but the precept of faith is greater and more steadfast; if it is not permitted to keep both, at least keep your soul pure, and I judge that this is what you must do, namely, that with your mind confirmed in Christ through faith, you expose your flesh to the insults and injuries of the wicked. Nicephorus, book 7 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 17. § To suffer violence without consent is not an action but a passion; therefore it deserves pardon and pity, not punishment. Whence Theodore Beza finely sang of the Roman Lucretia, who laid violent hands on herself because of the rape committed by Tarquin the Younger, in this epigram:

units.la: Si fuit ille tibi Lucretia gratus adulterImmerito ex merita pramia morte petit.Sin potius casto vi est illata pudoriQuis furor, alterius crimine velle mori.Frustra igitur laudem captas Lucretia: namqueVel scelerata ruit vel furiosa cadit.
units.tr: If that adulterer was pleasing to you, Lucretia, then undeservedly by death she seeks the reward her deeds have earned. But if rather violence was done to chaste modesty, what madness it is to wish to die for another's crime. In vain, then, Lucretia, do you seek praise, for she either falls wicked or falls mad.

units.la: Corollarii loco hanc quaestionem subjiciemus: An homo facinorosus, qui confidenter & intrepidè poenas patitur dicendum sit fortis? Resp. Non posse fortem dici propter has tres rationes: 1. Quia fortis suis praemia meretur, non poenam. 2. Quia non quaelibet violenta perpessio cadit in virum fortem, sed tantum ea, quae est honesta, illa vero poenarum perpessio ob aliquod facinus, est inhonesta & infamis, utpote quae juste infligitur homini flagitioso propter flagitia, ad deterrendum alios à similibus peccatis. 3. Vir fortis ex habitu fortitudinis omnia agit, facinorosus non item, cum ne micam quidem veræ virtutis in se habeat.
units.tr: By way of a corollary, we shall add this question: Can a wicked man who suffers punishment confidently and fearlessly be called brave? Answer: he cannot be called brave, for three reasons: (1) Because the brave man deserves rewards, not punishment. (2) Because not every violent suffering befits the brave man, but only that which is honourable; whereas the suffering of punishments for some crime is dishonourable and infamous, since it is justly inflicted on a shameful man for his shameful deeds, to deter others from similar sins. (3) The brave man acts in all things from the habit of fortitude; the wicked man does not, since he does not have in himself even a crumb of true virtue.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Sequitur hic tertium membrum hujus tractatus de Fortitudine, in quo Philosophus, postquam de objecto & oppositis fortitudinis egit, quinque adfert species fortitudinis non veras, sed apparentis, nempe fortitudinem civilem seu civicam, militarem seu experimentalem. 3. Jucundam. 4. Fiduciariam. Et 5. Insciam, & ponit differentiam inter has & veram fortitudinem. Partes capitis sunt quinque pro quinque speciebus fortitudinis apparentis, de quibus hoc loco agit Aristot. sic etiam lib. 3. Eud. cap. 1. & lib. 1. Magnor. Mor. cap. 21. & Pontanus de fortitudine à cap. 23. ad 32. Similitudo in genere in hoc consistit, quod tam in his, quam in vera fortitudine sit quaedam intimiditas, & animus ad pericula subeunda intrepidus. Dissimilitudo vero est in eo, quod vera fortitudo sit perpetua & constans, utpote quae sit habitus, ista non item. 2. Fortitudo honestatis gratia omnia agit, ista non item, sed alios atque alios sibi fines proponit.
units.tr: Here follows the third part of this treatise on Courage, in which the Philosopher, having dealt with the object of courage and its opposites, brings forward five kinds of false courage, that is, not true but apparent courage: (1) civic or civil courage; (2) military or experiential courage; (3) pleasant courage; (4) courage based on confidence; and (5) courage from ignorance. He also draws a distinction between these and true courage. The parts of the chapter correspond to the five kinds of apparent courage with which Aristotle deals here. So also Eudemian Ethics 3.1 and Magna Moralia 1.21, and Pontanus, On Courage, chapters 23 to 32. In general, the likeness lies in this: both in these and in true courage there is a certain fearlessness and a mind that is undaunted in facing dangers. The difference, however, is that true courage is lasting and constant, since it is a habit, whereas these are not. (2) True courage does everything for the sake of honour; these do not, but set themselves one goal after another.

units.la: In prima igitur parte capitis agit de prima specie fortitudinis apparentis, nempe de fortitudine civili seu civica, quae definitur ea fortitudo, quam leges a singulis civibus propositis poenis aut praemiis exigunt, in hoste propulsando & defendenda patria & Repub. Et hinc fit, ut cives illius Reipubl. habeantur omnium fortissimi, inquit Plato 4. de Repub. apud quos viris fortibus & strenuè se gerentibus praemia & honores proponuntur, ignavis vero & imbecillis animi hominibus poenae & infamia, ut videre est apud Lacedaemonios, teste Plutarcho in vita Chromenii, & apud Germanos teste Cornelio Tacito, de moribus Germanorum, et apud Romanos infames capitali afficiebantur supplicio, teste Arriano JCto ad l. omne delictum, ff. de re militari, tum etiam aliis infamiae generibus, ut Vegetius, Gellius, Cicero & alii referunt. Differt vero haec civilis a vera fortitudine in duobus. 1. Causa efficiente, quia hanc leges singulis imperant, sub comminatione poenae, si recusent, at vera fortitudo, non poenae aut legum metu, sed per se terribilia subit. 2. Causa finali, quia non tam honestatem, sicut vera fortitudo, quam praemii adoptionem, puta: honores, aut poenae & infamiae aversationem spectat: Tales inducit Homerus, Diomedem Iliad. 8. qui ideo non recusat cum Hectore congredi, ne Hector apud Trojanos dicat se fugasse Diomedem ad naves: & Hectorem Iliad. 22. qui ideo detractat hoc singulare certamen cum Achille, ne Polidamas redeuntem in urbem jurgiis & convitiis excipiat. Postea philosophus interserit quaedam de iis, qui fortiter pugnant & periculla subeunt, non tam sponte sua, quam Ducum & Imperatorum, quorum sub potestate sunt, jussu & coactu, quod variis modis fit. 1. Propositā gravissima mortis poena. Quod Agamemnon facit lib. 2. Iliad. & Hector 15. Iliad. verberibus & flagellis cives ad pugnam cogunt, sub quibus Persas olim pugnasse contra Lacedaemonios ad Thermopylas refert Herodotus lib. 7. Tertio, cum fossa a tergo exercitui subjicitur, ut vel invitę pugnare cogantur milites, quia nullus fugae pateat locus, cum a fronte sit hostis, a tergo fossa: Sicut Laconas contra Myscenios pugnasse refert Scholiastes Graecus ex Tyrtaeo Poeta. Quarto, cum portas occludunt, pontes rescinduntur, ne ad suos fugientibus sint receptus: Sicut olim Coronei pugnarunt contra Phocenses, teste Plutarcho: Huc etiam pertinent omnes alii modi, quibus milites invitę pugnare coguntur, ut Iliad. 4. Cum Agamemnon dux Graecorum equites collocat in prima acie, fortiores pedites etiam animosiores in extrema, ignaviores in media acie, ut nolentes volentes pugnare cogantur, cum utrinque qui cogant habeant.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter, then, he treats of the first kind of apparent courage, namely civic or civil courage, which is defined as the courage that the laws demand of individual citizens, under threat of penalties or with rewards held out, in repelling the enemy and in defending the fatherland and the commonwealth. Hence, as Plato says in Republic 4, the citizens of that commonwealth are regarded as the bravest of all, for whom rewards and honours are offered to brave men who acquit themselves vigorously, while penalties and infamy await the cowardly and feeble-minded. This may be seen among the Lacedaemonians, as Plutarch witnesses in the Life of Chromenius; among the Germans, as Cornelius Tacitus witnesses in On the Manners of the Germans; and among the Romans, who punished the infamous with capital punishment, as the jurist Arrian witnesses in on the law "omne delictum," Digest, on military affairs; and also by other kinds of infamy, as Vegetius, Gellius, Cicero and others report. This civic courage differs from true courage in two respects. (1) As to the efficient cause: the laws impose it on individuals under threat of punishment if they refuse, whereas true courage faces what is terrible in itself, not from fear of penalty or of the law. (2) As to the final cause: it looks not so much to honour, as true courage does, as to the gaining of rewards, such as honours, or to the avoidance of punishment and infamy. Homer introduces such men: Diomedes in Iliad 8, who does not refuse to engage Hector, lest Hector should say among the Trojans that he had put Diomedes to flight back to the ships; and Hector in Iliad 22, who declines that single combat with Achilles, lest Polydamas should meet him on his return to the city with reproaches and abuse. Next the Philosopher inserts some remarks about those who fight bravely and face dangers, not so much of their own accord as at the command and under compulsion of the commanders and generals under whose power they are, which is done in various ways: (1) by proposing the most severe penalty of death, as Agamemnon does in Iliad 2, and Hector in Iliad 15; (2) citizens are forced into battle with lashes and whips, under which Herodotus, in Book 7, reports that the Persians once fought against the Lacedaemonians at Thermopylae; (3) when a trench is placed behind the army, so that the soldiers are forced to fight even against their will, since there is no room for flight, the enemy being in front and the trench behind; so the Laconians, as the Greek scholiast reports from the poet Tyrtaeus, fought against the Messenians; (4) when the gates are shut and the bridges broken down, so that there is no retreat for those fleeing to their own side, as the Coronaeans once fought against the Phocians, according to Plutarch. To this also belong all other methods by which soldiers are compelled to fight against their will. So in Iliad 4, when Agamemnon, the leader of the Greeks, places the cavalry in the front line, the stronger and more spirited infantry at the extremity, and the weaker in the middle, so that the unwilling are forced to fight whether they will or no, since there are men on both sides to compel them.

units.la: X beant. Itaque hos omnes qui fortiter ducum jussa pugnant, ad primam speciem fortitudinis apparentis seu non verae referendos putat Aristoteles: Nam sicut cives poenarum & legum metu fortiter se gerunt, ita hi ducum minis & verberibus compulsi, strenuè pugnant. Civibus tamen deteriores, quod illi ob pudorem: hi ob metum tantum, cives turpitudinis vitandae gratia, isti poenarum & verberum eff giendorum causa strenuè pugnant.
units.tr: Aristotle thinks that all those who fight bravely at the commands of their leaders should be referred to the first kind of apparent courage, or courage that is not true. For just as citizens behave bravely from fear of penalties and laws, so these fight vigorously, driven by the threats and blows of their commanders. Yet they are inferior to citizens in this respect: the citizens fight vigorously from shame, which they wish to avoid as a disgrace, whereas these do so from fear alone, and only in order to escape punishment and blows.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis adfert secundam speciem fortitudinis apparentis, nempe fortitudinem militarem, ut vulgo dicitur, propterea, quod in veteranis & exercitatis militibus plerumque reperiatur, teste Phil. 3. Eud. c. 1. Hinc vocatur fortitudo per experientiam aut experimentalis, quod experientia & usu plerunque constet. Definitur ea fortitudo, quae milites propter experientiam & spem praedae in periculis ad eundis intrepidos reddit & explicat, in quibus locum habeat, cum in multis aliis rebus tum maximè in rebus bellicis, habet etiam locum in nautis malos scandentibus & adversus tempestates intrepidis. In medicis morbos desperatos curantibus. In urinatoribus aquas profundiores perscrutantibus. In Athletis & multis aliis.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he brings forward the second kind of apparent courage, namely military courage, as it is commonly called, because it is for the most part found in veteran and experienced soldiers, as the Philosopher witnesses in Eudemian Ethics 3.1. Hence this courage is called courage through experience or experiential courage, because it rests for the most part on experience and practice. It is defined as that courage which, through experience and the hope of booty, makes soldiers fearless and bold in going into dangers. It has its place in many other matters, but above all in matters of war. It is also found in sailors who climb the masts and are undaunted against storms; in physicians who treat desperate diseases; in divers who search deep waters; in athletes and many others.

units.la: In militibus vero, quantam vim habeat, usu & experientia conjicere licet, & ex milite veterano & Tyrone, quod adeo Platoni & Socrati placuit, ut hanc fortitudinem, usu & experientia acquisitam speciem non apparentis, sed proprie dictae fortitudinis esse putarint in Lachete & Protagora: nam peritiam & scientiam rerum formidabilium & con-tratrariarum statuebant veram fortitudinem, non recte tamen, nam usu & experientia fortes non ideo sunt vere fortes, quod pericula adire sciant, sed quod usus & peritia adjumenta adhiberi doceant, quibus se homines in maximis periculis tueri & munire possint, sicut docet Philosophus lib. 3. Eud. cap. 1. Et ratio est, cur maxime locum habeat in rebus bellicis, quia in bellis multi sunt subiti terrores & vani, quibus Tyrones & novitii milites facile perturbantur & conturbantur. Veterani vero, qui ista fortitudine experimentali praediti sunt, non item. Cujus rei elegans exemplum extat apud Caesarem lib. 1. de bello civili. Noctu, inquit, excitato in castris tumultu, novitii trepidare & confusis clamoribus omnia miscere coeperunt: Veterani paulatim & placide ad arma & prelium se accingere. Duo igitur praestat haec fortitudo militaris, primo ut ex peritia & rerum experientia milites vanos terrores & panicos (quibus ignari facile commoventur) cognoscant, cognitis non commoveantur, sed intrepidos sed gerant, & hac in parte veterani milites Tyronibus longe praestant, ut pote qui his jam afflueverint. 2. Quod armorum usum doceat, & quomodo hostium ictus declinare, & occasione commoda hostem invadere: nam peritia & usus, audaciam & animos faciunt, non secus ac si armatus cum inermi congrederetur, aut Athleta veteranus, cum pugili novitio.
units.tr: How much force it has in soldiers may be gathered from experience and practice, and from a veteran soldier as opposed to a raw recruit. This pleased Plato and Socrates so much that, in the Laches and the Protagoras, they thought this courage, acquired by practice and experience, belonged not to apparent courage but to courage properly so called. For they held that skill and knowledge of frightening and contrary things constitute true courage. This is not right, however. For those who are brave through experience and practice are not truly brave merely because they know how to approach dangers; rather, practice and skill teach them to use aids by which men can protect and fortify themselves in the greatest dangers, as the Philosopher teaches in Eudemian Ethics 3.1. The reason why it has its greatest place in matters of war is that in wars there are many sudden and groundless terrors, by which raw recruits and novices are easily upset and thrown into confusion, whereas veteran soldiers, who are endowed with this experiential courage, are not. A striking example of this is found in Caesar, On the Civil War, Book 1: "At night, when a tumult was raised in the camp, the novices began to tremble and to throw everything into confusion with confused cries; the veterans, gradually and calmly, prepared themselves for arms and battle." This military courage therefore does two things. First, through skill and experience of affairs, soldiers recognise empty and panic terrors, by which the inexperienced are easily moved; having recognised them, they are not moved, but carry themselves fearlessly. In this respect veteran soldiers far surpass recruits, since they have already grown accustomed to these things. Second, it teaches the use of arms, how to avoid the blows of the enemy, and how to attack the enemy at a favourable opportunity. For skill and practice produce boldness and spirit, just as when an armed man fights with an unarmed one, or a veteran athlete with an inexperienced boxer.

units.la: Differt vero a vera fortitudine in tribus: 1. Causa efficiente, quod sola rerum experientia nititur, non vero prudentia sicut vera fortitudo. 2. Causa finali quod honestatem sibi propositam non habeat. 3. In effo effectu: quod in fortitudine experimentali non sit constantia certa: nam milites veterani, qui praestant fortitudine ista experimentali, ubi hostem aut copiis, aut alio bellico apparatu superiorem vident, fugam capessunt, vere fortes non item, & hac perseverantia & periculorum perpessione fortitudinem civilem, de qua supra egimus, hac militari longe praestare (nam cives ad mortem usque pugnare solent pro patria) ostendit Philosophus exemplo praelii in Hermeo (Hermeum planities est, Mercurio sacra juxta Coronem Boeotiae urbem) commissi, in quo Coronei contra Onomarchum Phocensium hostium suorum ducem, qui proditione arcem urbis ceperat, fortiter pugnando ad unum omnes occubuerunt: Thebani vero milites licet essent veterani, & militari fortitudine excellerent, qui auxilio illis venerant, cognita Chironis ducis sui morte, fuga domum se receperunt, ut refert Thucid. lib. 5.
units.tr: It differs from true courage in three respects. (1) As to the efficient cause: it rests on experience of affairs alone, not on prudence, as true courage does. (2) As to the final cause: it does not have honour set before it as its aim. (3) As to the effect: experiential courage has no certain constancy. For veteran soldiers, who excel in this experiential courage, when they see the enemy superior in numbers or in other military equipment, take flight; they are not truly brave. The Philosopher shows that civic courage, of which we spoke above, far surpasses this military courage in perseverance and in enduring dangers (for citizens are accustomed to fight to the death for their country), by the example of the battle fought at Hermeum (Hermeum is a plain sacred to Mercury, near the city of Coronea in Boeotia), in which the Coronaeans, fighting bravely against Onomarchus, the leader of their Phocian enemies, who had seized the citadel of the city by treachery, were all killed to a man. The Theban soldiers, however, although they were veterans and excelled in military courage, had come to aid them; when they learned of the death of their leader Chiron, they retreated home in flight, as Thucydides reports in Book 5.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis agit de tertia specie fortitudinis non verae, nempe de fortitudine iracunda, quae hic in textu dicitur fortitudo per iram lib. 1, Mag. Mor. c. 21. fortitudo per affectus, unde & eorum fortitudo esse intelligitur, quae ira vel amore vel simili aliqua animi cupiditate ad pericula subeunda stimulatur. Definitur vero ea fortitudo, quam ira vel odium, ad cupiditatem vindictae sine certo consilio excitat, consentit cum vera fortitudine, quod in utraque sit animositas quaedam, & impetu quodam animi periculA suscipiantur, quod multis testimoniis Homeri declarat, quorum omnium haec vis est, ut iram & animosum impetum ad res praeclare gerendas & exequenquendas magnum habere momentum & itā, quod vulgò dicitur, cotem esse fortitudinis ostendat.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he deals with the third species of false fortitude, namely angry fortitude, which here in the text is called fortitude through anger (Mag. Mor. 1, c. 21), or fortitude through the passions, whence it is understood to be the fortitude of those whom anger, love, or some similar desire of the mind spurs on to face dangers. This fortitude, which anger or hatred excites toward the desire for vengeance without a settled plan, is defined as agreeing with true fortitude, in that both involve a certain spirit and impetus of mind by which dangers are undertaken. Homer demonstrates this by many testimonies, and the sum of them all is that anger and a spirited impulse carry great weight for performing and carrying out illustrious deeds, and thus show that anger is, as is commonly said, the whetstone of fortitude.

units.la: Notandum iram esse duplicem, unam immoderatam, quæ ex furioso quodam animi impetu oritur & de hac non loquitur Philosophus, cum iram vocat cotem fortitudinis: aliam moderatam, quæ à recta ratione regitur, & de hac hic sermo est, & hæc dicitur cos fortitudinis, propter has tres rationes. 1. propterææstum naturalem quem cōcitat. 2. propter cupiditatem vindictæ, quam ingenerat. 3. propter vires corporis, quas corroborat & confirmat, dum spirituum vitalium copias circa cor ex ebullitione sanguinis adducit. Differt verò à vera fortitudine quatuor modis: 1. Causa efficiente, quia à passione aliqua, ira puta vel odio excitatur, & caret destinata p oærefi & consilio: nam ab impetu quodam animi fluit, at hæc in vera fortitudine requiruntur, unde Cic. 1. offic. proprium, inquit, est irati, ei à quo læsus videatur, maximum innuere dolorem. 2. Subjecto, nam hæc fortitudo competit malis & insanis hominibus etiam similitudine quadam ipsis brutis, at vera fortitudo nō cernitur, nisi in prudentibus & probis hominibus. 3. Differunt causa formali: nam hæc non tam rectæ rationi obtemperat, quam ab affectu rapta in præceps inconsideratè fertur: at vera fortitudo à sola dependet recta ratione. 4. Causa finali, quia non tam honestatem sibi proponit, sicut vera fortitudo, quam cupiditatem vindictæ, unde iracundum sic definit Claudianus Poēta:
units.tr: It should be noted that anger is twofold: one kind is immoderate, arising from a certain frenzied impulse of the mind, and the Philosopher does not speak of this when he calls anger the whetstone of fortitude; the other is moderate, governed by right reason, and it is of this that the discussion here treats. This is called the whetstone of fortitude for three reasons: (1) because of the natural heat which it stirs up; (2) because of the desire for vengeance which it engenders; (3) because of the bodily strength which it strengthens and confirms, while by the boiling of the blood it draws the supply of vital spirits about the heart. It differs from true fortitude in four ways: (1) in its efficient cause, because it is excited by some passion, anger or hatred, and lacks a purpose fixed by choice and deliberation; for it flows from a certain impulse of the mind, whereas these things are required in true fortitude. Hence Cicero, De officiis 1: "It is the mark of an angry man to show the greatest pain toward the one by whom he seems to have been wronged." (2) in its subject, for this fortitude befits bad and mad men, and even brutes by a certain likeness, whereas true fortitude is seen only in prudent and upright men. (3) in its formal cause: for it does not so much obey right reason as, seized by passion, is carried headlong without consideration, whereas true fortitude depends on right reason alone. (4) in its final cause, because it sets before itself not so much honour as the desire for vengeance, as the poet Claudian thus defines the angry man:

units.la: In jaculum quodcunque gerit dementia mutat,
units.tr: Whatever madness takes up as a javelin, it changes.

units.la: Omnibus armatur rabies pro cuspide ferri, Cuncta volant dum dextra ferox in vulnera savit,Pro telo geritur quicquid suggesserit ira.
units.tr: Rage arms itself with every iron point for a spear. All things fly while the fierce right hand rages against the wounds; whatever anger has suggested is taken up as a weapon.

units.la: Tandem addit notam, qua haec species fortitudinis a reliquis dignosci & distingui possit, nempe quod facilime possit converti in veram fortitudinem, si accedat recta ratio, aut consilium tanquam principium, & honestas tanquam finis. 1. Haec fortitudo est maxime secundum naturam, nam fluit ab affectu quodam naturali, ab ira nempe quae est motus quidam, nobis a natura insitus. At reliquae fortitudinis apparentis species habent alias causas: nam oriuntur partim ex pudore & metu, ut prima species, partim experientia & usu ut secunda, partim ex spe ut quarta nempe fiduciaria, partim ex ignorantia ut quinta, quae neque sunt affectus neque causae naturales.
units.tr: Finally he adds a mark by which this species of fortitude may be distinguished and set apart from the rest, namely that it can very easily be turned into true fortitude if right reason, or counsel as its principle, and honour as its end, be added. (1) This fortitude is especially according to nature, for it flows from a certain natural affection, namely anger, which is a motion implanted in us by nature. But the other species of apparent fortitude have other causes: for they arise partly from shame and fear, as the first species; partly from experience and practice, as the second; partly from hope, as the fourth, namely the fiduciary; partly from ignorance, as the fifth; and these are neither affections nor natural causes.

units.la: In quarta parte cap. adducit quartam speciem fortitudinis non verae, nempe fortitudinem fiduciariam, quae hic in textu & 1. Eadem. cap. 3. vocatur fortitudo propter spem, propterea quod a spe maxime excitetur. Definitur ea fortitudo, quam externa praesidia in periculis praevisis propter certam spem animo conceptam excitant: nam quae confidentiam ad pericula subeunda ex variis victoriis sibi pepererunt, spem inde habent, ut quemadmodum saepe antea, sic etiam nunc superiores futuri sint, & hac spe victoriae ad pericula excitantur. Haec spes fortes nonnullos & confidentes facit, & in hoc maxime convenit cum vera fortitudine, quod in periculis adeundis homines reddat confidentes, & perseveratio-nem ex spe concepta addat.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he brings forward the fourth species of false fortitude, namely fiduciary fortitude, which here in the text, and in Eadem, chapter 3, is called fortitude through hope, because it is chiefly excited by hope. This fortitude is defined as that which external protections, in foreseen dangers, arouse by means of a sure hope conceived in the mind. For those who have gained confidence for facing dangers from various victories have hope from them, that, as often before, so now also they will be superior, and by this hope of victory they are roused to dangers. This hope makes some men bold and confident, and it agrees most with true fortitude in this, that it makes men confident in facing dangers and adds perseverance grounded in the hope conceived.

units.la: 1. Eadem. cap. 3. Differt verò à vera fortitudine in tribus. 1. Quia non tam à causæ bonitate & propositο honestatis oritur, quam à certa quadam spe externis auxiliis & præsidiis confirmata. 2. Differunt fine, quia vere fortes honestatis gratia, ut sæpe jam dictum est omnia agunt, & confidere honestum, non confidere & pericula non constanter adire turpe esse putant: At isti spe fortes propter certam spem utilitatis & gloriæ extra veram fortitudinē posti æ, & quia superiores se fore putant, & nihil incommodi passuros confidunt. Quod inde liquet ubi se inferiores fore vident, & vulnera aut damna accepturos, non perstiltunt aut perferunt pericula sicut vere fortes, sed statim refugiunt, unde non male comparatur hæc fortitudo à Philosopho cum ebrietate, nam ut
units.tr: (1) Eadem, chapter 3. It differs from true fortitude in three respects. (1) Because it arises not so much from the goodness of the cause and a purpose of honour, as from a certain sure hope confirmed by external aids and protections. (2) The ends differ, because truly brave men act for the sake of honour, as has often been said, and they think it shameful not to be confident about what is honourable and not to face dangers steadily; but these, brave through hope of a certain sure advantage and glory, are outside true fortitude, and because they think they will be superior and trust they will suffer no harm. This is clear from the fact that when they see they will be inferior and will receive wounds or losses, they do not persist or endure dangers as truly brave men do, but at once flee. Hence this fortitude is not badly compared by the Philosopher to drunkenness, for as

units.la: Vina parant animos, ut ait Ovid. &
units.tr: Wine prepares the spirits, as Ovid says, and

units.la: Spes juber esse ratas, ut ait Horat.
units.tr: Hope bids that they be fulfilled, as Horace says.

units.la: Eleganter Plat. lib.1 de Rep. quo quis plus vini hauserit, tantò majori spe impletur, & si vinum abesset, nihil prorsus consideret, nihil auderet, sic etiam isti spe fortes, cui uni innituntur destituti, omnem confidentiam & omne fortitudinem amittunt. Huius generis fortitudo maxime cernitur in adolescentibus, qui propter imperitiam rerum spe vana inflari quidlib et audent, sed non diu in hac audacia perstiunt. Unde Aristoteles lib. 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 7. Adolescentes, inquit, reliquis videntur fortiores, tum quia iracundiores exsistunt, tum quia spe pleni sunt, at non sunt constantes. Tertia differentia ducitur ab effecto, quod primum haec fortitudo in praevisis locum solum habeat, in subitis vero & repentinis ani-mum mū despondeat, vera fortitudo in subitis magis cernitur propter duas rationes: 1. Quia est habitus in quib. vero praeparationi aut praemeditationi nullus relinquitur locus ulla magis ex habitu fiunt, praevisa vero magis ex consilio & consultatione. 2. Quia praevisa sunt leviora, repentina autem graviora, quippe cum nictu quasi oculi super veniant, & ideo hominem perturbent, de quibus rationibus elegantER disputat Cic. lib.3. Tusc quaest. statim ab initio, exemplū hujus fortitudinis videre est cap.penult. Judicum, ubi Benjamitæ contra reliquos Israëlitas pugnant: & spe victoriæ duplicis tertiò, sed infeliciter pugnant.
units.tr: Elegantly Plato, Republic 1: the more wine a man has drunk, the more he is filled with a greater hope, and if the wine were absent he would dare nothing and undertake nothing. So too these men, brave through hope, when they are deprived of the one thing on which they rest, lose all confidence and all fortitude. This kind of fortitude is seen most in young men, who, through inexperience of affairs, dare to be puffed up by any empty hope, but do not persist long in this boldness. Hence Aristotle, Rhetoric 1, to Theodectes, chapter 7: "Young men," he says, "seem braver than others, partly because they are more prone to anger, partly because they are full of hope, but they are not steady." The third difference is drawn from the effect: this fortitude has a place only in foreseen dangers, while in sudden and unexpected ones it loses heart; true fortitude is more evident in sudden dangers, for two reasons: (1) because it is a habit, in which no room is left for preparation or premeditation, for the things foreseen arise more from counsel and deliberation. (2) because foreseen dangers are lighter, while sudden ones are heavier, since they come upon us as it were in the blink of an eye and so disturb a man. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3, at the very beginning, discusses these reasons elegantly. An example of this fortitude may be seen in the last chapter but one of Judges, where the Benjamites fight against the rest of the Israelites, and, with hope of a double victory, they fight unhappily as the third time.

units.la: In quinta parte capitis agit de quinta specie fortitudinis adumbratæ, nempe de fortitudine insciā, quæ hic in textu & lib.3. Eodem cap.1, vocatur fortitudo per insciitiam & ignorantiam. Definitur fortitudo apparēs, quæ ignorat periculi magnitudinem & circumstantias, & idcirco, si majus periculum ingruat, quam praevisum erat statim homines fugiunt, & mortem potius, quam ignominiā metuunt: magnam vero affinitatem habet cum superiori specie, propterea quod utraq; hac fortitudine præditi, nihil incommodi aut damni accepturos se putant, illi vero, id est, fiduciarii fortes propter spem quandam, quam ex variis victoriis conceperunt, isti vero, id est insci fortes spe quadam etiam incitantur, propter ignorantiam aut insciitiam, nihil putates subesse periculi, differunt vero in hoc, quod hæc fortitudo deteriores homines faciat, nam insci fortes nullam spem aut dignitatem verae fortitudinis habent, propterea quod intellecto statim periculo fugiant, mortem honestati praeferant. Fiduciarii vero fortes virorum more vere fortium ad pericula subeunda se parant, nec prius fugiunt, quam inferiores se fore prospexerint.
units.tr: In the fifth part of the chapter he deals with the fifth species of counterfeit fortitude, namely ignorant fortitude, which here in the text, and in Eadem, chapter 1, is called fortitude through ignorance and want of knowledge. It is defined as apparent fortitude which is ignorant of the magnitude and circumstances of the danger, and therefore, if a greater danger threatens than was foreseen, such men at once flee, and fear death rather than disgrace. It has, however, a great affinity with the preceding species, because those endowed with either kind of fortitude think they will suffer no harm or loss; but the fiduciary brave, through a certain hope conceived from various victories, and the ignorant brave, who are likewise moved by a certain hope arising from ignorance or want of knowledge and suppose there is no danger at all, differ in this: that this fortitude makes men worse, for ignorant brave men have no hope or dignity of true fortitude, since, as soon as the danger is understood, they flee and prefer death to honour. The fiduciary brave, however, prepare themselves to face dangers like true brave men, and do not flee until they perceive they will be inferior.

units.la: Differt vero a vera fortitudine in tribus, 1. Quod non consilio aut deliberatione pericula adeat, sed ex mera imprudentia. 2. Quod nullam in periculis constantiam praestet. 3. Quod mortem honestati praeferat. Exemplum habet Philosophus de Archivis, qui cum in Lacedaemonios, (quos Scycionios esse putabant, de quibus saepe antea multas reportarat victorias) incidissent, strenue primo ex insciitia & ignorantia pugnarunt, cognito demum se cum Lacedaemoniis pugnare, fugam arripuerunt. Simile habet exemplum Caesar lib. 6. de bello Gallico, ubi Trevirenses cum finitimis se pugnare putantes, cum in Romanos incidissent, strenue pugnarunt, postquam sensissent Romanos esse fugerunt. Similis etiam fraus fuit Patrocli, Achilleis armis induti, sed male illi ceciderunt, ut refert Homerus lib. 6. Iliad.
units.tr: There are three ways in which it differs from true courage: (1) it faces dangers not by counsel or deliberation but from mere imprudence; (2) it shows no constancy in dangers; (3) it prefers death to honour. The Philosopher gives an example in the men of Archivis, who, when they met the Lacedaemonians (whom they thought to be the Scyonians, over whom they had often won many victories before), at first fought vigorously out of ignorance and inexperience, but when they finally recognised that they were fighting with the Lacedaemonians, they took to flight. Caesar, in book 6 of the Gallic War, gives a similar example, where the Treveri, thinking they were fighting with their neighbours, fought vigorously when they met the Romans, but once they perceived that they were Romans, they fled. A similar trick was played by Patroclus, who put on the armour of Achilles, but he fell badly, as Homer relates in book 6 of the Iliad.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Omnis fortitudo est vel vera vel apparens.
units.tr: 1. Every courage is either true or apparent.

units.la: 2. Fortitudo civica legum & poenarum metu tantum, cives ad pericula subeunda excitat.
units.tr: 2. Civic courage, through fear of the laws and penalties alone, stirs citizens to undergo dangers.

units.la: 3. Multi ob timorem non ob pudorem fortiter se gerunt.
units.tr: 3. Many men behave bravely out of fear, not out of shame.

units.la: 4. Vir vere fortis, non necessitatu sed honestatis gratia omnia agere debet.
units.tr: 4. A man who is truly brave ought to do everything not from necessity but for the sake of honour.

units.la: 5. Fortitudo militaris hoc praestat, ut multa, quae alii metuunt, ex peritia militari fortiter subire quit possit.
units.tr: 5. Military courage achieves this, that through military skill a man can bravely undergo many things that others fear.

units.la: 6. Milites veterani vel crescente periculo, vel auxilii destituti, metuere maxime solent.
units.tr: 6. Veteran soldiers are usually most afraid when the danger grows, or when they are deprived of help.

units.la: 7. Fortitudo militaris mortem potius, quam ignominiam metuit.
units.tr: 7. Military courage fears death rather than disgrace.

units.la: 8. Fortitudo iracunda, quia eos est fortitudinis ira, ad pericula subeunda maximè excitat.
units.tr: 8. Angry courage, because anger is, as it were, the very stuff of courage, most of all stirs men to undergo dangers.

units.la: 9. Qui ira aut dolore in periculum aguntur, non sunt verè fortes.
units.tr: 9. Those who are driven into danger by anger or grief are not truly brave.

units.la: 9. Fortitudo iracunda homini à natura maximè insita videtur.
units.tr: 9. Angry courage seems to be most innate in man by nature.

units.la: 11. Fortitudo iracunda non honestatis gratia agit, neque ut recta ratio prascribit, sed ut affectus tantum dictitant.
units.tr: 11. Angry courage does not act for the sake of honour, nor as right reason prescribes, but only as the passions dictate.

units.la: 12. Fortitudo fiduciaria sola spe, cui innititur destituta, nihil prorsus agit.
units.tr: 12. Fiduciary courage, deprived of the hope on which it rests, achieves absolutely nothing.

units.la: 13. Viri fortis est, qua terribilia sunt per se & sua sponte subire, quia & agere est honestum, & non verò agere est turpe.
units.tr: 13. It belongs to the brave man to undergo terrible things in themselves and of their own accord, because both to act is honourable and not to act is shameful.

units.la: 14. Qua derepente fiunt, fortitudinem veram magis sapiunt, quam qua ex provisio.
units.tr: 14. Things that happen suddenly resemble true courage more than those foreseen.

units.la: 15. Prævisa magis, ex consilio & deliberatione fiunt, repentina verò magis ex habitu.
units.tr: 15. Things foreseen are done more from counsel and deliberation, while sudden things are done more from habit.

units.la: 16. Qui perignorantiam fortes sunt, qui si vel cognoverint vel suspicati fuerint, aliud esse, quam putabant, turpi fuga levitatem suam ostendunt.
units.tr: 16. Those who are brave through ignorance, if they had either recognised or suspected that the matter was other than they supposed, show their lightness by a shameful flight.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I.
