Quæritur: Quomodo quinque tantum fortitudinis non vera species enumeret & inter cæteras fortitudinem iracundam, qua ab ira animi affectu, ut dictum est excitatur, cum plures sint affectus, animique perturbationes æque potentes, ac ira, unde species quædam fortitudinis derivari possant, verbi gratia: Cacus amor qui impulit Medeam, ut patriam patriam & parentes proderet, fratrem membratim discerpe-ret, liberos tandem suos trucidaret. Sic etiam amplius Empe-docles Poëtam impulit, ut in Ætnam montem se conjiceret, unde Horatius in arte poët. Deus immortalis haberi Dum cupit Empedocles, ardentem fervidus Ætnam, Insiluit. Sic etiam ebrietas, ut ait Poëta. In prælia trudit inermem.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Why does he list only five species of fortitude, and among them the angry fortitude, which is roused by the emotion of anger as has been said, when there are more emotions and disturbances of the mind equally powerful as anger, from which certain species of fortitude could likewise be derived? For example, blind love, which drove Medea to betray her country and her parents, to tear her brother limb from limb, and finally to slaughter her own children. Likewise Empedocles was driven by it to throw himself into Mount Etna; whence Horace in the Art of Poetry: "While Empedocles, in his fervour, longs to be considered an immortal god, he leaps into burning Etna." So too drunkenness, as the poet says, thrusts the unarmed man into battle.

units.la: Et Philosophus in textu ait, ebrietatem homines reddere for-tes, unde jure plures enumerandae essent species quam quinque? Resp. Etsi plures sint impotentes animi affectus, proprie tamen & aperte à nullo animi affectu fortis quisquam dicitur, nisi à sola ira, propterea quod stimulus & cos-sit fortitudinis, deinde etiam ad speciem fortitudinis, quae dicitur iracunda, referuntur omnes alii affectus ab ipso Phil. lib. 1. Mag. Mor. c. 21. & proinde hac specie vocat ibi fortitudine per affectus. ἀνδρείαν ἀλγὼ πάθη.
units.tr: And the Philosopher says in the text that drunkenness makes men brave. Why then should more species be listed than five? Answer: although there are more emotions of the mind that are impotent, yet properly and plainly no one is called brave from any emotion of the mind except from anger alone, because anger is the spur and the impulse of fortitude. Moreover, all the other emotions are referred to the species of fortitude called angry, as Aristotle himself says in the Magna Moralia, book 1, chapter 21; and therefore there he calls this species fortitude through the emotions [ἀνδρείαν ἀλγὼ πάθη].

units.la: II. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat fortitudinem civicam magis assimilari fortitudini verae, quam fortitudinem militarem & experimentalem, cum militaris experientia nitatur, & majori nitatur prudentia in pugnando, quam civica, nam ut Phil. Sophus ait in textu, & ipsa experientia comprobat, milites veterani, quorum proprie est fortitudo militaris artem tenent pugnandi, & experientia rei militaris hostem graviter possunt offendere, seque ab eorum ferocitate tueri? Resp. Negandum est fortitudinem militarem, majori uti prudentia in pugnando, quam civicam, & si fallaci nitatur experientiae, unde nascitur animi impetus & vana confidentia, quae multos in exitium trahit: at vero civica fortitudo, & in periculis suscipiendis, & in honore appetendo magis accedit ad veram fortitudinem, quia & honestatem sibi proponit, & a causa honesta oritur, nempe ab amore patriæ, quæ sui defensionem a civibus jure quodam suo exigit.
units.tr: II. It is asked: how can he say that civic fortitude more closely resembles true fortitude than military and experiential fortitude does, since military experience rests on, and rests on greater prudence in fighting than civic fortitude does? For as the Philosopher says in the text, and experience itself proves, veteran soldiers, whose proper business is military fortitude, master the art of fighting, and through their experience of warfare can gravely wound the enemy and protect themselves from his ferocity. Answer: it must be denied that military fortitude uses greater prudence in fighting than civic fortitude does. Even if it rests on deceptive experience, from which arises the rush of spirit and empty confidence that draws many to ruin; but civic fortitude, both in undertaking dangers and in seeking honour, comes closer to true fortitude, because it sets honour before itself and arises from an honourable cause, namely love of the fatherland, which by a certain right demands from its citizens the defence of itself.

units.la: III. Quæritur: Quomodo asserit Philosophus, inrepentinis magis, quam in prævisis, aut præmeditatis veram videri fortitudinem: cum tamen supra cap. 8. huius libri dicat, eum vere esse fortem, qui considerato & consulte agit, & Cic. lib. 1. offic. fortitudinem definit consideratam periculorum susceptionem, & consultam laborum perpessionem: nam cum omnis vera fortitudo cum prudentia conjuncta esse debeat. Prudentia vero nihil nisi ex consulto & deliberato hominem agere docet: nam viri prudentis est, ut ait Seneca, non tantum quæ ante pedes sunt, sed etiam longe futura prospicere, proinde in prævisis potius & præmeditatis, quam in repentinis vera cernitur fortitudo? Resp. Fortitudo consideratur duobus modis: 1. Absolute secundum essentiam & sic in prævisis magis cernitur, quam in repentinis, quo etiam modo loca illa ex Cicerone & Aristotele allata sunt intelligenda. 2. Comparatè secundum existentiam, & sic postulante necessitate pugnandi in repentinis magis cernitur, idque propter tres causas: 1. Propter metum depulsum; nam ut vir fortis ubique metu, sic maxime in repentinis liber esse debet. 2. Propter periculum susceptum, a quo recedere turpe esse putat, cum honestatem in rebus omnibus sibi proponat, & mortem ignominiæ præferat. 3. Propter honorem inde comparatum, si periculo superfit.
units.tr: III. It is asked: how does the Philosopher assert that true fortitude appears more in sudden situations than in foreseen or premeditated ones, when yet in chapter 8 of this book he says that a man is truly brave who acts with consideration and deliberately, and Cicero in book 1 of On Duties defines fortitude as the considered undertaking of dangers and the deliberate endurance of toils; for since all true fortitude ought to be joined with prudence? Prudence teaches a man to act only from deliberate and considered judgement; for it is the mark of a prudent man, as Seneca says, to look not only at what lies before his feet but also to foresee what is far off. Therefore is true fortitude not seen rather in foreseen and premeditated circumstances than in sudden ones? Answer: fortitude is considered in two ways. 1. Absolutely, according to its essence, and in this sense it is seen more in foreseen situations than in sudden ones; and in this way those passages from Cicero and Aristotle are to be understood. 2. Comparatively, according to its existence; and in this sense, when the necessity of fighting demands it, it is seen more in sudden situations, and this for three reasons: 1. Because fear has been driven away; for just as a brave man ought to be free from fear everywhere, so especially in sudden situations he ought to be free. 2. Because of the danger he has undertaken, from which he thinks it shameful to withdraw, since he sets honour before himself in all things and prefers death to disgrace. 3. Because of the honour thereby gained, if he survives the danger.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: QVartum & ultimum hujus tractatus de Fortitu-dine membrum hoc cap. habetur, in quo quasdam proprietates fortitudinis & viri fortis adfert. Partes capitis sunt quatuor: In prima virum forte magis circa formidolosa, quam circa ea, quae fiduciam adferrunt versari ostendit. In secunda docet, quomodo vir fortis versetur circa dolorem. In tertia, quomodo circa voluptatem. In quarta demum corollarium infert; an scilicet vir fortis poterit esse bonus miles, ut qui omnes vires in bellum impendat.
units.tr: This chapter contains the fourth and last part of this treatise on Fortitude, in which the author sets out some further properties of fortitude and of the brave man. The chapter has four parts. In the first, he shows that the brave man is concerned more with frightening things than with those that inspire confidence. In the second, he teaches how the brave man deals with pain. In the third, how he deals with pleasure. In the fourth and last, he draws a corollary: whether the brave man can also be a good soldier, since he devotes all his strength to war.

units.la: In prima igitur parte dicit, etsi fortitudo versetur circa terribilia, & quae fiduciam adferunt, in formidolosis magis tamen spectatur: nam fortis vulgo habetur, qui imperterritum in rebus formidolosis se praestat, quam qui audacter se gerit in iis, quae fiduciam afferunt, & ratio haec est, quia duo sunt fortitudinis & viri fortis munera, aut periculum perferre, aut hostem invadere, & periculu perferre longe gravius & periculosius esse constat, quam hostem invadere: Nam qui hostem invadit, bona spe ducitur, fore, ut tandem aliquando victoria potiatur, qui sustinet periculu nec cedit, invicto plane videtur esse animo, & uno verbo, cu fortitudo versetur circa fiducia & metu, circa metum magis quam circa fiducia versatur.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he says that although fortitude is concerned with terrible things and with those that inspire confidence, it is judged more by its conduct in frightening situations. The man commonly regarded as brave is the one who shows himself undaunted in dangerous circumstances, rather than the one who acts boldly where there is ground for confidence. The reason is that the brave man has two tasks: either to endure danger or to attack the enemy. It is evident that enduring danger is far heavier and more perilous than attacking the enemy. For the one who attacks is led by good hope that he will at last gain the victory; but the one who sustains danger and does not give way seems to have a truly unconquered spirit. In a word, since fortitude is concerned with confidence and fear, it is concerned with fear more than with confidence.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis secundam adfert proprietatem, nempe cum dolore & molestia fortitudinem esse conjunctam (quod de fortitudinis actionibus tantum intelligi debet) & propterea maxime laudatur fortitudo, quia difficilius est circa aspera molesta verĭari, quam a rebus suavibus & jucundis abstinere, unde & praestantior habetur virtus fortitudo, quam temperantia, cum temperantia sit abstinentia a rebus jucundis & suavibus. Fortitudo vero sit perpessio molestiarum in periculis sufferendis. Notandum difficilius esse circa aspera & molesta versari, quam a suavibus & jucundis abstinere, propter duas rationes: 1. Propter naturam ipsam, quae omnem dolorem tanquam hostem fugit: nam ut voluptas est amica naturae, sic dolor est inimicus. 2. Propter periculum, quod inde provenit, nam dolor inducit timorem, timor mortem, naufragium vitae, naturae, voluptatis adfert.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he brings forward a second property: that fortitude is joined with pain and discomfort (which must be understood only of the actions of fortitude). For this reason fortitude is praised above all, because it is harder to deal with harsh and painful things than to abstain from pleasant and agreeable ones. Hence fortitude is considered a more excellent virtue than temperance, since temperance is abstinence from pleasant and agreeable things, whereas fortitude is the endurance of discomforts in facing dangers. It should be noted that it is harder to deal with harsh and painful things than to abstain from agreeable and pleasant ones, for two reasons: (1) because of nature itself, which shuns all pain as an enemy; for just as pleasure is nature's friend, so pain is its foe; (2) because of the danger that arises from it, for pain brings fear, fear brings death, and death brings the shipwreck of life, of nature, and of pleasure.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis tertiam adfert proprietatem, nempe in fortitudine esse etiam voluptatem, nam fines actionum viri fortis summam habent voluptatem, sed ipsae actiones no habent, quia sunt molestae & asperae, &, ut modo dictum est, cum dolore conjunctae, quod probat exemplo Athletarum, in ludis gymnicis, horum finis est corona, ex olea & lauro, victus publicus, statuae, honores, &c. Sed ad hunc finem assequendum, multae perferendae erunt molestiae, multae devorandae plagae. In summa finis fortitudinis est delectabilis, seu habet voluptatem conjunctam propter tres causas: 1. Propter habitum virtutis, quo fortis excellit. 2. Propter bonum civitatis, quae vir fortis solum quaerit. 3. Propter honoris praemium, quod inde acquirit.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he brings forward a third property: that pleasure is also present in fortitude. For the ends of the brave man's actions have the greatest pleasure, though the actions themselves do not, because they are troublesome and harsh and, as has just been said, joined with pain. He proves this by the example of athletes in the gymnastic games: their goal is the crown of olive and laurel, public maintenance, statues, honours, and so on. But to reach this goal many discomforts must be endured and many blows swallowed. In sum, the end of fortitude is delightful, or has pleasure joined to it, for three reasons: (1) because of the habit of virtue in which the brave man excels; (2) because of the good of the commonwealth, which the brave man alone seeks; (3) because of the reward of honour that he acquires from it.

units.la: Tandem disputat Philosophus contra Stoicos, qui dicebat, virum studiosum seu virtute praeditum nulli dolori, ne in ipsa quidem morte, esse obnoxium xium, contrariū asserit Philosophus nam quo quis fit plu- ribus instructior virtutibus, mor e tanto ęg ius fert, quippe cum magnis hujus vitæ bonis & commodis obari sc sen iat, & ipsa etiā luce, qua se dignissimū, utpore præstantissimum, judi cat, & quia per morte vir fortis magno bono scies privatur, nempe officiis fortitudinis & cæterarū virtutum, quæ si vita lōgior daretur, patriæ & R ip. diutius præstare posset, quā- to vero majori bono quis scies privatur, tanto magis in morte ipsa dolebit, uno verbo, vir fortis mortem ægre fert propter potissimum duas causas: 1. Respectu naturæ suæ, quæ mortem tanquam destructionem sui instinctu quodam indito fugit. 2. Respectu patriæ, cuicū potissimū se narū esse novit per mortem inservire diutius non posset, ad hanc Aristotelis sententiam accedit querela Theophrasti, quem moriențem scribit Cicero 1.Tusc. quaest. graviter de natura ipsa conquestum: quod cornicibus vitam longissimam, hominibus vero vita longe dignioribus, brevissimam sit largita. Et Aristippus Philosophus cum in mari esset tempestate deprehensus, & ex vectoribus aut nautis unus illum reprehenderet, quod oborta subita tempestate expellesceret, ipse vero minime formidaret: Respondit, nil mirum cum tu de vita vilissimi tantum nebulonis, ego vero de vita Philosophi sollicitus sim.
units.tr: Finally, the Philosopher disputes against the Stoics, who said that the virtuous man, that is, the one endowed with virtue, is subject to no pain, not even in death itself. The Philosopher asserts the contrary: the more virtues a man is furnished with, the more he dreads death, since he sees himself deprived of the great goods and advantages of this life, and even of the light itself, which he judges most worthy and most excellent. And because by death the brave man is deprived of a great good, namely the duties of fortitude and of the other virtues, which he could have continued to perform for his country and commonwealth if a longer life had been granted him: the greater the good of which a man is deprived, the more he will grieve even in death itself. In a word, the brave man bears death with difficulty, chiefly for two causes: (1) with respect to his nature, which by an inborn instinct shuns death as the destruction of itself; (2) with respect to his country, since he knows that by dying he can no longer serve it for long. To this opinion of Aristotle agrees the lament of Theophrastus, whom Cicero writes as having complained bitterly of nature as he was dying: that she had given crows the longest life, and to men, who are far more worthy, the shortest. And the philosopher Aristippus, when he was caught in a storm at sea, and one of the passengers or sailors rebuked him because he was alarmed by the sudden tempest while he himself showed no fear, replied: No wonder, since you are anxious only about the life of a most worthless scoundrel, but I am anxious about the life of a philosopher.

units.la: In quarta parte cap. hanc demum subjicit quæst. An fell. vir fortis posset esse bonus miles, nam quia supra jam dixerat, virū forte in morte maxime dolere, & propterea vitā suā magnifacere, ideo jure quæri potest, ut possit esse bonus miles, qui more caterorum hominum vitā suā timet? Resp. Nil obstaret, quo minus sit præstantissimus miles, quippe cum fortitudo maxime cernatur in periculis bellicis, ut ex cap.8. hujus libri patet, & quo quis confidentiori animo pericula sibi adeunda proponit, tanto habetur fortior, vir tamen fortis non debet esse vilis & mercenarius miles, qui vitam pro vili mercede aut lucelli gratia periculis exponat, sed tum demum militem se praestet, cum commune civitatis bonum, & honestas (quam semper sibi proponere debet) id postulant, & tandem concludit hunc tractatum de Fortitudine.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he finally puts this question: Can the brave man be a good soldier? For since he had already said above that the brave man grieves most at death, and therefore values his life highly, it may rightly be asked whether he can be a good soldier, when he fears his life as other men do. The answer: nothing prevents him from being the most excellent soldier, since fortitude is seen most clearly in the dangers of war, as appears from chapter 8 of this book. The more confidently a man undertakes dangers, the more he is considered brave. Yet the brave man ought not to be a cheap and mercenary soldier, who exposes his life to danger for a paltry wage or for the sake of a little gain; he shows himself a soldier only when the common good of the commonwealth and honour (which he must always set before himself) require it. And at last he concludes this treatise on Fortitude.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Fortitudo magis circa formidabilia, quam circa ea, quae fiduciam adferunt, versatur.
units.tr: 1. Fortitude is concerned more with things that are frightening than with things that inspire confidence.

units.la: 2. Omnis fortitudinis actio est cum dolore & molestia conjuncta.
units.tr: 2. Every action of fortitude is joined with pain and discomfort.

units.la: 3. Difficilius est in rebus asperis & molestis fortiter se gerere, quam a suavibus & jucundis abstinere.
units.tr: 3. It is harder to behave bravely in harsh and troublesome matters than to abstain from pleasant and agreeable ones.

units.la: 4. Fortitudo summam habet in fine voluptatem.
units.tr: 4. Fortitude has its greatest pleasure in its end.

units.la: 5. Non tam in ipsis virtutum actionibus, quam in fine cernitur voluptas.
units.tr: 5. Pleasure is discerned not so much in the actions of the virtues themselves as in their end.

units.la: 6. Quo quis fit pluribus instructior virtutibus, tanto magis in morte dolebit.
units.tr: 6. The more virtues a man is furnished with, the more he will grieve at death.

units.la: 7. Vir fortis, bonus poterit esse miles, etsi non sit vilis & mercenarius miles.
units.tr: 7. A brave and good man can be a soldier, even if he is not a base and mercenary soldier.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus, omnem fortitudinis actionem esse cum dolore & molestia conjunctam, cum tamen libro 2. hujus operis contrarium afferat, nempe omnes virtutis actiones esse suaves & delectabiles? Resp. Actio virtutis consideratur duobus modis, vel in se, in se, vel respectu finis, in se est molesta, & sic eam considerat hic Philosophus ratione finis est jucunda propter voluptatem adjunctam, & sic eam consideravit Philosophus lib. 1. vel sic responderi poterit. Actionem virtutis esse duplicem, unam internam, aliam externam. Interna est, qua ab ipso habitu profluit, & ratione habitus laudabilis & jucunda habetur. Interna dicitur respectu objecti, & sic virtutis actio molesta & tristis dicitur, maxime vero in fortitudine, quæ pro objecto habet mortem bellicâ.
units.tr: I. The question is: How does the Philosopher say that every action of fortitude is joined with pain and discomfort, when in the second book of this work he asserts the contrary, namely that all actions of virtue are pleasant and delightful? Answer: An action of virtue is considered in two ways, either in itself, in itself it is painful, and so the Philosopher considers it here; with respect to its end it is pleasant because of the pleasure joined to it, and so the Philosopher considered it in book 1. Or the answer may be given thus: the action of virtue is twofold, one internal and the other external. The internal is that which flows from the habit itself, and by reason of the habit it is held to be praiseworthy and pleasant. The external is so called with respect to the object, and so the action of virtue is called painful and sad, especially in fortitude, which has as its object death in battle.

units.la: 11. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat difficilius esse circa aspera & molesta versari, quam a suavibus & jucundis abstinere, cum facilius multo sit hostem apertum & manifestum vincere, utpote contra quem omni se modo præparare quis possit, quam inimicum tectum & dissimulatum, utpote a quo nescias paratas tibi insidias, at res molesta & aspera sunt velut hostes aperti, res vero injucunda, tanquam inimici tecti & dissimulati, proinde longe difficilius videtur a suavibus & jucundis abstinere, quam circa aspera versari? Resp. Verum id quidem est, si animum viri fortis habitu virtutis præditum spectes: at si tenerum mollemque naturam consideres, longe difficilius est dolores perferre, quâ voluptates vincere. Nam dolor est hostis naturæ, voluptas vero amica, ut sæpius jam dictum.
units.tr: 11. The question is: How does he say that it is harder to be occupied with harsh and troublesome things than to abstain from pleasant and agreeable ones, when it is much easier to conquer an open and manifest enemy, against whom one can prepare oneself in every way, than a hidden and disguised enemy, from whom you do not know what snares are laid for you? Troublesome and harsh things are like open enemies, while unpleasant things are like hidden and disguised enemies; therefore it seems far harder to abstain from pleasant and agreeable things than to deal with harsh ones. Answer: This is true if you look at the mind of a brave man endowed with the habit of virtue. But if you consider a tender and soft nature, it is far harder to endure pains than to overcome pleasures. For pain is the enemy of nature, but pleasure is its friend, as has been said often already.

units.la: Coronidis loco nonnullas subjiciemus quæstiones, in quib. vera fortitudo cerni possit, saltem magis illustrari: 1. An difficilius sit res secundas, quam adversas moderate ferre: Rationes sunt in utramque partem: Quidam enim difficilius esse res adversas moderate ferre, quam secundas probant his rationibus. 1. Quia in iis, quæ animos hominum maximaximè perturbare solent, in primis cernitur vis & robur animi, tales verò sunt adversæ. 2. Quia ut Philosophus ait hoc cap.11. fortes dicuntur, qui in formidabilibus (cujusmodi sunt res adversæ) magno & invicto sunt animo, & Cic. lib. 1. offic. ea, quæ peracerba sunt & adversa ita ferre, ut nihil à statu naturæ discedas, nihil à dignitate sapientis, robusti est animi magnæq; constantiæ.
units.tr: By way of a crown, we shall add some questions in which true fortitude may be seen, or at least more clearly illustrated. 1. Is it harder to bear prosperity moderately than adversity? There are arguments on both sides. Some hold that it is harder to bear adversity moderately than prosperity, and prove this by these reasons. (1) In those things which are wont to disturb the minds of men most greatly, the strength and vigour of the mind is chiefly seen, and such are adversities. (2) As the Philosopher says in this chapter 11, those are called brave who have a great and unconquered mind in dangerous things (of which kind adversities are). And Cicero, in the first book of On Duties, says that to bear the most bitter and adverse things so that you depart nothing from the state of nature, nothing from the dignity of the wise man, is the mark of a robust mind and great constancy.

units.la: Contrarium tuentur Pythagorei & Architas Tarentinus his innixi fundamentis. 1. voluptas quando adblanditur, & omnia quasi affatim suppeditat, tum difficillimum est modum tenere, propter has rationes. 1. Quia res secundæ & voluptates tacitè se nobis insinuant, & suavi subactos imperio, à circumspectione ad incogitantiam, à modestia ad insolentiam, à metu ad audaciam quasi aliud agentes plerumque deducunt. 2. Quia voluptatum illecebris non totus homo resistit, sed ipsa tantum ratio, quamvis & ipsa ægrè tandem repugnet. Hinc Aristoteles lib. 2. cap. 4. hujus operis, ex Heraclíti sententia majoris esse momenti pronunciat ipsi voluptati, quàm irae resistere. Et Pub. Mimographus: voluptas cum adblanditur, tunc captatum venit, nec male Poëta: Luxuriant animi rebus plerunque secundis, Nec facile est æqua commoda mente pati.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans and Archytas of Tarentum hold the contrary, relying on these foundations. (1) When pleasure flatters and supplies, as it were, everything in abundance, then it is most difficult to keep due measure, for these reasons. (a) Because prosperity and pleasures creep into us unnoticed, and having subjected us to their gentle rule, they lead us from caution to thoughtlessness, from modesty to insolence, and from fear to audacity, mostly while we are, as it were, doing something else. (b) Because the whole man does not resist the allurements of pleasures, but only reason itself, and even that at last resists with difficulty. Hence Aristotle, in the fourth chapter of the second book of this work, following the opinion of Heraclitus, declares that it is of greater importance to resist pleasure itself than anger. And the mime-writer Publilius says: when pleasure flatters, then it comes as a snare; nor does the poet speak badly: The minds of men run riot in prosperous circumstances, nor is it easy to bear equal fortune with an even mind.

units.la: Tertia ratio ducitur ab exemplis. Exemplo possunt esse in sacris David, Hezekias, in prophani Hercules, Alexander Magnus, quos res adversæ frangere nullo modo poterat, secundæ tamen fregerunt. Secundum fundamentum est, res adversæ quando nos adoriuntur, tum ius totus homo quatus quantus est reliresistit, ut non facile succumbere possit: Tertium fundamentum, quia res adversae animum elatum deprimunt, inflatum contrahunt, exorbitantem in viam reducunt, unde illa proverbia: Quae nocent, docent: Piscator ictus sapit: Phryx plagis emendatur. Et Cato Censorius in oratione pro Rodiensibus adversa res, inquit, se facile domant, & docent, quid facto opus sit.
units.tr: A third reason is drawn from examples. Examples may be found in sacred history in David and Hezekiah, and in profane history in Hercules and Alexander the Great, whom adversity could in no way break, yet prosperity broke. The second foundation is this: when adversities assail us, the whole man, shaken as he is, resists, so that he can hardly succumb. The third foundation: because adversities depress a lofty spirit, contract a swollen one, and lead one who has strayed back onto the road, whence those proverbs: What harms, teaches; the fisherman who is struck becomes wise; the Phrygian is corrected by blows. And Cato the Censor, in his speech for the Rhodians, says: adversity easily tames men and teaches them what must be done.

units.la: Pro decisione huius quaestionis notandum est, res adversas sumi tribus modis, pro triplici subiecto cui insunt, aliae enim sunt res adversae corporis, aliae animi, aliae fortunae, communiter res adversae animi & fortunae facilius ferri possunt, quam res secundae: At vero in malis seu rebus adversis, quae corpus ipsum & vitam concernunt, longe alia videtur esse ratio: In his enim mors ipsa, & quae mortem adducunt, sunt res maxime adversae, & difficilius est, res adversas corporis moderate ferre, quam secundas, propterea quod naturae ipsi contrariae videantur, & propterea Philosophus palmam & primas tribuit fortitudini inter virtutes morales, quod haec, quae corpori maxime adversa sunt, moderate ferre doceat, nam fortitudo illustrior & clarior redditur in adversis & asperis, quam in prosperis & secundis.
units.tr: To decide this question, it must be noted that adversities are taken in three ways, according to the three subjects in which they inhere. For some adversities are of the body, others of the mind, others of fortune. Generally, adversities of mind and fortune can be borne more easily than prosperities. But in evils, or adversities, which concern the body itself and life, the reasoning seems quite different. For in these death itself, and the things that bring death, are the most adverse things, and it is harder to bear bodily adversities moderately than prosperities, because they seem directly contrary to nature. For this reason the Philosopher gives the palm and the first place to fortitude among the moral virtues, because it teaches us to bear moderately those things which are most adverse to the body. For fortitude is rendered more illustrious and clearer in adversities and harsh things than in prosperous and favourable ones.

units.la: Unde Lipsius lib. 1. de Constantia cap. 8. inquit. Utenim aromata longe lateque odorem immittunt, si teras, sic virtutis fama diffunditur, si premas, & eleganter Ovid 1. Trist. Scilicet adversis probitas exercita rebus Tristi materiam tempore laudis habet. Si nihil infelici direxit vidisset Ulysses Penelope felix, sed sine laude foret.
units.tr: Hence Lipsius, in the first book On Constancy, chapter 8, says: For as spices send out their scent far and wide when you crush them, so the fame of virtue spreads when you press it down. And Ovid elegantly, in the first book of the Tristia: Surely in adversity tried uprightness has matter for praise in a sorrowful time. If Ulysses had seen nothing of unhappiness, Penelope would have been happy, but without praise.

units.la: Secunda quæstio. An viri fortis sit quævis pericula adire & suscipere?
units.tr: Second question. Is it the mark of a brave man to face and undertake any dangers whatever?

units.la: Statuitur verius negativa propter duas rationes. Ea pericula viro forti sunt adeunda, quæ recta ratio adire jubet, idest, quæ honesta sunt, & partim in laudem propriam, partim in utilitatem publicā cedere videntur. 1. Quia qui periculā adit absq; præscripto rectæ rationis, levis commodi gratia, nullo respectu honestatis habito, non vir fortis, sed temerarius & audax dici debet, ut fusè docet Philosoph. lib. 1. Mag. mor. cap. 3. Hinc sequentia consectaria inferuntur. 1. Mercatorem qui sui tantum quæstus gratia & commodi maxima adit pericula, & extrema quæque & adversa patitur, non esse dicendum virum, fortem propterea quod vir fortis ex præscripto rationis omnia agat, & ob sua facta laudem & honorem meretur, mercator verò non 2. Pugiles & gladiatores, qui levis lucelli gratia, ad gloriolam & aurarum populi captandam, duello aut monomachia congrediantur, non esse viros fortes, quia de re vide plura apud Pic. gradu 6. cap. 22. 3. Possea liquem tueri nomen viri fortis & laudem etiam, etsi ejusmodi duello se non sistat, in quo sive vincas sive vincaris, nulla in publicum possit redire utilitas. 4. Eos, qui in mala causa extrema pericula vitæ adeunt, & in mala causa militant non esse viros fortes. 5. Neque etiam milites mercenarios, qui hoc tantum fine militant, ut stipendium mereantur, & rapinam exerceant, nullo causæ aut honestatis respectu habito. 6. Eos etiam, qui ex desperatione ob debitam & meritam pœnam extrema quæque subsubeunt discrimina, fortium numero non esse addendos.
units.tr: The more accurate answer is negative, for two reasons. The brave man must face those dangers which right reason bids him face, that is, dangers that are honourable and seem to serve either his own praise or the public good. (1) Someone who faces danger without the guidance of right reason, for a small gain and with no regard for honour, should be called not a brave man but rash and reckless, as the Philosopher explains at length in Magna Moralia 1, ch. 3. From this the following corollaries follow. (1) A merchant who faces great dangers and suffers every hardship and misfortune solely for his own profit is not to be called a brave man, because a brave man acts in everything according to the dictate of reason and earns praise and honour for his deeds, whereas the merchant does not. (2) Boxers and gladiators, who fight in a duel or single combat for a small wage and to catch a little popular applause, are not brave men; on this matter see more in Pichler, Gradus 6, ch. 22. (3) A man cannot keep the name of brave man, nor the praise of it, if he engages in a duel of this kind, in which, whether he wins or loses, no advantage can return to the public. (4) Those who face the extreme dangers of life in an unjust cause, and fight in an unjust cause, are not brave men. (5) Nor are mercenary soldiers, who fight only to earn their pay and to plunder, with no regard to a just cause or to honour, brave men. (6) Nor should those be counted among the brave who, from despair, undergo the utmost perils to escape a deserved and due punishment.

units.la: Tertia sit quæstio, an fortitudo etiam cadat in fœminam. Negativam tuentur multi, propter duas rationes, quarum prima ducitur a ratione nominis, nam fortitudo Græcis dicitur ἀνδρεία, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνδρὸς, quod viri propria, non fœminæ sit virtus. 2. Quia fœminæ per naturam, (nam cato in iis est mollior & debilior quam in viris) sunt pusillanimes, molles & eorum, quæ periculum aut metum adferunt, admodum impatientes.
units.tr: The third question is whether fortitude also falls to women. Many defend the negative, for two reasons. The first is drawn from the meaning of the name: fortitude is called andreia [ἀνδρεία] by the Greeks, from andros [ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνδρὸς], so that it is a virtue proper to a man and not to a woman. (2) Women are by nature timid, weak and soft (for in them the body is softer and feebler than in men), and they are very impatient of anything that brings danger or fear.

units.la: Contraria tamen sententia veritati magis videtur consentanea, propter quatuor causas. 1. Quia omnis homo sane mentis, per naturam est capax cujusvis virtutis ordinariæ, unde Aristoteles cap. 1. lib. 2. hujus operis, & c. 3. lib. 6. dicit, quasdam virtutes inesse a natura. Ergo & fœminæ capaces sunt fortitudinis. Hinc Seneca elegantor. Epistola 31. ad Lucil. Nulli, inquit, virtutis via clausa est, omnes admittit, nec sexum, nec sensum eligit. 2. Ratio ducitur a contrariis, quicquid capax est vitii, idem & capax est virtutis vitio contrariæ, at fœminæ capaces sunt timiditatis, pusillanimitatis & ignaviæ. Ergo & ipsius fortitudinis. 3. Quia sicut quidam mares habent animum molem & effœminatum, sic quædam mulieres animum fortem & virilem, unde Ennius apud Cicer. 1. officiorum:
units.tr: The opposite view, however, seems more consistent with the truth, for four reasons. (1) Every sane person is by nature capable of any ordinary virtue; hence Aristotle, in chapter 1 of the second book of this work and chapter 3 of the sixth, says that some virtues are present in us by nature. Therefore women too are capable of fortitude. Hence Seneca elegantly says in Epistle 31 to Lucilius: "No way to virtue is closed to anyone; it admits all, and chooses neither sex nor station." (2) An argument from contraries: whatever is capable of a vice is also capable of the virtue contrary to that vice. But women are capable of timidity, pusillanimity and cowardice; therefore they are also capable of fortitude itself. (3) Because just as some men have a soft and effeminate spirit, so some women have a brave and manly spirit; hence Ennius, quoted by Cicero in the first book of On Duties:

units.la: Vos etenim juvenes animum gerite muliebrem: Illaque virgo viri.
units.tr: For you young men bear a woman's spirit; but that maiden has a man's.

units.la: Ergo in ejusmodi cadere potest fortitudo. 4. Avariis exemplis id confirmari potest, ut in sacris exemplo Deboræ, Jud. 4. Et Judithæ, in libro Judith. In prophanis exemplo Semiramidis Reginæ Assyriorum, Tomyridis Reginæ Scytharum, Cleriæ virginis Romanæ, Johannæ Lotaringicæ & aliarum.
units.tr: Therefore fortitude can fall to such women. (4) This can be confirmed by examples: in sacred history, the example of Deborah, Judges 4, and of Judith, in the book of Judith; in profane history, the example of Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, Tomyris, queen of the Scythians, Cloelia, the Roman maiden, Joan of Lorraine, and others.

units.la: Quarta quæstio sit. An cum vir fortis intrepido profu-sus in periculis adeundis debeat esse animo, illum quoque fit nihil omnino dolere. Sunt, qui affirmativam tuentur, exemplo Mucii Scevolæ, qui ut refert Liv. lib. 2. Dec. 1. manum rogo intulit, & quasi sensus omnis expers esset, sibi amburi passus est. Negativa tamen est verior, propter quatuor rationes. Prima, Nō est in potestate hominis per naturam nullum sentire dolorem, cum dolor & voluptas ex necessitate naturæ sensum requantur, nullus vero hominum sit sensuum expers. Secunda. Quia vir fortis non debet esse instar trunci aut lapidis, qui per naturam omni doloris sensu destituitur. Tertia. Quia fortitudo est virtus dolorem recte ferendi, & quo quis majorem percipit dolorem, tanto majorem fortitudinis gloriam habet. Quarta. Quia sic nulla esset fortitudinis laus, nam ut testatur ipse Philosophus in libello de virtutib. Fortitudo vera est virtus dolorem recte & cum laude ferendi. Proinde fortes nullo modo dici debent, sed timidi potius & ignavi, qui diabolicis artibus torporem aut stuporem inducunt membris, ne vel vulnerari omnino in bello possint, vel ullum exitu, sentire in corpore dolorem.
units.tr: The fourth question is this: Since the brave man must in facing dangers be fearless and bold, should he also be altogether without feeling of pain? Some defend the affirmative, citing the example of Mucius Scaevola, who, as Livy relates in book 2, decade 1, thrust his hand into the fire and let it be burnt, as if he had no sensation at all. The negative, however, is more true, for four reasons. First, it is not within the power of a human being, by nature, to feel no pain at all, since pain and pleasure are necessarily bound up with the sensation of nature, and no human being is without senses. Second, the brave man ought not to be like a stump or a stone, which by nature is deprived of all sense of pain. Third, because fortitude is the virtue of bearing pain rightly, and the more pain a man feels, the greater the glory of his fortitude. Fourth, because otherwise there would be no praise of fortitude at all; for, as the Philosopher himself testifies in his little book On Virtues, true fortitude is the virtue of bearing pain rightly and with praise. Therefore those who feel no pain should in no way be called brave, but rather timid and cowardly, who by diabolical arts induce numbness or insensibility in their limbs, so that they cannot be wounded at all in battle, or feel any pain in the body at all.

units.la: Quinta quæstio: An viro forti potius sit moriendum, quam fugiendum; Affirmativa placet multis & præcipue Stoicis, apud quos nulla fere est pagina, in quâ non inculcetur, virum fortem ab omni timore, & ob-tani inclinatione ad metum, & perconsequens à fugâ figa alienum esse oportere, & ideo vere dici forte, quod nihilo magis a morte sibi metuat, quam si jussu Imperatoris aut Ducis ab una statione in aliam se transferat, hinc illud Senecae Poëtae.
units.tr: The fifth question: Is it better for the brave man to die than to flee? The affirmative pleases many, and especially the Stoics, in whose works there is scarcely a page that does not insist that the brave man must be free from all fear and from any inclination to dread, and consequently a stranger to flight; and that he is therefore rightly called brave because he is no more afraid of death than if, at the command of a general or commander, he were moved from one post to another. Hence that saying of the poet Seneca:

units.la: Haud est virile terga fortuna dare.
units.tr: It is not manly to turn one's back to fortune.

units.la: Et Medea apud eundem;
units.tr: And Medea, in the same author:

units.la: Fortuna fortes metuit, ignavos premit.
units.tr: Fortune fears the brave, and oppresses the cowardly.

units.la: Prohac Stoicorum opinione facit consuetudo cuiusdam populi Celtarum nempe, qui, ut ut refert Aristoteles lib. 3. Eud. cap. 2. & Ælianus lib. 12. cap. 24. Turpe esse putarunt aedes corruentes deserere, & inundationes marinas tantisper expectarunt, donec submergerentur, ne si fugere nt, mortem metu sine viderentur, & sic probro aut pudori iis daretur, sic etiam Turcae, putant indecorum esse & hominis insani pestem aut lues infandis fugere, Babet. epist. 3. Distinctione poterit lis haec dirimi, ut viro forti potius sic moriendum, quam fugiendum, si ex illius fuga prodatur Religio, Resp. deseratur, leges violentur, infamia attrahatur, juniores ad ignaviam excitentur, verbi gratia: Demosthenes non erat vir fortis, cum in praelio Athenien sium, adversus Philippum Macedonum Regem abjecto clypeo mortem praesentissimam turpi fuga averteret, & cum hoc ei probro daretur. Respondit: Vir fugiens iterum pugnabit: At Æschines antagonista ex tempore respondit: At iterum fugiet. Ergo contra stultitiae esset mortem potius experiri, quam fuga sibi consulere, si plus commodi ex vita alicujus, quam ex morte Respubl. sit habitura. Fortes enim censendi sunt, non tantum qui ob salutem patriae vitam contemnunt & profundunt, sed etiam, qui vitam alioqui cōtem- nendam patriæ quoque gratia conservant, atque hoc nomine senatus Romanus Varroni cōsuli gratias egit, quod remale ad Cānas gSta fugere potius, seseque ad meliora Republ. tempora servare, quam una cum collega Paulo perire maluerit, ut restatur, Liv. Dec. 3. lib. 2. sub finem. Sic etiam Antigonus Rex Lacedæmonliorum cum hostibus cederet, negabat se fugere, sed opportunitatem à tergo sitam persequi. Stobæus sermon. 5.
units.tr: To this Stoic opinion the custom of a certain people of the Celts seems to accord, who, as Aristotle relates in Eudemian Ethics 3, ch. 2, and Aelian in book 12, ch. 24, thought it shameful to leave houses that were collapsing, and waited for sea floods until they were drowned, lest they seem to have fled from death out of fear, and so incur reproach or disgrace. So too the Turks think it unbecoming to flee from a pestilence or plague, which they consider a dreadful thing sent by a madman; see Babelius, epistle 3. This question may be settled by a distinction: the brave man should rather die than flee if by his flight religion would be betrayed, the commonwealth deserted, the laws violated, infamy incurred, and the young incited to cowardice. For example, Demosthenes was not a brave man when, in the battle of the Athenians against Philip, king of Macedon, he threw away his shield and by a shameful flight turned aside the death that was imminent, and when this was thrown in his face as a reproach. He replied: "A man who flees will fight again." But his opponent Aeschines replied on the spot: "And he will flee again." Therefore it would be foolish rather to seek death than to look to one's safety by flight, if the commonwealth is going to gain more advantage from the life of a man than from his death. For men are to be counted brave not only if they despise and pour out their life for the safety of their country, but also if they preserve a life that is otherwise to be despised for the sake of their country too. On this ground the Roman senate gave thanks to the consul Varro, because after the disaster at Cannae he preferred to flee and to save himself for better times for the commonwealth rather than to perish together with his colleague Paulus, as Livy relates in the third decade, book 2, near the end. So too Antigonus, king of the Lacedaemonians, when he was retreating before the enemy, denied that he was fleeing, but said that he was pursuing an opportunity lying behind him; Stobaeus, sermon 5.

units.la: Breviter si ex fuga sequatur ruina religionis Reipub. aut honestatis, in tali casu mors potius est expetenda, quam fuga, sic enim mortem fugæ domagnum scelus committitur, quod à viro forti longissime abesse debet: aut sequitur salus civitatis, totus exercitus, suaque vitæ, & sic fuga est magis laudabilis, non enim stultum esset, sed & turpe etiam mori, cum ex vita plus commodi in Rempub. redundare posset.
units.tr: In brief: if flight would bring about the ruin of religion, of the commonwealth or of honour, in such a case death is rather to be chosen than flight, for by fleeing from death one commits a great crime, which must be far removed from a brave man. But if the safety of the state, of the whole army, or of his own life follows from flight, then flight is more praiseworthy; for it would not be foolish but even shameful to die when more advantage might flow from his life to the commonwealth.

units.la: VI. Quæritur: An Sancti Dei martyres vere fortes fuerint? Resp. Si fortitudo proprie sumatur pro ea virtute, quæ versatur circa mortem bellicam, fortes proprie dici non possunt.
units.tr: VI. It is asked: were the holy martyrs of God truly brave? Answer: If fortitude is taken strictly for that virtue which is concerned with death in battle, the martyrs cannot properly be called brave.

units.la: 2. Fortitudo Moralis est habitus & mediocritas inter fiduciam & metum, ut ista martyrum fortitudo non est talis, est enim patientia quædam ex hujus vitæ contemtu & melioris futuræ spe, gratia Spiritus sancti ingenerata. Caeterum quia multa habet communia cum hac fortitudine Ethica, vulgo fortes dicuntur Martyres: nam primo, non temere & inconsulto se in periculad conjecerunt, sed prudentia quædam spirituali instructi.
units.tr: 2. Moral fortitude is a habit and mean between confidence and fear. The fortitude of the martyrs is not of this kind. It is rather a patience that springs from contempt of this life and hope of a better future, produced in them by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Yet because they share many things with this ethical fortitude, the martyrs are commonly called brave. First, they did not throw themselves into danger rashly and without thought, but were instructed in a certain spiritual prudence.

units.la: 1. In periculis & in morte ipsa constanter & decenter se gesserunt, divina enim gratia illos sustentabat.
units.tr: 1. In dangers and in death itself they conducted themselves steadily and with dignity, for divine grace sustained them.

units.la: 3. Causa bonitatis confisi, quod honestissimum erat, Dei nempe gloriam & proximi emolumentum ob oculos semper posuerunt. Quod testatur illud Tertuliani in Apologetico. Sanguis Martyrum est semen Ecclesiae, quo plures demetimur, plures evadimus. Et Justinus Martyr idem de se testatur, ut refert Nicephorus lib. 3. Ecclesiastica historia, cap. 26. Ego, inquit, qui Platonicis delectabar disciplinis, cum Christianos calumniose deferri audirem, videremq; eos esse impavidos & intrepidos ad mortem, & quaecunque horrenda videntur mortalibus, consideravi ipse mecum, fieri omnino non posse, ut illam flagitiis delicisque viverent. Idem etiam refert de Christianis Plinius Secundus, in quadam ad Trajanum Caesarem Epistola.
units.tr: 3. Trusting in the goodness of their cause, which was most honourable, they always kept before their eyes the glory of God and the benefit of their neighbour. This is witnessed by Tertullian's saying in the Apologeticus: "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church; the more we are mown down, the more we grow." Justin Martyr also bears witness to the same about himself, as Nicephorus reports, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 26: "I, who took delight in Platonic teachings, when I heard that Christians were slanderously accused, and saw that they were fearless and undaunted in the face of death and of all the things that seem dreadful to mortals, considered with myself that it was altogether impossible for them to live in vice and pleasure." Pliny the Younger also reports the same about the Christians, in a certain letter to the Emperor Trajan.

units.la: Ultimo & hoc quaeri potest: An major fuerit Martyrum fortitudo, quam eorum, qui in bello pro aris & focis fortiter pugnando occubuerunt? Resp. Si fortitudo, ut vulgo, pro intrepida animositate in periculis recte suscipiendis, & reb. adversis rite ferendis, sumatur, longe quidem majorem esse fortitudinem martyrum, propter quatuor rationes. Prima: Quia mors ista martyrum mortem bellicam longo intervallo superat, idque duabus de causis: 1. Quia in Martyribus cruciandis non una impedebatur hora, sed multi dies, multi etiam menses interdum. At vero in bello non diu sentitur dolor, nam ut canit Poeta: Aut cito mors venit, aut victoria laeta.
units.tr: Finally, this too may be asked: Was the fortitude of the martyrs greater than that of those who died fighting bravely in war for their altars and hearths? Answer: If fortitude is taken in the common sense, as an undaunted courage in facing dangers properly and in bearing adversity rightly, then the fortitude of the martyrs is indeed far greater, for four reasons. The first: the death of the martyrs surpasses a death in battle by a long interval, and this for two causes. (1) In torturing the martyrs, not one hour was consumed but many days, and sometimes many months. In battle, however, pain is not felt for long, for as the poet sings: "Either death comes swiftly, or victory comes joyfully."

units.la: 2. Quia in istum finem acerbissimi cruciatus excogitati sunt a Tyrannis, ut languenti & languido malo majorem inurerent dolorem, sicut testatur Nice-ph. lib. 6. cap. 6. 7 8. & 9. Secunda ratio, Qua n martyrum tormentus spes nulla est, sed mottem viden: praefentiffimam, nec ullum evadendi locum aut viam. At vero in bello spes evasionis est maxima, fiquidé incerti Martis dubiae sunt vices, & modo in hanc, modo in illam partem inclinat fortuna, ut quae modo in dubio est vita, spe evadendi & melioris fortunae erigi,& sustentari possit, ubi vero spes est reliqua, ibi minus est malum, ubi nulla: ibi majus. Spes enim dolorem omnem relevat, & melius fore femperait. Nam ut canit Tibullus lib. 2. eleg. 6. leg. ult.
units.tr: (2) Because the Tyrants devised the most bitter tortures for this very purpose, to inflict greater pain on a languishing and wasting affliction, as Nicephorus bears witness, book 6, chapters 6, 7, 8 and 9. The second reason: in the torments of the martyrs there is no hope, but death is seen as most immediate, with no place or way of escape. In battle, however, the hope of escape is very great, since the chances of uncertain Mars are doubtful, and fortune now inclines to this side, now to that. So while life is in doubt, a man can be raised up and sustained by hope of escape and of better fortune. Where hope remains, the evil is less; where there is none, the evil is greater. For hope relieves all pain and always promises that things will be better. As Tibullus sings, book 2, elegy 6, the last line:

units.la: Spes etiam duro solatur compede vinctum, Crura sonanti ferro, sed canit inter opus.
units.tr: "Hope also comforts the man bound in a hard fetter, while he sings at his labour, his legs clanking with iron."

units.la: 3. Ratio, quia ista Martyrum mors magis afficit animum & corpus. Animum, quod dolore vehementè capiat excausa Christi per impios & nefarios homines quasi superata: Corpus quoque exquisitissimi cruciatus, quantos fcil. poterit humana, excogitare malitia illis torquendis adhibeantur. 4. Qua in bello mortem inferenti licet resistere, & vindicta locum habet; at vero in Martyrum tormentis nihil est tale. Nam impune cruciantur, & acerbissimis tormentis absque omni vindictae spe subjiciuntur, ut omnes superioris & nostrae aetatis testantur historiae.
units.tr: 3. The reason: this death of the martyrs affects both mind and body more. The mind, because it is struck with violent grief that for the sake of Christ it is overcome by impious and wicked men; the body, because the most exquisite tortures, as many as human malice can devise, are applied to torment it. 4. In war it is permitted to resist the one who inflicts death, and there is room for vengeance; but in the torments of the martyrs there is nothing of the kind. For they are tortured with impunity and subjected to the most bitter torments with no hope of vengeance at all, as the histories of all the former and of our own age bear witness.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Sequitur tertius & ultimus hujus libri tractatus de Temperantia, quae ideo postponitur Fortitudini, quod dignitate & praestantia longe fit inferior, precedit. tedit vero reliquas virtutes duabus de causis: 1. Quia omni ætati, pueritiæ & adolescentiæ non minus quàm perfectæ convenit. Necesse enim est, ut omnes promisçuè sciant, quo nam modo modestè vivant, & suis cupiditatibus modum præscribant, reliquæ verò virtutes maturam tantum ætatem spectant. 2. Quia ad partem animæ appetitivæ (versatur enim circa appetitum in gula & Venere moderandum) pertinet: reliquæ verò ad partem animæ rationalem. Quæ verò sunt in parte appetitiva, præcedere debent ea, quæ sunt in parte animæ rationalis. Nam ut testatur Aristot. lib.7. Polit. cap.13 & lib.2. de anima, cap.5. putabant Philosophi animam hominis non totam simul & semel ingenerari homini, sed per partes, & naturâ priorem esse partem appetitivam seu irrationalem, propterea quod fit communis nobis cum aliis animalibus: postea demum progrediente ætate nasci in homine rationalem, ut scilicet appareret per effectus suos, & de hac opinione fusè etiam disputat Gell. lib.11. Noct. Attic. cap.5.
units.tr: Follows the third and last treatise of this book, on Temperance, which is placed after Fortitude, though it is far inferior to it in dignity and excellence, and it precedes the remaining virtues for two reasons: (1) because it suits every age, childhood and youth no less than maturity. For everyone without distinction must know how to live modestly and set limits to their desires, whereas the remaining virtues concern only mature age. (2) Because it belongs to the appetitive part of the soul (for it deals with restraining appetite in eating and in sexual pleasure), whereas the remaining virtues belong to the rational part. What belongs to the appetitive part ought to come before what belongs to the rational part. For, as Aristotle testifies in lib.7. Polit. cap.13 & lib.2. de anima, cap.5., the philosophers thought that a man's soul was not generated in him all at once, but in parts, and that the appetitive or irrational part is prior by nature, because it is shared with other animals; only later, as age advances, is the rational part born in man, so that it becomes apparent through its effects. Gellius also discusses this opinion at length in lib.11. Noct. Attic. cap.5.

units.la: Hujus tractatus membra sunt tria. In primo agit de materia circa quam versatur Temperantia, & extrema ei opposita. In secundo agit de operationibus, quæ procedunt à Temperantia & vitiis ei contrariis. In tertio corollarii loco confert intemperantiam cum Timiditate, & quærit in utra magis peccetur. Primum membrum continetur hoc capite duodecimo, cujus partes sunt: In prima ostendit, cur statim post doctrinam de Fortitudine egerit de Temperantia, quia utrumque pertinet ad partem animæ appetitivam, sicut & Fortitudo; & cum appetitiva sit dux ut lex: Ira, &c. Irascibilis nempe ad quam Fortitudo, & Concupiscibi-lis ad quam Temperantia, de qua nunc agit Philoso-phus spectat, reliquae vero virtutes sunt in ea parte animae rationalis, saltem quae rationi ipsi paret. In se-cunda parte ostendit materiam circa quam versatur Temperantia, & sicut antea cap. 8. lib. 2. huius operis, ficetiam hic docet in voluptatibus & molestiis seu doloribus versari, magis tamen circa voluptates quam dolores. Postea in tertia parte capitis ex voluptatum allata divisione investigat veram Temperantiae materiam, ut ostendat circa quas voluptates proprie versetur temperantia. Voluptates igitur aut sunt animi, aut corporis: Voluptates animi, quae fiunt absque aliqua perturbatione aut mutatione, ut ex solo animi motu procedunt, cujusmodi sunt eae voluptates, quae ex honorum, artium & contemplationis studio capiuntur, aut etiam ex divitiis, venationibus, confabulationibus, congressibus & caeteris percipiuntur. Voluptates corporis sunt, quae cum aliqua corporis mutatione & sensuum argumento fiunt, & hac divisione infra etiam utitur lib. 7. cap ult. huius operis. Et removet voluptates animi a Temperantia, propterea quod ab his nemo temperans aut intemperans proprie dicatur, sed aliis ex consuetudine nominibus insignitur. Sed cum voluptates corporis, circa quas proprie versatur Temperentia, sint multiplices, ideo adhibita subtiliore distinctione veram Temperantiae materiam exquirit, perlustratis singulorum sensuum voluptatibus, & 1. quidem eas, quae visu aut oculis percipiuntur, quales ex pictis tabulis, signis, statuis, ex oculis & forma mulierum capiunpiuntur, quibus voluptatibus depingit Cic. Verrem actio 4 in Verr. & Virgil. Æneam 1. Aeneid.
units.tr: This treatise has three parts. In the first it treats of the matter with which Temperance is concerned, and of the extremes opposed to it. In the second it treats of the actions that proceed from Temperance and from the vices contrary to it. In the third, by way of a corollary, it compares intemperance with Timidity and asks in which of the two more sin is committed. The first part is contained in this twelfth chapter, whose parts are these. In the first part he shows why he treats of Temperance immediately after the teaching on Fortitude: both pertain to the appetitive part of the soul, and since the appetitive part is, as it were, the leader, Anger, etc., the irascible part, to which Fortitude belongs, and the concupiscible part, to which Temperance belongs, and of which the Philosopher now treats, are both its concern; the remaining virtues, however, lie in the rational part of the soul, or at least in that which obeys reason itself. In the second part he shows the matter with which Temperance is concerned, and, as before in chapter 8 of book 2 of this work, he teaches here too that it is concerned with pleasures and pains or sufferings, though more with pleasures than with pains. Afterwards, in the third part of the chapter, from the division of pleasures just given, he investigates the true matter of Temperance, so as to show which pleasures Temperance is properly concerned with. Pleasures, therefore, are either of the mind or of the body. Pleasures of the mind are those that arise without any disturbance or change, as they proceed from the motion of the mind alone; such are the pleasures taken from the pursuit of honours, arts and contemplation, or also those derived from riches, hunting, conversation, company and the like. Pleasures of the body are those that arise with some change in the body and with a sensory cause; he uses this division also below in book 7, last chapter of this work. He removes the pleasures of the mind from Temperance, because no one is properly called temperate or intemperate on account of them, but they are labelled with other names by custom. But since the pleasures of the body, with which Temperance is properly concerned, are manifold, he therefore, by applying a finer distinction, seeks out the true matter of Temperance, going through the pleasures of each sense in turn. And first, those perceived through sight or the eyes, such as those drawn from painted pictures, images, statues, and from the eyes and the form of women; Cicero describes these pleasures in his Verrine Oration, action 4, and Virgil in Aeneid 1:

units.la: Oculos pictura pascit inani.
units.tr: Painting feeds the eyes with empty show.

units.la: Voluptates quoq; auditu aut auribus percipiuntur, ut quæ ab Histrionibus & Musicis proveniunt. Sed neque in his neque in superioribus proprie cernitur Temperantia, sed tantum abusive de ejusmodi subjectis prædicatur nomen Temperantiæ & Intemperantiæ, propterea lib. 3. Eudem. cap. 2. negat Philosophus eos, qui Sirenum cantu capti erant, fuisse intemperantes. Tertius sensus est odoratus, cujus quoq; suæ sunt voluptates, utpote quæ ex unguentis, suffitus, rosis, &c. percipiuntur, sed neq; in his versatur temperantia, nisi forte per accidens, quod nimirum voluptates ex gustu & tactu perceptas (quorum sensuum voluptates sunt proprium objectum temperantiæ & intemperantiæ) in memoriam revocent, verbi gratia: delectatur intemperans unguenti odore, non tam propter odorem unguenti, quam quod voluptatis propriæ ex gustu & tactu perceptæ memoriam excitet. Sic etiam gulosus aliquis voluptatem capit ex odore epularum, non tam propter ipsum odorem, quam propter objectum alterius sensus, gustus nempe, qui isto odore excitatur. Et ostendit Philosophus non in hominibus tantum, sed etiam in beluis hoc evenire, ut voluptates, q ex auditu, visu aut odoratu percipiuntur, non proprie per se, sed per accidens & ex eventu capiantur. Nam canis gaudet odore leporis, non tam propter ipsum odorem, quam propter esum. Similiter Leo gaudet audito bovis mugitu, non tantum tum per se, sed quia ex tali mugitu percipit in propinquo adesse nutrimentum. Sic etiam in visu lupus laetatur viso agno aut ove, sed hoc per accidens, quia nimium videt paratam escam. Relinquitur ergo Temperantiam cum opposita Intemperantia circa eas solum voluptates versari, quae ex gustu & tactu percipiuntur, quae duo sensus beluarum videntur proprii, quod ex his solis voluptatem beluae capiant, ut docet Philosophus Sect. 28. Probl. 5. & Gell. lib. 19. Noct. Att. cap. 11. At licet Temperantia versetur circa voluptates communissimas, quae ex gustu & tactu percipiuntur, proprie tamen & vere versatur circa voluptates ex solo tactu, quod praeclare docet Aristoteles lib. 3. Eudem. cap. 2. hoc verbis: Vulgo quidem & ex opinione multorum versatur temperantia circa duo sensibilia gustabile & tangibile, revera tamen circa tangibilia solum versatur: quod hic in textu ratione a contrario & exemplo confirmat. Ratio haec est, circa quam voluptatem maxime versatur Intemperantia circa eandem quoque Temperantia. At circa voluptatem ex tactu maxime versatur Intemperantia, quod probat exemplo Philoxeni cujusdam heluonis, qui ut refert Athenaeus lib. 1. cap. 6, optabat sibi ciconiae collum aut tricubitale, ut diutius sentiret cibi suavitatem. Hoc exemplo demonstrat Philosophus intemperantes magis gaudere voluptate tactus, quam judicio saporum. Optabat enim collum perlongum, ut perlongius spatium diutur-niorem caperet ex tactu voluptatem, & sic miram suam Intemperantiam magis in tactu, quam in gustu versari comprobaret. Cum igitur versetur temperantia maxime circa voluptates, quae ex sensu communissimo, tactu nempe (qui sensus est nobis communis cum omnibus aliis animalibus) percipiuntur, manifesto patet: Intemperantiam illi oppositam vitium esse vilissimum & plane bestiale. Nam homini competit, non quatenus est homo, aut rationalis, sed qua est animal tantum & irrationale. Et quamquam Temperantia versetur circa voluptates ex tactu, non tamen circa omnes. Nam ex calefactionibus, & frictionibus gymnasticis & balneariis voluptas summa capitur, ut ipse docet & Galenus lib. 3. de tuenda valetudine. Non tamen circa has versatur Temperantia, propterea quod modum in iis servare sit difficillimum, cum diversissimae sint hominum constitutiones, & pro diversis temperamentis magis & minus intendantur. Tandem concludit, temperatiam cum suo opposito versari circa eas voluptates, quae ex cibo, potu & Venere percipiuntur.
units.tr: Pleasures are also perceived through hearing or the ears, such as those that come from actors and musicians. But Temperance is not properly seen in these or in the previous ones; the name of Temperance and Intemperance is applied to such matters only in a loose sense. For this reason the Philosopher, in lib. 3. Eudem. cap. 2., denies that those who were captivated by the song of the Sirens were intemperate. The third sense is smell, which also has its own pleasures, such as those perceived from perfumes, incense, roses, etc. But Temperance is not concerned with these either, except perhaps by accident, namely in so far as they recall to memory pleasures perceived through taste and touch (the pleasures of these senses being the proper objects of temperance and intemperance). For example, an intemperate man takes delight in the scent of a perfume not so much because of the scent itself, as because it stirs the memory of a pleasure properly perceived through taste and touch. So too a glutton takes pleasure in the smell of a feast, not so much for the smell itself as for the object of another sense, namely taste, which is roused by that smell. The Philosopher shows that this happens not only in humans but also in beasts: pleasures perceived through hearing, sight or smell are taken not properly in themselves but incidentally and from the circumstance. For a dog rejoices in the smell of a hare not so much for the smell itself as for the prospect of eating it. Similarly a lion rejoices at the bellowing of an ox, not merely in itself, but because from such bellowing it perceives that food is near at hand. So too a wolf in sight rejoices at the sight of a lamb or sheep, but this is by accident, because it sees its food ready to hand. It remains, then, that Temperance and its opposite Intemperance are concerned only with those pleasures that are perceived through taste and touch, which two senses seem to be peculiar to beasts, since beasts take their pleasure from these alone, as the Philosopher teaches in Sect. 28, Probl. 5, and Gellius, lib. 19, Noct. Att. cap. 11. But although Temperance is concerned with the most common pleasures, those perceived through taste and touch, it is nevertheless properly and truly concerned with the pleasures of touch alone; Aristotle teaches this admirably in lib. 3. Eudem. cap. 2., in these words: "Commonly, and in the opinion of many, temperance is concerned with two sensible objects, the tasteable and the tangible; in truth, however, it is concerned with the tangible only," which he here confirms by an argument from the contrary and by an example. The argument is this: that about which intemperance is chiefly concerned, temperance is also concerned with. But intemperance is chiefly concerned with the pleasure of touch, which he proves by the example of a certain glutton, Philoxenus, who, as Athenaeus reports in lib. 1. cap. 6, wished that he had the neck of a crane or one of three cubits, so that he might enjoy the sweetness of food for longer. By this example the Philosopher demonstrates that the intemperate rejoice more in the pleasure of touch than in the judgement of flavours. For he wished for a very long neck, so that over a longer stretch he might receive pleasure from touch for longer, and thus showed that his remarkable intemperance lies more in touch than in taste. Since, then, temperance is chiefly concerned with pleasures perceived through the most common sense, namely touch (which sense we share with all other animals), it is clearly evident that the vice opposed to it, intemperance, is most base and plainly bestial. For it belongs to man not in so far as he is a man or rational, but in so far as he is merely an animal and irrational. And although Temperance is concerned with the pleasures of touch, it is not concerned with all of them. For from warming and from gymnastic and bathing rubbings great pleasure is derived, as he himself teaches, and Galen in lib. 3. de tuenda valetudine. Yet Temperance is not concerned with these, because it is most difficult to observe measure in them, since human constitutions differ greatly and are more or less intensely affected according to their different temperaments. Finally, he concludes that Temperance, together with its opposite, is concerned with those pleasures that are derived from food, drink and sexual love.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Temperantia est virtus circa voluptatem & dolorem.
units.tr: 1. Temperance is a virtue concerned with pleasure and pain.

units.la: 2. Circa idem obiectum versatur Temperantia & Intemperantia.
units.tr: 2. Temperance and intemperance are concerned with the same object.

units.la: 3. Voluptates omnes sunt aut animi aut corporis, quae scilicet homini proprie competunt.
units.tr: 3. All pleasures are either of the mind or of the body, that is, those which properly belong to a human being.

units.la: 4. A voluptatibus animi non mutatur, neque proprie patitur corpus.
units.tr: 4. The body is not changed by pleasures of the mind, nor does it properly suffer from them.

units.la: 5. Circa corporis solum voluptates, neque omnes tamen, sed quae aut naturales sunt, aut ex visu, auditu aut odoratu percipiuntur, versatur Temperantia.
units.tr: 5. Temperance is concerned only with bodily pleasures, and not all of them, but those that are natural or are perceived through sight, hearing or smell.

units.la: 6. Bruta ex nullis sensibus, nisi ex solo gustu & tactu voluptatem capiunt, nisi forte per accidens.
units.tr: 6. Brute animals take pleasure from no senses except taste and touch alone, unless perhaps by accident.

units.la: 7. Temperantia cernitur in iis voluptatibus, qua nobis cum belluis sunt communes.
units.tr: 7. Temperance is seen in those pleasures that we share with the beasts.

units.la: 8. Intemperantia beluinum maxime est vitium, cum homini non qua rationalis, sed qua irrationalis proprie competat.
units.tr: 8. Intemperance is above all a beastly vice, since it belongs to a human being not as rational but as irrational.

units.la: Caeterum Temperantiae nomen est ambiguum, & tribus modis vulgo sumitur. 1. Generalissime, ita ut no hominibus tantum, sed et brutis ipsis competat, quo sensu Ælianus lib. 5. de natur. animal. cap. 11. apibus temperantiam ascribit, quod nimirum ferarum eos odisse, qui unguentis sunt delibuti, & a recenti venere veniunt. Etl. lib. 2. cap. 26. aquilae temperantiam laudat, quod diuturniorem sitim patiatur, nec caeterarum avium more in pulvere se volutet. 2. Hac voce generaliter denotantur omnes reliquae virtutes: sic & justitia suam habet temperantiam circa actiones in bono & aequo constituendas. Unde Cic. lib. 1. de finibus, eam sic definit: Temperantia est virtus prima, qua in rebus appetendis aut fugiendis, ut rationem sequamur, monet. 3. Stricte sumitur pro secunda virtute morali, qua egulae ac Veneri modum praescribit. Unde definitur virtus mediocritate servans in appetendis, aut fugiendis corporis voluptatibus, quae ex tactu & gustu percipiuntur. Breviter, circa temperantiam illa quinque observanda sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the name of temperance is ambiguous, and it is commonly taken in three ways. (1) Most generally, so that it belongs not only to humans but also to the brutes themselves. In this sense Aelian, De natura animalium book 5, chapter 11, ascribes temperance to bees, because they naturally hate the wild beasts that have been anointed with perfumes and that come from recent intercourse. And book 2, chapter 26, he praises the eagle for temperance, because it endures thirst for a longer time and does not roll in the dust as other birds do. (2) In this word all the remaining virtues are generally denoted; thus justice too has its own temperance, in establishing actions in what is good and fair. Hence Cicero, in De finibus book 1, defines it thus: "Temperance is the first virtue, which bids us, in things to be sought or avoided, to follow reason." (3) Strictly it is taken for the second moral virtue, which prescribes measure for the appetite and for sexual love. Hence it is defined as the virtue that keeps the mean in seeking or avoiding the pleasures of the body that are perceived through touch and taste. In short, the following five points are to be observed concerning temperance.

units.la: I. Natura, quae est duplex, una communis, & sic in omnium virtutum actionibus cernitur, ut supra in in secunda significatione patuit. 2. Propria, & sic circa objectum gustus & tactus solum versatur, & sic a Philosopho hic tractatur. II. Consideratur munus temperantiae, quod in tribus consistit: 1. In conflictu cum dolore & voluptate. 2. in abstinentia à cibo & potu supra, quam requiritur. 3. in coë endis stimulis cupiditatis, & delitiis Venereis. III. Considerantur Opposita: Opponitur ei in excessu Intemperantia, in defectu ἀναισθησία stupor, insensibilitas seu stupiditas, aut uti à Cic. 1. Tusc. quaest. vocatur immanitas in aspernandis voluptatibus licitis, quae à natura homini non conceduntur. Unde Aristoteles lib. 1. mag. moral. cap. 22. & 3. Eudem. cap. 2.
units.tr: I. Its nature, which is twofold: one common, and in this sense it is seen in the actions of all the virtues, as was made clear above in the second sense; the other proper, and in this sense it is concerned only with the object of taste and touch, and in this sense it is treated here by the Philosopher. II. Its function is considered, which consists in three things: (1) in conflict with pain and pleasure; (2) in abstaining from food and drink beyond what is required; (3) in restraining the goads of desire and the delights of Venus. III. The opposites are considered. Opposed to it in excess is intemperance; in defect is [ἀναισθησία] insensibility, stupor, or stupidity; or, as Cicero in Tusculan Disputations book 1 calls it, savagery, in rejecting lawful pleasures which nature does not deny to a human being. Hence Aristotle, Magna Moralia book 1, chapter 22, and Eudemian Ethics book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: Temperantiam definit, ab extremis mediocritatem inter intemperantiam & stuporem. IV. Consideratur Obiectum, quod est vel commune & per accidens, & hic spectatur, non solum in omnibus sensibus externis sed etiā in internis: vel est proprium & per se, & hic tantum cernitur in gustu & tactu secundum quod hic definitur à Philosopho. V. Consideratur species. Etsi apud Aristotelem nulla reperiatur temperantiae divisio in species, à recentioribus tamen Philosophis variè dividitur, ut videre licet, apud Timplerum lib. 2. Syst. Eth. cap. 4. quaest. 3.
units.tr: He defines temperance as the mean between the extremes, intemperance and stupor. IV. The object is considered, which is either common and by accident, and in this sense it is looked at not only in all the external senses but also in the internal ones; or it is proper and per se, and in this sense it is seen only in taste and touch, according to how the Philosopher defines it here. V. The species are considered. Although no division of temperance into species is found in Aristotle, it is nevertheless divided variously by more recent philosophers, as may be seen in Timpler, Systema ethicum book 2, chapter 4, question 3.

units.la: Receptior divisio temperantiae est in frugalitatem & castitatem, quae quidem divisio complectitur illud, quod à Platone lib. 3. de Rep. dicitur, temperantia, inquit, in cibo, potu & Venere cernitur. Nam in cibo & potu moderandis occupatur Frugalitas, in Venere cohibenda Castitas. Frugalitas definitur temperantia in gula moderanda & regenda secundum rectae rationis praescriptum. Hac virtute inter Ethnicos plurimi reperiuntur celebres, ut Cyrus Persarum Rex, de quo Ammianus Marcellinus lib. 21. qui interrogatus ab hospite, quidnam in prandium apparere juberet? nihil aliud, inquit, quam panem, nam spero me prope rivum coenaturum. Mira frugalitas in Rege barbaro, cui panis erat pro obsonio & sitim aquae spe differebat in coenam. Talis fere fuit Philosophorum praesertim Cynicorum convictus, ut testatur Laërt. lib. 6. qui ait, eos herbis aqua frigida & oleis ut plurimum usos. De Cratete autem sic narrat, constat, inquit, aquam bibisse Cratetem, nam Demetrio Phalereo, qui panem & vinum miserat, convitiabatur, dicens utinam & fontes panem ferrent. Hanc in Diogene Cynico frugalitatem Alexander Magnus etiam laudavit, sicut his verbis testatur Juven. Sat. 14.
units.tr: The more accepted division of temperance is into frugality and chastity, a division which embraces what Plato, in Republic book 3, says: "temperance," he says, "is seen in food, drink and love." For frugality is occupied with moderating food and drink, and chastity with restraining love. Frugality is defined as temperance that moderates and governs the appetite of the belly according to the prescription of right reason. Among the heathen many famous men are found in this virtue, such as Cyrus, king of the Persians, of whom Ammianus Marcellinus, book 21, writes: when a guest asked him what he should order to be set out for dinner, he said, "Nothing but bread, for I hope to dine near a stream." Remarkable frugality in a barbarian king, for whom bread was his relish, and who put off his thirst with the hope of water for dinner. Such, more or less, was the way of life of the philosophers, especially the Cynics, as Laertius, book 6, testifies, who says that they mostly used herbs, cold water and olives. Of Crates, however, he relates thus: "It is agreed," he says, "that Crates drank water; for he reproached Demetrius of Phalerum, who had sent him bread and wine, saying: 'I wish that the springs too would bear bread.'" Alexander the Great also praised this frugality in Diogenes the Cynic, as Juvenal attests in Satire 14 in these words:

units.la: Sensit Alexander testa, cum vidit in illa Magnum habitatorem, quanto felicior hic qui Nil cuperet, quam qui totum sibi posceret orbem.
units.tr: Alexander felt it, when in that pot he saw the great inhabitant, how much happier was he who wanted nothing than he who demanded the whole world for himself.

units.la: Insignes etiam hoc nomine fuerunt Zeno, Pythagoras, Socrates, ipse etiam Epicurus, qui alias ob voluptates male vulgo audire solet, sed immerito, si Laërtio credimus, qui in ejus vita frugalitatis maximae testimonium de eo perhibet, quod & Juven. Sat. 14. aperte indicat: Mensura tamen qua Sufficiat sensus, si quis me consulat edam, In quantum sitis atque fames & frigora poscunt, Quantum Epicure tibi parvi suffecit in horto, Quantum Socratici coeperunt ante penates.
units.tr: Zeno, Pythagoras, Socrates, and even Epicurus himself were also famous under this name. Epicurus is usually ill spoken of by the crowd on account of his pleasures, but undeservedly, if we believe Laertius, who in his life of Epicurus bears witness to his greatest frugality; and Juvenal in Satire 14 plainly indicates this too: "Yet I would tell anyone who asks me the measure that suffices for the senses, as far as thirst and hunger and cold demand; how much, Epicurus, was enough for you in your little garden, how much the Socratics began with before their household gods."

units.la: De frugalitate pulcherrime Seneca, hanc inquit, salubrem & sanam vitae formam tenere, ut corpori tantum indulgeas, quantum bonae valetudini satis est, venter praecepta non audit, poscit & apellat, parvo tamen contentus, erit, si des illi, quod debes, non quod potes.
