D viditur rursus frugalitas in abstinentia & sobrietatem pro duplici objecto circa quod versatur, versatur namque circa cibum & potum. Definitur vero abstinentia, frugalitas in moderato cibi usu, seu ea virtus; quae in cibo capiendo modum tenet, naturae & rectae rationi convenientem. Hanc ita commendat lib. 10 apud Laert. Epicurus cibis simplicibus & non magnifice apparatis & salubritatis est, & hominem ad vitae usus necessarios impigrum reddit ac splendidis (si per intervalla furmantur) nos commodius apta atque adversus fortunam imperterritos reddit. Frugalitatis commoda, qui intelligere cupit ex Horatio lib. 2. sat. 2. facile percipiet: adeo autem frugalitatis studiosi erant Ethnici, ut Romani sumtuarias leges ferrent, quae modum viven di imponerent, ut refert Alex. ab Alex. lib. 3. cap. 11. Et ne fraus legibus fieret, cautum est, ut publice pranfitaretur. Idem a Lycurgo apud Spartiates factum est teste Xenoph. lib. de Repub. Lacedam. Fertur lata lex in Gallii Fannii coniulatu, ne quid volucrum apponeretur, praeter unam gallinam, quae altilis non esset, prorogata deinde lege Dydia & Fannia per totam Italiam, has quae Julius Caesar exercuit dispositis etiam circa Macellum custodibus, qui obsonia contra vetitum retinerent, & deferrent ad se, submissi quocunque lictoribus & militibus, qui si qua custodes fefellissent, extriclinio jam appositae auferrent. De aliis similibus legibus onsulendis est Gellius lib. 2. cap. 28. & lib. 4. cap. 16. Athenaeus etiam lib. 6. cap. 8. refert adeo temperatos fuisse
units.tr: On frugality, Seneca says very beautifully: "This is a healthy and sound form of life to keep: indulge the body only as much as good health requires. The belly does not heed precepts; it demands and clamours. Yet if it is content with little, it will be satisfied if you give it what you owe, not what you are able to give." Frugality is also seen in abstinence and sobriety, which have a twofold object, since they concern both food and drink. Abstinence, or frugality, is defined as the moderate use of food, that is, the virtue which keeps to a measure in taking food that agrees with nature and right reason. Epicurus commends this in book 10 of Laertius: simple foods, not elaborately prepared, are conducive to health and make a man vigorous for the necessary uses of life; and when we enjoy splendid feasts (if these are taken at intervals), they make us better suited and undaunted in the face of fortune. Whoever wishes to understand the benefits of frugality will easily perceive them from Horace, book 2, satire 2. The Gentiles were so devoted to frugality that the Romans passed sumptuary laws, which set a limit on the way of living, as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, book 3, chapter 11. And lest the law be evaded, it was provided that the midday meal be taken in public. The same was done by Lycurgus among the Spartans, as Xenophon witnesses in his work on the Lacedaemonian republic. It is said that a law was passed in the consulship of Gallius Fannius that no fowl be served except one hen that was not fattened. This law was afterwards extended throughout all Italy by the Lex Didia and the Lex Fannia, which Julius Caesar enforced, posting guards even around the Macellum. These guards would seize provisions contrary to the prohibition and carry them to him; he also sent out lictors and soldiers in every direction, who, if the guards had been eluded, would take away from the couches the dishes already set out. On other similar laws, consult Gellius, book 2, chapter 28, and book 4, chapter 16. Athenaeus also, book 6, chapter 8, reports that the early Romans were so temperate that by law a relish costing more than two and a half drachmas was forbidden to them.

units.la: illegible, ~3 letters sc priscos Romanos, ut lege prohiberetur illis obsonium, quod pluris duabus drachmis cum dimidia constaret. Ecclesiasticus cap. 38. de hac virtute praecipiens, inquit, noli avidus esse in epulis, in multis enim cibis est infirmitas. Et Cy us apud Xenophontem, do, inquit, primo operam, ut nunquam nimium me exp-leam, deinde ut in ventrem demissa bene digeram, hinc est, quod semper valeo.
units.tr: Ecclesiasticus, chapter 38, teaching this virtue, says: "Do not be greedy at feasts, for in many dishes there is sickness." And Cyrus in Xenophon says: "I take care first that I never overfill myself, and then that what is sent down into the belly is well digested; hence it is that I am always well."

units.la: Abstinentiae extremum in excessu dicitur gulosi-tas seu voracitas, in defectu nimia abstinentia a cibo. Voracitas definitur in eperantia in cibo quan-do scilicet plus cibi justo sumitur. Vitium hoc per-frequens, quae hominum immoderata est luxuries, esse solet, & quinque modis committitur. 1. In quan-titate cibi, ut cum plus accipitur quam fit necesse. 2. In nimia festinatione, cum scilicet certatim vora-tur prout canes famelici facere solent. 3. Si in eden-do suavitas & dulcia esculenta suavioribus prae-ponantur. 4. Si quis sibi delicatiora quam convi-vantibus opponat. 5. Denique si intempestive nul-la urgente fame major gulae quam graviorum negotio-rum habeatur ratio, ut notat Stephanus Niger in opere ex Musonio sumto de nimia obsonatorum appetentia.
units.tr: Gluttony or voracity is the extreme of abstinence in excess, and excessive abstinence from food is its extreme in deficiency. Voracity is defined as intemperance in eating, namely when more food is taken than is just. This vice is very common and is usually the immoderate luxury of men. It is committed in five ways: (1) in the quantity of food, when more is taken than is necessary; (2) in excessive haste, when people gulp down their food eagerly, as hungry dogs usually do; (3) when pleasant and sweet dishes are preferred to plainer ones while eating; (4) when someone sets more dainty food before himself than before his fellow diners; (5) finally, when, without any pressing hunger, more regard is paid to the pleasures of the palate than to weightier business, at the wrong time. Stephanus Niger notes this in his work, drawn from Musonius, on excessive appetite for delicacies.

units.la: In vitium hoc acerrime invecti sunt Ethnici sapien-tes. Unde Diogenes ventrem vitae Charybdim appellabat teste Laërt. lib. 6 de vitis philosophorum. Qua de re Senecam audi epist. 6. Taurus paucissimorum jugerum pascuis impletur, una sylva elephantibus plurib. sufficit, homo & terra pascitur & mari, quid ergo? an invariabilem nobis alvum natura dedit, cum tam modica corpora dedisset, ut vastissimorum edacissimorum q; animalium aviditate vinceremus? minime. Quantulum enim est, quod naturæ datur, parvo illa dimittitur non fames nobis ventris nostri magno constat, sed ambitio, homines itaque ventri obedientes animalium loco numeremus nō hominum, quo dam veró ne animalium quidem sed mortuorum: hoc nomine male audivit Aristippus, quem ut nim is delicatum Diogenes regium canem appellabat, ob quam causam & Timon eum acriter insectatur.
units.tr: The wise men of the Gentiles railed most bitterly against this vice. Hence Diogenes called the belly the Charybdis of life, as Laërtius reports in book 6 of the Lives of the Philosophers. On this matter, hear Seneca, Epistle 6: "A bull is filled by the pasture of a very few acres; one forest is enough for many elephants; man and earth are fed by land and sea. What then? Has nature given us an insatiable belly, when it gave us such small bodies, so that we might surpass the greed of the largest and most voracious animals? By no means. For how little is what nature demands, and it is satisfied with a small amount. The hunger of our belly does not cost us much; it is ambition that does. Therefore let us count those who obey their belly among the animals, not among men; and indeed some of them not even among the animals, but among the dead." For this reason Aristippus was ill spoken of, whom Diogenes, because he was too delicate, called the royal dog; and for this reason Timon also attacks him bitterly.

units.la: Qualis Aristippi mollis natura sophista Qui potuit tactu verum discernere falso, Autor est Laërt. lib. 2. de vit. Philosoph. Nec immerito hoc vitium tanto odio sunt prosecuti. Nam ut loquitur Seneca lib. 7. multis causam mortis fercula nostra ferunt, innumerabiles q; morbi innumerabiles coquo numerant. Quod confirmat Juven. sat. 1.
units.tr: "Such was the soft nature of the sophist Aristippus, who could distinguish true from false by touch alone." The author is Laërtius, book 2 of On the Lives of the Philosophers. Nor without reason have men pursued this vice with such hatred. For, as Seneca says in book 7, "Our dishes bring death to many; cooks count countless diseases." Juvenal confirms this in Satire 1.

units.la: Hinc subita mortes atque intefiata sine stus It, nova nec tristis per cuncta sabula canas Ducitur iratus splendendum sunt amicis.
units.tr: Hence come sudden deaths and old age that dies intestate; new (and not sad) ... through all the tables, you may sing; he is led away, angry, ... the splendid ones are to be friends.

units.la: Duo sunt præter alia inter infinita exempla satis illustria, unum Asini Celeris, qui, ut refert Dion Cassius lib. 47. sex millibus H.S. unius muli piscis obsonium deculit, alterum Marci Gabionis quem idem Cassius omnes homines luxuria superasse refert, qui cum ini sset rationem ut sciret quantum prodegisset, quantumq; superesset eam q; centum sestertium talentum restare comperisset, magno mœrore confectus quasi sibi fame fuisset perendum, seipsum interemit. Alterum extremum est nimia corporis maceratio & abstinentia à cibo, quo vitio laborabat
units.tr: There are two examples, among countless others that are quite famous. One is Asinius Celer, who, as Dio Cassius reports in book 47, spent six thousand sesterces on the fish course of a single mullet. The other is Marcus Gabinius, whom the same Cassius reports to have surpassed all men in luxury. When he had drawn up an account to learn how much he had squandered and found that only a hundred thousand sesterces remained, he was overcome with great grief, as if he must perish by hunger, and killed himself. The other extreme is excessive mortification of the body and abstinence from food, a vice from which Chrysippus suffered.

units.la: Chrysippus suis adeo immeisu⁠s studiis ut cibi & corporis cu⁠i æ proifus obl visceretu⁠. Hoc etiam vitio laborant sæpe, qui ira, an ore cæterisque affectibus animi irregula ibus intricantur. Sobrietas (quæ altera est frugalitatis species) definitur frugalitas in modera o potus usu. Nec diffitemur vocem hanc in latiore aliquando significatione accipi, ut frugalitate in genere significet, hæc tamen est frequentior ejus significatio, ut pro moderatione potus sumatur. Hanc adeo sibi commendatam Romani habuerút ut ante annum so. vinum bibere viris quoque crimini daretur, servo vero in interdum penitus, nisi sacrorum caus & solennibus festisque diebus, ut autor est Alexander l.b.1. cap.25. qui ibidem de Persis ait, licet natalem diem summo semper honore studio & conviviis celebrarint, filiis tamen indulgentissimi etiam parentes vinum prohibebant. De hac virtute eleganter Augustinus, Sobrietas rectí judicii & memoria conservatrix, secretorum custos, ingenii magistra, lectionis & memoria nutrix. Extrema sobrietatis sunt in excessu Ebrietas, in defectu nimia potus requisiti pro naturæ defectu supplendo avessatio. Veru̅m de hoc vitio in defectu quod nomine careat, cum sit perquam rarum, neque enim fieri potest, ut homo sana mente & corpore naturæ necessitati non prospiciat, ulla non egemus. Refertur tamen in historiis prodigiosis à Gulatio de quadam virgine Delphis in Belgio nata, quæ totos 27. annos ab que potu solo casci duris esu se sustinabat, sed ægrotabat continuo, & in pessima fuit corporis constitutione. Alterum extremum dicitur Ebrietas tas, quæ definitur intemperantia inpotu, & sicut contrarium hujus vitii est rarissimum, ita hoc frequentissimum esse solet, cujus tamen, si eff cta intuemur, maximè detestandum censeri debet. Ebrietatem sic depingit Basilius Magnus, qui quid esset ebrietas interrogatus? respondit: Ebrietas dæmon sponte admissus in animos per voluptatem, mater est malitiæ, impugnatio virtutis, ex forti timidum facit, ex modesto lasciv um, justitiam ignorat, prudentiam abolet, & sicut aquæ pugnat cum igne, sic immoderatio vini mentem sobriam extinguit, ut fumus fugat apes, sic ebrietas pellit spiritualia dona, & ideo Alphonsus Hispaniæ Rex vino abstinuit, quod sciret id Alexandri Magni gloriæ maximè obstuisse, ut refert Antonius Panormitanus lib. 2. cap. 7.
units.tr: Chrysippus was so absorbed in his studies that he completely forgot about food and the care of his body. People who are entangled in anger, love, or other irregular emotions of the mind often suffer from this same vice as well. Sobriety, which is the other kind of frugality, is defined as frugality in the moderate use of drink. We do not deny that this word is sometimes taken in a broader sense, so that it means frugality in general, but its more common meaning is moderation in drinking. The Romans held this virtue in such high regard that wine was a disgrace even for men before the age of sixty, while slaves were allowed no wine at all, except for sacred rites and solemn festivals, as Alexander reports in book 1, chapter 25. There he also says of the Persians that although they always celebrated their birthdays with the greatest honour, feasting and enthusiasm, even the most indulgent parents forbade their sons to drink wine. Augustine speaks elegantly of this virtue: Sobriety preserves right judgement and memory, guards secrets, teaches the mind, and nurses learning and memory. The extremes of sobriety are, on the one side, drunkenness as an excess, and on the other, too little drink, where a person refuses what is needed to supply the deficiency of nature. Concerning this defect, which has no name of its own, since it is extremely rare (for a person of sound mind and body cannot fail to provide for the necessities of nature, and we need none of this), it is nevertheless recorded in prodigious histories, by Gulatius, of a certain virgin born at Delft in Belgium, who for the whole of twenty-seven years sustained herself on hard food without any drink, but was constantly sick and was in very poor bodily condition. The other extreme is drunkenness, which is defined as intemperance in drink. Just as the opposite of this vice is very rare, so this one is usually very frequent, and yet, if we look at its effects, it ought to be judged most detestable. Basil the Great described drunkenness in this way: when asked what drunkenness was, he replied: Drunkenness is a demon willingly admitted into the minds of men through pleasure; it is the mother of malice, the enemy of virtue; it makes the brave timid and the modest lascivious; it knows nothing of justice and destroys prudence; and just as water fights with fire, so excess of wine extinguishes a sober mind, as smoke drives away bees, so drunkenness drives out spiritual gifts. For this reason Alphonso, king of Spain, abstained from wine, because he knew that it had been most harmful to the glory of Alexander the Great, as Antonius Panormitanus reports in book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: Quapropter Cato vocabat ebrietatē speciem furoris voluntariam, autore Marcellino lib. 15. Hinc factum, ut ebrii furiosis pejores seipsos interemerint, alii incauti ab aliis fuerint interemti, sicut de Bonosio Imperatore refert Vopiscus, qui extremæ gulæ & ebrietatis monstrum, cum se suspendio suffocasset, interrogatus quidam, qui temulentiam ejus noverat, quisnam esset suspensus? respondit non hominem, sed amphoram. Adversus ebrietatem hoc remedium adhibendum suasit Plato, ut auctor est Laërt. lib. 2. ut in speculo, si ebrii contemplarentur, ita futurum ut rei fœditatē à tam deformi vitio deterreantur, à quo non procul abest, quod de Lacedæmonibus recenset Plut. in vita Demetrii, qui ut ebrietatis turpitudinem demonstrarent, & liberos suos inde deterrerent, cogebant Helotas, i.e. agrestes homines quamplurimum bibere, deinde mero ingurgitatos
units.tr: For this reason Cato used to call drunkenness a voluntary form of madness, on the authority of Marcellinus in book 15. Hence it happened that drunkards, who were worse than madmen, killed themselves, and others, being unwary, were killed by others. Vopiscus reports this of the emperor Bonosus, a monster of extreme gluttony and drunkenness. When he had strangled himself by hanging, someone who knew of his drunkenness was asked who the man hanging there was, and he replied that it was not a man but a wine jar. Plato suggested this remedy against drunkenness, as Laërtius reports in book 2: that if drunkards were to look at themselves as in a mirror, they would be deterred by the foulness of the thing from so ugly a vice. Not far from this is what Plutarch recounts of the Lacedaemonians in the life of Demetrius: to show the shamefulness of drunkenness and to deter their children from it, they forced the Helots, that is, country folk, to drink a great deal, and then, when they were gorged with neat wine, made them sing ridiculous songs and perform foolish dances, so that they might teach their children in this brief way that sobriety is a most honourable thing and drunkenness most disgraceful.

units.la: gitatos carmina ridicula canentes saltationes ineptas instituere, ut sobrietatem rem honestissimam, ebrietate turpissimam hoc compendio liberos suos edocerent. Castitas est Temperantia in Venere moderanda, dum nempe ille servatur modus, quëDeus legesq; praescribunt extra & intra conjugium. Hujus virtutis proprium esse solet, quod inprimis ornat hominem adeo quod reliquarum virtutum veluti corona quaedam si & palma. Ejus effectum dicitur Pudicitia, quæ est vitatio verborum acgestuum ardorem Venereum vel significantium vel provocantium. Extremum Castitatis in excessu dicitur Libido, in defectu affectu ita omnis Veneris detestatio. Libido definitur intemperantia in venere modum omnem excedens. Sic appellamus tum luxum illum, qui extra conjugium exercetur, qui fornicato dicitur, tum in matrimonio commissam, quod proprio nomine adulterium vocatur. Hujus libidinis multa nefaria & execranda sunt effecta, sicut appareret in Samsone Jud. 16. in Salomone 1. Reg. 13. in Tarquinio Superbo propterea regno exuto Livius lib. 1, decad. 1. Notat hoc Cyrus Persarum Rex, ideo pro poena severissima, quae i bellibus debebatur luxuriosam vitam impoluit: Lydiis cum secundo rebellassent, te ste Justino lib. 1. arma & equi adempti sunt, jussiq; lenocinia exercere, & sic gens inductria quodam potens ac manu strenua effeminata mollitie & luxurie virtutem pristinam perdidit. Alterum extremum proprio nomine caret, quia res rarius accidit, nisi postremis hisce temporibus forte deprehendatur in monachis & monialibus virginitatem non sinceram affectantibus. Refertur tamen historia de quodam Guarino patritio Veneto, qui cum castam traduxisset adolescentiam vicesimo secundo aetatis anno in morbum incidit periculosissimum, a quo cum liberari non posset nisi exercitio Veneris castam: tamen mori, nitentibus contra Medicis, quam Venere aut libidine se nefaria polluere maluit. Poterit etiam Castitas dividi in Pudicitiam, quae servatur a copulatis in aut extra conjugium & virginitatem, quae servatur ab iis, qui nullam matrimonii societatem contraxerunt. Illa rursus in conjugalem quae servatur in legitimo conjugio, & Virtualem, quae extra conjugium post obitum alterius servatur, sed de his jam satis, nunc ad dubia, quae ex ipso occurrunt Aristotele.
units.tr: singing ridiculous songs and performing foolish dances, so that they might teach their children, by this short lesson, that sobriety is a most honourable thing and drunkenness most shameful. Chastity is temperance in moderating love, namely by keeping that measure which God and the laws prescribe both within and outside marriage. It is characteristic of this virtue that it adorns a man above all, and is, as it were, a crown and palm of the other virtues. Its effect is called modesty, which consists in avoiding words and gestures that either signify or provoke venereal ardour. The extreme of chastity in excess is called lust, and in deficiency a hatred of all sexual intercourse. Lust is defined as intemperance in sexual love, exceeding every measure. We call by this name both that debauchery which is practised outside marriage, which is called fornication, and that which is committed in marriage, which is called adultery by its proper name. This lust has produced many wicked and detestable effects, as appears in Samson (Judges 16), in Solomon (1 Kings 11), and in Tarquin the Proud, who for this reason was stripped of his kingdom (Livy, book 1, decade 1). Cyrus, King of the Persians, observed this and therefore, as the most severe punishment owed to rebels, imposed a life of luxury: when the Lydians had rebelled a second time, according to Justin, book 1, their arms and horses were taken away and they were ordered to practise prostitution, and so that people, once powerful and strong in hand, lost their former virtue through effeminate softness and luxury. The other extreme has no proper name, because the thing happens rarely, unless perhaps in these latter times it is found among monks and nuns who affect a virginity that is not sincere. Yet there is a story of a certain Guarino, a Venetian patrician, who, having spent his youth chastely, fell in his twenty-second year into a most dangerous illness, from which he could not be freed unless he practised sexual intercourse; though the physicians struggled against it, he preferred to die chaste rather than defile himself with love or unlawful lust. Chastity can also be divided into modesty, which is kept by those joined in marriage, or outside it, and virginity, which is kept by those who have entered into no married partnership. Modesty is again divided into conjugal modesty, which is kept in lawful marriage, and widowly modesty, which is kept outside marriage after the death of the other spouse. But enough of these matters; now let us turn to the doubts which arise from Aristotle himself.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An Temperantia jure possit dici virtus, cum omnis virtus sit habitus ratione definitus, ut patet ex cap. 7. lib. 2. huius operis: At Temperantia non est talis. Non enim ratione definitur seu quod idem est, non ad partem animae rationalem spectat, sed ad sensitivam tantum, ut expresse docet Philosophus in textu; Proinde jure non potest vocari virtus? Resp. Per negationem minoris. Nam etsi ad partem animae appetitivam seu ὀρεκτικὸν spectet, propterea quod ratione officii appetitus rationis imperio subjiciat: ratione tamen definitur cum voluntatem, quae est altera facultas animae rationalis, pro subjecto habeat.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Can temperance rightly be called a virtue, since every virtue is a habit defined by reason, as is clear from chapter 7 of book 2 of this work; but temperance is not such a habit? For it is not defined by reason, or what is the same, it does not pertain to the rational part of the soul but only to the sensitive part, as the Philosopher expressly teaches in the text. Therefore it cannot rightly be called a virtue? Answer: by denying the minor premise. For although it pertains to the appetitive part of the soul, or τὸ ὀρεκτικόν, inasmuch as by the function of appetite it submits to the command of reason, nevertheless it is defined by reason, since it has as its subject the will, which is the other faculty of the rational soul.

units.la: II. Quomodo neget Philosophus temperantiam versari circa voluptates animi, cum voluptates animi saepe sint immanio-res res corporeis voluptatib.v.g. Amor inhonestus aut libido animi qua Medeam, Syllam & alios complures in horrenda incidere flagitia coegit: Proinde magis circa voluptates animi quam corporis versatur temperantia, & ratio est, quia ut excap. 3. lib. 2. hujus operis patet. Virtus circa difficilia versatur: Multo enim difficilius est circa immanes animi voluptates, quam corporis versare. Resp. Negandum esse animi voluptates esse immaniores corporis voluptatibus. Nam etsi pravae voluptates animi videantur immaniores, non sunt tamen, quia originem a corporis voluptatibus, tanquam a causis suis trahunt. Sic Medea nunquam talem animi libidinem concepisset, nisi prius ex oculis tanquam corporis fenestris hujus mali originem imbibisset.
units.tr: II. How does the Philosopher deny that temperance is concerned with the pleasures of the mind, when the pleasures of the mind are often more monstrous than those of the body? For example, an unlawful love or a lust of the mind which drove Medea, Sulla and many others into horrible crimes. Therefore temperance is concerned more with the pleasures of the mind than of the body; and the reason is that, as is clear from chapter 3 of book 2 of this work, virtue is concerned with difficult things, and it is far more difficult to deal with the monstrous pleasures of the mind than those of the body. Answer: It must be denied that the pleasures of the mind are more monstrous than the pleasures of the body. For although wicked pleasures of the mind seem more monstrous, they are not so, because they draw their origin from the pleasures of the body, as from their causes. Thus Medea would never have conceived such a lust of the mind, had she not first drawn in the origin of this evil from her eyes, as from the windows of the body.

units.la: III. Quomodo negat illos intemperantes, qui Sirenum cantu capti fuerunt, tum etiam illos, qui luxum adhibent in pictis tabulis & statuis, in saltationibus & tripudiis, tum etiam in vestibus.
units.tr: III. How does he deny that those who were captured by the song of the Sirens were intemperate, and likewise those who indulge in luxury in painted pictures and statues, in dances and revelry, and also in clothing?

units.la: Nam & hi visu quoque peccant, & oculos ad lasciviam incitant. Unde nascitur libido & incontinentia: unde & hi videntur intemperantes: nam experientia & usus docet ex luxuria & concupiscentia oculorum natam esse intemperantiam. Resp. Jure negasse Philosophum istos per se esse intemperates, propterea prius exemplum lib. 3. Eadem cap. 2. relegat ab intemperantia, & dicit, tantum per accidens fuisse intemperantes, quatenus ex visu descendunt ad voluptatem tactus. Posterius vero exemplum relegat Philosophus libel. de moral. virt. ad prodigalitatem vitium libera litati in excessu oppositum.
units.tr: For these also sin by sight, and they incite the eyes to lasciviousness. From this arise lust and incontinence, and so these also seem to be intemperate, for experience and practice teach that intemperance is born of luxury and the lust of the eyes. Reply: the Philosopher rightly denied that these are intemperate per se. Therefore, in book 3, chapter 2, he first removes the former example from intemperance and says they were intemperate only per accidens, insofar as they pass from sight to the pleasure of touch. The latter example the Philosopher, in the little book on the moral virtues, refers to prodigality, a vice opposed to liberality by excess.

units.la: IV. Cur neget Philosophus canes & cetera animalia irrationalia voluptatem capere & sensibus alio, nisi ex solo tactu
units.tr: IV. Why the Philosopher denies that dogs and other irrational animals take pleasure from the senses other than touch alone

units.la: âtu & gustu, cum tamen sensus & experientia doceant ex aliis sensibus tam interni, quam externis voluptate in nasci, verbi gratia: Canis viso Domino redeunte adblanditur, unde voluptatem capit ex memoria: sic etiam instinctu quodam natura aranea visa praeda, ut musca aut bufo, statim invadit. Sic etiam ex auditu ut aves & ursi harmonia capiuntur. Sic etiam ex visu simia suos catulos, pavones suas plumas delectabiliter aspiciunt. Sic etiam ex odoratu canes, pisces, porci odoribus ad cadavera longissime pertrahuntur. Unde falsum videtur esse, quod Philosophus dicit, ex solo tactu & gustu voluptatem capere bruta. Respon. Non negavit Philosophus simpliciter ex aliis sensibus voluptate capere bruta, sed tantum per accidens hoc fieri ostendit, quia hoc faciunt propter fruitionem rei sensibus perceptae, ut in textu docetur.
units.tr: Touch and taste, although sense and experience teach that pleasure arises from the other senses, both internal and external. For example, a dog fawns on its master when it sees him returning, and so takes pleasure from memory. Likewise, by a certain natural instinct, a spider immediately attacks when it sees prey, such as a fly or a toad. Likewise, birds and bears are charmed by harmony heard. Likewise, a monkey delightedly looks at its young, and peacocks at their feathers, through sight. Likewise, dogs, fish and pigs are drawn from very far away to carcasses by smell. Whence it seems false that the Philosopher says brutes take pleasure from touch and taste alone. Reply: the Philosopher did not simply deny that brutes take pleasure from the other senses. He showed only that this happens per accidens, because they do it for the enjoyment of the thing perceived by the senses, as is taught in the text.

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: SEquitur secundum membrum huius tractatus de temperantia, ubi agit de effectibus & operationibus, quae procedunt a temperantia eiusque opposita Intemperantia. Partes capitis sunt quatuor. In prima, ex cupiditatum allata divisione ostendit, quomodo in iis delinquatur. In secunda ostendit, quomodo intemperans versetur circa molestiam & dolorem. In tertia agit de insensibilitate, quae temperantiae in defectu opponitur. In quarta ostendit, quomodo temperans iustum servet modum circa voluptates & dolores. In prima igitur ex cupiditatum divisione docet, quomodo in cupiditatibus delinquatur. Cupiditatum aliae sunt communes, quae apud omnes eaedem sunt, ut desiderium cibi & potus, & vocantur tur naturales, propterea quod naturæ Duce expetă-tur: Aliæ sunt proprię, quæ sunt posiræ in variis circumstantiis earum rerum, quæ appetuntur, ut in hoc cibo, hocpotu. Hæaliæ atque aliæ sunt apud varias hominum conditiones & varias corporis complexiones, & hac divisione cupiditatū utunturetiā Stoici tetle Cicer. lib. 2. de finib. tum etiam Plato lib. 8. & 9. de Repubi. Confirmat divisione usum explicat & dicit in communibus seu naturalibus à pauc s peccari, idque uno tantum modo, nempe in numio seu in excessu, cujusmodi sunt lurcones. Helluones, vettrem curantes qui cibis vulgaribus supra modū se in gurgitant. Talis fuit ille Philoxenus de quo supra egit Philosophus. Talis etiam ille Helluo, de quo refert Vopiscus, quod in mensa Imperatoris Aureliani integrum aprum & porcellum comederit, centum etiam panes & vervecem, & infundibulo ori appositio integrum vini cadum exhauserit. At vero in propriis multifariam peccatur secundum varias circumstantias earum rerum, quæ appetuntur, quarum quatuor modos enumerat Philosophus. 1. est, cū ea concupiscuntur, q omnino nefas sit appetere, ut cum quis alienam concupiscit uxorem. 2. cum plus justo quis concupiscit, etsi per se fit licitum, si modo justum non excedat, verbi gratia: cibum appetere omnibus est licitum: at vero lautiorem appetere, quàm tempori, loco aut personæ convenit, non est licitum. 3. cū more vulgi sive fine discrimine nulla honesti aut turpis habita ratione, quo morbo laborasse Parthos scribit Plin. lib. 17. cap. 18. quos quia summa cū aviditate quoslibet cibos indiscrete caperent, anima foeda fuisse, &c. 4. 4. cum non decenter (seu eo, quo decet, modo res appetuntur, licet sint licitae, verbi gratia: cibum capere in loco, sed tamen in lupanari aut in foro aut etiam cum sociis infamibus cibum capere non licitum est. Hoc etiam spectat, quod Philosophus refert in libel. de virtut. moral. Luxuriosos plerunque esse imprudentes, quod nullam decori habeant rationem. Et Cic. lib. 1. de finibus dicit, non est tam religiosos, quin de parvis cum canibus vescantur. In secunda parte capitis ostendit, quomodo temperantia versetur circa dolorem & molestiam pro quandam dissimilitudinem inter fortem & temperantem, timidum & intemperantem. Nam etsi fortitudo & ignavia non minus quam temperantia & intemperatia versentur circa dolorem & molestiam, longe tamen dissimili id fit modo. Vere foris non dolet, aut non magis, quam oportet: & sicut ratio recta dictat, dolet cum adsunt ea, quae dolorem & molestiam afferunt verbi gratia: periculum, vulnus, mors; temperans etiam non dolet, cum adsunt ea, quae voluptatem adferunt, timidus e contra dolet, cum adsunt ea, quae molestiam & dolorem afferunt: intemperans etiam molestè fert, si abstinet ea, ex quibus voluptate capere re possit. Proinde temperantia ex sola voluptatum abstentia & per accidens tantum circa dolorem versatur. In tertia parte capitis agit de insensibilitate altero extremo temperantiae, de qua supra egerat, cap. 8. lib. 2. huius operis & infra etiam agit, lib. 7. c. 4. Tales vero nullos reperiri argumento a minori ad maiores ducto probat, (tales inquam, qui, ut ait Cic. pro Cael. aspernentia oculos omnem pulchritudinem rerum
units.tr: Follows the second member of this treatise on temperance, where he deals with the effects and operations that proceed from temperance and from its opposite, intemperance. The chapter has four parts. In the first, from the division of desires, he shows how people go wrong in them. In the second, he shows how the intemperate person behaves with regard to distress and pain. In the third he treats of insensibility, which is opposed to temperance by way of defect. In the fourth he shows how the temperate person keeps the just mean with regard to pleasures and pains. In the first part, then, from the division of desires, he teaches how one errs in desires. Some desires are common, the same for everyone, such as the desire for food and drink, and they are called natural because they are sought under the guidance of nature. Others are proper, which arise from the various circumstances of the things desired, as in this food or this drink. These and those differ among different human conditions and different bodily constitutions. The Stoics also use this division of desires; see Cicero, De finibus, book 2, and also Plato, Republic, books 8 and 9. He confirms the division, explains its use, and says that in common or natural desires few sin, and that they sin in only one way, namely by excess. Of this sort are the gluttons and guzzlers, who stuff themselves beyond measure with ordinary foods and cater to their bellies. Such was that Philoxenus of whom the Philosopher spoke above. Such also was that glutton of whom Vopiscus reports that at the table of the Emperor Aurelian he ate a whole wild boar and a piglet, also a hundred loaves and a sheep, and with a funnel placed at his mouth drained an entire jar of wine. But in the proper desires people sin in many ways, according to the various circumstances of the things desired, and the Philosopher lists four modes: (1) when one desires things that it is utterly wrong to desire, as when someone desires another man's wife; (2) when one desires more than is just; even if a thing is lawful in itself, it becomes unlawful if one desires more than what is right. For example, to desire food is lawful for everyone, but to desire something more sumptuous than the time, place or person allows is not lawful; (3) when, after the manner of the common crowd, or without distinction, one takes no account of what is honourable or base. Pliny, book 17, chapter 18, writes that the Parthians were afflicted with this disease: because they took any food whatever indiscriminately and with the greatest greed, they were said to have a foul soul, etc.; (4) when things are not desired decently, that is, in the manner that is fitting. Though they are lawful, for example, to take food in a place, yet to take food in a brothel, or in the marketplace, or even with infamous companions, is not lawful. This also pertains to what the Philosopher reports in the book On the Virtues and Vices: that the voluptuous are for the most part imprudent, since they have no regard for propriety. And Cicero, book 1 of De finibus, says that they are not so scrupulous as to refrain from eating with dogs over trifles. In the second part of the chapter he shows how temperance is concerned with pain and distress, on account of a certain dissimilarity between the brave and the temperate, and between the timid and the intemperate. For although courage and cowardice are concerned with pain and distress no less than temperance and intemperance are, this happens in a far different way. The brave man does not grieve, or does not grieve more than he should; as right reason dictates, he grieves when those things are present that bring pain and distress, for example danger, wound, or death. The temperate man too does not grieve when those things are present that bring pleasure. The timid man, on the contrary, grieves when those things are present that bring distress and pain. The intemperate man too bears it with annoyance if he abstains from those things by which he could take pleasure. Therefore temperance is concerned with pain only through the abstaining from pleasures, and only incidentally. In the third part of the chapter he treats of insensibility, the other extreme of temperance, which he discussed above in chapter 8 of book 2 of this work, and which he also treats below in book 7, chapter 4. He proves, by an argument drawn from the less to the greater, that such people (such people, I say, who, as Cicero says in Pro Caelio, reject with their eyes all the beauty of things,

units.la: non odore ullo non tactu, non sapore capiatur, excludant auribus omnem suavitatem, quibus inter res jucundas & molestas nullum sit discrimen) probat Philosophus hoc modo: Quia homo principium sentiendi commune habet cum caeteris animalibus. Caetera animalia instinctu quod in natura inter convenientia & non convenientia naturae discernant, & haec appetant, ab illis abhorreant, tum multo magis hoc homo facere debet, cui ratio & judicium a natura supra caeteras creaturas sit concessum. Etsi vero raro aut nunquam detur talis vitium, quia tamen temperantia est virtus: omnis virtus sit medium quid, inter duo extrema necesse est, ut cum temperantia habeat vitium illi in excessu oppositum, quod vocatur intemperantia, habeat etiam extremum in defectu, quod vocatur insensibilitas. Et quoniam alia est cupiditas circa victum, alia circa Venerem, ideo pro duplici objecto duae constituuntur species, quarum altera vocatur nimia abstinentia victus, quae est stupiditas in cibo & potu a modo, quae naturae necessitas requirit, deficiens. Altera species dicitur abstinentia nimia Veneris, quae est stupiditas in Venere usurpanda a modo licito seu legitimo deficiens. In quarta parte capitis docet, quomodo ipsa temperantia circa voluptatem & dolorem versetur, & quomodo justum in iis servet modum & uno verbo explicat, nempe ut recta praescribit ratio. Nam voluptates sunt trium generum; alia enim sunt turpes seu inhonestae, quibus maxime delectantur intemperantes, ut sunt voluptates ex stupri, commessationibus, symphoniis, choreis, (quae instrumenta menta luxuriæ vocat Seneca) cibis inusitatis, eorumque condimentis aut obscœnis spectaculis, & ab his plane abstine: tëperans & odio potius habet. 2. Voluptates sunt honestæ, quæ bonam valetudinem & vires corporis conservât, ut sunt eæ voluptates, quæ ex cibis usitatis percipiuntur, ex ambulationibus, & variis ejusmodi exercitiis, & in his maximè versatur temperans, quas tamen voluptates honesto legitimoque modo expetit. 3. Voluptates sunt mediæ aut neutræ, quales capiuntur ex cibis paulo lautioribus & ex Venere, & in his versatur temperans, sicut recta præscribit ratio, id est, suo loco & tempore & modo, & cum decoro & pro modulo suarum facultatum. (Absurdum enim esset tenuioris conditionis hominem lautiores cibos, quam facultates ferant expetere.) Et in his omnibus honestatem tanquam ultimum finem semper sibi temperans proponit.
units.tr: take in no odour, no touch, no taste, shut out with their ears all sweetness, and make no distinction between agreeable and disagreeable things) are nowhere to be found. The Philosopher proves this thus: man has a principle of sensation in common with the other animals. The other animals, by instinct, which in nature distinguishes what is agreeable from what is not agreeable to their nature, seek the one and shun the other. Much more, then, ought man to do this, to whom reason and judgment have been granted by nature above the other creatures. And although such a vice is rarely or never found, yet because temperance is a virtue, and every virtue is a certain mean between two extremes, it is necessary that, just as temperance has the vice opposed to it in excess, called intemperance, so it also has an extreme in defect, called insensibility. And since one desire concerns food and another concerns Venus, two species are therefore set up for the twofold object. One is called excessive abstinence from food and drink, which is a deficient insensibility toward food and drink, falling short of the measure that the necessity of nature requires. The other species is called excessive abstinence from Venus, which is a deficient insensibility in the use of Venus, falling short of the licit or lawful measure. In the fourth part of the chapter he teaches how temperance itself is concerned with pleasure and pain, how it keeps the just mean in them, and he explains this in one word: it acts as right reason prescribes. For pleasures are of three kinds. Some are base or dishonourable, and in these the intemperate especially delight, such as the pleasures of fornication, carousing, music, and dancing (which Seneca calls the instruments of lust), unusual foods and their seasonings, or obscene spectacles. From these the temperate man entirely abstains and rather holds them in hatred. Second, some pleasures are honourable, those that preserve good health and bodily strength, such as the pleasures derived from ordinary foods, from walks, and from various exercises of this kind. In these the temperate man is chiefly occupied, yet he seeks these pleasures in an honourable and lawful manner. Third, some pleasures are intermediate or neutral, such as those taken from somewhat more sumptuous foods and from Venus. In these the temperate man is occupied as right reason prescribes, that is, in its proper place, time and manner, and with decorum and in proportion to his means. (For it would be absurd for a man of humbler condition to seek more sumptuous foods than his means can bear.) And in all these he always sets before himself honour as his ultimate end.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Omnes cupiditates sunt aut communes aut propriæ.
units.tr: 1. All desires are either common or proper to the individual.

units.la: 2. Communes sunt hominibus eadem cum cateris animalibus.
units.tr: 2. Common desires belong to men in the same way as to the other animals.

units.la: 3. In communibus raro delinquunt homines, nisi forte in excessu.
units.tr: 3. Men rarely go wrong in respect of common desires, except perhaps by excess.

units.la: 4. Propriæ cupiditates solis competunt hominibus, & in iis varie pro variis circumstantiis spectantur quadam.
units.tr: 4. Proper desires belong to men alone, and in them certain things are observed in various ways according to various circumstances.

units.la: 5. Intemperantia est excessus circa voluptates & frequenter in communi hominum vita accidit.
units.tr: 5. Intemperance is an excess concerning pleasures, and it frequently occurs in the common life of men.

units.la: 6. Temperans non dolet absentia voluptatis, intemperantia e contra. 7. Voluptas, si absit, est causa doloris: intemperati non temperati.
units.tr: 6. The temperate man does not grieve at the absence of pleasure; the intemperate man, on the contrary, does. 7. If pleasure is absent, it is the cause of pain: this belongs to the intemperate, not the temperate.

units.la: 8. Concupiscentia omnis propter metum, ne frustretur, est cum dolore & molestia conjuncta.
units.tr: 8. Every desire, because of the fear that it may be frustrated, is joined with pain and discomfort.

units.la: 9. Nulli delectari ex gustu & tactu voluptatibus non modo non humanum, sed belluinum quidem esse videtur.
units.tr: 9. To take no delight in the pleasures of taste and touch seems not only not human but indeed brutish.

units.la: 10. Sensus communis inter cibos convenientes & inconvenientes distinguere omnia animal docuit.
units.tr: 10. Common sense, which every animal has, has taught it to distinguish between suitable and unsuitable foods.

units.la: 11. In voluptatibus capiendis & molestiis rite perferendis versatur vere temperans sicut recta praescribit ratio.
units.tr: 11. The truly temperate man is concerned with taking pleasures and bearing discomforts rightly, as right reason prescribes.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Quomodo dicat Philosophus non spectaritam in communibus, quam propriis cupiditatibus, an sint à natura, nec ne, à qua nempe originem trahunt. Nam ab anima appetitiva proveniunt & naturam ducem sequuntur. Virtus verò & vitium non sunt à natura docente Philosophi Lib. 2. huius operis cap. 1. Resp. Cupiditates considerari bifariam vel secundum essentiam, & sic à natura proveniunt, & hoc modo homines raro in iis peccare dicuntur, quatenus scilicet ductum instinctumque naturæ bene affectæ cupiditates sequuntur. 2. Secundum exuperantiam & pravam dispositionem quatenus à voluntate prava & male affecta procedunt, & sic in iis homines peccant, quo sensu Aristoteles hic intelligi debet.
units.tr: I. The question is how the Philosopher can say that men do not sin in common desires but only in their own, whether or not these desires come from nature, since they indeed arise from the appetitive soul and follow nature as their guide. Yet, as the Philosopher teaches in Book 2, chapter 1 of this work, virtue and vice are not from nature. Answer: desires may be considered in two ways. First, according to their essence, and in this sense they arise from nature. Men are said to sin rarely in them, namely insofar as they follow the guidance and instinct of nature when their desires are well disposed. Second, according to excess and a depraved disposition, insofar as they proceed from a perverse and ill-affected will. In this sense men sin in them, and this is the sense in which Aristotle must be understood here.

units.la: II. Quomodo dicat, Voluptatem esse causam doloris, cum voluptas & dolor sint contraria: unū vero contrarium non posse esse causa alterius? Resp. Voluptate perse non esse causa doloris, nā hoc longe recedit à natura voluptatis, sed per accidens tantum, quatenus abientia sua intemperatis parit dolorem, quemadmodum diximus nauclerum esse causam submersionis navis (per accidens tantum, nam per se maris tempestas est causa) absentia sua, cujus praesentia fuisset causa contrarii effectus, nempe conservationis.
units.tr: II. How does he say that pleasure is the cause of pain, since pleasure and pain are contraries, and one contrary cannot be the cause of the other? Answer: pleasure is not per se the cause of pain, for this is far removed from the nature of pleasure, but only per accidens, insofar as its absence in the intemperate produces pain. Just as we said that the helmsman is the cause of a shipwreck (only per accidens, for the storm at sea is the cause per se), so by his absence, whose presence would have caused the contrary effect, namely preservation.

units.la: III. Quomodo dicat omnem concupiscentiam esse cum molestia & dolore conjunctam, cum omnis cupiditas sit vel naturalis vel propria, ut ex superioribus patet. At in neutra harum est dolor. Nam natura in naturalis & voluptas in propria cupiditate dolore omnem fugiunt? Resp. Cupiditates considerantur duobus modis, vel per se & sic cum voluptate non cum dolore sunt conjunctae: vel per accidens, & sic interdum habent conjunctum dolorem. Nam intemperans ex concupiscentia, si rem diutius aucupetur, nec tamen assequatur, cum velit, dolorem animi ac cruciatum excipit.
units.tr: III. How does he say that every concupiscence is joined with discomfort and pain, since every desire is either natural or proper, as appears from what was said above? But in neither of these is there pain. For do natural desires, and pleasure in one's own desire, flee all pain? Answer: desires are considered in two ways. Either per se, and so they are joined with pleasure and not with pain; or per accidens, and so they sometimes have pain joined to them. For the intemperate man, if he pursues a thing from desire for a long time and yet does not obtain it when he wishes, suffers anguish and torment of mind.

units.la: IV. Cur negat Aristoteles tales dari in rerum natura, qui temperantibus in defectu opponuntur, seu qui spernant voluptates victus & Veneris, cum tamen lib. 10. c. 6. h. operis contrarium afferat, & tales commendet tanquam Philosophiae & contemplationis studio aptissimos. Talis fuit Chrysippus Philosophus, qui tanto contemplationis studio tenebatur, ut ordinarium usum cibi & potus neglexerit. Talis etiam Zenon fuit, qui nullis blanditiis ad Venerem induci potuit, sicut testatur Diogenes Laertius lib. 7. de vita Philosophorum? Resp. Hominis statum considerari duobus modis, vel secundum intellectum speculativum, & nobilissimas illius operationes, & sic interdum homo negligit ordinarium usum victus, cibi & potus & omnes corporis voluptates, non propter infensib li-tatem
units.tr: IV. Why does Aristotle deny that there are in nature such people as are opposed to the temperate in deficiency, that is, who despise the pleasures of food and of Venus, when yet in Book 10, chapter 6 of this work he asserts the contrary and commends such people as most fit for philosophy and the study of contemplation? Such was the philosopher Chrysippus, who was so held by the study of contemplation that he neglected the ordinary use of food and drink. Such also was Zeno, who could not be induced to Venus by any allurements, as Diogenes Laertius testifies in Book 7 of the Lives of the Philosophers. Answer: the state of man may be considered in two ways. First, according to the speculative intellect and its noblest operations, and in this way a man sometimes neglects the ordinary use of food, drink and all bodily pleasures. This is not because of a certain insensibility opposed to temperance in deficiency, but because he has a calm appetite and such tranquil desires that he seems to delight in nothing but the pure study of contemplation.

units.la: Aa tatem quandam, quæ temperantiæ in defectu opponitur, sed quia habet appetitum sedatum & cupiditates ita tranquillas, ut nulla aliare nisi mero contemplationis studio delectari videatur: Secundo considerat homo, moraliter, seu secundum communem vivendi in hac vita usum, quo sensu dicitur cap. 5. lib. 1. huius operis natura animal Politicum, id est, ad hoc natus, ut in hominum communi societate vivat: & sic in hoc morali statu Philosophus recte negavit dari tales homines, qui aspernarētur corporis voluptates, seu ut vulgò dicuntur, qui essent stupidi & insensiles.
units.tr: Second, man is considered morally, or according to the common use of living in this life. In this sense it is said in chapter 5 of Book 1 of this work that man is by nature a political animal, that is, born to live in the common society of men. And so in this moral state the Philosopher rightly denied that there are such men as would despise bodily pleasures, or, as they are commonly called, men who would be stupid and insensible.

units.la: V. & ult. Cur insensibilitas vocetur vitium, cum nullum vitium prosit ad virtutem assequendam.
units.tr: V. and last. Why insensibility is called a vice, since no vice helps toward attaining virtue.

units.la: At insensibilitas maximè prodest: nam docet voluptates fugere ex quibus oriuntur, plerumque vitia. Proinde non vitium, sed aut virtus aut causa virtutis dici debet insensibilitas. Respon. Negandum est prodesse ad virtutem, cum doceat absque ordine & ratione omnes voluptates etiam licitas fugere.
units.tr: But insensibility is of the greatest help, for it teaches us to flee the pleasures from which vices mostly arise. Therefore insensibility should be called not a vice, but either a virtue or a cause of virtue. Answer: it must be denied that it helps toward virtue, since it teaches us to flee all pleasures, even lawful ones, without order and reason.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: SUperest tertium & ultimum huius tractatus de temperantia inembrum, in quo intemperantiam cum timiditate, quæ fortitudini in defectu opponitur confert Philosophus, & in utra magis peccetur, docet: Partes capitis sunt duæ: In prima triplex affertur dissimilitudo inter ignaviam & intemperantiam: In secunda origo nominis intemperantiæ declaratur. In prima igitur triplex affertur discrimen ignaviæ & intemperantiæ. Primum est, quod intemperantia fit magis magis voluntaria nostrique magis arbitrii, quam fit ignavia seu timiditas: id quod probat duabus rationibus: 1. est, quia Intemperantia est cum voluptate conjuncta: nam semper sibi voluptatem proponit: ignavia vero cum dolore est conjuncta. Nam propter metum mali semper sibi dolorem obversantem habet, ut ex cap.1. hujus lib. patet, queque cum voluptate fiunt, ea volentibus & cupientibus nobis fiunt, quae vero cum dolore & molestia, ea invitis & nolentibus nobis fiunt. 2. Ratio est, quod dolor ignaviae comes homines non sui compotes reddat, & mentem plerunque de sede sua perturbet, quod fusè explicat Cic. lib.4. Tusc. quaest. Voluptas vero Intemperantiae comes mentem itabiliat, & vires animi magis magisque confirmet, & sic voluntatem ad aliquid exequendum impellat. Secunda dissimilitudo est: quod cum Intemperantia sit magis voluntaria, ideo magis odio & reprehensione sit digna. Nam ut ex cap.1. lib.2. hujus operis constat, quae a volentibus vitia committuntur, poena, quae a nolentibus vero venia & commiseratione sint digna. Id probat ratione ducta a contrario hoc modo: Ad quam virtutem facilius homines assuefieri possunt, ejus contrarium majore reprehensione est dignum. Atqui ad Temperantiam facilius possunt assuefieri homines quam ad fortitudinem. Nam usus Temperantiae est quotidianus, & in omni aetate requiritur, & nullo cum periculo est conjuncta Temperantia: Fortitudinis vero rarior est usus & in bello tantum cernitur, & objectum habet vulnera, mortem & pericula: proinde Intemperantia Temperantiae op-posita posita majore reprehensione est digna, quam Timiditas, quæ opponitur fortitudini. Tertia similitudo est: quod Timiditatis habitum facilius expectant homines, quam ipsum obiectum. Quilibet enim timidus & ignavus dici mavult, quàm vulnera & mortem experiri: at contra intemperantiæ habitum nemo expetit, nemo enim intemperans dici cupit, at verò voluptate circa quam versatur Temperantia omnes expetunt.
units.tr: There remains the third and last part of this treatise on temperance, in which the Philosopher compares intemperance with timidity, which is opposed to fortitude as its deficiency, and teaches in which of the two more fault is committed. The chapter has two parts. In the first, three differences between cowardice and intemperance are set out. In the second, the origin of the name intemperance is explained. In the first part, then, three distinctions are drawn between cowardice and intemperance. The first is that intemperance is more voluntary and more within our choice than cowardice or timidity is. He proves this by two reasons: (1) intemperance is joined with pleasure, for it always proposes pleasure to itself, whereas cowardice is joined with pain, for on account of fear of evil it always has pain before it, as is clear from chapter 1 of this book; and things done with pleasure are done by us willingly and eagerly, but things done with pain and distress are done by us unwillingly and against our will. (2) The reason is that the pain which accompanies cowardice makes men not in control of themselves and mostly disturbs the mind from its seat, which Cicero explains at length in book 4 of the Tusculan Disputations. But the pleasure which accompanies intemperance makes the mind firm and strengthens the powers of the soul more and more, and so drives the will to carry something out. The second difference is that, since intemperance is more voluntary, it is therefore more deserving of hatred and rebuke. For, as is clear from chapter 1 of book 2 of this work, faults committed by those who are willing deserve punishment, while those committed by the unwilling deserve pardon and pity. He proves this by an argument drawn from the contrary, thus: the contrary of a virtue to which men can more easily be accustomed deserves greater reproach. But men can more easily be accustomed to temperance than to fortitude. For the practice of temperance is daily, is required at every age, and is joined with no danger; but the practice of fortitude is rarer, is seen only in war, and has as its objects wounds, death and dangers. Therefore intemperance, which is opposed to temperance, deserves greater reproach than timidity, which is opposed to fortitude. The third difference is that men desire the habit of timidity more readily than its object. For anyone would rather be called timid and cowardly than experience wounds and death; but, on the contrary, no one desires the habit of intemperance, for no one wishes to be called intemperate, whereas everyone desires the pleasure with which temperance is concerned.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis ratio nominis Intemperantiæ redditur. Intemperantia Græcis dicitur ἀκολασία, ab α privativa, & κολάζω coërceo, castigo, quod vitium puerorum male educatorum est proprium, quorum petulantia nondum sit castigata aut coërcita, ut docet Aristophanes Comicus in Pluto, & magna est convenientia inter intemperantes & pueros. Nam ut pueri cupiditate potius, quam recta ratione, quæ in iis admodum est infirma, propter tenerā ætatem & imbecilla corporis organa omnia gerunt, sic etiam intemperantes. 2. Cupiditates in pueris cum ætate incrementum capiunt, & nisi studio & diligentia coerceantur, in infinitum excrescunt, sic etiam intemperatorum cupiditates nullum servant modum, nisi rectæ rationis gyro flectátur. Nam recta ratio docet in omnibus actionibus honestatem, tanquam scopum ultimum sibi proponere, & cupiditates omnes ad veram temperantiam (quæ quemadmodum decet, quando & quæ decet, docet expetere) se accommodare. Et ratio, cur cupiditates non refrenatæ in infinitum excrescant est, quod à natura penè insitam voluptatum sitim inexpleexplebilem habeamus, ut præclarè docet hoc loco Philosophus & Plato lib.7.de Repub. Cic.lib.1. de finib. & paradoxo 7. Plura vide apud Keckerman. pag.188. Syftem. Eth.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter the reason for the name intemperance is given. Intemperance is called in Greek ἀκολασία [akolasia], from the alpha privative and κολάζω [kolazō], I restrain or chastise, which is the proper vice of ill-brought-up children, whose petulance has not yet been chastised or restrained, as the comic poet Aristophanes teaches in the Plutus; and there is a great likeness between the intemperate and children. For just as children do everything from desire rather than from right reason, which in them is very weak because of their tender age and feeble bodily organs, so too do the intemperate. 2. Desires in children grow with age, and unless they are restrained by zeal and diligence they swell without limit; so too the desires of the intemperate keep no measure unless they are bent by the turn of right reason. For right reason teaches us to set honour before ourselves as the ultimate goal in all actions, and to adapt all desires to true temperance, which teaches what is fitting to desire, and when and how. The reason why unrestrained desires grow without limit is that we have an almost innate thirst for pleasures that cannot be satisfied, as the Philosopher here teaches admirably, and Plato in book 7 of the Republic, and Cicero in book 1 of On Ends and in Paradox 7. See more in Keckermann, p. 188, System of Ethics.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Intemperantia est cum voluptate conjuncta, timiditas verò cum dolore.
units.tr: 1. Intemperance is joined with pleasure, but cowardice with pain.

units.la: 2. Dolor hominis animū perturbat, & de sua fede dejicit.
units.tr: 2. Pain disturbs a man's mind and drives it from its firm footing.

units.la: 3. Intemperantia est vitium majore reprehensione dignum, quam timiditas.
units.tr: 3. Intemperance is a vice more deserving of reproach than cowardice.

units.la: 4. Nemo intemperans dici cupit, voluptatem tamen omnes expetunt.
units.tr: 4. No one wishes to be called intemperate, yet all men desire pleasure.

units.la: 5. In pueris cupiditatum appetitus, non recta ratio bene cernitur.
units.tr: 5. In boys the appetite of the desires is clearly seen, not right reason.

units.la: 6. In pueris cupiditates, nisi studio & diligentia coercean-tur cum atate incrementum capiunt.
units.tr: 6. In boys the desires, unless they are restrained by zeal and diligence, grow with age.

units.la: 7. Ut pueri virgis & castigatione Padagogi sunt coercendi, sic intemperatorum cupiditates rationi recta subjici debent.
units.tr: 7. Just as boys must be restrained with rods and the correction of the tutor, so the desires of the intemperate must be made subject to right reason.

units.la: 8. Voluptates si magna & vehementes sint rationem ipsam expellunt.
units.tr: 8. Pleasures, if they are great and vehement, drive out reason itself.

units.la: 9. Recta ratio cupiditates omnes ad honestatem flectit & legitimo omnia modo expetere docet.
units.tr: 9. Right reason bends all desires toward honour and teaches us to seek everything in a lawful manner.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat intemperantiam magis esse voluntariam, seu magis in nostra voluntate sitam, quā timiditatem seu ignaviam, cum tamen lib.2.cap.8. hujus operis, disputans contra Platonem asseruerit aquè vitia ac virtutes esse in nostra potestate. Proinde non magis involuntaria videtur intemperantia, quam timiditas? Resp. Negatur turhocsequi. Nam etsi asseruerit loco citato non minus vitia, quum virtutes in nostra esse potestate (contra quod Plato volebat) non prohibet tamen, quo minus unum vitium sit magis voluntarium, quam alterum propter varias circumstantias, exempli gratia: Intemperantia magis est voluntarium vitium, quia voluptatem habet comitem, quam timiditas, quae dolorem habet conjunctum.
units.tr: I. It is asked: how can he say that intemperance is more voluntary, or more within our will, than cowardice or timidity, when in Book 2, chapter 8 of this work, disputing against Plato, he asserted that vices and virtues are equally in our power? Therefore intemperance does not seem more involuntary than timidity? Answer: The inference is denied. For although he asserted in the passage cited that vices are no less in our power than virtues (against what Plato held), he does not deny that one vice may be more voluntary than another because of various circumstances. For example, intemperance is a more voluntary vice than timidity, because it has pleasure as its companion, whereas timidity has pain joined to it.

units.la: II. An hoc verum sit, quod dicit dolorem corrumpere & labefactare animum hominis, voluptatem vero minime cum contrario experientia testetur. Nam incontinentes & luxuriosi sunt brevissima vita, & voluptas in iis magis labefactat animum quam dolor. Deinde Valerius Maximus lib. 4. cap. 7. de morte non vulgari refert, quendam Romanam cuius rumor erat filium in bello Canensi cecidisse, eam cum diu deflevisset, sed cum salvum vidisset reversum, prae nimia laetitia moribundam decidisse, ubi haec addit verba: quam dolor superare non poterat, laetitia extinxit. Proinde voluptas magis labefactat animum hominis, quam dolor? Resp. Divus Thomas duplicem esse voluptatem, vel secundum medium, vel secundum exuperantiam. Voluptas secundum medium non labefactat, sed conservat animum hominis propterea, quod spiritus vitales in suo tuentur vigore. At voluptas secundum exuperantiam magis, quam dolor labefactat & sic incontinentes & luxuriosi, quia voluptate supra modum seu secundum exuperantiam abuntur brevissimae sunt vitae.
units.tr: II. Is it true what he says, that pain corrupts and weakens the mind of a man, while pleasure does not, as experience shows to the contrary? For the incontinent and the dissolute have very short lives, and pleasure weakens their minds more than pain does. Again, Valerius Maximus, Book 4, chapter 7, reports an uncommon death: a certain Roman woman, who had been told that her son had fallen in the battle of Cannae, mourned him for a long time; but when she saw him return safe, she collapsed dying from excessive joy. Valerius adds these words: "what grief could not overcome, joy destroyed." Therefore pleasure weakens the mind of a man more than pain does? Answer: Thomas says there are two kinds of pleasure, one according to the mean and one according to excess. Pleasure according to the mean does not weaken but preserves the mind of a man, because it keeps the vital spirits in their proper vigour. But pleasure according to excess weakens more than pain does; and so the incontinent and the dissolute have very short lives, because they abuse pleasure beyond measure, that is, according to excess.

units.la: III. An cum veritate constet, quod dicit Aristoteles in textu voluptates, nempe vehementiores ipsam rationem expellere, ut hominem infamire faciant? cum tamen lib. 3. de anima cap. 5. teste eodem Philosopho, animus rationis com-
units.tr: III. Does it agree with the truth, what Aristotle says in the text, that the more intense pleasures drive out reason itself, so that they make a man mad? For, as the same Philosopher testifies in Book 3 of On the Soul, chapter 5, the mind, when it is in possession of reason, is free and immune from every disturbance. Therefore it cannot be so conquered by pleasures that it is reduced to madness?

units.la: pe pos liber & immunis fit ab omni perturbatione. Proinde nec a voluptatibus ita vinci poterit, ut ad insaniam redigatur? Resp. Animum considerari duobus modis; vel absolute, ut est spiritus, & sic liber est ab omni perturbatione & affectu, quo sensu intelligi debet locus ille ex 3. de anima cum animus vel extra corpus consideratur, & per se vel cum homo in hac vita constituitur: secundo consideratur animus comparatè, ut est actus corporis, & sic affectibus interdum ita vincitur, ut eorum impetu a rectae rationis sede deturbetur: voluptates vero vehementiores insanire hominé faciunt, propter quatuor causas. 1. Quia cerebrum hominis vehementia sui nimis concitant. 2. Quia spiritus animales in homine admodum pertubant. 3. Quia phantasiam multis & variis intentionibus vulnerant. 4. Quia immensos dolores in appetitu excitant.
units.tr: ... Answer: The mind may be considered in two ways. Either absolutely, as it is spirit, and so it is free from all disturbance and passion; in this sense that passage from the third book On the Soul must be understood, when the mind is considered outside the body, and in itself, or when man is placed in this life. Secondly, the mind is considered comparatively, as it is the act of the body, and so it is sometimes conquered by the passions, so that by their assault it is hurled from the seat of right reason. The more intense pleasures make a man mad for four reasons: (1) because by their very vehemence they greatly agitate the brain; (2) because they greatly disturb the animal spirits in a man; (3) because they wound the imagination with many and various intentions; (4) because they arouse immense pains in the appetite.

units.la: Corollarii loco & has adjiciemus quaestiones:
units.tr: By way of a corollary, we shall also add these questions:

units.la: 1. An cum Temperantia duae sint species, Frugalitas & Castitas (de quibus vide, quae superius dicta sunt.) Virginitas species castitatis vere dici possit? Non posse sequentes hae vincunt rationes. 1. Quia virginitas nihil aliud est, quam abstinentia foeminae non conjugatae a contactu virili, ideoque bonum naturale est, quod in iis foeminis esse potest, quae revera castae non sunt. Nam impudentissimae quaeque ante congressum sua fruuntur virginitate, at vero castitas species est temperantiae appetitum Veneris & usum legitime moderans. 2. Virginitas usu & exercitatione non acquiritur, sicut omnis virtus moralis. 3. Virtus moralis, ut ex definitione data cap.7. lib. 2. parte, est habitus, bitus, omnis vero habitus, ut difficulter acquiritur, sic etiam difficulter amittitur: Virginitas vero facile & una quidem actione.
units.tr: 1. Since there are two species of temperance, frugality and chastity (on which see what has been said above), can virginity truly be called a species of chastity? The following reasons show that it cannot. (1) Virginity is nothing other than the abstinence of an unmarried woman from contact with a man, and so it is a natural good that can be present in women who are not truly chaste. For the most shameless women enjoy their virginity before intercourse; but chastity is a species of temperance, which legitimately governs the appetite for Venus and her use. (2) Virginity is not acquired by use and practice, as every moral virtue is. (3) A moral virtue, as is clear from the definition given in chapter 7 of Book 2, is a habit; and every habit, as it is acquired with difficulty, so also is lost with difficulty. Virginity, however, is lost easily, and indeed by a single act.

units.la: II. An helluo febricitans, qui a vino abstinet, sit temperans dicendus, aut etiam illi, qui per naturam abstinent ab odoribus, a casco aut ab esu carnium aut hujusmodi aliis cibis. Et respondetur neutros temperantes esse dicendos; nam helluo febricitans coactus id facit, & ex medici tantum praescripto, nec promta accedit voluntas, quae ad omnem veram virtutis actionem adesse debet. 2. Metus gravioris periculi ne morbus diutius continuetur aut etiam pereat, in causa tantum est, cur abstineat: qui vero per naturam abstinent ab aliis cibis, id non faciunt ex temperantia, sed ex ἀδυναμία & naturae quadam infirmitate, atqui in temperantia nec coactio nec naturae infirmitas quicquam habet loci. Unde sequitur Carthusianos Monachos temperantes minime habendos, quod a carnibus abstineant & piscibus continuo vivitent, propter has rationes. Nam 1, accedit coactio. Id enim faciunt, quia voto se ad hoc adstringunt. 2. Mandatum seu regula ordinis hoc praescribit. 3. Major intemperantia saepenumero sequitur ex esu piscium, quam ex usu carnium. Nam pisces sunt plerumque natura feventioris & Veneris titillationem vehementer excitant, cujus rei fidem faciunt piscatores & nautae, qui admodum delectantur piscibus & in Venerem sunt proniores. Proinde abstinentia a carnibus & ingurgitatio piscium non est temperantia dicenda aut jejunium, sed gulositas potius & intemperantia.
units.tr: II. Is a glutton with a fever, who abstains from wine, to be called temperate, or also those who by nature abstain from smells, from cheese, from the eating of meats, or from other foods of this kind? The answer is that neither are to be called temperate. For the glutton with a fever does it under compulsion, and only on the doctor's prescription, and no ready will comes to it, which ought to be present in every true act of virtue. (2) The fear of a more serious danger, that the illness may continue longer or even end in death, is the only cause of his abstinence. Those who abstain by nature from other foods do not do so from temperance, but from [inability, ἀδυναμία] and a certain weakness of nature; yet in temperance neither compulsion nor weakness of nature has any place. Hence it follows that the Carthusian monks are by no means to be held temperate, because they abstain from meat and live continually on fish, for these reasons: (1) compulsion is present, for they do it because they bind themselves to it by vow; (2) the command or rule of their order prescribes it; (3) greater intemperance very often follows from the eating of fish than from the use of meat. For fish are generally of a more heating nature and vigorously stir up the titillation of Venus, as fishermen and sailors bear witness, who take great delight in fish and are more prone to Venus. Therefore abstinence from meat and the gorging of fish is not to be called temperance or fasting, but rather gluttony and intemperance.

units.la: III. An cum temperantia maximè versetur circa voluptatem tactus, summa verò tactus voluptas ex saltatione percipiatur, an temperanti saltare liceat? De hac quæstione variæ sunt variorum opiniones.
units.tr: III. Since temperance is chiefly concerned with the pleasure of touch, and the greatest pleasure of touch is found in dancing, is it lawful for a temperate person to dance? On this question there are various opinions among various authors.

units.la: Quidam enim omnem simpliciter saltationem licitâ esse contendunt, quidam verò simpliciter illicitam: quidam verò media viam tenent, & quandoq; licitam quandoq; illicitam esse affirmant. Rationes pro prima opinione sunt hæ: 1. Quia saltatio est motus artificiosus, quo corpus hominis exercetur. 2. Quia sanitatem conservat. Ut enim, inquit Seneca, ferrum nisi exercea rubiginem contrahit, sic corpus hominis nisi moderatè subinde exercitiis (inter quæ saltationi non infimus est locus) reficiatur, tabe inficitur & labascit. 3. Quia corpus hominis agile reddit & alacre: nam melancholiam discutit, & lætitiam adfert. 4. Quia hominem ab ebrietate abstrahit, etsi plus quam naturæ necessitas postulat biberit, crapulam excutit. 5. Quia finis illius est partim hilaritatem animi declarare, partim honore afficere eam personam cum qua instituitur saltatio. 6. Quia occasionem sæpe præbet ad legitima matrimonia contrahenda: sic enim juvenes & virgines ansam inter se colloquendi habent, & sensa mentis mutuo significandi. 7. Quia nusquam in Scripturis expresse prohibetur.
units.tr: Some hold that every dance is lawful without qualification, others that every dance is unlawful without qualification, and others take a middle course and affirm that dancing is sometimes lawful and sometimes unlawful. The reasons for the first opinion are these: (1) dancing is an artful motion by which the human body is exercised; (2) it preserves health. For, as Seneca says, "iron, unless it is used, contracts rust; so the human body, unless it is refreshed from time to time by moderate exercises" (among which dancing has no small place) "is infected by decay and grows weak." (3) It makes the body nimble and lively, for it drives away melancholy and brings cheerfulness. (4) It draws a man away from drunkenness, and even if he has drunk more than natural need requires, it shakes off the stupor. (5) Its purpose is partly to show the cheerfulness of the mind and partly to honour the person with whom the dance is performed. (6) It often provides an occasion for lawful marriages, for young men and maidens thus have an opportunity to talk together and to make known their thoughts to each other. (7) It is nowhere expressly forbidden in Scripture.

units.la: In contrariam partem, id est, pro eorum opinione, qui omnem saltationem prorsus illicitam esse contendunt; Rationes sunt multæ & variæ, nec minori fere ponderis, quam priores. Prima ratio est, Quia omnis saltatio est sua natura turpis & inhonesta: non enim bono honestoque fine instituitur, sed libidinis augendæ proritandæque gratia, nempe ut sic saltantes simul esse, se invicem tangere, colloqui, & reliqua facere possunt. Secunda ratio: Quia argumentum est levitatis oppositæ gravitati. Hinc Gallos leviculos judicabat Alphonsus Siciliæ Rex, quod choreis & saltationibus indulgerent, tantoque magis, quanto essent ætate provectiores. Tertia ratio: Quia fomentum & irritamentum est lasciviæ & libidinis: sæpe enim ibi, ut ait Petrarcha, matrona diu servatum decus perdidit, sæpe ibi infelix virguncula male didicit, quod melius ignorasset, multarum ibi fama periit, pudorq. multa inde impudica, plures ambiguæ domum redierę, castior autem nulla. Quarta ratio: Quia non solum bonis moribus obest, sed & publicæ etiam tranquillitati & in publicam vergit perniciem. Nam ut saltatio ex vino, compotationibus, & lascivia mentis plerumque oritur, sic relinquit post se stupra, cædes, aliaque nefanda, quibus tranquillitas publica turbatur. Hinc Johannes Baptista capite plectitur propter saltatriculam. Unde eleganter Chrysostomus homil. 43. in Matth. inquit: Saltationis libidinosæ precium factum est caput Johannis. Et tota gens Lapitharum & Centaurorum cum excommessationibus ad saltationes pervenire, pugna inter se orta periit, teste Ovid. 12. Metam. Sic etiam Israelitæ contemto vero Dei cultu cum vitulum in deserto sibi erexissent, cœperunt ludere & cantantes circa eum choreas ducere Exo. 32. cap. Quinta ratio: Patres quidam primitivæ Ecclesiæ nec infimæ etiam notæ omnem saltationem prorsus damnarunt. Hinc Chrysostomus homil. 48. in Genesin. saltationes omnes vocat diabolicas, & homil. 56. ibidem dicit, diabolum una saltasaltare. Et Augustinus graviter invehitur in corruptos clericorum mores, quod choreis se immiscerent, & cum mulierculis promiscuè saltarent: Melius, inquit, tota die sederent, quam die Sabbati saltarent. Et Bernhatd.serm. 14. in cap. Matth. Saltationem vocat circulum, cuius centrum sit diabolus, peripheria ejus Angeli. Sexta ratio: Quia in concilio Laodicensi & Illardensi Christianis saltatio est publicè interdicta. Septima ratio. Idem probatur iudicio prudentissimorum imperatorum. Hinc Fridericus I. Imperator teste Æneâ Sylvio in hist. Bohem. dicebat, se malle febricitare quam saltare. Et Albertus Imperator, venationem vocabat exercitium proprium virile, sed saltationem exercitium muliebre & tantum mulierculis dignum.
units.tr: On the other side, that is, in support of the opinion of those who maintain that all dancing is utterly unlawful, the arguments are many and varied, and of almost no less weight than the former. The first argument is that all dancing is by its nature base and dishonourable: it is not undertaken for a good and honest end, but for the sake of increasing and provoking lust, namely so that those dancing may be together, touch one another, talk, and do the rest. The second argument: it is a sign of levity, which is opposed to gravity. Hence Alphonso, King of Sicily, judged the French to be frivolous because they indulged in round dances and dancing, and all the more so the older they were. The third argument: it is a fomenter and incitement of wantonness and lust: "for often there," as Petrarch says, "a matron has lost the honour she had long kept, often there an unhappy young girl has learned badly what she would better have not known; the reputation of many has perished there, and much immodesty has come from it, and many have gone home dishonoured, and none has gone home more chaste." The fourth argument: it not only harms good morals but also tends to the ruin of public tranquillity. For just as dancing usually arises from wine, drinking parties and wantonness of mind, so it leaves behind it debauchery, murder and other abominable deeds, by which public peace is disturbed. Hence John the Baptist was beheaded on account of a dancing girl. Whence Chrysostom elegantly says in Homily 43 on Matthew: "The head of John became the price of a lewd dance." And the whole race of the Lapiths and Centaurs, coming to the dances with drunken revelry, perished in strife among themselves, as Ovid testifies in Metamorphoses 12.
