So too the Israelites, having despised the true worship of God, when they had set up a calf for themselves in the wilderness, began to play and to lead round dances singing about it, Exodus 32. The fifth argument: some Fathers of the primitive Church, and not those of least note, condemned all dancing utterly. Hence Chrysostom, in Homily 48 on Genesis, calls all dances diabolical, and in Homily 56 on the same says that the devil dances along with them. And Augustine rebukes sharply the corrupt morals of the clergy, because they mixed themselves with dances and danced promiscuously with silly women: "It would be better," he says, "for them to sit all day than to dance on the Sabbath." And Bernard, in Sermon 14 on the chapter of Matthew, calls the dance a circle whose centre is the devil and whose circumference is the angels. The sixth argument: dancing has been publicly forbidden to Christians in the councils of Laodicea and Illiberis. The seventh argument: the same is confirmed by the judgement of the most prudent emperors. Hence Emperor Frederick I, as Aeneas Sylvius reports in History of Bohemia, used to say that he would rather have a fever than dance. And Emperor Albert called hunting a proper and manly exercise, but dancing an exercise of women, fit only for silly females.

units.la: Octava ratio: Quia saniores Ethnici omnem saltationem exploserunt & irriserunt. Hinc Cicero dicit, Virum probum & honestum nolle in foro saltare, etsi eo modo ad maximum pervenire possit patrimonium. Et in Orat. pro L. Murena dicit, neminem saltare sobrium, nisi forte insaniat, neque in convivio moderato atque honesto intempestivi, inquit, convivii immoderati judicium turpium deliriarum comes est extrema saltatio. Et in orat. habita post reditum in senatum, Aulum Gabinium inimicum suum contumeliae causa vocat Calamistratum saltatorem. Et Salust. in conjuratione Catilinaria Sempronii improbrat, quod canere & saltare doctior esset, quam probae mulieri convenire. Et M. Cato Murenae, quod in Asia, dum ibi regeret, saltasset, pro maximo crimine objecit. Et Demosth. Olynth. 2. Socios Philippi Macedonum Regs gravissimè reprehensuros, saltatores vocat. Nona ratio: Qua
units.tr: Eighth reason: Because the wiser heathens also rejected and ridiculed every kind of dancing. Hence Cicero says: An honest and upright man would not want to dance in the forum, even if he could in that way acquire a very large fortune. And in his speech for L. Murena he says: No one dances while sober, unless perhaps he is out of his mind; and dancing to the very end is the companion of an immoderate feast, of shameful follies, not of a moderate and respectable dinner-party. And in the speech delivered after his return to the senate, he calls his enemy Aulus Gabinius a curled dancer, to insult him. And Sallust, in the Catilinarian conspiracy, criticises Sempronia because she was more learned at singing and dancing than suits a respectable woman. And Marcus Cato reproached Murena, as a very great crime, for having danced in Asia while he was governing there. And Demosthenes, in the second Olynthiac, calls the companions of Philip of Macedon dancers, when he is about to rebuke them most severely. Ninth reason: Because dancing seems to be a kind of voluntary madness and a sort of insanity. Hence Ludovicus Vives, in book 2 of De institutione feminae Christianae, says that some foreigners arrived in these parts and saw our people dancing from a distance, but could not hear the music; they thought that all of us, because we were seen running about together in a disorderly way, had been seized by some peculiar kind of madness. See more in Cornelius Agrippa, chapter 18, On the uncertainty of the sciences and arts.

units.la: Quia furoris voluntarii & insaniæ quoddam genus esse videtur. Hinc Ludov. Viv. lib. 2. de instit. fœminæ Christianæ, dicit peregrinos quosdam in has oras pervenisse, & saltantes nostrates vidisse ex longinquo, ita tamen ut Musicam non audirent, qui putabant omnes nostros (propterea quod promiscuè discurrentes, continuò vidissent) peculiari quodam genere furoris captos esse. Plura vide apud Cornel. Agrippam cap. 18. de incertitudine scientiarum & artium.
units.tr: Because it seems to be a kind of voluntary madness and a sort of insanity. Hence Ludovicus Vives, in book 2 of De institutione feminae Christianae, says that some foreigners arrived in these parts and saw our people dancing from a distance, but could not hear the music; they thought that all of us, because we were seen running about together in a disorderly way, had been seized by some peculiar kind of madness. See more in Cornelius Agrippa, chapter 18, On the uncertainty of the sciences and arts.

units.la: Argumenta pro tertia opinione, quam tanquam maximè probandam sequimur sunt hæc: Ergo quia non omnis saltatio est inhonesta, sed quædam est honesta, decora & moderata, & hæc est licita modò recte & ritè usurpetur, quod probatur exemplo sanctorum in Scriptura: Nam David coram arca Domini saltavit 2. Reg. 6. & puellæ Judaicæ victoriam ejus de Goliatho choreis & saltationibus celebrarunt 2. Sam. 24. & Miria sorore Moysis submersò cum exercitu Pharaone una cum aliis mulieribus Israeliticis choreas duxit Exod. 15. 2. Quia non omnis saltatio quoad saltatio est turpis impia aut illicita, sed quæ est lasciva & libidinosa, quæ etiam gravitati aliisque virtutibus est adversa; non secus ac aurum & vinum, quæ sua natura bona sunt, sed ubi mala usurpantur, mala esse incipiunt. Hinc Petrus Martyr in L. C. class. 2. cap. 2. dicit mihi sane non videtur hoc saltationis genus, quod lætitiæ gratia excitatur, esse sua natura vitiosum & prohibitum: & quoniam agilitas corporis est donum Dei, si aliquid artis accedat, nimirum ut corpus ordine, numero, aptè & cum decoro moveatur nō video, cur debeat reprereprehendi modò in tempore, & citra offensionem fiat. Quemadmodum canere licet & ad gratias Deo agendas, & ad laudes ejus celebrandas possumus uti cantu, sic moderata saltatione gaudium & laetitiam animi testari possumus. 3. Saniores etiam Ethnici quoddam saltationis genus, tanquam salubre corpori & Reipub. utile probarunt. Nam Pyrrhicam ad agilitatem corporis & facilitatem arma gestandi comparandam saltarunt, tum Graecitum Romani teste Vegetio in lib. de ftratag. militari. Et Polybius refert Laelium & Scipionem aliosq; Romanorum Ducum praecipuos, hoc saltationis genere vehementer delectatos. Et Josephus Scaliger in vita patris sui Julii refert patrem hanc Pyrrhicam saltaseapud Ludovicum XII. Gallicarum Regem. Breviter: Omnis saltatio est aut religiosa, aut politica, religiosam esse licitam exemplis supra allatis constat, modò quo spiritu illi in Scripturis sancti saltaruntsaltent homines. Politica rursus est aut socia aut solitaria. Solitaria etiam est licita, si ad laetitiam animi excitandam & sanitatem corporis conservandam instituatur. Socia etiam si recte & honesto fine usurpetur, damnari nullo modo potest.
units.tr: The arguments for the third opinion, which we follow as the one most worthy of approval, are these. First, because not every dance is dishonourable, but some dancing is honourable, decorous and moderate, and this is lawful provided it is rightly and properly practised. This is proved by the example of the saints in Scripture: for David danced before the ark of the Lord (2 Sam. 6), and the Jewish maidens celebrated his victory over Goliath with choral dances and leaping (1 Sam. 18), and Miriam, the sister of Moses, led the dances with the other Israelite women after Pharaoh and his army had been drowned (Exod. 15). Second, because dancing as such is not shameful, impious or unlawful, but only that which is wanton and lustful, and which is also opposed to gravity and other virtues; just as gold and wine, which are good by their nature, begin to be evil when they are misused. Hence Peter Martyr, in Loci communes, class 2, chapter 2, says: "It does not seem to me that this kind of dancing, which is performed for the sake of joy, is by its nature vicious and forbidden; and since bodily agility is a gift of God, if some art is added, so that the body is moved in order, measure, aptly and with grace, I do not see why it should be blamed, provided it is done at a suitable time and without giving offence. Just as it is permitted to sing both to give thanks to God and to use song to celebrate his praises, so by moderate dancing we can also show the joy and gladness of the mind." Third, even the wiser heathens approved a certain kind of dancing as beneficial to the body and useful to the commonwealth. For the Romans, as Vegetius teaches in his book on military matters, danced the Pyrrhic to acquire agility of body and ease in bearing arms, after the Greek manner. And Polybius reports that Laelius and Scipio and other leading Roman commanders took great delight in this kind of dancing. And Joseph Scaliger, in the life of his father Julius, reports that his father danced this Pyrrhic before Louis XII, king of the French. In brief: every dance is either religious or secular. That a religious dance is lawful is established by the examples cited above, provided men dance in the spirit in which those holy men danced in the Scriptures. A secular dance, in turn, is either social or solitary. A solitary dance is also lawful, if it is undertaken to rouse the joy of the mind and to preserve bodily health. A social dance also can in no way be condemned if it is used rightly and for an honest end.

units.la: IV. An idem fit Continentia quod Temperantia? Et videntur unum & idem esse ex opinione Aristot. propter duas rationes: Nam cap. 4. lib. 7. Nic. Continentiam definit virtutem per quam luctamur, cum cupiditate cibi, potus & Veneris. Et quidem ficluctamur, ut recta ratio superior evadat. 2. Opponit idem loco citato Continentiae in defectu virium quoddam nomine carens, per quod homo à licitis volup-tatipratibus abstinet, ita ut honestę voluptatis gratia nihil præclarum aut laudabile facere velit; in excessu vero opponit Incontinentiam, per quam homo in affectibus & cupiditatibus, & præsertim in cupiditate alimentaria & Venerea contra dictamen rectæ rationis modum excedit. Proinde cum testimonio ipsius Aristotelis & definitione & extremis conveniant, unum & idem esse videntur. At vero non esse idem quatuor hæ probat rationes: 1. est, quia Continentia non est virtus saltem perfecta, sed potius bonus affectus virtutem moderans secundum rectam rationem; Temperantia vero virtus est. De hac re vide plura apud Keckermann pag. 308. sylt. Ethic. 2. quia Philosophus loco citato duplicitér Continentiam sumit; modo generaliter pro ea virtute, imperfecta scilicet qua pravæ cupiditates omnes, & immoderati affectus subjiciuntur rectæ rationi, sed invitis modo sumit speciali ter pro ea virtute, quæ iram moderatur, tum eiā cupiditates reliquas cibi, potus & Veneris, sermonis & locomotivæ. 3. Objectum Continentiæ latius patet. Nam extendit se ad affectus omnes internos; Temperantia vero versatur circa voluptates tantum tactus & gustus. 4. In Continentia est lucta appetitus & rectæ rationis; in Temperantia vero non non.
units.tr: IV. Is Continence the same as Temperance? They seem to be one and the same, according to Aristotle's view, for two reasons. First, in Nicomachean Ethics book 7, chapter 4, he defines continence as a virtue by which we struggle against desires for food, drink and sex, and indeed we struggle so that right reason may prevail. Second, in the same passage he sets against continence, in its deficiency of strength, a nameless quality by which a man abstains from permitted pleasures, so that he will do nothing noble or praiseworthy for the sake of honest pleasure. In excess he sets incontinence, by which a man, in his passions and desires, and especially in his desire for food and sex, goes beyond the measure contrary to the dictate of right reason. Therefore, since both the definition and the extremes agree with Aristotle's own testimony, they seem to be one and the same. But that they are not the same, four reasons prove: (1) Continence is not a virtue, at least not a perfect one, but rather a good disposition which moderates the passions according to right reason, whereas Temperance is a virtue. On this matter see more in Keckermann, p. 308, Systema Ethicae. (2) Because the Philosopher, in the passage cited, takes Continence in two senses: in general, for that imperfect virtue by which all wicked desires and immoderate passions are made subject to right reason; but in a special sense he takes it for the virtue which moderates anger and also the remaining desires of food, drink, sex, speech and movement. (3) The object of Continence is wider in scope, for it extends to all inward passions, whereas Temperance is concerned only with the pleasures of touch and taste. (4) In Continence there is a struggle between appetite and right reason, but in Temperance there is no such struggle.

units.la: V. An, cum Philosophus dicat, in communibus cupiditatibus homines peccare tantum in excessu, ideo liceat uni homini plus edere & bibere, ita ut Temperantia finem & modum non excedat, quam alteri? Et affirmatur. Nam usus cibi & potus moderandus est partim ex natura indigentia & necessitate, partim ex virtutis digestivæ quanquantitate, tantaque alimentorum proportione unicuique uti licet, quantam natura ad sui conservationem requirit, seu quanta ad famis & sitis naturalis expletionem sufficit, quantaque bene digeri poterit. Jam autem unus homo, vel experientia teste, majore fame & siti naturali laborat quam alius, & majori alimentorum necessitate indiget, majoreque vim alimenta cocoquendi habet quam alius. Proinde uni homini licitum est plus edere & bibere quam alteri. Hinc Milo Crotoniates plus ciborum sumere poterat, quam alii sumere licuisset, & Phil. ait lib. 2. hujus operis cap. 6. illi decem libræ panis non sufficient, cum aliis una aut duæ libræ satis essent. Hinc illi, qui duris occupantur laboribus, majore fame & siti naturaliter laborant, quam qui in otio tantum vivunt. Examinanda igitur cuiq; est sua natura, stomachi, mensura pernoscenda, ut naturæ necessarium alimentum sine culpa & noxa supeditari possit. Nam turpe est, ut ait Seneca epist. 17. ad Lucil. stomachi suiratiocinem non nosse. Nam haec sana & salubris forma vitæ est tenenda, ut tantum corpori indulgeamus, quantum bonæ valetudini sufficit. In summa ratione constitutionis corporis humani plus sanguineis edere licet, quia propter majorem caloris naturalis vim plus digerere possunt, quam aliis: tum etiam ratione climatum. Hinc Septentrionalibus plus edere licet, quam Australibus, quia in his propter vicinitatem Solis calor naturalis est imbecillior & remissior, in illis vero propter distantiam Solis & antiperistasin frigoris fortior & robustior.
units.tr: V. Since the Philosopher says that men sin in common desires only through excess, is it therefore lawful for one man to eat and drink more than another, so that his Temperance does not exceed the proper end and measure? It is affirmed. For the use of food and drink is to be moderated partly by a person's nature, need and necessity, and partly by the quantity of his digestive power. Each person may use as much nourishment as nature requires for its preservation, that is, as much as suffices to satisfy natural hunger and thirst, and as much as he can digest well. Now one man, as experience bears witness, suffers from greater natural hunger and thirst than another, needs a greater quantity of food, and has a greater power to digest food than another. Therefore it is lawful for one man to eat and drink more than another. Hence Milo of Croton could take more food than others would be allowed, and the Philosopher says in book 2, chapter 6 of this work, that ten pounds of bread would not be enough for him, when one or two pounds would suffice for others. Hence those who are occupied with hard labour naturally suffer greater hunger and thirst than those who live only in idleness. Each man must therefore examine his own nature and learn the measure of his stomach, so that the food necessary to nature may be supplied without fault or harm. For, as Seneca says in Letter 17 to Lucilius, it is shameful not to know the capacity of one's stomach. This healthy and wholesome way of life must be kept, so that we indulge the body only as much as good health requires. In summary, given the constitution of the human body, those of a sanguine temperament may eat more, because on account of the greater strength of natural heat they can digest more than others. The same holds by reason of climates: people of the north may eat more than people of the south, because in the south, owing to the proximity of the sun, the natural heat is weaker and more relaxed, whereas in the north, owing to the sun's distance and the antiperistasis of cold, it is stronger and more vigorous.

units.la: VI. & ult. An, cum Temperantia, qua Veneri non minus
units.tr: VI. and last. Whether, since Temperance, which moderates lust no less than gluttony, the state in a well-ordered commonwealth should tolerate brothels?

units.la: nus, quam gula moderatur constet in Republ. bene constituta lupanaria tolerare? Pro affirmativa rationes hae afferuntur: 1. Quia remedium propriarum voluptatum est, ut ad communes voluptates transferantur. Unde Valerius Maximus lib. 7. c. 3. refert, patrem quendam, cum filium suum amore insano nobilis matronae correptum videret, filiumque de vita periclitari animadverteret, summis ab eo precibus contendisse, ut priusquam ad illam accederet, promisceua in lupanari Venere uteretur. Paruit filius restinctoque aliquatulum libidinis incendio vitae suae consuluit, omnemque metu patrem liberavit. Sic Diogen. Laert. lib. 6. cap. 6. de vitis Philosophorum refert, Cratem Cynicum Philosophum, cum filium suum adolescentem uxori insidias struentem vidisset, manu prehensum in lupanaria duxisse, & hic inquit: ibi patrius thorus esto, ubi citra offensionem cuiusdam cupiditatibus tuis indulgere possis. 2. Cum ex duobus malis neutrum sit eligendum, alterum tamen minus grave altero videtur, jam vero communis scortatio qualis in lupanaribus exercetur, inter omnes libidinum species majore venia digna judicatur, cum neminem injuria afficiat, qui cum meretrice miscetur, nam jure civili talis non reus habetur, neque etiam punitur aut coercetur. 3. Quia jus civile Romanorum attestante Danaeo lib. 2. Ethic. Christ. cap. 14. lupanaria non tollit, neque meretrices damnat, quas veluti usuras quoque majoris periculi vitandi gratia homines politici concedendas esse contendunt. Hinc Augustin. lib. 14. de civit. Dei, cap. 8. ex temporum suorum moribus scribit, scorta quidem a civitate terrena licita esse & permitti, adeo ut illis vim inferre lex civilis vetet, aut in earum invitarum aedes quenquam perrumpere, quemadmodum fase scribit Gellius lib. 12. Noct. Attic. cap 4. 4. Quia ut testis est Zwingerus in lib. 3. Nic. ad cap. 11. quidam ex sanctis Patribus lupanaria permiserunt, ne videlicet omnes domus incestis libidinibus polluerentur, matronae honestae aut virgines pudicae corrumperentur. Melius enim & consultius ipsis videbatur, ut una domus publice omnium libidini prostitueretur, quam ut omnes divitatis angulos homines pervagarentur. Plura vide apud Petrum Gregorium lib. 14. de Repub. cap. 1. Pro negativa parte firmiores sunt rationes: 1. Quia temperantiae adversatur; nam castitati, quae est altera species temperantiae, Veneris usum moderans legitime, directe opponitur. Proinde cum Temperantia nullo modo constare potest. 2. Non sunt facienda mala, ut inde eveniant bona, ad Rom. 3. v. 8. 3. Quia legi divinae contrariatur, nam Exod. 20. verf. 15. dicitur, Non moechaberis, quo praecepto expresse prohibetur omnis fornicationis genus & 1. ad Corinth. 6. verf. 18. dicit Apostolis, qui fornicatur, in corpus suum peccat. 4. Etsi jus civile Romanorum hoc permiserit, certum tamen est, verbo divino repugnare, Proverb. cap. 7. verf. 10. & cap. 8. verf. 13. & 1. ad Corinth. 6. verf. 16. ubi non minus simplex fornicatio, quam quodvis stupri genus prohibetur. 5. Imperator Theodosius Magnus, ut testis est Socrates lib. 5. cap. 18. Ecclesiast. hist. lupanaria omnia Romae subluit, quia pius, inquit, Imperator legerat Deuteron. 23. verf. 17. Ne sit meretrix de filiabus Israelis. 6. Patribus si qui forte fuerint, qui lupanaria naria tolleranda duxerint, aliorū Patrum aurorita- te facile opponimus, instar omnium unus erit Aug. qui lib. de adulterio & conjugio omne consortium & omnem concubinatum cum meretrice damnat. Et in quaest. ad Deuter. ad cap. 23. inquit, meretrices esse, & ad meretrices accedere lege divina expresse est prohibitum. Et Salvianus Episcop. lib. 7. dicit Romanorum leges, quae lupanaria permiserunt, deteriores longius fuisse institutis Gothorum & Vandalorum. Illi enim, inquit, omnem meretricum contactum prorsus abhorrent, & si quae forte fuerint in urbibus a se captis inventae ad maritalem thorum transire cogunt. Plura de Temperantia, qui volet legere, consulat Platonem in Charmide, Ambrosium lib. 1. officior. cap. 43. Clementem Alexandrinum lib. 2. stromatum per tot. Isidorum lib. 2 etym. Senecam lib. de quatuor virtutibus, D. Thomam in 2.2. quaest. 141.
units.tr: Whether, since Temperance, which moderates lust no less than gluttony, the state in a well-ordered commonwealth should tolerate brothels? The following reasons are offered for the affirmative. (1) Because the remedy for one's own pleasures is to be turned toward common pleasures. Hence Valerius Maximus, book 7, chapter 3, reports that a certain father, seeing his son seized by an insane love for a noble matron, and perceiving that the son's life was in danger, earnestly begged him to make use of a common prostitute in a brothel before he approached her. The son obeyed, and, with the fire of his lust somewhat quenched, he looked after his life and freed his father from fear. So too Diogenes Laertius, book 6, chapter 6, On the Lives of the Philosophers, reports that Crates the Cynic philosopher, seeing his young son plotting against his wife, took him by the hand and led him to a brothel, and said: "Let there be your marriage bed where you may indulge your desires without offence to anyone." (2) Since neither of two evils should be chosen, yet one seems less grave than the other, the common fornication practised in brothels is judged, among all kinds of lust, deserving of greater leniency, since it wrongs no one who consorts with a prostitute; for under civil law such a man is not regarded as guilty, nor is he punished or restrained. (3) Because Roman civil law, as Daneau attests in book 2 of his Christian Ethics, chapter 14, does not abolish brothels nor condemn prostitutes, and political men contend that these, like usury, are to be permitted in order to avoid a greater danger. Hence Augustine, in book 14 of The City of God, chapter 8, writes from the customs of his own times that prostitutes are indeed allowed and tolerated by the earthly state, to such an extent that civil law forbids anyone to use force against them, or to break into the houses of unwilling women, as Gellius reports in book 12 of his Attic Nights, chapter 4. (4) Because, as Zwinger testifies on book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, on chapter 11, certain of the holy Fathers allowed brothels, so that, namely, not all houses would be polluted by incestuous lusts and honourable matrons or chaste virgins would not be corrupted. For it seemed to them better and more prudent that one house be publicly given over to the lust of all, than that men wander through every corner of the city. See more in Peter Gregory, book 14 of On the Commonwealth, chapter 1. For the negative side the reasons are firmer: (1) Because it is opposed to temperance; for it stands directly against chastity, which is another species of temperance and which lawfully moderates the use of sex. Therefore Temperance cannot in any way exist alongside it. (2) Evil is not to be done that good may come of it, Romans 3:8. (3) Because it is contrary to the divine law, for Exodus 20:15 says, "You shall not commit adultery," by which precept every kind of fornication is expressly forbidden; and 1 Corinthians 6:18 tells us, "He who commits fornication sins against his own body." (4) Even if Roman civil law has permitted this, it is nevertheless certain that it is contrary to the divine word, Proverbs 7:10, 8:13, and 1 Corinthians 6:16, where simple fornication is forbidden no less than any kind of illicit lust. (5) The emperor Theodosius the Great, as Socrates attests in book 5, chapter 18 of the Ecclesiastical History, closed all the brothels at Rome, because, as the pious emperor had read in Deuteronomy 23:17, "There shall be no harlot of the daughters of Israel." (6) If there are any Fathers who thought that brothels should be tolerated, we easily set against them the authority of other Fathers; the chief of all is Augustine, who in his book On Adultery and Marriage condemns all association and all concubinage with a prostitute. And in Questions on Deuteronomy, on chapter 23, he says that harlots exist, and that to approach harlots is expressly forbidden by divine law. And Salvian, bishop, in book 7 says that the laws of the Romans, which permitted brothels, were far worse than the institutions of the Goths and Vandals. For those peoples, he says, utterly abhor all contact with harlots, and if any are found in the cities they have captured, they compel them to pass into lawful marriage. Whoever wishes to read more on Temperance may consult Plato in the Charmides, Ambrose, book 1 of On the Duties, chapter 43, Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the Stromata throughout, Isidore, book 2 of the Etymologies, Seneca's book On the Four Virtues, and Thomas Aquinas, in 2.2, question 141.

units.la: LIBER QVARTUS.
units.tr: BOOK FOUR.

units.la: UPRA egit Philosophus de iis Virtutibus, quae affectus corporis regunt, seu quae in homine tuendo & moderando sunt occupatae, hic agit de iis virtutibus, quae animum quidem gubernant, seu quarum eminentia in bonis aut malis tantum externis versatur. Dividitur hic liber ex D. Thoma in duas partes: in quarum priori agitur de variis virtutibus, in secunda de duobus affectibus Indignatione scili. scilicet & Verecundia cum ipsis virtutibus magnam affinitatem habentibus. Pars prior, quae de virtutibus agit, est longior, & se extendit ad caput decimumquintum & ultimum, subdivisurque in quatuor tractatus. In primo agitur de iis virtutibus, quae versantur circa voluptates seu sumtus modicos aut magnos, ut sunt Liberalitas & Magnificentia. In secundo agit de virtutibus, quae versantur circa honores meliores aut ingentes, ut sunt Magnanimitas & virtus quaedam Graecis proprie no nominata, Latinis dicitur Modestia; & hae 4. virtutes versantur circa bona externa, quae Cic. & alii munera fortunae vocant, propterea quod homini extrinsecus obveniant, & casu quodam fortunae accidere videantur. In tertio tractatu agit de Lenitate seu Mansuetudine, quae in malis externis cernitur, & quib. adiram facile excitamur. In quarto agit de iis virtutibus, quae ad communem conversationem, congressum puta & colloquium spectant, ut sunt Amicitia, Veritas, Urbanitas. Primi tractatus duo rursus sunt membra. In priori agitur de Liberalitate, in posteriori de Magnificentia.
units.tr: Above, the Philosopher treated of those virtues which govern the affections of the body, or which are occupied in preserving and moderating the human being. Here he treats of those virtues which indeed govern the mind, or whose excellence is concerned only with external goods. This book is divided, following St. Thomas, into two parts. In the first part, various virtues are discussed; in the second, two affections, namely Indignation and Shamefastness, which have great affinity with the virtues themselves. The first part, which treats of the virtues, is the longer, and extends to the fifteenth and last chapter; it is subdivided into four treatises. In the first, the virtues are treated which concern pleasures or moderate and great expenses, such as Liberality and Magnificence. In the second, he treats of the virtues which concern greater or grand honours, such as Magnanimity and a certain virtue which the Greeks have no proper name for and which the Latins call Modesty; these four virtues concern external goods, which Cicero and others call gifts of fortune, because they come to a man from outside and seem to befall him by some chance of fortune. In the third treatise he treats of Gentleness or Meekness, which is seen in external evils, and by which we are easily provoked to anger. In the fourth he treats of those virtues which pertain to common conversation, that is, to association and conversation, such as Friendship, Truthfulness, and Wittiness. The first treatise has two parts again: in the first is discussed Liberality, in the second Magnificence.

units.la: De Liberalitate agit Philosophus tribus primis capitibus, & quidem accuratissime de ea disputat, sicut & Cic. lib. 2. offic. propter duas causas: 1. Quod ejus usus in vita communi sit varius & multiplex; 2. Quia in iis rebus, quibus modum praescribit Liberalitas, plerunque versantur mortales.
units.tr: The Philosopher treats of Liberality in the first three chapters, and he disputes about it most carefully, just as Cicero also does in the second book of De Officiis, for two reasons: (1) because its use in common life is varied and manifold; (2) because mortals for the most part are occupied with those things in which Liberality prescribes a measure.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: PRimi capitis partes sunt duae: In prima materiam circa quam versatur Liberalitas exquirit: In secunda actiones Liberalitatis & vitiorum illi oppositorum docet. In prima igitur de materia seu objecto agit, (quo cognito natura & definitio Liberalitatis facile cognoscitur) & ait versari περὶ τὰ χρήματα, id est, circa pecunias: huius rei ratio hæc reddi potest, quia in pecuniis recte & cum laude liberalis tantum le gerit: nō enim laudatur, quod fortiter in bello egerit, nec quod temperanter vixerit, aut etiam in judiciis & pactis contrahendis justum se præbuerit, sed quod in pecuniis liberaliter se gesserit. Quæ ratio, ut melius intelligatur, repetendum est ex superioribus, nempe ex cap. 1. lib. 3. hujus operis virtutes ipsas ex factis ipsis dijudicari & cognosci. Unde ex quibusdam factis laus sequitur, ea pro objecto virtutis statuenda sunt. Et hanc proprie esse notam, qua cujusque virtutis objectum facile inveniri poterit, refert Scholiastes Græcus Eustathius, si nempe ad laudem, quæ ex factis sequitur, attendamus.
units.tr: The first chapter has two parts. In the first part he investigates the matter with which Liberality is concerned; in the second he teaches the actions of Liberality and of the vices opposed to it. In the first part, then, he treats of the matter or object (and once this is known, the nature and definition of Liberality are easily grasped). He says that it is concerned with τὰ χρήματα [peri ta chrēmata], that is, with money. The reason for this can be given thus: a person is rightly and commendably called liberal only in dealing with money. For a man is not praised for fighting bravely in war, nor for living temperately, nor for showing himself just in judgments or in making contracts, but for behaving liberally with money. To understand this reason better, we must recall what was said earlier, in chapter 1 of the third book of this work: the virtues themselves are judged and recognised from the deeds themselves. Hence, where praise follows from certain deeds, those deeds must be set down as the object of the virtue. The Greek scholiast Eustathius reports that this is properly the mark by which the object of each virtue can easily be found, namely if we attend to the praise that follows from the deeds.

units.la: Postea explicat, quid nomine χρημάτων intelligat, & ait denotare res omnes, quarum est aliquis in tota vita communi usus, seu æstimationem rerum. Unde & Jurisconsulti pecuniæ nomen sumunt non tantum pro nummis, sed pro omni eo, quod in supellectili habetur, ut agros, pecudibus, sylvis, &c. l. 4. l. 22. l. 222. & 225. ff. de verb. signif. Plura vide apud D. Keckermann. pag. 259. Inventa jam materia Liberalitatis, interim quaedam de extremis ejus nempe Prodigalitate & Avaritia, & ait circa unam eandemque materiam versari, propterea quod medium & extrema tanquam contraria circa idem versentur objectum, sed hæc ut recta præscribit ratio, illa vero magis & minus, quam recta ratio praescribit. In secunda parte capitis agit de operationibus liberalitatis, in quibus modus & usus materiae circa quam versatur Liberalitas, perspicue demonstratur. Etusum ait consistere tum in dando, tum in accipiendo, magis tamen in dando. nam ut ait Apostolus Paulus Act. 20. verf. 35. meminisse oportet verborum Jesu, quod ipse dixerit, beatius est dare, quam accipere: id quod Philosophus noster confirmat, octo rationibus. 1. est: Quia verus τῶν χρημάτων, seu pecuniarum usus in dando non in accipiendo consistit: nam accipere est custodire, custodire vero ad possessionem divitiarum potius spectat, quam rectum earum usum. 2. Quia virtutis magis est proprium benefacere quam pati, hoc enim agit virtus ut omnibus aliis benefaciat, nemini noceat, quod etiam infra lib. 8. cap. 13. iterat Philosophus: atqui dando non accipiendo aliquis aliis benefacere potest: Proinde dare magis, quam accipere liberalitatis est proprium. 3. Quia virtutis etiam proprium est honestè potius agere, quam turpiter non agere, magis enim laudatur, qui honestè quid egerit, quam qui a Fortitudine se abstinet: nam ut praeclare ait Cicero 2. offic. non satis est neminem injuria afficere, sed oportet omnes juvare mortales studio, opera, facultatibus. 4. Quia beneficio afficientibus seu danti bus gratiae agi solent, non vero accipientibus. 5. Magis etiam laudari solet is, qui aliquid donat, quam qui accipit, nam qui donat, beneficium impertit aliis hominibus, qui accipit, beneficium abstrahit. 6. Quia cum virtus, ut ex cap. 3. lib. 2. hujus operis patet, circa difficilius cilius versetur: difficilius est sua dare, quam aliena non accipere: non enim tam facile quis, quod suum est, alii is dat, quā ab alienis rebus fe abstinet. 7. Quia liberales vulgò felices habentur, qui non accipiunt aliena, justi tantum non felices, qui vero accipiunt injusti habentur. 8. & ultimò: Quia ex omnibus virtutibus liberalitas maxime laudatur: nam justi propter vigorem juris, quem exercent plerunque sunt molesti: prudentes, quod alios prudentia sua circumvenire videantur, pro callidis habentur: temperantes vero quod vitae austeritatem impulsent, odio haberi solent; soli omnium liberales gratissimi habentur, nam ut ait Cicero lib. 2. offic. Vir liberalis est commune omnium perfugium.
units.tr: Next he explains what he means by the word χρημάτων [chrēmatōn], and says that it denotes all those things of which there is some use in the whole of common life, or the valuation of things. Hence the jurists also take the word pecunia not only for coins but for everything that is held as household goods, such as fields, cattle, woods, and so on (Dig. 50.16, laws 4, 22, 222 and 225, De verborum significatione). More on this may be seen in D. Keckermann, p. 259. Having found the matter of Liberality, he says something in the meantime about its extremes, namely Prodigality and Avarice: he says that they are concerned with one and the same matter, because the mean and the extremes, as contraries, are concerned with the same object. But the mean is prescribed by right reason, whereas the extremes go beyond or fall short of what right reason prescribes. In the second part of the chapter he treats of the operations of liberality, in which the measure and use of the matter with which Liberality is concerned is clearly shown. He says that its use consists both in giving and in receiving, but more in giving. For, as the Apostle Paul says in Acts 20:35, we ought to remember the words of Jesus, who said: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Our Philosopher confirms this by eight reasons. (1) The true use of riches or money lies in giving, not in receiving; for to receive is to keep, and keeping looks rather to the possession of wealth than to its right use. (2) It is more proper to virtue to do good than to suffer, for virtue aims to do good to all and harm no one, which the Philosopher also repeats below, in book 8, chapter 13. But by giving, and not by receiving, one can do good to others; therefore to give rather than to receive is proper to liberality. (3) It is also proper to virtue to act honourably rather than to fail to act basely, for a man who has done something honourable is praised more than one who abstains from what is brave. As Cicero says excellently in De officiis 2: it is not enough to injure no one; one must help all mortals by zeal, labour and resources. (4) Thanks are usually rendered to those who confer benefits, that is, to givers, and not to recipients. (5) He who gives is also usually praised more than he who receives, for the giver bestows a benefit on others, while the recipient takes one away. (6) Since virtue, as is clear from chapter 3 of book 2 of this work, is concerned with what is more difficult, it is more difficult to give away what is one's own than not to take what belongs to others; for it is not so easy to give one's own property to another as to abstain from the goods of others. (7) Liberal people are commonly considered fortunate, while those who do not take what belongs to others are considered just, not fortunate; but those who take what belongs to others are considered unjust. (8) And lastly: of all the virtues, liberality is most praised. For the just, because of the severity of the law they exercise, are usually troublesome; the prudent, since they seem to outwit others by their prudence, are held to be cunning; the temperate, because they impose the austerity of life, are usually held in hatred; only the liberal are considered the most welcome of all. For, as Cicero says in De officiis 2, the liberal man is the common refuge of all.

units.la: Axiomata.
units.tr: Axioms.

units.la: 1. Liberalitas est virtus, quae versatur circa pecunias.
units.tr: 1. Liberality is a virtue which is concerned with money.

units.la: 2. Χρήματα seu pecunia sunt omnia ea, quorum astimationem nummus mensurat.
units.tr: 2. Chrēmata [Χρήματα], or money, are all those things whose value is measured by coin.

units.la: 3. Liberalitatis usus tum in dando, tum in accipiendo consistit.
units.tr: 3. The use of liberality consists both in giving and in receiving.

units.la: 4. Laus viri Liberalis in dando, non in accipiendo cernitur.
units.tr: 4. The praise of the liberal man is seen in giving, not in receiving.

units.la: 5. Prodigalitas & Avaritia sunt excessus & defectus circa pecunias.
units.tr: 5. Prodigality and avarice are excess and deficiency concerning money.

units.la: 6. Etsi prodigus multa scatet vitiis, proprie tamen is dicitur, qui facultates suas incaute dilapidat.
units.tr: 6. Although the prodigal man abounds in many vices, he is properly so called who carelessly squanders his resources.

units.la: 7. Prodigus & se & opes suas male perdit, profusione sua.
units.tr: 7. The prodigal man badly ruins both himself and his wealth by his extravagance.

units.la: 8. Quorum est aliquis in hac vita communi usus & bene & male uti licet.
units.tr: 8. Of those things which are in common use in this life, one may use them both well and badly.

units.la: 9. Virtutis est magis proprium bene agere quam pati.
units.tr: 9. It is more proper to virtue to act well than to suffer.

units.la: 10. Difficilius est sua dare, quam aliena non accipere.
units.tr: 10. It is more difficult to give away one's own things than not to accept what belongs to others.

units.la: 11. Magis etiam convenit virtuti honestè agere, quam turpiter non agere.
units.tr: 11. It is more fitting for virtue to act honourably than not to act basely.

units.la: 12. Qui beneficium accipiunt, & non rependunt & injusti & ingrati ab omnibus habentur.
units.tr: 12. Those who receive a benefit and do not repay it are regarded by all as unjust and ungrateful.

units.la: Breviter In Liberalitate consideranda sunt ista quinque. I. Natura, quae in vero divitiarum usu moderando consistit. II. Objectum, quod est duplex, internum concupiscentia divitiarum, cui liberalitas ex praescripto rectae rationis moderatur: Externum pecuniae, seu omnia ea, quae nummo mensurantur. III. Officium seu munus quod est duplex, commune quod in dando & accipiendo concernitur, & proprium quod in dando observare jubet varias circumstantias, quae possunt reduci ad sex. 1. Ut mens sit jocunda, quae laetitiam in dando praeferat. 2. Ut frons sit grata, quae animi hilaritatem & promtitudinem testetur. 3. Ut res quae datur sit propria non aliena: nam alienum dare summa est injustitia. 4. Ut justa sit proportio & secundum facultates quisque demus. 5. Cura sit honesta, ut honestatem in omni actione liberalitatis nobis proponamus. 6 Demum ut justa sit causa, quae nos ad largiendum impellat. IV. Consideratur in liberalitate extrema, prodigalitas nempe & Avaritia, de quibus vide Keckerm. pag.263.& 267. V. Consideratur usus, qui est duplex unus publicus conservatio nempe totius societatis, alius privatus ex quo emanat laus, bona fama, & dilectio viri liberalis. Dicta vero est liberalitas à libero, vel quod homine libero sit digna, vel quod vir liberalis alios beneficentia sua à necessitate liberet. Definitur demum virtus mediocritatem servans in dandis & accipiendis pecuniis modicis. In qua definitione objectum usus & differentia liberalitatis à magnificentia continentur.
units.tr: Briefly, five things are to be considered in liberality: I. Its nature, which consists in the moderate and true use of riches. II. Its object, which is twofold: the internal, the desire for riches, which liberality moderates according to the rule of right reason; and the external, money, or all those things which are measured by coin. III. Its duty or function, which is twofold: the common, which concerns giving and receiving, and the proper, which in giving requires attention to various circumstances, reducible to six: (1) that the mind be cheerful, showing joy in giving; (2) that the countenance be kind, attesting the cheerfulness and readiness of the mind; (3) that the thing given be one's own and not another's, for to give what is another's is the height of injustice; (4) that there be a just proportion, so that each gives according to his means; (5) that care be taken for what is honourable, so that we set before ourselves honour in every action of liberality; (6) finally, that there be a just cause which impels us to bestow. IV. In liberality one considers the extremes, namely prodigality and avarice, on which see Keckerm. pp. 263 and 267. V. Its use is considered, which is twofold: one public, namely the preservation of the whole society; the other private, from which comes praise, good repute and the affection of the liberal man. Liberality is so called from liber (free), either because it is worthy of a free man, or because the liberal man frees others from want by his beneficence. Lastly, virtue is defined as keeping the mean in giving and receiving modest sums of money. In this definition are contained the object, the use, and the difference of liberality from magnificence.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An rectè assignarit Philosophus pecunias pro objecto liberalitatis, cum apud varias gentes nullus sit pecuniæ usus, & tamen maximus est apud illas liberalitatis usus. Nam liberalitatem in dando & accipiendo seu in nummis commutandis exercent, verbi gratia: Varia gentes in Peruana Regione & America, summam ergo Hispanos & alios illuc navigantes liberalitatem exercent, & tamen omnē pecuniæ usum ignorant. Proinde Philosophus non rectè videtur assignasse objectum liberalitatis pecunias? Resp. Nomen pecuniæ duobus modis sumi: 1. Strictè pro signato numismate, & quia nullus est in hoc sensu pecuniæ usus apud varias gentes, ideo nec objectum liberalitatis esse potest. 2. Latè pro omni eo, quod nummus mensurat vel mensurare potest, ut hic in textu sumitur à Philosopho, & sic est ad æquatum liberalitatis objectum. Instantia. At pecunia non est adæquatum objectum: nam illud dicitur objectum adæquatum, quod toti naturæ rei, cujus est objectum, competit. At pecunia non toti liberalitatis naturæ competit, nam et liberalitas versatur circa concupiscentiā divitiarū, cui tanquā interno hominis affectui secundum rectam rationē moderatur? Resp. Objectum est duplex, internum concupiscentia divitiarum, externum pecuniæ quod hīc pro objecto adæquato ponit Philosophus tribus de causis. 1. Quia ex factis non ex causis virtutes judicari solent. 2. Quia hoc objectum maximè incurrit in sensus hominum. §. Quia circa objectum externum bene versatur, circa internum bene se gerit.
units.tr: I. Question: Did the Philosopher rightly assign money as the object of liberality, since among various peoples there is no use of money at all, and yet among them the practice of liberality is very great? For they exercise liberality in giving and receiving, or in exchanging coins. For example, the various peoples of Peru and America, and the Spaniards and others who sail there, practise the greatest liberality, and yet they are wholly ignorant of any use of money. Therefore the Philosopher does not seem to have rightly assigned money as the object of liberality? Answer: The name 'money' is taken in two ways. (1) Strictly, for the stamped coin. Since in this sense there is no use of money among these peoples, it cannot be the object of liberality. (2) Broadly, for everything that a coin measures or can measure, as the Philosopher takes it here in the text; and in this sense it is the adequate object of liberality. Objection: But money is not the adequate object. For that is called the adequate object which belongs to the whole nature of the thing of which it is the object. But money does not belong to the whole nature of liberality, since liberality is also concerned with the desire for riches, which it moderates according to right reason as an inward affection of the person? Answer: The object is twofold: internal, the desire for riches; and external, money. The Philosopher posits the external object as the adequate one for three reasons: (1) because virtues are judged by deeds, not by their causes; (2) because this object falls most directly under the senses of men; (3) because one deals well with the external object when one conducts oneself well with regard to the internal.

units.la: 11. An usus liberalitatis in dando & accipiendo consi-stat, cum dare & accipere differant non modò specie, sed & genere: proinde non possunt esse actus unius liberalitatis? Respond. Verùm est differre inter se, si per se consideretur, at verò si considerentur ratione subjecti, posse vere dici convenientes actus unius ejusdemq; subjecti. Nam etsi usus liberalitatis in his duobus consistat, aliter tamen consideratur Liberalitas in dando, aliter in accipiendo.
units.tr: II. Question: Does the use of liberality consist in giving and receiving, since giving and receiving differ not only in species but also in genus, and so cannot be acts of one and the same liberality? Answer: It is true that they differ from each other if they are considered in themselves. But if they are considered in relation to the subject, they can truly be called acts of one and the same subject that agree with each other. For although the use of liberality consists in these two, liberality is considered one way in giving and another way in receiving.

units.la: III. An usus liberalitatis magis consistat, in dando quàm accipiendo, quod vult Philosophus, cum nulla virtus naturæ vi ac propensioni repugnet, sed potius eam absolvat & perficiat: nam si virtus natura ipsi repugnaret, esset contra naturam, & tamen cap. 1. lib. 2. hujus operis dictum est, virtutem etsi non sit à natura, tamen non esse contra naturam, sed praeter naturam tantum. At dare potius quàm accipere natura vi ac propensioni repugnat, cum natura sedula rerum omnium conservatrix velit, ut potius nobis ipsis bene cupiamus, quàm aliis. Hoc autem fit accipiendo, non dando. Malè ergo dixit Philosophus liberalitatis usum in dando magis, quàm in accipiendo consistere? Resp. Bona esse duplicia interna & externa, interna ut sunt scientiæ, virtutes, artes & ex his plus nobis appetere licet, quam aliis dare, propterea quod natura, quæ ut rerum omnium conservationem intendit, sic etiam perfectionem, hisce verò internis bonis animus perficitur & ad veram suam naturam reducitur. Externa bona sunt rursus duplicia, vel enim sunt necessaria vitæ & familiaris liæ alendæ respectu & in his natura vult, ut melius nobis prospiciamus quam aliis: vel sunt superflua, quæ absque vitæ & conditionis detrimento aliis cedi possunt, & in his plura licet dare aliis, quam sibi retinere. Sic enim liberalitas naturæ non repugnat, sed ipsam naturæ benignitatem imitatur, & in his bonis superfluus intelligi debet Philosophus cumliberalitatem in dando maxime cōsistere dicit.
units.tr: III. Question: Does the use of liberality consist more in giving than in receiving, as the Philosopher holds, since no virtue opposes the force and propensity of nature, but rather completes and perfects it? For if virtue opposed nature, it would be against nature; yet in chapter 1 of the second book of this work it was said that virtue, although it is not from nature, is nonetheless not against nature, but only beyond nature. Now giving rather than receiving opposes the force and propensity of nature, since nature, the diligent conserver of all things, wishes us rather to desire good for ourselves than for others. But this comes about by receiving, not by giving. Did the Philosopher therefore speak wrongly in saying that the use of liberality consists more in giving than in receiving? Answer: Goods are of two kinds, internal and external. Internal goods are such things as knowledge, virtues and arts, and from these we may desire more for ourselves than we give to others, because nature, which intends the conservation of all things, also intends their perfection; and the mind is perfected by these internal goods and brought back to its true nature. External goods are again of two kinds. Some are necessary for sustaining life and the household, and in respect of these nature wills that we provide better for ourselves than for others. Others are superfluous, and can be yielded to others without harm to life or station, and in these it is lawful to give to others more than we keep for ourselves. For in this way liberality does not oppose nature, but imitates nature's own goodness; and the Philosopher, when he says that liberality consists chiefly in giving, must be understood to mean these superfluous goods.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: HOc capite secundo de conditionibus quibusdam & variis proprietatibus veræ liberalitatis agitur. Partes capitis sunt duæ. In prima conditiones istas, quas Cic. lib. 1. offic. cautiones vocat, adfert: In secunda proprietates liberalitati accommodat. In prima igitur quatuor adfert conditiones, quarum duæ priores sunt dantis, posteriores duæ sunt accipientis. I. Conditio est, ut largitio Viri Liberalis honeste fiat & honestatis gratia: & ratio redditur, quia omnium virtutum actiones honestæ sunt, & honestatem pro fine habent. Non est igitur Liberalis largitio, quæ fit aut majoris lucri aut honoris aspiquendi, aut libidinis aut voluptatis perfruendæ gratia: sed tales vel ambitiosi, vel prodigi, vel captatores, vel negotiatores, vel alio aliquo nomine insigniuntur, Liberales vero minime vocantur. II. Conditio seu cautio est, ut largitio fiat libenter absque omni molestia, & non gravatè, & ratio est, quia omnium virtutum actionum actiones jucundæ & absque omni molestia sunt, aut certè minima cum molestia conjunctæ. Unde Augustin. homil. 19. in Johan. ban. Manus non est tam munere vacua, si arca cordis fit plena bona voluntate, Et Apost. 2. Corinth. 9. verf. 7. Unusquisque benefaciat secundum propositum cordis sui, non ex dolore aut necessitate. Plura vide apud Keck. p. 260. III. Conditio, quae accipientem spectat, est, quod sicut Liberalis honestè & non gravatè largiri debet, sic etiam neque sumet aut accipiet a quo non accipere debet. Nam accipere aliquid unde non oportet, non est viri Liberalis, qui pecunias aut divitias parvi aestimat, sed avari potius, qui pecunias seipso chariores habet & qui suae unius utilitati, non omnium commoditati studet. IV. Conditio est, ut Liberalis non sit peetax seu procax, id est, ad accipiendum proclivis. Nam Liberalis, qui alios beneficiis afficere solet, non debet postulare, ut ab aliis afficiatur: atqui petax vel ad postulandum facilis est, ille non alios, sed seipsum beneficio afficere studet. In secunda parte capitis adfert proprietates quasdam Liberalitati convenientes, quantum 1. quod Liberalis in dando seu largiendo valdè excellat, adeò ut minimum sibi semper relinquat, (quod tamen de superfluis non de necessariis aut internis animi bonis intelligi debet) & ratio haec est, quia viri liberalis qua Liberalis haec est natura & indoles, ut nulla sui curam gerat, nihil se respiciat, sed totus ad largiendum & benefaciendum humano generi, ut supra cap. 1. probatum erat, propondeat: quamvis tamen ita in dando excedat, ut minus sibi relinquat, non omnibus aut quibuslibet nullo prorsus discrimine dabit, sed secundum rectam rationem, ut nempe habeat, unde aliquid semper det. Quin etiam quid, quando, & quibus dandandum fit, seu ubi honestum fuerit bene observabit. II. Proprietas est ex facultatibus judicandâ esse Liberalitatem, non in magnitudine aut multitudine donorum, sed ex animo & propensa voluntate spectari Liberalem, quod ex eo confirmatur, quia magis Liberalis habetur is, qui pauca ex re tenui dederit, quam qui multa ex magnis copiis & non pro rata expenderit: Exemplo esse potest vidua illa apud Euangelistam Lucam cap.21.verf.1. III. Proprietas est, magis esse Liberales, qui divitias à majoribus partas acceperunt, quam qui ipsi sua opera & industria pepererunt, quod etiam Plato 1. Polit. fuse docet. Et duas hujus rei rationes adfert Philosophus. Prima est, Quod tales inopiam nunquam sint experti. Nam ut illi qui nunquam bello interfuerunt, audaciores & projectores ad pericula esse solent, quam qui in quotidiano versantur belli discrimine, sic etiam, qui inopiam nunquam experti sunt ad opes suas profundendas proniores & faciliores sunt. Atque hoc argumento ostendit Philosophus 2. Rhet. cap.5. adolescentes magis esse liberales quam senes: nam hi longa experientia varias fortunæ vices didicerunt, illi per ætatem nullam adhuc experientiam habent. Secunda ratio est, quod suum cuique sit pulchrum, unicuique id maximè placet, quod suo labore pepererit, & hoc illustrat duplici exemplo: prius est ab amore parentum in liberos, quod quia pepererunt suos liberos intensissimè illos amant: alterum est ab exemplo Poëtarum, quibus sua scripta in primis placent, aliorum non item. Qua de re eleganter disputat Cic. lib.5. Tusc. quæst. & lib.14. epist. ad Attic. in variis variè epist. IV. & ult. Proprietas est, rarò fieri, ut liberales ditescant, seu hoc plerumque evenire ut liberales non sint ex ditioribus, cujus rei Aristoteles adferr quinque. 1. est, Quia Liberales ad accipiendum & acquirendum non sunt avidi: 2. Quia suis rebus conservandis non sunt intenti. 3. Ad dandum & largiendum sunt faciles & proni. 4. Bona non tam propter seipsa, quam largiendi causa cupiunt & quaerunt. 5. Nullum in divitiis congerendis studium aut operam ponunt: Nam uti alia res omnes, verbi gratia: bona valetudo, honores, eruditio, studio & opera parantur & conservantur, sic etiam divitiae.
units.tr: In this second chapter, Aristotle deals with certain conditions and various properties of true liberality. The chapter has two parts. In the first, he sets out the conditions which Cicero, in book 1 of De Officiis, calls cautions. In the second, he applies properties to liberality. In the first part, then, he gives four conditions, of which the first two belong to the giver and the last two to the recipient. I. The first condition is that the generous man's giving be done honourably and for the sake of honour. The reason given is that all the actions of the virtues are honourable and have honour as their end. So giving is not liberal when it is done for the sake of greater gain, or of winning honour, or of indulging lust or enjoying pleasure. Those who give for such reasons are called ambitious, prodigal, fortune-hunters, or traders, or are marked with some other name, but they are never called liberal. II. The second condition, or caution, is that giving be done willingly, without any grudging, and not reluctantly. The reason is that the actions of all the virtues are pleasant and free from all distress, or at least joined with very little distress. Hence Augustine, homil. 19 in John: "The hand is not so empty of gifts if the chest of the heart is full of good will." And the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 9 verse 7: "Let each one do good according to the purpose of his heart, not out of grief or necessity." See more in Keckermann, p. 260. III. The third condition, which concerns the recipient, is that just as the liberal man ought to give honourably and without reluctance, so he will neither take nor accept from anyone from whom he ought not to accept. For to receive something from where one ought not is not the mark of a liberal man, who values money and riches lightly. It is rather the mark of a covetous man, who values money more than himself and who cares for his own single advantage, not for the common good. IV. The fourth condition is that the liberal man should not be petax or procax, that is, prone to receiving. For the liberal man, who is accustomed to bestow benefits on others, ought not to ask that he himself be benefited by others. But the man who is ready to ask, or easy to demand, seeks to benefit himself rather than others. In the second part of the chapter, he sets out certain properties fitting to liberality. First, that the liberal man greatly excels in giving, so that he always keeps the least for himself. (This must be understood of superfluous goods, not of necessities or of the inner goods of the mind.) The reason is that the nature and disposition of the liberal man, as such, is that he takes no thought for himself and does not look to himself, but is wholly inclined to giving and doing good to mankind, as was proved above in chapter 1. Yet although he excels in giving so that he keeps less for himself, he will not give to all or to whomever without any distinction at all, but according to right reason, so that he always has something from which to give. Indeed, he will also observe carefully what should be given, when, and to whom, or where it is fitting to give. II. The second property is that liberality is to be judged by the faculties, not by the size or number of the gifts. The liberal man is to be judged by his spirit and his ready will. This is confirmed by the fact that he is held to be more liberal who gives a little from a modest estate than he who spends much from great wealth and not in proportion to what he has. The widow in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 21 verse 1, can serve as an example. III. The third property is that those are more liberal who have received riches inherited from their elders than those who have themselves acquired them by their own labour and industry. Plato also teaches this at length in book 1 of the Politics. The Philosopher gives two reasons for this. The first is that such men have never experienced want. For just as those who have never been in war are usually more daring and more ready to rush into dangers than those who live daily in the peril of war, so also those who have never experienced want are more inclined and more ready to squander their wealth. By this argument the Philosopher shows, in Rhetoric 2, chapter 5, that young men are more liberal than old men: the old have learned through long experience the various changes of fortune, while the young have as yet no experience through their age. The second reason is that each person's own is beautiful, and everyone is most pleased with what he has produced by his own labour. He illustrates this with a twofold example. The first is the love of parents for their children: because they have brought them forth, they love them most intensely. The other is the example of poets, who are most pleased with their own writings and not so with those of others. Cicero discusses this point elegantly in Tusculan Disputations book 5, and in the letters to Atticus, book 14, letters in various places, and last letter. IV. The last property is that it rarely happens that liberal men grow rich; that is, it generally happens that liberal men are not from the wealthier classes. Aristotle gives five reasons for this. (1) Liberal men are not eager to receive or to acquire. (2) They are not intent on preserving their possessions. (3) They are easy and ready to give and to bestow. (4) They desire and seek goods not so much for their own sake as for the sake of giving. (5) They take no zeal or effort in heaping up riches. For just as all other things, for example good health, honours, and learning, are obtained and preserved by study and effort, so too are riches.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Omnis virtutis actio honesta est & honestatem prosine habet.
units.tr: 1. Every action of virtue is honourable and has honour as its aim.

units.la: 2. Vir Liberalis quid, quibus & quando dandum sit, cum reliquis circumstantiis bene observabit, ne rationis limites egrediatur.
units.tr: 2. The liberal man will carefully observe what, to whom and when to give, together with the other circumstances, lest he go beyond the limits of reason.

units.la: 3. Omnis virtutis actio est aut jucunda, aut nullo cum dolore conjuncta.
units.tr: 3. Every action of virtue is either pleasant or not conjoined with any pain.

units.la: 4. Qui divitias honestis actionibus praeferunt non Liberales sed avari dici debent.
units.tr: 4. Those who prefer riches to honourable actions ought to be called not liberal but avaricious.

units.la: 5. Vir Liberalis res suas non negligit ut nempe aliquid aliis suppeditare possit semper habeat.
units.tr: 5. The liberal man does not neglect his own goods, so that he may always have something to supply to others.

units.la: 6. Liberalis in dando valde excellit, ita ut minimum sibi relinquat.
units.tr: 6. The liberal man excels in giving, so that he leaves very little for himself.

units.la: 7. Liberalitas ex facultatibus judicatur potius, quam ex rebus datis.
units.tr: 7. Liberality is judged by one's means rather than by the things given.

units.la: 8. Non ex multitudine aut magnitudine donorum, sed ex animo & propensione actio censetur Liberalis.
units.tr: 8. An action is judged liberal not from the number or size of the gifts, but from the spirit and disposition.

units.la: 9. Liberaliores sunt, qui divitias à maioribus partas acce-perunt, quam qui ipsi pepererunt.
units.tr: 9. Those are more liberal who received riches inherited from their elders than those who acquired them themselves.

units.la: 10. Raro evenit ut Liberalis ditescat, cum continuo sua aliis communicet.
units.tr: 10. It rarely happens that a liberal man grows rich, since he constantly shares his goods with others.

units.la: 11. Fortuna hoc vitio dari solet, quod maxime digni non sint maxime divites.
units.tr: 11. Fortune is usually given to this vice: that the most worthy are not the most wealthy.

units.la: 12. Principes & Tyranni etsi nimium expendant, cum tamen divitias affluant, non dicuntur prodigi proprie.
units.tr: 12. Princes and tyrants, although they spend too much, yet since their riches flow in abundance, are not properly called prodigal.

units.la: 13. Liberalis, si quid forte praeter decorum dederit, dolebit, sed moderate tamen & sicut debet.
units.tr: 13. If the liberal man gives something beyond what is fitting, he will grieve, but moderately and as he ought.

units.la: 14. Hoc etiam convenit Liberali, ut in vita societate sit perfacilis.
units.tr: 14. It also belongs to the liberal man to be very easy to live with in society.

units.la: 15. Vir Liberalis cum pecunias non magni aestimet injuria facile affici potest.
units.tr: 15. The liberal man, since he does not value money highly, can be easily affected by injury.

units.la: 16. Magis dolebit Liberalis si quid non dederit, quando decet, quam si quid dederit, quando non decet.
units.tr: 16. The liberal man will grieve more if he has not given when he ought, than if he has given when he ought not.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: .I Quaeritur: Quomodo dicat omnem Virtutis actionem esse jucundam, aut nulla cum molestia conjunctam, cum tamen lib. 3 cap. 11. hujus operis, hoc pro Fortitudinis proprietate assignarit, quod cum molestia & dolore omnis ejus actio conjuncta sit. Proinde centrarium sibi videtur Philosophus? Resp. Actiones Virtutis considerari duobus modis, vel respectu sui, vel finis. Respectu sui non sunt interdum jucundae, sed finis respectu sunt. Dein considerari possunt actiones virtutis vel ratione habitus, qui est in homine, vel ratione objecti externi in quod agunt. Ratione habitus (qui promptitudinem & facilitatem gignit) possunt dici omnes jucundae: Ratione objecti solius Fortitudinis actiones nes sunt cum dolore & molestia conjunctæ, & sic intelligi debet Philosophus supra loco citato.
units.tr: .I It is asked: how can he say that every action of virtue is pleasant, or is joined with no distress, when in book 3, chapter 11 of this work he has nonetheless assigned as a property of Courage that every action of it is joined with distress and pain? Does the Philosopher therefore seem to contradict himself? Answer: The actions of virtue may be considered in two ways, either with respect to themselves or with respect to their end. With respect to themselves they are not always pleasant, but with respect to their end they are. Next, the actions of virtue may be considered either in terms of the habit that is in a person, or in terms of the external object they act upon. In terms of the habit (which produces readiness and ease), all of them can be called pleasant. In terms of the object, only the actions of Courage are joined with pain and distress, and the Philosopher must be understood in this sense in the passage cited above.

units.la: II. Cur neget Philosophus dandum esse omnibus seu quibuslibet, aut ut Cic. interpretatur 2. officior. idoneos tantum, cum tamen natura Liberalitatis hoc requirat, ut omnibus benefaciamus, & nulli manus claudamus, & hoc ipse inculcat Philosophus cap. 1. huius libri, tum etiam cap. 13. lib. 8. tum etiam probari potest, à facto ipsius Aristotelis: nam ut refert Laërtius lib. 5. de vit. Philosoph. non tantum dignis & idoneis, sed etiam indignis eleemosynam dedit: unde non immerito videtur culpari à Lact. lib. 6. Instit. Christ. quod quibuslibet dandum esse prohibuerit? Resp. Non simpliciter negat omnibus dandum esse, sed tamen non promiscue quibusvis, non habita circumstantiarum ratione propter duas causas: 1. Ne vir Liberalis exhauriat fontem Liberalitatis. 2. Ne nimia profusione degeneret in prodigum aut redigatur in pauperem.
units.tr: II. Why does the Philosopher deny that one must give to all, or to whomever, or, as Cicero interprets it in De Officiis 2, only to the worthy, when the nature of Liberality nonetheless requires that we do good to all and close our hand to no one, which the Philosopher himself inculcates in chapter 1 of this book, and also in chapter 13 of book 8? It can also be proved from the practice of Aristotle himself: for, as Laertius reports in book 5 of Lives of the Philosophers, he gave alms not only to the worthy and suitable but also to the unworthy. Hence does Lactantius not seem to have rightly blamed him in Divine Institutes book 6 for forbidding that one must give to whomever? Answer: He does not simply deny that one must give to all, but not indiscriminately to whomever, without regard to circumstances, for two reasons: (1) so that the liberal man does not exhaust the source of his liberality; (2) so that by excessive lavishness he does not degenerate into a prodigal or be reduced to a pauper.

units.la: III. & ult. An verum sit magis esse Liberales eos, qui parva ex parvis copiis dant, quam qui magna ex magnis, cum tamen ratio contrarium doceat: nam qui magis & melius versatur circa objectum Liberalitatis, ille magis dicendus est Liberalis, quam qui minus. At qui multa ex magnis copiis expendit, magis & melius versatur circa objectum Liberalitatis: unde magis videtur dici Liberalis? Resp. In Liberalitate consideranda esse duo, objectum & personam dantis. Si solum objectum respiciatur, tunc procedit argumentum, at si simul objectum, cum persona dantis consideratur primo animus promptus & beneficus, secundo qualitas, ut largitio fiat secundum facultates, & sic qui pauca ex retenui donat, magis LibeLiberalis dici poterit, quam qui multa ex rebus magnis.
units.tr: III. And last. Is it true that those are more liberal who give small amounts out of small means than those who give large amounts out of large means, when reason teaches the contrary? For the one who deals more and better with the object of Liberality is to be called more liberal than the one who deals less. But the one who spends much out of large means deals more and better with the object of Liberality. Hence he seems more rightly to be called liberal? Answer: In Liberality two things must be considered, the object and the person of the giver. If only the object is regarded, then the argument holds; but if the object is considered together with the person of the giver, then, first, the mind must be ready and beneficent, and second, the quality must be such that the gift is made according to one's means. Thus the one who gives a little out of a slender estate can more fittingly be called liberal than the one who gives much out of great possessions.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: SEquitur tertium membrum huius tractatus de Liberalitate hoc capite, in quo agit de extremis Liberalitatis, de quibus etiam egerat lib. 2. huius operis, cap. 8. & lib. 1. magn. moral. cap. 24. Partes capitis sunt quatuor: In prima agit de Prodigalitate. In secunda confert prodigum cum avaro, & in utro magis peccetur, docet. In tertia agit de avaritia. In quarta demum extrema confert cum ipso medio, & utrum magis accedat aut recedat a medio, demonstrat.
units.tr: Now follows the third part of this treatise on Liberality, in this chapter, in which he treats of the extremes of liberality, which he had also discussed in book 2 of this work, chapter 8, and book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter 24. The chapter has four parts. In the first he treats of prodigality. In the second he compares the prodigal with the miser and shows in which of the two more fault is committed. In the third he treats of avarice. In the fourth he finally compares the extremes with the mean itself and shows which of them comes nearer to the mean and which departs further from it.

units.la: In prima igitur breviter agit de Prodigalitate, & ait illud esse vitium, quod Liberalitati in excessu opponitur: prodigum vero in omnibus iis peccare, in quibus Liberalis recte se gerit. Nam in dando modum excedit, in accipiendo modū deserit, omnémque verum Liberalitatis usum prorsus invertit: ideo non immmerito Græcis dicitur ἀσώτος seu non servatus aut perditus: nam ut supra cap. 2. docuerat, se & res suas prorsus perdit.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he briefly treats of prodigality and says that it is the vice opposed to liberality by excess, and that the prodigal sins in all those respects in which the liberal man acts rightly. For in giving he exceeds the measure, in receiving he falls short of it, and he entirely reverses the true use of liberality. Therefore he is not unjustly called by the Greeks asotos, that is, unsaved or lost [ἀσώτος]; for, as he had taught above, chapter 2, he utterly ruins both himself and his goods.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis confert prodigum cum avaro in duobus: 1. In effectis utriusque contrariis. Nam prodigus in dando modum excedit, in accipiendo modum deserit: in dando quidem quod temere dignis & indignis maximè det; accipiendo, quod nihil prorsus accipere curet; sed sua potius sine ullo discrimine profundar. Contra fit in avaro, in accipiendo modū excedit, nā undecunq; & quibuscunq; possit, modis semper accipit, in dando vero modū deserit, nam parum aut nihil prorsus dare solet. 2. Comparat cum dissimili: nam ut ex duobus malis alterum altero levius & minus esse solet, sic ex his extremis prodigum avaro minus peccare tribus rationibus docet: 1. est, quod prodigus fit curabilis, seu possit ad sanitatem & frugem reduci, aut, quod idem est, ad ipsam veram Liberalitatem, avarus econtra, sed deploratus & insanabilis, nec possit ad ullam veram frugem & mediocritatem reduci: nam experientia docet, multos fuisse prodigos, qui se in melius receperint, & veram liberalitatem amplexi sint, avaros vero paucos aut nullos, qui se ad liberalitatem aut largitionem revocari patiantur. Qua de re eleganter & fuse disserit Cic. pro Caelio. Hujus rationis duplex causa afferri poterit, prior est ab aetate: nam hoc vitium prodigalitatis cadit plerunque in adolescentes imperitos & petulantes, qui ubi adoleverint confirmato cum aetate judicio, vitam luxuriosam delinquere solent, cujus exemplum videre est in Polemone adolescente luxurioso, qui postea se in veram frugem receperit, ut testis est Laërt. lib. 4. in vitis Philosophorum in vita ipsius. Contra fit in avaris, nam hoc vitium plerunque cadere solet in senes, in quibus ut nulla est aetatis & judicii ratio, sic nulla etiam morum in melius mutatio, sed potius exaggeratio. 2. Ratio ducitur ab inopia, nam inopia adolescentes facultatibus exutos ad frugem revocare saepe solet, ita ut necessitate mera coacti verae virtuti incipiant studere: at in avaris nulla inopia, sed potius copiae quaeruntur, quibus ubi sibi prospexerint, non de mutando vitae genere, sed de nummis numme commorandis tantum studeant. 1. Ratio est, cur prodigus minus peccet, quam avarus, quia prodigus majore affinitatem & cognatione habet cum Liberalitate quam avarus, nam prodigus non est ad accipiendum proclivis sicut avarus, sed ad largiendum pronus est & facilis, sicut liberalis cum hoc tamen discrimine, quod liberalis cum ratione & honestatis tantum gratia largiatur, prodigus non item: 2. Ratio est, quia prodigus sua profusione multis tamen prodest, avarus autem nemini sua tenacitate, ne sibi ipsi quidem. Unde praeclare Publius Mimographus: in nullum avarus bonus, in se pessimus; & alibi, avarus, nisi cum moritur, nihil recte facit. Notandum tamen tria esse prodigorum genera: nam quidam sunt, qui ad largiendum tantum faciles sunt, quidam qui dant & accipiunt, sed sine ullo modo & discrimine, tertio quidam sunt, qui in luxuriosos degenerant, & qui ad voluptates & libidines perfruendas patrimonium & opes profundunt. Deprimi generis prodigis loquitur Phil. dum prodigum cum avaro confert: nam secundi generis prodigi partim sunt prodigi, quatenus scilicet sine discrimine dant, partim sunt avari, quatenus indiscrete accipiunt. Tertii generis sunt compositi ex diversis vitiis, veluti ex injustitia, intemperantia, illiberalitate, ideo cum avaritia, quae simplex vitium est, comparari recte non possunt. Breviter, Prodigus bifariam consideratur vel simpliciter seu qua est simplex nullis aliis vitiis depravatus, & hic avaro est melior quatuor de causis: 1. Propter faciliorem reductionem, quia facilius ad liberalitatem reduci potest idque tribus modis: in aetatis progressu. su. 2. sano & salubri consilio, ubi offectos suos rectæ rationi subjicit. 3. in gente necessi ate, quia pro virtute sæpe utitur. 11. Ca sa, quia major est similitudo & affinitas prodigi cum liberali quam avari. III. Quia sanior rem animum in judicio virtutis habet: nam in omnibus actionibus, si non veram honestatem umbram saltem honestatis præse fert. 1 V. Proper laudé & admiratione populi quam ad hæc duo sua profusione & beneficiis fac le allesceir: Secundò consideratur prodigus, ut est coposicus ex diversi generis vitiis, & hic cū avaro à Phil. non coparatur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he compares the prodigal with the miser in two respects: (1) in the contrary effects of each. For the prodigal exceeds the measure in giving and falls short of it in receiving: in giving, indeed, he gives rashly, mostly to the worthy and the unworthy alike; in receiving, he takes no care to receive anything at all, but rather squanders his own without any discrimination. The reverse happens with the miser: in receiving he exceeds the measure, for he takes always and by whatever means he can from anywhere and anyone; in giving he falls short of it, for he is accustomed to give little or nothing at all. (2) He compares unlike things: for, as of two evils one is usually lighter and less than the other, so he teaches that the prodigal sins less than the miser, for three reasons: (1) The prodigal can be cured, that is, he can be brought back to soundness and thrift, or, what is the same, to true liberality itself; the miser, on the contrary, is hopeless and incurable and cannot be brought back to any true thrift or moderation. For experience shows that many have been prodigal and have reformed themselves and embraced true liberality, but few or none of the misers allow themselves to be called back to liberality or generosity. On this matter Cicero argues elegantly and at length in Pro Caelio. This reason can be explained by a twofold cause. The first is age: for the vice of prodigality usually falls upon young men who are inexperienced and wanton, and when they have grown up and their judgment has matured with age, they usually abandon a luxurious life. An example of this is seen in the young and dissolute Polemo, who afterwards reformed himself to true thrift, as Laertius attests in book 4 of the Lives of the Philosophers, in his life. The reverse happens with misers, for this vice usually falls upon the old, in whom, as there is no consideration of age and judgment, so there is also no change of character for the better, but rather an increase of it. (2) The reason is drawn from want, for want often recalls young men, stripped of their means, to thrift, so that, compelled by sheer necessity, they begin to pursue true virtue. But in misers there is no want, but rather they seek riches, and once they have provided for themselves, they are concerned not to change their way of life but only to heap up money upon money. (2) The reason why the prodigal sins less than the miser is that the prodigal has a greater affinity and kinship with liberality than the miser does. For the prodigal is not prone to receiving as the miser is, but inclined and ready to give, as the liberal man is; yet with this difference, that the liberal man gives with reason and only for the sake of honour, while the prodigal does not. (3) The reason is that the prodigal, by his lavishness, still benefits many, whereas the miser, by his tightfistedness, benefits no one, not even himself. Whence the Publilius Mimographer says admirably: The miser is good to no one, and worst to himself; and elsewhere: The miser does nothing rightly unless when he dies. It must be noted, however, that there are three kinds of prodigals.
