For some are only ready to give; some give and receive, but without any measure or discrimination; and thirdly, some degenerate into luxurious men and squander their patrimony and wealth on enjoying pleasures and lusts. The Philosopher speaks of the first kind of prodigal when he compares the prodigal with the miser: for the prodigals of the second kind are partly prodigal, insofar as they give without discrimination, and partly miserly, insofar as they receive indiscriminately. Those of the third kind are compounded of various vices, such as injustice, intemperance and illiberality, and therefore cannot rightly be compared with avarice, which is a simple vice. In brief, the prodigal is considered in two ways: either simply, insofar as he is a simple man corrupted by no other vices, and in this respect he is better than the miser for four reasons: (1) because he can more easily be brought back, and this can happen in three ways: with the progress of age; by a sound and wholesome counsel, when he subjects his appetites to right reason; and by stern necessity, for he often uses this for virtue. (2) Because the likeness and affinity of the prodigal with the liberal man is greater than that of the miser. (3) Because he has a more sound mind and a judgment inclined to virtue: for in all his actions, if he does not bear the true honour, he at least bears the shadow of honour. (4) Because by his lavishness and benefactions he attracts the praise and admiration of the people, which are the two things he seeks. Secondly, the prodigal is considered as compounded of different kinds of vices, and in this respect the Philosopher does not compare him with the miser.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis agit de Avaritia Philosophus, de qua duo adfert: 1 est, avaritiam esse malum incurabile, nunquam posse revocari ad veram Liberalitatem, cujus rei duas adfert causas, quarum priorem sumit ab ætate: Nam hoc vitium plerunque cadit in senes, qui, ut testatur ipse lib.2. Rhet. cap.5. sunt avari & intractabiles, norunt enim senes cum longo usu & experientia didicerint, quid valeat nummus, quanti fiat pecunia, & quam non temere sit expendenda. 2. Causa, quia naturæ humanæ mag s est cognata avaritia quam prodigalitas, id quod probat à consuetudine vulgari: Nam plures pecuniæ studiosos quam ad largiendum faciles reperiri licet, semper què instinctu quodam naturalis providentiæ inculcant homines illud Bianus: Spera tanquam mortalis, sed parce tanquam immortalis. Secundum, quod adfert de Avaritia, est de generibus avarorum, & duo adfert genera: 1. est eorum, qui in dando peccant, nihil prorsus dant, & ideo vocantur parci, quod semper parcant tenaces, quod firmiter omnia teneant,
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter the Philosopher treats of avarice, and of it he brings forward two points. (1) That avarice is an incurable evil, which can never be brought back to true liberality. He gives two causes for this, the first of which he takes from age: for this vice usually falls upon the old, who, as he himself testifies in book 2 of the Rhetoric, chapter 5, are miserly and intractable; for old men, having learned by long use and experience what money is worth, how much it is valued, and how it is not to be spent rashly. (2) The second cause is that avarice is more akin to human nature than prodigality, which common custom proves: for more men are found who are eager for money than who are ready to give, and by a certain instinct of natural providence men always impress upon themselves that saying of Bias: Hope as one who is mortal, but spare as one who is immortal. The second point that he brings forward about avarice concerns the kinds of misers, and he gives two kinds: (1) of those who sin in giving: they give nothing at all, and are therefore called sparing, because they are always sparing and tenacious, because they hold everything fast.

units.la: Cc ollares qualem Plautus describit Euclionem cum sua olla, de quo sic ait, famem si utendum roges, nunquam dabit. Talis etiam fuit Hermocrates quidam, qui, teste Lucilio, tanto pecuniarum suarum amore tenebatur, ut morientem se scripserit haeredem bonorum suorum. Meminit etiam Athenaeus lib. 4. cap. 18. cujusdam insigniter avari, qui, ne nummos suos aliis relinqueret, multos aureos deglutivit, ut eos secum auferret, & reliquos in sago consuit, imperavitque, ut eo indutus sepelietur. Secundum genus Avarorum est eorum, qui nimiu accipiendo peccant, & quia nullu in accipiendo modu tenent, sed undecunq; possunt, lucru captant etiam minimu & cu infamia, quales plerunq; sunt opifices, lenones, foeneratores, viduarum testamentarii, assentatores, aleatores, fures etiam & grassatores, & G qui alii sint id genus homines turpis, injusti & illiberalis quaestus cupidi, quos Juvenal sat. 14. sic describit: Inde fere scelerum causa nec plura venena Miscuit, aut ferro grassatur saevius ullum Humanae mentis vitium, quam saeva Cupido Indomiti sensus, nam dives qui fieri vult Et citò vult fieri, sed quae reverentia legum? Quis metus aut pudor est, unquam properanti avari?
units.tr: Such misers as Plautus describes in Euclio with his pot, of whom he says: If you ask him for the use of fire, he will never give it. Such also was a certain Hermocrates, who, as Lucilius attests, was so possessed by love of his money that, being at the point of death, he wrote himself as heir to his own goods. Athenaeus also mentions, in book 4, chapter 18, a man remarkably miserly, who, so that he would not leave his gold coins to others, swallowed many gold pieces so that he might carry them away with him, and sewed the rest into his cloak, and ordered that he be buried wearing it. (2) The second kind of misers are those who sin by receiving too much; and because they keep no measure in receiving, but gather profit from wherever they can, they chase even the smallest gain, even with infamy. Such men are mostly craftsmen, panders, usurers, executors of widows' wills, flatterers, gamblers, even thieves and highwaymen, and all others of this kind, base, unjust men greedy for dishonourable and illiberal gain. Juvenal describes them in Satire 14 thus: Hence almost the cause of crimes; nor does a more cruel vice mix poisons or rage with the sword than the savage lust of an unbridled desire; for the man who wants to become rich and wants it quickly, what reverence for the laws is there? What fear or shame is there for one who is hurrying, in the case of the greedy?

units.la: Talis fuit Flavius Vespasianus, qui, ut refert Sueton. in vita ipsius, rapacissimum quemque ad honores & officia promovebat, moxque ditatos condemnare solebat, unde dictus est officiarios suos habere pro spongiis, quod & siccas made faceret, & humentes exprimeret.
units.tr: Such was Flavius Vespasian, who, as Suetonius reports in his life of him, promoted the most rapacious men to honours and offices and used to condemn them once they had grown rich. For this reason he was said to treat his officials as sponges: he squeezed them when they were wet and dried them out when they were dry.

units.la: Hisce duobus avarorum generibus tertium ex Ari-
units.tr: A third kind of avarice may be added to these two kinds, from the

units.la: Aristotelis libello de virtutibus addi potest, nempe qui nihil dando, & nimium accipiendo simul delinquunt, de quibus Cic. in paradox. 1. nunquam explentur cupiditas sitis in avaris, neque enim solum libidini augendæ ea, quæ habent cruciantur, sed etiam amittendæ metu. Exemplum habet lepidum Valerius Maximus lib. 7. cap. 6. Refert enim in Cassilini obsidione inter trecentos Prænestinos unum fuisse, qui murem à se captum ducentis denariis maluit vendere, quam ipse levandæ famis gratia comederet, atque ita cum pecunia miserè interiit. Plura de his vide apud Keckerm. à pag. 263. ad pag. 266.
units.tr: book of Aristotle On the Virtues: namely, those who sin on both counts, giving nothing and taking far too much. Cicero speaks of them in Paradoxa 1: "The desire of avaricious men is never satisfied, for they are tormented not only by the wish to increase what they have, but also by fear of losing it." Valerius Maximus, book 7, chapter 6, gives a charming example. He reports that during the siege of Casilinum, among three hundred men of Praeneste, there was one who preferred to sell a mouse he had caught for two hundred denarii rather than eat it himself to relieve his hunger; and so he died wretchedly, with his money. More on these men may be found in Keckermann from page 263 to page 266.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis confert extrema cum medio, & ostendit Avaritiam magis contrariari Liberalitati quam Prodigalitatem, idque confirmat tribus rationibus: 1. est, quia avaritia majus fit malum, quam prodigalitas, ut ex supra dictis patet. Ideo minorem affinitatem & similitudinem cum Liberalitate habet. 2. quia in profusione est umbra quædam honestatis, & prætextus benefaciendo generi humano, sicut in vera Liberalitate est vera intentio, in avaritia verò non. 3. quia magis in avaritia peccant homines, quam in profusione. Nam magis ad illam proclives quam ad hanc, quia naturæ humanæ magis congruere videtur, ut ex consuetudine vulgari supra probavit Philosophus.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he compares the extremes with the mean, and shows that avarice is more opposed to liberality than prodigality is. He confirms this by three reasons: (1) avarice is the greater evil than prodigality, as is clear from what was said above, and so it has less affinity and resemblance to liberality; (2) prodigality has a certain shadow of honourableness and a pretext of benefiting mankind, whereas true liberality has a true intention, and avarice does not; (3) men sin more in avarice than in prodigality, for they are more inclined to it than to the other, since it seems more in keeping with human nature, as the Philosopher proved above from common experience.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Prodigus in iis omnibus peccat, in quibus Liberalis recte segerit.
units.tr: 1. The prodigal sins in all those things in which the liberal man acts rightly.

units.la: 2. Prodigus in nimium dando modum excedit, in nihil accipiendo deserit modum, avarus contra.
units.tr: 2. The prodigal exceeds the measure in giving too much; the avaricious man falls short of the measure in accepting nothing, and the reverse holds for him.

units.la: 3. Prodigus quod semper det, & nihil accipiat ad pauperta-tem facile: ed g potest.
units.tr: 3. Since the prodigal always gives and accepts nothing, he can easily come to poverty.

units.la: 4. Prodigus multa de causis avaro melior habetur.
units.tr: 4. For many reasons the prodigal is held to be better than the avaricious man.

units.la: 5. Prodigus ab statu & ab indigentia curari poterit, avarus non item.
units.tr: 5. The prodigal can be cured of his condition and his want; the avaricious man cannot.

units.la: 6. Prodigus ad veram liberalitatem facile reduci potest, nec malis ipsi moribus videtur.
units.tr: 6. The prodigal can easily be brought back to true liberality, and his morals do not seem to be bad at heart.

units.la: 7. Avarus nulli prodest, ne sibi ipsi quidem, profusus tamen sua profusione multa.
units.tr: 7. The avaricious man benefits no one, not even himself; the prodigal, however, benefits many by his prodigality.

units.la: 8. Prodigi actiones per se nec honestae sunt, nec honestatis gratia fiunt, umbram tamen honoris habent.
units.tr: 8. The actions of the prodigal are not honourable in themselves, nor are they done for the sake of honour, yet they have a shadow of honour.

units.la: 9. Avarus plane est desperatus, nec ullo curari morbo poterit.
units.tr: 9. The avaricious man is wholly beyond hope and can never be cured of his disease.

units.la: 10. Plerique hoc natura indidit, ut avaritia potius quam prodigalitati studeant.
units.tr: 10. Nature has implanted in most people a greater inclination to avarice than to prodigality.

units.la: 11. Etsi multa sint avaritiae genera, ad hoc tamen tria revocari possunt, ut alius in nihil dando, alius in nimium accipien do, alius in utrumque simul peccent.
units.tr: 11. Although there are many kinds of avarice, they can nonetheless be reduced to three: one sins by giving nothing, another by accepting too much, and another by doing both at once.

units.la: 12. Qui alienis rebus metu abstinent, ne si forte aliquid accipiant, plus reddere cogantur, avari sunt & sordidi.
units.tr: 12. Those who out of fear abstain from other people's goods, lest, should they chance to accept anything, they be forced to give back more, are avaricious and sordid.

units.la: 13. Qui beneficium ab avaro accepit, nec rependit, non solum avarus est, sed ingratus etiam est & injustus.
units.tr: 13. Whoever accepts a benefit from an avaricious man and does not repay it is not only avaricious but also ungrateful and unjust.

units.la: 14. Qui aliena accipiunt, & undecunque possunt multa & magna rapiunt, ut tyranni solent, non tam avari, quam improbi & injusti sunt dicendi.
units.tr: 14. Those who take what belongs to others, and seize great amounts from wherever they can, as tyrants are wont to do, are to be called not so much avaricious as wicked and unjust.

units.la: 15. Lenones, assentatores, aleatores, fures etiam & grassatores ex avarorum genere sunt.
units.tr: 15. Pimps, flatterers, gamblers, and also thieves and highwaymen belong to the kind of avaricious people.

units.la: 16. Cum avaritia majus sit malum, magisque in ea peccent homines, Liberalitati ipsi magis contrariari videtur.
units.tr: 16. Since avarice is the greater evil, and men sin more in it, it seems to be more opposed to liberality itself.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: 1. Quæritur: An verum sit, quod in textu dicitur, Avaritiam esse deterius malum Prodigalitate, cum contrarium ratio evincat: nam qui non tantum alios, sed seipsum etiam ledit, deterior videtur, quam qui alios tantum, & non seipsum. At talis est prodigus: nam ut recte ait Philosophus, se & opes suas perdit, & ipse sibi in causa est paupertatis suæ, tum etiam sua profusione se exhaurit, ut in alios beneficium conferre possit: unde deterior videtur esse prodigus avaro? Respon. Negandum est gravius peccare prodigum quam avarum. Nam avarus nec sibi, nec aliis prodest, ut recte in textu dicitur; prodigus vero alios per pecuniam suam juvat, seipsum per benevolentiam, amorem & favorem populi, unde etsi se exhauriat, non tamen tam graviter peccat quam avarus.
units.tr: 1. Question: Is it true, as the text says, that avarice is a worse evil than prodigality, when reason proves the contrary? For one who harms not only others but also himself seems worse than one who harms only others. But the prodigal is such a man: as the Philosopher rightly says, he loses both himself and his wealth, and he is himself the cause of his own poverty. Moreover, by his lavishness he exhausts himself so that he can confer benefits on others. So is the prodigal not worse than the avaricious man? Answer: It must be denied that the prodigal sins more gravely than the avaricious man. For the avaricious man benefits neither himself nor others, as is rightly said in the text. The prodigal, however, helps others with his money and himself with goodwill, love and the favour of the people. So although he exhausts himself, he does not sin as gravely as the avaricious man.

units.la: II. An verum sit, quod dicit Philosophus prodigum non esse malum aut degenerem animi cum tamen id variis rationibus probari possit. Nam prodigus peccat in excessu Liberalitatis, & alius multis vitiis est implicatus: prodigus enim stimul & intemperans & injustus est? Resp. Vocatur prodigus non malus aut degeneris animi, propterea quod studeat bene facere generi humano sua profusione, & ita hoc sensu non poterit dici malus. Deinde prodigus, quem Philosophus vocat non degeneris animi, non est intricatus aliis vitiis, sed tantum profusione, & ideo in excessu tantum Liberalitatis supra modum & præter rationem se gerit.
units.tr: II. Is it true, as the Philosopher says, that the prodigal is not an evil or degenerate-minded man, when this can be proved by various reasons? For the prodigal sins by excess in liberality, and he is entangled in many vices: he is foolish, intemperate and unjust. Answer: The prodigal is called not evil or degenerate-minded because he strives to do good to mankind by his lavishness, and in this sense he cannot be called evil. Next, the prodigal whom the Philosopher calls not degenerate-minded is not entangled in other vices, but only in lavishness, and so he behaves excessively and beyond measure and reason only in the matter of liberality.

units.la: Instantia: Prodigi actiones non sunt honestæ, quippe quæ sine delectu exercentur & sapenumero ergo, eos, quibus omnino non est largiendum, conjusmodi sunt bistriones, musici, lenones, assentatores, aliiq; voluptatum corporis ministri. Ergo neque bonus esse potuit prodigus, neque generosi animi? Resp. Non vocatur simpliciter prodigus bonus, sed comparate tantum: nam si comparatur cum avaro illius respectu & non malus & generosi poterit dici animi, si quidem si non veram honestatem, umbram salte honestatis in actionibus suis prae se fert, & cum magis aliorum utilitati, quam suo commodo studeat, recte non degeneris animi a Philosopho dicitur.
units.tr: Objection: The actions of the prodigal are not honourable, since they are performed without discrimination and often toward those to whom nothing should be given at all, such as actors, musicians, pimps, flatterers and other servants of bodily pleasures. Therefore the prodigal could be neither good nor generous in spirit? Answer: The prodigal is not called good simply, but only comparatively. For if he is compared with the avaricious man, he can be called neither evil nor of ungenerous spirit. If he does not bear true honesty, he at least displays a shadow of honesty in his actions, and since he cares more for the advantage of others than for his own gain, he is rightly called by the Philosopher not degenerate-minded.

units.la: III. An vere Avaritia dicatur malum incurabile, cum incurabile aut quod curari non potest, etiam vituperari nequit: frustra enim vituperatur id, quod curari aut mutari in melius nullo modo potest. Proinde Avaritia cum sit incurabilis, male a Philosopho dicitur vitium, & quidem deterius vitium, quam prodigalitas? Resp. Incurabile dicitur duobus modis, vel simpliciter, quod curari nullo modo potest, & sic avaritia non dicitur incurabile malum. 2. Respective quod curari quidem potest, sed difficulter admodum, si nempe conferatur cum aliis vitiis, & hoc modo incurabile malum dicitur Avaritia.
units.tr: III. Can avarice truly be called an incurable evil? What is incurable, or cannot be cured, cannot be blamed either, for it is vain to blame what cannot in any way be cured or changed for the better. Therefore, since avarice is incurable, is it wrongly called a vice by the Philosopher, and indeed a worse vice than prodigality? Answer: "Incurable" is said in two ways. Either simply, of what cannot be cured in any way; and in this sense avarice is not called an incurable evil. Or comparatively, of what can indeed be cured, but with great difficulty, namely when it is compared with other vices; and in this way avarice is called an incurable evil.

units.la: IV. Cur etiam senectam vocet causam avaritiae? Nam si hoc verum esset, tunc omnes senes essent avari, sed ratio & experientia contrarium docent. Ratio quia contraxerunt habitum liberalitatis in florida aetate eum in senecta non facile amittunt. Experientia etiam docet multos senes esse liberales: nam ut testatur Suetonius in vita Augusti, gloriabatur Augustus, quod juvenis reperisset Romam ligneam, & senex jam moriturus reliquisset eam sua liberalitate auream. Unde male dicitur senecta causa avaritiae? Resp. Sene-ca &a non est causa avaritiæ per se, sed per accidens, quia hoc vitium avaritiæ plerunq; cadit in senes.
units.tr: IV. Why does he also call old age the cause of avarice? For if this were true, then all old men would be avaricious, but reason and experience teach the contrary. Reason, because they acquired the habit of liberality in the flower of their age and do not easily lose it in old age. Experience too teaches that many old men are liberal: for, as Suetonius attests in the life of Augustus, Augustus boasted that as a young man he had found Rome built of brick, and that as an old man, about to die, he had left it golden through his generosity. Whence is it wrongly said that old age is a cause of avarice? Answer: Old age is not the cause of avarice in itself, but only incidentally, because this vice of avarice generally falls upon old men.

units.la: V. Cur Philosophus fœneratores inter avaros numerarit, cum tamen fœneratores liberales sint. Nam viri liberalis munia exercent, quia beneficium in alios conferunt, dum pecuniam suam mutuo dant, & alios à necessitate liberant, quæ duo viri liberalis propria sunt munia? Resp. Per negationem, nullum munus liberalis viri fœnatores exercere: nam per pecuniæ erogationem nullum beneficium in alios conferunt, sed suam privatam utilitatem respiciunt: dein alios à necessitate non liberant, sed potius damno & detrimento premunt, dum fœnus illicitum exigunt. Breviter: Non immeritò inter avaros collocantur, quia nullam honestatem in actionibus suis præse ferunt, & non tam benefacere, quam malefacere generi humano aut nocere student.
units.tr: V. Why did the Philosopher number moneylenders among the avaricious, when moneylenders are yet liberal? For they perform the duties of the liberal man: they confer a benefit on others when they lend their money, and they free others from necessity, and these two are the proper duties of the liberal man. Answer: On the contrary, moneylenders perform no duty of the liberal man. For by paying out money they confer no benefit on others but look to their own private advantage. Next, they do not free others from necessity but rather burden them with loss and harm, when they exact illicit interest. In short, they are not unjustly placed among the avaricious, because they show no honesty in their actions, and they strive not so much to do good to mankind as to do it harm and injury.

units.la: Hinc exurgit hæc quæstio: An usura, quæ à Philosopho malum sub avaritia contentum dicitur, sit licita necne, seu iurene an iniuria, pro avaritia malo à Philosopho habeatur. Hæc quæstio, ut melius intelligatur, venit distinctio quædam observanda ex D. Thoma, nempe rerum quædam sunt, quarum usus & consumtio non distinguuntur, ut vinum, granum, oleum, & in his aliquid supra sortem exigere est id, quod non est, contra legem naturæ, vendere cum rei non existentis nulla naturaliter possit esse venditio, aut est idem omnis vendere, quod est contra legem iustitiæ, aut est violare charitatem Christianā, cum id, quod quis non dederit, ab alio exigit, aut alteri facit, quod sibi fieri nolit. Et in his omnibus usura plane est illicita, cum usus & consumtio harum rerum inter se non distinguantur. Secundò quæ-dam res sunt, quarum usus & consumtio inter se distinguuntur, verbi gratia: Usus domus est inhabitatio, ejus consumtio aut destructo domus longè distat ab isto usu: sic etiam usus fundi est fructus perceptio, non verò destructio fundi. Et in his (reservato interim suis Dominis proprio rei domino) licet aliquid supra sortem exigere, ita tamen ut fiat secundum qualitatem dantis, & rei usus non nisi ex ratione æstimetur; secus enim aliquid exigere sordida avaritia est. Breviter: Usura à Philosopho pro avaritiæ malo censetur, propter sex rationes. 1. est: Quia usum naturalem pecuniæ (qui usus in hoc consistit, ut sit mensura in rebus ultro citroque commutandis) pervertit: nam rem cum suo valore non tantum æstimat, sed supra valorem jus & æquū. 2. Quia monstrosum ortum pecuniæ ex pecunia quærit: nam partum quærit ex iis rebus, quæ naturaliter vim pariendi non habent, verbi gratia: Ex pecunia & omni substantia domestica, quæ cum res inanimatæ sint naturaliter parere non possunt. 3. Quia non ens, seu id, quod non est, dum id, quod supra sortem est, nusquam sit, vendit, & idem bis vendit: nam rem primo in suo valore vendit, postea supra valorem. 4. Quia usum rei à re ipsa, à qua tum naturaliter divelli non potest, distrahit. 5. Quia pecuniam infinitè quærit: nam nummum nummo fine fine adjicere non definit. 6. Quia legem Dei violat Deut. 23. verf. 29. non fœnerabis fratri tuo, neque pecuniam neque ullam aliam rem.
units.tr: Hence arises this question: Whether usury, which the Philosopher calls an evil contained under avarice, is lawful or not; that is, whether it is just or unjust, and whether it is to be regarded by the Philosopher as the evil of avarice. So that this question may be better understood, a certain distinction taken from St Thomas must be observed. Some things are such that their use and their consumption are not distinct, as wine, grain and oil. In these, to demand something above the principal is against the law of nature, since no sale of a thing that does not exist can naturally take place; or it amounts to selling what one does not possess, which is contrary to the law of justice; or it violates Christian charity, since one demands from another what he has not given, or does to another what he would not wish done to himself. In all these cases usury is plainly unlawful, since the use and consumption of such things cannot be distinguished. Secondly, there are certain things whose use and consumption are distinct from each other. For example, the use of a house is habitation, and its consumption or destruction is far removed from that use; so too the use of a field is the gathering of its produce, not its destruction. In these cases (the proper ownership of the thing being meanwhile reserved to its owners) it is lawful to demand something above the principal, provided this is done according to the quality of the giver, and the use of the thing is estimated only by reason. Otherwise, to demand more is sordid avarice. In short, the Philosopher counts usury as an evil of avarice for six reasons. (1) It perverts the natural use of money, which consists in this, that money is the measure in exchanging things back and forth: for it values a thing not merely at its worth but claims, beyond its value, a right that is not just. (2) It seeks a monstrous offspring of money from money: for it seeks increase from things which by nature have no power of bearing, such as money itself and all household goods, which, being inanimate, cannot naturally beget. (3) It sells what does not exist, namely what lies beyond the principal and is nowhere, and it sells the same thing twice: first at its value, then again beyond its value. (4) It separates the use of a thing from the thing itself, from which the use cannot naturally be divided. (5) It seeks money without limit: it never ceases to add coin to coin without end. (6) It violates the law of God, Deut. 23. vers. 29: "Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother, neither money nor any other thing."

units.la: Objectio. At leges humanæ permittunt hujusmodi mensuram, furam, quod non facerent, si illicita aut mala essent: nam cum leges fundentur super rationem ipsam & fini regula ipsius rationis, nihil malum aut illicitum permittunt? Resp. Aliud est permittere aut tolerare, aliud sancire & statuere tanquam licitum, leges quidem humanæ permittunt usuram, ne scilicet majus malum aut detrimentum in Republ. sequatur, ne ille, qui necessitate premitur, si pecuniam ad necessitatem levandã, mutuò non acceperit, ad illicitas artes descendat, & rapinam aut furtum exerceat: Malum tamen hoc usuræ quantum possunt in Rebuspub. beneformatis restringunt.
units.tr: Objection: But human laws permit such usury, which they would not do if it were illicit or evil; for since laws are founded upon reason itself, and reason is the rule of the end, they permit nothing evil or unlawful. Answer: It is one thing to permit or tolerate, and another to sanction and establish as lawful. Human laws indeed permit usury, lest a greater evil or harm follow in the commonwealth, and lest one who is pressed by necessity, if he has not received money on loan to relieve his need, turn to illicit arts and commit robbery or theft. Nevertheless, in well-ordered commonwealths they restrict this evil of usury as far as they can.

units.la: At objicitur II. Etiam lege divina permissum esse: nam Moses legislator Deut. 23. verf. 19. permittit ut à peregrinis & extraneis usura capiatur: unde prorsus non videtur illicita? Resp. Permisit quidem Moses, quia magna fuit infirmitas populi Judaici, & sicut divortium Deut. 24. verf. 1. permissum erat propter duritiê cordis ipsorum, sicut testatur Salvator Christus Matth. 19 verf 8 sic etiam & usura, sed tamen valdè restringebat hoc malum, ne scilicet à fratribus exigeretur, sed à peregrinis & extraneis. Jam verò cum templi velo scisso Matth. 27. verf. 25. viaque gentibus ad salutem patefacta, omnes in Christo fratres simus, jam Christiano ab aliis Christianis usuram hoc prætextu Scripturæ exigere non licet. Plura vide apud D. Keckerm. in synopsi Oecon. pag. 97. 98. & 99. & in Syst. Polit. pag. 121.
units.tr: Second, it is objected that usury is also permitted by divine law: Moses the lawgiver, in Deut. 23 verse 19, allows usury to be taken from foreigners and strangers, so it does not seem unlawful at all. Answer: Moses did indeed permit it, because the weakness of the Jewish people was great. Just as divorce was permitted because of the hardness of their hearts (Deut. 24 verse 1), as Christ the Saviour testifies (Matth. 19 verse 8), so too usury. Yet he greatly restricted this evil, so that it was not exacted from brothers but only from foreigners and strangers. But now that the veil of the temple has been torn (Matth. 27. verse 25) and the way to salvation has been opened to the Gentiles, and we are all brothers in Christ, it is no longer lawful for a Christian to exact usury from other Christians on the pretext of Scripture. More may be seen in D. Keckermann, in the Synopsis Oeconomica, pp. 97, 98 and 99, and in the Syst. Polit., p. 121.

units.la: II. An simpliciter liceat alteri communicare sua bona, quod vis & natura liberalitatis, per se effagitare videtur? Statuitur thesis negativa, propter quatuor rationes: I. Quia
units.tr: II. Whether it is simply lawful for one person to share his goods with another, which the force and nature of liberality seems to demand in itself? The negative thesis is laid down, for four reasons: I. Because

units.la: 1. Qu'a id est simpliciter honestum, quod ex præ- scripto rectæ rationis fit: communicare autem alte- ri sua bona, non fit semper ex præscripto rectę ratio- nis: rectà enim ratio non jubet, ut communicemus bona nostra, nisi quibus decet, cur, quomodo, quā- do, & quantum decet: hæ autem conditiones non semper observantur in qualibet bonorum communi- catione. 2. Ratio est: Quia prodigi communicant aliis sua bona, sed sine discrimine, & ita eorum hæc actio non est honesta, & laudabilis, sed turpis plerumque & vituperabilis. 3. Quia interdum honestum & laudabile est, non communicare quibusdam nostra bona, seu ut Philosophus loquitur cap. 2. hu- jus libri, non dare quibusvis, verbi gratia: Si parentes denegent liberis suis pecuniam, qua sciunt illos abusuros esse ad compotationem aut amorem illi- citum, ad rerum futilium & inutilium coemptionem aliàve peccata. Unde præclarè Seneca lib. 5. de beneficiis cap. 3. Quædam sunt nocitura impetranti- bus, quæ non dare, sed negare beneficiū est. 4. Quia si simpliciter honestum esset communicare alteri sua bona, tunc non opus esset liberalitate, quæ bonorum præscribit moderationem seu modum. At consequens est absurdum: nam absque virtute rebus velle bene præesse non tantum modum relin- quere, sed à via etiam rectæ rationis deflectere, sine qua nihil in rebus humanis rectè geri potest.
units.tr: 1. For that is simply honourable which is done according to the prescription of right reason. But to communicate one's goods to another is not always done according to right reason. Right reason does not bid us share our goods except with those to whom it is fitting, and for the reason, in the manner, at the time, and in the amount that is fitting. These conditions, however, are not always observed in every sharing of goods. 2. The reason is: prodigals share their goods with others, but without discrimination. Therefore their action is not honourable and praiseworthy, but generally base and blameworthy. 3. Because it is sometimes honourable and praiseworthy not to share our goods with certain people, or, as the Philosopher puts it in chapter 2 of this book, not to give to just anyone. For example: if parents refuse their children money which they know will be spent on drinking parties, on illicit love, on buying trivial and useless things, or on other sins. Hence Seneca rightly says in book 5 of On Benefits, chapter 3: "There are some things which harm those who ask for them, and to refuse them is a benefit, not to give them." 4. Because if it were simply honourable to share one's goods with another, there would be no need of liberality, which prescribes the moderation or measure of goods. But the consequence is absurd: for to wish to preside well over affairs without virtue is not only to leave out the measure, but also to turn aside from the path of right reason, without which nothing in human affairs can be done rightly.

units.la: III. An cum liberalitatis usus in dando maxime consi- stat, quis poterit esse liberalis in seipsum?
units.tr: III. Since the exercise of liberality consists chiefly in giving, who can be liberal towards himself?

units.la: Resp. Non pro- pter tres rationes: 1. Quia liberalitas est virtus communicativa, quæ naturâ suam exercet in alios lios. 2. Quia nemo proprie potest dici in se libera-litatem exercuisse, sed potius de bonis suis sibi profuisse. Unde præclare Seneca lib. 5. de benefic. cap. 4. Sicut nemo liberalis est, qui sibi dat, nec clemens, qui sibi ignoscit, nec misericors, qui malè suis tantum tangitur, sed qui in alios istas exercent virtutes: sic etiam, qui in se beneficium confert nõ liberalis est, sed natura suaparet, quæ monet fugiēda esse, quæ nocent & appetenda quæ prosunt. 3. Quia aliquid sibiipsi dare est illud ab aliis abstrahere, quod avari est, non viri liberalis.
units.tr: Answer: No, for three reasons: 1. Because liberality is a communicative virtue, which by its nature exercises itself on others. 2. Because no one can properly be said to have exercised liberality towards himself, but rather to have benefited himself with his own goods. Hence Seneca rightly says in book 5 of On Benefits, chapter 4: "Just as no one is generous who gives to himself, nor merciful who forgives himself, nor compassionate who is moved only by his own troubles, but those who exercise these virtues towards others: so too, one who confers a benefit on himself is not generous, but obeys his own nature, which warns us to avoid what harms and seek what profits." 3. Because to give something to oneself is to take it away from others, which is the mark of a miser, not of a liberal man.

units.la: IV. An pauper poterit esse liberalis? Et videtur non posse: nam liberalis ille vere dicitur, qui de bonis suis aliis aliquid communicat.
units.tr: IV. Can a poor man be liberal? It seems not, for he is truly called liberal who communicates something of his goods to others.

units.la: At pauper parum aut nihil bonorum proprium habet. Unde liberalis dici minimè videtur. Sed contrarium esse verum ratio duplex evincit. Nam primò, pauper potest esse officiosus seu officiis & obsequiis suis de aliis benemereri, & aliis gratificari. Secundò, licet pauper non eo modo quo divites liberalis esse possit, cum tamen liberalitas non secundum facultates, sed ex animo & affectu dantis æstimetur, liberalis esse suo modo pauper potest, si nempe animum promtum & benevolum benefaciendi habeat. Non enim in quantitate donorum, sed in hilaritate animi aut promtitudine dantis consistit liberalitas.
units.tr: But a poor man has little or nothing of his own goods. Hence he seems by no means to be called liberal. Yet the contrary is true, as a twofold reason proves. For, first, a poor man can be dutiful, that is, deserve well of others by his services and attentions, and show kindness to others. Second, although a poor man cannot be liberal in the same way as the rich, yet since liberality is judged not by the means but by the mind and disposition of the giver, a poor man can be liberal in his own way, if indeed he has a ready and kindly mind to do good. For liberality consists not in the quantity of gifts but in the cheerfulness of mind or readiness of the giver.

units.la: V. An Reges & Principes possint dici prodigi? Negat hoc Philosophus: contrarium rationibus quibusdam evincere conantur quidam Neoterici. 1. ratio est, quia prodigus in dando modum excedit & nullas circumstantias veræ liberalitatis observat, tales etiam possunt esse Reges. 2. Quia Reges nimia sua profusione bona sua possunt absumere, & hoc est proprium prodigi. At hæ rationes non magni sunt momenti. Nam Reges non immerito dicuntur non esse prodigi, propterea quod nimis opibus supra vel quos mortales affluant: & quæ aliis mera esset profusio, vix iis revera potest dici liberalitas. Nam etsi modum aliis consuetum in dando non observent, modum tamen supra facultates suas non excedunt. 2. ratio est planè falsa: Nam Reges nimia sua profusione nō possunt bona sua abstumere. Quicquid enim dant, vel dant peregrinis vel subditis. Si peregrinis id faciunt publicæ utilitatis gratia, ut nempe vel militem conducant, vel pacem redimant, vel fœdus ineant, ad commercia cum aliis gentibus tractanda: fi dent subditis, sic se bonis exuere non possunt: nam, ut omnes fluvii per occultos terræ meatus ab Oceano veniunt, & rursum illabuntur in eum: Sic Reges quicquid dant subditis, à subditis rursus per varias rationes recipiunt, ad Liberalitatem suam sustinendam. Dein' nullæ historiæ, aut experientia testatur Reges donis & largitionibus bona sua assumfisse. Immerito gitur culpatur Philosophus: nam cum liberalitas versetur circa opes modicas & homines mediocris conditionis requirat, non vero Magnates aut Principes; Ideo neq; Prodigalitas ejus extremum in excessu ad Reges proprie pertinere posset.
units.tr: V. Can kings and princes be called prodigals? The Philosopher denies it, and some modern writers try to prove the contrary by certain arguments. 1. The argument is that the prodigal exceeds the measure in giving and observes none of the circumstances of true liberality, and kings can be like this too. 2. Because kings, by their excessive lavishness, can use up their goods, and this is the mark of a prodigal. But these arguments are not of great weight. For kings are rightly said not to be prodigals, because they abound in wealth beyond what most mortals enjoy, and what would be sheer profusion in others can hardly truly be called liberality in them. For although they do not observe the measure customary for others in giving, they do not exceed their means. As for the second argument, it is plainly false: kings cannot use up their goods by excessive lavishness. Whatever they give, they give either to foreigners or to their subjects. If they give to foreigners for the sake of public utility, namely to hire soldiers, to buy peace, to make a treaty, or to conduct trade with other nations, then they cannot be stripped of their goods. If they give to their subjects, they likewise cannot be impoverished, for as all rivers come from the ocean through hidden channels of the earth and flow back into it, so kings, whatever they give to their subjects, receive back again from them by various means, to sustain their liberality. Next, no histories or experience testify that kings have consumed their goods through gifts and largesses. Therefore the Philosopher is unjustly blamed. For since liberality is concerned with modest means and requires people of middling condition, not magnates or princes, its extreme of excess, prodigality, could not properly pertain to kings.

units.la: VI. An Monachi Cacuzini sint liberales dicendi, qui ab aliis mendicant, quod aliu etiam tribuunt.
units.tr: VI. Whether the Cacuzine monks, who beg from others and yet give to others as well, are to be called liberal.

units.la: Et statuitur, quod non, propter quatuor rationes. 1. Quia liberalitas requirit, ut de nostris bonis aliquid tribuamus mus ibus aliis, non vero de alienis. Nam alienum dare injustitia est. 1. Qua sic debemus dare, ut aliquid semper habeamus, quod demus, ne fontem exhauriamus liberalitatis, at illi nihil fibiipsis relinquunt. 2. ratio, Qua omnis largitio & actio liberalitatis debet esse honestaris gratia: haec vero non est. Nam aut ambitionis aut supererogationis, ut loquuntur, gratia instituitur, nempe ut non tantum ista liberalitate sibi aliquid promereant, sed aliis etiam, quibus sua merita impertire dignentur. 4. ratio: Quia liberalitas debet exerceri secundum facultates de bonis superfluis, non vero necessariis. At illi necessaria, cibum nempe & potum aliis impertiunt, ut nihil fibiipsis relinquant.
units.tr: It is held that they are not, for four reasons. (1) Liberality requires that we give some of our own goods to others, not of others' goods, for giving what belongs to another is injustice. (2) We must so give that we always keep something to give, so that we do not drain the source of liberality; but these men leave nothing for themselves. (3) Every act and gift of liberality must be done for the sake of honour; but theirs is not. For they act for the sake of ambition or, as they put it, of supererogation, namely so that by this liberality they may earn merit for themselves and also for others, to whom they deign to impart their merits. (4) Liberality must be exercised according to one's means, out of surplus goods and not out of necessities; but these men give away the necessities, namely food and drink, to others, so that they leave nothing for themselves.

units.la: VII. Animidem sit benefacere alteri & prodesse; Et statuit ut thesis negativa.
units.tr: VII. Whether it is the same to do good to another and to benefit him; and it is held in the negative.

units.la: Nam licet omnis, qui bene facit alteri, eidem etiam prosit, non tamen vice versa, omnis qui prodest, benefacere etiam dicitur propter tres rationes. 1. est: Quia lapides, plantae, bestiae, aliis virtute & operatione sua prosunt, non tamen recte dicuntur benefacere. 2. Mercatores & opifices prosunt civitati, non tamen benefaciunt. Prosunt quidem quatenus opificia & mercaturam in civitate exercent, non benefaciunt, quia privatum suum commodum, non publicam totius civitatis utilitatem quaerunt. 3. Quia quidam inscii & nolentes prodesse aliis possunt, non vero benefacere, verbi gratia: refert Cicero de Nat. Deorum hostem Jasonem Phaereum gladio interficere voluisse, sed ille vomicam ejus apperuit, quam Medici sanare non poterant. Et ratio harum omnium rationum haec est: quia beneficium est id, quod scienter à rectæ rationis judicio bonaque voluntate gratuitò solius honestatis gratia proficiscitur, teste Seneca lib. 1. de Benef. cap. 2.
units.tr: For although everyone who does good to another also benefits him, the reverse does not hold: not everyone who benefits another is said to do good. This is for three reasons. (1) Stones, plants and beasts benefit others by their power and activity, yet they are not rightly said to do good. (2) Merchants and craftsmen benefit the commonwealth, yet they do not do good. They benefit it indeed insofar as they practise their crafts and trade in the state, but they do not do good, because they seek their private advantage and not the public utility of the whole commonwealth. (3) Some people can benefit others without knowing it and against their will, but cannot do good. For example, Cicero, in On the Nature of the Gods, relates that Jason of Pherae wished to kill his enemy with a sword, but the enemy opened his abscess, which the physicians could not cure. And the reason for all these is this: a benefit is that which proceeds knowingly, from a judgement of right reason and a good will, freely and for the sake of honour alone, as Seneca teaches in On Benefits, book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: VIII. An simpliciter turpe sit beneficiis vinci ab aliis?
units.tr: VIII. Whether it is simply shameful to be overcome by others in benefits?

units.la: Et statuitur, quod non, propter duas præcipuè rationes, 1. Quia in omnibus non est æquè perfectus liberalitatis habitus: nam quidam habitum in ortu, quidam in progressu, quidam in perfectione habent, unde magis vel minus rectè pro diversis in habitu gradibus actiones liberalitatis homines exercere possunt. 2. ratio est, quia non omnibus æqualis suppetit benefaciendi facultas idque propterea, quia diversæ sunt hominum conditiones & status, unde præclarè Seneca lib. 5. de beneficiis c. 4. non est turpe filium beneficiis à parente, quidni non sit turpe, cùm à nullo vinci turpe sit, quibusdam enim pares & impares sumus, pares animo, quem illi solum exigunt, & quem nos solum promittimus, impares fortuna, quæ, si cui obstitit, quo minus gratiam referre, non illi tanquam victo erubescendum est: non enim turpe est non assequi, dum modo sequaris, id est, animum & voluntatem benefaciendi habeas. Pro determinatione sciendum est, parem à pari beneficiis vinci turpe esse, & contra Liberalitatem, inter impares superiorem ab inferiori superari beneficiis esse turpissimum, cum ingratitudinem & avaritiam simul declaret; inferiore à superiori vinci beneficiis non est turpe, dummodo donis rependere beneficium non possit, animi tamen promtitudinem quibuscunque possit modis declaret.
units.tr: It is held that it is not, chiefly for two reasons. (1) Liberality is not equally perfect in everyone: some have the habit at its beginning, some in its progress, some in its perfection, whence people can exercise the acts of liberality more or less rightly according to the different degrees of the habit they have. (2) Not everyone has an equal ability to confer benefits, and this is because the conditions and states of men differ. Hence Seneca rightly says in On Benefits, book 5, chapter 4: "It is not shameful for a son to be overcome by his parent's benefits; why, then, should it be shameful to be overcome by anyone? For with some we are equals and with others unequal: equals in spirit, which is all they require of us and all we promise; unequal in fortune. If fortune has stood in someone's way so that he cannot repay the favour, he has no need to blush as if he were vanquished. For it is not shameful not to attain, provided you still pursue; that is, provided you have the spirit and will to do good." As a rule, it should be known that to be overcome in benefits by an equal is shameful, and contrary to liberality; but that to be overcome in benefits by one's inferior is most shameful, since it shows ingratitude and avarice at once. To be overcome in benefits by a superior is not shameful, provided one cannot repay the benefit with gifts, but still shows readiness of mind by whatever means one can.

units.la: IX. Et
units.tr: IX. And

units.la: IX. & ult. hoc etiam quæritur: An cuilibet licitum sit communicare aliis de bonis suis quantum velit? Non licere sequentes hę vincunt rationes: Prima est, quia liberalitas est virtus, quæ bonorum cum aliis communicationem moderatur, ne vel modum excedat, vel ab eo deficiat: at ista moderatione non opus esset, si liceret cuilibet de bonis suis communicare aliis quantum velit. 2. Ratio: quia omnis largitio, aut actio liberalitatis debet esse secundum facultates: secundum facultates vero fit, cum sine jactura & detrimento rei familiaris fit, id est, de bonis superfluis non necessariis vitæ aut familiæ alendæ. 3. Ratio est, quia nemini licet esse prodigum: at communicare aliis de bonis suis quantum quis velit, est esse prodigum: nam prodigus is est, non tantum qui certas in dando circumstantias non observat, sed etiam qui plus aliis dat, quam debet, non habita ratione vel personæ cui dat, vel facultatum suarum quas dat.
units.tr: IX. and last: this also is asked: Is it lawful for anyone to share with others as much of his goods as he wishes? That it is not lawful, the following reasons prove. The first is that liberality is a virtue which moderates the sharing of goods with others, so that one neither exceeds the measure nor falls short of it; but there would be no need of such moderation if anyone might share as much of his goods with others as he wished. (2) Every gift or act of liberality must be according to one's means; but it is according to one's means when it is done without loss or damage to one's household, that is, out of surplus goods, not out of those needed for living and supporting one's family. (3) No one is allowed to be prodigal; but to share with others as much of one's goods as one wishes is to be prodigal. For a man is prodigal not only if he fails to observe the set circumstances in giving, but also if he gives more to others than he ought, without regard either to the person to whom he gives or to the means he gives from.

units.la: At objicitur: Liberalitatis non certum esse modum, & cum præcipuus scopus liberalitatis sit benefacere humano generi, quanto quis magis benefacit mortalibus, tanto magis laudatur. Ideo neque certum in liberalitate modum servare licet. Secundo unusquisque habet plenariam potestatem dispensandi & elargiendi bona sua pro libitu. Ergo quid impedit, quominus aliquis de bonis suis communicet aliis, quantum velit? Resp. Neutram istam rationem esse veram. Nam ut omnis virtus, sic etiam liberalitas certum habet modum, certosque fines, quos ultra utraque nequit consistere rectum: neque in benefaciendo quis fontem liberalitatis exhaurire debet. Secunda vero ratio est plane falsa. Nam nemo habet potestatem dispensandi bona sua, nisi observaris circumstantiis, quae requiruntur ad veram dispensationem, nisi idem prodigus & vitiosus velit dici, non liberalis & virtuosus.
units.tr: But it is objected: Liberality has no fixed measure; and since the chief aim of liberality is to benefit mankind, the more one benefits mortals, the more one is praised. Therefore it is not lawful to keep a fixed measure in liberality either. Second, everyone has full power to dispense and bestow his goods at will. What, then, prevents anyone from sharing as much of his goods with others as he wishes? Reply: neither of these reasons is true. For, as with every virtue, so liberality also has a fixed measure and fixed limits, beyond which neither can remain right; nor should anyone exhaust the source of liberality in doing good. The second reason is plainly false. For no one has the power to dispense his goods unless he observes the circumstances which are required for a true dispensation; otherwise he wishes to be called prodigal and vicious, not liberal and virtuous.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Sequitur secundum membrum primi tractatus huius libri, in quo postquam Philosophus de Liberalitate egit, statim agit de Magnificentia, quia istae duae virtutes sunt admodum sibi invicem cognatae: nam versantur circa unam eandemque materiam, circa opes nempe auri sumtus. Partes huius posterioris membri sunt tres: In prima de materia circa quam versatur Magnificentia, cuius suis extremis agit. In secunda, ut natura Magnificentiae melius illustretur, varias operationes Magnificiadfert. In tertia demum de extremis agit. Prima pars continetur hoc capite quarto, cuius duae sunt partes: In prima differentiam inter Liberalitatem & Magnificentiam adducit. In secunda varias proprietates Magnifici explicat.
units.tr: There follows the second member of the first treatise of this book. In it, after the Philosopher has dealt with Liberality, he at once deals with Magnificence, because these two virtues are closely related to each other: they are concerned with one and the same matter, namely the spending of wealth. This second member has three parts. In the first he treats of the matter with which Magnificence is concerned, and of its extremes. In the second, so that the nature of Magnificence may be better illustrated, he presents its various operations. In the third, finally, he treats of its extremes. The first part is contained in this fourth chapter, which has two parts. In the first he draws out the difference between Liberality and Magnificence. In the second he explains the various properties of the magnificent man.

units.la: In prima igitur parte hoc ponit discrimen inter Liberalitatem & Magnificentiam, quod licet circa unam eandemque materiam versentur, in modo tamen differant. Nam Liberalitas in parvis, communibus & quotidianis sumtibus tantum cernitur. Magnificentia vero in rariss, magnis & insolitis, id quod probat a nomine Magnificentiae, nihil enim aliud significat, quam in magnitudine aut in rebus magnis sumtum decorum. Decorum vero in sumtu faciendo servatur, aut convenientia unicuique pro dignitate.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he lays down this distinction between Liberality and Magnificence: although they are concerned with one and the same matter, they differ in their manner. For Liberality is seen only in small, common and everyday expenses, whereas Magnificence is seen in rare, great and unusual ones. This he proves from the name Magnificence, for it signifies nothing other than a fitting expenditure on great things or in great matters. Fittingness, moreover, is observed in making an expense, or a suitability to each person according to his dignity.

units.la: d'gnidignitate & præstantia attribuuntur, idq; spectatur vel in opere, in quod sumtus impenditur, vel in persona: respectu operis, ut verbi gratia: major sumtus impendi debet in ludos publicos & solennes, quam in privatam aliquam triremem, quia in illis major ratio decori observari debet, sic etiam major sumtus fieri debet in basilica, quam in xenodochio exstruendo; respectu personæ major sumtus in Rege excipiendo, quam in Duce; majot tamen in Duce, quam in aliquo Barone.
units.tr: Dignity and eminence are assigned, and this is regarded either in the work on which the expense is laid out, or in the person. With respect to the work, for example: a greater expense ought to be laid out on public and solemn games than on some private trireme, because in the former a greater measure of fittingness must be observed; so too a greater expense ought to be made in building a basilica than in building a hospice for strangers. With respect to the person: a greater expense is to be made in receiving a king than in receiving a duke, but a greater one in receiving a duke than in receiving some baron.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis sex affert proprietates Magnifici, & ideo ut natura objecti circa quod versatur Magnificentia magis innotescat. 1. Proprietas est, quod Magnificus debeat esse scienti similis: nam sicut aliquis scientia præditus appositè & bene novit conclusiones resolvere in sua principia, & ex iisdem principiis easdem rursus reducere conclusiones: sic etiam Magnificus circa materiam suam novit invenire, quid deceat, & sumtus convenienter pro tempore & loco & persona rebus accommodare. II. Conditio est, ut Magnificus sumtus tantum faciat honestatis gratia, & ratio est, quia cum omnis virtus honestatis gratia agat, tum inprimis Magnificentia, quæ virtus est excellens & in gradu eminenti constituta. III. Conditio, ut cum voluptate sumtus faciat, non tantum ut promtitudinem & hilaritatem animi declaret, quod etiam liberalis facere solet, sed etiam ut excellentiam & generositatem animi in decoro rite observando ostendat. IV. Conditio est, quod in omni opere, in quod sumtus impendit, debet respicere, quo pacto fiat, an pulchrum & elegans, & maximè decorum sit, non verò quanti constet, & ratio est, quia hæc est natura Magnificentiæ: ut non sumtus ipsos, sed decorum in sumtu faciendo unicè respiciat. V. Conditio, quod licet interdum liberalis & Magnificus eosdem faciant in aliqua re sumtus, tamen dissimili hoc modo fit. Nam Liberalis utilitatem & precium rei spectat, Magnificus verò pulchritudinem & decorum, verbi gratia: si poculum donet Liberalis, quod centum aureis constat, ille utilitatem & precium poculi spectat: Magnificus verò si idem poculum det non tam utilitatem, quàm excellentiam operis & quantum cum decoro consistat quam donum. VI. Conditio quod etsi Magnificus modum liberalitatis in sumtu faciendo excedat, varias tamen circumstantias, sicut Liberalis in dando observabit, secus enim in vitia illi opposita degeneraret.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he sets out six properties of the magnificent man, so that the nature of the object with which Magnificence is concerned may become better known. (1) The first property is that the magnificent man ought to be like a man of learning: for just as one who possesses science knows how aptly and well to resolve conclusions into their principles, and from the same principles to derive the same conclusions again, so too the magnificent man knows how to discover, in his own matter, what is fitting, and to adapt his expenses suitably to the time, place and person. (2) The second condition is that the magnificent man should spend only for the sake of honour; and the reason is that, since every virtue acts for the sake of honour, Magnificence above all does so, being an excellent virtue placed on a lofty level. (3) The third condition is that he should spend with pleasure, not only to show the readiness and cheerfulness of his mind, which the liberal man also customarily does, but also to display the excellence and nobility of his mind in duly observing fittingness. (4) The fourth condition is that in every work on which he spends, he ought to look to how it is done, whether it is beautiful and elegant and above all fitting, and not to what it costs; and the reason is that this is the nature of Magnificence: that it regards not the expenses themselves but only the fittingness in making them. (5) The fifth condition is that although the liberal man and the magnificent man sometimes spend the same sum on some thing, they do so in a dissimilar way. For the liberal man regards the usefulness and price of the thing, whereas the magnificent man regards its beauty and fitness. For example: if the liberal man gives a cup that costs a hundred gold coins, he looks to the usefulness and price of the cup; but the magnificent man, if he gives the same cup, looks not so much to its usefulness as to the excellence of the workmanship, and to how far the gift is consistent with fitness. (6) The sixth condition is that, although the magnificent man exceeds the measure of liberality in making expenses, he will nevertheless observe various circumstances, as the liberal man does in giving; otherwise he would degenerate into the vices opposed to it.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Magnificentia est virtus, quæ versatur circa opes, non tamen sicut Liberalis circa quaslibet & modicas, sed circa magnas tantum.
units.tr: 1. Magnificence is a virtue concerned with wealth, yet not, as Liberality is, with any and every modest sum, but with great sums only.

units.la: 2. Magnificentia nihil aliud denotat, quam in magnitudine aut rebus magnis decorum magnum.
units.tr: 2. Magnificence signifies nothing other than great fittingness in great matters or in magnitude.

units.la: 3. Omnis Magnificus est Liberalis, sed non econtra.
units.tr: 3. Every magnificent man is liberal, but not conversely.

units.la: 4. Magnificus instar hominis scientifici quid, quibus & quantum expendere debeat, novit.
units.tr: 4. The magnificent man, like a man of learning, knows on what and how much he ought to spend.

units.la: 5. Magnifici sumtus, ut sunt magni & decori, sic etiam ejus actiones tales esse debent.
units.tr: 5. As the magnificent man's expenses are great and fitting, so his actions too ought to be of this kind.

units.la: 6. Magnificus non tantum honestatis & voluptatis gratia aliquid modicè expendit, sed etiam fusè & in magna copia.
units.tr: 6. The magnificent man spends something modestly not only for the sake of honour and pleasure, but also lavishly and in great abundance.

units.la: 7. Magnificus non tam precium aut præstantiam rei, quam pulchritudinem & decorum spectat.
units.tr: The magnificent man regards not so much the price or excellence of a thing as its beauty and fitness.

units.la: 8. Quicquid verè & magnificè fit, id magna plerunque admiratione dignum esse solet.
units.tr: Whatever is done truly and magnificently is usually worthy of great admiration.

units.la: Notandum nomen Magnificentia male iis attri- bui, qui in aliquo honoris gradu constituti sunt, ver- bi gratia: qui magistratum aut munus in Repub. ge- runt: nam proprie iis tantum competit, qui in ma- gnis sumtibus erogandis mediocritatem cum deco- ro servant. Differt verò Magnificentia à Liberalita- te in tribus: 1. Quod in sumtibus magnis cum deco- ro consistat; Liberalitas verò non. 2. Cum Libera- litas in dando & accipiendo consistat. Magnificen- tia in sumtibus solum faciendis munus exercet suū. 3. Poterit esse aliquis Magnificus in se & suos, dum verbi gratia: ædificat ædes amplas, hortos, pomaria, & ejusmodi sibi & posteris parat; in Liberalitate verò hoc fieri, sicut supra ostendimus, non potest.
units.tr: It should be noted that the name Magnificence is wrongly applied to those who hold some rank of honour, for example those who bear a magistracy or office in the commonwealth; for properly it belongs only to those who, in spending large sums, keep the mean together with fittingness. Magnificence differs from Liberality in three respects: (1) that it consists in large expenses together with fittingness, whereas Liberality does not; (2) that Liberality consists in giving and receiving, whereas Magnificence exercises its office in making expenses only; (3) that a man may be magnificent towards himself and his own, as when he builds a spacious house, gardens and orchards, and provides such things for himself and his posterity; but in Liberality this cannot be done, as we have shown above.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DIFFICULTIES.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Magnificentia possit dici virtus, cum omnis virtus in mediocritate sit posita, ut ex cap. 7. lib. 2. hu- jus operis patet. At Magnificentia non consistit in mediocri- tate. Nam excedit Liberalitatem. Ideo aut Liberalitas non erit virtus, aut Magnificentia, quæ ipsam excedit, virtus dici non potest? Resp. Per inficiationem minoris. Nam etsi excedat Liberalitatem, Mediocritatem tamen, in qua consistit virtus, non excedit; nam excedit tan- tum, quoad exigentiam & splendorem ornatus & decori, non verò quoad essentiam & naturam virtutis. Dein excedit in modo objecti, non verò in modo rectæ rationis, quam exactissimè & justissimè juxta ac liberelitas tenet.
units.tr: I. Whether Magnificence can be called a virtue, since every virtue is placed in the mean, as is clear from ch. 7 of book 2 of this work. But Magnificence does not consist in a mean, for it exceeds Liberality. So either Liberality will not be a virtue, or Magnificence, which exceeds it, cannot be called a virtue? Reply: I deny the minor premise. For although it exceeds Liberality, it does not exceed the mean in which virtue consists. It exceeds only in the amount and splendour of its ornament and decorum, not in the essence and nature of virtue. Moreover, it exceeds in the mode of its object, but not in the mode of right reason, which Magnificence holds as exactly and justly as Liberality does.

units.la: II. Cur Magnificentiam distinguat à Liberalitate, cum unum idemque sit utriusque objectum, idem etiam usus; nam utraque in dando & largiendo consistit? Resp. Nomen Liberalitatis bifariam accipi: 1. Late pro omni virtute, quæ versatur circa opes, ut apud Aristotelem 3. Eudem. cap. 2. & sic non distinguitur Magnificentia à Liberalitate. 2. Strictè pro virtute, quæ versatur circa opes tantum modicas, & sic distinguitur à Magnificentia; nam etsi idem sit utriusque objectum, modus tamen quo versantur circa hoc objectum ipsas differre facit, neque usus Magnificentiæ tam in dando & largiendo consistit, quam in sumtu recte & ritè faciendo.
units.tr: II. Why does he distinguish Magnificence from Liberality, when the object of both is the same and their use is the same too, since both consist in giving and bestowing? Reply: The name of Liberality is taken in two ways. (1) In a broad sense, for every virtue concerned with wealth, as in Aristotle, Eudem. cap. 2 of book 3; and in this sense Magnificence is not distinguished from Liberality. (2) In a strict sense, for the virtue concerned only with modest means; and in this sense it is distinguished from Magnificence. For although the object of each is the same, the manner in which they deal with this object makes them differ. Nor does the use of Magnificence consist so much in giving and bestowing as in spending rightly and properly.

units.la: III. An hoc possit consistere cum veritate quod dicit Philosophus omnem Magnificum esse Liberalem, sed non econtra. Nam si ad Magnificentiam necessario requiratur Liberalitas, tunc Liberalitas nihil aliud erit, quam prævia dispositio ad ipsam Magnificentiam. At hoc videtur absurdum, cum aque sit perfecta virtus ac ipsa Magnificentia? Resp. Magnificentiam considerari duobus modis, vel ratione subjecti, vel objecti. Ratione subjecti necessario requiritur prævia Liberalitas, & hoc innuit Philosophus, cum dicit, omnem Magnificum esse Liberalem, nempe ut cui insit Magnificentia præstans & excellens in summo gradu virtus circa opes, eidem etiam insit virtus minus præstans: At ratione objecti non requiritur Liberalitas tanquam præcedens dispositio ad Magnificentiam, quia ut Magnificentia versatur circa opes magnas suo quidem modo, sic etiam Liberalitas beralitas circa opes modicas, & à modo, quo versa-tur, diversam habet naturam & definitionem ad ipsam Magnificentiam.
units.tr: III. Can it be true, as the Philosopher says, that every magnificent man is liberal, but not conversely? For if Liberality is necessarily required for Magnificence, then Liberality will be nothing other than a preliminary disposition towards Magnificence itself. But this seems absurd, since it is as perfect a virtue as Magnificence itself? Reply: Magnificence may be considered in two ways, either with respect to its subject or with respect to its object. With respect to the subject, Liberality is necessarily required as a preceding disposition, and the Philosopher hints at this when he says that every magnificent man is liberal: namely, that the one in whom Magnificence, a virtue excelling and eminent to the highest degree in wealth, is present, must also have the less excellent virtue. But with respect to the object, Liberality is not required as a preceding disposition towards Magnificence. For just as Magnificence deals with great wealth in its own way, so Liberality deals with modest wealth, and by the manner in which it deals it has a different nature and definition from Magnificence itself.

units.la: IV. An etiam hoc verum sit, Magnificentiam esse praestantiorem & excellentiorem virtutem Liberalitate, cum bonum, quo est communius eo sit melius, ut ex c. 1. lib. 1. hujus operis, tum etiam ex cap. 1. lib. 5. & 3. Topic. cap. 5 patet. At Liberalitas est virtus communior: nam pluribus competit, quam Magnificentia, etiam pauperibus: at Magnificentia non, ut ex sequenti cap. patebit. Proinde male dicitur à Philosopho praestantior virtus Magnificentia quam Liberalitas? Resp. Aliquid communius dici duobus modis: vel respectu frequentioris actionis, & sic Liberalitas est communior quam Magnificentia; vel respectu insigniors usus, & sic Magnificentia poterit dici virtus praestantior Liberalitate, quia usus habet maximè insignes in Republ. In summa Magnificentia virtus est praestantior Liberalitate quatuor de causis: 1. propter magnitudinem rei seu objecti circa quod versatur. 2. propter dignitatem personae agentis, quae debet esse vel Rex, vel princeps, aut aliquis in honore & autoritate constitutus, ut ex sequentibus patebit. 3. propter splendorem actionis, quae tota decorum respicit. 4. propter usum, qui est plerunque totius civitatis.
units.tr: IV. Is it also true that Magnificence is a more excellent and outstanding virtue than Liberality, since the good which is more common is better, as is clear from ch. 1 of book 1 of this work, and also from ch. 1 of book 5 and ch. 5 of book 3 of the Topics? But Liberality is the more common virtue, for it applies to more people, even the poor, whereas Magnificence does not, as will be clear from the following chapter. Therefore the Philosopher wrongly calls Magnificence a more excellent virtue than Liberality? Reply: Something may be called more common in two ways: either with respect to the more frequent action, and in this sense Liberality is more common than Magnificence; or with respect to the more distinguished use, and in this sense Magnificence can be called a more excellent virtue than Liberality, because its uses are most distinguished in the commonwealth. In sum, Magnificence is a more excellent virtue than Liberality for four reasons: (1) because of the greatness of the matter or object with which it deals; (2) because of the dignity of the acting person, who must be a king, a prince, or someone placed in honour and authority, as will be clear from what follows; (3) because of the splendour of the action, which looks entirely to decorum; (4) because of its use, which generally extends to the whole state.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: SEquitur secunda pars hujus posterioris membri de Magnificentia, in qua postquam egit de materia & variis conditionibus, quae requiruntur ad Magnificentiam, agit statim de effectus seu operationibus
units.tr: This is the second part of this latter member on Magnificence. Having first treated its matter and the various conditions required for Magnificence, the author now turns straight to its effects or operations.

units.la: ejusdem. Partes capitis sunt duae: In prima, ut melius innotescat natura magnificentiae, distinguit genera impensarum seu sumtuum, quos facit Magnificus: In secunda, de persona magnifici, seu qualis debeat esse magnificus agit. In prima igitur impensas sic distinguit, ut aliae sint sacrae, aliae prophanae. Impensae sacrae sunt, quae in usus sacros propter cultum divinum a magnifico instituuntur, ut sunt donaria in aedes sacras seu templa, in hostias & sacrificia, in omnia ea denique, quae in Dei cultum & honorem fiunt. Hac Magnificentia excelluit Athenis Pericles, t ste Plutarcho, Romae Augustus Caesar, ut testis est Suetonius in vita ipsius. Talis etiam fuit structura sumtuosissima templi Dei a Salomone exstructi, 1.Reg.cap.6. Tales etiam sumtus fuerunt, Constantini Magni in aedes sacras Constantinopolitanas, ut refert Nicephorus, lib. 7.Eccles. histor.cap.49. Impensae profanae sunt, quae in opera profana seu non sacra a magnifico, propter cultum civilem instituuntur, & sunt duplices: vel enim sunt publicae, vel privatae, publicae sunt, quae in usum & commodum publicum fiunt. Sic plurimi Imperatores, Reges, Principes, aliique magnifici partim urbes fundasse & instituisse, partim renovasse, ornamentis & rebus variis locupletasse dicuntur. Sic Alexander Magnus Alexandriam de suo nomine in Aegypto condidit, testibus Ariano, Curtio & Plutarcho: Sic Constantinus Magnus urbe ad pontum Euxinum Byzantium de suo nomine Constantinopolin vocavit, ut refert Niceph.lib. 7.cap.48. Sic etiam non finis causa gloriari solebat Augustus Caesar, Romam lateritiam ... teritiam se accepisse, marmoream relinquere, ut autor est Pontanus in lib. de Magnific. cap. 22. Similia his sunt propugnacula, aquæ ductus, epulæ publicæ, theatra, spectacula, triremes, cæteraque ejusmodi, quæ & in usum & utilitatem totius civitatis à Magnifico fiunt. Impensæ privatæ sunt, quæ in opera privata fiunt, utpote quæ ad ipsum Magnificum aut posteros spectant, ut sunt ædificia privata, magnificè extructa, vestes, vasa, supellex aurea & argentea, horti amoeni, & id genus alia. Tale fuit ædificium Regis Salomonis, quod 1. Reg. cap. 6. exstruxisse dicitur. Tale etiam fuit palatium Constantini, quod Niceph. illum condidisse refert. Et ratio redditur à Philosopho ut hoc loco, sic etiam 3. Eadem. cap. 9. quia cum decorum proprie sit magnifici, quicquid splendorem & ornatum sferri possit, id proprium etiam erit Magnifici: Ideo quæcunque fiunt à Magnifico etiam privatim magnificè & splendidè fieri debent.
units.tr: The chapter has two parts. In the first, so that the nature of magnificence may be better understood, he distinguishes the kinds of expenses that the magnificent man makes. In the second, he deals with the person of the magnificent man, or what kind of man he ought to be. In the first part, then, he divides expenses so that some are sacred and others profane. Sacred expenses are those which the magnificent man incurs for sacred uses, for the worship of God, such as gifts to sacred buildings or temples, for victims and sacrifices, and, in short, for everything done for the worship and honour of God. Pericles excelled in this magnificence at Athens, according to Plutarch; at Rome, Augustus Caesar did so, as Suetonius witnesses in his life. Such was also the most sumptuous construction of the temple of God built by Solomon, 1.Reg.cap.6. Such also were the expenses of Constantine the Great on sacred buildings at Constantinople, as Nicephorus reports, lib. 7.Eccles. histor.cap.49. Profane expenses are those which the magnificent man incurs, for the sake of civil life, on profane or non-sacred works. They are of two kinds, for they are either public or private. Public expenses are those made for public use and benefit. Thus many emperors, kings, princes and other magnificent men are said to have founded and established cities, or to have rebuilt them and enriched them with ornaments and various goods. Thus Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in Egypt, named after himself, as Arrian, Curtius and Plutarch attest. Thus Constantine the Great called the city on the Black Sea Byzantium, after his own name Constantinople, as Nicephorus reports, lib. 7.cap.48. So also Augustus Caesar was accustomed to boast, not without reason, that he had received Rome of brick ... and was leaving it of marble, as Pontanus is the authority in lib. de Magnific. cap. 22. Similar to these are bulwarks, aqueducts, public feasts, theatres, shows, triremes, and other things of this kind, which the magnificent man provides for the use and utility of the whole city. Private expenses are those made on private works, namely those which concern the magnificent man himself or his descendants, such as private buildings splendidly constructed, clothing, vessels, gold and silver furniture, pleasant gardens, and things of that kind. Such was the building of King Solomon, which 1. Reg. cap. 6. says he built. Such also was the palace of Constantine, which Nicephorus reports he built. The reason is given by the Philosopher in this place, and likewise 3. Eadem. cap. 9.: because decorum is properly the magnificent man's, whatever can bring splendour and ornament will also be proper to him. Therefore whatever the magnificent man does should be done magnificently and splendidly, even in private.

units.la: Ad privatos etiam sumptus spectant ea, quæ raro fiunt, ut sunt impensæ, quæ fiunt in nuptiis, in dignitatis aut magistratus ingressu, aut funere, tum etiam quæ in hospitalitate exercenda impenduntur, de qua Theophrastus in lib. de divitiis fusè, Cic. 2. offic. vide etiam Keckerm. pag. 269. fyst. Eth. In summa opera Magnifici debent esse, quæcunque demum illa sint, & diuturniora & magis durabilia & in iis potissimum eloborare debet, propter duas potissimum rationes: 1. Quia splendidiora, & majori plerumque admiratione digna esse solent. 2. Quia nominis immortalitas (cujus veluti rei splendidæ inprimis studiosus debet esse Magnificus,) ex his conservatur, & ad posteros propagatur, de quibus fusè & per exempla docet Pontanus lib. de Magnificentia cap. 9. Sumtus etiam diuturniores magis ad magnificum spectant, & tales potius facere debet, quam eos qui citissimè pereunt, verbi gratia: Magis sumtus facere debet in templis, xenodochiis, aut moenibus urbis condendis, quam in spectaculis aut ludis publicis exhibendis, propter prædictas rationes.
units.tr: Among private expenses are also those which are made rarely, such as outlays at weddings, at the entry into a dignity or office, or at a funeral, and also those spent in exercising hospitality, on which Theophrastus writes at length in his book on wealth; see Cicero, 2 De officiis; see also Keckermann, p. 269, Systema Ethicae. In sum, the works of the magnificent man, whatever they may be, should be more lasting and more durable, and he should labour chiefly on these, for two main reasons: 1. because they are usually more splendid and more worthy of great admiration; 2. because the immortality of a name, of which the magnificent man should above all be eager as of something splendid, is preserved by these works and handed down to posterity. Pontanus teaches this at length and by examples, lib. de Magnificentia cap. 9. Lasting expenses also pertain more to the magnificent man, and he ought to make such rather than those which perish very quickly. For example, for the reasons stated, he ought to spend more on building temples, hospitals or city walls than on presenting shows or public games.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de persona Magnifici seu qualis debeat esse magnificus: & duas conditiones requirit in magnifico. 1. est: ut sit dives sive opera sua & industria, sive propinquorum & majorum opibus & labore fiat: nisi enim dives sit, sumtus quos requirit magnificentia facere non poterit. 2. conditio est, ut sit vir clarus & illustris ex nobili aut illustri familia, aut saltem in dignitate aliqua & magistratu constitutus: nam etsi opibus abundet, nisi dignitate, generis splendore, aut virtute cæteris antecellat: non poterit sumtibus suis decus & splendorem addere, siquidem dignitas, splendor, & decorum magnificentiæ individui sunt comites. Quare nullus pauper poterit dici magnificus, utpote cui desunt copiæ seu facultates ad sumtus faciendos, etsi quid magnificum suscipere velit, (quod plerunque facere conantur homines gloriosi,) non tam magnificus, quam stultus dici meretur, quippe qui contra honestatem & decorum in sumtibus faciendis aliquid attentet. Eadem ratio erit hominis plebei, quantumvis copiosi, qui si voler supra vires & conditionem suam magnificentiam affectare, ridiculus potius & odiosus erit, quam verè magnificus. Talis fuit fui: Lycinius quidam Romanus, qui cum nec genere, nec autoritate valeret, quia tamen opibus abundabat, marmoreum tumulum sibi exstruendum curavit: unde illum falsè ridet Martialis: Marmoreo Lycinius tumulo jacet, at Cato parvo Pompeius nullo, credimus esse Deos.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the person of the magnificent man, or what kind of man he should be, and he requires two conditions in the magnificent man. The first is that he be rich, whether his wealth comes from his own effort and industry or from the resources and labour of relatives and ancestors; for unless he is rich, he cannot make the expenses that magnificence requires. The second condition is that he be a distinguished and illustrious man, from a noble or famous family, or at least placed in some dignity or office.
