For even if he abounds in wealth, unless he surpasses others in dignity, splendour of birth or virtue, he will not be able to add grace and splendour to his expenses, since dignity, splendour and decorum are the inseparable companions of magnificence. Hence no poor man can be called magnificent, since he lacks the means or resources to make expenses. Even if he wishes to undertake something magnificent, which vainglorious men usually try to do, he deserves to be called not so much magnificent as foolish, since he attempts something against propriety and decorum in making his expenses. The same reasoning applies to a plebeian, however wealthy he may be: if he wishes to aspire to magnificence beyond his strength and condition, he will be ridiculous and hateful rather than truly magnificent. Such was a certain Roman, Lycinius, who, since he had neither birth nor authority, yet abounded in wealth, had a marble tomb built for himself. Hence Martial mocks him, though wrongly: "Lycinius lies in a marble tomb, but Cato in a small one and Pompey in none; we believe there are gods."

units.la: Notandum tamen cum Philosophus negat pauperem dici posse magnificum, id non de omni paupere intelligendum esse. Nam pauper sumitur duobus modis: 1. Pro homine indigente solum, & hic poterit dici magnificus, quod habitum animi quamvis adversæ fortunæ flatu, opibus ad exercendam magnificentiam careat, qualis fuit Priamus: aliqui Reges & Principes Regnis & fortunis exuti.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that when the Philosopher denies that a poor man can be called magnificent, this is not to be understood of every poor man. For "poor" is taken in two ways: 1. for a man who is merely in need. Such a man can be called magnificent, since, although he lacks the wealth to exercise magnificence because of the blast of adverse fortune, he has a generous state of mind. Priam was such a man, as were some kings and princes stripped of their realms and fortunes.

units.la: 2. Sumitur nomen pauperis pro homine, cui & animus excelsus & opes etiam desunt, & hic non poterit dici magnificus propter tres causas: 1. Quia non habet materiam, in quam agat: 2. Nullum habet usum, utpote cui nihil, unde addiscceret, suppetit: 3. Quia ignorat agere secundum habitum, quem nunquam contraxit.
units.tr: 2. The name of poor is taken for a man who lacks both a lofty spirit and wealth. Such a man cannot be called magnificent, for three reasons: (1) he has no material on which to act; (2) he has no opportunity for practice, since he has nothing from which he could learn; (3) he does not know how to act according to a habit which he has never acquired.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Omnes sumtus magnificentia verè honesti & laudabiles sunt, quippe qui in honestos & laudabiles usus conferuntur.
units.tr: 1. All expenditure of magnificence that is truly honourable and praiseworthy is so, since it is directed to honourable and praiseworthy uses.

units.la: 2. Maximè laudantur illi sumtus, qui in Deorum cultum & honorem erogantur, utpote qui hominum imprimis gratitudinem declarent.
units.tr: 2. Those expenses are most praised which are spent on the worship and honour of God, since they chiefly declare gratitude to men.

units.la: 3. In magnifico considerari duo debent, 1. quis sit, 2. qualis sit, id est, quas opes aut quæ bona habeat. 4. Nullus pauper, propterea quod unde sumtus decorè faciat, non habeat, magnificus dici poterit.
units.tr: 3. In the magnificent man two things must be considered: (1) who he is; (2) what sort he is, that is, what resources or goods he has. 4. No poor man can be called magnificent merely because he has no means from which he could make a fitting outlay.

units.la: 5. Qui aliquid supra vires aut opes aut conditionem suam suscipit, stultus habetur.
units.tr: 5. He who undertakes something beyond his strength, resources or station is held to be foolish.

units.la: 6. Quicquid secundum virtutem fit, id rectè & laudabiliter fit.
units.tr: 6. Whatever is done according to virtue is done rightly and praiseworthily.

units.la: 7. Magnificus debet esse opibus, vel a se vel majorum labore partis instructus: debet item vir esse clarus & illustris in aliqua dignitate, aut eminentia aut magistratu constitutus.
units.tr: 7. The magnificent man ought to be furnished with wealth, either acquired by himself or gained by the labour of his ancestors; he ought likewise to be a man renowned and illustrious, either in some dignity, eminence, or office of magistracy.

units.la: 8. Magnificus debet esse hospitalis & promtus admodum in muneribus dandis, & remunerationibus exercendis.
units.tr: 8. The magnificent man ought to be hospitable and very ready in giving gifts and in bestowing rewards.

units.la: 9. Debet etiam domum habere splendidam & magnificè, pro facultatibus & decoro ornatam.
units.tr: 9. He ought also to have a splendid house, adorned magnificently and in proportion to his means and his dignity.

units.la: 10. Magnificus impendit sumtus in opera maximè durabilia aut diuturniora, tum quia splendorem sapiunt, tum quia nominis etiam immortalitate importANT.
units.tr: 10. The magnificent man spends his money chiefly on works that are most durable or long-lasting, both because these savour of splendour and because they bring with them the immortality of a name.

units.la: 11. Magnificus etsi praparationem decori nihil faciat, alios tamen sumtus in rebus divinis alios in humanis facit.
units.tr: 11. Although the magnificent man does nothing to prepare for fitting display, he nonetheless makes one kind of outlay on divine matters and another on human ones.

units.la: 12. Magnificentissimus ille est, qui in re magna semper est magnus.
units.tr: 12. He is most magnificent who is always great in a great matter.

units.la: 13. Magnificus in quacunque opera sumtus faciat, & semper decorè & digrè & cum recta ratione faciat.
units.tr: 13. Whatever work the magnificent man undertakes in expenditure, he always spends fittingly, becomingly and with right reason.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Cur Philosophus neget pauperem posse dici Magnificum, cum tamen pauper possit esse prudens; & qui est prudens habet omnes virtutes inter se connexas, ut testatur Philosophus lib. 6. hujus operis cap. 7. Cum igitur pauper possit esse prudens, possit esse Magnificus, siquidem prudentia dentia una omnes virtutes continet? Resp. Prudentiam sumi dupliciter 1. Late pro corona omnium virtutum, & sic qui ea prudentia est instructus, habet omnes virtutes, & hoc modo intelligedus est Philosophus loco citato. 2. Stricte pro habitu tantum animi quo rebus recte praesse & sane aliis & nobis ipsis prodesse consilio possimus, & hoc modo pauper posset esse Prudens, nec tamen Magnificus, sed tamen per istam Prudentiam pervenire poterit ad opes & dignitatem, & sic veram exercere magnificentiam.
units.tr: I. Question: Why does the Philosopher deny that a poor man can be called magnificent, when a poor man can still be prudent, and the prudent man has all the virtues linked together, as the Philosopher testifies in Book 6, chapter 7 of this work? If a poor man can be prudent, and prudence alone contains all the virtues, then he could be magnificent. Answer: Prudence is taken in two senses. (1) Broadly, for the crown of all the virtues; and so the one who is equipped with that prudence has all the virtues, and it is in this sense that the Philosopher must be understood in the passage cited. (2) Strictly, for the mere habit of mind by which we can rightly preside over affairs and, by sound counsel, benefit both others and ourselves. In this sense a poor man could be prudent without being magnificent. Yet through this prudence he will be able to attain wealth and dignity, and so exercise true magnificence.

units.la: II. Cur neget Magnificum aliquem posse in seipsum esse, sed tantum in operapublica: cum tamen contrarium supra cap. 4. asseruit, tum etiam hoc capite jubet Magnificum habere domum splendidam, & cetera privata, qua quoque ad splendorem & ornatum Magnificentia spectant. Ergo sibi contrariari videtur Philosophus? Resp. Magnificentiam & sumtus, quos facit Magnificus considerari duobus primario & secundario. Primario nemo poterit in se exercere Magnificentiam, sed necesse est, ut conferat sumtus & vires suas in usum totius civitatis & hoc modo intelligi debet hic Philosophus. Secundario, Magnificentia exercetur in operibus privatis, sed ita tamen, ut ista privata serviant publicis usibus, verbi gratia: hospitalitati, totius civitatis splendori & decoro, & sic intelligendus est Philosophus, cum jubet Magnificam habere domum, & caetera privatim splendida.
units.tr: II. Why does he deny that a magnificent man can be magnificent toward himself, but only in public works, when he asserted the contrary above in chapter 4? And in this chapter too he bids the magnificent man to have a splendid house and other private possessions, which also belong to the splendour and adornment of magnificence. Does the Philosopher therefore seem to contradict himself? Answer: Magnificence and the expenses the magnificent man makes are to be considered in two ways, primarily and secondarily. Primarily, no one can exercise magnificence on himself; he must necessarily bestow his expenses and resources for the use of the whole state, and it is in this way that the Philosopher must be understood here. Secondarily, magnificence is exercised in private works, but in such a way that these private works serve public uses: for example, hospitality, and the splendour and decorum of the whole state. It is in this sense that the Philosopher is to be understood when he bids the magnificent man to have a house and other things privately splendid.

units.la: III. An Magnificus dici possit, qui in divinum cultum sumtus facit, cum tales sumtus ex debito faciat, siquidem omnia bona a Deo habet gratitudine exhibenda. Ergo partem reddere debet. Proinde non tam Magnificentia, qua est vir-tus, tus, & à libera voluntate proficiscitur, quam debitum, siquidem gratitudo hoc necessario requirit, hoc factum dici debet? Resp. Respectu beneficiorum à Deo acceptorum debitum quidem poterit vid r, at respectu facti, quod à libera voluntate proficiscitur, vera Magnificentia dici poterit, liquidem est in hominis voluntate, ut hoc agat, vel non agat, & ab hoc facto Magnifici dicuntur propter tres causas: 1. propter magnos sumtus quos expendunt: nam si decorum observari debeat in Magnificentia, & pro qualitate personæ sumtus sint faciendi, in nullum major sumtus fieri debet, quam in ipsum Deum. 2. propter res magnas quas faciunt: nam hoc etiam in Magnificentia observatur, ut opus personæ qualitati conveniat. 3. propter divinas laudes, quas intendunt & in quibus gratitudinem suam inprimis attestantur.
units.tr: III. Can one be called magnificent who makes expenses for divine worship, since he makes such expenses out of obligation? For he has all his goods from God, and these must be repaid with gratitude; therefore he ought to render a part. Hence, since gratitude necessarily requires this, should this act be called a duty rather than magnificence, which is a virtue and proceeds from free choice? Answer: With respect to the benefits received from God, it may indeed seem a duty; but with respect to the act, which proceeds from free will, it can be called true magnificence, since it lies in a person's will whether he does this or not. And men are called magnificent for this act for three reasons: (1) on account of the great expenses they lay out, for if decorum must be observed in magnificence, and expenses are to be made according to the quality of the person, then no greater expense should be made on anyone than on God himself; (2) on account of the great works they undertake, for this too is observed in magnificence, that the work should suit the quality of the person; (3) on account of the divine praises they intend, and in which they especially attest their gratitude.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: SEquitur tertia & ultima pars huius posterioris membri de Magnificentia, in qua agit de extremis ejusdem, de quibus supra egerat cap.8 lib.2.huius operis. Partes capitis sunt tres: In primo agit de altero extremo Magnificentiæ, quod opponitur ei in excessu quod Latinè dicitur Luxus seu Luxuria: Secunda agit de extremo, quod ei contrariatur in defectu, & dicitur Sordes seu Sordiditas: In tertia ostendit ista vitia non esse gravi admodum reprehensione digna. In prima igitur agit de Luxu, quod vitium est in magnis sumtibus indecore, & præter rationem excedens, cujus duas notas seu proprietates, quarum 1. sumitur à sumtibus, qui fiunt. 2. à fine cur fiant. I. Nota est hæc, quod qui hoc vitio sit præditus, in rebus parvis nugatoriis & indignis magnos sumatus, in magnis verò, & ubi oportet magnos sumtus facere, parvos faciat sumtus: & duo adfert exempla Philosophus: 1. est, ut si quis familiares & sodales suos cœna quotidiaria & communi excepturus convivio prorsus nuptiali exciperet. Alterum exemplum est de Megarensibus quorum is fuit luxus & ineptia potius, ut theatra, quæ pellibus tantum hœdinis aut id generis animalium intedi solebant, panno coccineo aut purpura intenderent. Idem etiam luxus reprehenditur in Verre act. 2. in Verrem, quod tentoria sua preciosis linteis insterneret. Idem etiam luxus Romæ percrebuit, de quo admodum graviter conqueritur Plinius lib. 19. cap. 1. quod nimirum ab hoc luxu labascere ceperint vires imperii Romani. Exemplum hujus immanissimi luxus insigne fuit in Regibus Ægyptiacis, qui Pyramides illas inter septem orbis miraculanotissimas condiderunt, quas Plinius lib. 36. cap. 12. vocat Regum pecuniæ stultam & otiosam ostentationem, quarum unam prægrandem 16000 millia hominum annis 20. constrvxisse refert: Reliquæ inquit, tres factæ sunt annis 74. pro alio & cœpis in operarios collatis impensa tunc 1080. talenta magna, quæ faciunt 115000. ducatorum Ungaricorum. Altera proprietas Luxus seu Luxuriosi est, quod non honestatis (quod quivis virtute præditus facere solet) sed ostentationis gratia sumtus faciat. Talis describitur a Luciano Nigrinus quidā Athenien-sis, quem vulgò Athenis propter ostentationem &c. & superbiam vocabant Pavonem, & oftētator pul-cherrimè describitur lib. 4. ad Heren. Tales fuerunt etiam Imperatores quidam Romani, ut Antonius Caracalla, qui ostentationis gratia 100. aprosin una cœna inter convivas distribuit. Sic etiâ Vitellius ut refert Sueton.in ejus vita 7000. avium, 2000. piscium in uno convivio amicis apposuit. Talis etiam Gajus Caligula, qui teste Lampridio pomis ac floribus gemas immiscuisse, & quantum ciborum convivis apposuerat, tantum per fenestros ejecisse dicitur, ut munificentiam aut potius luxuriam populo Romano ostentaret. In secunda parte capitis agit de altero extremo, quod opponitur Magnificētiæ in defectu nempe de sordibus seu sorditate, quod vitium est in sumtibus magnis indecorè deficiens, & quinque affert notas seu proprietates hujus vitii. 1. Quod qui hoc vitio laboret, minores semper, quâ deceat sumtus faciat. 2. Quod etsi interdū magnos sumtus faciat, in re tamen minuta & nullius penè momenti animum degenerem & sordes suas prodat. 3. Quod non promto hilariq;ue animo, sed ægrè admodum sumtus faciat. 4. Quod hoc sedulò semper agat, ut minima expendat. 5. Quod etsi minima expendat semper putet, se plus æquo expendere. Breviter committitur hoc vitium Sordiditatis, cum in magnis & splendidis operibus intempestiva adhibetur parsimonia, ut nec sumtus operi, nec opus personæ dignitati, respondeat; quod non tantum tum fit, dum opus aliquod inceptum non eodem tenore continuatur, sed etiam cum is, qui Magnificus esse debet, in quavis re mirè parcum se exhibet. Exemplum habet bet Cic.in orat.pro L.Murina,ubi Tuberonem praetura dejectum ostendit, quod dum populo Romano epulũ exhibere vellet, lectos pellibus haedinis straverit,vasa Samia seu figulina apposuerit,cum lectos purpura insternere, & aurea aut argentea vasa ponere debuisset: Odit, inquit Cicero,privatam luxuriam,publicam Magnificentiam diligit,non amat profusas epulas,sordes & inhumunitatem multò minus: distinguit rationem temporum ac officiorum, item vicissitudinem laboris ac voluptatis. In tertia parte capitis distinctis & explicatis jam extremis,docet ista quidem esse vitia, propterea quod aberrationes sint in majus aut minus ab ipso medio,in quo consistit ipsa Virtus,non tamen esse probrosa admodum aut graviore reprehensione digna propter duas rationes: 1. Quia nulli nocent,sed prosunt potius:nam etsi non ut decet, aliquo modo tamé sumtus faciunt,in quibus faciendis beneficium intendũt humano generi. 2.Quia non sunt turpia admodum aut deformia, non per se aut sua natura: nam omne vitium cum sit malum, quod adversatur bono, est turpe in se & deforme,sed respectu extremorũ libertalitatis: nam in luxuria est praetextus quidam decori,licet modum excedat, & in Sordiditate est umbra quaedam honesti, levis admodum, & quae tempori, loco, & personae non satis conveniat.
units.tr: There follows the third and last part of this second member on Magnificence, in which he treats of its extremes, which he had dealt with above in chapter 8 of book 2 of this work. The chapter has three parts. In the first he treats of the one extreme of Magnificence, which is opposed to it in excess and is called in Latin Luxus or Luxuria. The second treats of the extreme which is contrary to it in deficiency, called Sordes or Sordidity. In the third he shows that these vices do not deserve very grave reproof. In the first part, then, he treats of Luxury, which is a vice consisting in great expenditure that is unbecoming and exceeds reason. Its two marks or properties are: first, it is judged by the expenses that are made; second, by the end for which they are made. I. The first mark is this: the man who has this vice spends large sums on trifling, frivolous and unworthy things, but makes small outlays where great ones are needed. The Philosopher gives two examples. The first is of a man who, about to entertain his friends and companions at an ordinary daily dinner, received them with a wholly wedding-feast. The other example concerns the people of Megara, whose extravagance was rather foolishness: they stretched their theatre curtains with scarlet cloth or purple, when they used to be stretched only with goatskins or hides of that kind. The same extravagance is blamed in Verres, in the second speech against Verres, because he spread his tents with costly linen. The same luxury also became widespread at Rome, over which Pliny bitterly complains in book 19, chapter 1: that the strength of the Roman empire began to totter from this luxury. An outstanding example of this most monstrous luxury were the Egyptian kings, who built those pyramids, the most famous of the seven wonders of the world. Pliny, in book 36, chapter 12, calls them a foolish and idle display of royal wealth. He reports that one of them, very large, was built by sixteen thousand men over twenty years. "The other three," he says, "were made in seventy-four years for another purpose, and the expense, reckoned on the workmen's wages, was then 1080 great talents, which make 115,000 Hungarian ducats." The second property of the luxurious or extravagant man is that he makes his expenditure not for honour (which any virtuous person usually does) but for the sake of display. Such a man is described by Lucian in the person of a certain Athenian named Nigrinus, whom the people of Athens, on account of his display and pride, commonly called the Peacock. A vain man is also excellently described in the fourth book of the Herennius. There were also certain Roman emperors of this kind, such as Antoninus Caracalla, who, for the sake of display, distributed a hundred ostriches among the guests at a single dinner. So too Vitellius, as Suetonius reports in his life, set before his friends at one banquet seven thousand birds and two thousand fish. Such also was Gaius Caligula, who, according to Lampridius, is said to have mixed gems with fruit and flowers, and to have thrown out of the windows as much food as he had set before the guests, to display his generosity, or rather his extravagance, to the Roman people. In the second part of the chapter he treats of the other extreme, which is opposed to Magnificence in deficiency, namely meanness or stinginess. This is a vice of failing, in great expenditure, in a way that is unbecoming; and he gives five marks or properties of this vice. 1. The man who suffers from it always spends less than is fitting. 2. Even if he sometimes spends large sums, yet in a small and almost worthless matter he betrays his base spirit and his meanness. 3. He spends not with a ready and cheerful mind, but very grudgingly. 4. He takes great pains always to spend as little as possible. 5. Even when he spends very little, he always thinks he is spending more than is right. Briefly, the vice of Sordidity is committed when untimely thrift is applied to great and splendid works, so that neither the expense corresponds to the work nor the work to the dignity of the person. This happens not only when some undertaking that has been begun is not carried on in the same spirit, but also when the man who ought to be magnificent shows himself very sparing in every matter. Cicero gives an example in his speech for L. Murena, where he shows that Tubero was rejected from the praetorship because, when he wished to give a feast to the Roman people, he spread couches with goatskins and set out Samian or earthenware vessels, whereas he ought to have spread the couches with purple and set out gold or silver vessels. "He hates," says Cicero, "private luxury, he loves public magnificence; he does not love lavish feasts, and much less meanness and inhumanity:" he distinguishes the reason of times and duties, and likewise the alternation of labour and pleasure. In the third part of the chapter, having now distinguished and explained the extremes, he teaches that these are indeed vices, because they are departures in excess or defect from the mean itself, in which virtue consists; yet they are not very shameful or deserving of graver reproof, for two reasons: 1. Because they harm no one but rather benefit: for although they make expenditure not as it ought to be, still in some way they spend, and in spending they intend a benefit to mankind. 2. Because they are not altogether base or deformed, not in themselves or by their nature: for every vice, since it is an evil that opposes the good, is in itself base and deformed; but with respect to the extremes of liberality it is otherwise. For in luxury there is a certain pretext of decorum, though it exceeds the measure; and in sordidity there is a certain shadow of honour, very slight, and one that does not sufficiently suit the time, place and person.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Luxuriosus supra decorum sumtus semper facit.
units.tr: 1. The luxurious man always spends beyond what is fitting.

units.la: 2. Luxuriosus in rebus parvis magnos facit sumtus, & splendorem indecore seu praeter rationem affectat.
units.tr: 2. The luxurious man, in small matters, makes large outlays and affects a splendour that is unbecoming or beyond reason.

units.la: 3. Non honestatis,sed ostentationis gratia sumtus facere solet.
units.tr: 3. He is accustomed to make outlays not for the sake of honour but for the sake of display.

units.la: 4. Luxuriosus ubi pauca debet expendere, multa expendit, ubi vero multa pauca tantum.
units.tr: 4. Where the luxurious man ought to spend little, he spends much; where he ought to spend much, he spends only a little.

units.la: 5. Sordidus in omnibus prater rationem deficit, & sicubi sumtus facit, splendorem tamen & honestatem prorsus negligit.
units.tr: 5. The stingy man falls short in everything beyond reason, and wherever he does make an outlay, he utterly neglects splendour and honour.

units.la: 6. Sordidus non grato & hilari animo, sed agro & difficili semper aliquid expendit.
units.tr: 6. The stingy man never spends anything with a glad and cheerful mind, but always with a sour and grudging one.

units.la: 7. Sordidus etsi minimum expendat, putat tamen se plus aquo semper expendere.
units.tr: 7. Although the stingy man spends the least, he still thinks he always spends more than is right.

units.la: 8. Vitia ista non sunt probrosa admodum aut summa plane reprehensione digna, cum nulli noceant, minusque a decoro recedant.
units.tr: 8. These vices are not very shameful or deserving of the strongest censure, since they harm no one and depart less from what is fitting.

units.la: Hinc quaeritur: An verum sit, quod dicit Philosophus extrema ista Magnificentia non esse gravi reprehensione digna, cum sint vitia, & quaecunque talia sunt, quia contrariantur bono, reprehensione certe digna sunt? Resp. Per se quidem & absolute esse reprehensione digna; sed comparate, si conferantur cum extremis aliarum virtutum, praesertim cum extremis Liberalitatis, in quibus non est tantum benefaciendi studium, magisque ab omni honestatis praetextu receditur, gravem reprehensionem non merari dicuntur ista vitia. Secundo Philosophus videtur sequutus vulgi opinionem; nam vulgo sic excusari solent ista vitia, ut in luxu dicatur inesse amor quidam benefaciendi generi humano: in Sordiditate sit cura quaedam conservandi res suas, siquidem parsimonia, ut inquit Cicero, magni instar vectigalis esse solet. Et tertio demum reprehensio sumitur duobus modis: 1. Late & sic ista vitia non carent sua reprehensione. 2. Stricte pro tali reprehensione, cui innexa sit infamia, & sic graviorem reprehensionem non videntur mereri, propter rationes supra allatas.
units.tr: Hence the question is asked: Is it true, as the Philosopher says, that these extremes of Magnificence do not deserve serious reproach, since they are vices, and whatever is of this kind certainly deserves reproach because it is opposed to good? Answer: in themselves and absolutely they do deserve reproach; but comparatively, when they are set beside the extremes of other virtues, especially the extremes of Liberality, in which there is not merely a zeal for doing good and one departs further from every pretext of honour, these vices are said not to merit grave reproach. Secondly, the Philosopher seems to have followed the opinion of the common people, for among the people these vices are usually excused in this way: that in luxury there is said to be a certain love of doing good to mankind, and in stinginess a certain care for preserving one's own goods, since thrift, as Cicero says, is usually like a great source of revenue. And thirdly, finally, reproach is taken in two ways: 1. broadly, and in this sense these vices are not free of their reproach; 2. strictly, for such reproach as has infamy attached to it, and in this sense they do not seem to deserve a more serious reproach, for the reasons adduced above.

units.la: Coronidis loco & haec quaestio poterit adjici; Ad quam scilicet virtutem cardinalem cum quatuor vulgo numerentur virtutes cardinales, ut fusè lib. 6. conclus. c.17. docet Savanarola, referri debet Liberalitas & Magnificentia: Nam cum haec quatuor Temperantia scilicet, Justitia, Fortitudo, Prudentia sola cardinales habeantur virtutes, quaeritur ad quam istarum quatuor sint referenda? De hac te diversi entes sunt Philosophorum opiniones; Donatus Acciulus ad lib. 4. Nicom. Arist. cap 2. putat referendas esse ad Temperantiam propter duas potissimum rationes: 1. est, quia sicut Liberalitas & Magnificentia versantur circa cupiditatem pecuniarum, sic Temperantia circa cupiditatem voluptatum corporis. Ergo cum objecto interno cupiditatibus nempe convenire videantur, uno foedere facile conjungi possunt. 2. ratio est: quia Temperantia, teste Cicerone 2. Tusc. complectitur sub se omnes virtutes. Ergo etiam & Liberalitatem & Magnificentiam. Sed hae rationes non sunt tanti ponderis, ut hanc opinionem stabiliant. Nam quod ad primam, etsi utraque haec virtus versetur circa cupiditates, aliae tamen sunt cupiditates circa quas versatur Temperantia, aliae circa quas Liberalitas: Proinde neque objecto interno conveniunt. Quod ad secundam, etsi in omnibus virtutibus sit quaedam affectuum moderatio, quam vulgo Cicero Temperantiam vocat, Temperantiae vocabulo late accepto; non sequitur tamen omnes virtutes Temperantiae proprie dictae subesse, proinde neque Liberalitas.
units.tr: As a crowning point, this question too may be added: to which cardinal virtue should Liberality and Magnificence be referred? For though four cardinal virtues are commonly counted, as Savanarola teaches at length in book 6, conclusion 17, and since only these four are held to be the cardinal virtues, namely Temperance, Justice, Fortitude and Prudence, it is asked to which of these four they are to be referred. On this point the opinions of the philosophers differ. Donatus Acciaiuolus, on book 4 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 2, thinks they should be referred to Temperance, for two principal reasons: 1. because just as Liberality and Magnificence are concerned with the desire for money, so Temperance is concerned with the desire for bodily pleasures; therefore, since they seem to agree in their internal object, namely the desires, they can easily be joined under one bond. 2. The reason is that Temperance, as Cicero says in the second book of the Tusculan Disputations, embraces all the virtues under itself; therefore it embraces Liberality and Magnificence too. But these reasons are not of such weight as to establish this opinion. For as to the first, although each of these virtues is concerned with desires, nevertheless the desires with which Temperance is concerned are one set, and those with which Liberality is concerned are another; therefore they do not agree in their internal object. As to the second, although in all the virtues there is a certain moderation of the affections, which Cicero commonly calls Temperance, taking the word Temperance in its broad sense, it does not follow that all the virtues are subordinate to Temperance properly so called, and therefore neither is Liberality.

units.la: Ee 2 Liberalitas ralitatem. Secunda opinio est ipsius Savanarolæ, qui lib.cit.conclu. 42. Justitiæ dicit annexam esse Liberalitatem & Magnificentiam, cui adstipulatur eriam Cicero 2.offic. & triplex hæc ratio evincere videtur: 1. est, quia quemadmodum Justitia exercetur erga alios, sic etiam Liberalitas ad alios se extendit, & cum hoc discrimine, quod Justitia aliis tribuat, quod ipsos proprie spectat; Liberalitas vero, quod sibi proprium est, & de suo aliis communicet. 2. quia quemadmodum Justitia tantum aliis dat, quantum iis secundum proportionem & mensuram debetur: ita etiam Liberalitas hoc præceptum habet, ut aliis pro dignitate & necessitate aliisque circumstantiis largiatur. 3. quia sicut nemo vere Liberalis esse potest, qui non idem fit justus, & sicut nemo modum Liberalitatis excedere potest, qui nō idem fit in se, aut in aliós justus. Ergo cum tantam affinitatem & similitudinem inter se habeant istæ virtutes, altera ad alteram referenda videtur. Notandum tamen sub Justitia universali comprehendi tantum istas virtutes juxta illud; Justitia in sese virtutes continet omnes. Non vero sub particulari, quia natura, objecto & finibus distinguuntur, ut videre est apud Keckerm. lib.1.syst.Ethic.cap.5.& 6. & apud Picol. gradu.4.cap.51. Pro decisione dicendum, sicut diversa sunt objecta & distincta inter se diversarum virtutum, sic istæ virtutes, quæ versantur circa hæc objecta, diversæ & distinctæ sunt inter se, ideo nec una ad aliam commodè referri possit: sed sicut diversæ sunt viæ, quæ in unam aliquam magnam tendunt civitatem, & unaquæque via suos habet ductus &tus & tractus, quibus ab aliis viis distinguitur, sic diversæ & variæ virtutes, etsi inter se distinctæ sunt, ad unam tamen felicitatem & summum hujus vitæ bonum assequendum hominem unanimes ducunt.
units.tr: The second opinion is that of Savanarola himself, who in the book cited, conclusion 42, says that Liberality and Magnificence are annexed to Justice, and Cicero too agrees with him in the second book of De Officiis. This threefold reason seems to establish it: 1. because just as Justice is exercised towards others, so Liberality also extends itself to others, with this difference: Justice gives to others what properly belongs to them, whereas Liberality gives to others what is its own. 2. Because just as Justice gives to others only as much as is due to them according to proportion and measure, so Liberality has this precept, that it bestows on others according to their worth, their need and other circumstances. 3. Because just as no one can be truly liberal who is not at the same time just, so no one can exceed the measure of Liberality who is not at the same time unjust, either towards himself or towards others. Therefore, since these virtues have so great an affinity and resemblance to one another, one seems to be referred to the other. It must be noted, however, that these virtues are comprehended only under universal Justice, according to the saying: Justice contains all the virtues within itself. They are not comprehended under particular justice, for they are distinguished by nature, object and ends, as may be seen in Keckermann, book 1 of the System of Ethics, chapters 5 and 6, and in Piccolomini, grade 4, chapter 51. For the decision it must be said: just as the objects of the different virtues are diverse and distinct from one another, so the virtues that are concerned with these objects are diverse and distinct from one another, and therefore neither can conveniently be referred to the other. But just as there are different roads that lead into one great city, and each road has its own windings, turns and bends by which it is distinguished from the other roads, so diverse and various virtues, although they are distinct from one another, nevertheless lead man in harmony towards attaining one happiness and the highest good of this life.

units.la: II. Quæritur: An vera fuerit Magnificentia in Maximiliano II. Imperatore Romano, qui, ut refert Gaftius tom 2. convivali sermon. juveni, quem 20000. ducatorum decoxisse de sua pecunia norat, non tantum ignovit, sed Abbatiam præterea cum multis reditibus adjecit? Non fuisse vera: Magnificentiam hæ rationes videntur probare: 1. Quia ad oft ntationem, quod luxuriosus facere solet, no ad splendorem & ornatum, quibus Magnificus studet, hoc factum videtur. 2. Quia res fuit peffimi exempli: nam alios incitare poterat ad simile quid tentandum, & magnum detrimentum ærario inferedum, sicut de Hadriano Cæsare legimus, qui cum senem quendam pauperculum in balneo fricantem vidisset, servum illi dedit, à quo fricaretur: post alios hac benignitate licet non pari successu ad hoc faciendum excitavit. Sed tamen veram illustre Magnificentiam in hoc facto Cæsaris sequentes hæ probant rationes: 1. Quia fuit verum Magnificentiæ objectum, nempe sumtus magni in hoc facto. Subjectum etiam verum, nempe persona Imperatoria, quæ possit sumtibus magnis decorem ac splendorem addere. 2. Requisita habuit Magnificentiæ, nempe splendorem & ornatum, tum etiam amorem Cæsari, & benevolentiam apud omnes conciliavit. 3. Insigne fuit clementiæ exemplum in Imperatore & incitamentum juveni ad virtutem amplectendam, dehortamen{*}mentum à desperatione, in quam fortasse præci- pitaffet.
units.tr: II. It is asked whether Magnificence was real in the Roman Emperor Maximilian II, who, as Gastius relates in the second volume of his Convivial Sermons, when he learned that a young man had squandered 20,000 ducats of his own money, not only pardoned him but also added an abbey with many revenues? It was not real Magnificence, for these reasons seem to prove it: 1. because the deed seems to have been done for ostentation, which the luxurious man is accustomed to do, and not for splendour and adornment, which the magnificent man aims at. 2. Because the deed was of the worst example: it could incite others to attempt something similar and inflict great loss on the treasury, just as we read of the Emperor Hadrian, who, when he saw an old, poor man rubbing himself in the bath, gave him a slave to rub him; afterwards he incited others, though not with equal success, to do the same. But the following reasons prove that in this deed of the Emperor there was true and illustrious Magnificence: 1. because there was a true object of Magnificence, namely a great outlay in this deed; and a true subject too, namely the imperial person, who could add decorum and splendour to great outlays. 2. He had the requisites of Magnificence, namely splendour and adornment; moreover he won the Emperor's love and goodwill from all. 3. It was a notable example of clemency in an Emperor, and an incitement to the young man to embrace virtue, and a deterrent from despair, into which he would perhaps have plunged.

units.la: III. An deteriora sint vitia, & majori reprehensione digna extrema Magnificentia, quam extrema Liberalitatis, & minore reprehensione digna videntur Luxus & Sordes, quæ sunt opposita Magnificentia, quam opposita Liberalitatis ex sententia ipsius Aristotelis cap. 6 sub finem & omnium interpretum ad illum locum? Sed contrarium variationes evincunt, nempe deteriora longè esse vitia extrema Magnificentiæ quam Liberalitatis. 1. Ratio est, quia ut canit Poëta:
units.tr: III. Are the extremes of Magnificence worse vices, and more deserving of reproach, than the extremes of Liberality? And do Luxury and Stinginess, which are opposed to Magnificence, seem to deserve less reproach than the opposites of Liberality, according to Aristotle's own opinion in chapter 6, near the end, and that of all the interpreters on that passage? But the contrary is shown by the following arguments, namely that the extremes of Magnificence are by far worse vices than those of Liberality. 1. The reason is that, as the poet sings:

units.la: Tanto animi vitium semper conspectius in se Crimen habet, quanto major qui peccat habetur.
units.tr: The fault of the mind always carries the more glaring guilt in itself, the greater the man who sins is held to be.

units.la: Ideo cum illustriores sint, qui in extremis Magnificentiæ peccant, quam qui in extremis liberalitatis deteriora esse vitia necesse est. 2. Ratio, quia Prodigalitas & avaritia in privatum tantum peccant; Luxus vero & Sordes in publicum commodum. Ideo vitia sunt longè majora, quia ut ait ille;
units.tr: Therefore, since those who err in the extremes of Magnificence are more conspicuous than those who err in the extremes of Liberality, these vices must necessarily be worse. 2. The reason is that Prodigality and Avarice sin only against private advantage, whereas Luxury and Stinginess sin against the public good; therefore these vices are far greater, because, as he says:

units.la: Publica privatis anteferenda malis.
units.tr: Public evils are to be placed before private ones.

units.la: 3. Ratio, quia Luxus potissimum mutationis aut alterationis & interitus Reipubl. causa est; expensae enim inutilia, quæ fiunt in conv via superflua, in profusas personarum largitiones & id genus cætera, quæ luxuriem sapiunt, maximum detrimentum Reipublicæ adferunt, propterea, quod populus pro his multis onerandus sit tributis, quibus tandem lacessitus (neque enim tributa facile sibi imponi præter jus & æquum patitur populus) rebellandi occasionem arripit. 4. Ratio, Petrus Gregorius Tolosanus lib. de Repub. cap. 20. cap. 4. ubi diu & multum de hac hac re disserit, tandem ait: Quid his vitiis foedius, quid damnosius, quibus omnis virtus atteritur, victoria langue-scunt, gloria sopita, in infamiam convertitur, animique pari-ter ac corporis vires expugnantur, ut nescias ab illisne an ab hostibus capi perniciosius habendum sit. Scribunt auto-res fide digni Valerius Maximus lib. 9. cap. 1. & Cic. 3. Tusc. quaest. Xerxen Persarum Regem opum suarum ostentatione eximia ita luxuriantem, ut praemium publico edicto proposuerit ei, qui novum voluptatis genus reperire posset, dumque delitiis nimis captus esset amplissimo Regno & totius Asiae Monarchiae magnam ruinam dedit. Exempla ejusmodi eversionum ex luxu plurima videre licet apud Valerium Maximum loco citato, 5. & ult. Ratio. Aristot. 3. Polit. cap. 10. scribit varios Reges & Principes, dum luxuriae nimium indulgerent in contemtum suorum subditorum venisse, atque ita occasionem sibi opprimendi dedisse, quod etiam illustrat exemplo Sardanapali. Unde sequitur deteriora longe esse haec vitia, quam sunt Prodigalitas aut avaritia. Ergo fallitur Aristoteles, qui dicit ista vitia non esse probrosa: Falluntur etiam interpretes, qui eum comparate haec protulisse referunt, si nempe conferrantur cum extremis liberalitatis. Sed respondetur Aristotelem vulgi secutum hoc loco opinionem: vulgus enim propter rationes supra ad cap. 6. allatas minus probrosa vocare solet haec vitia. Dein interpretes non male illum comparate dixisse contendunt, nam considerantur haec vitia duobus modis, vel in natura recessus, vel in natura actus, ut loquuntur Scholastici. In natura recessus deteriora quidem sunt vitia, propterea quod sint declinationes à præstantissimo medio, & quanto medium est præstantius, in virtute tanto deteriora sunt extrema. Jam verò cum magnificentia longè præstantior & excellentior sit virtus liberalitate, ideo in natura recessus deteriora longè habet vitia. At in natura actus, id est, si considerentur actiones extremorum, utriusque virtutis, non ita probrosa sunt extrema vitia magnificentiæ, quam liberalitatis, propterea quod in his majus longè sit benefaciendi studium magisque prosit generi humano, nec cum aliis vitiis ita complicari solent, ut extrema liberalitatis. Prodigalitas namque plerunque conjuncta est cum injustitia: solet enim, ut supra c.5. asseruit Philosophus, prodigus ab aliis mutuare, quod aliis det, nec rependere: Avaritia injustitiam exercet non tantum in alios, sed etiam in se ipsum.
units.tr: 3. The reason is that luxury is above all the cause of change, alteration and ruin in a commonwealth. The useless expenses incurred at banquets, the superfluous outlays on lavish largesses to individuals, and the other things that smack of luxury cause the greatest harm to the commonwealth, because the people must be burdened with many taxes for them, and the people, provoked at last (for a people does not easily suffer taxes to be imposed on it beyond what is lawful and fair), seize the opportunity to rebel. 4. The reason is given by Pietro Gregorio of Tolosa, in his book on the commonwealth, chapter 20 (or chapter 4), where, after discoursing at length on this matter, he finally says: What is more foul, what more damaging than these vices, by which all virtue is worn away, victory grows weak, glory is lulled to sleep and turned into infamy, and the strength of mind and body alike is overcome, so that you would not know whether it is more dangerous to be captured by them or by enemies. Trustworthy authors, Valerius Maximus (book 9, chapter 1) and Cicero (Tusculan Disputations, book 3), write that Xerxes, King of the Persians, was so extravagant in displaying his wealth that he offered a prize by public edict to anyone who could devise a new kind of pleasure; and while he was too much captivated by his delights, he brought great ruin upon his ample kingdom and upon the monarchy of all Asia. Many examples of such overthrows through luxury may be seen in Valerius Maximus, in the place cited. 5. And the last reason: Aristotle (Politics, book 3, chapter 10) writes that various kings and princes, while they indulged too much in luxury, fell into the contempt of their subjects, and so gave themselves an occasion to be overthrown; he also illustrates this by the example of Sardanapalus. Hence it follows that these vices are far worse than prodigality or avarice. Therefore Aristotle is mistaken when he says that these vices are not shameful. The interpreters are also mistaken who report that he put them forward in comparison, namely if they are compared with the extremes of liberality. But it is answered that Aristotle here followed the opinion of the common people; for, for the reasons given above in chapter 6, the common people are accustomed to call these vices less shameful. Then the interpreters contend that he spoke not badly in making the comparison, for these vices are considered in two ways: either in the nature of deviation or in the nature of action, as the Scholastics put it. In the nature of deviation, the vices are indeed worse, because they are departures from the most excellent mean, and the further the mean is from the extremes, the worse the extremes are in virtue. Now since magnificence is a far more excellent and outstanding virtue than liberality, therefore in the nature of deviation its vices are far worse. But in the nature of action, that is, if we consider the actions of the extremes of each virtue, the extreme vices of magnificence are not so shameful as those of liberality, because in them there is a much greater zeal for doing good and it benefits the human race more, and they are not usually combined with other vices as the extremes of liberality are. For prodigality is for the most part joined with injustice: as the Philosopher asserted above in chapter 5, the prodigal is accustomed to borrow from others in order to give to others, and not to repay; avarice exercises injustice not only towards others but also towards oneself.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: SEquitur secundus tractatus hujus libri, in quo postquam Philosophus egit de iis virtutibus, quæ versantur circa opes modicas & magnas, statim agit de iis virtutibus, quæ versantur circa honores ingentes vel mediocres. Ratio verò, cur statim de his post illas agat, duplex reddenda videtur: 1. est: Quia in communi hominum usu evenit, ut opes earumque regimen prius acquirantur, quam ad honores, dignitates accedatur. 2. Quia qui opibus recte & ritè præesse possunt, aptiores ad dignitates & honores censentur, quippe qui facilius munera Reipub. obire possunt. Membra hujus tractatus sunt duo, in quoquorum priori egit de ea virtute, quae versatur circa honores magnos, & haec dicitur Magnanimitas. In posteriore de virtute, quae versatur circa honores tantum mediocres, sed apud Graecos caret nomine, Latinis dicitur Modestia. Ratio vero cur de Magnanimitate priore loco agat, haec forte reddi poterit, quia frequentiores sunt in vita communi magnanimitatis, quam modestiae actus, aut quod crebrior sit huius quam illius usus: paucos enim aut nullos reperire licet, qui mediocribus tantum contenti honoribus non ad majores & sublimiores subinde adspirent, id quod pater duabus de causis: 1. Ut fortuna comite nominis famam propagent, & immortalem sui memoriam ad posteros transmittant, id est, ut natura duce (cuius instinctu omnia demum quaecunque illa, sint finem & perfectionem suam quaerunt) praestantiam quandam & perfectionem inter caeteros homines appetant. Vel etiam praefert magnanimitatem modestiae, ut Alexandro Magno Imperium orbis affectanti, cujus, ut canit Poeta, pectus erat insatiabilis laudis & honoris, placeret, vel etiam ut homine ingenuo hanc virtutem maxime dignam esse ostenderet, & propterea ad eam maxime contendendum, quippe quod proximam ad ipsam felicitatem viam demonstret: vel etiam tertio ut arbitrario ordine pro cujusque libitu virtutes collocari possint: non enim, ut inquit Seneca, refert, quo ordine virtutes disces, sed quam bene & quam recte ad usum vitae melioris adhibeas. De Magnanimitate igitur priore loco agit, de qua etiam disserit lib. 2. Eudem. & in libel. de virtutib. & in lib. mag. mor. & Cic. lib. 2. offic. & Pontanus tanus lib. duobus quos inscribit de Magnanimitate: & Francifcus Patricius lib. 7. de regno cap. 8. Membra huius tractatus de Magnanimitate sunt tria. In prior more solito agit de obj-ecto, circa quod versatur magnanimitas, quia in eo cognoscendo rota vis & natura magnanimitatis constiftit. In secunda agit de operationibus seu proprietatibus magnanimitatis, ut nempe modus, quo haec virtus circa obiectum suū versatur liquidò appareat. In tertio demum de extremis magnanimitatis agit.
units.tr: There follows the second treatise of this book. Having dealt with the virtues concerned with moderate and great wealth, the Philosopher now treats at once of the virtues concerned with great or moderate honours. The reason why he treats these immediately after the former seems to be twofold: (1) In common human experience, wealth and its management are acquired before one comes to honours and dignities. (2) Those who can rightly and properly govern their wealth are considered better suited to dignities and honours, since they can more easily discharge the duties of the commonwealth. The treatise has two parts. In the first he deals with the virtue concerned with great honours, which is called Magnanimity. In the second he deals with the virtue concerned only with moderate honours, which has no name among the Greeks but is called Modesty by the Latins. The reason why he treats Magnanimity first may perhaps be given as follows: acts of magnanimity are more frequent in common life than acts of modesty, or its use is more common than that of modesty. For we can find few or no people who, content with moderate honours, do not from time to time aspire to greater and loftier ones. This happens for two reasons: (1) so that, with fortune as their companion, they may spread their fame and hand down an immortal memory of themselves to posterity; that is, so that, with nature as their guide (by whose impulse all things, whatever they may be, seek their end and perfection), they may aim at a certain pre-eminence and perfection above other men. Or again, he gives magnanimity precedence over modesty, as with Alexander the Great, who aimed at dominion over the world, whose breast, as the poet sings, was insatiable of praise and honour; or again, so that he might show that this virtue is most worthy of a free man, and that therefore one should strive most of all for it, since it points to the path nearest to happiness itself; or thirdly, so that the virtues may be arranged in an arbitrary order according to each person's liking. For, as Seneca says, it does not matter in what order you learn the virtues, but how well and how rightly you apply them to the use of a better life. He therefore treats Magnanimity first, on which he also discourses in the second book of the Eudemian Ethics, in the treatise on the virtues, in the Magna Moralia, and Cicero in the second book of De Officiis; and Pontanus in two books he entitles On Magnanimity; and Francesco Patrizi in the seventh book of De regno, chapter 8. The parts of this treatise on Magnanimity are three. In the first, as usual, he deals with the object with which magnanimity is concerned, since the whole force and nature of magnanimity consists in knowing this. In the second he deals with the operations or properties of magnanimity, so that the manner in which this virtue is exercised about its object may clearly appear. In the third, finally, he deals with the extremes of magnanimity.

units.la: Primum membrum continetur hoc cap. 7. cujus partes sunt tres. In prima agit de materia magnanimitatis in genere: In secunda ipsam declarat in specie: In tertia affert quasdam conditiones ipsius magnanimi.
units.tr: The first part is contained in this chapter 7, whose three sections are these. In the first he deals with the matter of magnanimity in general; in the second he declares it in particular; in the third he sets out certain conditions of the magnanimous man himself.

units.la: In prima igitur dicit materiam Magnaminitatis esse τὰ μεγάλα seu magna, aut omne id, quod magnum est in rebus humanis, id quod probat tribus rationibus. 1. Ducitur ab Etymologia Magnanimitatis, quia nomen ipsum indicat. 2. Sumitur a definitione Magnanimi, quae ei vulgo assignatur, nempe quod Magnanimus is sit, qui cum magnis dignus sit, magnis quoq; dignum se judicat. 3. Ratio est, quia extrema Magnaminitatis superbia nimirum & Pusillanimitas circa magna versantur, extrema vero & medium circa idem versari obiectum certo constat.
units.tr: In the first section, therefore, he says that the matter of Magnanimity is the great things [τὰ μεγάλα], or everything that is great in human affairs, which he proves by three reasons: (1) it is derived from the etymology of Magnanimity, since the name itself indicates this; (2) it is taken from the definition of the magnanimous man commonly given, namely that the magnanimous man is one who, being worthy of great things, also judges himself worthy of great things; (3) the reason is that the extremes of magnanimity, namely arrogance and pusillanimity, are concerned with great things, and it is certain that the extremes and the mean are concerned with the same object.

units.la: Sed objici poterat. Si Magnanimitas versatur circa id, quod maximum est in rebus humanis, non erit mediocritas, in qua consistit ipsa virtus, sed potius extremitas & excellentia, propterea quod magnarum rerum propria sit excellensellentia; nam res ideò magna dicuntur, quæ apra caterīs rebus præstantiam & perfectionem quandam habent. Resp. Philosophus distinguit respectu esse extremū & medium: nam ratione magnitudinis, quam in summo gradu appetit Magnanimus, Magnanimitas poterit dici extremum: ratione vero dignitatis aut quatenus ipsam Magnitudinis perfectionem respicit, poterit dici medium. Breviter: Magnanimitas Quantitatis respectu, id est, quatenus consistit inter nimium & parum, poterit dici mediocritas: at respectu Qualitatis, id est, quatenus in magnitudine summam perfectionem & præstantiam intendit, est extremitas. Vide idem dubium supra propositum cap. 7. lib. 2. hujus operis, ubi de virtute in genere agitur.
units.tr: But it could be objected: If magnanimity is concerned with what is greatest in human affairs, then it will not be a mean, in which virtue itself consists, but rather an extreme and excellence, since excellence is the proper quality of great things; for things are called great because they have a certain pre-eminence and perfection beyond other things. Answer: the Philosopher distinguishes extreme and mean with respect to different aspects. For with respect to the magnitude which the magnanimous man seeks at the highest degree, magnanimity can be called an extreme; but with respect to its worth, or insofar as it regards the perfection of greatness itself, it can be called a mean. In brief: with respect to quantity, that is, insofar as it lies between excess and deficiency, magnanimity can be called a mean; but with respect to quality, that is, insofar as it aims at the highest perfection and pre-eminence in greatness, it is an extreme. See the same question raised above, in chapter 7 of the second book of this work, where virtue in general is discussed.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de materia Magnanimitatis in specie, & dicit materiam esse honorem, & causam breviter reddit, quia honor est bonorum externorum maximum quid: nam ut ex supra dictis patet, Magnanimus is dicitur, qui cum magnus sit, magnis quoque dignum se judicat: nihil vero majus sit in rebus humanis, quo se dignum judicat honore, ideo honorem proprie appetit. Ratio vero cur honor bonorum externorum maximum dicatur, triplex reddi u: 1. Quia Deo tribuitur non proprie quidem, sed cum nihil majus Deo a creatura tribuit possit, ideo honore illi gratitudinis ergo exhibet, & propterea Plato lib. 4. de Repubi. honorem quiddam divinum vocat. Plura videapud Philosophum cap. 12. lib. 1. hujus operis. 2. Ratio est, quia Pontifices & ius, qui Dei vices in terris gerunt, id est, qui
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he treats of the matter of magnanimity in particular. He says the matter is honour, and briefly gives the reason: honour is the greatest of external goods. For, as is clear from what was said above, the magnanimous man is one who, being great, also judges himself worthy of great things. Nothing is greater in human affairs than the honour by which he judges himself worthy, so he properly seeks honour. The reason why honour is called the greatest of external goods is given as threefold: (1) Honour is given to God, not properly indeed, but since a creature can give God nothing greater, we offer him honour as a matter of gratitude. For this reason Plato, in book 4 of the Republic, calls honour something divine. See more in the Philosopher, chapter 12, book 1 of this work. (2) Honour is also paid to pontiffs and judges, who bear God's place on earth, that is, to those set in some dignity or magistracy. See above the Philosopher, chapter 5, book 1 of this work; and Cicero discusses this matter at length in book 2 of On Duties. (3) Honour is the reward of virtue. Only the most excellent things, such as the virtues, merit it, and honour impels all people to acquire virtue. Since honour is in general the reward of virtue, it will especially be the reward of the most excellent and outstanding virtue. This is magnanimity, on whose nature Pontanus disputes at length in book 1 On Magnanimity, chapters 2, 3 and 4.

units.la: [Marginal reference mark at bottom right: 13] in dignitate aliqua aut Magistratu sunt constituti etiam attribuitur. Vide supra Philosophum cap. 5. lib. 1. huius operis: & de hac re copiose disserit Cicero lib. 2. officior. 3. Ratio, quia honor virtutis est præmium: nam non nisi res præclarissimæ, quales sunt virtutes, eum merentur, & honor impellit omnes ad virtutem comparandam: Jam vero cum honor sit virtutis in genere præmium, tum excellentissimæ & præclarissimæ virtutis in primis erit præmiū; hæc vero est Magnanimitas, de qua ratione fuse disputat Pontanus lib. 1. de Magnanim. cap. 2. 3. 4.
units.tr: (margin 13) In the case of pontiffs and judges, honour is attached to some dignity or magistracy. See above the Philosopher, chapter 5, book 1 of this work, and Cicero's extended discussion of this matter in book 2 of On Duties. The reason is that honour is the reward of virtue: only the most distinguished things, such as the virtues, deserve it, and honour drives everyone to acquire virtue. Since honour is the reward of virtue in general, it will be the chief reward of the most excellent and distinguished virtue. This is magnanimity, on whose reasons Pontanus argues at length in book 1 On Magnanimity, chapters 2, 3 and 4.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis adfert quatuor conditiones Magnanimi. 1. est, quod cum rebus maximis dignissimus sit, vir etiam optimus & præstantissimus sit: nam honorem semper, quo dignus est, appetit, at non nisi præstantissimo cuique debetur honor, ut eleganter disserit Cicero in orat. pro Archia. 2. est proprium hoc esse magnanimi, ut id semper agat & intendat, quod in unaquaque virtute maximè eximium & excellens est, ut in Fortitudine gravissima quæq; pericula sucipere & cōtemnere, in Temperantia omnes voluptates spernere, in Magnificentia in id, quod maximum & dignissimum est, sumtus facere: & sic de reliquis Virtutibus. 3. est, quod Magnanimus propter excelsum & generosum animum, neque periculis se turpiter subducit, quod est veræ fortitudinis: neq; etiam alteri injuriam infert, quod est Justitiæ idq; propter duas rationes: 1. Quia nihil in rebus humanis satis magnum judicat, quo inducatur ad injuriam inferendum. 2. Quia nihili omnia facit, ex quibus injuriarum causæ oriuntur, ut pecupecuniam, lucrum, & id genus caetera, de quo infra uberius explicabitur. 4. est, quod difficile sit admodum esse vere Magnanimum: nam ut habet proverbium commune; Quae pulchra sunt, etiam difficilia sunt: nam in Magnanimo omnis probitas, omnis cumulata debet inesse Virtus, ideo non sine summa cum difficultate pervenit ad veram Magnanimitatem, ut fuse docet ipse Philosophus lib. 2. mag. mor. cap. 9. Rationem affert Philosophus, quae pulcherrima sit omnium virtutum Magnanimitas, quia est ornamentum caeterarum virtutum; nam caeteros omnes virtutes cumulatiores & ornatiores reddit. Unde a Cic. lib. 1. offic. vocatur splendidissima omnium virtutum, quod velut luna inter stellas, haec inter caeteras virtutes maxime splendeat: & a Pontano lib. 1. de Magn. cap. 3. comparatur corollae ex optimis quibusque virtutum floribus contextae: comparatur etiam fluviorum regi Danubio, quod sicut ille inter caeteros Europae fluvios maxime excellit, ita haec inter omnes virtutes.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he sets out four conditions of the magnanimous man. (1) Since he is worthy of the greatest things, he is also a man of the highest goodness and excellence. He always seeks the honour he deserves, but honour is due only to the most excellent, as Cicero elegantly argues in his speech for Archias. (2) It is characteristic of the magnanimous man always to do and aim at what is most outstanding and excellent in each virtue: in courage, to undertake and despise the gravest dangers; in temperance, to spurn all pleasures; in magnificence, to spend on what is greatest and most worthy; and so with the other virtues. (3) The magnanimous man, on account of his lofty and noble spirit, neither shamefully withdraws from dangers, which belongs to true courage, nor inflicts injury on another, which belongs to justice. This is for two reasons: first, because he judges nothing in human affairs great enough to induce him to inflict injury; second, because he counts as nothing all the things from which the causes of injuries arise, such as money, gain and that kind of thing, which will be explained more fully below. (4) It is exceedingly difficult to be truly magnanimous. As the common proverb says, "What is beautiful is also difficult." The magnanimous man must have every uprightness and every accumulated virtue, so he attains true magnanimity only with the greatest difficulty, as the Philosopher himself teaches at length in Magna Moralia, book 2, chapter 9. The Philosopher also gives the reason why magnanimity is the most beautiful of all the virtues: it is the ornament of the others, for it makes them all fuller and more adorned. Hence Cicero, in book 1 of On Duties, calls it the most splendid of all virtues, because just as the moon shines most brightly among the stars, so this virtue shines most among the rest. Pontanus, in book 1 On Magnanimity, chapter 3, compares it to a garland woven from the finest flowers of the virtues. It is also compared to the Danube, king of rivers, because just as that river excels all the other rivers of Europe, so magnanimity excels all the virtues.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Magnanimitas, ut ratio nominis indicat circa magna aut omne id, quod magnum est, in rebus humanis maxime versatur.
units.tr: Magnanimity, as the meaning of the name indicates, is concerned with great things, or with whatever is great, and it is most at home in human affairs.

units.la: 2. Nil refert, an de ipso virtutis habitu, an de eo, qui est virtutis habitu praditus in tractatione virtutum agatur.
units.tr: It makes no difference whether we treat of the habit of virtue itself or of the person who possesses that habit in the treatment of the virtues.

units.la: 3. Magnanimus is est, qui cum magnus dictus fit, magnis quoque dignum se judicat.
units.tr: The magnanimous man is one who, when he is held to be great, also judges himself worthy of great things.

units.la: 4. Qui cum parvis dignus fit, in contentum se ostendit, non Magnanimus, sed Modestus dicitur.
units.tr: One who, being worthy of small things, shows himself content with them is not called magnanimous but modest.

units.la: 5. In magnitudine ipsa perspicitur Magnanimitas, sicut pulchritudo in magno corpore.
units.tr: Magnanimity is seen in greatness itself, just as beauty is seen in a large body.

units.la: 6. Magnanimitas respectu perfectionis est extremum, respectu vero dignitatis secundum rectam rationem est medium.
units.tr: With respect to perfection, magnanimity is an extreme; with respect to worthiness, however, according to right reason, it is a mean.

units.la: 7. Magnanimitas versatur circa magnos honores tanquam proprium suum obiectum.
units.tr: Magnanimity is concerned with great honours as its own proper object.

units.la: 8. Honor bonorum externorum est maximum quid, quia etiam Deo & Politicis tribuitur, & verè virtutis praemium est.
units.tr: The honour of external goods is a very great thing, because it is paid even to God and to rulers, and it is truly the reward of virtue.

units.la: 9. Magnanimus cum rebus maximis fit dignissimus, vir etiam erit praestantissimus.
units.tr: When the magnanimous man is most worthy of the greatest things, he will also be the most outstanding of men.

units.la: 10. Et proprium est Magnanimi, ut in unaquaque virtute, quod excellentissimum maximeque eximium fit, intendat.
units.tr: It is also characteristic of the magnanimous man that in every virtue he aims at what is most excellent and most distinguished.

units.la: 11. Magnanimus neque turpe quid unquam agit, neque alteri injuriam infert.
units.tr: The magnanimous man never does anything base, nor does he inflict injury on another.

units.la: 12. Magnanimitas est ornamentum caeterarum omnium virtutum.
units.tr: Magnanimity is the ornament of all the other virtues.

units.la: 13. Difficile est admodum verè esse Magnanimum, utpote quia in ipso omnia cumulata requiritur virtus.
units.tr: It is very difficult truly to be magnanimous, since in him all virtue must be present in full measure.

units.la: Notandum Magnanimitatis nomen triplici ter vulgò accipi: 1. Latissimè admodum: Nam Cicero, Seneca, aliique Latini scriptores Magnanimitatem cum Fortitudine conjungunt, Cicero ait 1. offic. Fortes & Magnanimi sunt dicendi, non qui faciunt, sed qui propulsant injuriam. Et Seneca l. 4. de virtut. Fortis & Magnanimus erit, si pericula non appetas, ut temerarius, si non refor-mides, ut timidus, si non fugias. 2. Sumitur Magnanimitas pro ornamento caeterarum omnium virtutum, quo sensu circumducit eam Philosophus pet caetecæteras omnes virtutes cap.8.lib.4.hujus operis. 3. Proprie summitu pro ea virtute, quæ in magnis veisatur honoribus. Plura vide apud Keckerm. pag.203.sqq. Ethic.
units.tr: It should be noted that the name magnanimity is commonly taken in three senses. (1) Very broadly indeed: for Cicero, Seneca and other Latin writers join magnanimity with fortitude. Cicero says in De officiis book 1: Those are to be called brave and magnanimous not who inflict injury but who ward it off. And Seneca in De virtutibus book 4: A man will be brave and magnanimous if he does not seek out dangers, as a rash man does, if he does not dread them, as a timid man does, and if he does not flee. (2) Magnanimity is taken as the ornament of all the other virtues, and in this sense the Philosopher brings it in as the ornament of all the other virtues, ch. 8, book 4 of this work. (3) Properly, it is taken for that virtue which is concerned with great honours. See more in Keckermann, p. 203 ff., Ethics.

units.la: Versatur vero Magnanimitas circa magnos honores tribus modis: 1. in honoribus appetendis. 2. in iis accipiendis. 3. in perfruendis. Singuli isti modi suas habent conditiones & restrictiones. Debet Magnanimus appetere honores, sed cum his duabus conditionibus: 1. juste debet appetere, ne sit injuriosus. 2. modeste & moderate, ne aliorum incurrat odium. Debet etiam accipere honores, sed cum hac duplici restrictione: 1. ut fiat parce, ne ambitiosus videatur. 2. decore, ne superbus aut insolens audiat. In perfruendis etiam honoribus debent & istæ adhiberi tres limitationes: 1. ut sobrie iis perfruatur; nam qui sobrietati non studet, neque etiam modum in rebus tenere poterit, & qui non tenet modum, neque ipsam sequitur virtutem. 2. debet caute id agere respectu hostis, qui insidiatur, & qui ex qualibet vel levi suspicione, accusandi capiat occasionem. 3. fructuose debet perfrui honoribus propter commodum civitatis: Nam Magnanimitas ut omnis virtus ad civitatis bonum publicum ultimo collimare debet. Definitur vero Magnanimitas virtus in appetendis & contemnendis magnis honoribus modū servans. In qua definitione duo sunt maxime consideratu digna: 1. finis internus & objectum. Finis est appetere magnos honores, quos benefactis suis promeruit Magnanimus, & quibus se dignum judicat, vel etiam contemnere ejusmodi honores, quia infra statum & conditionem ipsius sunt, & qui illi minime conveniunt.
units.tr: Magnanimity is concerned with great honours in three ways: (1) in seeking them; (2) in accepting them; (3) in enjoying them. Each of these modes has its own conditions and restrictions. The magnanimous man ought to seek honours, but under two conditions: (1) he must seek them justly, lest he be unjust; (2) he must seek them modestly and with moderation, lest he incur the hatred of others. He ought also to accept honours, but under this twofold restriction: (1) that he accept them sparingly, lest he seem ambitious; (2) that he accept them becomingly, lest he be thought proud or insolent. In enjoying honours too, three limitations must likewise apply: (1) he should enjoy them soberly, for whoever does not strive for sobriety will not be able to keep measure in things, and whoever does not keep measure does not follow virtue itself; (2) he should act cautiously with regard to an enemy who lies in wait and who seizes on any occasion for accusation from even a slight suspicion; (3) he should enjoy honours fruitfully, for the good of the commonwealth, since magnanimity, like every virtue, must ultimately aim at the public good of the state. Magnanimity is defined as the virtue that observes measure in seeking and despising great honours. In this definition two things are especially worthy of consideration: (1) the internal end and the object. The end is to seek great honours, which the magnanimous man has earned by his good deeds and by which he judges himself worthy, or else to despise such honours, because they lie beneath his rank and condition and do not suit him at all.

units.la: Objectum sunt honores non quilibet sed magni, qua voce distinguitur à Modestia, quæ quidé versatur circa honores, sed modicos tantũ, unde non tam ipso objecto, quam modo, quo versatur circa ipsum objectũ, & causa efficiente differunt: nam sicut magni honores Magnanimo propter magna facinora debentur, sic etiā Modesto honores modici propter res modicè gestas. Hinc præclarè Seneca lib. 4. de virtutib. sicut quævis corona non quemvis decet victorem, sic quivis honor non quemvis hominem.
units.tr: The object is not just any honours but great ones, and this word distinguishes it from modesty, which is indeed concerned with honours, but only with modest ones. Hence they differ not so much in their object as in the manner in which each deals with it, and in their efficient cause: for just as great honours are due to the magnanimous man on account of great deeds, so modest honours are due to the modest man on account of modest achievements. Hence Seneca, in book 4 of De virtutibus, aptly says: just as no crown fits every victor, so no honour fits every man.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Magnanimitas possit recte dici virtus, cum nulla virtus virtuti contrarietur, quippe omnis virtus est bonum quid, & bonum bono non contrariatur. At Magnanimitas contrariatur cuidam virtuti, nempe Humilitati. Ergo virtus dici non poterit. Minor probatur, quia Magnanimus est is, qui magnos expetit honores, & indignos aut inferiores contemnit. At contraria hu facit humilis. Ergo sibi invicem contrariari videntur? Resp. In natura virtutis non contrariantur, sed in modo actus. Et in Humili duo veniunt consideranda: 1. est habitus internus, secundum quem novit, & judicat se dignum honoribus iis, qui ei ex præscripto rectæ rationis offeruntur: & hoc respectu non contrariatur Magnanimo. 2. consideratur actus externus secundum quem statum & dignitatem suam vivere, & se aliis postponere studet, quia nempe studio contemplativæ potius, quam activæ vitæ delectatur: Et hanc ut üt tranquillitati consulat suæ, magis eligit illam, cum tempus postulat, aut res etiam non negligit, & hoc modo contrariari videtur Magnanimus.
units.tr: Question: Can Magnanimity rightly be called a virtue, since no virtue is contrary to another virtue? Every virtue is a good thing, and a good is not contrary to a good. But Magnanimity is contrary to a certain virtue, namely Humility. Therefore it cannot be called a virtue. The minor is proved because the magnanimous man is one who seeks great honours and despises those that are unworthy or lower. The humble man does the opposite. Therefore they seem to be contrary to one another? Answer: They are not contrary in the nature of virtue, but in the mode of action. In the humble man two things must be considered. (1) There is an inner disposition, by which he knows and judges himself worthy of those honours which are offered to him according to the rule of right reason; in this respect he is not contrary to the magnanimous man. (2) There is an outward act, by which he takes care to live within his station and dignity and to put others before himself, because he delights in the study of the contemplative life rather than the active. When time requires it, or affairs cannot be neglected, he chooses the active life, in order to look after his own tranquillity; in this way the humble man seems to be contrary to the magnanimous man.

units.la: Instantia: Imò Magnanimitas non poterit dici virtus, quia omnis virtus versatur circa objectum, quod est in ipso agente, aut in eo, qui est virtute prædituus. At Magnanimitas non versatur circa ejusmodi objectum; nam versatur circa honorem, & honor non est in honorato seu in Magnanimo, sed in honorante, aut in eo, qui defert honorem. Major probatur, quia omnis virtutis objectum debet esse in eo ipso subjecto, in quo est ipsa virtus, secus enim non rectè & secundum ipsam rationem circa objectum suum versaretur virtus? Respon. Duplex esse objectum Magnanimitatis, unum internum, quod est moderata appetitio honoris secundum rectam rationem: & hoc est in ipso agente seu Magnanimo: aliud externum, nempe honor, qui est activè in honorante, passivè in honorato, qua de re vide plura ad cap. 3. lib. 1. huius operis: Et non requiritur, ut objectum hoc externum sit in ipso agente, sed ut agens in illud extra agat.
units.tr: Objection: Indeed Magnanimity cannot be called a virtue, because every virtue is concerned with an object which is in the agent itself, or in the one who has the virtue. But Magnanimity is not concerned with such an object; for it is concerned with honour, and honour is not in the honoured man or in the magnanimous man, but in the one who honours, or in the one who bestows the honour. The major is proved because the object of every virtue must lie in the very subject in which the virtue is; otherwise the virtue would not be concerned with its object rightly and according to its own nature? Answer: Magnanimity has a twofold object: one internal, which is the moderate desire for honour according to right reason, and this is in the agent, that is, the magnanimous man; the other external, namely honour, which is active in the one who honours and passive in the one honoured. On this matter see more at chapter 3 of book 1 of this work. It is not required that this external object be in the agent itself, but only that the agent act outwardly upon it.

units.la: II. An rectè hic statuerit Philosophus honorem pro objecto Magnanimitatis, cum tamen lib. 1. Rhet. cap 7. ad Theod. objectum Magnanimitatis beneficentiam aut benefacta statuerit. Ergo aut non rectè hic asserere videtur, aut sibi contrariari Philosophus?
units.tr: II. Whether the Philosopher rightly laid down honour here as the object of Magnanimity, when in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 7, addressed to Theodectes, he stated the object of Magnanimity to be beneficence or beneficent deeds. Therefore either he seems here to assert wrongly, or the Philosopher contradicts himself?

units.la: Respondeo. In Rhetoricis non ex professo de virtutibus agere, sed tantum pro subjecto materiæ, id est, quemadmodum Rhetori sufficit. Igitur pro vero objecto proprietatem quandam Magnanimitatis ponit, nempe quod hoc unicè agat, ut in omnes largus & beneficus sit.
units.tr: I answer: in the Rhetoric he does not treat of the virtues professedly, but only as far as the subject matter requires, that is, as much as suffices for a rhetorician. Therefore, for the true object he assigns a certain property of Magnanimity, namely that the magnanimous man acts so as to be generous and beneficent towards all.

units.la: III. An honor possit esse objectum Magnanimitatis cum honor
units.tr: III. Whether honour can be the object of Magnanimity, since honour

units.la: honor fit proprietas quaedam summi boni, ut expresse docet Philosophus lib. 1. cap. 12. huius operis. Et si Magnanimitas agat in honorem, qui est proprietas summi boni, necesse est, ut Magnanimus agat in ipsum summum bonum, & sic habeat illud pro obiecto suo, quod est absurdum, cum summum bonum non sit obiectum virtutum, sed finis tantum, & collective perfecta actio ex omnibus virtutibus: ideo honor non poterit esse verum obiectum Magnanimitatis? Resp. Honorem considerari duobus modis: 1. In summo gradu perfectionis, quatenus inter bona externa dicitur maximum, & ideo Deo & ei, quod est perfectissimum tribuitur, quo sensu Philosophus loco citato felicitatem vocavit bonum honorabile. 2. Consideratur in medio gradu perfectionis, quatenus nondum tetendit ad ultimum, & sic dicitur obiectum Magnanimitatis, in quod proprie agit, eo nempe sensu, quo viris magnis & Politicis adscribitur, & virtutis praemium habetur.
units.tr: honour is a certain property of the highest good, as the Philosopher expressly teaches in book 1, chapter 12 of this work. And if Magnanimity acts upon honour, which is a property of the highest good, it is necessary that the magnanimous man acts upon the highest good itself and so has it as his object. This is absurd, since the highest good is not the object of the virtues but only their end, and the perfect action arising collectively from all the virtues. Therefore honour cannot be the true object of Magnanimity? Answer: Honour may be considered in two ways. (1) At the highest degree of perfection, insofar as among external goods it is called the greatest, and so it is attributed to God and to what is most perfect; in this sense the Philosopher, in the passage cited, called happiness an honourable good. (2) At a middle degree of perfection, insofar as it has not yet reached the ultimate end; and so it is called the object of Magnanimity, at which it aims properly, in the sense in which it is ascribed to great and political men and regarded as the reward of virtue.

units.la: IV. & ult. An plene & vere hic assignarit obiectum Magnanimitatis Philosophus, cum in libel. de virtutib. definiens Magnanimitatem vocet virtutem animae, per quam homo ferre possit bonam & adversam fortunam. Ergo hic non satis plene assignavit obiectum magnanimitatis Philosophus? Resp. Duplex esse obiectum Magnanimitatis etiam externum primarium, quod est honor, & hoc maxime hic spectavit Philosophus, secundarium, quod est adversa vel bona fortuna, & quia hoc primarium illud sequitur, satis esse putabat de primario hoc loco agere.
units.tr: IV. and last: Whether the Philosopher here assigned the object of Magnanimity fully and truly, since in the little book On the Virtues, defining Magnanimity, he calls it a virtue of the soul by which a man can bear good and adverse fortune. Therefore the Philosopher here has not assigned the object of Magnanimity fully enough?
