Answer: Magnanimity has a twofold external object as well: the primary, which is honour, and this is what the Philosopher chiefly had in view here; and the secondary, which is adverse or good fortune. Because the primary is followed by the secondary, he thought it sufficient to treat of the primary in this place.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: SEquitur hoc capite secundum membrum hujus tractatus de Magnanimitate, in quo agit de operationibus seu proprietatibus magnanimitatis. Cognito enim objecto circa quod versatur magnanimitas, consequens videtur, ut quo modo circa istud versetur objectum, plenius ostendatur. Partes hujus capitis sunt quatuor. In prima proprietates circa objectum proprium magnanimitatis affert: In secunda officium circa duas virtutes in specie Fortitudinem & Liberalitatem docet: In tertia quomodo erga singulos homines magnanimus se gerere debeat, declarat: In quarta varias ex variis rebus proprietates desumtas in medium adducit. In prima adfert proprietates circa verum objectum magnanimitatis, sed cum objectum sit duplex primarium & secundarium, primo adfert proprietates duas circa objectum primarium, nempe circa honorem: 1. est: Quod magnanimus honores sibi a viris probis & gravibus delatos magni faciat, iisque admodum laetetur, propterea quod iis dignum le norit: non enim solent viri probi magnos honores tribuere immeritis, sed tamen honores a pravis aut a vulgo hominum delatos negligit, aut parvi pendit, propterea quod aut parvi sunt aut statu & conditione magnanimi longe inferiores: nam a malis honorari non magnus est honor. Hinc Achilles, ut est apud Homerum Iliad. 1. Nestori suadenti, ut ab Agamemnone delatos honores suscipéret, respondit: se à Jove tantum, non ab Agamemnone homine ignavo & inimico petere velle honores. res. 1. Proprietas est circa objectum primarium, quod magnanimus etsi à viris probis minores, quam pro merito honores, deferri videat, non egre ferat tamen, sed boni consulat, propterea quod majores quibus illum afficere possunt, forte non habent. Et ratio hujus rei redditur ex cap. 4. lib. 3. hujus operis, ubi ex intentione potius, quam ex factis judicari solere homines dicit Philosophus, & vir magnanimus animum potius deferentis honoré quam delatum honorem respicit, quod Æsopus in Apologia quadam Leonis & Elephanti eleganter expressit. Circa objectum secundarium, nempe potentiam, divitias, secundam & adversam fortunam, hanc proprietatem adfert Philosophus, quod magnanimus neque secunda fortuna efferatur, neque adversa animum despondeat, sed utramque decore & modeste ferat. Et ratio hæc est, quia cum honore (quem unice cha-rum habet magnanimus) non efferatur, tum multo minus hisce fortunæ bonis, quæ propter honorem solum acquiruntur, ideoque longe deteriora sunt. Cæterum etsi præ honoris studio potentiam & divitias contemnere videatur, ad magnanimitatem tamen sustinendam necessaria videntur: nam in excellentia quadam vulgo habentur, & status conditioque hominum non tantum ad virtutem, sed ad ipsam felicitatem comparandam his necessario indiget: unde à vulgo honorari solent, qui his bonis affluunt, propterea quod rebus suis gerendis decus & splendorem addere possunt, sola tamen virtus vere honoratum reddit hominem, ideoque magnanimus propter solam virtutem honoratur & honorat. rat. In secunda parte capitis declarat Philosophus officium magnanimi circa fortitudinem & liberalitatem. Et primò circa fortitudinē ita gerere se debet magnanimus, ut neq; de rebus exigui momenti, aut etiā crebro magna adeat pericula, propterea quod omnia al a praeter solum honorem flocci habeat: & hoc animum aut lucri cupidum aut desperatum arguit: at vero ubi periculā se digna videt, quibus salvo honore se subducere non potest, vitę suae minimè parcit, sed ultrò se in pericula offert, ut dignitatem & praestantiam tueatur suam. Circa liberalitatem vero aut beneficentiam diversa sunt veri magnanimi officia, nā primò ita se habet, ut studeat de omnibus bene mereri & in alios beneficia conferre; contra beneficium accipere illum pudet, seu in beneficiis accipiendis tardus & verecundus esse debet. Et ratio hujus rei est, quia illud est praestantioris & excellentioris animi, hoc vero deteriōris & inferioris seu animi degeneris: at constat inter omnes magnanimos esse excellentissimos, quia haec virtus est omnium virtutum maximè excellens. 2. In beneficiis conferendis debet esse largus, quia ut ex superioře capite patet, hoc proprium est magnanimi id intendere, quod in unaquaque virtute est maximè excellens: atqui in liberalitate nihil est excellentius, quam largum & munificum esse. 3. Meminit quibus beneficia dederit, non autem à quibus accepe-rit, audit etiam libenter commemorari, quae ipse in alios contulerit, non autem quae in illum alii. Et ratio horum est, quia prius illud ad excellentiam pertinet, & praestantiam animi declarat: posterius hoc imimbecillitatem & necessitatem, quod alios gravarit, & suo gravamine animi magnitudini multum detraxerit, quo arguit imbecillitatem & necessitatem. Et hæc illustrat duobus exemplis. 1. est, ex lib.1. Iliad. Hom. ubi Thetys Dea maris Jovem pro filio Achille contra Agamemnonem deprecatura, non commemorat sua beneficia in Jovem collata (nempè quod cũ Mars & Neptunus rebellassent in Jovem, ipsa Briaræum Gigantem auxilio Jovi miserit, cujus præsentia territi ab incepto destiterunt) quia Jovi ut magnanimo ingratam hanc commemorationem fore putabat. 2. Exemplum est de Lacedæmoniis ex lib. 1. rerum Græcarum à Calisthene descriptarum. Nam cum Thebani Epaminondα Duce Lacedæmoniū invalissent, & in angustias jam redegissent, Lacedæmonii missa legatione Athenienses auxilių rogabant, & cum multa ultro citroq; collata essent, beneficia sua non tamen in Athenienses tanquam magnanimos, sed potius Atheniensium in se beneficium commemorant. 4. Hoc etiam officium magnanimi est, ut à nullo vix ac ne vix quidem quicquam petat, etiamsi summa necessitate gravetur, propterea quod, qui aliis prodesse debet, alios gravare & ab iis petere non debet, cum hoc præstantiam magnanimitatis minimè deceat. Exemplū fuit in Miltiade Atheniensi, qui cum esset Atheniensium Imperator & variis victoriis eorum opes & potentiam auxisset, in summa tamen paupertate qua vixit, nihil ab Atheniensibus petere voluit, aurumq; obiatum recusaba. In tertia parte capitis quomodo ergo omnes in genere homines magnanimus se gerere debeat docedocetur. Nam etsi ad hoc natus videatur magna-nimus, ut promtè cuivis inserviat, quia omnib. prodesse debet: tamen hoc ita debet fieri, ut gravitatem suam non violet. Et cum tres sint hominum ordines, ut hoc loco & cap.11. lib.4. Polit. docet Philosophus, alii summi, alii infimi, alii medii, ergo hos omnes convenienter & pro dignitate sua se geret magnanimus. Ergo summos virosque Principes, qui dignitate aut opibus aut etiam genere caeteris antecellunt, magnitudine sua & gravitate uti debet magnanimus, idque propter conscientiam virtutis suae, qua se summis viris parem esse novit: Ergo medios & infimos facilis & humilis esse debet, & rationem utriusque hanc affert Philosophus, quia magnos viros superare difficile est, & nō nisi in difficilibus cernitur virtutum splendor, ut ex cap.3. lib.2. patet, viris etiam magnis antecellere res est magni momenti, & non nisi generosi pectoris. At ergo medios & infimos, qui in fastum & conditionem ipsius longe sunt, facile est modestum & humilem se praebere: quod probat a simili, quia non minus esse ineptum contra viros plebejos & humiles se efferre, quam adversus debiles & infirmos corporis robur experiri. Ideoq; insignis haec est viri magnanimi nota adversus superiores & aequales de honore contendere, adversus vero inferiores modeste se gerere, & magnitudinem animi dulcedine quadam & mitigatione temperare, quod de leone generosissimo animali scribit Plinius lib.7. cap.15. Leoni ex feris soli clementia in supplices, & in viros citius, quam infeminas savit, in infantes non, nisi magna percitus fame. In viris exemplum fuit Alexander Magnus adversus Po-rum Indorum Regem, ut testis est Curtius lib. 8. sub finem. In quarta parte capitis varias ex variis defumtas rebus proprietates viri magnanimi adducit. 1. est: Quod locum honoratum frequenter non adeat, nisi scilicet officii, aut conditionis ratio id postulet. Et ratio, cur non frequentet ejusmodi loca, est haec, ne videatur scilicet honorem ambire, & sic superbiae notam incurrat, aut etiam aliis se submittere videatur magis, quam gravitatem & virtutem suam deceat. 11. Quod magnanimus sit cunctator, nihil temere aggrediatur, sed examinatis ante diligenter circumstantiis, ne sua festinatione & properantia se & res suas perdat: quia hoc pertinet ad gravitatem magnanimi non continuo impelli omnibus de causis etiam levissimis ad aliquid aggrediendum: neq; debet res multas agendas suscipere, sed paucas tantum esq; praeclaras & magnas, quod in Fabio Maximo laudat Cic. 1. offic. ex versibus Ennii;
units.tr: This chapter takes up the second part of this treatise on Magnanimity, which deals with the operations or properties of magnanimity. Once the object with which magnanimity is concerned is known, it seems to follow that we should show more fully how that object is handled. The parts of this chapter are four. In the first he gives the properties of magnanimity's proper object; in the second he teaches its duty with regard to two particular virtues, Fortitude and Liberality; in the third he explains how the magnanimous man should conduct himself towards individual men; in the fourth he brings forward various properties drawn from various things. In the first he gives properties concerning the true object of magnanimity. But since the object is twofold, primary and secondary, he first gives two properties concerning the primary object, namely honour. 1. The first is this: the magnanimous man sets great store by honours conferred on him by upright and serious men, and he is greatly pleased by them, because he knows himself to be worthy of them. Upright men do not usually bestow great honours on the undeserving. But he disregards, or thinks little of, honours offered by wicked men or by the common crowd, because such honours are either worthless or come from people far below the magnanimous man in rank and standing. For to be honoured by bad men is no great honour. Hence Achilles, in Homer's Iliad 1, when Nestor urged him to accept the honours offered by Agamemnone, replied that he wished to seek honours from Jove alone, not from Agamemnon, a cowardly man and an enemy. 2. The second property concerns the primary object: although the magnanimous man sees that upright men offer him lesser honours than he deserves, he does not take it badly but accepts it graciously, because they may not have greater honours with which to honour him. The reason for this is given in chapter 4 of book 3 of this work, where the Philosopher says that men are usually judged by intention rather than by deeds. The magnanimous man looks to the mind of the one who confers honour rather than to the honour conferred, which Aesop elegantly expressed in a certain fable of the Lion and the Elephant. As to the secondary object, namely power, riches, and good and bad fortune, the Philosopher gives this property: the magnanimous man is neither puffed up by good fortune nor cast down by bad, but bears both with dignity and moderation. The reason is this: since he is not elated by honour, which alone he holds dear, he is much less elated by these goods of fortune, which are acquired only for the sake of honour and are therefore far inferior. Yet although he seems to despise power and riches for the sake of his zeal for honour, they seem necessary for sustaining magnanimity. For they are held in a certain esteem by the common people, and the standing and condition of men need them not only for acquiring virtue but for acquiring happiness itself. Hence those who abound in these goods are usually honoured by the common people, because they can add dignity and splendour to their undertakings. Yet virtue alone truly makes a man honourable, and therefore the magnanimous man is honoured and honours for virtue alone. In the second part of the chapter the Philosopher sets out the duty of the magnanimous man with regard to fortitude and liberality. First, with regard to fortitude, the magnanimous man must so conduct himself that he does not run into dangers over matters of slight moment, nor often seek out great perils, since he cares for nothing except honour. Such conduct would show a man who is greedy for gain or desperate. But when he sees dangers that he cannot escape without loss of honour, he does not spare his life at all, but offers himself freely to peril in order to protect his dignity and excellence. With regard to liberality or beneficence, the duties of the true magnanimous man are different. First, he is disposed to deserve well of all and to confer benefits on others; he is ashamed to receive a benefit, or at least must be slow and modest in accepting benefits. The reason is that conferring is the mark of a superior and more excellent mind, while receiving belongs to a baser and inferior, or degenerate, mind. Everyone agrees that magnanimous men are most excellent, since this virtue is the most excellent of all virtues. 2. In conferring benefits he must be generous, because, as is clear from the previous chapter, it is proper to the magnanimous man to aim at whatever is most excellent in each virtue. But in liberality nothing is more excellent than being open-handed and munificent. 3. He remembers to whom he has given benefits, but not from whom he has received them. He is also glad to have his own gifts to others mentioned, but not what others have given to him. The reason is that the former pertains to excellence and reveals the eminence of his mind, whereas the latter reveals weakness and need, and that he has burdened others, and by his burden has greatly diminished the greatness of his mind, which shows weakness and need. He illustrates this with two examples. 1. The first is from book 1 of Homer's Iliad, where the goddess Thetis, the sea-nymph, pleads with Jove for her son Achilles against Agamemnon. She does not mention the benefits she had conferred on Jove, namely that when Mars and Neptune had rebelled against Jove, she sent the giant Briareus to help Jove, whose presence frightened them from their undertaking. She thought this reminder would be unwelcome to Jove as a magnanimous god. 2. The second example concerns the Lacedaemonians, from book 1 of the Greek history written by Callisthenes. When the Thebans, led by Epaminondas, had overpowered the Lacedaemonians and had already driven them into straits, the Lacedaemonians sent an embassy and asked the Athenians for help. Although many good offices had been exchanged on both sides, they did not recall their own benefits to the Athenians as magnanimous men would, but rather mentioned the Athenians' benefit to themselves. 4. It is also the duty of the magnanimous man to ask almost nothing, scarcely anything at all, from anyone, even when he is weighed down by the greatest need, because one who ought to benefit others should not burden them or ask things from them, since this hardly suits the eminence of magnanimity. There was an example in Miltiades the Athenian, who, although he was general of the Athenians and had increased their wealth and power by various victories, yet in the great poverty in which he lived, wished to ask nothing from the Athenians, and refused the gold offered to him. In the third part of the chapter it is taught how the magnanimous man should conduct himself towards all men in general. For although the magnanimous man seems born to serve anyone readily, since he ought to benefit all, yet this must be done without violating his dignity. And since there are three orders of men, as the Philosopher teaches here and in chapter 11 of book 4 of the Politics, some highest, some lowest, some middling, the magnanimous man will conduct himself towards all of them fittingly and according to their dignity. Therefore he should use his greatness and gravity towards the highest men and princes, who surpass others in dignity, wealth, or even birth, and he does so on account of his awareness of his own virtue, by which he knows himself equal to the greatest men. Towards the middling and lowest, who are far beneath him in pride and condition, he should be easy and humble. The Philosopher gives the reason for each: it is difficult to surpass great men, and the splendour of virtues is seen only in difficult things, as is clear from chapter 3 of book 2; to surpass even great men is a matter of great moment, and belongs only to a noble breast. But to show oneself modest and humble towards the middling and lowest is easy. He proves this by analogy: it is no less absurd to exert oneself against common and humble men than to test the strength of one's body against the weak and infirm. Therefore it is a distinguishing mark of the magnanimous man to contend for honour against his superiors and equals, but towards inferiors to conduct himself modestly, and to temper the greatness of his mind with a certain sweetness and mildness. Pliny writes this of the lion, the most generous of animals, in book 7, chapter 15: "Among wild beasts the lion alone is merciful to suppliants, and rages more quickly against men than against women, and does not attack infants unless driven by great hunger." Among men, Alexander the Great provides an example against Porus, king of the Indians, as Curtius attests, book 8, near the end. In the fourth part of the chapter he brings forward various properties of the magnanimous man drawn from various things. 1. The first is this: he does not often go to honourable places, unless the reason of duty or condition requires it. The reason he does not frequent such places is that he should not seem to court honour, and so incur the mark of pride, or seem to submit himself to others more than his gravity and virtue befit. 2. The magnanimous man is a delayer; he undertakes nothing rashly, but carefully examines the circumstances beforehand, lest by his haste and precipitancy he ruin himself and his affairs. For it belongs to the gravity of the magnanimous man not to be pushed at once, for any reasons, even the most trivial, into undertaking something. Nor should he take on many tasks to be done, but only a few that are outstanding and great. Cicero praises this in Fabius Maximus in De officiis 1, from the verses of Ennius:

units.la: Unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem.
units.tr: "One man by delaying restored our state to us."

units.la: Et contra Cleombrotum vituperat, quod cum temere cum Epaminonda Duce Thebanorum confli xisset, se & opes suas everterit. 111. Proprietas est quod nihil occulte aut simulanter, sed aperte & candide omnia agat, propterea quod occultare quicquid animo volvunt, si timidi & degeneris animi, a quo long flime abesse debet magnanimus, quia mavult probus esse quam haberi: Unde Cic. 1. offic. circa sin, dicit: Viros magnanimos esse bonos & simplices, & veritatis amantes: & ipse Philosophus in libel. de virtut. hoc ipsum requirit. Exemplum fuit in Achil-le, le, qui apud Euripidem simplicem se profitetur, & qui nihil aliud dicat quam sentiat, & talis etiam ubique describitur ab Homero in Iliad. & Helvetii, ut refert Caesar in Comment. se hoc a patribus didicisse referunt, ut virtute magis quam dolo agerent, nec infidis niterentur, sed aperte hostem vincerent. Permittitur tamen magnanimo, ut interdum in dictis dissimulationem adhibeat, modo id Reipub. profuturum, & se inde virtutis fructum reportare posse viderit, quod de Lucio Paterculo Senatore Romano refert Livius lib. 1. decad. 1. IV. Proprietas est, quod magnanimus ad alterius nutum, nisi forte amici, cujus interdum monita sequi non recusat, non potest vivere nec debeat etiam, propterea quod alterius regi & vivere imperio servile admodum fit; id quod probat exemplo adulatorum, quales sunt scurrae & parasiti, quos ad alienum nutum & arbitrium vivere ideo constat, quia servili omnes sunt ingenio; At magnanimus, qui virtutis suae excellentia caeteris omnibus antecellit, servire indignum esse putat: Servile autem esse ad alienum nutum vivere, cum per se sit perspicuum, tum pluribus etiam docet Philosophus lib. 1. Polit. cap. 3. & 4. & 1. Metaph. cap. 2. eam sententiam dicit, videoesse praestantissimam, quod omnes aliae illi subsint, illa vero nulli. Hinc Pontanus lib. 1. de magnanimitate cap. 9. dicit, magnanimum esse libertatis amantissimum, servitutis vero impatientissimum, Plura vide apud Cic. lib. 1. offic. V. Proprietas est, quod nihil admiretur eorum, scilicet quae vulgo in admiratione magna sunt, nimirum caritatem supellectilis, delicias ciborum, comitatum multorum servorum, & cætera ejusmodi, propterea quod nihil ei fit magnum novum aut insolitum. Hinc Cic. 1. offic. ait, ea quæ plerisque eximia & præclara videntur, parvi ducere, & animo stabili firmiter contemnere fortis animi magniq; ducendum est. V 1. Proprietas est, (quæ est ad mansuetudinem spectat) quod magnanimus nō fit injuriarum memor, aut vindictæ pro injuriis illatis cupidus, quin potius omnes injurias contemnit, earumque prorsus oblivisci tur. Hinc egregiè Seneca lib.4.de virtut. ait, Magnanimus si fueris, nunquam judicabis tibi contumeliam fieri, de inimico dicis nō nocuit mihi, sed animum nocendi habuit: sed cum illum in potestate videris, vindictam putabis non vindicare voluisse, scito magnum & honestum esse vindictæ genus ignoscere. Quo pertinet etiam illud Ausonii.
units.tr: He also censures Cleombrotus, because he rashly engaged with Epaminondas, leader of the Thebans, and so ruined himself and his resources. III. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he does everything not secretly or with pretence, but openly and frankly. To hide whatever they have in mind belongs to a timid and degenerate spirit, from which the magnanimous man ought to be far removed, because he prefers to be good rather than to seem so. Hence Cicero says in offic. circa fin.: Magnanimous men are good, simple, and lovers of truth. The Philosopher himself demands the same thing in the little book de virtut. There was an example in Achilles, who in Euripides professes himself plain and says nothing other than what he thinks, and Homer describes him so everywhere in the Iliad. And the Helvetii, as Caesar reports in the Commentaries: they say they learned from their fathers to act by courage rather than by deceit, and not to rely on treachery, but to defeat the enemy openly. Still, the magnanimous man is permitted to use dissimulation in his words at times, provided he sees that it will benefit the commonwealth and that he can thereby gain a fruit of virtue. Livy reports this of Lucius Paterculus, a Roman senator, book 1 of the first decade. IV. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he cannot and ought not to live at another's nod, unless perhaps it is a friend whose advice he does not refuse to follow at times. To live under another's rule and command is altogether servile. This he proves by the example of flatterers, such as jesters and parasites, who are known to live at another's nod and will, because they are all of servile disposition. But the magnanimous man, who by the excellence of his virtue surpasses all others, thinks it unworthy to serve. That to live at another's nod is servile is clear in itself, and the Philosopher teaches it by many arguments in book 1 of the Politics, chapters 3 and 4, and in book 1 of the Metaphysics, chapter 2, where he says that this opinion seems the most excellent, because all other things are subject to it, while it is subject to nothing. Hence Pontanus says in book 1, de magnanimitate, chapter 9 that the magnanimous man is most fond of liberty and most impatient of servitude. See more in Cicero, book 1 of De Officiis. V. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he admires none of those things that are commonly held in great admiration, namely the dearness of furniture, the delicacies of food, a train of many servants, and other things of that kind, because nothing is great, new, or unusual to him. Hence Cicero says in book 1 of De Officiis: Things that seem remarkable and distinguished to most people, to regard as of little worth and to despise with a steady mind, is the mark of a brave and great spirit. VI. It is a property (which pertains to gentleness) that the magnanimous man is not mindful of injuries, nor eager for revenge for injuries inflicted, but rather despises all injuries and forgets them entirely. Hence Seneca admirably says in book 4 de virtut.: If you are magnanimous, you will never judge that an insult is done to you. Of an enemy you say: he did not harm me, but he had the intention to harm. But when you see him in your power, you will think you have not wished to take revenge; know that forgiving is a great and honourable kind of revenge. To this belongs also that line of Ausonius:

units.la: Quod prudentis opus? cum posset, nolle nocere.
units.tr: What is the work of a prudent man? When he could harm, to be unwilling.

units.la: Causa vero cur Magnanimus non debeat esse injuriarum memor hæc redditur à Philosopho, quia nō recordatur mala, sed ea potius propter animi magnitudinem contemnit, & quia suam famam aut æstimationem ab injuriis lædi non putat, ideo neque meminit, idque tribus de causis: 1. Propter excellentiam mentis suæ, quæ magna & generosa esse solet: ideoque injurias tanquam res vilissimas vili pedit. 2. Propter præstantiam virtutis suæ, quæ cæteris omnibus longè antecellit. 3. Propter prudentiam ipsius, quæ omnia adversa & mala in bonum usum convertere solet. VII. Proprietas est, quod Magnanimus non sit multiloquax seu non multum dicat, neque de aliis loquatur. De se non loquitur, sed hoc potius aliis relinquit, ne videatur gloriosus, aut vanus laudum suarum iactator, quia ut canit Poëta:
units.tr: The reason why the magnanimous man ought not to be mindful of injuries is given by the Philosopher: he does not recall evils, but rather despises them because of his greatness of spirit, and because he does not think his good name or esteem is harmed by injuries, so he does not remember them. This is for three reasons: (1) because of the excellence of his mind, which is usually great and noble, and so he counts injuries as the most worthless things and gives them no weight; (2) because of the eminence of his virtue, which far surpasses all others; (3) because of his prudence, which is wont to turn all adverse and evil things to good use. VII. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he is not talkative, that is, he does not say much, nor speak about others. He does not speak about himself, but leaves this to others, lest he seem boastful or a vain boaster of his own praises, since, as the poet sings:

units.la: Hoc faciunt stulti, quos gloria vexat inanis.
units.tr: They do this, the foolish, whom empty glory torments.

units.la: De aliis etiam non multa verba facit, ne videatur eis alludere aut adblandiri aut aliquo modo detrahere: nam longè dissimili est ab iis ingenio, qui alienavitia & reprehensiones suas putant esse laudes, alienas vero laudes suum interpretantur probrum & dedecus. VIII. Proprietas est, quod non sit maledicus, ne inimicis quidem, nisi forte ob contumeliam acceptam, ut honorem tueatur suum, ne si nimium ferat contumelias, iis dignus videatur, & sic sinistram de se apud homines concipiat opinionem. Hoc etiam confirmat alibi Philosophus lib. 7. cap. 7. Polit. ubi dicit, Viros Magnanimos non esse natura & ingenio asperos, nisi quum illos injuria affecerit, quae honori detrahere videatur. Hinc Pontanus lib. 2. de Magn. cap. 3. dicit. Magnanimos viros dedecorosos covitiis excipere, si nempe dicant aliquid, quod tendat in detrimentum Reipub. aut etiam decus & honorem magnatū obscurare possit. Exemplum fuit in Ulysse, qui, ut refert Homerus 2. Iliad. Therfitem convitiis excepit, quod sinistrum & turpe Græcis daret consilium, & illi etiam insultaret. Aliud etiam exemplum est apud Virgil. 2. Æneid. de Turno & Drance. IX. Proprietas est, quod de rebus ad vitam tuendam necessariis & parvis, etsi decent, non muliebriter querulus sit Magnanimus, aut de iis solicitè alios roget, propterea quod hoc illi faciant, qui toti in his rebus sunt, omnemque operam & studium in re familiari miliari acquirenda & augenda ponunt, ut faciunt vulgus & opifices: sed ab his longissime abesse debet Magnanimus, propterea quod hæc ut alia pleraque contemptui habeat, quia hæc magis dependentá fortuna, quam á vera virtute, quam solum magni æstimat Magnanimus. X. proprietas est, quod res elegantes & honestas, licet infructuosas, seu quæ non sunt tanta cum utilitate conjuncta, ut sunt horti amœni, voluptatis gratia comparati: tabulæ pictæ, signa sculpta aut liquefacta, equi, servorum comitatus, &c. habere & possidere mallet, quam res fructuosas aut majore cum utilitate conjunctas, verbi gratia: pecuniam, agros, pecudes, &c. & ratio est, quia prius illud est hominis nulla re indigentis, aut sibiipsi sufficientis, qualem constat esse Magnanimum; posterius illud animum lucri cupidum & utilia honestis præferentem magis arguit.
units.tr: Nor does he say many words about others, lest he seem to flatter them, to fawn upon them, or in any way to disparage them. For he is very unlike those who regard the faults and reproaches of others as their own praise, and who take others' praises as their own shame and disgrace. VIII. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he is not abusive, not even toward enemies, unless perhaps because of an insult received, so that he may defend his honour, lest, if he bears insults too much, he seem worthy of them and so conceive a bad opinion of himself among men. The Philosopher also confirms this elsewhere, book 7, chapter 7 of the Politics, where he says: Magnanimous men are not by nature and temper harsh, except when someone wrongs them in a way that seems to detract from their honour. Hence Pontanus book 2, de Magn., chapter 3, says that magnanimous men receive with reproaches those who say anything that tends to the detriment of the commonwealth, or that could obscure the honour and dignity of the great. There was an example in Ulysses, who, as Homer reports in book 2 of the Iliad, rebuked Thersites with reproaches, because he gave the Greeks a sinister and shameful counsel, and also insulted him. Another example is in Virgil, book 2 of the Aeneid, concerning Turnus and Drances. IX. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he is not querulous in a womanish way about things necessary for maintaining life, though they be small and fitting, nor does he anxiously ask others about them. For those do this who are wholly absorbed in such things and devote all their effort and zeal to acquiring and increasing family wealth, as the common people and craftsmen do. But the magnanimous man ought to be very far from these, because he holds these things in contempt, as most others, since they depend more on fortune than on true virtue, which alone the magnanimous man values highly. X. It is a property of the magnanimous man that he would rather have and possess elegant and honourable things, even if unproductive, or not so closely joined with usefulness, such as pleasant gardens made for pleasure, painted pictures, sculptures or cast figures, horses, a train of servants, and so on, than productive things or things more closely joined with usefulness, for example money, fields, livestock, and so on. The reason is that the former belongs to a man who needs nothing and is sufficient to himself, which is plainly the character of the magnanimous man, whereas the latter indicates a mind eager for gain and preferring the useful to the honourable.

units.la: XI. Proprietas tria in se continet, quæ spectant ad Magnanimum.
units.tr: XI. The property contains three things that pertain to the Magnanimous man.

units.la: 1. est, quod incessu tardo & gravi utatur non properante aut veloci, idq; propter duas causas. Nam celerior gressus aut mentis levitatem, (quia ut ait Cic. 1. offic. mentis habitus ex corporis statu cognoscitur) designat, quæ à gravitate viri Magnanimi longè abesse debet, aut negotiorum multitudine: nam ut ex superioribus patet, non multa agenda suscipit, sed pauca eaq; magna & præclara, & cum non sit πολυπραγμων, qui multis rebus se implicat, ideo nec properatu illi opus est.
units.tr: 1. It is that he uses a slow and grave gait, not hurried or quick, and this for two reasons. A quicker step indicates either lightness of mind, which, as Cic. says in book 1 of De officiis, is recognised from the condition of the body and must be far removed from the gravity of the Magnanimous man, or a multitude of business. For, as is clear from what has gone before, he does not undertake many tasks but few, and those great and outstanding. Since he is not a busybody [πολυπραγμων], who entangles himself in many affairs, he has no need of haste.

units.la: 2. Debet habere voce gravem & distinctam non nimis argutam aut intentam, quia res externas non tanti videtur facere Magnanimus, ut propter illas putet, magna vocis contentione lentione utendum: nam vocis contentio aut animum perturbatum aut ambitiosum aut ingenium iracundum & commotum plerunq; designat. 3. Demum oratione utitur firma & stabili, non varia & non inconstanti, quia varietas aut inconstantia in verbis aut levitatem, aut insipientiam denotat.
units.tr: 2. He should have a voice that is grave and distinct, not overly sharp or strained, because the Magnanimous man does not think external things so important that for their sake he would need to strain his voice greatly or let it fall slack. Straining of the voice usually indicates a troubled mind, an ambitious spirit, or an irascible and agitated temper. 3. Finally, he uses a firm and stable speech, not varied and not inconstant, because variety or inconstancy in words indicates either lightness or folly.

units.la: AXIOMATA:
units.tr: AXIOMATA:

units.la: 1. Magnanimitas magnis honoribus per magnos & probos viros tantum acquisitis delectatur.
units.tr: 1. Magnanimity takes delight in great honours, acquired only through great and upright men.

units.la: 2. Maxima & perfectissima virtuti, qualis est Magnanimitas, vix digna satis laus tribui potest.
units.tr: 2. The greatest and most perfect virtue, such as Magnanimity is, can scarcely be given praise worthy enough.

units.la: 3. Honores à parvis hominibus aut à vulgo collatos non magni facit Magnanimus.
units.tr: 3. The Magnanimous man does not value honours conferred by lowly people or by the common crowd.

units.la: 4. In omni rerum statu ita se gerit, ut neque prospera fortuna nimium efferatur, neque adversa nimium deprimatur.
units.tr: 4. In every state of affairs he conducts himself so that neither good fortune lifts him up too much, nor adversity casts him down too much.

units.la: 5. Divitiae & potentia propter honorem tantum expetenda sunt.
units.tr: 5. Riches and power are to be sought only for the sake of honour.

units.la: 6. Qui honorem non magnifacit, necq; catera, qua homini nem vere decent, recte astimabit.
units.tr: 6. He who does not value honour will not rightly judge the other things that truly befit a man.

units.la: 7. Divitiae & secunda fortuna ad Magnanimitatem comparandam multum conferre videntur.
units.tr: 7. Riches and good fortune seem to contribute much to the acquiring of Magnanimity.

units.la: 8. Etsi propter divitias vulgo honorentur homines, solum tamen bonus & virtute praditus vere honorari debet.
units.tr: 8. Although men are honoured by the common crowd on account of their riches, only the good man endowed with virtue ought to be truly honoured.

units.la: 9. Qui sine virtute divitias possidet, neq; honoribus dignus, neq; Magnanimus dici debet.
units.tr: 9. He who possesses riches without virtue deserves neither honour nor the name of Magnanimous.

units.la: 10. Fieri non potest, ut quis absq; vera virtute prosperos rerum succesus recte ferat.
units.tr: 10. It cannot happen that someone bears prosperous successes rightly without true virtue.

units.la: 11. Magnanimus, quia virtute praditus est, recte de rebus judicat; divites absq; virtute non item.
units.tr: 11. The Magnanimous man, because he is endowed with virtue, judges rightly about things; the rich without virtue do not.

units.la: 12. Magnanimus neque vili precio, neque crebro pericula adhibet, ubi tamen discrimen se dignum videt, majorem honorem, quam vitae curam habet.
units.tr: 12. The Magnanimous man does not expose himself to cheap danger, nor often; yet where he sees a peril worthy of himself, he has a greater regard for honour than for care of his life.

units.la: 13. Proprium est Magnanimi aliis benefacere, non item beneficium ab aliis accipere.
units.tr: 13. It is proper to the Magnanimous man to do good to others, not to receive a benefit from others.

units.la: 14. Magnanimus beneficia in alios a se collata libenter commemorari audit, non item quae in ipsum alii contulerunt, quia neccessitatem & indigentiam arguunt.
units.tr: 14. The Magnanimous man gladly hears benefits conferred by himself on others mentioned, but not those others have conferred on him, since these indicate need and want.

units.la: 15. Magnanimus, etsi summa urget necessitas, quod raro fit, a nullo tamen quicquam petere dignatur.
units.tr: 15. Although the greatest necessity presses, which seldom happens, the Magnanimous man nevertheless deigns to ask anything of no one.

units.la: 16. Erga omnes etiam in genere homines se recte gerit erga magnos magnum, erga mediocres mediocrem, erga infimos humilem se praestat.
units.tr: 16. He conducts himself rightly towards all men in general: towards the great he shows greatness, towards the middling he shows moderation, and towards the lowly he shows himself humble.

units.la: 17. Loca honorata raro, nisi necessitate urgente, adire solet, ne honorem ambire videatur.
units.tr: 17. He is accustomed to approach places of honour rarely, unless pressing necessity urges, lest he seem to be seeking honour.

units.la: 18. Cunctator etiam est, & circumstantias rerum gerendarum diligenter perpendit.
units.tr: 18. He is also slow to act, and weighs carefully the circumstances of the matters he conducts.

units.la: 19. Hoc maxime competit Magnanimo, ut tam odium quam amorem aperte profiteatur, nihil fucati gerat, sed veritatis certa, quam opinionis incerta, curam potius habet.
units.tr: 19. It is especially fitting for the Magnanimous man to profess openly both hatred and love, to do nothing feigned, but to take care of what is certain in truth rather than what is uncertain in opinion.

units.la: 20. Non poterit Magnanimus ad alterius nutum, nisi forte amici, cui interdum obsequitur, vivere.
units.tr: 20. The Magnanimous man cannot live at another's nod, unless perhaps at that of a friend, to whom he sometimes yields.

units.la: 21. Non est admirator rerum variarum, cum ei nihil in rebus humanis sit magnum, neque etiam injuriarum memor, cum mala despicere potius, quam recordari debeat.
units.tr: 21. He is not an admirer of various things, since nothing in human affairs seems great to him; nor is he mindful of injuries, since he ought rather to despise wrongs than to remember them.

units.la: 22. Neque de se, neq; de aliis multum loquitur, nec suas jactat laudes, nec alienas vituperat.
units.tr: 22. He does not speak much either of himself or of others, he does not boast of his own praises, nor does he disparage those of others.

units.la: 23. Non est etiam maledicus, ne inimicis quidem, quod raro tamen contingit, nisi forte ob acceptam contumeliam. 24. De parvis aut necessariis, etsi decent, non multum conqueritur, nec alios folicite de istis rogat.
units.tr: 23. Nor is he a slanderer, not even of his enemies, which however rarely happens, unless perhaps on account of an insult received. 24. He does not complain much about small or necessary matters, even if they are fitting, nor does he anxiously ask others about such things.

units.la: 25. Honesta utilibus prefert, quia sibi sufficiens esse solet.
units.tr: 25. He prefers the honourable to the useful, because he is usually sufficient to himself.

units.la: 26. Incessu, oratione, aut scripto utitur gravi & decente & ad magnitudinem virtutis sua composito.
units.tr: 26. In his gait, speech, or writing he uses what is grave, becoming, and composed in a manner befitting the greatness of his virtue.

units.la: 27. Neque multitudine negotiorum se obruit, nec ullam in rebus gerendis levitatem praefert.
units.tr: 27. He neither overwhelms himself with a multitude of business, nor shows any levity in the conduct of affairs.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DIFFICULTIES.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Magnanimitas virtus dici possit excellentissima, quod asserit Philosophus initio huius capitis, cū ne virtus quidem dici mereatur, neduexcellentissima: nam ut communis experientia probat, versatur circa appetitionem honorum: at in appetendis honoribus boni à malis non distinguuntur. Ergo Magnanimitas ne virtus quidem est, nedum excellentissima. Resp. Per negationem minoris: nam ex natura virtutis distinguit Magnanimitas bonos à malis, & quanquam promiscuè appetant honores, tam boni quam mali, boni tamen merito & digne & secundum rectam rationem soli id faciunt boni, mali econtra. Dein etiam dicit Philosophus in textu Magnanimum non appetere honores, qui conferuntur à quovis aut à vulgo hominum, sed à bonis & gravibus tantum viris, qui dignum virtute præmium referre possunt.
units.tr: I. It is asked whether Magnanimity can be called the most excellent virtue, as the Philosopher asserts at the beginning of this chapter, when it does not even deserve to be called a virtue, much less the most excellent. For, as common experience shows, it is concerned with the pursuit of honours, and in pursuing honours good men are not distinguished from bad. Therefore magnanimity is not even a virtue, much less the most excellent. Answer: I deny the minor premise. For by its nature magnanimity distinguishes good men from bad. Although both good and bad men seek honours indiscriminately, only the good seek them rightly, worthily and according to right reason, while the bad do not. Furthermore, the Philosopher says in the text that the magnanimous man does not seek honours conferred by anyone or by the common crowd, but only those given by good and serious men, who can render a reward worthy of virtue.

units.la: Iustantia: Quicquid versatur circa bonum fragile & caducum, quod ab aliis dependet, id non meretur dici virtus. At Magnanimitas, quia versatur circa honores ab aliis exhibendos, qui sunt in honorante magis quam honorato, ut aperte docet Philosophus lib. 1. huius operis cap. 3. Resp. Duplex est dependentia, alia est dependentia quoad merimeritum, alia quoad actum & collationem. Priori modo non dependet Magnanimitas a bono, quod in aliorum manu consistit: nam quoad meritum dependet a virtute & praestantia viti magni animi, qui factis suis sibi promeruit honorem. Posteriori modo, id est, quoad actum & collationem dependet ab aliis, sed a bonis praecipue, qui sponte beneficiis exhibere solent honorem tanquam praemium virtuti debitum, coacte etiam a malis, qui cogente virtutis merito, honorem exhibere vel inviti cogutur, alioqui ipsa virtus sibi merces pulcherrima, ut ait Claudianus.
units.tr: Objection: Whatever is concerned with a fragile and perishable good that depends on others cannot deserve to be called a virtue. But magnanimity is concerned with honours to be bestowed by others, and these lie more in the one who honours than in the one honoured, as the Philosopher clearly teaches in Book 1, chapter 3 of this work. Answer: Dependence is of two kinds: one with respect to merit, the other with respect to the act and bestowal. In the first way magnanimity does not depend on a good that lies in the hands of others, for with respect to merit it depends on the virtue and excellence of the great-souled man, who has earned honour for himself by his deeds. In the second way, that is, with respect to the act and bestowal, it does depend on others, but chiefly on good men, who are accustomed to offer honour willingly as a reward due to virtue, and also on bad men, who are compelled, though against their will, to offer honour because the merit of virtue constrains them. Otherwise virtue is its own most beautiful reward, as Claudian says.

units.la: II. Quomodo dicat Philosophus Magnanimitatem versari circa pericula, quae sunt objecta Fortitudinis, & circa beneficia conferenda, quae sunt objecta Liberalitatis, cum sic non esset distincta ab iis virtus.
units.tr: II. How the Philosopher can say that magnanimity is concerned with dangers, which are the objects of fortitude, and with benefits to be conferred, which are the objects of liberality, since in that case virtue would not be distinct from them.

units.la: Nam objectis distinguitur inter se virtutes constat, quia quot sunt diversa objecta, aut modi diversi, quibus tractantur objecta diversa, tot distinctae efficiuntur virtutes? Respondeo: Magnanimitatem considerari duobus modis, vel absolute, & sic versatur circa solum honorem tanquam proprium suum objectum; vel comparative, quatenus refertur ad suum subjectum, in quo est, & sic versatur circa objecta Fortitudinis, Liberalitatis, & aliarum virtutum, quia ut excap. 1. patet, omnis in viro magnanimo cumulata debet esse virtus. Et hoc ipsum Seneca etiam in libello de quatuor virtutibus cardinalibus, Magnanimitatem cum Fortitudine & ceteris virtutibus confundit.
units.tr: For it is agreed that virtues are distinguished from one another by their objects, since as many distinct virtues arise as there are different objects, or different modes by which different objects are handled. I answer: magnanimity may be considered in two ways. Either absolutely, and so it is concerned only with honour as its proper object; or comparatively, insofar as it is related to its subject in which it resides, and so it is concerned with the objects of fortitude, liberality and the other virtues, because, as chapter 1 above makes clear, every virtue must be heaped up together in the magnanimous man. Seneca himself also confuses magnanimity with fortitude and the other virtues in his little book on the four cardinal virtues.

units.la: III. Cur dicat Magnanimum non recordari debere beneficii accepti, cum oblivisci sit animi ingrati.
units.tr: III. Why he says the magnanimous man ought not to remember a benefit received, when forgetting is the mark of an ungrateful mind.

units.la: Nam ut praeclare ait Seneca: Vir ingratus beneficio est indignus, utpote qui cito oblivisci tur. Cum igitur ingratitudo sit vitium, gi-tur. tur à Magnanimo abesse debet; non igitur oblivisci, sed re-cordari debet beneficii? Resp. Hoc sensu intelligendum esse Philosophum, ut dicat non recordari beneficium, nempe ut novum accipiat, quia qui accipit beneficium, alterius ope indigere videtur, & necessitatem aut indigentiam arguit, sed ab his duobus maxime sibi cavet Magnanimus, quia sibi ipsi αὐτάρκης esse solet: recordatur tamen, si quod beneficium acceperit, ut rependat, & multo quidem cumulatius, quam accepit, quia hoc spectat ad excellentiam & splendorem Magnanimitatis.
units.tr: For, as Seneca rightly says, the ungrateful man is unworthy of a benefit, since he quickly forgets it. Since ingratitude is a vice, it must be absent from the magnanimous man; therefore he ought not to forget but to remember the benefit? Answer: The Philosopher must be understood in this sense, that he does not remember the benefit so as to receive it as something new, for the one who receives a benefit seems to need another's help and shows his necessity or want. The magnanimous man guards most carefully against these two things, because he is usually self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης]. Yet he does remember a benefit he has received, so as to repay it, and indeed with far greater abundance than he received it, because this belongs to the excellence and splendour of magnanimity.

units.la: IV. Cur dicat Magnanimum nihil admirari, cum admiratio non cadat, nisi in summa & praeclarissima quaeque ingenia. Admiratio enim peperit Philosophiam, ut testis est Philosophus lib. 1. Metaphys. cap. 1. & qui non admiratur Dei & naturae opera, ut per eorum admirationem in causarum cognitionem devenirat, non homo, sed stipes & truncus est, ut comment. 2. ad illum locum docet Averroes? Resp. Magnanimitatem sicut omnes virtutes circa tria bona versari, animi nempe corporis, & fortunae, ut diserte docet Philosophus cap. 8. lib. 1. hujus operis, Magnanimus nihil admiratur in bonis fortunae, propterea quod nihil in iis magnificat, aut nulla admiratione dignum putet; corporis & animi, si quib. inest, cum raritate quadam aut supra vulgus, sicut debet, suspicere solet, & tanquam Dei & naturae dotes agnoscit.
units.tr: IV. Why he says the magnanimous man admires nothing, since admiration falls only upon the highest and most distinguished minds. For admiration gave birth to philosophy, as the Philosopher testifies in Metaphysics Book 1, chapter 1; and one who does not admire the works of God and nature, so that by their admiration he may arrive at knowledge of causes, is not a man but a stock and a block, as Averroes teaches in his second commentary on that passage? Answer: Magnanimity, like all the virtues, is concerned with three kinds of good: those of the mind, of the body and of fortune, as the Philosopher expressly teaches in chapter 8 of Book 1 of this work. The magnanimous man admires nothing in the goods of fortune, because he attaches no greatness to them and thinks nothing in them worthy of admiration. But in the goods of body and mind, where such goods are present, he is accustomed to look up to them with a certain esteem, as is proper, since they are rare or above the common run, and he acknowledges them as gifts of God and nature.

units.la: V. Cur dicat in decima proprietate, Magnanimum res pulchras & inutiles potius respicere quam utiles, cum hoc non sit viri Prudentis. At in Magnanimo summa esse debet Prudentia, propterea quod cum Prudentia sit corona omnium virtuvirtutum & in magnanimo requiratur aggregatio omnium virtutum simul, ut ex lib. 7. huius operis, tum etiam ex 9. magnor. moral. patet. Proinde male asseveratur ipsam proprietatem videtur Philosophus? Resp. Res fructuosas seu utiles esse duorum generum. Alia enim sunt utiles & honestae simul, & istas inprimis respicit Magnanimus propter finem virtutis communem quem habent, nempe honestatem. Alia sunt utiles quidem, sed non honestae, & istas ies non tam respicit Magnanimus quam inutiles, sed ut ipse interpretatur, quae amoenitatem potius & delectationem efferunt, quam utilitatem, ut sunt horti amoeni, pomaria, &c. quia in his splendor & praestantia Magnanimitatis elucet, tamen etiam unaipsius avtapxeia.
units.tr: V. Why he says in the tenth property that the magnanimous man regards beautiful and useless things rather than useful ones, since this does not belong to the prudent man. But in the magnanimous man prudence must be supreme, because prudence is the crown of all the virtues, and magnanimity requires the combination of all the virtues together, as is clear from Book 7 of this work and from the Magna Moralia, Book 9. Therefore the Philosopher seems wrongly to assert this property? Answer: Fruitful or useful things are of two kinds. Some are both useful and honourable at once, and these the magnanimous man regards especially, because of the common end of virtue which they have, namely honour. Others are useful indeed but not honourable, and these the magnanimous man does not regard so much; but, as he himself explains, he regards those which bring forth pleasantness and delight rather than usefulness, such as pleasant gardens, orchards, and so on, because in these the splendour and excellence of magnanimity shines forth, and also in them lies a sign of its self-sufficiency [αὐταρκεία].

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: SEquitur tertium & ultimum membrum huius tractatus de Magnanimitate, in quo agit de extremis ipsius. Partes huius capitis sunt tres: Inprima dicit vitia ista non g aviadmodum reprehensione esse digna. Infecunda agit de ipsis extremis, & de variis ipsorum motus & proprietatibus. In tertia comparat extrema inter se cum ipso medio.
units.tr: Here follows the third and last part of this treatise on Magnanimity, in which he treats of its extremes. This chapter has three parts. The first says that these vices do not deserve severe reproof. The second treats of the extremes themselves and of their various movements and properties. In the third he compares the extremes with one another and with the mean itself.

units.la: Inprima igitur dicit gravi reprehensione non esse digna (quod ipsum supra de extremis Magnificentiae monuerat) propterea quod non sint in publicum mala, & quod, qui his vitiis laborant, non aliis, sed sibi ipsis noceant, quod tanquam verum concedi poterit, si ista vitia per se & absque aliorum mixtione considerentur, propterea quod in honoribus tantum venadis, sed magis vel munus, quā decet, occupenpentur. At vero si ut committa ab aliis vitiis perpendantur, gravissima sunt vitia, & maxima reprehensione digna, cum magnum Reipub. damnum inferant, ut variae historiae, ipsaq; experientia testantur.
units.tr: First, then, he says that they do not deserve severe reproof (as he had already noted above concerning the extremes of Magnificence), because they are not harmful to the public, and because those who suffer from these vices harm not others but themselves. This may be granted as true if these vices are considered in themselves and apart from any mixture with other vices, since they are concerned only with honours, and are occupied with them more or less than is fitting. But if they are weighed as joined with other vices, they are the most grievous vices and deserve the greatest reproof, since they inflict great damage on the commonwealth, as various histories and experience itself attest.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de ipsis extremis, & quidem primo de Pusillanimitate, quae Magnanimitati opponitur in defectu, de quo primo loco agit, propterea quod vitium sit deterius, & pluribus mendis laboret, quam superbia, ut sub finem cap. patebit. Definitur Pusillanimitas vitium in honoribus deficiens, cum scilicet quispiam virtute aut meritis claras honores sibi jure competentes rejicit. Hujus vitii notas seu proprietates quatuor adfert Philosophus: 1. est, quod hoc vitio laborantes injurii sint in Deum: nam cum praeclara Deus in ipso dona contulerit, & propterea honoribus dignos judicarit, dum istos spernunt, Deum eorum autore spernere videntur. 2. est: quod seipsos suspectos reddant, quasi sceleris alicujus sibi essent conscii, nam ut canit Poëta:
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he treats of the extremes themselves, and first of Pusillanimity, which is opposed to Magnanimity by deficiency. He treats of it first because the vice is worse and suffers from more faults than pride, as will appear towards the end of the chapter. Pusillanimity is defined as a vice that falls short in honours, namely when someone rejects honours rightly due to him on account of his virtue or merits. The Philosopher gives four marks or properties of this vice: (1) those who suffer from it are wrong towards God, for since God has bestowed excellent gifts upon them and so judged them worthy of honours, by spurning these they seem to spurn God, their author; (2) they make themselves suspect, as if they were conscious of some crime, for as the poet sings:

units.la: Conscia mens ut cuique sua est, ita concipit intra Pectora pro facto spemq; metumq; suo.
units.tr: Each mind, as it is its own, so conceives within its breast hope and fear for its deed.

units.la: Et cum honos sit indicium de cujusque, quem colimus, virtute, cur eo indignum sequis judicet? nisi malis intestinis laboret, & propter metum majoris mali aut conscientiam scelcris promeritum honore refugiat. 3. nota est, quod seipsos non bene perpendant, neq; sciant, quibus honoribus digni sint, nam si scirent, quibus bonis digni forent, utique appeterent tanquam virtutis praemium. Quam vero turpe sit seipsum non bene nosse in Phil. Plato & Cic. lib. 3. ep. famil. ad Q. fratrem docet. 4 est, quod Pusillanimi-
units.tr: And since honour is a sign of the virtue of the one we honour, why do you judge him unworthy of it? Unless he is troubled by inner torments and, out of fear of a greater evil or from a conscience of a crime he has earned, shrinks back from honour. 3. It is well known that men do not weigh themselves rightly, nor know what honours they deserve; for if they knew what goods they were worthy of, they would surely desire them as the reward of virtue. How shameful it is not to know oneself well, Plato and Cicero teach in the Philebus and in the third book of the letters to Familiares, to Quintus his brother. 4. Pusillanimity makes men's spirits sluggish and turns them away from doing noble deeds and from honourable pursuits, as from dignities and magistracies in the commonwealth; for just as glory stirs men to act nobly, so Ovid says:

units.la: Gg nimitas segnescere faciat hominum animos, & avo- cet a rebus præclarè gerendis ab honestis studiis, ut à dignitatibus & a Magistratibus in Repub. nam ut gloria excitat homines ad præclarè faciendum, & ut ait Ovidius:
units.tr: Pusillanimity makes men's spirits grow sluggish and calls them away from honourable pursuits and from doing notable deeds, and so from offices and magistracies in the commonwealth; for just as glory stirs men to do noble things, as Ovid says:

units.la: Excitat auditor studium, laudataq; virtus Crescit, & immensum gloria calcar habet.
units.tr: The listener's eagerness is roused, and praised virtue grows, and glory has an immense spur.

units.la: In gloriæ contemtus avocat à rebus bene gerendis. Hoc vitio notatus fuit à Suetonio Domitianus Cæ- sar, qui honorem sibi à Senatu propter merita obla- tum recusavit. Decretum scilicet erat, ut quoties consulatum gereret, equitem Romani, quibus fors obtigisset trabeati, & cum hastis militaribus illum præcederent interelictores apparitoresque. Alterum vitium, quod magnanimitati opponitur in excessu, dicitur Superbia aut Elatio. Definitur vitium in magnis honoribus modum excedens. Hujus notas etiam tres affert Philosophus, quod, qui hoc vitio laborat, stultus plerunque sit: ignorat namque seipsum, & quia magnis honoribus dignum se judicat, quibus non sit dignus, & majores sibi arrogat, quam debet, ideo est injustus. Exemplum hujus in sacris fuit Sennacherib, qui jactitat in robore fortitudinis suæ devicisse omnes gentes Esa.26. & Nebucadnezar Dan.4. In profanis Alexander Magnus, qui, ut Arianus, Curtius, & Plutarchus referunt, à Lacedæmoniis contendit, ut divini ei honores decernerētur. Talis etiam fuit Julius Cæsar, qui ut refert Suetonius in ejus vita honores, nō modò nimios recepit, ut perpetuum consulatum, perpetuam dictaturam, perpetuam censuram, insuper prænomen Impe-
units.tr: Through contempt of glory it withdraws them from doing good deeds. This vice was noted in Suetonius's account of Domitian Caesar, who refused the honour offered him by the Senate on account of his merits. It had been decreed, namely, that whenever he held the consulship, Roman knights, chosen by lot, should walk before him in triumphal togas with military spears, along with the lictors and attendants. The other vice, which is opposed to magnanimity by excess, is called Pride or Haughtiness. It is defined as a vice that exceeds due measure in great honours. The Philosopher also gives three marks of it: that the one who suffers from this vice is mostly foolish, for he does not know himself, and because he judges himself worthy of great honours for which he is not worthy, and claims for himself greater things than he should, he is therefore unjust. An example of this in sacred history is Sennacherib, who boasts that in the strength of his might he has conquered all nations (Esa.26.), and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan.4.). In profane history there is Alexander the Great, who, as Arrian, Curtius and Plutarch relate, demanded of the Lacedaemonians that divine honours be decreed to him. Julius Caesar was also such a man, who, as Suetonius relates in his life, received honours not only excessive, such as a perpetual consulship, a perpetual dictatorship, a perpetual censorship, and besides these the forename Impe-

units.la: Imperatoris, nomé Patris patriæ statuam supra Reges, sedampliora humano fastigio sibi decerni voluit. 2. nota est, quod vestitu & ornatu totoque corporis gestu, aliisque moribus externis non debitum sibi honorem asseciet. Sic Caligula referentibus Suetonio & Xiphelino ad tantamprocessit superbiam, ut Deorum vestimenta induceret, nunc virgine bellicosam, nunc mulierem habitu repræsentabat: in sacrificiis deorum ornatu utebatur, in plateis serico & triumphali vestitu incedebat. In sacris exemplum est Herodes Actor. 12. 3. nota est, quod se jactiret, & res suas secundas nimium ostentet, cujusmodi sunt fundus, divitiæ, possessiones, opes, eruditio, &c. quæ ideo ostentat, ut honoré & simam suam apud vulgus hominū sueatur, & in majus augear. Exempla occurrunt varia, sic Croesus Lydorum Rex opes suas ostentavit apud Solonem. Sic Palæmon Grammaticus eò processit superbiæ, ut literas secundas, & interituras dixerit. Talis etiam fuit Empedocles Poeta, de quo Laertius lib. 2. de vita Philosoph. & Horat. in arte Poëtica. Hinc præclarè Seneca lib. 4 de virtut. magnanimitas si supra modum se extollat, virum saciet minacem, turgidum, inflatum, inquietum, in quascun-que dictorum & factorum eminentiam neglectâ honestate sestivum, quibus omnibus momentis supercilia subrigens, ut bestiarius inquietat, excitat, alium serit, alium fugat. Plura vide apud Keckerm. pag. 213. In tertia parte capitis co-parat extrema inter se & Pusillanimitatem deterrimus longè vitium esse superbia duabus rationibus probat. 1. Quia frequentius accidit, ut in pluribus reperiatur: nam plures videre licet abjectianimi, qui honores
units.tr: rator, the title Father of the Fatherland, and a statue above the kings; but he wished still greater things to be decreed to him than human rank allows. (2) He is wrong in his clothing, adornment, whole bearing and other outward habits, claiming honour not due to him. Thus Caligula, as Suetonius and Xiphilinus relate, went to such pride that he introduced the garments of the gods; at one time he presented himself as a warlike virgin, at another as a woman; in the sacrifices to the gods he used divine adornment, and in the streets he walked in silk and triumphal dress. In sacred history the example is Herod (Acts 12.). (3) He boasts and makes too much display of his prosperous circumstances, such as estates, riches, possessions, wealth, learning and so on, which he displays so that he may win honour and esteem among the common people and increase it. Various examples occur. Thus Croesus, king of the Lydians, displayed his wealth before Solon. Thus Palaemon the grammarian went so far in pride that he called letters secondary and perishable. Such also was the poet Empedocles, of whom Laertius (book 2, On the Lives of the Philosophers) and Horace (in the Art of Poetry) speak. Hence Seneca admirably says (book 4, On Virtues): Magnanimity, if it raises itself beyond measure, makes a man threatening, swollen, puffed up and restless; eager for prominence in whatever words and deeds, neglecting honour, it raises its eyebrows at every moment, like a beast-fighter it disturbs, excites, binds one man and puts another to flight. More may be seen in Keckermann, p. 213. In the third part of the chapter he compares the extremes with one another, and proves by two reasons that pride is by far the worse vice than Pusillanimity: (1) because it happens more often and is found in more people. For one may see many men of abject spirit who spurn honours on account of their poverty, since maintaining honour requires great expense and great display. But all men are generally avaricious by nature, as was proved above in chapter 4 of this book.

units.la: Gg nores spernant ob paupertatem nimirum: nam ad honore tuendum magnis sumtibus magnaq; pompa opus est. At omnes sunt plerunq; natura avari, ut superius cap. 4. huius libri probatum fuit. 2. Deterius est vitium, quia longius recedit a medio quam superbia: nam nullum omnino convenientiam cum magnanimitate habet, ut ex cap. 12. lib. 2. ostentat Philosophus. Accedit etiam haec ratio, quod qui hoc vitio laborant, aliisq; malo exemplo praeeant, occultantes eas virtutes, quas Deus in alium finem iis communicarat.
units.tr: (2) It is the worse vice because it departs further from the mean than pride does; for it has no agreement at all with magnanimity, as the Philosopher shows in chapter 12 of book 2. To this is added the further reason that those who suffer from this vice set a bad example to others, hiding those virtues which God gave them for another purpose.

units.la: Axiomata.
units.tr: Axioms.

units.la: 1. Pusillanimitas & superbia, utut vitia sint Magnanimitati opposita, sed tamen in se non prorsus nociva.
units.tr: 1. Pusillanimity and pride, although they are vices opposed to magnanimity, are nevertheless not wholly harmful in themselves.

units.la: 2. Pusillanimus, quibus honoribus dignus est, se defraudat, & malam de se suspicionem excitat, quod honores se dignos refugiat.
units.tr: 2. The pusillanimous man defrauds himself of the honours he deserves, and arouses a bad suspicion about himself, in that he shrinks from honours that are his due.

units.la: 3. Non bene perpendit, quibus bonus dignus est, secus enim ista bona tanquam virtutis praemium appetere.
units.tr: 3. He does not weigh rightly what goods he deserves; otherwise he would seek those goods as the reward of virtue.

units.la: 4. Pusillanimi non tam sunt famai, quam cogitabundi semper in se cogitantes se hac aut illa laude & honore indignos esse.
units.tr: 4. The pusillanimous are not so much fearful of fame as always brooding, thinking within themselves that they are unworthy of this or that praise and honour.

units.la: 5. Pusillanimitas deterret a rebus praeclare gerendis, & aliis pessimo exemplo esse solet.
units.tr: 5. Pusillanimity deters men from doing things worthy of note, and is wont to be a very bad example to others.

units.la: 6. Superbi sunt stulti, quia seipsos ignorant, & quia majores quam quibus digni sunt, honores appetunt, injusti etiam sunt.
units.tr: 6. The proud are foolish, because they do not know themselves, and because they seek honours greater than those they deserve; they are also unjust.

units.la: 7. Superbus vestitu & ornatu honorem supra modum affectat, & res suas secundas nimium ostentat.
units.tr: 7. The proud man seeks honour beyond measure by his clothing and adornment, and displays his prosperous circumstances too much.

units.la: 8. Magnus opponitur Pusillanimitas, quam superbia Magnanimitati, quia longius a medio recedit, & deterius longe vitium est.
units.tr: 8. Pusillanimity is opposed to greatness of soul as pride is to magnanimity; because it departs further from the mean, it is by far the worse vice.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Pusillanimitas deterius sit vitium, quod vult Philosophus, quam elatio aut immoderata honoris cupiditas, cum tamen contrarium ratio evincat, nam in textu pusillanimes non [?]cuntur stulti, superbi vero dicuntur: secundo idem probatur ab affectis, nam superbia in Republ. multos excitat tumultus & turbas, quod probatur exemplo Cæsaris & Pompeii, de quibus canit Poëta Lucanus: Sed nullum jam ferre potest Cæsar ve prior em, Pompeiúsve parem.
units.tr: I. The question is whether pusillanimity is a worse vice, as the Philosopher holds, than vanity or immoderate desire for honour. Reason seems to prove the contrary: in the text the pusillanimous are not called foolish, but the proud are. Secondly, the same is shown from its effects: pride in the commonwealth stirs up many tumults and disturbances, as the example of Caesar and Pompey shows, of whom the poet Lucan sings: "But Caesar cannot bear a superior, nor Pompey an equal."

units.la: At contra pusillanimitas homines docet vita se quieta tradere, ut videre sint in Scipione juniore, sicut memi nit Plin. l. 7. nat. hist. cap. 13: multo ergo deterius vitium videtur esse elatio, quam Pusillanimitas? Resp. Deterius esse pusillanimitatem vitium præter rationes supra allatas tribus de causis. 1. Propter hypocrisin metam, quam in se rectam habet; solent enim hoc vitio laborantes tam diu se occultare, donec commodum le pudendi tempus reperiunt. 2. Quia omnem operam, quam Reip. debent, denegant Pusillanimes: Nam cum homo natura sit animal Politicum, sicut dicitur cap. 7. lib. 1. hujus operis, & cap. 9 lib. 9. & 1. Pol. cap. 2. ideo homo non tantum in societate cæterorum vivere debet, sed totum humanum genus, quā o possit studio juvare. 3. Quia majorem asshmationem cum Magnanimitate habet Superbia, quam Pusillanimitas: Nam Pusillanimes omnes honores indecorè & indiscretè fugiunt, Superbi quidem appetunt honores, sed supra modum tantum: quod vero superbi dicantur stulti in textu, id ideo fit, quia vitia sua non æquè occultare possunt ac pusillanimes: nam hi plerunque vita delectantur solitaria & quàtum possunt, turbis hominum se eximunt, illi econtra in ore totius populi continuò versantur: neque superbia per se dat turbas in Repub. sed per accidés tantum, quatenus scilicet est cum injustitia, rapacitate, aliisque vitiis conjuncta. Ad hunc tractatum de Magnanimitate non incommodè adjici possunt paucæ hæ quæstiones.
units.tr: But on the contrary, pusillanimity teaches men to give themselves up to a quiet life, as may be seen in the younger Scipio, as Pliny recalls in Natural History, book 7, chapter 13. Is pride, then, a much worse vice than pusillanimity? Answer: pusillanimity is a worse vice than pride, for three reasons besides those given above. (1) Because of the hypocrisy it carries within itself, for those afflicted with this vice usually hide themselves for as long as they can, until they find a convenient time to show themselves. (2) Because pusillanimous men deny all the service they owe the commonwealth. For since man is by nature a political animal, as is said in chapter 7 of book 1 of this work, in chapter 9 of book 9, and in the first book of the Politics, chapter 2, man must live not only in society with others but must also, with all his zeal, help the whole human race. (3) Because pride has greater affinity with magnanimity than pusillanimity does. The pusillanimous shun all honours, unbecomingly and indiscriminately, whereas the proud do seek honours, but only beyond measure. That the proud are called foolish in the text happens because they cannot conceal their faults as easily as the pusillanimous can. The latter usually delight in a solitary life and, as far as they can, withdraw from crowds of men; the former, on the contrary, are constantly in the mouths of the whole people. Nor does pride in itself cause tumults in the commonwealth, but only incidentally, insofar as it is joined with injustice, rapacity and other vices. To this treatise on magnanimity these few questions may fittingly be added.

units.la: I. Cum Magnanimitas sit virtus excellentissima, quæ versatur circa honorem, an Magnanimus majorem vitæ, quam honoris debeat habere rationem, aut econtra? Pro prima parte, quod scilicet major vitæ, quam honoris habenda sit ratio, militant sequentes hæ tres rationes: 1. Quia vita est præstantior honore, nam à vita totius hominis conservatio dependet, ab honore autem non. 2. Quia mors seu vitæ amissio hominis totius substantialem corruptionem seu destructionem secum trahit, honoris autem amissio minimè. 3. Quia ut ait Philosophus l. b. 3. hujus operis cap. 8. mors est maximè formidulosa, nam est extrema rerum omnium meta, & nihil post mortem homini superesse videtur, neque boni, neque mali. Pro posteriori parte, quod scilicet honoris haberi debeat major ratio, quam vitæ, sunt hæ rationes: 1. Quia, ut ait Philosophus cap. 7. hujus libri, honor est virtutis præmium, & cum major virtutis, à qua homo dicitur bonus & frugi, habenda sit ratio, quam vitæ, idem videtur quoque de honore statuendum. 2. Quia satius est mori, quam peccare, & peccando adversus Deum grave aliquid committere, id quod proprobatur exemplis: Nam summa laude digna censetur Susanna, quod maluerit potius mori, quam pudicitiam profiteri, & sic Deum graviter offendere. Contra vituperanda est Lucretia, quod maluerit cum Tarquinio juniore Tarquinii superbi filio adulterium committere, quam abeo trucidari. Pro decisione hujus quaestionis distinguendum est inter verum & falsum honorem, itemque inter veram & falsam infamiam: Major quidem ratio veri honoris conservandi, & verae huic oppositae infamiae fugiendae habeni ratio debet, quam vitae, non autem falsi honoris falsaeque infamiae. Proinde vir bonus, qui vera Magnanimitate est praeditus, veri honoris confervandi, veraeque infamiae declinandae gratia potius, quam vivere debet, si haec duo in discrimen veniant, & alterum necessario sit eligendum: non autem falsi honoris falsaque infamiae gratia; Cujus rei haec ratio esse potest, quia verus honor a virtutis verae meritis provenit, vera infamia a malis factis & indignis facinoribus, ideo quidem Virtutis est studiosus, veri honoris conservandi & verae infamiae declinandae studiosus esse debet, non ante a falsi honoris & infamiae, quia ab umbratili hominum opinione non a rebus ipsi, proficisci solent.
units.tr: I. Since magnanimity is the most excellent virtue, and it is concerned with honour, ought the magnanimous man to have greater regard for life than for honour, or the reverse? For the first part, that greater regard should be had for life than for honour, the following three reasons speak. (1) Because life is more excellent than honour, for the preservation of the whole man depends on life, but not on honour. (2) Because death, or the loss of life, brings with it the substantial corruption or destruction of the whole man, whereas the loss of honour does not. (3) Because, as the Philosopher says in book 3 of this work, chapter 8, death is most dreadful, for it is the extreme limit of all things, and nothing seems to remain for man after death, neither good nor evil. For the latter part, that greater regard should be had for honour than for life, these are the reasons. (1) Because, as the Philosopher says in chapter 7 of this book, honour is the reward of virtue; and since greater regard is to be had for virtue, by which a man is called good and upright, than for life, the same seems to be decided for honour. (2) Because it is better to die than to sin, and by sinning to commit something grave against God. This is proved by examples: Susanna is judged worthy of the highest praise because she preferred to die rather than to betray her chastity and so offend God gravely. Lucretia, on the contrary, is to be blamed because she preferred to commit adultery with Tarquin the younger, son of the proud Tarquin, rather than be slain by him. To decide this question, a distinction must be drawn between true and false honour, and likewise between true and false infamy. A greater regard must indeed be had for preserving true honour and for avoiding the true infamy opposed to it than for life, but not for false honour and false infamy. Accordingly, a good man who is endowed with true magnanimity ought rather to die than live, for the sake of preserving true honour and avoiding true infamy, if these two come into peril and one of them must necessarily be chosen. But he ought not to do so for the sake of false honour and false infamy. The reason for this may be that true honour arises from the merits of true virtue, and true infamy from evil deeds and unworthy crimes. Therefore he should be zealous for virtue, and zealous for preserving true honour and avoiding true infamy; he should not be zealous for false honour and false infamy, since these usually arise from the shadowy opinion of men rather than from the things themselves.

units.la: II. An ad verum & solidum honorem sufficiat unius hominis testimonium, an vero plurium consensus requiratur? Resp. Per distinctionem. Nam aliud est honoris ipsius natura, aliud est confirmatio & illustratio ejusdem. Ad honoris quidem veri & solidi naturam sufficit unius probi & prudentis hominis testimonium proprer duas rationes: 1. Quia judicū recte conformatum habet mentemq; recte dispositam, secundum quam non nisi bene meritis honorem exhibere solet. 2. Quia in uno viro prudenti omnes alios eius similes habemus, una enim est vox unaq; sententia, ut inquit Cic. 1. offic. omnium proborum hominum. Cæterum ad honoris illustrationem & confirmationem seu autoritatis incrementum non sufficit unius hominis testimonium, sed opus est plurium suffragio. Nam ut experientia docet, sicut ad honoris consecutionem multorum opus est consensu, sic etiam ad ejusdem conservationem plurium opus est auxilio & consilio. Plura vide apud Petrum Martyrem ad cap. 5. 1. Nicomach, pag. 92.
units.tr: II. Is the testimony of one man sufficient for true and solid honour, or is the consent of many required? Answer by distinction. For the nature of honour itself is one thing, and its confirmation and illustration is another. For the nature of true and solid honour, the testimony of one upright and prudent man is sufficient, for two reasons. (1) Because he has a rightly formed judgement and a rightly disposed mind, by which he is accustomed to bestow honour only on those who have deserved well. (2) Because in one prudent man we have all others like him; for, as Cicero says in De officiis, book 1, there is one voice and one judgement of all upright men. But for the illustration and confirmation of honour, or the increase of authority, the testimony of one man is not sufficient, but the suffrage of many is needed. For, as experience teaches, just as the consent of many is needed to acquire honour, so too the help and counsel of many are needed to preserve it. See more in Peter Martyr on chapter 5 of book 1 of the Nicomachean Ethics, p. 92.

units.la: III. An largitionibus uti & honores emere liceat? Resp.
units.tr: III. Is it lawful to use largesses and to buy honours? Answer.

units.la: Etsi corruptus iste mos ubique locorum hodie inoleverit, ut qui justis rationibus honores assequi non valeat, illos emere minimè dubitet, modo opes & facultates adsint, nefas tamen esse, ut honores emātur, multis rationibus probatur: 1. est, quia omnibus justis legibus hoc damnatur, qua de re multa extant in ff. ad l. Iuliam, ff. de ambitu. Hoc vero vitium apud Latinos dicitur Ambitus in temporalibus, in spiritualibus dicitur Simonia, à Simone Mago, qui utcst Act. 8. vers. 18. donum Spiritus sancti pecunia emere voluit. 2. Quia turpissimum & indignissimum est viris probis pecunia aut largitionibus populi corrogare suffragia, & non virtute. Nam ut egregiè ait Plautus: Virtute ambire oportet, non fautoribus, Sat habet fautorum semper qui recte facit. 3. Quia quonquondam ambitus convicti duplici poena afficiebantur, infamia scilicet & multa pecuniaria: Infamia propterea, quod honores quibus minime digni essent, illicitis modis affectarent, & sic Reip. magnum damnum inferrent: multa pecuniaria damnabantur, ut cum jactura rei familiaris ab ejusmodi vitiis abstinerent. 4. Quia in Repub. Romana hujus vitii poenae subinde auctae fuerunt, quoniam sine modo grassabatur hoc vitium, & crescente delicto crescere aut augeri etiam debent poenae. 5.
