Qua Ecclesiastici Canones aut jus Canonicum leges Romanas hic est imitatum, propterea quod hoc vitium etiam in Ecclesiam irrepserit, & hodie passim regnet, ideo multa praeclare sancita sunt contra Simoniam quaest. 1. & 5. decretalium & can. 3. quaest. 2. expresse prohibetur, ne ecclesiastici vices suas sub annuo censu aliis concedant. 6. & ult. Qua qui dignitates Ecclesiasticas vendunt, puerum Elisaei Prophetae Gehesi 2. Reg. cap. 5. ut ait Augustinus, imitantur, & qui emunt, Simonem Magum referunt, ideo diligenter iis ab utriusque poena cavendam. Plura vide apud Petrum Martyrem ad cap. 1. Nicom. pag. 95. & apud Junium parte 1. quaest. Polit. pag. 95. Errant igitur, qui bona Ecclesiae & officia quaecunq; Ecclesiastica certa quadam pecunia coemi afferunt. Errant etiam, qui subtilitate quadam praepostera inter officium ipsum & reditum officii distinguunt, & prius nefas esse, ut ematur, putant, posterius autem non. Nam utrumque nefas est emere, nemo enim in ossi ium Ecclesiasticum se intrudere debet, nisi legitime vocatus fuerit. Sicut Apostolus Rom. 10. verj. 19. docet, quoquomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint. Reditus vero officii ab ipso officio separari non debet: nam qui servit altari, vivere debet ex altari, & dignus est mercenarius mercede sua, Matth. 10. vers. 10. 1. ad Timoth. 5. vers. 18. secundo etiam apud saniores non tantum in primitiva Ecclesia, sed hodie etiamnum hoc ut simonia dominatur.
units.tr: Although this corrupt custom has now taken root in every place, so that a man who cannot win honours by just means hardly hesitates to buy them, provided he has the wealth and resources, it is proved on many grounds that buying honours is wrong. (1) First, it is condemned by all just laws, on which much is found in the Digest, under the Julian law and under the title on canvassing. Among the Latins this vice is called ambitus in secular matters, and in spiritual matters it is called simony, from Simon Magus, who, as Acts 8.18 tells, wished to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit with money. (2) Second, it is most shameful and unworthy for upright men to win votes by money or by largesses to the people, and not by virtue. For, as Plautus says admirably: "One ought to canvass by virtue, not by supporters; he who acts rightly always has enough supporters." (3) Third, those convicted of canvassing were once punished with a double penalty, namely infamy and a fine. Infamy, because they sought by illicit means honours they did not deserve, and so did great harm to the commonwealth; a fine, so that by the loss of their property they might abstain from such vices. (4) Fourth, in the Roman commonwealth the penalties for this vice were from time to time increased, because the vice spread without limit, and as the crime grows, the penalties too ought to grow or be enlarged. (5) Fifth, the ecclesiastical canons, or canon law, have imitated the Roman laws here, because this vice has crept into the Church too and today reigns everywhere; therefore many excellent decrees have been made against simony in Decretals, questions 1 and 5, and Canon 3, question 2, expressly forbids that clergy let out their offices to others for a yearly rent. (6) And last: those who sell ecclesiastical dignities imitate, as Augustine says, the servant of the prophet Elisha, Gehazi (2 Kings 5); and those who buy resemble Simon Magus. Therefore one must take diligent care against the penalty of both. More on this may be seen in Peter Martyr on chapter 1 of the Nicomachean Ethics, p. 95, and in Junius, part 1, question on politics, p. 95. Those therefore err who assert that the goods of the Church and any ecclesiastical offices whatever may be bought for a certain sum of money. Those also err who, by a kind of perverse subtlety, distinguish between the office itself and the income of the office, and think that the former may not be bought, but the latter may. For it is wrong to buy either, since no one ought to thrust himself into an ecclesiastical office unless he has been lawfully called; as the Apostle teaches in Romans 10.19: "How shall they preach, unless they be sent?" But the income of an office ought not to be separated from the office itself: for "he who serves the altar ought to live from the altar," and "the labourer is worthy of his wages," Matthew 10.10; 1 Timothy 5.18. Secondly, among the wiser sort this simony reigns not only in the primitive Church, but even today.

units.la: IV. & ult. Quid sentiendum sit de illo Philosophi verbo, quod habentur cap. 8. huius libri, nempe vir magnanimus loca honorata adire non debet, cum tamen ratio contrarium doceat.
units.tr: IV. And last. What is to be thought of that saying of the Philosopher, found in chapter 8 of this book, namely that the magnanimous man ought not to approach honoured places, when reason seems to teach the contrary?

units.la: Nam eo debet ire Magnanimus, ubi virtutis suæ exercitium haberet, et ubi ipsa Magnanimitas in objectum suum agere posset, hoc vero fit in loco honorato. Ergo non recte præcepisse videtur Philosophus? Resp. Duplex esse potest huius loci sensus: 1. Vel quod Magnanimus ea loca honorata adire non debeat, ubi omnes pari honoris genere quotquot præsentes sunt, affici solent, cuiusmodi sunt convivia publica, theatra & spectacula, &c. Nam quatenus omnes pari honore excipiuntur, eatenus virtute pares censentur: Atqui Magnanimus non patitur aliorum splendore suam famam & æstimationem obscurari, quod de Pompeio & Cæsare elegater protulit Lucanus, Sed nullius jam ferre potest, &c. Verum hic sensus non satis arridet; nam fieri non potest, ut qui sibi ipsi sufficiens sua virtute contentus sit, egre ferat, alios externa honoris significatione sibi adæquari, quos vera interna virtutis possessione minime pares esse videt. Posterior sensus est hic, quod adire loca honorata, non adire debeat, ubi nempe honores promiscue distribuuntur, ne debitum virtuti præmium effl agitaret, & ultro ambire videatur, quin quin potius virtutis suę splendore contentus, ut honorem sponte oblatum non repudiat, sic non oblatum ex ἀντιπρεπείας & rerum fortuitarum respectu exigere non dignatur. Breviter, hæc verba Philosophi sunt intelligenda: Non debet adire Magnanimus loca honorata, non quod aliis dignioribus & superioribus locum honoratum invideat (nam ad splendorem Magnanimitatis etiam & hoc spectat bona cum malis collata, si minores sint, candide fateri, sin majores aperte etiam profiteri) Sed quod loca honorata de industria adire non debeat, ubi nempe honores a turba hominum conferuntur. Vulgus enim de meritis cujusque non satis judicare potest. Deinde etiam Philosophus seipsum explicat, cum addit, ubi alii primatum obtinent, quia ut dictum est, propter conscientiam virtutis suæ summis viris novit se parem, ideo ubi virtus in contemtum venire possit, aut ejus gravitas vilescat, ejusmodi loca studiose evitare debet.
units.tr: The magnanimous man ought to go where he might exercise his virtue, and where magnanimity itself could act upon its proper object; but this happens in an honoured place. Therefore the Philosopher seems not to have taught rightly? Answer. This passage can have two senses: (1) Either the magnanimous man ought not to approach honoured places where all those present, however many, are customarily honoured with the same kind of honour, such as public banquets, theatres and shows, and so on. For insofar as all are received with equal honour, to that extent they are considered equal in virtue. But the magnanimous man does not suffer his own fame and esteem to be dimmed by the splendour of others, which Lucan put elegantly of Pompey and Caesar: "But he can bear no one's superiority..." etc. Yet this sense does not quite please; for it cannot be that one who is sufficient to himself, content with his own virtue, should take it ill that others are made his equals in outward marks of honour, when he sees they are by no means his equals in the inner possession of true virtue. The latter sense is this: that he ought not to approach honoured places where honours are distributed indiscriminately, lest he seem to be seeking the reward due to virtue and to be ambitious of it unasked; but rather, being content with the splendour of his virtue, as he does not refuse honour offered freely, so he does not deign to demand what is not offered, on account of relative worth [ἀντιπρεπείας] and the regard for chance circumstances. In brief, these words of the Philosopher are to be understood thus: the magnanimous man ought not to approach honoured places, not because he envies more worthy and superior men their place of honour (for it also belongs to the splendour of magnanimity to admit candidly, if the others are greater, that they are greater, and to profess it openly), but because he ought not to approach honoured places deliberately where honours are conferred by the crowd of men. For the common people cannot judge sufficiently of each one's merits. Moreover, the Philosopher explains himself when he adds "where others hold the first place": because, as has been said, on account of the consciousness of his own virtue he knows himself equal to the highest men; therefore, where virtue might fall into contempt or its dignity grow cheap, he ought carefully to avoid such places.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: EXplicatur hoc capite decimo altera in honore posita virtus, quæ apud Græcos caret nomine: Latine dicitur Moderatum honoris studium, seu uno verbo apud Ciceronem Modestia. De hac virtute breviter hic agit, propterea quod pauciores hujus virtutis studiosos quā Magnanimitatis reperire licet. Partes hujus capitis sunt duæ: In prima dari ejusmodi virtutem, quæ circa parvos & mediocres honores versetur, ostendit. In secunda comparatio hujus virtutis cum extremis, & extremorum inter se instituitur.
units.tr: In this tenth chapter another virtue concerning honour is explained, one that has no name among the Greeks. In Latin it is called moderate desire for honour, or in a single word, as Cicero calls it, modesty. The Philosopher treats this virtue briefly, because fewer people are found who are zealous for it than for magnanimity. The chapter has two parts. In the first, he shows that there is such a virtue, one concerned with small and middling honours. In the second, this virtue is compared with the extremes, and the extremes are compared with each other.

units.la: In prima igitur dari hanc virtutem duabus rationi-bus docet: 1. est, à coparatione cum Liberalitate: nam eadem elt ratio ad Magnanimitatem Modestiæ, quæ est Liberalitatis ad Magnificentiam: & sicut Liberalitas in modicis non in magnis opibus cernitur, si hæc circa parvos & mediocres honores tantum versatur, & in hoc conveniunt, quod utraque in parvis & modicis hominess secundum rectam rationem bene affectos reddat. 2. Ratio ducitur ab extremis hoc modo: Extrema dantur. Ergo & ipsum medium. Hujus consequentiæ ratio est, quia medium & extrema sunt relata, & uno relatorum dato, necesse est dari alterum. Extrema dari probat à communi experientia; nam mediocris honor interdum magis quam oportet, interdum minus expetitur, & vulgò vituperari solet, qui honorem magis, quam decet aut debeat, affectat, & Philotimus seu ambitiosus vocari. Contra vituperatur etiam, qui oem honorem etiā præclaris factis & meritis dignū respuit, & inambitiosus dicitur. Utrque tamen & φιλότιμος & ἀφιλότιμος interdum laudari solent, quoties scilicet hæc vita, quæ niis sunt, virtutis speciem induunt. Nam φιλότιμος vir strenuus & cupidus honestatis vulgò dicitur, quod ad honores viriliter adipiret, quibus consequendis omnes ingenii vires & acumen intendit; ἀφιλότιμος etiam, qui honores omnes dedignatur & sperat, vu gò moderatus & temperans habetur, ut pluribus explicavit Philosophus cap. 8. lib. 2. hujus operis.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he teaches that this virtue exists, and he proves it by two reasons. (1) The first is drawn from a comparison with liberality. For the relation of modesty to magnanimity is the same as that of liberality to magnificence. Just as liberality is seen in modest means rather than great wealth, so modesty is concerned only with small and middling honours. The two agree in this, that each disposes men of small and modest rank to be well affected according to right reason. (2) The second reason is drawn from the extremes, as follows. Extremes exist; therefore the mean also exists. The reason for this inference is that the mean and the extremes are relatives, and once one of two relatives is given, the other must be given too. That extremes exist he proves from common experience. For a middling honour is sometimes desired more than it should be, and sometimes less, and the man who seeks honour more than is fitting or proper is commonly blamed and called philotimos [φιλότιμος], or ambitious. On the other hand, the man who rejects every honour, even one deserved by distinguished deeds and merits, is also blamed and called unambitious. Yet both the philotimos [φιλότιμος] and the aphilotimos [ἀφιλότιμος] are sometimes praised, namely whenever these vices put on the appearance of virtue. For the philotimos [φιλότιμος] is commonly called a vigorous man and one eager for honour, because he pursues honours manfully and bends all the powers and keenness of his mind to attaining them. The aphilotimos [ἀφιλότιμος], who scorns and disdains all honours, is commonly regarded as moderate and temperate, as the Philosopher explained at length in chapter 8 of the second book of this work.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis confert hoc medium cum extremis, & extrema demum inter se. Hæc virtus, fi conferatur cum alterutro extremorum, induere videtur natura alterius extremi. Nam fi conferatur cum alterutro extremorum, quæ ei opponitur in excessu, videtur ei contrariari in de fectu, & contra, fi conferatur cum inambitione, videtur illi contrariari in excessu, quod etiam Philosophus de Fortitudine, Liberalitate, aliisque virtutibus supra dixerat. Extrema inter se, si conferuntur, ut videantur sibi invicem contrariari, tamen non ipsi medio, nam quia medium nomine caret, ideo nec esse videtur, ideo nihil ei esse contrarium, sed tamen dari medium, & si vacet nomine, quia dantur extrema, ex superioribus constat. Proinde extrema non tantum inter se contrariantur ratione graduum, quos recipiunt, sed etiam opponuntur ipsi medio idque duabus de causis: 1. Quia vitia sunt, & vitia virtutibus contrariantur. 2. Ratione situs, quia a medio, in quo consistit virtus, longius recedunt.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter, he compares this mean with the extremes, and the extremes with each other. If this virtue is compared with either of the extremes, it seems to take on the nature of the other extreme. For if it is compared with the extreme that opposes it by excess, it seems to be opposed to it by deficiency, and conversely, if it is compared with unambitiousness, it seems to be opposed to that by excess. The Philosopher had said the same above about courage, liberality, and the other virtues. If the extremes are compared with each other, they seem to be opposed to one another, yet not to the mean itself. Because the mean has no name, it does not seem to exist, and so nothing seems to be opposed to it. But from what was said above, it is clear that the mean does exist, even though it lacks a name, because the extremes exist. Therefore the extremes are opposed not only to each other, by reason of the degrees they admit, but also to the mean itself, and this for two reasons: (1) because they are vices, and vices are contrary to virtues; (2) by reason of position, because they stand further away from the mean in which virtue consists.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Modestia sicut & Liberalitas in parvis & mediocribus tantum hominibus bene affectos reddit.
units.tr: 1. Modesty, like liberality, makes men well affected only towards those of small and middling rank.

units.la: 2. Ambitiosus vituperari solet, quod honorem magis, quam oportet, & unde non oportet, affectet.
units.tr: 2. The ambitious man is commonly blamed, because he desires honour more than he ought, and from sources whence he ought not.

units.la: 3. Inambitio etiam datur vitio, quod honorem facit praclaris dignum respuat.
units.tr: 3. Unambitiousness is also a vice, because it rejects honour that is worthy of distinguished men.

units.la: 4. Ambitio interdum laudatur, quia hominem, ut virili prorsus animo honores affectet, excitare videtur: inambitio etiam commendatur, quod hominem Temperantia studiosum reddat.
units.tr: 4. Ambition is sometimes praised, because it seems to stir a man to pursue honours with a thoroughly manly spirit. Unambitiousness is also commended, because it makes a man zealous for temperance.

units.la: 5. Ex mutua Relatorum natura, ubi dantur extrema, ibi dari medium necesse est. 6. Mo-
units.tr: 5. From the mutual nature of relatives, where extremes exist, the mean must necessarily exist as well. 6. Mo-

units.la: 6. Modestia cum alterutro extremorum collata inducit vitem semper alterius extremi, sicut & in aliis virtutibus accidit.
units.tr: 6. Modesty, when compared with either extreme, always takes on the nature of the other extreme, as also happens in the other virtues.

units.la: Definitur Modestia virtus, quae in parvis & mediocris honoribus debitum modum servat. Modestia, quia nomine apud Graecos caret, appellari solet nomine alterius extremi φιλοτιμία, quae vox interdum in bonam partem sumitur, quando scilicet cum vera humilitate & simplicitate conjungitur, sic etiam rationis limites non excedit; interdum in malam etiam partem, quando scilicet hypocrisi & fuco est palliata, ut ex ipso textu hic patet; nam sic est vitium, quod ei opponitur in excessu. Modestiae vero nomen huic virtuti primus apud Latinos indidit Cicero, quae vox etiam ambigua est: nam sumitur vel naturaliter vel moraliter. Naturaliter pro verecundia, qui est affectus hominis a natura insitus in appetendis aut fugiendis honoribus, & talem Modestiam requirit Cicero in dictis & factis adolescentis lib. 1. officior. Moraliter vero nomen Modestiae multipliciter usurpatur. Nam 1. generaliter significat modum & legitimum omnium virtutum usum, ut apud Cic. lib. 3. ad Heren. ubi inquit: Modestia parcibus recte utemur, si nimias libidines honoris, pecuniae, similiumque rerum vituperabimus, & modum uniuscuiusque rei statuemus. 2. A Stoicis referente etiam Cic. 1. offic. sumitur pro εὐταξία (bona dispositione) quo sensu definitur rerum, quae dicuntur, quaeque aguntur, bene collocandarum recta dispositio. 3. Sumitur pro Temperantia 3. Tusc. quaest. ubi haec verba habentur: Verisimile est illud, quis sit vere temperans eamque virtutem, quam Graeci
units.tr: Modesty is defined as the virtue that keeps due measure in small and middling honours. Because modesty has no name among the Greeks, it is usually called by the name of the other extreme, philotimia [φιλοτιμία]. This word is sometimes taken in a good sense, when it is joined with true humility and simplicity, and thus does not exceed the limits of reason. Sometimes it is taken in a bad sense, when it is cloaked with hypocrisy and pretence, as is clear from the text here, for in that sense it is the vice opposed to modesty by excess. The name modestia was first given to this virtue among the Latins by Cicero. This word too is ambiguous, for it is taken either naturally or morally. Naturally, it means shame, which is an affection implanted in man by nature regarding the seeking or avoiding of honours. It is this kind of modesty that Cicero requires in the words and deeds of a young man, in Book 1 of De Officiis. Morally, however, the name modesty is used in several senses. (1) In general it means the measure and lawful use of all the virtues, as Cicero says in Book 3 of the Rhetorica ad Herennium, where he writes: "We shall make right use of moderation in sparing things if we condemn excessive desires for honour, money, and similar things, and set a measure for each thing." (2) As Cicero also reports in De Officiis 1, the Stoics took it to mean good order [εὐταξία], in which sense it is defined as the right arrangement of well-ordered words and deeds. (3) It is taken for temperance, in Tusculan Disputations 3, where these words occur: "It is probable that this is who is truly temperate, and that virtue which the Greeks call sophrosyne [σωφροσύνην]" [...]

units.la: {*} aut fugiendis honoribus Græci σωφροσύνην vocant. Modestiam Latinè appellare soleo. 4. & ult. Pro moderatione honorum mediocrium & modicorum, & sic in hac speciali significatione hoc loco tractatur. Dicitur verò modestia, quod in appetendis modicis honoribus modū scienter doceat, & velut habena quædam sit inter ambitionem & abjectionem animi.
units.tr: or call it, regarding the seeking or avoiding of honours, sophrosyne [σωφροσύνην] in Greek. I am accustomed to call it modestia in Latin. (4) And last, it means the moderation of middling and small honours, and in this special sense it is treated here. It is called modesty because it teaches, in seeking small honours, to know the measure, and it is a kind of bridle between ambition and abjection of spirit.

units.la: 1. Quæritur: Quomodo definiatur ista virtus per honores parvos, cum nullus sit honor parvus, propter duas rationes. Nam 1. honor dicitur virtutis præmium. At præmium virtutis non est parvum quid, sed magnum, quia magno labore opus est ad hoc præmium asequendum. 2. dicitur à Philosopho cap.8. hujus libri & 1. mag. moral. cap. 9. bonorum externorum maximum. Proinde honor parvus nullus est, ideo neque obiectum modestiæ esse poterit? Resp. Honorem vulgò tribus modis accipi. 1. Pro materia honoris, & sic nihil aliud est, quam res honorabilis. 2. Pro substantia honoris, & sic est signum alicui datum in testimonium virtutis promeritæ. 3. Pro effectu honoris, & sic nihil est aliud, quam opinio laudabilis, quæ oritur ex præclaris cujusque meritis. At istis omnibus tribus modis secundum varios gradus augeri vel minui potest, ut ratio & res postulat & communis experientia docet.
units.tr: 1. It is asked: how can this virtue be defined by small honours, when no honour is small, for two reasons? For (1) honour is called the reward of virtue. But the reward of virtue is not a small thing but a great one, since great labour is needed to obtain this reward. (2) The Philosopher, in chapter 8 of this book and in chapter 9 of the first book of the Magna Moralia, calls it the greatest of external goods. Therefore no honour is small, and so modesty cannot have it as its object. Answer: honour is commonly taken in three ways. (1) As the matter of honour, and in this sense it is nothing other than a respectable thing. (2) As the substance of honour, and in this sense it is a sign given to someone as testimony of merited virtue. (3) As the effect of honour, and in this sense it is nothing other than a praiseworthy opinion arising from a man's distinguished merits. But in all three of these senses honour can be increased or diminished according to various degrees, as reason and the nature of the thing require and common experience teaches.

units.la: II. An honor possit dici modestiæ obiectum, cum nullius virtutis obiectum proprie dici possit. Nam ut constat ex cap. 12. lib. 1. hujus operis, virtutis proprium sit laudari, non honorari: nam iis, quæ tendunt ad finem non honor, sed laus debetur. At finis proprium est honorari, propterea quod sit perfectio cujusque rei, & ideo felicitatem bonum honorabile dicit esse Philosophus. Hinc ergo ex hoc loco nulli virtuti competit honor. honor? Resp. Aliud est habere honorem pro objecto, in quod agat, aliud pro proprietate & affectione, quae virtuti accidat. Dein etiam honor consideratur duobus modis: vel inchoative in progressu, & sic debetur etiam virtuti, vel perfective in summo gradu, & sic solius felicitatis est proprium, quo modo etiam honorem loco citato consideravit Philosophus. Plura ibidem vide & ad cap. 7. huius libri.
units.tr: II. Whether honour can be called the object of modesty, when the object of no virtue can properly be called honour. For, as is clear from chapter 12 of the first book of this work, it is the proper function of virtue to be praised, not to be honoured, since praise, not honour, is owed to things that tend towards an end. But it is the proper thing of the end to be honoured, because it is the perfection of each thing; and for this reason the Philosopher says that happiness is an honourable good. Hence, from this passage, honour belongs to no virtue. Answer: it is one thing to have honour as the object towards which one acts, and another to have it as a property and affection that accompanies virtue. Further, honour is considered in two ways: either inchoatively, in its progress, and in this sense it is due also to virtue; or perfectively, in its highest degree, and in this sense it is the property of happiness alone, in the way the Philosopher also considered honour in the passage cited. See more on this in the same place, and on chapter 7 of this book.

units.la: III. An recte inter caeteras virtutes enumeravit Philosophus modestiam, cum nullum habeat in vita communi usum, & ea virtutes tantum debent tradi, non quae in mera imaginatione consistunt, sed quae ex praxi & consuetudine tanquam regula bene beateq; vivendi subinde discuntur.
units.tr: III. Did the Philosopher rightly count modesty among the other virtues, since it has no use in common life? Virtues should be taught only if they are not mere matters of imagination but are learned from practice and habit, as the rule of living well and happily.

units.la: At modestia non est talis virtus, cum nullos aut saltem paucissimos reperiri liceat, qui parvis honoribus sint contenti? Resp. Per negationem minoris: nam etsi non usquequaque reperiantur homines, qui intra veros modestiae limites se contineant, multos tamen fuisse & esse historiae testantur, sed illos praesertim, qui aut vita solitaria aut contemplationis studio fere delectantur. Ergo multis haec pauca exempla sufficiant. Pythagoras Samius modestiae causa non se σοφον sed φιλοσοφον dici voluit. Sic etiam Thales Milesius, propter scientias Mathematicas sapientissimus habitus, cum tripus aureus a piscatoribus inventus esset, cum hac inscriptione, Detur sapientissimo, modeste recusavit solum Apollinem sapientem esse dictitans, ut testatur Laertius lib. 1. in vita ipsius. Sic Socrates hoc unum scire dicebat, quod nihil sciret, &c.
units.tr: But is modesty not such a virtue, since few or hardly any people can be found who are content with small honours? Answer, by denying the minor premise. Although people who keep within the true limits of modesty are not found everywhere, history testifies that there have been many, and still are, especially those who delight in a solitary life or in the pursuit of contemplation. A few examples will suffice. Pythagoras of Samos wished to be called not wise [σοφόν] but a lover of wisdom [φιλόσοφον], out of modesty. So too Thales of Miletus, regarded as the wisest man because of his mathematical learning, when a golden tripod was found by fishermen with the inscription Let it be given to the wisest, modestly declined it, insisting that only Apollo was wise, as Laertius attests in book 1, in his life. So Socrates said that he knew this one thing, that he knew nothing, &c.

units.la: IV. & ult. Cur duas virtutes circa honores, itemq; circa divitias perfari dixerit Philosophus, & non itidem circa voluvoluptates & cateros affectus, cum non minus hi, quam illa suos recipiant gradus, ideoq; de singulis dua diversa virtutes erant statuenda? Resp. Ita factum esse duabus de causis: 1. Quia major difficultas est in divitiis & honoribus secundum gradus suos moderandis, quam in voluptatibus & cæteris affectibus. Nam quicunq; magnis voluptatibus bene moderari poterit, idem etiam & parvis recte præesse potest. At non item in honoribus & divitiis hoc fieri: nam experientia testatur, multos in magnis honoribus, & divitiis magnis bene & cum laude se gessisse, non item in parvis. 2. Quia voluptates cæteriq; affectus omnes omnibus communes sunt hominibus, nulliq; per ætatem aut sexum, quia à natura proveniunt, dengatur. At divitiæ & honores sunt bona externa, quæ à labore & industria proveniunt, & magis his, quam illis accidere solent. Proinde cum diversi hominum status & conditiones quibus contingunt honores & divitiæ, diversæ etiam de iis statuendæ erant virtutes.
units.tr: IV. and last. Why did the Philosopher say that there are two virtues concerning honours, and likewise concerning riches, but not in the same way concerning pleasures and the other passions, since these receive their degrees no less than those do, and so two different virtues should have been set up for each? Answer: this was done for two reasons. (1) Because it is more difficult to moderate riches and honours according to their degrees than pleasures and the other passions. For whoever can govern great pleasures well can also rightly govern small ones. This is not so with honours and riches, for experience shows that many have conducted themselves well and with praise in great honours and great riches, but not in small ones. (2) Because pleasures and the other passions are common to all men, and are denied to none on account of age or sex, since they arise from nature. But riches and honours are external goods, which come from labour and industry, and are wont to fall to some more than to others. Therefore, since the differing states and conditions of men, to which honours and riches come, are diverse, different virtues had to be set up concerning them.

units.la: Non incommodè post hunc tractatum de Magnanimitate & modestia subjici possunt, paucæ hæ quæstiones:
units.tr: It is not inappropriate to add to this treatise on magnanimity and modesty the following few questions:

units.la: 1. An cum magnanimitas & modestia doceant homines honores legitimo modo appetere, an rationi consentaneum sit honores appetere? Resp. Dissentientes esse de hac re opiniones. Nam quidam sunt (quibus etiam annumerari possunt Anabaptistæ,) qui omnes honores tanquam fumos & caligines mentem humanam obscurantes repellendos esse dictitant, & tanquam Sirenum scopulos & Circes pocula vitandos. Rationes quæ militant pro hac opinione sunt hæ: 1. Quia honor non in numero bonorū censeturnam poste- sorem sui non meliorem aut beatiorem reddit, quia ut vulgò definitur, honor nihil aliud est, quam signū externum alicui collatum in testimonium virtutis suæ: Ideo non honor, sed virtus ipsa, quæ causatur ho- norem, hominem reddit bonum. 2. Quia honoris pa ticipes sunt tam improbi, quam probi homines & sæpius improbi, ut communis experientia testa- tur. 3. Quia honor corrumpit mores hominum et- iam proborum. Multi enim, qui probi fuerunt in vi- ta privata, dum ad honores ascenderunt, variis vitiis inquinati fuerunt. Unde ortum illud proverbium: Honores mutant mores, raro tamen in meliores. 4. Quia non tantum in vita privata, sed etiam in publica tur- bas & tumultus excitat, pacem, concordiam & ami- citiam tollit. Hinc Cic. in Lælio amicitiam labefacta- riait, si duo amici in honoris contentionem incide- rint: constat enim nullam majorem amicitiis esse pestem, ut ait Seneca, quam in plerisque pecuniæ & divitiarum cupiditatem, in optimis quibusq; ho- noris & gloriæ certamen, ex quo inimicitiæ multò maximæ sæpe extiterunt, atq; hoc testatur Romuli & Remi duorū fratrum historia, qui ut testantur Li- vius, Dionysius Halicarnassæus & Plutarchus, dum uterque urbem recens fundaram à se cognominari cupit, in inimicitias ex ista honoris contentione in- ciderunt tantas, ut eorum discordiam non nisi alte- rius sola mors finire potuerit. Testatur & hoc i- psum historia Cæsaris & Pompeji, qui ex mutua ho- noris pugna non tantum præstantissimorum hominum, sed ipsius etiam Reipub. Romanae perniciem attulerunt. 5. Quia honoris contemtum non solum in laude ponunt ipsi Christiani, sed etiam sapientes Ethnici. Hinc ut testatur Apostolus ad Hebr. 11. verf. 18. maluit Moyses cum populo Dei affligi & exul fieri, quam prosilio Pharaonis haberi. Et Paulus Apostolus gentium 2. Corinth. 11. & 12. non commemorat honores, quibus propter propagationem Euangelii fit affectus, sed vulnera, carceres, plagas, infirmitates, &c. Et Christus ipse, ut restatur idem in Apost. ad Philip. 2. verf. 7. cum esset in forma Dei, se exinanivit forma servi assumta: Omnis vero, ut ait Augustinus, Christi actio, debet nostra esse institutio, & vitam ipsius quantum in nobis est imitari debemus.
units.tr: 1. Since magnanimity and modesty teach men to seek honours in a lawful manner, is it consistent with reason to seek honours at all? Answer: opinions on this matter differ. For some (among whom the Anabaptists may also be numbered) insist that all honours must be rejected as smoke and mists that darken the human mind, and avoided like the rocks of the Sirens and the cups of Circe. The reasons that support this opinion are these. (1) Because honour is not counted among the goods, nor does it make its possessor better or happier; for, as is commonly defined, honour is nothing other than an external sign bestowed on someone as testimony to his virtue. Therefore it is not honour but virtue itself, which is the cause of honour, that makes a man good. (2) Because the sharers in honour are as wicked as good men, and more often wicked, as common experience attests. (3) Because honour corrupts the morals even of upright men. For many who were upright in private life were stained with various vices once they rose to honours. Hence the proverb: Honours change manners, but rarely for the better. (4) Because honour stirs up disturbances not only in private life but also in public, and destroys peace, concord and friendship. Hence Cicero, in Laelius, says that friendship is weakened if two friends fall into a contest for honour. For, as Seneca says, there is no greater pest to friendships than, in most cases, the desire for money and riches, and among the best men the contest for honour and glory, from which very great enmities have often arisen. The history of the two brothers Romulus and Remus confirms this: as Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch testify, while each wished the city he had recently founded to be named after himself, they fell into such enmity over this contest for honour that their discord could be ended only by the death of one of them. The history of Caesar and Pompey also bears witness, who through their mutual struggle for honour brought ruin not only upon the most outstanding men but upon the Roman Commonwealth itself. (5) Because Christians themselves, as well as wise pagans, have placed the contempt of honour in praise. Thus, as the Apostle testifies in Hebrews 11:18, Moses chose to suffer affliction with the people of God and to be an exile rather than to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. And the Apostle Paul, apostle of the Gentiles, in 2 Corinthians 11 and 12, does not recount the honours with which he was rewarded for spreading the Gospel, but wounds, prisons, stripes, infirmities, &c. And Christ himself, as the same Apostle testifies in Philippians 2:7, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Now every action of Christ, as Augustine says, ought to be our instruction, and we ought to imitate his life as far as we are able.

units.la: Inter Ethnicos etiam pleriq; sapientes judicio praeditii honores plane contemserunt. Hinc Philosophus 4. Nicom. cap. 7. dicit, magnanimitatis esse proprium, honores quoivis negligere & contemnere, & Cato major, ut testatur Plutarchus in vita ipsius, malebat quaeri: cur non essent posita statua Catoni, quam cur essent posita, nempe, quia honorem a vulgo delatum studiose fugiebat. Et hic 3. Tusc. quaest. dicit, multos esse beatiores ob id, quod sint inhonorati, nempe quia vitae quietae & tranquillae se tradere possunt. Hinc ergo cum Poeta dicendum:
units.tr: Among the pagans too, most of the wise and judicious plainly despised honours. Hence the Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics book 4, chapter 7, says that it is the mark of the magnanimous man to neglect and despise honours of every kind. And Cato the Elder, as Plutarch attests in his life, preferred to be asked why no statue had been set up to Cato rather than why one had been set up, since he eagerly avoided honour offered by the common people. And here, in Tusculan Disputations book 3, he says that many are happier for being unhonoured, because they can give themselves over to a quiet and tranquil life. Hence we must say with the Poet:

units.la: Bene qui latuit, bene vixit.
units.tr: Whoever has lived hidden has lived well.

units.la: Et paulo post; Vive tibi quantumque potes praelustria vita, Savum sublimi fulmen ab arce venit.
units.tr: And a little later: Live for yourself as much as you can, the lightning that strikes the proud comes from a high citadel.

units.la: At econtra protheta affirmante plures sunt longe & firmiores rationes: 1. est, quia honor inter omnia bona externa principatum renet: nam ut diferte ait Philosophus 4.Nicom.cap.7. honor bonorum externorum est maximum, idque rationibus confirmat. 2. Quia honor est virtutis praemium: Cum igitur virtus, quae est honoris causa, bona sit & expetenda, honor etiam erit talis. 3. Quia honor infligat homines ad virtutem, & bonas actiones. Hinc non immeritò a quibusdam calcar virtutis dicitur, & a Valerio Maximo lib.1 tit.de instit. antiquis honor vocatur ubertimum virtutis alimentum, & hoc etiam te statur Plutarchus in libel de virtute morali, inquiens: Nemo, qui honorem & gloriam vere appetit, evadit malus. Et Cicero Tuscul. quaest. Honos alit artes omnesque incendunt ad studia gloria. Nec male etiam Ovidius 5. Fast.
units.tr: On the other hand, those arguing for the opposite position have far longer and firmer reasons. (1) Honour holds the first place among all external goods; for, as the Philosopher says clearly in Nicomachean Ethics 4, chapter 7, honour is the greatest of external goods, and he confirms this with reasons. (2) Because honour is the reward of virtue. Since virtue, for whose sake honour is given, is good and to be desired, honour too will be such. (3) Because honour spurs men on to virtue and good actions. Hence it is not unjustly called by some the spur of virtue, and Valerius Maximus, book 1, title on institutions, calls honour the richest nourishment of virtue among the ancients. Plutarch also attests this in his little book on moral virtue, saying: No one who truly seeks honour and glory turns out bad. And Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations: Honour nourishes the arts and kindles all to the pursuit of glory. Nor is Ovid wrong in book 5 of the Fasti:

units.la: Non parvas animo dat gloria vires.
units.tr: Glory gives no small strength to the mind,

units.la: Et fecunda facit pectora laudis amor.
units.tr: and the love of praise makes the breast fruitful.

units.la: 4. Quia optimi quique autores & inprimis celebriores Philosophi in scriptis suis hoc agunt unice, ut homines ad honoris & gloriae studium cohortentur, quod non facerent, si putarent honore non esse appetendum.
units.tr: (4) Because the best authors, and above all the most celebrated philosophers, in their writings aim solely at this, that they exhort men to the pursuit of honour and glory, which they would not do if they thought honour was not to be sought.

units.la: 5 Quia vita Politica, quae Reipub. tuetur & conservat, sine honore consistere non potest: nam sine Magistratu communio populi regi non potest: At in Magistratu necessario requiritur honor. Hinc Philosophus cap. 5. lib. 1. huius operis d cit, viro Politico in primis appetendum esse honorem, cujus rationem reddit Plato 4. de Repub. quia sine honore nullus in Politia erit ordo, & ordine sublato nihil praeter merum turbarum & tumultuum remanet chaos.
units.tr: 5. Political life, which protects and preserves the commonwealth, cannot exist without honour, for without magistrates a community of people cannot be governed, and in the magistracy honour is necessarily required. Hence the Philosopher, in chapter 5 of book 1 of this work, says that honour is especially to be sought by the political man. Plato gives the reason in book 4 of the Republic: without honour there will be no order in the state, and once order is removed nothing remains but sheer chaos of disorders and tumults.

units.la: 6. Quia laudari solent tanquam viri probi, qui honores legitime appetunt, ecotra vituperari, qui honores nores aut relpuunt aut negligunt. Quod & ipsum testatur Philosophus cap.5.& 9 hujus lib.4.& eleganter ait Augustinus lib.7. de civitate Dei, tria omnino necessaria sunt: Bona vita mihi opus est propter Deum, bona consuetudo propter meipsum, bona fama propter proximum. Ergo & honore opus erit, quia honor est bonae famae causa. Et Cic. 1. offic. ait, negligere quid de se quisque sentiat, non solum arrogantis est, sed animi omnino dissoluti & abjecti. Et receptissima est inter JCtos sententia: Honorem vitae, infamiam morti esse comparandam. 7. Quia honor auctoritatem conciliat viris magnis & gravibus, additumque parat ad praeclaras actiones edendas benéque de Republica merendum. 8. Quia testimonium est vitae honestae praesidiumque firmum, ut ait Cic. 1. Tusc. quaest. adversus improborum hominum calumnias: nam quia honora pluribus, isque melioribus tribuitur, ideo propter consensum plurium maledicis & obtrectatoribus os obstruit. 9. Quia Deus honore praecipit quinto praecepto Decalogi: Honora patrem & matrem: quod vero Deus jubet, id juste appetere licet. 10. Quia mandato Dei obtemperatur, cum quis honore dignus eo afficitur. Hinc Scriptura 1. Tim. 5. verf. 3. & 17. dicit, Presbyterum duplici honore esse dignum. Cum igitur quis honorem alicui exhibet, quo dignus est, verbo Dei paret. 11. Quia Deus in variis locis Scripturae honorem piis & timentibus se promittit: unde illud; Glorificantes me, glorificabo. 12. & ult. Idem probatur a contrariis, quia infamia est aversanda & fugienda, ideo ex lege contrariorum honor erit sequendus & appetendus.
units.tr: 6. People are usually praised as upright men when they seek honours lawfully, and on the other hand blamed when they reject or neglect them. The Philosopher himself testifies to this, in chapter 5 and 9 of book 4 of this work, and Augustine elegantly says in book 7 of The City of God, "Three things are altogether necessary: a good life for the sake of God, good conduct for my own sake, and a good name for the sake of my neighbour." Therefore honour too will be necessary, since honour is the cause of a good name. And Cicero, in book 1 of On Duties, says: "To disregard what others think of oneself is not only the mark of an arrogant man, but of a wholly dissolute and abject mind." And the most widely accepted opinion among the jurists is this: honour is to be weighed against life, and infamy against death. 7. Honour wins authority for great and serious men, and it prepares an addition to their noble deeds and to deserving well of the commonwealth. 8. Honour is a testimony of an honourable life and a firm defence against the slanders of wicked men, as Cicero says in book 1 of the Tusculan Disputations; for because honour is given by many, and by the better sort, it silences slanderers and detractors through the agreement of the many. 9. God commands honour in the fifth commandment of the Decalogue: "Honour your father and mother." What God commands, it is lawful to seek justly. 10. When someone is honoured with the honour he deserves, he obeys the command of God. Hence Scripture says in 1 Tim. 5. verses 3 and 17 that an elder is worthy of double honour. Therefore when someone shows another the honour he deserves, he obeys the word of God. 11. God promises honour in various places of Scripture to the pious and to those who fear him; whence that saying: "Those who glorify me I will glorify." 12. The same is proved from the contraries: since infamy is to be avoided and shunned, by the law of contraries honour is to be followed and sought.

units.la: Pro decisione hujus quaestionis sequentia aliquot nonotanda sunt theoremata. 1. Distinguendum esse inter verum & falsum honorem, quorum ille, ut virtutis praemium sequitur virtutem ipsam, & non nisi vera virtute praeditis debetur, hic, malis etiam & improbis tribuitur: prior propter rationes supra allatas est appetendus, posterior fugiendus. 2. Distinguendum etiam inter moderatum veri honoris appetitum, & immoderatum, & priorem esse honestum & licitum, posteriorem vero turpem & illicitum. 3. Verum honorem mores hominum non deteriores, sed meliores reddere, qui enim honorem juste, & ex virtutis merito consequitur, eo laetatur & alacrius agit ea per quae virtute est adeptus praeclaras nempe actiones, quae virtutis habitum efficiunt, & in quibus producendis voluptas maxima esse solet, voluptas vero adjuvat & perficit actionem, ex qua oritur, ut praeter experientiam testatur Philosophus lib. 2. cap. 2. hujus operis, & lib. 10. cap. 4. 4. Seditionem, discordias & rixas & reliqua etiam mala non provenire ex vero honore per se aut juste honoris desiderio, sed vel ex iniqua honorum distributione, cum unicuique pro meritis honor justus non attribuitur, vel ex falso honore, qui jure non debetur, vel ex improbitate quorundam, qui malis artibus honoris insignia affectant. 5. Honoris contemtum non semper in laude poni, sed vel habito respectu ad falsum honorem vel ad immodicum, cum quis majorem, quam pro meritis aut pro qualitate personae suae appetit. 6. Verum quidem honorem in se esse bonum, ut jam supra ostensum fuit, sed tamen quemlibet cuilibet non convenire, nec omnes ex aequo cujusvis honohonoris esse capaces. Unde praeclare Seneca epist. 17. ad Lucil. Sicut non omnium humeri quodlibet ferunt onus, sic nec quosvis ex aequo quivis ferre potest honores. 7. Honorem supra meritum & dignitatem alicui tributum saepius obesse, quam prodesse: unde natum illud proverbium:
units.tr: To decide this question, the following theorems are to be noted. 1. A distinction must be made between true and false honour. The former follows virtue itself as its reward, and is owed only to those endowed with true virtue; the latter is given even to the wicked and the dishonest. For the reasons given above, the former is to be sought, the latter to be fled. 2. A distinction must also be made between moderate desire for true honour and immoderate desire: the former is honourable and lawful, the latter base and unlawful. 3. True honour makes men's manners not worse but better. For whoever obtains honour justly and by the merit of virtue rejoices in it, and acts more eagerly in those things by which he has gained virtue, namely noble actions, which produce the habit of virtue, and in producing which the greatest pleasure is usually found. Pleasure in turn aids and perfects the action from which it arises, as the Philosopher testifies, beyond experience, in book 2 chapter 2 and book 10 chapter 4 of this work. 4. Sedition, discords, quarrels, and the other evils do not arise from true honour in itself, or from a just desire for honour, but either from an unfair distribution of honours, when honour is not justly assigned to each according to his merits, or from false honour, which is not rightly owed, or from the wickedness of certain people who seek the marks of honour by evil arts. 5. Contempt of honour is not always to be counted a praise, but this must be judged with respect to false honour or to immoderate honour, when someone seeks more than his merits or the quality of his person warrant. 6. True honour is indeed good in itself, as has been shown above, but it does not suit everyone, and not all are equally capable of every honour. Hence Seneca admirably says in letter 17 to Lucilius: "Just as not all shoulders can bear every burden, so not everyone can bear every honour equally." 7. Honour bestowed on someone beyond his merit and dignity more often harms than helps; whence that proverb arose:

units.la: Asperius nihil est humili, cum surgit in altum.
units.tr: The harsher thing for the lowly is when it rises to the heights.

units.la: Et hoc etiam probant exempla Tyrannorum in historiis propósita. 8. & ulc. Verum honorem non appellandum esse, qui ab improbis aut imperita plebe tribuitur, sed tantum, qui ex judicio virorum prudentium & bonorum defertur, sicut testatur Philosophus cap. 7. hujus lib. 4. & Cic. 3. Tusc. quaest. Platim sub initio. Stat ergo sententia, verum honorem jure appetendum esse, quia id lex divina & humana, tum etiam rationes variae praecipiunt. Plura vide de hac quaestione apud D. Thomam in 1 parte summae dist. inct. 2. quaest. 32. apud Picol. grad. 8. cap. 23. apud Zwingerum super 4. Eth. cap. 2. apud Petrum Martyrem ad c. 5. lib. 1. Nicom. pag. 95. Goclenium in quaest. Ethicis quaest. 17.
units.tr: These examples of tyrants set out in histories also prove this. 8. Finally, honour is not to be called honour when it is given by wicked men or by the ignorant crowd, but only when it is conferred by the judgement of prudent and good men, as the Philosopher testifies in chapter 7 of book 4 of this work, and Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3, at the beginning of Platim. The position therefore stands: true honour is rightly to be sought, since divine and human law, as well as various reasons, prescribe it. See more on this question in D. Thomas in part 1 of the Summa, dist. 2, quest. 32; in Piccolomini, grad. 8, cap. 23; in Zwinger, on Ethics 4, cap. 2; in Peter Martyr, on chapter 5 of Nicomachean Ethics book 1, p. 95; and in Goclenius, Ethical questions, quest. 17.

units.la: 11. An cum honor dicatur virtutis praemium, sit etiam individuus virtutis comes? Resp. Diversas etiam esse de hac re opiniones. Et sunt, qui censent inseparabiliter comitari virtutem, propter duas causas: 1. Quia honor a virtute provenit tanquam a sua causa, tuai etiam impellit ad virtutem consequendam. Ergo ut effectus, qui sequitur, virtutem, & ut causa, quae impellit ad virtutis actiones virtutem inseparabiliter comitari debet. 2. Ratio est, quia ut umbra sequitur corpus, sic etiam honos comitatur virtute.
units.tr: 11. Since honour is said to be the reward of virtue, is it also an inseparable companion of virtue? Answer: opinions on this matter also differ. Some hold that virtue is inseparably accompanied by honour, for two reasons: 1. Because honour arises from virtue as from its cause, and it also impels one to pursue virtue. Therefore, as an effect that follows virtue and as a cause that drives one to virtuous actions, honour ought to accompany virtue inseparably. 2. The reason is that, as a shadow follows a body, so honour accompanies virtue.

units.la: Hh
units.tr: Hh

units.la: At pro thesi negante tres sunt solidae rationes: 1.Ducitur ab experientia communi, quae docet multos vera virtute praeditos non honorari, sed potius negligi aut contemni. Non igitur honos, ut comes individuus sequitur virtutem. 2. Ratio est, quia honor est in libero honorantis arbitrio, ita ut possit eü ei, cui debetur, tribuere, vel non tribuere pro suo libitu. 3. Quia multi virtutem aliorum bene perspectam non habent, ideoque de ea, quam bene noverunt, recte judicare non possunt, & proinde neque honorem etiam dignum tribuere. 4. Etiam & haec ratio addi potest, quia hominum plerunque judicium est odio, invidia, malevolentia, aliis affectibus ita obrutum & depravatum, ut de meritis cujusque non sincere satis & candide sentiat, ideoque neque honorem dignum exhibeat. Pro decisione hujus quaestionis pauca haec notanda sunt theoremata.
units.tr: But for the thesis that denies it there are three solid arguments: 1. It is drawn from common experience, which teaches that many who are truly virtuous are not honoured but rather neglected or despised. Therefore honour does not follow virtue as an inseparable companion. 2. The reason is that honour lies at the free discretion of the one who gives it, so that he may grant or withhold what is due to a person as he pleases. 3. Many people do not have a thorough knowledge of others' virtue, and so cannot judge rightly of the virtue they know poorly, and consequently do not give it the honour it deserves. 4. This reason too may be added: people's judgement is for the most part so overwhelmed and corrupted by hatred, envy, malice and other passions that they do not think sincerely and candidly enough about each person's merits, and so they do not render the honour that is due. For deciding this question, the following few points are to be noted.

units.la: 1. Honorem viri probi semper ex merito debeti, licet non ipso actu semper exhibeatur: ideoq; honor insepabiliter comitatur virtutem, sinon de facto saltem de jure, ut loquuntur JCti.
units.tr: 1. The honour of an upright man is always owed on account of merit, even if it is not always actually paid. Therefore honour inseparably accompanies virtue, if not in fact, at least in law, as the jurists say.

units.la: II. Honorem esse ejusmodi virtutis praemium, quod non a quovis, sed a recte & competente ejus judice vere tribui potest: & licet multi sint homines, qui praejudiciis & affectibus excaecati de aliorum virtute non recte sentiant: ideoq; quem debent honorem, non exhibeant: honor tamen virtutem comitatur respectu eorum, qui recte de ea sentiunt, cujusmodi sunt viri probi, ut pluribus ostendit Philosophus cap. 7. lib. 4. hujus operis.
units.tr: II. Honour is a reward of virtue which can truly be bestowed not by just anyone, but by its right and competent judge. And although there are many men who, blinded by prejudices and passions, do not judge rightly of another's virtue, and so do not render the honour they ought to, nevertheless honour accompanies virtue with respect to those who judge rightly of it, such as upright men, as the Philosopher shows at length in chapter 7 of book 4 of this work.

units.la: III. Virtutem externo pauperatis velo, non secus, ac Solem obducta nube ita occultari, ut in aliorum conspectum saepenumero non veniat, ideoq; mirum mirum non esse, si cui honor jure debetur ipso facto non consequatur. IV. Demum honor sequi debet virtutem, sicut umbra corpus, sed non eodem semper modo, nam nonnunquam umbra praecedit corpus, nonnunquam jungitur a latere, & quasi incedit una, nonnunquam subsequitur corpus pro varia positione & vario radiorum solarium in corpus illapsu, ut docent Optici: sic quorundam virtus vix inchoata & subipsis quasi initiis in honore habetur, quorundam vero non suspicitur aut praedicatur, nisi ubi aucta & & perfecta fuerit virtus, aliquos deniq; videas non prius honoratos, quam in vivis esse desierint. Accidit enim, ut quę quotidie ob oculos versentur bona, obrepente sensim satietate fastidiantur, ubi vero elapsa semel fuerint, incredibile sui desiderium post se relinquant, & animos multo acrius & arctius licet sero requirat. Comitatur igitur honos virtutem tanquam praemium amplissimum, sed non semper eodem gradu, nec eodem splendore, nec omni etiam tempore: interdum enim praecedit virtutis perfectionem, interdum cum ipsa virtute conjunctus est, & pari incedit passu, interdum intervallo etiam aliquo subsequitur, interdum est obscurior, interdu est illustrior, ut varia exempla & ipsa experientia in quotidianis vitae negotiis passim docent. Plura vide apud Petrum Martyrem ad cap. 5 lib. 1. Nic. pag. 104.
units.tr: III. I veil virtue with outward poverty, just as the sun, when a cloud covers it, is hidden so that it often does not come into the sight of others, and therefore it is no wonder if someone who rightly deserves honour does not in fact receive it. IV. Lastly, honour ought to follow virtue as a shadow follows a body, but not always in the same way. Sometimes the shadow goes before the body, sometimes it walks alongside and seems to move with it, and sometimes it follows behind, depending on the body's position and on how the rays of the sun fall upon it, as the optical writers teach. So too, honour is given to some people's virtue when it has barely begun and is still in its first stages. Others are not esteemed or praised until their virtue has grown and reached perfection. Finally, you may see some who are not honoured until they have ceased to live. For it happens that goods which we see every day gradually become tiresome as satiety creeps in, but once they have slipped away, they leave behind an incredible longing for themselves, and although it comes late, the mind seeks them far more eagerly and earnestly. Honour therefore accompanies virtue as its very great reward, but not always at the same rank, with the same brightness, or at every time: sometimes it goes before the perfection of virtue, sometimes it is joined to virtue itself and keeps pace with it, sometimes it follows at some distance, sometimes it is dimmer and sometimes brighter, as many examples and experience itself show everywhere in the daily affairs of life. See more in Peter Martyr on chapter 5 of book 1 of the Nicomachean Ethics, page 104.

units.la: III. An cum honor sit virtutis praemium, ut supra jam diximus, cur se e in patria quisque minus floreat, aut minori apud suos in honore sit?
units.tr: III. Since honour is the reward of virtue, as we have already said above, why does a man often flourish less in his own country, or enjoy less honour among his own people?

units.la: Occasionem huic quaestioni praebent illa Salvatoris nostri verba, quae habentur in omnibus quatuor Euangeliis Matth. 13. verf. 57.
units.tr: This question is prompted by those words of our Saviour which are found in all four Gospels: Matt. 13. verse 57.

units.la: Marc.6. verf.4. Luc.4. verf.24. Johan.4. verf.44. Non est Propheta inhonoratus, nisi in patria sua, seu ut vulgaris habet versic. In patria non est laudatus gente Propheta. Ideo cum Christus Salvator ipsa veritas hoc dixerit, & experientia quotidiana idem probet, non immerito quæri possunt ejus rei causæ: 1. Sit, quia ut canit Poeta:
units.tr: Mark 6. verse 4. Luke 4. verse 24. John 4. verse 44. "A prophet is not without honour, except in his own country," or as the common version has it, "A prophet is not praised in his own nation." Since Christ the Saviour, who is truth itself, has said this, and daily experience proves the same, it is not unreasonable to ask the causes of this thing: (1) Is it because, as the Poet sings:

units.la: Advena fama venit semper majoribus alii.
units.tr: A stranger's fame always comes to others greater than their own.

units.la: & cum natura hominum sit novitatis avida hoc consuetudine vulgari evenire solet, ut
units.tr: And since human nature is eager for novelty, this usually happens in the ordinary way, so that

units.la: Formosas gestet penna peregrina volucris.
units.tr: A foreign bird wears the fine feathers.

units.la: 2. Quia boni hæc est natura, ut longius latiusque se propagKet; nam ut ait Philosophus 1. Nicom. 1. bonum quo communius, eo melius, ideo propter bonitatem sui extrema studet ad se allicere, allectaque, si locum suum tueantur, magnificare. 3. Quia apud nostrates liberius vivere & magis segnescere solemus, aut saltem segnius agere, quia ipsis interdum non minus quam nostræ virtuti confidimus; apud ignotos vero gravius & studiosius res gerimus, cum nostræ tantum virtuti nitamur: ideoque apud ignotos & externos gratiores fumus, & majori afficimur admiratione. 4. Quia, quod inde usque a pueritia fuit oculis objectum, solet vilescere, & velut satietate quadam fastidiri, juxta illud Publii Mimocrati: Nulla est voluptas, quæ non assiduitate fastidium pariat. 5. Quia quivis vir doctus aut singulari aliqua virtute prædit minori in precio & honore apud suos habetur, propter conditionem parentum & cognatorum, & propter vilitatem & obscuritatem stirpis suæ. Hinc cives Christi in Christo offendebantur, ut est apud Euangelistas,
units.tr: (2) Because it is the nature of goodness to spread itself further and wider. For as the Philosopher says in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics, the more widely a good is shared, the better it is; so, on account of its goodness, it strives to draw in those furthest away, and, once drawn in, to magnify them if they keep their ground. (3) Because we at home are accustomed to live more freely and to grow slack, or at least to act more lazily, since we sometimes trust our own people no less than our own virtue; but among strangers we conduct ourselves more gravely and diligently, since we rely on our virtue alone. Therefore we are more welcome among strangers and foreigners, and are regarded with greater admiration. (4) Because what has been before the eyes from boyhood tends to become cheap and to be despised with a kind of satiety, according to the saying of Publius Mimus: "No pleasure is so great that constant repetition does not produce weariness." (5) Because any learned man or man endowed with some singular virtue is held in lower esteem and honour among his own people, on account of the condition of his parents and kin, and the lowliness and obscurity of his family. Hence the citizens of Christ were offended at him in Christ, as the Evangelists report:

units.la: Nonne hic est faber ille filius Maria, &c. quod etiam de Cicerone refert Plutarchus in vita ipsius, cum ex Asia in Italiam obito provinciae munere, multis variisq; terra & mari laudibus insignis reverteretur, eum secuti sunt, propter praeclarissime gesta magnam de se famam & existimationem speraffe; & cum in locum quendam non procul Roma digressus esset, avidum famae de se explorandae obvium quemque interrogasse; Ecquid de Cicerone Proconsule in Asia inaudivissent? cumque quid hominis ille esset, nescire se omnes affirmarent, ingemuisse graviter ferunt Ciceronem, & hicne mea gloria fructus est? dixisse; cum foris nomen coelo adaequarit, domi sit nemo, qui illud agnoscat. Idem enim plerisque accidere solet, ut qui apud exteros in luce, in oculis, & ore omnium sunt, domi cum Cicerone, tanquam Nili caput, obscuri & aut testudinis instar meridianae latent. 6. Etiam haec causa reddi potest, sicut ex longinquo illustrior esse solet & instar stellae lucere, & sicut Luna terris proxima, a Sole licet longius dissito obscuratur: sic etiam in conspectu virorum illustrium domestici oculi hebetantur, peregrinorum obtutus clarior & vegetior est. 7. Quod de Pompejo & Caesare a Poëta dicitur, quod neminem, neque superiorem, neque parem ferre potuerint, idem de omnibus eodem loco natis & educatis dici poterit; solent enim sibi invicem mutuo esse impedimento ad honores capessendos. 8. Sicut qui ex unis carceribus ad propositam metam anhelant, & alter alterum turbare & impedire conantur; sic in circulo vitae communis cives vel & populares inter se faciunt; & sicut in theatro cum cū uni applauditur, reliqui competitores invidia fe-rè rumpuntur, mussitant, & alto premūt corde dolore, & quantum possunt, obtendunt & obiiciunt ad alterius palmam velificandam & minuendam, sic in hoc circulo civili, quod dicit Poeta: Virtutem incolumem odimus, sublatam ex oculis quaerimus invidi. 9. & ult. Ideo major in honore apud peregrinos, quam apud suos homines esse solent, quia natura iplorum in longè excellentiorem transmutatur, quod à simili in ramo alteri arbori insito, & in plantis sylvestribus alió transmutatis demonstrari possit. Nam si ramum ramus adoptet, ut ait Poeta, aut si unius arboris ramus alteri arbori inseratur, ille ipse ramus postea excrescet in justæ magnitudinis & altitudinis arborem, qui in sua arbore ramus semper mansisset, sic etiam plantæ sylvestres in aliam terram transportatæ naturam suam agrestem & sylvestrum exuunt, & mitiorem induunt, ut experientia docet.
units.tr: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, etc.? Plutarch also relates something similar of Cicero in his life. When Cicero returned from Asia to Italy after completing his provincial office, distinguished by many and varied praises by land and sea, his companions hoped that, because of his most splendid achievements, he would have great fame and reputation. When he had turned aside to a certain place not far from Rome, he asked each person he met, eager to learn what fame he had, Had they not heard of Cicero, the proconsul in Asia? And when everyone declared that they did not know what sort of man he was, Cicero is said to have groaned deeply and said, Is this the reward of my glory? Though his name had matched the heavens abroad, at home there was no one who recognised it. For it usually happens to many who are in the light, in the eyes and on the lips of all among foreigners, that at home, like Cicero, they lie obscure, like the head of the Nile or like a tortoise in the midday sun. (6) This cause too may be given: just as something is usually more conspicuous from a distance and shines like a star, and just as the Moon, which is near the earth, is obscured when it is far from the Sun, so too in the presence of illustrious men our own eyes grow dull, while the gaze of strangers is clearer and keener. (7) What the poet says of Pompey and Caesar, that they could bear neither a superior nor an equal, may be said of all who are born and brought up in the same place; for they tend to be a hindrance to one another in gaining honours. (8) As those who strain from the same starting gates toward the appointed goal try to disturb and hinder one another, so fellow citizens and neighbours behave among themselves within the circle of common life. And as in the theatre, when one man is applauded, the other competitors almost burst with envy, mutter, and press down their pain in their deep hearts, and as far as they can they put obstacles in the way and detract from the other's palm, so in this civic circle the poet's words hold: Envious, we hate virtue while it is safe, and seek it out once it is removed from our sight. (9) Finally, therefore, strangers usually hold a man in greater honour than his own people, because his nature is changed into a far more excellent one. This can be shown by the analogy of a branch grafted onto another tree, and of wild plants transplanted elsewhere. For if, as the poet says, a branch takes up another branch, or if a branch of one tree is grafted onto another tree, that same branch will afterwards grow into a tree of full size and height, whereas it would always have remained a mere branch on its own tree. So too wild plants transported into another soil put off their rough and wild nature and take on a gentler one, as experience teaches.

units.la: IV. An cum honor dicatur individuum virtutis comes, vir probus semper dignus sit honore? Et statuitur th is affirmativa propter quatuor rationes: 1. est, quia in viro probo, semper est meritum aut causa meritoria honoris, nempe virtus ejusque actio. 2. Quia nemo potest viro probo virtutem eripere, quia virtus est habitus, quem quisque propriis suis viribus non alienis acquisivit, & proinde neque honore, quia à virtute provenit, indignum efficere. 3. Ratio, quia licet vir probus injuria sive verbali, sive reali ab alio afficiatur, non minus tamen dignus est honore, quam prius fuerat; imò si injuriam eam patienter, ac ut decet, ferat, majore longè dignus est honore, sicut ut de Magnanimo docet Philosophus cap. 8. huius lib. 4. 4. Quia solum vitium morale, eiusque pravæ actiones hominem possunt honore indignum reddere: Ergo cum vir probus careat vitio morali, neque pravas actiones ex se edat, non poterit fieri indignus honore, nullo unquam tempore, nisi desinat esse probus, & incipiat esse malus. Proinde graviter hallucinantur, qui per aliorum injurias existimant se honore suo ita spoliari, ut eo sint indigni, cum honor propriam cujusq; virtute sequatur, non secus ac umbra corpus. Secundo errant etiā, qui aliorum injuria ereptum honorem recuperari non posse putāt, nisi parem aut majorem inferant injuriam. Nam qui injuste agit, tantum abest, ut honorem recuperet suum, ut omni potius honore se privet, eó que ipse indignum se efficiat. Interim tamen quia accidere solet, ut vir probus, qui est læsus ab aliis, judicetur non læsus, ideo pro veritate patefacienda laborandum est, ut omnes intelligant, illum injuste esse læsum, & summa ope niti debet, ut honorem tuera: tuum, non ut injuriam alteri inferat, sed ut in tuendo honore præscriptum legum secundum rectam rationem observet.
units.tr: IV. Since honour is said to be the companion of virtue, is an upright man always worthy of honour? It is affirmed for four reasons. (1) The first is that in an upright man there is always the merit, or meritorious cause, of honour, namely virtue and its action. (2) Because no one can take virtue away from an upright man, since virtue is a habit which each person acquires by his own powers and not by those of others; and so no one can make him unworthy of honour, since honour arises from virtue. (3) The reason is that, although an upright man is wronged by another, whether by words or by deeds, he is no less worthy of honour than before; indeed, if he bears the wrong patiently and as is fitting, he is far more worthy of honour, as the Philosopher teaches of the magnanimous man in chapter 8 of the fourth book of this work. (4) Because only moral vice and its wicked actions can make a man unworthy of honour. Therefore, since the upright man lacks moral vice and does not produce wicked actions from himself, he cannot become unworthy of honour at any time, unless he ceases to be upright and begins to be wicked. Accordingly, those are gravely mistaken who think that through the wrongs of others they are so deprived of their honour that they become unworthy of it, since honour follows each person's own virtue, just as a shadow follows a body. Secondly, those also err who think that honour taken away by the wrongs of others cannot be recovered unless they inflict an equal or greater wrong. For he who acts unjustly is so far from recovering his honour that he rather deprives himself of all honour, and by that very act makes himself unworthy of it. Nevertheless, since it usually happens that an upright man who has been wronged by others is judged not to have been wronged, one must work to bring the truth to light, so that everyone understands that he has been unjustly wronged, and he must strive with all his might to defend his honour, not in order to inflict injury on another, but so that in defending his honour he observes what the laws prescribe in accordance with right reason.

units.la: Poterit & huic quæstioni non incommodè subjici hoc: An aliquis propter improbitatem & infamiam suorum, puta parentum, cognatorum, liberorum, uxoris, &c. indignus possit esse honore? Resp. Minimè, nisi ipse occasionem ad ejusmodi improbitatem & infamiā aliquo modo præbuerit; nemo enim tenetur pro iis respondere, quæ non sunt in sua potestate, neque quisquā propter alterius actiones, sed propter suas proproprias, honore indignus efficitur. Sed tamen multum honorem alicujus obscurat infamia parentum & familiae: & licet honorem proprie non detrahat, iniqua tamen & prava consuetudo hoc obtinuit, ut honoris, nominisq; splendori tum etiam famę plurimum deroget, utin Salust i Invectiva contra Ciceronem videre licet.
units.tr: This question may also fittingly be joined with this one: Can someone be unworthy of honour because of the wickedness and infamy of his own people, such as his parents, kinsfolk, children, wife, and so on? The answer is: by no means, unless he has himself in some way provided the occasion for such wickedness and infamy. For no one is answerable for things that are not in his power, and no one becomes unworthy of honour because of another's actions, but only because of his own. Still, the infamy of parents and family greatly obscures a person's honour. Although it does not properly take away honour, an unjust and perverse custom has prevailed whereby it greatly detracts from the splendour of one's honour, name, and also reputation, as may be seen in Sallust's Invective against Cicero.

units.la: V. etiam quaeritur: An cum Vir Magnanimus non debeat esse injuriarum memor, sicut supra diximus, non debeat etiam honoris sui acerrimus esse defensor? Et statui tur affirmativa thesis propter quatuor rationes: 1. est quia honor est praemium & testimonium virtutis, ut cap. 7. hujus lib. 4. docuit Philosophus. Ergo cum pro confesso sit virtutem magni esse faciendam, quippe quae una ad veram felicitatem sit via, etiā honor, qui ob virtutem tribuitur, magnifieri debet, & per consequens etiam legitimo modo defendi. 2. Quia honor a JCtis vitae comparatur: ergo cum vitae (cujus conservationem & defensionem natura instinctu suo singulis animatibus indidit) tum etiam honoris unusquisque acerrimus defensor esse debet. 3. Qui a, adversus seipsum crudelis est, qui famam suam negligit, eamque pro viribus juste non defendit adversus quoscunque impetentes & calumniatores. Ergo etiam & qui honorem suum negligit, quia honor est bonae famae causa. 4. Quia infamia quantum fieri potest est fugienda & aversanda, propterea quod morti comparetur (nam sicut, qui jam naturaliter mortui sunt, in conspectu hominum esse desinunt, sic etiam qui infamia laborant, in conspectum hominum ultra venire non audent.) Ergo e contrario honor est appetendus & proinde defendendus. Un-de g[?] viter illi reprehendendi sunt, qui nihil curant, quid de iis alii sentiant, omnemque honoris tum acquirendi, tum conservandi & tuendi curam abiiciunt.
units.tr: Again it is asked: Since the magnanimous man ought not to be mindful of injuries, as we said above, ought he not also to be a most zealous defender of his own honour? The affirmative thesis is upheld for four reasons: (1) Honour is the reward and testimony of virtue, as the Philosopher taught in chapter 7 of this fourth book. Therefore, since it is agreed that virtue must be held in high esteem, being the one path to true happiness, honour, which is bestowed on account of virtue, must also be held in high regard, and consequently must be defended by lawful means. (2) Honour is compared to life. Therefore, since everyone is by nature's instinct inclined to preserve and defend his life, everyone ought also to be a most zealous defender of his honour. (3) He is cruel to himself who neglects his good name and does not defend it, as far as he can justly do so, against all who attack or slander him. Therefore whoever neglects his honour is likewise cruel to himself, since honour is the cause of a good name. (4) Infamy is to be fled and shunned as far as possible, because it is likened to death. For just as those who are already dead naturally cease to be in the sight of men, so those who labour under infamy dare not come any longer into the sight of men. Conversely, then, honour is to be sought and therefore defended. Hence those are rightly blamed who care nothing for what others think of them, and cast off all care both to acquire and to preserve and maintain their honour.

units.la: VI. & ult. quaeritur: An aliquis magis solicitus esse debeat detribuendo, quam recipiendo honore? Et affirmatur propter quatuor etiam rationes: 1. Quia melius est honorare quam honorari, non tantum quia actio praestat passioni, quod testatur ipsa ratio, & datio melior est acceptione sicut testatur Scriptura: Sed etiam quia debiti honoris collatio absque culpa & vitio a viro probo praetermitti non potest: nam is, cui honor virtute dignus non tribuitur, non peccat, fi-quidem admittere, cum datur, non studiose ambire honorem debet; sed ille tantum peccat, qui honorem virtuti debitum non defert. 2. Ratio: quia ambitiosi honorari potius malunt, qua honorare, proinde qui verae virtuti student, debent magis soliciti esse de tribuendo aliis honore, quam recipiendo & affectando ab aliis honorem. 3. Quia honor magis est honorantis, quam honorati, sicut docet Philosophus cap. 4. lib. 1. huius operis: nam honor tanquam actio honorantis ab honorantis judicio, affectu & praeelectione pendet. 4. & ult. Quia cum quis honorem debitum alicui tribuit, officio viri probi fungitur, sicut ait Philosophus, etsi ipse a nullo debitum honorem recipiat.
units.tr: Lastly, and sixthly, it is asked: Ought a person to be more concerned about giving honour than about receiving it? The affirmative is again supported by four reasons: (1) It is better to honour than to be honoured, not only because action is superior to passion, as reason itself attests, and giving is better than receiving, as Scripture testifies, but also because the bestowing of due honour cannot be omitted by a good man without fault or blame. For one to whom honour is not given, though he deserves it by virtue, does not sin, since in receiving it, when it is offered, he ought not to seek it eagerly; but he alone sins who does not render the honour due to virtue. (2) Because ambitious men prefer to be honoured rather than to honour, therefore those who strive after true virtue ought to be more concerned about bestowing honour on others than about receiving and craving honour from others. (3) Because honour depends more on the one who honours than on the one who is honoured, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 4 of the first book of this work; for honour, as an action of the one who honours, depends on his judgement, feeling and preference. (4) And lastly, because when someone bestows due honour on another, he discharges the duty of a good man, as the Philosopher says, even though he himself receives no due honour from anyone.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: SEquitur tertius tractatus prioris partis huius libri, in quo Philosophus agit de Mansuetudine, quae versatur circa iram rite & legitime moderandam. Cur vero de hac virtute statim post tractatum de Liberalitate & Magnanimitate egerit Philosophus, haec ratio videtur esse: quia nemo in vita communi divitiis & honoribus recte moderari poterit, nisi affectus suos, inprimis vero iram sedatam habeat: circa divitias vero & honores, sicut diximus, versantur Liberalitas & Magnanimitas, his statim subjiciendam putavit Aristoteles mansuetudinem, quae affectibus internis modum praescribit, vel etiam arbitraria usus est methodo, nec tam refert, quo ordine virtutes tradantur, sed quo modo & judicio in usum vitae communis adhibeantur.
units.tr: There follows the third treatise of the first part of this book, in which the Philosopher deals with Gentleness, which is concerned with rightly and lawfully moderating anger. The reason why the Philosopher treated this virtue immediately after the treatises on Liberality and Magnanimity seems to be this: no one can rightly moderate his use of riches and honours in ordinary life unless he controls his passions, and above all keeps his anger calm. As we have said, Liberality and Magnanimity are concerned with riches and honours, so Aristotle thought gentleness should be placed right after them, since it prescribes measure to the inner passions. Or perhaps he simply followed an arbitrary method. It matters less in what order the virtues are taught than how and with what judgement they are applied to the use of common life.

units.la: Membra seu partes huius tractatus sunt tres, & continentur omnes hoc cap. 11. In prima agit de ipsa virtute cum suo objecto: In secunda agit de extremis: In tertia collatio extremorum inter se & cum medio instituitur. In prima igitur parte virtutem ipsam definit a suo objecto, quod nempe sit, virtus quae versatur circa iras, aut quae irae in vindicando & puniendo modum praescribit. Objectum igitur Mansuetudinis internum, quod a Philosopho hic ponitur, est ira, quae per se quidem non est mala, siquidem sit affectus animi: omnes vero animi affectus, quia a natura proveniunt, sunt in se boni, sed tum demum ira dicitur mala, quando modum excedit: nam qui irascitur, in quibus oportet, sicut oportet, quando & & ubi oportet cum reliquis circumstantiis non dicitur modum excedere, sed intra limites rectæ rationis se continere, & ideo vera mansuetudine est præditus.
