Quod vero omnis ira non sit mala, hinc patet, quia Deo tribuitur, cui nullum vitium tribui potest. Dicitur enim in Scriptura sæpius Deus nostris peccatis irasci, & quanquâ humano more hæc de Deo dicantur, aliquid tamen mali Deo tribuere nefas est. Sic etiam Psal.4 v.15. Irascimini, sed nec peccetis, id est, nisi justa de causa, & secundum rectam rationem est iracundum, ne ira degeneret in vitium. Ira igitur est objectum Mansuetudinis, quæ duplicem habet originem externam & internam. Externè oritur ira ex contemtu, sicut Philosophus 1. Rhet. cap. 3. docet. Interne oritur ex effervescentia & ebullitione sanguinis circa cor. Acut mansuetus circa iram tanquam objectum suum proprium rectè versetur, necesse est, ut ab omni animi perturbatione & affectu irregulari vacet: Nam si affectus animi sunt turbulentiores, iram ilico concitant, ac ita quidem ut sæpenumero modum non servet. Nam ut rectè ait Seneca, affectus indomiti pessimi sunt in homine consiliarii.
units.tr: There are three parts to this treatise, and all of them are contained in this eleventh chapter. In the first, he defines the virtue itself together with its object. In the second, he deals with the extremes. In the third, the extremes are compared with each other and with the mean. In the first part, then, he defines the virtue by its object, namely that it is the virtue concerned with anger, or the one that prescribes the measure of anger in taking revenge and punishing. The inner object of Gentleness, which the Philosopher posits here, is therefore anger. In itself anger is not evil, since it is a passion of the mind. Indeed all passions of the mind, because they arise from nature, are good in themselves. Anger is called evil only when it exceeds the measure. For a man who is angry at the right things, in the right way, at the right time and place, and with the other circumstances, is not said to exceed the measure but to keep within the limits of right reason, and so he is endowed with true gentleness. That not all anger is evil is clear from the fact that it is attributed to God, to whom no vice can be attributed. Scripture often says that God is angry at our sins, and although these things are said of God in human fashion, it is wrong to ascribe anything evil to God. So also in Psal.4 v.15, "Be ye angry, and sin not": that is, one may be angry only for a just cause and according to right reason, lest anger degenerate into vice. Anger, then, is the object of Gentleness, which has a twofold origin, external and internal. Anger arises externally from contempt, as the Philosopher teaches in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 3. Internally it arises from the boiling and effervescence of the blood about the heart. For gentleness to be rightly concerned with anger as its proper object, it must be free from all disturbance of mind and from every irregular passion. For if the passions of the mind are more turbulent, they immediately stir up anger, and often in such a way that it does not keep measure. As Seneca rightly says, undisciplined passions are the worst counsellors for a man.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de extremis mansuetudinis, & primò de altero extremo, quod opponitur ei in defectu, quæ Græcis dicitur ἀοργησία, Latinè iræ vacuitas aut Lenitas, aut sicut à Lucretio reddittur Clementia, sed non satis commodè à Cicerone 3. Tusc. quæst. dicitur hoc vitium Lenitudo aut Lentitudo, quod definitur vitium, per quod ne justis quidem de causis ira commovetur, de quo D. Bernhardus sic ait: Non autem irasci quando debes, peccatum est, irasci autem quando non debes, peccatum peccato addere est. Hoc vitium duplici nomine vituperandum dicit Philosophus: 1. Quod qui hoc vitio laborant, fatui sunt & stupidi, propterea quod injurias sibi immerito illatas tanquam trunci & stipites non sentiant. 2. Quod servili & abjecto prorsus sint animo, cum quae veri hominis sint, non sapiant, omnemque famae & aestimationis suae curam abjiciant, sicut 3. Eadem. cap. 2. pluribus docet Philosophus. Poterit & haec ratio addi, cur vituperandum sit hoc vitium, nempe quod sit sicuti Philosophus dicit 7. Polit. cap. 4. ad res praeclaras bene gerendas prorsus inepti, quia stolido & hebeti plerumque sunt ingenio. Hoc vitio inter Imperatores Romanos notatus fuit Nerva Coccejus, de quo Julius Fionto Consul dixit: Malum esse sub Principe vivere, qui nihil prohiberet, omnia permitteret. Hoc vitio plurimum laborant parentes in educandis liberis, sed malo saepe eventu, ut eleganter docet Plinius lib. 9. natural. hist. cap. 54. Simia, inquit, amplexu enecat catulos, ita parentes nimio in liberos affectu & indulgentia corrumpunt illos. Unde vulgaris versiculus:
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the extremes of gentleness. He treats first the extreme opposed to it in deficiency. The Greeks call this aorgesia [ἀοργησία], which in Latin is "freedom from anger" or "mildness"; Lucretius renders it as "clemency." Cicero, in the third book of the Tusculan Disputations, does not very fittingly call this vice "slackness" or "sluggishness." It is defined as a vice by which anger is not stirred even for just causes. On this St Bernard says: Not to be angry when you ought is a sin, but to be angry when you ought not is to add sin to sin. The Philosopher says this vice deserves blame on two counts. (1) Those who suffer from it are foolish and dull, because they do not feel injuries undeservedly done to them, as if they were blocks and stumps. (2) They have a wholly servile and abject spirit, since they do not savour what belongs to a true man, and they cast off all care for their reputation and esteem, as the Philosopher teaches at length in the third book, chapter 2. This reason may also be added for why the vice deserves blame: as the Philosopher says in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 4, such men are wholly unfit for performing noble deeds well, because they are usually of a dull and sluggish disposition. Among the Roman emperors, Nerva Coccejus was noted for this vice, and of him the consul Julius Fionto said: It is a bad thing to live under a prince who forbids nothing and permits everything. Parents suffer greatly from this vice in bringing up their children, but often with a bad result, as Pliny elegantly teaches in the ninth book of the Natural History, chapter 54: "The ape," he says, "kills its young by embracing them; so parents ruin their children by excessive affection and indulgence." Hence the common verse:

units.la: Blanda patrum segnes facit indulgentia natos.
units.tr: The soft indulgence of fathers makes their sons slack.

units.la: Exemplum in sacris fuit Eli Sacerdos, de quo 1. Sam. 4. Alterum extremum Mansuetudinis, quod ei opponitur in excessu, dicitur Iracundia, quae definitur vitium in ira praeter justas causas modum excedens. Nam in iis omnibus, in quibus Mansuetudo recte & secundum rationem se gerit, ut supra modum peccat Iracundia. Sed ut hoc vitium melius declaret Phi-
units.tr: An example in sacred history is Eli the priest, of whom we read in 1 Samuel 4. The other extreme of gentleness, which is opposed to it in excess, is called irascibility, which is defined as a vice that exceeds the measure of anger without just causes. For in all those matters in which gentleness rightly and according to reason conducts itself, irascibility sins by going beyond the measure. But so that the Philosopher may explain this vice more clearly,

units.la: lofoIosophus, tres ejus affert species, quæ à diversis circumstantiis distinguuntur: 1. Dicitur Excandescentia. 2. Amaritudo seu Amarulentia. 3. Acerbitas aut Difficultas aut etiam Crudelitas, & de his speciebus Iracundiæ, non tantum hic agit Philosophus, sed etiam in libello de virtutib. & vitiis. Et Johannes Damascenus lib.2.de Orthod. fide cap.26. Prima igitur species est Excandescentia, quæ definitur Iracundia, qua subito & acerte ob levem aliquam causam irascimur, subitoq; placamur. Duo igitur in iis, qui hoc vitio laborant notat, Philosophus. 1. Quod subito & ob leviculam quamlibet causam, ob levissimum contemptum, aut contemtus suspicionem ad iram concitentur. Hujus rei causa naturalis hæc esse poterit, quia flava bilis (unde ἀχρογολοι dicuntur, quasi bilis sint in extremo) prædominatur in iis, quæ cum sit calida & subtilis admodum, subito accenditur & elevatur. 2. Quod notat in iis Philosophus, quod citò etiam desinant ab ira, cujus etiam hæc ratio est, quia iram non continent aut celant, sed effundunt simul & semel, & producunt animum, & quia celeritate magna in ira proclivia utuntur, valde sunt immobiles & inconstantes, sicut in libello de virtutib. & vitiis docet Philosophus, & ipsa quotidiana testatur experientia. Et quod citò irasci desinant optimum in iis dicit esse Philosophus: nam optimi quique hoc vitio plerunque laborant, ut ad irascendum sint faciles & propensi, sed illico rursus placabiles, quod & de se testatur Horatius:
units.tr: he brings forward three species of it, distinguished by their different circumstances: (1) the first is called hot-temperedness (excandescentia); (2) the second is bitterness or rancour; (3) the third is harshness, difficulty, or even cruelty. The Philosopher treats of these species of irascibility not only here but also in his little book On Virtues and Vices, and John of Damascus does so in the second book of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 26. The first species, then, is hot-temperedness, which is defined as irascibility by which we become angry suddenly and sharply over some slight cause, and are soon appeased. The Philosopher notes two things in those who suffer from this vice. First, they are stirred to anger suddenly and by any very trivial cause, by the slightest contempt or suspicion of contempt. The natural cause of this may be that yellow bile, which the Greeks call achrocholoi [ἀχρόχολοι] (as if they had bile at the extreme), predominates in them. Being very hot and subtle, it is quickly kindled and stirred up. Second, the Philosopher observes that these men also quickly cease from anger. The reason for this too is that they do not contain or hide their anger but pour it out all at once, and so they exhaust their spirit. And because they are very prone to anger, they are very unsteady and inconstant, as the Philosopher teaches in the little book On Virtues and Vices, and everyday experience confirms it. The Philosopher says it is best in such men that they cease quickly from anger. For the best men are for the most part afflicted with this vice, in that they are easy and inclined to anger, but immediately placable again. Horace bears witness to this about himself:

units.la: Irasci facilis tamen ut placabilis esset.
units.tr: Prone to anger, yet easy to appease.

units.la: Et Cic. 1. epist. ad Attic. ep. 16. nam li statueris & irritabiles esse animos optimorum saepe hominum, & cosdem rursus placabiles, & esse hanc agilitatem, ut ita dicam mollicies quae naturae bonitatem. Exemplum fuit in Davide 1.Sam 25. contra Nabal. Unde hanc speciem Iracundiae Stoici, ut est apud Laert. lib. 7. de vitis Philosophorum definierunt hoc modo: quod sit ira mox subnascens & mox subsistens. Secunda species Iracundiae Graecis dicitur ὀξυθυμία, Latine Amaritudo, seu Amarulentia. Definitur Iracundia qua homines tarde quidem irascuntur, sed iram semel animo conceptam tam diu retinent & fovent, donec vel vindictam fuerint consecuti, vel temporis diuturnitate eam concoxerint. Causa naturalis in his haec videtur esse, quia flavam bilem cum nigra cholera permixtam habent, quae cum sit humor viscosus & lentus ideo facile resolvi aut digeri non potest: unde Ira diutius in iis perseverat. Isti secundi, qui hac specie Iracundiae laborant, sunt prioribus contrario plane ingenio: nam non cito irascuntur ut priores, sed tarde admodum. 2. Irami non effundunt ut priores, sed eam diu retinent, & non nisi vindicta, quae voluptatem iis affert, pro dolore accepto iram aufert. Et quia tales tectae & reconditae plerumque sunt natura, nec iram suam aliis aperiunt, hinc fit, ut aliorum suasu & consiliis ipsorum ira levari aut minui minime possit; quare & sibi & amicis valde sunt molesti. Sibi, quod sanguinem semper effervescentem circa praecordia habeant: unde & complexionis mutatio & dolor perpetuo animo obversantur. Amicis sunt molesti, quia propter ira intus concitatam difficiles sunt & morosi: unde istam Amarulentiam Stoici apud Laërt. loco cit. definiunt, quod sit ira inveterata, sed tecta, plena odii, ulciscendi tempus expectans. Nam ut habet vulgaris versiculus: Licet ad tempus bilem sibi continet atram, Non tamen Ira animo excedit, nisi poena sequatur.
units.tr: And Cicero, in the first book of the Letters to Atticus, letter 16: "For you will find that the spirits even of the best men are often irritable, and again placable, and that this agility, as I may call it, is a softness that comes from the goodness of their nature." There was an example in David against Nabal, 1 Samuel 25. Hence the Stoics, as Laertius reports in the seventh book of the Lives of the Philosophers, defined this species of irascibility thus: it is anger that arises quickly and quickly subsides. The second species of irascibility is called by the Greeks oxythymia [ὀξυθυμία], in Latin bitterness or rancour. It is defined as irascibility by which men are indeed slow to become angry, but once anger has been conceived in the mind they retain and nurse it so long that they either obtain vengeance or digest it through the lapse of time. The natural cause in these men seems to be that they have yellow bile mixed with black bile. Since this is a viscous and sluggish humour, it cannot easily be resolved or digested, and so anger persists longer in them. Those who suffer from this second species of irascibility have a disposition plainly contrary to the first: they are not quick to anger as the former are, but very slow. (2) They do not pour out their anger as the former do, but retain it for a long time, and only vengeance, which gives them pleasure, removes their anger in return for the pain they have suffered. And since such men are by nature closed and secretive and do not reveal their anger to others, it follows that their anger can hardly be eased or lessened by the persuasion or counsel of others. Therefore they are very troublesome both to themselves and to their friends. To themselves, because they always have blood seething about the heart, whence a change of complexion and a constant pain disturb their mind. To their friends they are troublesome, because on account of the anger stirred up within them they are difficult and morose. Hence the Stoics, in the passage of Laertius already cited, define this bitterness as anger that has grown old, but is hidden, full of hatred, and waiting for the time of vengeance. For as the common verse has it: "Though for a time he restrains the black bile, his anger does not depart from his mind unless punishment follows."

units.la: Exemplum singulare habet Laërtius lib. 9. Phil. in Anaxarcho: Cum Alexander Magnus in convivio aliquando esset, & Anaxarchum, quid de hac cœna sentiret, interrogasset; cuncta, inquit, magnifice ô Rex, nisi quod strapæ cujusdam caput oportebat opponi; Nicocreonta Cypriæ Tyrannum inimicum suum innuens. Hoc ægrè ferebat astans Nicocreon & injuriæ memor, cum post Regis mortem Anaxarchus navi veheretur, invitusque applicuisset Cyprum, comprehensum cum in saxum concavum conjecit, & ferreis malleis illum feriri jussit, tum Anaxarchū ferunt celebre illud dictum ingeminasse: Tunde, tunde Anaxarchi hoc vasculum, nam Anaxarchi nihil terit: Jubente vero Nicocreonte linguam illi præscidi, famaest, præcisam mordicus linguam in os Tyranni conspuisse. Exemplo etiam in sacris sunt in Simeone & Levi contra Sichimitas Genef. 34. & in Absalomo contra fratrem suum Hamonem 2. Sam. 13.
units.tr: Laertius, in book 9 of his Philosophers, in the life of Anaxarchus, gives a singular example. Once, when Alexander the Great was at dinner and asked Anaxarchus what he thought of the banquet, he replied: "Everything is magnificent, O King, except that the head of a certain satrap ought to be served up," indicating Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, his enemy. Nicocreon, who was present, took this badly and remembered the insult. After the king's death, Anaxarchus was sailing home and, against his will, was driven onto Cyprus. Nicocreon seized him, threw him into a hollow rock, and ordered iron mallets to be brought to beat him. They say that Anaxarchus then repeated his famous saying: "Beat away, beat away at the case of Anaxarchus; you are not beating Anaxarchus himself." When Nicocreon ordered his tongue to be cut out, the story goes that he bit off the severed tongue and spat it into the tyrant's face. Examples of this in Scripture are Simeon and Levi against the Shechemites, Gen. 34., and Absalom against his brother Amnon, 2 Sam. 13.

units.la: Tertia species Iracundiæ dicitur βαρυθυμία, Latine, Acerbitas, Asperitas, & non male etiam à D. Thoma redditur Crudelitas. Definitur ve ô Iracundia pertinax & aperta, qua homines sævi & asperi diutius & gravius, quam oportet, irascuntur, & nô nisi vindicta memorabili & extraordinaria placari possunt. Qui hoc vitio laborant, sunt omnium deterrimi, & ex duobus prioribus conflati. Nam ut primi cito ad irã concitantur, & ut secundi diutius iŭ corinent, in hoc tamen sunt secundis pejores, quod apertè iras gerant, & magis sint vindictæ cupidi, nec longo temporis intervallo, nec ulla ratione placari possunt, nisi vindicta memorabili exacta. Hoc vitium Tyrannis familiare esse solet, sicut in Mezentio 8. Æneid. docet Virgil.
units.tr: The third species of anger is called barythymia [βαρυθυμία] in Greek, in Latin bitterness or harshness, and St Thomas rightly renders it cruelty. It is defined as a stubborn and open anger, by which savage and harsh people are angry for longer and more intensely than they ought, and can be appeased only by a memorable and extraordinary revenge. Those who suffer from this vice are the worst of all, being a mixture of the two former kinds. For like the first kind they are quickly stirred to anger, and like the second they hold on to it for a long time; yet they are worse than the second kind in this, that they openly display their wrath, are more eager for vengeance, and cannot be appeased by any long lapse of time or by any means, unless a memorable vengeance has been exacted. This vice is usually characteristic of tyrants, as Virgil teaches in the case of Mezentius in Aeneid 8:

units.la: Mortua quin etiam jungebat corpora viva, Componens manibusq; manus, atque oribus ora (Tormenti genus) & sanie tabq; fluentes Complexu in misero, longa sic morte necabat.
units.tr: "Nay, he even joined dead bodies to living ones, hand to hand and mouth to mouth, a kind of torture; and in that wretched embrace, with the corpses rotting and oozing with gore, he killed them with a long death."

units.la: Exemplum fuit in Ann. bale, qui co pecta fossa Romanorum militū sanguine plena, Pulchrum, inquit, est spectaculum, sicut refert Valerius Max lib. 9. cap. 2. & Baptista Fulgosius lib. 20. cap. 11. Varia etiam extant exempla in historiis, ut de Nerone, qui matrem suam interfecit: de Marco Antonio Philosopho, qui Senatores & amicos suos excoriabat: & maxime memorabile est illud exemplum, quod habetur 2. Maccab. cap. 7. de septem fratribus ab Antiocho Rege cruciatis. Cæterum quia circa iram tanquam objectum suum versatur Mansuetudo, & Iracundia ei opponitur in excessu, notandum dilgenter erit discrimen inter Iram & Iracundiam. Nam ut Vives lib. 2. de anima, cap. 6. notat, Ira proprie est motus & affectus naturalis animi: Iracundia est habitus proclivis ad malum. Dicerunt igitur, ut generale & speciale. Nam omnis Iracundia est Ira, sed non econtra, sermone tamen vulgari confunduntur.
units.tr: There is an example in Hannibal, who, when a ditch full of the blood of Roman soldiers had been dug, said: "It is a beautiful sight," as Valerius Maximus reports in book 9, chapter 2, and Baptista Fulgosus in book 20, chapter 11. Many other examples are found in histories, such as Nero, who killed his own mother; Marcus Antonius the Philosopher, who flayed his senators and friends; and most memorable of all, the story in 2 Maccabees, chapter 7, of the seven brothers tortured by King Antiochus. Moreover, since gentleness has anger as its object, and irascibility is opposed to it by excess, the difference between anger and irascibility must be carefully noted. As Vives notes in book 2 of De anima, chapter 6, anger properly is a natural motion and affection of the soul, while irascibility is a habit inclined to evil. Thus they differ as the general and the specific: all irascibility is anger, but not conversely; in ordinary speech, however, they are confused.

units.la: Intertia parte capitis instituitur comparatio extremorum
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter a comparison of the extremes

units.la: morum cum medio: & iracundiam, quæ opponitur in excessu Mansuetudini, magis illi contrariari, quâ Lentitudinem docet Philosophus, idque duabus rationibus: 1. Quia iracundia est malum frequentius & usitatius, in quo sæpius peccant homines, quam in Lentitudine; nam experientia docet homines ad irascendum & ulciscendum magis esse proclives, quam ad ferendum & ignoscendum. 2. Quia Iracundia malum est gravius & deterius. Nam cum lento seu cum eo, qui Lentitudine laborat, facilius quis vivere potest, non secus ac cum agno: at cum Iracundis præsertim illis sævioribus in secunda & tertia specie vivere nemo commodè potest, cū lupos, ursos & leones, ipsa crudelitate superare videantur. Tandem excusat se Philosophus, quod notas & proprietates ipsius medii subtilius non explicarit, quia omnia singillatim explicare cum suis circumstantiis magnæ esset difficultatis, idque propter duas rationes, quarum 1. ducitur ab usu communi; vulgo enim lentos seu eos, qui lentitudine laborant, mites & mansuetos vocare solemus, id est, nomine ipsius medii, quasi veræ Mansuetudini studerent unicè, contra iracundos & stomachantes tanquam fortes & viriles laudare solemus, & putamus ad imperandum maximè esse idoneos, quia ut ait Plato 2. Polit. Imperantibus stomachis, & iracundis esse solent ad pœnam de sontibus exigendam. 2. Ratio difficultatis est, quia variæ hæ circumstantiæ ut hujus, si aliarum virtutum versantur in singularibus, quæ non multis tantum, sed infinitis etiam modis pro varia temporis loci & personarum ratione variari possunt. Ideoque non tam Regulis & præceptis communibus quàm obseruatione & usu quotidiano dijudicanda venit ut sicut supra lib.2 cap.4. probatum fuit. Cæterum tantum hoc constat, medium, in quo consistit virtus, & veros irascendi modus, esse laudandum, extrema verò vituperanda, sed adhibita distinctione. Nam si extrema paululum recedant, non sunt graviter reprehendenda, sed minorem merentur reprehensionem; si longius, gravius; si longissimè, gravissimè sunt vituperanda, & tandem concluditur solum medium relictis extremis tanquam vitiis virtuti contrariis esse amplectendum.
units.tr: of character with the mean is set out. The Philosopher teaches that irascibility, which is opposed to gentleness by excess, is more contrary to it than is the lack of spirit, and he gives two reasons: (1) because irascibility is an evil that is more frequent and common, and in which people sin more often than in lack of spirit; for experience shows that men are more inclined to be angry and to take revenge than to bear with injuries and forgive them; (2) because irascibility is the graver and worse evil. For one can live more easily with a man lacking spirit, or with one who suffers from that defect, much as one lives with a lamb; but no one can live comfortably with irascible people, especially the fiercer kinds of the second and third species, who seem to surpass wolves, bears and lions in cruelty itself. Finally, the Philosopher excuses himself for not explaining more subtly the marks and properties of the mean itself, since to explain each point individually with all its circumstances would be of great difficulty; and this for two reasons, of which (1) the first is drawn from common usage. For we commonly call the lacking in spirit, or those who suffer from lack of spirit, mild and gentle, that is, by the name of the mean itself, as if they pursued true gentleness alone; whereas we are accustomed to praise the irascible and the fuming as brave and manly, and think them most fit for command, because, as Plato says in book 2 of the Politics, the fuming and irascible are wont to exact punishment from the guilty when they are in command. (2) The second reason for the difficulty is that these circumstances, as with those of the other virtues, concern particulars, which can be varied not only in many but in infinite ways, according to the varying circumstances of time, place and persons. Therefore they are to be judged not so much by common rules and precepts as by observation and daily practice, as was proved above in book 2, chapter 4. Meanwhile this much is certain: the mean, in which virtue consists, and the right manner of being angry, is to be praised, while the extremes are to be blamed, with a distinction made. For if the extremes depart slightly, they are not to be severely censured but deserve a lesser reproach; if further, a graver one; if very far, they are to be most gravely condemned. And finally it is concluded that only the mean, with the extremes rejected as vices contrary to virtue, is to be embraced.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Mansuetudo est Virtus, quæ iræ modum præscribit, ut ratio jubet.
units.tr: 1. Mildness is a virtue which prescribes the measure of anger, as reason commands.

units.la: 2. Ira etsi sit affectus à natura proveniens, à variis tamen causis & extra & intra concitari solet.
units.tr: 2. Although anger is an emotion arising from nature, it is nonetheless commonly stirred up by various causes, both external and internal.

units.la: 3. Qui irascitur, sicut debet, & quando debet, & cum reliquis circumstantiis non vituperari, sed laudari debet.
units.tr: 3. One who is angry as he ought, when he ought, and with the other circumstances, should not be blamed but praised.

units.la: 4. Mansuetus, quo rectè circa iram tanquam objectum suum versetur, omni animi perturbatione & affectu concitatiori vacare debet.
units.tr: 4. The mild person, if he is rightly to deal with anger as its proper object, ought to be free from every disturbance of mind and from any more agitated emotion.

units.la: 5. Mansuetus non ad ulciscendum, sed ad ignoscendum solet esse proclivis.
units.tr: 5. The mild person is usually inclined not to take revenge but to forgive.

units.la: 6. Mansuetudini opponitur in excessu Iracundia, in defectu Lentitudo.
units.tr: 6. Opposed to mildness, in excess, is irascibility; in defect, sluggishness.

units.la: 7. Qui, quando jure debent, non irascuntur, stolidi & insensiles, servili etiam & abiecto prorsus ingenio esse videntur.
units.tr: 7. Those who do not become angry when they rightly ought to be are seen to be dull and insensible, and to have a servile and utterly abject disposition.

units.la: 8. Iracundi in omnibus iis, in quibus mansueti bene & secundum rationem se gerunt, supra modum peccant.
units.tr: 8. Irascible people sin beyond measure in all those matters in which the mild behave well and according to reason.

units.la: 9. Iracundi plerunq; cito & prater omnem longe rationem irasci solent, sed quod optimum in iis esse videtur cito etiam irasci desinunt.
units.tr: 9. Irascible people usually become angry quickly and far beyond all reason, but what seems best in them is that they also quickly cease to be angry.

units.la: 10. Sunt quidam Iracundi, qui quavis de causa irascuntur, sed non diu, & vocantur Excandescentes, quidã tardè irascuntur, sed iram diu retinent & vocantur Amarulenti: quidam etiam pertinaces & apertas gerunt iras, & non nisi vindicta extraordinaria placari possunt, & dicuntur Acerbi & Crudeles.
units.tr: 10. Some are irascible, becoming angry for any cause whatever but not for long; these are called excitable. Some are slow to become angry but hold on to their anger for a long time; these are called bitter. Others also bear open and lasting anger and can be appeased only by an extraordinary revenge; these are called harsh and cruel.

units.la: 11. Mansuetudini magis opponitur Iracundia, quia malum est usitatius & deterius quàm Lentitudo.
units.tr: 11. Irascibility is opposed to mildness more than sluggishness is, because it is the more common and the worse evil.

units.la: 12. Difficile est omnes Mansuetudinis proprietates singillatim explicare, tum quia usus communis id non patitur, tum etiam, quia rerum singularium certa tradi regula non possunt.
units.tr: 12. It is difficult to explain all the properties of mildness one by one, both because common usage does not allow it and because particular matters cannot be given a fixed rule.

units.la: 13. Extrema, prout accedunt, & recedunt à medio, æstimari solent. Nam si parum recedant, non graviter reprehenduntur, si multum, gravius; si maximè ut vitia gravissima gravissimè vituperari solent.
units.tr: 13. Extremes are judged by how far they depart from the mean and how near they come to it. For if they depart a little, they are not severely blamed; if much, more severely; and if most, as the gravest vices, they are customarily condemned most severely.

units.la: Notandum Nomen Mansuetudinis variis modis accipi apud autores. Nam 1. omne id denotat, quod cicur seu cicuratum est, unde feræ cicures mansuetæ dicuntur à Columella, & antiqui pro cicurare dicebant manuefacere, ut testis est M. Varro lib. 3. de Latin. ling. unde omne illud, quod à fero discretum est, cicur & mansuetum dici solet. 2. Sumitur pro ipsa Lentitudine, quæ alias opponitur ei in defectu: nam proprie Lentitudo est nimia in lenitate & indulgentiam propensio. 3. Demum proprie virtutem tutem inter Iracundiam & Lentitudinem medium servantem denotat, & sic hoc loco usurpatur. Graece dicitur πραότης, Latine reddituræ Cicerone Mansuetudo aut Placabilitas, interdum etiam clementia, sed tamen non satis commode: quia ut ait Seneca in lib. de Clementia: Proprie clementia est actio superioris erga inferiorem in constituendis poenis vel praemiis dandis. Mansuetudo vero est moderatio irae unius hominis erga seipsum vel erga alios.
units.tr: It should be noted that the name of mildness is taken in various ways by authors. For (1) it denotes whatever is tame or tamed, whence tame wild animals are called mild by Columella, and the ancients used "manuefacere" for "to tame," as M. Varro attests in book 3 of On the Latin Language. Hence whatever is distinguished from the wild is customarily called tame and mild. (2) It is taken for gentleness itself, which is otherwise opposed to it in defect; for properly gentleness is an excessive tendency toward leniency and indulgence. (3) Finally, properly it denotes the virtue keeping the mean between irascibility and sluggishness, and in this sense it is used here. In Greek it is called [πραότης], which Cicero would render in Latin as mansuetudo or placabilitas, sometimes even clementia, but not very appropriately; for, as Seneca says in his book On Clemency: properly, clemency is the action of a superior toward an inferior in fixing punishments or bestowing rewards, whereas mildness is the moderation of anger of one man toward himself or toward others.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Mansuetudo vere possit dici Virtus, cum omnis virtus versetur circa duplex objectum, externum nempe & internum, sicut patet de reliquis virtutibus. Deinde etiam ratione probatur: quia omnis Virtus debet moderari & principio interno actionum suarum, tum etiam ipsis actionibus externis ut secundum rectam rationem procedant ne devient aut deflectant a medio. At Mansuetudo circa unum tantum versatur objectum, nempe circa iram, sicut hic dicitur in textu: Ergo aut vere Virtus dici non potest, aut saltem erit diversa natura Virtus a reliquis? Resp. Id verum est: omnem Virtutem habere duplex suum objectum, & Mansuetudo etiam suum habet, nempe injuriam, offensionem, damnum, contemptum nostri, & ignominiam illatam, ex quibus ira extrinsecus commovetur. Sed Philosophus posuit tantum internum objectum, quia qui irae intrinsecus recte moderari poterit, etiam iis externis facile moderari poterit.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Can mildness truly be called a virtue, since every virtue is concerned with a twofold object, external and internal, as is plain in the other virtues? Furthermore, it is proved also by reason: because every virtue ought to regulate both the internal principle of its actions and the external actions themselves, so that they proceed according to right reason and do not stray or deviate from the mean. But mildness is concerned with only one object, namely anger, as is said here in the text. Therefore either it cannot truly be called a virtue, or at least it will be a virtue of a different nature from the others? Answer: That is true: every virtue has a twofold object, and mildness too has its own, namely injury, offence, loss, contempt of ourselves, and dishonour inflicted, by which anger is stirred from without. But the Philosopher posited only the internal object, because whoever can rightly moderate anger within will also easily be able to moderate those external things.

units.la: II. An Ira recte dicatur objectum Mansuetudinis, cum Ira opponatur Mansuetudini in excessu: Ira enim & iracundia sunt idem, sermone enim vulgari confunduntur. Proinde cum idem objectum & oppositum esse nequeat, etiam Ira ManMansuetudinis obječtum esse non potest? Resp. Iram consideran duobus modis. 1. Ut est affectus animi regularis, qui rectæ rationi paret, & sic est materia Mansuetudinis. 2. Ut habitum ex multis actionibus sed pravis comparatum, & sic confunditur cum Iracundia.
units.tr: II. Is anger rightly called the object of mildness, since anger is opposed to mildness in excess? For anger and irascibility are the same, since they are confused in ordinary speech. Therefore, since the same thing cannot be both object and opposite, anger cannot be the object of mildness either? Answer: Anger is to be considered in two ways. (1) As a regular emotion of the mind, which obeys right reason, and so it is the matter of mildness. (2) As a habit acquired from many actions, but bad ones, and so it is confused with irascibility.

units.la: III. An Mansuetudo vera diciposit Virtus, qua in mediocritate versetur, cum tamen in textu dicatur defectio, aut quæ proprie inclinat ad Lenitudinem, id est, ad oppositum ipsius in defectu?
units.tr: III. Can mildness be rightly called a virtue which lies in the mean, when in the text it is called a defect, or one which inclines properly toward sluggishness, that is, toward its opposite in defect?

units.la: Resp. Dici quidem defectionem non quod declinet à mediocritate rectæ rationis, sed quod aliquid detrahat de severitate debitæ punitionis in ira exercenda: Sic enim sonant verba Philosophi: Mansuetus ut recte circa iram versetur, debet ad ignoscendum magis quam ulciscendum esse proclivis.
units.tr: Answer: It is indeed called a defect not because it departs from the mean of right reason, but because it takes something away from the severity of the punishment due in the exercise of anger. For so the words of the Philosopher run: the mild person, if he is to deal rightly with anger, ought to be more inclined to forgive than to take revenge.

units.la: IV. & ult. Cur tres tantum statuerit species Iracundia & non plures, cum plures esse possint. Dein etiam cur plures Iracundia species statuat, cum omnis Iracundia peccet in excessu, ut ex superioribus jam patet?
units.tr: IV. And last: why he set up only three species of irascibility and not more, though there could be more? Again, why does he set up several species of irascibility, since all irascibility sins in excess, as is already clear from what precedes?

units.la: Resp. Necessario id faciendum fuit: nam quotidiana experientia testatur homines non uno modo irasci, sed quot ferè sunt ingenia, tot esse diversos modos irascendi, & ideo plures erant constituendæ species. Dein etiam plures quam tres statuere non poterat, quia triplex tantum est causa iræ in excessu. Nam cum ira omnis sit ebullitio sanguinis circa cor, tribus tantum modis id fieri s detur. Nam 1. omnis ebullitio est tenuis & subtilis, in qua prædominatur flava bilis, & sic constituit speciem primam Excandescentiam. 2. Est media neque tenuis neque crassa, ubi cum flava bile perpermiscetur nigra cholera, & sic constituit secun- dam speciem, nempe Amarulentiam. 3. Demum est crassa admodum & lenta, ubi prædominatur sola melancholia aut atra bilis, & sic tertiam constituit speciem, quæ dicitur Crudelitas.
units.tr: Answer: This had to be done of necessity: for daily experience attests that men do not become angry in only one way, but as there are almost as many kinds of temper, so there are as many different ways of becoming angry, and therefore several species had to be established. Again, he could not posit more than three, because there is only a threefold cause of anger in excess. For since all anger is an effervescence of blood about the heart, this can happen in only three ways. (1) Every effervescence is thin and subtle, in which yellow bile predominates, and this constitutes the first species, Excitability. (2) There is one which is neither thin nor thick, where black bile is mixed thoroughly with yellow bile, and this constitutes the second species, namely Bitterness. (3) Finally, there is one which is very thick and sluggish, where only melancholy or black bile predominates, and this constitutes the third species, which is called Cruelty.

units.la: Coronidis jam loco discutiedæ veniunt hæ quæ- stiones: I. Cum Philosophus dicat materiam circa quam versatur Mansuetudo, esse Iram, & virum mansuetum, cur, quomodo, quantum, & quibus debeat irasci, tantum, ideo quaeri poterit, quousque ira hominis mansueti se extendat, ita ut modum non excedat? Resp. In Ira exercenda virum Mansuetum habere suos limites, quos ultra citraq; nequit consistere rectum. Nam 1. Non irascitur, sed tantum iis, qui ex destinata malitia peccant, & nulla scelerum suorum pœnitudine ducuntur: iis vero, qui per imprudentiam peccant, & culpam deprecantur, aut veniam petunt, quantum officii ratio postulat, ignoscit. 2. Non irascitur propter leves causas, sed tantum propter graves & arduas pertinentes ad defensionem religionis, legum, patriæ, proprii⁄que honoris. 3. Non nimis cito vel tardè irascitur, sed medium servat, & ex præscripto rectæ rationis iram suam dirigit. Nam qui citò irascitur, iræ suæ moderari nequit, qui vero tardè aut stupidior aut vindictæ cupidior esse videtur. 4. Inprimis cavet, ne in primo iræ furore aut impetu eò usque abripiatur, ut aliquid committat, quod sit vel contra honestatem vel utilitatem ipsius aut alterius, & cujus ipsum postea pœnitebit. Et ratio est, cur Mansuetus nihil in primo iræ impetu faciat, quia primi impetus minimè omnium sunt in nostra po- stea. testate. Nam ut vulgò dicitur, primi motus non sunt nostri juris: Quia ab ipsa naturæ violentia concitari videntur. Id quod prudenter inter alia Athenodorus Philosophus monuit Augustum Cæsarem: Cæsar, inquit, cum iratus fueris, ne quid prius dixeris, fecerisve, priusquam viginti quatuor Græcarum literarum nomina apud te recensueris. Unde Statius 8. Thebaid. inquit: Nec frena animo permitte calenti, Da spacium tenuemq; morã, mala cuncta ministrat Impetus.
units.tr: By way of a conclusion, the following questions now come up for discussion. I. Since the Philosopher says that the matter with which mildness is concerned is anger, and that the mild man ought to be angry, why, how, how much, and with whom only, one may ask: how far does the anger of the mild man extend, so that it does not exceed the measure? Answer: In exercising anger the mild man has his limits, beyond or short of which right cannot stand. For (1) he is not angry with those who sin from settled malice and are moved by no sorrow for their crimes; but with those who sin through imprudence, and deprecate their fault or seek pardon, he forgives as far as the demand of duty requires. (2) He is not angry on account of slight causes, but only on account of grave and weighty ones pertaining to the defence of religion, of the laws, of the fatherland, and of his own honour. (3) He is not angry too quickly or too slowly, but keeps the mean and directs his anger according to the prescription of right reason. For whoever becomes angry quickly cannot moderate his anger, while whoever is slow to anger seems either too dull or too eager for vengeance. (4) Above all he takes care that he is not carried away in the first fury or onset of anger so far as to commit something which is contrary either to honesty or to the advantage of himself or another, and for which he will afterwards repent. And the reason why the mild man does nothing in the first onset of anger is that first impulses are least of all in our power. For, as is commonly said, first motions are not under our control, because they seem to be stirred up by the very violence of nature. This is what the philosopher Athenodorus prudently warned Caesar Augustus, among other things: Caesar, he said, when you are angry, say or do nothing before you have recited to yourself the names of the twenty-four letters of the Greek alphabet. Whence Statius, in the eighth book of the Thebaid, says: Do not give the reins to a heated mind; give space and a little delay; onset furnishes every evil.

units.la: Cujus rationem Ovid. 1. de arte amand. hanc reddit: Ut fragili glacies interit ira morâ.
units.tr: Ovid gives this reason for it in the first book of the Art of Love: "As ice melts away in a brief delay, so anger dies with delay."

units.la: ʃ. Vir mansuetus non debet iram diu fovere, ne ira in odium degeneret. Nam ut præclarè ait Augustinus: sicut aceti in vas infusum, si unû aut alterû diem durauerit vas ipsum corrumpit, sic ira, si diutius inhæserit, hominem destruit. Scit enim inconveniens esse, ut homo mortalis immortales gerat iras. Quod consilio consentaneum est regulæ Apostolicæ Ephef. 4. vers. 26. Ne Sol occidat super iram vestram: Tum etiam Salvatoris nostri præcepto Luc. 17. ubi jubet, ut totiesfratri peccanti ignoscamus, quoties veniam deprecatus fuerit. Quod plurimi etiam Ethnici cum suaserunt, tum observarũt, Hinc Ovid. 1. de arte amandi: Sed nunquam dederis spatiosum tempus in iram: Sæpe simulates ira morata facit.
units.tr: § A gentle man ought not to nurse anger for long, lest anger degenerate into hatred. For as Augustine rightly says: "As vinegar poured into a vessel, if it stays there a day or another, corrupts the vessel itself, so anger, if it has clung on longer, destroys the man." For he knows it is unfitting that a mortal man should harbour immortal anger. This agrees with the counsel of the apostolic rule in Ephesians 4 verse 26: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath." It also agrees with our Saviour's precept in Luke 17, where he bids us forgive a brother who sins against us as often as he asks forgiveness. Many even of the heathen both urged this and observed it. Hence Ovid, in the first book of the Art of Love: "But never give anger a long span of time; a feigned anger, once delayed, often brings about its own end."

units.la: Quod similitudine perquam elegãti illustravit Plutarchus: ut flamma facilè & non magno negotio exstinguitur, in pilis leporinis aut scirpis, aut stipulis accendi cepta, non item si solida corripuerit, ut ligna sive sicca sive viridia: sic ira primum glíscens facilè cilè vel joco vel risu compescitur, cum fumantem adhuc videris, ut si ultra provocesserit, vix ullo negotio exstingui poterit. 6. Qua, ut ait Philosophus c.11.hujus lib.4. Ira est vehemens impetus, ideo mansuetus ad ignoscendum magis, quam ad ulciscendum debet esse propensus: quia prius illud animi moderationem & prudentiam non vulgarem, posterius hoc perturbationem animi, saepe etiam insipientiam, saepe furorem denotat. 7. & ult. Non tantum vindictam & poenam condonare debet vir mansuetus ei, a quo laesus est, sed etiam causam illius irritatricem offensam nempe & injuriam alta oblivione sepelire debet. Proinde neque irae moderari vere, neque Manstuetudinem recte colere possunt ejusmodi homines, qui ignoscere se profitentur injuriam, sed oblivisci non posse.
units.tr: Plutarch illustrated this with a very elegant comparison: as a flame is easily put out, without much trouble, when it has begun to kindle on rabbit's fur, or on rushes or straw, but not when it has seized on solid wood, whether dry or green, so anger, while it is first kindling, is easily checked by a joke or a laugh, while you still see it smoking; but if it has advanced further, it can hardly be put out with any effort. 6. To this, as the Philosopher says in chapter 11 of book 4 of this work: anger is a violent impulse, so the gentle man ought to be more inclined to forgive than to avenge; because the former indicates moderation of spirit and no ordinary prudence, while the latter indicates a disturbance of the mind, often also folly, and often madness. 7. and last. The gentle man ought not only to remit the vengeance and punishment owed by the one who has wronged him, but also to bury in deep oblivion the cause that provokes it, namely the offence and the injury itself. Therefore men of this sort, who profess that they forgive an injury but cannot forget it, can neither truly moderate their anger nor rightly cultivate gentleness.

units.la: II. Moveri poterit & haec quaestio: An quia Philosophus dicit, eum, qui injurias sibi immerito illatas non vindicat, stupidum esse & insensilem, vindicare injuriam sit licitum?
units.tr: II. A question may also arise here: "Because the Philosopher says that one who does not avenge injuries unjustly inflicted on him is stupid and insensible, is it lawful to avenge an injury?"

units.la: Resp. Hanc quaestionem tanquam dubiam disceptari in utramque partem. Nam pro affirmante septem militant argumenta: 1. Quia irasci juste & vindictam expetere est licitum, sicut pluribus jam docuit Philosophus. Ergo & vindicare injuriam. 2. Quia honestum quandoque, est vindicare injuriam, ut contra turpe est, non vindicare, cum scilicet honor aut bona fama in dubium propter injuriam non vindicatam devenire possint. 3. Quia vindicta nihil est aliud, quam injuriae contumeliaeque injuste illatae debita punitio, haec autem per se & simpliciter non est illicita; nam sic frustra statuerentur bonae leges de vindicta pro malis commissis exigenda. 4. Quia Deus ipse non tantum vindicat & coercet injurias sibi illatas, & proinde in Scripturis dicitur Deus ultor aut vindex; sed etiam Magistratum politicum vicarium suum ad puniendum & exigendum sibi aliisque injuriam illatam constituit. Roman. 13. vers. 1. & 2. 5. Quia absque punitione & vindicatione injuriarum, nulla disciplina aut securitas, neque publica, neque privata recte consistere potest, sicut experientia communis docet. 6. Quia nimia conniveнтia & indulgentia in condonandis & relaxandis poenis debitis est vitium morale. 7. Demum, quia non tantum Clementia, sed etiam Severitas moderata ex praescripto rectae rationis in puniendis & coercendis delictis adhibita virtus est moralis, & summa laude digna censetur, sicut hoc cap. 11. notat Philosophus & Plato lib. 2. Politicor. Pro thesi negante duo haec faciunt argumenta: 1. Quia sacra Scriptura non tantum prohibet, ut vindicemus injurias nobis illatas, sed etiam praecipit, ut maledicentibus benedicamus, malefacientibus benefaciamus, Levit. 19. Proverb. 24. Eccles. 28. Matth. 5. Rom. 13. & alibi. 2. Quia cum Mansuetudine & praesertim cum Clementia pugnat omnis vindicatio injuriae. Nam vindicta semper prae se fert asperitatem ingenii & crudelitatem. Proinde non incommode dixit Philosophus Mansuetum magis ad ignoscendum, quam ad ulciscendum esse proclivem. Pro decisione hujus quaestionis quidam distinguunt inter vindictam privatam & publicam, & priorem prorsus esse illicitam, posteriorem vero licitam dicunt. Sed neque omnis mnis vindicta privata est illicita, neque omnis publica est licita. Nam si id esset verum, sequeretur patrifamilias non concessum esse castigare vel punire liberos suos, aut domesticos peccantes, in quos tamen jure œconomias imperium habet herile. Neque ullum Magistratum in puniendis & coercendis hominum delictis errare posse, cujus contrarium experientia probat; tum etiam factum Cambysis Persarum Regis, qui iniquo judici cutem detraxit. Verius distinguendum erit inter vindictam justā & moderatam, & injustam & immoderatam. Prior illa est licita, sive sit publica, sive privata, quia secundum praescriptum legum humanarum & divinarū fit: posterior verò qualiscunque sit, est illicita. Et de priori vera est affirmativa pars quæstionis cum suis argumentis, de posteriori negativa. Notandum etiam sacra Scripturam nō simpliciter locis citatis prohibere vindictam injuriæ justam & moderatam, sed tantum injustam, nempe cum convitium convicio, maleficium maleficio, adeoque in genere malum malo contra jus & æquum compensatur.
units.tr: Answer: This question, being doubtful, is disputed on both sides. For the affirmative seven arguments stand: (1) because it is lawful to be angry justly and to seek vengeance, as the Philosopher has already taught at length; therefore it is also lawful to avenge an injury. (2) Because it is sometimes honourable to avenge an injury, just as it is shameful not to avenge it, since honour or good name may come into doubt on account of an unavenged injury. (3) Because vengeance is nothing other than the due punishment of an injury and insult unjustly inflicted; but this in itself and simply is not unlawful, for otherwise good laws concerning the exacting of vengeance for wrongs committed would be made in vain. (4) Because God himself not only avenges and restrains injuries done to himself, and therefore in Scripture God is called "avenger" or "vindicator"; but he also appoints the political magistrate as his vicar to punish and to exact for injuries done both to himself and to others, Romans 13 verses 1 and 2. (5) Because without punishment and vindication of injuries, no discipline or security, neither public nor private, can rightly stand, as common experience teaches. (6) Because excessive connivance and indulgence in remitting and relaxing deserved punishments is a moral vice. (7) Lastly, because not only clemency but also moderate severity, applied in punishing and restraining offences according to the prescription of right reason, is a moral virtue and is judged worthy of the highest praise, as the Philosopher notes in this chapter 11, and Plato in book 2 of the Politics. For the negative thesis these two arguments tell: (1) because Holy Scripture not only forbids us to avenge injuries done to us, but also commands us "to bless those who curse us, and to do good to those who do evil to us," Leviticus 19, Proverbs 24, Ecclesiasticus (Eccles.) 28, Matthew 5, Romans 13, and elsewhere. (2) Because every vindication of an injury fights against gentleness, and especially against clemency. For vengeance always displays harshness of temper and cruelty. Hence the Philosopher said, not inappropriately, that the gentle man is more inclined to forgive than to avenge. To decide this question some distinguish between private and public vengeance, and say that the former is altogether unlawful, but the latter lawful. But neither is every private vengeance unlawful, nor is every public vengeance lawful. For if that were true, it would follow that a head of a household is not permitted to chastise or punish his children, or the servants who sin, over whom he nonetheless has the authority of a master by right of household government. Nor can any magistrate err in punishing and restraining men's offences, which experience proves to be false; and so too the deed of Cambyses, king of the Persians, who flayed the skin from an unjust judge. It will be more correct to distinguish between just and moderate vengeance on the one hand, and unjust and immoderate vengeance on the other. The former is lawful, whether public or private, because it is carried out according to the prescription of human and divine laws; the latter, of whatever kind, is unlawful. Concerning the former, the affirmative part of the question with its arguments is true; concerning the latter, the negative part. It should also be noted that Holy Scripture, in the passages cited, does not simply forbid just and moderate vengeance for an injury, but only unjust vengeance, namely when reproach is repaid with reproach and wrong with wrong, so that in general evil is repaid for evil contrary to right and equity.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: SEquitur quartus hujus libri tractatus, in quo Philosophus agit de virtutibus Homiliticis, quæ ideo hoc nomine insigniuntur, quod earum usus in quotidiana consuetudine & convictu tam in dictis quam in factis cernatur. Nam cum homo sit natura animal Politicum sicut cap. 7. 1. Nicom. & 1. 2. Polit. dicitur, ideo necessariæ sunt ei illæ virtutes, quæ conversandi modum præscribunt. Membra hujus tractatu tus sunt tria: In primo agit de quadam virtute, quae apud Graecos proprio vacat nomine, Latine dicitur Affabilitas, Comitas, aut Humanitas. In secundo agit etiam de quadam virtute Graecis innominata, sed apud Latinos dicitur Veritas aut Veracitas, quae in rebus seriis plerunque versatur. In tertio demum agit de Urbanitate, quae in rebus ludicris & jocundis maximè cernitur.
units.tr: Here follows the fourth treatise of this book, in which the Philosopher deals with the social virtues. They are so named because their use is seen in everyday custom and companionship, both in words and in deeds. For since man is by nature a political animal, as is said in chapter 7 of the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics and in the first book of the Politics, those virtues are necessary to him which prescribe the manner of living with others. This treatise has three parts. In the first he deals with a certain virtue which among the Greeks has its own name, and which in Latin is called affability, courtesy, or humanity. In the second he also deals with a certain virtue that has no name among the Greeks, but which among the Latins is called truth or truthfulness, and which is mostly concerned with serious matters. In the third, finally, he deals with urbanity, which is seen chiefly in playful and pleasant matters.

units.la: Hoc capite duodecimo agit de prima virtute Homilitica, nempe de Affabilitate, cui cum satis aptum nomen non invenerit φιλίαν seu Amicitiam vocat, non quod Amicitia vera sit, quod quidam recentiores volunt, sed quod amicitiae edendae admodum accommodata sit virtus. Alias etiam vocatur φιλανθρωπία, Humanitas, propterea quod omnes in genere homines ad vitae societatem colendam maximè accommodatiis etiam, qui Reipub. praesunt, dicitur Popularitas, propterea quod qui hac virtute sunt praediti, toti populo vulgares & tractabiles se praebeant. Partes hujus capitis sunt tres: In prima dari ejusmodi virtutem cum suo objecto docet. In secunda varias adfert proprietates viri affabilis. In tertia ut magis innotescat ipsum medium, de extremis perspicue agit.
units.tr: In this twelfth chapter he deals with the first social virtue, namely affability. Not finding a name suitable enough for it, he calls it friendship [φιλίαν] or friendliness [Amicitiam], not because it is true friendship, as some more recent writers want, but because the virtue is very well suited to fostering friendship. It is also called philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] or humanity, because it makes all men in general most suited to cultivating life together. It is also called popularity (for those who preside over the commonwealth as well), because those who are endowed with this virtue show themselves common and approachable to the whole people. This chapter has three parts. In the first he teaches that there is such a virtue, with its object. In the second he brings forward several properties of the affable man. In the third, so that the mean itself may become better known, he clearly deals with the extremes.

units.la: In prima igitur dari, duabus rationibus ostendit, quarum prima ducitur ab experientia quotidiana. Videmus enim in congressibus & vitae societate quosdam tam blandos & faciles, ut omnibus placere, nullis molestiis causam aut displicentiae praebere studeant; quosdam vero e contra tam morosos, tam duros & difficiles, ut omnibus sint adversi & molesti. Cum igitur duo sint hominum genera, quae verfantur in extremis, & reprehensionem mereantur, necesse est reperiri quosdam, qui medium inter hæc duo teneant, & secundum rectam rationem agant; nam ut ex superioribus constat, ubi dantur extrema, ibi datur medium, quia medium & extrema sunt relata. 2. Ratio ducitur a nomine, quod vulgo huic virtuti imponitur. Nam ut videre est 2. Nicomach. cap. 8. & 3. Eudem. cap. 5. & 1. mag. moral. cap. 3. Amicitia vocatur, non quod vera Amicitia sit, sed quia magnam affinitatem & similitudinem cum Amicitia habeat: Tales enim sunt, qui hoc virtutis habitu sunt præditi, quales probos & honestos amicos volumus. Hinc Cic. 2. offic. ait, difficile dictu est, quantopere conciliet animos hominum Comitas, affabilitasq; sermonis. Et in Orat. pro Lucio Murena, idipsum iterat, ubi inquit, Comitas affabilitasq; sermonis maxime continent animos hominum. Ergo cum nomen ei datum sit certum, necesse est ipsam dari. Differt tamen a vera Amicitia in duobus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he shows that the virtue exists, by two reasons. The first is drawn from everyday experience. We see in social gatherings and common life some people so agreeable and easy-going that they take pains to please everyone and to give no one any cause of annoyance or displeasure. Others, on the contrary, are so peevish, so harsh and difficult, that they are hostile and troublesome to everyone. Since there are therefore two kinds of men who live at the extremes and deserve blame, there must necessarily be some who hold the middle between these two and act according to right reason. For, as is clear from what has been said above, where there are extremes, there is also a mean, because the mean and the extremes are relative to one another. The second reason is drawn from the name that is commonly given to this virtue. As may be seen in Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 8, Eudemian Ethics 3, chapter 5, and Magna Moralia 1, chapter 3, it is called friendship, not because it is true friendship, but because it has a great affinity and resemblance to friendship. For those who possess this habit of virtue are such as we want good and honest friends to be. Hence Cicero, in De Officiis 2, says: It is hard to say how greatly courtesy and affability of speech win the hearts of men. And in the oration For Lucius Murena, he repeats the same thing, where he says: Courtesy and affability of speech above all hold men's hearts. Therefore, since the virtue has been given a fixed name, it must necessarily exist. It differs, however, from true friendship in two respects.

units.la: 1. Quod Amicitia sit cum sincero affectu veroq; amore, hæc virtus vero non. 2. Quod hæc doceat homines, quomodo erga omnes in genere, tam ignotos, quam notos comiter & familiariter se gerant, Amicitia vero tantum erga notos & amicos. Poterit etiam & hæc differentia addi ex Seneca, quæ desumitur ab objecto, nempe quod Amicitia versetur circa amabile in vita & moribus: hæc virtus circa quod est delectabile tantum in dictis & factis.
units.tr: First, friendship is with sincere affection and true love, whereas this virtue is not. Second, this virtue teaches men how to conduct themselves courteously and familiarly towards all in general, both strangers and acquaintances, whereas friendship is only towards acquaintances and friends. This difference can also be added from Seneca, and it is taken from the object: friendship is concerned with what is lovable in life and character, whereas this virtue is concerned only with what is pleasant in words and deeds.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis quinque affert proprietates viri affabilis, ut magis innotescat natura affabilitatis. 1. est: Quod erga omnes in genere homines placidè & decorè, sicut decet & debet, se gerat juxta
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he brings forward five properties of the affable man, so that the nature of affability may become better known. The first is: that he conducts himself towards all men in general calmly and decorously, as is fitting and proper, in accordance with the

units.la: Regulam Apostolicam ad Coloss. 4. verf. 6. Sermo vester sit in gratia semper sale conditus, ut sciatis, quomodo invicem unusquisque aliis respondere debeat: cum etiam ad Ephes. 4. verf. 30. & 31. Exempla sunt e sacris, in Abigae e Davidem comiter excipiente 2. Sam. 25. & in Salomone, qui Regnam Sabae humaniter tractavit 1. Reg. cap. 10. In profanis ob hanc virtutem celebris est Trajanus Caesar, qui ut refert Brutonius lib 3 c 4. amicis multum accusantibus, qui Imperatoriae majestatis parum memor, omnibus comem familiarem se praebere respondit: Talem me praestabo Imperatorem privatis, qualem optarem ipse privatus. II. Proprietas est: Quod utilitatem & honestatem in actionibus suis semper sibi proponet: nam sic nulli, nisi multis displicere poterit. Unde Anthalcidas, ut Plutarchus in Apophtheg. a quodam interrogatus, quomodo quis omnibus maxime placere possit, respondit: si loquatur jucundissima, praeflat autem utilissima. III. Proprietas est: Quod studeat ejusmodi affere voluptates, quae sunt honestae & non damno sae, nec sibi qui affert, nec illi cui affertur, Nam si alterutri damnosae aut turpes sint, tum ut damnum & turpitudinem vitet, contrarium voluptatis, nempe dolorem potius afferet: existimat enim melius consultum fore tum sibi, tum etiam ei, cum quo ipse coversatur. IV. Proprietas est: Quod diversimode aut cum diversi generis hominibus versetur, aliter cum iis, qui in dignitate & eminentia sunt constituti, aliter cum privatis, cum notis, aliter cum ignotis, ubi utile fuerit conversum Epicteti Philosophi tenuisse, qui autore Stobaeo serm. 3. de Temperantia, homines, minem, cum quo conversari debemus, tribus modis considerandum esse suadebat, nempe ut majorem, ut minorem, & ut aequalem: majori auscultare & obtemperare recta monenti convenit: minori modeste persuadere, ne quid ei molestia afferas. Aequali consentire si quid justo & aequo consentaneum proferat. Hinc non incommode a D. Thoma 2. 2. quaest. 104. Affabilitas definitur virtus qua homo in conversatione erga omnes se gerit delectabiliter, sed non erga omnes aequabiliter.
units.tr: apostolic rule in Colossians 4, verse 6: Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man; and also Ephesians 4, verses 30 and 31. Examples from Scripture are Abigail receiving David courteously, 2 Samuel 25, and Solomon, who treated the Queen of Sheba humanely, 1 Kings 10. Among secular examples, Trajan Caesar is famous for this virtue. As Brutonius relates in book 3, chapter 4, when his friends complained much, saying that he was little mindful of imperial majesty, he replied that he showed himself courteous and familiar to all: I will show myself such an emperor to private men as I would wish to have been myself as a private man. The second property is: that he will always propose to himself usefulness and honesty in his actions, for in this way he will be able to displease no one, except many. Hence Anthalcidas, when asked by someone, as Plutarch relates in the Apophthegms, how a man could please everyone most, replied: if he speaks the most agreeable things, but intends the most useful. The third property is: that he takes pains to bring such pleasures as are honest and not harmful, neither to himself who brings them nor to the one to whom they are brought. For if they are harmful or shameful to either, then, in order to avoid the harm and the shame, he will rather cause the opposite of pleasure, namely pain, for he thinks it better provided both for himself and for the one with whom he is in company. The fourth property is: that he associates in different ways, or with different kinds of men: one way with those who hold rank and eminence, another with private persons, another with acquaintances, another with strangers. Here it is useful to hold to the saying of the philosopher Epictetus, who, according to Stobaeus, in Sermon 3, on Temperance, advised that a man with whom we must associate should be considered in three ways, namely as greater, as lesser, and as equal: it is fitting to listen to and obey the greater when he gives right counsel; to persuade the lesser modestly, lest you cause him any annoyance; to agree with the equal when he proposes something consistent with what is just and fair. Hence, not inappropriately, Thomas Aquinas, in 2.2, question 104, defines affability as the virtue by which a man conducts himself pleasantly towards all in company, but not equally towards all. The fifth property is: that he avoids, as far as he can, causing sadness and annoyance, and never omits this unless honesty and usefulness demand it; and he will always take greater care not to cause anyone pain, but rather will take pains to bring pleasure, which he sets before himself in all his actions as something delightful and agreeable. Or the property may be conceived in this way: that he does not grant everything to others, though he strives to please all; but if they put forward something that seems to offend against God or good morals, he will admonish them modestly and gently, especially if he sees that his admonition will bring more pleasure and usefulness in the future than annoyance or pain at present. See more in Keckermann, page 273.

units.la: V. Proprietas est: Quod tristitiam & molestiam afferre, quantum potest, caveat, nec unquam nisi ubi honestum & utile requirunt id deficiat, & semper magis cavere, ne excitet alicui dolorem, sed potius operam dabit, ut afferat voluptatem, quam tanquam delectabile & jucundum quiddam in omnibus actionibus sibi proponit. Vel poterit proprietas sic concipi, ut non omnia aliis concedat, etsi omnibus placere studeat, sed si quid proferant, quod in Deo & bonos mores peccare videatur, modeste & demisse admonebit, praesertim si admonitionem ipsius plus in futuro voluptatis & utilitatis allaturam videat, quam in praesentia molestiae aut doloris. Plura vide apud Keckerm. pag. 273.
units.tr: V. The property is this: he should take care, as far as he can, not to cause sadness and annoyance, and should never fail to do so unless honour and usefulness require it; and he should always take greater care not to give anyone pain, but rather make it his business to bring pleasure, which he sets before himself in all his actions as something delightful and agreeable. Or the property may be conceived thus: he does not grant everything to others, though he strives to please everyone, but if they put forward anything that seems to offend against God and good morals, he will admonish them modestly and humbly, especially if he sees that his admonition will bring more pleasure and usefulness in the future than annoyance or pain in the present. See more in Keckermann, p. 273.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis agit breviter de extremis, & dicit quidem medium sic qualicunque modo, prout ipsius natura ferebat, esse descriptum, extrema vero initio capitis leviter etiam adumbrata. Sed extremum in excessu duplici insignitur nomine, propterea quod duplicem habeat finem. Nam qui hoc vitio laborant, si solius voluptatis gratia & nulla alia ob causam placere studeant dicuntur Assentatores: fi lucri & pecuniarum studio dicuntur Adulatores. Extremum vero in defectu hoc habet vitii, quod omnibus molestiam exhibeat, & qui hoc vitio laborant, nullis dicto aut facto placere student, & dicuntur Morosi. Morositas vero magis opponitur affabilitati, quâ Assentatio, propter tres causas: 1. Quia nihil participat de natura medii. 2. Quia majus est vitium, cum majori reprehensione sit dignum. 3. Quia lites & discordias, non vero pacem & concordiam in hominum societate alere & fovere videtur.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he treats briefly of the extremes, and indeed says that the mean has been described in some general way, according to its own nature, while the extremes were only lightly sketched at the beginning of the chapter. But the extreme of excess is marked by a twofold name, because it has a twofold aim. For those who labour under this vice, if they strive to please solely for the sake of pleasure and for no other reason, are called Assentators; if for the sake of gain and money, they are called Flatterers. The extreme of defect, however, has this vice, that it causes annoyance to all, and those who labour under this vice strive to please no one by word or deed, and are called Morose. Moroseness, moreover, is opposed to affability more than assentation is, for three reasons: (1) because it shares nothing in the nature of the mean; (2) because it is the greater vice, and deserves greater blame; (3) because it seems to nourish and foster quarrels and discords, not peace and concord, in human society.

units.la: Breviter notanda sunt ista quatuor: I. Definitio, quæ est virtus, quædam in conversatione seria & oblectatione honesta mediocritatem servans. II. Objectum duplex, internum nempe voluptates & dolores animi, quæ ex rebus seriis in quotidiana hominum conversatione exsistunt: Externum communio dictorum & factorum in quovis congressu hominum. III. Notandum venit officium, quod in duobus præcipue consistit: 1. Ut affabilis sit facilis, facilemque se omnibus præbeat, sed cum hac conditione, ut unicuique pro dignitate status sui hæc facultas præstetur. 2. Ut suavis & blandus sit & sine molestia aut offensione cum aliis dicta & facta sua communicet, tum etiam ut in iis omnibus de quibus supra in proprietatibus dictum fuit, recte & secundum præscriptum rationis se gerat. IV. Extrema sunt observanda. Opponitur enim Affabilitati in excessu Adulatio Græcis ἀρέσκεια, in defectu Morositas, quæ definitur vitium in conversatione seria deficiens, quo ne in rebus quidem honestis aliis placere studemus. Ob hoc vitium inter alia, quam plurima male audiebat Nero, quem tam morosum & difficilem fuisse refert Xiphilinus in ipsius vita, ut neque cum servis, neque cum liberis versari dignatus sit, quin etiam si quid mandare vellet, id tabulis inscribere consueverit. Item Procopius Imperator, qui teste Cœlio lib 3.cap.28. diffugiebat conspectum hominum, & per morum tristium latebras habitum illius Crassi similem (quem semel in vita tantum risisse refert Lucilius) contraxit humum semper intuens. Talis etiam fuit Timon Atheniensis, qui vulgò μισάν-θρωπο dictus est. Assentatio vero, quæ, ut dictinus Affabilitati in excessu opponitur, est vitium in conversatione seria modum excedens, quo praeter rationem & honestatem omnibus in quibuscunque rebus placere unicè studemus. Hoc vitium in Regum & Principum aulis plurimum regnat, tales aulici esse conantur, qualem Comicus ille Poëta Gnathonem suum in Eunucho depingit: Est genus hominum, qui esse primos se omnium rerum volunt, nec sunt tamen, his ego non parem me ut arrideam, sed ultro iis arrideo, & ingenium admiror simul, si quid dicunt, laudo, & rursus si negant, laudo quoque. Negat quis, nego, ait, aio, postremo imperavi egomet mihi omnia assentari. Sed cum tales pestis & pernicies sint Principum, Regum & Magnatum, sic debet tractari, ut de Sigismundo refert Æneas Sylvius in lib.1 comment. de rebus gestis Alphonsi Aragonia Regis, narrat enim istum Sigismundum, cum quidam adulator aulicus eum supra modum laudaret. & Diis similem prædicaret, alapas aliquot impegisse, dicenti illi, cur me cadis Imperator? respondisse, cur me mordes adulator.
units.tr: Briefly, the following four points are to be noted. I. The definition: it is a virtue, a certain mean in serious conversation and honest recreation. II. The object is twofold: internally, the pleasures and pains of the mind that arise from serious matters in the daily conversation of men; externally, the sharing of words and deeds in any gathering of men. III. The duty to be noted consists chiefly in two things: 1. to be affable, easy to approach, and to make oneself accessible to all, but on the condition that this courtesy is extended to each person according to the dignity of his station; 2. to be pleasant and agreeable, and to share one's words and deeds with others without causing annoyance or offence, and also to conduct oneself rightly and according to the prescription of reason in all those matters of which we spoke above under the properties. IV. The extremes must be observed. For opposed to affability by excess is obsequiousness, which the Greeks call [ἀρέσκεια], and by defect is moroseness, which is defined as a vice that is lacking in serious conversation, by which we do not even in honest matters try to please others. Because of this vice, among many other faults, Nero was ill spoken of; Xiphilinus reports in his life that he was so morose and difficult that he did not deign to associate either with slaves or with free men, and that if he wished to give any order, he was accustomed to write it on tablets. Likewise the emperor Procopius, who, according to Caelius, book 3, chapter 28, shunned the sight of men, and, hiding in the lairs of gloomy manners, took on a habit like that of that Crassus (whom Lucilius reports laughed only once in his life), always staring at the ground. Timon of Athens was also of this sort, commonly called a misanthrope [μισάνθρωπος]. Flattery, however, which, as we said, is opposed to affability by excess, is a vice in serious conversation that exceeds the mean, by which we strive above all to please everyone in whatever matters, beyond reason and honesty. This vice reigns most of all in the courts of kings and princes, where courtiers try to be like that Gnatho of the comic poet, whom he depicts in the Eunuch: There is a kind of men who want to be first in everything, and yet are not; I do not smile along with them as an equal, but I smile at them of my own accord, and I admire their wit; if they say anything, I praise it; and again, if they deny it, I praise that too. If someone says no, I say no; if he says yes, I say yes; in short, I have trained myself to agree with everything. But since such people are a plague and ruin to princes, kings and great men, they should be treated as Aeneas Sylvius reports of Sigismund in the first book of his commentary on the deeds of Alphonsus, King of Aragon: for he narrates that when a certain courtier who flattered him beyond measure and called him like the gods, Sigismund gave him several slaps, and when the man said to him, Why do you strike me, Emperor?, he replied, Why do you bite me, flatterer?

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Quidam sunt, qui in congressibus in communi vita societate omnibus placere student, & isti vocantur placidi & faciles, quidam vero, qui omnibus displicere, & isti vere dicuntur morosi & difficiles.
units.tr: 1. Some people, in meetings and in the society of ordinary life, strive to please everyone. These are called agreeable and easy-going. Others strive to displease everyone; these are truly called surly and difficult.

units.la: 2. In virtutibus, quantum medium ipsum laudari solet, tantum extrema vituperantur.
units.tr: 2. In the virtues, the more the mean itself is usually praised, the more the extremes are blamed.

units.la: 3. Affabilitas amicitia non est absimilis, propterea quod qui ea sit praditus, talis solet esse, qualem honestum & probum amicum volumus.
units.tr: 3. Affability is not unlike friendship, because whoever possesses it usually turns out to be the kind of honest and upright friend we would want.

units.la: 4. Amicitia solet esse cum sincero affectu & amore, affabilitas non item.
units.tr: 4. Friendship usually involves sincere affection and love; affability does not necessarily.

units.la: 5. Amicitia ad amicos tantum & notos se extendit, affabilitas vero ad omnes ignotos juxta ac notos, non familiares & familiares.
units.tr: 5. Friendship extends only to friends and acquaintances, but affability extends to all, strangers as much as acquaintances, the unfamiliar as much as the familiar.

units.la: 6. Affabilis erga omnes decore se gerit, nihilq; committit, quod honestatem & utilitatem non sapiat.
units.tr: 6. The affable person behaves toward everyone with propriety and commits nothing that does not savour of honesty and usefulness.

units.la: 7. Affabilis etsi hoc unice agat, ut voluptatis in communi hominum societate afferenda studeat, turpi tamen voluptati, & quæ detrimentum, aut sibi aut aliis afferat, non studet.
units.tr: 7. Although the affable person aims solely at bringing pleasure in human society, he does not pursue shameful pleasure, or any pleasure that causes harm to himself or to others.

units.la: 8. Affabilis in dictis & factis plurimum afferre studet voluptatis, molestia & doloris minimum.
units.tr: 8. In word and deed the affable person strives to bring the greatest pleasure and the least annoyance and pain.

units.la: 9. Qui solius voluptatis gratia placere studen, dicuntur Assentatores, qui vero lucri & pecuniarum studio, dicuntur Adulatores.
units.tr: 9. Those who strive to please for the sake of pleasure alone are called flatterers (assentatores); those who do so for the sake of gain and money are called toadies (adulatores).

units.la: 10. Morosus in omnibus durus & difficilis esse solet.
units.tr: 10. The surly person is usually harsh and difficult in everything.

units.la: 11. Magis affabilitati opponitur Morositas, quam Assentatio, tum quia minus participat de natura medii, tum quia majore reprehensione sit digua.
units.tr: 11. Surliness is opposed to affability more than flattery is, both because it shares less in the nature of the mean and because it deserves greater reproach.

units.la: Kk 5 I. Quæ-
units.tr: Kk 5 I. Quae-

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Affabilitas vere possit dici virtus, cum nulla sit virtus, cujus non capax sit omnis homo. Nam etsi consuetudine & assuefactione acquirantur virtutes morales, ingenium tamen & indolem ad omnes virtutes capessendas & acquirendas natura unicuique indidit, sicut praeclare su-pra docuit Philosophus cap. 1. lib. 2. hujus operis, & lib. 6. cap. ult. At Affabilitatis non est omnis homo capax, verbi gratia: mutus quia Affabilitas in usu sermonis consistit solum: at sermonis usum muto natura denegavit, ideo non vere posse dici virtus? Resp. Duo in Affabilitate sicut in omni virtute esse consideranda. Primò habitum internum, qui muto non minus, quam aliis competere potest, & 2. actum externum secundum quem operationes virtutes seproducunt, & hic muto non competit. Dein etiam falsum est in solo sermonis usu Affabilitatem consistere. Nam in factis non tantum in dictis etiam consistit, & variis etiam gestibus, in quibus muti se faciles & affabiles exhibere possunt, & sicut in Tragœdiis & Comœdiis multa variis spectaculis involuta ad vivum exhibentur, sic etiam manus, oculi aliaeque corporis partes multa interdum suo modo loquuntur.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Can affability truly be called a virtue, since there is no virtue that every man is not capable of? For although the moral virtues are acquired by custom and habituation, nature has nonetheless implanted in each person the natural aptitude and disposition for taking up and acquiring all the virtues, as the Philosopher taught excellently above in chapter 1 of book 2 of this work, and in book 6, the last chapter.
