But not every man is capable of affability: for example, the mute. Since affability consists only in the use of speech, and nature has denied the use of speech to the mute, can it not truly be called a virtue? Answer: Two things must be considered in affability, as in every virtue: first, the inner habit, which can belong to the mute no less than to others; and second, the outward act, through which the operations of the virtue are produced, and this does not belong to the mute. Moreover, it is also false that affability consists only in the use of speech. It consists in deeds as well as in words, and in various gestures by which the mute can show themselves easy and affable. Just as in tragedies and comedies many things wrapped up in various spectacles are displayed to the life, so too the hands, eyes and other parts of the body sometimes speak in their own way.

units.la: II. An rectè dixerit Philosophus Affabilitatem versari circa voluptates & dolores, tanquam objectum suum proprium.
units.tr: II. Whether the Philosopher rightly said that affability is concerned with pleasures and pains as its proper object.

units.la: Nam lib. 2. cap. 3. hujus operis, vocat voluptatem & dolorem communia objecta omnium virtutum in genere, idque septem rationibus ibidem confirmat. Et lib. 3. cap. 13. Voluptatem & dolorem statuit objectum Temperantiæ. Ideo Affabilitatis objectum proprium esse non possunt. Resp. Voluptatem & dolorem considerari tribus modis, quatenus ad virtutes morales spectant: 1. Ut sunt comcommunes affectiones omnium virtutum, quia nēpe ex qualibet virtutis actione aut dolor aut voluptas in animo agentis excitati solet, & sic sunt communia obiecta omnium virtutum, quo etiam modo consideravit loco cit. lib. 2. Philosophus. 2. Consideratur, quatenus se extendunt ad affectiones duorum tantum sensuum exteriorum, nempe gustus & tactus, & sic de iis tanquam Temperantiae obiecto lib. 3. egit. Hic vero pro obiecto Affabilitatis ponuntur quatenus in quotidiano sermonis usu aut in conversatione seria in dictis & factis cernuntur.
units.tr: For in book 2, chapter 3 of this work he calls pleasure and pain the common objects of all the virtues in general, and he confirms this there by seven reasons. And in book 3, chapter 13, he establishes pleasure and pain as the object of temperance. Therefore they cannot be the proper object of affability. Answer: Pleasure and pain may be considered in three ways, insofar as they pertain to the moral virtues. 1. As they are the common affections of all the virtues, since from any action of a virtue either pain or pleasure is usually stirred up in the mind of the agent; and in this way they are the common objects of all the virtues, which is the way the Philosopher considered them in book 2 cited above. 2. They are considered insofar as they extend to the affections of only two outer senses, namely taste and touch; and in this way he treated them in book 3 as the object of temperance. But here they are posited as the object of affability insofar as they appear in the everyday use of speech, or in serious conversation, in words and deeds.

units.la: III. Quomodo dicat iflam Virtutem vocari quidem vulgò Amicitiam, sed non esse revera Amicitiam sed multis modis differre à vera Amicitia, cum tamen ratione probe-idem esse: nam habet eadem oppositas, nempe Assentationem & Morositatem seu Contentionem. Cum igitur eadem habeant opposita, non diversa, sed idem esse videntur.
units.tr: III. How does he say that this virtue is commonly called friendship, yet is in truth not friendship, but differs from true friendship in many ways, although by reason it is well the same? For it has the same opposites, namely flattery and surliness or contentiousness. Since they have the same opposites, they seem to be not different but the same.

units.la: Resp. Non habere eadem opposita. Nam Assentatio & Morositas directe opponuntur Affabilitati, Amicitiae vero indirecte & per accidens tantum, quatenus scilicet ex assentatione & morositate vera corrumpitur Amicitia, quod expresse docet Philosophus lib. 7. cap. 5. hujus operis. Deinde etiam ista opponuntur Affabilitati, ut sunt habitus pravi ex crebris actionibus comparati, Amicitiae vero ut sunt affectus naturales. Nam sunt quidam à natura placidi & faciles, sunt etiam à natura morosi & difficiles, sunt etiā, qui arte & consuetudine difficultatem aut severitatem in moribus affectant, sunt etiam, qui arte & consuetudine blandi & faciles fiunt.
units.tr: Answer: They do not have the same opposites. For flattery and surliness are directly opposed to affability, but to friendship only indirectly and accidentally, insofar as true friendship is corrupted by flattery and surliness, as the Philosopher expressly teaches in book 7, chapter 5 of this work. Next, these are opposed to affability as depraved habits acquired by frequent actions, whereas friendship is a natural affection. For some people are naturally agreeable and easy-going, and some are naturally surly and difficult; some, by art and custom, affect difficulty or severity in their manners; and some, by art and custom, become flattering and easy-going.

units.la: Coronidis loco hanc quaestionem adjiciemus:
units.tr: By way of a crown to the chapter, we add this question:

units.la: An Affabilitas consistere possit cum Gravitate: quia Philosophus dicit hoc esse Affabilitatis proprium & experientia ipsa etiam suadet, ut quantum recta velit ratio, omnibus se accommodet, & omnibus placere studeat? Resp. Etsi quidem sint hoc seculo, qui Stoicorum instar nolint moveri affectibus, sed veram Gravitatem ex vultus torvitate & morum severitate metiantur, & ideo cum haec affectiones Affabilitati repugnant: Nam affabilitas in vultus blanditie, & morum facilitate inprimis consistit; Ideo una istas duas virtutes consistere non posse autumant. Sed contrarium ratio ipsa evincit propter tres causas: 1. est, quia non in torvitate vultus, aut severitate morum, sed in apta & decora gestus externi moderatione consistit gravitas, id quod ex definitione gravitatis patet, Nam definitur Virtus externum corporis habitum, gestu & motum ad decorum dignitatem unicuique pro statu & conditionis ratione convenientem componens. Ideo non ex prioribus, sed ex posterioribus hisce circumstantiis commensurari debet gravitas.
units.tr: Can affability be combined with gravity? For the Philosopher says that this is a property of affability, and experience itself also suggests that, so far as right reason wills, one should accommodate oneself to all and strive to please all. Answer: Although there are in this age some who, like the Stoics, will not be moved by the affections, and who measure true gravity by a grim face and severity of manners, and who therefore think these affections are incompatible with affability (for affability consists above all in a pleasant countenance and easiness of manners), nevertheless reason itself proves the contrary, for three reasons. 1. Gravity consists not in a grim face or severity of manners, but in the fitting and seemly moderation of outward bearing; this is clear from the definition of gravity. For gravity is defined as a virtue that arranges the outward habit, gesture and motion of the body to a decorum and dignity suited to each person according to his station and condition. Therefore gravity must be measured not by the former circumstances but by these latter ones.

units.la: 2. Quia experientiae repugnat, non posse gravitatem cum Affabilitate consistere. Nihil enim gravitati alicujus detrahit summa ejus Affabilitas, quin potius gratiam & favorem addit.
units.tr: 2. Because experience is opposed to the claim that gravity cannot coexist with affability. For a person's great affability takes nothing away from his gravity; rather it adds grace and favour.

units.la: 3. Quia Gravitas cum affabilitate (aut quod idem est cum comitate) conjuncta fit illustrior, majoremque dignitatem & autoritatem homini conciliat. Hinc Cic. in Catone Major, commendaturus C. Fabricium & Quintum Fabium Max. dicit in iis cum comitate Gravitatem fuisse conjunctam. Tum etiam in Attico refert fuisse Affabilitatem severitate conditam, & Gravitatem cum Facilitate conjunctam.
units.tr: 3. Because gravity joined with affability (or, what is the same, with courtesy) becomes more illustrious and wins greater dignity and authority for a man. Hence Cicero, in Cato Major, wishing to commend Gaius Fabricius and Quintus Fabius Maximus, says that in them gravity was joined with courtesy. Also, in the Atticus, he reports that affability was seasoned with severity, and gravity was joined with ease.

units.la: II. & alt. An illud factum Carthusianorum qui se invicem non alloquuntur, neq; etiam, al os sed signis & nutu omnia peragunt, sit licitum, & cum vera affabilitate consiste re possit? Resp. Hanc quaestionem disceptari in utramque partem, sed veriorem esse negativam. Pro affirmativa sunt hae rationes: 1. Quia id fit ex Regula ordinis & praescripto superiorum, & cum inter omnia vota monachalia praecipua sit obedientia, ideo ut obedientiā & Regulae & superiori praestent, legitimo sermonis usu se privare possunt. 2. Quia ex silentio & taciturnitate quilibet meditationi & lectioni piae melius vacare potest. 3. Demum, quia in multo sermone multae solet esse vanitates, à quibus, ut fugiant, sermonis usum cohibere licet. At pro negativa parte sunt hae rationes: 1. Quia sermonis usus à natura unicuique inditus est, ideo quibus inest eum cohibere non debent, nisi ipsi naturae repugnare velint. 2. Quia homo est natura animal πολιτικόν, & natus ut in societate hominum degat: qui vero in societate hominum vivere potest, quomodo cum aliis Familiaritatem aut Amicitiam colere, si sermonis usu se privet. 3. Quia cum virtute morali pugnat, nempe cum Affabilitate in dictis nō facilem se & blandum praebere, & qui sermonis usum cohibet, quomodo aliis consilio aut salutaribus monitis prodesse poterit. 4. Quia Scriptura sacra contrarium probat. Nam Prov. 15. verf. 23. Sermo oportunus dicitur optimus, id est, qui suo tempore & loco pro convenienti personarum & rerum ratione profertur. Hinc Diogenes Cynicus dicit, verba opportunè prolata, esse velut poma aurea in argentea patina patina. Proinde cum & naturæ hoc repugnet, & ab Affabilitate, quæ in facilitate sermonis & blanditie consistit, longè discrepet, & Scriptura contrarium probet, illicitum esse & damnandum dicimus.
units.tr: II. Second question: Is that practice of the Carthusians, who do not address one another, not even by mouth, but do everything by signs and nods, lawful, and can it be combined with true affability? Answer: This question is disputed on both sides, but the negative is the truer. For the affirmative there are these reasons: 1. Because this is done by the rule of the order and the command of superiors, and since obedience is the chief of all monastic vows, therefore, in order to render obedience to the rule and to superiors, they may deprive themselves of the lawful use of speech. 2. Because by silence and taciturnity anyone can more freely devote himself to pious meditation and reading. 3. Finally, because much talk usually involves many vanities, and to avoid these it is lawful to restrain the use of speech. But for the negative there are these reasons: 1. Because the use of speech is implanted in each person by nature, therefore those in whom it is present should not restrain it, unless they wish to resist nature itself. 2. Because man is by nature a political animal [πολιτικόν], born to live in the society of men; but how can one who deprives himself of speech cultivate familiarity or friendship with others, if he cannot live in human society? 3. Because it conflicts with a moral virtue: namely, with affability, which in word does not show itself easy and pleasant; and one who restrains the use of speech cannot help others by counsel or salutary admonitions. 4. Because Holy Scripture proves the contrary. For Prov. 15 verse 23 says that a timely word is best, that is, one spoken at its proper time and place, according to the fitting circumstances of persons and things. Hence the Cynic Diogenes says that words spoken opportunely are like golden apples in a silver basket. Therefore, since this both opposes nature and differs widely from affability, which consists in easiness of speech and pleasantness, and since Scripture proves the contrary, we say that it is unlawful and to be condemned.

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: SEquitur secundum membrum quarti tractatus, in quo Philosophus agit de secunda virtute Homilitica, cui licet aptum & commodum nomen apud Græcos non sit repertum, vulgò tamen nec incommodè vocari solet ἀληθεια. Sic enim à Philosopho 3.Eudem. cap.5. & 1. magnor.moral. cap. 32. & supra cap. 8. lib. 2. propterea quod hujus virtutis proprium sit verum in communi vita sectari. Sed tamen hæc vox latius patet, quam hujus virtutis natura ferat. Latinè dicitur Integritas, Sinceritas, Candor, Veritas, ut sitato jam apud Ethicos nomine Veracitas, de qua agit hoc capite decimo tertio, & quatuor de ea adfert, ideo totidem erunt capitis partes. In prima de materia seu objecto circa quod versatur hæc virtus, agit. In secunda agit de ipsa virtute, quæ vulgò dicitur Veracitas. In tertia de extremis ejusdem. In quarta demum more consueto comparationem extremorum instituit & inter se & cum ipso medio.
units.tr: There follows the second part of the fourth treatise, in which the Philosopher deals with the second Homiletic virtue. Although the Greeks have found no apt and convenient name for it, it is commonly and not unsuitably called truth [ἀλήθεια]. The Philosopher calls it this in Eudemian Ethics 3.5, Magna Moralia 1.32, and above in book 2, chapter 8, because the proper task of this virtue is to pursue truth in common life. But this word has a wider range than the nature of this virtue allows. In Latin it is rendered integrity, sincerity, candour, truth. Since the name Veracity has already been used by the ethicists, and since this thirteenth chapter deals with it and gives four points about it, the chapter will have four parts. In the first part he deals with the matter or object with which this virtue is concerned. In the second he deals with the virtue itself, commonly called Veracity. In the third he deals with its extremes. In the fourth, as is his usual custom, he sets out the comparison of the extremes both with each other and with the mean.

units.la: In prima igitur, transitione facta à priori virtute nempe Affabilitate, nunc sibi agendum proponit de Veracitate, quæ verum in dictis & factis sectatur, falsum avertsatur. Unde hujus virtutis objectum à Philosopho ponitur verum, dictis & factis ita expressum, ut nihil fictum aut fucatum inveniatur. Ac ut melius innotescat natura objecti, operationes seu actus extremorum & medii in medium affert. Nam arrogans, qui veraci opponitur in excessu, fingit sibi ea inesse, quæ revera non insunt, & quæ bona revera insunt, majora semper, quam sunt, verbis facit. Econtra dissimulator, qui veraci in defectu opponitur, qui habet aut novit bona, aut prorsus negat, aut dissimulat, aut extenuat, aut minora, quam sunt, facit. Inter hos interjectus medius verax, quæ habet aut novit bona, tandem confitetur se habere & scire, nec negat aut dissimulat, non auget aut extenuat neque majora aut minora, quam sunt revera, facit. Proinde cum extrema modum circa verum non servent, medium vero modum cum recta ratione semper conjunctum respiciat, circa verum tanquam objectum suum hæc virtus versatur. Nam medium & extrema circa idem versantur objectum. Cæterum quia verum & falsum, quæ sunt objecta Veracitatis, multifariam dicuntur, ut constet, quomodo de iis hic agatur, distinctionem quandam de utrisque adhibet. Nam aut rei alicujus gratia aut nulluis ergo fiunt. Proinde hæc distinctio a fine eorum sumitur, verbi gratia: mentiuntur nonnulli aut metus aut commodi aut gloriolæ alicujus gratia: sunt etiam, qui nullo propositio præmio aut metu coacti, sed quia tam pravis & perversis sunt moribus, mentiri gaudent. Sunt etiam, qui verum dicunt aut metu coacti aut pactis adacti, quibus, ut pareant, ipsorum interest. Sunt etiam, qui nulla alia causa, quam quia probis & ingenuis sunt moribus, & tam bone præditi habitu, ut per se verum dicere ament. Hoc explicato jam discrimine veri & falsi, dicit priores illos, qui alicujus rei gratia verum aut falsum dicit, non huc pertinere, sed ad Justitiam, quae verum & fidem in pactis servat.
units.tr: In the first part, then, having passed from the previous virtue, namely Affability, he now sets himself to deal with Veracity, which pursues what is true in words and deeds and avoids what is false. Hence the Philosopher makes the object of this virtue the true, expressed in words and deeds so that nothing feigned or falsified is to be found. And so that the nature of the object may be better understood, he brings forward the operations or acts of the extremes and of the mean. For the boaster, who is opposed to the truthful man by excess, pretends to have qualities that are not really in him, and when good qualities really are in him, he always speaks of them as greater than they are. On the other hand, the dissembler, who is opposed to the truthful man by deficiency, when he has or knows good qualities, either denies them altogether, or conceals them, or belittles them, or makes them smaller than they are. Between these two lies the truthful mean, who, when he has or knows good qualities, admits that he has and knows them, neither denies nor conceals them, and neither exaggerates nor belittles them, nor makes them greater or smaller than they really are. Therefore, since the extremes do not keep a measure with regard to the true, while the mean always looks to a measure joined with right reason, this virtue is concerned with the true as its object. For the mean and the extremes are concerned with the same object. Moreover, since the true and the false, which are the objects of Veracity, are spoken of in many ways, so that it is clear how they are treated here, he makes a certain distinction between each of them. For they are done either for the sake of something or for no reason. Accordingly, this distinction is drawn from their end. For example, some lie for the sake of fear, or of advantage, or of some small glory. There are also some who, with no reward or fear put before them, but because they have such depraved and perverse characters, take pleasure in lying. There are also some who speak the truth, either compelled by fear or bound by agreements, which it is in their interest to obey. There are also some who, for no other cause than that they have upright and honourable characters, and are so well disposed in their habit that they love to speak the truth of their own accord. Having explained this distinction between true and false, he says that those first ones, who speak the true or the false for the sake of something, do not belong here, but to Justice, which keeps truth and faith in agreements.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de ipsa virtute, quae dicitur Veracitas, & cum duplex sit veracitas; una, quae in judiciis & pactis circa verum versatur, de qua hic non agitur, altera, quae in verbis & sermone & conversatione quotidiana verum spectat, de qua hic agendum sibi proponit, & definit virtutem, quae in veritate absque diminutione aut augmentatione mediocritatem servat. Et triplex describit viri veracis officium, quo melius de Veracitatis natura constet:
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the virtue itself, which is called Veracity. Since veracity is twofold: one kind, which concerns truth in judgements and agreements, is not dealt with here; the other, which concerns truth in words, speech and daily conversation, is what he sets himself to discuss here. He defines the virtue as that which, in truth, without diminution or exaggeration, keeps the mean. He also describes the threefold duty of the truthful man, so that the nature of Veracity may be better established:

units.la: 1. est, quod sit aut debeat esse justus aut probus propter privatum commodum nihil dicens aut faciens, quod revera non sit.
units.tr: 1. It is that he is, or ought to be, just and upright, saying or doing nothing for private advantage that is not really so.

units.la: 2. Quod sit caute castus, id est, per omnia verum sectetur, nihilque in aliorum gratiam a vero deflectat.
units.tr: 2. That he is cautiously chaste, that is, that he pursues the true in all things, and never turns away from the true for the sake of others.

units.la: 3. Quod non sit jactator, qui sua aut aliena nimium laudet, sed potius quantum rei veritas & ratio permittit, extenuet. Nam omnis jactatio pertinet ad Injustitiam, quia quanto plus sibi quis arrogat, tanto plus alii detrahit, & sic se injuste gerit, at extenuatio conjunctam plerunque habet modestiam, quia experientia docet paucos aut nullos sua extenuare, nisi modestiore sunt ingenio.
units.tr: 3. That he is not a boaster, who praises his own or others' things too much, but rather that he diminishes them as far as the truth of the matter and reason allow. For all boasting belongs to Injustice, because the more a man claims for himself, the more he takes from others, and so he acts unjustly. Whereas belittling usually has modesty joined with it, because experience teaches that few or none belittle their own things unless they are of a more modest disposition.

units.la: Nec aliter suadet Lactantius lib. 6. Instit. divin. cap. 10. qui veritati, inquit, studet, inimicas & anxias voluptates abjiciat, quae animum turbant & vincunt, praeferat vera falsis, aeterna caducis, utilia jucundis, nihil aspectu gratum sit, quod juste fieri non videas, nihil auditu suave, nisi quod animum teq; meliorem reddat. Exempla hujus virtutis in Scripturis sunt Josua & Caleb, qui cum peticulo vitæ veritatem defenderunt, ut est Num. 14. vers.6. Item Micheas Propheta, ut est 1.Reg.22. Exempla in profanis fuerunt in Persis, de quibus refert Herodotus lib.1. quod per omnes ætatis gradus liberis suis hoc inculcarint, ut mendacia fugientes, vera semper loquerētur, & saluberrimè apud illos constitutum fuit, ut qui tertio in mendacio deprehenderetur, is perpetuo silentii legē interdicerentur. Et Artaxerxes Persarum Rex mentientium linguas clavo trisulco affigendas curabat. Et Epaminondas etiàm Thebanus ne per jocum unquam mendacium dixit, & Pomponius Atticus ne mendacium quidem audire potuit, sicut refert Cornelius Nepos in vita ipsius.
units.tr: Lactantius urges nothing different, in Divine Institutes book 6, chapter 10: Let him who pursues truth cast off the hostile and anxious pleasures, which disturb and overcome the mind; let him prefer true things to false, eternal to fleeting, useful to pleasant; let nothing be pleasing to the sight that you see is not done justly, nothing sweet to the hearing except what makes the mind both better and more tranquil. Examples of this virtue in Scripture are Joshua and Caleb, who defended the truth at the risk of their lives, as in Num. 14.6. Likewise the prophet Micaiah, as in 1 Kings 22. Examples among the profane writers are found among the Persians, of whom Herodotus reports in book 1 that through every stage of life they instilled this into their children, so that, avoiding lies, they should always speak the truth; and it was most wholesomely established among them that whoever was caught in a lie a third time should be forbidden by a perpetual law of silence. And Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, had the tongues of liars fastened with a three-pronged nail. And Epaminondas the Theban never told a lie, not even in jest; and Pomponius Atticus could not even bear to hear a lie, as Cornelius Nepos reports in his life.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis agit de extremis Philosophus. Nam sicut mutua relatorum natura melius cognoscetur medium. Et primò agit de altero extremo, quod Veracitati opponitur in excessu, nempe Arrogantia, quæ definitur vitium in veritate modum excedens, quo ea, quæ revera non insunt inesse fingimus aut etiam majora quam sunt, nobis arrogamus. Ut hujus vitii definitio melius explicetur, tria eorum, qui hoc vitio laborant genera adfert. 1. est eorum, qui ea, quæ non insunt sibi aut aliis, effingūt & quidem nullius rei gratia, & tales dicit, vanos potius, & malis similes esse, quam revera malos, propterea, quod nullius emolumenti causa, quæ Veritas non permittit, effingunt. Ideoque solo mentiendi gaudent habitu, quales Aristoteles adolescentes quosdam procos inducit. 2. Genus eorum est, qui alicujus rei gratia majora, quam pro rei veritate, sibi ascribunt, verbi gratia: qui honoris aut gloriæ cau-
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter the Philosopher deals with the extremes. For, just as the mutual nature of correlatives is better known, so is the mean. And first he deals with the other extreme, which is opposed to Veracity by excess, namely Arrogance, which is defined as the vice that exceeds the measure in truth, by which we pretend that things which are not really in us are in us, or we claim for ourselves things greater than they are. To explain the definition of this vice better, he gives three kinds of those who suffer from it. (1) There are those who feign things that are not in themselves or in others, and this for no reason at all; he says such people are more like vain and foolish men than truly wicked ones, because they feign things for no advantage, which truth does not permit. For this reason they delight in the mere habit of lying, such as Aristotle introduces as certain young men who are suitors. (2) The second kind is of those who claim for themselves greater things than the truth of the matter allows, for the sake of something, for example, those who for the sake of honour or glory cau-

units.la: L1
units.tr: L1

units.la: a fa multa fingunt, & qui ea immerito sibi arrogant, quæ vulgò apud omnes laudari solent, ut sunt bona corporis & fortunæ, nimirum pulchritudo, vires, nobilitas, divitiæ, opes, d'gnirates: & tales etsi contra veracitatem peccent, summa tamen reprehensione non digitos esse dicit Philosophus, propter duas causas: 1. Quia honoris & gloriæ studio, instinctu quodam naturæ omnes incitantur. 2. Quia in publicum non sunt perniciosi, sed suavi quadam melancholia sibi ipsis illudunt. Talem describit Terentius Thrasonem suum in Eunucho. 3. genus est eorum, qui quæstus gratia veluti pecuniæ & majoris lucri ergo majora, quam pro vero de se jactitat. Et qui bona animi sibi arrogant, ex quibus usum & utilitatem capere possunt, ut qui de scientiis & cognitione varia se jactitant, & horum tres affert Philosoph. nempe Divinatores, Medicos, & Sophistas, qui omnes in summo gradu contra veracitatem peccant. De Divinatoribus agit Cic. lib. 1. de Divin. quibus, inquit, divitias magnas pollicentur, ab iis drachmam petunt. De Medicis multa ubique extant testimonia, & adstipulatur quotidiana experientia, præsertim circumforaneis illis. De Sophistis multa in variis Dialogis Plato, & præsertim in Gorgia, qui, inquit, omnium rerum scientiam sibi vendicant, ne umbram quidem scientiæ habent. & istos tertii ordinis, duos priores lógo post se intervallo relinquere dicit Philosophus, tum quia quæstus tantum gratia ista sibi bona vendicant, tum etiam quia suum non aliorum commodum solummodo respiciunt. Priusquam de altero extremo in defectu agat, Platonis sententiam re-præprehendit, qui in Hippia majore mendacem & veracem idem esse dicit, propterea, quod mendax verū, & verax falsum possit dicere. Hoc hic reprehendit Aristoteles. Nam mendacium & veritas non in potentia sicut volebat Plato, sed in proæresi, animi judicio & voluntate spectantur. Nam veritas, quæ in medio consistit, est habitus; extrema etiam, quæ opponuntur ei, sunt habitus. Habitus verò nō potentia constant, sed actu, quia actionibus comparantur, & destinatam habent animi proæresin & consilium adjunctum. Eandem etiam Platonis sententiam refutat lib. 4. Metaph. cap. 5. Alterum extremum in defectu dicitur Dissimulatio, quæ definitur vitium in defectu peccans, quando ea, quæ revera insunt, negantur, & contraria affinguntur. Cujus vitii duo adfert genera Philosophus; 1. est eorum, qui res magnas & illustres dissimulant, veluti magnam erudi- tionem, aut magnam prudentiam, & ejusmodi quidem omnia, de quibus aliis nō constat, an iis insint nec ne? Qui nō alio fine hoc faciunt, quam ut eům arrogantiæ suspicionem evitent. Et tales vocantur proprie Eirones vel Dissimulatores, qui res magnas & raras non omnibus notas aut obvias arte quadam singulari dissimulare norūt. Exemplum habet Philosophus de Socrate, qui cum esset omnium Græcorum doctissimus, fingebat se tamen literarum rudem, sicut fusè docet Xenophon in libris de dictis & factis Socratis. Talis etiam fuit Junius Brutus, qui ut refert Livius lib. 1. decad. 1. fingebat stultitiam, cum esset omnium prudentissimus. Alterum genus est eorum, qui res parvas, humiles, plebeias & vulgares quadam ... dissimulant, & quidem tales, quæ omnibus sunt bene notæ, & hoc ideo faciunt, ut dum se nimium extenuant, majorem modestiæ laudem consequantur, dum interim longè aliter de se sentiant, aliudque prorsus captent, quam verbis proferunt, & sic in jactantiam aut arrogantiam degenerat hoc vitium dum nimis affectate se suaque extenuant ejusmodi homines, & tales vocantur Verisipelles aut Veteratores, qui in rebus parvis & bene notis dissimulationem affectatam adhibent. Exemplum habet Philosophus de Laconica veste, quæ cum esset vilissima & sordidissima, ea inprimis superbiebat Lacedæmonii, quod pluribus referrt Xenophon in libello de Republ. Lacedæmoniorum. Talis etiam fuit Diogenes Cynicus, sicut testatur Ælianus lib. 3. varia historia. Hinc prædicare D. Hieronymus ad Paulinam, Sordida vestes candida mentis sunt judicia, mundi contemtum probat vilior tunica, sed sitamen, ne animus tumeat, ne habitus & sermo differant.
units.tr: They also invent many things, and they claim for themselves, undeservedly, the things that are usually praised among everyone: the goods of body and fortune, namely beauty, strength, nobility, riches, wealth and dignities. Even though such people sin against truthfulness, the Philosopher says they are not to be blamed severely, for two reasons: (1) because all people are driven by a certain natural instinct to seek honour and glory; (2) because they are not harmful to the public, but deceive only themselves with a kind of pleasant melancholy. Terence describes such a man in his Thraso in the Eunuch. (3) There is a third kind of people, who boast of more than the truth for the sake of gain, as if for money and greater profit. And those who claim for themselves goods of the mind, from which they can derive use and advantage, such as those who boast about the sciences and various kinds of knowledge: the Philosopher names three of these, namely diviners, physicians and sophists, all of whom sin against truthfulness to the highest degree. Cicero speaks of diviners in book 1 of On Divination: "They promise great riches, and ask a drachma from them." There are many testimonies everywhere about physicians, and daily experience confirms them, especially those wandering quacks. About sophists Plato says much in various dialogues, and especially in the Gorgias: "They claim for themselves the knowledge of all things, yet they do not even have a shadow of knowledge." The Philosopher says that the first two of these groups fall well behind the third, both because they claim these goods only for the sake of gain, and also because they look only to their own advantage and not to that of others. Before he treats the other extreme, which is the defect, he rebukes Plato's opinion, who in the Greater Hippias says that the liar and the truthful man are the same, because the liar can speak the truth and the truthful man can speak what is false. Aristotle criticises this here. For lying and truth are not to be judged by capacity, as Plato wanted, but by choice [προαίρεσις], by the judgement and will of the mind. For truth, which stands in the middle, is a habit; and the extremes which are opposed to it are also habits. Habits, however, do not consist in capacity but in act, because they are acquired by actions, and they have a settled choice of mind and an attached counsel. He also refutes this same opinion of Plato's in book 4 of the Metaphysics, chapter 5. The other extreme, in defect, is called Dissimulation, which is defined as the vice that sins by defect, when things that really are present are denied and their contraries are pretended. The Philosopher brings forward two kinds of this vice: (1) there are those who dissimulate great and illustrious things, such as great learning or great prudence, and generally all those things about which others are not certain whether they are present in them or not. They do this for no other end than to avoid the suspicion of arrogance. Such people are properly called Eirones or Dissimulators, who know how to conceal by a certain singular art great and rare things that are not known or obvious to all. The Philosopher gives an example from Socrates, who, although he was the most learned of all the Greeks, nevertheless pretended to be ignorant of letters, as Xenophon teaches at length in the books on the sayings and deeds of Socrates. Junius Brutus was also such a man, who, as Livy relates in book 1 of the first decade, feigned foolishness although he was the most prudent of all. The second kind is of those who dissimulate small, humble, common and ordinary things, and indeed such things as are well known to all; and they do this so that, while they belittle themselves too much, they may obtain a greater reputation for modesty, while meanwhile they think quite otherwise of themselves and aim at something entirely different from what they put into words. In this way the vice degenerates into boasting or arrogance, since such people, by affectedly belittling themselves and their own, go too far. Such people are called Verisipelles or Veteratores, who use affected dissimulation in small and well-known matters. The Philosopher gives the example of the Laconian garment, which, although it was very cheap and shabby, the Lacedaemonians were especially proud of; Xenophon reports this at length in the little book on the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians. Diogenes the Cynic was also such a man, as Aelian testifies in book 3 of Varied History. Hence Jerome teaches in his letter to Paulina: Shabby clothes are the judgements of a pure mind; a cheap tunic proves contempt of the world; yet let it be so, lest the mind swell with pride, lest dress and speech disagree.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis comparationem brevem instituit extremorum cum medio, & dicit Arrogantiam, quæ opponitur Veracitati in excessu magis illi contrariari, quam Dissimulationem propter duas causas: 1. Qui a deterius sit malum. Nam injustitiam secum habet conjunctam, qui enim plus æquo sibi arrogat, aliis detrahit. 2. Quia magis arrogas nocet. Nam cum alterius damno sæpe conjungitur, & aliis molestus & odiosus esse solet, quia mendaciis tantum delectatur. Dissimulator econtra nulli, nisi forte sibi ipsi obest, & Modestiæ & Humanitati studet, præsertim illi, qui sunt primi generis, de quibus modo dictum. Axio-
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he makes a brief comparison of the extremes with the mean, and says that Arrogance, which is opposed to truthfulness in excess, is more contrary to it than Dissimulation, for two reasons: (1) because it is the worse evil. For it has injustice joined with it; for the one who claims more for himself than is fair takes away from others. (2) Because arrogance does more harm. For it is often joined with another's loss, and it is usually troublesome and odious to others, since it delights only in lies. The dissimulator, on the other hand, harms no one except perhaps himself, and he aims at modesty and humanity, especially those of the first kind, of whom we have just spoken. Axio-

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Ut singularium inductione universalia cognoscuntur, sic ubi singulas in mediocritate consistere virtutes constiterit, tunc omnes in genere virtutes in mediocritate versari constabit.
units.tr: 1. As universals are known by induction from singulars, so when it has been established that each of the virtues consists in a mean, it will then be established that all the virtues in general lie in the mean.

units.la: 2. Arrogans, aut qua non habet, aut majora quam habet, semper sibi affingit: Dissimulator, qua habet, aut negat, aut minora, quam sunt, facit.
units.tr: 2. The arrogant man always ascribes to himself either what he does not have or more than he has; the dissembler either denies what he has or makes it less than it is.

units.la: 3. Verax, qui in medio duorum vitiorum consistit, qua habet, aut novit bona, nec auget, nec diminuit, nec majora, nec minora, quam sunt, facit.
units.tr: 3. The truthful man, who stands between two vices, neither increases nor diminishes what he has or knows to be good, and makes it neither greater nor less than it is.

units.la: 4. Omne mendacium est perse pravum & vituperabile, sicut econtra verum est honestum & laudabile.
units.tr: 4. Every lie is in itself wicked and blameworthy, just as, on the contrary, the truth is honourable and praiseworthy.

units.la: 5. Quidam quia ex habitu tales sunt, in vita & verbis verum semper profitentur, & tales dicuntur proprie Veraces.
units.tr: 5. Some men, because they are such by habit, always profess the truth in their life and words, and such are properly called truthful.

units.la: 6. Verax bene vir probus dicitur, quia quando debet, & sicut debet, verum profert, ideoque summa laude dignus habetur.
units.tr: 6. The truthful man is rightly called an upright man, because when he ought, and as he ought, he speaks the truth, and he is therefore held worthy of the highest praise.

units.la: 7. Arrogantes trium sunt generum, aut enim nullius rei gratia plus aequo sibi attribuunt, & sic vani potius quam mali habentur. 2. Aut alicujus rei gratia veluti honoris & gloriae, & nondum sunt magna reprehensione digni. 3. Quaestus & pecuniae gratia, & tales sunt omnium, qui laborant arrogantia pessimi.
units.tr: 7. Arrogant men are of three kinds. (1) Some ascribe more to themselves than is fitting for no reason at all, and so are considered vain rather than wicked. (2) Others do so for the sake of something, such as honour and glory, and these are not yet deserving of great reproach. (3) Others do so for the sake of gain and money; and such men are the worst of all who suffer from arrogance.

units.la: 8. Non mendax dicitur, qui posset falsum dicere, aut verax, qui posset verum, ut vult Plato, sed quia actu tales sunt.
units.tr: 8. A man is not called a liar because he could speak falsely, nor truthful because he could speak the truth, as Plato holds, but because they actually are such.

units.la: 9. Dissimulatores non lucri aut fastus, sed modestiae tantum gratia dissimulare solent.
units.tr: 9. Dissemblers are not wont to dissemble for the sake of gain or display, but only for the sake of modesty.

units.la: 10. Dissimulatores duûm sunt generum, aut enim res magnas & illustres nullis bene notas dissimulant, & sic proprie vocantur Eirones; aut res parvas & humiles omnibus constantes, & sic dicuntur versuti, callidi & arrogantes.
units.tr: 10. Dissemblers are of two kinds. Either they dissemble great and illustrious matters that are known well to no one, and so are properly called Eirones (self-deprecators); or they dissemble small and humble matters that are known to all, and so are called crafty, cunning and arrogant.

units.la: 11. Veracitati Arrogantia magis opponitur, quam Dissimulatio, quia deterius est malum magisque in communi nocet.
units.tr: 11. Arrogance is opposed to truthfulness more than dissimulation is, because it is the worse vice and does more harm in general.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An Veracitas recte posst dici Virtus, cum omnis virtus consistat in medio duorum extremorum. At Veracitas non, quia versatur circa verum. At in vero dicendo nemo potest neque modum excedere, neque in modo deficere? Resp. Etsi hoc verum sit, quod in vero dicendo modus certus servari debeat, tamen quia hoc verum consistit in medio duarum falsitatum, quarum altera affirmat id esse, quod non est, ut Arrogantia, altera, negat id esse, quod est, ut Dissimulatio. Ideo Veracitas, quae versatur circa hoc verum, recte posit dici Virtus.
units.tr: I. It is asked: can truthfulness rightly be called a virtue, since every virtue consists in the mean between two extremes? But truthfulness does not, because it is concerned with truth. Yet in speaking the truth, no one can either exceed the measure or fall short of it? Answer: Although it is true that in speaking the truth a fixed measure ought to be kept, nevertheless, because this truth lies between two falsehoods, of which one affirms that what is not is, as arrogance does, and the other denies that what is, is, as dissimulation does, therefore truthfulness, which is concerned with this truth, can rightly be called a virtue.

units.la: II. An Dissimulatio, quae Veracitati opponitur, in defectu possit dici vitium, cum omne vitium sit malum, & ideo Virtuti tanquam bono quippiam opponitur. At Dissimulatio non est mala, id quod probatur exemplo Socratis. Nam Philosophus in textu laudat Socratem propter dissimulationem. & Cicero etiam de claris Oratoribus, inquit: Socrates Protagoram, Hippiam, Prodigum, Gorgiam summis in caelum effert laudibus, se vero omnium rerum fingit inscium & rudem, quod mali ingenii esse non potest? Resp. Ex ipso Philosopho Dissimulationem esse duplicem, unam, quae lucri & ostentationis gratia fit, & haec dicitur mala propter intentionem mali, quam habet; alia est Dissimulatamulatio, quæ modestiæ tantum gratia fit, & hæc non dicitur mala, non simpliciter quidem, sed comparatively, si nempe conferatur cum altera Dissimulationis specie.
units.tr: II. It is asked whether dissimulation, which is opposed to truthfulness, can be called a vice by way of defect, since every vice is evil and so is opposed to virtue as to something good. But dissimulation is not evil, as the example of Socrates proves. For the Philosopher in the text praises Socrates on account of his dissimulation; and Cicero too, in his book on famous orators, says: "Socrates extols Protagoras, Hippias, Prodicus and Gorgias to the heavens with the highest praises, but he himself pretends to be ignorant and unskilled in everything." What, he asks, can this be but the mark of a bad character? Answer: From the Philosopher himself, dissimulation is twofold. One kind is done for the sake of gain and display, and this is called bad because of the evil intention it has. The other is done only for the sake of modesty, and this is not called bad, not absolutely indeed, but comparatively, namely when it is compared with the other kind of dissimulation.

units.la: III. An Arrogantia & Dissimulatio possint dici diversa extrema Veracitatis; cum tamen unum & idem esse videantur, propter duas causas: 1. Quia per idem definiuntur, nempe per falsum seu mendacium. 2. Quia eodem nomine insigniuntur. Nam in textu Dissimulatio dicitur Arrogantia, propterea quod aliquis dissimulando & extenuando minimum plus sibi arrogare, quam detrahere intendat? Resp. Esse diversa, quorum alterum opponitur in excessu, alterum in defectu. Nam non sequitur, definiuntur per idem genus, ergo sunt idem; nam diversæ species semper definiuntur per idem genus. Quod vero Dissimulatio dicatur arrogantia, id ideo fit, quia in rebus cognitis & obviis ostentationis potius & gloriolæ causa, quam modestiæ adhiberi solet; & sic, quia est cum superba intentione conjuncta, arrogantia non incommodè poterit dici: Quod tamen de Dissimulatione secundæ speciei intelligi debet.
units.tr: III. It is asked whether arrogance and dissimulation can be called different extremes of truthfulness, since they seem to be one and the same, for two reasons: 1. Because they are defined by the same thing, namely the false or the lie. 2. Because they are marked by the same name. For in the text dissimulation is called arrogance, because by dissembling and minimising, one intends to ascribe to oneself a little more than to detract? Answer: They are different, one of which is opposed in excess, the other in defect. For it does not follow that because they are defined through the same genus, they are the same; for different species are always defined through the same genus. That dissimulation is called arrogance happens because, in matters that are known and obvious, it is usually employed for show and vainglory rather than for modesty; and so, since it is joined with a proud intention, it can not inappropriately be called arrogance. This, however, must be understood of the second species of dissimulation.

units.la: Notanda vero de hac Virtute duo ista sunt: 1. Rectius dici Veracitatem quam Veritatem, idque propter quatuor rationes: 1. Quia Veritas est attributum generale Entis, quod partim in rebus, partim in verbis, partim in conceptibus inest. Veracitas vero prout hoc loco accipitur, est attributum tantum solius hominis. Quod veritas sit attributum Entis in genere, id fusè docet Aristoteles 2. Metaph. c. 5.
units.tr: Two things, however, are to be noted about this virtue. 1. It is more properly called truthfulness (Veracitas) than truth (Veritas), and that for four reasons. (1) Because truth is a general attribute of being, which is present partly in things, partly in words, and partly in concepts, whereas truthfulness, as it is taken here, is an attribute of man alone. That truth is an attribute of being in general, Aristotle teaches at length in Metaphysics 2, ch. 5.

units.la: 2. Quia Veritas est congruentia seu conformitas rei cum intellectu, sicut docet Philosophus 2. Met. cap. 1.
units.tr: (2) Because truth is the agreement or conformity of a thing with the intellect, as the Philosopher teaches in Metaphysics 2, ch. 1.

units.la: At Veracitas tantum est virtus moralis per quam homo ad verum dicendum & patefaciendum proclivis redditur. 3. Quia Veritas praesertim in verbis est objectum, circa quod versatur ipsa Veracitas, Objectū vero, & id, quod versatur circa objectum, uno nomine dici non debent. 4. Quia veritas sive sit in verbis, sive in conceptibus, sive in rebus, alia est complexa, alia incomplexa: at Veracitas hoc modo nō dividitur, sed tantum habitū dicendi verum in congressibus denotat, ita ut verba factis, & facta verbis consonent. Plura vide apud Goclenium disputat. Ethic. 8. Venit vero Veracitas à vero; & verum rursus à vere, quia verno tempore, Sole arietem ingresso, omnia vere nascuntur, quae aliis temporibus deficiunt.
units.tr: But truthfulness is only a moral virtue through which a man is made inclined to speak and disclose the truth. (3) Because truth, especially in words, is the object with which truthfulness itself is concerned; but an object and that which is concerned with the object ought not to be named by one word. (4) Because truth, whether it is in words, in concepts or in things, is some complex and some incomplex; but truthfulness is not divided in this way, and denotes only the habit of speaking the truth in dealings, so that words agree with deeds and deeds with words. For more on this see Goclenius, Disputations on Ethics, book 8. The word Veracitas comes from verum, and verum in turn from vere, because in the spring, when the sun enters Aries, everything is born anew, which fails at other times.

units.la: II. Notandum est, Veracitati in genere opponi falsum seu mendacium, quod in judiciis dicitur vel falsum testimonium, vel falsa sententia, vel falsa defensio: extra judicia vero retinet nomen suum, & dicitur Mendacium, quod ab Augusto in lib. de mendacio, & a Magistro sententiarum lib. 3 distinct. 38. & a D. Thoma 2. 2. quaest. 110. Triplex statuitur, nempe Officiosum, Jocosum, & Perniciosum. Officiosum mendacium est, quod aliàs perbenignum & utile vocatur, est illud, quando aliquid profertur, quod nulli obest, sed alicui prodest vel ad vitam, vel ad famam, vel ad bona externa tutanda. Et hoc genus mendacii venia dignum esse, nec peccatū proprie dici debere, contendunt Doctores Scholastici, quia cum damno alterius non sit conjunctum: tum etiam quia intentionem boni pro fine habet. Exempla in sacris fuerunt runt in obfterricbus Ægyptiis Exod. 1. verf. 19. tum etiā in Rachab meretrice 2. Ios. v.14. quod utrumq; sictum à fide profectum testatur Apostolus ad Hebr. cap.11.vers.34. Sic etiam Jehu Sacerdotes Baaliticoſ occisurus magnum zelum Baaliticis simulavit 2 Reg. 10.vers.18. & alia ejusmodi exempla enumerati pos-sunt. Iocosum mendacium est, quod sola mentiendi libidine fit, & delectandi non alterius imponendi gratia, cujusmodi sunt fabulæ Poëtarum, & parabolæ, neq; hoc proprie peccatum dici meretur. Tertium pernitiosum est, quando aliquid contra fidem & bonos mores proferetur, idque vel in damnum vel contumeliam proximi, & hujus mendacii tria sunt requisita. 1. Ut falsum aliquod proferatur. 2. Ut id fiat duplici corde, id est, ut constet illi, qui profert hoc mendacium esse revera falsum aliquid & fictū. 3. Ut sit contra proximum, id est, cum voluntate & intentione eundem decipiendi. Et hoc mendacium tam in sacris, quā in profanis damnatur autoribus, idque propter tres causas: 1. Propter intentionem falsi, quod sibi propositum habet. 2. Propter persuasionem mali, quod inde provenit. 3. Propter illationem damni, quod aliis accidit.
units.tr: II. It must be noted that falsehood or lying is opposed to truthfulness in general. In judicial matters it is called either false testimony, or a false sentence, or a false defence; outside judicial matters it keeps its own name and is called a lie (Mendacium). Augustine, in his book On Lying, the Master of the Sentences in book 3, distinction 38, and St Thomas in 2.2, question 110, set out a threefold lie: the officious, the jocose and the pernicious. The officious lie, which is elsewhere called very kindly and useful, is when something is said which harms no one but benefits someone, either for their life, their reputation, or the protection of their external goods. The Scholastic teachers contend that this kind of lie is worthy of pardon and should not properly be called a sin, because it is not joined with harm to another, and also because it has the intention of a good as its end. Examples in Holy Scripture are the midwives of Egypt, Exod. 1. vers. 19, and also the harlot Rahab, 2 Ios. v. 14, which the Apostle testifies were both done out of faith, Heb. 11. vers. 34. So too Jehu, about to slay the priests of Baal, feigned great zeal for Baal, 2 Reg. 10. vers. 18; and other examples of this kind may be listed. The jocose lie is that which is told from mere desire to lie and for amusement, not for the sake of deceiving another; such are the fables of the poets and parables, and this does not deserve to be called a sin properly. The third, the pernicious lie, is when something is put forward against faith and good morals, to the harm or disgrace of a neighbour; and three things are required for this lie. 1. That something false is put forward. 2. That it be done with a double heart, that is, that the one who utters the lie knows that what he says is in truth false and feigned. 3. That it be against the neighbour, that is, with the will and intention of deceiving him. This lie is condemned both in sacred and in profane authors, for three reasons: (1) on account of the intention of falsehood that it has in view; (2) on account of the persuasion of evil that comes from it; (3) on account of the damage that befalls others.

units.la: Post hunc deveracitate tractatum subjici poterunt hæ quæstiones.
units.tr: After this treatise on truthfulness, the following questions may be added.

units.la: I. An cum Philosophus Socratis factum, quod ubiq; in verbis dissimularit, non improbet, sed laudet potius, licitum sit viro probo simulare & dissimulare, ita ut virtutis limites non egrediatur? Resp. Dubiam esse hanc quæstionem, & rationes in utramque partem afferri. Nam pro parte negante tria hæc militant argumenta:
units.tr: I. Since the Philosopher does not disapprove of Socrates' conduct, in that he everywhere dissembled in his words, but rather praises it, is it lawful for an upright man to simulate and dissemble, so long as he does not go beyond the limits of virtue? Answer: This question is debatable, and arguments are brought forward on both sides. For the side denying it, these three arguments stand:

units.la: 1. Quia vir probus debet candide & sincere omnia agere, propter bonitatis suæ naturam. Qui autem simulat aut dissimulat non sincere & candide agit, sed fucate potius & callide, id quod probatur ex definitione simulationis & dissimulationis. Nam Simulatio nihil est aliud, quam rei non revera existentis fictio: Dissimulatio negatio rei vere existentis.
units.tr: 1. Because a good man ought to act candidly and sincerely in all things, on account of the nature of his goodness. But whoever simulates or dissimulates does not act sincerely and candidly, but rather deceitfully and craftily, as is shown from the definitions of simulation and dissimulation. For simulation is nothing other than the feigning of a thing that does not really exist; dissimulation is the denial of a thing that truly exists.

units.la: 2. Quia viro probo non licet fallere & decipere alios. Sic enim a virtute longe recederet. At qui simulat aut dissimulat, fallit & decipit alios, aut saltem animum fallendi habet. 3. Demum quia omnis hypocrisis & simulatio sunt vitia moralia, ex quibus simulare & dissimulare tanquam eorum effecta oriuntur. Cum ergo vitiis moralibus viro bono se implicare non liceat, quia virtuti ex diametro repugnant: Ergo neque simulare aut dissimulare, quæ sunt effecta vitiorum moralium, licet. At pro parte affirmante sunt rationes solidiores numero septimo: 1. Quia licet viro bono occultare consilia sua secretiora, ne ab aliis impediatur, quo minus in eff. ctum deducat, juxta illud Biantis: Quæ facturus es, ea nemini dixeris: hoc autem absque simulatione & dissimulatione fieri nequit. 2. Quia licet viro probo in ludis Scenicis alienam personam præ se ferre, aliorum gestus facta & actiones imitari, etsi revera talis persona non sit, quod etiam absque simulatione aut dissimulatione fieri nequit. 3. Quia prudenti Imperatori licet dissimulare aut simulare, nempe se vires habere majores & commeatus majores, quam revera habet, ut sic milites suos præstet tutos, & hostibus incutiat terrorem, & hoc a prudentissimis quibusque factum fictū esse summa cum laude etiam, testātur omnes subindè historiæ. 4. Id etiam confirmatur exemplis sacræ Scripturæ: nam non solum David apud Achis Regem Gad ad evitandum præsens periculum simulavit, dum vultum suum mutaret, & stultūm se esse fingeret; sed etiam Christus Luc. 24. v. 28. cum duobus discipulis Emaunta euntibus simulabat se longius iturum. 5. Quia licet ironicè loqui, nam inter tropos numeratur Ironia à Rhetoribus, hoc verò fieri non potest absque simulatione & dissimulatione, sicut ex definitione Ironiæ patet. 6. Qu'a nisi licitum esset, viro bono simulare & dissimulare, tunc male fecisset Socrates, qui simulatione & dissimulatione plerunque in dictis & factis usus est, dum sophistas supra modum laudaret, le vè omnium rerum insciūm & ignarum fingeret, & tamen hoc ejus factum laudat Philosophos cap. 13. hujus libri. Tum etiam ab Apollinis oraculo sapientissimus omnium habitus est. 7. & ult. Quia licet viro bono absque virtutis præjudicio jocari, & facetias in dictis adhibere: nam ut ait Poëta:
units.tr: 2. Because it is not lawful for a good man to deceive and mislead others; for in that way he would depart far from virtue. But whoever simulates or dissimulates deceives others, or at least has the intention of deceiving them. 3. Finally, because every hypocrisy and every simulation are moral vices, and simulating and dissimulating arise from them as their effects. Since it is not lawful for a good man to involve himself in moral vices, because these are wholly opposed to virtue, it follows that neither is it lawful to simulate or dissimulate, which are effects of moral vices. But for the affirmative side there are stronger arguments, seven in number: 1. Because it is lawful for a good man to conceal his more secret plans, lest he be hindered from carrying them out, according to the saying of Bias: "What you are about to do, tell to no one." But this cannot be done without simulation and dissimulation. 2. Because it is lawful for a good man in stage plays to present another person, and to imitate the gestures, deeds and actions of others, even though he is not really that person; and this too cannot be done without simulation or dissimulation. 3. Because a prudent commander may dissimulate or simulate, namely that he has greater forces and supplies than he really has, so that he keeps his soldiers safe and strikes terror into the enemy; and that this has been done, with feigning, by the most prudent men of every age, with great praise, all histories testify. 4. This is also confirmed by examples from Holy Scripture: for not only did David, before Achish king of Gath, simulate in order to escape present danger, when he changed his countenance and pretended to be a fool; but also Christ, Luke 24. vers. 28., when he was going with two disciples to Emmaus, pretended that he would go further. 5. Because it is lawful to speak ironically, for irony is counted among the tropes by the rhetoricians; but this cannot be done without simulation and dissimulation, as is clear from the definition of irony. 6. Because, unless it were lawful for a good man to simulate and dissimulate, Socrates would have done wrong, who very often in his words and deeds used simulation and dissimulation, while he praised the sophists beyond measure and feigned to be ignorant and unaware of all things; and yet the philosophers praise this deed of his in chapter 13 of this book. Also, by the oracle of Apollo he was judged the wisest of all men. 7. And last: because it is lawful for a good man to joke without prejudice to virtue and to use witticisms in his speech; for as the poet says:

units.la: Stultitiam simulare loco prudentia summa est.
units.tr: Stultitiam simulare loco prudentia summa est.

units.la: At hoc etiam absque simulatione aut dissimulatione fieri nequit. Pro decisione quæstionis distinguendum est, inter simulationem & dissimulationem licitam & honestam, & illicitam & turpem. Prior est, tum fingimus aliquid esse vel non esse, non animo injustè fallendi aut aliis nocendi, aut etiam consequendi majorem, quam par est honorem aut quæum: aut evitandi & detrectandi officia Deo & proximo debita, præsertim patriæ, parentibus, cognatis & amicis: sed animo juste probandi, vel juste reprehendendi alios, fi quid delinquant, vel declinandi impedimenta injuste objecta, aut imminentia pericula, aut repraesentandi aliorum mores ad imitandum vel fugiendum propositos, aut hostes reprimendi & superandi, aut denique jocandi vel delectandi animo. Posterior est cum fingimus aliquid esse vel non esse plane contrario fine & modo. Et de priori vera est thesis affirmativa, cum suis argumentis: de posteriori negativa.
units.tr: But this too cannot be done without simulation or dissimulation. To decide the question, one must distinguish between simulation and dissimulation that is lawful and honourable, and that which is unlawful and base. The former is when we feign that something is or is not, not with the intention of deceiving unjustly or of harming others, nor of gaining greater honour or profit than is right, nor of avoiding or evading the duties owed to God and neighbour, especially to country, parents, kin and friends; but with the intention of rightly commending or rightly rebuking others, if they do wrong, or of averting unjust obstacles or impending dangers, or of setting before others manners to be imitated or avoided, or of restraining and overcoming enemies, or finally with the intention of joking or giving pleasure. The latter is when we feign that something is or is not, with a plainly contrary end and manner. And of the former the affirmative thesis is true, with its arguments; of the latter the negative.

units.la: II. An cum Veritas sit virtus, qua versatur circa verum ita quidem, ut verum neque in majus, neque in minus torqueat, ideo Vir probus, qui veracitate sit praeditus, verum semper debeat dicere, & quidem universum quod novit?
units.tr: II. Since truthfulness is a virtue that deals with the true in such a way that it twists the truth neither to more nor to less, is the good man, who is endowed with truthfulness, therefore bound always to speak the truth, and indeed the whole of what he knows?

units.la: Resp. Hanc quaestionem habere etiam suas difficultates, in utramque partem disceptatas. Nam pro parte negante, id est, quod non debeat verum semper dicere quinque haec militant argumenta: 1. Quia arcana suae fidei commissa aliis vir bonus aperire non debet, hoc enim vitio & levitati cuilibet vertí solet, tum etiam multo magis viro bono: nam a vitio abhorrere debet, propter naturam virtutis, quae ipsi inest, & etiam a levitate, quia gravitati repugnat. 2. Quia non debet consilia sua aliis patefacere, praesertim quae sine damno & periculo patefieri non possunt, propter malum, quod ipsi aut aliis inde provenire possit. 3. Quia dona sibi a Deo collata passim, & apud omnes praedicare non debet, ne ineptus & futilis habeatur. Multi enim sunt, qui singularia Dei dona non intelligunt, multi etiam irrid• ent, multi quoque non credunt. 4. Quia errata rata tum sua, tum proximi sui quantum possit occultare debet, nec temere & sine graví urgente necessitate patefacere: hocautem fieri non potest, si universum quod novit verum, semper dicat. 5. Quia Christus etiam ipse in Novo Testamento saepenumero praecepit, ne miracula sua aliis patefacerent. Pro parte affirmante, nempe, quod debeat semper verum dicere sex contra faciunt rationes: 1. Quia veracitas est virtus, per quam homo ad verum patefaciendum proclivis redditur: cum ergo vir bonus sit verax, debet verum semper dicere. 2. Quia mendacii est, cum ea, quae non sunt, esse dicere, tum ea, quae sunt non esse dicere aut majora etiam, quam sunt, fingere. 3. Quia justum & aequum est, omne verum, quod proximo debetur illi dicere, ne si fraudetur suo debito, Vir bonus injustitiae crimen incurrat, & sic desinat esse bonus. 4. Qui a falsum testimonium contra proximum, non est dicendum, tum quia naturae bonitati repugnat, tum quia in Scripturis expresse prohibetur Exod. 20. verf. 16. At, qui verum celat, ille falsum testimonium contra proximum dicit, cum animus testetur, se non id dicere, quod res est. 5. Quia vir bonus debet imitari Deum, Deus cum ipsa veritas Johan. 14. verf. 6. verum semper dicit. 6. & ult. Quia tam sacri quam profani scriptores nos ad verum dicendum semper adhortantur. Hinc Servator Christus Matth. 5. dicit, Sit sermo vester est, est, non, non: quo innuit nihil esse dicendum, quod revera non sit, aut sic esse loquendum, sicut res se habet. Et Augustinus super locum illum, inquit: Utrumque peccare, & qui verum non dicit, & qui falsum profert: nam ille, inquit, aliud prodesse non vult, & iste aliud nocere desiderat. Apud profanos autores infinita exstant, quae nos ad verum simpliciter dicendum adhortantur. Hinc Hom. 1. Iliad. inducit Achillem Magnanimum heroa simplici veritate ita delectantem, ut inferorum portis pejus odisse se dicat ejusmodi homines, qui aliud ore dicunt, aliud in corde sentiunt.
units.tr: Answer: This question too has its difficulties, debated on each side. For the side denying it, that is, the view that he is not bound always to speak the truth, these five arguments stand: 1. Because a good man ought not to disclose to others the secrets entrusted to his faith; for this is usually imputed to anyone as a vice and as levity, and much more so to a good man: he ought to shun vice on account of the nature of virtue which is in him, and levity too, because it is opposed to gravity. 2. Because he ought not to reveal his plans to others, especially those which cannot be revealed without harm and danger, on account of the evil which might arise from this for himself or for others. 3. Because he ought not to proclaim everywhere the gifts God has bestowed on him, lest he be held foolish and frivolous. For there are many who do not understand God's particular gifts, many also who laugh at them, and many who do not believe them. 4. Because he ought to conceal, as far as he can, both his own errors and those of his neighbour, and not reveal them rashly and without a grave and pressing necessity; but this cannot be done if he always tells everything he knows to be true. 5. Because Christ himself in the New Testament very often commanded that his miracles not be disclosed to others. For the side affirming, namely that he ought always to speak the truth, six arguments speak against them: 1. Because truthfulness is a virtue through which a man is made inclined to disclose the truth; therefore, since the good man is truthful, he ought always to speak the truth. 2. Because it is a lie to say that things which are are not, and also to say that things which are not are, or to feign them to be greater than they are. 3. Because it is just and fair that he should tell the whole truth owed to his neighbour, lest, if he defrauds him of what is due, the good man incur the crime of injustice and so cease to be good. 4. That a false witness is not to be borne against one's neighbour is not only because it is opposed to the goodness of nature, but because it is expressly forbidden in the Scriptures, Exod. 20. vers. 16. But whoever conceals the truth, he bears false witness against his neighbour, since his mind testifies that he does not say what the matter is. 5. Because a good man ought to imitate God, and God, who is truth itself, John 14. vers. 6., always speaks the truth. 6. And last: because both sacred and profane writers everywhere exhort us to speak the truth always. Hence the Saviour Christ, Matt. 5., says, Let your speech be yea, yea; nay, nay: by which he implies that nothing is to be said that is not really so, or that one must speak as the matter stands. And Augustine, on that passage, says: Both sin, both he who does not speak the truth and he who utters a falsehood: for the one, he says, does not wish to benefit another, and the other desires to harm. Among profane authors there are countless passages that exhort us to speak simply the truth. Hence in the first book of the Iliad Homer introduces Achilles, the magnanimous hero, delighting so much in plain truth that he says he hates more than the gates of Hades those men who say one thing with their mouth and think another in their heart.

units.la: Prodecisione quaestionis notanda sunt sequentia quaedam Theoremata: 1. Verum non cuivis aut quovis tempore aut de qualibet re semper esse dicendum. 2. A nemine id exigi, ut universum, quod novit verum, nulla urgente necessitate depromat. 3. Viro bono verum dicendum esse quidem, sed caute & observatis Circumstantiis, nempe quibus, quomodo, cur, quantum & quando debet. 4. Viro bono non incumbere, ut illud verum dicat, quod jure optimo tacendum est, aut ad quod dicendum ratione officii non est obligatus. 5. Aliud esse verum non semper dicere, aliud falsum dicere: nam aliquis poterit verum non dicere, dum tacet, at falsum dicere non poterit, si taceat. 6. Distinguendum est etiam inter id, quod est diversum a Veracitate, & id, quod Veritati plane repugnat. Fieri enim poterit, ut aliquis dicat, quod sit diversum a veritate, verbi gratia: cum diversum ab eo, de quo quaeritur respondetur, aut et indirecte respondetur, & tamen falsum non dicat aut contrarium veritati. 7. Nudam apertam & simplicem veritatem in quibusdam casibus & Prudentia, quae est praecipua Virtus, & Taciturnitati repugnare. Ideo non semper verum, neque omne, quod quis novit, esse verum, debet proferre, nisi suo tempore & loco. Nam cum Veritas sit virtus, exigit, ut omnes ejus actiones ad rectae rationis nornormam dirigantur. Proinde secundum errare eos, qui in veritate patefaciendas, nulla habita ratione temporis, loci aut personarum liquidissime & planissime verum semper & ubiq; & apud quosvis dicendum esse contendunt.
units.tr: Before deciding the question, the following propositions should be noted: 1. Truth is not always to be told to everyone, nor at every time, nor about every matter. 2. No one may demand that a man bring out everything he knows to be true when no pressing necessity requires it. 3. A good man must indeed tell the truth, but cautiously and with the circumstances observed, namely to whom, how, why, how much and when he ought to tell it. 4. A good man is not bound to say that truth which is rightly to be kept silent, or which he is not obliged by his office to state. 5. To not always tell the truth is one thing; to tell a falsehood is another. For someone may fail to tell the truth by keeping silent, but he cannot tell a falsehood if he is silent. 6. One must also distinguish between what differs from truthfulness and what plainly contradicts truth. For it may happen that someone says something that differs from the truth, for example when a reply is given that differs from the matter asked about, or is given only indirectly, and yet he says nothing false or contrary to the truth. 7. In certain cases, bare, open and simple truth conflicts with prudence, which is the chief virtue, and with discretion. Therefore one ought not always to utter the truth, nor everything that one knows to be true, except in its proper time and place. For since truth is a virtue, it requires that all its actions be directed by the rule of right reason. Accordingly, those err who contend that the truth must be laid open most clearly and plainly, always, everywhere and before anyone, with no regard to time, place or persons.

units.la: III. An cum Mendacium triplex vulgo statuitur, sicut jam diximus, omne Mendacium in genere sit prohibitum, & nullum sit mendacium, quod possit cum vera virtute consistere?
units.tr: III. Whether, since lying is commonly divided into three kinds, as we have already said, every lie is forbidden in general, and there is no lie that can be consistent with true virtue?

units.la: Resp. De mendacio perniciosò non est dubitandum, quin prorsus sit prohibitum & illicitum, tum quia intentionem mali habet, tum quia cum damno & contumelia proximi est conjunctum. Jocosum vaniloquium potius, quam mendacium dici meretur, cum joci & delectandi alterius non lædendi gratia fiat. Restat, ut de mendacio officioso discutiamus, sitne licitum necne? Si officiosum mendacium fumatur pro eo, quod est contrarium veritati, nempe cum contra veritatem privati aut publici commodi gratia proferimus, sumatur, videtur esse prohibitum propter ejusmodi rationes: 1. Quia omnia mendacia cum sint falsa, vitii rationem obtinent, & gradu potius, quam specie differunt, ideo sunt illicita. Nam sicut virtus dicitur licita, quia est bona, sic vitium dici ut illicitum, quia est malum, quod etiam cap. 10. lib. 7. hujus operis docet Philosophus. 2. Qui a per mendacia fidem & autoritatem homo sibi abrogat, ita ut non facile ei credatur. Hinc Aristoteles, ut refert Laërtius in vita ipsius, interrogatus, Quid commodi proveniret hominï ex mendacio? Respondit, hoc nempe, ut cum verum dixerit, nemo ei credat, tum etiam, qui mendacijs delectatur, non possit a-lie lios admonere aut arguere, aut rectum consilium, sicut debet, cum fuctu d-re. 3. Quia omne mendacium est contrarium societati humanæ; quę enim societas inter homines conservari possit, si unusquisque animi sui sensa non vere, sed falso aliis communicet? Sic enim contractus & obligationes & promissiones quæ liber futuri essent nullius valoris. 4. Quia invertit finem verborum, propter quem inventa sunt. Nam ut docet Aristoteles cap. 1. de interpr. Verba in hunc finem instituta sunt, ut alter alteri sensa & cogitationes suas proferat, non ut alium alii decipiat, quod per mendacium fit. 5. Quia Deus odio habet, quicquid est naturæ suæ contrarium; Deus vero cum sit veritas, necesse est, ut odio habeat mendacium contrarium veritati, sicut dicitur Jac. 3. vers. 14. 6. Quia mendacium omne patrem habet Diabolum, sicut dicitur Johan. 8. vers. 44. 7. Quia mendacium non constat Christiana charitate. Nam ut ait Apostolus 1. Corinth. 13. vers. 6. Charitas veritati gaudet, nullaque injustitia patet; at omne mendacium est pars injustitiæ, cum suum cuiq; non tribuat, sed veritate contra jus & æquum celet. 8. Quia tam sacri quam profani autores nos ad fugiendum omne mendacium hortantur. Hinc Levit. 19. vers. 11. dicitur: Nec mentiamini, nec decipite unusquisque proximum suum. Sic Ephe. 4. Deponentes mendacium, loquimini veritatem unusquisque cum proximo suo. Et Augustinus in Enchirid. cap. 18. nullo facto, nullo fine, nulla dispensatione divina vel humana poterit licitè mendacium dici. At contra, quod Mendacium officiosum non sit prorsus prohibitum quatuor hæ faciunt rationes: 1. Quia est conconjunctum cum insigni utilitate, & sejunctum ab omni intentione mali, id quod ex definitione patet: nam definitur, quod nulli obest, sed alicui prodest.
units.tr: Answer: Concerning a harmful lie there can be no doubt that it is wholly forbidden and unlawful, both because it has the intention of evil and because it is joined with injury and insult to one's neighbour. A jesting idle talk deserves to be called a lie rather less, since it is done for the sake of joking and delighting another without harming him. It remains to examine the officious lie, whether it is lawful or not. If an officious lie is taken to mean what is contrary to the truth, namely when we utter what is contrary to the truth for the sake of a private or public advantage, it seems to be forbidden for the following reasons: (1) Because all lies, since they are false, have the character of vice, and differ by degree rather than by kind; therefore they are unlawful. For as a virtue is called lawful because it is good, so a vice is called unlawful because it is evil, which the Philosopher also teaches in book 7, chapter 10 of this work. (2) Because a man by lies strips himself of faith and authority, so that he is not easily believed. Hence Aristotle, as Laertius reports in his life, being asked what advantage accrues to a man from lying, replied: namely this, that when he tells the truth no one believes him; and also that one who delights in lies cannot admonish or rebuke others, or give good counsel as he ought, with profit. (3) Because every lie is contrary to human society; for what society could be preserved among men if each communicated the feelings of his mind to others not truly but falsely? For thus contracts, obligations and promises would be of no validity. (4) Because it inverts the purpose of words, for the sake of which they were invented. For as Aristotle teaches in chapter 1 of On Interpretation, words were instituted for this end, that one may set forth his feelings and thoughts to another, not that one may deceive another, which is done by lying. (5) Because God hates whatever is contrary to his nature; and God, since he is truth, must hate the lie that is contrary to truth, as is said in Jas. 3.14. (6) Because every lie has the Devil as its father, as is said in John 8.44. (7) Because a lie does not agree with Christian charity. For as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 13.6: Charity rejoices in the truth and is not seen in any injustice; but every lie is a part of injustice, since it does not give each his due but conceals the truth contrary to right and equity. (8) Because both sacred and profane writers exhort us to flee every lie. Hence it is said in Lev. 19.11: Ye shall not lie, nor deceive one another, each his neighbour. So in Eph. 4: Putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour. And Augustine in the Enchiridion, chapter 18, says that no lie can lawfully be told by any deed, any end, or any dispensation, divine or human. On the other hand, four reasons show that the officious lie is not wholly forbidden: (1) Because it is joined with a notable advantage and separated from every intention of evil, which is clear from its definition; for it is defined as that which harms no one but benefits someone.

units.la: 1. Quia non ex habitu aut animo nocendi aut fallendi proficiscitur, sed animo ad juvandum proximum propensio, neque prius committitur ejusmodi mendacium a viro bono, quam praesens periculum, in quo se aut proximum suum constitutum videt, necessario id requirat.
units.tr: 1. Because it does not arise from a habit or intention of harming or deceiving, but from an inclination of mind to help one's neighbour; and a good man does not commit such a lie before a present danger, in which he sees himself or his neighbour placed, necessarily requires it.

units.la: 3. Quia definitio mendacii, quae traditur ab Augustino cap.22. Enchir. non competit ei; definitur enim in genere ab Augustino mendacium sic: Est falsa vocis significatio, cum intentione fallendi & nocendi alius: atqui tantum abest, ut hinc quis fallat, aut alteri damnum inferat, ut potius proximum suum quocunque modo juvare & sublevare studeat.
units.tr: 3. Because the definition of a lie given by Augustine in chapter 22 of the Enchiridion does not fit it; for Augustine defines a lie in general thus: It is a false signification by voice, with the intention of deceiving and harming another. But so far is this from being the case with the officious lie, that one who tells it aims rather to help and relieve his neighbour in every way.

units.la: 4. Quia liquidam exemplorum copiam sacra Scriptura suppeditat, quae neque damnantur, neque tanquam illicita referuntur. Sic Abraham Genef.12. mentitur Saraм esse sororem suam, ut vitae suae consulat. Sic Isaacus etiam Genef.26. Sic & Jacob dicit se primogenitum Isaaci benedicendum Genef.47. cujus consilium recte successit.
units.tr: 4. Because holy Scripture supplies an abundant number of examples, which are neither condemned nor related as unlawful. Thus Abraham, in Gen. 12, lies that Sarah is his sister, to provide for his own life. Thus Isaac too, in Gen. 26. Thus also Jacob says that he is Isaac's firstborn, to be blessed, in Gen. 27, whose plan rightly succeeded.

units.la: Pro decisione distinguendum erit inter mendacium proprie dictum, & improprie dictum. Nam etsi omne mendacium sit falsiloquium, tamen contra omne falsiloquium non est proprie mendacium. De priori vero sunt argumenta superius allata, cujusmodi est mendacium perniciosum, quod quia & per mala media fit & malo fine, plane est prohibitum. At vero cum officiosum mendacium non sit proprie dictum mendacium, ideo poterit interdum esse licitum, cum hisce conditionibus: 1. Ut citra gloriæ divinæ diminutionem fiat. 2. Ut contra fidei datæ fœdus non committatur. 3. Ut nihil damni afferat, neque ipsi autori, neque etiam alii cuivis, & sic non tam contrarium veritatis, quod thesis superius affirmabat dici debet, quam diversum quid à veritate, & temperamentum quoddam inter Taciturnitatem & Prudentiam. Proinde non assentiri pos-sumus quibusdam rigidioribus Theologis, qui omne falsiloquium in genere prohibitum esse asseruerunt, cum viro bono simulare & dissimulare interdum liceat absque præjudicio veritatis, ut in 1. quæst. diximus: tum etiam ei non conceditur universum, quod novit verum dicere, nisi observatis probè circumstantiis, ut in 2. quæst. patuit.
units.tr: For the decision one must distinguish between a lie properly so called and a lie improperly so called. For although every lie is a falsehood, not every falsehood is properly a lie.
