Of the former there are the arguments set out above, such as the harmful lie, which, because it is done by bad means and for a bad end, is plainly forbidden. But since an officious lie is not properly a lie, it may sometimes be lawful, under these conditions: (1) that it be done without diminishing the glory of God; (2) that it not violate the covenant of a promise given; (3) that it bring no harm either to its author or to any other person; and so it should be called not so much something contrary to truth, as the thesis above affirmed, but something different from truth, and a certain middle course between discretion and prudence. Therefore we cannot assent to certain more rigid theologians, who have asserted that every falsehood is forbidden in general, since it is sometimes lawful for a good man to dissemble and to pretend, without prejudice to truth, as we said in the first question; and also he is not permitted to tell everything he knows to be true, unless the circumstances are carefully observed, as became clear in the second question.

units.la: IV. An cum in quotidiano sermone & vita communi usu multa hyperbolicè, ironicè, parabolicè, fabulosè & ambiguè dicta occurrant, viro bono absque mendacii suspicione ūs uti liceat?
units.tr: IV. Whether, since many things are said hyperbolically, ironically, parabolically, fabulously and ambiguously in everyday speech and common life, a good man may use these modes without suspicion of lying.

units.la: Resp. Et hanc quæstionem disceptari in utramque partem. Nam viro bono non licitum esse hisce modis uti hinc patet: quia qui sic loquitur, non verè dicit, sed falsum aut saltem nō directè verum dicet, quod inductione omnium probatur. Nam qui Hyperbolicè loquitur, rem magis, quam rei veritas & quidem supra modum exaggerare aut extenuare conatur: Qui etiam Ironicè aliquid profert, aliter, quam sentit, loquitur, & sic contra mentem suam falsum profert: Qui etiam Parabolicè & Fabulosè, multa, quæ neque fuerunt, neque fieri possunt, confingere solet: Sic etiam, qui ambiguè aliquid dicit, non directè verum profert, sed obscurè.
units.tr: Answer: This question is debated on both sides. That a good man may not use these modes is clear from the following: whoever speaks in this way does not speak truly, but says what is false, or at least does not say directly what is true. This is proved by induction over all cases. For the one who speaks hyperbolically tries to magnify or diminish a thing beyond its truth. The one who speaks ironically says something other than what he thinks, and so utters falsehood against his own mind. The one who speaks parabolically or fabulously usually invents many things that neither have happened nor could happen. Likewise, whoever speaks ambiguously does not state the truth directly, but obscurely, and only through circumlocutions.

units.la: & & per ambages tantum. At contra quod licitum sit, hinc constat, quia non tantum autores gravissimi tam sacri, quam profani passim in scriptis suis omnibus hisce loquendi generibus utuntur: sed etiam sacra Scriptura variis locis: & Christus Servator ipse doctrinæ suæ admiscet sæpenumero parabolas. Ut Veritas hujus quæstionis intelligatur, sciendum erit hyperbolicè, ironicè, & cæteris modis viro bono licitum esse, ita ut contra veracitatē nihil peccet, modo id fiat animo non malevolo, aut fallendi & nocendi cupido, aut vitio hypocrisis aut dissimulationis illicitæ scilicet, aut arrogantiæ aut assentationis aut detractationis: sed animo taxandi & reprehendendi vitia pravosque mores, aut docendi & instituendi alios in rebus utilibus & bonis: aut exornandæ orationis, aut auditorum excitandorum gratia, aut mali alicujus majoris vitandi gratia. Sin autem contrario modo & fine fiat, repugnare veracitati & proinde illicitum esse dicimus.
units.tr: On the other hand, that these modes are lawful is shown by the following. Not only do the most weighty authors, sacred and profane, use all these kinds of speech throughout their writings, but holy Scripture does so in various places, and Christ the Saviour himself often mingles parables with his teaching. To understand the truth of this question, it must be recognised that a good man may lawfully speak hyperbolically, ironically and in the other ways, so that he sins in nothing against truthfulness, provided he does so without a malicious mind, without a desire to deceive and harm, and without the vices of hypocrisy, unlawful dissimulation, arrogance, flattery or detraction; but with the intention of censuring and rebuking vices and wicked morals, or of teaching and instructing others in useful and good matters, or for the sake of adorning his speech, or of stirring up his hearers, or of avoiding some greater evil. But if it is done in the contrary manner and for the contrary end, we say that it is opposed to truthfulness and therefore unlawful.

units.la: V. & hoc discutiendum venit:
units.tr: V. And here the following must be discussed:

units.la: An aliquis possit verum dicere, & tamen mentiri? Resp. Etsi prima statim fronte hæc quæstio videatur absurda, & contradictionem implicare, nihilominus tamen fieri potest, ut sit vera. Nam si quis aliquid, quod in se verum est, falsum esse judicet, & animo fallendi & decipiendi hoc pronunciet, aliisque communicet, is verum dicendo mentitur, quia nō consentit oratio cum ipsius mente, cum aliud lingua proferat, aliud mens cogitet. Et hoc etiam testatur Goclenius disceptat. Eth. 8. Fieri, inquit, potest, ut aliquis verè dicat Logicè, quod nepe Antipodes sint, & tamen mentiatur Ethicè. fi
units.tr: Whether someone can speak the truth and yet lie? Answer: Although this question may at first sight seem absurd and to involve a contradiction, nevertheless it can happen that what is said is true. For if someone judges that something which is true in itself is false, and with the intention of deceiving and misleading announces it and communicates it to others, he lies by speaking the truth, because his speech does not agree with his mind, since his tongue utters one thing while his mind thinks another. Goclenius also bears witness to this in his Disputations on Ethics, book 8: "It can happen," he says, "that someone speaks truly in the logical sense, namely that there are Antipodes, and yet lies in the ethical sense."

units.la: Mm 4 (catchword-like marker at foot: "nempe") tempenon credat ipse Antipodes esse, sed animo fallendi hoc apud illos proferat.
units.tr: ... that is, if he himself does not believe that there are Antipodes, but utters this to others with the intention of deceiving them.

units.la: Huic quaestioni non incommode adjici poterit illud, quod est apud Scaliger Exercit. 2. An scilicet falsum dicat, qui se verum putat dicere, verbi gratia: qui nova ab alio conficta pro veris obtrudit, aliis, ille ne falsum dicat, cum putet se verum dicere? Resp. breviter: Etiam mendacium proprie dictum non proferat ejusmodi, falsum tamen profert. Nam sicut veritas, ita etiam falsitas a rebus ipsis dependet. Nam nisi hoc verum esset, sequeretur hoc absurdi, nempe ab opinionibus hominum naturam rerum dependere, et sic pro variis hominum phantasiis variis mutationibus subjicerentur res ipsae. Et sic verum esset dogma Pyrrhonis Philosophi, qui dixit, res esse tales, quales quisque putaret. Proinde etsi mendacium non committitur, cum abest intentio fallendi: Nam ad mendacium proprie dictum ἀληθεύω et judicium hominis requiritur; falsum tamen, quod revera sic res non sit, dicit.
units.tr: To this question there may fittingly be added what is found in Scaliger, Exercitations 2: namely, whether someone who thinks he is speaking the truth says what is false, for example, someone who foists on others inventions made up by another as if they were true; does he not say what is false, since he thinks he is speaking the truth? Answer briefly: although such a person does not properly tell a lie, he nevertheless utters what is false. For just as truth, so also falsity depends on the things themselves. For if this were not so, it would follow, absurdly, that the nature of things depends on men's opinions, and that the things themselves would be subject to various changes according to the various fancies of men. Then the doctrine of the philosopher Pyrrho would be true, who said that things are such as each man thinks them to be. Therefore, although a lie is not committed when the intention to deceive is absent (for a proper lie requires both the intention [ἀληθεύω] to speak the truth and the judgment of the man), he nevertheless says what is false, because in fact the thing is not so.

units.la: VI. An cum mendacium opponatur tanquam falsum veritati, Calumnia et, quae est species mendacii perniciosi opponatur Veracitati?
units.tr: VI. Whether, since a lie is opposed as falsehood to truth, slander, which is a kind of harmful lie, is opposed to truthfulness?

units.la: Resp. Affirmat, propter tres rationes: 1. Quia Calumnia partim illi nocet, quem defert quatenus scilicet malitiose traducit, et bonum illi debitum detrahit, et crimen fraudulenter affingit: partim illi apud quem defert quatenus pro veritate mendacium obtrudit: partim etiam ei, qui defert quatenus conscientiam ipsius atrociter laedit.
units.tr: Answer: It is affirmed, for three reasons. (1) Slander harms in part the one it accuses, insofar as it maliciously defames him, takes away the good that is owed to him, and fraudulently fastens a crime upon him; in part it harms the one before whom it accuses, insofar as it forces a lie upon him in place of the truth; and in part it harms the one who accuses, insofar as it grievously wounds his conscience.

units.la: 2. Quia omnis calumniator est fraudulentus, insidiosus et injurius, et simul etiam lividus. Hinc Lucanus canus in libello de non facile credendo calumnia, scribit ab Apelle pictorū Principe calumniæ imaginem hoc modo fuisse formatam: ut ad virum quendam gradibus & patulis auribus præditum, quem circumstant duæ mulieres suspicio scilicet & ignorantia: hunc accedit alia mulier calumnia videlicet, quæ altera manu facem ardentem gestat (quo magni incendium mali à calumnia ortum denotet) altera manu juvenem cœlo suspicientem & Deum in conscientiæ suæ testem invocantem capillis trahat, præcedunt fraus & insidiæ, comitantur livor & invidia, sequuntur a tergo lugubri veste pœnitentia, quæ virtutem juveni a latere affixam respiciēs, magno cum pudore eam intuetur. 2. Quia licet vulnus Sycophantæ morsu inflictum cicatrix tamen manet, quod elegantér exprimit Plutarchus in libel. de discrimine adulatoris & amici: verum enim illud esse solet, quod in primitiva Ecclesia frequenter usurpatum fuit, calumniare audacter, aliquid adhærebit. Et propterea etiam, ut refert Possidonius, in mensa Cæsaris hoc distichon inscriptum erat:
units.tr: (2) Every slanderer is fraudulent, treacherous and unjust, and at the same time also malicious. Hence Lucian, in his little work On Not Readily Believing Slander, writes that the image of Slander was formed by Apelles, the prince of painters, in this way: a man with a seat and open ears, around whom stand two women, Suspicion and Ignorance. Another woman, Slander herself, approaches him; in one hand she carries a blazing torch (to signify that great evil arising from slander is kindled), and with the other she drags by the hair a young man who looks up to heaven and calls God to witness his conscience. Fraud and Treachery go before her, Envy and Spite accompany her, and from behind follows Repentance in mournful dress, who looks back at Truth, which stands beside the young man, and gazes at her with great shame. (3) Although the wound inflicted by the bite of a sycophant is healed, a scar remains. Plutarch expresses this elegantly in his little work On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend. It is indeed true, what was often used in the primitive Church: "Slander boldly; something will always stick." And for this reason, as Posidonius reports, the following couplet was inscribed on Caesar's table:

units.la: — Quisquis amat dictis absentem rodere amicum, Hunc mensam vetitam noverit esse sibi.
units.tr: Whoever loves to gnaw at an absent friend with his words, let him know that this table is forbidden to him.

units.la: Nempe quia de absente nihil nisi bonum, ut ait Seneca: Optimum & præsentissimum remedium adversus calumnias præscribit Plato, ut nempe, quilibet recte vivere & recte facere discat: nam licet Calumnia viros probos & innocentes læat, & ad tempus arrodat, veritatis tamen obortā luce nebulæ instar evanescit: Veritas enim premitur, sed non opprimitur.
units.tr: For, as Seneca says, one should say nothing of the absent but what is good. Plato prescribes the best and most immediate remedy against slanders, namely that each man learn to live rightly and to act rightly. For although slander wounds upright and innocent men and gnaws at them for a time, it vanishes like a cloud once the light of truth has risen. "For truth is pressed down, but not crushed."

units.la: VII. An qui in locis Papatui aut contrariæ religioni ditis
units.tr: VII. Whether those who live in places under Papal rule or otherwise hostile to their religion may conceal their religion

units.la: ditis negotiorum suorum causa versantur Religionem suam dissimulare liceat? Resp. Arduam & difficilem esse hanc quæstionem, propter contrarias ultrò citroq; disceptatas sententias. Nam pro parte affirmativa quatuor hæc afferri solent argumenta: 1. Quia vitæ curam & conservationem unicuique natura instinctu suo indidit. Ergò ubi in ejusmodi loca devenitur, ubi vita periclitari posšit, ad vitæ incolumitatem tutandam dissimulare licet. 2. Quia iis tantum incumbit aperte & palàm profiteri Religionem suam, qui ad hoc à Deo vocati sunt, ut vel voce suam Religionem propagent: vel etiam, quos Deus hoc honore dignatus est, ut pro Religionis constanti confessione martyrii coronam subeant. Hoc verò cum Deus omnibus non concesserit, nam raro sunt hæc, quæ paucis contingunt bona. Ideo qui negociorum suorum causa apud diversæ Religionis homines versantur, dissimulare commodè possunt. 3. Quia fœdera inter diversarum Religionum gentes hoc exigunt, ut quilibet apud contrariæ religionis homines ex alterutra gente religionem suam occultet, ne aperta scilicet professione aliquid turbarum aut tumultuum ad turbanda fœdera excitetur. 4. Quia exempla sunt hujus dissimulationis in Scripturis: Nam 1. Reg. 5. Naaman Syro permisit Elisæus Propheta, ut Dominum suum ad templum idolorum comitaretur: Sic etiam Mauritius Saxonia Elector gladium præ[…] Carolo V. Missam aditurò, cum ipse esset contrariæ religionis, ut refert Sleidanus lib. 7. comment. At contra pro parte negativa rationes sunt gravissimæ: 1 Quia omnis hypocrisis est detestabilis lis in conspectu Dei: At cum omnis in religione dissimulatio sit mera tantum hypocrisis, dissimulare nullo modo licet. 2. Quia ut ait Apostolus Rom. 12. vers. 10. ore fit confessio ad salutem, proinde absque praejudicio salutis dissimulare non conceditur. 3. Quia est contra officium hominis Christiani, quod a Petro Apostolo exigitur Epist. 1. cap. 3. vers. 10. esto parati ad reddendam rationem spei, quae est in vobis, cuilibet petenti. 4. Quia Servator Christus Luc. 12. vers. 9. dicit, qui me abnegaverit coram hominibus, negabo illum coram Angelis Patris mei. Proinde cum omnis dissimulatio in Religione sit abnegatio Christi, homini Christiano nequaquam conceditur. Pro decisione huius quaestionis iciendum erit, aliud esse dissimulare in Religione, aliud silere seu parum aut nihil loqui de Religione nisi reporis, loci & personarum ratio id exigat.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to conceal one's religion when one lives among people of a contrary religion for the sake of one's business affairs? Answer: This question is difficult and hard to settle, because opinions on both sides have been argued back and forth. For the affirmative side, four arguments are usually brought forward: (1) Nature, by its own instinct, has implanted in everyone the care and preservation of life. Therefore, when one comes into such places, where life may be endangered, it is lawful to dissimulate in order to keep one's life safe. (2) Only those are bound to profess their religion openly and publicly who have been called by God to spread it by their voice, or whom God has deigned to honour with the crown of martyrdom for steadfastly confessing their religion. But God has not granted this to everyone, for these are rare goods that fall to few. Therefore those who live among men of a different religion for the sake of their affairs can conveniently dissimulate. (3) The covenants between nations of different religions require that whoever lives among people of a contrary religion from either nation should keep his religion hidden, lest an open profession should stir up some disturbance or tumult that would break those covenants. (4) There are examples of this dissimulation in Scripture: in Reg. 5, the prophet Elisha permitted Naaman the Syrian to accompany his master into the temple of the idols. So too Mauritius Elector of Saxony, when he was of a contrary religion, went before Charles V to the Mass, as Sleidan reports in lib. 7. comment. On the other hand, the arguments for the negative side are very weighty: (1) Every hypocrisy is detestable in the sight of God; but since all dissimulation in religion is mere hypocrisy, it is in no way lawful to dissemble. (2) As the Apostle says in Rom. 10.10, "with the mouth confession is made unto salvation"; therefore it is not permitted to dissemble without prejudice to salvation. (3) It is contrary to the duty of a Christian man, which the Apostle Peter requires in 1 Pet. 3.10, "Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you." (4) Christ our Saviour says in Luke 12.9, "Whosoever shall deny me before men, shall be denied before the angels of my Father." Therefore, since all dissimulation in religion is a denial of Christ, it is by no means allowed to a Christian man. To decide this question it must be noted that it is one thing to dissemble in religion, and another to keep silent, or to say little or nothing about religion, when the circumstances of time, place and persons require it.

units.la: 2. Licere interdum, pro ut nunc tempora sunt, ratione officii, aut graviorum negotiorum gratia connivere ad contrariam Religionem, seu non contradicere, aut palam carpere, modo animus sincerus & integer maneat: Sed cum his duabus limitationibus fieri debet: 1. Ut absque omni Religionis scandalo id fiat. 2. Ut magna necessitas aut officii, quod incumbit, aut rerum graviorum, quae accidunt, ad hoc impellat: sin autem aliter fiat nusquam homini vere Christiano conceditur. Proinde argumenta pro parte affirmativa sunt eatenus vera, quatenus cum hisce conditionibus consentiunt. Pro negativa sunt intelligenda argumenta, non de omni dissimulatione, sed tantum de illicita, quae fit aut utilitatis mundanae gratia, aut levitatis & in constantiae, tiæ, aut etiam à causis non necessariis provenit. Huic quæstioni propter affinitatem subjici poterit illud: An scilicet ritibus aut ceremoniis contraria Religionis, se quis attemperare aut interesse possit, ita ut non modo conscientiæ non lædat, sed contra veritatem etiam nihil peccet? Resp. Ritus esse duplices: nam alii sunt indifferentes, quorum usus cuilibet liber esse potest, absque religionis aut fidei suæ detrimento, cujusmodi sunt concio-nes, matrimonii celebrationes, aut etiam dierum festorum, & his interesse licet: alii sunt non indif-ferentes, qui peccant contra ipsum fundamentum Religionis, & manifestam in se continent impieta-tem aut idololatriam: & his interesse nullo modo licet, quia ut ait Apostolus, nulla communio lucì cum tenebris, Christo cum Belial. 2. etiam quia Spiritus san-ctus jubet nos abstinere ab omni specie mali; interim tamen, si accidat, ut aliquis vel ratione officii, vel alia quævis necessitas hoc exigit, ut quis interes-se cogatur, id debet ita fieri, ut neque præsentia sua approbet, neque de iis participet, sed quantum pos-sit, & tempus ferat animo vultuque aspernetur, Quod si etiam alicui novitatis gratia conceditur, ut intersit ejusmodi ritibus, id cautè admodum & ra-ro fieri debet, & hoc tantum fine, ut odio majore prosequatur. Nam sicut albedo opposita nigredini magis illucescit, sic ubi quis falsitatem directè repu-gnantem veritati viderit, majori falsitate odio haud dubio habebit. Sic Paulus, ut est Act.17. Athenien-sium perlustravit aras, ut hoc modo ipsorum cæci-tatem perstringeret, & Apostoli in primitiva Eccle-sia gentium ritibus intersuerunt, ut refert in histo-ria ria Ecclesiastica Eusebi lib. 2. sed hinc carpendi & abolendi ipsarum ritus ansam coeperunt.
units.tr: 2. It is sometimes permitted, as things now stand, for the sake of one's office or of weightier affairs, to tolerate the contrary religion, that is, not to contradict it, or to criticise it openly, provided the heart remains sincere and upright. But this must be done under two limitations: (1) that it be done without any scandal to religion; (2) that great necessity of one's duty, or of the weightier matters that arise, compels it to be done. If it is done otherwise, it is never permitted to a man who is truly a Christian. Accordingly the arguments for the affirmative are true only so far as they agree with these conditions. The arguments for the negative must be understood not of all dissimulation but only of the unlawful kind, which is done either for worldly advantage, or out of levity and inconstancy, or arises from causes that are not necessary. Because of its affinity with this question, the following may be added: Whether one may conform to, or take part in, rites or ceremonies of a contrary religion, so that not only does one not harm one's conscience, but also sins in nothing against the truth? Answer: Rites are of two kinds. Some are indifferent, and their use may be free to anyone without loss to his religion or faith, such as sermons, celebrations of marriage, or even festival days; and it is lawful to take part in these. Others are not indifferent: they sin against the very foundation of religion and contain manifest impiety or idolatry; and it is in no way lawful to take part in these, because, as the Apostle says, there is no communion between light and darkness, between Christ and Belial. Also, the Holy Spirit commands us to abstain from every appearance of evil. Yet if it happens that someone is compelled to be present, whether by reason of his office or by some other necessity, this must be done in such a way that he neither approves by his presence nor takes part in them, but, as far as he can and as the time allows, shows his disapproval in his heart and face. If, moreover, someone is permitted to attend such rites for the sake of a new convert, this must be done very cautiously and rarely, and only for the purpose of prosecuting them with greater hatred. For as white set against black shines all the brighter, so when someone sees a falsehood directly opposed to the truth, he will without doubt hold it in greater hatred. Thus Paul, in Act. 17, walked through the altars of the Athenians, so that by this means he might expose their blindness; and the Apostles in the primitive Church joined in the rites of the Gentiles, as Eusebius reports in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, but from this there arose an occasion for criticising and abolishing those rites.

units.la: VIII. & ult. An viro bono liceat fallere & decipere, cum hoc natura Veracitati repugnare videatur, utpote, quia fallacias omnes aversatur tam in dictis, quam infactis, & sola sinceritate gaudet, & hoc ipsum etiam afferunt, & contrarium strenuè impugnant quidam Theologi Petrus Martyr Loc. Commun. class. 2. cap. 51. & 58. Relp. Istam quaestionē Problematice à variis esse disceptatam. Nam pro parte affirmare, hæc tria adferuntur argumenta:
units.tr: VIII. and last. Whether it is lawful for a good man to deceive and mislead, since this seems by nature to be opposed to truthfulness, inasmuch as he shuns all deceit both in words and in deeds, and delights in sincerity alone. Some theologians, such as Peter Martyr in Loc. Commun., class 2, chapters 51 and 58, both assert this and vigorously oppose the contrary. Answer: This question has been argued on various sides as a problematic one. For the affirmative, three arguments are brought forward:

units.la: 1. Quia Viro bono licet simulare & dissimulare, ut jam dictum est: ergo etiam fallere & decipere cum hoc ex illo sequatur. Hinc dolus in genere à Servio Jurisconsulto definitur machinatio quaedam alterius decipiendi gratia, cum aliud agitur, aliud simulatur.
units.tr: 1. It is lawful for a good man to pretend and to dissemble, as has already been said; therefore also to deceive and mislead, since this follows from that. Hence the jurist Servius defines fraud in general as a certain contrivance for deceiving another, when one thing is done and another is pretended.

units.la: 2. Quia quidam dolus non pugnat cum charitate proximi, sed potius cum ea consenti, quippe qui legitimè usurpatur ad legitimam sui vitæ suæ defensionem, aut proximi vel juvandi vel conservandi, velætiâ à malis majoribus avertendi gratia. Ejusmodi dolus est, cū viator latronē decipit, simulando aliam viâ, vel à recta via deflectendo, ne in latronis manus incidat: Sic etiam cum Medicus decipit ægrotantem sanitatis restituendæ gratia, ut Galenus sterum se febricitantem circumvenisse, & pro vino aquam illi propinasse. Hoc etiam dolo usus est David adversus Regem Gad. 1. Sam. 21. vers. 13.
units.tr: 2. Some fraud does not conflict with love of neighbour but rather agrees with it, since it is lawfully used for the lawful defence of one's own life, or for the help or preservation of one's neighbour, or even to turn him away from greater evils. Such fraud is when a traveller deceives a robber, by pretending to take another road or by turning aside from the right road, so as not to fall into the robber's hands. So too when a physician deceives a sick man for the sake of restoring his health, as Galen reports that he deceived a man who was feverish and gave him water in place of wine. David also used this fraud against King Gath, 1 Sam. 21.13.

units.la: 3. Quia in bello bono Imperatori licet insidias struere, & omnis generis strategematis uti ad circumveniendum & fallendum hoste juxta illud Poëtæ: Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat:
units.tr: 3. In a just war it is lawful for a commander to lay ambushes and to use every kind of stratagem to outwit and deceive the enemy, according to the saying of the poet: "Whom, in an enemy, would one ask whether it is fraud or valour?"

units.la: At pro thesi negante hæ tres rationes faciunt: 1. Quia cum sinceritate, quæ in viro bono potissimum requiritur, pugnat omnis fallacia & deceptio: Nam, quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri non feceris: proinde cui quis nolit, ut sibi imponatur, neque aliis imponere debet. 2. Quia vir bonus debet esse expers omnis doli: Nam, cum dolus sit vitium oppositum virtuti, ideo a viro bono, qui sol virtute studet, longe abesse debet. 3. Qua non sunt facienda mala, ut inde eveniant bona: Nam ut regula JCtorum habet: Bona sunt bene agenda, quia nimirum omnis finis est bonus aut boni, & cum media mensuram suam habeant a fine, debent propter naturam finis etiam esse bona: unde concluditur, viro bono non licere ut alios fallat aut decipiat. Pro decisione huius quæstionis distinguendum est inter dolum bonum & malum: dolus bonus is dicitur, qui fit ex præscripto rectæ rationis nec ulli nocet: dolus malus econtra. Prior tanquam licitus viro bono conceditur, quia non tam fallacia aut deceptio dici debet, quam animi quædam sagacitas cum prudentia civili conjuncta, tum etiam nullam mali intentionem habet: & de hoc dolo vera est pars affirmativa quæstionis: dolus malus viro bono non conceditur: proinde neque fallere, nec decipere per dolum malum: & de hoc posteriori intelligitur pars negativa quæstionis. Sed rursus in dolo malo adhiberi solet quædam distinctio. Nam contendunt quidam, etsi simpliciter sit illicitus, tamen secundum quid posse esse licitum, & licet adversus amicos aut eos, qui familiaritate aut aliqua necessitudine conjuncti sunt dolo malo uti jure nemo mo possit: adversus hostes tamen, quos vel Deus vel Respubl. vel Magistratus legitimus tales declaravit, uti quis poterit, tanquam armis & telis, sed cum hac restrictione: 1. Ne juramentum in contrarium fit interpositum. 2. Ne fides hosti de eo non fallendo sancte fit data: In hoc enim casu ne adversus hostes quidem dolo malo uti licet, quod probatur exemplo Josuae, Gibeonitarum Jos. cap. 9. Sin autem altera pars quae juravit, a fide & pactis prior recesserit, tunc sententiam illam vulgo justam locum habere dicunt:
units.tr: On the other side, for the negative thesis, these three arguments count: (1) Every deception and every fallacy is at odds with sincerity, which is chiefly required in a good man. For "what you do not want done to you, do not do to another"; therefore one who would not want to be deceived himself ought not to deceive others. (2) A good man ought to be free of all fraud. For since fraud is a vice opposed to virtue, a good man, who strives after virtue alone, ought to stay far from it. (3) Evils are not to be done so that good may come of them. For as the rule of the lawyers has it: good things are to be done well, because every end is good or of a good, and since means receive their measure from the end, they must by the nature of the end also be good. From this it is concluded that it is not lawful for a good man to mislead or deceive others. To decide this question, one must distinguish between good fraud and bad fraud. Good fraud is that which is done according to the prescription of right reason and harms no one; bad fraud is the opposite. The former is granted to a good man as lawful, because it should not so much be called a fallacy or deception as a certain sagacity of mind joined with civil prudence, and moreover it has no intention of evil; and the affirmative part of the question is true of this fraud. Bad fraud is not granted to a good man; therefore neither to mislead nor to deceive by bad fraud; and the negative part of the question is understood of this latter. But again, a certain distinction is usually made regarding bad fraud. Some contend that although it is simply unlawful, it may nevertheless be lawful in a certain respect; and that while no one may rightly use bad fraud against friends, or those joined to him by familiarity or some close tie, one may use it against enemies, whom God, the commonwealth or the lawful magistrate has declared to be such, as one uses weapons, but with this restriction: (1) that no oath has been sworn to the contrary; (2) that no faith has been solemnly given to the enemy not to deceive him. For in this case one may not use bad fraud even against enemies, as is shown by the example of Joshua and the Gibeonites, Josh. 9. But if the other party, who has sworn, has departed from its faith and its pacts first, then they say that the saying commonly held just has its place:

units.la: Frangenti fidem, fides frangatur eidem.
units.tr: Let faith be broken to the one who breaks faith.

units.la: Cujus rationem reddere videtur Cic. 3. offic. ubi citat carmen ex Accio veteri Poeta: Fregistine fidem? Respondet Atreus, quem loquentem introducit, neque dedi, neque do, fidem infideli cuiquam. Sed tamen haec sententia, non est approbanda, quin potius struendum est dolo malo, qua talis est viro bono simpliciter uti non licere, tum quia intentionem mali semper habet conjunctam, tum quia mendacium perniciosum in malitia superat: Nam mendacium fit in dictis, dolus malus, in dictis & factis simul; & quia ad finem bonum & honestum, bonis & honestis mediis, non turpibus aut illicitis est contendendum, ideo Viro bono dolus malus nullo respectu utendus conceditur.
units.tr: Cicero seems to give the reason for this in De Officiis, book 3, where he cites a verse from the early poet Accius: "Have you broken faith?" Atreus, whom he introduces as speaking, replies: "I have neither given faith to any faithless man, nor do I give it." Yet this maxim is not to be approved. Rather, it must be held that deceit is not simply permitted to a good man, both because it always carries an intention of evil with it, and because a harmful lie surpasses malice in wickedness: "For a lie lies in words; deceit lies in words and deeds together." And because a good and honest end must be pursued by good and honest means, not by base or unlawful ones, deceit is granted to be used by a good man on no account whatever.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: AGit hoc capite Philosophus de tertia virtute Homilitica, nempe de Urbanitate, quae in jocis, in rebus ludicris & jucundis versatur. Partes capitis sunt quatuor: 1.In prima dari ejusmodi virtutem probat, quia nempe datur ejus objectum jucunda (scilicet conversatio in ludo & joco.In secunda agit de medio & extremis simul. In tertia adfert proprietates utriusque, & notas quibus a se invicem distinguantur. In quarta demum parte comparat virtutes homiliticas inter se.
units.tr: In this chapter the Philosopher treats of the third homiletic virtue, namely Urbanity, which is concerned with jests, play and pleasant matters. The chapter has four parts. 1. In the first he proves that such a virtue exists, because its object, pleasant things (namely conversation in play and jest), exists. In the second he deals with the mean and the extremes together. In the third he sets out the properties of each and the marks by which they are distinguished from one another. In the fourth he finally compares the homiletic virtues with one another.

units.la: In prima igitur parte dari hanc virtutem duabus rationibus docet: 1. est, quia ea est vitæ humanæ conditio, ut quiete & relaxatione opus habeat: nam ut canit Poëta:
units.tr: In the first part, then, he teaches by two arguments that this virtue exists. 1. It exists because it is the condition of human life to need rest and relaxation; for, as the poet sings:

units.la: Quod caret alterna requie, durabile non est.
units.tr: What lacks alternate rest does not endure.

units.la: Ideo cum ludus & jocus quietis & relaxationis gratia instituantur ad vitæ recreationem, sicut præest experientiam docet Philosophus fusè admodum lib. 8. Polit. cap. 3. & Cicero lib. 1. offic. Ludo, inquit, & joco sicut somno & cateris quietibus uti debemus: necesse dari aliquam virtutem, quæ modum in ludo & joco præscribat. 2. Ratio, quia dantur extrema, quæ in nimio vel in parvo circa ludum & jocum cernantur; ergo necesse est dari medium aliquod circa eandem materiam, quod, quæ, quemadmodum, & apud quos loqui & audire deceat, rationem præscribat: nam in personis etiam distinctio adhiberi solet & debet: aliter enim licet jocari apud familiares & notos, aliter apud ignotos: Facilius fertur sciommea alicujus magni viri, quam leviculi nugatoris, & sic de cæteris: proinde mediocritatem circa ludos & jocos dari necesse est.
units.tr: Therefore, since play and jest are instituted for the sake of rest and relaxation, to refresh life, as the Philosopher shows at length, and as experience itself teaches, in Politics book 8, chapter 3, and Cicero says in book 1 of De officiis: We ought to use play and jest as we use sleep and other kinds of rest, it is necessary that some virtue exists which prescribes the measure in play and jest. 2. The argument is that there are extremes, which are seen in excess or in deficiency in play and jest; therefore there must necessarily be some mean concerning the same matter, which prescribes what, how, and in whose presence it is fitting to speak and to listen. For a distinction of persons is also usually and rightly observed: one may jest one way among friends and acquaintances, and another way among strangers. A jest about some great man is more readily tolerated than one about a worthless trifler, and so on for the rest. Therefore a mean concerning jests and play must necessarily exist.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis agit de medio & extremis, & primo quidem de extremis, quia de iis nullum erat, dudubium, tum etiam magis in sensus incurrunt; & primo adfert extremum in excessu, quod dicitur Scurrilitas, & qui hoc vitio laborant, dicuntur scurrae & importuni, quorum haec est natura, ut ex omni re risum captent, & ideo modum excedant, & magis studeant ridicula dicere aut audire quantumlibet turpia, quae honesta & decora. Unde Diogenes tum vidisset adolescentem quendam, obscoena quaedam sine modo efferentem, non te pudet, inquit, adolescens ex eburnea vagina plumbeum educere gladium. Non enim isti scurrae laborant, ut aliis placeant, dum modo ridicula proferant. Alterum extremum in defectu dicitur Rusticitas, & qui hoc vitio laborant, tales sunt, ut neque ridiculi quid ipsi proferant, neque ridicula proferentes patienter audiant: unde duri & agrestes vocantur, propterea quod duro agrestiq; plerunq; sint ingenio, in quibus hoc vitium reperitur. Qui vero medium servant, ut neque deficiant, neque excedant, sed apte & moderate jocentur, sicut recta prescribit ratio, dicuntur Urbani & Versatiles, quia ad motionem & versionem animi, admodum sunt proclives: nam ut experientia docet, quidam ad festivitatem & jocos sunt promti admodum, quidam vero sunt tardi, nempe, quibus hoc natura negavit, & sicut ex moribus cognoscitur constitutio corporis, sic ne sanum corpus an infirmum, sic etiam ex jocis cognoscitur subtilitas aut stupiditas ingenii.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the mean and the extremes, and first with the extremes, because there was no doubt about them and they are also more evident to the senses. First he sets out the extreme in excess, which is called Buffoonery. Those who labour under this vice are called buffoons and tiresome fellows. Their nature is to catch laughter from every matter, so they exceed the measure and strive more to say or hear jokes, however foul, than what is honourable and decent. Hence Diogenes, when he saw a certain young man bringing out obscene remarks without restraint, said: "Are you not ashamed, young man, to draw a leaden sword from an ivory sheath?" For these buffoons do not labour to please others, provided only they utter jokes. The other extreme, in deficiency, is called Rusticity. Those who suffer from this vice are such that they neither utter anything laughable themselves nor patiently hear those who do. Hence they are called hard and boorish, because they are mostly of a hard and rustic disposition, in whom this vice is found. Those who keep the mean, neither falling short nor exceeding, but jesting aptly and moderately as right reason prescribes, are called Urbane and Versatile, because they are very inclined to the movement and turning of the mind. For, as experience teaches, some are very prompt to merriment and jokes, while others are slow, namely those to whom nature has denied this gift. And just as the constitution of the body is known from its habits, whether it is healthy or sick, so too from jests is the subtlety or the dullness of a mind known.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis adfert proprietates quasdam medii & extremorum, & primo tres proprietates seu notas medii: I. est, quod qui urbanus sit propter dexteritatem ingenii scienter & perite jocetur, id est,
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he sets out certain properties of the mean and of the extremes, and first three properties or marks of the mean. I. The first is that the urbane man, because of the quickness of his wit, jests knowingly and skilfully, that is,

units.la: se ad temporis, loci & personarum rationem accommodet, tantum dicat & audiat, quae libero homine sunt digna, & quae aliis minime displiceant: nam cum duplex sit jocandi genus, ut hoc loco Aristoteles, & Cicero l.offic.docet, unum nempe liberale & ingenuum libero & politico homine dignum; alterum illiberale flagitiosum & scurrile, honestoq; homine prorsus indignum, priori tantum gaudet vere urbanus propter naturam virtutis suae, tum etiam propter rectae rationis ductum quem sequitur; discrimen namque magnum esse solet inter viri eruditi & politici jocos, & viri indocti & non politici: id quod patet exemplo veterum & recentiorum Comoediarum, nam utraque joco utebatur, sed veteres illae Comoediae joco illiberali, turpi & aperto, recentiores liberali tantum, eleganti & recto, nam licet res turpes non turpiter dicere modo castas aures non offendant, inquit Cicero 2.deorat. & Stoici, ut idem restatur lib.9. epist.familiar.ad Patrum, imitabantur veteres Comoedias, turpia enim aperte profitebantur, Platonici econtra turpia honestis verbis involvebant. II. Proprietas est, quod etsi urbanus nullis displicere studeat, tamen non tam spectare debet, quid huic aut illi placeat, aut quid vulgo hominum arrideat, quam quod viro bono placeat, cuius judicium est recte dispositum, & ideo de factis cujusque recte judicare potest, quod fusius dilatat Philosophus lib.3. Eodem. cap.7, III. Proprietas est, quod cum duplex sit munus viri urbani, alterum dicere recte & rite jocos, alterum recte audire, tantum debet audire, quae libero & honesto homine sunt
units.tr: he adapts himself to the circumstances of time, place and persons, and says and hears only what is worthy of a free man and least displeasing to others. For since there are two kinds of jesting, as Aristotle here and Cicero teach, one liberal and well-bred, worthy of a free and civilised man, the other illiberal, shameful and buffoonish, utterly unworthy of an honest man, the urbane man rejoices truly only in the former, both on account of the nature of his virtue and on account of the guidance of right reason which he follows. For there is usually a great difference between the jests of a learned and civilised man and those of an unlearned and uncivilised man. This is clear from the example of old and recent comedies: both used jesting, but the old comedies used illiberal, foul and open jesting, while recent ones used only liberal, elegant and proper jesting. For, as Cicero says in book 2 of De oratore, although one may not speak shameful things shamefully, one may speak of them so long as chaste ears are not offended. And the Stoics, as the same author attests in book 9 of the Letters to Friends, to Paetus, imitated the old comedies, for they openly professed base things; the Platonists, on the contrary, wrapped base things in honourable words. II. The second property is that, although the urbane man strives to displease no one, he ought not look so much at what pleases this or that person, or what the common crowd laughs at, as at what pleases the good man, whose judgement is rightly disposed and who can therefore judge rightly of each man's deeds. The Philosopher explains this more fully in book 3 of the same work, chapter 7. III. The third property is that, since the office of the urbane man is twofold, one to tell jokes rightly and fittingly, the other to hear them rightly, he ought to hear only what is worthy of a free and honest man,

units.la: digna nō nimis flagitiosa aut injuriosa, quia flagitiosa audire intempestivā sapit, injuriosa, quæ nomen aut famam alicujus lædere possint, ignaviam ingenii arguit. Quis enim maledicta aut jocos absque ratione projectos æquanimiter ferre posset, ut non rependat, nisi idem scurra sit aut assentator, qui ab aliorum scommatis dependeat, & de quibus Juvenal. sat.5.
units.tr: not too shameful or injurious. For to hear shameful things savours of an untimely ..., and to hear injurious things, which can harm someone's name or reputation, shows a dull wit. For who could bear with equanimity slanders or jokes flung out without reason, and not return them, unless he were the same buffoon or flatterer who depends on the mockery of others? Juvenal speaks of such men in Satire 5:

units.la: Si potes illa pati, quæ nec Sarmenta iniquas Cæsaris ad mensas aut vilia Galba tulisse.
units.tr: If you can bear those things which Sarmentus himself did not bear at Caesar's unjust tables, nor vile Galba.

units.la: Hoc nomine inprimis laudantur Augustus Cæsar & Vespasianus Imperator, qui, ut refert Dion Cassius in sua epitome jocos non modo eleganter dicere, sed patienter etiam & absque molestia ferre aut audire poterant. Postea adfert proprietates extremorum, & primo extremi in excessu tres istas adfert notas: I. Quod scurra, quod hoc vitio laborat, ex omni objecto, quod occurrit, risum excitat, & absque delectu circumstantiarum ridicula semper proferat: unde à Stoicis definiri solet Scurrilitas, risus jociquè movens intempestivum & immoderatū studium. II. Quod Scurra, neque sibi, neque aliis parcat, dum pro ingenio scurrili ridicula proferat, quod de Mevio scurra quodam refert Horatius 1. epist.
units.tr: By this name especially are praised Augustus Caesar and the Emperor Vespasian, who, as Dio Cassius reports in his epitome, could not only jest elegantly but also bear or hear jests patiently and without annoyance. Next he sets out the properties of the extremes, and first of the extreme in excess, he gives these three marks. I. The buffoon, who labours under this vice, provokes laughter from every object that comes before him, and always utters jokes without regard to the circumstances. Hence the Stoics usually define Buffoonery as an untimely and immoderate eagerness to stir up laughter and jests. II. The buffoon spares neither himself nor others while he utters jokes according to his buffoonish nature. Horace reports this of a certain buffoon, Mevius, in Epistles 1:

units.la: Inprans sus civem, qui non dignoscere hoste:
units.tr: A shameless pig, who cannot tell a citizen from an enemy:

units.la: Qualibet in quemvis opprobria fingere savus.
units.tr: Savage enough to invent reproaches of every kind against anyone at all.

units.la: Hoc vitium in pleriq; notat & graviter taxat Cic. 2. de Orat. & in Cicerone ipso Plutarchus in vita Ciceronis & in Philippo Macedonia Rege Livius. III. Proprietas est, quod turpia & indecora ejusmodi profer-rat, à quibus Vir verè Urbanus prorsus abhorreat, tuna tum quia modum excedant, tum quia aliis in primis displicent. Alterius extremi in d fectu duas affert notas Philosophus: I. Quod qui Rusticitatis vitio laborant, ad colloquium humanum & conversationem quotidianam prorsus sint inepti, cum ludos & jocos dictis & factis suis tanquam sales admiscere non possint. II. Nota est, quod in utriumque urbanitatis genus peccant: nam neque jocos ipsi dicunt, neque alios dicentes libenter ferunt aut audiunt; unde vel ofores hominum cum Timone Atheniense sunt, quod donum hoc jocandi aliis invident, vel crasso & pecuario sint ingenio, cum ipsi jocos excogitare aut invenire non possint. Talis fuit Demea senex ille morosus apud Comicum. Tales plerunque sunt Melancholici isti, qui vita solitaria & silentio plurimum delectantur.
units.tr: Cicero, in book 2 of De oratore, notes this vice in most men and sharply censures it; and Plutarch, in the Life of Cicero and in the Life of Philip the Macedonian King, and Livy likewise, censure it in Cicero himself. III. The buffoon utters base and unseemly things of this kind, from which a man who is truly urbane shrinks entirely, both because they exceed the measure and because they especially displease others. Of the other extreme, in deficiency, the Philosopher sets out two marks. I. Those who suffer from the vice of rusticity are wholly unfit for human conversation and daily company, since they cannot mix jests and play into their words and deeds as a seasoning. II. It is noted that they fail in both kinds of urbanity: they neither utter jests themselves nor willingly bear or hear others uttering them. Hence they are either envious, like Timon of Athens, who begrudge others this gift of jesting, or they are of a gross and boorish wit, since they cannot devise or invent jokes themselves. Such was Demea, the morose old man in the comedy. Such for the most part are those melancholics who delight most in a solitary life and silence.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis confert tres istas homiliticas virtutes inter se: Primo quidem in simili, quod omnes in victu quotidiano & communione dictorum ac factorum versentur. Unde & homiliticae quasi conversativae dicuntur. 2. Comparat in dissimili: Nam objectis suis differunt, siquidem Veracitas circa veritatem in dictis & factis cernitur, reliquae duae Affabilitas & Urbanitas circa jucunditatem in quotidiana vita: hoc tamen inter istas duas ponitur discrimen, quod Affabilitas circa voluptatem in re seria cernatur, Urbanitas circa jucunditatem in jocis & rebus ludicris. Plura de hac comparatione vide ad cap. 8. lib. 2. huius operis.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter the author compares these three homiletic virtues with one another. First, they are alike in that all three are concerned with daily life and with the sharing of words and deeds; for this reason they are also called conversational virtues. Second, he compares them by their differences: their objects are different, since Truthfulness is exercised in words and deeds with regard to truth, while the other two, Affability and Urbanity, are concerned with pleasantness in everyday life. Yet there is this difference between those two: Affability is exercised with regard to pleasure in serious matters, Urbanity with regard to pleasantness in jests and playful things. For more on this comparison, see on chapter 8 of book 2 of this work.

units.la: De Urbanitate breviter notanda sunt ista quatuor: 1. Nomen, quod Graecis dicitur εὐτραπελία, Latinè FaciliFacilitas aut Flexibilitas morum à Cicerone, vel quia ex ludo & joco mores hominum facilè flectuntur, vel quia, qui hac virtute sunt præditi, omnia dicta & facta sua ad arbitrium aliorum facilè flectere possunt. Latinè dicitur Urbanitas ab urbe, quia in urbibus propter crebram hominum frequentiam frequentiores, qui hac virtute sunt præditi, reperiuntur, quam in pagis aut in agro: Nam ut ait Cic. 2. de Orat. in urbibus multò jucundius & suavius vivitur, quam ruri. II. Significatio hujus vocabuli, quæ triplex vulgò reperitur: Nam 1. Urbanitatis nomen sumitur pro insita quadam humanitate naturæ humanæ, & sic affectus potius, quam virtus dici debet. 2. Sumitur improprie, idq; duobus modis: 1. Ut idem sit, quod Civilitas & sic urbanus pro bene morato sumitur, ut in illo versiculo: Diceris urbanus, sed non urbanus haberis, Cum ceu vacca bibas, & suis instar edas.
units.tr: Four points about Urbanity should be noted briefly. 1. The name: in Greek it is εὐτραπελία [eutrapelia], in Latin affability or flexibility of manners, as Cicero calls it, either because people's manners are easily bent by play and jest, or because those who possess this virtue can easily bend all their words and deeds to the will of others. In Latin it is called Urbanitas from urbs, city, because people who possess this virtue are found more often in cities, owing to the frequent crowding of people there, than in villages or the countryside. For as Cicero says in On the Orator book 2, life in cities is far more pleasant and agreeable than life in the country. II. The meaning of this word, which is commonly found in three senses. For 1. the name Urbanity is taken for a certain innate humanity of human nature, and in this sense it ought to be called an affection rather than a virtue. 2. It is taken improperly, and in two ways: (a) so that it means the same as civility, and in this sense urbane is taken to mean well-mannered, as in that line: You are called urbane, but you are not thought urbane when you drink like a cow and eat like a pig.

units.la: 2. Sumitur in malam partem pro scurrilitate, quæ modum omnem in jocis excedit, & sic ab Apostolo nomen ἐὐτραπελία sumitur ad Ephes. 5. vers. 4. quia tempore Pauli ex hominum malitia in abusum jam venerat. 3. Proprie sumitur pro virtute quadam, quæ modum in jocis & ludis observet: nec est à ratione alienum, ut sit quædam virtus, quæ in rebus levibus & ludicris versetur, quia ut ait Philosophus 8. Polit. cap. 5. qui laborant, quiete & relaxatione opus habent ad vitam reficiendam, & hujus gratia inventus est jocus, in quo, ut in omnibus rebus, quæ à viro bono tractantur, modus certus determinari debet.
units.tr: (b) It is taken in a bad sense for scurrility, which goes beyond all measure in jests; and in this sense the Apostle uses the word εὐτραπελία [eutrapelia] at Ephesians 5:4, because in Paul's time it had already come into abuse through human malice. 3. It is taken properly for a certain virtue which observes measure in jests and games. Nor is it contrary to reason that there should be a virtue which is concerned with light and playful matters, since, as the Philosopher says in Politics book 8, chapter 5, those who labour need rest and relaxation to restore their lives, and jesting was invented for this purpose; and in it, as in all things handled by a good man, a fixed measure ought to be determined.

units.la: Hinc Cic. 2. de Orat. nullum, inquit, est vitæ tempus, in quo quo non decorum & jucunditatem adhibere possumus, modo certa cum ratione fiat. Hinc definitur Urbanitas virtus in ludis & jocis mediocritatem servans. III. Objectum duplex: Internum, nempe moderatio cupiditatum in ludis & jocis: Externum ludus & jocus, qui per se non contrariantur virtuti: Nam mentem adeoque hominem praeparant ad virtutem & vires ad actiones bene peragendas augent. Nam cum labor assiduus & occupatio ferå spiritus vitales exhauriant, & cor exsiccent: ideo ut labores continui melius ferantur, opus est quiete & relaxatione, & si his opus est, etiam ludo & joco opus erit, quibus cor dilatetur & spiritus vitales denuo reficiantur. IV. Consideratio da veniunt Extrema, quorum alterum in defectu dicitur Rusticitas, alterum in excessu Scurrilitas, quae definitur intempestivum & immoderatum, aliis risum movendi studium, Graecis dicitur βωμολόχος cuius nominis ratio varie a variis interpretibus reddITUR: Nam Scholiastes Graecus putat βωμολόχοι dici aves quasdam rapaces, quae aris insidiantur, & sicut istae aves ex qualibet occasione & quovis tempore cibum captant, sicuti scurrae ex qualibet re nata risum quaerunt. Suidas vero hanc reddit rationem, & dicit, homines esse quosdam nullius precii, qui aris dum victimae immolantur, adstant emendicantes particulam, & quia blandis verbis & risum excitant, quo facilius a sacrificante aliquid impetrent, hinc factum, ut omnes scurrae, qui intempestive & supra modum jocis delectarentur βωμολόχοι etiam dicantur: & hanc rationem approbat Caelius Rhodiginus lib. 10. lect. antiq. antiq.cap.6. Plura vide apud Keckerm.pag.277. Syst. Ethic. De altero extremo, quæ dicitur Rusticitas, vide cap.8.lib.2.hujus operis. De hac virtute cum suis extremis agit, non tantum hoc loco Philosophus, sed etiam cap.8 lib.2. ut jam diximus; & 1.mag.mor.cap.31. & 3. Eudem.cap.7.
units.tr: Hence Cicero, in On the Orator book 2, says: There is no time of life in which we cannot bring in propriety and pleasantness, provided it is done with sound judgement. Hence Urbanity is defined as a virtue that keeps the mean in play and jesting. III. Its object is twofold: internal, namely the moderation of desires in play and jesting; external, play and jesting, which in themselves are not contrary to virtue, for they prepare the mind, and therefore the man, for virtue, and increase his strength for performing actions well. For when constant labour and occupation drain the vital spirits and dry up the heart, then, so that continual labours may be better borne, there is need of rest and relaxation; and if there is need of these, there will also be need of play and jest, by which the heart is refreshed and the vital spirits are restored again. IV. The extremes must be considered: one of them, in deficiency, is called Rusticity, the other, in excess, Scurrility, which is defined as an untimely and immoderate eagerness to move others to laughter. In Greek it is called βωμολόχος [bomolochos]. The reason for this name is explained variously by various interpreters. For a Greek scholiast thinks that βωμολόχοι [bomolochoi] are certain rapacious birds which lie in wait around altars, and just as these birds seize food on any occasion and at any time, so scurrilous jesters seek laughter from any chance matter. Suidas, however, gives this explanation: that there were certain worthless men who, while victims were being slaughtered at the altars, stood about begging for a morsel, and because they excited laughter with flattering words, so that they might more easily obtain something from the one sacrificing, it came about that all jesters who delighted in jests untimely and beyond measure were also called βωμολόχοι [bomolochoi]; and Caelius Rhodiginus approves this explanation in Lectiones antiquae book 10, chapter 6. More on this may be seen in Keckermann, Systema Ethicae, page 277. As for the other extreme, which is called Rusticity, see chapter 8 of book 2 of this work. The Philosopher treats of this virtue with its extremes not only in this place, but also in chapter 8 of book 2, as we have already said; and in Magna Moralia book 1, chapter 31, and Eudemian Ethics book 3, chapter 7.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Cum vita humana quiete & relaxatione indigeat, necessaria illi videtur Urbanitas, quæ in ludis & jocis modum præscribat.
units.tr: 1. Since human life needs rest and relaxation, a certain urbanity seems necessary to it, one which sets bounds to play and jest.

units.la: 2. Medium & extrema etsi diversam longè habeant naturam, circa idem tamen versantur objectum.
units.tr: 2. The mean and the extremes, though they have very different natures, nonetheless are concerned with the same object.

units.la: 3. Qui jocis & ludis supra modum delectantur, scurra & importuni dicuntur, at verò qui à medio deficiunt, ut neque dicant, neque libenter jocos audiant, agrestes & duri nuncupantur, qui verè medium tenent, faceti & urbani recte vocantur.
units.tr: 3. Those who take too much pleasure in jests and play are called buffoons and tiresome persons; but those who fall short of the mean, neither making jokes nor willingly listening to them, are called rustic and harsh. Those who truly keep the mean are rightly called witty and urbane.

units.la: 4. Sicut ex motu corporis dignoscitur constitutio, sic etiam ex motibus animi ingenii dexteritas aut stupiditas.
units.tr: 4. Just as bodily constitution is recognised from the motion of the body, so too quickness or dullness of wit is recognised from the motions of the mind.

units.la: 5. Quia jocis & ludis, quidam nimium delectantur, hinc fit, ut scurra à quibusdam nomine ipsius medii, id est, elegantes & urbani vocentur.
units.tr: 5. Because some take too much pleasure in jests and play, it comes about that buffoons are called, by some, by the very name of the mean, that is, elegant and urbane.

units.la: 6. Proprium est viri urbani tantum dicere & audire ejusmodi jocos, qui virum bonum deceant, & cum ipsa ratione constent.
units.tr: 6. It is proper to the urbane man to say and hear only such jests as befit a good man and agree with right reason.

units.la: 7. Plurimum inter se differunt, viri docti & Politici, & indocti seu rudis scommata.
units.tr: 7. Learned and courtly men differ very much from the uneducated and coarse in their witticisms.

units.la: 8. Urbanus non tam respicere debet, quid huic aut illi placeat aut displiceat, sed tantum quid viro bono videatur, cujus nempe rectè dispositum sit judicium.
units.tr: 8. The urbane man ought not to look so much at what pleases or displeases this person or that, but only at what seems right to a good man, that is, one whose judgement is rightly disposed.

units.la: 9. Urbanus, quia fibiipsi lex est, dicit & audit tantum, qua recta prascribit ratio.
units.tr: 9. The urbane man, since he is a law to himself, says and hears only what right reason prescribes.

units.la: 10. Scurra, qui urbano in excessu opponitur, neque sibi, neque aliis parcit, dum modo ridicula dicat.
units.tr: 10. The buffoon, who is opposed to the urbane man in excess, spares neither himself nor others, provided only that what he says is laughable.

units.la: 11. Rusticus qui in defectu opponitur urbano, cum neque dicat, neque audiat libenter iocos, ad societatem & conversationem humanam prorsus est ineptus.
units.tr: 11. The rustic, who is opposed to the urbane man in deficiency, neither speaks nor willingly listens to jests, and is wholly unfit for society and human conversation.

units.la: 12. Tres ista virtutes homilitica licet inter se nomine consentiant, obiecto tamen differunt: Nam Veracitas circa verum versatur tantum: Affabilitas & Urbanitas circa voluptatem, sed ita ut prior voluptatem in rebus seriis, posterior in rebus ludicris & iocundis tantum respiciat.
units.tr: 12. These three virtues of social life, though they agree in name, differ in their object. Truthfulness is concerned only with the true; affability and urbanity are concerned with pleasure, but affability regards pleasure in serious matters, while urbanity regards it only in playful and pleasant matters.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An Urbanitas poterit recte dici virtus, cum ut ex cap. 2. lib. 2. huius operis patet, virtus circa difficilia versetur: at Urbanitas non versatur circa difficilia, quia tantum in ludis & iocis cernitur, qui propter voluptatem, quam pariiunt faciles admodum sunt? Resp. In ludis & iocis duo spectari: 1. naturam ipsorum, 2. modum quo circa naturam istam aliquid versatur: etsi sua natura ludi & joci videantur faciles, modum tamen in iis tenere est perquam arduum & difficile, nec poterit quis apte & decore ludos & jocos adhibere, nisi acutiore judicio & longa rerum experientia modum circumstantiarum observare didicerit.
units.tr: I. It is asked: can urbanity rightly be called a virtue, since, as is clear from chapter 2 of book 2 of this work, virtue is concerned with what is difficult, whereas urbanity is not concerned with what is difficult, since it is found only in play and jest, which, because of the pleasure they bring, are very easy? Answer: in play and jest two things are to be considered: first, their nature; second, the manner in which something is done concerning that nature. Although play and jest seem easy by their nature, to keep the mean in them is exceedingly hard and difficult, and no one can use play and jest fittingly and becomingly unless he has learned, by a more acute judgement and long experience of affairs, to observe the measure of the circumstances.

units.la: II. An possit dici virtus necessaria ad perfectionem vitae humanae, cum omnis talis virtus actione sua tendat ad felicitatem, ut ex cap. 6. lib. 1. huius operis liquet: At Urbanitas non tendit. Quid enim ludus & jocus conferunt ad felicitatem comparandam, cum summum bonum morale rebus tantum seriis comparetur, ut ex reliquarum virtutum inductio ductione patet? Dein etiam lib. 7. Polit. cap. 4. summum bonum nō immeritō dicitur acquisitu difficile, & pauci sunt, qui ipsum asequuntur: At si ludus & jocus aliquid conferrent, ad felicitatem, facile quis eam possit assequi: Unde nō videtur Urbanitas ad felicitatem necessaria? Resp. Aliquid tendere ad felicitatem duobus modis vel proximè vel remotè, proximè quidem non tendit Urbanitas, propter objectum circa quod versatur: remotè tamen dicitur tendere, quia ludus & jocus quietem animi gignunt & solvunt, ac curis & doloribus, quibus si quis obrutus sit, virtutum actionibus, & per consequens ipsi felicitati studere non potest.
units.tr: II. Can it be called a virtue necessary to the perfection of human life, since every such virtue by its action tends toward happiness, as is clear from chapter 6 of book 1 of this work; yet urbanity does not tend toward it? For what do play and jest contribute to the attainment of happiness, since the highest moral good is won only through serious things, as is clear from the induction of the other virtues? Furthermore, in book 7 of the Politics, chapter 4, the highest good is not without reason said to be difficult to acquire, and few are those who attain it. But if play and jest contributed anything to happiness, one could attain it easily. Hence urbanity does not seem necessary to happiness? Answer: to tend toward happiness may happen in two ways, either proximately or remotely. Urbanity does not tend toward it proximately, because of the object with which it is concerned; yet it is said to tend toward it remotely, because play and jest produce and loosen the quiet of the mind, and if a man is overwhelmed by cares and sorrows, he cannot devote himself to the actions of the virtues and, consequently, to happiness itself.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: An constet cum ratione, quod Philosophus dicit sub medium capitis, non spectandum esse urbano, quid hic aut ille de ludis & jocis sentiat, aut quid omnibus videatur, sed quid paucis tantum iis, bonis: cum, si hoc sit verum, Urbanitas non erit virtus, nam nulla virtus offendit, quia est bonum quid, tum & habet finem honestum. At Urbanitas, quae non omnibus placet, sed paucis offendit, & ideo non videtur esse virtus? Resp. Haec non absolutè & simpliciter à Philosopho dici, sed comparatè ad hominum statum & conditionem: Nam quia diversi sunt mores, diversa hominum ingenia, non debet Urbanus se omnium ingeniis attemperare, quia quod huic ludus & jocus est, illi serium videtur. Dein etiam fieri non potest, ut quis omnibus placeat, cum ut ait Euripides: Jupiter ipse omnibus non placet. Sed satis est, si ad ingenium viri boni se accommodet, quia recte dispositum habet judicium vir bonus, & potest tam de intentione interna, quam de actione extrema recte judicare, & sic seipsum exponit Philosophus lib. 3. Eudem. cap. 7.
units.tr: Does it agree with reason that the Philosopher says, about the middle of the chapter, that the urbane man must not look at what this or that man thinks of play and jest, nor at what all think, but only at what a few good men think? For if this is true, urbanity will not be a virtue: no virtue gives offence, since it is a good thing and has an honourable end. Yet urbanity, which does not please all but offends a few, does not seem to be a virtue? Answer: the Philosopher does not say this absolutely and simply, but in comparison with the condition and state of men. For since manners differ and human dispositions differ, the urbane man ought not to adapt himself to the dispositions of everyone, because what is play and jest to one seems serious to another. Furthermore, it cannot happen that one pleases everyone, since, as Euripides says: Jupiter himself does not please everyone. But it is enough if he accommodates himself to the disposition of the good man, since the good man has a rightly disposed judgement and can judge rightly both the inner intention and the outward action. And so the Philosopher himself explains it, in book 3 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 7.

units.la: Post tractatum hunc de Urbanitate quaedam discutienda veniunt, & 1. An cum Urbanitas, cum ludos & jocos tanquam objectum suum versari dicatur, Viro bono liceat dicere & audire jocos? Resp. Dubium esse hanc quaestionem, nam in utramque partem ventilari solet, & pro negativa parte afferuntur quinq; rationes: 1. Quia vir probus, propter naturam bonitatis suae, debet, rebus tantum seriis intentus esse, non vero jocosis, quae rebus seriis contrariantur: ideo cum res jocosae famae & aestimationi Viri boni & bonitati ipsius quodammodo detrahant, iis vacare non debet. 2. Quia Vir probus nihil dicere aut audire debet, quod non sit liberale & honestum, at joci & ludi sunt plerunque illiberales, inhonesti & turpes. 3. Quia nulli maledicere debet, at omne vitium scomma & maledictum a Philosopho vocatur hoc cap. 14. ideo cum omne maledictum sit vitium, & vitium bonitati repugnet, a jocis tanquam a maledictis abhorrere debet vir probus. 4. Quia vir probus fugere debet omnem occasionem alios offendendi & ad iram provocandi, hoc autem fieri non poterit, si sit scopticus, id est, salibus im tempestivis & dicteriis alios lacessat. 5. Quia sacra Scriptura vetat jocis & ludis uti aut verbis vanis futilibus aut inutilibus, hinc Apostolus ad Ephes. cap. 5. vers. 4. fatuem sermonem & scurrilitatem expresse prohibet: & Christus ipse Matth. 12. vers. 36. dicit, in extremo judicio de omni verbo otioso reddendam esse rationem. At pro parte affirmativa sunt rationes majoris momenti numero etiam quinque: 1. est, quia vir bonus semper rebus seriis intentus esse non debet, propter vitae humanae manæ conditionem, quæ alterna quietē nec sfariō indiget, ideoà ferjs quandoque quiescere potest, & animi recreandi gratia ludere & jocari, hinc Philosophus 3. Eudem. cap. 4. inquit, videtur ludus & quies in vita humana necessariò habere locum, & simul etiam traductionem temporis cum ludo, hujus rationem hanc reddit Seneca lib. 4. de virtutibus cap. 1. Ludus & jocus, aut vacatio à rebus seriis instar cotticulæ esse videtur, ad acuendum ingenium hominis. 2. Quia libanitas est virtus, quæ in ludis & jocis mediocritatem servat: Ergo cum viro bono urbanus esse licet, quippe, qui virtuti studere debet, ludos etiam & jocos dicere & audire debet. 3. Quia joci liberales & honesti, ut ait Philosophus hoc cap. 14. tum etiam 3. Eudem. cap. 4. & 7. efficiunt conversationem hominum apertam, jucundam & amabilē, ut contra Ruslicitas, quæ nec jocos dicere necaudire possit, ad societatem & conversationem hominum prorsus inepta & inutilis habetur. 4. Quia joci liberales & honesti sunt veluti condimetum laborum & oblectamentum, quo taedia tam animi, quam corporis ex laboribus contracta depelluntur: hinc Scipio Africanus major & Cato gravissimi Senatores, quā primum à curia aut à rebus gravioribus aliquid laxamenti sumpserunt, jocis & ludis se reficere solebant, ut testatur Cic. in Dial. de amicitia. 5. Quia in Scripturis sacris legimus viros etiam sinctos jocatos esse Gen. 26. vers 8. Pro decisione quæstionis distinguendum erit inter jocos moderatos & immoderatos: Joci moderati sunt, qui fiunt ex præscripto rectæ rationis, ubi, quando, apud quos, quātum, quomodo,cur & cujus gratia fiunt aut fieri debent: Immoderati econtra, qui peccant contra omnes istas circumstantias. In priori genere sunt joci liberales, honesti,tempestivi, salsi,venusti, lepidi, eruditi, jucundi,&id genus cæteri,& tales omnes sunt laudabiles & liciti, tum quia hominis reficiendi tantum gratia,instituti sunt, tū quia nulla çū malitia aut damno sui ipsius, autproximi sunt conjunćti, & de his intelligi debet locus illeapud Cic.1.offic.Ludo & jo-co uti quidé debemus sicut somno&vigilia,&cæte-ris quietibus tūc cū gravibus feriis q; reb. satisfeceri-mus: Ite illud apud Dionem Cassiumain vitaCæsaris Augusti:Ludo & joco tanquam vita sale moderatè quidem utebatur: Nam ut ait Seneca,non secus ac sal corruptionem aut putrefactionem à carnibus prohibet,ludi & joci tempestivi morbos à corpore arcent. In posteriori genere sunt joci illiberales & inhonesti, intempestivi, infulsi & molesti,qui omnes sunt vituperabiles & illiciti propter rationes contrarias: De jocis igitur moderatis vera est thesis affirmativa cum suis argumentis,de immoderatis negativa cum suis,
units.tr: After this treatment of urbanity, certain questions must be discussed. First: since urbanity is said to be concerned with play and jest as its object, is it lawful for the good man to say and hear jests? Answer: this question is disputed, for it is usually argued on both sides. On the negative side five reasons are brought forward: (1) because the upright man, by the nature of his goodness, ought to be occupied only with serious things and not with jocular ones, which are opposed to serious things; therefore, since jocular things in some measure detract from the good name and esteem of the good man and from his goodness itself, he ought not to give himself to them. (2) Because the upright man ought to say or hear nothing that is not liberal and honourable, but jests and play are for the most part illiberal, dishonourable and base. (3) Because he ought to speak evil of no one, but the Philosopher calls every vice a scoffing and slander, in this chapter 14; so since every slander is a vice, and vice is incompatible with goodness, the upright man ought to shrink from jests as from slanders. (4) Because the upright man ought to avoid every occasion of offending others and provoking them to anger; this cannot happen if he is a scoffer, that is, if he assails others with ill-timed witticisms and taunts. (5) Because Holy Scripture forbids the use of jests and play, or of vain, frivolous or useless words; hence the Apostle expressly forbids foolish talk and scurrility in Ephesians 5:4; and Christ himself says in Matthew 12:36 that at the last judgement an account must be given of every idle word. On the affirmative side, however, there are reasons of greater weight, likewise five in number: (1) the good man does not have to be always occupied with serious things, because of the condition of human life, which by turns needs rest and recreation; so he may sometimes cease from serious things, and play and jest for the sake of refreshing his mind. Hence the Philosopher in book 3 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 4, says: play and rest seem necessarily to have a place in human life, and likewise the passing of time with play. Seneca gives this reason in book 4 of On Virtues, chapter 1: play and jest, or relief from serious things, seems to be like a whetstone for sharpening the human mind. (2) Because urbanity is a virtue which keeps the mean in play and jest; therefore, since urbanity is permitted to the good man, he who ought to pursue virtue ought also to say and hear play and jests. (3) Because liberal and honourable jests, as the Philosopher says in this chapter 14, and also in Eudemian Ethics 3, chapters 4 and 7, make conversation among men open, pleasant and agreeable; whereas the rustic, who can neither say nor hear jests, is held wholly unfit and useless for society and human conversation. (4) Because liberal and honourable jests are, as it were, a seasoning of labours and a solace by which the weariness of mind and body contracted from labours is driven away. Hence Scipio Africanus the Elder and Cato, most grave senators, when they first took some relaxation from the senate-house or from weightier business, were accustomed to refresh themselves with jests and play, as Cicero testifies in his dialogue On Friendship. (5) Because in the sacred Scriptures we read that even holy men jested, Genesis 26:8. For the decision of the question one must distinguish between moderate and immoderate jests. Moderate jests are those made according to the prescription of right reason: where, when, before whom, how much, how, why and for whose sake they are or ought to be made. Immoderate jests, on the contrary, are those which offend against any of these circumstances. To the first kind belong liberal, honourable, timely, witty, pleasant, learned, agreeable jests and others of that kind, and all such are praiseworthy and lawful, both because they are instituted only for the sake of refreshing a man, and because they are joined with no malice or harm to oneself or one's neighbour. And the passage in Cicero, On Duties 1, should be understood of these: We ought to use play and jest just as we use sleep and waking and other forms of rest, when we have satisfied serious duties and affairs. Likewise that saying in Dio Cassius, in the life of Augustus Caesar: He used play and jest, as it were the salt of life, with moderation. For, as Seneca says, just as salt keeps flesh from corruption and putrefaction, timely play and jest keep diseases away from the body. To the second kind belong illiberal and dishonourable jests, ill-timed, insipid and offensive ones, all of which are blameworthy and unlawful for the contrary reasons. Therefore the affirmative thesis, with its arguments, is true of moderate jests, and the negative, with its arguments, of immoderate ones.

units.la: II. An cum ludo & joco uti licet, sicut jam distum est, ludi scenici, quales sunt Comœdia & Tragœdia in bene constituta Republ. liciti sint & ferendi? Resp. Hanc quæstionem sicut alias plerasq; non carere suis difficultatibus, nam pro diversis hominum ingeniis ultrò citroq; agitari solet: sunt enim, qui prorsus illicitos esse contendunt propter quatuor potissimum rationes: 1. Quia horum ludorum usus expresso Dei verbo repugnat, nam in iis fit plerunque,ut vir mulibri utatur veste, & mulier contra virili,at hæc abomiominatio dicitur coram Domino Deuter. 22. verf.5.
units.tr: II. Whether stage plays, such as comedies and tragedies, may be lawful and tolerated in a well-ordered commonwealth, along with play and jesting, as has already been said. Answer: Like most other questions, this one has its difficulties, and it is commonly debated back and forth according to the different judgments of men. Some maintain that such plays are wholly unlawful, chiefly for four reasons: (1) the practice of these plays conflicts with the express word of God, for in them it often happens that a man wears a woman's garment and a woman a man's, and this is called an abomination before the Lord (Deut. 22 v. 5).

units.la: 2. Quia actiones harum Comœdiarum plerunque conjunctæ sunt cum magno detrimento juventutis, cum depravatione gestuum & morum, cum intemperantiæ & superbiæ attractione, cum vitæ & famæ læsione, aliisque plurimis incommodis, ut experientia docet.
units.tr: (2) The actions of these comedies are usually bound up with great harm to young people: with corruption of gesture and morals, with the enticement of intemperance and pride, with injury to life and reputation, and with many other disadvantages, as experience teaches.

units.la: 3. Quia Ethnicismum redolet tales in Republic. ludos permittere. Ethnicos enim in Tragœdiis & Comœdiis vitæ publicæ & privatæ speculum exhibere solebant: at Christiani homines habent sacræ Scripturæ fontes, ad cujus imitationem vitam conformant, & vitæ suæ speculum depromant.
units.tr: (3) To allow such plays in a commonwealth smacks of heathenism. For the heathen used to hold up in their tragedies and comedies a mirror of public and private life, whereas Christians have the fountain of Holy Scripture, to whose pattern they shape their lives and from which they draw the mirror of their lives.

units.la: 4. Quia cum tertio præcepto Decalogi pugnant, ubi dicitur: Non assumes nomen Dei tui in vanum: Assumunt vero nomen Dei in vanum, non tantum, qui expresse hoc faciunt, sed qui ad hoc connivent dum ab aliis fit, ut plurib. docent recetiores quidam Theol.
units.tr: (4) They conflict with the third precept of the Decalogue, where it is said: You shall not take the name of your God in vain. Men take the name of God in vain not only when they do so expressly, but also when they connive at it while others do it, as several of the more recent theologians teach.

units.la: At contra quod liceat sint & ferendi in Rebus, optimè constituatur novem hæ rationes, multò firmiores probant:
units.tr: On the other side, that these plays are lawful and may be tolerated in a commonwealth is far more firmly proved by nine reasons, which are set out here very well:

units.la: 1. Quia magnam verborum & rerum selectissimarum supellectilem suppeditant; nam quæ verba solent esse exquisitiora aut elegantiora, quæ res etiam auditu & visu gratiores eæ omnes in iis ludis ad vivum exhiberi solent.
units.tr: (1) They supply a great stock of words and the choicest matter, for the more refined or elegant words, and the things that are more pleasing to hear and see, are all customarily presented to the life in those plays.
