units.la: 2. Quia memoriam rerum omnium thesaurum excolunt, & mirifice confirmant: Nam per duos sensus nobilissimos auditum scilicet & visum res menti humanæ suggerunt.
units.tr: (2) They cultivate the memory, which is a treasury of all things, and strengthen it wonderfully, for through the two noblest senses, hearing and sight, they bring things to the human mind.

units.la: 3. Quia timidiusculis animum addunt, & loquendi libertatem docent, ut enim usus rerum magister optimus, sic ex crebro usu & exercitio habitum coram quovis dicendi vel agendi perfectum acquirere possunt dimidioris aut verecundioris ingenii homines. 4. Quia linguam expeditam reddit actio horum ludorum, haesitantem omnem tollit, aliaque in sermone vitia corrigit: Ut enim fabricando fabri fimus, sic distinctè & saepe loquendo distinctum & expeditum loquendi habitum acquirimus.
units.tr: (3) They add courage to the timid and teach freedom of speech; for, as experience, the best teacher of things, shows, from frequent practice and exercise men of a slower or more diffident temper can acquire a settled habit of speaking or acting before anyone. (4) The performance of these plays makes the tongue ready, removes all hesitation, and corrects other faults of speech; for as we become smiths by smithing, so by speaking distinctly and often we acquire a distinct and fluent habit of speech.

units.la: 5. Quia mores non usquequaque probatos corrigunt & in melius reformant, dum veluti in speculo hos sequendos, illos fugiendos esse, unusquisque videt. 6. Quia animi recreationem magnam afferunt, quis enim est, qui ex multiplici rerum, quae exhibentur varietate summam non percipiat voluptatem, dum aliquid subinde novi oculos repraesentari videt. 7. Quia historias multas & res praeclaras gestas scitu dignissimas & necessarias apud vulgus hominum vel plane ignotas referunt, vel oblivioni traditas in memoriam revocant. 8. Quia Chinenses acutissimi Asiae majoris populi, sic juventutem suam educare solent ut in Comoediis & Tragoediis exhibendis primum se exerceant, hoc enim modo ad quodvis vitae genus ampliectendum faciliores & promptiores reddi putantur. 9. Quia nihil est, quod aeque homines a vitiis abster ret, quam si vitiorum deformitatem in personis repraesentari & exhiberi ad vivum videant, quod in Tragoediis & Comoediis fieri solet: atque hinc factum, ut Graeci filios suos a vitiis dehortaturi servum aliquem eodem vitio infectum in medium producerent, ut hoc quasi sensili argumento a vitiis facilius deterrerent. Atque huc procul dubio respexit Magistratus, dum praemia virtutum & poenas vitiorum in publico loco fieri voluit, ut hinc ad virtute excitaretur homines; illinc à vitiis aliorum exemplis deterrerentur. Unde ex his rationibus, quas ex variis aliis collegiis licitos esse ludos scenicos constat. Pro decisione huius quaestionis notanda sunt sequentia Theoremata: I. Comoedias & Tragoedias dijudicandas esse tum ratione finis, qui honestate semper respicit tu ratione materiae, quae ab omni impudicitia & immunditie, cuius longissime abesse debet. II. Distinguendos esse actus serios à non seriis & jocosis, in quibus omnino videndum est, ut omnia modeste & absque scandalo fiant, nam actus jocosi honestae tantum voluptatis & recreationis gratia, non contra instituti debent. III. Multa offendicula provenire ex vitio & obscoenitate agentium, non vero ex rebus ipsis, quae aguntur. Hinc ad primum argumentum, quod pro negativa parte adfertur, respondeti poterit cum Augustino: Non esse indecorum neque contra Scripturas, ut quis alterius sexus vestes induat, modo fallendi gratia id non fiat, & poterit quis meretricula vestes induere, ut vitia & peccata meretricia ostendat, neque monstrosum est vestes, sed mores scorti induere. In reliquis argumentis committitur fallacia finis & accidentis, nam Comoediis & Tragoediis non eveniunt, sed ex vitiis agentium.
units.tr: (5) They correct morals that are not altogether approved and reform them for the better, since everyone sees, as in a mirror, which conduct is to be followed and which to be avoided. (6) They bring great refreshment of mind, for who does not take the greatest pleasure from the manifold variety of things presented, while he sees something new set before his eyes from time to time? (7) They relate many histories and notable deeds, worth knowing and necessary, which are either wholly unknown to the common people or have been consigned to oblivion, and they recall them to memory. (8) The most shrewd of the Chinese, the people of Greater Asia, are accustomed to educate their young in such a way that they first train themselves in producing comedies and tragedies, for by this means they are thought to be made easier and readier to embrace any way of life. (9) Nothing deters men from vices as much as seeing the deformity of vices represented and exhibited to the life in persons, which is what happens in tragedies and comedies. Hence it came about that the Greeks, wishing to dissuade their sons from vices, brought some slave infected with the same vice into the midst of them, so that by this, as it were, sensible argument they might more easily deter them from vice. Undoubtedly the magistrate also had this in view when he wished the rewards of virtues and the punishments of vices to be made in a public place, so that men might be roused to virtue on the one hand and deterred from vices by the examples of others on the other. From these reasons, drawn from various other collections, it is clear that stage plays are lawful. To decide this question, the following theses are to be noted. I. Comedies and tragedies are to be judged both by their end, which always looks to honesty, and by their subject matter, which must be entirely free from all impurity and uncleanness, from which they ought to be far removed. II. Serious actions must be distinguished from those that are not serious and are jocular, and in the latter one must take care that everything is done modestly and without scandal, for jocular actions ought to be undertaken only for the sake of honest pleasure and recreation, and not contrary to their purpose. III. Many stumbling-blocks arise from the vice and obscenity of the actors, not from the things that are being performed. Hence to the first argument, which is brought on the negative side, one may reply with Augustine: It is not unbecoming, nor contrary to the Scriptures, for someone to put on the clothing of the other sex, provided it is not done for the sake of deceiving; and a man may dress as a harlot in order to show the vices and sins of harlots, and it is not monstrous to put on the clothing, but to put on the morals, of a whore. In the remaining arguments the fallacy of end and accident is committed, for these things do not befall comedies and tragedies, but arise from the vices of the actors.

units.la: III. An ista tres virtutes Homiliticae in virtutum numero sint habendae? Resp. Et hanc quaestionem probabiliter disceptari solitam. Nam pro negativa parte afferuntur rationes: 1. Est, quia Philosophus ipse lib. 1. Magnor. Moral. cap. 33. dubitat, sintne virtuvirtutes an affectus. 2. Quia regenerati Spiritu recreare se debent hymnis & Psalmis, ut restatur Apostolus Ephes. 5. verf. 19. & 20. At omnes Christiani sunt regeneråti Spiritu Rom. 5. verf. ult. Ideo hymnis & Psalmis non rebus istis ludicris oblectari se debent. Proinde cum Scriptura e numero virtutum istas homilitícas excludat, pro virtutibus veris haberi non debent. 3. Quia εντεξαπελια tertia harum virtutum ab Apostolo damnatur ad Ephes. 5. v. 4.
units.tr: III. Are these three homiletic virtues to be counted among the virtues? Answer: This question too is commonly disputed with probability. For the negative side the following reasons are brought: (1) the Philosopher himself, in the first book of the Magna Moralia, chapter 33, doubts whether they are virtues or affections. (2) Those who are regenerate by the Spirit ought to refresh themselves with hymns and psalms, as the Apostle urges in Eph. 5 vv. 19 and 20. But all Christians are regenerate by the Spirit (Rom. 5, last verse). Therefore they ought to delight themselves with hymns and psalms, not with these playful things. Accordingly, since Scripture excludes these homiletic virtues from the number of virtues, they ought not to be held as true virtues. (3) The buffoonery [εὐτραπελία] of the third of these virtues is condemned by the Apostle in Eph. 5 v. 4.

units.la: 4. Quia omnibus virtutibus propositum est praemium, ut vitiis contrariis poena; at hisce nihil tale est propositum. Quis enim, quod jocando & confabulando aliorum ingeniis se accommodare nesciat, poenam promeruit? aut ut hoc maxime calleat, quis inde ampla repotitat praemia? 5. Quia omnes virtutes interna maxime respiciunt, ut intrinsecus hominem perficiant; at istae tres homiliticae in externis potius consistunt, ut ex singularum objectis patet: unde caeteris virtutibus jure adnumerari non debent. 6. Quia omnis virtus circa difficilia versatur, ut cap. 2. lib. 2. hujus operis docet Philosophus. At istae tres homiliticae circa etiam jusmodi versantur objectum, in quo nulla plane cernitur difficultas: nam versantur vel circa voluptatem vel circa res ludicras, in quibus parum aut nihil unquam difficultatis reperitur. 7. Quia sunt potius consequentia aut appendices virtutum quam verae virtutes; nam qui Justitiae habitu est praeditus, & qui juste erga omnes se possit gerere, ut suum cuique tribuat, is procul dubio noverit, quomodo in conversatione quotidiana se gerere debeat; unde aut plane in Virtutum nuhumero non sunt habendæ aut superflue tantum possæ sunt. Pro affirmativa parte rationes sunt sex majoris ponderis: 1. Est, quia iis competit definitio virtutis à Philosopho tradita cap. 7. lib. 2. h. o. At cui competit definitio, eidem competit & definitū. 2. Cui forma alicujus rei convenit, eidem convenit & formatum, ut præter experientiam testatur Philosophus 2. Phys. cap. 1. At hïsce hominiticis competit forma virtutis, nempe mediocritas secundum rectam rationem, quod singularum inductione probari potest. 3. Quia consistunt inter duo extrema, sicut de singulis probat Philosophus: At hoc esse virtutis proprium, constat exc. 12. lib. 2. 4. Quia quicquid provenit ex mente & judicio, ex proæresi seu præelectione, id est aut virtus, aut actio, quæ gignit virtutem, sicut cap. 4. lib. 3. docetur: At ex his proveniunt tres illæ hominiticæ. 5. Quia magnus est earum in vita humana usus, & major fere quam reliquarum virtutum excepta sola Temperantia & Justitia universali. 6. Quia finem communem virtutis sibi propositum habent, nempe honestatem; unde & à Philosopho & à Platone in variis Dialogis pro virtutibus habentur.
units.tr: (4) Every virtue has a reward set before it, as its contrary vices have a punishment; but nothing of the kind is set before these. For who has earned a punishment for not knowing how to accommodate himself to the wits of others by jesting and conversing? Or who, to be most skilled in this, gathers from it any great rewards? (5) All virtues look chiefly to what is internal, so that they perfect a man inwardly; but these three homiletic virtues consist rather in external things, as is clear from the objects of each. Hence they ought not rightly to be numbered among the other virtues. (6) Every virtue is concerned with difficult things, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 2 of the second book of this work. But these three homiletic virtues are concerned with objects of such a kind in which no difficulty whatever is plainly seen; for they are concerned either with pleasure or with playful things, in which little or no difficulty is ever found. (7) They are rather consequences or appendages of the virtues than true virtues; for whoever has the habit of justice, and who is able to conduct himself justly towards all, so as to render to each his due, will doubtless know how he ought to conduct himself in daily conversation. Hence they are either not to be counted at all among the virtues, or they can be only superfluous. For the affirmative side there are six reasons of greater weight: (1) the definition of virtue handed down by the Philosopher in chapter 7 of the second book of this work applies to them, and whatever a definition applies to, the thing defined applies to as well. (2) What belongs to the form of a thing belongs also to the thing formed, as the Philosopher attests, apart from experience, in the second book of the Physics, chapter 1. But the form of virtue, namely the mean according to right reason, belongs to these homiletic virtues, which can be proved by induction over each of them. (3) They consist between two extremes, as the Philosopher proves of each of them; and this is known to be the property of virtue, from chapter 12 of the second book. (4) Whatever arises from the mind and judgment, from proairesis or prior choice, is either a virtue or an action that produces a virtue, as is taught in chapter 4 of the third book; but these three homiletic virtues arise from such things. (5) Their use in human life is great, and almost greater than that of the other virtues, except for Temperance and universal Justice. (6) They have as their common end the goal of virtue, namely honesty; hence they are held to be virtues by both the Philosopher and Plato in various dialogues.

units.la: Pro pleniori hujus quæstionis determinatione sciendum est, eminentiâ quidem & præstantiâ istas hominiticas virtutes reliquis cedere, at vero sive utilitatem spectes, sive ipsam virtutis formalitatem æquipollent reliquis virtutibus. 2. Non ubivis aut quovis loco concessa esse ludicra, circa quæ tertia harum virtutum, nempe Ubanitas versatur; non enim in loco sacro, non in foro, aut in loco publico, non etiam ubi moeror & tristitia magis decet, sed tantum concessa sunt in conviviis aut in iis locis, in quibus recreationis aut voluptatis gratia convenitur. Hinc Cicero 1. offic. Neque enim a natura itagenerati sumus, ut ad ludum & jocum facti esse videamur, sed ad veritatem potius & studia quaedam graviora & majora: ludo quidem & jocouri illis licet, sed sicut somno & vigilia & ceteris quietibus tunc cum gravibus seriisque rebus satisfecerimus. 3. Considerandas esse istas virtutes non tantum ratione objecti circa quod versantur, sed etiam ratione subjecti, cui insunt & & caeterarum circumstantiarum respectu: Nam ad sanitatem & animi & corporis propter magnam recreationem, quam subinde ferunt, necessarie ad modum & utiles sunt, ut pluribus docet Philosophus cap. 3. lib. 8. Polit. Hinc de valore contrariorum argumentorum facile judicari poterit. Nam quod ad primum, respondendum est, Philosophum loco citato non loqui ex sua, sed vulgi opinione, propterea quod vulgo putarentur a natura potius quam ab assuefactione & usu provenire: & proinde esse tantum affectus: Ipse vero Philosophus suam opinionem & hoc loco & cap. 8. lib. 2. tum etiam 1. Eudem. cap. f. satis declarat. Quod ad secundum, laudare Deum hymnis & Psalmis, item honeste modesteque jocari non contrariantur sibi invicem, sed potius subordinantur modo suo quaeque loco & tempore fiant. Tertium argumentum loquitur de ὑπερβολῇ in abusu: Nam temporibus Pauli in malam partem sumebatur, nepe pro altero extremo in excessu. Quartum argumentum omni consequentia vacat: nam non sequitur, his neq; poena, neq; præmiū propositū est, ergo non sunt virtutes, nā sæpenumero neq; Magnificentiæ neque Magnanimitati proponuntur præmia, & tamen sunt præcipuæ Virtutes. Quintum argumentum est falsum; nam in externis non tantum versantur, sed etiam in moderatione internorum affectuum, quia objectum habent duplex, sicut & cæteræ Virtutes. Justitiæ etiam usus maximè refertur ad alium, sic etiam reliquæ virtutes cum actiones suas ad extra edunt, in externis versantur, & tamen sunt veræ virtutes. Sexta etiam ratio falsitatis vitio laborat; nam non minus difficile est modum servare in hisce virtutibus, quàm in reliquis, nā si quis circumstantias bene observet, magnam difficultatem in hisce virtutibus reperiet. Septimum etiā nihil habet roboris, nam non sunt appendices virtutum, sed veræ & distinctæ à cæteris virtutes; & instantia, quæ affertur, probat tantum de Justitia universali, quæ comprehendit sub se omnes in genere virtutes, ut postea patebit.
units.tr: For a fuller determination of this question, it must be understood that these social virtues yield to the others in eminence and excellence, but whether you look at their usefulness or at the formal nature of virtue itself, they are on a par with the other virtues. Playful amusements are not permitted everywhere or in every place, and it is with these that the third of these virtues, urbanity, is concerned. They are not permitted in a holy place, in the forum, or in a public place, nor where mourning and sadness are more fitting, but only at banquets or in places where people gather for recreation or pleasure. Hence Cicero: "For we were not born by nature to be made for play and jest, but rather for truth and certain more serious and weighty pursuits; we may indeed indulge in play and jesting, just as in sleep and rest, when we have satisfied serious and weighty matters." These virtues must be considered not only in terms of the object they concern, but also in terms of the subject in which they inhere and of the other circumstances. For they are necessarily useful and suitable in due measure for the health of both mind and body, on account of the great recreation they sometimes bring, as the Philosopher teaches at length in Politics 8.3. From this, the value of the contrary arguments can easily be judged. As to the first, it must be answered that the Philosopher in the passage cited does not speak from his own view but from common opinion, because it was commonly thought that these virtues came from nature rather than from habituation and practice, and therefore were merely feelings. The Philosopher himself makes his own opinion clear both in this place and in Nicomachean Ethics 2.8, and also in Eudemian Ethics 1, last chapter. As to the second, praising God with hymns and psalms and jesting becomingly and modestly do not oppose one another, but rather are subordinated to one another, each being done in its own place and time. The third argument speaks of excess [ὑπερβολῇ] in abuse, for in Paul's time the word was taken in a bad sense, namely for the other extreme, excess. The fourth argument has no valid consequence: it does not follow that, because no punishment or reward is proposed for these virtues, they are therefore not virtues, since often no rewards are proposed for Magnificence or Magnanimity either, and yet these are principal virtues. The fifth argument is false, for these virtues are concerned not only with externals but also with the moderation of inner affections, since they have a twofold object, as do the other virtues. Justice too is especially directed toward another, and so the remaining virtues, when they perform their actions outwardly, are concerned with externals, and yet they are true virtues. The sixth reason also suffers from falsity, for it is no less difficult to keep the mean in these virtues than in the others; if one observes the circumstances well, one will find great difficulty in these virtues. The seventh likewise has no strength, for these are not appendages of the virtues but true virtues, distinct from the others; and the instance adduced proves only about universal justice, which comprehends under itself all the virtues in general, as will later become clear.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Sequitur hoc capite altera pars hujus libri, in qua Philosophus post tractationem quarundam virtutum agit de affectu quodam, nempe Verecundia, & de quadam imperfecta virtute, nempe Continentia. Gausa verò, cur de his hoc loco agat, triplex esse videtur: 1. Quia magnam cognationem & affinitatem cum ipsis virtutibus habent; nam sunt mediocritates secundum rectam rationem, sicut & ipsæ virtutes. 2. Quia sua laude etiam sunt dignæ, cum
units.tr: In this chapter the Philosopher begins the second part of this book. After treating certain virtues, he deals with an affection, namely Shame, and with an imperfect virtue, namely Continence. There seem to be three reasons why he treats of them here: (1) because they have a great kinship and affinity with the virtues themselves, for they are means according to right reason, just as the virtues are; (2) because they too are worthy of praise, since

units.la: ne que declinant ad excessum neque ad defectum: at laudabile & fle compertum proprie virtuti, sicut lib.1. cap.12. docet Philosophus. 3. Etiam quia a diversis Philosophorum sectis, praesertim a Stoicis & Academicis pro veris virtutibus habebantur: attamen non sunt virtutes, sed aut principia virtutum aut affectiones, ut posthac patebit. Partes huius capitis sunt duae: In prima prolixius agit de ipsa Verecundia. In secunda breviter admodum & succincte de Continentia, propterea quod lib.7. cap.4. huius operis fusius de ea agendum sibi proponit.
units.tr: they incline neither to excess nor to defect; and what is praiseworthy belongs properly to virtue, as the Philosopher teaches in Book 1, chapter 12. (3) Also because they were held to be true virtues by various schools of philosophers, especially the Stoics and the Academics. Yet they are not virtues, but either principles of virtues or affections, as will be clear hereafter. The parts of this chapter are two. In the first he treats more at length of Shame itself. In the second he treats very briefly and succinctly of Continence, because he proposes to treat of it more fully in Book 7, chapter 4 of this work.

units.la: In prima igitur de Verecundia agit, de qua tria adfert: 1. Est, quod non sit virtus, quicquid alii sentiant, quia non est habitus, idque confirmat duabus rationibus: 1. Sumitur a definitione Verecundiae, quia ab omnibus definitur metus infamiae seu ignominiae, sicut docet hoc loco Philosophus & 2. Rhetor. cap.5. & probat hanc ipsam definitionem Plato in Euth. cum qua etiam consentit definitio D. Thomae, Verecundia est metus turpitudinis exprobrabilis. Cum igitur sit metus, erit tantum affectio. 2. Ratio ducitur ab eventu, quia pudore & rubore afficere solet Verecundia, sicut metus in periculis solet afficere pallore. Cum igitur metus & pudor sint tantum affectiones, quae corpus afficiunt, Verecundia, quae & pudor & metus dicitur, non erit habitus, & si non sit habitus, neque etiam virtus, quia per habitum definitur virtus, sicut ex cap.7. lib.1. iam liquet. II. Quod adfert de Verecundia, est, quod non omni conveniat aetati, sed tantum adolescentibus & iis, qui in viridiori aetate sunt constituti, non autem senibus, id quod etiam Plato in Charmide affirmat, & Philosophus hic probat duabus rationibus: 1. est: Quia adolescentes Verecundia a peccatis, in quæ cupiditatibus impulsi incidunt facile abasterrentur, quod probat exemplo Polæmonis adolescentis, de quo Laërt. lib. 4. de vit. Philos. At senes quia non tam cupiditatibus, quam proæresi & mentis judicio omnia agunt sola Verecundia, à peccatis deterreri non possunt: nam longo rerum usu & experientia habitum in rebus agendis sibi comparârunt, proinde cum habitus difficulter amittatur non Verecundia aut persuasionibus ab incepto prohiberi possunt. 2. Ratio est hæc: Quia adolescentes non senes à Verecundia laudare solemus, unde illud apud Tert. in Adol. de Æschine adolescente: Erubuit, salva res est. Et Socrates, ut testatur Xenophon lib. 2. de dictis & factis Socratis, à Verecundia laudabat adolescentes, dicebat, indubitatum esse virtutis futurae in iis signum. III. De Verecundia hoc est, quod non competat viro bono, idque propter duas causas: 1. Quia Verecundia ex reb. malis & turpibus oritur, quæ viro bono nullo modo sunt faciendæ, sed fugiendæ, sive eæ res sunt re & natura sua turpes, sive opinione & consuetudine tantum. 2. Quia viri boni proprium est, ea quæ bona sunt agere, non autem sponte sua, ea committere, ob quæ pudore aut Verecundia afficiatur: quæ præcipuè videntur dicta in Platonem. Nam Plato lib. 1. de Repub. & in Prot. contrarium asserit, & hoc etiam addit, Verecundia & Justitia, tanquam præcipuis virtutibus totas conservari Respub.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he treats of Shame, and he brings forward three points about it. (1) It is not a virtue, whatever others may think, because it is not a habit. He confirms this with two arguments. (a) It is drawn from the definition of Shame, since by all it is defined as the fear of infamy or disgrace, as the Philosopher teaches here and in Rhetoric 2, chapter 5. Plato confirms this very definition in the Euthydemus, and the definition of St Thomas agrees with it: Shame is the fear of an disgraceful reproach. Since, then, it is a fear, it is merely an affection. (b) The argument is drawn from its effect, because Shame is accustomed to affect a man with blushing and redness, just as fear in dangers is accustomed to affect him with paleness. Since, then, fear and blushing are merely affections which affect the body, Shame, which is called both blushing and fear, will not be a habit; and if it is not a habit, neither is it a virtue, since virtue is defined by habit, as is already clear from Book 1, chapter 7. (2) What he says of Shame is that it does not suit every age, but only young people and those who are in the prime of life, not old men. Plato also affirms this in the Charmides, and the Philosopher proves it here with two arguments. (a) Young people, driven by desires, easily fall into sins, and Shame readily deters them from these. He proves this by the example of the young Polemon, of whom Laertius speaks in Book 4 of the Lives of the Philosophers. But old men do not act from desires so much as from deliberate choice and the judgement of the mind, and so they cannot be deterred from sins by Shame alone. For by long use of affairs and experience they have acquired a habit in doing things, and since a habit is hardly lost, they cannot be restrained from what they have begun by Shame or by persuasion. (b) The argument is this: we are accustomed to praise young people, not old men, for Shame. Hence that saying of Tertullian in De Adolescentia about the young Aeschines: He blushed; the thing is safe. And Socrates, as Xenophon testifies in Book 2 of the Memorable Sayings and Doings of Socrates, used to praise young people for Shame, saying that it was an undoubted sign of future virtue in them. (3) What he says of Shame is that it does not befit a good man, and this for two causes. (a) Shame arises from bad and base things, which a good man must by no means do but must flee, whether those things are base by their own nature or only by opinion and custom. (b) It is the proper mark of a good man to do the things that are good, and not willingly to commit those things for which he would be affected with shame or Shame. These seem to be said especially against Plato, for Plato in Book 1 of the Republic and in the Protagoras asserts the contrary, and adds that Shame and Justice, as the chief virtues, keep the whole commonwealth intact.

units.la: Cæterum quia paradoxa hæc sententia Philoso-phi phi videtur, & plane contraria vulgari & receptæ hominum opinioni, nempe quod Verecundia non conveniat viro bono, ideo tribus obiectionibus, quæ adferri poterant, occurrit & solvit etiam.
units.tr: Moreover, because this paradoxical opinion of the Philosopher seems to be wholly contrary to the common and received opinion of men, namely that Shame does not befit a good man, therefore he also meets and resolves three objections which could be raised.

units.la: I. Objectio est hæc: Turpia sunt duorum generum, aut re & natura sua, utpote, quæ contra principia communia boni & honesti peccant, ut sunt furtum, latrocinium, avaritia & catera ejusmodi vitia, quæ re & natura sua turpia esse communi omnium hominum consensu, ubicunque locorum aut regionum sint, confirmantur. Alia sunt turpia instituto lege consuetudine aut usu, quæ pro variis variarum gentium ingeniis, & moribus aliter atque aliter æstimarisolent, ut verbi gratia: Cantare in foro, hac aut illa veste uti contra humanitatem, aut civilem consuetudinem alicuius loci aut regionis, sic etiam in nutu, gestu, aut oratione peccare. Sic apud Græcos turpe erat mulieres adhibere virorum conviviis, ut testatur Cornelius Nepos in præfat. lib. de claris Imperatoribus Græciæ: Sed apud Romanos non erat turpe, teste Cicerone act. 3. in Verrem. Sic Romæ turpe erat saltare aut psallere, in Græcia non item, ut testatur idem Cornelius Nepos loco cit. & Sallust. initio conjurationis Catilinariæ, & Cic. 3 offic. Cum igitur turpia sint duorum generum, ut modo diximus, ad posterius tantum genus pertinere videtur Verecundia, id quod perspicuum fit ex definitione Verecundiæ, nempe quod fit metus infamiæ, quasi metus injustæ reprehensionis, ob peccata in consuetudinem civilem, & Cic. 1. offic. varius in locis ad posterius hoc genus turpium potissimum accommodat Verecundiam: At constat dici virum bonum respectu prioris generis, nempe quod ab iis, quæ re & natura turpia sunt, abstineat: vir enim bonus dicitur respectu virtutum suarum, non ratione morum civilium, quipropter
units.tr: I. The objection is this: Base things are of two kinds: either base by their own nature and substance, as they sin against the common principles of good and honour, such as theft, robbery, avarice and other vices of that sort, which are confirmed by the common consent of all men, wherever they live or in whatever region, to be base in their own nature; or they are base by institution, law, custom or usage, which men of various peoples and tempers are accustomed to judge differently in different ways. For example: to sing in the forum, to use this or that garment, is contrary to decency or to the civil custom of some place or region; so too to offend in gesture, bearing or speech. Thus among the Greeks it was base for women to be admitted to men's banquets, as Cornelius Nepos testifies in the preface to his book on the famous generals of Greece; but among the Romans it was not base, as Cicero testifies in the third action against Verres. So at Rome it was base to dance or to play the lyre, but not in Greece, as the same Cornelius Nepos testifies in the passage cited, and Sallust at the beginning of the Catilinarian conspiracy, and Cicero in De Officiis, Book 3. Since, then, base things are of two kinds, as we have just said, Shame seems to pertain only to the second kind; this is clear from the definition of Shame, namely that it is the fear of infamy, as it were the fear of unjust reproach for sins against civil custom; and Cicero in De Officiis, Book 1, variously applies Shame chiefly to this second kind of base things. But it is agreed that a good man is so called with respect to the first kind, namely that he abstains from those things which are base by their nature. For a good man is so called with respect to his virtues, not by reason of civil customs; for which reason

units.la: Ptet pter diversas opiniones hominum subinde mutantur, & proinde verecundia viro bono competit? Resp. Philosophus per negationem antecedentis: Nam vir bonus in neutro genere turpium peccare debet, quod etiam tesatur Cic. 1. offic. & cū in neutro genere peccare debeat, quia bonus nō tantū à malo revera, sed à specie etiam mali abstinere debet, ideò Verecundia ei non competit: nam ubi nō peccatū est, ibinon est pudor ob peccatū, & per cōsequens neq; Verecundia.
units.tr: Since the opinions of men are changed from time to time, does Shame therefore befit a good man? Answer: The Philosopher denies the antecedent. For a good man ought to sin in neither kind of base things, as Cicero also testifies in De Officiis, Book 1. And since he ought to sin in neither kind, because a good man must abstain not only from what is truly evil but also from the appearance of evil, Shame does not befit him. For where there is no sin, there is no shame for sin, and consequently no Shame.

units.la: 11. Objectio est: Quod etsi mens & voluntas viri boni sit ejusmodi, ut vitia quacunque detestetur, si tamen in vitia incidat, quod forte fieri potest, debet pudore affici, & ideo Verecundia ei competit? Resp. Philosophus hoc perabsurdum esse, ut in vitia incidat vir bonus, qua est talis: Namaut sponte aut invite incidit in vitia: si spōte, definit jam esse bonus, & incipit esse malus, si invite, cur pudere illum deber, cum pudor tatum ob sponte facta sequatur, utpote in quibus voluntatis consensus repertitur, & quae dolor & poenitentia plerunque comitantur: At ob invite facta veniam & commiserationem quivis meretur, ut constat ex cap. 1. lib. 3. hujus operis. Proinde neque hoc modo competit Verecundia viro bono.
units.tr: II. The objection is: Even if the mind and will of a good man is such that he detests vices of every kind, yet if he falls into vices, which perhaps can happen, he ought to be affected with shame, and so Shame befits him? Answer: The Philosopher says it is utterly absurd that a good man, as such, should fall into vices. For either he falls into vices willingly or unwillingly. If willingly, he now ceases to be good and begins to be bad. If unwillingly, why should he be ashamed, since shame follows only deliberate deeds, in which the consent of the will is found, and which are commonly accompanied by grief and repentance? But for deeds done unwillingly, anyone deserves pardon and pity, as is clear from Book 3, chapter 1 of this work. Therefore Shame does not befit a good man in this way either.

units.la: 111. Objectio est haec: Impudentia est mala, & ideo viro bono non convenit, Verecundia contra est bona & propterea viro bono competere debet, quia ex lege contrariorū alterutrū semper inesse debet? Resp. Hoc non sequi: nam hoc axioma tantum valet in subjectis contrariorum capacibus, & quibus per vices alterutrum inesse potest: At viro bono impudentia non competit, cum sit mala. Ergo neque Verecundia cum ob malefa&a sequatur, ut ex superioribus jam constat. Caeterum etsi Verecundia per se viro bono non conveniat, utpote quae ob sponte malefacta sequatur, ex hypothesi tamen & per aliud convenire viro bono interdum dicitur, nempe si praeter naturam bonitatis suae, in vitia, quod humanum est, labatur. Ut sententia Aristotelis melius intelligatur, notandum est, Verecundiam duobus modis accipi: 1. Proactu erubescendi, & sic hoc loco definitur a Philosopho, & 2. Rhet. cap. 5. merus seu perturbatio animi ob mala e-jusmodi, quae infamiam afferre possunt, multi enim sunt, qui licet peccatum non timeant, infamiam, quae peccatum ipsum sequitur, maxime timeant. 2. Sumitur pro dispositione naturali hominem ad istum actum erubescendi inflectentem, & sic rursus bifariam sumitur: 1. Communiter pro metu omni dedecoris, tam alieni quam proprii: Nam multi sunt qui aliorum infamia vulnerantur, multi qui aliorum rebus male gestis ad infamiam commoventur. 2. Proprie sumitur, pro metu dedecoris proprii, & sic hoc loco viro bono non competere dicitur: Nam vir bonus, qua talis, nullam causam Verecundiae aut pudoris in se habet, quia ut ex superioribus patet, ex malis rebus oritur.
units.tr: 111. The objection is this: "Shamelessness is bad, and therefore it does not belong to the good man; shame, on the contrary, is good, and so it ought to belong to the good man, since by the law of contraries one of two contraries must always be present?" Reply: This does not follow. For this axiom holds only of subjects capable of contraries, to which one or the other may belong in turn. But shamelessness does not belong to the good man, since it is bad. Therefore neither does shame belong to him, since it follows wrongdoing, as is already clear from what has gone before. Yet although shame does not belong to the good man in itself, inasmuch as it follows wrongs done willingly, it is nevertheless said sometimes to belong to him hypothetically and through something else, namely if, contrary to the nature of his goodness, he slips into vice, which is human. So that Aristotle's opinion may be better understood, it must be noted that shame is taken in two ways: (1) as the act of blushing, and in this sense the Philosopher defines it here; and (2) in Rhetoric, book 1, chapter 5, as a disturbance of mind arising from bad deeds of such a kind as can bring infamy. For there are many who, although they do not fear sin, greatly fear the infamy that follows sin itself. (2) It is taken as a natural disposition inclining a man to this act of blushing, and so again it is taken in two ways: (1) commonly, for fear of every dishonour, both another's and one's own; for there are many who are wounded by the infamy of others, and many who are moved to infamy by the ill deeds of others. (2) Properly, for fear of one's own dishonour; and in this sense it is said not to belong to the good man here. For the good man, as such, has no cause of shame or modesty in himself, since, as appears from what has gone before, it arises from bad things.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis paucis agit de Continentia, idque propterea, quod non tam propter se, quam propter Verecundiam de ea agat, & dicit non mirum esse, si Verecundia non sit virtus, cum etiam Continentia, in qua ratio pugnat cum appetitu, non sit virtus: Nam in Continentia duo concurrunt: 1. Affectus rationi rectae repugnantes, qui ad Virtutem pro-
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he treats briefly of Continence, and this because he discusses it not so much for its own sake as on account of shame; and he says it is no wonder if shame is not a virtue, since continence too, in which reason struggles with appetite, is not a virtue. For two things come together in continence: (1) affections opposed to right reason, which do not properly pertain to virtue;

units.la: p:oproprie non spectant. 2. Ratio, quae est regula Virtutum: & ideo cum Continentia sit mixtum quid, & recta ratio simul (nam affectus & ratio tam diu inter se pugnant, donec alteri victoria cedat.) Ideo non tam erit virtus, quam semivirtus, aut imperfecta quaedam virtus; De qua fusius infra agit Philosophus lib. 7. ab initio usque ad cap. 11.
units.tr: (2) reason, which is the rule of the virtues. And so, since continence is a mixed thing, and right reason at once (for the affections and reason struggle with each other until victory falls to one side), it will not be so much a virtue as a half-virtue, or an imperfect kind of virtue. Concerning this the Philosopher treats more fully below, book 7, from the beginning to chapter 11.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Verecundia cum sit affectus tantum, non debet dici virtus.
units.tr: 1. Since shame is only an affection, it ought not to be called a virtue.

units.la: A. Verecundia vulgo & non male definitur metus ignominiae seu infamiae, aut quod idem est pudor turpitudinis exprobrabilis.
units.tr: 2. Shame is commonly, and not badly, defined as fear of ignominy or infamy, or what is the same, a sense of shame at disgraceful conduct that may be reproached.

units.la: 3. Experientia docet Verecundos rubescere, ut metu correptos pallescere.
units.tr: 3. Experience teaches that the shamefaced blush, as men seized with fear turn pale.

units.la: 4. Verecundia non omni aetati competit, sed tantum adolescentia.
units.tr: 4. Shame does not belong to every age, but only to youth.

units.la: 5. Adolescentes, quia cupiditatibus facile ducuntur, facile etiam in peccata incidunt, sed tamen verecundia seu pudore a peccatis deterreri possunt.
units.tr: 5. Young people, since they are easily led by desires, easily also fall into sins, but nevertheless they can be deterred from sins by shame or modesty.

units.la: 6. Usus obtinuit, ut adolescentes a verecundia, non senes laudari soleant.
units.tr: 6. Custom has prevailed that young people, and not the old, are usually praised for shame.

units.la: 7. Verecundia viro bono non convenit, cum qua est talis nulla ei Verecundia causa, nempe peccatum proprie infit.
units.tr: 7. Shame does not belong to the good man, since where it exists there is no cause for shame in him, namely, sin has properly not arisen.

units.la: 8. Vir bonus, neque qua natura turpia sunt, neque qua instituto aut consuetudine talia habentur, committere debet.
units.tr: 8. The good man ought not to commit things that are shameful either by nature or by those that are held to be such by custom or practice.

units.la: 9. Vir bonus, cum neque sponte peccet, neque etiam ob invite facta pudore suffundi debeat, nullam in se causam verecundiae habet.
units.tr: 9. Since the good man does not sin willingly, nor ought he to be suffused with shame for things done unwillingly, he has no cause of shame in himself.

units.la: 10. Neque impudentia, neque Verecundia subjectum proprie capax est Vir bonus, cum alterum sit malum utpote vitium, alterum ex malo proveniat.
units.tr: 10. Neither shamelessness nor shame is properly a subject the good man is capable of, since the one is evil, being a vice, and the other arises from evil.

units.la: 11. Etsi Verecundia in bonum virum proprie non cadat, si tamen delinquat, cadere debet, & sic ex hypothesi seu conditione Verecundia bona & laudabilis dici poterit.
units.tr: 11. Although shame does not properly fall upon the good man, if nevertheless he offends, it ought to fall upon him, and so by hypothesis or condition shame may be called good and praiseworthy.

units.la: 12. Continentia cum sit mixtum quid, ex affectibus & ratione simul, non vera virtus, sed semivirtus aut imperfecta virtus dici meretur.
units.tr: 12. Since continence is a mixed thing, made up of affections and reason together, it deserves to be called not a true virtue but a half-virtue or imperfect virtue.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An recte Philosophus negarit Verecundiam esse virtutem, cum tamen contrarium ratio evincat: Nam propria virtutis ei competunt, & hic dicitur laudabilis: At laudabilem esse competit Virtuti, sicut cap. 12. lib. 1. hujus operis docet Philosophus. Deinde etiam sua habet extrema sicut & virtus, nam in defectu habet pavorem aut stuporem ingenii: in excessu Impudentiam, ex quibus constat esse virtutem? Resp. Per negationem, nam propria virtutis ei nullo modo competunt. Virtus enim dicitur laudabilis simpliciter & per se, Verecundia vero per accidens tantum, & ex consequenti, ut loquuntur, hinc in adolescente Verecundia laudatur, in sene vero vituperatur, quia in adolescente signum est virtutis indubitatæ, in sene est argumentum sceleris inveterati. Quod vero dicatur habere sua extrema, id non proprie competit virtuti tantum, sed etiam quibusdam affectibus mediocribus, ut cap. 8. lib. 2. subsinem docuit Philosophus: nam medium esse inter duo extrema non arguit virtutem esse, sed magis aut minus nus quam recta præscribit ratio, aut sicut recta ratio præscribit in homine reperiri: nam cum non sit habitus, sed affectus, qui à natura provenit, Virtus dici nullo modo debet.
units.tr: I. Question: Did the Philosopher rightly deny that Shamefastness is a virtue, when reason seems to prove the contrary? For proper virtues belong to it, and it is called praiseworthy; but being praiseworthy belongs to virtue, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 12 of book 1 of this work. Next, it also has extremes, as virtue does: in deficiency it has fearfulness or dullness of mind, and in excess shamelessness. From which it seems to be a virtue? Answer: By denial. For proper virtues do not belong to it in any way. Virtue is called praiseworthy simply and in itself, but Shamefastness only accidentally, and by consequence, as they say. Thus Shamefastness is praised in a young man but blamed in an old man, because in a young man it is a sign of virtue not yet doubted, while in an old man it is evidence of a wickedness long entrenched. As to its having extremes, this does not properly belong to virtue alone, but also to certain moderate affections, as the Philosopher taught in chapter 8 of book 2, near the end. For being in the middle between two extremes does not prove that a thing is a virtue; it shows only that it is more or less than right reason prescribes, or as right reason prescribes it to be found in a man. Since it is not a habit but an affection arising from nature, it ought in no way to be called a virtue.

units.la: 11. An recte definiatur Verecundia metus infamia cum omnem metum, seu timorem pallor sequatur, ut experientia docet: At Verecundiam non sequitur pallor, sed rubor ut sensus docent: Ergo male definitur metus infamia, seu ignominia? Resp. Timorem seu metum consideran duobus modis: 1. Quatenus procedit ex forti mentis imaginatione, dum scilicet spiritus à corde sursum ad cerebrum & phantasiam rapiuntur, qui illic non comprehensi propter vehementiam sui, statim per vultum aut per malas, se diffundunt, & sic Verecundia definitur per metum in hac significatione. 2. Sumitur metus pro vehementi cordis passione, dum scilicet spiritus ab externis relabuntur ad ipsum cor tanquam ad fontem suum, in quo conservantur, & quia iste metus pallore gignit, dum scilicet sanguis destitutus calore ruborem gignere non potest, ideo Verecundiæ iste metus non convenit.
units.tr: 11. Is Shamefastness rightly defined as fear of infamy? Since pallor follows every fear or dread, as experience teaches, but blushing and not pallor follows Shamefastness, as the senses show, it seems wrongly defined as fear of infamy or disgrace. Answer: Fear or dread may be considered in two ways. (1) As it proceeds from a strong imagination of the mind, when the spirits are driven upward from the heart to the brain and the imagination. There, not being held in, because of their violence, they immediately spread through the face or the cheeks. In this sense Shamefastness is defined through fear. (2) Fear is taken for a violent passion of the heart, when the spirits sink back from external things into the heart itself, as to their own source, where they are kept. Since this fear produces pallor, because the blood, deprived of heat, cannot produce redness, this fear does not suit Shamefastness.

units.la: 111. Cur Verecundiam viro probo denegarit Philosophus, cum tamen ipse lib. 3. hujus operis, cap. 10. dicat viro forti timendam esse infamiam: At verecundia nihil aliud est, quam metus infamia, tum etiam hoc lib. 4. cap. 8. dicit: Magnanimum verecundari debere in accipiendis beneficiis: At constat Magnanimum esse Virum probissimum, utpote in quo omnis fit cumulata virtus. Proinde aut Verecundia competit Viro bono, aut sui oblitus sibi contrariatur Philosophus? Resp. Non competere viro bono propter rationes supra allatas, neque sibi contrariatur Philosophus: nam, quod ad primum de viro forti sciendum est, metum sumi duobus modis: 1. Ut ex malo commissio oritur, & sic viro forti non convenit. 2. Sumitur pro metu invidiae, quae ut est Virtutis comes, sic virtuti plurimum adversatur, & sic vir fortis timere debet infamiam, quae immerito ex invidia oritur, non autem eam, quae ex rebus malis provenit. Quod ad secundum de Magnanimo pudor seu Verecundia interdum sumitur pro omni metu pudoris cujuscunque, & sic Magnanimus, verecundari debet in accipiendis beneficiis, ne scilicet magnitudinem & splendorem virtutis suae obscuret: interdum sumitur pro metu ex mala causa proveniente, & sic Magnanimo non convenit.
units.tr: 111. Why did the Philosopher deny Shamefastness to the good man, when in book 3 of this work, chapter 10, he himself says that infamy is to be feared by the brave man; and Shamefastness is nothing other than fear of infamy? Again, in book 4, chapter 8, he says that the magnanimous man ought to be ashamed in receiving benefits. But it is agreed that the magnanimous man is a most upright man, since in him all virtue is heaped up. Therefore either Shamefastness belongs to the good man, or the Philosopher, forgetting himself, contradicts himself? Answer: It does not belong to the good man, for the reasons given above, and the Philosopher does not contradict himself. As to the first point, about the brave man, we must know that fear is taken in two ways. (1) As it arises from an evil deed committed; and in this sense it does not belong to the brave man. (2) It is taken for the fear of envy, which, as it is the companion of virtue, so it is greatly opposed to virtue. In this sense the brave man ought to fear infamy, which arises undeservedly from envy, but not that which arises from bad deeds. As to the second point, about the magnanimous man: shame or Shamefastness is sometimes taken for every fear of shame of whatever kind, and in this sense the magnanimous man ought to be ashamed in receiving benefits, namely lest he obscure the greatness and splendour of his virtue. Sometimes it is taken for fear arising from a bad cause, and in this sense it does not belong to the magnanimous man.

units.la: IV. An jure fecerit, quod Verecundiam seni denegarit, cum etiam in sene sit utilis, propterea quod pudor vitii sit utilis: nam senem a turpitudine celeris revocat: At Verecundia nihil aliud est, quam pudor vitii, quia malum commissum, ut umbra corpus sequitur, sicut ait Bernhardus?
units.tr: IV. Did he act rightly in denying Shamefastness to the old man, since it is useful even in an old man, because the shame of vice is useful: for it recalls an old man from baseness? And Shamefastness is nothing other than the shame of vice, since, as Bernard says, the evil committed follows like a shadow the body?

units.la: Resp. Per negationem: nam pudor vitii proprie non competit seni, quia dum senex erubescit, signum est altius infixi scelleris, quam quod facile deleri possit, & ratio est, quia propter tarditatem spiritus (qui jam ex defectu caloris naturalis tardior multo redditur) non absque gravi sceleris suspicione ad erubescentiam aut Verecundiam commovetur.
units.tr: Answer: By denial. For the shame of vice does not properly belong to an old man. When an old man blushes, it is a sign of a wickedness more deeply fixed than can easily be removed. The reason is that, because of the slowness of his spirits (which, through the decline of natural heat, have become much slower), he is not moved to blushing or Shamefastness without a grave suspicion of wickedness.

units.la: V. An Verecundia non possit vere dici Virtus, cum quintuplex ratio idipsum probet: 1. Quia ei definitio virtutis, quae traditur lib. 2. cap. 7. competit. 2. Quia est habitus perse honestus & laudabilis. 3. Quia pudorem in dictis & factis moderatur, & media inter duo extrema versatur nemipe inter Impudentiam & Stuporem, sicut ipse testatur Aristoteles lib. 1. mag. moral. cap. 30. 4. Quia ad Verecundiam tanquam ad præcipuam Virtutem, tam sacri, quam profani autores nos hortantur: hinc D. Ambros. lib. 2. offic. inquit, Præcipua virtus est Verecundia & suavis quædam gratia pudoris, qua non in factis modo, sed in ipsis spectatur sermonibus, ne modum prætergrediaris loquendi, ne quid indecorum sermo resonet tuus. Et Theognes Poëta nullum Verecundiæ thesaurum homini meliorem esse dicit. ʃ. Quia omnibus temporibus, locis & personis apta est, utidem testatur Ambros. loco citato? Resp. Illas rationes non tanti esse momenti, ut à sententia Aristotelis discedamus. Nam ad primam, secundam & quintam, per meram negationem respondetur: nam primo cum non sit habitus, definitio Virtutis ei non competit, & secundo non dicitur laudabilis per se, sed per accidens quod nimirum sit affectus bonus, quia recta ratione regitur. In quinta Verecundiæ nomen improprie sumitur: nam proprie adolescentibus aut juvenibus tantum competit, sicut prætereatione supra allatas, testatur ipse Ambrosius lib. 2. offic. Imprimis vero, inquit, adolescentes & juvenem ætatem decet Verecundia. Tertia ratio etiam nihil probat, nam cap. 9. lib. 2. dictum est de quibusdam affectibus, quod inter duas extremitates versentur, qui tamen non sunt Virtutes propterea, quod à natura originem ducant. In quarta ratione apud Ambrosium & alios scriptores virtutis nomen latius sumitur, quam alioqui natura ipsius fert, nempe pro quolibet bono, quod intra rectæ rationis limites se continet.
units.tr: V. Can Shamefastness not truly be called a virtue, since five reasons prove this same point? (1) Because the definition of virtue given in book 2, chapter 7, applies to it. (2) Because it is a habit that is honourable and praiseworthy in itself. (3) Because it moderates shame in words and deeds, and stands between two extremes, namely between shamelessness and dullness, as Aristotle himself testifies in book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter 30. (4) Because both sacred and profane authors urge us to Shamefastness as a chief virtue. Hence St. Ambrose, book 2 of the Duties, says: "Shamefastness is a chief virtue, and a certain sweet grace of modesty, which is looked for not only in deeds but in words themselves, lest you go beyond the measure of speaking, lest your speech sound anything unseemly." And the poet Theognis says that no treasure is better for a man than Shamefastness. (5) Because it suits all times, places and persons, as Ambrose testifies in the passage cited? Answer: These reasons are not of such weight that we should depart from the opinion of Aristotle. To the first, second and fifth, a plain denial is given. For first, since it is not a habit, the definition of virtue does not belong to it; and second, it is not called praiseworthy in itself, but accidentally, namely because it is a good affection, being governed by right reason. In the fifth, the name Shamefastness is used improperly, for properly it belongs only to adolescents or young men, as Ambrose himself testifies in book 2 of the Duties, in the passage cited above: "Above all, Shamefastness becomes youth and the age of young men." The third reason also proves nothing, for in chapter 9 of book 2 it was said of certain affections that they lie between two extremes, which nevertheless are not virtues, because they take their origin from nature. In the fourth reason, in Ambrose and other writers the name of virtue is taken more widely than its nature otherwise bears, namely for any good thing that keeps within the limits of right reason.

units.la: Coronidis loco hæc quæstio moveri poterit: An pudor pudor seu verecundia sit laudabilis necne, an vero vituperabilis? Resp. Gravem hanc esse quaestionem, & inter Philosophos morales non satis convenire, utram partem sit potissimum sequenda. Nam alii statuunt omnem pudorem esse laudabilem, alii econtra omnem esse vituperabilem, quidam mediam viam tenent, & aliquam Verecundiam esse laudabilem, aliquam vituperabilem esse putant. Argumenta pro prima opinione sunt: 1. Quia pudor seu verecundia est timor turpitudinis, seu ut a Philosopho definitur metus infamiae: at ejusmodi metus est principium omnis virtutis moralis, quia nempe a rebus malis & turpibus hominem abstrahit, & ad virtutem praeparat. 2. Quia pudor virtutem custodit, vitium expellit; nam quamdiu animo obversatur, hominem intra recti & honesti fines continet; at semel animo ejectus ad omnia facinora & flagitia frenum laxat: nam ibi est scelus,
units.tr: By way of a crown to this question, the following may be raised: Is shame, or Shamefastness, praiseworthy or not, or is it rather blameworthy? Answer: This is a weighty question, and the moral philosophers do not sufficiently agree as to which side is to be followed. For some hold that all shame is praiseworthy; others, on the contrary, that all shame is blameworthy; some take a middle way, and think that some Shamefastness is praiseworthy and some blameworthy. The arguments for the first opinion are these: (1) Because shame or Shamefastness is fear of baseness, or, as it is defined by the Philosopher, fear of infamy. But such fear is the beginning of all moral virtue, because it indeed withdraws a man from evil and base things and prepares him for virtue. (2) Because shame guards virtue and expels vice; for as long as it is present to the mind, it keeps a man within the bounds of what is right and honourable; but once it is cast out of the mind, it loosens the bridle for every crime and disgrace, for there is wickedness there,

units.la: Cum pudor & probitas & metus omnis abest, ut ait Poeta. 3. Quia pudor est signum bonae naturae, & a vitiosa turpitudine abhorrentis. 4. Quia ubi pudor est, ibi est spes aliqua futurae emendationis, ubi vero non est, ibi neque est spes aliqua, unde praeclare Seneca epist. 15. ad Lucil. Nutriendus est pudor, qui, quamdiu duraverit, aliquis est bonae spei locus; & recte exclamat ille apud Plautum in Bacch. periit, cuiperiit pudor: Quia ut ait Plut. qui pudore vacat, non sentit dolorem a malefactis, & consequenter illa non avertatur. 5. Quia impudentia, quae opponitur verecundiae in excessu, est mala & vituperabilis: Ergo ex lege contrariorum ipsa verecundia (seu pudor erit laudabilis: unde Pythias Aristotelis filia, ut refert Laë tiun in vita Philosophi interrogata, quisnam esset color omnium optimus: quo ob pudorem, inquit, in genu innascitur. Argumenta pro secunda opinione sunt duo:
units.tr: "When shame and probity and all fear are absent," as the poet says. (3) Because shame is a sign of a good nature, one that abhors vicious baseness. (4) Because where there is shame, there is some hope of future amendment; where it is not, there is no hope at all. Hence Seneca admirably says in letter 15 to Lucilius: "Shame must be nurtured; as long as it endures, there is some ground for good hope." And rightly does that man in Plautus cry out: "He is lost, who has lost his shame." Because, as Plutarch says, "he who is without shame does not feel pain from wrongdoing," and consequently does not turn away from it. (5) Because impudence, which is opposed to Shamefastness in excess, is bad and blameworthy; therefore, by the law of contraries, Shamefastness itself, or shame, will be praiseworthy. Hence Pythias, the daughter of Aristotle, when asked, as Diogenes Laertius relates in the Life of the Philosopher, which colour was the best of all, answered: "The one that is born on the knee, because of shame." The arguments for the second opinion are two:

units.la: 1. Quia pudor non est comes virtutum, sed vitiorum, non honestarum, sed turpium actionum; nam rem male gestam subsequitur.
units.tr: 1. Because shame is not the companion of virtues but of vices, not of honourable actions but of shameful ones; for it follows an ill-performed deed.

units.la: 2. Quia pudor virum bonum non decet, neq; in eum cadit, sive praecedat, sive subsequatur actiones ipsius; nam cum virtutis habitu sit praeditus, nihil turpe cogitat aut agit, propter quod pudore suffundi necesse sit: proinde cum pudor in malis no in bonis reperiatur, vituperabilis tantum erit. Rationes itidem pro tertia opinione sunt duae: 1. Quia ut ait Philosophus hoc cap. ult. huius operis, lib. huius 4. in adolescente seu juvenili aetate pudor est honestus & ingenuus, nam peccatis facile adolescentes abstrahit, & nativa ingenii ad virtutem in iis propensionem denotat. In senilibus vero & adultioribus est turpis & vituperabilis, propterea quod malum commissum in iis sequatur, neq; agere quicquam debent, propter quod pudore suffundantur.
units.tr: 2. Because shame does not befit a good man, nor does it fall upon him, whether it precedes or follows his actions. For since he is endowed with the habit of virtue, he thinks and does nothing base, on account of which he would need to be suffused with shame. Therefore, since shame is found in bad men and not in good, it will be merely blameworthy. There are likewise two reasons for the third opinion: 1. Because, as the Philosopher says in the last chapter of this work, book 4, in a youth or young man shame is honourable and noble, for it draws young people away from sins and indicates a natural inclination of character towards virtue in them. In old men and those of more advanced age, however, it is base and blameworthy, because the wrong they have committed follows them, and they ought to do nothing for which they would be suffused with shame.

units.la: 2. Quia nisi quidam pudor esset laudabilis, quidam vituperabilis, frustra opus esset recta ratione, quae eam regat & dirigat; nam quod aliter se habere nequit, alterius ductu, ut in alteram naturam commutetur, opus non habet: at consequens est absurdum: igitur & antecedens.
units.tr: 2. Because unless some shame were praiseworthy and some blameworthy, right reason, which governs and directs it, would be needless. For what cannot be otherwise has no need to be led by another so as to be changed into another nature. But the consequent is absurd; therefore so is the antecedent.

units.la: Pro decisione quaestionis distinguendum erit inter pudorem naturalem & moralem, quorum ille est indifferens per se, id est, neque laudabilis, neque vituperabilis, quia tantum est affectus a natura proveniens, niens, hic est vel laudabilis vel vituperabilis, prout rectæ rationis regimen accessit vel recessit abeo. 2. Distinguendum erit inter pudorem moralem moderatum & immoderatum: Moderatum is dicitur, qui fit ex præscripto rectæ rationis, ubi, quando, ergα quos, quantum, quomodo & cur fieri debet, & hic est licitus & laudabilis: Immoderatum e contra, qui fit contra præscriptum rectæ rationis non observatis circumstantiis, & hic est illicitus & vituperabilis, quia tantum est metus justæ reprehensionis, qui ex conscientia malefacto oritur. In priori genere est pudor, le, qui peccatum hominis antecedit, eumque ab illo abstrahit: posteriori est pudor, qui subsequitur post perpetrationem scelerum: unde sequitur pudorem quendam esse laudabilem, quendam etiam vituperabilem, prout rectam rationem vel fugit vel sequitur.
units.tr: To decide the question, a distinction must be made between natural and moral shame. The former is indifferent in itself, that is, neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy, since it is merely an affection arising from nature. The latter is either praiseworthy or blameworthy, according as the guidance of right reason has been added to it or withdrawn from it. 2. A distinction must be made between moderate and immoderate moral shame. Moderate is that which arises in accordance with the prescription of right reason, where, when, toward whom, how much, how and why it ought to occur; and this is lawful and praiseworthy. Immoderate, on the contrary, is that which arises contrary to the prescription of right reason, the circumstances not being observed; and this is unlawful and blameworthy, since it is merely fear of just reproach arising from a guilty conscience. To the former kind belongs the shame which precedes a man's sin and draws him away from it; to the latter belongs the shame which follows the commission of wickedness. Whence it follows that some shame is praiseworthy and some also blameworthy, according as it flees from or follows right reason.

units.la: Poterit & hoc breviter quæri: An pudor in viro bono præcedat ipsam rationem necne? Et resp. breviter pudorem duobus modis considerari: 1. Pro imbecillitate naturæ, & sic quia est motus naturæ, non voluntatis rationem ipsam in bonis dicitur præcedere.
units.tr: This may also be briefly asked: Does shame in a good man precede reason itself or not? And the answer is that shame may be considered in two ways. (1) With respect to the weakness of nature; and so, since it is a movement of nature and not of the will, it is said to precede reason even in good men.

units.la: 2. Sumitur pro suspicione sceleris commissi, & sic non præcedit, quia boni, quà tales scelera non admittunt.
units.tr: (2) It is taken as the suspicion of a crime committed; and so it does not precede, since good men, as such, do not commit crimes.

units.la: LIBER
units.tr: BOOK

units.la: LIBER QVINTUS.
units.tr: BOOK FIVE.

units.la: OSTQVAM Philosophus egit de iis Virtutibus, quas lib. 2. cap. 8. sibi declarandas proposuit, demū hoc lib. f. per tot. agit de ipsa Justitia, quae cum sit praeclarissima & cognitu difficilima virtus, de ea fusius & accuratius agit, nec absque ratione posterior in ordine virtutum collocatur, quia cum sit quodammodo omnis virtus, & veluti aggregatum quid ex omnibus in genere virtutibus, tunc demum tractanda fuit, cum reliquae omnes cognitae & perspectae essent; nam ad ipsius meliorem notitiam & naturam commodè declarandam reliquarum omnium virtutum cognitione opus est. Poterit hic liber non incommode inscribi de Justitia & Jure, nam de utroque hic agitur, & alterum ad alterius cognitionem necessariò requiritur, sicut etiam titulus extat apud Jureconsultos de Justitia & Jure. Dividitur verò in tres partes: In quarum priori agit de Justitia propriè dicta sive ea sit universalis, sive particularis. In secunda de Aequo & bono, quae sunt affectiones Justitiae. In tertia de Justitia improprie dicta, quae tantum propter similitudinem, quam habet cum vera Justitia, nomen Justitiae sortitur. Prioris partis duo sunt tractatus: In primo de Justitiae ipsius natura fusè agit. In secundo Jus dividit in civile & oeconomicum, & utrumque membrum copiosè explicat. Primi tractatus, in quo de Justitia agitur, quinque sunt membra. bra. In primo de Justitia in communi agit, & quam dividit in universalem & particularem. In secundo agit de Justitia particulari, quam definit & subdivid in suas species, nempe in Distributivam & Commutativam. In tertio agit de Justitia Distributiva & modum inveniendi medii in ipsa prolixius declarat. In quarto agit de Commutativa & varias difficultates circa ipsum medium quoque explicat. In quinto errorem vulgo receptum circa medium Justitiae tam Distributivae, quam Commutativae excludit, & simul etiam opinionem Pythagoricorum refellit.
units.tr: Since the Philosopher has dealt with those virtues which, in book 2, chapter 8, he proposed to set out, he now in this book treats throughout of Justice itself. Since it is the most excellent virtue and the most difficult to know, he treats of it at greater length and with greater care. Nor without reason is it placed last in the order of the virtues: since it is in a way every virtue, and as it were a whole made up of all the virtues taken together, it had to be treated only when all the others were known and understood. For to explain its nature and understanding better and more conveniently, a knowledge of all the other virtues is needed. This book may not inappropriately be titled On Justice and Right, for both are treated here, and the one is necessarily required for knowledge of the other; just as the title On Justice and Right also stands among the jurists. It is divided into three parts. In the first he treats of Justice properly so called, whether it is universal or particular. In the second, of the Equitable and the good, which are affections of Justice. In the third, of Justice improperly so called, which takes the name of Justice only on account of its resemblance to true Justice. The first part has two treatises: In the first he deals fully with the very nature of Justice. In the second he divides Right into civil and economic, and explains each of these members at length. The first treatise, in which Justice is discussed, has five sections. In the first he deals with Justice in general, and divides it into universal and particular. In the second he deals with particular Justice, which he defines and subdivides into its species, namely Distributive and Commutative. In the third he deals with Distributive Justice and explains at greater length the manner of finding the mean in it. In the fourth he deals with Commutative Justice and also explains various difficulties concerning the mean in it. In the fifth he excludes the error commonly received concerning the mean of both Distributive and Commutative Justice, and at the same time refutes the opinion of the Pythagoreans.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CAPUT I.

units.la: PRimum membrum tribus primis absolvitur capitibus: In primo justitiam popularand & veluti in typo describit. Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima agendum sibi proponit de Justitia, ejusque contrario Injustitia. In secunda vulgarem utriusque descriptionem secundum receptam tum temporis opinionem affert. In tertia, ut viam muniat ad Justitiae divisionem, quam allaturus est, tres regulas proponit. In prima igitur de Justitia sibi agendum proponit: 1. Circa quos actus versetur seu quas actiones habeat, qua parte maxime distinguitur a reliquis Virtutibus: nam reliquae affectus potius moderantur internos, qua actus externos, non quod non habeat suas actiones externas, sed quia primo respiciant cupiditates internas, a quibus actiones externae profluunt. Justitia vero primario respicit actiones externas, quia ejus vis aut natura non tam perficit habentem quam alium, in quem exercetur. 2. Videndum, inquit qualis fit mediocritas, seu quale medium: nam reliquae versantur in medio rationis, ut singularum inductione patebit, hęc vero præsertim commutativa, in medio rei, ut infra patebit. 3. Circa quæ sit medium, aut quorum extremorum sit medium, quo etiam modo a reliquis distinguitur; nam non, ut illæ, nunc accedit, nunc recedit ab hoc vel illo extremo ratione nostri, sed æqualiter ab utroque distat.
units.tr: The first member is completed in the first three chapters. In the first he describes justice in its popular sense, as it were in outline. The chapter has three parts. In the first he sets out to treat of justice and its opposite, injustice. In the second he gives the common description of each, according to the opinion then accepted. In the third, to prepare the way for the division of justice that he is about to offer, he proposes three rules. In the first part, then, he proposes to treat of justice in three respects: (1) with what acts it is concerned, or what actions it has, and in what respect it is most clearly distinguished from the other virtues. The other virtues govern internal affections rather than external acts, not because they lack external actions of their own, but because they first regard the internal desires from which external actions flow. Justice, however, chiefly regards external actions, because its force or nature does not so much perfect the one who has it as the other person toward whom it is exercised. (2) We must consider, he says, what kind of mean or mediocrity it is: the other virtues lie in a mean of reason, as will be clear from an induction of each of them, but this virtue, especially the commutative kind, lies in a mean of the thing, as will be shown below. (3) With what things the mean is concerned, or of which extremes it is the mean, and in what way it is thereby distinguished from the others. For it does not, as they do, sometimes draw near to and sometimes recede from this or that extreme in relation to us, but stands equally distant from both.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis vulgarem Justitiæ & Injustitiæ descriptionem affert, nempe quod Justitia sit habitus, quo si quis sit præditus, possit agere, & agat & velit e iam justa: Injustitia vero econtra. In hac descriptione ad naturam Justitiæ constituendā tria requiruntur: 1. Propensio & aptitudo ad juste agendum, quæ ex ipso habitu proficiscitur, nam habitus & proclivitatem & facilitatem ingenerat. II. Requiritur actio, quæ agat, non enim satis est proclivitatem, & facilitatem ad juste agendum habere, nisi etiam quis agat. III. ut velit justa, id est, justas actiones exerceat, ex libera voluntate, facili propensione & certo judicio, secus enim nulla erit Justitiæ laus. Eodem etiam modo Plato in Gorgia Justitiam definit habitum, per quem justa agant, & velint homines, nam ad perfectionem Justitiæ non tantum externa actio, sed etiam internus voluntatis consensus requiritur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he gives the common description of justice and injustice, namely that justice is a habit by which a person who possesses it is able to act, and does act and wills things that are just; injustice is the reverse. In this description three things are required to constitute the nature of justice: (1) a propensity and aptitude for acting justly, which proceeds from the habit itself, for a habit produces both inclination and facility. (2) Action is required, for it is not enough to have an inclination and facility for acting justly unless one also acts. (3) That one wills just things, that is, performs just actions from free will, with ready inclination and sound judgment; otherwise there would be no praise for justice. In the same way Plato, in the Gorgias, defines justice as the habit by which men act and will what is just, for the perfection of justice requires not only external action but also the inward consent of the will.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis tres affert regulas generales, quibus rationem reddat descriptionis Justitiæ, quā modo attulit, & viam præmuniat ad divisionem Justitiæ, quam in sequentibus allaturus est. I. Regula continet discrimen inter facultates & scientias & inter ter ipsos habitus, quod nempe facultates & scientiae recipiant contraria, aut absque ullo naturae suae incommodo ad contraria juxta tendant, habitus vero non, verbi gratia: Sanitas est habitus corporis, a quo proficiscuntur actiones non laesae aut mutilae, sed integrae: nam qui bene sanus est recte & valenter ambulat: at ab eodem habitu non proficiscuntur actiones contrariae veluti actiones laesae aut mutilae: Qui enim sanus est, qua talis aegre aut infirmiter no ambulat. Facultates vero & scientiae per contraria definiri possunt, ut facultas visiva recipit simul albedinem & nigredinem, sic & eadem est scientia albedinis & nigredinis veri & falsi, boni & mali. Sed habitus Justitiae etsi actiones edat justas, non tamen edit injustas actiones illi contrarias, quod modo a simili in exemplo sanitatis docuit Philosophus. Plura vide de hac differentia lib. 9. Metaph. cap. 5. ubi ex professo hanc quaestionem tractat Aristoteles II. Regula est de modo cognoscendorum habituum, seu qua ratione cognoisci possint habitus, & duos prescribit modos: 1. Est ex natura ipsorum repugnante, verbi gratia: Si quis novit quid sit bona corporis constitutio, facile e contrario cognoscit, quid sit mala constitutio, quia isti duo habitus inter se natura sua pugnant. 2. Modus ducitur a natura subjectorum, quibus insunt habitus, quae si repugnent sibi invicem, docet etiam & habitus inter se pugnare, verbi gratia: Si densitas carnis sit causa bonae constitutionis in corpore, raritas carnis erit causa malae constitutionis. Usus hujus regulae est, ut doceat bene se describsisse supra Justitiam & Injustitiam, nam quia habitus sunt contrarii ex se invicem facile cognoscuntur. III. Regula est de homonymia, nam si unum contrariorum sit homonymum, & alterum erit ex lege contrariorum, quae traditur lib. 1. Topic. cap. 14. Proinde si Iustitia sit homonyma, ut infeqq. patet b.c, etiam Iniustitia erit.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he offers three general rules, by which he gives an account of the description of justice just offered and prepares the way for the division of justice that he will give in what follows. (1) The first rule concerns the difference between faculties and sciences, and between the habits themselves: faculties and sciences receive contraries, or without any harm to their nature incline toward contraries, whereas habits do not. For example, health is a habit of the body from which proceed actions that are not impaired or maimed but whole; for one who is healthy walks rightly and vigorously. But from the same habit there do not proceed contrary actions, such as impaired or maimed actions: one who is healthy, as such, does not walk painfully or weakly. Faculties and sciences, however, can be defined through contraries: the faculty of sight receives both whiteness and blackness at once, and the same is true of the science of whiteness and blackness, of true and false, of good and evil. But the habit of justice, although it produces just actions, does not produce unjust actions contrary to them, as the Philosopher has just taught by a similar example of health. See more on this difference in the ninth book of the Metaphysics, chapter 5, where Aristotle treats this question expressly. (2) The second rule concerns the way habits are known, or by what means habits can be recognised, and it prescribes two methods: (a) the first is drawn from the nature of the habits themselves, which are opposed: for example, if someone knows what a good bodily constitution is, he easily recognises from the contrary what a bad constitution is, because these two habits are opposed by their nature. (b) The second method is drawn from the nature of the subjects in which the habits inhere; if these subjects are opposed to one another, it also teaches that the habits are opposed. For example, if density of flesh is the cause of a good constitution in the body, rarity of flesh will be the cause of a bad constitution. The use of this rule is to show that he has described justice and injustice well above, for since habits are contrary to one another they are easily known from each other. (3) The third rule concerns homonymy: if one of two contraries is homonymous, the other will also be, by the law of contraries, which is set out in the first book of the Topics, chapter 14. Therefore, if justice is homonymous, as is clear in what follows at b.c, injustice will be so too.

units.la: Notandum Iustitiae nomen multis modis accipi, praecipuè vero quinque: 1. Generaliter prout brutis ratione carentibus etiam competit. Sic Ælian. lib. 2. de anim. cap. 18. Delphinos vocat iustos, quod ubi pisces venari fuerint in praedae distributione ita agant, ut majore parte ei relinquat, qui capturae causa fuit. Sic l. 5 idem 39. multa de Leonis Iustitia refert. 2. Sumitur Iustitia pro Legali sive Mosaica, & Euangelica sive Christiana, de qua tantum Theologi, nihil praeci-piunt Philosophi, propterea quod a causis secundis non proprie pendeat. 3. Sumitur pro eo officio, quod defunctis exhibetur: Sic apud Varronem lib. 1. de Ling. Lat. iusti dicuntur & iustitiarii, qui defunctis sua iusta solvunt, & eorum exequi recte obeunt. 4. Proaequali praedae distributione, quae inter praedones & latrones servatur, quomodo Cic. lib. 2. offic. dixit: Cum igitur tanta vis sit Iustitiae, ut etiam latronum opes augeat atque confirmet, quantam ejus vim inter leges & iudicia Reipub. fore putamus? 5. Pro eo aequali quod in communi hominum societate cernitur, & sic de ea toto hoc libro quinto agit Philosophus.
units.tr: It should be noted that the name justice is taken in many ways, but chiefly in five: (1) generally, as it also belongs to brute animals that lack reason. So Aelian, in the second book On Animals, chapter 18, calls dolphins just, because when fishermen are sharing out the prey they act so that they leave the larger part to the one who was the cause of the catch. Likewise, in the fifth book, chapter 39, he relates many things about the justice of the lion. (2) Justice is taken for legal or Mosaic justice, and for evangelical or Christian justice, of which only the theologians treat; the philosophers say nothing of these, because they do not depend properly on secondary causes. (3) It is taken for the duty owed to the dead. So in Varro, On the Latin Language, book 1, those are called just and dutiful (iustitiarii) who pay their due rites to the dead and properly perform their funeral observances. (4) It is taken for the equal distribution of plunder, which is kept among pirates and robbers, as Cicero said in the second book of On Duties: "Since, therefore, justice has such power that it even increases and strengthens the wealth of robbers, how great a power do we suppose it will have among the laws and courts of the Commonwealth?" (5) It is taken for that equality which is seen in the common society of men, and it is in this sense that the Philosopher treats of justice throughout this whole fifth book.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.
