units.la: 1. Iustitia est habitus, per quem iusta possunt agere, & agunt, & volunt homines, Iniustitia econtra.
units.tr: 1. Justice is a habit by which men are able to do just things, and do them, and want to do them; injustice is the reverse.

units.la: Pp 2.Fa-
units.tr: Pp 2.Fa-

units.la: 2. Facultates & Scientiæ ab habitibus differunt, quod illæ sint receptiva contrariorum, habitus vero non.
units.tr: 2. Faculties and sciences differ from habits in that the former admit of contraries, whereas habits do not.

units.la: 3. Habitus contrarii cognoscuntur vel ex natura ipsorum repugnante, vel ex natura subjectorum quibus insunt.
units.tr: 3. Contrary habits are known either from the repugnant nature of the habits themselves or from the nature of the subjects in which they inhere.

units.la: 4. Si unum contrariorum sit homonymum, etiam alterum erit, quia hoc lex & vis contrariorum jubet.
units.tr: 4. If one of two contraries is homonymous, the other will be too, since this is what the law and force of contraries require.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DUBIA.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Cur statim initio libri dicat videndum circa quas actiones versetur Justitia, cum tamen lib. 2. cap. 3. hujus operis circa affectus versari dixerit omnes virtutes: id, quod etiam Thiagines Pythagoricus apud Stob. serm. 5. de Justitia probat, Affectus, inquit, sunt materia omnium in genere virtutum. Hinc ergo contrariatur sibi Philosophus? Resp. Per negationem: nam lib. 2. dixit virtutes versari circa affectus tanquam internum suum objectum & commune, quia perturbationibus animi medetur virtutes, siquidem appetitum rectæ rationis subjiciunt: at vero considerat virtutes & inprimis Justitiam quoad extra, seu quatenus actiones externas edat, & propterea recte dixit distinguendas esse actiones Justitiæ, quia ab iis tota vis & natura Justitiæ dependet, & ab iis in hominum cognitionem devenit.
units.tr: I. It is asked why he says at the very start of the book that we must see which actions justice is concerned with, when in Book 2, chapter 3 of this work he said that all the virtues are concerned with the affections. Thiagines the Pythagorean also proves this in Stobaeus, Sermon 5, on Justice: "The affections," he says, "are the matter of all the virtues in general." Does the Philosopher then contradict himself? Answer: No. In Book 2 he said that the virtues are concerned with the affections as their internal and common object, because the virtues heal the disturbances of the mind, since they bring the appetite under right reason. But he considers the virtues, and above all justice, with respect to what is external, or insofar as they produce external actions. For this reason he rightly said that the actions of justice must be distinguished, since the whole force and nature of justice depends on them and through them justice comes to be known among men.

units.la: II. Cur in definitione Justitia dicat esse habitum, per quem res justas agunt homines, cum sic fit definienda, sequitur idem per idem definiri, quod vitium taxat idem Philosophus lib. 5. Top. cap. 4. nam idem per idem definire est, obscurum peraque obscurum explicare & petitio principii, ut ab Aristotele vocatur 2. anal. prior. cap. 16. Resp. Per nega-
units.tr: II. Why, when he defines justice as the habit by which men do just things, does he say it is defined in this way? It follows that the same thing is defined by the same thing, which the same Philosopher censures in Book 5 of the Topics, chapter 4. For to define the same thing by the same thing is to explain the obscure by the equally obscure, and is a petitio principii, as Aristotle calls it in the Prior Analytics 2, chapter 16. Answer: by denial.

units.la: [the word continues on the next page: negationem, nam etsi Justitiam per justa definiat, non identica est definitio, quia cum definitio nihil sit aliud, quam rei definiendae explicatio & enodatio, Justitiam in abstracto definivit per justum, in concreto tanquam per aliquid notius, siquidem subjectum citius devenit sub sensus, quam accidentia. Dein etiam justum in definitione Justitiae sumitur pro aequali in ordine ad bonum civitatis, quod est duplex, vel Arithmeticum, quando verbi gratia: tantum additur, quantum adimitur, unde jus naturale derivatur, secundo est Geometricum, idque rursus duplex vel privatum, quoad personam ex placito, cum scilicet unusquisque sua parte se contentum putat, nec ultra petit, vel est publicum, quoad Reipubl. ex praescripto Magistratus, quando scilicet res non privati uniuscujusque arbitrio, sed Magistratus tantum distribuuntur, unde jus positivum & municipale nascitur.
units.tr: For even though he defines justice through the just, the definition is not circular. A definition is nothing other than the explanation and unfolding of the thing to be defined. He defined justice in the abstract through the just, but in the concrete he defined it as through something better known, since the subject comes under the senses sooner than its accidents. Further, the just, as used in the definition of justice, means the equal with respect to the good of the state. This equal is twofold: either arithmetical, as when, for example, just as much is added as is taken away, and from this natural law is derived; or geometrical. The geometrical equal is again twofold, either private, with respect to persons, by agreement, when each man thinks himself content with his own share and seeks no more; or public, with respect to the commonwealth, by the prescription of the magistrate, when things are distributed not by the judgment of each private person but by the magistrate alone, and from this positive and municipal law arises.

units.la: III. Cur etiam in eadem definitione addat, per quam quis justa velit, cum sic videatur Justitia in sola voluntate esse collocata: juxta definitionem Ctorum, quae habetur apud Justinian. lib. 1. Instit. tit. 1. Justitia est constans & perpetua voluntas suum cuique tribuendi.
units.tr: III. Why also does he add, in the same definition, "by which someone wills just things," since justice would seem in this way to be placed in the will alone? This follows the definition of the jurists found in Justinian, Institutes, Book 1, title 1: "Justice is a constant and perpetual will to render to each his due."

units.la: Et Plutarchus in vita Catonis Uticensis Justitiam reliquis virtutibus praefert, quod sola resideat in voluntate, reliqua autem in appetitu. At vero Philosophus ipse cap. ult. lib. 1. hujus operis, dicit, omnes virtutes ad ὀρεκτικὸν, id est, appetitivam animae facultatem spectare, cum quo etiam consentiunt reliqui omnes Ethnici, qui de virtutibus egerunt, nam nihil certius quam tunc demum cepisse homines virtutes amplecti, cum pugnam inter affectus & rectam rationem deprehendissent, unde contra dicit sibi Philosophus? Resp. Nihilominus manere tamen in appetitu Justitiam, sicut & reliquas virtutes, quia in appetitu tria considerantur: 1. Cupiditas aliquid habendi. 2. Ira. 3. Voluntas, quae rectae rationi paret, & illius jus exequitur semper quae cum ratione & judicio conjuncta est & hominis propria. Nihil igitur contrarii admittit Philosophus, cum dicit, Justitiam esse in voluntate & appetitu seu ὀρέξει, quia appetitus est duplex, alius ratione destitutus in quo sunt cupiditas & ira, quae nobis cum belluis communes sunt: alius rationi parens, in quo est voluntas, & in quo tanquam in subjecto interno resident virtutes practicae.
units.tr: Plutarch, in the Life of Cato of Utica, also prefers justice to the other virtues because it resides in the will alone, while the others reside in the appetite. But the Philosopher himself, in the last chapter of Book 1 of this work, says that all the virtues look to the orektikon, that is, the appetitive faculty of the soul [ὀρεκτικὸν]. All the other Gentiles who have treated of the virtues agree with this, for nothing is more certain than that men first took up the virtues when they perceived the struggle between the affections and right reason. How then does the Philosopher not contradict himself? Answer: Justice nonetheless remains in the appetite, as do the other virtues, since three things are considered in the appetite: (1) desire to have something; (2) anger; (3) the will, which obeys right reason and carries out its command, and which is always joined with reason and judgment and is proper to man. The Philosopher therefore admits nothing contrary when he says that justice is in the will and the appetite, or in the orexis [ὄρεξις], because appetite is twofold: one kind is destitute of reason, and in it are desire and anger, which we share with the beasts; the other obeys reason, and in it is the will, and in it, as in an internal subject, the practical virtues reside.

units.la: IV. Quomodo in prima Regula dicat habitus non esse contrariorum, seu non tendere ad contraria, cum tamen ratio contrarium evincat.
units.tr: IV. How does he say in the first rule that a habit is not of contraries, or does not tend to contraries, when reason nonetheless proves the contrary?

units.la: Nam Temperantia versatur circa voluptatem & dolorem, Fortitudo circa fiduciam & timorem, & constat istas virtutes esse habitus. Dein etiam scientia est habitus, ut ex cap. 3. lib. 6. hujus operis satis liquet: At scientiam esse contrariorum, praeter experientiam probat hoc loco Aristoteles, nam quae scientia de uno contrariorum agit, de altero etiam agit? Resp. Habitum esse contrariorum duobus modis considerari, vel objective, vel operative ut loquuntur. Cum Philosophus diceret habitum no esse contrariorum, operative tantum intellexit. Nam etsi Temperantia & Fortitudo versentur circa contraria, id fit objective tantum, & in unoquoque objecto duo sunt: 1. Unum per se, 2. per accidens. Circa fiduciam versatur Fortitudo per se; circa timorem per accidens, quatenus scilicet eum avertatur: At vero eadem Fortitudo non proproducit actiones simul fortes & contrarias. Quod ad secundam Instantiam de scientia, sciendum est, habitus esse triplices, nempe Contemplativos, Ethicos & Practicos: Philosophus vero hic de habitibus Practicis & Ethicis loquitur, non vero de Contemplativis qualis est scientia, sed de iis ex professo agit lib.6.seqq.
units.tr: For temperance is concerned with pleasure and pain, fortitude with confidence and fear, and it is agreed that these virtues are habits. Again, science is a habit, as is quite clear from chapter 3 of Book 6 of this work. But Aristotle proves here, apart from experience, that science is of contraries: for whatever science treats of one of two contraries, does it not also treat of the other? Answer: A habit can be considered in relation to contraries in two ways, either objectively or operatively, as they say. When the Philosopher said that a habit is not of contraries, he understood it only operatively. For although temperance and fortitude are concerned with contraries, this happens only objectively, and in each object there are two things: (1) one thing per se, (2) one per accidens. Fortitude is concerned per se with confidence, and per accidens with fear, insofar as it averts it. But the same fortitude does not produce actions that are at once brave and contrary. As for the second objection, about science, it must be understood that habits are of three kinds, namely contemplative, ethical and practical. The Philosopher here speaks of practical and ethical habits, not of contemplative ones such as science; he treats of these ex professo in Book 6 and following.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: POstquam attulit definitionem Justitiae in communi, pergit hoc caput secundum ad divisionem explicandam, & nominalem potius, quam realem Justitiae hic divisionem affert, ex qua tamen divisio Justitiae secundum naturam non parum illucescit. Partes capitis sunt duae: In prima divisionem homonymorum adfert hoc consilio, ut ostendat utro in genere fit Justitia & Injustitia; In secunda divisionem Justitiae adducit, & singulas partes breviter & succincte explicat.
units.tr: After giving the definition of justice in general, this second chapter goes on to explain the division. It offers a nominal rather than a real division of justice, though from it the division of justice according to its nature is not a little clarified. The chapter has two parts. In the first he gives the division of homonyms, to show under which genus justice and injustice fall. In the second he gives the division of justice and briefly and succinctly explains each part.

units.la: In prima igitur divisionem homonymorum (quae nomen unum & commune, sed naturae rationem & essentiam secundum illud nomen habent diversam) adfert, nempe quod homonyma vulgo sint duplicia: Alia enim sunt perspicua & cognitu facilia, utpote quae propter diversitatem naturae longissime a se invicem distant, & ideo fortuita homonyma, vel a fortuna dicuntur, ut verbi gratia: clavis est simul instrumentum, quo ostium clauditur, & aiculum quoddam parvum inter humeros & jugulicomissuram. Secundo alia sunt homonyma obscura & cognitu difficilia, utpote quae propter cognatio-nem nem & similitudinem à se invicem ilicò & ab omnibus non discerni possunt, & ista vocantur secundū analogiam homonyma, ut verbi gratia: Cum Magnificentiæ & Liberalitati idem nomen Liberalitatis imponitur, & Temperantiæ & Continentiæ idē etiam nomen. Sed de hac homonymorum divisione, plura vide ad cap. 4. lib. 1. hujus operis, tum etiam lib.7.Phys. Acroas. cap.ult. & cap.15.lib.1.post. anal. Hanc divisionem ideò attulit Philosophus, ut ostenderet ad secundum genus homonymorum spectare Justitiam & Injustitiam, propterea quod altera ab altera non sit ita separata, ut ab omnibus intelligi possit discrimen, sicut in progressu patebit.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he gives the division of homonyms (words that are one and the same name but have a different account of nature and essence under that name). Homonyms are commonly of two kinds. Some are plain and easy to recognise, since because their natures differ so widely they are far apart from one another; these are called chance homonyms, or homonyms from chance. For example, "key" is both an instrument by which a door is locked and a small bone between the shoulder and the joint of the neck. Others are obscure and hard to recognise, since because of kinship and similarity they cannot readily be distinguished from one another by everyone; these are called homonyms according to analogy. For example, the same name "liberality" is given to Magnificence and to Liberality, and the same name is also given to Temperance and Continence. For more on this division of homonyms, see chapter 4 of book 1 of this work, and also Physics book 7, last chapter, and Posterior Analytics book 1, chapter 15. The Philosopher offered this division in order to show that justice and injustice belong to the second kind of homonyms, because one is not so separated from the other that the difference can be grasped by everyone, as will become clear in the course of the work.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis divisione Justitiæ adducit, ex contrario ipsius, nempe Injustitia, propterea quod vitia, ut frequentiora, sint etiam notiora, magisque propter similitudinē ipsorum in hominum cognitionem deveniant, nam injustus, qui Injustitia laborat dicitur duobus modis, & qui leges transgreditur, & qui iniquus est, seu plurris, quam debet aut æquum sit, cupidus est: ergo etiam à contrario Justus dicetur: 1. Qui leges non transgreditur. 2. Qui plus quam quod sui ipsius est, aut quod ratio & æquitas postulat, non cupit: sed ne quis putet Philosophum per injustum intellexisse eum, qui simpliciter aliquid magis cupit, in quibusvis rebus, restringit hanc cupiditatem ad bona tantum externa, ut sunt divitiæ & honos, quæ vulgò vocantur bona fortunæ, & in quibus solis Justitia, cum suo contrario Injustitia, tanquam in sua materia proprie versantur. Cæterum quia fit interdum, ut quis non plus sed minus sibi appetat, verbi gratia: in simpliciter malis, ut in infortuniis, miserius & id genus cæteris, quæritur, ad quid spectare hoc factum debeat, ad Justitiam ne, an ad injustitiam? Respondet ad injustitiam pertinere: nam qui minus appetens est mali, magis est appetens boni, & ideo erit pluris cupidus, quam æquum aut justum sit, & proinde iniquus legum transgressor, si quidem leges Justitiæ universalis hoc exigunt, ut quod quisq; fecit aut promeruit, sive in bonis, sive in malis, id etiam merito ferat.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he gives the division of justice by way of its opposite, injustice. Vices, being more frequent, are also better known, and through their resemblance they come more readily to human knowledge. An unjust man, one who suffers from injustice, is spoken of in two ways: (1) one who transgresses the laws, and (2) one who is unfair, that is, greedy for more than he ought or than is fair. By contrast, then, the just man will be called: (1) one who does not transgress the laws; (2) one who does not desire more than what is his own, or more than reason and equity demand. But lest anyone think the Philosopher meant by the unjust man one who simply desires more of anything whatever, he restricts this desire to external goods, such as riches and honour, which are commonly called goods of fortune. Justice, together with its contrary injustice, is properly concerned with these alone, as with its own matter. Moreover, since it sometimes happens that someone desires less rather than more for himself, for example in things that are simply bad, such as misfortunes, poverty and the like, the question arises whether such an act belongs to justice or to injustice. He answers that it belongs to injustice. For one who desires less of evil is more eager for good, and so will be greedy for more than is due or just, and therefore an unfair transgressor of the laws, if indeed the laws of universal justice require that each person should rightly bear whatever he has done or deserved, whether in goods or in evils.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Justitia & Injustitia dicuntur multifariam, & sunt homonyma.
units.tr: 1. Justice and injustice are spoken of in many ways, and they are homonyms.

units.la: 2. Homonyma sunt duorum generum, alia enim sunt cognitu facilia, & vocantur fortuita homonyma, alia sunt cognitu difficilia propter cognationem, & vocantur secundum analogiam homonyma.
units.tr: 2. Homonyms are of two kinds: some are easy to know and are called chance homonyms; others are hard to know because of kinship, and are called homonyms according to analogy.

units.la: 3. Injustus dicitur duobus modis, & qui leges transgreditur, & qui plus quam debet aut æquum est, cupit, Justus econtra.
units.tr: 3. The unjust man is spoken of in two ways: one who transgresses the laws, and one who desires more than he ought or than is fair. The just man is the opposite.

units.la: 4. Justitia cum suo contrario Injustitia non versatur simpliciter circa omnia bona, sed tantum circa bona externa.
units.tr: 4. Justice, together with its contrary injustice, is not concerned with all goods simply, but only with external goods.

units.la: 5. Qui minus appetit malis, & plus boni, quam debet, iniquus est legum transgressor & injustus.
units.tr: 5. One who desires less of evil and more of good than he ought is unfair, a transgressor of the laws, and unjust.

units.la: 6. Iniquitas est affectio communis omnis injustitia, sicut æquitas Justitia.
units.tr: 6. Unfairness is the common affection of all injustice, as equity is of justice.

units.la: Quæritur: Rectè Philosophus negarit, illum justum esse, qui minus appetit mali, & plus sibi boni, cum sequatur ductum naturæ, quæ ut provida rerum parens & sui & rerum omnium à se conditarum conservationem intendit.Cum ergo naturam sequatur, injustè non agit, nam super jus naturæ fundantur omnes leges humanæ? Respond. Falsum esse,quod sequatur ductum naturæ, Nam Justitia non versatur circa bona naturæ, sed circa bona fortunæ seu externa. Qui igitur in bonis externis minus appetit mali, quam debet aut promeruit, plus appetit boni, & ideo erit injustus, nam Justitia,ut in sequentib. patebit,suum cuique tribuit.
units.tr: Question: Did the Philosopher rightly deny that a man is just who desires less of evil and more of good for himself, since he follows the guidance of nature, which, as the provident parent of things, intends the preservation both of itself and of all the things it has created. Therefore, since he follows nature, he does not act unjustly, for all human laws are founded upon the law of nature? Answer: It is false that he follows the guidance of nature. For justice is not concerned with goods of nature, but with goods of fortune, that is, external goods. So one who, in external goods, desires less of evil than he ought or has deserved, desires more of good, and therefore will be unjust. For justice, as will become clear in what follows, gives to each his own.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: DEscripsit jam in communi Justitiam 1.cap. & homonymiam distinxit secundo capite, hoc tertio capite Justitiam dividit in suas species, nempe in Universalem & Particularem. Partes capitis sunt tres: In prima de justo agit in genere,propterea quod subjectum solcat esse notius ipso habitu, qui inest subjecto,& ideo non de Justitia,sed de justo in concreto agit. In secunda parte de Justitia universali tractat. In tertia dubium quoddam solvit,quod contra istam doctrinam afferri poterat.
units.tr: In the first chapter he has already described justice in general, and in the second he distinguished the homonymy of the term. In this third chapter he divides justice into its species, namely universal and particular. The chapter has three parts. In the first part he treats of the just in general, because the subject is usually better known than the habit that inheres in it; so he deals not with justice but with the just in the concrete. In the second part he treats of universal justice. In the third part he resolves a certain difficulty that could be raised against this doctrine.

units.la: In prima igitur parte de Justo in genere agit hoc quidem consilio, ut materiam circa quam versatur Justitia universalis inveniat, & ait illud justum esse, quod legibus determinatur aut definitur non quidem simpliciter, sic enim iniquæ leges materiam continerent Justitiæ, sed quodammodo, quia diversa sunt hominum ingenia, diversi mores, & quia varia est in variis Rebus p. gubernandi forma, ideo variant leges, ut quod hic justum est, illic sit injustum, stum,& econtra. Justa igitur illa dicuntur, quæ legibus determinatur, sed cum restrictione, & ideo declarat Philosophus, quot sint legū partes, seu quam longè lateque pateant leges, & dicit leges de omnibus rebus agere, quæ ad utilitatem publicam spectant, sive ad utilitatem omnium, ut in Democratia sive populari statu, sive quorundam optimorum, ut in Aristocratia, sive aliorum, qui imperium tenent, vel ex virtute, ut in regno Regis, vel aliis de causis, aut ob divitias, aut nobilitatem, aut ob potentiam, ut in tyrannide & oligarchia, quæ de re fusius disputat Phil. lib. 8. h.oper. & lib. 4. Pol. Nam leges hoc præcipuè spectant, ut utilitatē publicā conservent, & malis moribus frenum, bonis vero limites & metā imponant, sicut hoc loco ex Platone lib. 1. & 3. de Rep. docet Phil. & Cic. 3. etiā de Rep. & leges civiles in tit. de justitia & jure per tot. Quicquid igitur virtutibus præcipitur, aut legibus definitur aut determinatur, id omne justum esse affirmat Philosophus, ex quibus perspicuum est, quam latè pateat materia Justitiæ universalis, nempe ut materia virtutum omnium, & legum etiam omnium illi sit materia. Unde cum tam late pateat, ut materiam omnium legum & omnium virtutum sub se comprehendat, non male à Xenophonte definitur habitus, per quem obedientiam omnibus legibus præstamus, & earum beneficio omnes virtutum habitus recte colimus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he treats of the just in general, with this aim: to find the matter with which universal justice is concerned. He says that the just is that which is determined or defined by laws. Not simply, however, for then unjust laws would contain the matter of justice; but in a qualified sense. Men's dispositions differ, their customs differ, and the form of government differs from place to place, so laws vary, and what is just here is unjust there, and conversely. Those things are therefore called just which are determined by law, but with a restriction. So the Philosopher states how many parts of law there are, or how far and wide laws extend, and he says that laws deal with all those matters that concern the public advantage, whether the advantage of all, as in a democracy or popular state, or of some of the best, as in an aristocracy, or of others who hold power, whether by virtue, as in the kingdom of a king, or for other reasons, whether wealth, nobility or power, as in tyranny and oligarchy. He discusses this more fully in the eighth book of his Ethics and the fourth of his Politics. For laws aim chiefly at preserving the public advantage, and at putting a bridle on bad morals and setting limits and bounds on good ones; the Philosopher teaches this here from Plato, Laws books 1 and 3, and from Cicero, On the Republic book 3, and the civil laws throughout the title on justice and law. Whatever is commanded by the virtues, or defined or determined by laws, the Philosopher affirms that all of it is just. From this it is clear how widely the matter of universal justice extends: it is the matter of all the virtues and of all the laws. Since it extends so far, embracing under itself the matter of all laws and all virtues, Xenophon rightly defines it as the habit by which we render obedience to all the laws and, by their benefit, rightly cultivate all the habits of virtue.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis proprie tractat quasdam Justitiæ universalis affert: 1. Quod sit præstantissima omnium virtutum. 2. Quod at perfectissima non quidem in se, sed in usu & ordine ad alium. Præstantissima tissimam esse probat duabus autoritatibus & ratione quadam: 1. desumitur ex Euripide Poëta, qui Justitiam dicit esse hesperò & lucifero (una eadémque stella est, sed propter diversos effectus, diversa sortitur nomina: nam quia Solem occidentem sequitur, dicitur Hesperus, à Varrone, & quia orientem precedit, dicitur Lucifer) pulchriorem & mirabiliorem. 2. est Theognidis, cujus meminit Jambichus ferm. 6. de Just. apud Stobaum.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals properly with certain features of universal justice. He asserts: (1) that it is the most excellent of all the virtues; (2) that it is the most perfect, not indeed in itself but in its use and in its relation to others. He proves its excellence by two authorities and a certain reason. First, he draws on the poet Euripides, who says that justice is more beautiful and more wonderful than the evening star and the morning star (it is one and the same star, but because of its different effects it takes different names: because it follows the setting sun it is called Hesperus, by Varro, and because it goes before the rising sun it is called Lucifer). Second, he cites Theognis, whom Iamblichus mentions in his sixth sermon on justice, preserved by Stobaeus.

units.la: Justitia in se fe virtutes continet omnes.
units.tr: Justice in itself contains all the virtues.

units.la: Sic etiam apud varios autores, propter naturae suae praestantiam variis insignitur nominibus. Cic. 3. ossi. vocat, virtutum omnium Reginam, quod aequitatis suae sceptro omnes reliquas regat & dirigat. Athenaeus etiam lib. 12. dicit, apud varias gentes illi aras & focos exstructos fuisse. Et constat apud Graecos & Romanos pro Dea habitam esse, unde illud Ovidii Metam.
units.tr: So also among various authors, because of the excellence of its nature, it is distinguished by various names. Cicero, in De officiis book 3, calls it the queen of all the virtues, because by the sceptre of its equity it rules and directs all the others. Athenaeus also says in book 12 that altars and hearths were set up to it among various peoples. And it is well established that among the Greeks and Romans it was regarded as a goddess, whence that line of Ovid in the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Vita jacet pietas, & terras cademadentes
units.tr: Piety lies dead, and Astraea, the last of the heavenly dwellers,

units.la: Ultima coelicolum terras Astraea reliquit:
units.tr: has left the falling earth:

units.la: Id est, Dea Justitiae. Ratio, qua probat praestantiam Justitiae, ducitur à contrario; nam sicut ille pessimus dicitur, qui nulli bene facit, sed omnib. injuste nocet, sic ille dicitur optimus, qui omnibus bene facit, & juste prodest. Perfectissimam esse probat etiam duabus rationibus: 1. Est, quia omnium virtutum usus inest, & debetur Justitiae: nam actiones suas ad extra exserere non possunt virtutes absque Justitiae regula, quae modum in illis praescribit. 2. Ratio, quia Justitia non tantum uti licet erga seipsum, sed maxime erga alium, quia respicit bonum publicum, quod quanto difficilius, tanto etiam est quid perfectius, & perfectionem Justitiae denotat. Con-
units.tr: That is, the goddess of Justice. The reason by which he proves the excellence of justice is drawn from the contrary. For just as he is called the worst who does good to no one but harms everyone unjustly, so he is called the best who does good to all and benefits them justly. He proves its perfection also by two reasons: (1) because the use of all the virtues belongs to justice and is owed to it; for the virtues cannot put their actions forth outwardly without the rule of justice, which prescribes the measure for them. (2) Because justice is not only to be exercised towards oneself but above all towards another, since it regards the common good; and the more difficult this is, the more perfect it is, and this denotes the perfection of justice.

units.la: Confirmat id etiam ab experientia quotidiana, quia multos videre licet, qui in privata vita bene & cum laude degerant, qui tamen ad civilem societatem prorsus inepti, qualis ille durus Demea apud Terent. in Adelph. Id etiam probat proverbium vulgo jactatum, quod Bianti inventori ascribitur: Ex Magistratu cognosci unumquemque, id est, cognoscitur bene quails unusquisque, sit bonusne an improbus, cum ad tractandam Rempublicam accesserit, quia in vita privata aliquis bene latere potest, & non multae occurrunt difficultates, poterit enim quis suos & suorum mores, quibus ab ineunte aetate assuescit bene exploratos habere, qui tamen diversissima singulorum in Repub. membrorum ingenia satis explorata habere nequit. Unde ex his cognoscere licet, Justitiam non esse partem aliquam virtutis, sed omnem omnino virtutem, sicut econtra justitia non est pars aliqua vitii, sed omnis in genere vitiositas.
units.tr: He confirms this also from everyday experience, since we may see many who live well and with credit in private life, yet who are wholly unfit for civil society, like that harsh Demea in Terence's Adelphi. The proverb commonly repeated, which is ascribed to Bias the inventor, also proves it: Each man is known from his magistracy, that is, one is known as to what kind of man he is, good or wicked, when he takes up the government of the commonwealth. For in private life a man can easily lie hidden, and few difficulties arise. One may well have his own and his family's manners thoroughly examined, to which he has been accustomed from early youth, yet he cannot have examined well enough the very diverse dispositions of the individual members of the commonwealth. From this, therefore, we may recognise that justice is not some part of virtue but altogether every virtue, just as, conversely, injustice is not some part of vice but all vice in general.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis solvit dubium, quod contra istam doctrinam afferri poterat: nam si Justitia universalis sit omnis virtus, superfluè traduntur omnes reliquae virtutes, frustra etiam de iisdem egit lib.1. cap.8. & lib.3. & 4. satis enim esset, de una Justitia agere, liquidem omnis in genere est virtus, nam frustra fiunt per plura, quae fieri possunt per pauciora. Respondet esse omnem virtutem, & non esse diversso respectu, nam re & subjecto convenit cum omni virtute, at ratione & usu differt: Nam si unaquaeque Virtus consideretur secundum propriam suam perfectionem quam in se habet, & ad intra, ut loquuntur:
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he resolves a difficulty that could be raised against this doctrine. For if universal justice is every virtue, then all the other virtues are handed down superfluously, and he has treated them in vain in book 1, chapter 8, and in books 3 and 4; for it would be enough to treat of justice alone, since in general it is every virtue, for things done by more are done in vain when they can be done by fewer. He replies that it is every virtue, and yet not in every respect. For in reality and in subject it agrees with every virtue, but it differs in aspect and in use. For if each virtue is considered according to the perfection it has in itself, and as directed inwards, as they say:

units.la: Jam Justitia non est omnis virtus: at si consideretur & ordine & usu ad alium, & ad extra quatenus tendit ad bonum publicum, jam poterit Justitia dici omnis virtus, quia re & subjecto non differunt, sicut in doctrina Physica intellectus practicus & Theoreticus re & subjecto coveniunt: at ratione, usu, & fine differunt. Poterit virtus duobus modis considerari, vel absolute & per se, ut est habitus, per quem disponitur homo in ordine ad bonum proprium, & sic Justitia non est omnis virtus; vel comparate, ut est habitus, per quem disponitur homo ad bonum publicum civitatis, & sic Justitia hoc loco poterit dici omnis virtus, quia velut lex & norma singularum virtutum bonas actiones praecipit, & contrarias prohibet. Est enim duplex uniuscujusque virtutis consideratio, propria scilicet seu absoluta & communis seu respectiva: secundum illam priore distinguitur Justitia a reliquis virtutib. Secundo hanc reliquae virtutes ad Justitiam referuntur tanquam ad totum universale, verbi gratia: Temperans qui talis, caste & sancte vivit & hoc est bonum proprium & singulare secundum quod Temperantia distinguitur a Justitia universali: at idem temperans caste sanctequeque viven-do in Republ. membro damnum aut injuriam inferr, & hoc est bonum publicum & commune, secundum quod ad Justitiam universalem tanquam ad suam perfectionem refertur Temperantia. Solent interpretes aliter etiam ad hoc dubium respondere, nempe etsi Justitia universalis reipsa non distinguatur a reliquis virtutibus, Particularis tamen, quae in Distributivam & Commutativam dividitur, quæque potissimum toto hoc lib. f. explicatur, reipsa differat à reliquis virtutibus, sed quia hæc responsio dubium non solvit, nam an Justitia universalis sit idem, an vero diversum quid, à reliquis virtutibus, quæstio est, ideo prior responsio magis placet.
units.tr: Then justice is not every virtue. But if it is considered both in its order and use towards another, and outwardly insofar as it tends to the public good, then justice can be called every virtue, because in reality and in subject they do not differ, just as in the Physical doctrine the practical and the theoretical intellect agree in reality and in subject, but differ in aspect, use and end. A virtue can be considered in two ways: either absolutely and in itself, as a habit by which a man is disposed towards his own good, and so justice is not every virtue; or comparatively, as a habit by which a man is disposed towards the public good of the state, and so justice here can be called every virtue, because, like a law and rule of the individual virtues, it commands good actions and forbids their opposites. For there is a twofold consideration of each virtue: the proper or absolute, and the common or relative. According to the former, justice is distinguished from the other virtues. According to the latter, the other virtues are referred to justice as to a universal whole. For example: the temperate man, as such, lives chastely and holily, and this is his proper and particular good, according to which temperance is distinguished from universal justice. But the same temperate man, by living chastely and holily, inflicts harm or injury on a member of the commonwealth, and this is the public and common good, according to which temperance is referred to universal justice as to its own perfection. The interpreters usually answer this difficulty in another way too, namely that although universal justice is in reality not distinct from the other virtues, particular justice, which is divided into distributive and commutative, and which is chiefly explained in this whole fifth book, does differ in reality from the other virtues. But since this answer does not resolve the difficulty (for the question is whether universal justice is the same as the other virtues or something different from them), the former answer pleases me more.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: Quicquid legibus determinatur, id omne justum est non simpliciter, sed quodam modo tantum.
units.tr: Whatever is determined by laws, all of that is just, not simply, but only in a certain way.

units.la: Leges conferunt communi omnium utilitati in quocunque Republica sive in Democratia, sive Aristocratia, sive Monarchia.
units.tr: Laws contribute to the common utility of all in any commonwealth, whether a democracy, an aristocracy, or a monarchy.

units.la: Id vere justum est, quod conservat totam Remp. & singulas tuetur ejus partes in communi hominum societate.
units.tr: That is truly just which preserves the whole commonwealth and guards each of its parts in the common society of men.

units.la: Justum in genere sive virtutibus sive legibus tantum definiatur, materia est justitiae universalis.
units.tr: Justice in general, whether defined by virtues or by laws alone, is the matter of universal justice.

units.la: Justus in genere consideratus praecipit, & quid vir temperans, & quid vir fortis, & quid quivis quæque virtute præditus agit aut agere debet.
units.tr: Justice in general, considered, prescribes both what the temperate man and what the brave man, and what each man endowed with any virtue, does or ought to do.

units.la: Leges sunt duplices bona aut mala. Bona bene & consulto latæ sunt, mala vero tumultuarie tantum & male.
units.tr: Laws are of two kinds, good or bad. Good laws are enacted well and deliberately; bad ones only in tumult and badly.

units.la: Justitia dicitur virtutum omnium perfectissima, non in se & absolute sed respective tantum ad alium.
units.tr: Justice is called the most perfect of all the virtues, not in itself and absolutely, but only relatively, in relation to another.

units.la: Justitia etiam dicitur virtutum præstantissima, quod cateras omnes regat & dirigat ad bonum publicum.
units.tr: Justice is also called the most excellent of the virtues, because it governs and directs all the others to the public good.

units.la: Multi in privata vita bene & cum laude se gesserunt, qui tamen ubi ad Remp. accesserunt, justitiam prodiderunt suam.
units.tr: Many have conducted themselves well and with praise in private life, who nevertheless, when they came to public office, betrayed their justice.

units.la: Ut ille pessimus dicitur, qui omnibus in uste nocet, sic ille optimus, qui omnibus juste prodest.
units.tr: As he is called the worst who harms all unjustly, so he is the best who benefits all justly.

units.la: Si-
units.tr: Si-

units.la: II. Sicut Justitia universalis dicitur omnis in genere virtus, sic Injustitia universalis omnis in genere vitiositas.
units.tr: II. As universal justice is called every virtue in general, so universal injustice is every vice in general.

units.la: 12. Justitia universalis & omnis virtus inter se hoc modo differunt, quod illa ad alium semper referatur, haec vero ad habentem seu possessorem sui tantum.
units.tr: 12. Universal justice and every virtue differ from one another in this way: the former is always referred to another, but the latter only to the one who has or possesses it.

units.la: DUBIA.
units.tr: DOUBTS.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An recte hic dicatur Justitia omnium virtutum praestantissima, cum tamen lib. 3. cap. 10. Fortitudinem vocarit omnium virtutum praestantissimam, & addidit rationem, quia nempe circa praestantissimum objectum versatur, nempe mortem bellicam, & lib. 4. cap. 7. Magnanimitatem dicit omnium virtutum praestantissimam. Ergo aut hic aut illic lapsus est, cum plures in superlativo gradu res ejusdem ordinis dari non possint, sicut ipse docet 2. de anima, textu 17. Resp. Dignitatem & praestantiam alicujus virtutis considerari diversimode, prout a diversis causis oritur. Nam interdum consideratur praestantia objecti, & sic lib. 3. Fortitudinem vocavit praestantissimam, propterea quod circa objectum praestantissimum versetur, nempe circa mortem bellicam, quae a causis praeclaris exiit, nempe a defensione religionis, patriae, parentum, cognatorum, amicorum, & similium. 2. Consideratur praestantia respectu subjecti, & sic Magnanimitas est virtutum omnium praestantissima, quia nempe inest ejusmodi subjecto, in quo omnis bonitas, omnis cumulata virtus inesse debet, sicut loco citato docet Philosophus. 3. Consideratur praestantia respectu finis, & sic hoc loco Justitia dicitur omnium praestantissima, propterea quod ejus finis est ad commune civitatis bonum tendere.
units.tr: I. It is asked whether it is rightly said here that Justice is the most excellent of all the virtues, when in book 3, chapter 10, he called Courage the most excellent of all the virtues and gave the reason, namely that it is concerned with the most excellent object, namely death in battle; and in book 4, chapter 7, he calls Magnanimity the most excellent of all the virtues. Therefore he has erred either here or there, since several things of the same kind cannot be given in the superlative degree, as he himself teaches in De anima 2, text 17. Answer: The dignity and excellence of a virtue is considered in different ways, according to the different causes from which it arises. First, the excellence of the object is considered, and so in book 3 he called Courage the most excellent, because it is concerned with the most excellent object, namely death in battle, which proceeds from noble causes, namely the defence of religion, country, parents, kinsfolk, friends and the like. Second, the excellence is considered with respect to the subject, and so Magnanimity is the most excellent of all the virtues, because it inheres in such a subject, in whom all goodness and every accumulated virtue ought to be present, as the Philosopher teaches in the passage cited. Third, the excellence is considered with respect to the end, and so in this place Justice is called the most excellent of all, because its end is to aim at the common good of the state.

units.la: II. An recte Justitia universalis possit dici omnis virtus, sicut hoc capite vult Philosophus, cum tamen ratio doceat differre inter se, proinde non posse esse idem, nam unum & idem a seipso non differt, quod vero inter se differant, hinc probatur, quia virtus & objectum virtutis inter se differunt, sicut de Liberalitate & pecunia, Magnanimitate & honore, & caeteris etiam virtutibus constat. At reliquae virtutes sunt tantum objectum Justitiae universalis, sicut hoc cap. 3. initio docet Philosophus, ubi de justo in genere agit tanquam de materia & objecto Justitiae; Ergo idem esse non possunt? Resp. Exipso Philosopho virtutes considerari duobus modis, vel quoad habitum seu essentiam in ordine ad personam, cui insunt, & sic non sunt objectum Justitiae universalis, sed unaquaeque seorsim & separatim consideratae a Justitia universali differt. 2. Consideratur quoad actum externum seu modum & usum in ordine ad Rempub. & sic sunt objectum Iustitiae universalis seu legalis; nam lex praesupponit in homine habitum, qui jubet actum usumque uniuscujusque virtutis in civitate. Proinde etsi virtus & objectum inter se differant; Iustitia tamen universalis omnis virtus dici poterit, propterea quod usus sui ratione omnes in se continet virtutes.
units.tr: II. Whether universal Justice can rightly be called every virtue, as the Philosopher wishes in this chapter, when reason teaches that they differ from one another, and therefore cannot be the same; for one and the same thing does not differ from itself. That they do differ from one another is proved as follows: a virtue and the object of the virtue differ from each other, as is plain about Liberality and money, Magnanimity and honour, and the other virtues as well. But the remaining virtues are only the object of universal Justice, as the Philosopher teaches at the beginning of this chapter 3, where he treats of the just in general as the matter and object of Justice. Therefore they cannot be the same? Answer: From the Philosopher himself, virtues are considered in two ways. Either they are considered with respect to the habit or essence in relation to the person in whom they inhere, and in this way they are not the object of universal Justice; rather, each one considered separately and by itself differs from universal Justice. Second, they are considered with respect to external act, that is, their mode and exercise in relation to the Commonwealth, and in this way they are the object of universal or legal Justice. For the law presupposes in a man the habit, which commands the act and exercise of each virtue in the state. Therefore, although a virtue and its object differ, universal Justice can still be called every virtue, because by reason of its exercise it contains all the virtues within itself.

units.la: III. An recte dicatur Injustitia omnis vitiositas seu omne in genere vitium, cum, si hoc verum esset, sequeretur, cuilibet, cui inesset Injustitia, inesse etiam contraria vitia, quia propter naturam diversissimam & longissimè a se distant, & uni subjecto inesse non possunt, verbi gratia: Timiditas & Audacia, Prodigalitas & Avaritia, quae ex legecontrariorum una inesse non possunt, nam cum se mutuo destruant, simul consistere non possunt? Resp. Recte asseruisse ruisse Philosophum Injustitiam esse omnem vitio- sitatem, sicut econtra Iustitia est omnis virtus, quia ex lege contrariorum contraria contrarius accidunt: Neque est absurdum contraria inesse eidem subjecto, nempe universali, ubi nulla circumstantiarum habetur ratio, licet particulari subjecto sei vatis circumstantiis inesse non possint: At Injustitia, quae opponitur Iustitiae, intelligitur inesse subjecto universali & indeterminato, non vero particulari & ad certas circumstantiis restricto.
units.tr: III. Whether it is rightly said that injustice is every viciousness, or every vice in general, since, if this were true, it would follow that whoever has injustice would also have contrary vices, for vices which are very diverse in nature and very far apart from one another cannot inhere in one subject; for example, timidity and rashness, prodigality and avarice, which by the law of contraries cannot be in one person, since they destroy each other and cannot exist together? Answer: The Philosopher rightly asserted that injustice is all viciousness, just as, conversely, justice is all virtue, because contrary things belong to contraries by the law of contraries. Nor is it absurd for contraries to inhere in the same subject, namely the universal subject, where no regard is had to circumstances, although they cannot inhere in a particular subject with certain circumstances. But injustice, which is opposed to justice, is understood to inhere in a universal and indeterminate subject, not in a particular one restricted to certain circumstances.

units.la: IV. An rectè Iustitia dicatur bonum alienum hoc cap. & 1.Polit. cap.6. & 3.Polit.cap.8. ubi hoc discrimen inter Iustitiam & cateras virtutes adsert, nempe quod reliqua possidentem respiciant; Iustitia vero ad alium semper referatur, & hoc confirmat etiam Cicero 2.de Repub,ubi ait: Iustitiam totam ad alienas se porrigere & explicare utilitates.
units.tr: IV. Whether justice is rightly called the good of another, in this chapter and in Politics 1, chapter 6, and Politics 3, chapter 8, where he draws this distinction between justice and the other virtues: that the others regard the possessor, but justice always refers to another. Cicero also confirms this in De republica 2, where he says that all justice extends itself and is directed to the advantages of others.

units.la: Sed hoc impugnatur & contrarium statuitur tribus rationibus: 1. Quia absurdum esset eum, cui Iustitia habitus inesset, alteri tantum tribuere, quod suum est, sibi vero suum non tribuere. Iustitia nideo justa dicitur, quod non solum aliis, sed & sibi, & ei, cui inest, æqua & justa sit; Ergo qui aliis prodest, sibi ipsi etiam prodest, proinde Iustitia non ad alium tantum est referenda. 2. Quia omnis virtus habentem, possidentem, utentem perficit, sicut cap. 4.lib.1.hujus operis docet. Si ergo Justitia ad alium tantum referatur, & non ad possidentem virtus esse negabitur. 3. Quia, qui justus in alios est, in seipsum justus fit, necesse est: relata enim non unius, sed alterius respectu dicuntur, ut ex Logicis patet. Ergo ut quis vere justus sit, necesse est, ut à seipso incipiat esse justus, & postea Justitiam suam extendat ad alium? Resp. Justitiam dici bonum alienum, & dici etiam proprium, sed diver-so fo respectu. Nam primariò dicitur alienum, propter- ea quod Justitiae primarius scopus sit, proximum juvare & ad utilitatem Reip. tendere: Secundariò vero dicitur bonum proprium, quod tantum secundario posse ssorem sui respiciat, sicut Medici primarius scopus est alium curare, secundarius tantum seipsum si aegrotet.
units.tr: But this is challenged, and the contrary is maintained by three arguments. 1. Because it would be absurd for the one who has the habit of justice to give to another only what is his own, and not to give to himself what is his own. Justice is therefore called just because it is just and fair not only to others but also to oneself and to the one in whom it inheres. Therefore, one who benefits others also benefits himself, and so justice is not to be referred to another only. 2. Because every virtue perfects the one who has it, possesses it and uses it, as chapter 4 of book 1 of this work teaches. If, then, justice is referred only to another, and not to the possessor, it will be denied to be a virtue. 3. Because one who is just towards others must necessarily be just towards himself; for relatives are spoken of with respect not to one but to the other, as is clear from the logicians. Therefore, for someone to be truly just, it is necessary that he begin by being just to himself, and afterwards extend his justice to another? Answer: Justice is called the good of another, and it is also called one's own, but in different respects. For it is called primarily another's, because the primary aim of justice is to help one's neighbour and to aim at the advantage of the Commonwealth. Secondarily, however, it is called one's own good, because it regards the possessor of it only secondarily, just as the primary aim of a physician is to care for others, and his secondary aim only for himself if he falls ill.

units.la: V. Quia in hoc cap. 3. de Justitia universali agit Philo- sophus, quari poterit, an ista universalis Justitia species sit virtutis moralis? Resp. Dubiam esse hanc quaestionem, & disceptari in utramque partem ab interpretibus. Nam pro negativa parte afferuntur sex rationes: 1. Quia Justitia universalis sub se comprehendit reliquas omnes virtutes, aut tanquam species suas aut tanquam partes, quod testatur vulgatus versiculus Theog. b Arist. hoc cap. 3. citatus:
units.tr: V. Since the Philosopher treats of universal Justice in this chapter 3, it may be asked whether this universal Justice is a species of moral virtue. Answer: This question is doubtful, and the interpreters dispute it on both sides. For on the negative side six arguments are advanced. 1. Because universal Justice comprehends all the other virtues under itself, either as its species or as its parts, as the commonly quoted verse of Theognis, cited by Aristotle in this chapter 3, bears witness:

units.la: Justitia in se virtutes continet omnes.
units.tr: Justice contains all the virtues within itself.

units.la: Ergo cum unaquaeque virtus specialiter sumta, sit Justitia, species virtutis moralis Justitia universalis esse non poterit: aut saltem hoc sequetur absurdum, nempe aut genus unius speciei respectu dici, cujus contrarium docetur in Logicis, aut saltem omnes species in una contineri aut ab una pedere, & sic virtus esset genus imperfectu. 2. Quia Justitia est mater & nutrix caeterarum virtutum teste Polo Pythagoreo, cujus verba citantur a Luciano in libro de Justitia hoc modo: Videtur mihi Justitia inter homines mater & nutrix caeterarum omnium virtutum appellanda: ubi etiam ad confirmandam hanc suam assertionem duas subjicit rationes: quarum prima est, quod abs; Justitia, neque Temperans, neque Prudens, neque Fortis quisquam fieri possit: Secunda quod Justitia fit pax & tráquillitas animi cum suavi quadam harmonia & eleganti concinnitate conjuncta. Et hoc ipsum testatur etiam Cic.1 offic. ubi ait: Sine Justitia nihil posse unquam esse laudabile, nihilq; utile honestum esse, quod Justitia vacat. Item alibi: Sine Prudentia multum posse Justitiam, sine Justitia nihil valere Prudentiam. Unde Scaliger. exerc.307.sect.3. Justitia est mater & conservatrix conjunctionis humanae, quae conjuncto una est ad beatitudinem via. Haec igitur omnia testimonia huc spectant, ut Justitiam propter latitudinem naturae suae speciem virtutis moralis non esse demonstrent.
units.tr: Therefore, since each virtue taken specially is justice, universal Justice cannot be a species of moral virtue; or at least this absurdity would follow: either the genus would be predicated of one of its species, which is taught to be contrary in the Logicians, or else all the species would be contained in one and depend on one, and so virtue would be an imperfect genus. 2. Because Justice is the mother and nurse of the other virtues, according to the Pythagorean Polus, whose words are quoted by Lucian in the book on Justice in this way: It seems to me that Justice should be called among men the mother and nurse of all the other virtues. There he also adds two reasons to confirm this assertion: the first is that no one can become temperate, prudent or brave without Justice; the second is that Justice brings about peace and tranquillity of soul, joined with a certain sweet harmony and graceful fitness. Cicero also bears witness to this in De officiis 1, where he says: Without Justice nothing can ever be praiseworthy, and nothing that lacks Justice can be honourable or useful. Likewise elsewhere: Without Prudence Justice has great power; without Justice Prudence is worth nothing. Hence Scaliger, Exercitationes 307, section 3: Justice is the mother and preserver of human fellowship, which, being joined together, is the way to blessedness. All these testimonies therefore tend to show that Justice, on account of the breadth of its nature, is not a species of moral virtue.

units.la: 3. Quia omnis species virtutis moralis medium servat inter duo extrema vitia, ut singularu inductione patet; Justitia autem non, cum ei tantum opponatur Injustitia, nihilque aliud in rerum natura dari posset, quod ei adversetur, praeter solam Injustitiam, quae non duo, sed unum extremum esse videtur.
units.tr: 3. Because every species of moral virtue keeps the mean between two extreme vices, as the induction of individual cases makes clear; justice does not, since only injustice is opposed to it, and nothing else in the nature of things could be opposed to it apart from injustice alone, which seems to be one extreme rather than two.

units.la: 4. Quia etiam omnis species virtutis moralis est proprium hominis bonum, & possessorem sui intrinsecus perficit: Justitia autem est bonum alienum, sicut hoc cap.5. docet Philosophus, cum ad aliud tatum referatur eaq; agat, quae aliis sunt utilia.
units.tr: 4. Because every species of moral virtue is the proper good of the human being and perfects its possessor inwardly; justice, however, is another's good, as the Philosopher teaches in this chapter 5, since it is directed wholly toward another and performs those things that are useful to others.

units.la: 5. Quia omnis species virtutis moralis, aliquem hominis affectum aut motum animi internum moderatur, sicut ex cap.5.&4.lib.2. constat: Iustitia vero nullum internum hominis affectum regit, sed tantum in actionis ad extra cernitur, sicut ex definitione supra c.1.data liquet.
units.tr: 5. Because every species of moral virtue regulates some affection of the human being or some inner motion of the mind, as is established from chapters 4 and 5 of book 2; but justice governs no inner affection of the human being and is seen only in external action, as is clear from the definition given above in chapter 1.

units.la: 6. & ult. Ratio ducitur à contrario, quia Injustitia non est species vitii moralis, sed sub ea omnia vitia tanquam species sub genere comprehenhendit. Proinde neque iustitia species erit virtutis moralis. Pro affirmativa parte tria adferuntur argumenta: 1. Quia definitio virtutis, quae traditur lib. 1. cap. 6. iustitiae competit. 2. Quia eandem habet finem cum virtute in genere, nempe honestatem: Cum igitur eandem habeat naturam, eundem finem, aut species sit virtutis moralis necesse est, aut genus: Non genus, quia cum reliquis comprehenditur sub natura virtutis in genere. 3. Quia omnes morales Philosophi quotquot unquam de virtutibus scripserunt, iustitiam inter cæteras etiam annumerant. Unde a Philosopho comparative vocatur perfectissima & praestantissima omnium virtutum, & a Cic. 3. offic. excellentissima & splendidissima, omnium quae in genere virtutum Regina ac Domina, quod non fieret, nisi species etiam virtutis moralis esset.
units.tr: 6. and last. The argument is drawn from the contrary: injustice is not a species of moral vice, but it comprehends all vices under itself as species under a genus. Therefore justice will not be a species of moral virtue either. For the affirmative side three arguments are brought forward: (1) the definition of virtue given in book 1, chapter 6, applies to justice; (2) justice has the same end as virtue in general, namely honesty. Since it therefore has the same nature and the same end, it must be either a species or a genus of moral virtue. It is not a genus, because it is included with the rest under the nature of virtue in general. (3) All the moral philosophers who have ever written about the virtues also count justice among the others. Hence the Philosopher calls it, comparatively, the most perfect and most excellent of all the virtues, and Cicero (De Officiis 3) calls it the most excellent and splendid, the queen and mistress of all the virtues. This would not be so unless it were also a species of moral virtue.

units.la: Pro decisione distinguendum erit inter universalem & Particularem Iustitiam, universalis quidem species iustitiae moralis virtutis dici non potest, propterea quod omnis sit in genere virtus, & nihil aliud, quam obedientia generalis, quam homo praestat erga leges, aut habitus proprescticus, quo unusquisque vitam & mores instituit secundum praescriptum legum: & de hac vera est negativa pars quaestionis cum suis argumentis. Nam cum omnis species naturam habeat suo genere angustiorem, ut ex Logicis patet, haec vero naturam aeque latam acipia virtus moralis, species ejus dici non potest, sed particularis iustitia cum sit distincta a reliquis virtus, & aeque participet de natura virtutis in genere, ac reliquae virtutes, species virtutis moralis merito dicitur, tur, & de ea vera est pars affirmativa cum suis rationibus.
units.tr: For the decision, a distinction must be made between universal and particular justice. Universal justice cannot indeed be called a species of moral virtue, because it is virtue in general and nothing other than the general obedience which a person renders to the laws, or the habit by which each person orders his life and morals according to the precept of the laws. Concerning this, the negative part of the question, with its arguments, is true. For since every species has a nature narrower than its genus, as is clear from the logicians, while this virtue of moral virtue has a nature equally broad, it cannot be called a species of it. But particular justice, since it is distinct from the other virtues and shares equally in the nature of virtue in general, as the other virtues do, is rightly called a species of moral virtue, and concerning it the affirmative part, with its reasons, is true.

units.la: Huic quaestioni propter affinitatem adjici poterit & haec, quae a multis serio movetur, & etiam creditur: An scilicet divisio Justitiae in Universalem & Particularem sit distributio generis in species? Resp. Negative propter tres rationes: 1. Quia distinctio vocabuli aequivoci in sua aequivocata non facit divisionem generis in species: At haec nihil est aliud: Nam justitiae nomen interdum ita late sumitur, ut omnes comprehendat sub se virtutes, interdum stricte, ut quandam a caeteris distinctam tantum complectatur. 2. Quia, quae sunt species ejusdem generis, earum una non includit essentialiter alteram, ut ex Logicis patet: At Iustitia Universalis totam in se includit naturam Particularis ut ex supra dictis patet. 3. Quia Iustitia universalis nihil est aliud, quam virtus moralis generatim sumta: Cum igitur Virtus moralis in genere, & Iustitia Particularis non sint species ejusdem generis proximi, ideo neq; Iustitia Universalis & Particularis.
units.tr: To this question, because of its affinity, may be added this one, which is seriously raised by many and also believed: Whether the division of justice into universal and particular is a distribution of a genus into its species? Answer: No, for three reasons: (1) the distinction of an equivocal term into its equivocal senses does not make a division of a genus into species; yet this is what it is, for the name of justice is sometimes taken so broadly that it embraces all the virtues under itself, and sometimes strictly, so that it comprehends only one particular virtue distinct from the others. (2) Species of the same genus are such that one does not essentially include the other, as is clear from the logicians; but universal justice includes within itself the whole nature of particular justice, as is clear from what has been said above. (3) Universal justice is nothing other than moral virtue taken generally. Since moral virtue in general and particular justice are therefore not species of the same proximate genus, neither are universal and particular justice.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: SEquitur secundum membrum tractatus primi hujus libri, in quo Philosophus incipit agere de Iustitia Particulari, cujus potissimum gratia totam hanc de Iustitia disputationem instituit. De universali vero parcius hic agit, propterea quod toto lib. 2. & etiam magna parte 3. ubi in genere de virtute egit, & ubi etiam de singulis virtutibus in specie tractavit deca egisse videatur. Partes hujus capitis sunt duae: i. primi prima de Iustitia Particulari agit, & hanc adducit quæstionem: An scilicet talis sit Iustitia necne: In secunda Iustitiam Universalem cum Particulari tam in similitudine, quam dissimili comparet.
units.tr: There follows the second part of the first treatise of this book, in which the Philosopher begins to deal with particular justice, for the sake of which chiefly he has undertaken this whole discussion of justice. Universal justice, however, he treats more sparingly here, because he has dealt with it in the whole of the second book and a large part of the third, where he treated of virtue in general, and where he seems to have treated of each individual virtue in particular. The parts of this chapter are two. In the first, he deals with particular justice and raises this question: whether there is such a justice or not. In the second, he compares universal justice with particular justice, both in their likeness and in their unlikeness.

units.la: In prima igitur parte de Iustitia Particulari agit, & primò quæritur: An sit talis Iustitia: quæ quæstio tum temporis necessaria videbatur: Nam Stoici & Platonici exiguum aut penè nullum discrimen inter Universalem & Particularem Iustitiam ponebant, & sicubi de Iustitia universali ageret, satis sibi detota Iustitiæ natura egisse videbantur. Probat verò esse à contrario habitu, nempe Injustitia Particulari, quam quotidiana experientia & sensus communis dari probant, siquidem illius effecta nulli non sunt obvia & cognita: & quò magis constet dari Injustitiam Particularem simul cum Iustitia triplicem hæc suæ assertionis affert rationem: 1. Quia licet multorum virorum facta sint injusta, non tamen sunt pleonectica, id est, quod plus æquo affectant, seu quæ simul cum Injustitia cupiditatem ultra habendi connectunt, idque probat tribus exemplis:
units.tr: In the first part, then, he deals with particular justice, and first he asks whether there is such a justice. This question seemed necessary at that time, for the Stoics and the Platonists put little or almost no difference between universal and particular justice, and wherever they treated of universal justice they seemed to think they had sufficiently explained the whole nature of justice. He proves that there is such a justice by its contrary habit, namely particular injustice, whose existence daily experience and common sense prove, since its effects are everywhere obvious and known to all. And in order that it may be more clearly established that there is particular injustice together with justice, he brings forward a threefold reason for his assertion: (1) Although the deeds of many men are unjust, they are not nonetheless grasping, that is, they do not aim at more than their due, or combine with injustice a desire to have more. He proves this by three examples:

units.la: 1. Qui clypeum aut arma in bello abjecit, propter timiditatem aut ignaviam, dicitur timidus & ignavus.
units.tr: (1) He who throws away his shield or arms in battle, out of timidity or cowardice, is called timid and cowardly.

units.la: 2. Qui aliis propter linguæ asperitatem & ingenii malitiam maledicit, dicitur maledicus.
units.tr: (2) He who curses others because of the harshness of his tongue and the malice of his mind is called abusive.

units.la: 3. Qui avaritiam & sordiditatem amat, & neminem juvat, dicitur Avarus. Isti omnes tres, licet sint injusti, tamen nō sunt πλεονέκται seu qui aliquid sibi de alienis bonis usurpant. Sic aliquis poterit esse πλεονέκτης, qui tamen neq; sit timidus neque maledicus aut ullo alio vitio in specie præditus. Hæc ratio, ut melius intelligatur, repetendum erit ex cap.2. & initio cap 3. duo esse Injustitiae facta, unum paronomum, quod leges transgreditur, aliud pleoneticum, quod plus aequo de bonis alienis concupiscit. Cum igitur haec duo Injustitiae facta saepenumero non incurrant, fit ut duplex nascatur Injustitia, una Communis & Universalis, quae respondet Paronomae, altera particularis, quae respondet pleonexiae: sic etiam e contra duplex erit Iustitia, una Universalis, quae universas leges moderatur, & iis obedientiam praestat, altera Particularis, quae de bonis alienis, nihil nisi ex justo & aequo usurpandum suadeat. 2. Ratio explicatur comparatione duorum adulterorum, verbi gratia: ponantur duo adulteri, quorum alter pecunia impulsus adulterium committit alioqui non commissurus, alter vero ut committat pecuniam insuper addat, & sic damnum sibi in bonis suis faciat. Posterior iste proprie dicitur Intemperans, quia ob libidinem suam hoc factum committit: prior vero qui pecunia im pulsus, dicetur mere injustus, quia ob lucrum tantum hoc facit: Cum igitur dissimili ratione isti duo sint injusti, alter, qui Intemperans dicitur, quia leges violat, alter qui ob lucrum facit, quia plus aequo usurpat, necessario statuenda erunt duo Injustitiae, & e contrario Iustitiae genera. 3 Ratio, quia omnis injuriae qualescunque, eae demum sint, possunt ad suum quaeque referri vitiu seu sunt in aliquo genere vitiorum, ut, verbi gratia: timidus, qui ob ignaviam peccat, ad ignaviam, quod vitium est Fortitudinis in defectu oppositum, sic qui adulterium committit ob libidinem ad Intemperantiam referreferri possit, & sic de cæteris vitiis. At injuriæ pleonecticæ, quæ plus æquo de bonis alienis usurpant ad nullum aliud peculiare vitium sunt referri possunt, sed necesse est, ut suo proprio vitio gaudeant. Proinde non immerito duplex statuitur Injustitia, una Universalis & communis omnibus, altera singularis propria huic autem illi, & econtra duplex etiam Iustitia, una Universalis, altera Particularis, de qua posteriori insequentibus sibi agendum proposuit Philosophus.
units.tr: (3) He who loves avarice and meanness and helps no one is called avaricious. All three of these, although they are unjust, are nonetheless not πλεονέκται, that is, those who appropriate to themselves something from the goods of others. So someone may be a πλεονέκτης who is neither timid, nor abusive, nor endowed with any other vice in particular. This reason, so that it may be better understood, must be recalled from the second chapter and the beginning of the third chapter: there are two kinds of unjust deeds, one lawless [παρανομία], which transgresses the laws, and the other grasping [πλεονεξία], which desires the goods of others more than is fitting. Since these two kinds of unjust deed do not often coincide, it follows that a twofold injustice arises: one common and universal, which corresponds to lawlessness, and the other particular, which corresponds to grasping. So too, conversely, there will be a twofold justice: one universal, which governs all the laws and renders obedience to them, and the other particular, which counsels that nothing be taken from the goods of others except what is just and equitable. (2) The reason is explained by a comparison of two adulterers, for example. Let there be two adulterers, of whom the one, driven by money, commits adultery which he would otherwise not have committed, and the other adds money in order to commit it, and so does harm to his own goods. This second is properly called intemperate, because he commits this deed on account of his lust; the first, who was driven by money, is called merely unjust, because he does this only for gain. Since these two are unjust for different reasons, the one who is called intemperate because he violates the laws, and the other who acts for gain because he takes more than is fitting, two kinds of injustice must necessarily be established, and conversely two kinds of justice. (3) The reason is this: every injury, of whatever sort it may be, can be referred to its own vice, or lies within some kind of vice. For example, the coward who sins through cowardice is referred to cowardice, which is the vice opposed to fortitude by defect; so he who commits adultery from lust may be referred to intemperance, and so with the other vices. But grasping injuries, which take more than is fitting from the goods of others, cannot be referred to any other particular vice, but must rejoice in their own proper vice. Therefore it is not unreasonably established that there is a twofold injustice: one universal and common to all, the other singular and proper to this or that person; and conversely a twofold justice also, one universal, the other particular, concerning which latter the Philosopher proposed to treat in what follows.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis confert Iustitiam Universalē & Particularem inter se: 1. Quidem in simili, nempe quod idem iis sit nomen: utraque enim Iustitia appellatur, una etiam sit proprietas finis, nempe quod ad alium utraque referatur. 2. In dissimili: nam differunt ratione objecti seu materiæ circa quam versantur, & à diversa natura objecti pendet etiam singularum virtutum natura diversa. Differre objecto, hinc probat, quia Injustitia universalis versatur circa omnia ea, quæ legibus in genere præscribuntur, aut ab omnibus virtutibus præcipiuntur: Iustitia vero particularis circa bona tantum externa, seu ut vocatur munera fortunæ, cujusmodi sunt divitiæ, honos, lucrum, & si quæ sunt alia ejus generis. Justitia vero particularis tantum versatur circa bona fortunæ, quæ in fortunæ arbitrio videntur posita, propter hanc causam, quia in iis expetendis cum damno nostri aut alterius possunt modum excedere & peccare. At non versatur circa bona animi aut interna propter duas causas: 1. quia in iis expetendis, cum animum perficiant, absque alterius damno, nostri vero sumsummo cum lucro nō possumus excedere modum.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he compares universal and particular justice with each other: (1) first in likeness, namely that they have the same name, for both are called justice, and also that they share one property of their end, namely that each is referred to another. (2) In unlikeness: for they differ in respect of the object or matter with which they are concerned, and the nature of each virtue depends also on the diverse nature of its object. He proves that they differ in object for this reason: universal injustice is concerned with all those things which are prescribed by the laws in general, or enjoined by all the virtues; but particular justice is concerned only with external goods, or what are called the gifts of fortune, such as riches, honour, gain, and any others of that kind. Particular justice is concerned only with the goods of fortune, which seem to lie in the power of fortune; for this reason, that in desiring them we can exceed the measure and sin, to our own or another's loss. But it is not concerned with goods of the soul or internal goods, for two reasons: (1) because in desiring these, since they perfect the soul, we cannot exceed the measure without harm to another, while to ourselves they bring the greatest gain.

units.la: 2. Quia non possumus ea ita aliis tribuere, ut propterea dicamur injusti, quia cum nostra plane sint, possumus tantum dare, vel non dare, quantum nobis libuerit. Bona verò ista externa duobus modis considerari possunt: 1.Simpliciter & in se, & sic sunt & dicuntur bona, propterea quod à Deo sunt creata, & à Deo in hominum usus concessa, Vidit enim Deus cuncta, quae fecerat, & erant bona, Genes. 1. vers. 31.
units.tr: (2) Because we cannot so give them to others that we are called unjust for it; since they are wholly our own, we can give only as much as we please, or not give at all. These external goods, however, can be considered in two ways: (1) simply and in themselves, and so they are and are called goods, because they were created by God and granted by God for the use of men: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good," Genesis 1:31.

units.la: 2. Considerantur comparatè, respectu hominum, & sic nec semper, nec simpliciter, nec omnibus sunt bona, sed neutra tantum seu indifferentia, id est, nec bona nec mala, nisi quatenus iis bene vel male homines utuntur. Unde si quis bene iis utatur, & hic usus se extendat ad alium, hic usus dicitur Iustitia, si verò male, hic abusus dicitur Injustitia.
units.tr: (2) They are considered comparatively, with respect to men; and so they are neither always nor simply nor for all men goods, but are neutral, that is, neither good nor evil, except insofar as men use them well or badly. Hence, if anyone uses them well, and this use extends to another, this use is called justice; but if badly, this abuse is called injustice.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Datur Injustitia particularis, sicut experientia probat, ergo etiam econtra Iustitia particularis.
units.tr: 1. Particular injustice exists, as experience proves; therefore, conversely, particular justice exists too.

units.la: 2. Poterit aliquis esse ἀπλεονέκτης, qui non peccet contra leges in genere, & contra, unde cum duplex ex hisce factis sequatur Injustitia universalis & particularis, duplex etiam erit Iustitia.
units.tr: 2. There can be a covetous man [ἀπλεονέκτης] who does not sin against the laws in general, and conversely. Since from these facts two kinds of injustice follow, universal and particular, there will also be two kinds of justice.

units.la: 3. Qui sola libidine impulsus adulterium committit, dicitur proprie intemperans, qui verò lucri cupiditate, dicitur merè injustus.
units.tr: 3. One who commits adultery, driven only by lust, is properly called intemperate; but one who does so from greed for gain is called simply unjust.

units.la: 4. Iustitia universalis & particularis licet idem habeant nomen, naturam tamen sortiuntur longè diversam.
units.tr: 4. Universal and particular justice, although they have the same name, nevertheless have by nature very different characters.

units.la: 5. Synonyma non tantum sunt quorum nominis definitio eadem, sed etiam quorum usus ad idem tendit.
units.tr: 5. Synonyms are not only those things whose definition of the name is the same, but also those whose use tends to the same end.

units.la: 6. Universalis & particularis Iustitia obiecti seu materia circa quam versantur, respectu differunt: Nam universalis versatur circa omnia ea, quae a legibus determinantur, aut a virtutibus praecipiuntur; Particularis vero circa bona tantum externa, seu ut vocantur fortuna.
units.tr: 6. Universal and particular justice differ in respect of their object or matter, with which they are concerned. For universal justice is concerned with all those things which are determined by laws or enjoined by the virtues; but particular justice is concerned only with external goods, or what are called fortunes.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An recte Philosophus distinxerit Iustitiam Particularem ab Universali, cum duplex ratio suadeat non posse distingui: 1. Quia pars a toto separari non potest, utpote in quo existentia suam habet: At Iustitia particularis est pars quaedam Iustitiae Universalis, ut ex fine cap. 3. jam patet.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Did the Philosopher rightly distinguish particular justice from universal, when two reasons suggest that they cannot be distinguished: (1) because a part cannot be separated from the whole, since it has its existence in the whole; but particular justice is a certain part of universal justice, as is already clear from the end of chapter 3;

units.la: 2. Quia Iustitia Universalis sufficit ad instituendum hominem in iis omnibus, quae referuntur ad alium: Atqui in hoc tota Iustitia vis & natura consistit. Proinde male particularem ab universali separarunt Philosophi? Resp. Per negationem non male egisse, cum experientia & usus quotidianus doceat, ista duo a se invicem separari; & quod ad primam rationem, verum est, partem a toto separari non posse re & subiecto, ut maneat pars, sed ratione tamen potest & pars in toto, nō nisi indistincte & confuse cognoscitur: ideo ut distincte & perfecte consideretur, necesse est, ut quantum natura ipsius fert, a toto separetur. Quod ad secundam, etsi sufficiat Iustitia universalis ad instituendum hominem in iis, quae sunt ad alium, hoc tamen plane diverso modo a Iustitia particulari accidit; Nam universalis instituit hominem primario in ordine ad Rempubl. secundario in ordine ad personam: Particularis econtra, primario in ordine ad personam, secundario in ordine ad Rempublicam.
units.tr: (2) because universal justice is sufficient to form a man in all those things which relate to another; but in this the whole force and nature of justice consists.
