Therefore, have the philosophers wrongly separated particular from universal? Answer: By denial, they did not act wrongly, since experience and daily use teach that these two are separated from each other. As to the first reason, it is true that a part cannot be separated from the whole in reality and subject so that it remains a part; but in thought a part can be separated within the whole, and it is known only indistinctly and confusedly. Therefore, in order to consider it distinctly and perfectly, it is necessary that it be separated from the whole as far as its nature allows. As to the second, although universal justice is sufficient to form a man in those things which concern another, this comes about in a manner entirely different from particular justice. For universal justice forms a man primarily in relation to the commonwealth and secondarily in relation to the person; particular justice, on the contrary, forms him primarily in relation to the person and secondarily in relation to the commonwealth.

units.la: II. An recte divisnone Iustitiam in Universalem, quae tam tam respicit Rempub. & Particularem, qua respicit personas privatas, cum dari possit tertia species ab iisdem duabus distincta, nempe Iustitia Oeconomica, qua domum vel familiam respicit: nam constat familiam esse diversum quid & a privata persona & a tota civitate? Resp. Domus & familia in Oeconomicis dicitur parva civitas vel pars civitatis, ideo cum domus comprehendatur sub civitate, etiam Iustitia, quae regit domum sub communi aequitate, quae totam regit civitatem, comprehendi debet, & proinde non opus erat tertiam ab his duabus distinctam Iustitiae speciem statuere.
units.tr: II. Whether the division of justice into universal, which respects the commonwealth, and particular, which respects private persons, was rightly made, since a third kind distinct from these two could exist, namely economic justice, which respects the household or family: for it is clear that the family is something different both from a private person and from the whole state? Answer: In economics the household or family is called a small state or a part of the state. Therefore, since the household is included under the state, justice too, which governs the household under common equity, which governs the whole state, ought to be included, and so there was no need to set up a third kind of justice distinct from these two.

units.la: III. An recte Philosophus neget illum esse injustum, qui libidine impulsus adulterium committit, cum tamen maxime sit injustus, utpote qui suum unicuique non tribuit, sed id quod alterius est injuste viloat?
units.tr: III. Did the Philosopher rightly deny that the man who commits adultery, driven by lust, is unjust, since he is nevertheless most unjust, inasmuch as he does not give to each his due but unjustly violates what belongs to another?

units.la: Resp. Non simpliciter negare Philosophum illum esse injustum, sed quia particulariter non fit injustus, cum potius propter concupiscentiam, quam alterius rei cupiditatem, ad intemperantiam magis spectet, & ideo potius intemperans, quam particulariter injustus dici meretur.
units.tr: Answer: The Philosopher did not deny outright that this man is unjust; but because he is not unjust in a particular way, since he is inclined to intemperance rather through desire than through a craving for another thing, he deserves to be called intemperate rather than particularly unjust.

units.la: IV. & ult. Quomodo Iustitiam & Injustitiam hic vocet Synonyma, cum tamen cap. 2. homonyma vocarit & jure quidem: Nam utriusque nomen, non unum quid, sed multa significat, unde sibi contradicere videtur?
units.tr: IV. and last. Why does he here call justice and injustice synonyms, when in chapter 2 he called them homonyms, and rightly so? For the name of each signifies not one thing but many, so that he seems to contradict himself?

units.la: Resp. Justitiam diverso respectu dici homonymum quid & synonymum. Synonyma hic vocat Iustitiam universalem & particularem, propterea quod sub uno communi nomine eundem habent finem seu usum, nempe quod utraque ad alium referatur: At veró respectu objecti seu materiae, circa quam versantur recte dicuntur homonyma, quia cum diversa sortiuntur objeobjecta, diversam etiam naturam & definitionem habent, quod proprie homonymis competit, sicut 1.Categ. docet Aristoteles.
units.tr: Answer: Justice is called a homonym or a synonym according to a different respect. He calls universal and particular justice synonyms here, because under one common name they have the same end or use, namely that each relates to another. But with respect to the object or matter with which they are concerned, they are rightly called homonyms, because, since they have different objects, they also have a different nature and definition, which properly belongs to homonyms, as Aristotle teaches in the first book of the Categories.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: POstquam ordine naturae praemisit quaestionem: An sit Iustitia particularis? jam quaerit, quid sit & quod illius sint species hoc cap. quia ad Ethicam maxime spectat explicare, quid sit Iustitia particularis, & quae ejus natura, cum sit distincta a caeteris virtus, & talis quidem, ut tota ad salutem & commodum totius civitatis propendeat. Partes capitis sunt duae: In prima facta brevi repetitione eorum, quae tribus superioribus capitib. egerat, discrimen quoddam ponit inter universalem & particularem Iustitiam: In secunda particularem definit, & in suas species dividit.
units.tr: After the author had raised the question in natural order, whether there is particular justice, he now asks what it is and what its kinds are, in this chapter. Since it belongs chiefly to Ethics to explain what particular justice is, and what its nature is, as a virtue distinct from the others, and one that is wholly directed toward the welfare and advantage of the whole state. The chapter has two parts. In the first, after a brief recap of what he had treated in the three preceding chapters, he draws a certain distinction between universal and particular justice. In the second, he defines particular justice and divides it into its species.

units.la: In prima igitur parte dicit se jam explicasse, quid sit Iustitia in genere, quid etiam iniquum, seu id quod leges transgreditur, quia ad naturam universalis Iustitiae explicandam non parum affert momenti, siquidem facta injusta in sensus maxime incurrunt, cum corpus animoque hominum maxime feriant. Et jam ostendit Iustitiam universalem esse totum quid, de quo, ut de omnibus in genere virtutibus tractat, agere videtur, proinde nihil opus esse, ut speciali ipsius explicatione diutius inhaereat, & cum sit obedientia universalis erga omnes leges, qua praecipitur aliquid faciendum, aut prohibetur, ut non faciendum, de ea varii egerunt autores, sed tantum fuse, ut ipsam nusquam a particulari Iustitia distinxerint. rint: discrimen tamen in hoc potissimum consistit, quod universalis totam primario respiciat Remp. particularis vero personas privatas in Repub. siquidem non parum inter se differunt civis bonus, & vir bonus, civis enim denotat membrum Reipub. à toto corpore non avellendum, vir vero bonus nullam considerationem ad Remp. habet, qua talis. Proinde de particulari Iustitia hic seorsim & distincte agendum est, de qua caeteri autores aut nihil, aut saltem confusè tantum egerunt.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he says that he has already explained what justice is in general, and also what is unjust, that is, what transgresses the laws. This contributes no little weight to explaining the nature of universal justice, since unjust acts most of all strike the senses, as they most of all injure the body and soul of men. He now shows that universal justice is a whole thing, and he seems to treat it as he treats all virtues in general. Therefore there is no need for him to dwell longer on its particular explanation. Since it is the general obedience to all laws, by which something is commanded to be done or forbidden to be done, various authors have dealt with it, but only at length, and they have never clearly distinguished it from particular justice. The difference, however, consists chiefly in this: universal justice looks primarily to the whole commonwealth, while particular justice looks to private persons in the commonwealth. Indeed, a good citizen and a good man differ not a little. For "citizen" denotes a member of the commonwealth who must not be torn from the whole body, whereas the good man, as such, has no regard to the commonwealth. Therefore particular justice must be treated here separately and distinctly, which the other authors have either not treated at all or only confusedly.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis Iustitiam particularem definit & dividit in suas species. Definitio est talis: Quod sit virtus in rerum distributione & commutatione mediocritatem servans. Unde cum duo sint genera actionum quae in particulari Iustitia considerantur, rerum nempe distributio & commutatio, duae emergunt ejus species Distributiva scilicet & Commutativa. Distributiva Iustitia definitur talis Iustitia particularis, quae in rerum externarum distributione respectu dignitatis personarum, & coaequalitatis rerum suum cuique tribuit. Objectum igitur seu materia Iustitiae Distributivae in duobus potissimum consistere videtur: 1. In honoribus, quales sunt, Magistratus, dignitates, victus publicus, coronae, statuae, & id genus caetera honorum signa, de quibus Philosophus lib. 1. Rhet. cap. 7. agit. 2. In re, ut pecuniae, agri, vineae, possessiones, &c. Sed haec distributio, quae in hac Iustitia spectatur debet esse publica non privata, nam privata distributio, quae fit inter personas privatas ad alteram Iustitiae speciem pertinet, nempe ad Commutativam. Commutativa vero definitur nitur lustitia particularis, quæ in rerum commutatione nullo habito personarum respectu eam servat æqualitatem, ut suum unusquisque consequatur & nulla parte defraudetur. Dicitur alias a Philosopho Correctiva, quod rerum commutationem ita corrigat, & magis & minus ad æqualitatem & medium reducat, ut nulla pars injuriam sibi fieri juste afferat. Objectum seu materia hujus justitiæ est omne negocium, quo nos invicem res & facultates nostras permutamus, si omne commercium, quod utriusque partis consensu necessitat, indigentiæ, aut alterius respectu transigitur, sicut lib. 9. cap. 1. hujus operis, & Iurisconsultus Ulpianus adl. 17. ff. de iustitia & iure docet. Sed commercia, in quibus potissimum cernitur iustitia ista Commutativa, sunt duorum generum, respectu principiorum a quibus sumuntur, nam alia commercia sunt spontanea, quæ libera voluntate & pleno contrahentium consensu transiguntur: alia fiunt invite, & retracto aut abstracto voluntatis consensu. Ad prius genus commerciorum pertinet, emtio, venditio, mutuum, accommodatum, depositum, pignus, locatio, sponsio, & si quæ sunt alia contractuum genera, in quibus nullum injicitur impedimentum ad prohibendum utriusque partis consensum. Posterius genus rursus subdividitur, quia ut ex cap. 2. lib. 5. patet, Invitum etiam est duplex, per vim, & per ignorantiam. Sic commercia alia sunt clandestina, quæ aliis, ad quos nō spectant, insciis fiunt, & sic respondent invito per ignorantiam, in hoc genere sunt, furtum, adulterium, veneficium, lenocinium, quod est alicujus ad turpe in-temtemperantiæ facinus incitatio seu perfusio, servi item abductio: violenta commercia à vi aperta prodeunt, ubi vis ipsis partibus infertur, aut utrique aut alterutri saltem: adhuc genus spectant, vincula, mors, verberatio, rapina, mutilatio, contumelia, convitium, quod est tàm in dictis quàm in factis alterius nominis insidiosa detectatio, & si quæ sunt ejusmodi. In commerciis quidem spontaneis versatur per se Iustitia Commutativa, quia ibi revera cernitur permutatio, cum utrimque causæ dantur, quæ voluntatem promtam & paratam reddant: in posterioribus, nempe in vitiis non item versatur, sed tantum per accidens, & potius Iustitia Commutativa in iis cernitur, propterea quod suum cuique, ut debetur non tribuatur, ut in sequentibus patebit. De Iustitia particulari breviter ista duo sunt notanda:
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he defines particular justice and divides it into its species. The definition is this: it is a virtue keeping the mean in the distribution and exchange of goods. Hence, since there are two kinds of actions considered in particular justice, namely the distribution and the exchange of goods, two species arise: distributive justice and commutative justice. Distributive justice is defined as that particular justice which, in the distribution of external goods, gives each his own according to the worth of persons and the equality of the things. The object or matter of distributive justice seems chiefly to consist in two things: (1) in honours, such as magistracies, dignities, public maintenance, crowns, statues, and the other tokens of honour of this kind, of which the Philosopher treats in book 1 of the Rhetoric, chapter 7; (2) in property, such as money, fields, vineyards, possessions, and so on. But this distribution, which is considered in this justice, must be public, not private, for private distribution, which is made between private persons, belongs to the other species of justice, namely commutative. Commutative justice is defined as that particular justice which, in the exchange of goods, preserves equality without any regard to persons, so that each obtains what is his own and is defrauded in no part. The Philosopher also calls it corrective, because it corrects the exchange of goods, reducing what is more or less to equality and the mean, so that no party can rightly claim to have been wronged. The object or matter of this justice is every transaction by which we exchange goods and resources with one another, if every dealing that requires the consent of both parties is carried on out of need or for the sake of another. So teaches book 9, chapter 1 of this work, and the jurist Ulpian, ad l. 17 ff. de iustitia et iure. But the dealings in which commutative justice is chiefly seen are of two kinds, with respect to the principles from which they arise. For some dealings are voluntary, carried out by free will and the full consent of the contracting parties; others are made against one's will, with the consent of the will withdrawn or taken away. To the first kind of dealings belong buying, selling, lending for use, loans, deposit, pledge, letting and hiring, promise, and any other kinds of contract in which no hindrance is placed against the consent of both parties. The second kind is again subdivided, since, as is clear from chapter 2 of book 5, the involuntary is also twofold: by force and by ignorance. Thus some dealings are secret, done without the knowledge of those to whom they do not pertain, and in this way they correspond to the involuntary through ignorance. Of this kind are theft, adultery, poisoning, procuring, which is the incitement or drenching of someone into a shameful deed of intemperance, and likewise the abduction of a slave. Violent dealings arise from open force, where force is applied to the parties themselves, either to both or at least to one. Of this kind are chains, death, beating, robbery, mutilation, insult, reproach, which is the insidious disclosure of another's name in words or deeds, and any others of this sort. In voluntary dealings commutative justice is properly at work, because there an exchange truly takes place, since on each side reasons are given that make the will ready and prompt. In the second kind, namely in injuries, it is not at work in the same way, but only by accident; rather, commutative justice is seen in them because each person is not given what is owed to him, as will become clear below. Concerning particular justice, these two things are to be noted briefly:

units.la: 1. Finis seu scopus ipsius, qui est in rerum tam publicarum, quam privatarum distributione & permutatione æqualitatem rectam servare, unde duæ istæ oriuntur species Distributiva & Commutativa, de quibus prolixius & singillatim cap. 6. & 7. agit Philosophus.
units.tr: 1. Its end or aim, which is to preserve right equality in the distribution and exchange of public as well as private goods. From this arise the two species, distributive and commutative, which the Philosopher treats more fully and individually in chapters 6 and 7.

units.la: 2. Notanda sunt opposita: Opponitur enim Iustitiæ particulari tantum Injustitia particularis, quæ licet propter defectum vocabulorum unum habeat nomen, res tamen plures longè inter se dissitas denotat: nam interdum Injustitia ita exercetur, ut alteri plus æquo, alteri minus æquo tribuatur, & sic tam in excessu, quam in defectu contra Iustitiam ipsam peccatur, sed de hac re infra cap. 12.
units.tr: 2. The opposites are to be noted. For only injustice in the particular sense is opposed to particular justice. Although, because of a lack of words, it has one name, it nevertheless denotes several things that are far apart from one another. For sometimes injustice is practised in such a way that more than what is fair is given to one person and less than what is fair to another, and thus one sins against justice both by excess and by deficiency. But concerning this matter, see below, chapter 12.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Sicut inaequale seu paronomum secundum majus & minus minus differt à pleonexia, ut totum à parte, sic etiam Iustitia universalis à particulari.
units.tr: 1. As the unequal, or paronymous, differs from pleonexia by more and less, as the whole differs from the part, so also universal justice differs from particular justice.

units.la: Iustitia universalis prescribit, quomodo unusquisque secundum unamquamque virtutem vivere debeat, Iustitia particularis non item.
units.tr: Universal justice prescribes how each person ought to live according to each virtue; particular justice does not do this.

units.la: Aliud est esse virum bonum, & civem bonum, siquidem vir bonus ad Ethicam in genere spectat, civis verò bonus ad Politicam.
units.tr: Being a good man and being a good citizen are different things, since the good man belongs to Ethics in general, but the good citizen belongs to Politics.

units.la: Iustitia particularis, propter diversas actiones, quas edit duas diversas species habet Distributivam, nempe & Commutativam.
units.tr: Particular justice, on account of the different actions it produces, has two different species: distributive and commutative.

units.la: Distributiva in rebus tantum publicis, quae ad commune totius civitatis bonum spectant, cernitur: Commutativa verò in rebus privatis, quae privatas respiciunt personas.
units.tr: Distributive justice is seen only in public matters, which concern the common good of the whole state; commutative justice is seen in private matters, which concern private persons.

units.la: Quia Iustitia Commutativa in commerciis cernitur, quae aliis sponte, aliis invitè fiunt, ideo in spontaneam & invitam dividitur, non tamen per se, sed objecti tantum respectu.
units.tr: Because commutative justice is seen in dealings, some of which are done voluntarily and others involuntarily, it is divided into voluntary and involuntary. This division is not made in itself, but only with respect to the object.

units.la: Commercia sex commutationes tales sunt, quales sunt ipsarum principia à quibus fluunt.
units.tr: Dealings are exchanges of such a kind as their originating principles are.

units.la: Commercia occulta sunt, quae aliis ad quos non spectant ignorantibus fiunt, violenta verò à vi externa procedunt, nec tamin iis cernitur Iustitia, quam Injustitia.
units.tr: Some dealings are secret: they are done without the knowledge of those to whom they do not pertain. Violent dealings proceed from external force; yet in neither is justice seen any more than injustice.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Iustitia Distributiva & Commutativa recte possint dici species Iustitia Particularis, cum species duae eidem subiecto numero inesse simul non possint, utpote, quae sunt contraria, & contraria simul inesse non possunt ut habet axioma Logicum. Sed Commutativa & Distributiva eidemque homini numero inesse simul possunt. Pot enim unus idemque simul distribuere & permutare, ut experientia docet, unde propter hanc causam species dici non merentur? Resp. Duplex esse subjectum, unum praedicationis, alterum inhaesionis; Contraria quidem eidem subjecto praedicationis inesse non possunt, ut verbi gratia: homo & brutum simul Socrati; at possunt inesse eidem subjecto inhaesionis, sed diverso respectu, & per diversas circumstantias, & sic Commutativa & Distributiva Iustitia inesse possunt uni homini, sed ita ut distributionis respectu intelligatur persona publica, commutationis vero persona privata.
units.tr: I. It is asked: can distributive and commutative justice rightly be called species of particular justice, since two species cannot be numerically present in the same subject at once, being contraries, and contraries cannot be present together, as the logical axiom holds? But commutative and distributive justice can be present together in the same man numerically. For one and the same person can at once distribute and exchange, as experience teaches. Why then do they not deserve to be called species for this reason? Reply: there is a double subject, one of predication and one of inherence. Contraries cannot indeed be present in the same subject of predication, as for example man and brute together in Socrates. But they can be present in the same subject of inherence, though with a different respect and under different circumstances. And so commutative and distributive justice can be present in one man, but in such a way that the person considered in distribution is a public person, and the person considered in exchange is a private person.

units.la: II. Cur duas tantum species Iustitiae Particularis protulerit Philosophus & non plures, cum tamen in libel. de virtut. tria enumeret Injustitiae genera, nempe impietate, injuriam, & petulantiam, cum scilicet aliquis ex mera petulantia nullo proposito commodo alium laedit.
units.tr: II. Why did the Philosopher set forth only two species of particular justice and not more, since in the book on the virtues he enumerates three kinds of injustice: impiety, injury, and wantonness, when someone, out of sheer wantonness and with no intended gain, harms another?

units.la: Si ergo tres sunt Injustitiae species, econtrario tres etiam erunt species Iustitiae propter mutuam legem contrariorum. Praeterea Cicero lib. 5. de finibus & in Partit. Orat. & lib. 2. ad Heren. plures enumerat Iustitiae species, verbi gratia: religionem, pietatem, gratiam, observantiam, liberalitatem, veritatem, comitatem, bonitatem, fidem, lenitatem. Et Plato etiam in Dialog. de sanctitate, numerat sanctitatem inter cateras species, sine qua, inquit, Iustitia natura nullo modo consistere potest. Resp. Philosophum recte duas tantum constituisse Justitiae particularis, propterea quod tantum sit illius scopus, nempe prodesse publice aut privatim. Quod vero ad ista enumerata, non sunt verae species, sed appendices & officia Justitiae Universalis, quae omnem in se, ut diximus complectitur Virtutem. At ad Iustitiam Particularem pleraque horum pertinere non possunt, utpote, cuius munus in duobus tantum versetur, nempe in distributione rerumpublicarum, quae ad salutem totius civitatis spectant, (nam rerum privatarum nulla est proprie distributio per Iustitiam, sed tantum permutatio) & in rerum privatarum permutatione inter personas privatas.
units.tr: If there are therefore three species of injustice, then by the mutual law of contraries there will also be three species of justice. Moreover, Cicero in book 5 of On Ends, in the Partitions of Oratory, and in book 2 of the Rhetoric to Herennius enumerates several species of justice: for example, religion, piety, gratitude, observance, liberality, truthfulness, courtesy, goodness, faithfulness, and gentleness. And Plato too, in the dialogue on holiness, counts holiness among the other species, without which, he says, justice cannot in any way exist by nature. Reply: the Philosopher rightly set up only two species of particular justice, because its sole aim is to benefit either the public or the private. As for those enumerated, they are not true species but appendices and duties of universal justice, which, as we have said, embraces in itself the whole of virtue. Most of these cannot belong to particular justice, since its office lies in two things only: the distribution of public goods, which concern the welfare of the whole state (for there is properly no distribution of private goods by justice, but only exchange), and the exchange of private goods between private persons.

units.la: III. An etiam legitima sit ista divisio in Distributivam & Commutativam, cum omnis legitima divisio debeat esse adaequata divisio, sicut docet Philosophus 2. post anal. cap. 3. & Z. ethic. lib. 1. de prop. necess. cap. 5. At hoc non est adaequata, cum sit & angustior & latior; Angustior inde esse probatur, quia omnes species Iustitiae suo ambitu non complectitur, verbi gratia: Gratitudinem, Veracitatem, & Innocentiam, quae tamen a Stoicis Iustitiae species esse dicuntur. Est latior, quia plures species Iustitiae, quam debet, sub se comprehendit, nam cum Iustitia sit virtus, suum cuique tribuens, sola Distributiva debet vere Iustitia dici, utpote, quae per distributionem suum unicuique tribuit, unde sola Distributiva dici debet Iustitia Particularis tantum? Resp. In utroque argumento committi fallaciam Petitionis principii, siquidem falsum pro vero assumitur in utroq;: nam quod ad primum istae non sunt verae species, quia Gratitudo spectat ad Iustitiam Distributivam, tanquam causa aliqua impellens, aut etiam ut affectio aliqua, quae comitari debet. Veracitas vero est virtus a Iustitia Particulari distincta, & inter homilitias lib. 4. a Philosopho numeratur cap. 13. in essentia vero non est tam proprietas alicujus virtutis, quae hominis virtute praediti, siquidem omnis bonus virtute præditus propter naturam bonitatis suæ innocenter agere & hemini consulto nocere debet. Quod ad secundum etsi Iustitia suum cuique tribuat, tamen non sequitur omnem esse Distributivā; nam in contractibus & rerum permutationibus nō minus unicuique suum tribuitur, quam in distributione, ut experientia docet.
units.tr: III. Is this division into distributive and commutative justice also legitimate, since every legitimate division ought to be an adequate division, as the Philosopher teaches in the Posterior Analytics book 2, chapter 3, and in the Ethics book 1 on necessary propositions, chapter 5? But this division is not adequate, since it is both narrower and broader. It is narrower, because it does not embrace all the species of justice within its scope, for example gratitude, truthfulness, and innocence, which are nevertheless said by the Stoics to be species of justice. It is broader, because it includes under itself more species of justice than it ought; for since justice is a virtue giving each his due, only distributive justice should truly be called justice, since it is by distribution that each is given his own. Hence only distributive justice ought to be called particular justice? Reply: a fallacy of begging the question is committed in both arguments, since in each a falsehood is taken for a truth. For as to the first, these are not true species, because gratitude pertains to distributive justice, either as some impelling cause or as an affection that ought to accompany it. Truthfulness, however, is a virtue distinct from particular justice, and the Philosopher numbers it among the virtues in book 4 of the Ethics, chapter 13. Indeed, in its essence it is not so much a property of any one virtue as of a man endowed with virtue, since every good man, endowed with virtue, ought by the nature of his goodness to act innocently and not knowingly harm anyone. As to the second: although justice gives each his own, it does not follow that every justice is distributive. For in contracts and exchanges of goods each person is given his own no less than in distribution, as experience teaches.

units.la: IV. & ult. An verum sit hoc permutationem esse rerum tantum privatarum & non publicarum, cum tamen ratio & experientia doceat contrarium: Historia enim testantur, Regna commutasse inter se Provincias, Resp. urbes & pagos, salus & agros, & id genus similia, & ista omnia sunt publica non privata: Proinde etiam in rebus, non minus publicis, quam privatis versatur permutatio? Resp. Solent interpretes distinguere, inter res permutatas & personas commutantes, & res quidem esse privatas, licet personæ sint publicæ dicunt. Sed commodius sic respondeti potest, quod permutatio sit duplex, alia propria alia impropria, in Rebuspub. datur permutatio impropriè dicta, utpote, quæ propter commoditatem aut voluptatem, non propter indigentiam aut necessitatem instituitur; alia est propria, quæ necessitatis & indigentiæ causa fit, de qua infra cap. 7. Philosophus, & ista tantum cernitur in rebus privatis & inter privatas personas, aut saltem tanquam privatas personas.
units.tr: IV. and last. Is it true that exchange concerns only private and not public goods, when reason and experience teach the contrary? For histories bear witness that kingdoms have exchanged provinces, cities and villages, fields and lands, and similar things with one another, and all these are public, not private. Therefore exchange also takes place in public matters no less than in private? Reply: the commentators are accustomed to distinguish between the things exchanged and the persons exchanging, and say that the things are private although the persons are public. But it can be answered more conveniently thus: exchange is twofold, one proper and the other improper. In the commonwealth there is an exchange improperly so called, which is made for convenience or pleasure, not from need or necessity. The other is proper, and is done for the sake of necessity and want, concerning which the Philosopher speaks below in chapter 7. This proper exchange is seen only in private matters and between private persons, or at least as between private persons.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: TErtium hoc capite prioris tractatus hujus libri membrum habetur, in quo alteram Iustitiæ Particularis superius divisæ speciem, nempe Distributivam vam accurate explicat Philosophus. Ratio vero, cur de hac priori loco agat, triplex esse videtur: 1. Quia haec Justitiae species commune civitatis totius bonum inprimis respicit, & primario ipsi prodest Reipub. secundario singulis membris ejusdem; Commutativa vero econtra. 2. Quia sine hac nulla Respub. consistere potest, ubi enim dignitas personarum, & aequalitas rerum non bene attenditur, ibi nulla vere poterit esse societas, sine altera consistere potest, praesertim si talis vigeret Respub. qualem finxit Plato, ubi omnia sint communia, nec uni deest, quod alteri adest, aut etiam ubi rebus nō superfluis, sed necessariis, quas ipsa requirit naturae necessitas, sunt contenti homines, ut in Utopia Thomas, &c. 3. Etiam quia haec species consistit in medio Geometrico, seu quoad nos: altera vero in Arithmetico; seu in medio rei. Cum ergo res propter personas, non vero personae propter res sunt creatae, ideo ea Justitiae species, quae personas respicit, dignitate & excellentia illam debet praecedere, quae inprimis respectum habet ad res. Partes hujus capitis sunt tres: In prima Justitiam Distributivam, seu quod idem est, justum distributivum (nam & hic & in magnis moralib. Justitiae & justi promiscue utitur vocabulis & speciebus concreto, q abstracto, quia concretum cum sub sefus cadat, est notius abstracto.) In secunda declarat, secundum q similitudine seu proportione sit medium. In tertia de extremis hujus Justitiae breviter agit.
units.tr: The third part of this first treatise of the book is found in this chapter, in which the Philosopher carefully explains the other species of Particular Justice mentioned above, namely Distributive justice. There seem to be three reasons why he deals with it first: (1) This kind of justice concerns above all the common good of the whole state, and benefits the commonwealth first and foremost, and its individual members only secondarily; commutative justice, on the contrary, does not. (2) No commonwealth can exist without this kind of justice. Where the dignity of persons and the equality of things are not properly regarded, no true society can exist; commutative justice, however, can exist without distributive justice, especially under the kind of commonwealth Plato imagined, where all things are held in common and one lacks nothing that another has, or where people are content with necessities rather than superfluities, which natural need itself requires, as Thomas does in his Utopia, and so on. (3) This kind also consists in the geometrical mean, or the mean relative to us, whereas the other kind consists in the arithmetical mean, or the mean of the thing. Since, therefore, things were created for the sake of persons and not persons for the sake of things, that kind of justice which regards persons ought to take precedence in dignity and excellence over that which regards things first of all. The parts of this chapter are three. In the first, he shows that distributive justice, or what is the same thing, the distributive just (for here, as in the Great Ethics, he uses the words and species of justice and the just interchangeably, the concrete for the abstract, since the concrete falls under the senses and is better known than the abstract). In the second, he declares in what respect it is a mean by similitude or proportion. In the third, he briefly treats of the extremes of this justice.

units.la: In prima igitur Justitiam Distributivam esse medium seu aequale (nam ista duo inter se aequivalent) probat duabus rationibus: 1. Ducitur a contrario,
units.tr: In the first part, then, he proves by two arguments that distributive justice is a mean or equal (for these two are equivalent to each other): (1) It is drawn from the contrary:

units.la: quia injustum est inæquale, utpote, quod circa majus & minus, quam recta velit ratio, cernitur. Ergo justum erit æquale,cum neque in majus, neque in minus deflectat, sed mediam viam solummodo teneat. 2. Ducitur ab autoritate populari. Nam communi omnium consensu, quod est æquale,idem justum, & econtra vocatur, & quod est justum, idem etiam est medium, id quod Plato confirmat lib. 5. & 6. de legib. & Cicero 1. offic. ubi inquit, Servare unusquique æquitatem debet, quæ est Justitiæ maximè propria. Sed non satis est probasse Justitiam Distributivam esse medium, propterea quod sit æqualitas inter majus & minus, nisi etiam doceat, quale sit medium, quia ex qualitate medii maximè dependet vis & natura hujus Justitiæ, & dicit non simpliciter aut absolutè, sed comparatè tantum esse medium, nempe secundum analogiam & proportionem rationis : idque confirmat duabus rationibus: Prior est, quia hæc similitudo in quatuor ad minimum terminis consistit, nempe in duabus personis & duabus rebus, ita inter se affectis & dispositis, ut ubi Justitia servari debet, majus & minus æquo pro extremis habeant: nam Justitia homines seu personas, in quas exercetur, respicit: æqualitas verò in Justitia ipsas res, quarum respectu æqualitas consistit. Quod verò personæ debeant esse æquales, hinc probat, quia nisi sint personæ inter se æquales, neque res etiam ipsæ erunt æquales, utpote quæ æqualitatem personarum, ut ipsæ ad æqualitatem reducantur, maximè respiciunt, & si res sint inæquales, hinc turbæ, seditiones, rixæ & tumultus in Repub. exorientur, quod defundefumfit, ut rotam fere hanc disputationem ex Platonis lib. 6. de legib. ubi Plato pulcerrime disputat de hac quaestione, & Isocrates etiam in Areopagitico dicit, nisi hac aequalitas servetur, turbas & tumultus non posse in Rebuspub. vitari. Ideo Plutarchus in libel. de fraterno amore taxat Solonem, quod neglecta hac, quae inter personas & res servari debet aequalitate, tota Rempubl. Atheniensium seditionibus & motibus impleverit, & ideo non immerito ipse propter leges male latas in exilium ejectus sit. Altera ratio, qua probat Justitiam Distributivam esse medium secundum analogiam, est haec: Quia secundum dignitatem maxime exercetur, qua potissimum ratione a Iustitia commutativa differt: Nam licet Iustitia in genere definiatur Virtus quae suum cuique tribuit, in sola tamen Distributiva dignitatis personarum habetur ratio, sicut in commutativa merae aequalitatis inter res, & licet in hoc omnes conveniant, quod secundum dignitatem exerceri debeat haec Iustitia Distributiva, tamen secundum quam dignitatem, an in divitiarum, an in honorum distributione sit exercenda, non satis conveniunt, quia cum alia sit apud alios dignitas, & suo diversis Rerumpublicarum formis, diversa est est dignitas: Nam in Democratia insola libertate putatur esse sita: in oligarchia, in divitiis & nobilitate, quae duae sunt verae notae omnis oligarchiae, ut testatur Philosophus 7. Pol. cap. 4. & Isocr. ad Nicoclem: in Aristocratia & Monarchia, quae optimae sunt Rerumpublicae formae, in sola virtute consistit dignitas, sicut eleganter disputat idem Isocrates in Areopagetico & ad Nicoclem. Tertiam rationem, quam hîc omittit Philosophus lib.1. mag.mor cap.13. addit, ideo nempe secundum analogiam seu proportionem rationis cernitur, hæc Iustitia, quia analogia continet vincula Reipub.dum unicuiq; suum pro dignitate tribuitur: nisi enim meriti & dignitatis habeatur ratio, nullæ inter se consistere possunt societates, & his sublatis tolluntur omnes Respubl. quia Respublica nihil est aliud, quam societas hominum sub eisdem legibus & institutis viventium.
units.tr: because the unjust is unequal, since it is found to deviate toward more and less than right reason wills. Therefore the just will be the equal, since it does not swerve toward more or less, but keeps only the middle way. (2) It is drawn from popular authority. For by the common consent of all, what is equal is called the same as the just, and conversely, and what is just is also the same as the mean; Plato confirms this in Laws, books 5 and 6, and Cicero in De Officiis 1, where he says: Each person ought to observe equity, which is most proper to justice. But it is not enough to have proved that distributive justice is a mean because it is an equality between more and less, unless he also teaches what kind of mean it is, since the force and nature of this justice depend chiefly on the nature of the mean. He says it is a mean not simply or absolutely, but only comparatively, namely according to analogy and proportion of reason. He confirms this by two arguments. The first is that this similitude consists in at least four terms, namely two persons and two things, so related and arranged to each other that where justice ought to be observed, the greater and the less hold the place of the extremes in relation to what is equal. For justice regards men, or persons, on whom it is exercised; but equality in justice regards the things themselves, with respect to which equality consists. That persons ought to be equal he proves thus: unless the persons are equal to each other, the things themselves will not be equal either, since they especially regard the equality of persons so that they may be brought back to equality; and if the things are unequal, tumults, seditions, quarrels and riots will arise in the commonwealth. This argument, which is almost the whole of this disputation, is taken from Plato's Laws, book 6, where Plato discusses this question most beautifully; and Isocrates also, in the Areopagiticus, says: unless this equality is kept, tumults and riots cannot be avoided in the commonwealth. Therefore Plutarch, in the little book on brotherly love, censures Solon because, having neglected this equality which ought to be kept between persons and things, he filled the whole Athenian commonwealth with seditions and disturbances, and for that reason he was not unjustly driven into exile on account of the badly passed laws. The second argument, by which he proves that distributive justice is a mean according to analogy, is this: it is exercised chiefly according to dignity, which is the main respect in which it differs from commutative justice. For although justice in general is defined as the virtue that gives each his due, in distributive justice alone is regard had to the dignity of persons, as in commutative justice regard is had only to mere equality between things. And although all agree that this distributive justice ought to be exercised according to dignity, they do not sufficiently agree as to which dignity it is to be exercised in the distribution of wealth or of honours, since dignity differs among different peoples, and according to the diverse forms of commonwealths it is diverse. For in a democracy it is thought to consist in liberty alone; in an oligarchy, in wealth and nobility, which are the two true marks of every oligarchy, as the Philosopher attests in Politics 7, ch. 4, and Isocrates to Nicocles; in an aristocracy and a monarchy, which are the best forms of commonwealth, dignity consists in virtue alone, as Isocrates himself elegantly argues in the Areopagiticus and to Nicocles. The third argument, which the Philosopher here omits, is added in lib. 1 Magna Moralia, ch. 13: namely that this justice is perceived according to analogy or proportion of reason, because analogy holds the bonds of the commonwealth together, while to each is given what is his according to his worth. For unless regard is had to merit and dignity, no societies can exist among men, and with these removed all commonwealths are dissolved, since a commonwealth is nothing other than a society of men living under the same laws and institutions.

units.la: Sed quia objici poterat analogiam tantum habere locum in numeris Mathematicis, non vero in rebus & factis humanis, respondet & in his suum habere locum, non tam per se, id est, ratione rerum & factorum, quam ex eventu, id est, ratione numeri, qui rebus adhæret: nam non tantum in numero solitario seu in numerante, ut loquuntur, sed etiam in numerato & rebus applicato reperitur analogia, quia definitur rationis similitudo & æqualitas, quæ in μαθήσει spectatur per se, in rebus humanis per accidens tantum, id quod hinc patet, quia ratio consistit in duobus terminis, ideo similitudo rationis, quæ unam rationem cum alia confert, consistit in quatuor terminis, ut verbi gratia: inter duo & quatuor est respectus quidam quantitatis, qui dicitur ratio dupla, sic etiam inter tria & sex: at analogia rationis confert istas duas rationes inter se, & ideo ad minimum quatuor requirit terminos, ut verbi gratia: sicut se habent duo ad quatuor, sic tria ad sex, utrobique enim est ratio dupla.
units.tr: But because it could be objected that analogy has a place only in mathematical numbers and not in human affairs and deeds, he replies that it has its place in these too, not so much in itself, that is by reason of things and deeds, as by its outcome, that is by reason of number, which adheres to things. For analogy is found not only in a solitary number, or in the counting number, as they say, but also in the counted number and in number applied to things. For the similitude and equality of ratio is defined as something that is considered in itself in mathematics [μαθήσει], but in human affairs only incidentally. This is clear from the fact that a ratio consists of two terms, so a similitude of ratio, which compares one ratio with another, consists of four terms. For example, between two and four there is a certain relation of quantity, which is called a double ratio; so too between three and six. But an analogy of ratio compares these two ratios with each other, and therefore requires at least four terms. For example: as two is to four, so three is to six, for in both there is a double ratio.

units.la: Sic etiam constituantur duæ personæ dignitatis & meriti, Achilles nempe & Ajax, ut Achilles sit 12. Ajax 6. sic etiam duæ res precii & valoris, quarum una sit 8. altera 4, hæc similitudo seu proportio interista servabitur, ut sicut se habet Achilles 12. ad Ajacem, qui est 6. sic res Achillis, quæ sunt 8. ad res Ajacis, quæ sunt 4. Aut si personæ cum rebus conferantur, sicut se habet, Achilles 12. ad rem 8. sic Ajax 6 ad rem 4. utrobique enim est ratio sesquialtera, sicut in priori proportione ratio erat dupla. Exemplis utitur Philosophus Mathematicis non Historicis, quia tum temporis erant notissima. Nam statim ab incunte ætate Mathesin discebant apud Græcos.
units.tr: In the same way, two persons of dignity and merit may be set up, Achilles and Ajax, so that Achilles is 12 and Ajax 6. Likewise two things of price and value, one of which is 8 and the other 4. This similitude or proportion will be kept between them so that, as Achilles, 12, is to Ajax, who is 6, so Achilles' things, which are 8, are to Ajax's things, which are 4. Or if persons are compared with things: as Achilles, 12, is to the thing 8, so Ajax, 6, is to the thing 4. For in both there is a sesquialter ratio, just as in the former proportion the ratio was double. The Philosopher uses mathematical examples rather than historical ones, because at that time these were most familiar, for from early childhood the Greeks studied mathematics.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis docet, secundum quam analogiam & proportionem rationis Iustitia Distributiva sit medium, quod, ut melius faciat, duas adfert ἀναλογίας divisiones, ut doceat, ad quod certum genus analogia hujus iustitiæ referatur. Prima divisio est in Continentem & Devinctam, seu ut in Logica vocatur, in Continuam & Discretam. Discreta analogia est, ubi nullum datur commune per minorem extremum, ut verbi gratia: duo ad quatuor, tria ad sex; hic est discreta analogia, quia communi termino non copulantur. Continua seu Continens analogia est, quando datur unum commune extremum per minorem, ut duo ad quatuor, quatuor ad octo, hic quartus est communis terminus, & licet actu tres tantum sint termini, potestate tamen sunt quatuor, quia commune extremum bis repetitur, & sustinet vicem duorum terminorum. Secunda divisio analogiæ est in Arithmeticam & Geometricam proportionem. Arithmetica dicitur, ubi sola ratio quantitatis titatis & excellentia numeri considerarur, ut verbi gratia: duo, tria, quatuor, quæ inter se superant, & superantur unitate. In Geometrica proportione habetur respectus personarũ & etiam rerum ipsarum secundum personas. Has divisiones ideo attulit, ut ostendat, non ad Continuam, sed ad Discretam spectare Iustitiam Distributivam, cum in quatuor ejus modi terminis versetur, qui communi extremo copulari non possunt, nam sunt duæ personæ, & duæ res à se invicem separatæ & discretæ: tum etiam, ut doceat, solam Geometricam analogiam hic spectari, ubi personarum & rerum simul habetur mutuus respectus, ita tamen ut magis habeatur personarum ratio, quibus aliquid datur, quam rerum ipsarum, quæ dantur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he teaches, according to what analogy and proportion of reason distributive justice is the mean. To make this clearer, he brings forward two divisions of analogy [ἀναλογίαι], so that he may show to which definite kind the analogy of this justice belongs. The first division is into continuous and disjunct analogy, or, as it is called in Logic, into continued and discrete. A discrete analogy is one where no term is common as the lesser extreme, for example, two to four, three to six. This is a discrete analogy, because the terms are not joined by a common term. A continuous or continued analogy is one where there is a single common extreme as the lesser term, for example, two to four, four to eight. Here the fourth term is the common term. Although only three terms are actually present, there are potentially four, because the common extreme is repeated twice and stands in the place of two terms. The second division of analogy is into arithmetical and geometrical proportion. It is called arithmetical when only the quantitative difference and the excess of number are considered, for example, two, three, four, which exceed one another and are exceeded by a unit. In geometrical proportion, regard is had to the persons and also to the things themselves in relation to the persons. He brought forward these divisions in order to show that distributive justice belongs not to the continuous but to the discrete kind, since it deals with four such terms, which cannot be joined by a common extreme, for there are two persons and two things, separate and distinct from one another. He also wished to teach that only geometrical analogy is considered here, where there is at the same time a mutual regard of persons and things, yet in such a way that more regard is had to the persons to whom something is given than to the things which are given.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis de extremis Iustitiæ Distributivæ breviter agit, & dicit, Iustitiæ distributivæ in genere opponi Injustitiam Distributivam; nam cum ipsa Iustitia Distributiva servet proportionem Geometricam, ut jam dictum est: ipsa Injustitia non servat sed plus aut minus quam tribuere debet, unicuique tribuit in præmiis & honoribus, & id genus ceteris, quæ ad Iustitiam Distributivam spectant, id quod melius patebit in actione injusta, nam injustus, qui injustè agit, in una eadem que actione secundum majus & minus peccat, sive sit in bonis, sive in malis, verbi gratia: qui alteri injuriam infert, sibi plus tribuit boni, alteri, cui injuria infertur, minus; in malis econtra minus sibi tribuit mali, alteri vero, qui injuriam patitur, plus: & si duo sint mala (cum ex duobus malis minus sit eligendum) sibi minus nus assumit, alteri majus tribuit. Proinde cum in actione injusta concurrant ista duo, nempe injuriae illatio respectu agentis, & injuriae perpessio respectu patientis, ideo Injustitia Distributiva peccabit secundum majus & minus seu in excessu & defectu contra Iustitiam ipsam Distributivam, quae medium Geometricum ubique servat.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he treats briefly of the opposites of distributive justice, and he says that distributive injustice is opposed to distributive justice in general. For since distributive justice itself keeps a geometrical proportion, as has already been said, injustice does not keep it, but gives to each person more or less than it ought to give in rewards and honours and the like, which belong to distributive justice. This will be clearer in an unjust action. For the unjust man, who acts unjustly, sins in one and the same action according to more and less, whether in goods or in evils. For example, he who inflicts an injury on another gives himself more of the good and the other, who suffers the injury, less. In evils, on the contrary, he assigns to himself less of the evil and to the one who suffers the injury more. And if there are two evils (since of two evils the lesser is to be chosen), he takes the lesser for himself and gives the greater to the other. Therefore, since these two things meet in an unjust action, namely the infliction of injury on the part of the agent and the suffering of injury on the part of the one who is wronged, distributive injustice will sin according to more and less, that is, by excess and defect, against distributive justice itself, which everywhere keeps the geometrical mean.

units.la: De Justitia Distributiva notanda sunt breviter ista sex: Primo Definitio, de qua supra cap. 5. Secundo Objectum. Objectum vero faciunt res inter plures distribuendae, sive sint bonae, cujusmodi sunt honores, dignitates, officia, magistratus, pecuniae item & praemia, sive sint malae, ut castigationes, poenae, vincula, supplicia, &c. de quibus, ubi de contractuum generibus, supra quoque mentionem fecit Philosophus. Tertio notandae sunt personae, quibus haec Iustitiae species competit: eae vero sunt plerunque publicae, quia ipsa tendit primario ad commune civitatis bonum, ut sunt magistratus, item paterfamilias, qui licet Reipub. respectu videatur persona privata; familiae tamen ratione, cujus est caput, est persona publica, & si quae sunt personae publicae, quae publicum in Rep. munus gerunt, huc etiam referuntur. Quarto observanda est proportio, quam haec virtus observat, ea vero est Geometrica, ubi personarum, inter quas fit distributio, & rerum, quae distribuuntur, pretium & valor spectatur; atqui haec quidem proportio necessario observari debet, quia absque ea nulla societas consistere potest, siquidem ex diversis hominum generibus consistit omnis Respub. non ex mercatoribus tantum, aut artificibus tantum, ideo cum non fit una eademque eorum dignitas, Iusti- tiæ Distributivæ munus erit, personas & res inter fe comparare, & ita rem cum persona comparan- do omnia partiri, ut æqualia æqualibus, & inæ- qualia inæqualibus tribuantur. Atque hoc est, quod Plato requirit lib. 6. de legib. ubi dicit, necessario ad societatem continedam observandam esse proportionem Geometricam, quanquam fui oblitus in commentitia sua Rep. lib. 1. statuat observandæ esse proportione Arithmetica, nempe ut omnia inter oës sunt communia, nulla perfonarū dignitas, nulla rerū æqualitas observetur, quod quomodo cum legibus aut cum societate hominum consistere possit, Ariftoteles negat fe videre. Cicero etiam 2. offic. ait, propter hanc proportione Geometrica constitutos initio fuisse Reges; nam cū multitudo opprimeretur ab iis, qui magnas facultates & divitias habebat, ad unum aliquem confugiebat virtute præstantem, qui cum prohiberet injuria tenuiores, in æquitate constituenda fummos cum infimis pari jure retinebat. Quinto observandus est modus, quo ista proportio fieri debet, fit enim duobus modis: 1. Separatim cum singuli termini inter fe comparantur, ut verbi gratia: persona cum persona, ut consul cum prætore: aut cum res cum re confertur, ut consulatus cum præsura; aut etiam personæ cum rebus, ut consul cum consulatu aut præsura, aut prætor etiam cum utroque. Atque hic Iustitia Distributiva suis defungetur partibus, fi personis dignis digna assignet officia, & fingulorū merita digno modo remunerabitur. 2. Fit hic modus proportionis conjunctim &im, quando scilicet totum cum toto confertur, ut quando persona & res cum alia persona & recomparatur, sic in spoliorum distributione personam Ducis cum persona militis comparando, plus Duci quam militi pro ratione spoliorum, & rursus militum huic plus, quam illi, prout quisque meritis & rebus gestis excelluit, tribuit. Sic Imperatori corona triumphalis decernebatur, ut ipsi tanquam capiti solus triumphus competere videretur: aliis alia pro rei gestae magnitudine & meritis, unde corona muralis ei dabatur, qui primus hostium muros per vim ascendisset, corona civica ei, qui civem servasset hostemque interfecisset: Corona castrensis ei, qui primus armata manu in hostium naves transiisset, de quibus vide Gell. lib.5. noct. Att. cap. 6. Huc etiam pertinet apologia Æsopi de Leone, Urso, Asino, & Vulpe. Attingit etiam hujus Justitiae proportionem seu Analogiam Paulus Apostolus 2. Corinth. 8. verf. 14. ubi monet Ecclesias, ut unam aliam juvet, servata, inquit, aequitate, quae maxime personas respicit. Sexto, hoc est observandum Aristot. hujus Iustitiae materiam angustiorem facere, quam vulgo solent alii. Nam ad honores & facultates publicas tantum restringit: alii vero faciunt latiorem & quidem latissime patentem, & ad omnes privatorum actiones qualescunque accommodant etiam ad divinas, ut ad motionem & creationem mundi, sicut Plato in quibusdam Dialogis, ad omnes denique res, in quibus ordo aliquis aut descriptio servanda sit, idq; quinque modis: 1. Ad cultum & observantiam, quae unicuique debetur, ut alia Deo, alia Magistratibus, alia parentibus,&c. debetur. 2. Ad victum & vestitum ut alius publici, alius privati, alius hujus, alius illius ordinis victus & vestitus esse debet, qua de re disserit Cic. in orat. pro Mil. 3. Accommodant etiam ad congressum in theatris & locis ejusmodi publicis, qua de re lex fuit Roscia apud Romanos, quam diserte tractat. Dion. Cassius lib. 42. histor. 4. Ad conventum & congressum, iq due duobus rursus modis: 1. In consiliis, ut potiori & digniori Princeps detur locus, si duo vel plures Reges, vel etiam Magnates, dignitate & potentia pares conveniant, ut de rebus magnis deliberent. 2. In conviviis, de qua quaestione pulcherrime disputat Plutarchus lib. Symposi. cap. 2 & 3. 5. Deniq; accommodant hujus Iustitiae materia eousque, ut unusquisque suo munere recte defungatur, & in eo se contineat, alterius munere abstineat, ne, cui non sit aptus, se immiscent, ne scilicet πολυπραγμοσύνης vitium incurrat. Solent etiam accommodare ad congressum in sermonibus & disputationibus, ut omnes circumstantiae pro decoro serventur, de quo Cic. pluribus disputat 1. offic. sub finem. In summa tam late aliis patet hujus Iustitiae materia, ut omnis actionum, tam privatarum, quam publicarum descriptio & modus, quo fieri debet, ab hac dirigatur. Sed quia hae res partim ad alias virtutes spectant, partim ex ratione naturali proficisci videntur, partim denique ad Iustitiam universalem, non particularem pertinent, Philosophus, quia ad Politica, sicut ipse cap. 1. lib. 1. hujus operis docet, totam hanc doctrinam Ethica maxime accommodat tantum in honoribus & facultatibus publipublicis, hujus Justitiæ materiâ versari asserit, quia in hís tanquam bonis externis Justitiæ publicæ usus maximè cernitur.
units.tr: Six points about distributive justice should briefly be noted. First, the definition, which was discussed above in chapter 5. Second, the object. The object is the things to be distributed among several persons, whether they are good things, such as honours, dignities, offices, magistracies, also money and rewards, or bad things, such as punishments, penalties, chains, executions, etc., of which the Philosopher also made mention above, when he dealt with the kinds of contracts. Third, the persons to whom this species of justice applies must be noted. These are for the most part public persons, because it aims primarily at the common good of the state, such as magistrates. Likewise the head of a household, who, although with respect to the commonwealth he may seem a private person, is by reason of the family, of which he is the head, a public person. And if there are any public persons who discharge a public duty in the commonwealth, these too are referred to here. Fourth, the proportion which this virtue observes must be noted. It is geometrical, where the worth and value are considered of the persons among whom the distribution is made and of the things that are distributed. This proportion must necessarily be observed, because without it no society can exist. For every commonwealth consists of various kinds of men, not of merchants only or craftsmen only. Therefore, since the dignity of these is not one and the same, the task of distributive justice will be to compare persons and things with one another, and so, by comparing thing with person, to divide everything so that equals are given to equals and unequals to unequals. This is what Plato requires in book 6 of the Laws, where he says that geometrical proportion must necessarily be observed to maintain society. Yet he forgot this in his fanciful Republic, book 1, where he lays down that arithmetical proportion must be observed, namely that all things are common to all, that no dignity of persons and no equality of things is observed. Aristotle says he does not see how this could agree with laws or with human society. Cicero also says, in book 2 of De officiis, that kings were originally established on account of this geometrical proportion. For when the multitude was oppressed by those who had great means and wealth, they fled to one man who excelled in virtue, and he, by restraining the injuries of the humbler sort, kept the highest and the lowest on an equal footing in establishing equity. Fifth, the mode in which this proportion must be made must be noted. It is made in two ways. 1. Separately, when the individual terms are compared with one another: for example, person with person, as consul with praetor; or thing with thing, as consulship with praetorship; or also persons with things, as consul with consulship or praetorship, or even praetor with both. And here distributive justice will discharge its parts if it assigns worthy offices to worthy persons, and rewards the merits of each in a fitting manner. 2. This mode of proportion is made jointly, when the whole is compared with the whole, that is, when a person and a thing are compared with another person and another thing. Thus in the distribution of spoils, by comparing the person of the general with the person of the soldier, he gives the general more than the soldier in proportion to the spoils, and again gives more to one soldier than to another, according as each has excelled in merit and deeds performed. So a triumphal crown was decreed to the commander, so that the triumph seemed to belong to him alone as the head. To others other honours were given according to the greatness of the deed and their merits: thus the mural crown was given to him who first by force had scaled the enemy's walls, the civic crown to him who had saved a citizen and killed an enemy, and the camp crown to him who first with armed hand had crossed into the enemy's ships. On these matters see Gellius, book 5 of the Attic Nights, chapter 6. To this also belongs the apology of Aesop about the Lion, the Bear, the Ass and the Fox. The Apostle Paul also touches on the proportion or analogy of this justice in 2 Corinthians 8:14, where he admonishes the churches that one should help another, keeping, he says, equality, which chiefly regards persons. Sixth, it must be observed that Aristotle makes the matter of this justice narrower than others commonly do. For he restricts it to public honours and resources only. Others make it broader, indeed very broad, and apply it to all the actions of private persons of whatever kind, even to divine matters, such as the motion and creation of the world, as Plato does in certain dialogues, and finally to all things in which some order or arrangement must be kept. And they do this in five ways: 1. To the worship and reverence owed to each person, for different reverence is owed to God, different to magistrates, different to parents, etc. 2. To food and clothing, for public persons, private persons, and persons of this or that rank ought to have different food and clothing. Cicero discusses this matter in his speech For Milo. 3. They also apply it to gatherings in theatres and similar public places. On this matter there was among the Romans the Roscian law, which Dio Cassius treats fully in book 42 of his History. 4. To assembly and gathering, which again is of two kinds: 1. In councils, so that the leading and more worthy person is given the place of honour, if two or more kings or magnates, equal in dignity and power, meet to deliberate on great affairs. 2. In banquets, a question which Plutarch disputes most beautifully in book 2 of the Symposiacs, chapters 2 and 3. 5. Finally, they apply the matter of this justice so far that each person discharges his own office rightly and keeps himself within it, abstaining from another's office, so that he does not meddle in what he is not fitted for, and so falls into the vice of busybodying [πολυπραγμοσύνη]. They also commonly apply it to gatherings in conversations and disputations, so that all circumstances are observed for propriety. Cicero discusses this at length in book 1 of De officiis, near the end. In sum, the matter of this justice extends so widely to other things that the whole description of actions, both private and public, and the manner in which they must be done, is directed by it. But since these matters partly pertain to other virtues, partly seem to arise from natural reason, and partly finally belong to universal rather than particular justice, the Philosopher, because he is writing about Politics, as he himself teaches in chapter 1 of book 1 of this work, adapts this whole doctrine to Ethics only as far as honours and public resources go. He asserts that the matter of this justice consists in these, because in them, as in external goods, the use of public justice is most clearly seen.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. In quacunque re datur inæqualitas secundum majus & minus, datur etiam æqualitas secundum medium.
units.tr: 1. In whatever thing there is inequality according to more and less, there is also equality according to the mean.

units.la: 2. Cum justum sit æquale, erit etiam medium inter injustum, quod secundum majus & minus cernitur.
units.tr: 2. Since the just is the equal, there will also be a mean between the unjust, which is perceived according to more and less.

units.la: 3. Justitia Distributiva in quatuor terminis versatur, nempe duabus personis, & duabus rebus.
units.tr: 3. Distributive justice is concerned with four terms, namely two persons and two things.

units.la: 4. Nisi servetur in hac Justitia personarum æqualitas, turba, tumultus & rixa in Repub. exorientur.
units.tr: 4. Unless equality of persons is preserved in this justice, uproar, tumult and strife will arise in the commonwealth.

units.la: 5. Justitia Distributiva pro personarum dignitate suas actiones exercere solet.
units.tr: 5. Distributive justice is accustomed to exercise its actions according to the dignity of persons.

units.la: 6. Alia in aliis hominum statibus observatur dignitas, alia in Democratia, ut Libertas, alia in Aristocratia ut virtus.
units.tr: 6. Different dignity is observed in different states of men: in democracy one kind, such as liberty; in aristocracy another, such as virtue.

units.la: 7. Analogia seu proportio non tantum cernitur in numero numerante seu formali, sed etiam in numerato seu materiali.
units.tr: 7. Analogy or proportion is found not only in the numbering number, which is formal, but also in the numbered, which is material.

units.la: 8. Analogia est vel continens, vel sejuncta, seu ut in Logicis vocatur continua vel Discreta.
units.tr: 8. Analogy is either continuous or disjunct, or, as it is called in logic, continuous or discrete.

units.la: 9. Continua proportio licet actu tantum tribus constet terminis, potestate tamen habet quatuor, quia terminus communis bis repetitur.
units.tr: 9. A continuous proportion, although it actually consists of only three terms, has four potentially, because the common term is repeated twice.

units.la: 10. Omnis etiam proportio est vel Geometrica, quæ respicit personas, vel Arithmetica, quæ ipsas considerat res, & circa priorem tantum versatur Justitia Distributiva.
units.tr: 10. Every proportion is either geometric, which regards persons, or arithmetic, which considers things themselves; and distributive justice is concerned only with the former.

units.la: 11. Justitia Distributiva opponitur Injustitia, quæ secundum majus & minus cernitur.
units.tr: 11. Distributive justice is opposed to injustice, which is perceived according to more and less.

units.la: 12. Qui injuste agit in bonis sibi plus attribuit, alteri minus, in malis vero e contra.
units.tr: 12. He who acts unjustly assigns to himself more of the goods and less to another, and the reverse in the case of evils.

units.la: 13. Ex duobus malis, cum minus respectu majoris obtineat rationem boni, injustus sibi minus semper eligit.
units.tr: 13. Of two evils, since the lesser holds the aspect of a good in comparison with the greater, the unjust man always chooses the lesser for himself.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An Iustitia Distributiva vere possit dici Iustitia, cum ei Iustitia definitio non competit. Nam Iustitia definitur, quasi suum cuique tribuit: at distributio non tribuit suum cuique, sed alienum tantum bonum & commune, quia versatur circa Respub. ut sunt facultates & honores, ergo Iustitia nomine non videtur appellanda? Resp. Suum cuique tribuere duobus modis posse considerari: Pro eo, quod ad unumquodque proprie spectat, & in sua potestate habet. 2. Pro eo, quod suo sibi merito quis acquisivit, & ratione quadam ei debetur, & secundo modo Distributiva dicitur suum cuique tribuere. Nam licet commune bonum inter plures distribuat, hoc commune possit dici proprium, & suum respectu singularum partium, quæ ad communitatem spectant.
units.tr: I. Question: Can distributive justice truly be called justice, since the definition of justice does not apply to it? For justice is defined as giving each his own, but distribution does not give each his own; it gives only another's good and the common good, since it is concerned with the commonwealth, such as offices and honours. Therefore it seems it should not be called by the name of justice? Reply: Giving each his own can be considered in two ways: (1) in respect of what properly belongs to each and is in his power; (2) in respect of what someone has acquired by his own merit and is due to him by a certain reason. It is in the second sense that distributive justice is said to give each his own. For although it distributes a common good among many, this common good can be called one's own with respect to each of the parts that belong to the community.

units.la: II. Quomodo dicat respiciendam esse personarum dignitatem in remuneratione, quæ fit per Iustitiam Distributivam, cum tamen lib. 4. cap. 8 dixerit, virtuti nullam mercedem dignam tribui posse, id quod etiam experientia docet: ergo virtuti viri boni proportio munerum respondere nullo modo potest? Resp. Licet ipsa nulla merces digna virtuti tribui possit, quomodo intelligendus est locus ille citatus, ratione tamen potest, cum scilicet munus aliquod (quo veluti calcari ad virtutis cursum persequendum excitantur homines) beneficiis viri reponditur.
units.tr: II. How does he say that the dignity of persons is to be regarded in the reward made through distributive justice, when yet in book 4, chapter 8, he said that no worthy reward can be given to virtue, which experience also teaches? Therefore a proportion of rewards can in no way correspond to the virtue of a good man? Reply: Although no reward worthy of virtue can be given to it, that passage cited can be understood in terms of reason, namely when some office (by which men are roused, as with a spur, to pursue the course of virtue) is rendered in return for the services of a good man.

units.la: III. &c ult. An verum sit hoc, quod Iustitia Distributiva ti̇va exer̈ eri debeat secundum dignitatem personarum, cum hinc hoc sequatur, nempe Justitiam esse personarum respectu, qui cum in nulla virtute fieri debeat, tum multo minus in Justitia, quae est praecipua virtus; quod vero in nulla virtute profopolephia sit admittenda, hinc patet, quia virtutes tantum sunt regulae rectae rationis, & ubi ratio dominatur, ibi perso-na secundum dignitatem non sunt respicienda, sed ipsa facta aut merita exprafcripto rectae rationi? Resp. Non inde hoc sequi, Justitiam scilicet esse personarū respectum, cum Justitia pro dignitate cujusque exercetur, nam natura Justitiæ Distributivæ hoc exigit, ut benefactis præmium, malefactis pœna tribuatur: hoc autem fieri non potest, nisi dignitas & merita personarum bene perpendantur: nam facta justa vel injusta ratione causæ & principii, a quo veniunt, illustrantur vel obscurantur: Dein etiam qualitates sunt duplices in singulis personis: aliæ sunt, quæ pertinent ad ipsam dignitatem illustrandam, & si istæ considerentur, non est vere personarum respectus, nisi ex præscripto rectæ rationis, quæ jubet, ut pro meritis suum cuique tribuatur. Secundò aliæ sunt alienæ & non pertinentes, ut verbi gratia: cum quæstio est de hæreditate, de homicidio, &c. & in istis casibus non debet fieri personarum respectus. Sic enim natura justi & æqui violabitur.
units.tr: III. &c., last. Is it true that distributive justice ought to be exercised according to the dignity of persons? For it follows from this that justice has respect of persons, which ought not to be done in any virtue, and much less in justice, which is the chief virtue. That respect of persons must not be admitted in any virtue is clear, because virtues are only rules of right reason, and where reason rules, persons are not to be regarded according to dignity, but the deeds themselves or merits according to the prescription of right reason. Reply: It does not follow from this that justice is a respect of persons, since justice is exercised according to each one's dignity. For the nature of distributive justice requires that reward be given to good deeds and punishment to evil ones. But this cannot be done unless the dignity and merits of persons are weighed carefully, for just or unjust deeds are illuminated or obscured by the reason of the cause and principle from which they come. Then, too, qualities are twofold in each person. Some pertain to illustrating dignity itself, and if these are considered, it is not truly a respect of persons, but accords with the prescription of right reason, which bids that each be given his own according to his merits. Secondly, others are foreign and not pertinent, as for example when the question concerns an inheritance, a homicide, and so on; and in such cases no respect of persons should be shown. For otherwise the nature of the just and the equal would be violated.

units.la: Ut natura Justitiæ Distributivæ melius intelligatur, quæritur: An Gratitudo & Reverentia, quæ à plerisque Ethicis inter species Justitiæ Distributivæ numerantur, sint revera species ejusdem? Quod ad primam, ideo existimant, quòd cognationem quandam cum ipsa Justitia Distributiva habeat, idq; propter tres rationes: 1. Quia definitio Justitiæ Iustitia ei competit. 2. Quia vulgo & recepto definitur: Iustitia retribuens unicuique benemerito jucundam acceptï beneficii memoriam: & 3. Quia Ingratitudo est species Injustitiæ, ergo ex lege contrariorum Gratitudo erit species Iustitia? Resp. Per negationem, nam non tam est species, quàm effectio & proprietas insequens lustitiâ, & cernitur potius in privatis, quàm in publicis rebus. Ad Reverentiam vero quod attinet, distinguendum est inter reverentiam actívam & passivam, & rursus quatenus sumitur, vel pro actu vel pro habitu reverendi eos, qui dignitate & potentia sunt nobis superiores, & in hac significatione ponitur pro specie Iustitiæ Distributivæ, in reliquis pro specie honoris superioribus debiti, sed revera species nō est, prout Iustitia Distributiva à Philosopho consideratur, nisi forte ex consequenti, quatenus scilicet circa honores, in quibus etiam Iustitia cernitur publicè aut privatim versatur.
units.tr: To understand the nature of distributive justice better, it is asked: Are gratitude and reverence, which most ethicists count among the species of distributive justice, truly species of the same? As to the first, they think so because it has a certain kinship with distributive justice itself, for three reasons: (1) Because the definition of justice applies to it; (2) because it is commonly defined and received as justice rendering to each deserving person a pleasant memory of the benefit received; and (3) because ingratitude is a species of injustice, therefore by the law of contraries gratitude will be a species of justice? Reply: Denied. For it is not so much a species as an effect and property following from justice, and it is seen rather in private than in public matters. As for reverence, one must distinguish between active and passive reverence, and again according as it is taken either for the act or for the habit of revering those who are superior to us in dignity and power. In this meaning it is placed as a species of distributive justice; in the other senses, as a species of the honour owed to superiors. But in truth it is not a species as distributive justice is considered by the Philosopher, except perhaps by consequence, namely insofar as it concerns honours, in which justice too is exercised, publicly or privately.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: QUartum hoc capite prioris tractatus hujus libri habetur membrum, in quo Philosophus alteram speciem particularis Iustitiæ, nempe Commutativam, quæ in rerum commutatione tota versatur, explicat. Dicitur alias Corrective commerciorum, quod rerum commutationem ita corrigat, ut nulla pars injuriam sibi fieri justè asserat, vel ut ait Philosophus, hoc ipso capite, quia personarum dignitate seposita sic ita inter se comparat, ut omnis inæqualitas tollatur, vel etiam, ut quibusdam placet, quia res inæquales ad æqualitatem reducit, vel sententia iudicis, vel privato hominum arbitrio absque omni iudicis sententia. Partes capitis sunt quatuor: In prima de obiecto huius Iustitiae paucis agit: In secunda differentiam inter hanc & priorem speciem affert: In tertia de medio tractat & de proportione, quae servatur in hac Iustitia: In quarta demum, quo pacto inveniri possit medium huius Iustitiae, perspicue declarat.
units.tr: Here begins the fourth section of the first treatise of this book, in which the Philosopher explains the other species of particular justice, namely Commutative justice, which is wholly concerned with the exchange of goods. It is also called the corrective justice of transactions, because it so corrects the exchange of goods that no party can justly claim to have been wronged. Or, as the Philosopher says in this same chapter, it is because, setting aside the dignity of persons, it treats the parties as equals so that all inequality is removed. Or, as some prefer, it is because it reduces unequal things to equality, either by the sentence of a judge or by the private judgement of men without any sentence of a judge. The chapter has four parts. In the first, the author briefly treats the object of this justice. In the second, he sets out the difference between this and the former species. In the third, he deals with the mean and with the proportion observed in this justice. In the fourth, finally, he clearly explains how the mean of this justice may be found.

units.la: In prima igitur hanc speciem Iustitiae versari in rerum contractibus docet: qui ut ex superioribus patet, vel sponte vel invite fiunt, & proinde multum refert scire de modo, quo commercia contrahuntur inter homines, quia ab isto modo tota huius Iustitiae ratio pendet. Obiectum igitur sunt res omnes, de quibus inter se contrahere, quocunque modo sive sponte, sive coacte fiat, id possunt homines: de quo vide plura supra ad caput f.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he teaches that this species of justice is concerned with contracts over goods. As is clear from what was said above, these contracts are made either voluntarily or under compulsion. It therefore matters a great deal to know the manner in which dealings are contracted between men, since the whole account of this justice depends on that manner. The object, then, is all those things about which men can contract with one another, in whatever way the agreement is made, whether freely or by compulsion. On this, see more above, at the chapter marked f.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis discrimen adfert inter hanc Iustitiam & priorem. Discrimen vero constat potissimum in quatuor rebus: 1. Quia Iustitia Distributiva versatur circa facultates publicas & honores inter personas publicas distribuendos, haec vero respicit res privatas & personas etiam privatas. 2. Differentia sumitur a ratione medii, quia haec non versatur circa medium secundum proportionem Geometricam, ut prior, sed circa medium secundum proportionem Arithmeticam. 3.
