Differentia est ratione officii: nam huius est res tantum inter se commutare, servata rerum ipsarum aequalitate tantum nullo ad personas habito respecta, prioris vero e contra. 4. Etiam ratione usus & finis distinguun-tur, tur, quia hæc singula Reipub. membra, non ipsam Rempub. primario respicit: in Iustitia Distributiva econtra fit.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he draws the distinction between this justice and the former one. The difference consists chiefly in four points: (1) Distributive justice is concerned with public resources and with honours to be distributed among public persons, whereas this justice concerns private goods and private persons too. (2) The difference is taken from the nature of the mean: this justice does not work with the mean according to geometrical proportion, as the former does, but according to arithmetical proportion. (3) The difference lies in the function: it is the task of this justice merely to exchange goods with one another, keeping the goods themselves equal, with no regard to persons; the task of the former is the reverse. (4) They are also distinguished by their use and end, because this justice looks primarily at the individual members of the commonwealth and not at the commonwealth itself; distributive justice, on the contrary, does so.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis docet, hanc speciem Iustitiæ medium servare secundum proportionem Arithmeticam, quia rerum ipsarum non personarum, ut in priori hic habetur ratio, idque confirmat duobus exemplis: 1. Est quod de duobus inter se contrahentibus, & si in contracta alter alterum defraudaret, non quæritur de isto defraudatore sitne vir probus an improbus, illustri aut ignobili familia, sed tantum quanta sit fraus aut damnum, quod alteri intulit, quia de personis quærere ad alteram Iustitiæ speciem pertinet. 2. Exemplum erit de adultero, nam qui adulterium comisit, de ipso non quæritur, qualis sit bonusne an malus, sed tantum de facto & re ipsa, non de persona, quia natura Justitiæ Commutativæ hoc exigit, ut damni & jacturæ, quæ rebus ipsis accidit, tantum habeatur ratio, personas eodem loco habet & pro iisdem utitur, non magis huic quam illi tribuit, nisi facti ipsius ratio postulet. Proinde non immerito Cyrum Persarum Regem futurum castigavit Præceptor ejus, ut testatur Xenoph. lib. 1. instit. Cyri, quod neglecta hac proportione Arithmetica usus sit in rebus ipsis commutandis proportione Geometrica, nempe dum tunicam longiorem brevioris daret longiori, & longiorem econtra breviori. Sic pulcherrimus extat locus apud Gell. lib. 12. noct. Attic. cap. 2. Sed quia Justitia Commutativa diversissimæ est naturæ à Distributiva, nam contrarium fere habet medium, ideo ne quis putaret, non esse virtutem, quod medium singulare & distinctū à cæteris virtutibus obtineat, ideo probat consistere in medio duabus rationibus: 1. Quia hoc medium Arithmeticum sit æquale etiam inter majus & minus, nam si quæ sit in rebus ipsis inæqualitas, judex emendare studet, ut e.g. Si alter sit percussus alter sit occisus, hęc perpessio cū sit in æqualiter distributa, judex damno & lucro exæquare studet, atq; ita ad æqualitatē perducere, ut nulla passim injuriā sentiat, quod exemplum ideo adducit, ut ostendat Justitiam Commutativam non habere tantū usum in commodis aut incommodis externarū facultatū, sed etiam ad corpus ipsum spectare, postquā nempe injuria, autoritate Iudicis per damnum & lucrum emensa & emendata fuerit, nam damnum & lucrum sunt extrema inter quæ tanquam inter excessum & defectum hęc Justitia versatur, sed contrario modo: nam cui inest lucrum, illi plus boni minusque mali inesse dicitur, & sic lucrum pro excessu habetur: cui inest damnum, illi plus mali & minus boni inest, & sic damnum pro defectu opponitur. Cum igitur inter damnum & lucrum mediam teneat viam Iustitia commutativa, medium non minus erit inter excessum & defectum, quam reliquæ virtutes licet diverso plane modo. 2. Ratio ducitur à nomine, quod Iudici imponitur (qui Iudex justis minister, executor, interpres, & jus quoddam animatum hīcá Philosopho dicitur, & à Cic. 3. de leg. & in tit. de Iustitia & Iure apud Iurisconsultos:) nam Iudex dicitur mediatus quasi sit medius, aut quia exæquat obortam damni & lucri æqualitatem, per
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he teaches that this species of justice keeps the mean according to arithmetical proportion, because it takes account of the goods themselves and not of persons, as the former did. He confirms this by two examples. (1) Take two parties contracting with each other. If in the contract one defrauds the other, one does not ask whether this defrauder is an upright or a wicked man, or of a famous or obscure family, but only how great the fraud or loss is that he has inflicted on the other, because to inquire about persons belongs to the other species of justice. (2) The example will be of an adulterer. For one who has committed adultery is not asked what sort of man he is, good or bad, but only about the deed and the thing itself, not about the person. The nature of commutative justice requires this: it takes account only of the damage and loss that befall the things themselves, and it treats persons on the same footing, using them alike, assigning no more to one than to the other, unless the nature of the deed itself demands it. Therefore his tutor rightly rebuked Cyrus, the future King of the Persians, as Xenophon reports in the first book of the Cyropaedia, because he had neglected this arithmetical proportion and used geometrical proportion in exchanging the things themselves, namely when he gave a longer tunic to the taller man and a shorter one to the shorter man, and conversely. There is also a very fine passage on this in Gellius, Attic Nights, book 12, chapter 2. But since commutative justice is of a very different nature from distributive justice (for its mean is nearly the opposite), lest anyone think that it is not a virtue because it has a mean of its own, distinct from the other virtues, he proves that it consists in a mean on two grounds. (1) This arithmetical mean is equal even between greater and lesser, for if there is inequality in the things themselves, the judge seeks to correct it. For example, if one man has been struck and the other killed, since this suffering has been unequally distributed, the judge seeks to balance the loss and gain and so bring them to equality, that no party feels wronged. He gives this example to show that commutative justice does not have its use only in the advantages or disadvantages of external goods, but also concerns the body itself, once the injury has been measured by loss and gain and corrected by the authority of the judge. For loss and gain are the extremes between which this justice operates, as between excess and deficiency, but in the opposite way: for one who has gain is said to have more good and less evil, and so gain is taken as excess; one who has loss has more evil and less good, and so loss is set against deficiency. Since commutative justice therefore holds the middle course between loss and gain, the mean will be no less between excess and deficiency than in the other virtues, though in a quite different way. (2) The argument is drawn from the name given to the judge, who is called (as the Philosopher says, and Cicero in De legibus book 3, and in the title on Justice and Law among the jurists) a just minister, executor, interpreter, and a sort of living law. The judge is called mediator as though he were the middle, or because he equalises the inequality of loss and gain that has arisen, by a certain middle reckoning, just as if someone, wishing to make unequal lines equal, were to take some part from the longer one so as to make it equal to the shorter, or were to add to the shorter just as much as would make it equal to the longer.

units.la: rationem quandam mediam, non secus ac si quis lineas inæquales exæquaturus longiori portionem aliquam demat, ut sic breviori æqualis fiat, vel etiam breviori tantum addat, quantum longiori æqualem facere possit.
units.tr: a certain middle proportion, just as someone who wishes to make unequal lines equal cuts off some portion of the longer one, so that it becomes equal to the shorter, or else adds to the shorter just as much as can make it equal to the longer.

units.la: In quarta parte cap. docet, quomodo inveniri possit medium in hac Justitia, quod sit æquale inter majus & minus secundum proportionem Arithmeticam. Docet vero quadam similitudine, nempe quemadmodum lineariū inæquales partes quis inæquatur, qua altera longior breviore superat, eam portione totam illi demit, vel etiam tantundem alteri breviori addet, ut sic linearum inæqualitas ad justam æqualitatem perducatur, ut neque una superet alteram, neque superetur ab altera: sic etiam Judex in hac Justitia Commutativa facere debet, ut si quis lucrum cum alterius damno habeat, id totum illi detractum Judex alteri attribuere debet, ut sic æqualitate in rebus constituta, nulla pars injuriam sibi fieri asserat. Et hanc similitudinem confirmat ratione ab etymo nominis Justitiæ deducta, & exemplis trium linearum. Ratio hæc est: Justum Græcis dicitur δίκαιον, quasi δίχαιον, id est, in duo æqualia divisum, & Judex dicitur δικαστής, id est, divisor continui in duas partes æquales, ita ut nulla superet nec superetur, quanquam Plato in Cratylo hanc notationem Justitiæ non probet; sed dicit δίκαιον ideo vocari, quod sit quasi διὰ πάντα transiens, quia Justitia sua bonitate omnia æquè transit, vel quia, ut idem ait, ex sententia Anaxagoræ, omnium bonorum causa sit. Exemplum de tribus lineis est hoc: Sumantur tres lineæ, quarum prima sit longissima, secunda brevior, tertia brevissima. Si igitur una pars auferatur, & addatur tertiae, nempe qua secundam superat, ambae erunt aequales ipsi mediae, & sic Judex ad medium tanquam ad scopum ita respicere debet, ut omnis inaequalitas inexcessu & defectu ad aequalitatem reflectis jam inaequalibus perducatur. Et hac ratione justum modum inveniendi medii secundum proportionem Arithmeticam in hac Justitia praescribit.
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter he teaches how the mean can be found in this Justice, which lies equally between the greater and the lesser according to arithmetical proportion. He teaches this by a certain likeness: just as, when one makes unequal lines equal, one takes from the longer line the portion by which it exceeds the shorter, or else adds to the shorter as much as it lacks, so that the inequality of the lines is brought to a just equality, neither exceeding the other nor being exceeded by it, so too the judge in this commutative Justice ought to act. If someone has a gain at another's loss, the judge must take all of that gain away from him and assign it to the other, so that, with equality established in the matter, no party can claim that an injury has been done to him. He confirms this likeness by an argument drawn from the etymology of the name of Justice, and by the example of three lines. The argument runs thus: what is just is called by the Greeks δίκαιον [dikaion], as if δίχαιον [dichaion], that is, divided into two equal parts, and the judge is called δικαστής [dikastes], that is, a divider of a continuum into two equal parts, so that neither exceeds nor is exceeded. Yet Plato in the Cratylus does not approve this derivation of justice; he says that δίκαιον [dikaion] is so called because it is, as it were, διὰ πάντα [dia panta] passing through, since justice by its goodness passes equally through all things, or because, as the same writer says, following the opinion of Anaxagoras, it is the cause of all good things. The example of the three lines is this: let three lines be taken, the first the longest, the second shorter, the third the shortest. If one part is taken away from the first and added to the third, namely that part by which the second exceeds the third, then both will be equal to the middle line. So the judge, looking to the mean as to a goal, ought to act in such a way that every inequality, by excess and by defect, is brought back to equality, the unequal things being reshaped. By this argument he prescribes the just method of finding the mean according to arithmetical proportion in this Justice.

units.la: De hac lustitiæ specie ista 5. sunt breviter notanda: 1. Definitio, de qua supra cap. 5. 11. Differentia, de qua etiā hoc cap. actum fuit, qua distinguitur ab altera specie, nempe Distributiva. 111. Modus observari debet, quo medium servat secundam proportionem Arithmeticam; Modus vero consistit in debita rerum inter se collatione, ut quantum una res alteram dignitate precio aut valore superat, aut ab altero superatur, tantum in excessu & defectu compensetur, servata semper ipsarum rerum proportione, ut verbi gratia: si mercator & agricola vinum & ferrum inter se commutent pondo ferri aestimetur quinque g. amphora vini decem g. Cum igitur proportio, qua vini amphora pondo ferri superat, sit dupla, mercator pro singulis vini amphoris duo ferri pondo dabit, ut sic justa ratio ipsarum rerum exaequata valore & precio habeatur, & justum medium in Commutativa Iustitia observetur. Hac Iustitia excelluit Q. Mutius Scævola, qui, ut refert in vita ipsius Rutilius, cum sibi fundus, cujus erat emptor, ut aestimaretur, rogasset, idque fecisset venditor, dixit sepluris aestimare, ideo sponte sua addidit 100000. ne si minoris, quam res esset, fundum coemisset, hanc Iustitiam Commutativam violasset. Hoc etiam elogio Thuriacos populos commendat Stob. serm. 42. quod mercaturam exercentes absque omni dolo emerent, & venderent omnia, apud quos, si quis domum emisset in Apollinis templo sacra facere tenebatur, & Deum testari, nihil se iniqui commisisse in hac emtione: si vero vicum aut hortum in praedio, quod inhabitabat, coram Magistratu jurare solebat, quod juste & recte emisset, & non fraudulenter egisset, aut arte aut dolo malo usus esset. Eodem etiam modo & vendentem jurare cogebat Magistratus, quod absque omni dolo vendidisset. IV. Observandum venit objectum hujus Iustitiae; Objectum vero sunt res omnes, quae commutari possunt ad necessitates & indigentias hominum supplendas, atque adeo non tantum res externae, sed etiam qualitates aut affectiones corporis, in quibus damnum aut lucrum spectari possit, sed de objecto plura vide ad cap. f. V. & ult. Consideratur media, quibus rerum precium ac valor in hac Iustitia aestimatur. Hujusmodi vero sunt duo, natura nempe & institutum hominum. Res enim vel secundum necessitatem, quam natura importat, aestimari solent, vel secundum utilitatem & commodum hominum, & sic ab instituto dependent. Natura majoris precii sunt, quarum major est usus majorque ad vitam humanam necessitas. Atque haec fuit prima mercaturae instituendae occasio, cum enim in diversis regionibus habitarent homines, nec singula ad vitam necessaria in singulis gigneretur mundi parpartibus, commercia natura duce instituta sunt. Namque, ut aiit eleganter Poëta:
units.tr: There are five points to note briefly about this species of justice. (1) The definition, discussed above in chapter 5, 11. (2) The difference, which was also treated in this chapter, by which it is distinguished from the other species, namely Distributive justice. (3) The mode that must be observed, by which the mean keeps the second, arithmetic proportion. This mode consists in a due comparison of things with one another: whatever amount one thing exceeds another in dignity, price or value, or is exceeded by it, must be balanced by the excess and deficit, the proportion of the things themselves always being preserved. For example, if a merchant and a farmer exchange wine for iron, let a weight of iron be valued at five gold pieces and an amphora of wine at ten. Since the proportion by which an amphora of wine exceeds a weight of iron is double, the merchant will give two weights of iron for each amphora of wine. In this way the just relation of the things themselves is kept, equal in value and price, and the just mean is observed in Commutative justice. Q. Mucius Scaevola excelled in this justice. As Rutilius reports in his life, when the seller was asked to value an estate that Scaevola was buying, and had done so, Scaevola said that he would value it at a higher figure. Accordingly he of his own accord added 100,000, lest by buying the estate for less than it was worth he should violate Commutative justice. Stobaeus, Sermon 42, also commends the Thurini by this praise: that those who practised trade bought and sold everything without any deceit. Among them, if someone had bought a house, he was bound to perform a sacrifice in the temple of Apollo and to call God to witness that he had committed no wrong in this purchase. If he had bought a vicus or a garden on an estate he lived on, he was accustomed to swear before the magistrate that he had bought justly and rightly, and had not acted fraudulently or used craft or evil deceit. In the same way the magistrate also compelled the seller to swear that he had sold without any deceit. (4) The object of this justice must be considered. The object is all things that can be exchanged to supply the needs and wants of men, and so not only external things but also qualities or affections of the body, in which loss or gain may be looked at. More on the object may be seen at chapters 5 and 6 below. The means by which the price and value of things are estimated in this justice is to be considered. There are two such means, namely nature and human institution. For things are customarily valued either according to the necessity that nature imposes, or according to the utility and advantage of men, and so depend on institution. Those things are of greater price whose use is greater and whose necessity for human life is greater. This was the first occasion for establishing trade: since men lived in different regions, and not every necessity of life was produced in every part of the world, commerce was established under the guidance of nature. For, as the poet elegantly says:

units.la: Non omnia fert omnia tellus,Sed hic segetes illic veniunt felicius uva, &c.
units.tr: No land bears all things; here grain comes more fruitfully, there the grape, and so on.

units.la: ita ut quod in diversis regionibus nascitur, natura effecit, ut id omne ad necessitatem supplendam permutaretur, & quod in una regione majore copia proveniret, aliis eo indigentibus impertiretur, effecit provida rerum parens, ut iidem rebus apud exteros majori proventu nascentibus, opus etiam habe ret, & sic mutua permutatione sibi mutuo succurrerent. Et haec fuit prima rerum permutatio priusquam pecuniae usus inveniretur. Hinc etiam Seres populi, ut referunt Plinius, Solinus & alii, rerum permutationem instituisse dicuntur, & cum scirent adventare mercatores, ad litus descendebant, & sericum suum, quo maxime abundabant, in loco conspicuo deponebant, postea abeuntes ipsius pretium mercatorum arbitrio relinquebant, unde Virg.
units.tr: So that what is born in one region, nature has so arranged that all of it may be exchanged to meet necessity, and what comes in greater abundance in one region may be shared with others who lack it. The provident parent of things has also arranged that those who have a greater yield of things born among foreigners should also need them, and so by mutual exchange they should help one another. This was the first exchange of things, before the use of money was discovered. Hence also the Seres, as Pliny, Solinus and others report, are said to have instituted the exchange of goods: when they knew that merchants were approaching, they went down to the shore and laid out their silk, of which they had the greatest abundance, in a conspicuous place. Afterwards, withdrawing, they left its price to the judgment of the merchants. Whence Virgil:

units.la: Ignoti facie, sed noti vellere feras.
units.tr: Wild creatures unknown in face, but known for their fleece.

units.la: 2. Media dependent ab instituto hominum, quibus rerum pretium & valor aestimatur, hujusmodi vero medium est nummus, de quo prolixius cap. seq.
units.tr: (2) The means depend on human institution, by which the price and value of things are estimated. Such a means is money, of which more at the following chapter.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Justitia Commutativa in contractibus aut commerciis non tantum spontaneis, sed etiam invitis cernitur.
units.tr: 1. Commutative justice is seen in contracts or dealings not only voluntary but also involuntary.

units.la: 2. Haec species Justitiae a priori Distributiva in duobus maxime differt, objecto nempe & medio.
units.tr: 2. This species of justice differs from Distributive justice, as stated before, chiefly in two respects, namely object and means.

units.la: 3. Quia in Iustitia Commutativa non personarum, sed rerum habetur ratio, nil refert bonusne malum, an malus bonum virum suo debito defraudarit.
units.tr: 3. Because in Commutative justice regard is had not to persons but to things, it makes no difference whether a good man or a bad man has defrauded another of his due.

units.la: 4. Iudex autoritate sua omnia in hac Iustitia ad aequali- tatem & Iustum conatur perducere.
units.tr: 4. In this justice the judge, by his authority, strives to bring everything to equality and what is just.

units.la: 5. Etsi damnum aut lucrum ad facultates externas proprie spectant, ad commoda tamen & incommoda corporis etiam referri possunt.
units.tr: 5. Although loss or gain properly concerns external resources, they can also be referred to the advantages and disadvantages of the body.

units.la: 6. Iustitia Commutativa inter damnum & lucrum tanquam inter excessum & defectum consistit.
units.tr: 6. Commutative justice lies between loss and gain as between excess and deficit.

units.la: 7. Lucrum in bonis habet locum excessus, damnum vero locum defectus: & in malis econtra fit.
units.tr: 7. In goods, gain has the place of excess and loss the place of deficit; and in evils it is the other way round.

units.la: 8. Iudex est jus quoddam animatum, seu, ut ajunt Iuris-consulti, viva legum civilium vox, utpote a cujus ore legum executio dependet.
units.tr: 8. The judge is a kind of animate law, or, as the jurists say, the living voice of the civil laws, since the execution of the laws depends on his mouth.

units.la: 9. Totum in Iustitia Commutativa aequaliter dividi dicitur, cum una pars tantum habet quantum altera, nec una excedit alteram, aut exceditur.
units.tr: 9. The whole is said to be divided equally in Commutative justice when one part has no more than the other, and one does not exceed or is exceeded by the other.

units.la: 10. Ut justum medium inveniatur, demere, quod excedit, & addere, quod defuit, sicut in lineis inaequalibus sit, debemus.
units.tr: 10. To find the just mean, we must take away what exceeds and add what was lacking, as is done in unequal lines.

units.la: 11. Unusquisque nec majus nec minus, quam debet habere dicitur, cum neque damnum, neque lucrum in rebus ipsis proprie patitur.
units.tr: 11. Each person is said to have neither more nor less than he ought, when he suffers neither loss nor gain in the things themselves.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An Iustitia Commutativa possit dici virtus, cum non consistat in mediocritate rationis, seu quoad nos, aut quod idem est, non versatur circa medium Geometricum, quod requirit in omni virtute Philos. cap. 7. lib. 2. huius operis, sed tantum versetur, circa medium Arithmeticum, sicut ex hoc textu patet. Ergo aut non est virtus, aut saltem et definitio virtutis non competit, quam supra tradidit Philosophus? Resp. Vetari circa medium Iustitia Commutativa dicitur duobus modis: Primario & sic res ipsa secundum naturam suam, aut saltem nulla habita ratioratione nostri respicit. Et hoc modo definitio virtutis vix ei competit: Secundariò, quatenus mensuram rerum considerat, & sic etiam versatur circa ejusmodi medium, quod refertur ad nos, quia mensura rerum dependet plerunque ab arbitrio hominum. Plura videad cap. 7. lib. 2. hujus operis.
units.tr: I. It is asked: can Commutative justice be called a virtue, since it does not consist in a mean of reason, that is, relative to us, or what is the same, it is not concerned with the geometrical mean, which the Philosopher requires in every virtue (Book 2, chapter 7 of this work), but is concerned only with the arithmetic mean, as is clear from this text? Therefore either it is not a virtue, or at least the definition of virtue, which the Philosopher laid down above, does not apply to it? Answer: Commutative justice is said to be about the mean in two ways. Primarily, and so the thing itself, according to its own nature, or at least without any regard to us, looks to the mean. In this way the definition of virtue hardly applies to it. Secondarily, insofar as it considers the measure of things, and so it is also concerned with a mean of this kind, which is related to us, because the measure of things depends for the most part on the judgment of men. See more at Book 2, chapter 7 of this work.

units.la: II. An rectè dixerit istam Commutativam à priori nempe Distributiva specie differre, propter hanc præcipuè rationem, quod diversa habeant obiecta, sed hac ratio est falsa, nam unum habent obiectum, nempe facultates externas aut etiam pecuniam. Ergo neque specie differunt, cum obiectum unum & idem habeant? Resp. Objectum consideratur duobus modis, formaliter & materialiter: materialiter non differunt secundum obiectum, sed tantum formaliter, quia licet unum habeat obiectum, non uno tamen eodemque modo circa hoc obiectum versantur, sed Commutativa respicit res ipsas quatenus commutantur, aut quatenus de rebus contrahere possunt homines: Distributiva verò respicit distributionem rerum inter plures, non quoad res, sed quoad dignitatem personarum.
units.tr: II. Whether he rightly said that this Commutative justice differs in species from the other, Distributive justice, chiefly for this reason, that they have different objects? But this reason is false, for they have one object, namely external goods or even money. Therefore they do not differ in species either, since they have one and the same object? Answer: An object is considered in two ways, formally and materially. Materially they do not differ according to object, but only formally, because although they have one object, they are not concerned with that object in one and the same way. Commutative justice looks at the things themselves insofar as they are exchanged, or insofar as men can make contracts about things. Distributive justice, however, looks at the distribution of things among several persons, not as to the things but as to the dignity of the persons.

units.la: III. Quomodo dicat Justitiam Commutativam esse medium inter damnum & lucrum tanquam inter extrema, cum si hoc esset verum, sequeretur, damnum & lucrum esse vitia: at vitia dici non possunt, cum eis definitio virtutis non competat, nam vitia, quæ oppònuntur virtutibus, sunt habitus ex multis actionibus pravis comparati: damnum verò & lucrum dici non possunt ejusmodi habitus, cum tantùm incrementum vel decrementum externarum facultatum denotent? Resp. Damnum & lucrum considerari posse duobus modis, vel respectu personæ, cui accidunt, & sic vitia non sunt. 2. Respectu rei circa quam versantur, & sic possunt dici vitia, siquidem damnum est defectus rei infra justum, lucrum vero est excessus rei supra lucrum, & hoc etiam modo pro externis Justitiae Commutativae a Philosopho ponuntur.
units.tr: III. How does he say that Commutative justice is a mean between loss and gain as between extremes, since if this were true it would follow that loss and gain are vices? But they cannot be called vices, since the definition of virtue does not apply to them. For the vices which are opposed to virtues are habits acquired from many wrong actions; but loss and gain cannot be called habits of this kind, since they denote only an increase or decrease of external resources? Answer: Loss and gain can be considered in two ways. Either with respect to the person to whom they happen, and so they are not vices. Or secondly, with respect to the thing with which they are concerned, and so they can be called vices, since loss is a deficiency of a thing below what is just, and gain is an excess of a thing above what is just. And in this way too the Philosopher reckons them among the external goods of Commutative justice.

units.la: IV. Quomodo statuat hanc differentiam inter Iustitiam Commutativam & Distributivam, quod Distributiva respiciat Rempublicam, Commutativa vero res privatas, cum omnis virtus in genere debeat tendere ad utilitatem Reipublicae & ad commune omnium hominum bonum, secus enim virtutes ipsae non essent media ad assequendam felicitatem, quod pro principio in Ethicis ponitur, ut patet in lib. 1. & 2. docet Philosophus?
units.tr: IV. How does he hold this difference between Commutative and Distributive Justice, that Distributive Justice concerns the commonwealth, while Commutative Justice concerns private matters, when every virtue in general ought to aim at the benefit of the commonwealth and the common good of all men? Otherwise the virtues themselves would not be means to attaining happiness, which is laid down as a principle in Ethics, as the Philosopher teaches in Books 1 and 2.

units.la: Resp. Verum omnes virtutes tendere ad utilitatem Reipublicae, sed non uno eodemque modo. Quaedam primario ut Distributiva Iustitia, quae commune totius civitatis bonum in primis respicit: quaedam secundario & sic etiam Commutativa, licet primo respiciat privata membra Reipublicae.
units.tr: Reply: It is true that all the virtues tend towards the advantage of the commonwealth, but not in one and the same way. Some do so primarily, such as distributive justice, which chiefly regards the common good of the whole state; others do so secondarily, and so also commutative justice, although it first regards the private members of the commonwealth.

units.la: Poterit & hoc non incommode quaeri: An Iustitia Commutativa recte dicatur versari circa contractus in communi hominum societate, sicut Philosophus cap. 5. & hoc cap. 7. docet. Et statuitur thesis affirmativa propter 5. potissimum rationes: 1. Quia objectu Iustitiae hujus sunt res omnes de quibus inter se contrahere, quocunque modo possunt homines, ergo & circa contractus versatur. 2. Quia haec Iustitia in contractibus absque omni personarum respectu, rerum duntaxat ipsarum, de quibus fiunt contractus, servat aequalitatem, ut neutra pars habeat, quod possit vel de nimio gloriari, vel de nimis parvo conqueri.
units.tr: It may also not unprofitably be asked: whether commutative justice is rightly said to be concerned with contracts in human society in general, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 5 and here in chapter 7. The affirmative thesis is upheld chiefly for five reasons: (1) Because the objects of this justice are all the things about which men can make contracts with one another in any way whatever; therefore it is also concerned with contracts. (2) Because this justice, in contracts, without any regard to persons, observes equality only with respect to the things themselves that are the subject of the contracts, so that neither party has grounds either to boast of too much or to complain of too little.

units.la: §. Quia omnem inæqualitatē, quæ respectu damni & lucri in rebus ipsis oboritur, ad æqualitatem reducit, dum nempe habita ratione proportionis Arithmeticæ tantum de lucro uni detrahit, quantum alteri de damno per injuriam accessit & vice versa, tantum damni uni addit, quantum alteri de lucro alterius per injuriam accessit, idq; inprimis autoritate & arbitrio Iudicis, qui propterea, quod justum & æquale in rebus ipsis statuat, mediator seu mediarius à Philosopho dicitur. 4. Quia Iustitia Commutativa efficit ut personæ contrahentes justam inter se servent æqualitatem, sine qua nulli omnino contractus de rebus ipsis subsistere possunt. 5. Quia à contrario omnis contractus est injustus, quem Justitia Commutativa non moderatur, propterea quod, ut jam diximus, sola rebus ipsis certam præscribat æqualitatem.
units.tr: Because it reduces every inequality that arises in the things themselves, with respect to loss and gain, to equality: namely, by taking into account arithmetical proportion, it subtracts from the gain of one party as much as the other has gained through injury, and conversely adds to the loss of one party as much loss as has come to the other through injury; and this chiefly by the authority and judgement of the judge, who, because he establishes the just and equal in the things themselves, is called by the Philosopher a mediator or middleman. (4) Because commutative justice brings it about that contracting persons keep just equality between themselves, without which no contracts at all concerning things can stand. (5) Because, on the contrary, every contract is unjust which commutative justice does not regulate, since, as we have just said, it alone prescribes a fixed equality in the things themselves.

units.la: Poterit & hoc quæri: An cum Iustitia Commutativa res ipsas ita respiciat, ut nullum habeat personarum respectum, qui plus minusve alicui tribuit, quam par est, aut qui plus minusve recipit, quâ par est, injustè agat? Resp. Distinguendum esse partim inter personas, quibus plus minusve tribuitur, partim inter res, quæ tribuuntur, sive eæ res sint bonæ sive malæ eæque propriæ vel alienæ: 1. Igitur non injustè agit is, qui plus minusve de bonis suis propriis uni tribuit, quam alteri, cum neutri quicquam debeat, sed pro libitu suo tantum gratis det. 2. Neq; injustè etiam agit, qui minus de rebus sibi debitis quam par est, recipit, cum possit recipere, vel nō recipere pro libitu suo. 3. Qui minus bonorum & plus malorum in se recipit, hic etiam non injustè agit, modò bono fine hoc a-gat. At contra Injustè agit: 1. Qui de bonis alie-nis ad se non spectantibus uni plus, alteri minus, quam par est, tribuit, cū natura Justitiæ hoc exigat, ut suū cuiq; tribuatur, id est, neq; magis neq; minus, quam æquitatis ratio postulat. 2. Injustè etiam agit, qui plus bonorum sibi tribuit, minus verò aliis relinquit, aut econtra minus malorum sibi tribuit, aliis plus relinquit: nam ut præclarè ait Philosophus hoc cap. 7. Injustè ille agit, qui iniquè aliquid tribuit: Iniqua verò omnis distributio non in accipiente, sed in dante primò locum habet, siquidem initium illius iniquæ actionis à dante, non ab accipiente proficiscitur: non enim injuriam proprie pati dicitur, qui debita sua parte sciens & volens se defraudat, licet damnum patiatur: nam aliud est injuriam pati, aliud damnum pati. Damnum patitur, qui debito suo sciens & volens se privat: Injuriam verò is patitur, cui invito & nō consentienti præter jus aut æquum aliquid infertur, ut infra cap. 9. clarius declarabitur.
units.tr: This too may be asked: Does a person act unjustly if, since commutative justice regards the things themselves in such a way as to have no regard for persons, it gives to someone more or less than is fitting, or receives more or less than is fitting? Reply: One must distinguish partly between the persons to whom more or less is given, and partly between the things that are given, whether those things are good or bad, and whether they are one's own or another's. (1) Therefore he does not act unjustly who gives more or less of his own goods to one person than to another, since he owes nothing to either, but may give freely as he pleases. (2) Nor does he act unjustly who receives less than is due to him, since he may receive or not receive as he pleases. (3) He who receives less good and more evil for himself does not act unjustly either, provided he does so for a good end. On the contrary, one acts unjustly: (1) who, from goods belonging to others and not to himself, gives more to one and less to another than is fitting, since the nature of justice requires that to each his own be given, that is, neither more nor less than the reason of equity demands. (2) One also acts unjustly who assigns more good to himself and leaves less to others, or conversely assigns less evil to himself and leaves more to others; for, as the Philosopher rightly says in this chapter 7: He acts unjustly who distributes something unequally. Now every unequal distribution has its place primarily in the giver, not in the recipient, since the beginning of that unequal action proceeds from the giver, not from the recipient. For he is not properly said to suffer injury who knowingly and willingly defrauds himself of his due part, although he suffers loss; for it is one thing to suffer injury, another to suffer loss. He suffers loss who knowingly and willingly deprives himself of what is his due; but he suffers injury to whom something is inflicted against his will and without his consent, contrary to right or equity, as will be declared more clearly below in chapter 9.

units.la: Coroni dis loco poterit & hæc quæstio subjici: An quicquid Justum est, congruat ad Analogiam Geometricam aut Arithmeticam; aut, an in Justitia particulari nulla servetur proportio, præter Geometricam aut Arithmeticam? Resp. Justitiam particulare considerari duobus modis: 1. Separatim in singulis suis speciebus, & sic nulla omnino est proportio, quæ non sit vel Arithmetica vel Geometrica, nam duas tantum habet species: Distributivam, in qua servatur analogia Geometrica: & Commutativam, in qua Arithmetica. 2. Consideratur conjunctim, quatenus nempe utraq; species cies in suo genere perpenditur simul & semel, seu quatenus Justitia ex æquitate & lege coalescit, ad commune totius civitatis bonum, & sic datur tertia quædam proportio, quæ vocatur Harmonica, cū nempe ex utraque supra dicta exurgit ejusmodi quædam proportio, quæ suavem concentum & harmoniam in Repub. efficit, & hoc vult Bodinus, cum dicit: legem, quæ in civitate omnibus est eadem, congruere ad proportionē Arithmeticam: quæ vero æquitatem secundum personas respicit, aptari ad res Geometricas. Justitiam vero ipsam analogiam servare Harmonicam ex utraque superiore conflata, ut elegantí temperatura integrū Reipub. servetur corpus: Et hoc non in actionibus tantum humanis, sed & divinis observari, exemplis liquido demonstrari potest. Deus in electione fidelium ex universo genere humano proportione servat Harmonicam, cum scilicet ex beneplacito nunc hos, nunc illos ex hac aut illa gente eligit: In oblatione salutis toti humano generi proportionem servat Arithmeticam: offert enim eam omnibus absq; personarum respectu. At in distributione bonorum corporalium proportionem observat Geometrica, nec unicuique pro eadem mensura bona sua distribuit, sed uni magis, alteri minus, verbi gratia: divitias, honores, &c. prout illi visum fuerit. Sic etiam in humanis actionibus triplex ista proportio facile apparet, & ex jure civili exempla desumi possunt: nam in l. Capital. § fervorum, ff. de pœnit, exemplum habetur proportionis Geometricæ, ut nempe persona-rum habeatur respectus, & magis puniatur servus, si delinquat, quam liber. Sic etiam in tit. de obligat. ligat. & action. lege obligamur, statuitur exemplū proportionis Arithmeticæ, ut nempe in obligationibus aut contractibus eadem apud omnes seruetur lex, nullo habito personarum respectu: at vero proportionis Harmonicæ exemplum extat lib. 4. C. l. eos. ff. de usuris, ubi ex lege & æquitate mitigantur usuræ, & conceditur, ut aliquis paupertate pressus, qui nihil habet, unde vivat, præter exiguam summam pecuniæ, usuram sumat: divitibus vero & opulentis ejusmodi usura non conceditur.
units.tr: As a corollary, this question may also be raised: Does whatever is just accord with geometrical or arithmetical analogy, or in particular justice is no proportion observed other than geometrical or arithmetical? Reply: Particular justice may be considered in two ways. (1) Separately, in its individual species; and so there is no proportion at all that is not either arithmetical or geometrical, for it has only two species: distributive justice, in which geometrical analogy is observed; and commutative justice, in which arithmetical analogy is observed. (2) It is considered jointly, that is, insofar as each species is weighed in its own kind at once and together, or insofar as justice arises from equity and law toward the common good of the whole state; and so a certain third proportion is given, which is called harmonic, since indeed from both of the above there arises a proportion of this kind which produces a sweet concord and harmony in the commonwealth. This is what Bodin means when he says: the law, which is the same for all in the state, accords with arithmetical proportion; but that which regards equity according to persons is fitted to geometrical things. Justice, moreover, preserves harmonic analogy, compounded from both of the above, so that the whole body of the commonwealth is kept in elegant balance; and that this is observed not only in human actions but also in divine ones can be clearly demonstrated by examples. God, in choosing believers from the whole human race, preserves harmonic proportion, since he chooses now these, now those, from this or that nation, according to his good pleasure. In offering salvation to the whole human race he preserves arithmetical proportion, for he offers it to all without regard to persons. But in the distribution of bodily goods he observes geometrical proportion, and does not distribute his goods to each by the same measure, but more to one and less to another, for example riches, honours, and so on, as it seems good to him. So also in human actions this threefold proportion readily appears, and examples can be drawn from the civil law: for in the law Capital, § servorum, Digest, de poenis, there is an example of geometrical proportion, namely that regard is had to persons, and a slave is punished more heavily than a free man if he offends. So too in the title de obligationibus et actionibus, the law obligamur lays down an example of arithmetical proportion, namely that in obligations or contracts the same law is kept for all, with no regard to persons. But an example of harmonic proportion is found in book 4 of the Code, law eos, Digest, de usuris, where interest is moderated by law and equity, and it is allowed that someone oppressed by poverty, who has nothing to live on except a small sum of money, may take interest; but such interest is not allowed to the rich and wealthy.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: SEquitur quintum & ultimum membrum prioris tractatus hujus libri, in quo Philosophus errorem quorundam, præcipuè verò Pythagoreorum de medio Justitiæ Correctivæ seu Commutativæ refellit. Hi enim Justitiam Commutativam non in proportione Arithmetica, sicut hic à Philosopho statuitur, sed in æqualitate repassionis, aut, ut vulgò vocatur, Talionis, sitam esse dicebant; hoc autem potissimum agit, ut sententia Pythagoreorum refutata suam, quam superiori cap. de Justitia Commutativa attulit sententiam magis confirmet. Partes hujus capitis sunt quatuor: In prima opinionem Pythagoricorum adducit, & accuratè etiam refellit. In secunda suam de Talione opinionem, & in quibus rebus locum habeat, quibus non, perspicuè declarat. In tertia formam seu modum, quo in rerum permutationibus hæc talio observari possit, cum exemplis, tum rationibus docet. In quarta demum Justitiam esse mediocritatem probat, & comparationem instituit inter me-
units.tr: There follows the fifth and last member of the first treatise of this book, in which the Philosopher refutes the error of certain men, chiefly of the Pythagoreans, concerning the mean of corrective or commutative justice. For these men held that commutative justice lies not in arithmetic proportion, as the Philosopher here lays down, but in equality of requital, or, as it is commonly called, talion. His main aim is to refute the opinion of the Pythagoreans, so that his own opinion, which he set out in the earlier chapter on commutative justice, is confirmed more firmly. This chapter has four parts. In the first he presents the opinion of the Pythagoreans and refutes it carefully. In the second he states clearly his own opinion about talion, and the cases to which it does and does not apply. In the third he teaches, by examples and by reasons, the form or manner in which this talion may be observed in exchanges of goods. In the fourth he proves at last that justice is a mean, and draws a comparison between the mean of justice and the mean found in the other virtues.

units.la: mediocritatem Justitiæ, & eam quæ in aliis reperitur virtutibus.
units.tr: the mean of justice, and that which is found in the other virtues.

units.la: In prima igitur parte opinionem Pythagoricorum de Talione adducit, quæ opinio sententia Rhadamanti confirmatur (cujus ab omnibus prædicatur Justitia, & ideo propter summam Justitiam à Poëtis fingitur unus ex tribus inferorum judicibus, ut videre licet apud Senecam in Hercule furente) cujus sententia seu jus hoc versiculo Hsiodi comprehensum est, Si quis quid fecerit, patiatur, jus erit æquum. Nam Talio vulgò definitur, qua, quod alteri facimus, idem vicissim patimur, & ideo hic Rhadamatus, cujus opinione nituntur Pythagorici, idé unicuiq; reppendebat, quod fecisset nō variatis aut observatis circumstantiis. Quod vero talio ejusmodi non sit medium in Justitia Commutativa, hoc modo probat Philos. quia nullius Justitiæ est medium, & proinde neque Commutativæ; nam cum omnis Justitia, ut ex superioribus patet, sit vel Distributiva vel Commutativa, neutri tamen competit hæc talio, id quod & exemplis & rationibus probat. Exempla sunt: si quis Magistratum gerens privatum percusserit, non est statim repercutiendus, quia multum est differentiæ inter personam publicam & privatam. Sic etiam si quis privatus Magistratum pulsaverit, non est iterum pulsandus simpliciter tantum, id quod natura talionis exigit, sed est insuper puniendus, propterea quod in persona publica totam læserit Remp. Rationes vero sunt hæ duæ: Prima, quia multum inter se differunt injuria sponte & invitè commissa, aut factum aliquod sponte aut non sponte patratum, ideo non uno eodemq; modo puniri debent, quod tamen fieret, si Talio hæc Pythagoreorum in nulla Justitia locu haberet: nam non tam delictum quam animus delinquentis in pœnis irrogandis considerari debet, siquidem pro diversis principiis internis quædam facta sunt commiseratione digna & venia, quædam nullam merentur veniam, ut excap.1. & 2. lib 3. patet. Altera ratio, cur in nulla Justitia medium sit Talio, est hæc, quia non semper fieri potest permutatio rerum simpliciter æqualium, nec eadem pro iisdem semper reddi possunt, id quod tamen fieri debet, si Iustitia secundum talionem exercenda esset.
units.tr: In the first part he presents the opinion of the Pythagoreans about talion. This opinion is supported by the judgment of Rhadamanthus, who is praised by everyone for his justice; for this reason the poets, because of his outstanding justice, make him one of the three judges of the underworld, as may be seen in Seneca in Hercules Mad. His judgment, or this law, is summed up in the verse of Hesiod: If someone does something, he shall suffer it; that will be just. For talion is commonly defined as that by which we in turn suffer the same thing that we do to another. Therefore this Rhadamanthus, on whose opinion the Pythagoreans rely, used to repay each person with the very same thing he had done, without varying or observing the circumstances. The Philosopher proves in the following way that such talion is not the mean in commutative justice: because it is not the mean of any justice, and so not of commutative justice either. For since, as is clear from what has gone before, every justice is either distributive or commutative, talion applies to neither; he proves this by examples and by reasons. The examples are these: if someone who holds public office strikes a private citizen, he must not be struck back at once, because there is a great difference between a public person and a private one. Likewise, if a private citizen strikes a magistrate, he must not simply be struck again, as the nature of talion demands, but must moreover be punished, because by harming a public person he has harmed the whole commonwealth. The reasons are these two. The first is that injuries done willingly and those done unwillingly differ greatly, and so do acts done deliberately and acts done without intention; therefore they ought not to be punished in one and the same way. Yet this would have to happen if this talion of the Pythagoreans had any place in justice. For in inflicting penalties one ought to consider not so much the offence as the mind of the offender, since some deeds, from different inner motives, deserve pity and pardon, while others deserve no pardon at all, as is clear from the first and second chapters of Book 3. The second reason why talion is not the mean in any justice is this: an exchange of things that are simply equal cannot always be made, nor can the same things always be repaid for the same, though this would have to be done if justice were to be exercised according to talion.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis suam de Talione opinionem adducit; nam licet per se & simpliciter Talio non sit necessaria, seu non sit medium ullius Justitiæ, est tamen necessaria in rebus contrahendis & in commerciis, quæ spectant ad Iustitiam Commutativam (quod vero ad Distributivā attinet, quia personas, non res respicit, ut ex superioribus patet, ideo in ea talio locum non habet) Hinc vero necessariam esse probat, quia mutuis dationibus & acceptionibus omnes continentur Respub. id quod abiq; officiorum, aut operarum, aut rerum contrahendarum mutua vicissitudine, aut, ut uno verbo dicatur, absque commerciis nulla consistere posset Respubl. id quod etiam non tantum hoc loco, sed lib.2. Politic. cap.1. Philosophus docet, & Cicero 1. & 3. offic. non tamen eadem specie compensatio, sed æquivalens & proportione quadam adæquata ratio continet Respub. & in suo vigore conservat, id quod exem-plis plis probat, verbi gratia: si quis malo afficiatur, non statim conatur malum malo rependere secundum jus talionis, sed si juste id faciet, rependit secundum proportionem rationis, ut sic a Justitiae limitibus nunquam reflēat, & sic etiam si quis bono afficiatur, conatur id rependere pro merito, sicut recta praescribit ratio, secus enim ingrati animi erit symbolum, quod meram Injustitiam vocat Socrates libro 2. apud Xenophontem, propterea ait Philosophus, veteres in propatulo urbis loco sacrarium gratiis (quae tres fingunt̄ur beneficiorum praesides, Aglaja, Thalia, Euphrosyne) erexisse, ut ejus intuitu cum in loco publico esset, de remuneratione beneficiorum, & de gratitudine commonefierent homines, & hac ratione mutua, nempe rerum dandarum & accipiendarum vicissitudine omnes societates & Respub. contineri scirent. Qui plura volet de loco Gratiis sacrato legere, consulat Vitruvium lib. 1. de architect. cap. ult.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he sets out his own opinion about talion. For although talion is not necessary in itself and simply speaking, or is not the mean of any justice, it is necessary in making contracts and in trade, which concern commutative justice. (As for distributive justice, since it regards persons rather than things, as is clear from what has gone before, talion has no place in it.) He proves that talion is necessary in this way: all the commonwealth is held together by mutual giving and receiving, and without the mutual exchange of services, labours, or goods to be contracted, or, to say it in one word, without commerce, no commonwealth could exist. The Philosopher teaches this not only in this place but also in Book 2 of the Politics, chapter 1, and Cicero does so in Books 1 and 3 of De Officiis. Yet the commonwealth is held together and kept in its strength not by compensation of the same kind, but by an equivalent and by a reckoning adjusted in a certain proportion. He proves this by examples. For instance, if someone is harmed, he does not at once try to repay the harm with harm according to the law of talion; but if he does so justly, he repays in proportion to the reason of the case, so that he never strays from the limits of justice. Likewise, if someone receives a benefit, he tries to repay it according to its worth, as right reason prescribes; otherwise he would be a sign of an ungrateful mind, which Socrates, in the second book, as reported by Xenophon, calls plain injustice. For this reason, the Philosopher says, the ancients set up a shrine of the Graces (whom they imagine as the three guardians of benefits: Aglaia, Thalia, and Euphrosyne) in an open place of the city, so that people, seeing it in a public place, might be reminded of repaying benefits and of gratitude, and might know that all societies and commonwealths are held together by this mutual exchange, namely the giving and receiving of things. Whoever wishes to read more about the place sacred to the Graces should consult Vitruvius, Book 1 of On Architecture, last chapter.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis docet modum secundum quem haec Talio observari debet, in commerciis aut in Justitia Commutativa, nempe ut fiat secundum proportionem rationis, & congruat ejusmodi Talio ad regulam aequalitatis, quam recta praescribit ratio, id quod confirmat primo exemplis, dein a rebus objectis, in quibus ipsa versatur Talio. Primum exemplum est de architecto seu domorum opifice & de furore & eorum operibus. Quod si talio haec Pythagoraeorum simpliciter in rebus permutandis haberet locum, & eadem pro iisdem semper permutaretur, sequeretur domus, quae est opus architecti, per-
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he teaches the manner in which this talion ought to be observed in commerce or in commutative justice: namely, that it be done according to the proportion of reason, and that such talion agree with the rule of equality which right reason prescribes. He confirms this first by examples, and then by the things with which talion itself is concerned. The first example is of the architect, that is, the builder of houses, and of the shoemaker and their works. If this talion of the Pythagoreans had a place in exchanging things simply, and the same things were always exchanged for the same, it would follow that a house, which is the work of an architect, would have to be exchanged for a shoe, which is the work of a shoemaker; yet this cannot be done, since they are not equal in price and value. For it is plain by common sense that a house is worth far more than a shoe. But so that the exchange may be just according to the analogy of right reason, as many shoes…

units.la: Tt mutādam esse pro calceo, qui est opus sutoris, quod tamen fieri non potest, cum precio & valore non æquivaleant: constat enim sensu longè pluris esse domum, quam calceum, sed ut justa fiat permutatio secundum analogiam rectæ rationis, tot calcei pro domo permutandi sunt, quot ei precio & valoi respondent: nam ratio in rebus permutandis hunc servat ordinem, ut prius æqualitas rerum statuatur, & postea talio adhibeatur, quod etiam hac ratione confirmari potest, cum res, quarum fit permutatio, sint inter se inæquales, & quantitate, id est, magnitudine & numero & qualitate id est, valore & pretio, nisi pro analogia rectæ rationis ad certam æqualitatem revocentur, nulla fieri potest, prorsus rerum permutatio, & si nulla permutatio, nulla etiā commercia, &his sublatis nulla etiam hominum inter se societas aut communio, & si tollatur societas, nullæ consistere possunt Respubl. Quod verò res sint dissimiles & natura sua plerunq; inæquales, donec ratio ipsa ad æqualitatem reducat, probat exemplo omnium urbium aut civitatum, in quibus reperitur hominū societas: neq; enim Resp. constant ex iisdē, sed plane dissimilibus & specie differentibus membris: nō enim constant ex solis Medicis, ex solis sutoribus aut artificibus, sed ex diversi generis hominib. inter se mistis, ut ex ista diversitate hominum maxima tamen existat secūdum regulam rationis in corpore Reipub. concordia; & cum homines, qui Reipubl. membra constituunt, sint inter se dissimiles & inæquales, res etiam inter se differentę & inæquales esse satis constat, neq; etiam fit permutatio earundem dem rerum,cum iisdem rebus,propterea quod nulla necessitas hoc requirat, verbi gratia Medicus non permutat opus suum cum Medico, neq; sutor cum sutore, sed Medicus cum sutore, sutor cum agricola & aliis,rebus tamen ad æqualitatem certam ante reductis, & hoc etiam modo, quod membra Reipubl. sint plane inter se dissimilia,disputat Philosophus contra Plat. lib. 3. Politic. cap. 3. quod nempe ubi dissimilitudo est, ibi nulla sit paritas, & ubi nulla paritas,omnia non possunt esse communia omnibus,quod voluit in sua Republ. Plato. Secundò probat modum in Talione servandum esse secundum proportionem rectæ rationis à rebus objectis, in quibus cernitur ipsa talio: Res verò sunt comparabiles,id est, quæ aliquo modo inter se comparari possunt,si non directè & per se semper, saltem ex eventu & per accidens,aut per aliquod tertium ut loquuntur(de qua comparatione plura videapud Euclidem lib.5.Geomet. in principio) sed cum rerum permutandarum, de quibus inter se contrahere homines possunt, ea sit natura, ut non semper commode comparari inter se possint propter diversitatem naturæ: idcirco repertus est nummus, quo veluti communi res inter se plane dissimiles comparari, & inæquales ad æqualitatem reduci facilius possint. Metitur enim nummus in rebus permutandis extrema,& ad certam æqualitatem revocat, ut quantum unum extremorum ab altero extremo superatur, ipsius interventu æquale reddatur,sicut in exemplo superius allato facilè patet: nam licet calceus longè infra valorem domus & ideo sit admodum inæqualis, interventu tamen nummi posset æquivalere domui, & sic res inter se inæquales per nummū ad æqualitatem reducuntur. Cæterum cū mensura secundū proportionem rationis in rebus permutandis sit opus, ut res inæquales & natura valdè differentes ad æqualitatem & consensum reducantur, videndum erit, quotuplex sit hæc mensura, quæres inter se comparat. Ea verò est duplex: Prima, Indigentia, quæ vere & natura sua rerum permutandarum mensura dicitur, nam absque hac nulla esset omnis rerum permutatio, id quod patet duabus rationibus: 1. est, quia nemo nisi aliqua re indigens, cum alio quicquam comutaturus aut contractus esset, non possum enim aliquid permutare, nisi necessitas urgeret, & sic communi quasi indigentiæ vinculo hominum inter se conservantur societates. 2. quia ex providentia naturæ, cum omnes omnibus non abundarent, permutatio rerum est inducta, multo ante nummum inventum, & si fuit multo ante permutatio, necesse est etiam, ut fuerit aliqua rerum mensura, quæ æqualitatem in iis constitueret: hæc vero fuit Indigentia, quæ necessitatis explendæ gratia ad conservandam inter homines societatem ad permutationem mutuam homines impulit. Secunda rerum mensura est Nummus, qui in locum Indigentiæ, quasi communi hominum pacto successit, & idcirco nomisma rectè dicitur νόμισμα à lege, quia lege & instituto hominum non natura valet, & penes est homines valorem ejus augere vel minuere, vel etiam pro libitu inutilem reddere, sicut variarum gentium & Rerumpub. histo-riæ riæ testantur. De Nummo vero ista duo observan- da veniunt: 1. Inventio ubi primò inventus fit. 2. Utilitas seu quibus rebus sit utilis. De inventione varia variì referunt autores, ut videre est apud Polyd. Virg lib.1. de rerum invent.cap.22. Alexander vero ab Alexandro lib. 15. general.dier.cap.6. Lydi hoc inventum refert, quanquam alii Ægyptij, primò nummum excusum credant, quod etiam testatur Ovid. 2. Fast. Qui plura de nummi inventione legere volet, consulere potest autores supra dictos locis citatis. Ut nummi utilitatem doceat Philosophus, hoc modo procedit, quod experientia testatur, nullam esse societatem inter homines, nisi sit aliqua rerum permutatio, neque ulla sit rerum permutatio, saltem secundum rectam rationem, nisi justa in rebus statuatur æqualitas: ut hæc habeatur, opus erit communi mensura, ex instituto hominum, quæ mensura dicitur nummus, hujus quatuor præcipuè sunt utilitates: 1. est: Quod ejus beneficio res omnes metiamur, atque ita quidem, ut solius nummi interventu æqualitas in rebus admodum inæqualibus reperiatur: Hinc æra gravi jam signato utebantur in principio Romani, quo appenso ad libram nō numerato debita exsolvebant, & rerum permutationes peragebant. 2. Utilitas est, quod sponsoris vices subeat, & venditori pro emtore spondeat, ut si alii rem nobis necessariā, illis vero superfluam concedant, nos nummo mediante, eorum necessitatibus pro facultate subventuros. 3. Contractus conservat & eam inæqualitatem demit, nam quia per res, neque ejusdem generis, neque etiam diversas fidem saepenumero exsolvere non valemus: per nummum tamen tanquam communem mensuram hoc possimus. 4. Demum quia hominum inter se societatem tuetur ac fovet, nam cum singuli rebus plurimis nunc magis nunc minus, prout indigentia occurit, indigeant, nummus ex copia vel inopia certum in genere precium rebus imponit, atque ita hominum inter homines societates conservat. Proinde cum res sua natura sint dispares & magna dissimilitudine laborent, nummus tamen res diversissimas pro proportione quadam respondentes facit. Exemplum habet Philosophus de domo, de decem minis, & de lecto, quos terminus sic adaequat, ut domus constet quinque minis, id est, sit dimidium decem minarum, lectus vero sit tantum decima pars decem minarum, & ideo erit unius minae, ideo ut justa permutatio fiat inter domum & lectum necesse est, ut pro domo commutetur, non tantum lectus, sed insuper adjiciantur quatuor minae, quae simul cum ipso lecto domui precio & valore aequivalent.
units.tr: That the house would have to be exchanged for a shoe, which is the work of the cobbler. This cannot be done, since they do not match in price and value. It is plain to the senses that a house is worth far more than a shoe. But for an exchange to be just, according to the analogy of right reason, as many shoes must be given for a house as correspond to it in price and value. Reason observes this order in exchanging goods: first the equality of the things is established, and only then is retaliation applied. This can also be confirmed as follows. Goods that are exchanged are unequal to one another in quantity (that is, in size and number) and in quality (that is, in worth and price). Unless they are brought to a fixed equality according to the analogy of right reason, no exchange of goods can take place at all. Without exchange there is no trade, and without trade there is no association or fellowship among men, and if association is removed, no commonwealth can exist. That things are unlike and, by their nature, mostly unequal until reason itself reduces them to equality, is shown by the example of all cities and states in which human society is found. For commonwealths are not made up of the same kind of members, but of members that are wholly dissimilar and different in kind. They do not consist only of physicians, or only of cobblers or craftsmen, but of men of different kinds mixed together, so that from this diversity there arises, according to the rule of reason, the greatest harmony in the body of the commonwealth. Since the men who make up the members of the commonwealth are unlike and unequal to one another, it is quite clear that their works are also different and unequal. Nor is the same thing exchanged for the same thing, because no necessity requires it. For example, a physician does not exchange his work with another physician, nor a cobbler with a cobbler, but a physician exchanges with a cobbler, and a cobbler with a farmer and others, though the goods have first been reduced to a fixed equality. The Philosopher argues in this way too, against Plato, that the members of a commonwealth are wholly unlike one another: lib. 3. Politic. cap. 3. Namely, where there is dissimilarity there is no parity, and where there is no parity, all things cannot be common to all, which Plato wished in his own commonwealth. Secondly, he proves that the measure to be observed in retaliation must follow the proportion of right reason, drawn from the things in which retaliation itself is seen. Things are comparable, that is, they can in some way be compared with one another, if not directly and always in themselves, at least by their result and incidentally, or through some third thing, as they say (more on this comparison may be found in Euclid, lib.5.Geomet. in principio). But since the nature of the goods that men can contract to exchange is such that they cannot always be conveniently compared with one another, because of the diversity of their natures, money was therefore invented, so that goods wholly unlike one another could be compared, as by a common standard, and unequal things could more easily be reduced to equality. For money measures the extremes in exchange and brings them to a fixed equality, so that, through its intervention, the amount by which one extreme exceeds the other is made equal, as is easily seen in the example given above. For although a shoe is far below the value of a house and is therefore very unequal to it, yet through the intervention of money it could match the house, and so things unequal to one another are reduced to equality by means of money. Moreover, since a measure according to the proportion of reason is needed in exchanging goods, so that things unequal and very different in nature may be brought to equality and agreement, we must consider how many kinds of measure there are by which they are compared. There are two. The first is need, which is truly and by its nature called the measure of goods exchanged, for without it there would be no exchange of goods at all. This is clear for two reasons: (1) no one who is not in some need would want to exchange or make any contract with another, for a man cannot exchange anything unless necessity urges him, and in this way societies are preserved among men by the common bond, as it were, of need. (2) Because, by the providence of nature, since not all men had abundance of everything, exchange of goods was introduced long before money was invented. And if exchange existed long before, there must also have been some measure of goods that set equality among them. This measure was need, which, for the sake of satisfying necessity and preserving society among men, drove men to mutual exchange. The second measure of goods is money, which took the place of need, by a sort of common agreement of men. For this reason it is rightly called nomisma [νόμισμα], from law [νόμος], because it has its value by law and human institution, not by nature, and it is in the power of men to increase or diminish its value, or even to make it worthless at will, as the histories of various peoples and commonwealths bear witness. Concerning money, two things are to be noted: (1) where it was first invented; (2) for what things it is useful. Different writers give different accounts of its invention, as may be seen in Polydore Virgil, lib.1. de rerum invent. cap.22. Alexander ab Alexandro lib. 15. general. dier. cap.6. Lydi attributes the invention to the Lydians, though others believe the Egyptians first struck coin, which Ovid also attests, Fast. 2. Whoever wishes to read more about the invention of money may consult the authors cited above in the places named. To teach the usefulness of money, the Philosopher proceeds as follows. Experience shows that there is no society among men unless there is some exchange of goods, and there is no exchange of goods, at least according to right reason, unless a just equality is established among the things. To obtain this, a common measure is needed by human institution, and this measure is called money. Its uses are chiefly four: (1) by its benefit we measure all goods, and in such a way that equality is found among very unequal things through money alone. Hence the Romans at the beginning used bronze, already stamped by weight, which they weighed on a scale, and so paid debts without counting and carried out exchanges of goods. (2) Its use is that it takes the place of a surety and stands for the buyer to the seller, so that if others give us what we need and they have something superfluous, we, through money, will come to their needs according to our means. (3) It preserves contracts and removes that inequality, for since we cannot often pay a debt with goods that are neither of the same kind nor even of different kinds, we can do so through money as a common measure. (4) Lastly, because it guards and cherishes the society of men. For since individuals need very many things, now more and now less, as need arises, money, from abundance or scarcity, places a fixed price on goods in general, and so preserves the society of men with one another. Therefore, although things are by their nature unlike and suffer from great dissimilarity, money makes the most diverse things correspond in a certain proportion. The Philosopher has an example of a house, of ten minae, and of a bed, which the standard so equates that the house is worth five minae, that is, half of ten minae, while the bed is only a tenth part of ten minae, and so is worth one mina. Therefore, for a just exchange between the house and the bed, it is necessary that for the house there be given not only the bed but also four minae added, which together with the bed are equal to the house in price and value.

units.la: In quarta parte capitis
units.tr: In the fourth part of the chapter

units.la: docet Philosophus, qualis mediocritas sit Justitia ex comparatione Justitiae cum aliis virtutibus in dissimili; nam dicit, sit in Justitia quaedam mediocritas, quae consistat inter duo extrema, longe tamen se aliter habet, quam in caeteris virtutibus, quia caeterae omnes duobus distinctis nominibus duo distincta habent extrema, & sicut sunt duo diversa vitia, sic duplici insigniuntur nomine, ut ve bigratia: Fortitudo est mediocritas inter ignaviam & audaciam, Liberalitas inter Prodigadigalitatem & avaritiam, & sic de caeteris. At vero Justitia licet sit mediocritas, cum sit virtus non tamen versatu inter duo extrema duobus nominib. distincta, sed uno tantum Injustitiae nomine insigniuntur. Nam sicut Justitia le habet ad medium & ad aequum, sic Injustitia secundum magis & minus ad extrema in excessu & defectu pertinet, id quod patet ex definitione utriusque tam Justitiae quam Injustitiae: Justitia enim, ut ex superioribus patet, est habitus, quo quis praeditus redditur aptus ad juste agendum, consul o & ex proaresi five in aliorum actionibus recte distribuendis, five etiam in iisdem recte judicandis, nempe ne quis sibi plus bonorum, malorum vero minus tribuat, aliis vero ecostra plus malorum & minus bonorum, & unicuique sua tribuat, secundum jus & aequum aequaliter: Injustitia vero est deficientiae & excedentiae habitus, quo quis in sua causa sibi plus boni & lucri, aliis plus mali & damni tribuit, in aliena vero causa inaequalitatem universaliter observat, fortuito casu nunc huic nunc illi plus aut minus boni, aut mali attribuens, quam justum & aequum postulet, ita ut actiones Injustitiae sic distinguantur, ut qui plus aequo alteri tribuit dicatur peccare in excessu cum injuriam inferat, qui minus aequo, dicatur Injustitia exercere in defectu, cum non tantum contra naturam ipsius Justitiae agat, sed etiam in causa sit, ut alter injuriam patiatur. Tandem concludit & dicit ista omnia, quae de Justitia & Injustitia in genere dixerit, tam Oeconomicis quam Politicis actionibus accommodari posse, exactiora vero & magis specialia in Politicis edie quærenda : nam morali Philosopho incumbit, ut tantum agat universaliter de virtutibus, quæ possunt accommodari tam ad familiam, quam Remp. singularia verò quæ ad Legumlatores, Judices & Jurisconsultos spectant, hîc in Ethica esse prætermittenda, propter duas causas: 1. Quia, ut jam dictum est, ad Politicam spectant. 2. Quia præceptis universalibus vix contineri possunt, tum quia sunt penè infinita, tum etiam quia pro variis temporum, locorum, & personarum circumstantiis variari solent, & ideo propter insignem mutationem, quam subinde patiuntur, regulis generalibus comprehendi non possunt.
units.tr: The Philosopher teaches what kind of mean justice is, by comparing justice with the other virtues, where it differs from them. He says that justice has a certain mean, lying between two extremes, but it stands in a different relation from the other virtues. For all the others have two distinct extremes, each with its own name, and just as there are two different vices, so they are marked by two names. For example: courage is the mean between cowardice and rashness; liberality is the mean between prodigality and avarice; and so on for the rest. But justice, although it is a mean and a virtue, does not lie between two extremes that have two names. It is marked by only one name, that of injustice. For just as justice relates to the mean and the equal, so injustice relates to the extremes, in excess and deficiency, by degrees of more and less. This is clear from the definitions of both. Justice, as is clear from what was said above, is a habit by which a person is made apt to act justly, both wishing and choosing [προαίρεσις] to distribute rightly the actions of others, or to judge them rightly, namely so that no one takes more of the good and less of the bad for himself, gives more of the bad and less of the good to others, and gives each his due according to right and equity equally. Injustice, on the other hand, is a habit of deficiency and excess, by which a person, in his own cause, assigns more good and gain to himself and more evil and loss to others, and in another's cause observes inequality in general, by chance assigning now to one and now to another more or less good or evil than what is just and equal requires. The actions of injustice are distinguished thus: one who gives another more than is equal is said to sin by excess, since he inflicts injury; one who gives less than is equal is said to practise injustice by deficiency, since he not only acts against the nature of justice itself, but is also the cause of the other suffering injury. Finally, he concludes and says that all these things which he has said about justice and injustice in general can be applied both to domestic and to political actions, but that more exact and more specific points are to be sought in the Politics. For it falls to the moral philosopher to treat only in general terms of the virtues which can be applied both to the household and to the commonwealth. The particulars, which concern lawgivers, judges and jurists, are to be omitted here in Ethics, for two reasons: (1) because, as has already been said, they belong to Politics; (2) because they can scarcely be contained in universal precepts, both because they are almost infinite, and because they are usually varied according to the different circumstances of times, places and persons, and so, on account of the remarkable changes they undergo from time to time, cannot be comprehended by general rules.

units.la: In hoc capite notanda sunt ista tria: I. De jure Talionis, quod non tantum à Pythagoræis & Ethnicis Philosophis constitutū fuit, sed etiam in Lege Mosaica viguit, ut videre licet Exod. 21. verf. 24. 25. Levit. 24. verf. 19. & 20. Deuter. 19. verf. 19. Ibi enim statuitur, ut oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente, pes pro pede, &c. reddatur, quod etiam Deum in exigendis pœnis observasse tam ex sacris quam profanis historiis est manifestum. Insigne exemplum in sacris est 1. Judic. Adonibesecus occisus est amputatis digitis manuum & pedum, sicut ille 70. Reges ante occiderat. Sic etiam David, qui, ut videre est 2. Sam. 11. uxorem Uriae adulterio polluerat, adulterio etiam punitur, dum Absalon filius ejus medio die contaminat ejus uxores, cap. 26. ibidem. In profanis memorabile est exemplum de Agamemnone. Agamemnon inter fl. & Tantalo Thyestę filio, uxorem ejus Clytemnestram rapuerat, & duxerat in conjugem, postea absente Agamemnone (profectus enim erat ad bellum Trojanum) Ægystus Tantali fratet Clytemneftram corrupit, & postea Agamemnone rede unte interfecit, paulò post&Clytemneftra mater, & Ægyftus adulter ab Oreste Agamemnonis filio sunt interfecti, sicut refert Eurip.in Iphig. Aulid. & Æschyl.in Agam. Et certe ratione naturali videtur, ut quod quis alteri fecerit, idem vicissim patiatur, notum enim illud est ex jure naturæ defumtū principium, Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris: Et Jurisconsultus Cecilius apud Gellium lib. 20. Noct. Attic. cap.1. inquit,quæ, obsecro, ista est acerbitas, quæ est severitas, ut quod tu alii feceris tute in teipso feras: sic etiam leges duodecim tabularum apud Romanos jus talionis statuebant; exstat enim ibi hæc lex: Si quis membrum alterius rupit, ni pháctt (id est, paciscatur aut transigat cum læso) talio esto: sic etiam in jure Civili exstant variæ leges pro Talione confirmada l.quod quisque 5. ff.de jure in alium,l.itidem 59.ff.de periculis,& administratione tutorum. Sed severitatem talionis,cum ratione semper non nitatur, revocavit clementia juris prætorii, ut refert Gel. loco cit. & causa revocationis fuit difficultas retaliandi; fieri enim no potest, ut semper eadē pro iisdem reddantur, neq; et ut eadem pœna pro eodem delicto rependatur, cum sint diversæ & personarum & actionum circumstantiæ. Ariftoteles etiam ipse, licet in criminalibus, ubi pro injuria corpori humano illata pœna rependitur, non admittat talionem, propterea quod personarum hic inprimis habeatur respectus, in civilibus tamen, & rerum permutationibus admittit, modo fiat secundū analogiam rationis & prorsus secundum æqualitatem tem rem rei, ut videre licet ex initio hujus capitis. In summa, Talio simpliciter non admittenda videtur propter quatuor potissimum rationes: 1. Propter inaequalitatem personarum. Nam alia sunt privatae, quae nullum in Repub. gerunt munus: alia sunt publicae, quae gerunt munus, & inter istas talio observari non potest. 2. Propter aequitatem legum & judicum, qui in omni causa, lite & damno arbitri statuuntur, non eo quidem fine, ut ad aequalitatem rei partes dissentientes cogant, sed ut secundum regulam rectae rationis inter se conveniant. 3. Propter diversitatem & dissimilitudinem actionum humanarum, quarum alia sunt invitae, alia voluntariae, ut ex mitio lib. 3. patet. 4. Demum propter periculum seditionis & dissidii, ne cuilibet quidlibet audere liceret, sub praetextu aequalitatis, sicut eleganter disserit Favorinus Philosophus contra Sextum Caecilium Jurisconsultum, teste Gellio lib. 20. Noct. Attic. cap. 1.
units.tr: In this chapter three things are to be noted. I. On the law of retaliation, which was established not only by the Pythagoreans and the pagan philosophers, but also flourished in the Mosaic Law, as may be seen at Exod. 21 verses 24 and 25, Lev. 24 verses 19 and 20, and Deut. 19 verse 19. For there it is laid down that eye shall be given for eye, tooth for tooth, foot for foot, etc. That God also observed this in exacting punishments is clear from both sacred and secular histories. A notable example in the sacred history is at Judg. 1: Adonibezek was killed, his thumbs and big toes having been cut off, just as he had done to seventy kings before. So too David, who, as is seen at 2 Sam. 11, had defiled the wife of Uriah by adultery, is punished by adultery, when his son Absalom in broad daylight defiles his wives (ch. 16 of the same book). In secular history a memorable example concerns Agamemnon.
