Agamemnon, having carried off Clytemnestra, the wife of Thyestes' son Tantalus, and having taken her as his wife, later, while Agamemnon was away (for he had gone to the Trojan War), was seduced by Aegisthus, the brother of Tantalus. Afterwards, when Agamemnon returned, Aegisthus killed him. Shortly afterwards, the mother Clytemnestra and the adulterer Aegisthus were killed by Orestes, the son of Agamemnon, as related by Euripides in the Iphigenia at Aulis and Aeschylus in the Agamemnon. And indeed it seems in accordance with natural reason that whatever one has done to another, one should in turn suffer the same, for that principle taken from the law of nature is well known: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. And the jurist Caecilius, in Gellius, Attic Nights book 20 chapter 1, says: What, I beg you, is this harshness, what severity is it, that what you have done to another you should yourself bear? So too the Laws of the Twelve Tables among the Romans established the law of retaliation; for there this law stands: If anyone has broken another's limb, unless he comes to terms with the injured party, let there be retaliation. So too in civil law there are various laws confirming retaliation: l. quod quisque 5 ff. de jure in alium, l. itidem 59 ff. de periculis, et administratione tutorum. But the severity of retaliation, since it does not always rest on reason, was revoked by the clemency of the praetorian law, as Gellius relates in the passage cited. The reason for the revocation was the difficulty of exacting retaliation. For it cannot happen that the same things are always returned for the same things, nor that the same penalty is repaid for the same offence, since the circumstances of persons and actions are different. Aristotle himself, although in criminal matters, where punishment is repaid for injury inflicted on the human body, he does not admit retaliation, because respect of persons is chiefly to be had here, nevertheless in civil matters and exchanges of goods he admits it, provided it is done according to the analogy of reason and wholly according to equality, thing for thing, as may be seen from the beginning of this chapter. In sum, retaliation does not seem to be admissible simply, for four chief reasons: (1) because of the inequality of persons: some are private individuals who bear no office in the commonwealth, others are public persons who bear an office, and between these retaliation cannot be observed; (2) because of the equity of laws and judges, who are appointed as arbiters in every cause, suit and loss, not indeed for the purpose of compelling the disagreeing parties to equality of the thing, but so that they may agree among themselves according to the rule of right reason; (3) because of the diversity and dissimilarity of human actions, of which some are involuntary and others voluntary, as is clear from Aristotle, book 3; (4) finally, because of the danger of sedition and discord, lest anyone should be allowed to dare anything under the pretext of equality, as the philosopher Favorinus argues elegantly against the jurist Sextus Caecilius, as witnessed by Gellius, Attic Nights book 20 chapter 1.

units.la: 11. Notandum veniy, commensurabilia, de quibus in hoc cap. agit Philosophus duobus modis considerari: 1. Respectu essentiae & proprietatum suarum, & sic sunt diversorum generum, & hoc etiam respectu sub commensurationem aut comparationem non veniunt.
units.tr: 11. It is to be noted that commensurable things, of which the Philosopher treats in this chapter, may be considered in two ways: (1) with respect to their essence and their own properties; and in this way they belong to different kinds, and in this respect they do not come under commensuration or comparison.

units.la: 2. Respectu usus humani, & sic commensurari possunt, quaedam tamen ex iis juste commutari possunt, verbi gratia: vinum, oleum, triticum, & ejusmodi, quibus ad necessitatem explendam diversae regiones mutuo indigent, quaedam ex iis juste commutari non possunt, licet usibus humanis inserviant, idque propter duas causas: 1. Quia jure municipali seu lege civitatis talis commutatio est prohibita, ut verbi gratia: commutatio sacerdotii aut sacri muneris cum profano. 2. Quia lege naturae etiam est prohibita haec commutatio, ut verbi gratia: commutatio uxorum, de qua quaestione eleganter disputat Philosophus lib.3 Polit. cap.6. contra Platonem.
units.tr: (2) With respect to human use; and in this way they can be commensurated. Yet some of them can be justly exchanged, for example wine, oil, wheat and the like, which different regions mutually need to meet their necessities. Some of them cannot be justly exchanged, although they serve human uses, and this for two reasons: (1) because such an exchange is forbidden by municipal law, or the law of the state, for example the exchange of a priesthood or a sacred office for a secular one; (2) because this exchange is also forbidden by the law of nature, for example the exchange of wives, a question which the Philosopher discusses elegantly against Plato in Politics book 3 chapter 6.

units.la: III. Et hoc notandum venit, mensuram rerum, quae permutantur, esse duplicem: Unam naturalem, quam natura ipsa induxit, ut esset vinculum humanae societatis; ea vero est Indigentia: Aliam esse civilem, quae non natura, sed legibus et instituto mensura fit, et dicitur Nummus. Quod vero duae tantum sint mensurae, experientia ipsa probat, et Philosophus hoc ipso capite plurimus differt. Nummus vero propter tres causas mensura rerum dicitur: 1. est, propter adaequationem, quia suo interventu res inaequales ad precii et valoris aequalitatem reducit. 2. propter communionem personarum, ut hoc modo ad societatem et amicitiam excitarentur homines. 3. demum propter mutuam negotiorum translationem seu permutationem, qua permutatione societas et amicitia inter homines conservatur.
units.tr: III. It must be noted here that the measure of goods that are exchanged is twofold: one is natural, which nature itself introduced so as to be the bond of human society; this is need. The other is civil, made not by nature but by law and convention, and it is called money. That there are only these two measures experience itself proves, and the Philosopher in this very chapter argues at length. Money is called the measure of goods for three reasons: (1) it makes things equal, since through its intervention it reduces unequal goods to equality of price and value; (2) it serves the common life of persons, so that men are roused to fellowship and friendship in this way; (3) finally, it serves the mutual transfer or exchange of business, and through this exchange society and friendship between men are preserved.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Talio cum neque Distributiva neque Commutativa Justitia proprie conveniat, Injustitia simpliciter adhiberi nequit.
units.tr: 1. Since retaliation belongs properly neither to distributive nor to commutative justice, injustice cannot be simply applied to it.

units.la: 2. Lex Rhadamanti fuit, ut quod quis fecisset, idem vicissim pateretur, et sic talio stricte in rebus retribuenda observaretur.
units.tr: 2. The law of Rhadamanthus was that whatever a man had done, he should in turn suffer the same, and so retaliation was to be strictly observed in the exchange of goods.

units.la: 3. Cum multum inter se differant injuriae sponte et invitè commissae, ideo in iis reparandis talio locum habere non potest.
units.tr: 3. Since voluntary and involuntary injuries differ greatly from each other, retaliation cannot have a place in making reparation for them.

units.la: 4. Talio in rerum permutatione locum habet, cum res secundum analogiam rationu, non secundum aequalitatem rei permutantur.
units.tr: Retaliation has a place in the exchange of goods, when goods are exchanged according to proportion of reason, not according to equality of the thing.

units.la: 5. In loco urbis publico Gratiarum templum statuebant veteres, ut eo viso beneficii accepti memores redderentur homines.
units.tr: The ancients set up a temple of the Graces in a public place of the city, so that men, seeing it, would be mindful to repay the benefits they had received.

units.la: 6. Cum opus unius alterius opere multum praestet, precio & valore sunt sibi invicem adaequanda, ut justa rerum permutatio instituatur.
units.tr: Since one man's work far surpasses another's, they must be made equal to each other in price and value, so that a just exchange of goods may be established.

units.la: 7. Non ex uno hominum genere, ut ex Medicis & artificibus, sed ex diversis hominum generibus constituto omnis Respub.
units.tr: Every commonwealth is constituted not out of one kind of men, such as physicians and craftsmen, but out of different kinds of men.

units.la: 8. Quae sub proportionem veniunt, ea necesse est ut inter se comparari possint, si non per se semper, saltem respectu alicujus tertii & per accidens.
units.tr: Things that come under proportion must necessarily be comparable with one another, if not always in themselves, at least with respect to some third thing and accidentally.

units.la: 9. Nummus veluti communis omnium rerum mensura medium in rebus permutandis statuitur, quia res omnes suo interventu metitur.
units.tr: Money is set up in the exchange of goods as the common measure of all things, as a mean, because it measures all things by its intervention.

units.la: 10. Nulla esset societas inter homines, nisi esset rerum permutatio, neque ulla foret permutatio, nisi res inaequales ad aequalitatem perducerentur.
units.tr: There would be no society among men unless there were an exchange of goods, nor would there be any exchange unless unequal things were brought to equality.

units.la: 11. Revera Indigentia est prima rerum mensura, qua prima permutationem induxit, nisi enim aliqua re indigerent homines, aut nulla prorsus, aut certe non talis foret rerum permutatio.
units.tr: Indeed, need is the first measure of goods, by which the first exchange was introduced; for unless men needed some things, there would be no exchange at all, or certainly not such an exchange.

units.la: 12. Nummus dicitur Graecis νόμισμα ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμος, quod lege & instituto, non natura constet.
units.tr: Money is called in Greek νόμισμα [nomisma], from νόμος [nomos], because it rests on law and convention, not on nature.

units.la: 13. Nummus sponsoris vices subit, valorem tamen nunc majorem, nunc minorem pro libitu hominum habet.
units.tr: Money takes the place of a surety, yet it has a value now greater, now less, according to the pleasure of men.

units.la: 14. Nisi esset rerum permutatio non esset societas, neque esset permutatio, nisi esset rerum aequalitas, neque aqualitas foret nisi res, inter se commode comparari possent.
units.tr: Unless there were an exchange of goods there would be no society, nor would there be exchange unless there were equality of goods, nor equality unless the goods could be fitly compared with one another.

units.la: 15. Nummus res inter se diversas & natura differentes proportione quadam & commensuratione consentientes facit.
units.tr: Money makes things that are diverse in themselves and different by nature agree by a certain proportion and commensuration.

units.la: 16. Indigentia prior fuit rerum mensura propterea, quod antequam nummus inventus esset, rerum permutationem induxerit.
units.tr: Need was the earlier measure of goods, because it introduced the exchange of goods before money was invented.

units.la: 17. Justitia seu justa actio est medium quid, inter injuste agere tanquam excessum, & injuste pati tanquam defectum.
units.tr: Justice, or the just act, is a mean between acting unjustly, as an excess, and suffering injustice, as a defect.

units.la: 18. Justitia differt a reliquis virtutibus respectu medii, propterea quod ei sola opponatur Injustitia uno quidem nomine, sed duobus diversis naturis distincta.
units.tr: Justice differs from the other virtues with respect to the mean, because only one thing is opposed to it, injustice, which bears one name but is distinguished by two different natures.

units.la: 19. Justitia justum agit, & docet ita quidem, ut aequalia aequalibus tribuat, secundum jus & aequum, nec bonorum sibi plus, malorum minus assumat, aut contra alii bonorum minus, malorum plus concedat: Injustitia vero contraria hoc omnibus facit.
units.tr: Justice does what is just and teaches it in such a way that it gives equal things to equals, according to right and fairness, and does not take for itself more of the goods or less of the evils, or conversely grant to another less of the goods or more of the evils. Injustice, on the contrary, does all these things.

units.la: 20. De Justitia & Injustitia agere in communi & indeterminate pertinet ad Ethicam, determinate vero ad Oeconomicam & Politicam maxime tamen ad Politicam.
units.tr: To treat of justice and injustice in general and indefinitely belongs to Ethics; to treat of them definitely belongs to Economics and Politics, but chiefly to Politics.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An juste Philosophus damnaverit Pythagoraos, quod talionem in Justitia servandam statuerint, cum ratio hoc idem suadeat, nempe ut eadem pro iisdem tribuantur: tum etiam hoc Justitiae proprium est, ut nec plus nec minus aequo, sed aequalia aequalibus tribuat, sicut docet Philosophus cap. 6. hujus libri. Atqui talio nihil est aliud, quam aequalitas inter majus & minus, docente Philosopho hoc ipso cap. Cum igitur nullibi melius, quam in talione Iustitia
units.tr: I. It is asked: Did the Philosopher justly condemn the Pythagoreans for holding that retaliation was to be observed in justice, since reason itself suggests this same thing, namely that the same things should be rendered for the same; and also since it is proper to justice that it give neither more nor less than what is equal, but equal things to equals, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 6 of this book. But retaliation is nothing other than equality between greater and lesser, as the Philosopher teaches in this same chapter. Since therefore justice is nowhere better preserved than in retaliation,

units.la: sititia stitia æqualitas serve tur, injustè damnati videntur Pythago-rai? Resp. Philosophumnon damnare Pythagoraeos, quod talionem servandam statuerint (hoc enim ipse statuit) sed quod absque omni restrictione & conditione Justitiæ in genere talionem adcomodarint: nā licet in Justitia Commutativa locum habere possit, modò non secundum æqualitatem rei, sed analogiam rectæ rationis adhibeatur, in Distributiva tamen, ubi pœnarum & delictorum secundum personarum respectum habetur ratio, locum habere non potest, propter rationes & loca superiùs allata.
units.tr: are the Pythagoreans seemingly condemned unjustly? Answer: The Philosopher does not condemn the Pythagoreans for holding that retaliation was to be observed (for he himself holds this), but for having applied retaliation in general, without any restriction or condition of justice. For although it can have a place in commutative justice, provided it is applied not according to equality of the thing but according to the proportion of right reason, it cannot have a place in distributive justice, where account is taken of penalties and offences according to regard for persons, for reasons and places stated above.

units.la: II. Quomodo Indigentiam statuat mensuram omnium rerum, quæ inter se commutari possunt, cum experientia doceat, multa ad ornatum & dignitatem, multa ad divitias & voluptatem quotidie ultrò citròq; commutari, in quibus Indigentia locum non habet, cum non tam necessitatis, quam superfluitatis gratia hæc commutatio instituatur?
units.tr: II. How does he set need as the measure of all things that can be exchanged with one another, when experience teaches that many things are daily exchanged back and forth for ornament and dignity, many for riches and pleasure, in which need has no place, since this exchange is made not so much for the sake of necessity as of superfluity?

units.la: Resp: Indigentiam considerari duobus modis: 1. Respectu necessitatis, quæ causa fuit, ut mensura rerum statueretur, & sic in istis mensura dici non potest. 2. Respectu dignitatis & honestatis, & sic in istis, quæ ad voluptatem aut divitias commutantur mensura dici potest, cum non minus purpura deceat Regem, quam pannus aliquis rudiore filo textus pauperem, diversæ enim conditiones & status, diversas res necessariò requirunt.
units.tr: Answer: Need is to be considered in two ways: (1) with respect to necessity, which was the cause for setting up a measure of goods, and in this sense it cannot be called a measure in those cases; (2) with respect to dignity and decency, and in this sense it can be called a measure in those cases which are exchanged for pleasure or riches, since purple becomes a king no less than a coarse cloth woven from a rougher thread becomes a poor man; for different conditions and states necessarily require different things.

units.la: III. Quomodo dicat res omnes, quæ in commutationem veniunt esse commensurabiles seu inter se comparari, cum tamen multa res subinde commutentur, quæ comparari inter se nullo modo possunt, propterea quod diversorum sunt gene-rum rum, & naturarum plane diversarum. Proprie namq; inter fe comparari dicuntur, qua fiunt generis ejusdem aut speciei, propter similes vel dissimiles qualitates & affectiones quas habent? Resp. Non dixit res omnes plane esse comparabiles, quae inter se commutantur, sed necesse esse, ut ad aequalitatem reducantur, si modo Justitia in iis commutandis locum haberet, hoc autem fieri non posse, nisi aut per se sub comparationem veniant, aut saltem respectu alicujus tertii & per accidens.
units.tr: III. How does he say that all the things which come into exchange are commensurable or comparable with one another, when nonetheless many things are sometimes exchanged which in no way can be compared with one another, since they are of wholly different kinds and natures? For properly those things are said to be comparable with one another which are of the same genus or species, on account of the similar or dissimilar qualities and affections they have? Answer: He did not say that all things exchanged with one another are wholly comparable, but that they must necessarily be brought to equality, if justice were to have a place in exchanging them; and this cannot be done unless they come under comparison either in themselves or at least with respect to some third thing and accidentally.

units.la: IV. Quomodo etiam nummus statuatur rerum mensura cum, ut recte annotavit hic Philosophus, permutatio rerum fuerit multo ante nummum inventum saeculo. Dein etiamnum multi sunt populi, qui usum nummi prorsus ignorant, & tamen apud illos permutatio rerum viget, sicut apud Indos orientales & occidentales ex variis navigationibus deprehensum est?
units.tr: IV. How is money also set up as the measure of goods, since, as the Philosopher here rightly notes, the exchange of goods was in existence many centuries before money was invented? Furthermore, there are still many peoples who are entirely ignorant of the use of money, and yet among them the exchange of goods flourishes, as has been discovered from various voyages to the East and West Indies?

units.la: Resp. Nummus statuitur mensura rerum permutandarum non natura, sed lege & instituto hominum, sicut antea jam diximus. Neque hoc valet, multis ante nummum inventum saeculis fuit permutatio, ergo nummus mensura esse non potest, quia propter commoditatem & utilitatem hominum nummus in locum Indigentiae successit, cum ab uno loco in alium non tam commode res quam nummus deferri posset.
units.tr: Answer. Money is set up as the measure of goods to be exchanged not by nature but by the law and convention of men, as we have already said above. Nor does it follow that, because there was exchange many centuries before money was invented, money therefore cannot be a measure; for money took the place of need because of the convenience and usefulness of men, since goods could not be carried from one place to another as conveniently as money could.

units.la: V. & ult. Quomodo pecuniam seu nummum dicat res omnes metiri, & ad aequalitatem reducere, cum res animatae, verbi gratia: homines, bella, plantae, pluries sunt aestimandae, quam omnes divitiae aut pecuniae, orbis terrarum sicut praeter rationem & experientiam docet ipse Philosophus lib. 12. Metaph. cap. 3. & D. Thomas 2. part. sum. qu. 2. quaest. 43. Ergo
units.tr: V. and last. How does he say that money measures all things and brings them to equality, when living things, for example men, wars, and plants, are valued many times more than all riches or money in the world, as the Philosopher himself teaches, beyond reason and experience, in Metaphysics book 12, chapter 3, and St Thomas, 2 part, Summa, question 2, article 43? Therefore

units.la: ... go res omnes inter se nummo commensurari non possunt, cum nulla rerum inanimatarum ad res animatas sit proportio aut analogia? Resp. In rebus animatis duo consideranda: 1. Naturam & essentiam, & sic quaelibet musca pluris est aestimanda, quam quaevis divitiae, quantumvis maximi sint valoris & precii, nempe propter naturae suae excellentiam & dignitatem, habet enim in se vitam & motum & functiones suas recte obire potest, quod nullae divitiae unquam praestiterunt. 2. Consideratur usus respectu vitae humanae, & sic animatae respectu usus non praestant divitiis & pecunia, & hoc modo secundo sub commensurationem cadunt.
units.tr: ... so can all things not be measured against one another by money, since there is no proportion or analogy between inanimate things and animate things? Answer: In animate things two aspects are to be considered. First, their nature and essence; and so any fly is to be valued above any riches, however great their worth and price, namely on account of the excellence and dignity of its nature, for it has life and motion in itself and can perform its functions properly, which no riches have ever done. Second, their use with respect to human life; and in this respect animate things do not surpass riches and money, and in this way they fall under commensuration in the second sense.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: SEquitur secundus tractatus primae partis huius libri, in quo Philosophus de iure agit, & juris definitionem, divisionem, & proprietates adducit, sicut in priore sigillatim egerat Philosophus de Justitia. Membra huius tractatus sunt quatuor. In primo de jure ipso agit, & in quibus consistat, docet: In secundo dividit jus in suas species: In tertio dubia, quaedam de jure proposita solvit: In quarto demum varias quaestiones, quae ex doctrina de jure oriri poterant, movet, & ad omnes sigillatim respondet. Primi membri, quod hoc cap. 9. continetur tres rursum sunt partes, in quarum priori dubitationem quandam proponit, quam latius in tertio membro huius tractatus discutit & solvit: In secunda de jure ipso proprie dicto accurate agit, & inter quos reperiatur, ostendit: In tertia de jure per quandam similitudinem nem,cp cum jure proprie dicto cognatione & affinitate habere videtur nempe de œconomico tractat.
units.tr: There follows the second treatise of the first part of this book, in which the Philosopher treats of law (ius), and brings forward its definition, division and properties, just as in the former he had treated of justice one by one. This treatise has four members. In the first he treats of law itself and teaches what it consists in. In the second he divides law into its species. In the third he resolves certain doubts raised about law. In the fourth he finally raises various questions that could arise from the doctrine of law, and answers each one separately. The first member, which is contained in this ninth chapter, has three parts. In the first of these he puts forward a certain doubt, which he discusses and resolves more fully in the third member of this treatise. In the second he treats accurately of law properly so called, and shows among whom it is found. In the third he treats of the law that, by a certain likeness, seems to have kinship and affinity with law properly so called, namely domestic law.

units.la: In prima igitur parte dubium quoddam proponit,nempe,quod fieri possit, ut aliquis injuste agat, & tamen non sit injustus,verbi gratia : aliquis libidine inflammatus committit adulterium : aliquis fame aut necessitate coactus,res alienas invadit,&sic furtum committit. Utrque hic injuste agit, neuter tamen est injustus. Quid ita? quia, nempe nö ex tonsilio & proxerte si agunt ( quae duo ad omnem habitu ut ex cap. 4.lib.2. patet, necessario requiruntur ) sed tantum ex cupiditate & affectu. At ut aliquis proprie injustus dicatur, ex habitu injuste agere debet, quia cum Justitia sit habitus, etiam Injustitia erit. Proinde, qui proprie secundum Injustitiam agit, habitualiter tantum agit,una vero actio habitum non facit; Sic etiam boni interdum dicuntur ipso facto, ut verbi gratia: Cambyses Persarum Rex, qui iniquo judici pellem detraxit, ipso facto erat bonus, revera tamen non erat bonus,quia non ex habitu agebat: revera enim bonitas,quae est communis virtutum affectio,ab habitu provenire debet, sicut lib. 7. Eudem. cap. 3 prolixe docet Philosophus. Sed de hac quaestione hic propositia latius infra agit Philosophus,sicut in progressu patebit.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he puts forward a certain doubt: whether it can happen that someone acts unjustly and yet is not unjust. For example: someone, inflamed with lust, commits adultery; someone, compelled by hunger or necessity, seizes another's goods and so commits theft. Both act unjustly here, yet neither is unjust. Why so? Because they do not act from deliberate choice and deliberately (which two things are required for every habit, as is clear from book 2, chapter 4), but only from desire and passion. But for someone to be called unjust in the proper sense, he must act unjustly from a habit, because since justice is a habit, injustice too will be a habit. Therefore, one who acts properly according to injustice acts only by habit, whereas a single action does not make a habit. So too some are sometimes called good merely by the fact itself: for example, Cambyses, king of the Persians, who flayed an unjust judge, was good by the fact itself, yet in truth he was not good, because he did not act from a habit. For goodness, which is the common affection of the virtues, must truly arise from a habit, as the Philosopher teaches at length in book 7 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 3. But the Philosopher treats this question more fully below, here merely proposed, as will become clear as we go on.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis incipit agere de Jure ipso, & primo definit, quid sit Jus, quia a definitione naturae cujusque rei cognitio potissimum dependet. Definitur vero hoc modo Justitiae effectum, quod in mutuae societatis usu hominibus recta praescribit ratio: sicut etiam apud Diog.Laert.lib.10.de vit.Phil. in vita Epicuri, & à Cic. lib. 1. de leg. definitur recta quæ-dam ratio, quæ in jubendo & vetando, quid sit licitum, & quid illicitum, præscribit. Verùm non de omni Jure hîc agit Philosophus, sed de jure tantum absoluto & simpliciter dicto, quod aliis Politicum aliis civile dicitur. De jure Oeconomico verò non proponit sibi agendum, propterea quod, ut infra patebit, non sit jus simpliciter, sed secundum quid tatum. Et quia aut ex cap. 7. lib. 1. huius operis, videre est, tota tractatio Ethica ad Reipubl. salutem & Politicam maximè refertur. Ratio verò, cur de jure civili hîc tantum agat, ducitur à personis ad quas proprie spectat, quia inter ejusmodi tantum homines cernitur, qui in eadem societate sunt inter se devincti, & qui eadem civitate iisdemq; leg bus utuntur, & sunt æquales proportione & numero, seu communione, quadam libertatis & æqualitatis inter se gaudent. Hujus rei ratio hæc redditur, quia nempe inter homines, qui eadem societate vivunt, est legum communio, lex verò communis tunc esse dicitur, cum singulis & universis aut omnibus idem justum & injustum communi consensu habetur, & propterea, ut jus verè sit, requiritur communis quædam societas, sicut in definitione diximus. Rationem etiâ aliam affert in magna moral. lib. 1. cap. 24. quod nempe Juris Politici æqualitas inter plures & æquales tantum reperiatur. Quæ ratio à priore parû discrepare videtur; at cum jus Oeconomicum non sit ejusmodi, ut sub finem capitis patebit, de eo hîc sibi tractandû non proponit, nam proprie est inter dominum & servum, patrem & filium, maritum & uxorem, xorem, inter quas personas nulla proprie requiritur æqualitas, & propterea non eadem omnibus conceditur libertas. Sed ut jus politicum constanter & uniformiter constituatur, & ab injusto distinguatur, lex ipsa seu ratio illius norma esse debet, quæ Justitiam sectari, nec cupiditatibus depravari solet, nec plus aut minus quo huic aut illi tribuit. Verum homo ipse regula juris esse non debet, quia ejus judicium subinde variat, & in horas pene mutatur, & sæpius fit, ut affectu & cupiditatibus potius, quam recto judicio ducatur. Sed cum Magistratus sit juris custos, debet etiam æqualitatis esse custos, seu debet æqualiter jus sibi concreditum omnibus administrare, quod & hoc loco affert Philosophus, & Plato lib. 4. de leg. & leges Civil. l. 17. ne idipsum jus, ff. de Justitia & Jure: & hoc proprie munus est Judicis seu Magistratus, ut in jure dicendo, non sibi sed aliis consulat, neque bonorum sibi plus, aliis minus tribuat, sed ex præscripto Justitiæ suum cuique concedat, & hinc constat, cur Justitia dicatur bonū alienum, quod nempe ab uno exerceatur in alium, verbi gratia: à Magistratu in populum, qua de re supra disseruit Philosophus cap. 3. sub finem: ne tamen frustra laboret Magistratus, aut invanum videatur operam navasse Reipubl. pro quæstu & lucro, seu potius pro mercede honor & reverentia ei debentur, quibus si non contententus sit, sed aliquid ultra expetat, sive per defraudationem, sive aliis modis in tyrannū degenerat. Verus enim Magistratus honestatem pro fine suo, & salutem populi pro fine Reipubl. semper habet. Quod ve o leges in singulis civitatibus dominari & præesse: Magistratus iis subesse, sed exequi tamen: populus parere & servi-re debeat, præter rationem eleganter docet Plato lib. 4. & 9. de leg. & Aristoteles 4. Polit. sparsim per totum, & 1. lib. Rhet. ad Theod. c. 1. Quare præclarè Impp. Romanorum Alexander scilicet Severus & Antoninus inquiunt: Licet legibus soluti sumus, legibus tamen viviimus. §. ult. tit. 17. lib. 3. Instit. quibus modis testamentum infirmetur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he begins to treat of law itself, and first defines what law is, since knowledge of the nature of each thing depends chiefly on its definition. It is defined in this way: a rule of right, which dictates to men in the practice of mutual society the effect of justice; just as also in Diogenes Laertius, book 10, On the Lives of the Philosophers, in the life of Epicurus, and by Cicero, On the Laws, book 1, a certain right reason is defined, which, in commanding and forbidding, prescribes what is lawful and what unlawful. Yet the Philosopher does not treat here of all law, but only of law that is absolute and simply so called, which some call political and others civil. He does not propose to treat of economic law, because, as will become clear below, it is not law simply, but only in a certain respect. And as can be seen from chapter 7 of book 1 of this work, the whole ethical treatment is chiefly directed to the welfare of the commonwealth and to politics. The reason why he treats here only of civil law is taken from the persons to whom it properly pertains: because it is found only among such men as are bound to one another in the same society, who use the same city and the same laws, and are equal in proportion and number, or enjoy a certain shared liberty and equality among themselves. The reason for this is given as follows: among men who live in the same society there is a community of laws; and a law is said to be common when the same thing is held just and unjust by all and each by common consent. Therefore, for law to be truly law, a certain common society is required, as we said in the definition. He gives another reason in the Great Ethics, book 1, chapter 24, namely that equality is found in political law only among many and equal persons. This reason seems to differ somewhat from the former; but since economic law is not of such a kind, as will be clear toward the end of the chapter, the Philosopher does not propose to treat it here. For it properly exists between master and slave, father and son, husband and wife, and between these persons no equality is properly required, and therefore the same liberty is not granted to all. But so that political law may be constituted constantly and uniformly, and distinguished from the unjust, its law, or the reason of it, must be the rule, one that pursues justice, is not corrupted by desires, and does not give more or less to this man or that. A man himself ought not to be the rule of law, because his judgment varies from time to time, and changes almost hour by hour, and it often happens that he is guided by passions and desires rather than by sound judgment. But since the magistrate is the guardian of law, he ought also to be the guardian of equality, that is, he ought to administer equally the law entrusted to him to all; and the Philosopher brings this forward in this place, as does Plato in On the Laws, book 4, and the civil laws in Digest 17, "that the same law" (ff. de Iustitia et iure). And this is properly the office of the judge or magistrate: that in pronouncing law he consult not himself but others, nor give himself more of goods and others less, but grant each his own according to the prescription of justice. Hence it is clear why justice is called another's good: because it is exercised by one toward another, for example by the magistrate toward the people, a matter on which the Philosopher discussed above in chapter 3, near the end. Yet lest the magistrate labour in vain, or seem to have spent effort on the commonwealth for profit and gain, honour and reverence are due to him as his reward, or rather as his wage; if he is not content with these but seeks something beyond, whether by defrauding or by other means, he degenerates into a tyrant. For a true magistrate always has honesty as his aim, and the welfare of the people as the aim of the commonwealth. That laws should rule and preside in each city, that magistrates should be subject to them yet carry them out, and that the people should obey and serve, Plato elegantly teaches beyond reason in On the Laws, books 4 and 9, and Aristotle in Politics, book 4, scattered throughout, and in Rhetoric, book 1, to Theodectes, chapter 1. Wherefore the Roman emperors Alexander Severus and Antoninus rightly say: "Although we are released from the laws, yet we live by the laws" (Institutes, book 3, title 17, last section, on the ways in which a testament is invalidated).

units.la: In tertia parte capitis de jure agit, quod similitudinem & affinitatem cum jure Politico habet, nempe de œconomico, quod respectu personarum ad quas spectat, varie nominatur: nam vel inter dominum & servum colitur, & sic dicitur δεσποτικὸν, seu herile; vel patri in filium competit, & dicitur patrium, vel inter maritum & uxorem cernitur, & vocatur jus maritale. Differt verò à jure civili, licet nomine communi utrumque conveniat, in hoc potissimum, quod illas personas attingat, inter quas lex & justitia proprie non viget, talis scilicet Justitia, qualis in jure civili cernitur, ut supra jam probatum fuit, quod inde apparet, quia servi sunt propria possessio domini sui, ut ex lib. 3. Polit. cap. 5. & 1. Rhet. cap. 7. probat Philosophus: liberi verò præsertim minorennes & nondum emancipati, cum sint veluti membra parentum, una persona cum patre ipso censentur, nō tantum hîc à Philosopho, sed etiam in jure civili §. item vero, tit. 20. lib. 3. Instit. de inutilibus titulationibus, l. nati 2. C. de contrahenda stipulatione, l. omnis 9. ff. de stipulationibus, l. quod verò 130 ff. de verbor. oblig. Nemo verò in res suas jus exercere dicitur, neq; etiam proprie Justitiam stitiam, cum Justitia sit bonum alienum, quod in aliios exercetur. Proinde juri civili proprie dicto in œconomica societate locus esse non potest, cum ibi tantum locum habeat, ubi parendi imperandique vicissim potestas conceditur. Hoc autem in jure œconomico non reperitur, cum servi & liberi, qua tales, semper parere & subesse debeant; Patri vero regere & imperare conveniat, non econtra. Sed tertia species juris œconomici, quod vocatur jus maritale, majorem affinitatem cum jure civili ceteris duabus speciebus habet, quia cum inter maritum & uxorem fit, illis competit mutua parendi & imperandi vicissitudo: nam in quibusdam actionibus & rebus dominatio convenit uxori, non marito, in quibusdam etiam conjunctum habet imperium, sicut infra lib. 8. cap. 10. hujus operis, & in œconomicis latius declarat Philosophus. Differt vero a jure civili finis potissimum respectu, quod hoc commune civitatis bonum quaerat, illud vero bonum privatum, & domesticum sibi tantum proponat, de qua differentia pluribus agit Philosophus lib. 1. Polit. c. 1. & 5.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he treats of law which has a likeness and affinity with political law, namely economic law, which, with respect to the persons to whom it pertains, is variously named. For it is either practised between master and slave, and so is called herile [δεσποτικὸν]; or it belongs to a father over his son, and is called paternal; or it is seen between husband and wife, and is called marital law. It differs, however, from civil law, although both agree under a common name, chiefly in this: that it concerns those persons between whom law and justice properly do not hold sway, namely that justice of the kind seen in civil law, as has already been proved above. This is clear because slaves are the property of their master, as the Philosopher proves from Politics, book 3, chapter 5, and Rhetoric, book 1, chapter 7. But free persons, especially minors not yet emancipated, since they are as it were members of their parents, are regarded as one person with the father himself; this is taught not only here by the Philosopher but also in civil law (Institutes, book 3, title 20, on useless stipulations; Code, on entering into stipulation; Digest, on stipulations; Digest, on verbal obligations). Moreover, no one is said to exercise law over his own things, nor properly justice either, since justice is another's good, exercised toward others. Therefore civil law properly so called cannot have a place in the economic society, since it has a place only where the power of commanding and obeying is granted in turn. But this is not found in economic law, since slaves and free persons, as such, must always obey and be subject; whereas it is fitting for the father to rule and command, not the reverse. But the third species of economic law, which is called marital law, has greater affinity with civil law than the other two species, because between husband and wife there is a mutual interchange of obeying and commanding: for in some actions and matters dominion belongs to the wife, not the husband, and in some matters they share authority, as the Philosopher declares more fully in book 8, chapter 10 of this work, and in his Economics. It differs from civil law chiefly in its end, because the one seeks the common good of the state, while the other proposes to itself only private and domestic good. The Philosopher treats of this difference at more length in Politics, book 1, chapters 1 and 5.

units.la: Notanda sunt in hoc cap. praeter supra dicta haec tria: I. Aliquem injuste agere, aut injuriam facere posse quatuor modis: 1. Furenter propter immoderatos affectus, idque vel cum affectus rationem penitus e fede dejiciunt, quod fit per insaniam, vel cum non prorsus dejiciunt, sed non parent, quod fit per aliquam cupiditatem, iram puta, odium aut amorem. 2. Inscienter per nativam ignorantiam, cum aliquis injuste agit, sed propter naturae impedimenta ignorat, se injuste agere, ut plerunque fit a stultis.
units.tr: These points should be noted in this chapter, besides those mentioned above. I. Someone can act unjustly, or do an injustice, in four ways. (1) Furiously, on account of immoderate passions. This happens either when passion entirely throws reason from its seat, as occurs through madness, or when passion does not wholly dislodge reason but reason fails to obey, as occurs through some desire, such as anger, hatred or love. (2) Unknowingly, through innate ignorance: when someone acts unjustly but, because of impediments of nature, does not know that he is acting unjustly, as usually happens with fools.

units.la: 3. Cum invitè aut fortuitò aliquid committitur per coactionem aut casum, cum vis externa aut etiam fortuna factum contra leges aut rationem elicit. 4. Demum spontaneè & consultò per malitiam fit aliquid injuste, & qui hoc modo peccat, injustus dici potest ab una etiâ actione licet non habitualiter, actualiter tamen. II. Notandū, Jus civile seu politicum multò latius à Philosopho, quam à Jureconsultis accipi, nam hic Philosophus sumit pro omni jure publico, quod tendit ad commune bonum civitatis, sive id sit naturale, sive politicum, ut & seqq. cap. manifestum erit. Apud JCtos verò jus civile id proprie dicitur, quod quisq; populus sibi constituit lib. 1. Institut. tit. 2. §. 2. & 11. l. 9. omnes populi, ff. de justitia & jure, l. 1. omnes gentes, ff. de legib. Id enim proprie civile vocant Latini, quod cujusq; civitatis est proprium, ut ibidem explicatur. III. Et hoc observatu dignum, quod Magistratus hoc esse proprium dicat, ut aliis non sibi consulat, idque propter tres causas: 1. Propter munus suum, quia publicum gerit munus in Repub. idque hoc fine, ut cum sit Reipub. caput omnibus membris prospiciat. 2. Quia exemplum & vitam ejus intuentur omnes, juxta illud:
units.tr: (3) Unwillingly or by accident, when something is done through compulsion or chance, when external force, or even fortune, brings about an act contrary to laws or reason. (4) Finally, something is done unjustly willingly and deliberately, through malice. Someone who sins in this way can be called unjust from a single action, even though not by habit, yet in act. II. It should be noted that the Philosopher takes "civil law," or "political law," far more broadly than the jurists do. For here the Philosopher means all public law that aims at the common good of the state, whether it is natural or political, as will be clear in the following chapters. Among the jurists, however, "civil law" properly means that which each people has established for itself: Inst. lib. 1, tit. 2, §§ 2 and 11; l. 9, "omnes populi," ff. de justitia et jure; l. 1, "omnes gentes," ff. de legibus. For the Latins call that properly "civil" which belongs peculiarly to each state, as is explained in the same place. III. It is also worth observing that the Philosopher says a magistrate's characteristic is that he does not look after his own interests but those of others, and this for three reasons: (1) because of his office, since he holds a public office in the commonwealth, and this for the purpose that, being the head of the commonwealth, he may provide for all its members; (2) because all men look to his example and his life, according to that saying:

units.la: Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis.
units.tr: The whole world is shaped after the example of the king.

units.la: 3. Quia maximum honorem mercedis loco habet, ut aliis non sibi prosit, si enim privatim sibi tantum prospiceret, non jam judex aut magistratus, sed tyrannus & rapax diceretur, sicut eleganter Plato lib. 2. de Rep. disserit.
units.tr: (3) Because he regards the greatest honour as his reward, namely that he does good to others and not to himself. For if he cared only for his private advantage, he would no longer be called a judge or magistrate, but a tyrant and a plunderer, as Plato argues elegantly in the second book of the Republic.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: Axioms

units.la: 1. Poterit aliquis injustè agere, qui tamen hac una actione non statim fit injustus. 2. Mul-
units.tr: 1. A person may act unjustly, yet by this one action he does not at once become unjust. 2. Mul-

units.la: 2. Multa inter se differunt facta exproaresi & deliberatione, & ea, quae à cupiditatibus aut affectu proveniunt.
units.tr: 2. Many things differ from one another: deeds done from choice and deliberation, and those that proceed from desires or passion.

units.la: 3. Jus civile seu politicum in communi hominum societate consistit & inter homines non modo liberos, sed etiam aequales & proportione & numero cernitur.
units.tr: 3. Civil or political law consists in the common society of men, and is found among men who are not only free but also equal, both in proportion and in number.

units.la: 4. Iniustè agere proprie est de bonis plus aequo; de malis minus aequo sibi attribuere, sive ea sint bona corporis, sive fortunae.
units.tr: 4. To act unjustly properly means to claim for oneself more than one's fair share of goods, and less than one's fair share of evils, whether these are goods of the body or of fortune.

units.la: 5. Non debet permitti, ut homo ipse in Repub. regat, sed ut recta ratio tantum regat, aut saltem homo secundum rectam rationem.
units.tr: 5. It should not be allowed that a man himself rule in the commonwealth, but only right reason should rule, or at least man according to right reason.

units.la: 6. Magistratus est iuris & aequi custos, ita tamen, ut non sibi, sed aliis inprimis prospiciat.
units.tr: 6. The magistrate is the guardian of law and equity, yet in such a way that he looks chiefly to others and not to himself.

units.la: 7. Iudex etsi legum executionem in manu habeat, non minus tamen ipse legibus paret aut parere debet, quam alios secundum legem iudicat.
units.tr: 7. Although a judge has the execution of the laws in his hand, he nonetheless submits to the laws no less than he judges others according to the law, or ought to submit.

units.la: 8. Magistratus in Repub. frustra laborare debet, sed ei mercedis loco honor & reverentia debentur, quibus si contentus non sit, in tyrannum & iniustum degenerat.
units.tr: 8. The magistrate in the commonwealth must not labour in vain, but honour and reverence are owed to him as his wage; if he is not content with these, he degenerates into a tyrant and an unjust man.

units.la: 9. Jus oeconomicum est simile quidem iuri politico, non tamen est idem.
units.tr: 9. Economic law is indeed similar to political law, yet it is not the same.

units.la: 10. Habet ius oeconomicum locum in iis personis tantum, in quibus mutua parendi imperandi, potestas concedit ditur.
units.tr: 10. Economic law has its place only among those persons in whom the power of mutual obeying and commanding is granted.

units.la: 11. Differt à iure civili finis potissimum respectu, quod civile ad commune civitatis bonum tendat, oeconomicum vero bonum domesticum & privatum imprimis respiciat.
units.tr: 11. It differs from civil law chiefly in its aim: civil law tends to the common good of the state, whereas economic law looks chiefly to the domestic and private good.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: Recténe asserat Philosophus, illum non esse injustum, qui injuste agit, cum injuste agere, & juste age-
units.tr: I. The question is: Does the Philosopher rightly assert that one who acts unjustly is not unjust, since to act unjustly and to act justly are opposites, and therefore if he who acts justly is just, he who acts unjustly must necessarily be unjust? For the consequence of opposites is opposite.

units.la: re sint opposita, & ideo si justus sit, qui juste agit, necesse est, ut injustus sit, qui injuste agit. Oppositorum enim opposita est consequentia? Resp. Injuste agere bifariam sumi: 1. Perse & respecta voluntatis & qui hoc modo injuste agit, poterit dici injustus, licet non ex habitu injustus sit. 2. Per accidens respectu vel affectus, vel ignorantiae, vel fortunae, & sic non poterit dici injustus, cum ἀκούσιον, quae requiritur, vel ad ipsum habitum, vel ad omne actionem habitus non praecedat, & hoc modo intelligitur Philosophus, cum dicit, aliquem injuste agere, & tamen non esse injustum. Sed de hac quaestione fusius & accuratius infra tractabit. cap. 12.
units.tr: Answer: To act unjustly is taken in two ways. (1) Per se, with respect to the will, and one who acts unjustly in this way can be called unjust, though he is not unjust by habit. (2) Per accidens, with respect to passion, ignorance or fortune, and in this sense one cannot be called unjust, since the involuntary [ἀκούσιον], which is required either for the habit itself or for every action, does not precede the habit. It is in this way that the Philosopher is to be understood when he says that someone acts unjustly and yet is not unjust. But he will treat this question more fully and accurately below, chapter 12.

units.la: II. Quomodo neget, jus œconomicum esse simpliciter jus aut jus absolutum, cum duplex ratio id evincat: Nam 1. non minus habet suas leges, quam politicum aut civile. 2. Tempore & natura praecedit politicum, ideo magis absolutum dici debet. Quod tempore praecedat, hinc manifestum est, nam ut videre est, Genes. 2. inter Adamum & Evam erat jus œconomicum, nempe maritale, & tamen nullum erat adhuc politicum, cum nulla etiam essent personae, quibus competeret. Natura etiam praecedit, nam ex variis familiis, in quibus œconomicum jus vigebat, conflata est omnis Resp. & per consequens omne jus politicum? Resp. Ideo Philosophum negare esse absolutum, quia non tendit primario ad salutem aut commodum totius civitatis, quem ille scopum juris ex opinione omnium legatorum Graciae statuit. Quod ad secundam rationem, non ideo sequitur, esse magis absolutum, quod tempore & natura praecedat, cum & embryo in generatione foetus praecedat hominem, & tamen non est magis absolutum quid, quam est ipse homo.
units.tr: II. How does he deny that economic law is law simply or absolute law, since there are two reasons that prove it? For (1) it has no less laws of its own than political or civil law has. (2) In time and in nature political law comes first, and so it ought to be called more absolute. That it comes first in time is clear from this: as may be seen in Genesis 2, between Adam and Eve there was economic law, namely marital law, and yet there was as yet no political law, since there were no persons to whom it could apply. It also comes first in nature, for every commonwealth was formed from various households in which economic law prevailed, and consequently all political law. Answer: The Philosopher denies that it is absolute because it does not tend primarily to the welfare or advantage of the whole state, which he, by the common opinion of the Greek lawgivers, set down as the aim of law. As for the second reason, it does not follow that something is more absolute because it comes first in time and in nature, since the embryo also precedes the man in the generation of the foetus, and yet it is no more absolute a thing than the man himself is.

units.la: III. Cur Philosophus dicat, hoc boni Magistratus esse, ut magis alii quam sibi consulat, cum tamen nemo bonus legi naturae refragari debeat: atqui talis hoc facit. Est enim a natura unicuique hoc insitum, ut sibi prospiciat melius quam alii: natura enim & propter sui conservationem & propter boni intentionem, quod ergo creatur as suas intendit, mirum amorem, unumquemque querei ergasepsum excitat? Resp. In Magistratu duplicem consideran naturam, unam hominis privati, & sic ex naturae instinctu magis sibi, quam aliis prospicere debet: aliam hominis Politici & sic respectu muneris, quod in Republ. geri, plus aliis quam sibi consulere debet, propter rationes jam supra allatas. IV. Et hoc vocatur in dubium: An homo ipse non debeat regere in Repub. sed tantum recta ratio, cum recta ratio nihil aliud sit, quam ipse homo, aut saltem realiter non differat, cum sit forma cujusque hominis. Ideo si homo non debeat regere, sed ratio ipsa, hoc sequeretur absurdi, aut compositum esse absque forma sua, aut formam esse absque composito suo, quod utrumque est perabsurdum? Resp. Hominem considerari variis modis, & 1. quidem dupliciter, vel respectu naturae & essentiae suae, quomodo non est Ethicae considerationis: vel respectu qualitatum, quae sunt in ipso, & hoc modo spectat ad Ethicam. Sed hic rursus duplicem induit respectum: vel enim consideratur in gradu perfectionis, vel in gradu imperfectionis: In gradu perfectionis, quatenus nempe iis omnibus qualitatibus est praeditus, quae ad humanam felicitatem requiruntur, cujusmodi sunt virtutes omnes morales, & sic Ethicè non differt homo a recta ratione. 2. In gragradu imperfectionis quatenus nondum eas habet qualitates, quae ad bene beateque vivendum requiruntur, & hoc modo intelligi debet Philosophus, cum dicit non hominem, sed rectam rationem debere regere, quia ratio est regula omnium virtutum moralium, sicut ex definitione virtutis supra jam data patet.
units.tr: III. Why does the Philosopher say that it is the duty of a good magistrate to look to others rather than to himself, when yet no good man ought to resist the law of nature; but such a man does this? For nature has implanted in each person that he should look after himself better than others; for nature, both for its own preservation and for the intention of good, stirs up in each the wondrous love by which each seeks what is his own. Answer: In the magistrate there are two natures to be considered: one of a private man, and so by the instinct of nature he ought to look more to himself than to others; the other of a political man, and so with respect to his office, which he performs in the commonwealth, he ought to look more to others than to himself, for the reasons already given above. IV. And this is called into doubt: whether man himself ought not to rule in the commonwealth, but only right reason, since right reason is nothing other than man himself, or at least does not really differ from him, since it is the form of each man. So if man ought not to rule, but reason itself, it would follow that either the compound is without its form or the form is without its compound, both of which are most absurd? Answer: Man may be considered in various ways. First, indeed, in two ways: either with respect to his nature and essence, which does not belong to ethical consideration; or with respect to the qualities that are in him, and in this way it belongs to Ethics. But here again he takes on a twofold aspect: for he is considered either in the degree of perfection or in the degree of imperfection. In the degree of perfection, namely insofar as he is endowed with all those qualities required for human happiness, such as all the moral virtues, and so ethically man does not differ from right reason. (2) In the degree of imperfection, insofar as he does not yet have those qualities that are required for living well and blessedly; and it is in this sense that the Philosopher must be understood when he says that not man but right reason ought to rule, because reason is the rule of all the moral virtues, as is plain from the definition of virtue given above.

units.la: V. & ult. Quomodo jus civile seu politicum ab Oeconomico distinguat hoc loco, cum tamen lib.1. Polit. cap.1. Oeconomicum sub civili comprehendat. Ergo aut hic male facit aut sibi, aut sibi contrariatur? Resp. Hic proprie & stricte sumit nomen Juris politici, pro jure tantum publico, quod tedit ad commune civitatis bonum, illic improprie & late pro omni jure sive publico, sive privato, quod legibus & institutis constat, & sic sibi non contrariatur.
units.tr: V. & ult. How does he here distinguish civil or political law from the household law (Oeconomicum), when yet in the first book of the Politics, chapter 1, he includes the household under the civil? Therefore either he acts badly here, or he contradicts himself or is inconsistent? Answer: Here he takes the name of political law properly and strictly, for public law only, which tends to the common good of the state; there he takes it improperly and broadly, for all law, whether public or private, which consists of laws and institutions; and so he is not contradicting himself.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Continetur hoc cap.10. secundum membrum secundi tractatus hujus libri, in quo Phil. distincto jure civili ab Oeconomico sive illud sit maritale, sive patrium sive herile; Jus Politicum dividit in suas species, & singulas singillatim explicat: Partes hujus capitis sunt tres: In prima Jus Civile dividit in suas species: In secunda docet jus naturale esse proprie dictum jus, contra quod multi opinabantur, nempe nihil juris nomen mereri, quod non a legibus, institutis, & voluntate hominum dependeret: In tertia de factis justis & injustis, & eorum cum jure & injuria discrimine paucis agit.
units.tr: This tenth chapter contains the second part of the second treatise of this book. In it Philosophus (Aristotle), having distinguished civil law from economic law, whether marital, paternal or servile, divides political law into its species and explains each one separately. This chapter has three parts. In the first, he divides civil law into its species. In the second, he teaches that natural law is properly called law, against the view of many who held that nothing deserves the name of law unless it depends on laws, institutions and the will of men. In the third, he briefly treats of just and unjust acts and of the distinction between them and right and wrong.

units.la: In prima igitur parte, quia Jus Politicum vel a natura vel à natra vel legibus & consuetudine provenit, dividit in duas species, nempe in naturale & legitimū. Et primò jus naturale, (propterea quod originis & causæ suæ ratione multò sit dignius legitimo) describit à suis notis & proprietatibus, & duas potissimum admfert, quarum prima est respectu loci vel effectus sui, nempe quod ubique sit idem jus naturale, & eandem etiam habeat vim, de quo Cic.3. de Republ. & Lactant: lib.6.cap.8. de jure naturæ eleganter disputant. Sub hac etiam nota comprehendi poterit & proprietas temporis, nempe quod jus naturale semper sit perpetuum & constans, nec ullo unquam tempore mutetur, id quod etiam præclarè docet Sophocles in Oedipo Tyranno, & Imperator Justinianus lib. 1. Instit.tit. 2.§. 2. & 11. & l. adoptivus 24. ff.de ritu nuptiarum,l. Jura 8 ff. de Regulis Juris. Altera nota est respectu causæ efficientis, nempe quod cū à natura natum sit hoc jus per se & sua vi tantum valeat, non quod hic aut ille sic statuat, aut ab opinione hominum natum aut inditum sit, sed quod ex ipsa veritate dependeat, id quod etiam Philosophus disputat cap. 2. lib. de Soph. Elench. & Plato in Minoe & Cic. lib.2. Rhet. sub finem. Utriusq; notæ certæ reddi possunt causæ: prioris quidem hæ, quod naturæ hoc sit proprium tanquam communis omnium rerum parentis, unam eandemq; vim semper & in omnibus locis servare, quia generalis est causa rerum omnium, & specialem habet providentiam in rebus à se productis conservandis, sicut Philosophus docet sect. 15. problem. problem. 5. Alterius hæc etiam ratio esse poterit, quia sibi invicem repugnant, natunatura esse & opinione esse, quae enim à natura dependet sunt necessaria, nec aliter se habere possunt, quae vero ab opinione, sunt contingentia, & aliter atque aliter plerunque se habent, sicut Sophist. Elench. loco jam citato docet Philosophus. Secundo describit alteram speciem juris Politici, nempe jus legale, quod alias suo nomine vocatur à Jurisconsultis civile. Describit vero à duabus etiam notis seu proprietatibus, quarum prima ducitur à vi & potestate, quam in limitandis hominum actionibus habet, nempe quod juris legitimi haec sit vis & natura, ut prius quam decreto lanciatur, sit ἀδιάφορον & indifferens, quod nullam per se vim ante legislationem habeat, sed liberum plane sit hoc vel illo modo negotia disponi. Altera ducitur à causa efficiente, quod nempe non à natura, sicut prius illud naturale, sed à voluntate hominum dependeat, & ut melius illustret hasce proprietates, duo adseri exempla, quorum primum desumitur ex Herodoto in Erato, & ex Thucyd. lib. 5. hist. de jure quodam inter Lacedaemonios lato, ut nempe captivi duobus redimerentur minis: alterum continet institutum Acrorum, qui, ut scribit Herodotus in Euterpe, hunc habuerunt morem, ut Jovi Hammonio non auribus, ut apud caeteras gentes, sed capita tantum sacrificarent. Haec exempla ideo adducit, ut ostendat ista ante legis promulgationem fuisse libera, ut fieri vel non fieri hoc modo potuerint. Postea tamen non ita fuisse libera, & proinde esse de jure legali seu legitimo, non vero de naturali. Ad hoc jus legitimum pertinent etiam privilegia, de singularibus personis & rebus propter certas caucausas introductæ, ut verbi gratia: cum Lacedæmoni Brasidi ipsorum Duci privilegium esset concessum, ut illi divini exhiberentur honores; tum et cum apud Indos Libero Patri seu Baccho sacrificia quotannis fierent, sicut refert Thucyd. lib. 5. hist. Item omnia illa, quæ suffragiis & decretis populi, item Senatusconsultis, plebiscitis & edictis prætorum in variis Rebusp. constituuntur. Unde duplex erit jus legitimum, unum Commune, quod in omnes communiter, statuitur, cujusmodi sunt illa omnia, quæ in libris Jurisconsultorum habentur: aliud singulare, quo certis de causis uni, non multis fuit concessum, tanquam aliquod proprium, cujusmodi sunt eæ leges, quæ de bello propter certas causas suscipiendo, de legatione mittenda, de hoc vel illo in Magistratum assumendo & cæteris ejusmodi leges feruntur, quales plerasque e Republica Romana congessit in librum Paulus Manutius lib. de legibus Romanis. Et huic Aristotelis divisioni, quæ nempe dividit jus in naturale & legitimum, consentanea est illa divisio Jurisconsultorum, quæ habetur lib. 1. Institut. tit. 2. §. 10. & non inelegantER & l. 9. singularia ff. de legib.
units.tr: In the first part, then, since political law arises either from nature or from laws and custom, he divides it into two species, namely natural and legitimate. First he describes natural law, which by reason of its origin and cause is far more worthy than legitimate law, by its marks and properties. He chiefly admits two properties. The first, with respect to its place or effect, is that natural law is everywhere the same and has the same force. Cicero (On the Republic, book 3) and Lactantius (Divine Institutes, book 6, chapter 8) discuss this elegantly concerning the law of nature. Under this mark may also be included the property of time: natural law is always perpetual and constant and is never changed at any time. Sophocles also teaches this admirably in Oedipus Tyrannus, as does the Emperor Justinian in Institutes, book 1, title 2, §§ 2 and 11, and in the law adoptivus 24, Digest de ritu nuptiarum, and in the law Jura 8, Digest de regulis iuris. The second mark, with respect to the efficient cause, is that since this law is born of nature and has force through itself and its own power alone, it does not depend on this or that man's decreeing it, nor is it born of or imposed by human opinion, but it depends on truth itself. The Philosopher also argues this in Sophistical Refutations, chapter 2, as does Plato in Minos, and Cicero in Rhetoric, book 2, near the end. The causes of both marks can be made clear. The cause of the first is that it is proper to nature, as the common parent of all things, to preserve one and the same force always and in all places, since it is the general cause of all things and has a special providence for preserving the things it has produced, as the Philosopher teaches in Problems, section 15, problem 5. The reason for the second may also be this: nature and opinion are mutually opposed. Things that depend on nature are necessary and cannot be otherwise, whereas things that depend on opinion are contingent and for the most part are variously otherwise, as the Philosopher teaches in the Sophistical Refutations already cited. Secondly, he describes the other species of political law, namely legal law, which the jurists elsewhere call civil law by its own name. He also describes it by two marks or properties. The first is derived from the power and authority it has in limiting human actions: the nature and force of legitimate law is such that, before it is issued by decree, it is indifferent [ἀδιάφορον], having in itself no force before legislation, and it is entirely free for affairs to be arranged in this or that way. The second is derived from the efficient cause: legitimate law depends not on nature, as the former natural law does, but on the will of men. To illustrate these properties better, he adduces two examples. The first is taken from Herodotus in Erato and from Thucydides, History, book 5, concerning a certain law passed among the Lacedaemonians, namely that captives were to be redeemed for two minae. The second is the custom of the Acrians, who, as Herodotus writes in Euterpe, had the custom of sacrificing to Jupiter Ammon not ears, as among other nations, but only heads. He adduces these examples in order to show that such things were free before the promulgation of the law, so that they could be done in this way or not done. Afterwards, however, they were no longer free in this way, and so they belong to legal or legitimate law, not to natural law. To this legitimate law also belong privileges, introduced for particular persons and things for certain causes. For example, when the Lacedaemonians granted to Brasidas, their commander, the privilege that divine honours be paid to him; and when sacrifices were offered yearly among the Indians to Liber Pater, or Bacchus, as Thucydides, book 5, relates. Likewise, all those things which are established in the various commonwealths by the votes and decrees of the people, and likewise by decrees of the Senate, plebiscites and edicts of the praetors. Hence legitimate law will be twofold: one common, which is enacted for all in common, of which sort are all those things found in the books of the jurists; and another particular, by which for certain causes something has been granted to one person and not to many, as a kind of private right. Of this sort are those laws which are passed concerning undertaking war for certain causes, sending an embassy, or appointing this or that man to a magistracy, and other such laws, most of which Paulus Manutius gathered from the Roman commonwealth into his book On Roman Laws. To this division of Aristotle, which divides law into natural and legitimate, that division of the jurists corresponds, which is found in Institutes, book 1, title 2, § 10, and not inelegantly in the law singularia, 9, Digest de legibus.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis refutat eorum opinionem, qui putabant, omnia jura esse legibus & consuetudinis introducti, nullum esse naturale, nihil a natura rectum aut pravum, nihil justum & injustum esse. Eorum præcipua ratio hæc fuit, quia omnia naturalia sunt immutabilia, ut verbi gratia: ignis hic & apud Persas similiter urit, & eandem habet vim: jura autem quotidie mutantur, & in diversis locis diversa subinde fiunt, ut communis experientia testatur, verbi gratia: apud plerasque gentes, nefas est ducere matrem in uxorem, apud Persas tamen justum id fuit, nam & consuetudine & legibus erat sanctum, testibus Herodoto & Cicerone. Sic etiam apud varias gentes nefas est ducere sororem, apud Ægyptios tamen id justum fuit, ut refert Philo Iudæus de ritibus Ægyptiorum. Sic etiam apud Athenienses licebat ducere sororem ex eodem patre, non autem ex eadem matre, quia id legibus Solonis erat veritum: apud Lacedæmonios econtra legibus Lycurgi licebat ducere sororem ex eadem matre, sed non ex eodem patre: apud Ægyptios utramque habere uxorem justum fuit. Respondet Philosophus ad hanc rationem supra allatam per negationem, & negat omnia naturalia esse simpliciter immutabilia, quia naturalia sunt duorum generum, aut saltem bifariam considerari possunt, vel quoad Deos, in quos cum nulla cadat mutatio, neque apud illos naturalia mutantur: vel secundum homines, & sic naturalia pro variis casibus etiam mutantur, quod probat familiari exemplo, verbi gratia: Dextra est natura fortior siniistra, & tamen fieri potest, ut usu & exercitatione siniistra antecellat robore dextræ, quod fit in scævolis, atque adeo fieri potest, ut quis pæneque utraque manu utatur & fiat ambidexter. Cum igitur naturalia quædam mutentur, ut hæc instantia probat, possunt quædam jura esse naturalia, licet aliquid mutationis patiantur. Quæ vero sint ejusmodi Jura naturalia hoc signo dignoscenda proponit, quæ nempe ad eundem modum semper se habent, neque apud ullas gentes, nisi raro admodum aliter se habent. Ubi & hoc praecipuè notandum, jura naturalia quoad genus suum & in idæa non esse mutabilia, sed tamen in individuo seu respectu singularum circumstantiarū nonnihil subinde mutationis admittere possunt, ut verbi gratia: de jure naturæ est, parentibus esse obediendū, & hoc semper verum est, nec usquam mutatur quoad genus suum, fieri tamen potest, ut in singulari aliquo casu hoc mutetur, ut verbi gratia: Si parentes jubeant liberos agnitam fidem abnegare, patriam prodere, in Deum blasphemare, & ejusmodi, hic non tenentur liberi parentibus obedire, & tamen manet illud semper verū, parentibus scilicet esse obediendum. Cæterum de hac quæstione, an scilicet jus aliquod sit à natura, necne (quod tamen negavit Archilaus Præceptor Socratis, teste Laërt. lib. 2. de vit. Phil. & Callides Sophista, teste Platone in Gorgia, & Epicuræi omnes testibus Platone in Thraf. & Laërt. lib. 10. in vit. Epicuri, & contra quos omnes hic disputat Philosophus,) videatur Plato in Minoe & in Gorgia & lib 1. & 10. de leg. & Cic. 1. de leg. & Alex. Aphrodisi. lib. 2. de anima, & Simplicius in prafat. ad Physicam auscultationem Aristotelis. Disputavit etiam pulcherrimè Cicero in libris de Repub. sicut testatur Lactant. lib. 5. Instit. Christ. Jura verò legalia nō perinde ad eundem modum se habent, sed in omnibus fere locis sunt diversa, & non secus mutantur, quam mensuræ esculentorum aut poculentorum, seu aut mensuræ frugum aut liquidorum, quas pro variis locis, temporibus, & personis variari præter experientiam testatur lex 3. offic. omnium, ff. de eo quod certo loco. Cur verò jura ista legilegitima crebram habeant mutationem, rationem adfert Philosophus istam, quia diversa est diversarum civitatum ratio, variæ sunt variarum Rerump. formæ, quarum aliæ sunt corruptiores, aliæ meliores, quæ nempe ad naturæ leges proximè accedunt, & ubi omnia instituta & leges à communi hominũ consensu latæ ad naturæ rationem & modum quantum fieri possunt, accommodantur. Et de jure legali hoc etiam notandum, licet sua natura & in fe fit mutabile, non tamen temere esse mutandum, sed caute admodum & fervatis istis duabus conditionibus: 1. Utrarò admodum & non nisi magna urgente necessitate mutetur, ne crebra mutatio aliquod periculum Reipub. afferat, sicut de Atheniensium Republica refert ipse Philosophus lib. 4. Polit. cap. 2. Ut sensim & prudenter, ne subita mutatio naufragium civitati inferat.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he refutes the opinion of those who thought that all laws were introduced by laws and custom, that there is no natural law, that nothing is right or wrong by nature, and that nothing is just or unjust. Their chief argument was this: all natural things are unchangeable. For example, fire burns here and likewise among the Persians, and it has the same force. But laws change daily, and in different places different things come about from time to time, as common experience testifies. For example, among most nations it is wicked to marry one's mother, yet among the Persians this was just, for it was sanctioned both by custom and by laws, as Herodotus and Cicero testify. Likewise, among various nations it is wicked to marry a sister, yet among the Egyptians this was just, as Philo the Jew relates in On the Customs of the Egyptians. Likewise, among the Athenians it was permitted to marry a sister from the same father but not from the same mother, because this was forbidden by the laws of Solon. Among the Lacedaemonians, on the contrary, by the laws of Lycurgus it was permitted to marry a sister from the same mother but not from the same father. Among the Egyptians it was just to have both as wives. The Philosopher answers this argument, adduced above, by denying its premise. He denies that all natural things are simply unchangeable, because natural things are of two kinds, or at least can be considered in two ways. They may be considered with respect to the gods, in whom no change falls, and so among them natural things are not changed. Or they may be considered with respect to men, and so natural things are changed according to various cases. He proves this by a familiar example: the right hand is by nature stronger than the left, and yet it can happen that, through use and practice, the left surpasses the right in strength, as happens with left-handed people, and so it can happen that someone uses both hands almost equally and becomes ambidextrous. Since, therefore, some natural things are changed, as this instance proves, some laws can be natural even though they undergo some change. Which such natural laws are he proposes to recognise by this sign: those which always stand in the same way and are not otherwise among any nations, except very rarely. Here this especially must be noted: natural laws are not changeable as to their genus or in idea, but with respect to the individual, or as to the particular circumstances, they can admit some change at times. For example, it is by the law of nature that parents are to be obeyed, and this is always true and is never changed as to its genus. Yet it can happen that in some single case this is changed. For example, if parents command their children to deny the faith they have acknowledged, to betray their country, to blaspheme God, and such things, the children are not bound to obey their parents here; and yet that remains always true, namely that parents are to be obeyed. As for the question whether there is any law by nature or not, which Archelaus, the teacher of Socrates, denied (as Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, book 2, testifies), and Callicles the Sophist, as Plato testifies in Gorgias, and all the Epicureans, as Plato testifies in Theaetetus and Diogenes Laertius, book 10, Life of Epicurus (and against all of whom the Philosopher argues here), see Plato in Minos, Gorgias, and books 1 and 10 of Laws, Cicero, On Laws, book 1, Alexander of Aphrodisias, On the Soul, book 2, and Simplicius in the preface to Aristotle's Physics. Cicero also argued most beautifully in his books On the Republic, as Lactantius testifies in Divine Institutes, book 5. But legal laws do not stand in the same way everywhere; rather, they are different in almost all places, and they are changed no less than the measures of food or drink, or the measures of grain or liquids, which, as experience proves, vary according to places, times and persons, as the law Lex 3 officium omnium, Digest de eo quod certo loco, testifies. Why these legitimate laws undergo frequent change, the Philosopher gives this reason: the constitution of different states is diverse, and there are various forms of various commonwealths, of which some are more corrupt and others better. The better ones are those which come nearest to the laws of nature, and where all institutions and laws enacted by the common consent of men are accommodated, as far as they can be, to the reason and manner of nature. And concerning legal law this also must be noted: although by its nature and in itself it is changeable, it must not be changed rashly. It must be changed very cautiously, observing these two conditions: first, that it be changed very rarely, and only when great necessity presses, lest frequent change bring some danger to the commonwealth, as the Philosopher himself relates concerning the commonwealth of the Athenians, Politics, book 4, chapter 2; second, that the change be gradual and prudent, lest a sudden change bring shipwreck upon the state.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis duo potissimum facit. 1. Discrimen adfert inter jus ordinans & præscribens humanas actiones, & jus illud quod ordinatur, cum utrumque communi juris nomine gaudeat. 2. Facta justa, quæ proveniunt à jure, cum ipso jure comparat. Ad primum hoc modo responder: Jus quidem ordinans & præscribens humanas actiones esse in se unum quid omnes universaliter obligans, quia est norma, qua definiuntur & diriguntur omnia singularia; Jus vero ordinatum esse varium, respectu variarum & pene infinitarum actionum, quarum singulæ justæ existunt, cum scilicet à jure universali originem & modum suum trahant, verbi gratia: jus est universale, reddere depositum: singularia sunt reddere. dere huicaut illi depositum. Interim fi fur aliquid deponat apud aliquem, & justus dominus, a quo hoc surreptum fuit, repetat, & furipse, quaeritur, utri fit reddendum? De hujus generis quaestionibus disceptantur multa in variis legibus ff. depositi, & a Cic. lib. 1. & 3. offic. Secundo loco facta justa cum jure comparat, in dissimili: Nam jus ipsum provenit aut a natura aut ab instituto hominum (quia ut ex superioribus patet) jus est vel naturale, vel legitimum, nec requiritur in jure, ut aliquid actu fiat, sed ut possit demum fieri secundum rectam rationem, justa aut facta tum demum esse dicuntur, cum in externam actionem prodierint. Atque ita ut jus cum suo opposito injuria ad Categoriam qualitatis referatur, quo spectant Justitia & Injustitia: Justum vero & Injustū ad Categoriam actionis inprimis pertinent.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he does two main things. (1) He distinguishes between law that orders and prescribes human actions and the law that is ordered, although both share the common name of law. (2) He compares just deeds, which arise from law, with law itself. As to the first point, he answers as follows: the law that orders and prescribes human actions is, in itself, one thing binding all people universally, since it is the rule by which all particular things are defined and directed. The law that is ordered, however, is various, with respect to the many and almost countless actions, each of which is just, since they derive their origin and form from the universal law. For example: the law is universal, to return a deposit; the particulars are to return it to this person or that. Meanwhile, if a thief deposits something with someone, and the rightful owner, from whom it was stolen, demands it back, and the thief himself also demands it, the question arises: to which of them is it to be returned? Many things are debated about questions of this kind in the various laws of Digest, on deposit, and by Cicero in book 1 and 3 of On Duties. (2) Second, he compares just deeds with law, though in an unlike way. For law itself arises either from nature or from human institution (as is clear from what was said above). Law is either natural or positive. Nor is it required of law that something be actually done; rather, it is that it can be done in accordance with right reason. Actions are called just only when they have come forth into external performance. And so, just as law, together with its opposite, injustice, is referred to the category of quality, to which justice and injustice belong, so the just and the unjust pertain chiefly to the category of action.
