units.la: Dicerunt et apud Græcos in communi usu δίκαιωμα καὶ δικαιοτέχνημα tanquam genus & species; quod nempe δίκαιωμα significet specialem actionem justam in Commutativa Justitiae parte corrigentem obortam ibidem injuriam: δικαιοτέχνημα in genere significat quamlibet actionem in quaubet Justitiae specie. Sed de his vocibus, cum apud Latinos non sint tanti usus, nisi forte apud Jurisconsultos, nihil ultra erit disputandum.
units.tr: The Greeks, in common usage, say dikaiōma and dikaiotechnēma [δίκαιωμα καὶ δικαιοτέχνημα] as genus and species: namely, that dikaiōma [δίκαιωμα] signifies a particular just action, in the commutative part of justice, correcting an injury arising in the same sphere, whereas dikaiotechnēma [δικαιοτέχνημα] signifies in general any action in any species of justice. But since these words are not in such common use among the Latins, except perhaps among the jurists, nothing more will be said about them.

units.la: In hoc capite tria hæc sunt observanda: 1. Cum jus hoc politicum, quod contra distinguitur jure communi ⁊ naturæ & legitimo, longe aliter ju naturale, sumi à Philosopho quam à Jureconsultis. Nam illi volunt bruta etiam esse commune & nihil aliud revera est, quam naturæ instinctum inditum omnibus à natura animalibus §. i. tit. 2. lib. 1. Instit. §. jus naturale, l. 2. ff. de justitia & jure, l. non minus 13. ff. de alimentis & cibariis legatis; & in jure Canonico in Decretalium canone 2. distinct. 1. Contrarium hîc asserit Philosophus, & supr. lib. 8. cap. 3. & 1. Polit. cap. 1. & Cicero 2. offic. cujus hanc reddit rationem, nempe quod licet sic, ut caeterarum virtutum umbrae reperiantur in brutis, Justitiae tamen nulla appareat imago, quia nulla Justitia absque societate consistere potest; nulla vero societas absque ratione & oratione, quae duo hominibus, non brutis proprie competunt. II. Et hoc notandum, Jus legale seu legitimum pro variis Rebus publicis in quibus locum habet, diversa sortiri nomina: nam in Democratia ubi populus regit, vocatur Plebiscitum, quia plebis & totius populi concursu sancitur. In Aristocratia, ubi optimates senatu constituunt, dicitur Senatusconsultum. In Monarchia vero, ubi unus praeest omnibus, dicitur Edictum, quod solius Principis mandato edicatur aut statuatur: quod si voluntate alicujus viri prudentis prodeat, dicitur Responsum viri prudentis, de quibus omnibus vide tit. 2. lib. 1. Instit. Justin. III. Et hoc observatu dignum, quod jus naturale ubique vigeat, & apud omnes gentes habeat locum, & ubi fiat defectus a jure naturae, quod interdum accidit, habere iltas quatuor conditiones: 1. Quod sit perpaucorum tantum (nam, ut jam diximus, quoad genus suum nunquam deficit, licet quoad singularia aliquid defectus patiatur) ita interdum fit, ut quae sunt alicui speciei communia, in singularibus tamen desiderentur, ut verbi gratia: audiendi, videndi, lo-quendi. quendi, generandi, &c. facultas. 2. Quod sit eorum ab hoc jure deficere tantum, qui sunt scelera-tissimi & proximi naturæ beluarum; non enim reperitur hic defectus à jure naturæ, nisi inter tales, qui ad enormia flagitia sunt parati, quales sunt ingenio admodum feroci, idque vel educatione & consuetudine, quod de Nerone scribitur, vel natura & constitutione, ut pote in quib. plurimū choleræ dominatur, & sanguinis est summa copia, ut in tyrannis, latronibus, sicariis & id genus malefici is. 3. Quod hic defectus non tam sit mentis aut intellectus, in quo dominatur ratio, quam appetitus, qui in corrupto hoc statu rationem ipsam cui subesse debet, non modo deserit, sed etiā ita transversam rapit, ut jam ex Monarchia rectæ rationis fiat Democratia ancillantium affectuum. 4. Demum quod hic defectus fit à corrupto hominis statu post lapsum, vel ab instinctu Diaboli, vel à consuetudine depravata, quæ omnia ipsi naturæ vim certam inferre possunt.
units.tr: In this chapter there are three things to be noted. (1) Since this political law, which is distinguished from common law, natural law, and legitimate law, is taken by the Philosopher in a quite different sense from the way the jurists take natural law. For the jurists want even brute animals to share it, and it is really nothing other than the instinct of nature implanted by nature in all animals (Inst. 1.2.1, Digest 1.1.1.3, Digest 34.1.13, and in the canon law, Decretals, distinction 1, canon 2). The Philosopher asserts the contrary here, and above in book 8, chapter 3, and in Politics 1, chapter 1. Cicero, in On Duties 2, gives this reason: although the shadows of the other virtues are found in brutes, no image of justice appears in them, because justice cannot exist without society, and no society can exist without reason and speech, which properly belong to humans, not to brutes. (2) It should also be noted that law, whether legal or legitimate, takes on different names according to the various commonwealths in which it holds sway. In a democracy, where the people rule, it is called a plebiscite, because it is sanctioned by the assembly of the common people and the whole populace. In an aristocracy, where the best men constitute the senate, it is called a senatus consultum. In a monarchy, where one man presides over all, it is called an edict, because it is issued or enacted by the command of the prince alone; but if it comes forth by the will of some wise man, it is called the response of a wise man. Concerning all of these, see Institutes 1.2. (3) And this is worth observing: natural law holds everywhere and has force among all peoples; and where there is a failure of natural law, which sometimes happens, the following four conditions obtain. (a) It is found in only a few people (for, as we have already said, with respect to its kind it never fails, though with respect to particulars it may suffer some defect). Thus it sometimes happens that things common to a species are lacking in individuals, as for example the faculty of hearing, seeing, speaking, generating, and so on. (b) This failure of the law affects only those who are most wicked and closest to the nature of beasts. For this failure of natural law is found only among such as are ready for monstrous crimes, who are of a very fierce disposition, whether by upbringing and habit, as is written of Nero, or by nature and constitution, namely those in whom anger rules most and the quantity of blood is great, as in tyrants, robbers, assassins, and malefactors of that sort. (c) This failure concerns not so much the mind or intellect, in which reason rules, as the appetite, which in this corrupt state not only deserts reason, to which it ought to be subject, but even twists it aside and carries it off, so that the monarchy of right reason becomes a democracy of servile passions. (d) Finally, this failure arises from the corrupt state of man after the Fall, either from the prompting of the Devil or from depraved custom, all of which can do certain violence to nature itself.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Jus Civile seu Politicum dividitur in naturale & legitimum, seu in id, quod natura & institutio hominum constat.
units.tr: 1. Civil or political law is divided into natural law and legitimate law, that is, into what consists in nature and what consists in human institution.

units.la: 2. Jus naturale eandem ubique habet vim, nec ab opinione hominum dependet.
units.tr: 2. Natural law has the same force everywhere and does not depend on the opinion of men.

units.la: 3. Jus legale ante promulgationem nullam habet per se vim, sed est quid ἀδιάφορον, post promulgationem non item.
units.tr: 3. Legitimate law has no force in itself before promulgation; it is something indifferent [ἀδιάφορον]. After promulgation it is not so.

units.la: 4. Ad jus legitimum seu ut à Jurisconsultis vocatur, Civile referantur, privilegia, decreta, edicta prætorum & ejusmodi.
units.tr: 4. To legitimate law, or civil law as the jurists call it, belong privileges, decrees, the edicts of praetors, and the like.

units.la: 5. Naturalia licet respectu sui primi principii non dicantur mutabilia, respectu tamen objecti, & quoad extra posunt mutabilia dici.
units.tr: 5. Natural things, although with respect to their first principle they are not called changeable, can nevertheless be called changeable with respect to their object and as far as external things are concerned.

units.la: 6. Manus dextra natura sua est promtior & fortior ad actiones obeundas, quam sinistra, fieri tamen potest, ut consuetudine & usu hic cursus natura invertatur.
units.tr: 6. The right hand is by nature readier and stronger than the left for carrying out actions, yet it can happen that by custom and practice this natural course is reversed.

units.la: 7. Jura legalia, quia ab hominum voluntate libera dependent, sunt mensuris rerum non absimilia, quos pro variis circumstantiis subinde variari constat.
units.tr: 7. Legitimate laws, because they depend on the free will of men, are not unlike measures of things, which, as is known, are varied from time to time according to various circumstances.

units.la: 8. Jura naturalia, licet ubique maneant eadem, jura tamen legalia pro diversis Rerumpub. formis diversas subeunt mutationes.
units.tr: 8. Natural laws, although they remain the same everywhere, legitimate laws nevertheless undergo various changes according to the different forms of commonwealths.

units.la: 9. In jure id, quod praescribit, subit vicem rei universalis, id vero, cui praescribitur, denotat aliquid singulare.
units.tr: 9. In law, that which prescribes takes the place of a universal thing, while that to which it is prescribed denotes something singular.

units.la: 10. Sicut jus partim a natura, partim ab instituto hominum provenit, sic etiam injuria & injustum, non tamen ut natura autor sit iniuria, sed quod praeter scopum & intentionem naturae injuria fieri dicatur.
units.tr: 10. Just as law arises partly from nature and partly from human institution, so too injury and the unjust do; yet nature is not the author of injury, but injury is said to be done beside the aim and intention of nature.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An aliquod sit jus naturale, sicut hic vult Philosophus, cum nulla sit Iustitia naturalis, ergo a lege coniugatorum uno sublato alterum tollitur. Quod nulla sit Iustitia naturalis hinc patet, quia omnis Iustitia est virtus, virtus vero est a consuetudine & usu, non a natura, sicut disserte docet Philosophus lib. 2. cap. 1. hujus operis? Resp. Id non sequi, nullum esse jus a natura, quia nulla sit Iustitia, quia Iustitia cum sit habitus, provenit ab actionibus humanis; jus vero est regula, quae dirigit istas actiones, & licet Iustitia non sit a natura tanquam causa proxima, est tamen a natura tanquam causa remota sicut omnis virtus, ut loco citat. probat Philosophus. Dein etiam jus naturale dicitur, non quod a natura tantum habeat originem, sed quod eandem ubique habeat vim, & ab omnibus communiter recipiatur gentilibus: nam eiusmodi innititur principiis, quae apud omnes pro certis & veris habentur.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Is there any natural law, as this Philosopher wills, since there is no natural justice? So by the law of correlatives, when one of the married pair is removed, the other is removed too. That there is no natural justice is plain from this: all justice is a virtue, and virtue comes from custom and practice, not from nature, as the Philosopher clearly teaches in Book 2, chapter 1 of this work? Answer: It does not follow that there is no natural law because there is no natural justice. Justice is a habit and arises from human actions; law, however, is the rule that directs those actions. And although justice is not from nature as its proximate cause, it is from nature as its remote cause, as all virtue is, as the Philosopher proves in the passage cited. Moreover, natural law is so called not merely because it has its origin in nature, but because it has the same force everywhere and is commonly received by all nations, since it rests on principles that are held to be certain and true among all people.

units.la: II. An recte etiam dixerit Ius naturale non dependere ab hominum arbitrio, sed ab ipsa natura, cum tamen contrarium ratio evincere videatur, quia omnis Iustitia dependet a voluntate hominum, nam consistit vel in distributione, vel in commutatione rerum, tot enim numerantur species Iustitiae cap. 5 huius lib. Ergo cum actiones Iustitiae sint omnes voluntariae etiam & ius ipsum erit voluntarium, & per consequens hoc naturale dependebit a voluntate hominum? Resp. Neque hoc etiam sequi, quia distributio & commutatio sunt species Iustitiae particularis non universalis, quae proxime dependent a iure legali aut civili, remote autem a iure naturali, & licet respectu obiectiaut etiam principii proximi actiones Iustitiae sint voluntariae, respectu tamen primi fundamenti, nempe iusti & aequi, super quae primum fundantur, non tam sunt voluntariae, quam naturales, quia hoc sensu eandem ubique habent vim.
units.tr: II. Did he also rightly say that natural law does not depend on the will of men but on nature itself? Reason seems rather to show the contrary, since all justice depends on the will of men: it consists either in the distribution or in the exchange of goods, for so many kinds of justice are counted in chapter 5 of this book. Therefore, since all the acts of justice are voluntary, law itself will also be voluntary, and consequently natural law will depend on the will of men? Answer: This does not follow either, because distribution and exchange are species of particular justice, not universal justice; they depend proximately on positive or civil law, and remotely on natural law. And although with respect to the object, or the proximate principle, the acts of justice are voluntary, with respect to the first foundation, namely the just and the equitable on which they are first grounded, they are not so much voluntary as natural, because in this sense they have the same force everywhere.

units.la: III. Quomodo dicat ius naturale esse immutabile, cum tamen ipse contrarium docet exemplo dextrae & sinistrae? Resp. Non simpliciter dicit ius naturale esse immutabile, sed comparare tantum si conferatur, nempe cum iure legali, quod dicit mensuris esse simile, quae subinde pro variis circumstantiis ubique locorum mutantur.
units.tr: III. How can he say that natural law is unchangeable, when he himself teaches the contrary by the example of right and left hand? Answer: He does not say simply that natural law is unchangeable, but only makes a comparison, namely with legitimate law, which he says is like measures, which are varied from time to time according to circumstances in different places.

units.la: IV. &c ult. Quomodo dicat dextram esse naturaliter validiorem, sinistra, cum tamen Plato 7. de leg. contrarium docet a communi experientia, & etiam adducit Scythas, qui valivalidiores sunt sinistra quam dextra, & hoc totum fieri refert non à natura, sed à consuetudine & exercitio: Tum etiam plerique Medici probant opinionem Platonis, quod nempe natura neutri manui majorem vim indidit, sed æqualem, & quod unafit fortior altera, hoc fieri semper ab exercitio? Resp. Philosophum hoc asserere propter varias causas: 1. Quia sensus & experientia docet animalia prius movere dextrum latus, quam moveant sinistrum in progressu, qua de re disputat lib. de progressu animal. cap. 1. & 2. 2. Etiam quia epar est collocatum in dextra parte animalis, quod majorem sanguinis copiam propter vicinitatem suam dextræ infundit, quam sinistræ: tum etiam quia major vis caloris naturalis primo infunditur dextro hominis lateri, sicut in fœtibus recens formatis aut animatis deprehenderunt Anatomici: Unde cum major sit copia sanguinis, majorque vis calidi naturalis in dextra, quâ in sinistra parte, hinc fit, ut natura dextra sit validior sinistra. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Keckerm. disputat. Phys. 19 problem. 3.
units.tr: IV. And last. How can he say that the right hand is naturally stronger than the left, when Plato in the seventh book of the Laws teaches the contrary from common experience, and also adduces the Scythians, who are stronger in the left hand than in the right, and refers all this not to nature but to custom and exercise? Moreover, many physicians support Plato's opinion, that nature has given neither hand greater strength but equal, and that one becomes stronger than the other always through exercise. Answer: The Philosopher asserts this for several reasons: (1) because sense and experience show that animals move the right side first when they advance, a matter he discusses in the book On the Progression of Animals, chapters 1 and 2; (2) because the liver is placed on the right side of the animal, and because of its proximity it supplies more blood to the right than to the left; (3) because a greater force of natural heat is first infused into the right side of the human body, as anatomists have found in newly formed or animated foetuses. Hence, since there is a greater supply of blood and a greater force of natural heat on the right than on the left, the right hand is naturally stronger than the left. See more on this question in Keckermann, Physics disputation 19, problem 3.

units.la: Coronidis loco poterunt & hæc breviter quæri:
units.tr: By way of appendix, these points too may briefly be asked:

units.la: 1. An jus naturale tantum cadat in homines, quod vult hic Philosophus, an etiam competat brutis, quod volunt Jurisconsulti? Rationes pro Philos. sunt quatuor: 1. Quia jus naturale nihil est aliud, quam jussum & decretum rectæ rationis, ergo quæcunque sunt rationis expertia, in ea jus naturale cadere nullo modo potest. 2. Quia Jurisconsulti dum jus naturale bruto affingunt, & sibi & veritati contradicunt: nam sic definiunt jus naturale, quod nempe naturalis ratio inter homines constituit §. 3. tit. 2. lib. 1. Institut. Ergo in brubrutis locum non habet, alioqui bruta erunt ratione praedita: Atqui contradictio est in adjecto dicere, irrationale esse rationale. {3}Quia quadrupes aut brutum non dicitur injuriam facere, si damnum aut detrimentum aliquod intulerit, sed tantum pauperie, ut est in toto sit. Si quadrupes pauperiem fecerit. Proinde si bruta injuriam facere non dicuntur, quia injuria iis proprie non competit, neque etiam jus iis competet ex lege conjugatorum. {4}Quia quae Jurisconsulti juri naturali attribuunt, veluti seipsum conservare, generare, similiter, defendere seipsum, &c. ad naturalem potius et ff. actionem aut institutum omnibus animalibus a natura inditum pertinere videntur, non ad jus ipsum, quod ut supra diximus est regula rectae rationis.
units.tr: 1. Does natural law fall only upon men, as this Philosopher wills, or does it also belong to brutes, as the jurists maintain? There are four reasons for the Philosopher's view: (1) because natural law is nothing other than the dictate and decree of right reason; therefore it can in no way fall upon whatever lacks reason. (2) Because the jurists, while they ascribe natural law to brutes, contradict both themselves and the truth: for they define natural law as that which natural reason has established among men (Institutes, book 1, title 2, §3). Therefore it has no place among brutes, otherwise brutes would be endowed with reason; but to say that the irrational is rational is a contradiction in terms. (3) Because a quadruped or a brute beast is not said to do an injury if it inflicts some loss or damage, but only pauperies (damage by a beast), as the text has it: "If a quadruped has committed pauperies." Therefore, if brutes are not said to do injury, because injury does not properly belong to them, neither will law belong to them under the law of correlatives. (4) Because the things the jurists attribute to natural law, such as preserving oneself, generating, defending oneself, and so on, seem to pertain rather to the natural action or institution implanted by nature in all animals, and not to law itself, which, as we said above, is the rule of right reason.

units.la: Pro decisione hujus quaestionis, ut lis haec inter Philosophos & Jurisconsultos tollatur, sciendum est, Jus naturale considerari bifariam: 1. Proprie & stricte quatenus nempe est regula rationis & voluntate concipienda & dirigenda, & sic solis hominibus competit: quia soli homines sunt rationis, voluntatis, regularum & conclusionum & ejusmodi capaces tantum, & hoc sensu Philosophus hoc loco, & Cic. 1. offic. & e veteribus Carneades, Pyrrho, & omnes Cynici solis hominibus jus proprie assignant. 2. Late sumitur & improprie quatenus nepe non tantum revera inest, sed etiam per similitudinem quandam, & hoc modo Jurisconsulti brutis etiam attribuunt, in quibus simulachra virtutum omnium, pietatis, prudentiae, fortitudinis, castitatis, &c. & si Plinio & Solino credimus, Justitiae ipsius cognitionem & memoriam deprehendere licet.
units.tr: To decide this question, so that this dispute between the Philosophers and the Jurists may be settled, it must be understood that natural law is considered in two ways. (1) Properly and strictly, insofar as it is a rule of reason to be grasped and directed by the will; and in this sense it belongs to men alone, because men alone are capable of reason, will, rules, conclusions, and the like. In this sense the Philosopher here, Cicero in On Duties book 1, and among the ancients Carneades, Pyrrho, and all the Cynics assign law properly to men alone. (2) It is taken broadly and improperly, insofar as it is not only truly present but also present by a certain resemblance; and in this way the jurists also attribute it to brutes, in which are found the images of all the virtues: piety, prudence, fortitude, chastity, and so on. And if we believe Pliny and Solinus, one may even detect in them some knowledge and memory of justice itself.

units.la: Poterit etiam & hoc quæri: An cum jus hoc quod in naturale & civile dividitur, inter Ethnicos habuit locum, in Christianorum Rebuspubl. adhiberi possit, ita ut Christianis Ethnicorum legibus uti liceat? Resp. Hanc quæstionem esse dubiam & disceptari in utramq; partem. Nam pro negativa afferuntur tres potissimum rationes: 1. Quia Ethnicorum leges summam continent impietatem, id quod variis exemplis demonstrari potest. Apud Lydos & Cyprios lex erat, ut mulieres ante nuptias corpora prostituerent, & hoc quæstu dotem sibi colligerent, unde seipsas elocarent. Sic etiam apud Lacedæmonios legibus Lycurgi permissum erat adulterium interveniente pacto cum marito. Utrumque tamen hoc pugnat cum 7. præcepto Decalogi: Non mœchaberis. Sic etiam apud Indos lex erat, teste Æliano, ut liberi parentes jam senio confectos interficerent, & postea honeste sepelirent. Sic etiam apud Lacedæmonios in conviviis & ludis publicis mancipia per jocum tollebant de medio: & apud Romanos ubiq; in theatris permittebatur laniena servorum fugitivorum, ista tamen laniena 6. præcepto Decalogi prohibetur: Non occides. Sic & apud Lacedæmonios furari non dabatur vitio, sed deprehendi in furto tantum, quod repugnat 8. præcepto Decalogi: Non furaberis. Plurima ejusmodi exempla apud Johannem Bohemum de moribus gentium, & apud Alexandrum Sardum de ritibus populorum videre licet. 2. Quia in jure civili, quo utebantur Ethnici, multa sunt, quæ juri naturali rali repugnant. Id quod variis instantiis demonstrari potest: 1. Usucapio & praescriptio sunt modi legitime res acquirendi a legibus approbati, & tamen locupletant praescribentem cum damno illius adversus quae fit praescriptio aut usucapio, id quod testatur Imperator Justin. §. 1. tit. 6. lib. 2. Instit. tum etiam l. 13. tit. de usucapionibus, l. 41. ff. At locupletari cum damno & jactura alterius repugnat legi naturae, huic nempe: Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris, Sic libertas est juris naturalis, & est servituti contraria: At servitus est juris civilis, teste Justiniano tit. 3. lib. 1. Instit. §. 2. & l. 9. ff. de statu hominum. 3. Quia in jure civili multa sunt sibi invicem repugnantia, multa sibi contradicentia, quae diligenter Laurentius Valla, Budaeus & alii annotarunt contra Juris consultos. Cum igitur leges Ethnicorum contineant impietatem, quae juri repugnat divino, & juri naturali & sibi invicem contrariantur, iis in Christianorum Rebuspubl. uti non licet. Pro affirmativa parte sunt quinque rationes: Quia mandatis Principum aut superiorum honestati & pietati consentaneis est obediendum, ut testatur Scriptura Josua 22. verf. 12. At ejusmodi sunt mandata Principum, & responsa Prudentum, quae Corpori juris inseruntur a Jureconsultis, & ab Ethnicis sunt translata: Ergo ejusmodi Ethnicorum legibus uti licet. 2. Quia Evangelium non tollit Politias aut evertit Respub. sanis & bene constitutis legibus bene fundatas Matth. 21. verf. 21. Marc. 12. verf. 17. Luc. 20. verf. 25. Neque legitur unquam Apostolos, dum praedicarent Evangelium per orbem terrarum, jussisse gentes, ut abolerent lerent leges suas, sed potius, ut a cultu idolorum ad verum Deum converterentur, utre-statur tota historia Actorum. 3. Quia Apostolus Paulus ad Caesarem Imperatorem Ethnicum appellat, Act.22. verf 3. quod non fecisset, si putasset nefas esse Christianis Ethnicorum legibus uti. 4. Quia dum Ecclesia viveret sub Monarchis, qui a fide Christiana alienissimi erant, ut sub Persicis, Babylonicis, Graecis & Romanis, usque ad Constantinum Magnum non tantum pro salute Imperatorum orarunt, juxta praeceptum Pauli, 1.Tim. 2. verf. 4. sed etiam legibus ipsorum debitam obedientiam praestiterunt. Id quod restatur Tertullianus in Apologet.cap.39. Cum Imperatores Ethnici in Christianos saevissime desaevirent, nullus tamen repertus fuit, qui vocem hanc Christi, reddite, quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, non exacte & ad amussim servandam praeceperit, & pro salute & incolumitate omnium, sicut decebat, orandum non monuerit. s.Quia Ethnicorum legibus uti debet Christiani, nō jam ut Ethnicis, sed propter auctoritatem & approbationem Imperatorum Christianorum ut suis, idque propter duas causas: 1. Quia varios & multiplices habent in vita humana usus. 2. Quia super justum & aequum tanquam communia fundamenta naturae & rectae rationis ejusmodi leges fundantur.
units.tr: This question may also be raised: Since this law, divided into natural and civil, had its place among the heathen, can it be applied in the commonwealths of Christians, so that Christians may make use of the laws of the heathen? Answer: this question is doubtful and is disputed on both sides. For the negative, there are chiefly three reasons: (1) The laws of the heathen contain the greatest impiety, as can be shown by various examples. Among the Lydians and the Cypriots it was law that women should prostitute their bodies before marriage and gather a dowry for themselves by this gain, whence they hired out themselves. So too among the Lacedaemonians, by the laws of Lycurgus, adultery was permitted with the agreement of the husband. Yet both of these conflict with the seventh precept of the Decalogue: You shall not commit adultery. So too among the Indians, as Aelian witnesses, it was law that children should kill their parents once they were worn out with age, and afterwards bury them with honour. So too among the Lacedaemonians, at banquets and public games, slaves were put to death for sport; and among the Romans, in the theatres everywhere, the butchering of runaway slaves was permitted; yet such butchery is forbidden by the sixth precept of the Decalogue: You shall not kill. So too among the Lacedaemonians, stealing was not counted a fault, but only being caught in theft, which is contrary to the eighth precept of the Decalogue: You shall not steal. Many examples of this kind may be seen in Johannes Bohemus, On the Customs of the Nations, and in Alexander Sardus, On the Rites of the Peoples. (2) Because in the civil law which the heathen used, there are many things which conflict with the natural law. This can be shown by various instances: (1) Usucapion and prescription are legitimate modes of acquiring property, approved by the laws; yet they enrich the one who prescribes, to the loss of the one against whom prescription or usucapion is made. The Emperor Justinian bears witness to this in Institutes 2.6, §1, and also in the law 13, title On Usucapions, and law 41 of the Digest. But to be enriched with the loss and injury of another conflicts with the law of nature, namely this: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. So liberty is a part of natural law, and is contrary to slavery; yet slavery belongs to the civil law, as Justinian testifies in Institutes 1.3, §2, and in the law 9 of the Digest, On the Status of Men. (3) Because in the civil law there are many things mutually opposed and many things contradicting themselves, which Laurentius Valla, Budaeus and others have noted against the jurists. Therefore, since the laws of the heathen contain impiety, which conflicts with divine law and with natural law, and are contrary to one another, it is not lawful to use them in the commonwealths of Christians. For the affirmative there are five reasons: (1) Because obedience is to be given to the commands of princes or superiors that agree with honesty and piety, as Scripture testifies, Joshua 22.12. But such are the commands of princes and the responses of the learned, which are inserted into the body of the law by the jurists and were carried over from the heathen. Therefore it is lawful to use such laws of the heathen. (2) Because the Gospel does not abolish polities nor overthrow commonwealths that are well founded on sound and well-constituted laws, Matt. 21.21, Mark 12.17, Luke 20.25. Nor is it ever read that the Apostles, when they preached the Gospel throughout the world, ordered the nations to abolish their laws; rather, they urged that they be converted from the worship of idols to the true God, as the whole history of the Acts attests. (3) Because the Apostle Paul appealed to Caesar, the heathen Emperor, Acts 22.3, which he would not have done if he had thought it wrong for Christians to use the laws of the heathen. (4) Because while the Church lived under monarchs who were most alien to the Christian faith, as under the Persian, Babylonian, Greek and Roman rulers, right up to Constantine the Great, it not only prayed for the salvation of the emperors, according to the precept of Paul, 1 Tim. 2.4, but also rendered due obedience to their laws. Tertullian bears witness to this in his Apology, chapter 39: when the heathen emperors raged most savagely against the Christians, yet no one was found who did not command that this saying of Christ, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, be kept exactly and to the letter, and who did not, as was fitting, admonish that prayers be offered for the safety and welfare of all. (5) Because the laws of the heathen ought to be used by Christians not as heathen laws, but on account of the authority and approval of Christian emperors, as their own; and this for two reasons: (1) because they have various and manifold uses in human life; (2) because such laws are founded upon what is just and equitable, as common foundations of nature and right reason.

units.la: Pro decisione quaestionis affirmativam partem esse magis veritati consentaneam propter rationes supra allatas. Nam jus civile, quo utebantur Ethnici per se neque juri divino neque naturali repugnat, sed est tantum conclusio quaedam ex jure naturali deducta & determinatio, quae quod jus naturale in genegenere dicit, in specie explicat, & ad varios vitæ humanæ usus, & factorum singulorum themata accommodat, prout usus quotidianus & salus publica postulat, sicut infra cap. penult. patebit. Si forte quid deprehensum fuerit in hisce legibus, quod vel juri divino vel naturali contrarium videatur, tu prorsus admitti nō debet, sed potius audieda est vox illa Evangelii, Deo magis obedire oportet, quam hominibus Actor. f. verf. 29. & danda est opera magnus, sed non cum vulnere mentis. Quod vero ad rationes in contrarium allatas, non sunt tanti ponderis, ut propter utilitatem, quā habent, leges Ethnicorum prorsus à Christianis amentur. Nam prima loquitur tantum de abusu, non de legitimo usu legum, siquidem illa quæ proferuntur nō à recta ratione, sed à libidine & appetitu profluebant. Ad secundam rationem respondent per negationem Jurisconsulti, & negant quicquam esse in jure civili, quod directè repugnet juri naturali. Et ad primam institutiam de usucapione sic respondent, ut usucapio sit duplex, una illegitima, quæ ab injustis causis & usu passim est introducta, & hæc repugnat juri naturali, altera est legitima, quæ à certis & justis causis oritur, & hæc non repugnat. Legitimæ causæ sunt: 1. negligentia illius adversus quē adhibetur usucapio, ut hoc modo puniatur. 2. bonam publicum, ne ut inquit Imperator Justinianus, §. 3. lib. 2. Inst. tit. 6. rerum dominia semper essent incerta, & ut finis esset litiū, quia nisi daretur hic modus componendarum litium excrescerent in infinitum. Exemplum ejusmodi prescriptionis legitimæ exhibet nobis sacra pagina cap. 11. Jud. verf. 15. in Jephta, de quo vide Petrum Martyr. clas. i. L. C. cap. 10, p. 62. Quod ad secundam instantiam de servitute, servitus etiam sit juris civilis, tamen naturae prorsus non repugnat, sed est tantum diversum quid, & veluti praeterintentionem naturae, quae de re eleganter disputat Philosophus lib. 1. Polit. cap. 2. & 3. Tertia etiam ratio nihil facit, quia revera non contradicunt sibi leges, sed in specie & apparenter tantum, & nihil est in iis absolute contradictorium, ita ut utrumque pro lege stricte observetur, quin si unum praecipiatur, alterum expresse prohibetur, aut implicite, si quae leges, quod saepenumero fit, ex diametro inter se pugnare videantur.
units.tr: As for deciding the question, the affirmative side is more consistent with the truth, on account of the reasons set out above. For the civil law which the heathen used is not, in itself, contrary either to divine or to natural law; rather, it is only a certain conclusion deduced from natural law and a determination of it, which explains in particular what natural law states in general, and adapts it to the various uses of human life and to the individual matters of fact, as daily practice and the public welfare require, as will be made clear in the last chapter but one. If perhaps anything is found in these laws which seems contrary to divine or natural law, that must by no means be admitted; rather, that saying of the Gospel should be heeded: We ought to obey God rather than men, Acts 5.29, and care must be taken, but not with a wound to the mind. As for the arguments brought to the contrary, they are not of such weight that, on account of the usefulness they have, the laws of the heathen should be wholly rejected by Christians. For the first speaks only of the abuse, not of the lawful use of the laws, since those laws which were put forward did not flow from right reason, but from lust and appetite. To the second reason the jurists respond by denial, and deny that there is anything in the civil law which directly conflicts with natural law. And to the first instance, concerning usucapion, they respond thus: usucapion is twofold: one is illegitimate, introduced from unjust causes and by common practice, and this conflicts with natural law; the other is legitimate, arising from certain and just causes, and this does not conflict. The legitimate causes are: (1) the negligence of the one against whom usucapion is employed, so that he may be punished in this way; (2) the common good, so that, as the Emperor Justinian says, Institutes 2.6, §3, the ownership of things should not always remain uncertain, and so that there might be an end to lawsuits, since otherwise lawsuits would grow without limit. An example of such a legitimate prescription is presented to us by Sacred Scripture, Judges 11.15, in the case of Jephthah; on this see Peter Martyr, class 1, L.C., chapter 10, p. 62. As for the second instance, concerning slavery: even if slavery belongs to the civil law, it is nonetheless by no means contrary to nature, but is only something different, and as it were a deviation from the intention of nature, which the Philosopher discusses elegantly in Politics 1.2 and 3. The third reason also proves nothing, for the laws do not really contradict one another, but only in appearance and in particular cases; and nothing in them is absolutely contradictory, so that both may be strictly observed as law, unless one commands and the other expressly or implicitly forbids, if certain laws, as often happens, seem to clash diametrically with one another.

units.la: Poterit & hoc breviter quaeri: An justum & honestum, quae sunt fundamenta juris, sint a natura nec ne? Respon. Etsi Callides Sophista apud Platonem in Gorgia acriter disputet, nullum justum & honestum esse a natura, sed tantum a lege & instituto hominum contrarium tamen esse magis verum, quia utrumque a natura originem suam trahit: Nam quod simpliciter justum & honestum est, id omnes insitino quodam naturae scire videntur sicut contra Callidem ibi disputat Socrates: Sed quoad determinationem & ad perfectionem seu ad applicationem, qua nempe justum & honestum pro variis circumstantiis ad varios vitae humanae usus accommodantur, possunt dici abusu & instituto hominum provenire.
units.tr: It may also be asked briefly: are the just and the honourable, which are the foundations of law, from nature or not? Answer: Although the crafty Sophist in Plato's Gorgias argues sharply that nothing just and honourable is from nature but only from the law and institution of men, it is nevertheless more true that both have their origin from nature. For what is simply just and honourable, all men seem to know by a certain innate instinct of nature, as Socrates argues there against the crafty Sophist. But as to determination and as to perfection, or application, by which the just and the honourable are fitted to the various uses of human life according to various circumstances, these may be said to arise from the abuse and institution of men.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Sequitur tertium membrum secundi tractatus hujus libri, in quo Philosophus dubitationem quaedam dam supra cap. 9 hic accuratè solvit, & simul etiam propter quæ facta quis justus aut injustus dici debeat, declarat. Partes hujus capitis sunt tres: Inprima quæ facta sint justa aut injusta per se, quæ itidem per accidens, ostendit. In secunda inquirit, quæ sint illæ injuriæ, propter quas injustus quis dici mereatur, allata eorum, quæ sponte fiunt divisione. In tertia de de iis, quæ à nobis invitis fiunt, aut fieri videntur, pro variis circumstantiis breviter, sed accuratè agit, hoc scilicet fine, ut actiones verè justas & injustas à se invicem distinguat.
units.tr: The third part of the second treatise of this book follows, in which the Philosopher accurately resolves the doubt raised above in chapter 9 and at the same time declares for what reasons a person ought to be called just or unjust for what he does. This chapter has three parts. In the first he shows which deeds are just or unjust in themselves and which are so only by accident. In the second he inquires which injuries are those on account of which a man deserves to be called unjust, setting out a division of those things that are done voluntarily. In the third he treats briefly but accurately of those things that are done, or seem to be done, by us against our will, under various circumstances, with the aim of distinguishing truly just and unjust actions from one another.

units.la: In prima igitur ea demum dicit esse justè & injustè facta proprie & per se, quæ sponte & promta voluntate fiunt; quæ verò fiunt invitè, ea proprie nec justa nec injusta esse dicenda, nisi forte contingenter & per accidens seu ex eventu tantum, & quæ de factis jam dixit, eadem de facientibus intelligenda esse asserit, quia agentes tum demum dicuntur justi & injusti cum aliquid agunt cum ratione vel contra rationem sponte sua non viaut externo metu. Sed de hac re prolixius disputat lib. 1 Rethor. ad Theod. cap. 2. Cum etiam de factorum & facientium varietate supra accuratè egit ab initio lib. 3. usque ad cap. 6. Caeterum ex hac factorum & facientium distinctione pro- fluunt utilissimæ, illæ disputationes apud Jurisconsultos de casu fortuito, de incendio, ruina, inundationibus, negligentia, diligentia, custodia, vi & metu: Tum etiam de ira & ebrietate, & cæteris ejusmodi negotiorum fortuitorum eventibus, de quibus videre licet varia loca in jure civili, ut præsertim l. 7 contractus, ff. de lustitia & jure, l. 24. Nerva, ff. depositi l. 35. l.35. aut certa, ff. depœnû, l.12. aut patta, ff. commodati. Sed quia præcipua Justitiæ visin eo potissimū consistit ut quis sciat, nō modò, qua ratione actiones producantur, sed etiam à quibus principiis & quomodo affectis profluat, id est, Spontanea an invita fiant. Ideo breviter pro instituti sui ratione definitorem tum spontanei tum inviti ex lib.3. repertit, & id spontE factum esse dicit, quod cum in sua sit potestate sciens prudensque quis fecerit, id est, non ignoratis circumstantiis, quo instrumento, cuius gratia & cæteris ejusmodi id factum sit: Dein etiam ut neq; casu fortuito neque vi aut metu coactus, quid faciat, quæ enim sic fiunt, non sunt in facientis potestate: nam casus & fortuna extra nos sunt, quia præter intentionem & scopum nostrū proveniunt: vis quoque & metus cum extrinsecus accedant, libertatis voluntati ciusque potestati, maximè repugnant. Ad facta igitur voluntaria duo potissimum requiruntur; Scientia nempe & libertas arbitrii, alterutrum si defit, non erit quid sponte factum, & proinde per se nec justum nec injustum. Invitè factum econtra definitur, & ex natura voluntarii facti facilè intelligitur, sit enim aut ab ignorante aut à sciente, sed ita quidem sciente, ut in sua potestate nō habeat, ut aliter id agat, aut non agat, cum tantum coactus à vi extrema agat. Sed ne quis miretur, quod dixerit aliquid scienter fieri posse, & tamen invitè, id confirmat ab experientia quotidiana in actionibus & perpessionibus naturalibus, quæ homini quotidie fieri solent, verbi gratia: senescere, canescere, mori, cibum capere, & cætera eiusmodi fiunt scientibus quiquidem nobis, quia non tantum in intellectum, sed infe sui etiam externos incidunt, sed invitis tamen fiunt, quia nolimus vel imus, natura cuiusum suum in nobis peragi. Relinquitur ergo, ut ea dicimum fiunt juste vel injuste facta per se, quae sponte & aliberata voluntate proveniunt, quae vero invite fiunt, quod neque justa neque iniusta per se sint dicenda, probat duobus exemplis: 1. Est de injusto facto, sed invito, alterum de iusto verbi gratia: Qui vi aut metu coactus depositum reddit, neque iuste neque iniuste viri officio fungi dicitur, etsi quaedam in redditione appareat Justitia, quia invitus hoc facit. Sic etiam qui aliquo modo impeditus depositum ad promissum tempus non reddit, non dicitur iniuste agere, nisi forte per accidens & ex eventu, quia impedimentum aliquod intercessit, quo minus promissum exsolvere it.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he says that those things are properly and in themselves done justly or unjustly which are done willingly and with a ready will. Those which are done unwillingly are not to be called properly just or unjust, except perhaps contingently and by accident, or merely from the outcome. What he has said about deeds he asserts must likewise be understood of doers, since agents are then called just and unjust when they act with reason, or against reason, of their own accord and not under external fear. He disputes this more fully in the first book of the Rhetoric to Theodectes, chapter 2. He also treated at length above, from the beginning of book 3 to chapter 6, the variety of deeds and doers. Moreover, from this distinction of deeds and doers flow those most useful disputations among the jurists concerning chance, fire, collapse, floods, negligence, diligence, custody, force and fear; and also concerning anger, drunkenness and other such accidental events, on which one may see various passages in the civil law, especially l. 7 contractus, ff. de justitia et jure; l. 24 Nerva, ff. depositi; l. 35 aut certa, ff. de poenis; l. 12 aut pacta, ff. commodati. But since the chief business of justice consists especially in this, that a person knows not only by what reason actions are produced but also from what principles and in what disposition they proceed, that is, whether they are done spontaneously or unwillingly, he therefore briefly sets out, in keeping with his purpose, a definition of both the spontaneous and the unwilling from book 3. He says that something is done spontaneously when someone does it knowingly and wittingly, while it lies in his power, that is, without ignorance of the circumstances: by what instrument, for whose sake, and the like. And he does it neither by chance nor compelled by force or fear. For things done in this way are not in the power of the doer: chance and fortune lie outside us, since they occur beyond our intention and purpose; and force and fear, since they come from outside, are most opposed to the freedom of the will and its power. For voluntary deeds, therefore, two things are chiefly required, namely knowledge and freedom of choice. If either is lacking, there will be nothing done spontaneously, and so nothing just or unjust in itself. The unwilling deed, on the other hand, is defined in the opposite way, and from the nature of the voluntary deed it is easily understood: it is done either by one who is ignorant or by one who knows, but knows in such a way that he does not have it in his power to act otherwise or not to act, since he acts only under compulsion by extreme force. But lest anyone wonder that he said something can be done knowingly and yet unwillingly, he confirms this from everyday experience in natural actions and passions that commonly befall a man: to grow old, to grow grey, to die, to take food, and other things of this kind happen to us knowingly, since they fall not only upon the intellect but also upon our external senses; yet they happen unwillingly, because we do not wish them, but nature wills that its course be carried out in us. It remains, therefore, that we say those things are done justly or unjustly in themselves which proceed spontaneously and from free will, while those that are done unwillingly are not to be called just or unjust in themselves. He proves this by two examples: (1) one of an unjust deed done unwillingly, and (2) the other of a just one. For instance, one who, compelled by force or fear, returns a deposit is said neither justly nor unjustly to discharge the duty of a good man, although some justice appears in the return, because he does it unwillingly. So too, one who, hindered in some way, does not return a deposit at the promised time is not said to act unjustly, unless perhaps by accident and from the outcome, since some obstacle has intervened that prevented him from paying what he had promised.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis inquirit, quae sint illae iniuriae, ex quibus aliquis dicitur proprie iniustus, quia hinc potissimum dependet solutio dubitationis propositae initio capitis 9. An scilicet aliquis sit iniustus dicendus, qui iniuste agit, tum etiam quia non uno modo sed variis modis fit sponte aliquid. Fit enim vel ex proposito & praecedente deliberatione, vel absque eadem. Sed ut melius intelligatur, ob quos actiones, quis proprie dicatur iniustus tria affert factorum genera, quae iniuste fieri videtur cum sponte etiam fiant. Vel enim fiunt per ignorantiam circumstantiarum, & haec dicuntur proprie Errata, cum scilicet aliquid fit, quod ab interno principio provenit, ut nulla intellectus operatio ad hanc actionem ctionem producendam accedere videatur. Secundo quædam inopinato & casu fortuito fiunt, ut verbi gratia: cum quis de tecto decidens alium suo casu opprimit prætereuntem, & hæc dicuntur Fortuita, quia prorsus præter intentionem agentis fiunt. Sed ab horum neutro delictorum genere quispiam dicitur esse injustus, cum ad ejusmodi actionum productionem neque scientia, neque promta accedat voluntas, quæ duo requiruntur ad omnem actionem injustam, à qua quis dicatur verè injustus. Tertiò quædam sunt facta, quæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocantur ἀδικήματα seu injustè facta, quæ cum scientia & cognitione sunt conjuncta, sed ea rursus dupliciter fiunt, vel ex proæresi & præcedenti deliberatione, vel absque eadem, verbi gratia: cum quis ira, odio, amore, libidine, cupiditate, & cæteris animi perturbationibus commotus: alteri injuriam infert, hic quidem injustè agit, non tamen propter hæc & similia facta statim dicitur injustus, quia non ex improbitate & malitia seu nocendi studio hoc facit, sed prout effectus tantum dicitat: Verùm quando re prædeliberata, aliquis alteri injuriam infert non ex affectu, sed ratione perversa, tunc illud actum, verè dicitur injustum & ipse faciens & injustus & improbus dicitur. Quod verò aliquis scienter & sponte posset agere, sed quia non ex proæresi & industria peccat, & propterea nō fit injustus proprie dicendus, cōfirmat illud vulgare dictum ab omnibus usurpatum, quæ ex ira, & sic de cæteris animi perturbationibus iudicandum, gerunt, ea non ex providentia seu consulto geri dicuntur,idque probat duabus rationibus: 1. Quia iratus seu qui ad iram excitatur, non a priori laedit aliquem, neque priorem infert iniuriam, sed illepotius qui occasionem irae illi praebuit. Nam quod primus autor mali non sit ipse iratus, sed ille, qui ad iram provocat, haec duo signa liquido demonstrant: 1. Quia intentio mali non ab irato provenit, sed ab eo qui ad iram provocat. 2. Etiam quia prior actio mali in excitante ad iram non in irato originem suam habet. Altera ratio est, quia non de facto ab irato ipso commisso, sed de iure tantum quaestio esse solet: nam satis superque constat, ipsum factum imprudenter et absque deliberatione esse patratum: at in iis, quae consulto fiunt, et quae proprie sunt iniuste dicenda, non de iure ipso, sed de facto tantum quaeritur. Et ex hoc loco fundamentum habent illae quaestiones, quae crebro a Jurisconsultis usurpantur, ut videre licet in l. 1. Juris, ff. ad Ulpianum, ubi multa de iure et facto disceptantur. Quod vero in his, quae per iram geruntur, non de facto, sed de iure quaestio esse solet, a dissimili contractuum voluntariorum exemplo explicat: nam in contractibus, qui pleno sensu utriusque partis fiunt, longe dissimilis est ratio; non enim de iure ibi quaeritur, sed tantum de facto ipso, ut verbi gratia: an pecunia sit soluta necne? an res sit praestita secundum promissum et factum necne? Quia de iure ex pacto convento constat. Quod si vero aliqs a pacto recesserit, ut saepenumero, nisi ex oblivione aut casu aliquo deliquerit, improbus habetur, et in illa anima de vertitur ratione non juris, sed facti, quod scilicet ipso facto patuit. initum violavi t. Siceiam, si quis de industria & ex professo aliquem læserit, de facto ipso cum iam constet, de iure tamen dubitatur, iure ne an iniuria sit factum, verbi gratia: iratus, qui alterum læsit, putat se non læsisse, qui læditur, putat se iniuria effectu. Hic de iure tandem incidit quæstio, An iniuria sit illata necne? Et tandem concludit Philosophus, ea quoque esse iuste & iniuste facta (id quod initio capitis propositum erat) quæ sponte & deliberato fiunt, & illum esse iniustum, qui sponte aliis nocet contra legem, ut contra illæ iustus est, qui ex seria deliberatione & consulto Iustitiæ munera exequitur.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he inquires which injuries are those from which a man is properly called unjust, since the solution of the doubt proposed at the beginning of chapter 9 depends chiefly on this: namely, whether one who acts unjustly is to be called unjust, and also because something is done spontaneously not in one way only but in various ways. For something is done either from a prior deliberate choice [προαίρεσις] and previous deliberation, or without it. But that it may be better understood for which actions a man is properly called unjust, he sets out three kinds of deeds which seem to be done unjustly although they are also done spontaneously. (1) For they are done either through ignorance of the circumstances, and these are properly called errors, when something is done that arises from an internal principle, so that no operation of the intellect seems to have contributed to producing the action. (Secundo) Some things are done unexpectedly and by chance, as when someone falling from a roof crushes a passer-by with his fall; these are called accidental, since they occur altogether beyond the intention of the agent. A person is not called unjust for either of these kinds of wrongdoing, since neither knowledge nor ready will contributes to the production of such actions, and these two are required for every unjust action by which someone is truly called unjust. (Tertiò) There are some deeds which are called by way of eminence ἀδικήματα [adikēmata], that is, unjust deeds, which are joined with knowledge and awareness. These again are done in two ways, either from prior deliberate choice and previous deliberation, or without it. For example, when someone, moved by anger, hatred, love, lust, desire and other disturbances of the mind, inflicts an injury on another, he indeed acts unjustly, yet on account of these and similar deeds he is not at once called unjust, because he does not do this from wickedness and malice or a desire to harm, but only as the effect dictates. But when someone, having first deliberated, inflicts an injury on another not from passion but from a perverse reasoning, then the deed is truly called unjust, and the doer himself is called both unjust and wicked. That someone could act knowingly and willingly, yet because he does not sin from prior choice and deliberate purpose is therefore not to be called unjust properly, he confirms by that common saying used by everyone: those things which are done from anger are said not to be done from forethought or deliberately, and the same is to be judged of the other disturbances of the mind. He proves this by two reasons. (1) Because the angry man, or one who is provoked to anger, does not harm someone first, nor does he offer the first injury, but rather the one who gave him the occasion of anger. For that the angry man is not the first author of the evil, but the one who provokes him to anger, these two signs clearly demonstrate: first, because the intention of the evil does not arise from the angry man but from the one who provokes him; second, because the first act of evil in the one who provokes to anger has its origin not in the angry man. (2) Altera ratio est: the question is usually not about the deed committed by the angry man himself, but only about the law. For it is quite sufficiently and abundantly clear that the deed itself was done imprudently and without deliberation. But in those things which are done deliberately, and which are properly to be called unjust, the question is not about the law itself but only about the fact. From this passage those questions have their foundation which are often raised by the jurists, as one may see in l. 1. Juris, ff. ad Ulpianum, where many things about law and fact are disputed. That in those things which are done through anger the question is usually about the law and not the fact, he explains by the dissimilar example of voluntary contracts. In contracts, which are made with the full consent of both parties, the reasoning is far different. For there the question is not about the law but only about the fact itself: for example, has the money been paid or not? has the thing been delivered according to the promise, or not? For the law is settled by the agreement made. But if someone has departed from the agreement, as often happens, unless he has erred through forgetfulness or some chance, he is held dishonest, and in that case the question turns not on the law but on the fact, which is plain from the very fact that he has violated the agreement. So too, if someone has harmed another deliberately and openly, the fact itself is now established, yet doubt remains about the law, whether the deed was an injury or not. For example, the angry man who has harmed another thinks he has not harmed him, while the one who is harmed thinks he has been injured by the effect. Here at last the question arises about the law: whether the injury was inflicted or not? And finally the Philosopher concludes that those things also are done justly and unjustly (which was the proposition at the beginning of the chapter) which are done spontaneously and deliberately, and that he is unjust who harms others willingly against the law, just as he is just who carries out the duties of justice from serious deliberation and purpose.

units.la: Notandum vero ut aliquis vere iustus & injustus dicatur tria esse observanda: 1. Animum agentis, quia ab animo seu ab intellectu provenit intentio prima omnis actionis. 2. Observandam esse voluntatem, quæ intentionem intellectus persequitur & in actionem deducit. 3. Demum ipsum habitum, qui facilitatem actioni addit. Si duæ priores conditiones desint, actio proprie nec iusta nec injusta est; quod si tertia non adsit, poterit quidem dici actio aliqua singularis, sed à qua neque iustus neque injustus aliquis proprie dicatur, nisi actualiter tantum.
units.tr: It must be noted that three things are to be observed if someone is to be truly called just or unjust. (1) The mind of the agent, since the primary intention of every action arises from the mind or intellect. (2) The will, which pursues the intention of the intellect and carries it into action. (3) Lastly, the habit itself, which adds ease to the action. If the first two conditions are lacking, the action is properly neither just nor unjust. If the third is lacking, it may indeed be called a single action, but no one is properly called just or unjust on account of it, except in act only.

units.la: II. Et hoc notandum; Omne id quod lædit, seu quod alteri damnum infert provenire à tribus principiis: Vel enim ex ignorantia provenit, cum quis ignoratis circumstantiis aliquem lædit, & hoc proprie dicitur Erratum: Secundò vel ex affectu, ut cum quis ira vel libidine, vel aliis perturbationibus alteri nocet: Tertiò à malitia, cum quis de industria & ex professo alteri malum infert, & sic in rebus distri-buendis vel commutandis non modo æquitatem, sed ipsam justitiam læsdit. Et ex his tribus delicto-rum generibus tertium solum ita comparatum est, ut qui hoc faciat, & injuriam facere & injustus verè esse dicatur, priora vero duo non item. Nam pri-mum quod ab ignorantia provenit, est invitum sal-tem, non promta accedit voluntas; quod enim quis ignoranter facit, id non prorsus sponte agit. Secun-dum vero, quod ab affectu originem trahit, est quidem spontaneum, sed non constituto & deliberato factum, & proinde etiam neque injuriam proprie inferre dici ur. Tertium vero cum non tantum à malitia procedat, sed omnia etiam requisita veræ injuriæ habeat, minimè omnium veniam meretur.
units.tr: II. This too must be noted. Everything that harms, or causes loss to another, arises from three sources. (1) It may arise from ignorance, when someone harms another while ignorant of the circumstances; this is properly called an error. (2) It may arise from passion, as when someone harms another out of anger, lust, or other disturbances of the mind. (3) It may arise from malice, when someone deliberately and purposely inflicts evil on another, and so in distributing or exchanging goods violates not only equity but justice itself. Of these three kinds of wrongdoing, only the third is of such a nature that the one who does it is truly said to do an injury and to be unjust, whereas the first two are not. For the first, which arises from ignorance, is at least involuntary, and the will does not readily consent; for what someone does in ignorance, he does not do wholly willingly. The second, which takes its origin from passion, is indeed voluntary, but it is not done with settled and deliberate purpose, and therefore it is not properly said to inflict an injury either. The third, however, since it proceeds not only from malice but also has all the requisites of a true injury, deserves no pardon at all.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis, postquam jam ostendit, quæ justè, & quæ injustè fiant, quæ item punieнda, aut quæ non sint, distinguit invitè facta (quæ supra dixerat neque justa neq; injusta esse per se) ut scilicet alia mercantur veniam, quæ non tantum ab igno-rantibus, sed etiam per ignorantiam fiunt, & qui e-jufmodi delicta committunt, venia digni censentur propter duas rationes: 1. Respectu ipsius ignorantiæ, quæ est triplex, aut naturalis seu à natura insita, verbi gratia: quando infans aut morio aliquis aliquē læ-dunt. 2. aut fortuita seu casualis, ut verbi gratia: quā-do filius mittens telum in aciem hostiū adversorū, occidit casu patrem, quē nescivit in adversa acie sta-re: tertia est violenta, quando quis vi morbi aut vio-lentioris in corpore aut animo passionis non tan-tum otiose loquitur, sed etiam convicii aut contumeliis alium proscindit. 2, Tales censentur venia digni respectu infirmitatis humanae, quae in plurimis labi solet. Sed hic lapsus veniam habet, si modo poenitentiam comitem sortiatur. Secundo invita nullam merentur veniam, quae scilicet non ab ignorantia seu ignoranter fiunt, ut verbi gratia: quae a perturbationibus prorsus in humanis aut belluinis causantur. Sed de hac factorum divisione supra egit Philosophus c. 2. & 3. lib. 3. tum etiam lib. 1. mag. moral. c. 7.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter, after showing which things are done justly, which unjustly, and which are to be punished or not, he distinguishes things done unwillingly (which he had said above are neither just nor unjust in themselves). Some of these deserve pardon, namely those done not only by people who are ignorant but also through ignorance, and those who commit such offences are judged worthy of pardon for two reasons. (1) With respect to the ignorance itself, which is threefold: either natural, that is, implanted by nature, as when an infant or a madman harms someone; or accidental, or incidental, as when a son, hurling a missile into the battle line of the enemy, kills by chance his father, whom he did not know to be standing in the opposing line; or the third is violent, when someone, under the force of illness or of a more violent passion in body or mind, not only speaks idly but even tears another apart with reproaches or insults. (2) Such people are judged worthy of pardon with respect to human weakness, which is wont to stumble in many things. Yet this lapse is pardonable only if it is accompanied by repentance. Secondly, those things done unwillingly deserve no pardon at all, namely those that do not arise from ignorance, or are not done in ignorance, such as those caused entirely by passions, whether human or brutish. But the Philosopher treated of this division of actions above in chapters 2 and 3 of book 3, and also in book 1 of the Magna Moralia, chapter 7.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Juste & injuste demum ille agit, qui sponte agit; qui vero invite aliquid agit, nec juste nec iniuste proprie agere dicitur, nisi forte per accidens.
units.tr: 1. A person acts justly or unjustly only when he acts willingly; one who acts unwillingly is not properly said to act either justly or unjustly, unless perhaps by accident.

units.la: 2. Quando aliquid malisponte patiatur, tunc illud vituperatur, & injustum proprie dicitur.
units.tr: 2. When someone suffers something evil willingly, then that thing is blamed and is properly called unjust.

units.la: 3. Fieri potest, ut aliquid fit injustum in se, quod tamen non fit injuste factum, nisi etiam haec conditio accedat, ut scilicet sponte fiat.
units.tr: 3. It may happen that something is unjust in itself, and yet is not done unjustly unless this further condition is added, namely that it is done willingly.

units.la: 4. Spontaneum hoc proprie dicitur, quod scienter & cognitis circumstatiis fit, invitum vero econtra.
units.tr: 4. That is properly called willing which is done knowingly and with the circumstances known; the unwilling is the opposite.

units.la: 5. Quae per naturam fiunt, nec sponte nec invite fieri dicuntur, nam ista duo sunt propria requisita actionum humanarum non naturalium.
units.tr: 5. Things that happen by nature are said to be done neither willingly nor unwillingly, for these two are the proper requisites of human actions that are not natural.

units.la: 6. Quando quis invitus aut coactus depositum reddit, non injuste agere dicitur, nisi per accidens tantum, respectu scilicet actionis externae.
units.tr: 6. When someone unwillingly or under compulsion returns a deposit, he is not said to act unjustly, except only by accident, namely with respect to the external action.

units.la: 7. Ex spontaneis, quae prompta voluntate fiunt, alia fiunt cum electione, alia vero non.
units.tr: 7. Of voluntary actions, which are done with a ready will, some are done with choice and some are not.

units.la: 8. Cum electione ea fiunt, quae precedente deliberatione aut consultatione geruntur, absque electione econtra.
units.tr: 8. Those are done with choice which are carried out after prior deliberation or consultation; those without choice are the opposite.

units.la: 9. Que
units.tr: 9. Which

units.la: 9. Quae inscienter & contra legem fiunt, non tam injuria quam infortunii nomen merentur, quia ignoratia est causa transgressionis.
units.tr: 9. Things done in ignorance and against the law deserve the name not so much of injury as of misfortune, because ignorance is the cause of the transgression.

units.la: 10. Si ad cognitionem accedat consultatio & electio, & tunc aliquid praeter legem & rectam rationem gerātur, injuria proprie fieri dicitur.
units.tr: 10. If consultation and choice are added to knowledge, and something is then done beyond the law and right reason, it is properly said to be done as an injury.

units.la: 11. Ira aliiqʒ in homine affectus, cum a natura proveniant, qua tales nihil mali agunt.
units.tr: 11. Anger and other affections in man, since they arise from nature, do no evil as such.

units.la: 12. Quae ab ira caeterisq; animi perturbationibus geruntur, licet injuste fieri videantur, non tamen statim hominem injustum reddunt.
units.tr: 12. Things done from anger and other disturbances of the mind, although they may seem to be done unjustly, do not at once make the man unjust.

units.la: 13. Quando iratus alteri nocet, non tam a seipso, quam ab eo, qui ad iram provocavit initium hac injuria habet.
units.tr: 13. When an angry man harms another, the injury has its beginning not so much from himself as from the one who provoked the anger.

units.la: 14. In iis, quae ab irato committuntur, non de facto ipso, de quo constat, sed de jure quaestio esse solet.
units.tr: 14. In the things committed by an angry man, the question is usually not about the deed itself, which is clear, but about the law.

units.la: 15. In iis, quae invite fiunt, venia quaedam merentur, in quibus ignorantia & ignorans sunt simul causa, quaedam vero non, in quibus scilicet ignorantia ad actionis pravae productionem non accedit.
units.tr: 15. In things done unwillingly, some deserve a degree of pardon, in which ignorance and the ignorant person are together the cause; but some do not, namely those in which ignorance does not contribute to the production of the wrong action.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An jure neget Philosophus illos, qui ex ira aut ignorantia, aut aliquo etiam affectu aliquid agunt contra legem, aut rectam rationem committunt, injuriam agere, cum tamen experientia repugnet, & tales etiam legibus puniantur. Nam contra ejusmodi delinquentes multa sunt severa leges lata, ut videri licet ff. de poenis? Resp. Injuriam agere sumitur duobus modis: 1. Latē, 2. Strictē. Si strictē & per se & proprie, seu ut loquuntur Jurisconsulti, plenē sumatur, tunc illi injuriam agere dicuntur, qui sponte & voluntate sua aliis nocent, sicut hoc loco & lib. 2. Topic. cap. 4. docet Philosophus, & hoc modo, quia ex affectibus peccant, injuriam proprie non agunt. Si communiter & per accidens sumatur nomen injuriæ, & iratus, & ignorans, si aliquid mali commiserint, injuriam agere dicuntur, ita tamen, ut quæ leges contra ipsos sunt latæ, secundum æquitatem adhiberi debeant & pro variis circumstantiis & casibus, qui incidunt.
units.tr: I. It is asked whether the Philosopher rightly denies that those who act against the law or right reason out of anger, or ignorance, or some other passion, do an injury, since experience contradicts this, and such offenders are punished by the laws. For many severe laws have been passed against such offenders, as may be seen in the Digest, de poenis? Answer: to do an injury is taken in two ways: (1) broadly, (2) strictly. If it is taken strictly, and in itself and properly, or, as the jurists say, fully, then those are said to do an injury who harm others willingly and by their own will, as the Philosopher teaches here and in Topics book 2, chapter 4; and in this sense, since they sin from passions, they do not properly do an injury. If the name of injury is taken commonly and accidentally, then both the angry man and the ignorant man, if they have committed some evil, are said to do an injury; yet in such a way that the laws passed against them ought to be applied according to equity and according to the various circumstances and cases that arise.

units.la: II. An recte Philosophus neget, iratos & alios aliis affectibus laborantes esse iniustos, licet iniuste agant, cum tamen natura coniugatorum hoc doceat, ut si unum infit, & alterum inerit, sicut testatur Philosophus 2. Topic. cap. 4. Proinde si quis iniuste agat, iniustus sit necesse erit? Resp. Iram & alias animi perturbationes bifariam consiliderari: Vel quoad naturam, a qua primam habent originem, & sic non sunt causæ iniuriarum, neque docent homines iniuste agere, cum natura nihil nocivum perse condiderit. Secundo considerantur relatè, quatenus scilicet usu accrescunt in habitum, & sic qui ex ira, aut alia animi perturbatione iniuste aliquid agit, etiam iniustus dici potest, quia malitiam & scientiam destinatè una coniungit, dum scilicet ex habitu agit. At dum Philosophus negat iratos esse iniustos, licet iniuste agat, intelligit de una actione, non de habitu.
units.tr: II. Whether the Philosopher rightly denies that the angry, and those affected by other passions, are unjust, although they act unjustly, since the nature of related things teaches this, that if one is present and the other is in it, as the Philosopher testifies in Topics book 2, chapter 4? Therefore, if someone acts unjustly, he must necessarily be unjust? Answer: anger and the other disturbances of the mind are to be considered in two ways: either with respect to their nature, from which they have their first origin, and so they are not causes of injuries, nor do they teach men to act unjustly, since nature has established nothing harmful in itself. Secondly they are considered relatively, namely insofar as by use they grow into a habit; and so one who acts unjustly from anger or another disturbance of the mind can also be called unjust, because he joins malice and knowledge together in purpose, when he acts from habit. But when the Philosopher denies that the angry are unjust although they act unjustly, he means a single action, not a habit.

units.la: III. & ult. Quomodo affectus inter invita numeret sub finem capitis, cum tamen in medio inter voluntaria recenseat; affert enim exempla eorum, qui ex affectibus delinquunt contra legem aut rectam rationem. Tum etiam probari potest, affectus ad voluntaria tantum facta esse referendos, tum quia habent principium internum, nempe animam, tum etiam quia cum cognitione agere solent, quæ duo sunt requisita factorum spontaneorum. Cum igitur & inter invita & inter spontanea numeret, sibi contradicat necesse est? Resp. Affectus sectus duobus modis posse considerari: 1. Late, ita ut sub se complectantur omnia ea, quae sine consultatione & electione fiunt, & sic Philosophus sub fine capitis inter invita facta numeravit, quia certo constat, omnia invita absque ulla consultatione aut electione fieri. Secundo considerantur stricte, respectu principii, quia principium habent internum, inter spontanea sub medio capitis numeravit Philosophus. Proinde cum diverso respectu & ad invita, & ad spontanea referri possint, ubi non contradicit.
units.tr: III. and last. Why does he number the affections among involuntary acts at the end of the chapter, when in the middle he lists them among voluntary ones? For he gives examples of those who, from their affections, offend against the law or right reason. It can also be proved that affections are to be referred only to voluntary acts: both because they have an internal principle, namely the soul, and because they usually act with knowledge, which are the two requisites of spontaneous acts. Since he counts them both among involuntary and among spontaneous acts, must he not contradict himself? Answer. Affections can be considered in two ways. 1. Broadly, so that they embrace everything that is done without deliberation and choice; and in this sense the Philosopher numbered them among involuntary acts at the end of the chapter, because it is certain that all involuntary acts are done without any deliberation or choice. 2. Strictly, with respect to their principle, since they have an internal principle; and in this sense the Philosopher numbered them among spontaneous acts in the middle of the chapter. Therefore, since they can be referred to both involuntary and spontaneous acts under different respects, there is no contradiction.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Quartum & ultimum membrum secundi tractatus huius libri hoc capite & duobus sequentibus habetur, in quo Philosophus varias dubitationes seu quaestiones, quae vel ex supradictis oriri, vel etiam contra naturam Justitiae obiici poterant, proponit, & accurate etiam solvit.
units.tr: The fourth and last part of the second treatise of this book is contained in this chapter and the two that follow. In it the Philosopher proposes and also accurately resolves various doubts or questions, which could arise from what has been said above or be raised against the nature of Justice.

units.la: Subdividitur hoc membrum in tres rursum partes: In priori tres quaestiones proponit & etiam solvit hoc cap. 12. In secunda duas insigniores quaestiones, quae plurimum ad naturam Iustitiae illustrandam faciunt, movet, & dextre etiam ad utramque respondet. In tertia demum refellit vulgi opinionem existimantis iustum & iniustum rem esse facilem, seu non minus iuste agere, quam iniuste, non tantum esse nostri arbitrii, sed etiam absque omni cura & labore fieri posse cap. 15.
units.tr: This part is again divided into three sections. In the first, he proposes and also resolves three questions in this chapter, 12. In the second, he raises two more notable questions, which contribute greatly to clarifying the nature of Justice, and he also answers both skilfully. Finally, in the third, he refutes the opinion of the common people, who think that the just and the unjust are an easy matter, or that acting justly is no less easy than acting unjustly, and that it lies not only in our power but can also be done without any care or effort, chap. 15.

units.la: In prima igitur parte, quae habetur hoc cap. 12. tres adfert quaestiones. Partes capitis (sunt duae: In prima istae istas quæstiones proponit. In secunda eadem soluit, & potissimum primam, quia ex eadem reliquæ duæ inprimis dependent.
units.tr: In the first part, which is found in this chapter 12, he brings forward three questions. The parts of the chapter are two. In the first he sets out these questions. In the second he resolves them, and above all the first, because the other two chiefly depend on it.

units.la: In prima igitur occasione sumta ex Euripidis in Bellerophe dictis, qui inducit Bellerophontam matricidium superbè excusantem: Matrem quomodo occiderim, quaeris? Breviter dicam: Volens volentem, vel volentem non volens. Ideo cum hoc non tantum rationi, sed sensui etiam communi repugnet, ut aliquis sponte patiatur se interfici, quaerit: An quis sponte accipiat injuriam, seu, ut loquuntur Jurisconsulti; An volenti fiat iniuria, l. 1. ff. usque adeo, ff. de iniuriis. Quaerit igitur Philosophus, An sicut iniuria illatio est voluntaria; nemo enim alteri damnum infert, nisi sponte sua, ita etiam iniuria perpessio fit voluntaria nec ne? seu, An sicut sponte fit iniuria, ita etiam sponte sustineatur? Secunda quaestio est de juris perpessione; An scilicet aliquis sponte, an invite ius subeat aut patiatur, aut An aliquis quod revera est justum, nolens aut volens subeat? Et respondet primo breviter ad utramque quaestionem, & iuste & iniuste agere, esse quidem voluntarium, sicut supra iam cap. 11. determinavit: sed iniuriam perpeti aut ius etiam subire aut sustinere, interdum esse voluntarium, interdum vero non. Quomodo autem utrumque hoc fiat infra pluribus declarat. Tertia quaestio est; An quirem patitur iniustam, seu qui aliquid aliquo modo iniuste fert, idem etiam patiatur injuriam? Et respondet fieri posse, ut aliquis patiatur aliquid injuste, & tamen non statim dicatur pati injuriam, quia nulla injuria sponte admittitur. Potest tamen aliquis aliquid injuste sponte sua admittere, verbi gratia: ad-ulteultera, quæ polluit maritalem thorum, patitur aliquid injusti ab adultero, nam omnes leges hoc vetant, non tamen patitur injuriam, cum sponte sua hoc injustum admittat. Præterea requiritur etiam non tantum, ut sit aliquis, qui patiatur injuriam, sed etiam qui inferat, & quidem talis, qui sponte sua inferat, sicut jam cap. superiore comprobatum fuit.
units.tr: In the first, then, the occasion is taken from the words of Euripides in the Bellerophon, who introduces Bellerophon proudly excusing his matricide: You ask how I killed my mother? I will say it briefly: willing her, or unwilling while she is willing. Since this is contrary not only to reason but also to common sense, that anyone should willingly suffer himself to be killed, he asks: Does anyone willingly receive an injury? or, as the jurists put it, Is an injury done to one who is willing? Law 1, ff. Usque adeo, ff. de iniuriis. The Philosopher therefore asks: Just as the inflicting of an injury is voluntary (for no one does harm to another except of his own accord), is the suffering of an injury also voluntary or not? or, Just as an injury is done willingly, is it also willingly endured? The second question concerns the undergoing of right: Whether, that is, someone undertakes or suffers justice willingly or unwillingly, or Does someone undergo what is really just, willing or unwilling? He answers first, briefly, to both questions: to act justly and unjustly is indeed voluntary, as he has already determined above in chapter 11; but to suffer an injury, or to undertake or endure what is right, is sometimes voluntary and sometimes not. How each of these happens he explains at length below. The third question is: Does one who suffers what is unjust, or who bears something unjustly in some way, also suffer an injury? He answers that it can happen that someone suffers something unjustly and yet is not at once said to suffer an injury, because no injury is willingly accepted. Yet someone can willingly accept something unjust. For example, an adulteress, who defiles the marriage bed, suffers something unjust from the adulterer, for all laws forbid this; yet she does not suffer an injury, since she herself willingly admits this injustice.
