Moreover, it is required that there be not only one who suffers an injury but also one who inflicts it, and one who does so willingly, as was already shown in the preceding chapter.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis adfert solutionem prima quæstionis potissimum: An scilicet volenti fiat injuria? Et respondet per negationem, fieri non posse, ut injuriam proprie, quis sponte patiatur: nam cum omnis injuria sit malum quid, utpote quod non tantum à malitia procedit, sed etiam damnum & detrimentum alteri adfert, etiam plerunq; sit turpe: sed quia contra omnes leges fæde committitur, ideo ab injuria sustinenda omnes naturę quodam instinctu abhorrent. Et quo magis hoc probet Philosophus duo adfert exempla de hominibus vitiosis seu qui vitiis plurimum laborant, & quibus injuria fieri videtur sponte sua & tamen non fit. Primum est de incontinente, qui sponte sua in cibo, potu, & aliis rebus sibi nocet: hic quidem injuriam accipere videtur, non tamen accipit, propterea ꝯ injuriam accipere is dicatur, cui nolenti recusanti & prorsus repugnanti aliquid injuste fit, contra legem aut rectam rationem: id quod ex definitione injuriæ accipiendæ & faciendæ patet: Nam injuriam ferre aut accipere, est contra voluntatem, & coacte aliquid iniustum pati, sicut iniuriam facere, est sponte sua alicui damnum inferre aut alteri nocere. At ista de incontinente dici non possunt, cum sponte sua ruat in hæc vitia, quibus sibi ipsi detrimentum infert. Alterum exemplum est de Prodigo aut de eo, qui rem suam alteri largitur, cum suo ipsius damno, hic etiā injuriam accipere videtur eo, quod damnum sentiat, & alteri lucrum tribuat, quod sibi ipsi retinere debet, quemadmodum Homerus Iliad. 6. de Glauco refert, qui Diomedi veteri hospiti iam agnito in signum amoris arma sua aurea pro ferreis aut æneis dedit, & ut ait Poëta.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he gives the solution to the first question chiefly: namely, whether an injury is done to one who is willing? And he answers in the negative: it cannot happen that someone properly suffers an injury willingly. For since every injury is an evil thing, inasmuch as it proceeds not only from malice but also brings loss and harm to another, it is also generally shameful; and because it is committed in violation of all laws, therefore all men by a certain natural instinct shrink from enduring an injury. And to prove this the more, the Philosopher adduces two examples of vicious men, or of those who are greatly burdened by their vices, and to whom injury seems to be done willingly and yet is not. The first is of the incontinent man, who of his own accord harms himself in food, drink and other things. He seems indeed to receive an injury, yet he does not receive one, because a person is said to receive an injury when something unjust is done to him against his will, when he refuses and utterly resists, contrary to law or right reason; this is clear from the definition of receiving and of doing an injury. For to bear or receive an injury is to suffer something unjust against one's will and by force, just as to do an injury is to inflict harm on another or injure him of one's own accord. But these things cannot be said of the incontinent man, since he rushes into these vices of his own accord, by which he inflicts loss on himself. The other example is of the prodigal, or of one who gives his property to another to his own loss. He too seems to receive an injury, in that he feels the loss and bestows on another a gain which he ought to keep for himself. Homer relates this in the Iliad 6 of Glaucus, who, when he recognised his old guest Diomedes, gave him his golden armour in exchange for bronze, as a sign of love; and, as the poet says,

units.la: Próque novem centum pro ferro tradidit aurum.
units.tr: And for iron he gave gold worth nine hundred oxen.

units.la: Atque hic nulla affectus est injuria, licet damnum sit passus, propterea quod iniuria affici ab alio, nempe a patiente dependeat, & in aliena potestate sit situm: at vero rem nostram aliis largiri a nobis dependet ipsis, & in nostra voluntate est positum, velimus ne an nolimus rem nostram aliis dare, unde tandem hoc sequitur, etiam homines vitiosos iniuria proprie & sponte non affici, etsi sponte aliquid mali plerumque agant & in seipsos quidem agant. Notandum vero volenti non fieri iniuriam, propter quatuor potissimum rationes: 1. Ducitur a definitione iniuriae accipiendae, quia iniuria definitur voluntaria & malitiosa alicuius laesio contra iustum & aequum: Nemo autem sponte & malitiose laedit seipsum. Proinde nemo volens patitur iniuriam.
units.tr: Here, however, no injury is done to the one who suffers a loss, because being injured by another depends on the one who suffers it and lies within another's power. But giving our property to others depends on us, and it lies in our own will whether we wish or do not wish to give our property to others. Hence it follows that even wicked men are not injured properly or of their own accord, although they often do harm willingly, and indeed do it to themselves. It must be noted, however, that no injury is done to one who is willing, for four main reasons: 1. It is drawn from the definition of injury, since injury is defined as a voluntary and malicious harm done to someone contrary to what is just and fair. But no one harms himself willingly and maliciously. Therefore no one who is willing suffers injury.

units.la: 2. Quia omnis iniuria est malum quid, ut iam diximus: Nemo autem sponte velit, nisi quod bonum sit, propter duas praecipue causas: 1. Quia natura omnes inclinant ad hoc, ut sui conservationem & bonum quaerant. 2. Quia, ut ex 3. lib. cap. 4. patet, voluntas per se & recte dispósita, semper fertur ad bobonum, nemo igitur iniuriam, cum sit malum quid, sponte sua ferre velit. 3. Ratio sumitur a contrariis, quia nemo, nisi sponte infert alteri iniuriam: Ergo a contrario nemo, nisi invite patitur iniuriam. 4. Ratio, quia experientia docet, nullum esse neque unquam fuisse, qui sponte sua admiserit iniuriam propter φιλαυτίαν omnibus innatam. Sed haec sententia Philosophi intelligi debet de voluntate recte disposita & tunc quidem volenti nulla fit iniuria, qua talis, propter rationes supra allatas: Verum voluntate non recte disposita aut depravata fieri potest iniuria etiam volenti, verbi gratia: Si quis insano praebeat cultrū, quo se confodiat, aut desperabūdo & mortem optandi telum ministret, quo se vita privet, aut etiam illi necem inferat: Sed quia hic voluntas non est sana, sed aegra & male affecta: ideo non tam voluntas hoc admittere dicitur, quam appetitus, qui rationem & ipsam voluntatem plane rejecisse videtur. Secundo etiam alicui volenti iniuria infertur, si alio fine & modo, quam ipse velit, laesio inferatur, & sic Martyribus Christi iniuria illata est a Tyrannis persecutoribus. licet illi promptissima voluntate mortem oppetierint, quia mortem oppetebant pro gloria Christi & testimonio veritatis, sed non hoc fine illis hanc poenam irrogarant, sed tantum, ut libidini & suo ipsorum furori satisfierent. Distinguunt Jurisconsulti inter damnum leve, & damnum grave, & dicunt volenti quidem non fieri iniuriam, etsi accedat aliqua laesio, modo damnum aut laesio non sit gravis, verbi gratia: Si quis volenti & consentienti alapam impingat, hic cum non accedat damnum, ideo non dicitur accepisse injuriam, cui alapa infliſ̄ctifuit, & ideo juste contra infligentem actionem juris instituere non poterit. At vero si damnum aut læsio gravis accedat, tunc etiam volenti fit injuria, verbi gratia; Si quis consentienti & etiam jubenti manum aut aliquod membrum corporis detruncat, hic poterit injuriæ illatæ justissime accusari: nam etsi alter voluerit, non ita tamen, ut debuit, voluit, cum nemo sanæ mentis, in quo est voluntas recte dispositia hoc vellit, ut aliquod corpori inferatur damnum: neque etiam ita quisquam, sit dominus sui corporis, ut possit aliquod membrum pro libitu suo detruncare aut contra legem & præscriptum rectæ rationis auferre: nemo enim jure de membris suis dispensare potest, quia qui hoc facit quatuor modis peccat: 1. Contra naturam ipsam, quæ alio fine atque usu hæc illi membra concessit, quam ut ea abjicere aut contemneret. 2. Contra rectam rationem, quia rem per se integram & perfectam mutilam & imperfectam reddit. 3. Contra seipsum, cui hoc damnum infertur, dum se membrorum privatione inhabiliorem & ineptiorem ad munia vitæ peragenda reddit. 4. Etiam contra Rempubl. peccat, cui detrimentum accessit per mutilationem alicujus membri ipsius.
units.tr: 2. Because every injury is an evil, as we have already said. But no one would willingly choose anything except what is good, for two chief causes: (1) by nature all creatures tend to seek their own preservation and good; (2) as is clear from Book 3, chapter 4, a will that is in itself rightly disposed always tends toward the good. Therefore no one who wills it would of his own accord bear an injury, since an injury is an evil. 3. The argument is taken from the contrary: no one inflicts an injury on another except willingly; therefore, conversely, no one suffers an injury except unwillingly. 4. The argument is that experience teaches that there is, and never has been, anyone who of his own accord has allowed an injury, because of the self-love innate in all. But this saying of the Philosopher must be understood of a will rightly disposed, and then indeed no injury is done, as such, to one who is willing, for the reasons given above. But an injury can be done even to one who is willing when the will is not rightly disposed or is depraved; for example, if someone offers a knife to a madman so that he may stab himself, or gives a weapon to a despairing man who longs for death, so that he may deprive himself of life, or even inflicts death on him. But because the will here is not sound but sick and ill-disposed, it is said that it is not so much the will that admits this as the appetite, which seems to have utterly rejected both reason and the will itself. Secondly, an injury is also done to someone who is willing if harm is inflicted for an end or in a manner other than he himself wishes. Thus an injury was done to the martyrs of Christ by the tyrant persecutors, although they met death most readily and willingly, because they faced death for the glory of Christ and the testimony of the truth; but the tyrants did not impose this punishment on them for that end, only that they might satisfy their own lust and fury. Jurists distinguish between a slight loss and a grave loss, and they say that no injury is done to one who is willing, even if some harm is involved, provided the loss or harm is not grave. For example: if someone strikes a willing and consenting person with a slap, since no serious loss follows, the one who was slapped is not said to have suffered an injury, and therefore he cannot justly bring an action of law against the one who struck him. But if a grave loss or harm follows, then an injury is done even to one who is willing. For example: if someone cuts off the hand or some other limb of a person who consents and even orders it, the one who did it can be most justly accused of an injury. For although the other person willed it, he did not will it as he ought, since no one of sound mind, whose will is rightly disposed, wishes that some harm be done to his body. Nor is anyone so much master of his own body that he may cut off any limb at his pleasure or remove it contrary to the law and the rule of right reason. For no one can rightly dispose of his own limbs, because whoever does so sins in four ways: 1. Against nature itself, which granted these limbs for a purpose and use other than that they should be cast off or despised. 2. Against right reason, because he makes a thing that was whole and perfect mutilated and imperfect. 3. Against himself, to whom this harm is done, since by the loss of his limbs he makes himself less able and less fit to perform the duties of life. 4. He also sins against the Commonwealth, to which a loss has come through the mutilation of one of its members.

units.la: Secunda quæstio est: An aliquis sponte patiatur aliquid injustum nec ne? Resp. Quatuor modis id fieri posse, ut aliquis etiam sponte patiatur id, quod sit injustum: 1. Cum voluntas sit tacita & non expressa, ut cum quis consentit in damnum suum, sed praetextu majoris boni, verbi gratia: Cum invidus aliquis libeter cuperet aliquid a se tolli non magni gni momenti, hoc quidem fine,ut ab alio, cui invidet, aliquid majus & majoris mométi tollatur. Quo pertinet Apologia Æsopi de duobus Invidis, qui dona à Jove simul petebant, quorum votis Jupiter annuit, hac quidem lege & conditione, ut quodcunque primus acciperet, alter duplum referret, petiit primus, ut oculum illi erueret Jupiter, hoc fine, ut alterum utroque oculo privaret. 2. Cum voluntas accedit quidem, sed ex parte tantum & non integrè, ut cum quis volens cruciatum & dolorem patitur, pro boni majoris assecutione, ut de Martyribus supra jam constat. Voluntas quidem in iis accedebat ad ferendum supplicium, non tamen integrè, quia natura abhorrebat ab ejusmodi malo, sed quia spes majoris boni illos excitabat ad hanc patientiā, ideo sponte etiam dicuntur injuriam tulisse. 3. Cum voluntas ex conditione quadam accedit & non est absoluta, verbi gratia: Cum quis magna necessitate coactus fundum aut aliquid aliud oppignorat edaci fœneratori, hac quidem conditione, ut nisi redimat intra tale temporis spacium, depositum amittat: hic quidem consentit in id, quod est injustum, sed nisi necessitas premeret, planè non faceret. 4. Injustum etiam aliquis sponte pati dicitur, cum voluntas non est prorsus libera propter aliquod impedimentum, aut ætatis aut morbi aut similium rerū, quæ actiones voluntatis liberas impedire possunt, verbi gratia: Cum puer aliquis aut infirmus ab alio nocitura petens, ab eo etiam ea impetrat. Breviter notandum: Injustè aliquid pati duobus modis considerari potest: 1. Absolutè, cùm scilicet aliquis simplicipliciter contra voluntatem aliquid, quod repugnat aut legi aut rectæ rationi subire cogitur, ut cum injuste & malitiosè vulneratur ab hoste. 2. Aliquid injuste dicitur aliquis pati, comparatè, cùm scil. uno respectu, nempe necessitatis in gruentis sit plané voluntarium, quod agit, & posset hoc vel illo modo agere pro libitu suo: verum altero respectu, nempe conditionis aut pacti, est plané involuntarium, ut verbi gratia: cum aliquis à prædonibus deprehensus, pecuniam suam iis dat, ne vitam amittat, aut hosti tradit, quæcunque habet, ut periculum aut mortem instantem evitet. Primo casu, nempe respectu necessitatis, possunt hoc agere vel non agere, pecuniam dare vel vitam amittere, & sic injustum dicuntur pati (ponte sua, altero vero respectu conditionis non possunt non sic agere, quia sic pactum est, & sic contra voluntatem suam injustum patiuntur. Tertia quæstio est: An omnis, qui patitur aliquid injustum, patiatur statim injuriam? Et Resp. Licet conversim aut è converso valeat, ut omnis, qui patitur injuriam, dicatur pati injustum, non tamen omnis, qui patitur aliquid injustum, patitur semper injuriam propter tres causas: 1. Quia injustum latius patet, quam injuria; Nam injustum illud dicitur, quicquid contra legem aut rectam rationem committitur, & quocunq; modo; Injuria vero dicitur, quando aliquid ex proæresi & certa cognitione delinquitur, ita ut injustum & injuria differant tanquam species & genus. 2. A contrario idem probatur: nam omnis, qui patitur injustum, non statim patitur injuriam, ut exemplo adulteri supra docuit Philosophus. Ergo etiā qui sponte sua patitur aliquid injustum, non spon-te patitur injuriam, sed invite, quia volenti poterit aliquid fieri injustum, injuria vero fieri non potest.
units.tr: Second question: Does anyone willingly suffer something unjust or not? Answer: This can happen in four ways, so that someone willingly suffers what is unjust: 1. When the will is tacit and not expressed, as when someone consents to his own loss for the sake of a greater good. For example, when an envious man gladly wishes that something of little importance be taken from himself, with the purpose that something greater and of greater importance be taken from the one he envies. To this belongs Aesop's fable of the two envious men who asked Jove for gifts together; Jupiter granted their prayers on this condition, that whatever the first received, the other should receive double. The first asked that Jupiter put out one of his eyes, with the purpose that the other be deprived of both. 2. When the will is present, but only in part and not wholly, as when someone willingly endures torment and pain in order to obtain a greater good, as has already been established above concerning the martyrs. In them the will was indeed moving toward enduring punishment, but not wholly, because nature shrank from such an evil; but the hope of a greater good stirred them to this patience, and therefore they are said to have borne an injury willingly. 3. When the will comes from a certain condition and is not absolute. For example: when someone, compelled by great necessity, pledges a farm or something else to a grasping moneylender, on this condition, that unless he redeems it within a certain space of time he will lose the pledge. Here he does consent to what is unjust, but unless necessity pressed him he would plainly not do it. 4. A person is also said to suffer what is unjust willingly when the will is not entirely free because of some impediment, whether of age, sickness, or similar things that can hinder the free actions of the will. For example: when a child or a sick person asks another for something harmful, and receives it from him. In brief, it should be noted: to suffer something unjustly can be considered in two ways: 1. Absolutely, namely when someone is forced against his will to undergo something that is contrary either to the law or to right reason, as when he is unjustly and maliciously wounded by an enemy. 2. A person is said to suffer something unjustly in a comparative sense, namely when, in one respect, that is, of necessity pressing upon him, what he does is wholly voluntary, and he could do this or that as he pleased; but in another respect, that of a condition or agreement, it is wholly involuntary. For example: when someone, seized by robbers, gives them his money so as not to lose his life, or surrenders to an enemy whatever he has, so as to avoid imminent danger or death. In the first case, namely with respect to necessity, they can do this or not do it, give the money or lose their life; and so they are said to suffer what is unjust willingly. But in the other respect, that of the condition, they cannot but act in this way, because it was so agreed, and so they suffer what is unjust against their will. The third question is: Does everyone who suffers something unjust suffer an injury at once? Answer: Although it holds conversely, or the other way round, that everyone who suffers an injury is said to suffer what is unjust, not everyone who suffers what is unjust always suffers an injury, for three reasons: 1. Because what is unjust has a wider range than injury. For what is unjust is called whatever is committed against the law or right reason, and in any way at all; but injury is called what is done from deliberate choice and with certain knowledge, so that the unjust and injury differ as species and genus. 2. The same is proved by the contrary: for everyone who suffers what is unjust does not at once suffer an injury, as the Philosopher taught by the example of the adulterer above. Therefore also one who of his own accord suffers something unjust does not suffer an injury willingly, but unwillingly, because something can be done unjustly to a willing person, whereas an injury cannot be done to him.

units.la: 3. Quia injuriam is propriè patitur, cui ab alioqui sponte & animo injuriandi damnum infert, contra jus & æquum nocetur.
units.tr: 3. Someone properly suffers injury when another, willingly and with intent to injure, inflicts loss on him, harming him contrary to right and equity.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Voluntate recte disposita & recte volenti nulla propriè fit injuria, licet perperam volenti & voluntate depravata nonnunquam fiat.
units.tr: 1. When the will is rightly disposed and the person wills rightly, no injury is properly done to him, although it sometimes is done when he wills wrongly and his will is depraved.

units.la: 2. Sicut afficere injuria non prorsus spontaneum, sic injuria affici est plane invitum.
units.tr: 2. Just as inflicting injury is not altogether voluntary, so suffering injury is plainly involuntary.

units.la: 3. Multi sunt, qui invitè jus subeunt, ut sunt fures, latrones, & id genus malefici, qui pœnam sibi ex jure paratam vident.
units.tr: 3. There are many who undergo the law unwillingly, such as thieves, robbers, and malefactors of that kind, who see the punishment prepared for them by law.

units.la: 4. Non omnis, qui injustum patitur, statim patitur injuriam, quia alterum altero latius patet.
units.tr: 4. Not everyone who suffers what is unjust suffers injury at once, because the one extends more widely than the other.

units.la: 5. Injuria afficere definitur vulgo sponte aliquem ladere: sponte vero is ladit, qui habet cognitionem circumstantiarum, ut nempe sciat, quem, quomodo, & quo fine, quibus mediis & instrumentis ladat.
units.tr: 5. To inflict injury is commonly defined as wilfully harming someone. A person harms wilfully, however, when he knows the circumstances, namely whom he harms, how, for what end, and by what means and instruments.

units.la: 6. Incontinens etsi seipsum ladere videatur, quia tamen cognitione circumstantiarum nō habet, nescit enim, quod seipsum ladat, injuriam sibi propriè non infert.
units.tr: 6. Although an incontinent person may seem to harm himself, since he lacks knowledge of the circumstances and does not know that he is harming himself, he does not properly inflict injury on himself.

units.la: 7. Nemo id propriè vult, quod bonum esse non existimat, quia à malo quodam instinctu abhorrent.
units.tr: 7. No one properly wills what he does not judge to be good, since they recoil from it by a certain evil impulse.

units.la: 8. Qui rem suam alteri cum suo ipsius damno dat, injuriam sibi non facit, cum sit in potestate sua, ut hoc faciat, vel non faciat.
units.tr: 8. A person who gives his own property to another at his own loss does himself no injury, since it is in his power to do this or not to do it.

units.la: 9. Injuria illata sicut ab externo principio provenit, sic contra voluntatem patientis propriè committitur.
units.tr: 9. An injury inflicted proceeds from an external source, and so it is properly committed against the will of the one who suffers it.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An jure neget Philosophus, volenti non fieri injuriam, cum multa sit rationes, quæ idipsum probent: 1. Quia qui jugulum suum aliorum mucronibus offerunt volentes, sicut de Saule in Scripturis & aliis dicitur, sponte sua patiuntur injuriam: quod verò patiantur injuriam, hinc putet, quia lex interfectorem ejusmodi severissime punit, quod tamen non faceret, nisi injuria contra eos & æquum committeret. Cum igitur lex illum, qui volentem interficit, pro injuria illata puniat, injuriam volenti factam esse constat? Resp. Per negationem consequentiæ. Nam executio legum non arguit volenti esse factam injuriam, sed civitati aut naturæ tantum: Lex enim interfectores ejusmodi punit, quod & naturæ ipsi & civitati, non vero ei, cui damnum intulit, injuriam intulerit. Naturæ infert injuriam, quia contra scopum & intentionem naturæ, naturæ opus destruit; civitati vero, quia uno illam membro privat. 2. Instantia. Multi innocentes contumelias & injuriam mortis sponte patiuntur, sicut historiæ variæ testantur. Ergo manet illud verum volenti fieri injuriam? Resp. Licet injusta aliquid patiantur, tamen non patiuntur injuriam, & hæc perpessio poterit dici voluntaria & involuntaria diverso respectu. Nam respectu naturæ, quæ semper sui conservationem intendit, poterit dici involuntaria; at vero respectu finis, quem innocentes sibi proponunt, poterit dici voluntaria, quia innocentes malunt ejusmodi perpessiones sponte sua subire, quam nomini & famæ, aut etiam pietati maculam inurere. 3. Instantia. Modestus, qui alii plus tribuit, quam sibi relinquit, sicut Philosophus 4. Nicom. cap. 12. sponte sua patitur injuriam. Ergo etiam poterit aliquis non
units.tr: I. The question is: Whether the Philosopher rightly denies that injury is done to one who is willing, since there are many reasons which prove the very thing: 1. Those who offer their throat willingly to the swords of others, as is said of Saul in the Scriptures and elsewhere, suffer injury voluntarily. That they do suffer injury is shown by the fact that the law punishes the slayer of such a person most severely, which it would not do unless injury were committed against them contrary to right and equity. Since, then, the law punishes one who kills a willing person as for an injury inflicted, is it not clear that injury is done to the willing person? Answer: by denying the consequence. For the execution of laws does not prove that injury is done to the willing person, but only to the commonwealth or to nature. For the law punishes such slayers because they have injured nature itself and the commonwealth, not the person to whom they caused loss. They injure nature because they destroy the work of nature, contrary to its aim and intention; they injure the commonwealth because they deprive it of one of its members. 2. Instance. Many innocent people willingly suffer insults and deadly injury, as various histories attest. Therefore, is it still true that injury is done to the willing person? Answer: Although they suffer what is unjust, they do not suffer injury, and this suffering can be called voluntary and involuntary in different respects. For with respect to nature, which always intends its own preservation, it can be called involuntary; but with respect to the end which the innocent set before themselves, it can be called voluntary, because innocent people prefer to undergo such sufferings willingly rather than stain their name, reputation, or even piety. 3. Instance. The modest person, who gives more to others than he keeps for himself, as the Philosopher says in Nicomachean Ethics 4, ch. 12, willingly suffers injury. Therefore can someone also not

units.la: Nicom. cap. 12. tantum in bonis anima & corporis, sed etiam fortuna volens pati injuria? Resp. Etsi modestus, qui vel humilitatis vel amoris vel charitatis gratia, plus aliis tribuat, quam sibi relinquat, & sic videatur sibi injuriam facere, non facit tamen, sicut docet Philosophus hoc capite exemplo Glauci & Diomedis, quia in potestate sua ipsius est hoc facere vel non facere. Dein etiam capite 7. hujus libri, distinguit Philosophus inter damnum & injuriam: damnum quidem talis patitur, quod de suo commodo aliquid detrahat: injuriam proprie non patitur, cum omnis injuria contra voluntatem patientis proprie fiat.
units.tr: Nicom. ch. 12. only in goods of soul and body, but even in fortune, be willing to suffer injury? Answer: Although the modest person, who from humility, love, or charity gives more to others than he keeps for himself, and so seems to do himself an injury, does not in fact do so, as the Philosopher teaches in this chapter by the example of Glaucus and Diomedes, because it is in his own power to do this or not to do it. Then also, in chapter 7 of this book, the Philosopher distinguishes between loss and injury: one who suffers loss has something taken from his advantage, but he does not properly suffer injury, since every injury is properly done contrary to the will of the one who suffers it.

units.la: II. Contra secundam quaestionem: An etiam verum illud fit, aliquem interdum sponte sua pati, cum ipsa ratio contrarietur.
units.tr: II. Against the second question: Whether it is also true that someone sometimes suffers something willingly, even though reason itself opposes it.

units.la: Nam nemo sponte sua patitur malum, ut docet Philosophus hoc cap. At omne injustum est malii quid, quia est vitium oppositum ipsi Justitiae. Proinde nemo patitur injustum quid sponte sua? Resp. Injustum esse duplex, vel per se, vel per accidens. Injustum quidem per se, quod ex proaeresi & cum cognitione circumstantiarum fit, est malum, sicut Phil. docet: at vero per accidens, cum absque omni proaeresi & judicio fiat, tunc proprie malum non dicitur. Secundo etiam respondari solet, licet omne injustum sit malum, tamen iniustum pati semper non est malum, quia potest aliquis iniustum aliquid pati praetextu majoris boni, & sic sponte sua pati injustum, quod voluit Philosophus.
units.tr: For no one willingly suffers evil, as the Philosopher teaches in this chapter. But every unjust thing is some evil, since it is the vice opposed to Justice itself. Therefore no one willingly suffers anything unjust? Answer: Unjust is twofold, either in itself or by accident. What is unjust in itself, which is done from deliberate choice [προαίρεσις] and with knowledge of the circumstances, is evil, as the Philosopher teaches; but what is done by accident, without any deliberate choice or judgement, is not properly called evil. Secondly, it is also commonly answered that although every unjust thing is evil, to suffer what is unjust is not always evil, because someone may suffer something unjust under the pretext of a greater good, and so willingly suffer what is unjust, as the Philosopher intended.

units.la: III. Contra tertiam quaestionem: An non verum etiam sit, quod omnis, qui patitur injustum aliquid, etiam pati-
units.tr: III. Against the third question: Is it not also true that everyone who suffers something unjust also suffers

units.la: patiatur injuriam, cum natura conjugatorum hoc postulet, sicut docet Philosophus 2. Top. cap. 4. ut stuprum infit, etiam & alterum infit? Resp. Hoc axioma non est necessario verum, sed contingenter tantum. Nam habet suas conditiones & restrictiones, sicut docet Philosophus 2. Nicom. cap. 4. quia in iis tantum valet, quorum alterum altero non latius patet: at vero injustum multo latius patet, quam injuria, sicut supra in textu probavit Philosophus. Proinde fieri potest, ut aliquis pariatur iniustum quid, & tamen non patiatur injuriam.
units.tr: injury, since the nature of married persons requires this, as the Philosopher teaches, Top. 2, ch. 4, that where fornication occurs, adultery occurs too? Answer: This axiom is not necessarily true, but only contingently so. For it has its conditions and restrictions, as the Philosopher teaches, Nicom. ch. 4, book 2, since it holds only for those things of which one is not broader in extent than the other. But the unjust is far broader in extent than injury, as the Philosopher proved above in the text. Therefore it can happen that someone suffers something unjust and yet does not suffer injury.

units.la: Caeterum cum volenti nulla fiat iniuria, sicut Philosophus hic asserit, & ratio etiam evincit, poterit haec quaestio non incommode subiici: An scilicet, qui volentem & consentientem virginem abducit invitis insciisque parentibus, volenti fiat iniuria, necne? Resp. In virgine consideranda duo: 1. Personam ipsam virginis. 2. Jus in personam. Et licet simpliciter volenti & consentienti nulla fiat iniuria quoad personam, sit tamen iniuria quoad ius in personam quam parentibus (qui proprie ius in virginem habent, & in quorum potestate omnes liberi, praesertim minorennes sunt, ut testatur Justinianus tit. 9. lib. 1. Instit. de patria potestate, & l. 3. item in potestate, ff. de hn, qui sui vel alieni juris sunt & l. 12. Paulus, ff. de statu hominum) apertissime iniuria fit, quoniam iis iniquissima vi clam eripitur, ideo eiusmodi raptus & abductio iure Caesareo sub poena atroci est prohibita, ut testatur variae historiae C. de raptu virginum, dicitur simpliciter volenti, quia etsi aliquis rapiat virginem, tenetur illi promissa non tantum praestare ex pacto conventu, sed etiam omnia ea, quæ ad fidem faciendam serviunt l. una 13. C. de raptu virginum. Nam si ex una parte accedat expressa & libera voluntas, ex altera dolosa persuasio is, qui per dolum decipitur, pro non volente habetur, imo dolosa persuasio magis est, quam violenta coactio in iure civili l. 3. §. si quis volentem, ff. de libero homine. Proinde ut paucis dirimatur quæstio, etsi simpliciter consentiat virgo, sed dolosa persuasio impulserit ad consensum, volenti dicitur fieri iniuria, non tantum quoad ius in personam, sed etiam, quia alio fine & modo voluit, quam ut dolose à parentibus abduceretur.
units.tr: However, since no injury is done to one who is willing, as the Philosopher asserts here, and reason also proves, this question may fittingly be raised: Is injury done to a willing person when someone leads away a virgin who is willing and consenting, against the wishes and without the knowledge of her parents, or not? Answer: Two things must be considered in the virgin: 1. the virgin's person itself; 2. the right over the person. And although, absolutely speaking, no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting as regards the person, yet injury is done as regards the right over the person to the parents, who properly hold the right over the virgin, and in whose power all children are, especially minors, as Justinian testifies, tit. 9, lib. 1, Instit., de patria potestate, and l. 3, item in potestate, ff. de his qui sui vel alieni juris sunt, and l. 12, Paulus, ff. de statu hominum. Injury is done to them most plainly, since she is secretly snatched from them by the most unjust violence; therefore such abduction and rape is forbidden under severe penalty by imperial law, as various histories attest, C. de raptu virginum. It is said that she is willing in the absolute sense, because even if someone abducts a virgin, he is bound to perform not only the promises made in the agreement, but also all those things which serve to make good faith, l. una 13, C. de raptu virginum. For if on one side there is express and free will, and on the other a deceitful persuasion, the one who is deceived by fraud is held to be unwilling; indeed deceitful persuasion is considered worse than violent coercion in civil law, l. 3, §. si quis volentem, ff. de libero homine. Therefore, to settle the question briefly: even if the virgin absolutely consents, but was driven to consent by deceitful persuasion, injury is said to be done to one who is willing, not only as regards the right over the person, but also because she willed it for another purpose and in another manner than to be secretly led away by her parents.

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XIII.

units.la: Continetur hoc capite duæ insignes quæstiones, quæ spectant ad quartum membrum secundi tractatus huius libri. Partes capitis sunt duæ: In prima duas istas quæstiones proponit. In secunda eas etiam solvit, potissimum vero primam, quia ex eius solutione & decisione facilis erit responsio ad secundam quæstionem.
units.tr: This chapter contains two notable questions, which concern the fourth member of the second treatise of this book. The chapter has two parts. In the first part, he sets out these two questions. In the second he also resolves them, chiefly the first, because from its solution and decision the answer to the second question will be easy.

units.la: In prima igitur duas ait restare quæstiones ex iis, quas supra de inferenda aut ferenda iniuria proposuerat: 1. est; An qui distribuit, aut dat aliquid; an verò qui accipit plus æquo, iniuriam faciat? 2. Quæstio, quæ ex hac oriri videtur, est hæc; An scil. cum modesti homines hoc plerunque facere soleant, ut sibi minus, aliis plus concedant, aliquis in rebus distribuendis sibi facere possit iniuriam? Quæ duæ quæstiones cum ad naturam Juris & Iustitiæ illustrandam plurimum faciant, hic non immerito disquirendæ videntur.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he says that two questions remain from those he had raised above about inflicting or suffering injury: (1) Does the one who distributes or gives something do wrong, or rather the one who receives more than his due? (2) The question that seems to arise from this is: Since modest people usually make a practice of allotting less to themselves and more to others, can someone do himself an injustice in the distribution of goods? Since these two questions contribute greatly to clarifying the nature of right and justice, they seem not undeservedly to be investigated here.

units.la: In secunda parte redit ad primam & principalem quæstionem tractandam, quæ quæstio, ut melius intelligatur, & ex mente Philosophi dissolvatur, sciendum est, duo esse distribuentium genera, seu duo esse genera eorū, qui aliquid partiuntur aut distribuunt, nam vel duo homines privati aliquid inter se dividunt, vel arbiter aut judex inter alios. De primo genere tribuentium statuit Philosophus, partientem aut tribuentem non facere injuriam, etsi minus sibi, aliis plus concedat, idque probat duabus rationibus: 1. Quia multos reperire licet, qui minorem & deteriorem partem libenter sibi assumant, vel ostentationis, vel gloriolæ, vel laudis captandæ gratia, ut scilicet hoc modo videantur faciles & liberales, & hac ratione multos sibi amicos parant. Quam rationem fusius dilatat i magn.moral cap. 13. quod nempe ejusmodi homines sint plerunque ambitiosi & honoris cupidi, & dum sic iniquè res distribuunt, ut nempe minorem partem sibi assumant, viam faciliorem ad ambitionem sumant. 2. Ratio, quia licet neque ambitionis neque gloriæ causa hoc faciant, nullam tamen sibi faciunt injuriam, cum sponte sua & libera voluntate hoc faciant. Atqui ex superioribus patet, quæ cap. 11. sunt tradita, injuriam proprie non fieri, nisi contra ejus, cui infertur, voluntatem. De altero genere tribuentium, quales sunt arbitri & Judices, ut supra jam diximus, sic statuit Philosophus: tribuentem quidem facere injuriam, accipientem verò non. Idque confirmat trib us rationibus: 1. Quod initium hujus actionis sit in tribuente, à quo primum provenit hæc largitio aut distributio, tio, non vero in accipiente, cum ille sit tantum patiens, & primus in eo non consistat tribuendi modus. Notandum tamen & accipientem facere posse injuriam, licet no directe, tamen indirecte, idq; duobus modis: 1. Si inter distribuendum, majore aut meliore partem sibi assumat, quam par sit, aut etiam aliquid, quod aliis dari debet, sibi refervet. 2. Si distribuentem ad iniquè distribuendum pecunia, vel alia aliqua re impulerit. II. Ratio, qua probat tribuentem, non accipientem facere injuriam, petitur ab homonymia τῷ ἀδικεῖν. Nam injustè facere interdum significat rem injustam agere, interdum verò injuriam facere, ut exc. 11. sup. patet, idq; duobus modis Vel principaliter, vel instrumentaliter, v.g. lignû, lapis, & ejusmodi instrumenta, inanimata, itè animata instrumenta, ut manus, alio impellente, aut servus jubente domino, dum aliquè laedunt aut interficiunt, rè quidem injustâ agunt, injuriâ tamen non faciunt, cùm illi non sint causæ principales: sed aut ille, qui inanimata illa instrumenta excitavit, ad hoc malum agedum, aut qui manum intulit, aut qui servo mandavit, illi tanquam causæ principales injuriam solam faciunt. Sic qui alteri plus æquo tribuit, est causa principalis inæqualitatis, accipiens verò tantum instrumentalis. Ideo tribuens proprie facere dicitur iniuriam, non verò accipiens, licet qui plus æquo accipit, iniustè etiam hoc modo facere dicatur. III. Ratio est hæc, Distribuens aut tribuens considerari poterit duobus modis: Vel quatenus insciens, vel sciens iniustè aliquid agit, id quod in exemplis melius patebit, verbi gratia: Judex imprudenter aliquâdo iudicat, & plus æquo alicui attribuit imprudenter, sed tamen ex præscripto iuris civilis. Hic neque iniuriam facit, neque iudicium eius in hac distributione iniustum dicitur, respectu nempe iuris civilis aut legitimi, quod hic sequitur, quia nescit, se contra ius & æquum peccasse; Iniuriam vero agere, requirit non tantum proæresin, sed cognitionem circumstantiarum. At vero si hæc distributio imprudenter facta & a sententia Judicis confirmata, repugnet iuri primævo seu naturali, hic tamen utcunque iniuriam facit, cum ab ipso initium huius malæ actionis proveniat; Jus enim naturale neque ignorari potuit neque debuit. Et qui sic peccat, ignorantiam sibi hanc de industria accersit, ut testatur Philosophus lib. 3. cap. 2. Quid si scienter agat, & cognoverit ius civile cum omnibus circumstantiis, & tamen inæqualiter distributionem administret, hic plane iniuriam facit per se. Plus enim sibi tribuere videtur in eo, quod vel propter favorem alicuius partis hoc agat, ut sic sibi alteram partem conciliet, vel ut iniquo hoc iudicio iniuriam sibi aut suis allatam vindicet, aut etiam partem aliquam iniqua hac distributione reservet, atque ita sciens & prudens peccat, non tantum tribuendo, sed etiam accipiendo, verbi gratia: dum Judex aliquis aut arbiter iniustus agrum, aut agri aliquam partem inter duos iniquè distribuit, nō sumit sibi fortasse pro labore aliquam agri partem, sed aut pecuniā, aut aliquid tale, quod pecuniæ aut agro respondeat, & sic dum largitionibus se corrumpi patitur, nō tantum hominibus privatis, sed etiam toti Reip. damnum & detrimentū infert. Proinde hoc tandem sequitur, quia alicui plus aut minus æquo dat aut distribuit, interdum non facere iniuriam, si nemo fit aliquis privatus: interdum vero facere, si in dignitate publica fit collocatus, propter rationes supra allatas. Plura vide de hac quæstione supra ad cap. 7. ubi de Justitia Commutativa. De altera vero quæstione; An scilicet in rerum distributione sibi quis facere possit injuriam? infra agit cap.ult. propterea quod cum Justitia proprie dicta sit bonum, quod se extendit ad alios, & ideo proprie nemo sibi facere possit iniuriam, unde de hac quæstione in Justitia improprie dicta, pluribus agit.
units.tr: In the second part he returns to treat the first and principal question. So that this question may be better understood and resolved according to the mind of the Philosopher, it must be known that there are two kinds of those who distribute, or two kinds of those who divide something out: for either two private persons divide something between themselves, or an arbiter or judge divides between others. Concerning the first kind of distributors, the Philosopher holds that the one who divides or allots does not do wrong, even if he gives himself less and others more, and he proves this by two reasons: (1) Because one may find many who willingly take to themselves the smaller and worse share, either for show, for a little glory, or to win praise, so that by this means they may seem easygoing and generous, and by this method they gain many friends. The Magna Moralia, cap. 13, enlarges on this reason more fully, namely that such men are for the most part ambitious and eager for honour, and while they distribute goods so unequally as to take the smaller share for themselves, they take the easier road to ambition. (2) The second reason is that, although they do not do this for the sake of ambition or glory, they still do themselves no injury, since they do it of their own accord and by free will. Yet it is clear from what was delivered above, in cap. 11, that injury is properly not done except against the will of the one to whom it is inflicted. Concerning the other kind of distributors, such as arbiters and judges, as we have already said above, the Philosopher holds as follows: the distributor indeed does wrong, but the recipient does not. He confirms this by three reasons: (1) Because the beginning of this action lies in the distributor, from whom this giving or distribution first proceeds, and not in the recipient, since he is merely the one who suffers, and the manner of distributing does not first arise in him. It should be noted, however, that the recipient too can do wrong, though not directly, yet indirectly, and this in two ways: (a) if, while the distribution is being made, he takes for himself a larger or better share than is fitting, or even keeps back for himself something that ought to be given to others; (b) if he has induced the distributor to distribute unjustly by means of money or some other thing. (2) The reason by which he proves that the distributor, and not the recipient, does wrong is drawn from the ambiguity of the word "to do wrong" [ἀδικεῖν]. For to act unjustly sometimes means to perform an unjust deed, and sometimes to inflict injury, as is clear from exc. 11 above, and this in two ways: either principally or instrumentally. For example, wood, stone and such inanimate instruments, or animate instruments such as a hand moved by another, or a slave acting at his master's command, when they harm or kill someone, do an unjust thing, yet they do not inflict injury, since they are not the principal causes. But he who stirred up those inanimate instruments to do the evil, or he who laid on the hand, or he who ordered the slave, alone inflicts injury as the principal causes. Thus the one who gives another more than his due is the principal cause of the inequality, while the recipient is only an instrumental cause. Therefore the distributor is properly said to inflict injury, and not the recipient, although the one who takes more than his due is also said in this way to act unjustly. (3) The third reason is this: the distributor, or the one who allots, may be considered in two ways: either insofar as he acts unjustly unknowingly, or insofar as he acts unjustly knowingly, which will be clearer in examples. For instance: a judge sometimes judges imprudently and imprudently assigns more than due to someone, but yet in accordance with the prescription of civil law. Here he does no injury, nor is his judgement in this distribution called unjust, namely with respect to civil or statutory law, which he follows, since he does not know that he has sinned against law and equity. But to do injury requires not only deliberate choice but knowledge of the circumstances. If, however, such an imprudently made distribution, confirmed by the judge's sentence, conflicts with the primeval or natural right, he nevertheless does injury in some sense, since the beginning of this evil action comes from himself; for natural law could neither be unknown nor ought to be. And one who sins in this way brings this ignorance upon himself deliberately, as the Philosopher testifies in lib. 3, cap. 2. What if he acts knowingly, and has understood the civil law with all its circumstances, and yet administers the distribution unequally? Then he plainly does injury in himself. For he seems to give himself more in that he does this either for the favour of some party, so as to win that party to himself, or in order to avenge by this unjust judgement an injury done to himself or his own, or even to keep back some part for himself through this unjust distribution. And so he sins knowingly and deliberately, not only by giving but also by receiving. For example: when some unjust judge or arbiter unjustly divides a field, or some part of a field, between two parties, he perhaps takes for himself, as payment for his labour, not a part of the field but money, or something of that kind which is equivalent to money or to the field; and so, by allowing himself to be corrupted by bribes, he inflicts loss and harm not only on private persons but on the whole commonwealth. Accordingly this finally follows: when someone gives or distributes to another more or less than his due, sometimes he does not do injury, if no one is a private person; but sometimes he does, if he has been placed in public dignity, for the reasons adduced above. See more on this question above, at cap. 7, where he speaks of Commutative Justice. As for the other question, namely whether someone can do injury to himself in the distribution of goods? He treats it below, in the last chapter, because since justice properly so called is a good that extends to others, therefore properly no one can do injury to himself; hence he treats this question at greater length under justice improperly so called.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Ad cognitionem juris plurimum interest, scire, an qui plus minus ve dat aut distribuit, faciat injuriam: an vero qui accipit: Item, an quis in rerum distributione sibi facere possit injuriam?
units.tr: 1. For the knowledge of law it matters greatly to know whether he who gives or distributes more or less does an injustice, or rather he who receives. Likewise, can someone do an injustice to himself in the distribution of goods?

units.la: 2. Qui alteri plus tribuit sciens, volensque, quam sibi retinet, iniuria sibi sum non afficit, cum nihil contra voluntatem hic faciat.
units.tr: 2. He who knowingly and willingly gives another more than he keeps for himself does not wrong himself, since in this he does nothing against his will.

units.la: 3. Modesti hoc plerunque facere solent, ut de jure suo cum suo etiam ipsorum damno, alteri cedant.
units.tr: 3. Modest people generally do this, that they yield their right to another, even with loss to themselves.

units.la: 4. Qui aut gloria aut ostentationis ergo plus alii tribuit, quam sibi assumit, injuria nulla afficitur, cum sponte sua tantum hoc faciat.
units.tr: 4. He who gives another more than he takes for himself, out of vainglory or for show, suffers no injury, since he does this of his own accord.

units.la: 5. Multi sunt, qui damnum patiuntur, qui tamen iniuriam non patiuntur, cum alterum plena voluntate, alterum non nisi coacta voluntate sustineatur.
units.tr: 5. There are many who suffer loss but do not suffer injury, since one bears it with a full will and the other only with a constrained will.

units.la: 6. Qui alteri plus justo tribuit, ille tantum injuriam facit, non vero qui accipit, quia ab eo principium pravæ actionis non provenit.
units.tr: 6. He who gives another more than is just does the injustice, but not he who receives, because the origin of the wrongful action does not lie with him.

units.la: 7. Inanimata instrumenta, ut lignum, lapis, &c. item animata, ut servus aut manus, iniusta quadam facta instrumentaliter committere dicuntur, non vero principaliter in iure hoc facere, cum aliorum impulsu, non suo tantum agunt.
units.tr: 7. Inanimate instruments, such as wood, stone, etc., and likewise animate ones, such as a slave or a hand, are said to commit certain unjust deeds instrumentally, not principally in law, since they act at the impulse of others and not only of themselves.

units.la: 8. Qui contra ius naturale peccat, & secundum ius civile recte iudicat, inscienter quidem peccat, sed ita aut ignorantia pro excusatione admitti non potest.
units.tr: 8. He who sins against natural law, yet judges rightly according to civil law, sins indeed unknowingly, but such ignorance cannot be admitted as an excuse.

units.la: 9. Multum inter se differunt ius naturale & civile, quia naturale est tantum fundamentum Juris civilis, & veluti generale includit in se, alterum tanquam speciale.
units.tr: 9. Natural law and civil law differ greatly, because natural law is only the foundation of civil law and includes it within itself as the general includes the special.

units.la: 10. Qui scienter contra ius civile peccant, sicuti iudices & arbitri quidam iniusti, aut favoris aut vindictae aut lucri gratia facere solent, iniuriam non modo faciunt, sed damnum & privatis & toti etiam Reipub. inferunt.
units.tr: 10. Those who knowingly sin against civil law, as certain unjust judges and arbitrators are wont to do for the sake of favour, revenge or gain, not only do an injustice but also inflict loss both on private persons and on the whole commonwealth.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An recte Philosophus inanimata instrumenta, ut sunt lapis, lignum, &c. iniusta quadam facta patrare posse statuat, licet ex habitu non iniuste agant, cum, cui non competit unum contrariorum, ei etiam nec alterum competere possit. At Justitia solis competit animantibus, ut volunt Jurisconsulti tit. 2. lib. 1. Instit. aut solis hominibus, ut supra cap. 10. docuit Philosophus, cui etiam astipulatur Cic. lib. 1. offic. cum igitur iuste agere seu Iustitia solis convenit hominibus: Ergo etiam ex lege contrariorum, Iniustitia, & per consequens inanimatis instrumentis ligno, lapidi, & caeteris eiusmodi, falso ascribitur Iniustitia a Philosopho? Resp. Verum illud quidem, Justitiam & ejus contrarium Injustitiā, nempe solis competere hominibus, propterea quod iis solis competat ratio: sed hic Philosophus sophus allusisse videtur ad veterum Græcorum mo- res & instituta, cū dicit res inanimatas injusta quæ- dam facinora committere posse. Nam Athénis lege Draconis (Dracon verò & Solon Legislatores erant Atheniensium, quorum ille de delictis & pœnis le- ges severißimas tulit, & omnia morte multanda es- se voluit: unde illud proverbium: Draconis leges non atramento, sed sanguine sunt scripta: hic verò leges istas severas mitigavit, & ad ius & æquum magis reduxit) pœna constituta fuit in res inanimatas, ut in ligna, lapides, &c. Si quis eorum lapsu aut projectu læ- sus aut vulneratus esset, in mare tanquam res nefa- rias præcipitari jubebat. Sanxit item pœnas in res animatas, sed rationis expertes ut in beluas. Nam si sus aut bos aliquem læsissent aut occidissent, suspen- dere statim jubebat, & sic de aliis etiam statuit fa- ciendum, teste Suida in verbo Nicon. & Demosthene in oratione contra Aristocratem, & Pausania in libello de securi Buonis, (Buon verò dicebatur is, qui bovem mactabat in honorem Neptuni & postea securim, qua bovem mactabat, quia sanguinem fuderat in mare aut aquam, projiciebat:) Item etiam statuit Plato lib.9.de legib. Neque tantum hoc apud Ethni- cos viguit, sed etiam jure divino in beluas saltem pœna constituta fuit, ut videre est Genef. 9. v. 5. Exod. 21. vers.29. Levit.20 vers.15. Item in iure civili præser- tim in tit.si quadrupes pauperiem fecerit.
units.tr: I. Question: Did the Philosopher rightly state that inanimate instruments, such as stone, wood, etc., can commit certain unjust deeds, even though they do not act unjustly from a disposition? For where one of two contraries does not belong, the other cannot belong either. But Justice belongs only to living beings, as the jurists hold, Inst. tit. 2, lib. 1, or only to human beings, as the Philosopher taught above in ch. 10, to which Cicero also agrees, lib. 1 Offic. Therefore, since acting justly, or Justice, belongs only to human beings, then by the law of contraries Injustice, and consequently injustice, is falsely ascribed by the Philosopher to wood, stone and the like? Answer: It is true that Justice and its contrary, Injustice, belong only to human beings, because reason belongs to them alone. But here the Philosopher seems to have alluded to the customs and institutions of the ancient Greeks when he says that inanimate things can commit certain unjust deeds. For at Athens, under the law of Draco (Draco and Solon were the lawgivers of the Athenians; the former enacted most severe laws on crimes and penalties and wanted all of them punished by death, whence the proverb: Draco's laws were written not in ink but in blood; the latter mitigated those severe laws and brought them back more toward right and equity), a penalty was established against inanimate things, such as wood and stones. If anyone was harmed or wounded by their fall or throwing, he ordered them to be cast into the sea as guilty things. He also laid down penalties against animate beings lacking reason, such as beasts. For if a pig or an ox had harmed or killed someone, he at once ordered it to be hanged, and he decreed that the same should be done in other cases, as witnessed by Suidas in the word Nicon, by Demosthenes in the speech against Aristocrates, and by Pausanias in the little book on the axe of Buon. (Buon was the name given to the man who slaughtered an ox in honour of Neptune and afterwards threw into the sea the axe with which he had slaughtered it, because it had shed blood in the sea or water.) Plato also laid this down in book 9 of the Laws. Nor did this prevail only among the heathen; a penalty was also established against beasts by divine law, as may be seen Gen. 9:5, Exod. 21:29, Lev. 20:15. Likewise in civil law, especially in the title "if a four-footed animal has caused damage".

units.la: Poterit & hoc etiam propter affinitatem, quam habet cum hisce quæstionibus, hoc capite proposi- tis, breviter quæri: An scilicet pater filio, maritus uxori, herus servo injuriam facere possit? Resp. Etsi Philosophus cap. 9. huius libri neget ejusmodi personas injuriam facere posse, propter duas potissimum rationes. Sunt tamen, qui contrarium tuentur, & ideo pro & contra disceptari poterit haec quaestio. Rationes Philosophi sunt hae: 1. Quia inter patrem & filium, maritum & uxorem, dominum & servum non est proprie jus, sed improprie & tantum secundum similitudinem juris civilis: Ubi vero jus proprie non est, ibi neque injuria, quia ubi unum contrariorum non reperitur, ibi nec alterum habere locum proprie potest. 2. Quia nemo sibiipsi facere potest injuriam, sicuti infra capite ultimo, pluribus disceptabit: Ergo inter ejusmodi personas fieri non potest injuria. Consequens inde probatur, quia filius, praesertim minorennis, est pars patris ex jure civili, l. 2. ff. de stipulationibus: Uxor etiam est dimidium mariti; servus est propria heri possessio, ut supra iam cap, 9. probatum fuit. Cum igitur in jure non distinguantur a se invicem istae personae, injurii sibi invicem facere non possunt. Pro contraria sententia quatuor adferuntur rationes: 1. Quia non minus a Deo & recta ratione leges patri, marito, & hero praescriptae sunt, secundum quas illis vivendum est, quam aliis: ubi vero sunt leges, ibi etiam ius locum habet: Nam nihil aliud sunt leges, quam iuris ipsius regulae & conditiones. 2. Quia proprie loquendo neque filius est pars patris, neque uxor dimidium mariti, neq; servus heri possessio: Sed improprie tantum sic sumuntur a legibus. 3. Quia iniuriam facere definitur cap. 11. sponte aliquem laedere contra ipsius & voluntatem, & contra legem: At ejuseiusmodi personis competere potest hoc, ut sponte laedant: Ergo etiam ut iniuriam faciant. 4. Quia sic sequeretur e contrario, neque filium patri, neque uxorem marito, neq; servum hero iniuriam facere posse, quod non modo absurdum est, sed omnibus legibus tam divinis quam humanis prohibitum. At vero ex distinctione iniuriae facile salvari poterit Aristoteles. Nam iniuria consideratur bifariā, quatenus nempe vel publice vel privatim fit, seu quatenus committitur in personam, quae est membrum Reipub. aut in personam, quae tantum consideratur ut membrum familiae, quae familia uni tantum subest capiti. Priori modo negat Philosophus, patrem filio, maritum uxori, herum servo posse facere iniuriam, propterea quod inter eiusmodi personas ius civile seu Politicum non reperiatur: posteriori modo non negat. Proinde prima & tertia ratio in contrarium allata, loquuntur de legibus privatis & domesticis, non vero publicis, & directe pro Republ. ipsa latis, & ideo nihil contra Philosophum concludit. Secunda ratio sumit partes naturaliter, non vero legaliter, sicut in iure ubique sumuntur, nam quaecunque constituunt personam, aut ad unā personam spectant, vulgo partes illius personae in iure vocantur. Quarta ratio est penitus falsa, nam etsi pater filio, &c. iniuriam Politice inferre nequeat, non sequitur, filium patri econtra non posse, quia huiusmodi iniuria & iure naturali & gentium & civili passim est prohibita.
units.tr: This may also briefly be asked, because of its affinity with the questions proposed in this chapter: Can a father do an injustice to his son, a husband to his wife, a master to his slave? Answer: Although the Philosopher, in chapter 9 of this book, denies that such persons can do an injustice, chiefly for two reasons, there are nonetheless those who hold the contrary, and so this question can be debated for and against. The Philosopher's reasons are these: (1) Between father and son, husband and wife, master and slave there is not properly right, but only improperly and merely by resemblance to civil right. Where right does not properly exist, neither can injustice properly exist, since where one of the contraries is not found, the other cannot properly have a place. (2) No one can do an injustice to himself, as in the last chapter we shall discuss at length. Therefore injustice cannot occur between such persons. The consequence is proved thus: a son, especially a minor, is a part of the father by civil law, l. 2 ff. de stipulationibus; a wife is also half of the husband; a slave is the master's property, as already proved in chapter 9. Since these persons are therefore not distinguished from one another in law, they cannot do injustice to one another. For the contrary opinion four reasons are offered: (1) Laws are prescribed by God and right reason no less to the father, the husband and the master than to others, and they must live according to them; but where there are laws, right also has its place, for laws are nothing other than the rules and conditions of right itself. (2) Strictly speaking, a son is not part of the father, a wife not half of the husband, nor a slave the master's property; but the laws take these terms only improperly. (3) Injustice is defined in chapter 11 as wilfully harming someone against his will and against the law; but such persons are able to harm one another wilfully, and therefore also to do injustice. (4) For otherwise it would follow, conversely, that a son cannot do an injustice to his father, a wife to her husband, or a slave to his master, which is not only absurd but forbidden by all laws, divine and human. But Aristotle can easily be saved by a distinction of injustice. For injustice is considered in two ways: namely, as it is done publicly or privately, that is, as it is committed against a person who is a member of the commonwealth, or against a person who is considered only as a member of a household, which is subject to a single head. In the former way the Philosopher denies that a father can do an injustice to his son, a husband to his wife, or a master to his slave, because no civil or political right exists between such persons; in the latter way he does not deny it. Accordingly, the first and third reasons brought to the contrary speak of private and domestic laws, not of public ones, and laws given directly by the commonwealth itself, and so they conclude nothing against the Philosopher. The second reason takes parts naturally, not legally, as in law they are everywhere taken; for whatever constitutes a person, or belongs to one person, is commonly called in law a part of that person. The fourth reason is entirely false, for although a father cannot inflict injustice on his son politically, etc., it does not follow that a son cannot inflict it on his father, since such an injury is forbidden everywhere by natural law, by the law of nations and by civil law.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: SEquitur hoc capite tertia & ultima pars, quæ spe‐ctat ad quartum membrum secúdi tractatus hu‐jus libri, in qua Philosophus tres vulgi errores refu‐tat, ut naturam ipsam Juris & Justitiam magis illu‐stret. Partes capitis sunt duæ: In prima hos tres errores accuratè refellit, ut sic omnium animis eximat: Nam & Plato & plerique Athenjensium hos errores am‐plectebantur. In secunda corollarium infert de Justi‐tia, & in quibus personis jus proprie locum habeat, perspicuè docet.
units.tr: Following this chapter comes the third and last part, which relates to the fourth member of the second treatise of this book. In it the Philosopher refutes three errors of the common people, so as to make the nature of Law and Justice itself clearer. The chapter has two parts. In the first, he carefully refutes these three errors, so as to free the minds of all from them, for both Plato and most of the Athenians embraced these errors. In the second, he draws a corollary about Justice and clearly teaches the persons in whom law properly has its place.

units.la: In prima igitur errores istos singillatim refellit, & primum, qui fuit talis: Existimabant vulgò, & injuriam facere, & iustitiam exercere, in sua cuique potestate situm esse, & proinde utramque rem esse facilimam. Quàm vulgi opinionem commemorat etiam Plutarchus in vita Catonis Uticensis, disputans, Cur iniusti omnium deterrimi habeantur? & hanc affert rationem, propterea quod vulgò creditum sit, quemlibet iustum esse posse, qui velit, fortem & prudentem non item, ut pote quibus naturæ quædam bonitas sit necessaria; ut verò aliquis iustè agat certa tantum requiritur voluntas, quæ cum in cuiusque arbitrio sit posita, facile quis iuste aut iniuste agere possit. At licet sic vulgò existiment homines, longe tamen falluntur: Nam quanquam singularis aliqua actio, ut verbi gratia: uxoris alienæ violatio, proximi verberatio aut pulsatio (quæ spe‐ctant ad Iniustitiam) item debiti solutio, eiusq; generis alia præstare officia, quæ ad Justitiam pertinet, non sit operosum admodum & difficile, quia semel & illico fit: ex habitu tamen certaque animi proaeresi & constantia agere est operosum admodum & perquam difficile, cum a nullo habitus (cuiusmodi sunt iuste & iniuste agere, perite & scienter agere, quaeque habitum vitiorum aut virtutum constituunt) nisi longo usu & assidua agendi consuetudine, sicut praeclare lib. 2. cap. 4. huius operis docet Philosophus, comparari possit. Constat tamen habitum vitiorum cum in natura hac corrupta omnes in malum proniores sint, facilius multo comparari posse quam virtutes, & ideo maxime respexit Philosophus habitum Iustitiae non Iniustitiae, cum diceret, rem esse perquam difficilem perite & ex habitu Iustitiam exercere. In summa, licet actio tam Iustitiae quam Iniustitiae non sit difficilis, habitus tamen utriusque est difficilis, difficilior etiam multo habitus virtutis quam vitii, quia a virtute ingenii quadam pravitate abhorrere solent homines, sicut cap. 10. lib. 2. huius operis docet Philosophus.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he refutes these errors one by one. The first was this: people commonly thought that both doing injustice and practising justice lie within each person's power, and that therefore both are very easy. Plutarch also records this popular opinion in the Life of Cato of Utica, where he discusses Why are the unjust considered the worst of all? He gives this reason: it is commonly believed that anyone who wishes can be just, but not brave and prudent, since these require a certain natural goodness. To act justly, however, only a certain will is required, and since this lies in each person's power, anyone can easily act justly or unjustly. But although people commonly think this way, they are greatly mistaken. For although a single action, for example violating another man's wife, beating or striking a neighbour (which belong to injustice), or likewise paying a debt and performing other duties of that kind which pertain to justice, is not very laborious or difficult, since it is done once and at once, yet to act from a settled habit, with a fixed moral purpose and constancy, is very laborious and extremely difficult. A habit of this kind, such as acting justly or unjustly, acting skilfully and knowingly, and whatever constitutes the habit of vices or virtues, cannot be acquired by anyone except through long practice and constant custom of acting, as the Philosopher teaches admirably in Book 2, chapter 4 of this work. Yet it is clear that, since all are more inclined to evil in this corrupt nature, the habit of vice can be acquired much more easily than virtues. For this reason the Philosopher principally had in view the habit of Justice, not of injustice, when he said that it is very difficult to practise justice skilfully and from habit. In sum, although acting justly or unjustly is not difficult, the habit of either is difficult, and the habit of virtue is much more difficult than that of vice, because men usually shrink from virtue on account of a certain perversity of character, as the Philosopher teaches in Book 2, chapter 10 of this work.

units.la: Secundus error est, de cognitione Iuris: Existimant enim vulgo iuris & iniuriae cognitionem esse rem perquam facilem, propterea quod iusta & iniusta legibus publice praescriptis, quae iusta praecipiunt, & iniusta prohibent, continentur, & ideo quivis facile & per se scire potest, quid iustum & iniustum sit. Respondet Philosophus aliud esse indeterminate scire quid iustum & iniustum, aliud determinate: Nam licet prius illud non sit prorsus difficile, utpote ad quod natura quadam curiositate propendent homines, sicut docent lex 1. ff. de iuris & facti ignorantia; determinatè tamen & pro variis circumstantiis scire quo tem- pore, quo loco, cui personæ, cui etiam fini leges pro iusto & iniusto latæ adhiberi debeant, est perquam difficile, & ideo iustum & iniustum cognoscuntur duobus modis: 1. Per se & in suo valore, hoc est perquam difficile, quia singularem prudentiam, longam experientiam, & maximum rerum usum postulat. 2. Per accidens & ex eventu, & hoc non est difficile, quia cuivis obvium esse poterit cum confusa rerum notitia & iuris generalis cognitio, naturæ quodam instinctu omnibus innascatur. Hanc iuris & iniuriæ cognoscendæ difficultatem illustrat Philosophus similitudine quadā ducta ab arte medica: Nam sicut vinum, mel, helleborum, item usus aut sectio corporis facile per se cognoscuntur, cum in sensus externos incurrant: at vero medicinam ex prioribus facere aut posteriora convenienter adhibere pro sanitate vel recuperanda vel conservanda est summæ difficultatis, sicut docet Galenus lib.2.de facult.aliment. Tertium error est, quod vulgò existimenthomines, iustos peræque ac iniustos iniuriam facere posse, propter hanc rationem, quod experientia doceat, iustum aliquem alium pulsare aut verberare, uxorem alienam violare, convitia dicere, &c. non minus quam iniustum, & cum unum contrarium bene norit iustus, id est, recte agere, multò facilius possit alterum, nempe indirecte seu iniuste agere, quia sub praetextu Iustitiæ & Amicitiæ facilius lædi possunt homines, cum à iustis & amicis nihil sibi prorsus metuant. Verùm utut concedat Philosophus, quod iustus interdum præter scopum & naturam virtutis suæ aliquem lædere possit, injustè tamen agere aut injuriam facere negat, propterea quod, ut ex superioribus patet, ad injuriam inferendam, necessarius sit habitus, ad læsionem non item. Deinde etiam facta viri justi & injusti multum differunt: nam injustus injustè agit ex habitu; justus verò non item: cum duo contrarii habitus eidem semel & simul inesse non possint. Proinde licet interdum rem injustam facere possit vir justus ex imbecillitate naturæ, & quia labi humanum est, injuriam tamen proprie non facit, quia injuria, quæ directè opponitur Justitiæ, ex habitu, sicut jam diximus, & proœresi proficiscitur: sicut in arte medica purgare, urere, secare, non sunt idem, quod mederi, licet actiones quædam sint medicæ, sed tum demum habitum constituunt medicum, cum promtè & paratè & ex certa scientia & longo usu peraguntur.
units.tr: The second error concerns the knowledge of law. People commonly think that knowledge of what is right and wrong is a very easy matter, because just and unjust things are contained in laws publicly prescribed, which command what is just and forbid what is unjust, and therefore anyone can easily and by himself know what is just and unjust. The Philosopher replies that it is one thing to know in an indeterminate way what is just and unjust, and another to know it determinately. For although the former is not altogether difficult, since men are inclined to it by a certain natural curiosity, as the law 1, Digest, on ignorance of law and fact teaches, yet to know in a determinate way, and according to varying circumstances, at what time, in what place, for what person, and even for what end the laws enacted concerning just and unjust things ought to be applied, is extremely difficult. Therefore, just and unjust things are known in two ways: (1) through themselves and in their own worth, and this is very difficult, because it requires singular prudence, long experience and very great familiarity with affairs; (2) by accident and from the outcome, and this is not difficult, because anyone can come upon it with a confused knowledge of things and a general knowledge of law, since this is implanted in all by a kind of natural instinct. The Philosopher illustrates this difficulty of knowing what is right and wrong by a comparison drawn from the medical art. For as wine, honey, hellebore, and likewise the use or cutting of the body are easily known in themselves, since they fall under the external senses, yet to make medicine from the former, or to apply the latter suitably for the recovery or preservation of health, is of the greatest difficulty, as Galen teaches in Book 2 of On the Properties of Foods. The third error is that people commonly think that just men can do injury just as much as unjust men, for this reason: experience shows that a just man strikes or beats another, violates another man's wife, utters abuse, and so on, no less than an unjust man. And since the just man well knows the one contrary, namely to act rightly, he can much more easily do the other, namely to act indirectly or unjustly, because under the pretext of justice and friendship men can be harmed more easily, since they fear nothing at all from just men and friends. Yet, however much the Philosopher concedes that a just man may sometimes harm someone beyond his aim and the nature of his virtue, he denies that he acts unjustly or does injury, because, as is clear from what precedes, a habit is necessary for inflicting injury, but not for harm. Moreover, the deeds of a just man and of an unjust man also differ greatly, for the unjust man acts unjustly from habit, but the just man does not, since two contrary habits cannot be in the same person at once and together. Therefore, although a just man may sometimes do an unjust thing because of the weakness of his nature, and because it is human to slip, he nevertheless does not properly do injury, because injury, which is directly opposed to justice, proceeds from habit and moral purpose, as we have already said. Just as in the medical art, purging, burning and cutting are not the same as healing, although they are certain medical actions, but only then do they constitute the physician's habit, when they are performed readily, skilfully, from certain knowledge and long practice.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis de iis personis agit, inter quas locum ius habet: Nam non satis est naturam ipsius Juris ostendere, nisi etiam quibus proprie competit, ostendatur; & sicut supra cap.; huius lib. de bonis, circa quæ Justitia servatur, tractavit, ita etiam hic de personis commodè agendum erit. Jus verò proprie iis personis competere docet, quæ bonorum externorum (aliàs ista bona vocantur Fortunæ, & proprie sunt objecta Justitiæ) ita sunt participes, ut inter nimium & parum, excessum & defectum, sicut recti præscribit ratio, recte & rite versentur. Quod, ut magis perspicuum reddat, duo adfert personarum genera (ut ita dicam) in quibus jus proprie locum habere videtur. Nam jus competit vel Diis,
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with those persons among whom law has its place. For it is not enough to show the nature of Law itself unless it is also shown to whom it properly belongs. And just as above, in the chapter of this book, he treated the goods in which justice is observed, so here too it will be fitting to deal with persons. He teaches that law properly belongs to those persons who so share in external goods (which are otherwise called goods of fortune, and are properly the objects of justice) that they deal rightly and duly with them, in accordance with the excess and deficiency, the too much and the too little, as right reason prescribes. To make this clearer, he brings forward two kinds of persons, so to speak, in whom law seems properly to have its place. For law belongs either to gods

units.la: yel vel hominibus: Diis vero jus non competit, quia licet bonis superabundent, utpote qui omnia mortalibus suppeditant, nunquam tamen plus justo habent, & ideo neque nimium, neq; excessus in iis reperitur; & proinde neque jus, quia cum medium & extrema sint relata, cui unum non competit, neque alterum etiam competere potest. Adfert & aliam rationem infra cap.8. lib.10. hujus operis, cur nullum in Diis jus locum habeat, quia nempe indignæ sunt Diis actiones rerum contrahendarum, quippe necessitatem aliquam important, quam Diis affingere nemo sine impietate potest; ubi etiam neque cæteras virtutes Diis attribui recte posse, docet. Cuietiam adstipulatur Cicero lib.3. de natura Deor. Quæ omnia contra Platonem illata videntur, qui in variis Dialogis & 1. de legib. Justitiam & ius sicut & reliquas virtutes Diis inesse fingit. Secundum genus personarum statuit homines, qui rursus sunt duorum generum: Nam quidam sunt tam perverso ingenio, ut nulla re, quantumvis exigua bene utantur, quos hic in textu insanabiles, perditos & deploratos vocat Philosophus, apud quos cum nullus sit legitimus bonorum externorum usus, ius proprie locum non habet. Nam non, nisi ex coactione aut legibus impositis; non vero ex animo, aut proaresi aut etiam habitu bene agendi Justitiam ipsum in rebus ipsis servant. Alii sunt homines, qui in fortunæ bonis nunc nimium, nunc parum habent, & nunc bene nunc male iis utuntur, quo in genere sunt plerique mortales, qui recte rationis ductum sequuntur, & in his proprie locum ius habet, cum nempe medio Justitia tiæ inter excessum & defectum student, internúmque animi habitum externis actionibus perficiunt.
units.tr: or to men. Law does not belong to the gods, because although they abound in goods, as those who supply all things to mortals, yet they never have more than is just, and therefore there is neither too much nor excess in them; and consequently neither is there law, since, as the mean and the extremes are related, the one to which the other does not belong cannot have the other belonging to it either. He also gives another reason, in chapter 8 of Book 10 of this work, why law has no place in the gods: namely, that actions of contracting things are unworthy of the gods, since they imply some kind of necessity, which no one can ascribe to the gods without impiety; there he also teaches that the other virtues too cannot rightly be attributed to the gods. Cicero also agrees with this in Book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods. All these arguments seem to be aimed against Plato, who in his various Dialogues and in the First Book of the Laws imagines that justice and law, like the other virtues, are present in the gods. The second kind of persons he sets up is men, who in turn are of two kinds. For some are of so perverse a disposition that they make no good use of anything, however small; these the Philosopher here in the text calls incurable, lost and hopeless, and among them, since there is no lawful use of external goods, law does not properly have its place. For they keep justice in things only by compulsion or by imposed laws, and not from the heart, or from moral purpose, or even from a habit of acting well. Others are men who at one time have too much and at another too little of the goods of fortune, and who at one time use them well and at another badly. Most mortals belong to this class, and they follow the guidance of right reason.
