In these, law properly has its place, since they strive for the mean of justice between excess and deficiency, and bring their inner habit of mind to completion in outward actions.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Licet plerique existiment iustè & iniustè agere esse perquam facilè, difficultas tamen inest, quod, ut ritè & servatis circumstantiis utrumq; fiat, habitus necessario requiratur.
units.tr: 1. Although most people think that acting justly and unjustly is quite easy, there is a difficulty: to do either rightly and with the circumstances observed, a habit is necessarily required.

units.la: 2. Licet quivis facilè scire possit, quid iustum & iniustum sit indeterminatè, determinatè tamen pro tempore, loco & personis non facilè scire poterit.
units.tr: 2. Although anyone can easily know what is just and unjust in general, one cannot easily know it in particular, that is, for the time, place and persons involved.

units.la: 3. Justus peraquè ac iniustus iniustè agere non poterit, cum habitu vitiorum, proinde ac iniustus, nō contraxerit.
units.tr: 3. A just person, no less than an unjust one, cannot act unjustly, since he has not acquired the habit of vices, as the unjust person has.

units.la: 4. Jus in iis personis proprie locum habet, quæ bonorum externorum ita sunt participes, ut medium inter excessum & defectum, sicut recta præscribit ratio, observent.
units.tr: 4. Right (ius) properly applies to those persons who share in external goods in such a way that they observe the mean between excess and defect, as right reason prescribes.

units.la: 5. In Diis licet bonis superabundent, cùm bonis nusquam abutantur, ius proprie, quod voluit Plato, locum non habet.
units.tr: 5. In the gods, although they abound in goods, since they never misuse goods, right in the proper sense, which Plato wanted, does not apply.

units.la: 6. Est quoddam genus hominum ita deploratum, ut nullum in rebus humanis medium, sicut recta præscribit ratio, observent, & in his jus locum non habet, nisi quoad coactionem & pœnam.
units.tr: 6. There is a certain class of men so depraved that they do not observe any mean in human affairs, as right reason prescribes; and for these men right does not apply, except with respect to compulsion and punishment.

units.la: 7. Directè & proprie ius inter eiusmodi homines locum habet, qui ab extremis omnia ad medium & aequalitatem dirigunt.
units.tr: 7. Right applies directly and properly among those people who direct all things from the extremes to the mean and to equality.

units.la: I. Quæritur: An recte Philosophus neget, iustè & iniustè agere situm esse in nostra potestate, cum tamen lib.3. capite 5. disputans contra Platonem, contrarium affirat, cum & virtutes & vitia in nostra esse potestate varijs rationibus docet. Nam & iustè agere & iniustè proveniunt ab actionibus nostris, quarum actionum principium est ipsa voluntas. Proinde cum actiones omnes tam bona quam mala in nostra sint potestate, etiam & iuste & iniuste agere erunt, & per consequens, & sibi & rationi contrariari videtur Philosophus? Resp. Non negat Philosophus simpliciter ista non esse sita in nostra potestate, sed quia non possumus facile & ex habitu aut juste ut injuste agere, ideo habitum & ipsam facilitatem agendi negat esse in nostra potestate, contra quod tamen pleriq; opinabantur.
units.tr: I. It is asked: Does the Philosopher rightly deny that acting justly and unjustly lies within our power, when yet in book 3, chapter 5, disputing against Plato, he affirms the contrary, teaching in several ways that both virtues and vices are within our power? For acting justly and acting unjustly both arise from our actions, and the principle of these actions is the will itself. Therefore, since all actions, both good and bad, are within our power, acting justly and unjustly will also be within our power, and consequently the Philosopher seems to contradict both himself and reason? Reply: The Philosopher does not simply deny that these things are within our power; but because we cannot easily act justly or unjustly from a habit, he denies that the habit itself and the ease of acting are within our power, although many thought otherwise.

units.la: II. An recte etiam neget, justum perinde ac iniustum agere posse iniuriam, cum contrarium, & sensus communis, & quotidiana doceant exempla. Nam Davidut est 1 Reg 11. non minus poterat uxorem Uriæ polluere, quod & fecit, quia alius. Sic & plurima exempla idem testantur apud Ethnicos. Unde male hac in parte vulgi opinionem damnare videtur? Resp. Exempla ista nihil probant: nam facilitas agendi in rebus humanis provenit ab habitu tanquam à sua causa: Cum igitur justus æquè habitum vitiorum non contraxerit ac injustus, jure negavit Philosophus justum peræquè facere injuriam, posse ac injustum, licet quoad singularem aliquam actionem labi & errare interdum justus non minus possit, quam injustus, sed quoad habitū non potest.
units.tr: II. Does he also rightly deny that a just person, just as much as an unjust one, can commit injustice, when common sense and everyday examples teach the contrary? For David, as is said in 1 Reg. 11, could no less defile Uriah's wife, and did so, than another could. Likewise many examples to the same effect are found among the heathen. Hence he seems to condemn the opinion of the common people wrongly on this point? Reply: Those examples prove nothing. For the ease of acting in human affairs arises from the habit as from its cause. Since therefore the just person has not acquired the habit of vices any more than the unjust person has, the Philosopher rightly denied that a just person can commit injustice just as readily as an unjust one. Although a just person may sometimes slip and err in a particular action, no less than an unjust one, he cannot do so in respect of the habit.

units.la: III. Cur Philosophus ista fortuna bona, in quibus, ut ex cap. 3. huius libri patet, Justitia proprie cernitur, hic simpliciter vocet bona in hoc textu, cum ratio repugnet: nam cum casu quodam aut fortuna aliqua homini accidant, ideo fortuna vocantur bona; tum etiam ipse Philosophus 1. mag. moral. cap. 21. vocat ἀδιάφορα, idest, neque per se bona aut mala, nisi quatenus iis bene vel male utuntur homines? Resp. Ideo vocavit bona sine adjectione, quia toto hoc lib. de Justitia potissimum agit, & respectu Justitiæ possunt dici bona simpliciter, cum circa nulla alia bona versetur Justitia. Secundo etiam respectu usus sui, nam in bono usu & apud viros bonos possunt dici etiam bona simpliciter, quo sensu à Jurisconsultis hæc externa bona simpliciter & absque omni adjectione bona nuncupantur.
units.tr: III. Why does the Philosopher here simply call those fortunate goods, in which, as appears from chapter 3 of this book, justice is properly discerned, "goods" in this passage, when reason opposes this? For since they happen to a man by some chance or fortune, they are called fortunate goods; and the Philosopher himself, in Magna Moralia 1, chapter 21, calls them indifferent things [ἀδιάφορα], that is, neither good nor bad in themselves, except insofar as men use them well or badly? Reply: He called them goods without qualification because in this whole book he treats chiefly of justice, and with respect to justice they can be called goods simply, since justice is concerned with no other goods. Secondly, also with respect to their use: in good use and among good men they can also be called goods simply, and in this sense the jurists call these external goods simply and without any qualification "goods".

units.la: IV. & ult. Cur in Diis, & in quibusdam hominibus ius locum habere neget, cum tamen utrumque manifestè ratio evincat: Nam Dii sunt principia omnis boni, & proinde ipsius etiam iuris, quod non fieret, nisi ius in iis locum haberet: quomodo enim quis ius in aliū transfundere posset, quod ipse non habet? Quod verò ad homines, si qui tales sint, quibus jus proprie non competit, tunc enim ex hisce duob. absurdis sequitur, aut oës homines non esse capaces felicitatis, cū non sint capaces virtutum, quæ tendunt ad felicitatem, nam hic quidem excluduntur à iure ipsius Justitiæ effecta: aut secundo sequitur, Justitiam non esse virtutem, quod utrumq; est perabsurdum? Resp. Ideo negavit ius proprie cöpetere Diis, quod de virtute humana hic agat, quæ Diis affingi proprie nequit. Dein etiam ibi jus locum proprie habet, ubi extrema nempe vitia cernuntur, quæ Diis etiam asscribere est nefas. Quod ad homines, ideo negat jus in quibusdam habere locum, quod, ut ipse in textu refert, quidam prorsus sint incurabiles & ita vitiis immersi, ut ab iis ad virtutem revocari nullo modo possint. Dein etiam, licet quidam recedant à Justitia & Jure, quoad habitum & perfectionem, non tamen quoad singularem aliquam actionem semper & ubique recedunt: neque valet illud ababsurdum, quod nisi jus in omnibus individuis hominibus locum habeat, ideo non esse omnes felicitatis capaces: nam non omnes individuo seu singulari, sed in Idæa & specie sunt summi boni capaces, & quo modo finis homini competit, eodem etiam modo media ipsa competere dicuntur. Cum igitur felicitas sit hominis in genere bonum, & non hujus aut illius proprium, etiam & media, quæ ad ipsam tendunt, ad hominem in genere spectabunt.
units.tr: IV. and last. Why does he deny that right applies to the gods and to certain men, when reason clearly proves both? For the gods are the principles of all good, and therefore of right itself, which would not come about unless right applied to them; for how could anyone transfer to another a right that he himself does not have? As for men, if there are any to whom right properly does not belong, then from these two absurdities follows either that all men are incapable of happiness, since they are incapable of the virtues which tend to happiness (for these are indeed excluded from the effects of right itself, which is justice), or, secondly, that justice is not a virtue; and both of these are utterly absurd? Reply: He denied that right properly belongs to the gods because this passage deals with human virtue, which cannot properly be ascribed to the gods. Next, right properly applies where extreme vices are observed, and to ascribe these to the gods is also impious. As for men, he denies that right applies in certain people because, as he himself reports in the text, some men are utterly incurable and so immersed in vices that they cannot in any way be recalled from them to virtue. Furthermore, although some depart from justice and right with respect to habit and perfection, they do not always and everywhere depart from it with respect to every single action. Nor does that absurd conclusion hold, namely that unless right applied to all individual men, not all would be capable of happiness: for not all men are capable of the supreme good as individuals or singly, but in idea and in species they are. And just as the end belongs to man, so in the same way the means to it are said to belong to him. Therefore, since happiness is a good of man in general, and not the property of this or that individual, the means that tend towards it will also be regarded as belonging to man in general.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: TRactatur hoc capite secunda pars hujus libri, in quo Philosophus agit de Bono & Æquo, quæ sunt affectiones Justitiæ, & quomodo utrumque ad homines se habeat, breviter tamen explicat, ut hoc loco, sic 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 2. & 2. mag. moral. cap. 1. Cæterum etsi Philosophus breviter de utroque hic agat, propterea quod de Justitia potissimum sibi agendum proposuerit, & in gratiam Justitiæ de bono & æquo, cum tamen in vita communi & causis forensibus maximus sit utriusque usus, de utroque copiose & accurate agunt Jurisconsulti tam veteres, quam recentiores, ut videre licet apud Oldendorpium in tractatu de iure & æquo. Membra huius secundæ partis sunt tria, & quia continetur hoc capite, totidem etiam erunt hujus capitis partes: In prima ut naturam boni & æqui melius explicet, controversiam quandam proponit: An scilicet æquum sit idem cum iure necne? In secunda parte istam controversiam dextre discutit & solvit: In tertia, quid justum & æquum sit, & quis vir justus & æquus dici debeat, præclare docet. In
units.tr: This chapter treats the second part of this book, in which the Philosopher discusses the Good and the Equitable, which are affections of Justice, and how each relates to human beings. He explains them briefly here, as in 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 2. & 2. mag. moral. cap. 1. Although the Philosopher treats both only briefly, because he had proposed to deal chiefly with Justice and treats the good and the equitable for the sake of Justice, nevertheless both have very great use in common life and in legal cases. Therefore the jurists, both ancient and more recent, treat both copiously and accurately, as may be seen in Oldendorp in tractatu de iure & aequo. The members of this second part are three, and since they are contained in this chapter, there will be as many parts of this chapter too. In the first, in order to explain the nature of the good and the equitable better, he sets out a certain controversy: whether the equitable is the same as law or not. In the second part he skilfully discusses and resolves that controversy. In the third, he teaches admirably what is just and equitable, and who ought to be called a just and equitable man. In

units.la: In prima igitur dubitationem hanc seu controversiam proponit: An scilicet æquum sit idem cum jure, de quo superius egit, an vero diversum quid? Quod non sit idem probat duabus rationibus: Quarum prior ducitur ab adjuncta laude; quia longe majori laude extollere solet communis experientia bonum & æquû; Item viros bonitate & æquitate præstantes, quam Jus & Justitiam, ut viros justos. Cum igitur juris & æqui longe díspar locus sit, non possunt esse unum & idem, namque unum & idem secundum magis & minus laudare non solemus. Posterior ratio, quia vulgò melius habetur æquitas seu æquum, quam jus, propterea quod æquitas magis se accommodet ad vitæ humanæ utilitatem, quam jus quod secundum rigorem Justitiæ ipsam Justitiam administrare docet. Econtra quod non sint plane diversum quid, hinc probat ab absurdo, quod inde sequeretur, quia si æquum aut æquitas esset quid bonum & diversum aut contrarium juri, tunc sequeretur esse malum quid. Proinde etsi affectionibus quibusdam differant, genere tamen communi conveniunt, alias sequeretur absurdum modo allatum.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he sets out this doubt or controversy: whether the equitable is the same as law, which he treated above, or something different. He proves that it is not the same by two arguments. The first is drawn from the praise attached to each. For common experience is accustomed to extol the good and the equitable with far greater praise, and likewise men excelling in goodness and equity, than law and justice, or just men. Since, then, law and equity have very different standing, they cannot be one and the same, for we do not usually praise one and the same thing by degrees of more and less. The second argument is that equity, or the equitable, is commonly held to be better than law, because equity adapts itself more closely to the usefulness of human life, whereas law, which according to the strictness of justice teaches how to administer justice itself, does not. On the other side, he proves from the absurd that they are not altogether something different, because it would follow from this that if the equitable or equity were something good and different from, or contrary to, law, then it would follow that it is something bad. Therefore, although they differ in certain affections, they agree in a common genus, otherwise the absurdity just mentioned would follow.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis istam controversiam jam propositam accurate diluit, & dicit, etsi alterum altero sit melius quid, non tamen hoc sequitur genere inter se differre: nam & homo præstat bruto, & tamen sunt species sub uno animali, & genere inter se conveniunt. Docet vero, unde hæc controversia originem traxerit; nempe quod æquitas, seu æquum non sit idem cum jure civili, de quo superius cap. 10. fuit actum, sed sit juris tantum civilis correctio & emendatio quaedam, nam jus civile (quod aliàs καθ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur Lex à Jurisconsultis) cum universaliter latum fit, per æquitatem in quadam quasi speciali-tate corrigitur. Quod verò lex universaliter lata fit, testatur jus civile l. quia, ff. de legibus, quod idem & Plato lib. 1. de legib. & in Politico, & Aristoteles 3. Polit. cap. 7. & 1. Rhet. cap. 1. pulcherrimè docent; Ideo propter universalitatem suam singularibus quibusdam casibus ob infinitam eorum multitudinem rectè accommodari nequit: nam quod in hoc singulari justum esse dicitur, alibi in alio singulari injustum reprehenditur, hic Judex sententia sua diversum quid à jure universali constituit, quod dicitur æquitas seu jus æquum, quod tamen à jure universali seu à lege scripta, licet sit diversum, nô tamen ei contrariatur, verbi gratia: Jus universale est ut parricidæ, qui patres interficiunt, culeo insuantur, & in mare præcipitentur. At verò si furiosus aliquis patrem interfecerit, æquitas illum à juris universalis pœna liberat. Est enim æquitas quasi legis (quæ est veluti regula & commune præceptum, de hac vel illa re ad vitam humanam spectante, vel facienda vel omittenda) exceptio quædam, quæ non contrariatur legi, sed subordinatur ad mitigationem pro variarum circumstantiarum ratione. In negotiis igitur ejusmodi, ubi universalis quædam legis positio requiritur, nec tamen lex de singularibus quibusdam casibus rectè promulgari potest, ibi tum lex assumit illa, quæ communiter contingere solent, cum interim fiat, ut singulares quidam casus emergant, in qui-bus bus, si lex universaliter scripta adhiberetur, plane foret injusta; lex tamen in se & sua natura manet justa, neque enim in lege aut in legislatore, sed in negotii ipsius natura vitium residet, nam eorum, quae sub actionem cadunt ob infinitam eorum multitudinem, materia est perquam variabilis, adeo ut nulla lex certa de iis constitui possit, quod exemplis melius demonstrari poterit, verbi gratia: Lex ratum habet & firmum testatoris testamentum tanquam ipsius voluntatem ultimam, & vult, ut bona ab ipso legata, secundum ipsius voluntatem distribuantur: interim aliquis moriturus relinquit uxorem gravidam, & pro infante nascituro trecentos relinquit florenos: lex vult, ut certum & ratum hoc maneat, interim tamen accidit, ut gravida non unum aut alterum infantem pariat, sed tres, quatuor, quinque; forte; hic lex si adhiberetur de voluntate testatoris praestanda, respectu illus casus emergentis, plane foret injusta, nihilominus tamen lex in se manet justa, quia leges non de iis, quae raro, sed quae communiter & plerunque in vita communi accidunt, feruntur: Id quod testatur jus civile l. 3. cum tribus seqq. ff. de leg. ea enim proprie spectant leges, quae communiter & plerunque, non quae raro & extraordinarie accidere solent l. antiquitus, ff. de hered. pet. cui adstipulabatur etiam Plato in Politico. Cum igitur lex aequaliter de rebus ipsis pronunciet, neque certum singularum rerum eventum respiciat, aequitas secundum rectam rationem pro casuum incidentium respectu legem ipsam restringit, & ideo ipso jure aequitas aliquid melius esse videtur, non tamen omni jure, sed universali tantum & indeterminato, cujus est emendatio & interpretatio, si forte lex propter universalitatem suam vim & naturam casus singulares subinde incidentes, neglexisse videatur: quae correctio juris partim fit sententia & autoritate ipsius judicis, si adsit tunc singularem etiam legem aut potius decretum, de singulari aliquo casu ferre solet, ut experientia docet: partim etiam haec correctio fit ab aequitate ipsa, quae pro variis circumstantiis secundum rectam rationis pro tempore regulam, legem ipsam restringit.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he accurately resolves the controversy now proposed, and says that although one of the two is better than the other, it does not follow from this that they differ from each other in genus: for man excels the brute, and yet there are species under one animal, and they agree with each other in genus. He teaches, moreover, whence this controversy arose, namely that equity, or the equitable, is not the same as civil law, which was treated above in chapter 10, but is merely a certain correction and emendation of civil law. For civil law (which is otherwise called, by way of eminence [καθ' ἐξοχὴν], Law by the jurists), since it is enacted in universal terms, is corrected by equity in a certain kind of special case. That law is enacted universally is attested by the civil law, l. quia, ff. de legibus, and Plato lib. 1. de legib. & in Politico and Aristotle 3. Polit. cap. 7. & 1. Rhet. cap. 1. teach this most beautifully. Therefore, because of its universality, it cannot be rightly applied to certain single cases, given their infinite multitude. For what is said to be just in one single case is found unjust in another single case elsewhere. Here the judge, by his sentence, establishes something different from universal law, which is called equity or the equitable law. Yet although it is different from universal law, or from written law, it is not contrary to it. For example: the universal law is that parricides, who kill their fathers, be sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea. But if some madman has killed his father, equity frees him from the penalty of universal law. For equity is, as it were, an exception to law (which is like a rule and common precept concerning this or that matter touching human life, to be done or omitted), not contrary to law, but subordinate to it, for the sake of mitigation according to the circumstances of various cases. In affairs of this kind, therefore, where a universal enactment of law is required, yet the law cannot rightly be promulgated concerning certain single cases, then the law takes those things which commonly happen. Meanwhile it comes about that certain single cases emerge, in which, if the universally written law were applied, it would plainly be unjust. Yet the law remains just in itself and in its own nature, for the fault lies not in the law or in the lawgiver, but in the nature of the affair itself. For the material of those things which fall under action is, because of their infinite multitude, exceedingly variable, so that no fixed law can be laid down concerning them. This can be shown better by an example: the law holds a testator's will valid and firm as his last wish, and wills that the goods bequeathed by him be distributed according to his will. Meanwhile a man about to die leaves a pregnant wife, and leaves three hundred florins for the infant about to be born. The law wills that this remain certain and valid. Yet it happens that the pregnant woman bears not one or two infants, but three, four, perhaps five. Here, if the law were applied so that the testator's will had to be carried out with respect to that emerging case, it would plainly be unjust. Nevertheless the law remains just in itself, because laws are made not concerning those things which happen rarely, but concerning those which happen commonly and for the most part in common life. The civil law attests this, l. 3. with the three following, ff. de leg., for laws properly regard those things which commonly and for the most part, not those which happen rarely and extraordinarily, l. antiquitus, ff. de hered. pet. Plato in the Politicus also agreed with this. Since, then, the law pronounces evenly about the things themselves, and does not regard the certain outcome of individual things, equity, according to right reason, restricts the law itself with respect to the cases that arise. Therefore equity by its own right seems to be something better, not indeed better than all law, but only than universal and indeterminate law, whose correction and interpretation it is, if perhaps the law, because of its universality, seems to have neglected the force and nature of the single cases that arise from time to time. This correction of law is partly made by the sentence and authority of the judge himself, who, if he is present, is accustomed to issue also a special law, or rather a decree, concerning some single case, as experience teaches. Partly, too, this correction is made by equity itself, which, according to the various circumstances and according to the rule of right reason for the time, restricts the law itself.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis explicat, quid sit aequum seu aequitas, nempe quod sit juris universalis quaedam correctio & emendatio ea parte, qua lex deficit. Lex enim propter universalitatem suam omnes circumstantias & casus incidentes satis observare nequit, & ideo ad commoditatem vitae humanae assiduis opus est decretis & plebisscitis (quae secundum aequitatem sunt juris quaedam emendationes) quae in horas pene singulas variant, prout alia atque alia negotia emergunt, ut sic infinitis negociis propter rerum universitatem regula accommodetur variabilis, non secus ac structurae Lesbiae plumbea seu flexilis adhibetur regula: Lesbii enim in aedificiis exstruendis propter lapidum asperitatem plumbeam adhibebant regulam, quae ad lapidum formā se accommodaret, cum alias lapides potius ad regulam dirigi & conformari deberent) sic etiam decreta, quae subinde feruntur, variis vitae negotiis sese accommodant, cum alioqui varia vitae negotia legibus ipsis secundum rectam rationem latis, se accommodare dare deberent. Tandem concludit hinc, ex his, quæ de bono & æquo dicta sunt, facilè intelligi potest, quis sit vir bonus & æquus, quem describit à quatuor potissimum proprietatibus: 1. Quod consultò & exproætersi tam in sua, quam in aliena causa æquitatem sequatur. 2. Quod non secundum rigorem juris, sed secundum æquitatem actiones suas dirigat. 3. Quod non sit severus summi juris aut extremi exactor, & 4. demum, quod in defectu potius peccet, & ad defectum declinata juris scripti severitate omnia accommodet, etsi juris auxilio niti tuto possit, neque propterea æquitas, secundum quam vir bonus & æquus agit, habitus toto genere à Justitia discrepans aut diversum quid dici poterit, cum sit Justitia quædam particularis, pro variis circumstantiis & singularibus, qui incidunt casibus ad res ipsas accommodata. Cæterum de æquitate, de qua tanquam juris universalis laxamento hic agit Philosophus tria ista præcipuè notanda sunt: 1. Definitio, quæ ut ex hoc cap. colligitur, est juris universalis correctio, qua propter generalitatem deficere videtur. Dicitur autem Lex deficere, non quod in lege scripta ullus sit proprie defectus, cum plurium prudentum, secundum rectæ rationis regulam, consensu feratur, sed quia lex in genere tantum sancit, nec quicquam in specie propter circumstantiarum & negotiorum varietatem constituit: hic æquitas intervenit, & in specie exponit & determinat, quæ generaliter à lege scripta, seu à jure universali constituta sunt. Unde & à Jureconsultis definitur: Moderatio & benigna juris interpretatio l. placuit 8. ff. de judiciibus & l. 17. bona fides, ff. depositi. Vocatur legum ipsarum bona fides, quòd secundum utilitatem hominum & sinceram Legislatoris fidem, leges explicet. Pendet autem haec aequitas à prudentia judicis arbitrio, qui sua prudentia & multiplice rerum variarum experientia, certis adductus rationibus, legem benignè interpretatur, & ad hominum utilitatem accommodat. Exemplum illustre habet Valerius Maximus lib. 6. cap. 5. Zaleucus, inquit, urbe Locrensium a se salubberrimis atque utilissimis legibus munita, cum filius ejus adulterii crimine damnatus, secundum jus ab ipso latum utroque oculo carere deberet, ac tota civitas in bonorem patris necessitatem poena adolescentulo remitteret, aliquamdiu repugnavit, ad ultimum precibus populi victus, suo primum, dein filii oculo eruto, usum videndi utriquē reliquit, atque ita per singularem modum Justitiae satisfecit: aequitatis mirabili temperamento se inter misericordiam patrem & justissimum Legislatorem partitus. H. Notanda veniunt aequitatis effectα, quae propter humanae vitae utilitatem efficere solent. Haec autem à Philos. 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 13. duplicia constituuntur, Generalia nempe & Specialia. In genere aequitatis effecta sunt: 1. Jus scriptum benignius & mitius interpretari. 2. In Juris interpretatione non ad legem scriptam, sed ad Legislatorem: non ad orationem & verba, sed ad sensum & mentem Legislatorum respicere. 3. Si quid in jure scripto sit omissum supplere, atque ita corrigere & emendare jus scriptum. In specie vero effecta sunt varia: 1. Non ad actionem ipsam, sed ad intentionem & proaresin agentis, non ad partem actionis, sed ad totam re-spicere. spicere, neq; etiá perpendere, qualis is nunc fit, qui delinquit, sed qualis semper & plerunq; fuerit, atq; itafi semel fuerit bonus, adhuc bonum præsuppo- nere. 2. Non iisdem pœnis digna judicare omnia delicta, cum diversa sint delictorum genera, nam ut ex cap. 11. superiori patet: alia sunt delicta, quæ vocantur infortunia, & quæ præter opinionem & absque omni malitia fiunt: alia sunt errata, quæ licet non semper præter opinionem, sine omni tamen malitia committuntur: alia sunt quæ vocantur flagitia, quæ ex proæresi fiunt, & destinata cum malitia sunt conjuncta, & ideo æquitas pro diversis delictorum generibus diversas etiam solet constituere pœnas.
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he explains what the equitable, or equity, is: namely, a certain correction and emendation of universal law in the respect in which law is deficient. Because of its universality, law cannot observe all circumstances and incidental cases sufficiently. Therefore, for the convenience of human life, there is constant need of decrees and enactments (which, according to equity, are certain emendations of law), which vary almost every hour as different business arises. In this way a rule that is variable is adapted to the infinite variety of affairs arising from the nature of things, just as the leaden or flexible rule of the Lesbians is used in building. For the Lesbians, in constructing buildings, used a leaden rule because of the roughness of the stones, a rule that would adapt itself to the shape of the stones, whereas otherwise the stones would have to be directed and shaped to the rule. So too the decrees that are issued from time to time accommodate themselves to the various affairs of life, whereas otherwise the various affairs of life ought to accommodate themselves to the laws enacted according to right reason. Finally, he concludes from this that, from what has been said about the good and the equitable, it can easily be understood who the good and equitable man is. He describes him chiefly by four properties: (1) he follows equity deliberately, both in his own cause and in another's; (2) he directs his actions not according to the strictness of law but according to equity; (3) he is not severe, nor an exacter of the utmost right; and (4) above all, he errs on the side of deficiency, setting aside the severity of the written law and accommodating everything to circumstances, although he could safely rest on the help of law. Nor, for this reason, will the equity by which the good and equitable man acts be a habit differing in kind from Justice, or be called something other than it, since it is a certain particular Justice, adapted to the things themselves and to the single cases that arise according to the various circumstances. Moreover, three things are especially to be noted about equity, of which the Philosopher here treats as a relaxation of universal law. 1. The definition, which, as is gathered from this chapter, is a correction of universal law, by which it seems to fall short on account of its generality. Law is said to fall short not because there is any true defect in written law, since it is enacted by the consensus of many prudent men according to the rule of right reason, but because law lays down only in general terms and establishes nothing in particular, on account of the variety of circumstances and affairs. Here equity intervenes and sets out and determines in particular what has been laid down in general by written law, or universal law. Hence the jurists also define it as "the moderation and kindly interpretation of law" (l. placuit 8. ff. de judiciis, and l. 17. bona fides, ff. depositi). It is called the good faith of the laws themselves, because it explains the laws according to the usefulness of men and the sincere good faith of the Lawgiver. This equity, however, depends on the judgment of a prudent judge, who, guided by certain reasons, through his prudence and his manifold experience of various things, interprets the law kindly and adapts it to the usefulness of men. Valerius Maximus (lib. 6. cap. 5.) gives a notable example. Zaleucus, he says, having fortified the city of the Locrians with most wholesome and useful laws, when his son, condemned for the crime of adultery, ought by the law he himself had enacted to lose both eyes, and the whole city, out of respect for the father, was remitting the penalty to the young man, resisted for some time. At last, overcome by the entreaties of the people, he had one of his own eyes and then one of his son's torn out, leaving each of them the use of sight, and so satisfied Justice in a singular manner, dividing himself with a wonderful moderation of equity between a merciful father and a most just Lawgiver. H. The effects of equity, which it usually produces for the usefulness of human life, are to be noted. Philosophers (1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 13) set these out in two kinds, general and particular. The general effects of equity are: (1) to interpret written law more kindly and mildly; (2) in interpreting law, to look not to the written law but to the Lawgiver, not to the wording and words but to the sense and mind of the lawgivers; (3) to supply whatever has been omitted in written law, and so correct and amend written law. The particular effects are various: (1) to look not to the action itself but to the intention and deliberate choice of the agent, and not to a part of the action but to the whole; and not to weigh what kind of man the offender now is, but what kind he has always and generally been, so that if he has once been good, one still presumes him to be good. (2) Not to judge all offences worthy of the same penalties, since there are different kinds of offences. For, as is clear from the eleventh chapter above, some offences are called misfortunes, which happen beside expectation and without any malice; others are errors, which, although not always beside expectation, are nevertheless committed without any malice; others are called crimes, which are done from deliberate choice and are joined with a settled malice. Therefore equity is accustomed to assign different penalties to the different kinds of offence.

units.la: 3. Et hoc ad æqualitatem spectat, aliquid de suo jure remittere, veniamque dare delinquentibus in omnibus iis, in quibus decet, & in quibus ratio non repugnat. 4. Meminisse potius bonorum acceptorum quam malorum: quia prius illud summam animi moderationem, posterius hoc ingenii ferociam & vindictæ cupiditatem denotat. 5. Patienter injuriam illatam ferre, eamque verbis potius, quam factis judicare velle, ita demum ut a lege scripta non nimis recedat, sed secundum rectæ rationis regulam rem disceptati cupiat. 6. Si quid ipso jure fit tentandum, ad arbitrium potius, quam ad judicem referre, quia arbiter ipsam æquitatem & mitigationem respicit, judex vero stricte rigorem juris observat.
units.tr: (3) It also belongs to equity, for the sake of fairness, to remit something of one's right and to pardon offenders in all those cases in which it is fitting and in which reason does not oppose. (4) To remember good things received rather than evil ones, because the former denotes the highest moderation of mind, the latter the savagery of temper and the desire for vengeance. (5) To bear patiently an injury done, and to wish to judge it by words rather than by deeds, but only so that one does not depart too far from the written law, and desires to settle the matter according to the rule of right reason. (6) If something must be attempted by the law itself, to refer it to an arbiter rather than to a judge, because the arbiter looks to equity itself and to mitigation, whereas the judge observes the rigour of law strictly.

units.la: III. Notanda veniunt, extrema æquitatis, quæ ei opponuntur, in excessu opponitur ἀχρεῖος, id est, strictum, severum & rigorosum jus: In defectu repugnat Sycophantia, id est, malitiosa & callida juris interpretatio. Ἀκριβοδίκαιον definitur strictò juris legitimi seu universalis sine ulla commoda interpretatione explicatio, cum scilicet leges severæ sine ulla mitigatione retinentur, etiamsi propter certas circumstantias probabilis sit mitigationis ratio. De hac inquit Terentius: verum illud Chreme dicunt: Summum jus summa saepe injuria est. Et Cic. in orat. pro Cecin. hoc vit um copiosè describit & quid damni aut detrimenti Reipub. afferat, prolixè docet. Exemplum insigne extat apud Livium lib. 8. decad. 1. de Manlio Torquato, qui filium suum decollandū curavit, quod absque ipsius permissu cum hoste cōflixisset, etiamsi gloriosam reportasset victoriā. Alterum extremum in defectu Sycophantia definitur callida & malitiosa juris interpretatio ad dolum & fraudem instituta: à Jureconsultis vocari solet Calumnia, cum scilicet verba legis in alium longè sensum torquentur, quam à Legislatore erant intellecta. De hac, inquit Cic. 1. offic. exīstunt saepe injuria calumnia quadam & malitiosa iuris interpretatione, & paucis interjectis addit haec verba: Quo in genere etiam multa in Repub. peccantur, ut ille qui cum triginta dierum cum hoste pacta essent inducia, noctu populabatur agros, quod dierum non noctium facta essent inducia. Et paulo post simile habet exemplum, de quodam qui in secundo Punico bello peccavit.
units.tr: III. The extremes of equity opposed to it are to be noted. In excess, the opposite is akhreios [ἀχρεῖος], that is, strict, severe and rigorous law. In deficiency, the opposite is Sycophancy, that is, a crafty and malicious interpretation of law. Akribodikaion [Ἀκριβοδίκαιον] is defined as the explanation of legitimate or universal law strictly, without any kindly interpretation, when severe laws are kept without any mitigation, even though, because of certain circumstances, there is a probable reason for mitigation. Of this Terence says: "Verum illud, Chreme, dicunt: Summum jus summa saepe injuria est" ("They rightly say, Chremes: the highest law is often the highest injustice"). Cicero, in his oration pro Caecina, describes this vice at length and teaches at length what harm or detriment it brings to the commonwealth. A notable example stands in Livy (lib. 8. decad. 1.) concerning Manlius Torquatus, who had his own son beheaded because he had fought with the enemy without his permission, even though he had brought back a glorious victory. The other extreme, in deficiency, Sycophancy, is defined as a crafty and malicious interpretation of law, directed to fraud and deceit. The jurists usually call it Calumny, when the words of the law are twisted to a meaning far different from that which the Lawgiver intended. Of this Cicero says (1. offic.): "Injuria saepe exsistunt calumnia quadam et malitiosa iuris interpretatione" ("injuries often arise from a certain calumny and malicious interpretation of law"), and after a few words he adds these: "Quo in genere etiam multa in republica peccantur, ut ille qui cum triginta dierum cum hoste pacta essent indutiae, noctu populabatur agros, quod dierum non noctium factae essent indutiae" ("In this kind also many faults are committed in the commonwealth, as he who, when a truce of thirty days had been made with the enemy, plundered the fields by night, because the truce had been made for days, not for nights"). And a little later he gives a similar example, of a certain man who sinned in the Second Punic War.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMATA.

units.la: 1. Æquum seu æquitas ad ius & iustitiam, ita se habet, ut neque plane sit idem, neque toto etiam genere quid diversum.
units.tr: 1. The equitable, or equity, stands in relation to right and justice in such a way that it is neither plainly the same as them nor of a wholly different kind.

units.la: 2. Æquitas cum iure universali non coincidit, sed est iuris tantum correctio & emendatio.
units.tr: 2. Equity does not coincide with universal law but is only a correction and emendation of law.

units.la: 3. Quia lex universaliter fertur, ideo fieri non potest, ut de omnibus, qui inciderunt, casibus decernat.
units.tr: 3. Because law is enacted universally, it cannot possibly decide on all the cases that may arise.

units.la: 4. Licet ius universaliter latum sit, & ideo in particularibus casibus rite fatis iudicare nequeat, manet in se tamen iustum & rectum.
units.tr: 4. Although a law is laid down universally, and so cannot judge rightly in particular cases, it nonetheless remains in itself just and right.

units.la: 5. Defectus iuris universalis non in ipsa lege aut legislatore, sed in negotii ipsius natura residet.
units.tr: 5. The defect of universal law lies not in the law itself or the lawgiver, but in the very nature of the matter.

units.la: 6. Quando ius universaliter aliquid determinat, & praeter universalitatem aliquid contingit singulare, tunc quod ius omisit, aequitas ipsa supplet & corrigit.
units.tr: 6. When a law determines something universally, and some singular case arises beyond that universality, then equity itself supplies and corrects what the law has left out.

units.la: 7. Æquitas cum sit Iustitia quadam particularis existens, ideo videtur iure ipso aliquid praestantius, non tamen absolute, sed respectu usus humani & defectuum variorum, qui propter varios casus subinde incidunt.
units.tr: 7. Since equity is a kind of particular justice, it seems to be something more excellent than the law itself, not absolutely, but with respect to human use and the various defects that from time to time arise from the diversity of cases.

units.la: 8. Hæc est æquitatis natura, ut quà ius propter universalitatem suam deficere videtur, rite & recte corrigat.
units.tr: 8. It is the nature of equity that it rightly and properly corrects that in which the law seems to be deficient because of its universality.

units.la: 9. Quia omnia legibus determinari non possunt, hinc decreta & plebiscita pro variis circumstantiis subinde emergentibus ferri ubique solent.
units.tr: 9. Because not all things can be determined by laws, decrees and plebiscites are commonly enacted everywhere to meet the various circumstances that from time to time emerge.

units.la: 10. Æquitas velut regula Lesbia, ad res ipsas se accommodat, cum alias res ipsa ad ius scriptum aut saltem ad aequitatem se accommodare debeant.
units.tr: 10. Equity is like the Lesbian rule, which adapts itself to the things themselves, whereas things ought otherwise to adapt themselves to the written law, or at least to equity.

units.la: 11. Vir æquus is dicitur, qui ius scriptum mitigat & consultò benignam legis interpretationem sequitur.
units.tr: 11. A man is called equitable who softens the written law and deliberately follows a generous interpretation of the law.

units.la: 12. Vir æquus neque severè ius strictum urget, neque exequitur, sed potius de iure suo remittit, licet legem scriptam sibi auxiliantem habeat.
units.tr: 12. An equitable man neither presses the strict law severely nor enforces it, but rather remits something of his own right, although he has the written law on his side.

units.la: 13. Æquitas definitur Iustitia Particularis existens rebus ipsis accommodata, non tamen à Justitia Universali toto genere discrepans.
units.tr: 13. Equity is defined as a particular justice, adapted to the things themselves, yet not differing from universal justice in its whole genus.

units.la: I. Quæritur: Quomodo hic in textu dicat, aquitatem esse iure ipso seu Justitia, quid melius, seu praestantius, cum tamen cap. 3. huius libri Justitiam vocarit virtutum omnium perfectissimam & praestantissimam, propterea quod sit norma societatis humanae & directrix omnium virtutum, unde hic sibi contrariari videtur? Resp. Per negationem Consequentiae. Nam considerat hic æquitatem, non tanquam diversum quid ab ipsa Justitia, sed tanquam affectionem quandam Justitiæ rebus ipsis accommodatæ, & propterea quid melius vocat, quia res singulas pro variis circumstantiis singillatim respicit, quod justitia propter universalem suam naturam facere non potest. Dein justitia etiam consideratur bifariam: 1. Quoad universalem suam perfectionem, quam in omni virtutum genere habet, & sic eam supra cap. 3. consideravit Philosophus. 2. Quoad particularem defectum in sententia aut scriptura legis, dum scilicet rebus ipsis applicatur, & sic hoc loco intelligitur Philosophus.
units.tr: I. It is asked: How does he here say that equity is better, or more excellent, than law itself or justice, when in chapter 3 of this book he called justice the most perfect and excellent of all the virtues, because it is the rule of human society and the director of all the virtues? Hence he seems to contradict himself here? Answer: by denying the consequence. For he considers equity here not as something different from justice itself but as a certain affection of justice adapted to the things themselves; and he calls it better for this reason, that it regards individual things one by one according to their various circumstances, which justice cannot do because of its universal nature. Further, justice is considered in two ways: (1) as to its universal perfection, which it has in every genus of virtue, and in this sense the Philosopher considered it above in chapter 3; (2) as to the particular defect in the wording or the text of the law, when it is applied to the things themselves, and in this sense the Philosopher is understood here.

units.la: II. Quomodo etiam dicat, Virum bonum æquitatis studiosum de ipso aliquid minuere, cum si hoc fit, verum sequitur aut æquitatem non esse affectionem Justitiæ, aut saltem intra limites rectæ rationis non manere, quia de iure ipso diminuit aliquid, quod ius est regula rectæ rationis? Resp. Non simpliciter Philosophum hoc dicere, sed quod viri boni fit proprium, dum æquitati studet, de jure suo potius diminuere aliquid, quam severe & rigide jus scriptum & summum persequi. Dein etiam diminutio est duplex, alia est secundum rectam rationem, quæ à prudentia descendit. Alia deficit ab utraque; harum & degenerat in vitiū. Prior diminutio viro bono cōcedītur, propterea quod nihil sit aliud quam legis moderatio & benigna interpretatio, posterior non item, cum Injustitiam habeat adjuncta.
units.tr: II. It is also asked: How does he say that the good man who studies equity diminishes something of his own right? For if this is so, it follows either that equity is not an affection of justice, or at least that it does not remain within the limits of right reason, since it diminishes something from the right itself, which is the rule of right reason. Answer: the Philosopher does not say this absolutely, but that it is proper to the good man, while he studies equity, to diminish something of his own right rather than to pursue the written and strict law severely and rigidly. Further, diminution is of two kinds: one is according to right reason, which comes from prudence; the other departs from both, and in these it degenerates into vice. The former kind of diminution is granted to the good man, because it is nothing other than moderation of the law and a kindly interpretation; the latter is not granted, since it has injustice joined to it.

units.la: Poterunt hūc etiam propter affinitatem hæ quæstiones referri: 1. Cum Philosophus dicat, Virum bonum æquitatis studiosum, non esse severum iuris summi exactorē, propterea quod summum ius summa fit iniuria, an hæc ratio valeat nec ne? Resp. Etsi communi jactetur provérbio & pro vera passim habeatur, sunt tamen argumenta tria in contrarium, quæ probare nituntur hanc rationem esse falsam. 1. Quia justum & injustum sunt contraria: Ergo ex natura & vi contrariorum sequitur id, quod sit justum, non posse esse injustum, nisi unum contrarium degeneret in alterum, cui etiam ratio & experientia & natura ipsa repugnant. 2. Quia summe justum est in genere bonorum, & summe injustum in genere malorum. Proinde sicut summum bonum non poterit esse summum malum, ideo neque summum jus poterit esse summa injuria. 3. Quia summe justus non poterit esse summe injustus, sicut jam cap. 14. comprobatum fuit. Ergo per consequens neque summum jus poterit esse summa injuria. Pro decisione quæstionis distinguendum venit inter jus verum, quod cum æquitate nō pugnat, & jus falsum seu adulterinum, quo illi cōtrariatur, & propterea ab ea est corrigendum & emendandum. Thesis verò, qua statuitur, Summum ius esse summam iniuriam loquitur de jure falso, non autem de vero, quia hoc à lege rectæ ratiorationis decedit, & ideo in excessu aut defectu non peccat. Proinde argumenta in negativam partem allata, fallaciam committunt ex ignoratione Elenchi. Loquuntur enim de jure nō vero, sed falso, & ideo nihil concludunt. Hinc facile intelligi poterit dictum illud Augustini, quod habetur in lib. de Religione vera: Nimia Justitia incurrit peccatum, temperata Justitia facit perfectos. Intelligit enim per nimiam Justitiam, non veram, & perfectam Justitiam, quæ jus scriptum rite observat, in eo casu, de quo lex principaliter loquitur, hanc enim vocat temperatam lustitiam: Sed intelligit falsam & apparentem, quæ jus scriptum rigidè observat in eo potissimum casu, de quo lex principaliter non loquitur, hæc enim injustitia potius & iniquitas, quā Justitia dici debet.
units.tr: These questions may also be referred here because of their affinity: 1. Since the Philosopher says that the good man who studies equity is not a severe exactor of the highest right, because the highest right becomes the highest injury, does this reason hold or not? Answer: although it is bandied about in common proverb and is everywhere held to be true, there are three arguments to the contrary, which strive to prove that this reasoning is false. (1) Because the just and the unjust are contraries. Therefore from the nature and force of contraries it follows that what is just cannot be unjust, unless one contrary degenerates into the other; and reason, experience and nature itself are opposed to this. (2) Because what is supremely just belongs to the genus of goods, and what is supremely unjust to the genus of evils. Therefore, just as the supreme good cannot be the supreme evil, so neither can the supreme right be the supreme injury. (3) Because the supremely just man cannot be supremely unjust, as has already been proved in chapter 14. Therefore, consequently, neither can the supreme right be the supreme injury. To decide the question, one must distinguish between true right, which does not conflict with equity, and false or counterfeit right, which is opposed to it and therefore must be corrected and amended by it. The thesis, however, which lays down that the supreme right is the supreme injury, speaks of false right and not of true, because true right departs from the rule of right reason, and therefore does not err in excess or defect. Hence the arguments brought against this thesis commit a fallacy, the ignoratio elenchi. For they speak not of true right but of false, and therefore conclude nothing. From this it can easily be understood what Augustine says, in his book On True Religion: Excessive justice incurs sin; tempered justice makes men perfect. For by excessive justice he means not true and perfect justice, which rightly observes the written law in the case that the law principally concerns, for that he calls tempered justice; but he means false and apparent justice, which rigidly observes the written law especially in the case with which the law is not principally concerned. For this is injustice and iniquity rather than what ought to be called justice.

units.la: II. Cum viri boni proprium esse dicat Philosophus, ut non sit severus & rigidus juris summi exactor, sed potius de jure ipso minuat, an liceat sibi aliquid de jure suo remittere, ita ut recta rationis cancellos non transgrediatur? Et statuitur thesis affirmativa propter quinque potissimas rationes:
units.tr: II. Since the Philosopher says that it is proper to the good man not to be a severe and rigid exactor of the highest right, but rather to diminish the right itself, the question is whether it is lawful for a man to remit something of his own right, so that he does not overstep the bounds of right reason. The affirmative thesis is laid down, for five principal reasons:

units.la: 1. Quia neque cum honestate, neque cum justitia pugnat, de jure suo remittere: non cum honestate, quia tendit ad utilitatem proximi: Non cum Justitia, quia spectat ad æquitatem, quæ est Justitia quædam particularis, ut jam supra diximus.
units.tr: 1. Because to remit something of one's own right conflicts neither with honesty nor with justice: not with honesty, because it tends to the advantage of one's neighbour; not with justice, because it pertains to equity, which is a kind of particular justice, as we have said above.

units.la: 2. Quia opus est & argumentū singulare humanitatis, mansuetudinis, liberalitatis, misericordiæ & æquitatis, aliquid de jure suo remittere, cum possit quis severius jus ipsum persequi. Proinde Philosophus hoc capite dicit, hoc provenire à bonitate, quæ inest viro æquitatis studioso, ut aliquid nempe de jure suo remittat.
units.tr: 2. Because to remit something of one's own right is the work and a singular mark of humanity, gentleness, liberality, mercy and equity, although one could pursue the right more severely. Therefore the Philosopher says in this chapter that this comes from the goodness that is in the man who studies equity, namely that he remits something of his own right.

units.la: 3. Quia qui de jure suo remittit, neque sibi, neque alteri facit injuriam. Non sibi, quia sponte hoc facit. Omnis verò injuria fit contra voluntatē illius, cui infertur. Non alteri, quia ad alterum non spectat. 4. Quia Deus plurimum de suo jure remittit, dum hominibus sua peccata ignoscit, & pœnas iis dignas non infligit, aut non eo modo, quo possit, infligit. Quod autem Deus facit, id licitè poterit homo quivis imitari. f. Quia Scriptura sacra homines Christianos hortatur, ut aliquid de suo jure remittāt, & ad exemplum Dei offensa sua proximo condonent Matt. f. verf. 40. & 45. & alibi. Hoc autem Scriptura non juberet, nisi justum & licitum esset aliquid de suo jure remittere. At contra hanc sententiam adferri solent argumenta quædam: 1. Quod non liceat seipsum aliquo bono fraudare, cum Justitiæ munus sit, suum cuique tribuere, & alterum non lædere, ut testatur Justinianus lib.1. Instit.tit.1.§.3. 2. Quia non licitum est magistratui impunitos relinquere homines faci-norosos & delinquentes, quod tamen liceret, si permissum esset de jure suo remittere. Verùm non sunt tanti ponderis ista. Nam ad primum responderi poterit per distinctionem, quia duplicia sunt bona, alia sunt, quæ spectant ad vitam & salutem hominis, alia quæ non, & ideo vocantur externa seu bona fortunæ. De prioribus procedit argumentum, iis enim, ut aliquis se defraudet, non licet, quia sic peccaret non tantum contra Justitiam, sed contra naturam ipsam. De posterioribus autem non ita procedit, & ideo iis se poterit aliquis fraudare pro libitu suo, si nempe non tantum ad necessitatem, sed etiam ad superflui-tatem tatem aut ad copiam iis abundet. Secundum argumentum non directè impugnat thesin. Nam jus, quod habet magistratus in facinorosos, non est proprium seu suum ipsius, sed aliorum nempe Dei, cujus vicem hic in terris Magistratus gerit, & ideo verum illud, de jure alieno nemo poterit aliquid remittere, de suo tamen remittere, quando & quoties velit, poterit.
units.tr: 3. Because the one who remits something of his own right does wrong neither to himself nor to another. Not to himself, because he does this of his own accord; but every injury is done against the will of the one to whom it is inflicted. Not to another, because it does not concern another. 4. Because God remits a great deal of his own right, when he forgives men their sins and does not inflict the punishments they deserve, or does not inflict them in the way in which he could. But what God does, any man may lawfully imitate. 5. Because holy Scripture exhorts Christians to remit something of their right, and to forgive their neighbour's offences after the example of God: Matt. 5. vers. 40 and 45, and elsewhere. Scripture would not command this unless it were just and lawful to remit something of one's own right. But against this opinion certain arguments are usually brought: (1) that it is not lawful to defraud oneself of any good, since the office of justice is to give each his own and not to harm another, as Justinian attests, Institutes book 1, title 1, §3. (2) Because it is not lawful for the magistrate to leave criminals and wrongdoers unpunished, which would nevertheless be lawful if it were permitted to remit one's own right. But these arguments are not of such weight. For to the first it can be answered by distinction: goods are twofold, some being those that pertain to the life and salvation of a man, others those that do not, and which are therefore called external goods or goods of fortune. The argument holds for the former, for it is not lawful to defraud oneself of these, since in doing so one would sin not only against justice but against nature itself. But it does not hold for the latter, and so a man may defraud himself of these at his pleasure, provided he has an abundance of them not merely for necessity but also for superfluity or plenty. The second argument does not directly attack the thesis. For the right which the magistrate has over criminals is not his own but belongs to others, namely to God, whose place the magistrate here on earth takes; and therefore, although it is true that no one can remit anything of another's right, yet one can remit something of one's own right whenever and as often as one wishes.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: SUpereft tertia & ultima pars huius libri hoc capite explicanda, in qua Philosophus agit de Justitia improprie dicta, quæ cum ipsa Justitia, quam toto hoc libro tractavit, magnam affinitatem & similitudinem habere videtur. Nam & Justitia & Injustitia considerantur bifariam: Vel quatenus sunt inter diversos homines, & sic proprie sumuntur; Vel quatenus sunt unius hominis ad seipsum, & sic improprie & metaphoricè tantum dicuntur. De hac Justitia improprie dicta, hic agit Philosophus, maximè propter Platonem, qui in Gorgia & 4.de legib. Justitiam dicit, aliam esse unius hominis ad seipsum; aliam unius hominis ad alium. Hoc autem repugnat doctrinæ Aristotelis, nam c.3. h. libri Justitiam vocat bonum alienum, id est, quæ ad alios se extendit, & ideo per hanc proprietatem Justitiam distinguit à cæteris virtutibus. Partes huius capitis sunt tres: In prima hanc proponit quæstionem; An sibi ipsi quis facere possit injuriam? Ex qua quæstione dependet solutio dubitationis motæ; An sit Justitia unius hominis erga seipsum? In secunda parte comparatio injuriæ faciendæ & accipiendæ instituitur. stituitur, & in utro magis peccetur, ostenditur. In tertia redit ad præcpuâ dubitatione, & ostendit improprie & metaphoricè tantū nō proprie aliquē sibi ipsi injuriā facere posse, & proinde neq; Justitiā neq; Injustitiā nisi improprie erga seipsum exercéri posse.
units.tr: There remains the third and last part of this book, to be explained in this chapter, in which the Philosopher treats of justice improperly so called, which seems to have great affinity and resemblance with justice itself, the subject of the whole of this book. For both justice and injustice are considered in two ways: either as they hold between different men, and so are properly so named; or as they hold of one man towards himself, and so are named only improperly and metaphorically. It is this improperly named justice that the Philosopher treats here, chiefly on account of Plato, who in the Gorgias and the fourth book of the Laws says that justice is one thing for a man towards himself and another thing for a man towards another. But this contradicts the teaching of Aristotle, for in c.3 of this book he calls justice another's good, that is, what extends itself to others, and for this reason he distinguishes justice from the other virtues by this property. The parts of this chapter are three. In the first, he puts forward this question: Can anyone do injustice to himself? On this question depends the solution of the doubt raised: Is there a justice of one man towards himself? In the second part, a comparison is made between doing injustice and suffering it, and it is shown in which of the two one sins more. In the third, he returns to the main doubt and shows that one can do injustice to oneself only improperly and metaphorically, not properly, and therefore that justice and injustice can be exercised towards oneself only improperly.

units.la: In prima igitur quæstionem superius etiam capite 13. motam; An scilicet sibi ipsi aliquis facere possit injuriam? explicat. Asserit hoc quidem Plato loco supra citato; negat verò hîc Aristoteles. Quia si aliquis sibi ipsi facere possit injuriam, vel facerer contra Justitiam universalem vel particularem. Non contra universalem, quod probat duabus rationibus: 1. Quia talis injuria legibus & Reipub. ipsi infertur, & autor talis injuriæ dicitur Paronomus, id est, legibus in genere contrarius, sicut supra c. 4. huius libri docuit Philosophus. Cum igitur non sibi ipsi, sed Reipub. faciat injuriam, non poterit dici hoc modo, injuriam sibi facere posse. 2. Quia, qui irâ commotus, sponte seipsum lædit, & proinde sibi non facit injuriam, nam ad omnem injuriam duo potissimum requiruntur, Vis nempe externa & voluntatis coactio: ille sponte se lædit, sed quia contra legem peccat, civitati facere injuriam dicitur. Nam solet civitas animadvertere in ejusmodi delinquentes. Proinde secundum Justitiam universalem, nemo sibi facere potest injuriam. Neque etiam secundum Justitiam particularem (quod secundo probandum fuit) aliquis sibi facere posse injuriam, idque docet quatuor rationibus: 1. Ducitur ab absurdo, quia sic sequeretur uni eidemq; personæ plus minusve æquo accedere & decedere simul posse, & naturæ contrariorum priorsus repugnat. Nam jus & injuria inter plures semper reperiuntur, nec, qua tales, in uno eodemque subjecto cerni possunt. 2. Quia omnis injuria hic ex praeresi & dedita opera, & tempore prior est inferens injuriam eo, cui infertur: At qui sibi ipsi facit injuriam, simul facit & patitur laesionem, & sic alius a seipso esse videtur, & tempore seipso prior & posterior, quod nusquam concedi debet. 3. Quia nemo sponte patitur injuriam, cum sit malum quid, quod adversatur ipsius naturae, sicut docet Philosophus cap. 3. lib. 3. & c. 13. hujus lib. Ergo nemo etiam sibiipsi facit injuriam. 4. Quia omnis injuria secundum Justitiam Particularem consistit in particularibus damnis, quando quis πλεονεξίας, sive cupiditatis gratia alteri damnum & detrimentum infert, dum sibi plus attribuit, alteri minus attribuit. At ejusmodi generis injuria nemo sibiipsi inferre poterit, nemo enim dicitur uxorem suam adulterare, nemo rem suam suffurari, nemo parietem suum contra voluntatem perfodere. Proinde neque secundum Justitiam particularem, quis sibi facere possit injuriam.
units.tr: In the first part, then, he explains the question raised above too in chapter 13: Can anyone, then, do an injury to himself? Plato asserts this in the passage cited above; Aristotle here denies it. For if anyone could do an injury to himself, he would act against either universal or particular justice. Not against universal justice, which he proves by two arguments: (1) Because such an injury is done to the laws and to the commonwealth, and the author of such an injury is called a paronomus, that is, one opposed to the laws in general, as the Philosopher taught above in chapter 4 of this book. Since, therefore, he does an injury not to himself but to the commonwealth, he cannot be said in this way to be able to do an injury to himself. (2) Because one who, moved by anger, voluntarily harms himself does not thereby do himself an injury. For two things are chiefly required for every injury: external force and the coercion of the will. He harms himself voluntarily, but because he sins against the law he is said to do an injury to the state, for the state is accustomed to punish such offenders. Therefore, according to universal justice, no one can do an injury to himself. Nor, secondly, can anyone do an injury to himself according to particular justice, which had to be proved in the second place, and this he teaches by four arguments: (1) It is reasoned from the absurd, for it would follow that the same person could at once gain and lose more or less than his due, and this is wholly contrary to the nature of opposites. For right and injury are always found between several persons and cannot, as such, be seen in one and the same subject. (2) Because every injury of this kind is premeditated and deliberate, and the one who inflicts the injury is prior in time to the one on whom it is inflicted. But one who does an injury to himself at the same time both does it and suffers the harm, and so he seems to be other than himself, and prior and posterior to himself in time, which must in no way be granted. (3) Because no one voluntarily suffers an injury, since it is an evil thing that is contrary to nature, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 3 of book 3 and chapter 13 of this book. Therefore no one does an injury to himself either. (4) Because every injury according to particular justice consists in particular losses, when someone, for the sake of covetousness [πλεονεξίας] or greed, inflicts loss and damage on another, while assigning to himself more and to the other less. But no one can inflict an injury of this kind on himself. For no one is said to commit adultery with his own wife, no one to steal his own property, no one to dig through his own wall against his will. Therefore, neither according to particular justice can anyone do an injury to himself.

units.la: In secunda parte capitis de extremis Justitiae agit, nempe de injuriae illatione & perpessione, quarum illa, nempe injuriae illatio obtinet vicem excessus: haec injuriae perpessio vice defectus. Et primo comparat inter se in similib, & dicit utrumque quidem esse malum, quia utrumque sit vitium, quod a lege ipsa, nempe a Justitia aberret, ultra praescriptum rectae rationis, idque docet duobus similibus exemplis, uno Medicinae, altero artis Gymnasticae, in quibus plus aut minus aequo solet damnum aut detrimentum tum inferri, etiam perniciosum esse, medium vero ipsum & affectivum & conservativum est, tum sanitatis, tum bonae habitudinis in corpore. Sanitas igitur & bona habitudo in ipsa mediocritate consistunt. Secundò conferr in dissimili, quod nempe, licet utrumq; sit malu, facere tamen injuriâ longè deterius sit malum quam pati. Quin re assentitur Platoni, cujus prolixa & copiosa de hac quæstione exstat disputatio in Gorgia. Adstipulatur etiam Cicero Philip 9. Et rationem hanc adfert Aristoteles: Cur faciem injuriam longè sit deterius, quam perpeti? Quia illud est cum improbitate, & malitia, multiq; viciis, in quibus interdum promta accedit voluntas, simul cum proæresi & electione, interdum voluntatem non sequitur electio, est conjunctum: & proinde minore venia & majore vituperio dignum: Injuriam vero accipere seu pati, nihil horum annexum habet, ut experientia docet. Verùm licet injuriam facere per se sit magis malum, fieri tamen potest, ut per accidens & ex eventu injuriam pati sit magis, si nempe majus inde malum sequatur, verbi gratia: Si injuriæ perpessionem sequatur mors, aut morbus incurabilis, aut aliquid tale, quod certâ perniciem inferat, & hoc etiam illustrat simili ex arte medica desumto. Pleuritis seu dolor lateris ab omnibus habetur, & est revera magis malum quam læsio pedis: sed tamen accidere potest, ut læsionem pedis plus mali sequatur quam pleuritis, verbi gratia: Si salus celeritate pedum sit quærenda, & aliquis vitæ suæ consulere nequit, nisi fuga, interim si impingat propter læsionem pedis, & sic in hostium manus deveniat niat aut interficiatur, hîc læsio pedis magis poterit dici malum per accidens, quam pleurisis.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter he deals with the extremes of justice, namely the infliction and the suffering of injury, of which the first, the infliction of injury, takes the place of excess, and the second, the suffering of injury, takes the place of deficiency. And first he compares them with each other in respect of likeness, and says that both are indeed evils, because both are vices, which stray from the law itself, that is from justice, beyond the prescription of right reason. He teaches this by two similar examples, one from medicine, the other from the art of gymnastics, in which a loss or damage greater or less than is fitting is usually inflicted and is also harmful, whereas the mean itself is both productive and preservative, both of health and of good condition in the body. Health and good condition therefore consist in the very mean. Secondly he compares unlike things: that, although both are evils, to do an injury is far worse an evil than to suffer one. Indeed he agrees with Plato, whose long and copious disputation on this question is found in the Gorgias. Cicero too agrees, in the ninth Philippic. And Aristotle gives this reason why to do an injury is far worse than to suffer one: because the former is attended with wickedness and malice, and with many vices, in which sometimes a ready will is present together with deliberate choice and decision; sometimes choice, which is not accompanied by the will, is joined to it. It is therefore deserving of less pardon and greater blame. But to receive or suffer an injury has none of these things attached to it, as experience teaches. Yet although to do an injury is in itself the greater evil, it can happen that to suffer an injury is by accident and by its outcome the greater, if namely a greater evil follows from it, for example: if death, or an incurable disease, or something of that kind which brings certain ruin, follows the suffering of the injury. He illustrates this too by a comparison drawn from the medical art. Pleurisy, or pain in the side, is regarded by all as an evil, and is indeed a greater evil than an injury to the foot. But it can happen that an injury to the foot brings more evil than pleurisy does. For example: if safety must be sought by speed of foot, and someone cannot look to his life except by flight, and meanwhile he stumbles because of the injury to his foot, and so falls into the hands of his enemies or is killed, here the injury to the foot can rather be called an evil by accident than the pleurisy.

units.la: In tertia parte capitis redit ad primam quæstionem, & dicit fieri posse, ut aliquis sibi injuriam inferat, sed improprie tantum: ita etiam aliquis Justitia & Injustitia non solum erga alios, sed erga seipsum uti poterit, verum non proprie sed metaphoricè. Atq; ita breviter cōpleditur copiosam & prolixam Plat. disputationem, quæ habetur lib.4.de Rep.sub sin. Ibi duo facit Justitiæ genera, aliâ vocat Iustitiâ interiore, aliâ exteriore interioré: vocat triû animæ partiû nempe rationis, iræ, libidinis harmoniâ & consensum, ita ut imperiû teneat ipsa ratio, pareât reliquæ partes & suum cuique relinquatur officium à natura tributum. Exteriorem vocat istam, de qua hoc libro agit Philosophus, nempe Politicam. Admittit quidem Aristoteles, concordiam & consensionem trium istarum animæ partium dici posse Iustitiam, sed improprie & metaphoricè tantum, & propter similitudinem, quam habet cum vera Iustitia, de qua hoc libro actum fuit. Nam fieri potest, ut una animæ partium aliquid mali ab alia præter appetitionē & quasi voluntatem patiatur: Atqui injuriam pati, nihil est aliud, quam contra voluntatem pati: ubi injuriam pati invenitur, ibi etiam injuriam facere, & ubi ista duo extrema, ibi etiam & medium, nempe Iustitia, & ubi Iustitia, ibi etiam jus, quod est effectum Iustitiæ; verùm jus improprie dictum & œconomicum seu herile tantum, non verò Politicum seu civile, quod ut ex cap. 9. hujus libri patet jus proprie dicitur. Nam quæ est ratio dominii in servos, parensparentis in liberos, cujusvis imperantis in eos, qui ejus imperio subjiciuntur: eadem est ratio ipsius rationis in reliquas animae partes, qua de re infra fusius & prolixius disputat Philosophus capite 6. lib. 1. Polit. prout etiam Cic. 3 Tusc. quaest. Sicut igitur in Politica societate est communio quaedam juris qua & imperantes & parentes, seu qui imperantium imperio subjiciuntur, uti vel non uti possunt: sic etiam inter animi facultates seu partes reperitur interdum Justitia quaedam, dum nempe suum unaquaeque facit officium, interdum iis discrepantibus Injustitia quaedam oboriri poterit, qua quis in seipsum injurius esse dicatur, dum nempe appetitiva animae pars rectae rationis praescripto non paret, sed contra rationem ipsam in libertatem se vendicat, ut in illa pugna Medeae:
units.tr: In the third part of the chapter he returns to the first question and says that it can happen that someone inflicts an injury on himself, but only improperly. So too one may make use of justice and injustice not only towards others but towards oneself, yet not properly but metaphorically. And thus he briefly sums up the long and copious disputation of Plato, which is found in book 4 of the Republic, at the end. There Plato makes two kinds of justice: one he calls inner justice, the other outer. Inner justice he describes as the harmony and agreement of the three parts of the soul, namely reason, anger and desire, so that reason itself holds rule, the other parts obey, and each is left its own duty assigned by nature. The outer justice he calls that which Aristotle treats of in this book, namely political justice. Aristotle does admit that the concord and agreement of these three parts of the soul may be called justice, but only improperly and metaphorically, and on account of the likeness it bears to true justice, of which this book has treated. For it can happen that one part of the soul suffers something evil from another, beyond its appetite and, as it were, its will. But to suffer an injury is nothing other than to suffer against one's will. Where suffering an injury is found, there too doing an injury is found; and where these two extremes are, there too is the mean, namely justice; and where justice is, there too is right, which is the effect of justice. But this right is improperly so called and is merely domestic or servile, not political or civil, which, as is clear from chapter 9 of this book, is properly called right. For the principle that governs the rule of a master over slaves, of a parent over children, and of any ruler over those subject to his command, is the same as the principle by which reason rules the remaining parts of the soul. On this matter the Philosopher disputes more fully and at length below, in chapter 6 of book 1 of the Politics, as Cicero also does in the third book of the Tusculan Disputations. Just as, therefore, in political society there is a certain common participation in right, by which both rulers and parents, or those who are subject to the command of rulers, can either use it or not use it, so too among the faculties or parts of the soul there is sometimes a certain justice, namely when each performs its own duty; and when they disagree, a certain injustice may arise, by which someone is said to be unjust towards himself, namely when the appetitive part of the soul does not obey the prescription of right reason, but claims for itself liberty against reason itself, as in that struggle of Medea:

units.la: Sed trahit invitam nova vis, aliudque cupido, Mens aliud suadet.
units.tr: But a new force drags me unwilling, and desire pulls one way, while my mind counsels another.

units.la: Et tandem concludit Phil. se tam in genere, quam in specie hucusque de virtutibus moralibus egisse.
units.tr: And at last the Philosopher (Phil.) concludes that he has so far treated of the moral virtues, both in general and in particular.

units.la: In hoc capite duo haec breviter notanda sunt: I. An quis sibi ipsi facere possit injuriam? Quod disceptatur in utramque partem. Nam pro negativa quam hic tuetur Philosophus faciunt septem hae rationes: 1. Quia nemo vult, cum nemo id proprie velit, quod sit malum, seipsum sponte laedere contra legem: ideo neque injuriam sibi ipsi facere. 2. Quia ibi injuria proprie reperitur, ubi uni aliquid eripitur, & alteri additur: At uni eidem quae idem simul addi & eripi non potest, cum sint duo contraria a contrariis terminis profecta. 3. Quia nemo sibi ipsi popoterit esse contrarius, esset autem, si sibi ipsi facere possit injuriam, quia simul esset volens & nolens, volens, quatenus injuriam sibi ipsi facit, nolens, quatenus eandem patitur, quę duo miram in homine pugnam excitarent, si simul & eodem tempore inessent. 4. Quia nemo poterit seipso prior & posterior esse, cum ista duo implicent contradictionem: At verò is, qui facit injuriam, prior est tempore eo, cui infertur, aut qui patitur injuriam, cum omne agens natura prius sit patiente. 5. Quia necesse est, & jus & injuria esse inter plures; distinguitur n. is, qui injuria facit, ab eo, qui patitur, re & subjecto, sicut docet Phil. c. 13. h.l. At verò non essent inter plures, si quis sibi ipsi facere possit injuriam. 6. Quia nemo ergo seipsum jus proprie exercere potest, propterea quod Justitia sit boni alienum, quod ad alios se extendit, sicut sup. c. 5. ofte ium fuit. Hinc nemo dicitur conjugis suae adulter, sed alienae, nemo facultatum suarum fur, sed alienarum proprie, sicut hoc loco Phil. docet, & jus civile etiam lib. 4. Inst. tit. 2. §. 1. & li. & 4. ff. de obligation. & actionib. l. 52. §. 13. ff. de facti. 7. Quia nemo sibi ipsi facit malum quid, quia malu, cum ab eo naturae quodam instinctu omnes abhorreant: At omnis injuria est malum quod, & ab omnibus sic judicatur. Ergo sibi ipsi non facit injuriam. At pro affirmativa parte tres afferuntur rationes. 1. Ducitur ab auctoritate Platonis qui lib. 4. Repub. dicit, nullum posse injurium esse erga alium, nisi prius in seipsum sit injurius. 2. Quia idipsum exempla multa docent eorum, qui seipsos interficiunt aut corrumpunt vulnerando, mutilando, indulgendo pravis affectibus & cupiditatibus, potando & intemperanter vivendo aut pericula etiam temere adeundo & caetera ejusmodi. 3. Quia qui contra jus naturale agit, quod praecipit, ut homo seipsum amet, conservet & perficiat quantum potest, suumq; appetitum rectae rationis imperio subjiciat, ille sponte seipsum laedit, & ideo sibi ipsi facit iniuriam, propterea quod jus naturale violavit. Verum istae rationes non sunt tanti momenti, ut Aristotelis sententia rejiciatur: Nam quod ad primam rationem, quae ducitur ab auctoritate Platonis, ibi verbum ἀδικεῖν improprie sumitur, non proprie, & ideo nihil concludit. Secunda rationis consequentia laborat, nam etsi quis seipsum sponte laedit, non tamen sibi ipsi facit iniuriam, sed tum demum cum ad istam ἐξ-ηῆσιν accedit vis externa & violenta coactio, quae in uno eodemque homine non reperiuntur.
