Tertia ratio est falsa, nam qui jus naturale violat, non sibi ipsi, sed Deo, Magistratui & toti civitati facit injuriam. Sunt tamen, qui ista utuntur distinctione, ut dicant, neminem voluntate plene & recte constituta sibi facere posse iniuriam, licet voluntate perturbata & male affecta possit, ut cum quis male sibi consulit aut male velit, aut aliquid contra dictamen rectae rationis agit, verbi gratia: cum ex ira, odio, amore, desiderio, caeterisque affectibus quis cibo potu aut aliis vitae commoditatibus se privat.
units.tr: Two points in this chapter should be briefly noted. I. Can someone do an injury to himself? This is disputed on both sides. For the negative, which the Philosopher here defends, there are seven reasons: (1) No one wills, since no one wills properly what is evil, to harm himself voluntarily and against the law; therefore neither does he do an injury to himself. (2) Injury properly exists where something is taken from one person and added to another; but the same person cannot have the same thing added and taken away at once, since these are two contraries proceeding from contrary terms. (3) No one can be opposed to himself, yet he would be if he could do an injury to himself, for he would be both willing and unwilling at once: willing, insofar as he does the injury to himself; unwilling, insofar as he suffers it. These two would produce a remarkable conflict in a person if they were present together at the same time. (4) No one can be both prior and posterior to himself, since these two imply a contradiction. But the one who does an injury is prior in time to the one to whom it is done, or who suffers it, since every agent is by nature prior to the patient. (5) Both right and injury necessarily exist between several persons. For the one who does the injury is distinguished from the one who suffers it, in thing and in subject, as the Philosopher teaches in chapter 13 of this book. But they would not exist between several persons if someone could do an injury to himself. (6) No one, therefore, can properly exercise right over himself, because justice concerns the good of another, and extends to others, as was said above in chapter 5. Hence no one is called the adulterer of his own wife but of another's; no one is properly the thief of his own goods but of another's, as the Philosopher teaches in this place; and civil law also teaches this, in book 4 of the Institutes, title 2, §1, and in book 4 of the Digest on obligations and actions, law 52, §13, on theft. (7) No one does himself harm, since harm is evil, and all people shrink from it by a certain instinct of nature. But every injury is an evil, and everyone judges it so. Therefore no one does an injury to himself. On the affirmative side, three reasons are advanced. (1) It is drawn from the authority of Plato, who says in book 4 of the Republic that no one can be unjust toward another unless he has first been unjust toward himself. (2) Many examples of those who kill themselves or ruin themselves, by wounding, mutilating, indulging depraved passions and desires, drinking, and living intemperately, or by rashly facing dangers and other such things, teach the same. (3) Whoever acts against natural law, which commands that a man love himself, preserve himself and perfect himself as far as he can, and subject his appetite to the command of right reason, he harms himself willingly, and so does an injury to himself, because he has violated natural law. But these reasons are not of such weight as to overturn the opinion of Aristotle. For as to the first reason, which is drawn from Plato's authority, the word ἀδικεῖν [adikein] is there taken improperly, not properly, and so it proves nothing. The consequence of the second reason is faulty: for even if someone harms himself willingly, he does not do an injury to himself, but only when an external force and violent compulsion is added to that habit [ἕξιν], and these are not found in one and the same man. The third reason is false, for whoever violates natural law does an injury not to himself but to God, the magistrate and the whole commonwealth. Yet there are some who use this distinction, saying that no one can do an injury to himself when his will is fully and rightly disposed, but that he can when his will is disturbed and ill-affected: as when someone takes poor counsel for himself, or wills badly, or acts against the dictate of right reason, for example when, out of anger, hatred, love, desire or other passions, someone deprives himself of food, drink or other conveniences of life.

units.la: II. Quod notandum erat, fuit hoc, An facere iniuriam sit deterius malum, quam pati?
units.tr: II. What was to be noted was this: Is it a worse evil to do an injury than to suffer one?

units.la: Et affirmatur propter quatuor rationes: 1. Quia facere iniuriam est cum malitia & improbitate coniunctum, pati vero non item. 2. Quia facere injuriam repugnat omni in genere honesto, & peccat tam contra universales quam particulares: pati vero repugnat tantum honesto, jucundo & utili. 3. Quia facere injuriam reddit hominem simpliciter malum, non vero pati, nam male agendo aliquis fit malus & improbus, non vero male patiendo. 4. Quia meliorem animi partem vitiat & corrumpit, nempe voluntatem, nam sine promta voluntate nulla proprie infertur injuria.
units.tr: And it is affirmed on four grounds: (1) To do an injury is joined with malice and wickedness, but to suffer one is not. (2) To do an injury is opposed to every kind of honourable conduct, and it sins against universal as well as particular duties; but to suffer an injury is opposed only to what is honourable, pleasant and useful. (3) To do an injury makes a man bad absolutely, but to suffer one does not; for by acting badly a man becomes wicked and depraved, but not by suffering badly. (4) It corrupts and spoils the better part of the soul, namely the will, for no injury is properly inflicted without a ready will.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: 1. Fieri potest, ut quis seipsum injuria afficiat, non proprie sed improprie & per quandam similitudinem.
units.tr: 1. It is possible for someone to injure himself, not properly but improperly and by a certain similitude.

units.la: 2. Qua lex non iubet, ea prohibet, non simpliciter tamen, sed in malis tantum.
units.tr: 2. What the law does not command, it forbids; yet not absolutely, but only in the case of bad things.

units.la: 3. Qui sibi ipsi violentas manus infert, non sibi, sed toti civitati cuius est membrum iniuriam facit, cum & civitatem uno membro privarit contra leges mique egerit.
units.tr: 3. He who lays violent hands on himself does injury not to himself but to the whole state of which he is a member, since by depriving the state of one member he acts against its laws.

units.la: 4. Nemo sua sponte patitur iniuriam, cum ab externa vi & violenta coactione proveniat.
units.tr: 4. No one suffers injury of his own accord, since it comes from external force and violent compulsion.

units.la: 5. Quod nemo sibi proprie infert iniuriam, inde constat, quia unum & idem eidem subiecto simul addi & detrahi non potest.
units.tr: 5. That no one properly inflicts injury on himself is clear from this: one and the same thing cannot be added to and taken away from the same subject at the same time.

units.la: 6. Jus & & iniuria inter plures non in uno eodemque subiecto reperiuntur.
units.tr: 6. Right and injury are not found, between several people, in one and the same subject.

units.la: 7. Qui ex proposito male agit, & ideo iniuriam infert, tempore prior est eo, qui iniuriam patitur.
units.tr: 7. He who acts badly on purpose, and so inflicts injury, is prior in time to him who suffers the injury.

units.la: 8. Quod nemo sibi proprie facere potest iniuriam, definitio iniuria docet, definitur enim damnum seu lasio quam quis non sibi ipsi, sed alteri tantum infert.
units.tr: 8. That no one can do injury to himself properly, the definition of injury shows: for injury is defined as a loss or harm that someone inflicts not on himself but only on another.

units.la: 9. Licet utrumque & facere iniuriam & pati sit malum, deterius tamen est facere, cum sit cum improbitate & malitia coniunctum, pati vero non item.
units.tr: 9. Although both doing injury and suffering it are evil, doing it is the worse, since it is joined with wickedness and malice, whereas suffering is not.

units.la: 10. Utut pati iniuriam per se minus sit malum, per accidens tamen & ex consequenti poterit dici magis malum, si nempe maius inde malum sequatur.
units.tr: 10. Although suffering injury is in itself the lesser evil, it can nonetheless be called the greater evil by accident and as a consequence, if a greater evil follows from it.

units.la: 11. Quae fiunt per accidens non traduntur proprie in artibus, sed ea tantum quae plerumque aut communiter aut semper eveniunt.
units.tr: 11. Things that happen by accident are not properly taught in the arts, but only those that happen for the most part, or commonly, or always.

units.la: 12. Poterit aliquis sibi ipsi facere iniuriam impropriè & metaphoricè cum inferiores animi partes ipsi rationi tanquam Domina & Duci non parent.
units.tr: 12. Someone can do injury to himself improperly and metaphorically when the lower parts of his soul do not obey reason, which should rule them as mistress and leader.

units.la: 13. Ratio in cateras animi partes ius habet, non civile aut Politicum, sed Oeconomicum aut herile aut aliquid tantum simile.
units.tr: 13. Reason has a right over the other parts of the soul that is not civil or political, but domestic, like a master's, or something merely similar.

units.la: 14. Quando aliquis praeter appetitionem & voluntatem aliquid in se ipso patitur mali, ut quando affectus regunt, & ratio ipsa servit, tunc ex opinione Platonis aliquis seipsum iniuria afficere dicitur.
units.tr: 14. When someone suffers some evil within himself against his appetite and will, as when the passions rule and reason itself is enslaved, then, according to the opinion of Plato, he is said to injure himself.

units.la: 15. Quod imperium seu ius Princeps habet in subditos, dominus in servos, parens in liberos: idem habet aut saltem habere debet ratio in reliquas animae partes.
units.tr: 15. The power or right that a prince has over his subjects, a master over his slaves, and a parent over his children, reason has, or at least ought to have, over the remaining parts of the soul.

units.la: I. Quaeritur: An recte hoc sit dictum a Philosopho, quae lex non iubet, ea vetat: cum sexcenta sint imo infinita, quae lex nusquam iubet, & tamen non prohibet, verbi gratia uxorem ducere, non iubet, res necessarias vendere, aut emere, gratias pro beneficio accepto agere & cetera eiusmodi, & tamen ista non prohibet. Falsum ergo videtur quod Philosophus phus hic protulit? Respond. Ista verba Philosophi intelligi posse bifariam: 1. Generaliter de rebus omnibus tam bonis quam malis, & sic falsum erit, ut quæcunque lex non jubeat, ea prohibeat, cum propter universalitatem naturæ suæ singularia omnia pro variis circumstantiis comprehendere non possit. 2. Specialiter, ut tantum intelligantur ista verba de malis, & sic verum erit, ut quæcunq; lex r ö jubeat, ea etiā prohibeat, in malis scilicet, ut nō jubet scortari, res alienas suffurari, ergo etiam prohibet.
units.tr: I. It is asked: was this rightly said by the Philosopher, that what the law does not command, it forbids? For there are six hundred, indeed infinitely many, things which the law nowhere commands and yet does not forbid: for example, the law does not command a man to take a wife, to sell or buy necessities, to give thanks for a benefit received, and the like, and yet it does not forbid these. So what the Philosopher Philosophus hic protulit? says here seems false? Answer: these words of the Philosopher can be understood in bifariam: two ways. 1. Generally, of all things, good and bad alike; and so it will be false that whatever the law does not command, it forbids, since by the universality of its nature it cannot comprehend all particulars under their varying circumstances. 2. Specifically, so that the words are understood only of bad things; and so it will be true that whatever the law does not command, it also forbids, namely in the case of bad things: for the law does not command fornication or the theft of another's goods, and therefore it forbids them.

units.la: II. Quomodo etiam dicat cum, qui iniuria lacessitus, alteri damnum aut detrimentum infert, non facere iniuriam, cum Plato in Critone contrarium doceat, & ratio idipsum evincat: Tum etiam Scriptura sacra repugnet huic opinioni, Matth. enim 5 verf. 39. dicitur; ne rependite malum malo. Ergo hic labitur Philosophus?
units.tr: II. How can he also say that one who, provoked by injury, inflicts loss or damage on another does not do injury, when Plato in the Crito teaches the contrary and reason itself proves it? Holy Scripture too opposes this opinion, for Matthew 5:39 says: "Do not repay evil with evil." Does the Philosopher therefore err here?

units.la: Resp. Aristotelem hic non loqui absolutè, sed comparatè tantum respecta temporis, nempe quod non priorem faciat injuriā, sed ille potius, qui occasionem dedit, ut injuriam ulcisceretur, licet absolutè loquendo, cum contra legem peccet, & ex proæresi malum alteri inferat, injuriam verè facere dicatur.
units.tr: Answer: Aristotle is not speaking absolutely here, but only comparatively, with respect to time: namely, that it is not the one who first does injury, but rather the one who gave occasion for taking revenge, who is in the wrong. Yet speaking absolutely, since he sins against the law and deliberately inflicts evil on another, the first man is truly said to do injury.

units.la: III. Quomodo etiam dicat iniuriam pati esse malum, sed levius tamen malum quam iniuriam facere, cum nullo modo sit malum, quia est in potestate patientis, ut iniuriam sibi illatam in bonum suum transferat, modo patienter ferat.
units.tr: III. How does he also say that suffering injury is an evil, but a lesser evil than doing injury, when it is in no way an evil at all, since it lies in the power of the one who suffers to turn the injury done to him into his own good, provided he bears it patiently?

units.la: Multi enim viri patientes per patientiam suam lucrantur Christum, ut ait Bernhardus, quod de Martyribus constat. At vero si pati iniuriam esset malum, hoc non eveniret? Respond. Malum esse duplex, scilicet malum culpæ & malum pœnæ. Et injuriam, pati est tantum malum lum pœnæ, non culpæ. Quod vero sic intellexerit Philosophus, ex ipso textu patet, cum dicit: pati injuriam esse remotum ab omni malitia: Nam in agente tantum, non in patiente omnis malefacti cernitur improbitas.
units.tr: For many patient men gain Christ through their patience, as Bernard says, and this is evident in the martyrs. But if suffering injury were an evil, would this not be impossible? Answer: evil is twofold, namely evil of fault and evil of punishment. Suffering injury is an evil of punishment only, not of fault. That the Philosopher understood it this way is clear from the text itself, where he says that suffering injury is remote from all malice: for the wickedness of any wrongdoing is seen only in the agent, not in the one who suffers.

units.la: IV. An deterius sit malum facere iniuriam, quam pati, quod vult Philosophus, cum contrarium ratio evincat: Nam pati seu accipere iniuriam, est cum damno & detrimento coniunctum, facere vero non: & dare damnum, minus semper habetur malum, quam accipere, ut ipsis etiam sensibus patet, minus enim semper habetur malum, vulnus infligere, quam vulnus ferre. Huc etiam accedunt testimonia gravissimorum autorum. Nam Thrasymachus apud Platonem lib. 1. de Repub. & Carneades apud Cic. lib. 1. etiam de Republ. teste Lactantio lib. 5. Instit. Christian. cap. 7. idem affruere conantur? Resp. Primò ad rationem, per distinctionem mali, ut supra. Nam licet sit magis malum pœnæ, accipere injuriam, non tamen est magis malum culpæ, cum in patiente nihil sit culpæ, quæ ista promereat injuriam: quod inde manifestum evadit, quia in facientes injuriam pœnam & animadversionem statuunt leges, non vero in patientes. Secundò quod ad testimonia attinet, non sunt tanti momenti, ut contra sensum & experientiam quotidianam admittantur. Dein etiam hisce testimoniis opponimus testimonia graviorum Philosophorum, ut Platonis 1. de Rep. Aristotelis hoc loco, & 1. Eudem. cap. 11. & Cicer. Philip. 9. qui omnes contrarium no modo statuunt, sed hanc sententiam, quod scilicet pati injuriam, sit magis malum, quam facere, tanquam absurdam multis rationibus refellunt.
units.tr: IV. Is doing injury a worse evil than suffering it, as the Philosopher wills, when reason proves the contrary? For to suffer or receive injury is joined with loss and harm, but doing it is not; and inflicting harm is always held to be a lesser evil than receiving it, as even the senses show: to inflict a wound is always considered less evil than to bear one. To this are added the testimonies of very weighty authors. For Thrasymachus in Plato, Republic book 1, and Carneades in Cicero, also in book 1 of the Republic, as Lactantius testifies in Divine Institutes book 5, chapter 7, try to maintain the same. Answer: first, to the argument, by distinguishing evil as above. For although suffering injury is more an evil of punishment, it is not more an evil of fault, since in the one who suffers there is nothing of fault that deserves the injury. This is plain from the fact that laws impose penalty and punishment on those who do injury, not on those who suffer it. Second, as to the testimonies, they are not of such weight that they should be admitted against sense and daily experience. Moreover, we set against these testimonies those of weightier philosophers, such as Plato in Republic book 1, Aristotle here, and Eudemian Ethics book 1, chapter 11, and Cicero in the Philippics book 9. All of them not only maintain the contrary but refute, with many arguments, this opinion as absurd: that suffering injury is a greater evil than doing it.

units.la: V.&c
units.tr: V. etc.

units.la: V. & ult. An illud consistere possit, quod dicit Philosophus sub finem capitis, Rationalitatem nempe idem habere jus in partes animæ inferiores, quod habet dominus in servos, aut paterfamilias in suam familiam, cum contrarium experientia testetur; nam illi habent jus absolutum in suos inferiores, ratio vero non item, nam affectus & appetitus sæpius rectæ rationi imperant, quam in recta ratio, ut in morbis animi, & intemperatura laborantibus videre licet? Resp. Philosophum hoc non absolutè dicere, sed jus habere per quandam similitudinem seu metaphoram non idem plane quod œconomicum, sed veluti simile. Deinde falsum etiam illud absolutum omni tempore jus habere aut dominum in servos, aut patrem familias in familiam. Nam & servos dominis & familiam ipsi capiti seu patrifamilias repugnare, neque imperium ullum agnoscere, præter infinitas historias quotidiana testatur experientia.
units.tr: V. and last. Can that hold which the Philosopher says at the end of the chapter, namely that reason has the same right over the lower parts of the soul that a master has over slaves, or a householder over his household? Experience shows the contrary. For those have absolute right over their inferiors, but reason does not, since the passions and appetites often command right reason more than right reason commands them, as may be seen in those suffering from diseases of the mind and from intemperance. Answer: the Philosopher does not say this absolutely, but that reason has a right by a certain similitude or metaphor: not altogether the same as the domestic right, but something like it. Next, it is also false that a master always has absolute right over his slaves, or a householder over his household. Daily experience, apart from countless histories, testifies that slaves resist their masters and the household resists the head of the family, and acknowledge no command at all.

units.la: Coronidis loco, ut huic tandem libro finis imponatur, hoc poterit quæri: An cum Justitia constet, quod vulgo jactatur; Vim vi repellere licet? Resp. Trita & vulgata hanc inter plerosq; esse sententia, cujus veritas inde pendet, quod, ut Cicero 1. offic. ait, unicuique animantium generi à natura tributum sit, ut se, vitam, corpusque tueatur, declinetque ea, quæ ei nocitura videantur. Cum igitur juris sit naturæ, vim vi repellere, cum Justitia recte constare poterit. 1. Quia licet Justitiæ munus sit, neminem læd ere, ut habetur lib. 1. Inst. tit. 1. §. 3. tamen illud videtur hic esse limitandum, ne scilicet, cui quis noceat, nisi lacessitus injuriâ, sicut Cicero interpretatur 1. offic. Verùm huic sententiæ repugnat sacra Scriptura Matt. 5. vers. verf. 39. Ad Rom. 12. verf. 17. quæ vult, ut homo Christianus non malum pro malo, sed bonum pro malo reddat, & germinam potius patiatur injuriam quam unam repedaret vindicet. Ut igitur veritas hujus quæstionis melius intelligatur, sciendum est; Licere homini Christiano, ut se & proximum suum defendat, omnibus mediis licitis, non autem ullis illicitis. Media vero licita sunt ea, quæ honesta & justa sunt, & legi divinæ concessa; illicita vero e contra, quæ honesta & injusta & legi divinæ sunt prohibita. Proinde non licet injuriā injuriâ, convitiū convitio retaliare aut rependere, neq; et licet homini privato sui defendendi gratia aliū injustè in se impetū facientem impune occidere, licet tamen injuriā suā à se propulsare, inculpatæ tutelæ moderatione, ut loquitur JC. id est, ut quantum possit, se defendat, ita ut nemini nocere cupiat, neq; animo pravo alii petat. Licet et injuriæ sibi illatæ vindictā à legitimo magistratu expetere, quia ad hoc à Deo deputatus est, ut Justitiā administret, & innocentes ab injuriis defendat. Si posteriori hoc modo intelligatur, dictum illud verum erit; si priori, erit falsum, omnique Justitiæ contrarium.
units.tr: By way of a crown, so that this book may at last be brought to an end, it may be asked: Is it consistent with justice, as is commonly asserted, that force may be repelled by force? Answer: among most people this is a hackneyed and common opinion, whose truth depends on this: as Cicero says in De Officiis 1. offic. book 1, nature has given to every kind of living creature the task of protecting itself, its life and body, and avoiding what seems likely to harm it. Therefore, since it is a law of nature to repel force by force, it can rightly be consistent with justice. 1. Although the office of justice is to harm no one, as is stated in Institutes lib. 1. Inst. tit. 1. §. 3. book 1, title 1, §3, this seems to need limiting here: namely, that one should harm no one unless provoked by injury, as Cicero explains in De Officiis book 1. But this opinion is contradicted by holy Scripture, Matthew 5:39 and Romans 12:17, which wills that a Christian not repay evil for evil but good for evil, and rather suffer injury than avenge himself by repaying it. So that the truth of this question may be better understood, it must be known that a Christian may defend himself and his neighbour by all lawful means, but not by any unlawful means. Lawful means are those that are honourable and just and permitted by divine law; unlawful means, on the contrary, are those that are dishonourable and unjust and forbidden by divine law. Therefore it is not lawful to repay injury with injury or insult with insult, nor is it lawful for a private man, for the sake of self-defence, to kill with impunity another who unjustly attacks him. It is lawful, however, to ward off injury from oneself with the moderation of blameless defence, as the jurists say, that is, to defend oneself as far as one can, without wishing to harm anyone or attacking another with a wicked mind. It is also lawful to seek vengeance for an injury done to oneself from the lawful magistrate, since he is appointed by God to administer justice and to defend the innocent from injuries. If that saying is understood in the latter sense, it will be true; in the former, it will be false and wholly contrary to justice.

units.la: LIBER SEXTUS.
units.tr: BOOK SIX.

units.la: De Virtute Intellectuali.
units.tr: On Intellectual Virtue.

units.la: Ucusque de Virtutibus Moralibus ex mente & methodo Aristotelis, actum fuit, supersunt Intellectuales quinque, de quibus toto libro sexto agitur. Nos breviter de iis, ut Aristoteles ab aliorum vindicetur cetur calumniis, tractabimus: nō enim injuria (quicquid alii dicant) de virtutibus intellectualibus praecepta in Ethicis traduntur, siquidem felicitas seu summum hominis bonum non tantum virtutibus moralibus, sed etiam intellectualibus tanquam suis mediis acquiritur; nam ut ex cap. 4, lib. 10. Nicom. patet, duplex est Felicitas una Practica, quae virtutibus moralibus comparatur, & haec alias καθ' ἑξοχὴν Felicitas dici solet, propterea quod, ut ait Seneca, non tam bene sciendo, quàm bene agendo felices evadunt homines, & ut habet vulgaris versiculus:
units.tr: Thus far the moral virtues have been treated according to the mind and method of Aristotle. Five intellectual virtues remain, and these are the subject of the whole of the sixth book. We shall deal with them briefly, so that Aristotle may be vindicated from the calumnies of others. For the precepts about the intellectual virtues are not, whatever others may say, handed down in the Ethics without reason, since happiness, or the highest good of man, is acquired not only by the moral virtues but also by the intellectual virtues, as its means. For, as ex cap. 4, lib. 10. Nicom. makes plain, happiness is twofold. One is practical, which is won by the moral virtues, and this is usually called happiness par excellence [καθ' ἑξοχήν], because, as Seneca says, men become happy not so much by knowing well as by acting well; and as the common little verse has it:

units.la: Non qui multa tenet, sed qui scit idonea vita, Hic, dici felix cur merearur, habet.
units.tr: It is not he who holds many things, but he who knows the fitting way of life, who has the merit of being called happy.

units.la: Altera dicitur Theoretica, quae in sola contemplatione consistit, & haec virtutibus intellectualibus tanquam propriis suis mediis comparatur. Cum igitur de Felicitate in genere in Ethicis tractandum sit, de mediis etiam in genere tractandum videtur.
units.tr: The other is called theoretical, which consists in contemplation alone, and this is related to the intellectual virtues as to their own proper means. Since, then, happiness in general must be treated in the Ethics, the means in general seem also to require treatment.

units.la: 1. Ratio est haec, quod Prudentia, quae inter virtutes intellectuales non habetur postrema, sit omnium moralium Dux & moderatrix, sive qua neutiquam recte suo munere defungi possunt; & ideo Plato in Menone vocat eam caeterarum virtutum Ducem. Aristoteles in hoc lib. 6. variis in locis, appellat virtutum moralium Principem aut rectricem. Cicero, virendi artem & magistram 1. offic. quoniam rel quis virtutibus tanquam administris ad sapienter agendum, utitur, & earum ordinem opportunitatem agendique rationem demonstrat; ipsa vero tanquam mentis oculus, quod verum atque decus est, curat & omnis in hoc est, ut eleganter ait Horatius. 2. Accedit & haec ratio, cur de intellectualibus in Ethica agatur, quia lib. 2. Nicom. cap. 7. definita fuit, virtus moralis per rectam rationem, quæ pars definitionis rectè intelligi nō poterit, absq; cognitione virtutum intellectualiū. Nam illæ solæ sunt, quæ ratione ipsam dirigunt & informant post lapsum primorum parentum, & quantum humanis licet viribus, ad primævam integritatem reducere conantur.
units.tr: 1. The reason is this: Prudence, which is not counted the least among the intellectual virtues, is the leader and governor of all the moral virtues, without whose direction they cannot rightly perform their office. Hence Plato, in Menone, calls it the leader of the other virtues. Aristotle, in hoc lib. 6., in various places calls it the chief or director of the moral virtues. Cicero calls it the art and teacher of living well, 1. offic., since the man of wisdom uses the other virtues as his servants for acting wisely, and shows their order, their timing and the manner of acting; prudence itself, like the eye of the mind, takes care of what is true and fitting, and everything is directed to this, as Horace elegantly says. 2. There is also this reason why the intellectual virtues are treated in Ethics: lib. 2. Nicom. cap. 7. defines the moral virtue as a state governed by right reason, and this part of the definition cannot be rightly understood without knowledge of the intellectual virtues. For these alone direct and shape reason after the fall of our first parents, and strive, so far as human powers allow, to restore it to its original integrity.

units.la: 4. Duæ sunt mentis facultates, intellectus & voluntas, & istæ facultates ita sunt inter se connexæ & conjunctæ, ut una ab altera rectè sejungi non possit, ut variis rationibus docet Zabarel. lib. 1. de ordine intellectus cap. 1. Proinde rationi convenientissimum videtur, ut istarum facultatum virtutes sint connexæ & connexim tradantur, & cum omnium consensu voluntatis virtutes in Ethicis tradantur etiam de intellectivis, propter cognationem & affinitatem, in Ethicis agendum erit, cum ille non minus sint virtutes, quàm morales, sicut docet Philosophus 1. magn. moral. cap. 23. Proindè facilè dilui possunt rationes, quæ in contrarium afferuntur; ideo non esse tractandum de iis in Ethica: 1. Quia diversum ab Ethica habent finem. 2. Quia circa aliud occupantur objectum. 3. Quia harum virtutum præcepta magna ex parte pertinent ad Theoriam, quæ non est medium necessarium felicitatis humanæ. Verùm istæ rationes non sunt tanti ponderis, ut Intellectuales ab Ethica excludantur. Nam quod ad primam, licet diversum ab Ethica habeant finem, non tamen à summo hominis bono, quod partim in theoria, partim in praxi consistit, ut jam diximus, & ideo ut homo plenariam haberet fe-
units.tr: 4. Two are the faculties of the mind, the intellect and the will, and these faculties are so connected and joined with one another that one cannot rightly be separated from the other, as Zabarella shows by various arguments, lib. 1. de ordine intellectus cap. 1. Therefore it seems most reasonable that the virtues of these faculties should be connected and handed down together; and since all agree that the virtues of the will are treated in Ethics, the intellectual virtues must also be treated there, on account of their kinship and affinity, since they are no less virtues than the moral ones, as the Philosopher teaches, 1. magn. moral. cap. 23. Accordingly, the arguments brought against this can easily be dissolved: that the intellectual virtues should not be treated in Ethics, (1) because they have a different end from Ethics; (2) because they are concerned with another object; (3) because the precepts of these virtues pertain for the most part to theory, which is not a necessary means to human happiness. But these arguments are not of such weight as to exclude the intellectual virtues from Ethics. For as to the first, although they have a different end, it is not different from the highest good of man, which consists partly in theory and partly in practice, as we have already said; and therefore, in order that a man may have full knowledge of happiness, these intellectual virtues too must be treated in their own way.

units.la: Ccc liei licitatis cognitionem, de iis etiam intellectualibus suo modo tractandum fuit. Quod ad secundam non hic tractantur propter objectum, sed propter finem ad quem tendunt, & ideo nihil ista ratio concludit. Ad tertiam respondetur, nullum unquam negasse ad theoriam spectare istas virtutes; sed hoc tantum quaeritur, annon in gratiam virtutum moralium de iis in Ethica sit agendum, & praesertim propter Prudentiam, sine qua virtutes morales plene & perfecte percipi non possunt. Secundo etiam quia ex professo in nulla disciplina de iis tractatur, nisi in Ethica. Tertio, quia per comparationem virtutum Intellectualium cum doctrina moralium ipsae morales magis elucescunt, & melius cognoscuntur. Plures rationes cur de iis in Ethica sit agendum, vide apud Picol. grad. f. cap. 3. & 4. Interim tamen fatemur, plenariam harum virtutum cognitionem, hic non esse exspectandam: sed quanta facit ad meliorem & pleniorem felicitatis in genere adeptionem, & mediocritatis (quae secundum rectam rationem in virtutibus moralibus observatur) directionem; reliqua partim e Metaphysicis, partim e Mathematicis, partim e Physica, partim ex aliis disciplinis illis, quas vulgo vocant artes liberales inferiores, sunt petenda. Jam vero cum constet, de iis in Ethica tractandum esse, consequens videtur, ut quid sit virtus intellectualis per definitionem explicemus, siquidem ut ait Cic. 1. offic. omnis cognitionis fons a definitione pender. Definitur vero Virtus Intellectualis a Philosopho lib. 6. Nicom. cap. 3. & 3. Eudem. cap. 5. habitus animae rationalis, quo mens nostra affirmando vel negando verum, seu omne id, quod cum rebus ipsis cötentit, enunciat. Sed ut natura istius virtutis melius intelligatur, singulæ partes hujus definitionis discutiendæ veniunt: 1. ipsum definitum. 2. definitio. Definitum vero est virtus ἕξις προαιρετικὴ ἀ λόγοι, quæ vox proprie mentis discurtum significat, quo sensu alteri tantum animæ rationalis parti, ei nempe, quæ ratione utitur, respondet, quanquam sint, qui λόγον latius hoc loco sumi putent, ut quamvis in genere cognitionem significet, & in quavis animæ rationalis parte præter testimonia Ciceronis ex 1. offic. ubi inquit: Homo autem quoniam rationis est particeps, per quam consequentia cernit, principia & rerum causas videt, earumque progressus & quasi antecessiones non ignorat, similitudine comparat, rebusque præsentibus annectit, atque adiungit futuras, facile totius vita cursum videt, ad eamque degendam respraparat necessarias, eademque natura vi rationis hominem conciliat homini & ad orationis & ad vitæ societatem. Sed de hac quæstione infra fusius. 2. Considerant venit ipsa definitio, quæ quatuor hisce constat nempe genere, subjecto, fine & objecto. Genus huic virtuti cum morali est commune: habitus nempe, propterea quod sint species ejusdem generis. Subjectum est ea animæ pars, quæ rationalis dicitur, sicut ipse Philosophus 1. Nicom. cap. ult. & 6. Nicom. cap. 1. docet. Objectum vero sunt res omnes, in quibus verum aut falsum locum habent, sive eæ res sint à Deo & natura productæ, quæ vulgo dicuntur Necessariæ: sive ab hominum pendeant arbitrio, aut aliunde proveniat, & dicuntur Contingentes. Finis est veritatem affirmando
units.tr: ...a full knowledge of happiness, these intellectual matters too had to be treated in their own way. As to the second objection, these virtues are not treated here because of their object but because of the end to which they tend, so that argument proves nothing. To the third objection it is answered that no one has ever denied that these virtues belong to theory. The only question is whether they should also be dealt with in Ethics for the sake of the moral virtues, and especially for the sake of prudence, without which the moral virtues cannot be grasped fully and perfectly. Second, because they are not treated ex professo in any discipline except Ethics. Third, because by comparing the intellectual virtues with the doctrine of morals, the moral virtues themselves stand out more clearly and are better known. For more reasons why they must be treated in Ethics, see Piccolomini, grad. f. cap. 3. & 4. Meanwhile we admit that a full knowledge of these virtues is not to be expected here. What bears on the better and fuller attainment of happiness in general, and on the direction of the mean (which is observed in the moral virtues according to right reason), has been set out. The rest must be sought partly in Metaphysics, partly in Mathematics, partly in Physics, and partly in those other disciplines which are commonly called the lower liberal arts. Now, since it is established that these matters must be treated in Ethics, it seems to follow that we should explain by definition what an intellectual virtue is, since, as Cicero says in De officiis 1, the source of all knowledge depends on definition. The intellectual virtue is defined by the Philosopher in Nicomachean Ethics 6, chap. 3, and Eudemian Ethics 3, chap. 5, as a habit of the rational soul by which our mind, in affirming or denying, states what is true, that is, whatever agrees with the things themselves. But so that the nature of this virtue may be better understood, the individual parts of this definition must be examined: (1) the thing defined itself; (2) the definition. The thing defined is virtue, a state of choice with reason [ἕξις προαιρετικὴ μετὰ λόγου]. This word properly signifies the discourse of the mind, and in this sense it corresponds only to the other part of the rational soul, namely the part that uses reason. Yet some think that logos is taken more broadly here, so that it signifies knowledge in general and belongs to any part of the rational soul. Cicero also bears witness to this in De officiis 1, where he says: Man, since he shares in reason, through which he discerns consequences, sees the first principles and causes of things, and does not ignore their progress and, as it were, their antecedents; he compares like with like, connects and joins present things to future ones, easily sees the whole course of his life, and prepares what is necessary for living it; and by the same power of reason nature binds man to man for both speech and fellowship of life. But this question will be discussed more fully below. (2) Next comes the definition itself, which consists of four parts, namely genus, subject, end, and object. The genus is common to this virtue and to the moral virtue, namely habit, since they are species of the same genus. The subject is that part of the soul which is called rational, as the Philosopher himself teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 1, last chapter, and 6, chap. 1. The object is all those things in which the true or the false has its place, whether they are produced by God and nature, which are commonly called necessary, or depend on human choice or arise from elsewhere, and are called contingent. The end is to state, by affirming or denying, the truth; and in one word, truth, a term which should not be wrongly dragged over to words, but rather referred to the source of the word itself, namely right reason. For these virtues are said to attain their end only when our mind has conformity and agreement with the things that exist outside the mind.

units.la: Ccc vel negando enunciare, & uno verbo, Veritas, quæ vox non est perversè ad verba trahenda, sed potius ad fontem ipsius vocis, nempe ad rectam rationem referri debet. Nam tum demum finem suum assequi dicuntur istæ virtutes, cum mens nostra conformitatem & consensum habet cum rebus ipsis, quæ extra mentem sunt. Cæterum etsi virtutis Intellectualis vulgò finis statuatur Veritas: quidam sunt, qui veritate nullius rei finem esse contendunt, propterea quod veritatem prorsus incomprehensibilem esse putent, qualis fuit Pyrrho Philosophus cjusque sectatores, de quibus Laërtius lib. 6. in vita Pyrrhonis. Empedocles etiam & Democritus veritatem in profundo demersam esse statuebant, & ideo nos nihil scire posse, sed totum nostrum scire esse merum ignorare. Hinc Lactant. lib. 3. Instit. divin. cap. 6. ait: ut nihil sciri posse sciendum sit, aliquid scire necesse est, nam si nihil omnino scias, & ipsum hoc nihil scire tollitur. Et Metrodorus Chius, ut refert Cicero in orat. pro Lucullo initio libri illius, qui est de natura: Nego, inquit, nos aliquid scire, sciamusne, an nescimus idipsum nescire aut scire nos an aliquid omnino sit, an nihil omnino sit. Verum licet multi e veteribus in hac fuerint sententia, nempe quod nihil sciri possit, & propterea nulla rerum veritas haberi, propterea quod pro variis variorum locorum conditionibus & variis etiam hominum opinionibus res subinde variari viderentur: tamen ut eleganter ait Cicero 1. offic. Aristonis, Pyrrhonis, & Perilli & aliorum similiter sentientium jam pridem explosa sententia est. Jam expositâ definitione, sequitur divisio visio (de numero enim nihil attinet hîc dicere, nam vulgò quinque numerantur, Intellectus, Scientia, Sapientia, Prudentia & Ars,) & quia res in quibus verû aut falsum cernitur, sunt duplices, aliæ necessariæ, aliæ contingentes, & circa istas res versatur virtus intellectualis, ideo pro duplicis objecti respectu duplices et constituuntur habitus, ut alii dicantur versari circa res necessarias, alii circa contingentes Arist. 6.Nicom.cap.1.&3. Habet & aliam divisionem à subjecto sumtam 1.Nicom.cap,ult.ut alii dicantur esse in parte animæ intelligibili: aliæ in parte rationali, non quod anima rationalis sic in se dividatur, sed quod illi habitus, qui versantur circa res necessarias, certam pariant scientiam, qui verò circa res contingentes, discursum tantum pariunt & rationis modum. Sed de hac divisione vide ibi locum. Vulgò verò (sed hæc divisio reipsa cum cæteris coincidit) dividitur Virtus Intellectualis à fine, in Contemplativam & Practicam ex Savanorola lib.4 Epit. Ethica, conclus. 8. Contemplativa dicitur, quæ res necessarias cognitionis tantum gratia investigat. Objectû igitur sunt res necessariæ tantum, quæ arbitrio humano non subjacent, sed à Deo & natura producuntur. Finis verò est sola cognitio ad nudam tantum praxin relata. Ejusmodi habitus sunt tres, Intelligetia sive Intellectus specialiter sic dictus: Scientia & Sapientia: qui habitus rursus subdividuntur in simplices nempe & copositos. Simplices sunt, qui uno simplici habitu & respectu constant; nempe duo sunt Intelligentia & Scientia: sola Sapientia dicitur Compositus habitus, quod ex duobus prioribus cōstet & componatur. Nunc singulos suo ordine per-sequemur habitus, &primò de Contemplativis agemus propter duas causas: 1. Quia versantur circa obiectu dignius, nempe res necessarias. 2. Quia per contemplationem inducunt hominem ad rerum cognitionem, & per istam cognitionem coformant intellectum humanum menti divinæ, aut saltem, quàm proximè possunt, perducunt.
units.tr: Although the end of the intellectual virtue is commonly set as truth, there are some who contend that truth is the end of nothing, because they think truth is utterly incomprehensible. Such was the philosopher Pyrrho and his followers, of whom Laertius speaks in Lives of the Philosophers 6, in the life of Pyrrho. Empedocles and Democritus also held that truth was sunk in the depths, and therefore that we can know nothing, and that all our knowing is pure ignorance. Hence Lactantius, Divine Institutes 3, chap. 6, says: for it to be known that nothing can be known, something must be known, for if you know absolutely nothing, even this "knowing nothing" is taken away. And Metrodorus of Chios, as Cicero reports in his speech For Lucullus, at the beginning of that book which is on nature: "I deny," he says, "that we know anything: whether we know, or do not know, that very not-knowing, or whether we know that anything at all exists, or that nothing at all exists." But although many of the ancients were of this opinion, namely that nothing can be known and therefore no truth of things can be held, because the same things seemed to vary from time to time according to the various conditions of places and the various opinions of men, nevertheless, as Cicero elegantly says in De officiis 1, the opinion of Aristo, Pyrrho, Perillus, and others who thought alike has long since been exploded. Now that the definition has been set out, there follows the division. (For there is no need to say anything here about the number, since they are commonly counted as five: Understanding, Science, Wisdom, Prudence, and Art.) And because the things in which the true or false is discerned are of two kinds, some necessary and some contingent, and the intellectual virtue is concerned with these things, therefore, according to the difference in object, two kinds of habit are constituted: some are said to be concerned with necessary things, others with contingent things (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chaps. 1 and 3). He also has another division, taken from the subject, in Nicomachean Ethics 1, last chapter: some are said to be in the intelligible part of the soul, others in the rational part. This is not because the rational soul is divided in itself in this way, but because those habits which are concerned with necessary things produce certain science, whereas those concerned with contingent things produce only discursive reasoning and a mode of reason. But see the passage there about this division. Commonly, however (though this division in fact coincides with the others), the intellectual virtue is divided by its end into contemplative and practical, following Savonarola, Epitome of Ethics 4, conclusion 8. That is called contemplative which investigates necessary things merely for the sake of knowledge. Its object, therefore, is only necessary things, which are not subject to human choice but are produced by God and nature. Its end is knowledge alone, related only to bare practice. Such habits are three: Intelligence, or Understanding as it is specially so called; Science; and Wisdom. These habits are further subdivided into simple and compound. Simple habits are those which consist of a single simple habit and respect; there are two, namely Intelligence and Science. Wisdom alone is called a compound habit, because it consists of and is composed of the two former. Now we shall follow each habit in its order, and first we shall treat of the contemplative ones, for two reasons: (1) because they are concerned with the more worthy object, namely necessary things; (2) because through contemplation they lead man to the knowledge of things, and through that knowledge they conform the human intellect to the divine mind, or at least bring it as near as they can.

units.la: Primus Habitus dicitur Intelligentia, quæ definitur habitus rationis,per quem principia scientiarum & demonstrationum cognoscimus: Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 3. & 1. Metaph. cap. 1. & 5. Eadem. cap. 6. Hunc habitum Philosophus vocat νοῦς, qui generaliter mentem & ipsam rationem adeoque præcipuam & nobilissimâ animæ partem denotat: specialiter verò significat habitum animæ rationalis, quo principia primum in notitiam intellectus deveniunt. De hoc habitu tria observanda docet Philosophus: 1. Objectum, quod constituunt principia & axiomata scientiarum & artium, quæ vulgo vocantur communes notiones seu principia nobiscum nata. Hæc verò, licet nobis naturaliter insita sint, & à natura habeant suam inchoationem, ab hoc tamen habitu perficiuntur, & ad ultimum suum finem perducuntur, cujusmodi sunt: bis duo esse quatuor: quodlibet est, aut non est: Deus est colendus, &c. 2. Et hoc observandum, istam principiorum notitiam esse quidem nobis naturalem, sed tenuem admodum & obscuram propter naturæ imbecillitatem, ideo varia illi declaratione opus esse, ut certior & evidentior evadat, & mentem ipsam perficiat. Nam cum ista principia fluant Quant ex reliquiis illius imaginis divinæ, quam homo habuit ante lapsum, ideo pro tenebris menti humanæ ex lapsu illatis, necesse est, ut variis modis illustretur & ad priorem perfectionem reducatur.
units.tr: The first habit is called Understanding (Intelligentia), defined as a habit of reason, by which we know the principles of the sciences and demonstrations: Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 3, and 1. Metaph. cap. 1, and 5. Eadem. cap. 6. The Philosopher calls this habit nous, a word which in general denotes the mind and reason itself, and so the chief and most noble part of the soul. More specifically, it signifies the habit of the rational soul by which first principles come to be known by the intellect. The Philosopher teaches three things to be observed about this habit. 1. Its object, which consists of the principles and axioms of the sciences and arts, commonly called common notions or principles implanted in us by nature. Although these are naturally within us and take their beginning from nature, they are perfected by this habit and brought to their final end. Examples are: twice two is four; whatever is either is or is not; God is to be worshipped, and so on. 2. It must be observed that this knowledge of principles is indeed natural to us, but very faint and obscure because of the weakness of nature. It therefore needs various explanations to become more certain and evident and to perfect the mind itself. For since these principles flow from the remains of that divine image which man possessed before the Fall, it is necessary, because of the darkness brought upon the human mind by the Fall, that it be illuminated in various ways and restored to its former perfection.

units.la: 3. Et hoc dignū consideratu, q; notitia hæc principiorū in adultis, in sensibus, in hominibus longo retum usu exercitatis, multo reperiatur perfectior & præstantior, quam in pueris & juvenibus, qui experientia, usu & exemplis destituuntur. Nam per ætatem teneriorem ista nec satis observare, neq; per judicium immaturum satis assequi aut capere possunt. Notandum etiam & hoc, quod Cic. lib. 2. de Invent. Intelligentiam partem prudentiæ constituat & sic definiat: quod Intelligentia sit ea pars prudentiæ per quam animus prospicit, & contemplatur ea, quæ jam sunt: sed revera tamen proprie usurpatur in priori sensu, & à Philosopho & ab omnibus, qui de Intelligentia agunt. Plura vide apud Zabarel. lib. 1. de nat. Log. cap. 4.
units.tr: 3. This is also worth considering: this knowledge of principles is found to be much more perfect and excellent in adults, in the wise, and in men practised by long use of affairs, than in children and young people, who lack experience, practice and examples. For at a tender age they can neither observe these things sufficiently nor grasp them with immature judgment. It should also be noted that Cicero, in Book 2 of De Inventione, makes understanding a part of prudence and defines it thus: understanding is that part of prudence by which the mind looks forward and contemplates things that already exist. But in truth the word is properly used in the former sense, by the Philosopher and by all who treat of understanding. See more in Zabarella, Book 1 De natura logicae, cap. 4.

units.la: Secundus habitus est Scientia: quæ definitur habitus mentis demonstrativus, per quem conclusiones necessarias percipimus, per causas veras primas immediatas & priores ipsis conclusionibus. Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 3. 1. mag. moral. cap. 5. 5. Eudem. cap. 6. 1. post. anal. cap. 2. & 1. Phys. Acroas. statim in proœmio. Nomen vero huic habitui primo indidit Zeno, qui ut autor est Cicero 1. Acad. quaest. omne id, quod tam certum & firmum est, ut nulla ratione convelli aut refutari possit, scientiam vocabat. Alias vulgo Scientia significat quamvis animi cognitionem, quovis modo perceptam & hoc sensu & latiore hac significatione Aristoteles Grammaticam, Rhetoricam & Logicam & inferiores istas disciplinas vocat Scientias lib. Categor. cap.8. Proprie tamen nulli competit cognitioni, nisi ei, quæ fit per ejusmodi causas, de quibus in definitione dictum fuit. De hoc habitu observanda docet Philosophus lib. 6. Nicom. cap. 7. 1. Objectum, circa quod versantur: 2. Causam efficientem seu quo pacto comparari possit. Objectum vero est scibile sive omne id, quod sciri aut scientia comprehendi possit. Ea autem sunt, quæ aliter atque aliter se habere non possunt, cujusmodi sunt necessaria, æterna, ingenerabilia & incorruptibilia & cætera ejusmodi. Et ratio duplex est, cur circa ejusmodi objectum versetur scientia: 1. Quia ea tantum scire se arbitrantur homines, quæ nullam mutationem propter certitudinis suæ constantiam sentiunt. Nam quæ aliter atque aliter se habere possunt, sciri certo modo nequeunt, propter ipsarum rerum inconstantiam, levitatem, quæ subinde variari solent: ubi vero est variatio, ibi est dubitatio, & ubi hæc, ibi nulla est scientia: nā ois dubitatio venit ex ignoratione, ignoratio vero opponitur scientiæ. 2. Quia scientia est certa & immutabilis rei cognitio, quæ ad res contingentes se extendere non potest: nam cum crebrā subeant mutationem, & sæpius non sint, quàm sint, fieri non potest, ut aliquid certi mens de iis constituat, & per consequ. aliquid sciat, Aristoteles 6. Nic. cap. 3. & 1. post. cap. 2. 2. Quod ad causam efficientem attinet, hanc ponit Philosophus, nempe cognitionem quandam & doctrinam ex præcognitis 1. post. anal. cap. 1. statim initio, dum enim nota quædam proponuntur, quæ autsensibus sunt obvia aut intellectus ipse statim percipit, ibi mens per ejusmodi nota in rerum ignotarum cognitionem devenit, & propterea oportet discentem aut eum qui aliquid cognoscere velit, generale quandam secum afferre τροχωσι & inchoatâ quodammodo ejus rei, quâ discere velit notitiâ: alioqui non poterit docente perfectè satis assequi: nam non sufficit aptitudo ad discendum, neque etiâ cupiditas aut ardor discendi, nisi etiâ communia quædam principia & scintillas veluti quasdam rei discendæ aut cognoscendæ nobiscum afferamus. Cæterum cum duo sint præcognitorum genera, unum singulare, quæ solo sensu cognoscuntur: alterum universalium seu ejusmodi principiorum, quæ sola mente & intellectu percipiuntur: ideo etiam duo erunt modi ad perfectionem rei cognoscendæ ducentes, Inductio videlicet & Syllogismus: quorum prior Inductio ex singularibus jam bene cognitis, ut pote, quæ sub sensum cadunt, ipsa principia à sensib. remota colligit & confirmat: posterior vero Syllogismus ex principiis per inductionem jam cognitis, cognitione rei per causam suam docet, & sic veram scientiam ostendit, Phil. loc. citatis.
units.tr: The second habit is Science (Scientia), defined as a demonstrative habit of the mind, by which we perceive necessary conclusions through true, first, immediate causes which are prior to the conclusions themselves. Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 3, 1. Mag. Moral. cap. 5, 5. Eudem. cap. 6, 1. Post. Anal. cap. 2, and 1. Phys., at the very beginning of the proem. The name of this habit was first given by Zeno, who, as Cicero reports in 1. Acad. Quaest., used the word scientia for whatever is so certain and firm that it cannot be overturned or refuted by any argument. Otherwise, commonly, scientia signifies any knowledge of the mind, however obtained, and in this wider sense Aristotle calls grammar, rhetoric, logic and such lower disciplines sciences (Categ. cap. 8). Strictly, however, it belongs to no knowledge except that which comes through the kind of causes mentioned in the definition. Concerning this habit the Philosopher teaches that two things are to be observed (Nic. 6, cap. 7): 1. the object with which it is concerned; 2. the efficient cause, or how it may be acquired. The object is what is knowable, that is, whatever can be known or grasped by science. These are things which cannot be otherwise than they are, such as necessary, eternal, ungenerated and incorruptible things, and the like. There are two reasons why science is concerned with such objects. 1. Men think they know only those things which, because of their constancy of certainty, undergo no change. For things which can be otherwise cannot be known with certainty, because of the inconstancy and levity of the things themselves, which often vary. Where there is variation there is doubt, and where there is doubt there is no science; for all doubt comes from ignorance, and ignorance is opposed to science. 2. Science is a certain and unchanging knowledge of a thing, and it cannot extend to contingent things. Since these often undergo change and are often not what they were, it is impossible for the mind to establish anything certain about them and so to know anything (Arist. 6. Nic. cap. 3 and 1. Post. cap. 2). As for the efficient cause, the Philosopher posits a certain cognition and teaching from things already known (1. Post. Anal. cap. 1, at the very beginning). For when certain things are set forth which are either obvious to the senses or which the intellect perceives at once, the mind by means of such known things arrives at knowledge of unknown things. Therefore the learner, or one who wishes to know something, must bring with him some general notion [τροχωσι] and a kind of inchoate grasp of the thing he wishes to learn; otherwise he will not be able to follow the teacher fully. Aptitude for learning is not enough, nor even desire or eagerness to learn, unless we also bring with us certain common principles and, as it were, sparks of the thing to be learned or known. Since there are two kinds of prior knowledge, one singular, known by the senses alone, and the other universal, that is, such principles as are perceived by the mind and intellect alone, there will also be two ways leading to the perfection of knowledge: Induction and Syllogism. The former, Induction, gathers and confirms the principles, remote from the senses, from singulars already well known because they fall under the senses. The latter, Syllogism, from principles already known through induction, teaches knowledge of a thing through its cause, and so shows true science (Phil. loc. cit.).

units.la: Tertius Theoreticus habitus est Sapientia, ex utroque priori Intelligentia scilicet & Scientia conflatus, & ideo ordine naturæ & doctrinæ posterius tractanda venit. Definitur verò à Philosopho 6. Nicom. cap. 7. & 1. mag. moral. cap. 35. & 5. Eudem. cap. 8. Habitus ex Intelligentia & Scientia compositus, quierum bonestissimarum cognitionem sibi vendicat. Quam definitionem & ex veterum sententia sic expressit Cic. offic. Sapientia vero est (sicut à veteribus Phil. definita fuit)rerum divinarum humanarumq;& causarum,quibus hæres continentur, scientia. Verum circa Sapientiam, prout à Philosopho tractatur, quinq; hæc observanda veniunt. 1. Nomen. 2. Genus. 3. Objectum. 4. Requisita seu proprietates. 5. Discrimen & in quibus potissimum differat à Prudentia, nam quia in quibusdam conveniunt, à plerisque pro uno eodemque habitu censentur. Quod ad nomen, ut est magnum per se, sic etiam est latissimum: nam omne id, quod præclarum est, aut illustre aut honore dignum, id Sapientiæ nomine vulgò honoratur. Græcis dicitur σοφία, quod venit à σέβομαι, colo, quod cultum ac venerationem exhibere significat. Sumitur hæc vox tripliciter: 1. Pro certæ alicujus artis perfectione, peritia aut excellentia: Sic cum Polyclerum sapientem fuisse statuarium, aut Apellem sapientem fuisse pictorem, dicimus, nihil aliud innuimus, quam utrumque in arte sua perfectum & excellentem excitisse. 2. A Platone in Phædro usurpatur pro Philosophia: nam ubi definit Philosophiam, quod nempe sit appetitio cognitionis divinæ, per quam homo ipsi assimilatur Deo: ibi statim subjungit: eademque rectè Sapientia dici poterit, propterea quod ad veram Sapientiam homines adducat. 3. Proprie & strictè sumitur pro absoluta rerum cognitione, quæ ex principiis & causis deducitur, cum non modo conclusiones rerum per principia cognoscimus, quod præstat habitus Scientiæ; sed etiam ipsa principia per intelligentiæ habitum perfectè cognoscimus, & in hac significatione proproprie hîc à Philosopho usurpatur. Qui plura de nomine legere velit, consulat Picolom. grad 5. cap. 20. Secundò observandum venit genus, quod est habitus ex Intelligentia & Scientia compositus. Ex Intelligentia, quatenus principia & causas rerum perfectè cognoscit. Ex scientia, quatenus ipsarum conclusionum, quæ ex principiis & causis deducuntur, perfectam docent cognitionem. Tertiò obiectum sunt res omnes earumque causæ, quæ sub mentis humanæ cognitionem veniunt, cujusmodi sunt principia rerum & causæ: tum etiam conclusiones, quæ ex principiis inferuntur. Uno verbo, quicquid Intelligentiæ & Scientiæ subjacet, circa id omne versatur Sapientia, quæ causa fuit, ut veteres Philosophi, Philosophiam vocarent Sapientiam, nam in sola contemplatione sitam esse Philosophiam putabant, quod testatur Plato in Phædro. Hoc tamen constat, Sapientiam esse illum habitum, qui Philosophiæ Theoreticæ æquivalet: non enim ad Theoreticum Philosophum hoc tantum spectat, ut res per causas cognoscat, sed ut etiam ipsas causas & principia cognita habeat: unde male vulgò definitur Philosophia compages Scientiarum & Prudentiarum, siquidem nullius Intelligentiæ hic fit mentio, sine qua Philosophia Theoretica, cognosci & haberi nō poterit. Quartò requisita sunt potissimum tria: 1. Ut sit maximè exquisita & certissima, utpote quæ non tantum conclusiones, sed etiam ipsa rerum principia & causas investigat: & quantum menti humanæ perficiendæ sufficit, & diligenter exquirit, & cognoscere intendit. 2. Ut versetur circa res præstantissimas. tissimas, & sit veluti caput habituum contemplati- vorum, propterea, quod circa res praestantissimas, quae à Deo & natura producuntur, versetur. 3. Ut ad summam cognitionis verae praestantiam, adeoq; summum in rebus cognoscendis gradum perfectionis hominem elevet, Aristot. 6.Nicom.cap.7. Discrimen à Prudentia in tribus maxime cernitur: 1.Quod communi loquendi usu differant Sapientes à Prudentibus, siquidem Thales, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, illi veteres Philosophi, qui in rerum obscurarum & causarum earum investigatione erant occupati, Sapientes tantum dicebantur: Prudentes verò illi solum, & proprie appellari solent, qui in rebus bene agendis ad honeste vivendum, recte consulere possunt. 2. Differunt etiam objecto, nam Prudentia versatur circa res contingentes: Sapientia verò circa res necessarias. 3. Quod prudentia tam ad singularia, quam ad universalia se extendat, & potissimum ad singularia: nam versatur circa actiones humanas: at omnis vis actionum humanarum in singularibus & eorum circumstantiis rite observandis potissimum consistit: Sapientia verò tantum ad universalia se extendit, nam principia & causae, ut naturam universalem habeant, necesse erit, conclusiones etiam, quae ex iis deducuntur, eorum imitantur naturam à quibus descendunt. Arist. 6. Nicom.cap.7. Savanorol.lib.4.epit.ethic.concl.8. Plura vide de Sapientia apud Piccol.gra.5.àcap.21. usque ad cap.26.
units.tr: The third, theoretical habit is Wisdom (Sapientia), compounded of both the former, Understanding and Science, and therefore it comes to be treated later in the order of nature and of teaching. The Philosopher defines it (6. Nicom. cap. 7, 1. Mag. Moral. cap. 35, 5. Eudem. cap. 8) as a habit compounded of Understanding and Science, which claims for itself the knowledge of the most honourable things. Cicero also expressed this definition in the manner of the ancients: Wisdom is (as the ancient philosophers defined it) the science of divine and human things and of the causes in which these are contained. But concerning Wisdom, as the Philosopher treats it, five points are to be considered: 1. the name; 2. the genus; 3. the object; 4. the requisites or properties; 5. the distinction, and in what chiefly it differs from Prudence, since because they agree in some respects, most people regard them as one and the same habit. As to the name: as it is great in itself, so it is also very wide in its application, for whatever is excellent, illustrious or worthy of honour is commonly honoured by the name of wisdom. In Greek it is called sophia, which comes from sebomai, to honour, meaning to show worship and reverence. The word is used in three ways. 1. For the perfection, skill or excellence in some particular art. Thus when we say that Polyclitus was a wise sculptor, or Apelles a wise painter, we mean nothing other than that each excelled and was perfect in his art. 2. Plato in the Phaedrus uses it for philosophy. For when he defines philosophy as the desire for knowledge of the divine, by which man becomes like God, he immediately adds that the same could rightly be called wisdom, because it leads men to true wisdom. 3. Properly and strictly it is taken for absolute knowledge of things deduced from principles and causes. For we know not only the conclusions about things through principles, which the habit of science accomplishes, but also the principles themselves perfectly through the habit of understanding. It is in this sense that the Philosopher uses it here, properly. Whoever wishes to read more about the name may consult Piccolomini, Grad. 5, cap. 20. Second, the genus to be observed is a habit compounded of Understanding and Science: from Understanding, insofar as it perfectly knows the principles and causes of things; from Science, insofar as it teaches the perfect knowledge of the conclusions deduced from principles and causes. Third, the objects are all things and their causes which fall under human knowledge, such as the principles and causes of things, and also the conclusions inferred from principles. In a word, whatever lies under Understanding and Science, Wisdom is concerned with all of it. This is the reason why the ancient philosophers called philosophy wisdom, for they held that philosophy consisted solely in contemplation, as Plato attests in the Phaedrus. Yet it is established that Wisdom is that habit which corresponds to theoretical philosophy. For it concerns the theoretical philosopher not only to know things through causes, but also to have the causes and principles themselves known. Hence it is wrongly defined in common usage as a compact of the Sciences and Prudences, since no mention is made of Understanding, without which theoretical philosophy cannot be known or possessed. Fourth, three requisites are chiefly needed: 1. that it be most exact and most certain, since it investigates not only conclusions but also the principles and causes of things themselves, and as far as suffices for perfecting the human mind it inquires diligently and intends to know them; 2. that it be concerned with the most excellent things, and be as it were the head of the contemplative habits, because it deals with the most excellent things which are produced by God and nature; 3. that it raise man to the highest excellence of true knowledge, and so to the highest degree of perfection in knowing things (Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 7). The distinction from Prudence is seen chiefly in three ways. 1. In common usage, wise men differ from prudent men: Thales, Anaxagoras and Pythagoras, those ancient philosophers who were occupied in investigating obscure things and their causes, were called only wise, whereas those are properly called prudent who can rightly advise in the conduct of affairs for living honourably. 2. They also differ in object, for prudence is concerned with contingent things, wisdom with necessary things. 3. Prudence extends both to singulars and to universals, and chiefly to singulars, since it is concerned with human actions, and the whole force of human actions consists chiefly in rightly observing singulars and their circumstances. Wisdom extends only to universals, for principles and causes, in order to have a universal nature, must necessarily be such, and the conclusions deduced from them imitate the nature of those from which they descend (Arist. 6. Nicom. cap. 7; Savonarola, lib. 4 Epit. Ethic., concl. 8). More on Wisdom may be found in Piccolomini, Grad. 5, from cap. 21 to cap. 26.

units.la: Sic de Intellectualibus speculativis, quae versantur circa res necessarias; sequuntur habitus Practici, qui verversantur circa res contingentes, & quorum finis est praxis & ad actionem referTur, suntq; duo: Prudentia & Ars. Differunt vero a prioribus tribus potissimum: 1. Respectu subjecti, quod priores tres in parte animi intelligibili, id est, quae solam mentis contemplationem requirit, versentur, isti duo in parte animi rationabili, id est, quae praeter discursum mentis requirit etiam voluntatis consensum, ut etiam aliquid ultra producatur, Aristot. 1. Nic. cap. ult. & 6. Nicom. cap. 2. 2. Differunt objectis; nam priores tres versantur circa res necessarias, ut jam dictum fuit, hi vero circa res contingentes. 3. Respectu finis: nam priores habent solam speculationem pro fine, isti duo habent praxin. Ubi etiam hoc notandum, nomen praxeos hic late sumi, ut non solu actioni proprie dictae conveniat, sed etiam effectioni & operationi, nam a Philosopho 6. Nicom. cap. 4. Contingens duplex statuitur: 1. ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, quod in operatione & affectione consistit, alterum κατὰ συμβεβηκός, quod in actione specialiter sic dicta cernitur, unde alius erit habitus, qui versatur circa contingens ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, ut Ars, alius, qui versatur circa contingens κατὰ συμβεβηκός, ut Prudentia: tot enim contingentiū diversi debent constitui habitus, quot sunt rerum contingentium diversi fines & differentiae. At ex his constat, duos esse fines rerum contingentium: ideo duo etiam erunt habitus diversi. Unde ex his colligitur, Artem & Prudentiam partim inter se convenire, partim etiam discrepare. Conveniunt in duobus: 1. in objecto communi: nam utraque versatur circa contingentia. 2. fine generali, quod utraque non in theoria, sed in operatione finem habeat positum. Differunt etiam in tribus: 1. respectu finium specialium, quos istæ duæ virtutes sibi habent proprios: nam Prudentia proprie respicit actionem solam, id est, ea solum agit, quæ ad virtutem moralem & civilem societatem spectat; Ars vero pro fine habet operationem seu effectionem, quæ in externo plerunq; cernitur subjecto. 2. Ars cum sit mere virtus Intellectualis & ad morales proprie non spectet, à virtute morali poterit separari; nam ut præclare ait Philosophus 2. Nicom. cap. 4. nemo ab arte dicitur vir bonus, sed tantum peritus, aut bonus artifex: at Prudentia cum ab ea denominetur vir bonus, ita cum virtute morali est conjuncta, ut ab ea non magis separari possit, quam calor aut lumen à sole Arist. 6. Nic. cap. 5. & 13. Imo est norma, qua virtutes morales diriguntur; lapis Lydius, quo probantur; regina, qua reguntur. 3. Qui in arte peccat sponte sua, ille minus reprehenditur, quam qui invitè, propterea quod in isto appareat inscitia, in altero quædam tantum dissimulatio certis de causis instituta. At contra in Prudentia fit: nam qui sponte peccat, majore reprehensione dignus habetur, quâ qui invitè, propterea quod illud sit malitiæ indicium, hoc verò non item, Aristot. 6. Nicom. cap. 7. Savanorola lib. 4. Ethic. Epit. conclus. 9. Picol. gradu 5. cap. 29. Priusquam autem de Arte & Prudentia separatim agatur, operæ precium esset ad naturam utriusque illustrandam duo hæc præmittere: Primus, quid sit discriminis inter actionem & effectionem. Posterius, quæ sint requisita utriusque. Discrimen in quatuor capitib. potissimum cernitur: 1. Differunt consequente: Nam affectio post operationem suam reliquit aliquod opus tanquam finem; actio vero nil, nisi forte per accidens. 2. Differunt principiis: Nam actionis principium est πρόαιρεσις; effectionis vero, intellectus tanquam causa remota, proxima ipsa aut alia aliqua facultas, quae aut arti aequivalet, aut respondet, Aristot. 6 Metaphys. cap. 1. & lib. 11. cap. 7. 3. Differunt etiam adjunctis: nam actio praestantium bona, priusquam appetitus bene domitus fuerit & subjectus rectae rationi, non fit sine aliqua animi perturbatione & intrinsecus, id est, in ipsa voluntate perficitur: effectio vero fit sine aliqua insigni animi perturbatione cum ab habitu proficiscatur, & extrinsecus tantum absolvitur. 4. Differunt etiam objectis: nam effectio in rebus corporeis aut externis per corporea instrumenta peragendis plerunque consistit; actio vero est in virtutibus & vitiis: est enim actio humanae libertatis operatio in iis, quae ad vitam humanam regendam spectant, & provenit ex ratione & proaeresi, & ejus tantum gratia, quod in operatione includitur, institui solet Aristot. 6. Nicom. cap. 8.
units.tr: Thus, as the speculative intellectual habits are concerned with necessary things, so the practical habits follow, which are concerned with contingent things. Their end is practice, and they refer to action. There are two of them: Prudence and Art. They differ from the former three chiefly in three respects: (1) with respect to the subject, since the former three lie in the intelligible part of the soul, which requires only the contemplation of the mind, whereas these two lie in the rational part of the soul, which requires, besides the reasoning of the mind, also the consent of the will, so that something may further be produced; Aristotle, 1. Nic. cap. ult. & 6. Nicom. cap. 2. (2) they differ in their objects, for the former three are concerned with necessary things, as has already been said, but these two with contingent things; (3) with respect to the end, for the former have only speculation as their end, while these two have practice. Here it should also be noted that the word "practice" is used broadly in this place, so that it applies not only to action properly so called but also to making and doing. For the Philosopher, 6. Nicom. cap. 4., says that the contingent is twofold: (1) that which is as for the most part [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ], which consists in operation and affection; and the other, by accident [κατὰ συμβεβηκός], which is seen in action specifically so called. Hence there will be one habit that is concerned with the contingent as for the most part [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ], such as Art, and another that is concerned with the contingent by accident [κατὰ συμβεβηκός], such as Prudence. For as many different habits must be posited for contingent things as there are different ends and differences of contingent things. But from these points it is clear that there are two ends of contingent things, and therefore there will also be two different habits. From this it is gathered that Art and Prudence partly agree with each other and partly differ. They agree in two respects: (1) in the common object, for both are concerned with contingent things; (2) in the general end, since both place their end not in theory but in operation. They differ also in three respects: (1) with respect to their special ends, which these two virtues have as their own. For Prudence properly regards action alone, that is, it deals only with those things which pertain to moral virtue and civil society; but Art has as its end operation or production, which for the most part is seen in an external subject. (2) Since Art is purely an intellectual virtue and does not properly concern the moral virtues, it can be separated from moral virtue. For, as the Philosopher rightly says, 2. Nicom. cap. 4., no one is called a good man because of his art, but only skilled or a good craftsman. But Prudence, since a man is called good from it, is so joined to moral virtue that it can no more be separated from it than heat or light from the sun; Aristotle, 6. Nic. cap. 5. & 13. Indeed it is the rule by which the moral virtues are directed, the touchstone by which they are tested, and the queen by which they are ruled. (3) He who sins in art of his own will is blamed less than he who sins unwillingly, because in the latter ignorance appears, while in the former there is only a certain pretence, adopted for certain reasons. But the reverse is true in Prudence: for he who sins willingly is considered more deserving of blame than he who sins unwillingly, because the former is a sign of malice, while the latter is not; Aristotle, 6. Nicom. cap. 7.; Savonarola, lib. 4. Ethic. Epit. conclus. 9.; Piccolomini, gradu 5. cap. 29. Before Art and Prudence are treated separately, it would be worthwhile to premise two things in order to illustrate the nature of each: first, what the difference is between action and production; second, what the requisites of each are. The difference is seen chiefly in four respects: (1) they differ in their consequence: for production, after its operation, leaves some work behind as its end, whereas action leaves nothing, except perhaps by accident. (2) They differ in their principles: for the principle of action is choice [προαίρεσις]; of production, the intellect as the remote cause, and the proximate cause is the faculty itself or some other faculty which either corresponds to or answers to art; Aristotle, 6. Metaphys. cap. 1. & lib. 11. cap. 7. (3) They differ also in their circumstances: for the action of good men, before their appetite has been well tamed and made subject to right reason, does not take place without some disturbance of the mind, and is accomplished inwardly, that is, in the will itself; but production takes place without any notable disturbance of the mind, since it proceeds from a habit and is completed only outwardly. (4) They differ also in their objects: for production consists for the most part in things that are bodily or external and are to be done through bodily instruments; but action is concerned with the virtues and vices. For action is the operation of human freedom in those things which pertain to the governing of human life, and it arises from reason and choice, and is usually undertaken for the sake of that which is included in the operation itself; Aristotle, 6. Nicom. cap. 8.

units.la: Alterum vero, quod observandum diximus, sunt requisita actionis & effectionis. In utraque tria necessario requiruntur: 1. In effectione intellectus arte perfectus, aut qui artis habitu sit praeditus: nam intellectus est primum principium & prima causa artis. 2. Requiruntur externa membra, tanquam instrumenta exsequentia, quae intellectus praecipit. 3. Finis aliquis post operationem permanens, verbi gratia: opus aliquod in externo aliquo subjecto. In actioactione itidem sunt tria requisita: 1. Intellectus dirigens seu ipsa ratio, quae intendit actionem. 2. Proaeresis exsequens imperium rationis in producenda actione. 3. Appetitus utrique obediens, qui veluti ancilla statim peragit, quod ratio domina ex proaeresi praecipit. Atq; his de utraque tam de Arte quam de Prudentia generaliter praemissis, consequens est, ut de singulis singulatim agatur: ac primo de Arte, non quod ars praestantius aut dignius quid sit Prudentia, sed ut eae virtutes Intellectuales primo removeantur, quae nullam sine solo nomine affinitatem habent cum virtute morali, quales sunt speculativae illae tres, de quibus actum fuit, & inter practicas ars, de qua quinque haec observanda breviter veniunt: 1. vocabulum artis. 2. definitio. 3. objectum circa quod in specie versatur. 4. officium & artis & artificis. 5. proprietates nonnullae. Primo vocabulum artis varie significat. Nam interdum ponitur pro quavis in genere agnitione aut quavis etiam cognitione, ita ut scientiae etiam competat, unde Cicero etiam 2. de Orat. ait: Ars propriè est earum rerum, quae propriè sciuntur; ibi artis nomen late sumitur. 2. Significat variorum praeceptorum collectionem ex mentis habitu profectorum, quomodo eam definit Lucianus in Parasito: Ars est collectio praeceptorum usu cognitorum ad utilem aliquem rerum humanarum finem, quae tantum est idea quaedam & magnum ad artem addiscendam adminiculum. 3. Nomen artis significat habitum mentis, qui affectionem proprie spectat, & hoc sensu sumitur à Philosopho 5. Eadem, cap. 4. Secundò consideranda veniunt definitio: definitur ars à Philosopho habitus recta cum ratione effectivus. In qua definitione duo consideranda sunt: 1. quod dicatur habitus non simpliciter, sed effectivus, qua voce distinguitur à Prudentia: nam Prudentia non efficit, sed agit tantum, sicut in discrimine effectionis & actionis jam diximus. 2. additur cum ratione, qua particula ars distinguitur à naturali appellatione: nam natura quidem in eo subjecto, in quo inest, rationem non sibi tenet, neque ex proaeresi agit, cum hoc ad solum hominem spectet, cui proprie competit anima rationalis, intellectus & judicium. Verum si haec definitio dextre & sano modo intelligatur, non tantum artibus mechanicis, sed etiam ingenuis & liberalibus accommodari poterit.
