Nam effectio, quae est finis artis, est duplex; alia materialis, quae instrumenta externa & corporea & materiam externam & sensibilem ad sui productionem requirit, qualis effectio proprie cernitur in artibus mechanicis: alia est immaterialis, nō quod omni materia aut objecto destituatur, sed cp externa materia, ut opus suum fabricet & perficiat, non requirat, neq; et instrumentis corporeis & externis indigeat: & hoc posteriori modo artes liberales, quae a Cic. vocatur Logicae, artis nomen merito sibi vendicant, suffragante Arist. l. 1. soph. Elench. c. 11. Et de hac distinctione effectionis prolixius agit Scal. l. 1. de art. Poet. Unde Grammatica, Rhetorica & Logica hoc sensu recte Artes appellari possunt. Tertio notandum est, Objectu artis, cp duplex à Phil. statuitur, unum commune, aliud proprium. Commune sunt res contingentes, quae varia mutatione subire possunt propter naturae suae inconstantiam: cū artis hoc sit proprium, ut materiæ sibi subjectæ alia atq; aliā inducat formā. Objectū proprium sunt res contingentes quidē, sed quæ principium ac causam sui efficientem habent, seu non à seipso habent, ut producuntur, sed ab artifice, qui materiā ipsam movet, ut formam aliā admittat secundū artē. Quarto officiū artificis circa causam naturalē in tribus a Phil. constituitur 6.Nic.c.4. 1.in contemplatione secundū idea. 2. in operatione secundū artē. 3. in opere producendo secundum habitū artis. Dicitur in contemplatione, quia artifex priusquam aliquod opus producat aut aggrediatur, etiā debet rectè apud se perpendere & meditari, quomodo in materia subjecta formam secundum artē producat, id est, debet habere ideā quandam operis futuri in mente sua, secundū quam ranquam regulam opus aliquod artis producat. Additur autem in operatione, ut hempe secundum præscriptum artis operetur, & talem producat formam, qualem ars ipsa requirit. Hæc autē, ut fiat legitimè, tribus opus est medii: 1. Ablatione, ut nempe auferat omnia superflua, quæ scopo suo inservire nequeunt. 2. Additione, ut nimirum addat omnia necessaria, sine quibus finis artis comparari non potest, aut opus ipsum, quod intenderat, in effectum non possit deduci. 3. Opus est immutatione, ut nempe vi & virtute artis formam materiæ subjectæ transmutet in aliam, qualem & mente intenderat & ars postularat. Tertium officium est, ut ep*s producatur secundum habitum artis, quod ut fiat non tantum præcepta ipsa, sed etiam usum tenere necesse est: nam sunt brevia præcepta & cito etiam addisci possunt. usus vero non nisi longo temporis intervallo, longa etiam experientia & diuturna exercitatione comparatur, & hinc fit, ut artem non in præceptis, sed in usu constare afferat Hippocrates Aphorif. 1. Quintò obseruandæ sunt quædam proprietates Artis, imprimis vero iste quatuor: 1. Quod ars sit imitatrix naturæ, teste Philosopho, & quod instar naturæ opera varia producat: & licet naturæ proprie conveniat, ut rerum formas producat, hoc etiam arti tribuitur, dum per imitationem quandam quascunque naturā ipsa in substantiis formas constituit, eadem etiā ars effingere conatur, ut in pictoria, sculptoria, &c. videre licet. 2. Quod natura producat formas substantiales & internas: ars vero accidentales tantum & externas: neque enim artifex novam aliquam substantiam propria sua virtute efficere poterit, sed substantias à natura productas varia forma accidentali excolit & subinde mutat. Verùm de hac quæstione, an scilicet Ars substantiam efficiat? accuratè disputat Goclenius in disput. Phil. & Scalig. lib. 1. Latantii p. 226. & Zabarella lib. 2. de meth. cap. 9. 3. Causa impulsiva artium inveniendarum, fuit indigentia, adeo ut indigentiæ humanæ vera medicina artes dici possint, nam cum multis rebus se indigere videbant homines, verbi gratia: frugibus ad alimentum, calceis & vestibus ad tegumentum ædificiis ad habitationem & conservationem, ad unamquamque rem comparandam, quæ indigentiam supplerent, certas invenerunt artes, cujusmodi sunt agricultura, sartoria, sutoria, &c. de quibus omnibus earumq; causis inventricibus vide Polyd. Virgil. lib. 1. de invent. rerum. 4. Quod arti opponatur ἀπειρία (seu inscitia & quod ars nullum habeat osorem, nisi ignorantem & merainscitia laborantem. Cujus rei illustre extat exemplum in Johanne Basilide Moscovitarum tyranno, cum Christianus ejus nominis III. Daniæ Rex Livonis pacem impetrare cupiens, unà cū aliis muneribus globulum cœlestem assabre factum, in quo singulæ sphæræ & orbes suum peragebant motum ad placandum ei obtulit, Moscovita reliqua quidè munera libenter admisit, sed globum cœlestem cōtumeliosè derisum remisit, inquiens, Regem Daniæ stultè de cœlo cogitare cum de terra armis foret certandum.
units.tr: The second point, which we said should be observed, concerns the requisites of action and of making. Three things are necessarily required in each. (1) In making: an intellect perfected by art, or one endowed with the habit of the art, for the intellect is the first principle and first cause of art. (2) External members are required as executing instruments, which the intellect directs. (3) Some end that remains after the operation, for example, some work in an external subject. In action there are likewise three requisites: (1) the directing intellect, or reason itself, which aims at the action; (2) proaeresis [προαίρεσις], executing the command of reason in producing the action; (3) appetite, obeying both, which, like a handmaid, immediately carries out what reason, as mistress, prescribes through proaeresis. Having laid down these things in general about each, both about art and about prudence, it follows that we should treat each one separately. First we shall treat of art, not because art is nobler or more worthy than prudence, but so that those intellectual virtues which have no affinity with moral virtue beyond the name are set aside first, such as the three speculative virtues already discussed, and, among the practical ones, art. Five things about art are to be observed briefly: (1) the word art; (2) its definition; (3) the object with which it is specifically concerned; (4) the office of both art and artist; (5) certain properties. First, the word art has various meanings. Sometimes it is used for any knowledge in general, or indeed for any cognition, so that it also applies to science; whence Cicero also says in 2. de Orat.: Art properly belongs to those things which are properly known; there the name of art is taken broadly. (2) It signifies a collection of various precepts arising from a habit of the mind, as Lucian defines it in Parasito: Art is a collection of precepts known through use, directed to some useful end of human affairs, which is only a certain idea and a great aid to learning the art. (3) The name of art signifies a habit of the mind which properly regards the making, and in this sense it is taken by the Philosopher in 5. Eadem, cap. 4. Second, the definition must be considered. Art is defined by the Philosopher as a productive habit accompanied by true reason. In this definition two things are to be considered: (1) it is called a habit, not simply, but productive, a word by which it is distinguished from prudence; for prudence does not produce but only acts, as we have already said in the distinction between making and acting. (2) The words accompanied by reason are added, by which particle art is distinguished from natural faculty; for nature, in the subject in which it inheres, does not hold reason and does not act by proaeresis, since this belongs to man alone, to whom properly belong a rational soul, intellect and judgment. But if this definition is understood rightly and soundly, it can be applied not only to mechanical arts but also to the liberal and noble arts. For making, which is the end of art, is twofold: one is material, which requires external and bodily instruments and external and sensible matter for its production, such as is properly seen in the mechanical arts; the other is immaterial, not because it lacks all matter or object, but because it does not require external matter to fabricate and perfect its work, nor does it need bodily and external instruments. In this latter manner the liberal arts, which Cicero calls the Logical arts, rightly claim the name of art, with Aristotle agreeing in l. 1. soph. Elench. c. 11. Scaliger treats this distinction of making at greater length in l. 1. de art. Poet. Hence grammar, rhetoric and logic may rightly be called arts in this sense. Third, it must be noted that the object of art is set down by the Philosopher as twofold, one common and the other proper. The common object is contingent things, which can undergo various changes because of the inconstancy of their nature, since it is the property of art to introduce one form after another into the matter subject to it. The proper object is contingent things indeed, but which have their efficient principle and cause of themselves, or do not have from themselves that they are produced, but from the artist, who moves the matter itself so that it admits another form according to art. Fourth, the office of the artist with respect to the natural cause is set out by the Philosopher in *Nic.* 6, c. 4 as threefold: (1) in contemplation according to the idea; (2) in operation according to art; (3) in producing the work according to the habit of art. It is said "in contemplation" because the artist, before he produces or undertakes any work, ought first rightly to weigh and meditate within himself how he is to produce a form in the subject matter according to art; that is, he ought to have in his mind a certain idea of the future work, by which as a rule he produces some work of art. But it is added "in operation," so that he works according to the prescription of art and produces such a form as art itself requires. For this to be done lawfully, three kinds of means are needed: (1) removal, that is, he must take away all superfluous things which cannot serve his purpose; (2) addition, that is, he must add all things necessary, without which the end of art cannot be attained or the work he intended cannot be brought to effect; (3) change, that is, by the power and virtue of art he must transform the form of the subject matter into another, such as he intended in his mind and art demanded. The third office is that the work be produced according to the habit of art, which, for this to happen, requires that one hold not only the precepts themselves but also practice; for the precepts are brief and can be learned quickly, but practice is acquired only over a long interval of time, with long experience and continual exercise; hence Hippocrates, in Aphorism 1, says that art consists not in precepts but in practice. Fifth, certain properties of art are to be observed, especially these four: (1) that art is an imitator of nature, as the Philosopher testifies, and that, in the manner of nature, it produces various works; and although it properly belongs to nature to produce the forms of things, this too is attributed to art, since by a certain imitation art endeavours to fashion the same forms that nature constitutes in substances, as can be seen in painting, sculpture, etc. (2) That nature produces substantial and internal forms, but art only accidental and external ones; for the artist cannot by his own power produce any new substance, but polishes substances produced by nature with various accidental forms and changes them from time to time. But concerning this question, whether art produces substance, Goclenius disputes it accurately in his Disputations on Philosophy, and Scaliger in lib. 1, Lactantius, p. 226, and Zabarella in lib. 2, de meth., cap. 9. (3) The impelling cause of discovering arts was need, so that the arts may be called the true remedy of human need; for when men saw that they lacked many things, for example, grain for food, shoes and clothing for covering, buildings for habitation and preservation, they found certain arts for procuring each thing which would supply their need, such as agriculture, tailoring, shoemaking, etc. On all these and their inventive causes see Polydore Vergil, lib. 1, de invent. rerum. (4) That art is opposed to inexperience [ἀπειρία], or ignorance, and that art has no enemy except the ignorant and those labouring under sheer inexperience. A famous example of this exists in John Basilides, tyrant of the Muscovites: when Christian III, King of Denmark, wishing to obtain peace, offered him, along with other gifts, a celestial globe skilfully made, in which each sphere and orb performed its motion, to please him, the Muscovite willingly accepted the other gifts but sent back the celestial globe with contemptuous mockery, saying, The King of Denmark is foolish to think about heaven when he ought to be fighting with arms over the earth.

units.la: Tale etiam fuit factum Gottorum & Vandalorum cū Roma capta de Bibliothecis cōsulerent, utrū servare, an verò igni tradere deberent, tū quidā in medium prorūpit, inquiens: nugas istas esse servandas ad enervandos Romanorum animos, arma verò ipsis esse tractanda.
units.tr: The same thing happened when the Goths and Vandals, after Rome had been taken, were deliberating about the libraries, whether they ought to be preserved or handed over to the fire. Then one of them stepped forward and said: "Those trifles should be kept, so that they will weaken the spirits of the Romans, but arms must be the things they are given to handle."

units.la: Restat jam Prudentia, quinta Virtutum Intellectualium, quam ideo in ultimum locum rejecimus, quòd majori explicatione indigeat, cum sit Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum moralium, & ideo ad doctrinam Ethicam, quam hîc tractamus, maximè spectat. Definitur verò Prudentia à Philosopho 1.mag.moral.cap.35. Habitus verus cum ratione agendi ea, quæ sunt homini bona vel mala. De Prudentia hoc modo definita sex hæc observanda breviter veniunt: 1. Nomen. 2. Genus. 3. Forma. 4. Objectum. 5. Species. 6. Cognata. Primò verò quod ad Nomen attinet, dicitur φρόνησις ἀπὸ τῆς φρενὸς à mente, quia hæc virtus mentis præcipuum est ornamentum: nam dum homo ad bene beateq; vivendum tendit, mentem illi per virtutes morales excolit & informat. Latinè dicitur Prudentia quasi providentia, ut autor est Cic. 1. de leg. quia per hanc virtute unusquisque sibi providet, quid fugiendum, quid eligendum sit: vel quod praecipuus huius virtutis effectus & scopus consistat in providendis futuris; nam ille vere prudens dicitur, qui non tantum ea, quae ante pedes sunt, sed et longè futura prospicit. Nomen vero Prudentiae diversimodè sumitur, nam varias apud varios autores habet significationes: Aelian. de nat. anim. cap. 2. lib. 1. Prudentiam brutis animalibus tribuit, ut formicis, quod in futuru sibi prospiciant, & in aestate colligant, quibus hyeme fruantur, & quod adversus pericula & frigus se praeclarè muniant, dum non dos instruunt. Verum ut rectè annotavit D. Thomas in lib. de memoria & reminiscentia, lect. 1. haec brutorum perspicientia non tam prudentia, quam naturalis sagacitas quaedam, quae non actionibus comparatur, sed naturae instinctu ingeneratur, dici debet. 2. Sumitur nomen Prudentiae pro sagacitate & calliditate ingenii in solo homine, unde is Prudens vulgò dici solet, qui aliis solertia & acumine mentis antecellit, sive id fiat in rebus bonis, sive malis. Talis fuit prudentia in Ulysse, qui per quandam ingenii solertiam Palamedem & Ajacem praecipuos Graecorum Duces è medio tollendos curavit. 3. Sumitur Prudentia pro habitu mentis, qui secundum rectam rationem agit, & actiones hominum secundum regulam rectae rationis dirigit, & sic hoc loco definita fuit. Secundò consideratur Genus, quod est habitus, cum adjectione, nempe practicus, in qua voce includitur finis Prudentiæ,& per quam distinguitur à tribus virtutibus speculativis, nempe ab Intelligentia,Scientia,Sapientia,quarum finis in theoria,non in praxi cōsistit, & per voce praxeʋs distinguitur ɛt ab Arte, quæ effectionem non actione pro fine habet. Tertiò consideráda venit forma,quæ in ratione cōsultandi de rebus humanis cōsistit, idque non tantum universaliter, sed etiam particulariter. Non enim sufficit ad formam prudentiæ cognoscendam, scire in genere res humanas, sed necesse est, ut in singularibus & per circumstátias temporis, loci & personarum cognoscantur, Aristot. 6. Nic.cap.8. Et hinc etiam contingere videmus,ut sæpenumero homines indocti & plebei,sed rerum singularium periti in negotiis Reipub. gerendis, longè antecellant viris doctis,quirerum singularium non adeo sunt periti, Savanarola lib.4. Epit. Ethic.conclus. 1. Quartò, objectum Prudentiæ, sunt τὰ ἐνδεχόμενα πραγματικά, contingentia activa,id est,quæ sub actione cadunt, quæq; homini sunt bona vel mala; neq; enim naturam bonitatis aut malitiæ à seipsis sortiuntur, sed à modo agendi & à proærefi per quam primò eduntur. Aristot. 6.Nicom. cap.8. Hinc Cicero lib. 2. de inuent. Prudentiam definit, quod sitrerum bonarum & malarum, & utrarumque, prout aguntur,cognitio. Totidem verbis extat apud Diogen.Laërt. lib.7.in vita Zenonis, qui ex sententia Stoicorum Prudentiam sic definiebat: Prudentiam versari circa agibilia seu res agendas, probat Philosophus loco citato inductione eorum, qui propter negotia dextrè perité & sapienter administrata, prudentes apud omnes habiti fuerūt, quales inter Græcos fuerunt Themistocles, Solon, Lycurgus, & alii, ubi etiam Sapientes à Prudentibus distinguit, & Thaletem vocat Sapientem, quod in consideratione syderum plurimum præstarit, sed in negotiis Reipub. parum aut nihil sciverit. Cæterum de Prudentiæ objecto; hoc inprimis observari debet, quod cum versetur circa contingentia, & potius circa singularia & individua quam universalia, & ideo cernatur in rebus inconstantibus, caducis & ambiguis, ideo nemo sue prudentiæ nimium confidere debet, cum videat pendere à rebus admodum lubricis, quę infinitis mutationibus obnoxiæ sunt, & qui nimiū prudentiæ suæ confidunt, sæpenumero in infinitas miserias incidunt, sicut historiæ Romanæ testantur.
units.tr: We now come to Prudence, the fifth of the intellectual virtues, which we have put in the last place because it needs a fuller explanation. It is the leader and guide of all the moral virtues, and so it bears most directly on the ethical teaching we are treating here. The Philosopher defines Prudence in 1 Magna Moralia, chapter 35, as "a true habit, together with a reasoned way of acting in regard to what is good or bad for a human being." Prudence, so defined, calls for six matters to be briefly observed: (1) the name; (2) the genus; (3) the form; (4) the object; (5) the species; (6) its kindred virtues. First, as to the name: it is called phronesis, derived from the mind [φρόνησις ἀπὸ τῆς φρενός], because this virtue is the chief ornament of the mind; for when a person strives to live well and happily, he cultivates and shapes his mind through the moral virtues. In Latin it is called prudentia, as if it were providentia (foresight), as Cicero says in De legibus, book 1, because through this virtue each person foresees for himself what is to be avoided and what is to be chosen; or because the chief effect and aim of this virtue lies in providing for the future, since he is rightly called prudent who looks not only at what is before his feet but also far ahead. The name Prudence, however, is used in different ways, for it has various meanings among various authors. Aelian, in On the Nature of Animals, book 1, chapter 2, ascribes prudence to brute animals, as to ants, because they look ahead for themselves, gather in summer what they may enjoy in winter, and protect themselves well against dangers and cold, since they do not build houses. But as Thomas Aquinas rightly observed in his commentary On Memory and Reminiscence, lecture 1, this foresight of brutes ought to be called not so much prudence as a certain natural sagacity, which is not acquired by actions but implanted by the instinct of nature. Second, the name Prudence is used for the shrewdness and cleverness of mind found in man alone; hence he is commonly called prudent who surpasses others in skill and sharpness of mind, whether this is applied to good or to bad ends. Such was the prudence of Ulysses, who by a certain cleverness of mind saw to it that Palamedes and Ajax, the chief leaders of the Greeks, were removed from the way. Third, Prudence is taken for a habit of mind that acts according to right reason and directs human actions by the rule of right reason, and it is in this sense that it has been defined here. Second, we consider the genus, which is "habit," with the addition "practical," a word which includes the end of Prudence and by which it is distinguished from the three speculative virtues, namely Understanding, Knowledge and Wisdom, whose end lies in contemplation, not in practice; and by the word praxis [πρᾶξις] it is also distinguished from Art, which has production rather than action as its end. Third, the form must be considered, which consists in the reasoned deliberation about human affairs, and this not only in general but also in particulars. For it is not enough, in order to know the form of prudence, to know human affairs in general; they must be known in particular cases and through the circumstances of time, place and persons (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 8). And from this we often see that untaught and common people, who know particular affairs, far surpass learned men in managing the business of the commonwealth, since the learned are not so skilled in particular matters (Savonarola, Epitome of Ethics, book 4, conclusion 1). Fourth, the object of Prudence is ta endechomena pragmatika [τὰ ἐνδεχόμενα πραγματικά], contingent things that are active, that is, things that fall under action and are good or bad for a human being; for they do not derive the nature of goodness or badness from themselves, but from the manner of acting and from the choice [proairesis] through which they are first brought about (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 8). Hence Cicero, in De inventione book 2, defines Prudence as the knowledge of good things, bad things, and those which are neither, as they are done. The same words are found in Diogenes Laertius, Life of Zeno, book 7, where he defines Prudence in accordance with the opinion of the Stoics. That Prudence is concerned with things to be done, the Philosopher proves in the passage cited by induction from those who, because they conducted affairs skilfully, expertly and wisely, were held to be prudent by everyone; among the Greeks such were Themistocles, Solon, Lycurgus and others. There, too, he distinguishes the wise from the prudent, and calls Thales wise because he excelled in the study of the stars, but knew little or nothing of the business of the commonwealth. Moreover, concerning the object of Prudence, this above all must be observed: since it is concerned with contingent things, and with particulars and individuals rather than universals, and so is found in things that are changeable, perishable and uncertain, therefore no one should place too much confidence in his prudence, since he sees that it depends on very slippery matters, which are subject to endless changes; and those who put too much trust in their own prudence often fall into endless misery, as Roman history bears witness.

units.la: Quintò, cognoscendæ veniunt species Prudentiæ, quæ respectu rerum & personarum, in quibus ipsa cernitur Prudentia, diversę constituuntur. Nam dividitur primò in privatā, qua quis utitur erga seipsum, & ideo à Philosopho 6. Nicom. cap. 8. dicitur Prudentia ad unum aut ad seipsum: & in publicam, quæ ad alios se extendit, & ibidem dicitur Prudentia ad alios atque alios. Prudentia privata seu erga seipsum est, qua quis sibi ipsi sapit, & quæ ad suam unius ipsius utilitatem, solerter & dextrè providere potest. Rectè enim Cicero ad Trebat. epist. 16. lib. 1. famil. Illud semper memento, ne quicquam sapit, qui sibi ipsi sapiens prodesse nequit. Et nota sunt proverbia: Odi sapientem, qui sibi ipsi non est sapiens: Tunica vicinior est pallio: Omnes sibi melius malunt, quàm alteri: Charitas ordinata incipit à seipsa. Hanc Prudentiam recte ut teneamus, amplectendum est illud, quod lib. 4. de virtut. præcipit Seneca: Si prudens fit animus omnes vitæ actiones tribus temporibus dispensat; præfentia ordinat, futura præuidet, præterita recordatur: nam qui præsentia recte non disponit, in miseriam temere cadit, qui de præteritis nihil cogitat, vitam perdit, & obli-uiscitur sui; qui de futuris nihil præmeditatur, in omnia periculainca utus incidit. Altera dicitur Publica, & est prudentia communis, qua quis non sibiipsi tantum, sed & aliis de rebus utilibus & bonis recte consulit. Quare præclarè scriptum est à Platone (verba sunt Ciceronis 1. offic.) non solum nobis nati sumus, sed ortus nostri partem patria vendicat, partem parentes, partem amici, atque ut placet Stoicis, quæ in terris gignuntur omnia hominum causa creari, homines verò hominum causa essegeneratos, ut ipsi inter se alii alii prodesse possint: in hac natura debemus sequi Ducem, & communes vitæ utilitates in medium afferre. Vbi ex Stoicorum sententia & secundum rei veritatem docet, Prudentiam proprie esse illam, quæ aliis, non sibi tantum consulit. Dividitur rursus hæc Prudentia communis in œconomicam & politicam, quia duos istos diversos habet scopos, ut nempe vel familiæ vel Reipublicæ inserviat. Prudentia œconomica est prudentia communis de rebus utilibus & bonis, & quâ consulitur & prospicitur iis omnibus, quæ sunt necessaria familiæ, & hæc vel consistit in personis, quæ familiam ipsam constituunt, cujusmodi sunt pater & materfamilias, liberi, mercenarii & mancipia: vel in rebus ipsis, quibus alenda & sustentanda est familia, cujusmodi sunt agricultura, venatus, piscatus, aliæque officia & artes, quibus humanæ vitæ necessitatibus succurritur. Hujus Prudentiæ plures constituuntur species aut partes, quas tamen Cato apud Cicer. 2. offic. paucis complexus est. Ex eo enim cum quæreretur, quid maximè in re familiari expediret? respondit, benefacere: secundum quid? satis benefacere, quid tertium, bene vestire, quid quartum? bene arare, adeo ut Prudentiæ œconomicæ species in tribus constare asseruerit, in pastoria, agricultura, & in lanificio. Succinctius Pittacus, qui illam domum optimè constitutam pronunciabat, cui superfluum nihil redundet, & necessarium nihil desit, referente Stobæo serm. 4. de Justitia. Plura de hac Prudentia in œconomicis. Prudentia Politica est prudentia communis, qua & Reipublicæ & civitati in qua nati sumus, de utilibus & bonis rectæ consulere possumus: estque hæc prudentia propria bonorum civium, quibus solis Respub. curæ & cordi esse solet Aristot. 6. Nicom. cap. 8. sciunt enim viri boni, ad hoc se esse natos, ut Reip. inserviant, & cum sint membra Reipublicæ, illi tanquam suo corpori prospectum inprimis cupiunt, quo nomine Plato in Alcibiade eleganter dxit, hinc sanè Prudentem rectè dixerimus, qui non sibi tantum, sed & Reipubl.in qua natus est rectè consulere possit. Est enim Res. publ.ut ait Cicero 2.de leg. nomen universæ civitatis proqua nos mori & cui totos nos dare, & in qua omnia nostra ponere & quasi consecrare debemus. Subdividitur hæc rursus in νομοθετικὴν seu Legislatoriam, & quæ proprie versatur in universalibus & in πραγματικὴν, quæ respicit singularia. Nam circumstantia bene confiderat & ponderat, Ariftot. 6. Nicom. cap. 8. Legiflatoria, quæ alias dicitur Jurifprudentia, est ea, quæ versatur circa rectam legum interpretationem, & quæ nõ modo benignè fecundum æquitatem leges explicat, sed & leges salutares & utiles Reipublicæ condit. Hæc Prudentia est Magistratui inprimis necessaria, namque ut ait Cicero 1.de legib. cui Reip. cura fit commissa, & oratione & prudentia inprimis indiget, qua & populos sibi subjectos regat, & leges à fe latas stabiliat, improbos, ne in malitia perseverent, castiget, & bonos, ut in suo bonitatis vigore pergant, tueatur. Hac prudentia præreliquis laudantur inter Græcos Solon Atheniensis & Lycurgus Lacedæmoniorum legislator, ex quorum legibus, propterea quod super jus naturæ & fecundum rectam rationem latæ erant, pleraque Latini mutuati sunt, ut ex utrarumq; collatione facile patebit. Prudentia practica, quæ est altera species politicæ prudetiæ, illa dicitur, quæ in recte administrandis Reipub. negotiis tota ternitur, idque particulariter & fecundum varias circumstantias, qua in re potissimum differt à legiflatoria: namque ea versatur circa Reipub. negotia, sed universaliter tantum & indistinctè: hæc verò Practica distinctè confiderat omnes circumstantias non tantum temporis, loci & personarum, sed etiam principia, media & finem singularium actionum. Hanc intellexit Cicero 2.offic. ubi ait, hi, qui Rempubl. tuebuntur, inprimis operam dabunt, ne quid Refpub detrimenti capiat, ut juris & judiciorum æquitate suum quifq; teneat, ne aut tenuiores circumveniatur, aut locupletibus aut sua vel tuenda vel recuperanda obsit invidia, adeo ut qui rationem rerum singularium non teneat, hac prudentia praeditus esse nequeat. Haec iterum pro vario scopo & fine ad quem tendit duplex à Philosopho statuitur 6. Nicom. cap. 8. Senatoria nempe & Judiciaria. Senatoria quae à Philosopho βουλευτικὴ dicitur sive Consultatoria, quod in consiliis recte dandis & expediendis tota versetur, est ea prudentia, quae de futuris Reipub. negotiis, recte deliberat, quid scilicet Respub. quaevis debeat suscipere vel omittere, quid utile quid non sit. Dicitur vero Senatoria vel à Senatu, in quo necessario requiritur, vel à senibus, in quibus propter aetatem & experientiam maxime reperitur. Hac prudentia prae ceteris in Romana Repub. excelluit Cato, qui, ut testatur Cicero in dialogo de senectute plurimum Reipub. profuit; & sic de seipso loquitur: Non enim viribus, inquit, aut velocitatibus aut celeritate corporum res magnae geruntur, sed consilio, auctoritate & prudentia. Et paulo post: Nisi forte ego vobis, qui & miles & tribunus & legatus & consul in vario bellorum genere versatus sum, cessare nunc videor, cum bella non gero; at Senatui, quae sunt praestanda & perficienda praescribo. Altera dicitur Judiciaria, Graecis δικαστικὴ, id est, ea quae de praeteritis Reipub. negotiis recte aliquid constituit, & vel in poenis aut praemiis decernendis tota cernitur, & ad judicem maximè spectat. Nam, ut refert Cicero pro Roscio: Judex est is, quem non minus bene pro nobis, quam secundum nos judicare velimus, adeo ut recte dicat Plato 2. de leg. Judicis munus in duobus maximè consistere, nempe in distribuendis praemiis inter bonos, ut ad virtutem magis magisque incitentur: & in constituendis poenis in malos, ut vel ipsi a malo deterreantur, vel alios suo exemplo & castigatione a malo deterreant. Sexto consideranda veniunt cognata Prudentiae, quae a Philosopho lib.6.cap.9.& 11. quatuor enumerantur, ut sunt ista, Eubulia seu bona consultatio: Perspicacitas: Gnome seu sententia: Solertia, quibus in libel.de virtut.& vit. adjungit Memoriam & Experientiam. Dicuntur vero cognata Prudentiae, non tantum quod magnam affinitatem & convenientiam habeant cum ipsa Prudentia, sed etiam quod tam sint necessaria viro prudenti, ut absque iis prudentiae habitum comparare non possit. Primum igitur Eubulia est, quae definitur rectitudo consilii, qua media celerita ad bonum finem ducentia sicut & quando & quomodo oporteat dextre & expedite perquirimus. Unde ille bonus consultator erit, qui bonum finem per bona media assequi poterit. Aristoteles loco citato. Rectum vero consilium (cujus in definitione fuit facta mentio) quatuor modis dici posse docet Philosophus loco citato: 1. Cum quis propositum suum, sive id bonum sit, sive malum quocunque modo assequitur. Tale fuit consilium Pharisaeorum de tollendo Christo Johan. 11. Tale etiam fuit illud filiorum Jacobi Patriarchae de perdendo fratre Josepho Genef.27. Tale fuit etiam consilium Davidis de interficiendo Uria 2. Sam.11.ubi etiam hic Canon in primis notatu dignus videtur: Non omnis, qui recte consultat, bene etiam consulat. Nam ille recte consultat, qui illud, de quo consultat, assequitur, & ad destinatum scopum perducit, sive id fiat licitis, sive illicitis modis: at vero bene consultare is dicitur, quando ex sua consultatione bonum aliquod, quod modo civi, modo Reipub. prodest, aliquitur aut alteque conatur, verbi gratia: Tarquinius junior recte consultat, dum callidum captat consilium de inferendo Lucretiae stupro, & voto suo potitur, ergo cum scopum suum attigerit, recte consultasse dicitur. Verum cum finis hujus facti turpis sit & inhonestus, sicut & ipsum factum, non bene consultasse dicendus est, namque Eubulia seu recta consultatio est non tantum agnata Prudentiae, sed illius veluti species quaedam: at vero & ipsa Prudentia, & quicquid cum prudentia conjunctum est, a virtute nunquam separari poterit, & proinde recta consultatio Prudentiae saepe adversatur; consultatio vero bona nunquam, Aristot. c. ult. lib. 6.
units.tr: Fifthly, we must consider the kinds of Prudence. These are distinguished according to the things and persons with which Prudence is concerned. It is first divided into private prudence, which a person exercises toward himself, and which is why the Philosopher at Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 8 calls it prudence toward one's own self, and public prudence, which extends to others, and which he there calls prudence toward others. Private prudence, or prudence toward oneself, is the wisdom by which a person is wise for himself and can skilfully and adroitly provide for his own advantage alone. Cicero rightly says in Letters to Trebatius, Letter 16, Book 1 of Familiar Letters: "Always remember this: he is not wise who cannot benefit himself by his wisdom." There are also well-known proverbs: I hate the wise man who is not wise for himself; a tunic is nearer than a cloak; everyone prefers himself to another; ordered charity begins with oneself. To hold fast to this prudence, we should embrace what Seneca teaches in On Virtues, Book 4: "If the mind is wise, it arranges all the actions of life across three times: it orders the present, foresees the future, and remembers the past. For he who does not rightly arrange the present rashly falls into misery; he who thinks nothing of the past loses his life and forgets himself; he who premeditates nothing of the future rushes headlong into every danger." The second kind is called public prudence, and it is the common prudence by which a person rightly takes counsel not only for himself but also for others concerning useful and good things. Hence Plato is well quoted (these are Cicero's words in On Duties, Book 1): "We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims one part of our being, our parents another, our friends another. And, as the Stoics hold, all things that grow on earth are created for the sake of men, and men are born for the sake of men, so that they may be of use to one another. In this nature we ought to follow the guide, and bring our common advantages into the open." In this passage, following the Stoic view and the truth of the matter, he teaches that prudence properly speaks of that which takes thought not only for oneself but for others. This common prudence is again divided into economic and political, because they have two different aims, namely to serve either the household or the commonwealth. Economic prudence is the common prudence about useful and good things, by which all those things that are necessary for the household are considered and provided for. This concerns either the persons who make up the household, such as the father and mother of the family, the children, hired workers and slaves, or the things by which the household must be fed and sustained, such as farming, hunting, fishing, and other trades and crafts by which the needs of human life are met. Several species or parts of this prudence are distinguished, though Cato, as cited by Cicero in On Duties, Book 2, summed them up briefly. When he was asked what was most profitable in household affairs, he answered: to do good; in what way? to do good enough; what third? to dress well; what fourth? to plough well. So he asserted that the species of economic prudence consist in three things: pasturage, agriculture, and wool-working. Pittacus spoke more succinctly, calling that house best ordered in which nothing superfluous abounds and nothing necessary is lacking, as Stobaeus reports in his Sermon 4 on Justice. More on this prudence is said in the treatise on economics. Political prudence is the common prudence by which we can rightly take counsel about useful and good things for both the commonwealth and the state in which we were born. This prudence is the proper prudence of good citizens, to whom alone the commonwealth is usually a care and a concern (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 8). For good men know that they are born to serve the commonwealth, and since they are members of the commonwealth, they desire above all to look after it as their own body. Plato in the Alcibiades elegantly calls this the thing by which we may rightly say that a man is prudent: he who can rightly take counsel not only for himself but also for the commonwealth in which he was born. For the commonwealth, as Cicero says in On the Laws, Book 2, is the name of the whole state for which we ought to die, to which we ought to give ourselves wholly, and in which we ought to place, as it were consecrate, all that is ours. This is subdivided again into [nomothetikēn] (legislative) and [pragmatikēn] (practical). The legislative sort is concerned with universals, while the practical sort regards particulars, for it considers the circumstances well and weighs them (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 8). Legislative prudence, which is also called jurisprudence, is that which deals with the right interpretation of laws, and which not only explains the laws kindly and according to equity, but also enacts laws that are wholesome and useful to the commonwealth. This prudence is especially necessary for the magistrate, for, as Cicero says in On the Laws, Book 1, he to whom the care of the commonwealth has been entrusted especially needs speech and prudence, by which he may both rule the peoples subject to him and make firm the laws he has proposed, check the wicked lest they persist in wickedness, and protect the good so that they may continue in the vigour of their goodness. Among the Greeks, Solon of Athens and Lycurgus, lawgiver of the Lacedaemonians, are praised above the rest for this prudence. Because their laws were enacted above the law of nature and according to right reason, the Latins borrowed much from them, as will easily be clear from comparing the two. Practical prudence, which is the other species of political prudence, is that which is wholly occupied with the right administration of the affairs of the commonwealth, and this particularly and according to the various circumstances. In this it chiefly differs from legislative prudence: the latter is concerned with the affairs of the commonwealth but only in a universal and undifferentiated way, whereas the practical sort considers distinctly all the circumstances, not only of time, place and persons, but also the principles, means and end of particular actions. Cicero understood this in On Duties, Book 2, where he says: "Those who defend the commonwealth will above all take care that it suffers no harm, so that by the equity of law and judgments each keeps what is his, and so that the humbler are not cheated, nor the wealthy hindered by the envy that attends either the defence or the recovery of their property." So, unless a man understands the reasons of particular affairs, he cannot be endowed with this prudence. This prudence is again set out, according to its varying aim and end, in a twofold way by the Philosopher (Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 8): namely senatorial and judicial. Senatorial prudence, which the Philosopher calls [bouleutikē], or consultative, because it is wholly occupied with giving and carrying out sound counsel, is that prudence which rightly deliberates about future affairs of the commonwealth: what any commonwealth ought to undertake or omit, and what is useful and what is not. It is called senatorial either from the Senate, in which it is especially required, or from the old men, in whom it is most found on account of their age and experience. Among the Romans, Cato excelled above all others in this prudence, and, as Cicero attests in his dialogue On Old Age, he was of very great service to the commonwealth. He speaks of himself thus: "For great deeds are not done by strength, nor by speed, nor by the quickness of the body, but by counsel, authority and prudence." And a little later: "Unless perhaps I seem to you, who have been soldier, tribune, legate and consul, and have been engaged in many kinds of war, to be idle now because I do not wage wars; yet I prescribe to the Senate what is to be undertaken and carried out." The other is called judicial prudence, [dikastikē] in Greek, that is, the prudence which rightly decides something about past affairs of the commonwealth, and which is seen wholly in deciding punishments or rewards, and belongs chiefly to the judge. For, as Cicero reports in For Roscius: "A judge is one whom we would wish to judge for us no less well than according to our own cause." So Plato rightly says in On the Laws, Book 2 that the office of a judge consists chiefly of two things, namely distributing rewards among the good, so that they may be urged more and more toward virtue, and imposing penalties on the wicked, so that either they themselves may be deterred from evil, or by their example and chastisement they may deter others from evil. Sixthly, we must consider the things akin to prudence, which the Philosopher enumerates in Book 6, chs. 9 and 11 as four: namely good counsel (eubulia), sharpness of perception, judgment (gnōmē), and quickness of wit (solertia); to these, in the little book On Virtues and Vices, he adds memory and experience. They are called akin to prudence not only because they have great affinity and agreement with prudence itself, but also because they are so necessary to the prudent man that without them he cannot acquire the habit of prudence. First, then, good counsel is defined as the rightness of deliberation, by which we seek out, skilfully and expeditiously, the means that lead to a good end, as well as when, how and in what way it is fitting to do so. Hence he will be a good counsellor who can attain a good end by good means (Aristotle, loco citato). The Philosopher, in the same place, teaches that right counsel (of which mention was made in the definition) can be said in four ways: (1) when someone attains his purpose in any manner, whether it be good or bad. Such was the counsel of the Pharisees about removing Christ (John 11). Such too was the counsel of the sons of the patriarch Jacob about destroying their brother Joseph (Genesis 37). Such also was David's counsel about killing Uriah (2 Samuel 11), where this rule seems especially worth noting: not everyone who counsels rightly counsels well. For he counsels rightly who attains what he counsels about and brings it to the intended end, whether this is done by lawful or unlawful means. But he is said to counsel well when, by his counsel, he attains or strives for some good which profits either a citizen or the commonwealth. For example, Tarquin the Younger counselled rightly when he devised a cunning plan for the rape of Lucretia and gained his desire; therefore, since he attained his aim, he is said to have counselled rightly. But since the end of this deed is base and dishonourable, as is the deed itself, he must not be said to have counselled well. For good counsel, or right deliberation, is not only akin to prudence but is, as it were, a certain species of it. Prudence itself, however, and whatever is joined with prudence can never be separated from virtue; and so right deliberation is often opposed to prudence, but good deliberation never is (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, last chapter).

units.la: Incontinens igitur aut aliquo vitio laborans callidi tatis suae recte consulens, rectum captat consilium de fine asequendo, sed non bonum, quia ille recte consultat, qui illud, de quo consultat, asequitur; bene vero non. Unde isti vitiosi, cum ex sua consultatione non adipiscantur bonum, sed malum quid, interdum damnum, interdum turpitudinem, & semper vitiositatem, recte non bene consultasse dicuntur. Zwingerus ad cap. 9. lib. 6. Nicom. 1. Modo rectum consilium dicitur, cum quis voti sui fit compos per media illicita & illegitima, verbi gratia: Si quis liberos aut familiam alat furto aut rapina, aut etiam liberos educet ad furtum, aut rapinam exercendam, sicut de quodam fure refert Herodotus lib. 2. sub Rhambsinito Aegyptiorum Rege: aut etiam si quis incantamentis aut diabolicis artibus procu- rét sibi aut aliis sanitatem, & de modo consultatio- nem adhibeat. 3. Rectum consilium etiam dicitur, cum propositum obtingit per bona quidem & licita media, sed intempestive seu tempore minus commodo, verbi gratia: Bonum & honestum est pro patria pugnare, eamque armis tueri, & de ea tuenda consultationem dextre adhibere, sed nimis intempestivum est, si Troilus congrediatur cum Achille, id est, si aliquis aetate, viribus aut experientia congrediatur cum superiori: unde maxima requiritur Prudentia tanquam necessaria ad fortitudinem. 4. Denique consilium rectum capi dicitur, cum propositum bonis & licitis mediis obtingit & tempestive satis seu tempore satis accommodato variis circumstantiis. Et sic hoc sensu rectum consilium sumitur a Philosopho cap.9 lib. 6. ubi de Eubulia agit: & in hac significatione sumitur etiam a Stoicis, ut videre est apud Laert. lib.7. de vit. Philos. in vita Zenonis. Caeterum & hoc notandum de consultatione quod duplex vulgo statuatur, una simplex seu generalis, alia ad finem seu specialis Aristoteles, cap. 9. lib. 6. Consultatio simpliciter illa dicitur, quando de fine ultimo actionum humanarum seu de ipsa felicitate per sua media acquirenda deliberamus, quae consultatio generalis dicitur, quod ad omnes in genere homines spectet aut spectare debeat, cum nemo sit hominum, qui non bene & honeste vivere cupiat, etsi hanc de isto fine assequendo consultationem adhibeat. Consultatio vero ad finem illa dicitur, quando deliberatio suscipitur propter certum aliquod bonum per medium aliquod justum & legitimum acquirendum: cujusmodi sunt omnia ea, de quibus vulgò consultant homines, excepto summo bono, de quo deliberatio simpliciter instituitur, verbi gratia; quando de divitiis, potentia, dignitate, de honoribus & cæteris ejusmodi consultant homines. Plura vide de Consultationis speciebus apud Keckerm.pag. 89.& tribus seqq.Syst.Eth.
units.tr: The incontinent man, or one who labours under some vice, therefore takes good thought for his own cleverness and seeks a right plan for attaining his end, but not a good one, since a man takes good counsel only when he attains what he takes counsel about, and not otherwise. Hence such vicious men, when their deliberation does not win them a good, but something evil, sometimes loss, sometimes shame, and always depravity, are said to have deliberated rightly but not well. Zwinger on Nicomachean Ethics book 6, chapter 9. Sometimes a plan is called right when someone gets his wish by unlawful and illegitimate means, for example: if someone feeds his children or household by theft or robbery, or even trains his children to carry on theft or robbery, as Herodotus, book 2, reports of a certain thief under Rhampsinitus, king of the Egyptians; or if someone seeks health for himself or others by incantations or diabolical arts, and applies his deliberation to that means. (3) A plan is also called right when the purpose is attained by good and lawful means, but at an unseasonable time, or at a time less suitable; for example, it is good and honourable to fight for one's country and defend it by arms, and to deliberate skilfully about its defence, but it is far too unseasonable if Troilus engages Achilles, that is, if someone engages in combat with a superior in age, strength or experience. Hence the greatest prudence is required as necessary for courage. (4) Finally, a plan is said to be taken rightly when the purpose is attained by good and lawful means and at a time sufficiently fitting, given the various circumstances. In this sense the Philosopher takes a right plan in chapter 9 of book 6, where he treats of eubulia, and the Stoics also take it in this sense, as may be seen in Diogenes Laertius, book 7, in the life of Zeno. Moreover, this must also be noted about deliberation: it is commonly held to be twofold, one simple or general, the other directed to an end or particular. Aristotle, chapter 9 of book 6. Deliberation is called simple when we deliberate about the ultimate end of human actions, or about happiness itself, to be acquired by its means; this is called general, because it concerns, or ought to concern, all men in general, since there is no man who does not desire to live well and honourably, even if he deliberates about attaining that end. Deliberation directed to an end is that in which a decision is undertaken for the sake of acquiring some particular good by some just and lawful means; of this kind are all those things about which men commonly deliberate, except the supreme good, about which deliberation is instituted simply; for example, when men deliberate about riches, power, rank, honours and other such things. See more on the species of deliberation in Keckermann, p. 89 and the following three, Systema Ethicae.

units.la: Secundum cognatum Prudentiæ est Perspicacitas, quæ definitur à Philosopho cap.10.6. Nic. affectio quædam Prudentiæ, quæ eas res rectè intelligit & colligit, & etiam judicat, in quibus ipsa cernitur prudentia, unde circa unum idemque objectum cum prudentia versatur. Convenit verò cum prudetia in quibusdâ, in quibusdâ et discrepat. Convenit in duobus: 1. In objecto, quòd circa idem & unum versentur objectum, nempe circa contingentia practica, seu res agendas, quarum eventus dubius esse solet & incertus. 2. Conveniunt causa efficiente, nam utraque usu & experientia comparanda & confirmanda est, & licet perspicacitas requirat necessario quàdam corporis temperaturam, quæ aciem ingenii excitet acumen: ista tamen perspicaitas, quæ ad prudentiam necessario requiritur, non nisi usu & longa experientia & frequenti rerum gerendarum exercitio comparatur. Differt verò à prudentia in hoc, quod prudentia quid agendum aut non agendum sit, perspiciat; Perspicacitas verò de prudentiæ decretis jam latis aut etiam ferendis, rectum ferat judicium, & limam iis poliendis adhibeat, unde persequendi actum suum exerit post prudentiæ actum jam absque. absolutum. Arist.cap.11.6.Nic. Differetia à scientia & ab opinione, licet in multis conveniant, quod illæ in hominibus plerunq; cadant oēs: nemo enim est hominum, qui non aliquam cognitionem aut scientiam de rebus, & nemo est etiam qui non habeat opinionem modò convenientem, modò discrepantem cum aliis: perspicacitas verò in paucos cadit hominės, quia pauci reperiuntur ingeniosi, pauci etiā qui per varios gradus ad summam rerum experientiam veniunt. Differt etiam à scientia respectu objecti, quod scientia versetur circa necessaria, quæ aliter se habere nequeunt: perspicacitas verò circa ea, quæ dubitationem habent & in consultationem veniunt, adeo ut subinde pro variis casibus mutari possint, Aristot. loco cit. Tertium cognatum prudentiæ est Gnome seu sententia, quæ definitur à Philosopho cap. 11. lib. 6. facultas quædam animi aliorum dicta & facta in meliorem semper partem interpretantis, & si quid erratum sit, benigne ignoscentis: Munus verò seu officium sententiæ in duobus consistit: 1. Quæ ab aliis dicuntur & fiunt benigne interpretari. Unde à Philosopho ibidem viri prudentes dicuntur εὐγνώμονες, id est, bene de aliis sentientes, propterea quod virorum prudentum sit optima quæque de omnibus sentire, et si aliter dicta aut facta aliorum promereantur, tum cadit gare non ad destructionem, sed ad correctionem & emendationem, adeo ut non prudentes de his male judicent, sed secundum sua ipsorum facta aut dicta judicentur. 2. Munus sententiæ consistit in hoc, ut iis peccatis, quæ per ignorantiam aut infirmitatem fiunt, benigne
units.tr: The second kindred quality of prudence is perspicacity, which the Philosopher defines in chapter 10 of book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics as a certain affection of prudence, which rightly understands, gathers and also judges those matters in which prudence itself is discerned; hence it is concerned with one and the same object as prudence. It agrees with prudence in some respects, and differs in others. It agrees in two things. (1) In its object, in that both are concerned with the same and one object, namely practical contingencies, or things to be done, whose outcome is usually doubtful and uncertain. (2) They agree in their efficient cause, for both must be acquired and strengthened by practice and experience; and although perspicacity necessarily requires a certain temperament of the body which sharpens the edge of the mind into acuteness, yet that perspicacity which is necessarily required for prudence is acquired only by practice, long experience and frequent exercise in doing things. It differs from prudence in this: prudence perceives what is to be done or not to be done, whereas perspicacity passes right judgement on the decisions of prudence already made or yet to be made, and applies the file to polish them, so that it exerts its activity of pursuing them after the act of prudence is already complete. Aristotle, chapter 11 of book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics. It differs from science and from opinion, although they agree in many respects, in that those two generally fall to all men: for there is no man who has no knowledge or science of things, and no man who does not have an opinion, now agreeing, now disagreeing with others; but perspicacity falls to few men, because few are found to be gifted, and few who come by various degrees to the highest experience of affairs. It also differs from science with respect to its object, in that science is concerned with necessary things, which cannot be otherwise, whereas perspicacity is concerned with those things which admit of doubt and come into deliberation, so that they can be changed from time to time according to various circumstances. Aristotle, in the place cited. The third kindred quality of prudence is gnome, or judgement, which the Philosopher defines in chapter 11 of book 6 as a certain faculty of mind that interprets the words and deeds of others always in the better part, and benignly pardons whatever has been done amiss. The office or duty of judgement consists in two things: (1) to interpret kindly what is said and done by others. Hence the Philosopher in the same place calls prudent men eugnomones [εὐγνώμονες], that is, those who think well of others, because it is the mark of prudent men to think the best of everything and everyone; and if the words or deeds of others deserve otherwise, then the fault falls not on destruction but on correction and amendment, so that prudent men do not judge them ill, but are judged according to their own words and deeds. (2) The duty of judgement consists in this: that sins committed through ignorance or weakness are benignly

units.la: gnē gnè ignoscatur & venia detur,& propterea prudentes dicuntur συγγνωμονικοί, id est, ad ignoscendum & condonandum faciles & proclives cap.15.lib.6.Nicom. Differt vero sententia à perspicacitate in hoc, quod perspicacitas de rebus simpliciter pronuciet, quales nimirum per se & sua natura sint, nec postea mutet: sententia vero adhibeat æquitatem moderatricem, ut sicut se habet æquitas ad Justitiam, sic etiam gnome ad perspicacitatem. At æquitas dicta & facta non secundum rigorem juris & quoad externam faciem examinat, sed ex proæresi & interna dispositione agentis aut dicentis præponderat, & in defectu potius peccat quam in excessu, ita etiam in hisce ipsis se habet sententia seu gnome Arist.cap.11.6.Nicom. Quartum cognatum est Solertia, quæ definitur cap.15.lib.6. naturalis vis intelligendi & agendi ea, quæ ad propositum à nobis scopum recte & rite persequendum & assequendum pertinent. Unde de ista solertia tria notanda docet Philosophus: 1. Quod à natura suam habeat originem & inchoationem, licet perfectionem assequatur ab usu & experientia. Talis fuit solertia in dispensatore iniquo, de quo Luc.16. Talis etiam fuit in muliere Thekuita, quæ instructa à Joabo apud Regem Davidem fingit se duos habuisse filios, quorum unus alterum per imprudentiam occiderit, & petit, ut superstiti tanquam unico filio ignoscatur, annuente Rege, ipsa parabolam exponit, & de reducendo Absolomo filio Regis serio agit 2.Sam.14. Tales etiam fuit inter Ethnicos Themistocles Atheniensium Imperator, de quo Thucyd. lib.1. hist. Themistocles, inquit, quit, & acire mentis suæ non diu præmonitus, nec diu considerans optima quæq; consilia de rebus omnibus capiebat, & de futuris, quid maxime eventurum esset, rectissime conjiciebat, quæ in præsentia præ manibus habebat dexterrime expedire poterat, & quæ non noverat, non destitit inquirere: in obscuris autem rebus quid deterius, quid melius omnium maxime perspiciebat: ut in summa dicam, & naturæ viribus & solerti deliberatione id semper eligebat, quod in primis profuturum erat. 2. Et hoc notandum de solertia, quod pro similitudine scopi ad quem tendit, duplex sit, bona nempe vel mala, Philosophus loco cit. Solertia bona ea dicitur, quæ bonum finem & bonû scopum sibi propositum habet, & bona etiam media ad bonum asequendum finem investigat: & talis solertia est & publice & privatim utilis. Solertia vero mala econtra se habet, qualis fuit in Ulyffe, qui per astutiam & calliditate Palamedem Græcorum Imperatorem e medio tollendum curavit, & Ajacem ad desperationem adegit. Unde a Philosopho hæc solertia dicitur πανουργία astutia, versutia, calliditas & dolus. 3. Notandum quomodo solertia se habeat erga prudentiam, cum qua partim convenit, partim etiam ab ea discrepat. Convenit cum Prudentia in hoc, quod tantum inter se affinitatem & cognationem habeant, ut sine hac Prudentia comparari nullo modo possit: nam in quibus non reperitur naturalis hæc sagacitas, quales sunt ii, qui natura sunt stupidi & hebetes, illi prudentiam comparare nunquam possunt, etiamsi diutissime vivant & plurima videant, multa loca perlustrent, quia ut habet vulgaris versiculus: Parifios stolidus si transmittatur asellus, Sifuit hic asinus, non ibi fiet equus.
units.tr: pardoned, and forgiveness is granted; and therefore prudent men are called syngnomonikoi [συγγνωμονικοί], that is, ready and inclined to pardon and condone. Chapter 15 of book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics. Judgement differs from perspicacity in this: perspicacity pronounces simply on things as they are in themselves and by their nature, and does not afterwards change; whereas judgement applies a moderating equity, so that as equity stands to justice, so judgement stands to perspicacity. Equity does not examine words and deeds according to the strictness of law and their external appearance, but weighs them according to the choice and inner disposition of the doer or speaker, and it errs rather in defect than in excess; so too judgement or gnome stands in these same respects. Aristotle, chapter 11 of book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics. The fourth kindred quality is shrewdness, which is defined in chapter 15 of book 6 as the natural power of understanding and doing those things which pertain to attaining and pursuing rightly and fittingly the goal we have set ourselves. Concerning this shrewdness the Philosopher teaches that three things are to be noted. (1) That it has its origin and beginning from nature, although it reaches perfection from practice and experience. Such was the shrewdness in the unjust steward, of whom we read in Luke 16. Such too was that of the Tekoite woman, who, instructed by Joab, feigned before King David that she had two sons, one of whom had killed the other through carelessness, and asked that the survivor, as her only son, be pardoned; the king assenting, she explained the parable and seriously treated of bringing back Absalom, the king's son, 2 Sam. 14. Such among the heathen was Themistocles, general of the Athenians, of whom Thucydides, book 1 of his history, writes: Themistocles, he says, having had little prior instruction, and without long consideration, grasped the best counsels about all matters; and he conjectured most accurately what would most likely happen in the future; what lay before him at the moment he could very skilfully manage, and what he did not know he did not cease to inquire into; in obscure matters he discerned most clearly which course was worse and which better. To sum up, he always chose, by the powers of nature and shrewd deliberation, that which would be most advantageous. (2) And this must be noted about shrewdness: that according to the character of the goal it aims at, it is twofold, namely good or bad, as the Philosopher says in the place cited. Shrewdness is called good when it has set before itself a good end and a good goal, and also seeks good means for attaining that end; and such shrewdness is useful both publicly and privately. Bad shrewdness, on the other hand, is of the kind found in Ulysses, who by cunning and craft saw to it that Palamedes, the leader of the Greeks, was removed from the way, and drove Ajax to despair. Hence the Philosopher calls this shrewdness panourgia [πανουργία], that is, craftiness, guile, cunning and deceit. (3) It must be noted how shrewdness stands towards prudence, with which it partly agrees and partly differs. It agrees with prudence in that they have such mutual affinity and kinship that without this shrewdness prudence cannot be acquired in any way; for those in whom this natural sagacity is not found, such as those who are dull and slow by nature, can never acquire prudence, even if they live a very long time and see very many things, and travel through many places; for as the common verse has it: "If a dull donkey is sent to Paris, he will come back a donkey, not a horse."

units.la: Ideoque Philosophus solertiam comparat oculo: nam ut sine oculo nemo videre potest res objectas, aut etiam cognitionem earum rerū habere, quæ per visionē acquiruntur: sic absq; naturali hac solertia mens non potest percipere aut satis assequi, quæ ad Prudentiam comparandam sunt necessaria. Differt verò à Prudentia in duobus potissimum: 1. Causa efficiente, quod solertię causa efficiens sit ipsa natura, siquidem sit naturalis quædam facultas naturæ instinctu edita: Prudentiæ verò causa est usus & exercitatio, cum sit habitus usu & exercitatione comparandus. Aristoteles cap.13.lib.6. Differunt etiam subjectis; nā solertia pro diversitate scopi, ad quem tendit, est vel bona vel mala, & ideo tam in malis quā in bonis locum habet: Prudentia verò cum bona tantū sit, & cum virtute morali conjuncta in viris bonis tantummodo locum habet. Atque hæc causa est, cur Philosophus cap.penult. dixerit, impossibile est, ut quis sit Vir prudens, qui non sit Vir bonus. De prudentia etiam hoc notari debet, quod non nisi longa observatione & rerum singularium experientia acquiratur, & propterea Philosophus in libel. de virtut. & vit. experientiam requirit tanquam aliquid necessarium ad Prudentiam comparandam. Et hinc conjicere licet, cur Juvenis non possit esse prudens, quia per ætatem teneram & immaturam nondum habet rerum usum & experientiam, licet Ma-
units.tr: Therefore the Philosopher compares shrewdness to the eye: just as no one can see visible things, or have knowledge of those things which are acquired through sight, without an eye, so without this natural shrewdness the mind cannot grasp or sufficiently attain what is necessary for acquiring prudence. Prudence differs from shrewdness chiefly in two respects. (1) As to efficient cause: the cause of shrewdness is nature itself, since it is a natural faculty brought forth by the impulse of nature, whereas the cause of prudence is use and practice, since it is a habit to be acquired by use and practice. Aristotle, ch. 13, book 6. They also differ in their subjects. For shrewdness, according to the diversity of the aim to which it tends, is either good or bad, and so it has a place both in bad men and in good; but prudence, since it is always good and is joined with moral virtue, has a place only in good men. This is the reason why the Philosopher said, in the last chapter, that it is impossible for someone to be a prudent man who is not a good man. Concerning prudence it must also be noted that it is acquired only through long observation and experience of particular things, and therefore the Philosopher, in the little book On Virtues and Vices, requires experience as something necessary for acquiring prudence. And from this one may conjecture why a young man cannot be prudent: because by his tender and immature age he does not yet have the use and experience of things, although he can easily master the mathematical disciplines, since for learning those only judgment and keenness of mind are needed (Aristotle, ch. 8, book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics). This too is the reason why he called the young man not a suitable hearer of Ethics (1 Nicomachean Ethics, ch. 1).

units.la: Ece thematicas disciplinas facilè assequi possit, quia ad illas discendas solo judicio & mentis acumine opus est, Aristot. cap. 8. lib. 6. Nicom. Atque hæcetiam causa est, quod Juvenem non satis idoneum auditorem Ethices vocarit 1. Nicom. cap. 1. Quod verò prudentia solis senibus competat aut competere debeat, docet Cicero in Dialog. de Senect. ubi senatum (in quo maximè Prudentia requiritur) à senibus denominatum ostendit, utpote in quibus propter ætatem & experientiam consilium & ratio maximè vigent. Apud Lacedæmonios, inquit, qui summum Magistratum gerunt, ut sunt, sic appellantur etiam senes, & paulò post: Quod si legere & audire voletis externa, maximas Respub. ab adolescentibus labefactatas & deletas, à senibus verò restitutas & sustentatas reperietis. Idem etiam ex instituto Romuli primi Romanorum Regis docet Ovid. f. Fast. Et Cic. 1. Tusc. quaest. nihil profecto est homini prudentia dulcius, quā, ut cæteræ opera, affert certè senectus. Requiritur etiam Memoria ad Prudentiā tanquam summè necessaria. Nemo enim vir prudens esse poterit, qui de præteritis non cogitat, & præsentia cum præteritis non coformat, prout tempus postulat & res, qui etiam de futuris non cogitat, quomodo ipsi aut toti Reipublicæ sint profutura: hoc autem absq; memoria fieri non potest, & proinde etiam variarum historiarum lectione & temporis accurata supputatione opus est viro prudenti, siquidem verisatur circa actiones humanas & singulares, in quibus necessario exponendæ veniunt circumstantiæ, quæ absq; duobus his fulcris nec satis intelintelligi nec accommodari rebus singularibus possunt. Plura de Memoria & quomodo se ad prudentiam adeoque omnes qualitates animi habeat, videantur apud Philosophum in libello de Memoria & Reminiscentia.
units.tr: That prudence belongs, or ought to belong, only to old men, Cicero teaches in his Dialogue on Old Age, where he shows that the senate (in which prudence is most required) is named from the elders, since in them counsel and reason flourish most, on account of their age and experience. "Among the Spartans," he says, "those who hold the highest magistracy are, as they are, also called elders," and shortly afterwards: "If you want to read and hear of foreign states, you will find that the greatest commonwealths were weakened and destroyed by young men, but restored and sustained by old men." Ovid, in the Fasti, teaches the same from the institution of Romulus, the first king of the Romans. And Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations, book 1: "Nothing, indeed, is sweeter to a man than prudence, which old age certainly brings, as it does its other fruits." Memory, too, is required for prudence as most necessary. For no one can be a prudent man who does not think about past things and does not fit present things to past ones, as the time and the matter demand, and who does not also think about future things, how they will be of advantage to himself or to the whole commonwealth. This cannot be done without memory; and therefore the prudent man also needs the reading of various histories and the careful reckoning of times, since he is concerned with human and particular actions, in which circumstances must necessarily be set out, and these cannot be sufficiently understood nor applied to particular things without these two supports. More on memory, and how it relates to prudence and thus to all the qualities of the mind, may be seen in the Philosopher's little book On Memory and Reminiscence.

units.la: Haec de Virtutibus intellectualibus in genere dicta sint: restant paucae quaestiones de iis discutiedae breviter, quarum prima sit: Utrum virtutes intellectuales recte postponantur moralibus nec ne? Et Resp. Hanc quaestionem facile dirimi posse ex distinctione utilitatis & praestantiae sive dignitatis: Nam si utilitatis spectetur ratio, quae ad humanae felicitatis fastigium tendit, non immerito de moralibus virtutibus primo singillatim egisse videtur Philosophus, cum sint ipsa media, quae ad bene beateque vivendum tendunt, & per quae homo felicitatem ipsam assequitur. Proinde utilitatis rationem habuit Philosophus, cum morales intellectualibus virtutibus praemiserit. At vero praestantiae dignitatis & naturae respectu, Intellectuales praecedere debet virtutes morales, quia omne dirigens natura prius est directo, & mensura, prior est eo, cujus est mensura, sicut praeter multiplicem rationem docet Scalig. exerc. 353. sect. 2. Est enim Intellectus voluntatis quasi regula & mensura & haec ab illo dependet, & est Intellectus quasi natura prior & praestantior. Idem exerc. 307. sect. 26. Unde illud Scholasticorum: Voluntas ab officio suo non discedit, nisi intellectus ipse a recta via discesserit: & non est peccatum in voluntate, nisi sit prius defectus in ipsa ratione. Plura vide de hac quaest. apud D. Thom. 1. part. sum. 2. q. 19.
units.tr: These things have been said about the intellectual virtues in general. A few questions about them remain to be briefly discussed, the first of which is: Are the intellectual virtues rightly placed after the moral ones or not? Answer: This question can easily be settled by the distinction between usefulness and excellence or dignity. For if we regard the consideration of usefulness, which tends to the summit of human happiness, the Philosopher seems not undeservedly to have treated the moral virtues first and individually, since they are the very means which tend to living well and blessedly, and through which man attains happiness itself. Accordingly, the Philosopher had regard to usefulness when he put the moral virtues before the intellectual ones. But with respect to excellence, dignity and nature, the intellectual virtues ought to precede the moral ones, because whatever directs is by nature prior to what is directed, and a measure is prior to that of which it is the measure, as Scaliger teaches, besides many other reasons, Exercise 353, section 2. For the intellect is, as it were, the rule and measure of the will, and the will depends on it, and the intellect is, as it were, prior by nature and more excellent. Likewise Exercise 307, section 26. Hence that saying of the Scholastics: the will does not depart from its duty unless the intellect itself has first departed from the right way; and there is no sin in the will unless there is first a defect in reason itself. See more on this question in St. Thomas, 1 part, Summa 2, q. 19.

units.la: II. An recte statuantur quinque tantum virtutes intellectuales? Etrespondetur affirmative, id quod probat Philosophus cap. 3.6. Nicom. tribus hisce rationibus, quarum: 1. ducitur a forma seu ratione formali istarum virtutum intellectualium: quia quinque tantum modis affirmando vel negando mens verum enunciat aut enunciare potest: at isti quinque modi sunt quinque istae virtutes: Intelligentia nimirum, Scientia, Sapientia, Prudentia & Ars, neque in vero enunciando ab his quinque reperitur modus, qui non ad aliquem horum quinque referri possit. 2. Ratio ducitur ab objectis, circa quae versantur virtutes intellectuales: ea sunt duplicia, vel necessaria, circa quae intellectus, specialiter sic dictus, Scientia & Sapientia versantur: vel contingentia, circa quae Prudentia & ars, sed cum hoc tamen discrimine, ut Ars versetur circa contingens factivum. Prudentia vero circa contingens activum. 3. Ratio ducitur a natura istorum habituum. Hi enim vel sunt simplices, vel compositi. Simplices vel cognoscunt rursus aliquid simpliciter & absque medio seu ratiocinatione, ut Intelligentia, qua nuda ipsa principia unico intuitu & simplici apprehensione percipimus, verbi gratia: bis duo sunt quatuor. Omne totum est maius sua parte. Vel habitus isti simplices simpliciter aliquid cognoscunt per medium seu ratiocinationem, idque duobus modis, vel per discursum demonstrativum, quando nempe effecta ex causis cognoscuntur, quod facit Scientia, vel per discursum Dialecticum seu probabilem, quando intelligimus vel ea, quae sunt agenda, quod fit adminiculo prudentiæ, vel quæ sunt facienda, quod fit Arte. Atqui hi habitus sunt cognitionis simplicis. Compositus ex his habitus dicitur Sapientia, qua non tantum ipsa ratio absq; medio, sed etiam conclusiones, quæ ex principiis efficiuntur & deducuntur intelligimus. Cæterum quinarius hic numerus virtutum intellectualium arguitur duobus laborare vitiis, redundantia nempe & defectu, quæ duo vitia sibi invicem contrariantur. Redundantiæ vitio arguitur propter tres rationes: 1. Quia Intellectus numeratur inter virtutes intellectuales: At intellectus est altera animæ rationalis facultas, docente Philosopho lib. 3 de anim. cap. 4. & 8. & si sit facultas anima, est de essentia hominis: at nulla virtus est de essentia hominis, cum sit accidens, & neque sit de materia neque de forma hominis, sicut præter multiplicem rationem docet Zabarella lib. de constitut. Individ. cap. 2. & Scalig. exerc. 10. & 307. sect. 27. Sed ex homonymia Intellectus discussa facile dissolvitur hoc dubium: nam intellectus vocabulum est multiplex: Interdum enim ex defectu vocabulorum, denotat alteram animæ rationalis partem, quæ opponitur voluntati: interdum denotat cognitionem, quæ in præcipua animi parte reperitur, & quæ res apprehensas judicare & intelligere facile mens possit uno quasi intuitu: Et sic hoc loco sumitur, dum inter virtutes intellectuales refertur. 2. Quod Sapientia non sit distinctus habitus à reliquis, propterea quod ex Intelligentia & Scientia sit conflatus, & proinde ad utramque debet referri: & Philosophus ipse cap. 7. 6. Nicom. & cap. 7. 5. Eudem. Sapientiam vocat meram scientiam, & sic ad solam spectat scientiam: unde quaternarium tantantum erit numerus virtutū intellectualium? Sed resp. nihil hinc concludi: nā etsi Sapientia sit habitus copositus ex aliis habitibus, non inde sequitur, non esse diversum ab iis habitum: nam homo componitur ex materia & forma, & tamen est diversum quid ab utraque. Vocat vero Philosophus Sapientiam locū citatū, Scientiam, propterea quod quasdam mutuetur proprietates scientiæ, quia etiam conclusiones per ipsa principia & causas cognoscit. Dein etiam Scientiæ nomen ibi latius sumitur pro qualibet cognitione in perfectissimo gradu, & sic soli Sapientiæ competit.
units.tr: II. Are five intellectual virtues rightly laid down, and no more? It is answered in the affirmative, which the Philosopher proves in chapter 3 or 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics by three reasons. (1) The first is drawn from the form, or formal reason, of these intellectual virtues: for the mind utters or can utter a truth by affirming or denying in only five ways, and these five ways are those five virtues, namely Understanding, Science, Wisdom, Prudence and Art; nor is there any mode of uttering truth which cannot be referred to one of these five. (2) The second reason is drawn from the objects with which the intellectual virtues are concerned. These objects are of two kinds: either necessary, with which the intellect, so called specifically, Science and Wisdom are concerned; or contingent, with which Prudence and Art are concerned, with this difference, however, that Art is concerned with the contingent as factive, and Prudence with the contingent as active. (3) The third reason is drawn from the nature of these habits. For they are either simple or compound. The simple ones know something either simply, without a medium or reasoning, as Understanding, by which we perceive the bare first principles with a single intuition and simple apprehension, for example, twice two is four, the whole is greater than its part; or these simple habits know something through a medium or reasoning, and this in two ways: either through demonstrative discourse, when effects are known from causes, which Science does; or through dialectical or probable discourse, when we understand either the things that are to be done, which is done with the help of prudence, or the things that are to be made, which is done by Art. And these habits are of simple knowledge. Compounded from these is the habit called Wisdom, by which we understand not only the principle itself without a medium, but also the conclusions which are produced and deduced from the principles. Moreover, this quinary number of intellectual virtues is argued to suffer from two faults, namely excess and deficiency, which two faults are contrary to each other. The charge of excess is argued on three grounds. (a) Because Intellect is numbered among the intellectual virtues; but intellect is another faculty of the rational soul, as the Philosopher teaches in De Anima book 3, chapters 4 and 8; and if it is a faculty of the soul, it belongs to the essence of man; but no virtue belongs to the essence of man, since it is an accident, and is neither of the matter nor of the form of man, as Zabarella teaches besides many other reasons in his book on the constitution of individuals, ch. 2, and Scaliger, Exercises 10 and 307, section 27. But this doubt is easily resolved by sifting the ambiguity of the word intellect: for the word intellect is manifold. Sometimes, for want of words, it denotes the other part of the rational soul, which is opposed to the will; sometimes it denotes the knowledge which is found in the principal part of the mind, and by which the mind can easily judge and understand apprehended things with a kind of single glance. And it is in this sense that it is taken here, when it is reckoned among the intellectual virtues. (b) Because Wisdom is not a habit distinct from the others, since it is compounded of Understanding and Science, and therefore must be referred to both; and the Philosopher himself, in chapter 7 of book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics and chapter 7 of book 5 of the Eudemian, calls Wisdom mere science, and so it concerns only science. Whence the number of intellectual virtues would be only four. But I answer that nothing follows from this: for although Wisdom is a habit compounded of other habits, it does not follow that it is not a habit distinct from them; for man is composed of matter and form, and yet is something different from both. The Philosopher calls Wisdom "science" in the passage cited, because it borrows some of the properties of science, since it also knows conclusions through the principles and causes themselves. Furthermore, the name science is there taken more broadly for any knowledge in its most perfect degree, and in this sense belongs only to Wisdom.
