units.la: 3. Quod virtutes intellectuales sint, sicut docet Philos. cap. 2. 6. Nicom. quibus affirmando vel negando verum enunciare possumus, & ideo consistunt in affirmatione vel negatione. At Prudentia non est ejusmodi habitus, cum non in affirmatione vel negatione consistat, sed in conformitate rectæ rationis cum recto appetitu, sicut docet Philosophus cap.ult.lib.6. Nicom. & sic Prudentia excluditur e numero virtutum intellectualium cum ei definitio non competat? Resp. Hoc ipso, quod dicatur consistere in conformitate ipsius rationis cum recto appetitu, intelligitur vim suam habere in affirmatione & negatione: nam dum ipsa ratio praescribit appetitui, ut aliquid amplectatur, prout revera existit vel non existit, hoc ipso vim suam in affirmando & negando exerit. Dein etiam affirmatio & negatio considerantur duobus modis vel respectu rerum, in quibus aliquid enunciant vel non enunciant: vel respectu actionum humanarum, quæ fiunt vel non fiunt, & sic Prudentia posteriori hoc modo in affirmatione & negatione cernitur, dum scilicet expriscripto recte rationis dictitat aliquid esse agendum vel non agendum. Plura vide de hoc argumento, apud Piccol. grad. 5. cap. 2. & 3. Econtra defectus vitio laborare quinarium numerum virtutum intellectualium, docent hae duae rationes: 1. Quia praetermittuntur habitus instrumentales, & sic stante hoc numero quinario Grammatica & reliquae disciplinae, quae scientiae non sunt, ad nullum horum habituum referri possunt. 2. Quia omittuntur etiam opinio & suspicio, cum sint habitus mentis, quibus aliquid affirmare vel negare possumus? Resp. Ad priorem ratione per negationem: nam non praetermittuntur habitus instrumentales, siquidem omnes ad artem referri possunt propter finem similem, quem habent, ne npe effectionem, quae duplex est interna & externa, cum duplex sit ars alia materialis, & alia immaterialis, & ad posterius genus referri possunt Grammatica, Rhetorica & aliae disciplinae. Quod ad secundam, opinio & suspicio licet aliquam habeant aut habere videantur cum virtutibus ipsis intellectualibus cognationem, inter ipsas tamen numerari non possunt, propterea quod principia sint plerunque malarum & incertarum actionum: nam per ista falli & decipi possunt homines: Opinio enim nihil certi statuit, sed semper vacillatur & fluctuat in dubiis: suspicio etiam pessimam quaeque apprehendit, nam raro datur suspicio, nisi in pessimam partem. At haec naturae istorum habituum repugnant. Unde concluditur quinque tantum esse virtutes intellectuales nec plures nec pauciores, & propter rationes a Philosopho allatas.
units.tr: 3. Whether the intellectual virtues are as the Philosopher teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 2, namely that they are the habits by which we can state the truth by affirming or denying, and so consist in affirmation or negation. But Prudence is not a habit of this kind, since it does not consist in affirmation or negation, but in the conformity of right reason with right appetite, as the Philosopher teaches in the last chapter of Nicomachean Ethics book 6. And so Prudence is excluded from the number of intellectual virtues, since the definition does not apply to it? Reply: From the very fact that it is said to consist in the conformity of reason itself with right appetite, it is understood that its power lies in affirming and denying. For when reason prescribes to the appetite that it embrace something, as it truly exists or does not exist, it thereby exerts its power in affirming and denying. Furthermore, affirmation and negation are considered in two ways: either with respect to things, about which we affirm or deny something, or with respect to human actions, which are done or not done. In the second way, Prudence is seen to affirm and deny, since by the rule of right reason it pronounces that something is to be done or not to be done. For more on this argument, see Piccolomini, grade 5, chapters 2 and 3. On the other side, the following two arguments show that the number of five intellectual virtues suffers from a defect: 1. Because instrumental habits are passed over, and so, with this number of five standing, Grammar and the other disciplines, which are not sciences, cannot be referred to any of these habits. 2. Because opinion and suspicion are also omitted, although they are habits of the mind by which we can affirm or deny something? Reply: To the first argument, the answer is by denial: for instrumental habits are not passed over, since all of them can be referred to art, because of the similar end they have, namely production, which is twofold, internal and external, since there are two kinds of art, one material and one immaterial. Grammar, Rhetoric and the other disciplines can be referred to the latter kind. As to the second, although opinion and suspicion have, or seem to have, some kinship with the intellectual virtues themselves, they cannot be counted among them, because their principles are for the most part of bad and uncertain actions; for men can be deceived and misled by these. Opinion settles nothing certain but always wavers and fluctuates in doubts. Suspicion also grasps at the worst of everything, for suspicion is seldom given except in the worse part. But these habits are contrary to the nature of the intellectual virtues. Hence it is concluded that there are only five intellectual virtues, neither more nor fewer, and for the reasons given by the Philosopher.

units.la: III. De subjecto virtutum Intellectualium: An
units.tr: III. On the subject of the intellectual virtues: Whether

units.la: in phantasia & memoria, an vero in intellectu ipso tanquam in suo subjecto sint ista virtutes? Resp. Hanc quaestionem esse controversam, nam quidam negant in intellectu esse, quidam afferunt. Priorem partem tuetur Piccolom. qui cum cap. 6 grad. 5. tres aliorum de hoc quaesito recensuisset, opiniones tandem concludit contra D. Thomam & alios, has mentis virtutes in sola phantasia & memoria esse tanquam in suo subjecto. Colligamus igitur, inquit, has rationis virtutes in sola phantasia recipi, & in memoria conservari, & tum demum dici hominem ejusmodi habitu praeditum cum longo studio, cura & diligentia iteratisque actionibus phantasmata ita firmaverit, digesserit ac in ordinem redegerit, ut ad libitum valeat communes notiones mente colligere, speculari ac per eas vel ad actionem vel ad effectionem dirigere. Negat vero in intellectu ullam ex hisce virtutibus locum habere, ex hoc fundamento, quia mens hominis seu intellectus contra distinguitur a phantasia, & cum mens per se sit aeterna nihil in ea, ut in subjecto, recipiatur. Quod enim immortale est, & a materia non pendet, nulli novo accidenti subiici potest: Sat enim menti est, inquit, cum per se pura sit & congruenter se habeat, ut ea sola recte parentur, quae ad phantasiam ac memoriam ac phantasmatum ordinem ac dispositionem requiruntur; his enim recte compositis sublatisque impedimentis, quae obstabant omnibus, mens recte suo munere fungitur, non secus ac Geometra, qui discussa ebrietate aut a somno expergefactus congruenter speculatur. Posteriorem partem tuetur D. Tho-
units.tr: they are in the imagination and the memory, or rather in the intellect itself as in their subject? Reply: This question is disputed, for some deny that they are in the intellect, and some affirm it. The former view is defended by Piccolomini, who, after listing three other opinions on this question in grade 5, chapter 6, finally concludes, against St. Thomas and others, that these intellectual virtues are in the imagination and the memory alone as in their subject. "Let us conclude, then," he says, "that these virtues of reason are received in the imagination alone and preserved in the memory; and a man is said to be endowed with such a habit only when, by long study, care and diligence, and by repeated actions, he has so firmed up, arranged and put in order the images that he can at will gather common notions in his mind, contemplate them, and direct them either to action or to production through them." He denies, however, that any of these virtues has a place in the intellect, on this ground: that the mind or intellect of man is distinct from the imagination, and since the mind is eternal in itself, nothing can be received in it as in a subject. For what is immortal and does not depend on matter cannot be made subject to any new accident. For it is enough for the mind, he says, that it is pure in itself and disposed in a fitting way, so that only those things are prepared which are required for the imagination and memory and for the order and arrangement of images. For when these are properly composed and the obstacles that hindered everything are removed, the mind rightly performs its function, just as a geometer, once his drunkenness has been shaken off or he has been woken from sleep, contemplates in a fitting way. The latter view is defended by St. Tho-

units.la: D. Thomas aliiq; præclarissimi Philosophi, & statuunt istas virtutes intellectuales, cum sint habitus in prima specie qualitatis esse in solo intellectu, tanquam in suo subjecto, idque probant tribus rationibus: 1. Quia nisi essent in intellectu, frustra Intellectuales dici mererentur. Quorsum enim nomen Intellectualis iis imponeretur, nisi in ipso intellectu vim suam exercerent, & ibi sedem suam haberent? 2. Quia medicina parti patienti aut affectæ debet applicari non alii: At in intellectu est morbus, nempe inscitia seu ignorantia, ut apud omnes pro confesso est. Proinde cum intellectus sit pars affecta, quæ medicina indiget, necesse est, ut istæ virtutes sint in intellectu, cui medicinam afferant. 3. Quia si phantasia istas virtutes tantum reciperet & non ultra pergerent, tunc ratione solius phantasiæ homo diceretur Sapiens, Sciens, Intelligens, & non ratione Intellectus aut mentis, à qua sola res scire & in suo valore & vigore unumquodque percipere inditum est unicuique. At posterius hoc est absurdum: nam alias nihil obstabit, quo minus etiam bruta dicantur rationalia, cum in brutis sit phantasia, atqui irrationale dici rationale includit contradictionem. Poterit tamen sententia Piccolominei quodammodo tolerari, si nempe ipsa harum virtutum intellectualium consideremus principia à sensibus, siquidem plerunque deducuntur ad ipsam phantasiam & memoriam, & per eam demum ad intellectum & mentem. Falsa autem erit, quod statuat, in phantasia semper hærere, nec ulterius ufpiá elevari, propter rationes jam allatas. Fundamentum
units.tr: St. Thomas and other most distinguished philosophers, and they hold that these intellectual virtues, since they are habits of the first species of quality, are in the intellect alone as in their subject. They prove this by three arguments: (1) If they were not in the intellect, they would deservedly be called intellectual in vain. For why would the name "intellectual" be given to them, unless they exercised their power in the intellect itself and had their seat there? (2) Because medicine ought to be applied to the suffering or affected part and not to another. But there is a disease in the intellect, namely unlearning or ignorance, as is admitted by all. Therefore, since the intellect is the affected part, which needs medicine, it is necessary that these virtues be in the intellect, to which they bring the remedy. (3) Because if the imagination received these virtues only and did not proceed further, then a man would be called wise, knowing, and understanding by reason of the imagination alone, and not by reason of the intellect or mind, by which alone it is given to each person to know things and to perceive each in its worth and force. But this latter is absurd; for otherwise nothing would prevent even brute beasts from being called rational, since the imagination is in brutes, and yet to call the irrational rational involves a contradiction. Nevertheless, the opinion of Piccolomini could be tolerated to some extent, if we consider the principles of these intellectual virtues as coming from the senses, since they are for the most part led down to the imagination itself and memory, and through these at last to the intellect and mind. But it will be false if it asserts that they always remain in the imagination and are never raised further, for the reasons already given.

units.la: tum autem hoc, cui maximè innititur Piccolom, nempe quod mens, cum sit æterna & à materia non pendeat, nulli novo accidenti subjici possit, est planè frivolum & falsum, eiq; opponimus expressum Aristotelis textum lib.2.de anim. ubi text.2. 3. & 4. intellectum seu mentem antequam intelligat omnia, esse potestate statuit, & propterea comp rat tabulæ rasæ, in qua etsi nihil scriptum sit, quicquid tamen scribi poterit. Et text 8. ibidem, intellectum vocat locum recipiendarum specierum, & text.9. omnia intellectum fieri, expresse docet, non quidem essentialiter aut formaliter, quod voluit Cardanus, sed tantum subjectivè, ut elegantèr explicat Scalig. exerc. 307. sect.6. Plura vide de hac quæstione cap.6. & 7. gradu 5.
units.tr: But the foundation on which Piccolomini chiefly rests, namely that the mind, since it is eternal and does not depend on matter, cannot be made subject to any new accident, is plainly frivolous and false, and we oppose to it the express text of Aristotle in On the Soul 2, where, in text 2, 3 and 4, he states that the intellect or mind, before it understands all things, is in potentiality, and for this reason he compares it to a writing tablet, on which, although nothing is written, whatever can be written may be written. And in text 8 of the same book he calls the intellect the place for receiving the species, and in text 9 he plainly teaches that all things become intellect, not indeed essentially or formally, as Cardanus wished, but only subjectively, as Scaliger elegantly explains in Exercitations 307, section 6. Consult more on this question in Grade 5, chapters 6 and 7.

units.la: IV. An Prudentia è numero aut censu virtutum sit tollenda nec ne?
units.tr: IV. Is Prudence to be removed from the number or the rank of the virtues, or not?

units.la: Resp. Etsi multi sint, qui hoc statuunt, quia putant Prudentiam nihil aliud esse quam vim & notitiam ipsius intellectus, aut rem cum ipso intellectu unam naturam nobis insitam: hoc tamen falsum esse duabus rationibus evincitur: 1. Quia si Prudentia esset vis tantum natura nobis insita, tunc sequeretur, omnes homines æquè esse prudentes, propterea quod naturâ æquè omnibus communicetur, & cum in singulis rebus quibus inest, sit forma, & forma non recipit intentionem aut major aut minus, ideo nullus esset prudentior alio; contrarium cuivis experientia testatur. 2. Quia quæ nobis naturâ insunt, ab iis proprie non laudamur, utpote quæ ipsius tantum naturæ sint: at à prudentia laudamur, sicut ab alia aliqua virtute. te. Aristoteles 1. Nicomach. capite 12. Nam prudentia cum sit omnium regina virtutum, homines ad bene beateq; ie vivendum inprimis aptos & habiles reddit. Quod vero e numero virtutum non sit tollenda, quatuor hæ docent rationes: 1. Quia media ad ultimum finem vitæ humanæ sive ad summum bonum consequendum maximè inquirit & demonstrat. 2. Quia non tantum in contemplatione, sed in praxi etiam & maximè in praxi consistit. Nam cum versetur circa actiones humanas, necesse est, ut ad praxin omnem vim suam dirigat. 3. Quia absque prudentia nulla poterit esse virtus moralis, cum sit Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum, & idem præstet inter virtutes morales, quod clavus in nave aut frenum in equo. 4. Quia non minus est habitus crebris actionibus comparatus, quam reliquæ virtutes, & variis requisitis ad sui constitutionem indiget, ut supra jam probatum fuit. Accedit huc etiam testimonium Philosophi, qui lib. 1. magnor. moral. cap. 35. prudentiam non modo inter virtutes recenset, sed etiam inter Ethicas, propterea quod circa actiones hominum dirigendas non secus ac virtus moralis versetur. Adstipulatur etiam Cicero 5. de finib. Alterum, inquit, genus magnarum verarum que virtutum, quas appellamus voluntarias, sunt Justitia, Fortitudo, Temperantia & Prudentia.
units.tr: Answer: Although many hold that it should be removed, because they think Prudence is nothing other than the power and knowledge of the intellect itself, or a single nature implanted in us together with the intellect, this is shown to be false by two reasons. (1) If Prudence were only a power implanted in us by nature, then it would follow that all men are equally prudent, since nature is communicated equally to all. And since in each thing in which it is present, it is a form, and a form does not admit of more or less, no one would be more prudent than another. Experience testifies to the contrary for everyone. (2) We are not praised properly for those things that are implanted in us by nature, since they belong only to nature itself. But we are praised for prudence, just as for any other virtue. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1, chapter 12: "For prudence, since it is the queen of all the virtues, makes men especially fit and able to live well and happily." That it is not to be removed from the number of the virtues, these four reasons teach: (1) It most of all seeks out and demonstrates the means to the ultimate end of human life, that is, to the attainment of the highest good. (2) It consists not only in contemplation but also in practice, and most of all in practice. For since it is concerned with human actions, it must direct all its power toward practice. (3) Without prudence there can be no moral virtue, since it is the leader and governor of all the virtues, and among the moral virtues it does what the rudder does in a ship or the bridle does in a horse. (4) It is no less a habit acquired by frequent actions than the other virtues, and it needs various requisites for its constitution, as was already proved above. The testimony of the Philosopher also agrees with this, who in the first book of the Magna Moralia, chapter 35, counts prudence not only among the virtues but among the ethical virtues, because it is concerned with directing human actions no less than moral virtue is. Cicero also agrees, in the fifth book of De finibus: "The other kind of great and true virtues, which we call voluntary, are justice, fortitude, temperance and prudence."

units.la: Unde & hæc V. quæstio emergit: An scilicet Prudentia sit virtus Moralis, an Intellectualis. Nam Philosophus 6. Nicom. cap. 5. inter Intellectuales enumerat, & ut Intellectualem definit, & à morali distinguit: sed 1. magnor. moral. cap. 35. virtutem vocat moralem, nam & Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum moralium ab omnibus habetur? Respon. Esse mixtam virtutem ex Intellectuali & Morali. Esse intellectualem propter duas causas: 1. Respectu subjecti, quia in mente seu intellectu sedem suam habet. 2. Respectu causæ efficientis, quia ab hominis ingenio & judicio dependet, & ab ipsa mente oritur. Esse Moralem propter duas etiam rationes: 1. Respectu objecti, quia versatur circa actiones humanas, sicut omnis virtus moralis. 2. Respectu finis, quia non tam perficit intellectum, cui inest, quam appetitum & voluntatem: nam parti animæ appetitivæ, sicut virtutes morales inservit. Philosoph. cap. ult. 1. Nicom. & ipsum appetitum ad rectæ rationis imperium perducit; nec tam tendit ad felicitatem theoreticam, quam ad practicam seu bonum morale & civile. Idem confirmare videtur Aristot. 6. Nicom. cap. 6. ubi hoc discrimen inter Artem & Prudentiam ponit, quod Ars reipsa a virtute morali separari potest, & quod quis artis habitu perfecte posset esse præditus, qui nulla tamen virtute morali sit instructus. Unde c. 4. 2. Nic. poterit aliquis esse pictor & artifex bonus, qui idem sit facinorosus & improbus: At vero prudentia indissolubiliter est cum virtute morali conjuncta, ita ut nemo possit esse vir prudens, qui idem sit vir malus c. ult. lib. 6. Nicom.
units.tr: Hence also arises this fifth question: whether prudence is a moral or an intellectual virtue. For the Philosopher, in the sixth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 5, counts it among the intellectual virtues, defines it as intellectual, and distinguishes it from the moral virtues. But in the first book of the Magna Moralia, chapter 35, he calls it a moral virtue, for it is held by all to be the leader and governor of all the moral virtues. Answer: it is a virtue mixed of the intellectual and the moral. It is intellectual for two reasons: (1) with respect to its subject, since it has its seat in the mind or intellect; (2) with respect to its efficient cause, since it depends on a man's talent and judgment, and arises from the mind itself. It is moral also for two reasons: (1) with respect to its object, since it is concerned with human actions, as is every moral virtue; (2) with respect to its end, since it perfects not so much the intellect in which it resides as the appetite and the will. For it serves the appetitive part of the soul, as the moral virtues do, and it brings the appetite itself under the command of right reason. Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 1, last chapter. And it does not tend so much toward theoretical happiness as toward practical happiness, that is, the moral and civic good. Aristotle seems to confirm this too, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 6, where he draws this distinction between art and prudence: art can in fact be separated from moral virtue, and a man may be furnished with the habit of an art perfectly while being equipped with no moral virtue at all. Hence, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 4, a man may be a good painter and craftsman while being at the same time wicked and dishonest. But prudence is inseparably joined to moral virtue, so that no one can be a prudent man who is at the same time a bad man, Nicomachean Ethics 6, last chapter.

units.la: VI. An recte definiatur Prudentia a Philosopho 6. Nic. cap. 5. habitus verus cum recta ratione activus, & an itaque habitus verus, ut ei falsum subjici non possit?
units.tr: VI. Whether Prudence is rightly defined by the Philosopher (6 Nic. ch. 5) as a true habit active with right reason, and whether, for that reason, a true habit cannot have falsehood subjoined to it.

units.la: Ratio vero dubitandi inde venit, quod prudentia habeat pro objecto contingentia, quæ in utramque partem cadere dere possunt, & ita etiam judicium nostri intellectus falli-ere. Unde cur dicatur habitus verus, cum circa objectum varium & mutabile versetur, jure quæ i potest. Pro determinatione hujus dubii tenendum erit quod D. Thomas habet adversum 3.de Anim. part. 1. quæst. 79. part. 11. duplicem esse veritatem respectu finis, theoreticam nempe & practicam. Prior consistit in conformitate cognitionis seu intellectus cognoscentis ad rem cognitam seu qua intellectus rem ipsam percipit, prout revera existit, nec ei aliquid affingit. Aristot. 2. Met. cap. 2. Posterior cernitur in adæquatione rectæ rationis ad recti appetitū, id est, cum appetitus & ratio ita inter se conveniunt, ut, quod jubet ratio, exsequatur appetitus, & nihil exsequatur appetitus, quod non jubeat ratio. De hac adæquatione seu conformitate rationis cum appetitu, loquitur Philosophus 6. Nic. c. 2. ex hac duplici notione veritatis fit, ut nullus habitus specula-tivus per se & absolute sit verus, nisi quatenus circa objectum necessarium, & quod aliter se habere nequit, versatur, quia ejus veritas a conditione & natura objecti pendet. Habitus vero practicus etsi ad objectum contingens tendat, id est, circa ejusmodi versetur objectum, quod aliter atque aliter subinde se habere potest, poterit tamen nihilominus veritati esse consentaneus, si recto appetitui secundum rectam rationem dispositio adæquetur, quicquid sit de conformitate ad objectum secundum se, & sua natura spectatum. Proinde concludimus prudentiam esse habitum verum & in vero semper consistere, nec digitum latum ab eo unquam exorbitare, re, quia præsupponit rectitudinem voluntatis & conformitatem intellectus cum ipsa voluntate, & ideo oportet ejus actum practicè esse verum, quia ordinem habet ad rectam voluntatem, cui conformatur, licet in objectum contingens tendat, & ita respectu objecti dubium incidat; & licet speculativè etiam falsus deprehendi possit, cum non à conditione objecti, ut habitus speculativus, sed à principiis actionum humanarum & à fine ipsarum dependeat. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Philosophum cap.2. 6.Nicom. & apud Conimbricenses in epit.Ethic.disp.18.quaest.1.art.2.
units.tr: The reason for doubt arises from the fact that prudence has contingent things as its object, which can go either way, and so the judgment of our intellect can also err. Hence it is reasonably asked why it is called a true habit when it is concerned with a varied and changeable object. To settle this doubt we should hold what St Thomas holds, in De Anima, part 1, question 79, part 2: truth is twofold with respect to the end, namely theoretical and practical. The former consists in the conformity of the cognition, or of the knowing intellect, to the thing known, by which the intellect perceives the thing itself as it really exists, and adds nothing to it. Aristotle, Metaphysics 2, ch. 2. The latter is seen in the adequation of right reason to right appetite, that is, when appetite and reason so agree with each other that the appetite carries out what reason commands, and carries out nothing that reason does not command. The Philosopher speaks of this adequation or conformity of reason with appetite in Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 2. From this twofold notion of truth it follows that no speculative habit is true in itself and absolutely, except insofar as it is concerned with a necessary object, one that cannot be otherwise, because its truth depends on the condition and nature of its object. A practical habit, however, although it is directed to a contingent object, that is, one concerned with the kind of object that can at various times be one way or another, can nonetheless be consonant with truth, provided that the disposition of the right appetite is made adequate to right reason, whatever the conformity to the object considered in itself and by its nature. Accordingly we conclude that prudence is a true habit and always consists in truth, and never departs from it by a finger's breadth. For it presupposes rectitude of the will and the conformity of the intellect with the will itself. Therefore its act must be practically true, because it is ordered to the right will, to which it conforms, even though it is directed to a contingent object and so, with respect to the object, doubt may arise. And although it may also be found false speculatively, it is not dependent on the condition of the object, as a speculative habit is, but on the principles of human actions and on their end. For more on this question see the Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 2, and the Coimbra commentators, in Epitome of the Ethics, disputation 18, question 1, article 2.

units.la: VII. An Prudentia recte dicatur Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum, imprimis verò moralium?
units.tr: VII. Whether Prudence is rightly called the leader and governor of all the virtues, and especially of the moral virtues?

units.la: Resp. Licet vulgò sic habeatur, disceptari tamen solet hæc quæstio in utramque partem. Nam sunt, qui contrarium tuentur, & pro negativa afferunt quatuor rationes: 1. Ducitur à simili: sicut cognitio salubrium & insalubrium, nihil conducit ad sanitatem corporis: ita etiam prudentia nihil confert ad sanitatem animi seu ad virtutem moralem, quæ veluti medicina quædam expellit vitia animi. Nam prudentia nihil aliud est, quam cognitio bonorum & malorum, seu ejusmodi scientia, qua res cum bonæ, tum malæ pro variis circumstantiis inter se discerni possunt: At ut cognitio nihil prodest in medicina absque praxi, ita etiam prudentia nihil proderit virtuti morali, cum in sola cognitione, non in actione consistat, ut putant Stoici. 2. Quia communis experientia testatur, multos esse homines prudentes, hoc est, cognitione rerum expetendarum & fugiendarum beneinstructos, structos, qui tamen in vita & moribus sint improbi, & virtutis moralis expertes. Econtra multos esse imprudentes, id est, plane ignaros earum rerum, quae expetendae aut fugiendae sunt, qui tamen sunt probi & virtutis moralis participes, quales sunt plerunque adolescentes, idiotae, de quibus Seneca, quia parum sciunt, ideo minus patrant mali, & sat esse putant, si secundum naturae legem vivant, & neminem laedant. Proinde cum subiecto distinguantur prudentia & virtus moralis, prudentia poterit esse sine virtute morali, & virtus moralis absque prudentia. 3. Quia virtus moralis videtur potius esse Dux ipsius prudentiae, quatenus scilicet finem rectum ejus consultationi praescribit eamque dirigit, ut media honesta & utilia ad illum finem ducentia inquirat ac decernat. Nam sicut vitium perverti ac depravat judicium intellectus, efficitque, ut de principiis practicis male sentiamus, sic virtus econtra perficit judicium rectae rationis, efficitque, ut de principiis practicis bene sentiamus, Aristot. cap. ult. 6. Nicom. ubi statim adjungit, fieri non poterit, ut quis sit vir prudens absque virtute morali, innuens virtutem moralem requiri tanquam certum Ducem ad prudentiam. 4. Quia Socrates apud Platonem in variis dialog. ut in Menone & in Phaedro statuit, omnes virtutes esse prudentias, quod docet Aristoteles loco ante cit. Proinde prudentia non poterit esse Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum moralium, cum singulae sint prudentiae per se & sic sibi ipsis Duces sint. At pro affirmativa parte rationes sunt longe firmiores numero novem: 1. Ducitur a definitione prudentiae,
units.tr: Reply: Although this is commonly held, the question is usually disputed on both sides. Some defend the contrary view and bring forward four reasons for the negative. (1) It is argued by analogy: just as knowing what is healthy and unhealthy contributes nothing to the health of the body, so prudence contributes nothing to the health of the soul, that is, to moral virtue, which like a kind of medicine expels the vices of the soul. For prudence is nothing other than the knowledge of good and evil, or a kind of science by which good and bad things can be distinguished from one another according to their various circumstances. But just as knowledge is of no use in medicine without practice, so prudence will be of no use to moral virtue, since it consists in knowing rather than in acting, as the Stoics think. (2) Common experience shows that many men are prudent, that is, well informed about what is to be sought and avoided, yet are wicked in life and conduct and lack moral virtue. On the contrary, many are imprudent, that is, altogether ignorant of what is to be sought or avoided, yet are upright and share in moral virtue. Such are mostly young people and simple folk, of whom Seneca says that because they know little, they do little wrong, and think it enough to live according to the law of nature and harm no one. Therefore, since prudence and moral virtue are distinguished by their subject, prudence can exist without moral virtue, and moral virtue without prudence. (3) Moral virtue seems rather to be the guide of prudence itself, in so far as it prescribes the right end for its deliberation and directs it, so that prudence seeks out and decides upon the honourable and useful means that lead to that end. For just as vice perverts and corrupts the judgement of the intellect, so that we think wrongly about practical principles, so virtue on the contrary perfects the judgement of right reason, so that we think rightly about practical principles. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, last chapter, where he immediately adds that a man cannot be prudent without moral virtue, implying that moral virtue is required as a sure guide to prudence. (4) Socrates, in various dialogues of Plato, such as the Meno and the Phaedrus, held that all the virtues are forms of prudence, as Aristotle teaches in the passage cited above. Therefore prudence cannot be the guide and regulator of all the moral virtues, since each of them is prudence in itself and so is its own guide. But for the affirmative side the arguments are far stronger, nine in number. (1) It is drawn from the definition of prudence,

units.la: Fff tiæ, quia prudentia secundum Aristot. c. 5. lib. 6 Nicom. est habitus intellectualis cum ratione vera agendi ea, quæ sunt homini bona aut mala, & secundum Stoicos teste Laërtio lib. 7. de vit. Philosoph. in vita Zenonis. Prudentia est cognitio bonorum & malorum & neutrorum simul, adeo ut doceat discernere interres per se aut bonas aut malas, & inter ejusmodi etiam res, quæ neque per se sunt bonæ aut malæ, sed quatenus in usum bonum aut malum adhibentur: Et secundum Lipsium lib. 1. cap. 7. civil. doct. Prudentia est intellectus & delectus earum rerum, quæ publice privatimque expetendæ, aut fugiendæ sunt seu est cognitio vera bonorum aut malorum, ut delectus habeatur honestorum & turpium, utilium & inutilium: quæ omnes definitiones nihil aliud innuunt, quam prudentiam esse Ducem & moderatricem omnium virtutum moralium, propterea quod virtus versetur circa bonum, & per prudentiam posse discerni bonum a malo. 2. Quia facultatem hominis suppeditat recte consultandi de mediis ad bene beateq; vivendum conducentibus, & sic tam sibi quam aliis consulendi. Aristoteles 1. mag. moral. cap. 33. Proinde cum virtutes morales sint illa media, quæ tenduntad bene beateque vivendum, & per prudentiam dirigantur ad suum finem, necessario Dux & regula virtutum moralium erit prudentia. 3. Quia terminos actionibus hominum præscribit, quos egredi non licet, & medium in iis statuit ac decernit, ut inter excessum & defectum, hoc est, secundum virtutem moralem, tanquam viam regiam, omnes actiones procedant. 4. Quia voluntatem tatem & proærefin hominis dirigit ac moderatur, ut non nisi ad id, quod bonum & honestum est, seu quod legi naturæ & rectæ rationi fit consentaneum feratur, & quicquid iis repugnat aut etiam discrepat, id plane aversetur. 5. Quia rationem monstrat domandi & coercendi omnes perturbationes & appetitiones pravas, adeoq; ipsos affectus, qui per se sunt irrationales, cuiusmodi in parte animæ inferiore nempe ὁρεκτικὴ, ad rectæ rationis normam revocet.
units.tr: ...of prudence, since according to Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 5, prudence is an intellectual habit, joined with true reason, of doing those things that are good or bad for man, and according to the Stoics, as Diogenes Laertius reports in Book 7 of the Lives of the Philosophers, in the life of Zeno, prudence is the knowledge of good and bad things and of indifferent things at once, so that it teaches us to distinguish among things that are good or bad in themselves, and also among those things which are neither good nor bad in themselves but become so according to the good or bad use to which they are put. And according to Lipsius, Civil Doctrine, Book 1, ch. 7, prudence is the discernment and choice of those things that are to be sought or avoided in public and private life; or it is the true knowledge of good and evil, so that there may be a choice between the honourable and the shameful, the useful and the useless. All these definitions imply nothing other than that prudence is the guide and regulator of all the moral virtues, because virtue is concerned with the good, and through prudence good can be distinguished from evil. (2) It supplies man with the ability to deliberate rightly about the means that lead to living well and happily, and so to take counsel both for himself and for others. Aristotle, Great Ethics 1, ch. 33. Therefore, since the moral virtues are those means that tend to living well and happily, and are directed to their end through prudence, prudence will necessarily be the guide and rule of the moral virtues. (3) It prescribes the limits of human actions, which it is not permitted to exceed, and it fixes and decides the mean in them, so that all actions proceed between excess and deficiency, that is, according to moral virtue, as along a royal road. (4) It directs and governs the will and the choice of man, so that it is borne only towards what is good and honourable, or what agrees with the law of nature and right reason, and wholly turns away from whatever is opposed or even discordant with these. (5) It shows the way of taming and restraining all the disturbances and wicked appetites, and indeed the affections themselves, which are in themselves irrational, of the kind found in the lower part of the soul, namely the appetitive part [ὁρεκτικὴ], and brings them back under the standard of right reason.

units.la: 6. Quia judicium hominis informat in æstimandis rebus singulis, ut singula recte æstimet, nec pluris nec minoris, quam fieri debet. Ex hoc enim fonte omnis error oboritur, quod de rerum ipsarum valore & preciis non rectum ferant homines judicium. 7. Idipsum demonstratur ab officiis prudentiæ, quia præsentia ordinat, futura prævidet, præterita recordatur, quæ tria prudentiæ esse officia apud omnes pro confesso est. 8. Quia recte & exacte præponderat rerum circumstantias, in quibus versantur actiones humanæ, easq; ad amussim dijudicat & pro tempore loco & personis rebus ipsis accommodat.
units.tr: 6. Because judgment shapes our estimate of each single thing, so that we value each one rightly, neither more nor less than it should be valued. For every error arises from this source: people do not form a correct judgment about the worth and price of things themselves. 7. This is shown also from the offices of prudence, since it orders present matters, foresees future ones, and recalls past ones; everyone agrees that these three are the offices of prudence. 8. Because it weighs exactly and correctly the circumstances in which human actions take place, judges them precisely, and fits them to the time, place, persons and the matters themselves.

units.la: 9. Demum, quia omnis virtus moralis est habitus rectæ rationi consentaneus, & cum recta ratione conjunctus, docente Philos. cap. 7. lib. 2. Nicom. & c. ult. lib. 6. Proinde cum prudentia ipsam rationem informet, ad eamque ducat virtutes morales, sequitur Ducem esse & moderatricem omnium in genere virtutum moralium. Et hoc etiam testantur præclarissimi Philosophi Plato & Aristoteles, quorum ille in Menone inquit: Prudentia sola præit, & ducit ad bene beateq; vivendum & ad actiones bene agendas, das. Et in 3. de leg. Prima & omnis virtutis Dux est prudenti.Hic Arist.nempe c. ult.lib. 6.subfin. expressè affirmat, virtutem moralem nō esse sine prudentia, fieri enim non potest, ut quis sit prudens absq; virtute morali, aut et virtute morali praeditus absq; prudentia. Alicubi etiam à Plat. propter hanc ipsam causam prudentia vocatur auriga vitæ humanæ: quia appetitus indomitos & affectus irregulares nō secus ac equos ferocientes nec frenum audientes, sed petulanter excurrentes frenat & moderatur, ne hominem in vitia præcipitem trahant. Alicubi etiam dicitur nauta in puppi sedens, quia totius vitæ humanæ cursum in manibus tenet, & in mediis perturbationum & appetitionum variarum fluctibus homines à naufragio vitiorum salvos & incolumes reddit. Ab aliis etiam omnium actionum nostrarum, omnium consiliorum, omnium operum & laborum, totius denique vitæ humanæ regula Dux & magistra non immerito dicitur. Unde elegantèr Lipf.lib. 1. civ. doct. cap. 8. ut architectus nullum opus procedit absque libella & linea, qua opus dirigatur: sic nobis in opere actionum nostrarum absque norma hac directrice nempe prudentia. Proinde affirmativam, quaafferitur, prudentiam esse Ducem & moderatricem omnium virtutum moralium, propter rationes supra allatas, veram esse statuimus. Ac ut ad argumenta pro negativa & contraria parte adducta breviter respondeatur, observanda sunt sequentia theoremata: 1. Non simpliciter id verum esse, quod scientia salubrium & insalubrium nihil conferat ad sanitatem corporis. Nam licet non sit causa proxima sanitatis vel recuperandae vel conservandae, poterit tamen esse causa remota, siquidem is, qui bene & dextre novit, quae sint salubria, quae insalubria, vel sibi vel aliis, poterit eo melius vel sua vel aliorum sanitatem, usu salubrium & declinatione insalubrium conservare vel restituere. 2. Neque illud esse simpliciter verum, quod prudentia sit mera cognitio bonorum & malorum, sed potius est ejusmodi notitia, quae intellectum hominis de bonis & malis informat, ut iis commode utatur ad bene honesteque agendum & mentem hominis flectat ad bonum appetendum & persequendum: malum vero aversandum & fugiendum, id quod patet etiam ex definitione prudentiae, cum dicitur habitus agendi cum ratione ea, quae sunt hominibus bona vel mala. Aristot. 6 Nicom. cap. 5. 3. Homines improbos non vere & proprie esse prudentes, sed potius callidos, versutos & malitiosos, qui sua prudentia & cognitione abutuntur ad malum. Hinc Lipsius lib. 1. civ. doct. cap. 2. inquit: Prudentia absque virtute est tantum calliditas aut versutia, & quidvis potius quam vera prudentia. Id quod exemplo Caesaris Gordiae satis liquet, qui proprie opinionem prudentiae ad Reipub. administrationem evectus, sed mera calliditate, dolis & versutia laborare tantum in vita & moribus demonstravit. 4. Neminem esse probum virtutisque moralis participem, qui idem sit plane imprudens, id est, bonorum & malorum prorsus ignarus, sicut rationes supra allatae demonstrant. Cum igitur adolescens aliquis, aut idiota rerum non adeo periculus dicitur secundum leges naturae & rectam ratiotionem vivere, non poterit vere esse probus, nisi notitiam ejusmodi turpis & honesti habeat, cujus vi fuerit excitatus ad virtutem ipsam appetendam & persequendam. Nam ut vulgo dicitur, Ignoti nulla cupido, qui enim fieri potest, ut aliquis sponte suaid appetat, quod prorsus ignorat? Hinc insciria & virtus moralis simul esse nequeunt, cum ad virtutem moralem requiratur parata voluntas ab intellectu ipso informata, teste Philosopho 2. Nicomach. cap. 4. 5. Prudentiam esse Ducem & moderatricem virtutis moralis ab homine jam acquiredae, sed eam rursus acquisitam esse quodammodo Ducem & moderatricem ipsius prudentiae, quatenus eam perficit, & ne in abusum deflectat, aut in versuriam degeneret, prohibet. 6. Virtutes morales omnes a Socrate quidem dici prudentias, non tamen, ut recte annotat Philosophus cap. ult. lib. 6. proprie, sed improprie quia scilicet prudentiae norma dirigunntur, & nulla absq; prudentia acquiri potest virtus moralis. Hinc Goclenius in quaest. Eth. quaest. 39. dicit, virtutes morales vocari prudentias propter duas potissimum causas: 1. Respectu dependentiae & acquisitionis, quia a prudentia dependent omnes & ad virtutes morales acquirendas necessario requiruntur. 2. Respectu connexionis sive consensu conspirationis, quia prudentia & virtus moralis ita inter se conspirant, ut una absque altera esse non possit, sed in dissolubili nexu inter se conjunctae sint.
units.tr: 9. Lastly, because every moral virtue is a habit agreeing with right reason and joined with right reason, as the Philosopher teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 7, and in the last chapter of book 6. Therefore, since prudence shapes reason itself and leads the moral virtues by it, it follows that prudence is the leader and governor of all the moral virtues in general. This is also attested by the most distinguished philosophers, Plato and Aristotle. Plato says in the Meno: "Prudence alone goes before and leads one to live well and happily, and to act well." And in Laws 3: "Prudence is the first and leader of every virtue." Aristotle himself, in the last chapter of book 6, near its end, expressly affirms that moral virtue is not without prudence: it cannot happen that someone is prudent without moral virtue, or endowed with moral virtue without prudence. Elsewhere Plato, for this very reason, calls prudence the charioteer of human life: just as a charioteer restrains and governs wild horses that are unruly and will not hear the bit but rush wantonly about, so prudence checks and moderates the unruly appetites and irregular passions, lest they drag a man headlong into vices. Elsewhere it is called the sailor sitting at the stern, because it holds the course of the whole of human life in its hands and, amid the waves of the various disturbances and appetites, brings men safe and sound through the shipwreck of vices. Others rightly call it the leader and mistress of all our actions, all our counsels, all our works and labours, and in short the rule of the whole of human life. Hence Lipsius neatly says, in Political Doctrine, book 1, chapter 8, that as an architect proceeds with no work without a level and a line by which the work is directed, so in the work of our actions we have nothing without this directing rule, namely prudence. Therefore we hold that the affirmative proposition, which is asserted, namely that prudence is the leader and governor of all the moral virtues, is true, for the reasons given above. And so that the arguments adduced for the negative and opposing side may be answered briefly, the following propositions must be noted: 1. It is not simply true that the knowledge of wholesome and unwholesome things contributes nothing to bodily health. For although it is not the proximate cause of preserving or recovering health, it can still be a remote cause, since one who knows well and skilfully what is wholesome and unwholesome, for himself or for others, can better preserve or restore his own or others' health by using wholesome things and avoiding unwholesome ones. 2. Nor is it simply true that prudence is mere knowledge of good and evil; rather it is that sort of knowledge which shapes the human intellect about good and evil, so that it may use them suitably for acting well and honourably, and which turns the mind to pursue the good and to shun and flee evil. This is also clear from the definition of prudence, when it is said to be a habit of acting with reason in matters that are good or bad for men (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 5). 3. Wicked men are not truly and properly prudent, but rather clever, crafty and malicious, who abuse their prudence and knowledge for evil. Hence Lipsius, Political Doctrine, book 1, chapter 2, says: "Prudence without virtue is merely cunning or craftiness, and anything rather than true prudence." This is sufficiently clear from the example of Caesar Gordianus, who, though raised to a reputation for prudence in the administration of the commonwealth, showed in his life and conduct that he laboured only under mere cunning, tricks and craftiness. 4. No one is upright and a partaker of moral virtue who is wholly imprudent, that is, utterly ignorant of good and evil, as the reasons given above demonstrate. Therefore, if some young man or unlearned person who is not so well versed in affairs is said to live according to the laws of nature and right reason, he cannot truly be upright unless he has knowledge of what is base and honourable, by the power of which he is roused to desire and pursue virtue itself. For, as the common saying goes, "there is no desire for what is unknown"; for how can it happen that someone willingly desires what he entirely does not know? Hence ignorance and moral virtue cannot exist together, since moral virtue requires a will ready and shaped by the intellect itself, as the Philosopher testifies, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 4. 5. Prudence is the leader and governor of moral virtue in a man who has already acquired it; but that virtue, once acquired, is in some measure the leader and governor of prudence itself, insofar as it perfects prudence and prevents it from turning to abuse or degenerating into craftiness. 6. All the moral virtues are indeed called prudences by Socrates, but not properly, as the Philosopher rightly notes in the last chapter of book 6; they are so called improperly, because they are directed by the rule of prudence, and no moral virtue can be acquired without prudence. Hence Goclenius, in Questions on Ethics, question 39, says that the moral virtues are called prudences chiefly for two reasons: 1. With respect to dependence and acquisition, because all of them depend on prudence and are necessarily required for acquiring the moral virtues. 2. With respect to connection, or agreement and joint action, because prudence and moral virtue so agree with one another that one cannot exist without the other, but they are joined together in an indissoluble bond.

units.la: VIII. An Prudentia praestet Sapientia, an vero contra? Resp. Hanc quaestionem pro variis hominum conditionibus & pro ingeniis varie affectis (quidam
units.tr: VIII. Does Prudence excel Wisdom, or the reverse?

units.la: dam enim contemplatione & foltudine delectan-tur, quidam magis actione & hominum societate) esse dubiam & dilceptari in utramque partem: nam pro negativa septem adferuntur argumenta: 1. Quia Prudentia est proles Sapientiae, & ab ea principia sua accipit; nam absque intelligentia & certa rerum cognitione (quae duae efficiones constituunt Sapientiam) nulla haberi poterit prudentia. Quantum igitur causa praestat causato, principium principiato, tantum dicetur Sapientia praestare Prudentia.
units.tr: Answer: This question is open to dispute and is argued on both sides, depending on the varying conditions of men and their differently disposed minds. Some delight in contemplation and solitude, others more in action and human society. For the negative side, seven arguments are brought forward: (1) Prudence is the offspring of Wisdom and receives its principles from it. Without understanding and sure knowledge of things, which are the two components of Wisdom, no prudence can exist. Therefore, as much as a cause excels what it causes, and a principle excels what proceeds from it, so much will Wisdom be said to excel Prudence.

units.la: 2. Quia Sapientia est quieta & otiosa, utpote quae in sola contemplatione consistat, & negotiis quotidianis se non implicet: Prudentia vero est inquieta & negotiosa, utpote quae non in actione solum consistat, sed circumstantias singulares omnium actionum perpendat, & Reipub. imprimis curam gerat, ubi infinita pene ingruunt negotia.
units.tr: (2) Wisdom is quiet and leisurely, since it consists in contemplation alone and does not entangle itself in the daily business of life. Prudence, however, is restless and busy, since it does not consist in action alone but weighs the particular circumstances of all actions, and above all takes care of the commonwealth, where almost endless business presses in.

units.la: 3. Quia objectum Sapientiae est praestantius Prudentiae; nam Sapientia versatur in rebus divinis & naturalibus, quae sunt stabiles & constantes: Prudentia vero in rebus tantum humanis, quae infinitis mutationibus sunt obnoxiae. Quantum igitur res divinae & naturales praestant humanis, tantum Sapientia superabit prudentiam.
units.tr: (3) The object of Wisdom is more excellent than that of Prudence. For Wisdom is concerned with divine and natural things, which are stable and constant, whereas Prudence is concerned only with human things, which are subject to endless change. Therefore, as divine and natural things surpass human things, so much will Wisdom surpass Prudence.

units.la: 4. Quia Sapientia sibi ipsi est sufficiens minusque naturae & fortunae bonis indiget, quam prudentia: nam cum in sola contemplatione consistat, non indiget divitiis, tanquam mediis ad finem suum aequendum, non caeteris ejusmodi, quae prudentia necessario requirit bonis, sed solus naturae apparatus illi sufficit, & ad naturam referre cooponit, & astris esse putat, si homines no ad ... cessi-
units.tr: (4) Wisdom is sufficient in itself and needs fewer of the goods of nature and fortune than Prudence does. For since it consists in contemplation alone, it does not need riches as means to attain its end, nor other such goods which Prudence necessarily requires. Only the equipment of nature is enough for it, and it thinks that it is related to nature and resembles the stars, if men ... [the rest is illegible].

units.la: [The final lines of the page are partly illegible.] cessitatem instruat. s. Subjecti utriusq; dignitas id ipsum evincit: nam Sapientia mentem & intellectum hominis perficit; prudentia vero appetitum & voluntatem. Cum vero intellectus sit animi facultas longe præstantior ipsa voluntate: Nam voluntas ab eo defendit & regitur, sequitur Sapientiam absolutè consideratam esse quid longè præstantius prudentia. 6. Quia theoria seu vita contemplativa, in qua cernitur Sapientia, longè præstantior habetur praxi seu vita practica, circa quam occupatur prudentia. Proinde & hoc etiam respectu præserri debet Sapientia prudentiæ. 7. Quia Sapientia elevat hominem ad summum bonum in contemplatione sicum. Nam est præcipuum medium, per quod homo tendit ad felicitatem theoreticam: Prudentia vero ad summum bonum tantum in actione positum. Quantum igitur bonum contemplativum, cū sit idea divinæ perfectionis & proximus ad summam beatitudinem gradus, superat bonum practicum, tantum Sapientia præstabit prudentiæ. At pro contraria parte steruntur plures & firmiores rationes, quarū quædam ducuntur ab objectis, quædam à proprietatibus utriusque, quædã ab effectis, quædam ab extremis. 1. Ratio sumitur ab objectis utriusque, quia prudentia versatur in perspicientia boni & mali: Sapientia vero in perspicientia veri & falsi. Semper autem ratio boni præsertur rationi veri, propter majorem, quam præstat humanæ vitæ utilitatem. 2. Quia prudentia est cum virtute morali indissolubili nexu conjuncta, nec ab ea separari unquam poterit, sicut cap. ult. 6. Nicom. docet Philosophus phus, Sapientia vero non item. Et hæc causa fuit cur Plato 1. Politi. Prudentia prætulerit Sapientiæ cū Anaxagoram, Anaximenem, & Diogenem vidisset in vita & moribus non satis fuisse bonos, & tamen ab omnibus habebantur Sapientes: Socratem econtra vitæ inculpatæ semper animadvertisset, qui prudentiæ potius quam Sapientiæ operam dabat.
units.tr: [The final lines of the page are partly illegible.] ... [necessity] instructs. (5) The dignity of each subject proves this very point: for Wisdom perfects the mind and intellect of man, whereas prudence perfects the appetite and the will. But since the intellect is a faculty of the soul far more excellent than the will itself (for the will is defended and governed by it), it follows that Wisdom, considered absolutely, is something far more excellent than prudence. (6) Theory, or the contemplative life, in which Wisdom is seen, is held to be far more excellent than practice, or the practical life, with which prudence is occupied. Therefore, in this respect also, Wisdom ought to be preferred to prudence. (7) Wisdom raises man to the highest good in contemplation as its chief means, through which man strives toward theoretical happiness. Prudence, however, reaches the highest good only in action. Therefore, as the contemplative good, since it is the idea of divine perfection and the nearest step to supreme blessedness, surpasses the practical good, so much will Wisdom excel prudence. But on the opposite side, more and firmer arguments are advanced, some drawn from the objects, some from the properties of each, some from the effects, and some from the extremes. (1) The argument is taken from the objects of each: prudence is concerned with discerning good and evil, but Wisdom with discerning truth and falsehood. Now the consideration of good is always preferred to the consideration of truth, on account of the greater usefulness it brings to human life. (2) Prudence is joined to moral virtue by an indissoluble bond and can never be separated from it, as the Philosopher teaches at the end of the sixth book of the Nicomachean Ethics; Wisdom is not so. And this was the reason why Plato, in the first book of the Republic, preferred prudence to wisdom, when he had seen that Anaxagoras, Anaximenes and Diogenes, though held by all to be wise, were not good enough in life and morals; whereas he had always observed that Socrates was of blameless life, and he devoted himself to prudence rather than to wisdom.

units.la: 3. Quia prudentia est Dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum moralium, ut jam supra probatum fuit: Sapientia non item: nam nihil cum moralibus virtutibus habet rei, sed illi sufficit, si, quæ ad contemplationem necessaria sunt, in promtu habeat.
units.tr: (3) Prudence is the leader and regulator of all the moral virtues, as has already been proved above; Wisdom is not so. For it has nothing to do with the moral virtues, but it is enough for it to have ready at hand what is necessary for contemplation.

units.la: 4. Quia prudentia absque sapientia est utilis vitæ humanæ & honorabilis etiam, Sapientia vero absq; prudentia est damnosa & perniciosa sæpe, cum nihil utilitatis communi hominum societati soleat afferre. Unde Plato 4. de leg. Sapientiam destitutam prudentia comparat gladio acuto in manu furentis, qui nec gerenti nec aliis prodest.
units.tr: (4) Prudence without wisdom is useful and even honourable in human life, whereas wisdom without prudence is often harmful and destructive, since it usually brings no benefit to the common society of men. Hence Plato, in the fourth book of the Laws, compares wisdom lacking prudence to a sharp sword in the hand of a madman, which profits neither the one who wields it nor others.

units.la: 5. Quia prudentia reddit hominem bonum, Deoque & aliis propter hanc bonitatem amabiliorem & gratiorem, Sapientia non: Nihil enim bonitatis affert homini, sed aliquid tantum cognitionis & modum veritatis indagandæ demonstrat.
units.tr: (5) Prudence makes a man good, and on account of this goodness more lovable and pleasing both to God and to others; Wisdom does not. For it brings no goodness to man, but only some knowledge and shows the method of searching out truth.

units.la: 6. Quia prudentia usum omnium bonorum recte docet, adeo ut nihil nobis bonum esse queat absque prudentia: Sapientia autem non: non enim in usu boni exquirendo, sed in veri natura perlustranda versatur.
units.tr: (6) Prudence rightly teaches the use of all good things, so that nothing can be good for us without prudence; but Wisdom does not. For it is concerned not with seeking out the use of the good, but with investigating the nature of truth.

units.la: 7. Quia prudentia totius civitatis puppi præsidet & ejus gubernaculum tenet & moderatur: Sapientia vero tantum unius paucis prodesse solet, non se extendit ad totius civitatis bobonum; at vero bonum, quo communius, eo melius, docente Philos. 1. Nicom. cap. 1. 8. Qua prudentia est auriga vitae humanae, & Dux omnium actionum nostrarum: nam sine prudentia actiones nostrae ad finem suum recta tendere no possunt: Sapientia non item, nullam enim habet curam actionum nostrarum, neque docet, quomodo aut nobiscum aut eum aliis conversemur, sed tantum hoc agit, ut mens in rerum cognitione & ardua contemplatione perficiatur. 9. Qua prudentia hominem reddit sibiipsi constantem, adeo ut nullis fortunae procellis ita deijci possit, quin sui semper similis sit, quod de Socrate inprimis legitur, qui quod esset prudentia instructissimus, eodem semper vultu eodemque animi tenore conspiciebatur, teste Lactio in vita ipsius lib. 6. Sapientia autem non, id quod videre licet in Boetio in lib. de consolat. Philosoph. qui exilium sibi indictum iniquissimo ferebat animo. 10. Quia prudentia est magis necessaria humanae conditioni hominiq; ad futuram vitam se praeparanti, longe utilior & accommodatior, quia hominem docet, non tantum, ut praeterita ruminer, praesentia disponat, sed etiam ut de futuris sibi prospiciat, & hinc fit, ut hominem hac prospicientia rerum futurarum ad futuram vitam praepararet. 11. Qua omnis prudens est bonus, at omnis sapiens non est talis, & ratio haec est, quia prudens semper est virtute morali instructus, quae praesupponit semper bonitatem in homine: At Sapiens non est semper praeditus virtute morali, quia poterit aliquis scientia & intelligentia satis esse instructus, qui tamen satis nequiet vitam
units.tr: (7) Prudence presides over the stern of the whole state, holds its helm and steers it; Wisdom usually benefits only a few individuals and does not extend to the good of the whole state. But the good is better the more widely it is shared, as the Philosopher teaches in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 1. (8) Prudence is the charioteer of human life and the leader of all our actions, for without prudence our actions cannot tend rightly to their end. Wisdom is not so; for it has no care of our actions, nor does it teach how we should conduct ourselves either with ourselves or with others, but it only aims at this, that the mind be perfected in knowledge of things and in lofty contemplation. (9) Prudence makes a man constant with himself, so that he cannot be cast down by any storms of fortune without always remaining like himself. This is read above all of Socrates, who, because he was most thoroughly equipped with prudence, was always seen with the same countenance and the same composure of mind, as Laertius bears witness in his Life of him, book 6. Wisdom, however, does not do this, as may be seen in Boethius in his book On the Consolation of Philosophy, who bore with a very unjust mind the exile imposed upon him. (10) Prudence is more necessary to the human condition and to a man preparing himself for the life to come, and far more useful and suitable, because it teaches him not only to brood over past things and arrange present ones, but also to provide for the future; and thus, by this foresight of future things, it prepares a man for the life to come. (11) Every prudent man is good, but not every wise man is such; and the reason is that the prudent man is always furnished with moral virtue, which always presupposes goodness in a man. But the wise man is not always endowed with moral virtue, since someone may be sufficiently furnished with knowledge and understanding and yet be unable to live his life well ... [as Plato relates of Timon of Athens in the first book of the Republic, and of Epicurus in Laertius's Life of him].

units.la: non alio tempore. vitam agat, quod de Timone Atheniensi refert Plato lib.1. Polit. & de Epicuro Laërt in vita ipsius. 12. Idipsum probatur ab extremis utriusque, nam Imprudentia, quæ opponitur Prudentiæ, longe deterior est, quam Insipientia, quæ opponitur Sapientiæ, propterea quod Imprudentia conjuncta sit semper cum vitio morali & defectu voluntatis rectè dispositæ: insipientia vero nō sed tantum arguit defectū cognitionis in mente. Pro decisione quæstionis notandum, Sapientiam absoluté confideraram longè præstare prudentia, tum propter materiam circa quam versatur, nam pro objecto habet res divinas & naturales, tum propter magnam affinitatem & cognationem, quam habet cum mente divina, cum sit veluti idea quædam perfectionis divinæ, dum res cœlestes & naturales contemplando, hominem ad aliquod majus & sublimius seipso elevat, adeo ut jam statum hominis transcendisse putetur, & non homo, sed ut inquit Plato, aut Deus aut Semideus habeatur. At verò ratione utilitatis & societatis humanæ longè præstantior erit prudentia, quia actiones hominum dirigit, & ad rectum semper finem adducit, & viam ad virtutes morales comparandas & assequendas demonstrat. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Picol.grad. 5. à cap. 44. usque ad so.
units.tr: ... at another time. (12) The same is proved from the extremes of each. For imprudence, which is opposed to prudence, is far worse than foolishness, which is opposed to wisdom, because imprudence is always joined with moral vice and a defect of a rightly disposed will, whereas foolishness indicates only a defect of knowledge in the mind. To settle the question, it should be noted that Wisdom, considered absolutely, far excels prudence: first, on account of the matter with which it is concerned, for its objects are divine and natural things; and second, on account of the great affinity and kinship it has with the divine mind, since it is as it were an idea of divine perfection, while by contemplating heavenly and natural things it raises man above himself to something greater and more sublime, so that he seems to have passed beyond the state of a man, and is considered, as Plato says, either a god or a demigod. But in respect of usefulness and human society, prudence will be far more excellent, because it directs men's actions, always leads them to the right end, and shows the way to acquire and attain the moral virtues. Look for more on this question in Piccolomini, Grade 5, from chapter 44 to the end.

units.la: IX. Cur prudentia magis cadat infenilem quam juvenilem ætatem, & cur prudentiores senes sint juvenibus? Respond. Triplicem esse hujus rei causam: 1. Temperamentum, 2. doctrinam, 3. rerum variarum usum & experientiam. Quod ad primam nempe ad temperamentū attinet, ideo prudetiores sunt senes juvenivenibus, quia magis contemperatus solet esse in iis fervor ille sanguinis, qui turbaverat metem & proærefin, pervertebat q; judicium & rectam rationem, quo minus super affectus & inferiores animi facultates imperium recta ratio teneret. 2. Quia lenita sunt omnes jam perturbationes, quæ animum distrahere solent, & in varias rapere partes, ut hincaf-sectus, illinc ratio tanquam in adversa acie stare videantur: harum vero perturbationum quiera & amica compositione animus dicitur fieri prudens, dum res singulas non secundum affectus suos, sed secundum rectam rationem perpendit, & in suo valore & vigore examinat. 3. Qua prudentia requiritur temperamentum ad frigidum & siccum inclinans, atra bile contemperata (quod formicæ, apes & id genus similia animalia satis nobis perfaciunt.) At ejusmodi temperamentum reperitur in solis senibus: nam copia sanguinis non patitur temperamentum in juvenibus esse frigidum, & abundantia humorum non patitur esse siccum. Quod vero propter doctrinam & rerum usum prudentiores solent esse senes, id satis constat; nam quia diu vixerunt, ideo propter longiore ætatem multa discere, multa videre, multa observare, & multiplicem rerum variarum usum habere poterunt. Et hæc causa fuit, cur Aristot. 7. Nicom. cap. 9. dicat, natura juvenibus vires, senioribus, & qui diu vixerunt, largitur prudentiam. Exemplo esse possunt patres primitivi seculi, qui vixerunt ante diluvium, nam quia diu vixerunt, ut testatur Scriptura, ideo per ætatis decursum plurima observarunt, & ex ista observatione artes omnes & disciplinas plinas inveneiunt,t/-te Josepho lib.1. antiq. Jud. cap. 5. Adstipulatur etiam Polydorus Virg. lib.1. de rerum inventi. variis in locis. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Piccol. gradu 6. cap. 29.
units.tr: IX. Why does prudence fall more to old age than to youth, and why are the old more prudent than the young? Answer: there is a threefold cause of this: (1) temperament, (2) learning, (3) the use and experience of various things. As to the first, temperament, the old are more prudent than the young because in them that fervour of the blood is more tempered, which disturbed the mind and choice [προαίρεσιν], corrupted judgement and right reason, and so kept right reason from ruling over the passions and the lower faculties of the soul. Second, all the disturbances which are wont to distract the soul and drag it in different directions have now been calmed, so that on one side the passions and on the other reason seem to stand as in opposing battle lines. The soul is said to become prudent through the quiet and friendly settling of these disturbances, when it weighs each matter not according to its passions but according to right reason, and examines it in its true worth and strength. Third, prudence requires a temperament inclining to cold and dry, with the black bile tempered, as ants, bees and similar animals sufficiently show us. But such a temperament is found only in the old: for the abundance of blood does not allow the temperament of the young to be cold, and the abundance of humours does not allow it to be dry. That the old are for the most part more prudent because of learning and the use of things is quite clear; for because they have lived long, they can, through their longer life, learn much, see much, observe much, and have a manifold use of various things. This was the reason why Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 9, says that nature gives strength to the young and prudence to the old, and to those who have lived long. The patriarchs of the primitive age, who lived before the flood, can serve as examples: for because, as Scripture attests, they lived long, they observed very many things over the course of their years, and from that observation they invented all arts and disciplines, as Josephus testifies, Antiquities of the Jews book 1, ch. 5. Polydore Vergil, On the Discovery of Things, book 1, in various places, also agrees. See more on this question in Piccolomini, grade 6, ch. 29.

units.la: X. Cum Scientia & Prudentia simul sint habitus, & habitus non facile possint amitti, cur Scientia & non Prudentia possit fieri oblivio? Respon. Etsi Philosophus quæstionem hanc paucis attingat lib. 6. Nicom. cap. 5. ubi hoc discrimen ponit inter scientiam & prudentiam, nempe quod Prudentiæ non possit fieri oblivio, cum tamen experientia ipsa testetur, multis viris magnis accidisse propter morbum aut casum aliquem, ut omnium rerum, quas sciebant, oblivisce rentur, & omnem prorsus amitterent scientiam & memoriam de rebus antea bene cognitis. Exemplum poterit esse in Messalo Cordino, qui cum esset oratorum Romanorum disertissimus & in omni doctrinæ genere versatissimus, in tantam incidit oblivionem, ut proprii oblivisceretur nominis; tamen quia causas hujus rei non assignat Philosophus, nos duas assignabimus. Quarum prima ducitur à subjecto, quia ejus, quod in sola mente seu prima seu præcipua animæ rationalis parte & in nuda animi cognitione consistit, fieri potest oblivio, non autem ejus, quod simul cum ipsa mente appetitum rectum trahit, & voluntatem secum conjunctam habet: voluntas autem non potest amitti, nam in furentibus, & qui ratione destituuntur, manet voluntas, licet non satis recte disposita. At scientia in sola ratione & mera animi consideratione consistit, neque voluntatis aut appetitus præsupponit rectitudinem.
units.tr: X. Since science and prudence are both habits, and habits cannot easily be lost, why can science be forgotten but not prudence? Answer: although the Philosopher touches on this question only briefly in Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 5, where he draws this distinction between science and prudence, namely that prudence cannot be forgotten, experience itself shows that for many great men it has happened, through illness or some accident, that they forgot everything they knew and lost altogether all science and memory of things previously well known. Messalla Corvinus can be an example: though he was the most eloquent of Roman orators and versed in every branch of learning, he fell into such forgetfulness that he forgot his own name. Since the Philosopher does not assign causes for this, we shall assign two. The first is taken from the subject. What consists in the mind alone, whether in the first or the principal part of the rational soul and in bare knowledge of the mind, can be forgotten; but what at the same time draws the appetite rightly along with the mind and has the will joined to it cannot be forgotten. The will cannot be lost: for in the insane and those deprived of reason the will remains, though not rightly disposed. But science consists in reason alone and mere consideration of the mind, and does not presuppose rectitude of will or appetite.

units.la: Poterit enim æque pravus ac bonus scientiam sibi addiscere & vndicare, cum ad scientiam nuda tantum mentis dispositio, nō voluntatis simul consensus requiratur. At prudentia non in sola mente aut ratione consistit, sed simul etiā voluntatis & appetitus præsupponit rectitudinem & consensum, & sic duas ad minimum animę facultates requirit, & propterea q̈ in pluribus versetur facultatibus, tenacius animis hominum inhæret. Secunda ratio ducitur ab obj-ecto, quia sæpe, imò semper occurrit materia operandi circa prudentiam, nam versatur in actionibus hominum quotidianis, quæ semper occurrunt, & sensibus ipsis obviæ sunt, & hinc fit, ut propter operationis assiduitatem prudentiæ non fieri possit oblivio. At non tam frequens occurrit materia operandi circa scientiam, cum versetur in rebus universalibus abstrusis & arduis, quæ hominum sensibus plerunque remotæ sunt, & hinc fit, ut considerationis intermissione & absentia operationis fieri possit scientiæ oblivio. Neque obstat, quod dicit Philosophus lib. 1. poster. cap. 2. sub finem scientiam esse immutabile quā hoc intelligitur respectu rerum circa quas versatur, non autem respecta subjecti, in quo cernitur. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Picol. gradu 5. cap. 29. & apud Goclenium inexercit. Ethic. exercit. 63.
units.tr: For the wicked person can learn and acquire science for himself just as well as the good, since for science only a bare disposition of the mind is required, not also the agreement of the will. But prudence does not consist in the mind or reason alone; it also presupposes rectitude and consent of the will and appetite, and so requires at least two faculties of the soul; and for that reason, because it inheres in more faculties, it clings more tenaciously to human minds. The second reason is taken from the object: the matter of action concerning prudence often, indeed always, arises; for it is concerned with the daily actions of men, which always occur and lie open to the very senses, and hence, owing to the constancy of the operation, prudence cannot be forgotten. But the matter of action concerning science does not arise so frequently, since it is concerned with abstruse and difficult universal things, which for the most part are remote from human senses; and hence it happens that, through interruption of consideration and absence of operation, science can be forgotten. Nor does it stand in the way that the Philosopher says in Posterior Analytics book 1, ch. 2, near the end, that science is unchangeable; this is understood with respect to the things it is concerned with, not with respect to the subject in which it resides. See more on this question in Piccolomini, grade 5, ch. 29, and in Goclenius, Exercitationes Ethicae, exercise 63.

units.la: XI. An Intemperantia recte dicatur causa corrumpens Prudentia?
units.tr: XI. Whether Intemperance is rightly said to be a cause that corrupts Prudence?

units.la: Et statuitur thesis affirmativa ex Philosopho lib. 6. Nicom. c. 5. & 7. ubi Temperantiam causam conservantem Prudentiæ statuit, quæ propter ea dicitur Græcis σωφροσύνη, quasi σῴζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν; θν; illa enim notitiam & judicium de principiis rerum agendarum, hoc est, de bonis & malis circa quę versatur Prudentia, tuetur ac conservat, tum etiam hominę in æquabili tenore corporis & animi custodit, ut actiones prudentiæ & omnium virtutum recte edere possit. Ergo à contrario causam prudentię corrumpentem constat esse Intemperantiam, quæ per voluptatem & dolorem intempestive adhibitum, judicium hominis corrumpit, de principiis rerum agendarum, quatenus scilicet voluntatem ipsam depravat, ut non possit jam verum finem velle, quem nemperatio ipsa exigit, quoniam autem vero fine aberratur, qui est principium & causa impellens omnium rerum agendarum, necesse est, ea omnia, quæ ad istum finem diriguntur, prava esse & vitiosa. Vide 2. cap. 1. Nic. & qui in principiis aberrat, necesse est; ut in omnibus iis, quæ principia ipsa consequuntur, continuo etiam aberret, & si in principiis paululum fit erroris, ut infiniti postea subsequatur, necesse est, Aristot. in Phys. Acroas. cap. 3. Picol. gradu 1. cap. 31. Cæterum hoc inprimis notandum, quod ipse loco cit. observavit Philosophus, intemperantiam non corrumpere hominis judicium de principiis omnibus, sed tantum de principiis practicis, nam ad praxin sive ad actionem non tantum requiritur notitia rei peragendæ, sed etiam voluntatis & appetitus consensus, qui intemperantibus deesse solet, & fieri potest, ut aliquis intemperanter satis vivat, qui tamen de principiis theoreticis sanum habeat judicium, verbi gratia: poterit recte judicare, an natura abhorreat vacuum, an corpus grave sua natura tendat deorsum.
units.tr: The affirmative thesis is laid down from the Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics, bk. 6, chs. 5 and 7, where he states that Temperance [σωφροσύνη] conserves Prudence. The Greeks call it sōphrosynē for this reason, as if it were sōzousa tēn phronēsin, "preserving prudence." For temperance keeps safe the knowledge and judgement about the principles of things to be done, that is, about the good and evil with which Prudence is concerned, and it also keeps a person in an even state of body and mind, so that he can rightly perform the actions of prudence and of all the virtues. It follows, then, that by contrast Intemperance is the cause that corrupts prudence. Through pleasure and pain applied out of season, it corrupts a person's judgement about the principles of action, insofar as it depraves the will itself, so that the will can no longer desire the true end that temperance requires. And since one goes astray about the true end, which is the principle and the impelling cause of all actions, it is necessary that all the things directed to that end be depraved and vicious. See Nic. 2, ch. 1. And whoever goes astray in principles must necessarily go astray continually in all the things that follow from those principles; and if there is a small error in the principles, an infinite error must necessarily follow from it. Aristotle, Physics, Acroasis 3, ch. 3; Piccolomini, grade 1, ch. 31. Moreover, the following point must especially be noted, which the Philosopher himself observed in the passage cited: intemperance does not corrupt a person's judgement about all principles, but only about practical principles. For action, or practice, requires not only knowledge of the thing to be done but also the consent of the will and appetite, which intemperate people usually lack. And it can happen that someone who lives intemperately still has sound judgement about theoretical principles. For example, he may judge rightly whether nature abhors a vacuum, or whether a heavy body by its nature tends downward,

units.la: Vide 2. cap. 1. Nic. Vide Picol. gradu 1. cap. 31. orsum;an omnes lineæ à centro ad circumferetiam ductæ,sint æquales, & cætera ejusmodi, & hinc fit, ut Epicuræi alii intemperanter viventes, de principiis theoreticis, physicis nempe & mathematicis acute admodum & judiciose philosophati sint, cum tamen circa res agendas depravatum habuerint judicium, & salsissima principia practica, nempe eo, quod ad voluptatem omnia retulerint, tanquam ad summum bonum. Vide Piccol.gradu 5.cap.38 & 39.
units.tr: See Nic. 2, ch. 1; see Piccolomini, grade 1, ch. 31; whether all lines drawn from the centre to the circumference are equal, and other things of this kind. Hence it happens that some Epicureans, though they lived intemperately, philosophized very keenly and wisely about theoretical principles, physical and mathematical, while about things to be done they held a corrupt judgement and most foolish practical principles, namely that they referred everything to pleasure as the highest good. See Piccolomini, grade 5, chs. 38 and 39.

units.la: XII. An rectè Socrates statuerit omnes virtutes esse prudentias,sicut refert Plato in Protagora,& Aristotel. ult.cap. 6.Nicom.cum prudentia vox non sit homonyma, quæ possit omnibus virtutibus attribui: neque etiam sit genus omnium virtutum, ut possit naturam suam omnibus communicare; sed potius prudentia vox est plana & perspicua, & prudentia est specialis quædam virtus à cateris distincta. Resp. Philosophus loco cit. hanc sententiam Socratis partim esse falsam, partim veram ait.
