Falsam esse; quatenus omnes in genere virtutes simpliciter statuerit esse prudentias,propter duas rationes: 1. Quia sic nulla virtus esset moralis, sed omnis virtus esset intellectualis, propterea quod prudentia ipsa sit intellectualis virtus. 2. Quia quæliber moralis virtus simul esset intellectualis, & sic species virtutis in genere sibi invicè oppositæ inter se confunderentur, quas tamen natura seu definitione, subjecto & fine differre & distingui ex superioribus constat. Veram esse statuit,quod scilicet virtutes omnes possint dici prudentiæ,verùm non essentialiter, sicut Plotinus & alii Platonici voluerunt,sed tantùm accidentaliter idque propter duas causas: 1. Respectu dependentiæ. pendentię & acquisitionis, quia omnis virtus moralis dependet à prudentia tanquam à sua regula & mensura : & prudentia est perquam necessaria ad virtutis acquisitionem, adeo ut in quibus prudentię vestigia non elucent, illi judicium rectè constitutum & voluntatem bene dispositam nò habeant, ad bonas actiones edendas & virtutes ritè comparandas. 1. Ratione consensionis & conspirationis, nulla quidem virtus moralis per se & proprie est prudentia, nulla tamen absque prudentia esse poterit, & sicut in una radice omnes partes plantę uniuntur, & incrementum suum habent, licet quaelibet pars non sit ipsa radix : sic in una prudentia omnes virtutes uniuntur, licet inter se separatę maneant & distinctę, & quemadmodum mirum non est, videri multas vires seu facultates in una anima humana conjunctas, multas lineas ad unum centrum tendentes : sic mirum non est, videre multas virtutes in una prudentia, tanquam omnium Duce esse unitas, respectu cujus unionis singulas licet appellare prudentias. At ne aliquis excipiat, Virtutem intellectualem distinctam esse à morali, prout una species ab alia distingui solet. 2. Naturalem virtutem à naturali prudentia differre etiam subjecto ; nam in pueris prius videre licet Liberalitatis vestigia, quam prudentiae, & proinde Prudentiam non conspirare cum omnibus virtutibus prout vult Philosophus? Respond. 1. Species istas manere inter se distinctas secundum naturam specificam, sed actionibus suis non ita separari, quin simul reperiantur. Nam prudentia actu à virtute morali separari nequit, siquidem virtus moralis recta ratione, à qua dirigi solet, uti-tur; tur: Recta autem ratio dependet à prudentia, adeo ut necesse sit, prudentiam comitari continuò virtutes morales. Et hinc Socrates apud Platonè se explicans, qui prudentiam, inquit, habet, omnes virtutes habere videtur, nam rectam rationem in promtu habet, quæ voluntatem dirigit & recte disponit, per voluntatem recte dispositam facilis ad virtutum actiones est via. Quod ad secundum respondetur, non fieri hic mentionem virtutis moralis, quæ quodam instinctu naturæ actiones suas producit, & actiones tantum imperfectas non ab habitu proficiscentes; sed tantum de virtute acquisita, quæ cum variis actionibus acquiritur, ut prudentiam habeat, à qua regatur, necesse est. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Aristot. 6. Nicomach. cap. ult. & Goclen. in exercit. Ethic. exercit. 39.
units.tr: XII. Did Socrates rightly hold that all the virtues are prudences, as Plato reports in the Protagoras, and Aristotle at the end of Nicomachean Ethics 6, ch. 6? For the word "prudence" is not equivocal, so that it could be attributed to all the virtues, nor is it the genus of all the virtues, so that it could communicate its nature to all of them. Rather, "prudence" is a plain and clear word, and prudence is a particular virtue distinct from the others. Reply: the Philosopher in the passage cited says that this opinion of Socrates is partly false and partly true. It is false insofar as he simply stated, in general, that all the virtues are prudences, for two reasons: (1) because then no virtue would be moral, but every virtue would be intellectual, since prudence itself is an intellectual virtue; (2) because every moral virtue would at the same time be intellectual, and so the species of virtue, which are opposed to one another within the genus, would be confused with one another, although by their nature or definition, their subject and their end, they are known from what has been said above to differ and be distinguished. He holds it to be true that all the virtues can be called prudences, not essentially, as Plotinus and the other Platonists maintained, but only accidentally, and for two causes: (1) with respect to dependence and acquisition, because every moral virtue depends on prudence as on its rule and measure, and prudence is very necessary for the acquisition of virtue, so that those in whom no traces of prudence shine forth do not have a rightly ordered judgement and a well-disposed will for performing good actions and rightly acquiring the virtues; (2) by reason of agreement and conspiracy. No moral virtue is in itself and properly prudence, yet none can exist without prudence. And just as in one root all the parts of a plant are joined and have their growth, although no single part is the root itself, so in one prudence all the virtues are united, although they remain separate and distinct from one another. And just as it is no wonder to see many powers or faculties joined together in one human soul, many lines tending to one centre, so it is no wonder to see many virtues united in one prudence, as it were the leader of all, with respect to which union each of them may be called a prudence. But lest anyone object, "The intellectual virtue is distinct from the moral, as one species is usually distinguished from another," and, "The natural virtue differs from natural prudence also in subject; for in children one can see traces of liberality earlier than of prudence, and therefore prudence does not agree with all the virtues, as the Philosopher wishes," I reply to the first: these species remain distinct from one another according to their specific nature, but in their actions they are not so separated that they cannot be found together. For prudence cannot in act be separated from moral virtue, since moral virtue makes use of right reason, by which it is usually directed; and right reason depends on prudence, so that it is necessary for moral virtues to accompany prudence continually. And hence Socrates, explaining himself in Plato, says that whoever has prudence seems to have all the virtues, for he has right reason at hand, which directs the will and rightly disposes it, and through a rightly disposed will there is an easy path to the actions of the virtues. To the second objection it is answered that no mention is made here of a moral virtue that produces its actions by a certain instinct of nature, and only imperfect actions not proceeding from a habit; but only of an acquired virtue, which must, along with the various actions by which it is acquired, have prudence by which it is ruled. More on this question may be seen in Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, last ch., and Goclenius, Exercitationes Ethicae, exercise 39.

units.la: XIII. An ars suum semper æquatur finem? Et ratio dubitandi hinc oritur, quia objectum artis, ut jam dictum est, sunt res contingentes quæ aliter atque aliter se habere possunt.
units.tr: XIII. Does art always attain its end? The reason for doubting arises from this: the object of art, as has already been said, is contingent things, which can be and not be otherwise.

units.la: 2. Quia ars magnam cognationem habet cum fortuna, à qua interdum juvatur, interdum impeditur. Et hinc fit, ut artifices modo fortunati, modo infortunati dicantur, prout alii aliis in operando sunt feliciores vel infeliciores? Sed resp. ad hoc dubium per distinctionem, nam ars poterit considerari duobus modis: 1. Respectu formæ, quatenus est habitus intellectualis, qui recta ratione utitur, & in animo nostrum instituit, ut verum æquatur fine, & scopo suo satisfaciat, neque hoc respectu à fortuna impediri potest, quo minus ad id, quod intendebat, recta perveniat: nam in arte, quia ars est, respectu formæ fortuna non cadit. 2. Consideraturas respe-
units.tr: 2. Because art has a great affinity with fortune, by which it is sometimes helped and sometimes hindered. Hence it happens that craftsmen are called now fortunate and now unfortunate, according as some are more or less successful than others in working. But I answer this doubt by a distinction, for art can be considered in two ways: (1) with respect to its form, insofar as it is an intellectual habit that uses right reason and is established in the mind, so that it attains the truth and satisfies its end and aim. In this respect fortune cannot prevent it from reaching straight to what it intended, for in art, since it is art, fortune does not fall upon the form. (2) With respect to the particular matter it is applied to, which, since it is varied and inconstant, can admit fortune. Therefore, since fortune befalls an art not through a fault of its form but through the fault of its subject, it comes about that, habitually or formally, it always attains its end.

units.la: { } respectu materiae particularis subjectae, cui applicatur, quae cum sit varia & inconstans, ideo fortunam admittere potest. Idcirco cum in artem non ipsius formae vitio, sed subjecti culpa fortuna cadat, fit, ut habitualiter seu formaliter semper suum assequatur finem, cum a recta ratione dirigatur, & omnia media ad certum finem dirigatur, licet subjectivè, cum subjectum sit varium & inconstans, & fortunam etiam habeat plerunque comitem, non semper assequatur.
units.tr: the particular matter to which it is applied, which, since it is varied and inconstant, can admit fortune. Therefore, since fortune falls upon art not through a defect of its form but through the fault of its subject, it comes about that art always attains its end habitually and formally, since it is directed by right reason and directs all its means to a certain end; but subjectively, since the subject is varied and inconstant, and usually has fortune as its companion, it does not always attain it.

units.la: XIV. An ars aliqua valeat efficere & producere novam per se subsistentiam?
units.tr: XIV. Can some art produce and bring forth a new substance in itself?

units.la: Et statuitur thesis negativa propter tres rationes: 1. Quia novae substantiae a Deo & natura tantum producuntur, nam ut patet 1. Genes. Deus novas substantias primo produxit, & ut videre licet ex communi rerum cursu a principio hucusque, natura, quae est Dei ordinatio, substantias novas effingit. 2. Quia si ars produceret novam aliquam substantiam, id efficeret aut per creationem novae substantiae ex nihilo, & si cadaequaret Dei potentia, nam Dei solius est aliquid ex nihilo producere, & quilibet artifex esset vel Deus, vel Deo in potentia similis, quod utrumque est blasphemum: aut per transmutationem substantiae unius speciei in aliam. Atqui hoc non datur, ut variis demonstrationibus demonstrare licet. Nam apud omnes pro confesso est, transitum unius speciei in aliam nullo modo dari posse. 3. Quia nullum accidens insita vi & propria facultate sua substantia aliquam producere potest. At omnis, ars cum sit habitus mentis, est accidens in prima specie qualitatis, & ideo nullam subsubstantiam producere poterit. Ratio huj is rationis est hæc, quia fieri non potest, ut aliquid proprium sua facultate illud producat, quod superet gradum perfectionis suæ, sic enim effectus præstantia sua superaret causam suam. At omnis substantia gradu suæ perfectionis superat accidens, & hinc fit, ut ab accidente produci nequeat. Neque obstat, quod contra objicitur nonnulla metalla confici arte Chymica, & aliis etiam artibus variis novas materias producí, ut sunt calx, gypsus, lateres & similia. Nam arte contingit aliquid fieri duobus modis, principaliter, vel instrumentaliter. Priori modo nulla nova substantia ab arte effici potest, propter rationes jam allatas; posteriori modo fieri potest, cum ars, ut natura æmula dicitur, sicut 2. Phys. capite 8. natura impedimenta removet, ut operationem suam absolvat, aut etiam dum varias res, quæ inter se temere coierunt, à se invicem separat, verbi gratia: Aurum ab argento, stannum à plumbo, æs à ferro: nihil tamen hic erit, quod nova substantia respectu artis dici possit, cum remotio impedimentorum naturæ, aut separatio rerum à se invicem non substantiam, sed accidentia tantum constituant. Quod vero ad illa exempla de calce & gypso; Resp. Duplicem in rebus considerari formam, unam internam & naturalem, quam ars in rebus istis non producit, aliam externam & accidentalem, quam licet ars producat, nullam tamen substantiam novam efficit.
units.tr: The negative thesis is laid down for three reasons: 1. Because new substances are produced only by God and by nature; for, as is plain from Genesis 1, God first produced new substances, and, as can be seen from the common course of things from the beginning until now, nature, which is the ordering of God, brings forth new substances. 2. Because if art were to produce some new substance, it would do so either by the creation of a new substance out of nothing, and then it would equal the power of God (for to produce something out of nothing belongs to God alone, and every artisan would be either God or like God in power, both of which are blasphemous); or by the transmutation of a substance of one species into another. But this does not happen, as can be shown by various demonstrations. For it is admitted by all that the passage of one species into another can in no way occur. 3. Because no accident can by its inherent force and proper faculty produce any substance. But all art, since it is a habit of the mind, is an accident in the first species of quality, and therefore it can produce no substance. The reason for this reason is that it cannot happen that something produces by its own faculty something that surpasses the degree of its own perfection; for thus the effect would surpass its cause in excellence. But every substance surpasses an accident in the degree of its perfection, and hence it comes about that it cannot be produced by an accident. Nor does it stand in the way that is objected, that some metals are made by chemical art, and that various new materials are produced by other arts, such as lime, gypsum, bricks and the like. For something happens through art in two ways: principally, or instrumentally. In the first way no new substance can be made by art, for the reasons already given; in the second way it can, since art, as the rival of nature, as stated in Physics 2, chapter 8, removes the hindrances that nature may complete its operation, or even separates from one another various things that have come together by chance, for example gold from silver, tin from lead, bronze from iron. Nevertheless, there will be nothing here that can be called a new substance with respect to art, since the removal of hindrances to nature, or the separation of things from one another, constitutes not substance but accidents only. As for those examples of lime and gypsum: the answer is that in things there are to be considered a twofold form, one internal and natural, which art does not produce in these things, and another external and accidental, which art, although it produces it, nevertheless does not make a new substance.

units.la: XV. An ars præstantia sint superet naturam, an vero natura superet artem, cum utraque ars & natura in omnibus penè rebus operationes suas edant? Resp. Hanc quæstio-
units.tr: XV. Does art surpass nature in excellence, or rather does nature surpass art, since both art and nature carry out their operations in almost all things? The answer: this question

units.la: stionem esse difficilem & dubiam, nam disceptatur in utramque partem, & tam hinc quam illinc rationes sunt graviss-imę. Pro praestantia artis, quod nempe ars longe superet naturam, sferuntur satis graves rationes numero septem, quaium 1. Ducitur a modo operandi: nam ars consultatione utitur & cū cognitione operatur: neut um vero facit natura, nam lapis dū tendit per naturā dē orsum, hoc non facit ex proæresi, nescit enim, quo tendat: sed ex naturæ quodam instinctu propter gravitatem sibi insitam deorsum tanquam ad locum suum ferrur, quia omnia gravia tendunt deorsum. 2. A definitione utriusque idipsum probatur. Nam ars definitur habitus cum recta ratione effectivus: natura vero ut ex 2. Phys. cap. 1. text. 3. principium motus & quietis: neque natura tenet rationem facti, aut potest expedire causas, cum hoc aut illo modo agat; sed uniformi cursu res omnes, nisi impediatur producit, sicut inductione rerum omnium naturalium facile patet: Ars autem cum ratione utatur in operando, & rationem facti tenet, & causas satis exacte expedire potest. Proinde quantum causa superat causarum, tantum cognitio causae superabit ignorantiam ejusdem, & per consequens ars erit praestantior natura. 3. Ab officiis utriusque id quoque demonstratur, quia quoties & ars & natura simul concurrunt ad aliquid producendū, ars obtinet locum Ducis, mensurae & regulae, natura ipsa ducitur, formatur & dirigitur ab arte, ut patet in iis, qui arte saltat, aut cantant, aut similia etiam faciunt. Ibi natura dat tantum principium & inchoationem seu dispositionem ad habitum: ars ftam dispositionem dirigit ad habi- tum & perfectionem. Ideo Ariftoteles 1. Rhet. ad Theod. cap. 1. inquit: Duin aliquid natura & arte fi- mul fit, id multò exactius fieri arte, quâ natura tan- tum propterea quod ars naturam perficiat. Et Cic. 4. de sin. disertis verbis docet, artem Ducem esse lon- gè certiorem, quam fit natura, quia ars ex habitu o- peratur, natura ex levi dispositione, quæ facilè mu- tatur. 4. A subjectis in quibus insunt, seu à rebus, quibus competunt ars & natura. Ars est propria hominis, cum fit habitus animæ rationalis, natura in rebus homine longè vilioribus maximè elucet, & in ipso homine opera naturæ, verbi gratia: nutritio, accretio, sunt vilia respectu operum artis, quæ à me- te & ab anima rationali proficiscuntur, & proinde opera naturæ perficiunt & dirigunt in homine, nea scopo suo aberrent. Quantum igitur homo præstat cæteris creaturis, quantum etiam operationes ani- mæ corporis operationibus antecellunt, tantum ars superabit naturam. ƒ. Ratio ducitur à similitudine operationum Dei & artis: nam ars exactius imita- tur modum operandi, quo Deus in rebus producen- dis utitur, quam natura: operatur enim Deus co- gnitione eminentissima mente & voluntate: sic etiâ ars, cum sit habitus mentis & ratione dirigatur, vo- luntatis expressum habet consensum, & cum cogni- tione certa operatur. Hinc Plato 10. de leg. illos da- mnat, qui naturam præferebant arti, & cum veteri- bus Philosophis Democrito seu Leucippo & Em- pedocle mundum asserebat fieri ex atomis seu cor- pusculis sponte motis & cæco concursu res produ- centicentibus: tamen etiam materiæ quadam necessitate conspirantibus: Nam si hoc esset verum, præcipua naturæ operatio, nepe mudi fabrica, esset postponenda cuilibet artis operationi vel infimæ, cum cæco tantũ concursu, absq; cognitione fiat. 6. Ratio desumitur ex ordine & origine rerum: Ea enim, sunt quæ origine posteriora, sunt p æstatiora & nobilitate priora, propter hanc rationé, quia prioribus addunt finem & perfectionem, sicut docet Philosophus 8. Phys.cap. 5. Et cum ars naturam sequatur, & sit origine posterior, ideo erit perfectione præstatior & prior, id quod etiam ex obiectis utriusq; videre licet, nam natura versatur circa materiam vel primam vel secundam, quæ utraque est rudis & imperfecta respectu rerum, quæ ex iis fiunt: Ars verò in corporibus jam absolutis & perfectis vires exercet suas: jure igitur præseitur naturæ. 7. Quia opera & effecta artis sunt præstantiora quam naturæ: effecta enim patefaciunt naturam & conditionem suarum efficientium causarum. Quod verò artis effecta sint potiora, hinc patet, quia,ut dicitur 2. Phys.text.79. ars perficit naturam. Omne autem perficiens præstantius est eo, quod perficitur, sicut causa præstantior est causato. Deinde etiam initio quast. mech. cap.1. docet Philosophus, nos arte multa superare à quibus per naturam vincimur, verbi gratia: Cum simus natura imbelles & vires non sufficiant ad gravissima onera tollenda, arte tamen valemus elevare & portare, quo velimus. Sic arte tauros & equos domamus & vires leonum, & ferocissimorum animalium frangimus, quod per naturam efficere
units.tr: is difficult and doubtful, for it is disputed on both sides, and the arguments on both sides are most weighty. For the excellence of art, that art far surpasses nature, seven fairly weighty arguments are brought forward, of which 1. The first is drawn from the mode of operating: for art uses deliberation and works with knowledge, whereas nature does not do so; for a stone, while it tends downward by nature, does not do this from deliberate choice, for it does not know where it is heading, but by a certain instinct of nature it is carried downward, to its own place, on account of the heaviness implanted in it, because all heavy things tend downward. 2. The same is proved from the definition of each. For art is defined as a habit effective with right reason; nature, however, as in Physics 2, chapter 1, text 3, the principle of motion and rest. Nor does nature hold the reason of a deed, or is able to set out its causes, as it acts in this or that way; but by a uniform course it produces all things, unless it is hindered, as is easily seen from the induction of all natural things. But art, since it uses reason in working, holds the reason of the deed and can set out its causes quite exactly. Accordingly, as far as cause surpasses causes, so far will knowledge of the cause surpass ignorance of it, and consequently art will be more excellent than nature. 3. This is also shown from the offices of each: for whenever both art and nature concur together to produce something, art takes the place of leader, of measure and of rule, and nature itself is led, formed and directed by art, as is seen in those who dance by art, or sing, or do similar things. There nature gives only the principle and beginning, or disposition towards the habit; art directs that disposition towards the habit and perfection. Therefore Aristotle, in Rhet. ad Theod. chapter 1, says: when something happens both by nature and by art together, it is done far more exactly by art than by nature, for the reason that art perfects nature. And Cicero, in de sin. 4, teaches in plain words that art is by far the more certain leader than nature, because art works from habit, nature from a slight disposition, which is easily changed. 4. From the subjects in which they inhere, or from the things to which art and nature belong. Art is proper to man, since it is a habit of the rational soul; nature is most evident in things far baser than man, and in man himself the works of nature, for example nutrition and growth, are base in comparison with the works of art, which proceed from the mind and from the rational soul; and therefore they perfect and direct the works of nature in man, so that they do not go astray from their end. Therefore, as man surpasses other creatures, and as the operations of the soul surpass the operations of the body, so far will art surpass nature. 5. The argument is drawn from the similarity of the operations of God and of art: for art imitates more exactly the mode of operating which God uses in producing things than nature does; for God operates with most eminent knowledge, mind and will; so too art, since it is a habit of the mind and is directed by reason, has the express consent of the will, and works with certain knowledge. Hence Plato, in de leg. 10, condemns those who preferred nature to art, and who, with the ancient philosophers Democritus or Leucippus and Empedocles, asserted that the world was made from atoms, or little bodies moved of their own accord, and that things were produced by blind concourse, though also by a certain necessity of matter conspiring together. For if this were true, the chief operation of nature, namely the fabric of the world, would have to be ranked below any operation of art, even the lowest, since it comes about by blind concourse alone, without knowledge. 6. The argument is taken from the order and origin of things: for those things which are later in origin are more excellent, and prior in nobility, for the reason that they add an end and perfection to the earlier things, as the Philosopher teaches in Physics 8, chapter 5. And since art follows nature and is later in origin, it will therefore be superior and prior in perfection; which can also be seen from the objects of each. For nature is concerned with matter, either primary or secondary, both of which are crude and imperfect in relation to the things that are made from them; but art exercises its powers on bodies already finished and perfect. Rightly, then, art is preferred to nature. 7. Because the works and effects of art are more excellent than those of nature: for effects reveal the nature and condition of their efficient causes. That the effects of art are the more excellent is plain from this, that, as is said in Physics 2, text 79, art perfects nature. But everything that perfects is more excellent than that which is perfected, just as a cause is more excellent than what is caused. Then also, at the beginning of the Mechanics, chapter 1, the Philosopher teaches that by art we surpass many things by which we are overcome by nature: for example, since we are by nature feeble and our strength does not suffice to lift the heaviest burdens, yet by art we are able to raise and carry them wherever we wish. So by art we tame bulls and horses, and break the strength of lions and of the most ferocious animals, which we cannot do by nature.

units.la: non possumus. Idipsum in homine inprimis videre licet: homo enim in lucem editur rudis & impotens ad omnia, & potius ad malum quàm ad bonum proclivis, propterea quod naturæ vis in ipso statim edito tantum eluceat. At verò cum ars accedit, tunc formatur & perficitur, & potens redditur ad quælibet, & ad utilia & bona dirigitur. Cujus rei exemplum illustre fuit in sylvestribus illis, qui nuper à Hispanorū navigatione in America & novis Insulis orientalibus reperti sunt, quia tantū naturæ ductū sequebantur, rudes omnium rerum erant: at postea cum didicissent ab Hispanis artes, & subtilitate ingenii assequi & perfectione in rebus ceperunt. Hinc Plato 1. de Repub. & 7. de leg. & Aristot. 1. Polit. cap. 1. dicunt hominem perperam educatum, longè deteriorem evadere feris. Proinde ut mens præfertur animæ, anima naturæ, sic ars pertinens ad mentem competentibus animæ & naturæ longè præferenda videtur, & potissimum cum natura ad infimam materiam descendat plerunque, & iis competat, quæ à materia pendent, & circa eam versantur: Ars verò supra materiam ejusque formam erigatur, nam proprietates & perfectiones varias utrique superaddere solet. At pro contraria parte, nempe pro præstantia naturæ supra artę rationes afferuntur & firmiores & plures numero novem: 1. Ducitur à modo operandi, quia natura intrinsecus operatur, & est internū rei principium, sicut docetur 2. Phys.c.1. cont. 3. ars verò extrinsecus tantum operatur & externam solam permutat formam rei. Unde quantum essentialis forma præstat accidentali, tantum natura præstabit arte. 2. Quia natura dicitur ars Dei lib. 1. de cœlo text. 31. & quæ à natura fiunt, divina arte fieri dicuntur, ibid. text. 32. Natura dicitur etiam Dei ordinatio teste Scalig. exerc. 188. sect. 1. & exerc. 358. sect. 11, propterea quod seriem causarum secundum Dei institutum disponat ac ordinet: ars verò licet sit habitus mentis, & à ratione recta diligatur, tamen propter hominis imbecillitatem & materiæ, circa quam versatur, inconstantiam multis, imò penè infinitis erroribus solet esse obnoxia, ita ut non semper certum assequatur finem sicut natura, quæ Dei ordinatio est. 3. Idipsum probatur ab ordine operandi seu res producendi, quia quoties natura & ars simul concurrunt pro aliquo opere conficiendo: natura obtinet primum locum, & primò ad rem producendam concurrit: ars demum succedit vel ad naturam juvandam vel ad impedimenta removenda. Hinc & dignitatis & ordinis respectu natura præferetur arti. 4. Quia ars imitatur naturam & naturæ operibus similia plane producere conatur: e contra natura nō æmulatur artem, nec ei se conformat, cum verò natura sit idea quædam seu exemplar, ad cujus imitationem ars sua opera producit, sequitur naturam esse præstantiorē arte, quia quod aliquid imitatur, sperat se aliquid pei sectionis exista imitatione consecuturum, quod ars dum imitatur naturam, etiam facit. 5. Quia sublatis viribus naturæ, ars prorsus evanescit, & nullas vires ad operandum habet: econtra subductis viribus artis, natura in suo vigore remanet & proprias suas vires retinet, id quod videre licet in automatis seu horolo-giis, giis, in quibus sublatis artis machinationibus natu- ralis vis iis insita adhuc manet integra: Nam ferrum, ex quo cóficiuntur rotæ, licet nō moveatur ad mo- tū artis, naturaliter tamē movetur & non minus fer- tur deorsum quam antea, dum per artem operare- tur. 6. Quia nihil fit per artem, quod non prius fit per naturam & à natura tanquam principe causa suâ habet inchoationem, verbi gratia: in eo, qui saltat, ædificat, aut aliquid ex habitu artis facit, per naturá primò movetur ad hoc ipsum agendum, & natura primò ei res suas & facultates impertitur, postea ars modum quendam & figuram externam tantum ad- dit. 7. Quia natura est substantia & essentia cujusq; rei, in qua inest, cum fit rei ipsius forma, sicut 2.Phys. cap.1. probat variis rationibus Philosophus. Ars est tantum accidens, cum fit qualitas. At verò omnis substantia quovis modo præstantior & dignior est arte, sicut 7.Metaph.cap.2. docet Philosophus. 8. Idipsum ex ordine causarum inspicere licet: nam in omni serie causarum prior origine & dignitate præfertur posteriori, sicut asseritur 8. Phys cap. 6. & jure perfectionum secundæ causæ sunt posteriores primis, & à primis dependent, nec sine iis operantur: Nam necesse est, ut primæ causæ influant in secundas, & secundæ cooperentur primis. Deus dicitur & est prima causa omnium rerum: illi subjicitur natura, cùm sit Dei ordinatio, quæ ad præscriptum divinum res producit. Naturæ subest ars, cum naturam imitetur, quæ à natura fiunt, à Deo & natura simul producuntur: quæ verò ab arte, à Deo & natura & arte simul. Nam ut secunda causa præsupponit primam,sic tertia praefupponit fecundam. Quare & huius ordinis respectu natura praeferetur arti. 9. Idipsum evincitur ex conditione operum utriusque & naturae & artis; nam natura efficit substantiā, cum fit interna causa rei cujusque res omnes naturaliter producens: ars vero tantum accidens efficit, cum modum quendam & figuram tantum externa rebus addat. Natura producit res ferias, verbi gratia: metalla, plastas, jumenta & ipsum hominem: ars vero umbras & imagines tantum rerum. Natura producit omnes mundi partes ipfasq; conservat, & omnia proximè in Deum dirigit: arsve ò in viliori-bus tantum versatur, neq; in Deum proximè omnia dirigit, sed in solum hominem, propterea quod fit habitus mentis humanae & necessitatis humanae; ergò ars primum inventa fuit. Proinde ut substantia praefertur accidenti, res feria rei umbrae, artifex suo instrumento, causa principalis suae instrumentali, & ut res certa & constans longè praestantior habetur re incerta aut mutabili, sic natura praeferetur arti, adeò ut non immeritò Galen. lib.6.de morbis vulgaribus, dixerit, quamlibet vim naturae quantumvis exiguam longè praestantiore esse vi aut facultate artis. Pro determinatione hujus quaestionis sciendum, artem dupliciter considerari posse: 1. Per fe, quatenus scilicet contradiftincta à natura ipsa aliquid operatur, & sic longè inferior est natura. 2. Consideratur ars ut cōjuncta cum ipsa natura, quatenus naturam ipsam includit, & quia aliquid naturae addit, verbi gratia: perfectionem quandam, nam quicquid alicui rei aliquid addit ad finem assequendum, id per-f ctiosectionem adhibet, & sic ars natura praestantior dici posset. Breviter. Natura per se quatenus suis viribus operatur, longè praefertur arti, & sic intelligendae sunt rationes pro praestantia naturae. Ars vero quatenus non per se & absolutè seduna cum natura operatur, longè praefertur naturae propter rationes supra allatas.
units.tr: cannot do. This is especially easy to see in man. A human being is born rudimentary and unable to do anything, and inclined more to evil than to good, because the power of nature shows itself in him only at birth. But when art is added, he is formed and perfected, becomes able to do all things, and is directed to what is useful and good. A famous example of this was those savages recently found by the Spanish voyages to America and the new eastern islands. Because they followed nature alone, they were rude in everything; but afterwards, when they had learned the arts from the Spaniards, they came to attain and perfect things by the subtlety of their minds. Hence Plato (Republic 1 and Laws 7) and Aristotle (Politics 1, ch. 1) say that a man badly brought up turns out far worse than the wild beasts. Therefore, just as mind is preferred to soul, and soul to nature, so art, which belongs to the mind, seems to be far preferable to the soul and nature together. This is especially so because nature for the most part descends to the lowest matter and belongs to those things that depend on matter and are concerned with it, whereas art rises above matter and its form, for it usually adds various properties and perfections to both. On the other side, however, firmer arguments, and more in number, are brought forward for the superiority of nature over art, namely nine: (1) It is drawn from the mode of operating. Nature works from within and is the internal principle of a thing, as is taught in Physics 2, ch. 1 [cont.]. Art works only from outside and changes only the external form of a thing. Hence, as far as essential form surpasses accidental form, so far nature will surpass art. (2) Because nature is called the art of God (On the Heavens 1, text 31), and things that are produced by nature are said to be made by divine art (ibid., text 32). Nature is also called the ordinance of God, according to Scaliger (Exercitation 188, sect. 1, and Exercitation 358, sect. 11), because it arranges and orders the series of causes according to God's appointment. Art, however, although it is a habit of the mind and is guided by right reason, is nevertheless, because of human weakness and the inconstancy of the matter with which it deals, liable to many, indeed almost countless, errors. So it does not always attain its end with certainty, as nature does, which is the ordinance of God. (3) The same is proved from the order of operating, or of producing things. Whenever nature and art concur together to accomplish some work, nature takes the first place and joins first in producing the thing; art comes in last, either to help nature or to remove hindrances. Hence, with respect to dignity and order, nature is preferred to art. (4) Because art imitates nature and tries to produce things entirely similar to the works of nature. On the contrary, nature does not imitate art or conform itself to it. Since nature is a kind of idea or pattern, to whose imitation art makes its works, it follows that nature is superior to art, because whatever imitates something hopes to obtain by that imitation some perfection, which art also does while it imitates nature. (5) Because when the powers of nature are taken away, art vanishes altogether and has no power to work; on the contrary, when the powers of art are taken away, nature remains in its own vigour and keeps its own powers. This can be seen in automata or clocks: when the mechanisms of art are removed, the natural force inherent in them remains entire. For iron, of which the wheels are made, although it is not moved by the motion of art, is nevertheless moved naturally, and falls downward no less than before, while it was working through art. (6) Because nothing is made by art that is not first made by nature, and it has its beginning from nature as its principal cause. For example, in one who dances or builds, or does something from a habit of art, he is first moved by nature to do this very thing, and nature first bestows on him his materials and faculties; afterwards art adds only a certain manner and external shape. (7) Because nature is the substance and essence of each thing in which it inheres, since it is the form of the thing itself, as Aristotle proves by various arguments in Physics 2, ch. 1. Art is only an accident, since it is a quality. But every substance is in every way more excellent and worthier than art, as Aristotle teaches in Metaphysics 7, ch. 2. (8) This can also be seen from the order of causes. For in every series of causes, what is prior in origin and dignity is preferred to what is posterior, as is asserted in Physics 8, ch. 6. And by right, the secondary causes of perfections are posterior to the primary and depend on them, and do not work without them. For it is necessary that the primary causes flow into the secondary, and that the secondary cooperate with the primary. God is called and is the first cause of all things; nature is subject to him, since it is God's ordinance, which produces things according to the divine prescription. Art is subject to nature, since it imitates nature; things that come from nature are produced at once by God and nature; things that come from art, by God, nature and art together. For just as a second cause presupposes a first, so a third presupposes a second. Therefore, with respect to this order too, nature is preferred to art. (9) The same is proved from the condition of the works of each, both of nature and of art. For nature produces substance, since it is the internal cause of each thing, producing all things naturally; art produces only accident, since it adds only a certain manner and figure to things from outside. Nature produces the noble things, for example metals, plants, beasts of burden and man himself; art produces only the shadows and images of things. Nature produces all the parts of the world and preserves them, and directs all things immediately to God; art is concerned only with lesser things, and does not direct all things immediately to God, but only to man, because it is a habit of the human mind and of human need; therefore art was first invented. Accordingly, just as substance is preferred to accident, the noble thing to the shadow of a thing, the craftsman's instrument to its principal cause, and a certain and constant thing is held to be far more excellent than an uncertain or changeable one, so nature is preferred to art. Hence Galen (On Common Diseases, book 6) said not without reason that any power of nature, however small, is far more excellent than the power or faculty of art. To determine this question, it must be known that art can be considered in two ways. (1) In itself, that is, insofar as it works distinct from nature itself; and so considered it is far inferior to nature. (2) Art is considered as joined with nature itself, insofar as it includes nature and adds something to nature, for example a certain perfection; for whatever adds something to a thing to attain its end, applies more perfection to it, and so art could be called superior to nature. Briefly. Nature, considered in itself, insofar as it works by its own powers, is far preferred to art, and in this way the arguments for the superiority of nature are to be understood. Art, however, insofar as it does not work by itself and absolutely apart from nature, but works together with nature, is far preferred to nature on account of the arguments brought forward above.

units.la: Poterit & hoc propter affinitatem magnam huic quaestioni subjici: An scilicet ars cum natura aliquam habeat similitudinem vel convenientiam? an vero ars ita a natura discrepet ut nulla utriusque conformitas reperiatur? Resp. Artem cum natura in quibusdam convenire, in quibusdam etiam prorsus discrepare. Conveniunt in hisce septem: 1. Sicut natura res omnes producit, aut sicut naturae opera praecedunt certa quadam praescriptione ratis legibus compositè & suo quaeque ordine, ita ut posterius non eripiat locum priori, nec prius etiam posterius suo jure defraudet; ita & opera artis & ratio ex hoc axiomate dependet, quia ars imitatur naturam. 2. Sicut formae naturales primò habent suam existentiam in agente, in quo insunt potestate, quod vulgò dicitur a Scholasticis esse virtuale, postea vero in materia ipsa, quam agens praeparat ad formam recipiendam, ita etiam formae artificiales, primò habent suum esse in mente artificis, quod vulgò dicitur esse Ideale: postea in materia ipsa, quam artifex praeparavit ad formam artificialem recipiendam: 3. Conveniunt in hoc, quod sicut ars naturam praesupponit, sic natura Deum, si quidem ars nihil operatur, nisi suppeditato sibi aliquo quo naturali compositio, in quod formam artificiatlem inducat: Sic natura nihil gignit, nisi præjacente materia a Deo creata, in qua naturalem formam effingit, adeo ut hoc ordine, hoc modo & ratione res in lucem prodeant,primo Deus ex nihilo omnia creat, natura ex Ente potentia, ars ex Ente perfecto opus suum producit: Deus creando, natura generando, ars concinnando & conformando ad naturæ scilicet imitationem. 4. Quia tam a sensim res producit & ab imperfectioribus ad perfectiora paulatim progeditur, verbi gratia: ars pictoria ptimo opus suum leviter adumbrat, postea in omnem colorum conformitatem paulatim inducit ac tandem perficit: Sic naturain effingende fœtu (quod etiam in cæteris rebus suo modo facere consuevit) primo rude aliquid sine membrorum distinctione producit, postea paulatim expolit, donec animal perfectissimis lineamentis in decentem speciem statuto tempore absolvat, adeo ut non minus ars quam natura suos habeat gradus, & progressus in rebus producendis, & ad finis consummationem perducendis. 5. Sicut natura imitatur Deum aut divinam operationem, sic ars imitatur naturam, & sicut divina operatio, quæ alias à Platone ars divina dicitur, naturæ exemplar est, & natura ipsa divini archetypi exemplum vocatur: Ita ars humana interdum alter natura, interdum naturæ simia appellari solet, propterea quod ad naturæ modum & imitationem multa effinxerit, & ex naturæ operibus plurima humanæ vitæ necessaria primum invenerit, verbi gratia: ex umbra picturam, ex antris domos, mos, ex avium volatu vela pro navibus, ex piscium pinnis remos, quibus propellantur cymbæ & rates, & cætera hujusmodi. Et sicut natura, quo magis divinæ artis substantiam exprimit, eo altiorem gradu obtinet, ita ars tanto amplius commendatur: quanto ad naturam magis accedit. Sic Zeuxis inter Græcos veteres pictores facile primas obtinet, veritate ita repræsentata, ut volucres cœli deciperet, quæ cum accederent propius, ratæ veras esse uvas carpere volebant. Sic Apelles Alexandrum Magnum fulmen manu tenentem in tabella exhibuit, ita ut digiti eminere & fulmé extra tabellam esse viderentur, tanto operis & famæ successu, ut vulgo diceretur duos esse Alexandros, unum Philippi filium nullis viribus superabilem, alterum Apellis opus, nulla arte imitabilem.
units.tr: This question may also be raised, since it is closely related: Does art have any likeness or agreement with nature, or does art differ from nature so completely that no conformity between them can be found? Answer: art agrees with nature in some respects and differs from it entirely in others. They agree in these seven: (1) Just as nature produces all things, and natural works proceed by a certain fixed order, composed according to fixed laws and each in its own place, so that the later does not seize the place of the earlier, nor the earlier defraud the later of its right, so also the works of art and their reasoning depend on this axiom, because art imitates nature. (2) Just as natural forms first have their existence in the agent, in which they inhere potentially (which the Scholastics commonly call "virtual"), and afterwards in the matter itself, which the agent prepares to receive the form, so also artificial forms first have their being in the mind of the artist (commonly called "ideal" being), and afterwards in the matter itself, which the artist has prepared to receive the artificial form. (3) They agree in this, that just as art presupposes nature, so nature presupposes God. For art produces nothing unless some natural thing is supplied to it, into which it introduces an artificial form; and likewise nature begets nothing unless matter created by God lies beneath, in which it fashions a natural form. Hence things come into the light in this order, manner and reason: God first creates all things out of nothing, nature produces from being in potency, and art produces its work from a finished being: God by creating, nature by begetting, art by fitting together and shaping, namely in imitation of nature. (4) Because nature produces things little by little, and progresses gradually from the less perfect to the more perfect. For example, the art of painting first sketches its work lightly, afterwards gradually brings it into full conformity of colours, and at last finishes it. So nature, in forming the foetus (which it is also accustomed to do in other things in its own way), first produces something rough without distinction of limbs, afterwards gradually refines it, until at the appointed time it completes the animal with the most perfect outlines in a fitting form. Thus art has no fewer stages and progressions than nature in producing things and bringing them to the completion of their end. (5) Just as nature imitates God, or the divine operation, so art imitates nature. And just as the divine operation, which Plato elsewhere calls "divine art," is the pattern of nature, and nature itself is called the image of the divine archetype, so human art is sometimes called another nature, sometimes the ape of nature, because it has fashioned many things after the manner and imitation of nature, and has first discovered from the works of nature many things necessary for human life. For example: from a shadow, painting; from caves, houses; from the flight of birds, sails for ships; from the fins of fishes, oars by which boats and rafts are propelled; and other things of this kind. And just as nature holds a higher rank the more closely it expresses the substance of divine art, so art is commended all the more the nearer it comes to nature. Thus Zeuxis, among the ancient Greek painters, easily takes the first place, having represented the truth so well that he deceived the birds of the air, which, approaching more closely, thought the grapes were real and wanted to peck at them. Thus Apelles exhibited Alexander the Great holding a thunderbolt in his hand on a panel, so that the fingers seemed to stand out and the thunderbolt seemed to be outside the panel, with such success in the work and its fame that it was commonly said there were two Alexanders: one the son of Philip, who could be conquered by no force, and the other the work of Apelles, which could be imitated by no art. (6) As in natural things, so also in those things which are worked out with artful care, chance finds a place. Among natural things many examples occur everywhere, such as frogs, lizards, flies and that kind of little animal being enclosed in a piece of amber. Among artificial things, various cases are also recorded by writers, concerning which see Pliny, Natural History, book 35, chapter 10, and Plutarch, in the book On Fortune and Chance.

units.la: 6. Sicut in rebus naturalibus, ita etiam in iis, quæ artificioso studio elaborantur, casus locum invenit & in naturalibus multa passim occurrunt exempla, ut quod in particula electri includantur ranæ, lacertæ, muscæ & id genus animalcula. In artificiosis variaetiam commemorātur a scriptoribus de quibus Plin. lib. 35. nat. hist. c. 10. & Plut. in lib de fort. & casu.
units.tr: (7) Because neither nature (here "nature" is taken as distinguished from the intellectual soul) nor art, as Philoponus reports, Physics book 2, chapter 8, comment 87, deliberates about or takes counsel concerning attaining its end. This, however, ought not to be understood of every art in general. For medicine, navigation and other arts of this kind, which are commonly called conjectural, do take counsel about the end, not about their own end, but about the means to it, because they do not have certain and fixed means for attaining their end. Since the means usually vary according to the various circumstances of individual subjects, it is necessary that they deliberate about which of the means and methods they should use to attain their end.

units.la: 7. Quia neq; natura (sumitur vero hic natura prout ab anima intellectrice distinguitur) neq; ars, ut refert Phil. 2. Phys. Acroas. c. 8. cont. 87. cō ultantaut deliberāt de fine assequendo, quod tamē de qualibet arte in genere intelligi non debet. Nam medicina, navigatoria & cæteræ ejusmodi artes, quæ vulgo conjecturales dicuntur, de fine (no aut pro fine suo consultant, propterea quod certa & statuta media ad finem suum assequedum non habeant, sed quia
units.tr: But, as Aristotle himself explains in Nicomachean Ethics book 3, chapter 4, this must be understood of those arts which attain their end by certain and determined means. For example, the arts of dancing, writing letters or painting do not take counsel about their end, since they have the means at hand by which they reach it. Likewise neither the carpenter nor the stonemason deliberates how to attain his end, provided he performs his task rightly, since he knows his own work to be fixed and determinate, and does not ignore the order that leads to the proposed end. So much for the agreement of art and nature. They also differ in some respects, and especially in these six:

units.la: pro variis circumstantiis singulorum subjectorum media variare solent, ideo necesse est, ut in medium consultent, quibus potissimum modis & mediis finem suum assequantur. Verum sicut Aristoteles ipse explicat lib. 3. Nicomach. cap. 4. hoc intelligi debet de iis artibus, quae percerta & determinata media finem suum attingunt, verbi gratia: ars saltandi, scribendi aut pingendi literas non consultant de fine suo, cum media in promtu habeant, quibus ad illum perveniant. Sic neque faber, neque lapicida deliberant, quomodo finem suum assequantur, si modo munere suo recte defungantur, cum suum sibi certum finitum que sit opus & verum ad finem propositum non ignorat ordinem. Haec de convenientia actus & naturae. De screpat etiam in quibusdam & potissimum in hisce sex: 1. Natura res veras producit, ars vero non, ut verbi gratia: non producit veras arbores aut verum jumentum, sed res veri imitatrices, dum variis ludit modorum pigmentis ad veri speciem referendam apte & concinne collocatis. Et hinc fit, ut picturas nonnulli appellarint vigilantium insomnia, propterea quod non res verae, quoad esse suo proprio, sed rerum tantum imagines & umbrae quoad esse imaginativo in iis sese exhibeant. 2. Quoties natura & ars ad opus aliquod efficiendum conspirat, ars perficit naturam, non econtra natura perficit artem, sicut Aristoteles docet 2. Phys. cap. 8. text 79. Id quod in omnibus habitibus, quos homo contrahit, videre licet, ut verbi gratia: in habitu saltandi aut canendi natura tantum primam inchoationem dat, postea ars accedit & perfectionem adhibet. 3. Quia ut ait D. Thomas lib. 1. contra gentes cap. 76. formæ per artem inductæ non possunt aliam sibi similem producere, sicut formæ à natura conditæ, verbi gratia: domus non potest producere aliam domum, sicut equus gignit alium equum: Et ratio hui jus discriminis hæc esse poterit: Formæ naturales ut eundem in gignente & regenita obtinent essendi modum, ita etiam eandem sortiuntur agendi vim. At vero formæ artificiales longè aliter in mente & idea artificis quam in rebus ipsis insunt. Nam in mente artificis habent essentiam quandam Idealem, in rebus ipsis vero realem. 4. Quia cum forma rei, quæ instanti generationis interit, pereat aut decidat & omnia simul illius accidentia aboleantur, hinc fit, ut formæ naturales superveniant Enti in potentia seu nudæ tantum materiæ: At vero formæ artificiales superveniunt Enti in actu seu rei absolutæ & perfectæ seu toti composito. Nam ars nihil operatur, nisi suppeditato sibi naturali aliquo pei facto veluti subjecto, in quod operatione inducat, ut jam diximus, adeò ut vere dicatur, ubi natura definit, ibi ars operari incipit. 5. Qui a ut annotavit Plotinus Ennead. 8. lib. 8. cap. 4. Et Averrhoës in secundum lib. de ortu & interitu comment. 11. Ars in externa superficie præcipuè versatur, quia externam faciem & elegantiam inprimis affectat, natura vero in abditioribus & interioribus elaborandis impensius occupatur, quia magis sunt necessaria & majoris momenti, & idcoab optimo patente maximè cum ari debent. 6. Quia formæ naturales sunt actuosæ & quasi vivæ, propterea quod vitam & motum rebus omnibus impertiant, formæ vero artificiales sunt quasi emortuae, nullam vim effectricem in se habentes, propterea quod nihil sint aliud quam compositio, ordo, figura, modus quidam & determinatio quantitatis in iis rebus, quibus insunt, sicut ex iis liquet, quae docet Ariftot. 1. Phyf. cap. 5. text. 64. Et hinc fit, ut res naturales in se motionis & quietis principium habeant, res vero artificiales, qua tales, non item, docente Philosopho 2. Phyf. cap. 1. text. 2. 6. Nicomach. cap. 4. 11. Metaph. cap. 3. text. 14.
units.tr: (1) Nature produces true things, but art does not. For example, art does not produce true trees or a true beast of burden, but things that imitate the truth, while it plays with various kinds of pigments, arranged aptly and neatly to represent the appearance of the true. Hence some have called pictures "the dreams of those awake," because the things shown in them are not real things as to their own proper being, but only images and shadows of things as to an imaginary being. (2) Whenever nature and art combine to bring about some work, art perfects nature, not conversely, as Aristotle teaches in Physics book 2, chapter 8, text 79. This can be seen in all the habits that a human acquires; for example, in the habit of dancing or singing, nature gives only the first beginning, and afterwards art comes in and adds perfection. (3) Because, as Saint Thomas says in Against the Gentiles book 1, chapter 76, forms introduced by art cannot produce another form like themselves, as forms established by nature can. For example, a house cannot produce another house, as a horse begets another horse. The reason for this difference may be this: natural forms have the same mode of being in the one who begets and in what is begotten, and so they also receive the same power of acting. But artificial forms exist very differently in the mind and idea of the artist than in the things themselves. For in the mind of the artist they have an ideal essence, but in the things themselves a real one. (4) Because the form of a thing, which perishes at the instant of its generation, is destroyed or falls away, and all its accidents are abolished at once, it follows that natural forms come upon a being in potency, or upon bare matter only, whereas artificial forms come upon a being in act, that is, upon a thing already absolute and perfect, or upon a finished composite. For art produces nothing unless some natural thing is supplied to it as a kind of prepared subject, into which it introduces its operation, as we have already said. So much so that it is truly said: where nature ends, there art begins to work. (5) As Plotinus noted, Ennead 8, book 8, chapter 4, and Averroes on the second book of On Generation and Corruption, comment 11: art is concerned chiefly with the outer surface, because it especially aims at the external face and elegance, whereas nature is more intensely occupied in working out the hidden and inner parts, because these are more necessary and of greater importance, and therefore they should be exposed to the best light most of all. (6) Because natural forms are active and, as it were, alive, since they impart life and motion to all things, whereas artificial forms are, as it were, lifeless, having no effective power in themselves, since they are nothing other than a composition, order, figure, a certain mode and determination of quantity in those things in which they inhere. This is clear from what Aristotle teaches in Physics book 1, chapter 5, text 64. Hence it follows that natural things have in themselves the principle of motion and rest, but artificial things, as such, do not, as the Philosopher teaches in Physics book 2, chapter 1, text 2; Nicomachean Ethics book 6, chapter 4; and Metaphysics book 11, chapter 3, text 14.

units.la: XVI. Poterit & hoc quaeri: An cum natura & ars partim inter se conveniant, partim discrepent, ars propter similitudinem quam habet cum natura, possit opera quadam natura moliri aut producere? Et respond. per distinctionem. Nam ars poterit considerari duobus modis: Vel quatenus per se & sua vi aliquid efficit, aut quatenus aliena vi seu ope & adminiculo ipsius naturae. Priori modo ars nulla naturae opera producere poterit propter duas potissimum rationes: 1. Quia natura est Dei ordinatio & secunda causa immediate Deo subjecta: Ars cum sit habitus mentis humanae, non tam ex praescripto mentis divinae, quam voluntatis humanae res producit, unde opera naturae producere non poterit. 2. Quia ars cum artifice non aliter concurrit, quam ut aliquid tradens seu praescribens regulas & praecepta operis faciundi. Atqui ejusmodi regulae potestatem inducendi formam aliquam naturalem non habent. Nam, ut ex superioribus patet, ars per se nullam ad agendum vim habet: Verum licet ars nullum in rebus motum per se efficiat, modum tamen & via adhiberi poterit, ut hoc vel illo pacto fiat. Sic saltatio, quia a facultate motrice in membris corporis haerente primo provenit, ab arte habet, ut eleganter, cocinnè & numerosè exerceatur. Sic dum aliquid per artem ex plano fit acutum, artis adminiculo habet, ut facilius acutum moveatur quam planum, non quod figura plana aut acuta efficienter ad motum concurrat, sed quia plano corpori plus opponitur medii seu resistentiæ, quàm acuto. Et hinc fit, ut hoc facilius quam illud moveatur, propterea quod corporis interjecti repugnantiam facilius vincat, qua de re videatur Aristoteles lib. 4. de Cœlo sub finem. Utut ars per se & sua vi nulla naturæ opera producat; aliena tamen vi (quæ secunda pars est distinctionis) seu applicando naturalia activa passivis, poterit varia opera naturæ moliri, ut patet in medicina, quæ ex nativa herbarum facultate, ægris corporibus sanitatem restituit, & in aliis artibus, quæ adhibito igne aut aliis etiam caulis naturalibus varias materias & varias res naturales variè etiam immutant. Unde constat artem per se & sua vi nulla naturæ opera producere, quia neque eius vires neque facultatem, quam natura habet, sortitur. Natura enim potentiam proximè operandi à Deo ipso habet, ars autem non. At verò dum ars operatur aliena vi, quatenus scilicet naturam aut adjuvat aut promovet ad perfectionem, aut etiam perficit, quæ natura propter impedimenta quædam objecta aliquando ad finem perducere nequit. Hoc sensu poterit tolerari, ut dicatur ars naturæ quædam opera producere, proinde nihil valent argumenta in contrarium allata, quod scilicet ars sua vi & propria pria facultate naturæ quædam opera moliri possit, quorum primum ducitur à variis instantiis. Dædali statuæ, quas in Creta Insula fabricavit, sponte sua huc illuc discurrebant, non secus ac si vivi fuissent homines. Sic etiam legimus apud Philostratum in vita Apollonii Pryanei aureas quasdam mensas Hyarchi Gymnosophistæ Indi sponte sua se motasse & in gyrum se vertisse & aureos quosdam pincernas operam suam convivis præstitisse: Item quia teste Phavorino apud Gellium lib. 10. Noct. Attic. Architas Tarentinus ligneam fecit columbam ponderibus atq; aura intus inclusa, ita fabricata, ut medio aëre suspensa volitaret. Constat etiam Archimedem Siculum vitreum confecisse globum, in quo astrorum omnium ortus & occasus, defectus item Solis & Lunæ, omnes etiam sphærarum cœlestium & syderum cursus seu revolutiones, rata ordinis constantia & certa æquabilitate distinctæ, cernebantur, quod miraculum humani ingenii postea imitatus est Possidonius, sicut testatur Cicero 1. de natura Deor. Secunda ratio ducitur à majori ad minus, quia ars multos edere possit effectus, ad quos natura non pertingit. Cum ergo aliquid majus, quam natura ipsa possit, cur non etiam effectus naturæ producere possit? Antecedens probatur exemplo annulorum & imaginum Astronomicarum, quæ certo syderum influxu & situ conficiuntur, quas varias supra usitatum naturæ cursum, imò supra omnes naturæ vires producere effecta referunt auctores quidam. Porphyrius apud Augustinum lib. 10. de civit. Dei, cap. 11. Platonis 2. dial. de justo. Et Plotinus Ennead. 4. lib. 4. cap. 44. 3. Id ipsum conconvinci poterit testimonio artis Chymicæ, cûjus professores aurum & alia metalla à se confici asse-runt. Verisimile autem non est omnem eorum opera-m & sumtus in sumum semper abire, quin aliquid producant. Quare non videtur negandum, multa vi artis naturæ opera confici, cum & motum rebus addat, & res plane naturales, cujusmodi sunt metalla, producat, imò in quibusdam rebus naturam non modo æmulatur, sed etiam perficit & superat. Sed ista facile diluuntur. Nam primum argumentum nihil concludit, quia statuæ & id genus arte facta, nõ à suis formis neque arte, sed à natura ipsa moventur compositis latente intus artificio machinulis quibusdam, & argento vivo immisso & cætera ejusmodi, quæ à natura hoc habent, ut motum aliquem cansentur, sicut videre licet in automatis & horologiis, quæ libratis certa ratione ponderibus, rotas suas circumagunt & moventur. Itaque motum istum ars ipsa nõ efficit, sed modificat, seu modum quendam præscribit, ut hac vel illa ratione fiat, & ad tempora aut dirigit naturalem motum ad hunc vel illum finem. Ad secundum etiam per negationem responde-tur. Nam neque annulos neque imagines Astrono-micas ullam ex se ad tales effectus vim habere, aut è cœlo excipere, ut superent omnes naturæ vires, variis rationibus probat D. Thomas in 2.part.summa, quast. 96. art. 2. Itaque quæ de his rebus circumfe-runtur, aut ad fabulas aut ad Dæmonum pertinent præ-stigias. Ad tertium respondetur per distinctionem. Nam ars Chymica non producit verum aurum per se & sua vi, sed aliena tantum, dum scilicet applicat naturalia actiua passivis. Et licet perquam dif- ficilè sit Chymicæ rationis artificio verum aurum producere, aut etiam inferiora metalla in superiora transmutare, non videtur tamen impossibile, cum & factum esse multi testentur, & rationes fieri posse probent. Prima ducitur à majori ad minus, quia cum ars æmula & imitatrix naturæ, non apparet, cur natu- ram in vero auro efformando imitari non possit, quam sæpe in aliis rebus, quæ sunt multo operosio- res, ad vivum expressit. Constat enim quædam ani- malcula artis beneficio progigni & ita quidem, ut perfectiora natura ipsa non edat, verbi gratia: Ex ventribus boum recentibus & fimo obrutis aut etiā ex juvencorū corpore exanimato, ars aut industria humana potest producere Apes. Sic etiam ex elixa- tura anatis sub dio positæ nascuntur bufones, ex serpentibus cum oleo olivarum cocti scorpiones, de quibus vide Plinium lib. 10. natural. histor. cap. 20. Secundò quia plumbum, stannum, argentum & cæ- tera inferiora metalla respectu auri, sunt cruda & impura, id quod experientia & ocularis inspectio demonstrat. Hæc verò cruditas & concoctio venit ab ipsorum imperfectione, sicut docet Philosophus 4. Meteor. cap. 4. At verò possunt purgari, defecari & ad perfectionem suam deduci beneficio artis & in- strumentis ad id commodè adhibitis, præsertim vi ignis. Nec sanè refert artem Chymicam seu ratio- nem auri conficiendi esse obscuram & difficilem, adeo ut multi putêt ex fornace Chymico nondum verum aurū prodiisse, sed aut aurum adulterinum, aut aliquod inferius metallum tinctura auri fucatū. Sic
units.tr: This too may be asked: Since nature and art agree with each other in some respects and differ in others, can art, because of the likeness it has to nature, bring about or produce certain works of nature? The answer is given by distinction. Art can be considered in two ways: either insofar as it effects something through itself and its own power, or insofar as it works through another's power, that is, with the help and assistance of nature itself. In the first way, art can produce no work of nature, for two main reasons. (1) Nature is God's ordinance and a secondary cause immediately subject to God. Art is a habit of the human mind, and it produces things less by the prescription of the divine mind than by the human will, so it cannot produce the works of nature. (2) Art concurs with the artist only by giving rules and precepts for making the work. But such rules do not have the power to induce any natural form. For, as appears from what was said above, art has no power of acting in itself. Yet although art does not of itself produce any motion in things, it can still supply the manner and way in which a thing is done in this or that fashion. Thus dancing, since it comes first from the motive faculty inherent in the members of the body, owes to art that it is performed gracefully, elegantly and rhythmically. Likewise, when something is made sharp from flat by art, it has this through the aid of art, so that a sharp object is moved more easily than a flat one. This is not because the flat or sharp shape contributes efficiently to the motion, but because more resistance of the medium opposes a flat body than a sharp one. Hence it is that one is moved more easily than the other, since it overcomes the resistance of the intervening body more easily. On this matter see Aristotle, On the Heavens, book 4, near the end. Although art by itself and through its own power produces no work of nature, yet by another's power (which is the second part of the distinction), that is, by applying active natural agents to passive ones, it can bring about various works of nature. This is clear in medicine, which restores health to sick bodies by the natural power of herbs, and in other arts which, by the use of fire or other natural means, variously change various materials and natural things. From this it is established that art by itself and through its own power produces no work of nature, because it has neither the powers nor the faculty which nature possesses. For nature has the power of operating immediately from God himself, but art does not. But when art works by another's power, namely insofar as it helps or promotes nature towards its perfection, or even completes what nature, because of certain obstacles, sometimes cannot bring to its end, then in this sense it may be allowed that art produces certain works of nature. Accordingly, the arguments brought to the contrary carry no weight, namely that art, by its own power and its proper faculty, can bring about certain works of nature. The first of these is drawn from various instances. The statues of Daedalus, which he made in the island of Crete, ran here and there of their own accord, no differently than if they had been living men. Thus too we read in Philostratus, in the Life of Apollonius of Tyana, that certain golden tables of Hyarchas, an Indian gymnosophist, moved of their own accord, turned themselves round, and that certain golden cupbearers performed their service for the guests. Likewise, since according to Favorinus, as reported by Gellius in book 10 of the Attic Nights, Archytas of Tarentum made a wooden dove with weights and air enclosed within it, fabricated so that it flew suspended in mid-air. It is also well known that Archimedes of Sicily made a glass globe in which the risings and settings of all the stars, likewise the eclipses of the sun and moon, and also the courses and revolutions of all the celestial spheres and stars, distinguished by a fixed order of constancy and a certain regularity, could be seen; and this marvel of human ingenuity was later imitated by Posidonius, as Cicero attests in book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods. The second argument is drawn from the greater to the less: art can produce many effects which nature does not reach. Since art can therefore do something greater than nature itself, why should it not also be able to produce the effects of nature? The antecedent is proved by the example of rings and astronomical images, which are made under a certain influence and position of the stars, and which some authors report to produce effects beyond the usual course of nature, indeed beyond all the powers of nature: Porphyry, as cited by Augustine in book 10 of The City of God, chapter 11; Plato's second dialogue On the Just; and Plotinus, Enneads 4, book 4, chapter 44. This same point can be confirmed by the testimony of the chemical art, whose practitioners claim that they make gold and other metals. It is not likely, however, that all their labour and expense always go up in smoke without producing anything. Therefore it does not seem to be denied that many works of nature are accomplished by the power of art, since it adds motion to things and produces things that are plainly natural, such as metals; indeed, in some things it not only imitates nature but even perfects and surpasses it. But these points are easily answered. For the first argument proves nothing, because statues and things of that kind, made by art, are moved not by their own forms nor by art, but by nature itself, since they are composed with certain hidden little machines built inside them, with quicksilver introduced and other such things, which by nature have the property of producing some motion. This can be seen in automata and clocks, which turn their wheels and move when weights are hung in a certain proportion. Thus art itself does not produce this motion but modifies it, or prescribes a certain manner of its occurring in this or that way, and either directs natural motion to this or that end or regulates it in time. To the second argument also, the answer is given by denial: rings and astronomical images have no power of their own to produce such effects, nor do they draw from the heavens a power to surpass all the powers of nature. St Thomas proves this for various reasons in the Summa, part 2 of part 2, question 96, article 2. Therefore what is circulated about these things belongs either to fables or to the illusions of demons. To the third argument the answer is given by distinction. The chemical art does not produce true gold through itself and its own power, but only through another's, namely when it applies active natural agents to passive ones. And although it is extremely difficult by the craft of chemical reasoning to produce true gold, or even to transmute inferior metals into superior ones, it does not seem impossible, since many attest that it has been done and prove that it can be done by reasoning. The first reason is drawn from the greater to the less: since art is a rival and imitator of nature, it does not appear why it could not imitate nature in forming true gold, when nature has so often expressed it to the life in other things which are far more elaborate. For it is certain that some tiny animals are generated with the help of art, and in such a way that nature itself does not produce them in a more perfect form. For example, from the fresh dung of oxen buried in manure, or even from the carcass of a dead calf, art or human industry can produce bees. Likewise, from the boiled broth of a duck set out in the open air, toads are born, and from serpents boiled with olive oil, scorpions: on these see Pliny, Natural History, book 10, chapter 20. The second reason is that lead, tin, silver and the other inferior metals, compared with gold, are crude and impure, as experience and visible inspection demonstrate. This crudity and lack of concoction comes from their imperfection, as the Philosopher teaches in Meteorology, book 4, chapter 4. But they can be purified, refined and brought to their perfection with the help of art and instruments suitably applied to it, especially by the power of fire. Nor indeed does it matter that the chemical art, or the reasoning for making gold, is obscure and difficult, so much so that many think that no true gold has yet come out of the chemist's furnace, but only counterfeit gold or some inferior metal coloured with a gold tincture. So

units.la: Sit ita: poterit tamen progressu temporis haec ars ad hucad perfectionem deduci, cum multa in iis hominum solertia atque industria reperiantur prioribus saeculis plane ignota, verbi gratia: Usus bombardarum, & pulveris tormentarii, usus itidem pixidis nauticae, ars typographica, ratio separandi unū metallum ab alio, & ratio extrahendi oleum ex metallis & mineralibus: Item Saccharum ex arundinibus excoquendi & caetera ejusmodi. Verum prodiisse & verum & certum aurum arte Chymica restantur à sua experientia varii auctores Raimundus Lullius in testamento longissimo. Theophrastus Paracelsus lib.1. Philosophia magna cap.4. aliiq; complures.
units.tr: Granted, it may be so. Nevertheless, as time goes on this art may be brought to perfection, since many things have been discovered through human ingenuity and industry in later ages that were quite unknown to earlier centuries. For example: the use of bombards and gunpowder; likewise the use of the nautical compass; the art of printing; the method of separating one metal from another; the method of extracting oil from metals and minerals; also the boiling of sugar from reeds, and other things of this kind. Moreover, several authors attest from their own experience that real and true gold has been produced by chemical art: Raimundus Lullius in his very long Testament; Theophrastus Paracelsus, Philosophia magna, book 1, chapter 4; and many others.

units.la: Coronidis loco quaeritur: An ars sit praestantior virtute morali? Et statuitur thesis negativa propter quatuor potissimum rationes: 1. Quia ad artem sola sufficit cognitio & peritia. Ad virtutem vero non. Nam cognitio parum aut nihil praestat in virtute morali. Aristoteles 6. Nicom. cap.7. 2. Quia virtus hominem facit meliorem & ad honestatem instruit. Ars autem non. Nam multi sunt pessimi & perditissimi homines, qui artes optime callet. Et hinc fit ut Phil. 2. Nicom. cap. 4. dicat aliquem posse esse bonum artificem, qui tamen sit vir improbus. At virtus moralis in malis locum nullum habere poterit. 6. Nicom. cap.ult. 3. Quia ars, ut ancilla inservit virtuti & materiam illi suppeditat, qua prudenter uti possit, verbi gratia: Ars fartoria suppetitat vestes, quibus homo virtute praeditus decenter utatur: coquinaria condit cibos, quibus temperanter vescatur: Ars fabrilis armea, quibus fortiter ie gerat. 4. Quia virtutibus nemo poterit abuti ad malum. At artibus quibus poterit abuti pessime, verbi gratia: Arte medica ad venena miscenda. Arte fabrili ad claves conficiendas & cætera ejusmodi instrumenta, quibus furtum, fluprum, latrocinium committant. Unde sequitur virtutem longe esse præstantiorem & digniorem arte. Sed non leve hic oritur dubium: Quomodo dicat Philosophus notitiam parum facere ad virtutem, cum tamen prudentia, quæ est dux & moderatrix omnium virtutum, requirit imprimis notitiam & rerum cognitionem, sicut docet Philosophus 6. Nicom. cap. 6. Cui etiam adstipulantur omnes Stoici, teste Laërtio lib. 6. de vitis Philosophorum in Zenone? Respondet Petrus Martyr duplicem esse notitiam, unam simplicem & nudam, quæ in sola Theoria consistit, & hanc intellexisse Philosophum, cum diceret notitiam parum conferre ad virtutem: aliam esse non simplicem, sed conjunctam, quæ cum cognitione mentis requirit & consensum voluntatis & appetitus, siquidem ad prudentiam pertinet non tantum de destinatis ad finem consultare, sed consultatione jam peracta & determinata imperare, ut hoc vel illo modo fiat. Quod fieri nō poterit sine voluntate, quæ ad id non adduceretur, nisi appetitus inferior urcunque dominitus & coërcitus esset. Et sic in voluntate tanquam duci & rationi tanquam dominæ in omnibus se subjiciat, &c.
units.tr: As a kind of conclusion, the question is raised: Is art superior to moral virtue? The negative thesis is affirmed, chiefly for four reasons: (1) Art requires only knowledge and skill, but virtue does not. For knowledge contributes little or nothing to moral virtue. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 7. (2) Virtue makes a man better and trains him in honesty, but art does not. For there are many most wicked and deprave men who are most skilled in the arts; and hence it is that Philosophus, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 4, says that someone may be a good craftsman and yet be a wicked man. But moral virtue can have no place in the wicked, Nicomachean Ethics 6, last chapter. (3) Art serves virtue as its handmaid and supplies it with material to use prudently: for example, the tailor's art supplies clothing with which a virtuous man may dress becomingly; the cook's art prepares food with which he may eat temperately; the smith's art makes arms with which he may fight bravely. (4) No one can abuse the virtues for evil, but arts can be abused most wickedly: for example, the medical art to mix poisons; the smith's art to make keys and other such tools with which people commit theft, adultery and robbery. Hence it follows that virtue is far more excellent and worthier than art. But here a no small doubt arises: How does the Philosopher say that knowledge contributes little to virtue, when yet prudence, which is the guide and governor of all the virtues, requires above all knowledge and understanding of things, as the Philosopher teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 6? All the Stoics also agree with this, as Laertius testifies in book 6 of the Lives of the Philosophers, in the life of Zeno? Peter Martyr answers that there are two kinds of knowledge: one simple and bare, which consists in mere theory alone, and it is this that the Philosopher understood when he said that knowledge contributes little to virtue; the other is not simple but joined with action, which requires along with the knowledge of the mind also the consent of the will and of the appetite. For prudence pertains not only to deliberating about the means to an end, but, once deliberation is complete and a decision made, to commanding that this or that be done. This cannot be done without the will, and the will would not be brought to it unless the lower appetite were in some way mastered and restrained; and so the will submits itself in all things to reason as its leader and the appetite to the will as its mistress, etc.

units.la: TRACTATUS IN QVO CONTINETUR SUMMA LIBRI VII. VIII. & IX.
units.tr: A Treatise Containing the Summary of Books VII, VIII and IX

units.la: Νικομαχείων.
units.tr: Nicomachean [Νικομαχείων].

units.la: OSTQVAM Philosophus toto libro sexto de Virtutibus mentis, quaeque iis accidere solent, fusè egit, libro septimo ad morales regreditur, ac initio statim libri de Continentia & Tolerantia tractare incipit. Iis subjicitur virtus quaedam cum eminentia quadam & dignitate singulari conjuncta, quae vulgò dicitur Heroica. Dehinc libro octavo & nono de Amicitia unà cum accidentibus & proprietatibus variis agit. Nos de singulis seorsim, sed succinctè tantum pro Philosophi scopo agere decrevimus: Et primò
units.tr: After the Philosopher has treated at length, throughout the whole of the sixth book, of the virtues of the mind and the things that usually accompany them, he returns in the seventh book to the moral virtues and, right from the beginning of the book, begins to treat of Continence and Tolerance.
