To these is subjoined a certain virtue joined with a particular eminence and singular dignity, which is commonly called Heroic. Then, in the eighth and ninth books, he deals with Friendship together with its various accidents and properties. We have decided to treat of each of these separately, but only briefly, in keeping with the Philosopher's aim. And first, concerning Continence and Tolerance in general.

units.la: De Continentia & Tolerantia in genere.
units.tr: Concerning Continence and Tolerance in General

units.la: VOcantur istae Virtutes quidem, sed imperfectè tantum, quarum discrimen à perfectis hoc ponit Philosophus, quod in his sit continua luctaa inter appetitum & rectam rationem, & quod nondum cupiditates plane & plenè rationis freno sint subjectae. In perfectis econtra se habet, & ideo istae perfectarum respectu, quae ex habitu proficiscuntur, sunt veluti dispositiones quaedam & praeparationes ad perfectionem habitus; unde a Picol.gradu 3.cap.1.dicun- tur etiam Semivirtutes, quod dimidiata quasi viam ad veram & perfectam virtutem demonstrent. Distinguuntur vero ratione objecti, ut & virtutes perfectae, de quibus agit Philosophus: Nam una earum versatur circa voluptatem & dicitur continentia, altera circa dolorem & dicitur Tolerantia. Nam ut illa in voluptatibus animi & corporis modum praescribit quendam, sic haec dolorem circa eosdem deceter & cum ratione, licet non plena, perferre docet.
units.tr: These are indeed called virtues, but only imperfectly. The Philosopher sets this distinction between them and the perfect virtues: in these there is a continual struggle between the appetite and right reason, and the desires are not yet fully and completely subject to the bridle of reason. In the perfect virtues it is the reverse, and so these, compared with the perfect virtues that proceed from habit, are as it were certain dispositions and preparations for the perfection of the habit. Hence they are also called, by Piccolomini [Picol.] Grade 3, chapter 1, "half-virtues," because they show, as it were, a half-way road to true and perfect virtue. They are distinguished, however, by their object, as are the perfect virtues of which the Philosopher treats. For one of them is concerned with pleasure and is called continence; the other is concerned with pain and is called tolerance. For as the former prescribes a certain measure in the pleasures of mind and body, so the latter teaches a person to bear pain about the same things becomingly and with reason, though not with full reason.

units.la: De Continentia in specie.
units.tr: Concerning Continence in Particular

units.la: CONtinentia Graecis ἐγκράτεια quasi dicat, virtus appetitum refrenans recta cum ratione pugnante, & inde Latinis dicitur Cotinentia, qp appetitu intra rationis cancellos cotinere studeat. Sumitur vero duob. modis vel generaliter pro virtute quadam qua pravae cupiditates & inordinati affectus rectae rationi subjiciuntur 7. Nicom.cap.1. Vel specialiter pro virtute imperfecta, qua luctamur cum ira, cupiditate cibi, potus, Veneris, item cum cupiditate sermonis & locomotivae, & sic luctamur, ut tamen virtus superior sit, Aristoteles loco cit. & cap. 4. ejusdem libri. Unde & haec vera ipsius definitio ex ipso Philosopho eruitur. Opponitur vero Continentiae in defectu semivitium quiddam nomine carens, cum quis voluptates adeo aversatur, ut ne propter honestam quidem voluptatem aliquid laude dignum suscipere velit: Unde aut raro aut nunquam hoc vitium reperitur. In excessu vero opponitur incontinentia
units.tr: Continence, from the Greek ἐγκράτεια [enkrateia], means as it were a virtue restraining the appetite when it strives against right reason; and from this it is called in Latin continentia, because it strives to keep the appetite within the bounds of reason. It is taken in two ways: either generally, for a certain virtue by which depraved desires and disordered affections are made subject to right reason (Nicomachean Ethics 7, chapter 1); or specially, for an imperfect virtue by which we struggle against anger, the desire for food, drink and sexual pleasure, and likewise against the desire for speech and for movement; and we struggle in such a way that the higher virtue nonetheless prevails (Aristotle, in the place cited, and chapter 4 of the same book). Hence this true definition of his is drawn out from the Philosopher himself. Opposed to continence in defect is a half-vice with no name, when someone so shrinks from pleasures that he is not willing to undertake anything praiseworthy even for the sake of an honourable pleasure; hence this vice is found rarely or never. In excess, on the other hand, incontinence is opposed to continence, when someone exceeds the due measure in other affections, but above all in gluttony and lust, so that he is drawn into sin somewhat against his will by depraved desires. In general, it must be noted about continence that a person acts partly knowingly and partly ignorantly. Knowingly, indeed, insofar as in general he knows that shameful things are to be shunned; ignorantly, he acts insofar as he does not apply this general knowledge to his own action, and this on account of the conflict between appetite and reason and on account of the various perturbations of the mind, by which, overwhelmed, he very often does not sufficiently grasp what he ought to, as the Philosopher teaches throughout Nicomachean Ethics 7, chapter 3.

units.la: Hhh 5 n.n. nentia, quatum affectibus aliis, tum inprimis in gula & Venere modum quis excedit, ita ut à pravis cupiditatibus quodam modo invitus ad peccandum pertrahatur. In genere de Continentia hoc notandum venit, quod partim sciens agat, partim ignorans: Sciens quidem quatenus in genere novit, turpia esse fugienda, ignorans agit quatenus generaliter istam noticiam non applicat ad suam actionem idq; propter repugnantiam appetitus & rationis, & propter varios animi perturbationes, quibus obrutus saepenumero id, quod debet, non satis apprehendit, sicut docet Philosophus 7. Nicomach. cap. 3 per totum.
units.tr: Hhh 5 n.n. ...nentia (incontinence): a man exceeds the proper measure in his other passions, but above all in gluttony and lust, so that he is drawn into sin by wicked desires, somewhat against his will. Regarding incontinence in general, it should be noted that a person acts partly knowingly and partly ignorantly. He acts knowingly insofar as he knows in general that shameful things are to be avoided, but he acts ignorantly insofar as he does not apply this general knowledge to his own action. This happens because of the conflict between appetite and reason, and because of the various disturbances of the mind, by which he is often overwhelmed and so does not sufficiently grasp what he ought to do, as the Philosopher teaches in Nicomachean Ethics book 7, chapter 3, throughout.

units.la: Statuitur incontinentia pro diversis, quibus committitur modis duplex: Praecipitantia nempe & Infirmitas. Praecipitantia definitur, qua quis subito & quasi per imprudentiam ad peccandum abripitur, antequam posit cogitare: Et hinc hoc nominis sortitum videtur, quod temere & praecipitanter hoc vitium committatur. Aristoteles 2. cap. 7. Nicomach.
units.tr: Incontinence, considered in relation to the different ways in which it is committed, is twofold: namely, precipitancy and weakness. Precipitancy is defined as that by which a person is suddenly and, as it were, through want of thought carried away into sin before he is able to reflect. And it seems to have received this name because the vice is committed rashly and headlong. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics book 7, chapter 7.

units.la: Hinc minus reprehendendam putat hanc incontinentiam Philosophus, propterea quod antequam de remedio cogitari potuit ab affectu vehementiori quis in eam praeceps feratur, libri citati cap. 7. Infirmitas altera incontinentiae species definitur, qua quis affectibus & cupiditatibus pravis aliquandiu resistens tandem succumbit, & cupiditatibus suis quasi victus ad peccandum seducitur. Hoc vitium majorem reprehensionem incurrit quam praecipitantia, quia infirmitas habet spacium & moram sese muniendi adversus cupiditates & pravos affectus. Aristoteles loco citato. Rursus incontinentia sub sin. cap. 5. lib.7. dividitur in humanam seu κατ' ἄνθρωπον & non humanam seu ὑπὲρ τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Humana dicitur, quæ frequenter in homines cadit, idq; κυρίως seu principaliter, nempe circa voluptates naturales & necessarias, utputa alimenti & Veneris vel κατὰ τὴν ἡδονὴν ... ἐνδεχόμενον, secundum quod & per additionem ut in continentia honoris, pecuniæ, lucri, &c. Non humana incontinentia dicitur, vel θηριώδης bestialis, cujusmodi reperitur in monstrosis hominibus, &c. quorum plurima reperiuntur apud varios auctores exempla vel νοσηματώδης, morbosa, qualis inesse solet mulieribus nonnullis gravidis pica laborantibus & in viris βαλανίζ vexatis, vel denique dicitur ἔθισμὴ consuetudinaria, quam homines contrahunt ex depravata & inveterata consuetudine, ut cum homines per consuetudinem pravam fiunt gulosi. Aristoteles loco dicto.
units.tr: For this reason the Philosopher thinks that this incontinence is less to be blamed, because a person is carried headlong into it by a more violent passion before he can think of a remedy (the passage cited, chapter 7). Weakness is defined as the other species of incontinence, by which a person, resisting evil passions and desires for a while, at last gives way and, as if overcome by his desires, is led into sin. This vice incurs greater blame than precipitancy, because weakness has the space and time to fortify itself against desires and evil passions. Aristotle, in the passage cited. Again, incontinence is divided, near the end of chapter 5 of book 7, into human, or according to man [κατ' ἄνθρωπον], and non-human, or beyond man [ὑπὲρ τὸν ἄνθρωπον]. It is called human when it frequently befalls men, and this properly [κυρίως], namely concerning natural and necessary pleasures, such as food and sex, or according to pleasure [κατὰ τὴν ἡδονὴν] as it may happen [ἐνδεχόμενον], and in the way that it is also by addition, as in incontinence regarding honour, money, gain, and so on. Non-human incontinence is called either bestial [θηριώδης], such as is found in monstrous men, of which many examples are found among various authors; or morbid [νοσηματώδης], such as is commonly found in some pregnant women who suffer from pica, and in men afflicted with a disease of the groin; or finally it is called habitual [ἔθισμὴ], which men contract from a depraved and long-standing custom, as when through bad habit men become gluttons. Aristotle, in the passage mentioned.

units.la: De Tolerantia.
units.tr: On Tolerance.

units.la: HÆc de Continentia cum suis oppositis: sequitur Tolerantia, quæ definitur virtus imperfecta, qua res adversas & laboriosas honestatis gratia quidem perferimus, sed perferimus cum dolore, cū molestia, & cum lucta animi. Aristot. 7. Nicom. cap. 1. cui succinit Picolhomineus grad. 3 cap. 14. Unde ut continentia voluptatem continet cum lucta rationis & appetitus, ita tolerantia dolorem tolerat cum eadem lucta. Differt vero tolerantia a fortitudine, de qua sup.lib 3.capp.8.9. & o.egit Philosophus, non tantum ut dispositio ab habitu, imperfectum a perfecto, sed etiam quia fortitudo in adeundis quoq; peripericulis, tolerantia verò in impositis perferendis est occupata.
units.tr: These are the points on continence and its opposites. Next comes tolerance, which is defined as an imperfect virtue by which we bear adverse and burdensome things for the sake of honour, but bear them with pain, with distress, and with a struggle of the mind. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 1; Piccolomini agrees, grad. 3 cap. 14. Just as continence restrains pleasure by a struggle between reason and appetite, so tolerance endures pain by the same struggle. Tolerance differs from fortitude, which the Philosopher treated sup. lib. 3 capp. 8, 9., not only as a disposition differs from a habit, or the imperfect from the perfect, but also because fortitude is concerned with facing dangers, whereas tolerance is concerned with enduring what is imposed.

units.la: Opponitur Tolerantiae in excessu pertinacia, seu ut ab aliis vocatur, durities, in defectu mollitiei. Pertinacia est vitium modum excedens in adversis, quo quaevis sine honestatis ratione perferimus. Hoc vitio Spartanos laborasse refert Cicero 2. Tusc. quaest. Spartae, inquit, pueri ad aram sic verberibus excipiuntur, ut multus e visceribus sanguis exeat, nonnunquam etiam, ut cum ibi essem, audiebam, ad necem usque, quorum nemo non tantum exclamabat unquam sed ne ingemuit quidem. De Spartano et puero refert Plutarchus cum vulpeculam esset furatus, eamque sub veste abditam teneret, et bestia illius latus ad intestina roderet, tacite dissimulavit, et quibusdam eum objurgantibus et dicentibus: Praestat detegere vulpeculam quam ad necem servare: Nequaquam dixit, quin potius praestat dolo-ribus immori, quam committere ut ob mollitiem, luci fecisse vitam dicat. Hoc vitium non tantum in factis, sed et in verbis esse testatur experientia, et horum, qui hoc vitio in verbis laborant, tria genera referuntur. Quidam enim sunt, qui singulares et proprias suas opiniones fovent et obstinate defendunt hoc solo nomine, quod propriae ipsorum sint, et hos vocat Philosophus ἰδιογνώμονας. 2. Quidam sunt pertinaces indocti (vulgo ἀμαθεῖς) qui licet non possint suas opiniones defendere, nec aliorum rationes solvere, aut ad eas respondere, tamen praejudicio quodam in proposito perseverant. 3. Denique quidam sunt ἀγεέλκοι, agrestes, qui plane nō curant, utrum bene vel male sentiant, alii autem veritatem & honestatem non amant, sed tantum perfistunt in iis, quibus sunt assueti, aut quibus delectantur. Rationes autem non volunt audire plane, nec possunt etiam audītas intelligere: Ut breviter dicam, pertinax sic distinguitur, quod sit vel singularis, vel indoctus vel profanus. Cum singularibus & indoctis utcunque adhuc disputari potest, quamvis difficulter & raro cum fructu: Cum profanis vero non esse disputandum, monet Philosophus saepius 7. & 8. Topic.
units.tr: Opposed to tolerance by excess is obstinacy, or as others call it, hardness, and by deficiency, softness. Obstinacy is the vice that exceeds the proper measure in adversity, by which we endure anything without any reason of honour. Cicero, in the second book of the Tusculan Disputations, reports that the Spartans suffered from this vice: "At Sparta," he says, "boys are flogged at the altar so that much blood flows from their bodies; sometimes, as I heard while I was there, they are beaten to death, and not one of them ever cried out, or even groaned." Plutarch tells of a Spartan boy who had stolen a little fox and was hiding it under his cloak, and the beast gnawed his side down to the intestines. He kept silent and concealed it. When some men rebuked him and said that it was better to reveal the fox than to keep it to his death, he replied, "By no means; rather it is better to die of the pains than to commit an act by which, through softness, he might say he had lived for the light." This vice is shown by experience to exist not only in deeds but also in words, and three kinds of those who suffer from this vice in words are reported. Some cling to their own singular opinions and stubbornly defend them for this one reason, that they are their own; the Philosopher calls these idiognomones [ἰδιογνώμονας]. (2) Some are obstinate ignorant people [vulgo amathes ἀμαθεῖς], who, although they cannot defend their opinions, nor refute the arguments of others, nor answer them, nevertheless persist in their position out of some prejudice. (3) Finally, some are agroikoi [ἄγροικοι], rustics, who simply do not care whether they think rightly or wrongly; others do not love truth and honour, but only persist in those things to which they are accustomed or in which they delight. Such people do not wish to hear reasons at all, nor can they understand them when heard. To state it briefly: the obstinate person is distinguished thus, that he is either singular, or ignorant, or profane. One may still dispute in some way with the singular and the ignorant, though with difficulty and rarely with profit; but with the profane one must not dispute at all, as the Philosopher warns in the Topics, books 7 and 8, more than once.

units.la: Mollities Tolerantiae in defectu oppositae definitur vitium, quo plane nullos labores aut dolores etiam minimos honestatis gratia subire aut perferre volumus: Et duplex statuitur, nempe vel insita, vel quaesita, 7. Nic.c.7. Insita dicitur qua nonnulli homines propter naturam loci, in quo habitant, vel propter aetatem & sexum laborant, & sic distinguit Philosophus sub finem cap. 7. Et sunt exemplum hujus mollitiei Persae, qui natura fuerunt molliores: Unde proverbium; Mollities Persica. Ita etiam de hac mollitie male audiebant Jones, utpote qui primo unguenti item coronarum ad mensam, item mensarum secundarum usum introduxerunt. De mollitie Sybaritarum vide Danaeum lib.2.cap.6. Sic mollitie laborant infantes, item feminae, item quae diuturnis morbis enervantur. Notandum vero hanc insitam mollitiem, cum sit quodammodo naturalis, & a causis naturalibus plerumque veniat non proprie vitium esse morale, cum non a pravis actionibus promanet, ut vitia illa, quae opponuntur virtutibus Ethicis, thicis, sed à prava quadam dispositione aut animi aut corporis, ut experientia & exempla late testantur. 2. Quia fi insita mollities effet vitium naturale, sequeretur in varia brutorum genera, ut catellos Melitenfes, equos Persicos & id genus alia animalia cadere vitium morale, & per consequens, etiam virtutem: Nam in quodcunque cadit unum horum, cadit & alterum. At hoc absurdum & contra experientiam est. Vide cap. 6. 2. Nicom. Quaesita mollities seu voluntaria dicitur, quae non tam natura qua nostra culpa contrahitur, dum scilicet ex prava dispositione animi & ineptitudine aut socordia corporis illas redimus actiones, quae virtuti repugnant. Et haec mollities proprie vitium morale dicitur. Exemplum huius notat Strabo lib. 5. Geograph. Et Valerius Maximus lib. 9. cap. 1. in Campanis Italiae populis, qui cum aere gauderent molliore, etiam studium & affectationem mollitiei addiderunt. Philosophus cap. 7. 7. Nicom. refert hoc vitio laborare voluptarios ignavos & qui luxui deditii sunt. Nam hinc vires & corporis & animi frangunt, & inhabilitatem bonarum actionum sibi accersunt.
units.tr: Softness, the deficiency opposed to tolerance, is defined as a vice by which we are wholly unwilling to undergo or endure even the slightest labours or pains for the sake of honour. It is held to be twofold, namely either innate or acquired, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 7. Innate softness is that by which some men suffer because of the nature of the place where they live, or because of age and sex; the Philosopher distinguishes it thus at the end of ch. 7. Examples of this softness are the Persians, who by nature were softer; hence the proverb, Persian softness. The Ionians too were ill-spoken of for this softness, since they were the first to introduce perfumed ointment and garlands at table, and the custom of second courses. On the softness of the Sybarites see Daneau, lib. 2 cap. 6. Thus infants suffer from this softness, as do women, and those who are weakened by long illnesses. It should be noted, however, that this innate softness, since it is in some way natural and generally comes from natural causes, is not properly a moral vice, since it does not flow from wicked actions, as those vices do which are opposed to the moral virtues, but from some wrong disposition either of mind or of body, as experience and examples widely attest. (2) For if innate softness were a natural vice, it would follow that a moral vice, and consequently also a virtue, would fall upon the various kinds of brute beasts, such as Maltese lapdogs, Persian horses, and other animals of that kind; for wherever one of these falls, the other falls too. But this is absurd and contrary to experience. See Nicomachean Ethics 2, ch. 6. Acquired softness, or voluntary softness, is that which is contracted not so much by nature as by our own fault, when, through a wrong disposition of mind and a sluggishness or indolence of body, we shun those actions that are opposed to virtue. This softness is properly called a moral vice. Strabo, Geography book 5, notes an example of this, and Valerius Maximus, lib. 9 cap. 1, among the peoples of Campania in Italy, who, since they delighted in a softer air, also added a zeal and affectation for softness. The Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 7, reports that this vice afflicts the lovers of pleasure, the idle, and those given over to luxury; for by it they break down both the strength of body and of mind, and bring upon themselves an incapacity for good actions.

units.la: Absoluta sic doctrina harum semivirtutum subjici possunt quaestiones nonnullae: Et 1. An verum illud sit, quod dicit Philosophus cap. 3. lib. 7. incontinentem scilicet peccare scienter? Nam contrarium defendit Plato, ut videre licet in Protagora, ubi Socratem inducit hac de re disputantem, & scienter incontinentem peccare negatem, hoc in primis fretum fundamento. Si scientia sit fortissimum & potentissimum quid in homine ab inferiore concupiscentia scilicet vinci non poterit, quia nimirum scientia est dux appetitionum & actionum, estque boni & mali index. Aristoteles contra experientiae testimonio nititur, & omnium sensibus id patere affirmat. Sed nulla remanebit difficultas, si vocabulum scientiae sano sensu accipiatur: nam vel habitum vel actum denotat. Habitus scientiae incontinens praeditus esse solet. Non enim ignorat, quid apprehendendum rejiciendumque sit, sed actu destituitur, cum ob perturbationem vim & impetum impeditus in porta veritatis rationis permanere non valet, sed cum videat meliora, deteriora sequitur. 1. Deinde peccat quoque incontinens scientia generali, quando nempe explorat tu habet, turpia esse fugienda, voluptatum incantamenta esse condemnanda: Interim in specie ignorat hoc vel illud cujus amore capitur, esse vitandum. 2. Distinctis temporum intervallis considerari debet. 1. Ante actionem, tamque praeditus est scientia tam generali quam speciali. 2. In actione ipsa: Tunc enim similis est ignoranti, quia animus perturbatus est pravis affectibus, ut non possit ea noticia, quam habet frui. 3. Post actionem: Tunc enim redit ad noticiam, quam antea habuit, quod inde deprehenditur, quia poenitentia ducitur & pudore facti suffunditur. Plura de hac quaestione vide apud Picol. grad. 3 cap. 13.
units.tr: With this doctrine of these half-virtues fully set out, several questions may be raised. First: Is it true, as the Philosopher says in ch. 3 of book 7, that the incontinent man sins knowingly? For Plato defends the contrary, as may be seen in the Protagoras, where he introduces Socrates disputing on this matter and denying that the incontinent man sins knowingly, relying chiefly on this foundation: if knowledge is the strongest and most powerful thing in a man, it cannot be overcome by inferior desire, since knowledge is surely the guide of appetites and actions, and the judge of good and evil. Aristotle relies on the testimony of experience and affirms that this is evident to the senses of all. But no difficulty will remain if the word "knowledge" is taken in a sound sense, for it denotes either a habit or an act. The incontinent man usually possesses the habit of knowledge. For he does not fail to know what is to be pursued and what rejected, but he lacks the act; for, hindered by disturbance and violence, he cannot remain at the gate of truth and reason, but though he sees the better things, he follows the worse. (1) Again, the incontinent man also sins with general knowledge, when he indeed understands that shameful things are to be shunned and the enchantments of pleasures to be condemned, yet in particular he does not know that this or that thing, by whose love he is captured, is to be avoided. (2) The time intervals must be distinguished. (1) Before the action, a man has knowledge both general and particular. (2) In the action itself: then he is like one ignorant, because his mind is troubled by evil affections, so that he cannot enjoy the knowledge he has. (3) After the action: then he returns to the knowledge he had before, which is shown by the fact that he is led to repentance and is overcome with shame for what he has done. More on this question may be found in Piccolomini, grad. 3 cap. 13.

units.la: Secunda quaestio: An incontinens alimenti & Veneris, & qui nullum in illis modum servat, sit deteriorior incontinenti ira? Et assi mativam tuetur Ariստoteles 7. Nicomach. cap. 6 quatuor potissimum argumentis: r.
units.tr: The second question: Is the man who is incontinent in food and in sexual love, and who observes no measure in these, worse than the man who is incontinent in anger? Aristotle defends the affirmative in Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 6, chiefly with four arguments.

units.la: Quia incontinens nae aliquam ex parte audit rationem, hem, ejusq; mandatum conatur exequí, quæ jubet illatam injuriam vindicari, verum in eo potissimum peccat, quod nimis cito, antequam plenum ratio-nis mandatum acceperit aut etiam nimis acerbe ad vindictam properat: Qui propter & celeribus comparatur ministris, qui primùm sensa Domini sui perceperint excurrunt tamen postea; officiū minus recte faciunt: Incontinens aut cibi & Veneris nullo modo audit rationē, sed solo sensu fertur, & prolectatur voluptate gustus & tactus. 2. Quia incontinens irae magis aperte agit, voluptarii autem agunt callidè & occultè. 3. Irae incontinentia proficiscitur à temperamento, & ideo cum sit quodammodo quid naturale, quodammodo excusari poterit. At incontinentia Veneris & alimenti à voluptate provenit, quam quis, si rationem audiat, declinare potest, & si nō declinet, majori reprehensione dignus habetur. 4. Quia justo dolore incontinens irae videtur excitari ad vindictam, voluptuarius autem nullum habet honestum prætextum, sed ex mera perulantia peccat.
units.tr: (1) Because the incontinent man in anger in some measure hears reason and tries to carry out its command, which bids that the injury done be avenged; but he sins chiefly in this, that he hastens to vengeance too quickly, before he has received the full command of reason, or too harshly. He is therefore compared to hasty servants, who, having just grasped their master's intention, rush off, and yet afterwards act less rightly. But the man who is incontinent in food and in sexual love does not hear reason at all, but is carried by sense alone and is enticed by the pleasure of taste and touch. (2) Because the man incontinent in anger acts more openly, whereas those given to pleasures act cunningly and secretly. (3) Incontinence in anger proceeds from temperament, and so, since it is in some way natural, it can in some measure be excused. But incontinence in sexual love and food arises from pleasure, which a man can avoid if he listens to reason; and if he does not avoid it, he is held more deserving of reproach. (4) Because the man incontinent in anger seems to be stirred to vengeance by a just pain, whereas the lover of pleasure has no honest pretext, but sins from sheer wantonness.

units.la: Tertia quæstio. His propter affinitatem non incommode poterit hæc subjici: Quis peccet magis, num qui sponte vel invitus aberrat? Movet hanc difficultatem Plato in Hippia majori, & primò ostendit Socrates, quem ibi loquentem inducit, illos, qui sponte mendacium dicunt, meliores esse, quam qui non sponte: Mox Hippias ei objicit, inquiens: Quoniam pacto Socrates, qui scientes volentesque injuriantur, seducunt, lædunt, meliores esse possunt, quam qui hæc propter animi sententiam faciunt?
units.tr: The third question. Because of its affinity with the preceding, this may conveniently be raised here: who sins more, the one who errs knowingly or the one who errs unwillingly? Plato raises this difficulty in the Greater Hippias. There Socrates, whom he introduces as speaking, first shows that those who lie deliberately are better than those who do not. Then Hippias objects to him, saying: "How can it be, Socrates, that those who wrong and harm others knowingly and willingly can be better than those who do these things from a mistaken opinion?"

units.la: Nam multum ignoscitur illi, qui per ignorantiam injuria infert aut mendacium profert, vel aliud quicquam mali committit, legesq; in eos severius animadvertunt, qui volentes mala faciunt quam qui nolentes. Ex adverso Socrates cursorem sponte tardum, & in palæstra luctatorem, qui spõte cadit, ei præfert, qui invitus hæc facit, & idipsum de plurimis ita se habere inductione demonstrat. Ratione hac utitur Socrates, quia aberrans sponte, præditus est Scientia & Potentia recte agendi, qui aberrat invitus vel uno vel altero caret. At sciens non sciente, potens impotente præstantior habetur. Et inde colligit: Si quis igitur hominum sit, qui sponte aberret, turpiaque & injusta committat, haud aliud sit ô Hippia quam vir bonus. Ac ita cum pro omni parte dubitasset, rem sub dubio derelinquit. Aristoteles per distinctionem ad hanc quæstionem respondet 6. Nic. cap. 5. In artibus hoc esse verum, in morali disciplina e contra. Eandem sententiam protulit Seneca Epistola 96. inquiens: Vis scire, quam difficilis sit aliarum artium conditio & hujus nempe moralis scientiæ: In illis excusatius habetur voluntate peccare quam casu, in hac maxima culpa erit sponte delinquere: Grammaticus non erubescit solœcismum si iciens facit, erubescit vero si nesciens. Ratio pro confirmanda Aristotelis sententia hæc esse poterit, quia in attinentibus ad scientias contemplativas & artes perfectio consistit in cognitione exacta; possessione habitus, in attinentibus vero ad morales actiones consistit præsertim in præelectione. Ex ea enim consurgit probitas vel improbitas actionis. Attifex cum sciens peccat in arte, aut occultat artem suam, aut aliorum explorat ingenia an illum errore possint deprehendere. At vero moralis scientiae studiosus si sciens male agat, scienter se malum reddit, & non tam scientiam quam malitiam aut depravationem voluntatis demonstrat. Verum hic objici potest: Medicum sponte veneno necantem judicari poena dignum, non autem si nesciens & invitus id faciat? Resp. Id contingere quia tunc medicus praesertim peccat, ut vitiosus non autem ut ignarus, & errat in attinentibus admodum, non aut quae spectant artem medicam.
units.tr: For much indulgence is shown to one who commits an injury or tells a lie through ignorance, or does some other wrong, and the laws punish more severely those who do wrong willingly than those who do so unwillingly. On the other hand, Socrates prefers a runner who is slow on purpose, and a wrestler who falls on purpose, to one who does these things unwillingly, and he demonstrates by induction that this holds true in most cases. Socrates reasons thus: one who errs knowingly has the knowledge and the power to act rightly, whereas one who errs unwillingly lacks one or the other of these. And the one who knows is considered superior to the one who does not know, and the one who is able superior to the one who is unable. From this he concludes: "If there is therefore anyone among men who errs knowingly and commits shameful and unjust deeds, my Hippias, he is no other than a good man." Having doubted this on every side, he leaves the matter in doubt. Aristotle answers this question by a distinction in Nicomachean Ethics 6, chapter 5: that this is true in the arts, but in moral discipline the opposite holds. Seneca gives the same opinion in Epistle 96, saying: "Would you know how difficult the condition of the other arts is, and of this moral science in particular? In the other arts it is considered more excusable to sin willingly than by accident; in this one, to offend knowingly will be the greatest fault. The grammarian is not ashamed of a solecism if he makes it unknowingly, but he is ashamed if he makes it knowingly." The reason for confirming Aristotle's view may be this: in matters pertaining to the contemplative sciences and the arts, perfection consists in exact knowledge, and in possessing the habit; but in matters pertaining to moral actions, it consists especially in the choice (prohairesis). For from this arises the goodness or badness of an action. When a craftsman knowingly errs in his art, he either conceals his art, or tests the abilities of others to see whether they can detect the error. But when a student of moral science acts badly knowingly, he knowingly makes himself bad, and shows not so much his knowledge as his malice or the depravity of his will. Yet here it may be objected: "Is a physician who knowingly kills with poison judged worthy of punishment, but not if he does it unknowingly and unwillingly?" Answer: this happens because in that case the physician sins as a wicked man, not as an ignorant one, and errs in matters that concern not the medical art at all, but ... [no: see note] Correction for the final sentence of [2], which should read: The answer is that this happens because in that case the physician sins as a wicked man rather than as an ignorant one, and he errs in matters very far removed from the medical art itself.

units.la: 2. Objici & hoc potest ex sententia Platonis hominem in iis, quae ad mores spectant peccantem sponte non posse malum dici, cum nemo sponte fiat malus, ut ille asserit in Hippia minore. Aliud est inficiari hominem sponte reddi malum, & inficiari sponte agere actiones pravas, ut furari & similia scelera patrare, potest homo ex sententia Platonis sponte furari, adulterare & laedere: At non ob id dicitur sponte fieri malus, quia nō patrat ea scelera, ut per ea improbus reddatur, sed ob bona, quae in iis reperiri judicat. Picolhomineus gradu 3. cap. ultimo.
units.tr: 2. This may also be objected, from Plato's opinion: a man who sins knowingly in those things which concern morals cannot be called bad, since no one becomes bad willingly, as he asserts in the Lesser Hippias. It is one thing to deny that a man is made bad willingly, and another to deny that he willingly performs wicked actions, such as stealing and committing similar crimes. According to Plato's opinion, a man can willingly steal, commit adultery and do harm; yet he is not said to become bad willingly because he perpetrates these crimes in order to be made wicked by them, but because of the goods which he judges to be found in them. Piccolomini, book 3, last chapter.

units.la: De Virtute Heroica.
units.tr: On Heroic Virtue

units.la: HActenus de Virtute Morali ordinaria, quae ab aliis dicitur communis: sequitur extraordinaria, quae spectatur in gradu eminentiae & summae excellentiae, quae vocatur Heroica vulgo, de qua agit Philosophus 7. Nicom. sparsim, sed breviter tantum, de qua hoc ordine agemus, ut 1. De nominis origine unde scilicet nomen habeat, & quot modis summatur. matur demonstremus. 2. De causis. 3. De subje-ćto,in quod cadit hæc virtus. 4. De obje&to,quod ab aliis dicitur subjectum occupans, sed non satis commodè. 5. De proprietatibus seu requisitis ad hanc virtutem. 6. De oppositis cum suis accidentibus. 7. Quæstiones quasdam subjiciemus.
units.tr: So far we have dealt with ordinary moral virtue, which others call common. Next comes extraordinary virtue, which is found in a degree of eminence and supreme excellence, and which is commonly called heroic. The Philosopher discusses it in scattered places in the seventh book of the Nicomachean Ethics, but only briefly. We shall treat it in this order: (1) we shall show the origin of the name, from what it is derived and in how many senses it is taken; (2) the causes; (3) the subject in which this virtue inheres; (4) the object, which others call the subject-matter, though not very suitably; (5) the properties or requisites for this virtue; (6) its opposites, with their accompanying features; (7) we shall add some questions.

units.la: De Nomine virtutis Heroicæ, & quot modis dicatur. Dicitur hæc Virtus Heroica ab Heros, quæ vox Græca est, quam quia Latini satis exprimere non possunt, retinere sunt consueti. ἥρως unde venit hæc virtus, derivatur vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἡρέτης, quæ derivatio duriuscula esse videtur, cum hac ratione oēs virtutes dici possint Heroicæ. Alii deducunt à voce ἀήρ, quia nempe Herou animæ antiquitus creditæ sunt, cum Dæmonibus manere in aëre, & ibi res humanas à vicino contemplari, sicut etiam Xenon apud Laertium lib.7.de vit.Philosoph. Heroas vocat animas sapientum corporibus solutas & in aëre ita obvagantes: Unde Pythagoras Dæmonas istos, qui vulgo vocantur aërei, nihil aliud quam Heroum esse animas dicebat. Alii derivant ab ἥρα, à terra, quia Heroës sunt terrestres quidam Dii, sicut etiam Lucianus Heroum definit ὃς μήτε θεὸς μήτε ἄνθρωπος ἀλλὰ συμφόρτον. Alii derivant ab ἥρα, id est, à Junone, quæ Dea præses aëris à veteribus fingitur, quod nempe Heroës terras superent, & ad Deos accedere videantur: Vel potius quod existimo, quia Heroes habent naturam aëream & impetus vehementes instar ventorum, quam etymologiam ampleƈtitur Augustinus lib.10.de civit.Dei, cap.21. Sed omnium optima videtur esse derivatio ἀπὸ τῆς ἐρωτῶ, quod amor & studium virtutis in Heroicis naturis sit vehemens: quam etymologiam etiam Plato tradidit in Cratylo. Haec de origine Nominis. Caeterum late se extendit Heroica virtus, ita ut alia sit Heroica virtus intellectualis, qualis est in excellenter doctis & sapientibus, praesertim vero disciplinarum inventoribus: alia vero sit spiritualis, qualis fuit excellens virtus Abrahami, alia denique sit excellens virtus moralis, qualis ad institutum hoc nostrum pertinet: nam de aliis speciebus excellentissimi huius virtutis non in Ethica, sed alibi in suis quibuscunque disciplinis tradendum erit.
units.tr: On the name of heroic virtue and the senses in which it is used. This virtue is called heroic from Heros, a Greek word, which Latins, since they cannot express it adequately, are accustomed to keep as it is. The word ἥρως [heros], from which this virtue comes, is derived either from ἡρέτη [aretē, virtue], which derivation seems rather harsh, since on this reasoning all virtues could be called heroic. Others derive it from ἀήρ [aēr, air], because the souls of heroes were believed in antiquity to remain in the air with the demons and from there to contemplate human affairs nearby, as Xenon also does in Laertius, book 7 of Lives of the Philosophers, where he calls heroes the souls of the wise, released from their bodies and wandering thus in the air. Hence Pythagoras said that those demons which are commonly called aerial were nothing other than the souls of heroes. Others derive it from ἥρα [hēra, earth], because heroes are certain earthly gods, just as Lucian also defines a hero as one who is "neither god nor man but a mixed being" [ὃς μήτε θεὸς μήτε ἄνθρωπος ἀλλὰ συμφόρτον]. Others derive it from ἥρα, that is, from Juno, the goddess whom the ancients imagined as presiding over the air, because heroes surpass the earth and seem to draw near to the gods. Or rather, as I think, because heroes have an airy nature and vehement impulses like the winds; Augustine embraces this etymology in On the City of God, book 10, chapter 21. But the best derivation seems to be from ἐρωτῶ [erōtō, to love, to desire], because the love and zeal for virtue is vehement in heroic natures. Plato also gave this etymology in the Cratylus. So much for the origin of the name. Heroic virtue, moreover, extends widely, so that there is a heroic intellectual virtue, such as is found in men of outstanding learning and wisdom, especially the inventors of the disciplines; there is a spiritual heroic virtue, such as the excellent virtue of Abraham; and finally there is an excellent moral virtue, which is the concern of our present undertaking. For the other kinds of this most excellent virtue must be treated not in ethics but elsewhere, in whichever disciplines they belong to.

units.la: II. De Causis inquirendum erit, quae duplices statuuntur, efficientes nempe & finales. Efficiens rursus est duplex: Prima nempe peculiaris Dei afflatus & ductus, quo incitatae Heroicae naturae altissima quaeque sibi proponunt, & propter quae ductum numinis nancisci tur oportunitates, successus & felicitates, quas alii non nanciscuntur. Secunda, quae consideratur vel ut remota, utpote partim singulare temperamentum, & dispositio corporis, partim peculiaris naturae impetus ab ejusmodi temperamento pendens: vel ut propinqua, quae consistit partim in optima institutione, & quae inde oritur sapientia & doctrina eminente, partim in amore ardenti & desiderio felicitatis & divinae conditionis. Proxima causa est actionum Heroicarum frequens iteratio. Nam ut omnis virtus ex iteratione bonarum actionum oritur, ita haec inprimis quae sublimes & supereminentes spectat actiones. Finalis causa consistit partim in rerum magnarum suscepione & gestione, quae dicitur finis proxiproximus, partim in summa hominis cum Deo assimilatione, quae ad ipsam felicitatē maximè refertur, & dicitur ei finis cum reliquis virtutibus communis, sed majori cū dignitate & excellentia ei competens.
units.tr: II. The causes must be inquired into; these are reckoned as twofold, namely efficient and final. The efficient cause is again twofold. The first is the particular inspiration and guidance of God, by which heroic natures, stirred up, propose to themselves the highest aims, and on account of which, being guided by the divine power, they obtain opportunities, successes and felicities which others do not obtain. The second, which is considered either as remote or as proximate, is remote in so far as it consists partly in a singular temperament and disposition of the body, and partly in a peculiar impulse of nature depending on such a temperament; it is proximate in so far as it consists partly in the best upbringing, and the outstanding wisdom and learning which arise from it, and partly in a burning love and desire for happiness and a divine condition. The proximate cause of heroic actions is their frequent repetition. For just as every virtue arises from the repetition of good actions, so this virtue especially arises from the repetition of actions that are lofty and surpassing. The final cause consists partly in the undertaking and accomplishing of great things, which is called the nearer end, and partly in the highest likeness of man to God, which refers most of all to felicity itself; this is called its end, which it shares with the other virtues, but which belongs to it with greater dignity and excellence.

units.la: Subjectum Heroicae virtutis sunt Heroës & Heroînae, hoc est, personae illustres ob eximiam virtutem supra communem hominum conditionem & sortem elevatae. Nam quando Deus aliquid singulare vult efficere, & Regna & Respublicas vel fundare, vel collapsas restaurare, tum excitat singularia ingenia, quae id sua virtute & felicitate praestant. Nam ad magna effecta magnis opus erit causis.
units.tr: The subject of heroic virtue is heroes and heroines, that is, illustrious persons raised above the common condition and lot of men on account of their outstanding virtue. For when God wishes to bring about something singular, and either to found kingdoms and commonwealths or to restore those that have fallen, then he raises up singular geniuses, who excel in this by their virtue and good fortune. For great effects require great causes.

units.la: Objectum sunt oēs illæ res, circa quas virtutes ordinariæ versantur, sed quatenus in iis excellentia & eminentia quaedam cernitur, inprimis verò quae bona publica, gloriam Dei, Reipub. felicitatem, salutemq; hominum, praesertim aeternam concernunt, & evidentem humano generi utilitatem adferunt.
units.tr: The object is all those things with which the ordinary virtues are concerned, but in so far as a certain excellence and eminence is discerned in them; and especially those which concern the public good, the glory of God, the welfare of the commonwealth, and the salvation of men, above all their eternal salvation, and which bring evident advantage to the human race.

units.la: Proprietates seu requisita sunt tria potissimum : 1. Impetus & facultas inchoandi praeclara & eximia facta. 2. Singularis celeritas & constantia efficiendi. 3. Felicitas seu successus valde secundus perficiendi. Hoc in exemplis videre licet. Ita summus Heros fuit Alexander Magnus, itē Julius Caesar, quoad omnia tria requisita virtutis Heroicae impetum, nempe celeritatem & successum. Talis etiam ab Hom. describitur Achilles & à Virgilio Æneas, quanquam Laēt. lib. 9. c. 8. de Just. contradicat. Vide Picol. grad. 6. c. 8.
units.tr: The properties, or requisites, are chiefly three: (1) an impulse and ability to begin illustrious and outstanding deeds; (2) a singular speed and steadfastness in carrying them out; (3) felicity, or a very favourable success in completing them. This can be seen in examples. Thus Alexander the Great was the supreme hero, and likewise Julius Caesar, in respect of all three requisites of heroic virtue: impulse, namely, speed and success. Achilles is described in this way by Homer, and Aeneas by Virgil, although Lactantius, book 9, chapter 8, On Justice, contradicts this. See Picolhomineus, degree 6, chapter 8.

units.la: Opposita Heroicae virtutis sunt in defectu summa ignavia seu ineptitudo ad omnem virtutis impetum (de quo vitio, cum raro aut nunquam contingat, nihil hic ultrà dicemus: Nullus.n. tà hebes aut stu-pido reperitur ingenio, qui non ex instinctu natura aliquid boni intesdum moliatur, & aliquam virtu-tis actionem proferat: (quanquam alii aliis rariores reperiantur.) In excessu feritas seu bestialitas 7.Nic. cap.1. Definitur feritas ibidem vitium summum & extremum, quo homo excusso rectæ rationis judi-cio omniquę humanitate abjecta turpissimè & ne-fandè perpetrat, à quibus alias natura humana ab-horret. Tales fuerunt apud veteres Scines, Proaru-stes, Phalaris & inter Imperatores Romanos Nero. Statuitur verò feritas hæc duplex: alia est sine omni ratione, alia cum ratione, sed læsa aut depravata: Ari-stoteles loco cit. Picolhomineus gradu 6.cap.14. Feri-tas absque ratione vel nihil prorsus habet rationis, quàs hominum feritas μανία aut insania laboran-tium, quales homines interdum horrenda patrant. Talis fuit feritas Herculis, cum furore correptus uxorem & liberos occideret, ut testatur Seneca in Hercule furente. Talis etiam fuit in Agave, quæ Thracias mulieres in filium suum Penthea armavit, illumque membratim discerpsit. Talis etiam in Medea proprios suos filios cum se à Jasone despectam videret, interficiente. Vel ex parte tantum excludit rationem, cujusmodi feritas ex morbo humorum si; depravatione consurgit, qualis soler esse mulierum pica laboriantium, vel ex naturali quadam sive à pri-mis incunabulis orta consuetudine, quæ est vel in-tegrorum populorum nempe eorum, qui in silvis & montibus instar bestiarum oberrant, vel singulo-rum, qui è societate civili præ desperatione civili se subsubducentes instar bestiarum degunt, & vel pilos sibi evellunt, vel ungues erodunt; alii aut corpus proprium suum horribiliter tractant. Philosophus 7.Nic.c.1. & 5. Picolh. prolixe grad. 6: cap.14. Et de hac feritate hoc notandum, quod cum sit aut naturalis aut morbosa licet in se horribil or videatur, tamen est minus malum quam vitium morale. Feritas cum ratione conjuncta dicitur, quam homines patrant ex eminentia quadā vitiosi habitus sine morbo aut barbarie quadam, sive quando nec morbosi sunt, nec in barbarie vivunt. Ejusmodi feritas reperitur in iis qui ex uore inimicorum pascunt oculos, qui se obleCtant aspectu suppliciorum, qui de miseris sumuntur. Tales homines depinxerunt Poëtae, quando dicunt fuisse per veneficium Circes mutatos in feras. Etenim tales, ut Erasmus inquit lib. 2. de copia, praeter hominis nomen nihil habent, sed degenerant libidine in ursos, ferocitate in sues, ferocia in leones, crudelitate in Tigres. Haec feritas tanto deterior vitio habetur morali, quanto altiori gradu illud superat.
units.tr: The opposites of heroic virtue are, in defect, utmost sloth or unfitness for every impulse towards virtue. (Of this vice, since it rarely or never occurs, we shall say nothing further here. For no one is found so dull or stupid in mind that he does not, by natural instinct, sometimes undertake something good and perform some action of virtue, although some are found rarer than others.) In excess there is ferocity or brutishness, Nicomachean Ethics 7, chapter 1. There ferocity is defined as the supreme and extreme vice, by which a man, having cast off the judgement of right reason and abandoned all humanity, commits the most shameful and unspeakable deeds, from which human nature otherwise shrinks. Such were, among the ancients, Sinis, Procrustes and Phalaris, and among the Roman emperors Nero. Now this ferocity is held to be twofold: one kind is without any reason, the other is with reason, but impaired or corrupted. Aristotle, in the place cited; Picolhomineus, degree 6, chapter 14. Ferocity without reason either has no reason at all, as in the ferocity of men suffering from madness or insanity, which men sometimes commit in horrible acts. Such was the ferocity of Hercules, when, seized by fury, he killed his wife and children, as Seneca testifies in Hercules Furens. Such also was the ferocity of Agave, who armed the Thracian women against her son Pentheus and tore him limb from limb. Such too was that of Medea, who, when she saw herself scorned by Jason, slew her own sons. Or it excludes reason only in part, as the ferocity that arises from a disease or corruption of the humours, such as is wont to be found in women suffering from pica, or from some natural custom, or one arising from the earliest upbringing, which is found either in whole peoples, namely those who wander in forests and mountains like beasts, or in individuals who, withdrawing from civil society out of despair, live like beasts, and either tear out their own hair or gnaw their nails, while others handle their own bodies in a horrible way. The Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 7, chapters 1 and 5; Picolhomineus at length, degree 6, chapter 14. And concerning this ferocity it should be noted that, since it is either natural or morbid, although in itself it may seem very horrible, it is nevertheless a lesser evil than moral vice. Ferocity is said to be joined with reason when men commit it out of a certain eminent vicious habit, without disease or any barbarity, that is, when they are neither diseased nor living in barbarism. Such ferocity is found in those who feed their eyes on the blood of their enemies, who delight in the sight of the punishments inflicted on the wretched. Poets depicted such men when they say that they were changed into beasts by the poisons of Circe. For such men, as Erasmus says in De copia, book 2, have nothing but the name of man; they degenerate in lust into bears, in ferocity into swine, in fierceness into lions, in cruelty into tigers. This ferocity is considered so much worse than moral vice as it surpasses it in degree.

units.la: Pro declaranda melius virtutis Heroicae natura adjiciendae erunt quaestiones quaedam. I. Cum haec virtus dicatur cum eminentia quadam transcendere reliquas, quae vulgo dicuntur communes, an virtus moralis recipiat magis & minus? Resp. in utramque partem hoc disputari solet. Nam alii negant propter has rationes: 1. Quia perfectum illud dicitur 7.Phys.Acroas tex.18. 1.de coelo text.12.5 Metaph.text.2. Nic. capp. 7. & 8. cui nihil addi vel demi potest. Quaelibet autem virtus perfecta est, imo ipsa perfectio 1. Nicom. c.13. & lib.2. cap. 6. lib. 4. cap. 3. Non igitur recipiet magis & minus, imò statuere semper unius est, inquit Seneca Epistola 71. 2. Recto nihil rectius, alioquin nihil esset rectum: idem Seneca Epistola 66. Virtus vero dicitur recta, quia est habitus recta cum ratione conjunctus 2. Nicom. cap. 6. Quemadmodum igitur amussim quoquo flectas, flectis incurvas, sic virtus recta linea est, & quorsum flexeris, augendo vel detrahendo nocet. Omnis modus certa mensura est & graduum omnium expers, Cicero lib. 2. & 3. de finibus, Seneca Epistola 66. & 74. & lib. 2. natur. quaest. cap. 34. Virtus autem est mediocritas seu mensura quaedam 2. Nicom. cap. 6. Seneca de vita beata cap. 3. Ergo magis aut minus non recipit. Alii contra affirmant propter has rationes: 1. Quia acquiritur per assuefactionem honestarumque actionum exercitationem. Aristoteles 2. Nicom. cap. 1. Scal. Exerc. 307. sect. 4. Ergo quo major vel minor assuefactio honestarumque exercitatio, eo magis etiam & minus virtutis moralis habitus comparatur. 2. Honor est virtutis praemium 4. Nicom. cap. 8. Atqui non omnes boni viri aeque digni honore censentur. Ergo nec virtus omnibus aequaliter inest. 3. Delectatio qua afficimur in obeundo virtutis munere, est signum habitus contracti 2. Nicom. cap. 3. Atqui haec delectatio non aequalis in omnibus reperitur, siquidem unus magis alter minus actionibus probis delectatur. Ergo nec virtus. 4. Denique in nobis ipsis & aliis deprehendimus virtutem moralem, per gradus recipi & in uno magis, in alio minus esse perfectam. Unde tandem concluditur virtutem moralem ralem recipere magis & minus. Cæterum pro conciliatione harum opinionū distinguendū erit inter perfectionem virtutis essentialem & accidentalem. Secundum priorem non recipit magis & minus, quia quod innuunt argumenta negantis sententiæ unius cujusque rei essentia est certa & definita, & se habet instar numeri, cui sine variatione speciei nihil veladdi vel detrahi potest, ut tradit Aristot. 8. Metaph. cap. 3. Et unicuique est unum & idem esse, & neque intentionem neque remissionem recipit, ut docet Porphyrius cap. de differentia. Secundum posteriorem modum virtus omnio magis & minus recipit, quia per gradus ob actionum aliarumq; circumstantiarum varietatem acquiritur: Unde etiam non solum unum hominem altero, sed etiam unū eundemque hominem seipso alio atque alio tempore consideratō virtuosiorem esse experientia docet. Vide Picolhom. gradu 5. capite 45. Hinc recte Keckerm. in Logicis lib. 1. cap. 9. qualitates magis & minus recipiunt, non ratione essentiæ seu definitionis, quæ nullibi variatur, sed ratione υπόρξεως seu singularis inhæsionis in hoc vel illo subjecto hoc vel illo modo dispositō.
units.tr: To explain more clearly the nature of heroic virtue, some questions must be added. I. Since this virtue is said to surpass the others, which are commonly called ordinary, with a certain eminence, can moral virtue admit of more and less? Reply: this is usually disputed on both sides. For some deny it, for these reasons: 1. Because what is perfect is said to be so in Physics 7, text 18, On the Heavens 1, text 12, Metaphysics 5, text 2, and Nicomachean Ethics, chapters 7 and 8, and nothing can be added to or taken from it. Now every virtue is perfect, indeed perfection itself, Nicomachean Ethics 1, chapter 13, and book 2, cap. 6. lib. 4. cap. 3. Therefore it will not admit of more and less. Rather, as Seneca says, Epistola 71., to set a standard is always the work of one thing only. 2. Nothing is more right than the right; otherwise nothing would be right: Seneca again, Epistola 66. Virtue is called right because it is a habit joined with right reason, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 6. Just as, whichever way you bend a rule, you bend it crooked, so virtue is a straight line, and whichever way you deviate, by increasing or diminishing, you do harm. Every measure is a fixed standard and free of all degrees: Cicero, lib. 2. & 3. de finibus, and Seneca, Epistola 66. & 74. & lib. 2. natur. quaest. cap. 34. Virtue, however, is a mean or a certain measure, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 6; Seneca, On the Happy Life, chapter 3. Therefore it does not admit of more or less. Others, on the contrary, affirm it, for these reasons: 1. Because it is acquired by habituation and by the practice of honourable actions, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 1; Scaliger, Exercitationes 307, section 4. Therefore the greater or lesser the habituation and practice of honourable actions, the greater or lesser the habit of moral virtue acquired. 2. Honour is the reward of virtue, Nicomachean Ethics 4, chapter 8. But not all good men are considered equally worthy of honour. Therefore virtue is not equally present in all. 3. The pleasure we feel in performing the duty of virtue is a sign of an acquired habit, Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 3. But this pleasure is not found equally in all, since one takes more delight in upright actions than another. Therefore neither is virtue equal. 4. Finally, in ourselves and in others we perceive that moral virtue is received by degrees, and is more perfect in one and less perfect in another. From which it is at last concluded that moral virtue admits of more and less. But to reconcile these opinions, a distinction must be made between the essential and the accidental perfection of virtue. In respect of the former, it does not admit of more and less, because, as the arguments of the negative opinion imply, the essence of each thing is fixed and defined, and it stands like a number, to which nothing can be added or taken away without a change of species, as Aristotle teaches, Metaphysics 8, chapter 3. For each thing has one and the same being, and it admits neither intension nor remission, as Porphyry teaches in the chapter on difference. In the latter respect, however, virtue admits of more and less in every way, because it is acquired by degrees on account of the variety of actions and other circumstances. Hence experience teaches that not only one man is more virtuous than another, but also one and the same man is more virtuous at one time than at another, when he is considered in himself. See Piccolomini, degree 5, chapter 45. Hence Keckermann, in his Logic, book 1, chapter 9, rightly says that qualities admit of more and less not by reason of their essence or definition, which never varies, but by reason of their hyparxis, that is, their singular inherence in this or that subject disposed in this or that way.

units.la: Cum virtus consideratur secundum perfectionem suam accidentalem, consideratur vel quatenus omnibus numeris est absoluta, vel quatenus non. Priori modo non recipit magis & minus. Posteriori modo omnino recipit pro intensione seu remissione rerum, quæ ad virtutem vel constituendam vel exercendam requiruntur, & sic unaquæque virtus sola & seorsim consideratā ex circumstanstantiarum varietate magis vel minus cognosci potest.
units.tr: When virtue is considered according to its accidental perfection, it is considered either as it is absolute in every respect or as it is not. In the former way it does not admit of more and less. In the latter way it wholly admits of it, by intension or remission of the things required to constitute or exercise virtue; and so each virtue, considered alone and by itself, can be known to be greater or lesser according to the variety of circumstances.

units.la: II. Hoc etiam commodè quæri potest: An cum, ut ex ante dicta quæstione patet, multi existiment, virtutem non recipere magis & minus, ideo vitia virtutibus opposita sint omnia paria? Resp. Etsi hoc Stoicis placet, non omnibus tamen arridere. Stoici enim, ut testatur Cicero pro Murena, id plane statuebant: Placet inquit Stoicis omnia peccata esse paria, nec minus delinquere eum, qui gallum gallinaceum cum opus non fuerit, quam qui patrem suffocaverit. Laërtius in Zenone cansam addit: Ut enim (ait) verum vero magis tale non est, neque falsum falso, ita nec fraus fraudi, nec peccatum peccato. Nam & qui centum stadiis Canopo abest, & qui uno, pariter non est in Canopo: Sic qui parvum vel magnum deliquit, pariter abest à recto. Apud Ciceronem 4. de finibus alia habetur similitudo. Nihil adjuvat procedere, inquit, & progredi in virtute, quò minus miserrimus sit, priusquam ad eam pervenerit, quoniam in aqua nihilo magis respirant, qui jam ad summitatem appropinquant, quam qui sint in profundo: Et quoniam catuli qui jam despecturi, sunt cæci æquè ut ii qui modo nati. Hanc Stoicorum sententiam sunt quidam Christiani, qui tueri conantur, idque his rationibus: 1. Quia unius reus omnium reus, Jac. 2. vers. 10. 2. Quia puriores Theologi orta nuper luce utiliter dixerunt, nullum peccatum sua natura veniale esse, sed mortifera in se omnia si à Deo judice ponderentur. Nam quæ idem & æquè infinitum objectum lædunt, quidni æqualia. 3. Quia magni usus hoc Paradoxon, & quo nil valentius, quod à flagitiis hominem absterreat. Ille enim resistet peccato, qui novit modum & magnitudinem peccati.
units.tr: II. This question may also conveniently be asked: since, as the preceding question shows, many think virtue does not admit of more and less, are therefore all vices opposed to virtues equal? Reply: although this pleases the Stoics, it does not please everyone. For the Stoics, as Cicero testifies in pro Murena, held exactly this: It pleases the Stoics, he says, that all sins are equal, and that a man who kills a cock when there was no need is no less at fault than one who has suffocated his father. Laertius adds a reason in his life of Zeno: just as truth is not more true than truth, nor falsehood more false than falsehood, so neither is fraud more fraudulent, nor sin more sinful. For whether one is a hundred stades from Canopus or one stade, one is equally not in Canopus. So whoever has done wrong in small things or great is equally distant from the right. Cicero, 4. de finibus, gives another comparison: it is no help, he says, to advance and progress in virtue, so as to be less wretched before one has attained it, since those who are near the surface in the water breathe no more easily than those who are in the depths; and puppies that are about to open their eyes are as blind as those just born. Some Christians try to defend this Stoic opinion, and they do so for these reasons: 1. Because whoever is guilty of one is guilty of all, James 2:10. 2. Because the purer theologians, since the light has lately dawned, have rightly said that no sin is venial by its own nature, but all are deadly in themselves if they are weighed by God as judge. For those which injure the same and equally infinite object, why should they not be equal? 3. Because this paradox is of great use, and nothing is more powerful for keeping a man from wickedness. For he will resist sin who knows the measure and the magnitude of sin.

units.la: 4. Peccare est quasi transfire lineas, aut ut definitur peccatum ab Apostolo ἀνομία 1. Joh. 3.4. Quod si lineas semel transieris, culpa commissa est quam lógè progrediare, quâ semel transieris ad augendam transeundi culpam nihil pertinet. Cicero Parad. 3.
units.tr: 4. To sin is as it were to cross lines, or, as sin is defined by the Apostle, lawlessness [ἀνομία], 1 John 3:4. If you have crossed a line once, the fault is committed, and how far you go on afterwards makes no difference to the guilt of having crossed it once. Cicero, Paradoxes 3.

units.la: 5. Quod non licet, nec magis nec minus fit. Satis enim in eo peccatum si non licet. Cicero loco dicto. At peccare licet nemini, cum nemini liceat esse malum, utpote quod legibus non tantum divinis, sed & humanis prohibetur.
units.tr: 5. What is not permitted is not made more or less so. For in that case the sin is enough, if it is not permitted. Cicero, in the passage cited. But no one is permitted to sin, since no one is permitted to be wicked, as wickedness is forbidden not only by divine law but also by human law.

units.la: 6. Scelera animo æstimantur non eventu, Seneca lib. 16. de benef. cap. 8. Animus enim brutus est ipsa essentia, ut sic loquar vitiorum, sicut recta ratio virtutum. Aristoteles lib. 1. magnor. moral. cap. 4. Imo omnia scelera ante effectum operis quantum culpæ satis est, perfecta sunt. Seneca de constant. sapientis cap. 7.
units.tr: 6. Crimes are judged by the mind, not by the outcome, Seneca, On Benefits book 6, chapter 8. For the wicked mind is itself the very essence, so to speak, of vices, just as right reason is of virtues. Aristotle, Magna Moralia book 1, chapter 4. Indeed, all crimes are complete before the effect of the deed, as far as guilt goes. Seneca, On the Constancy of the Wise Man, chapter 7.

units.la: Hocigitur animo bruto tanquam regula omnia scelera æquantur.
units.tr: Therefore by this wicked mind, as by a rule, all crimes are made equal.

units.la: 7. Nullum scelus habet rationem, non terminatur, non limite distinguitur: Cicero 4. Tusc. quaest. 8. Omnia vitia sunt vacua & orba bonæ mentis. Ergo uti in vacuo, sic neque in vitiis datur ulla differentia propriis & remotioris, quæ cum ira se habeant, sequitur vitia omnia esse paria.
units.tr: 7. No crime has a measure; it is not bounded, it is not distinguished by a limit. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, question 8: All vices are empty and bereft of a good mind. Therefore, just as there is no difference in a vacuum, so neither is there any difference among vices between what is proximate and what is more remote; and since these are related as they are, it follows that all vices are equal.

units.la: Verum pro contraria sententia sunt Phalanges rationum: 1. Quia virtus una altera est præstantior: Unde cum contrariorum eadem sit ratio, sequitur unum vitium esse altero deterius.
units.tr: But for the opposite opinion there is a whole phalanx of arguments: 1. Because one virtue is more excellent than another; hence, since the reasoning for contraries is the same, it follows that one vice is worse than another.

units.la: 2. Quia diversa objecta faciunt etiam diversitatem ipsarum rerum. Ergo & vitia quæ pro objecto habent bent ipsum hominem, graviora erunt iis, quæ pro objecto habent bona hominis externa. 3. In Theologia hoc valde tritum, magis peccasse Judam, qui Christum prodidit, quam Petrum, qui auriculam Malchi abscidit. 4. Si parricidiū nihil differt a promissa cæde, quod volunt Stoici, cur majori pœnæ illud puniturin jure civili, l. 9. ff. de parricid. 5. Sublato peccatorum discrimine tantum abest, ut homines arceantur ab impietate, ut etiam multo magis confirmentur. Quibus enim persuasum est nullum esse peccatorum discrimen, tantidem faciunt parricidium atque simplex homicidium, incestum atque scortationem simplicem, sacrilegium atque furtum commune, quibus omnibus, ut diversum discrimen, sic diversæ statuuntur pœnæ in scripturis. 6. Quia pare desperationis materia habebunt, qui semel tantū carnis illecebris quasi tempestate quadam abrepti in peccatum inciderunt cum illis qui perpetua peccati mancipia fuerunt membra sua tradentes arma injustitiæ: Rom. 6 vers. 13. 7. Ipsi Ethnici hanc opinionem tanquam portentum aliquod exploserunt. Cicero 4. de finibus sub finem & Plutarchus lib. de Stoicis. Et ex Christianis Bellarminus toto lib. 1. de amiss. gratia: Et Goclenius in quaest. Ethic. 59. & 100. 8. Etiam ipsi Stoici, inquit Plutarchus in libello de profectu in virtute, dum clamant, parem esse injustitiam Aristidis & Phalaridis, parem imp. obitatem Melii & Platonis, in vita tamen & rerum usu illos declinant, his adhærent & audiunt. & fidem habent. Vide Lipsium Menudus. lib. 3. diff. penult.
units.tr: 2. Because different objects also make for different kinds of things. So the sins that have human beings themselves as their object will be graver than those that have external goods as their object. 3. It is a commonplace in theology that Judas, who betrayed Christ, sinned more gravely than Peter, who cut off the ear of Malchus. 4. If parricide differs in no way from a murder that has been merely planned, as the Stoics hold, why does civil law punish it with a heavier penalty? (Digest, law 9, de parricidiis.) 5. If the distinction between sins is removed, men are not restrained from impiety at all; rather, they are made far more confident in it. For those who are persuaded that there is no distinction between sins regard parricide and simple homicide as the same, incest and ordinary fornication as the same, sacrilege and common theft as the same. Yet Scripture establishes different penalties for these, corresponding to their different degrees of guilt. 6. Those who have fallen into sin only once, as if swept away by some storm of fleshly desire, will have no cause for despair; and neither will they be placed on the same footing as those who gave their members over as perpetual slaves of sin, offering their limbs as weapons of unrighteousness (Rom. 6.13). 7. Even the heathen themselves rejected this opinion as a monstrous thing: Cicero, De finibus book 4, near the end, and Plutarch in his book On the Stoics. Among Christians, Bellarmine throughout book 1 of De amissione gratiae, and Goclenius in his Quaestiones ethicae 59 and 100. 8. Plutarch, in his little book On progress in virtue, says that the Stoics themselves, while they cry out that the injustice of Aristides and of Phalaris is equal, and that the cruelty of the Melians and of Plato is equal, nevertheless in their lives and in their dealings avoid the former and cling to and listen to and trust the latter. See Lipsius, Manuductio, book 3, the penultimate diatribe.

units.la: Verum diffidentes hæ sententiæ: dhibito distinctioâionum fœdere componi possunt. Peccata enim in se ratione essentiæ & respectu generis considerata, æquè paria dici possunt, quo sensu forte Stoici hoc asseruerunt, interim tamen magna peccatorum inæqualitas deprehenditur, sive diversę peccata inter se conferantur, sive singula seorsim considerentur, suis ipsorum circumstantiis & gradibus, quibus à parvis initiis paulatim assurgunt, quod manifestissimè apparebit, si circumstantiæ personarum, locorum, temporum, rerum & mediorum inspiciantur, & quis, in quem, ubi, quando, quomodo, qua in re, quo animi propósito, & quibus de causis delinquat, consideretur, verbi gratia: ratione personæ, quo quis maiora accepit dona, eo major requiritur gratitudo & obedientia: Et ita gravius peccat Princeps, quà plebejus quisquâ, minister verbi, quà quivis ex auditoribus, senes quam juvenes. Ratione obiecti, quo præstantiora sunt peccatorum objecta, eo ipsa peccata sunt graviora. Sic atrociora peccata in hominum animas quam in corpora incidunt, item in Deum quam in homines, 1. Sam. 2. verf. 25. Hebr. 10. verf. 26. Ratione loci, gravius peccavit Absalom, quod uxores patris stuprarit coram Sole in spectante toto populo, quà si id fecisset clam. Ratione materiæ: Gubernatorum unus navē paleis alter auro onustam obruit, licet pariter utriusque imperitia, hujus tamen culpæ grande momentum materia addit, quam perdidit, cum sic detrimētum maximum Reip. intulerint. Cic. Parad. 3.
units.tr: But these opposing opinions, if they are rightly distinguished, can be reconciled. For sins considered in themselves, according to their essence and in relation to their genus, may indeed be called equal, and in this sense the Stoics perhaps asserted it. Nevertheless, a great inequality of sins is apparent, whether different sins are compared with one another or each is considered separately, with its own circumstances and degrees, by which they rise gradually from small beginnings. This will be most clearly seen if the circumstances of persons, places, times, things and means are examined, and if we consider who sins, against whom, where, when, how, in what matter, with what purpose of mind, and for what causes. For example: in respect of the person, the more gifts someone has received, the greater the gratitude and obedience required of him. Thus a prince sins more gravely than any commoner, a minister of the Word more gravely than any of his hearers, and elders more gravely than the young. In respect of the object, the more excellent the object of a sin, the graver the sin itself. Thus sins that strike against men's souls are more atrocious than those against their bodies, and sins against God more atrocious than those against men (1 Sam. 2.25; Heb. 10.26). In respect of place, Absalom sinned more gravely in that he defiled his father's wives in the sight of the sun, with the whole people looking on, than if he had done it in secret. In respect of the matter: of two pilots, one sinks a ship laden with straw and the other a ship laden with gold. Although both are equally unskilled, the great weight of the matter adds to the guilt of the second, since the cargo he lost was greater and so he inflicted the greatest damage on the commonwealth (Cicero, Paradoxa 3).

units.la: III. An virtus Heroica specie differat à mediocri?
units.tr: III. Does heroic virtue differ in species from ordinary virtue?

units.la: Resp. Discrepantes esse hac de re sententias. Nam sunt, qui statuunt, non differre specie, sed tantum gradu perfectionis accidentalis, sicut fervor a tempore: Et hoc inde probant, quod virtus Heroica nihil aliud sit, quam virtus communis, quatenus adjunctam sibi habet excellentiam & eminentiam quandam. Unde à plerisque culmen, apex, & splendor virtutis communis appellatur. Verum pro contraria opinione sunt hæ rationes: 1. Quia virtus Heroica elevat hominé supra communem naturæ humanæ conditionem. Id autem non facit virtus communis. 2. Quia ex actius, firmius & splendidius finem suum attingit, quam communis. 3. Quia communis in quosl bet homines cadit ratione valentes aut cadere saltem potest: Heroica non item. 4. Quia Heroica à peculiari Dei afflatu in homine excitatur, communis autem non. 5. Quia virtus Heroica præstabilior & honoratior habetur communi. Aristoteles 2. Nicom. cap. 1. 6. Quia feritas specie differt à vitio communi, ut ibidem testatur Philosophus. Proinde cum virtus Heroica opponatur feritati, sequitur illam quoque specie à communi virtute differre, sicut feritas differt à vitio communi. Verior tamen videtur esse illorum sententia, qui gradu, non specie differre contendunt, idque propter duas potissimum rationes: 1. Quia utraque virtus idem habet genus nempe habitum: neque enim casu quodam hæc virtus Heroibus inest, sed multo labore multoque sudore acquiritur, ut exempla Heroum varia docent. 2. Circa idem versantur objectu nempe voluptatem & appetitum rationalem, & ad eundem finem collimant, nempe felicitatem civilem. Plura vide de hac quæstione apud Picolhomineum grad. 6. cap. 4. & 5.
units.tr: Answer: opinions on this question disagree. For some hold that it does not differ in species but only in the degree of its accidental perfection, as warmth differs from heat. They prove this from the fact that heroic virtue is nothing other than common virtue, insofar as it has joined to it a certain excellence and eminence. For this reason it is commonly called the summit, the peak and the splendour of common virtue. But for the contrary opinion the following reasons are offered: (1) Heroic virtue raises a man above the common condition of human nature; ordinary virtue does not do this. (2) It attains its end more actively, more firmly and more splendidly than ordinary virtue does. (3) Ordinary virtue falls, or at least can fall, to any men who are endowed with reason; heroic virtue does not. (4) Heroic virtue is stirred up in a man by a special inspiration of God; ordinary virtue is not. (5) Heroic virtue is regarded as more excellent and more honourable than common virtue (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2, ch. 1). (6) Brutishness differs in species from common vice, as the Philosopher testifies in the same place. Therefore, since heroic virtue is opposed to brutishness, it follows that it also differs in species from common virtue, just as brutishness differs from common vice. Nevertheless, the view of those who contend that it differs in degree and not in species seems the truer, and this for two principal reasons: (1) Both virtues have the same genus, namely a habit. For this heroic virtue is present in heroes not by some chance, but is acquired by great labour and great sweat, as the examples of the heroes variously show. (2) Both are concerned with the same objects, namely pleasure and the rational appetite, and both aim at the same end, namely civil happiness. See more on this question in Piccolomini, Grade 6, ch. 4 and 5.

units.la: IV. An virtus Heroica reperiatur in quibuslibet personis, & an in fœmina? Resp. Quod ad priorem partem quæstionis attinet, sententiam negantem omnes Philosophi defendunt. Nam iis tantum competit, qui & præclaro ingenio & afflatu divino supra vulgus hominum ad conditionem sublimem elevatur. Nam nisi hoc esset virtus Heroica, ne gradu quidem, quod jam probatum fuit, nedum specie à virtute communi differret.
units.tr: IV. Is heroic virtue found in all persons, and is it found in a woman? Answer: As to the first part of the question, all philosophers defend the negative opinion. For it belongs only to those who are raised above the common crowd to a lofty condition by an outstanding intellect and a divine inspiration. For if this were not heroic virtue, it would not differ from common virtue even in degree, which has already been proved, let alone in species.

units.la: Quod ad secundam partem quæstionis, etsi quidam sint, qui in fœminis hanc virtutem reperiri negent, experientia tamen contrarium docet. Nam si natura fœminam solertem, si industria literatam, si educatio piam, si experientia sapientem fecit, quid ni etiam Heroicam virtutem illi concessi? Semiramis, Zenobia & aliæ è vetustate testes citari possunt plane Heroicæ virtutis fœminæ: Et ne longius abeundum sit (cum multa omnis ætatis & temporis exempla suppeditet experientia) in medio prodeat illa Angliæ Regina Elisabetha, cujus ingenii aciem cum promta animi magnitudine ad stuporem usque mirantur, aut saltem mirari debent homines. Verum hac laude spoliari videntur fœminæ ab Aristotele, qui 1. Politic. cap. 4. nulla ratione eam mulierum, quam virorum virtutem esse ait. Res vero tota limitatione determinatur. Nam fœminarum natura dupliciter consideratur, vel ordinarie, quatenus nempe hic sexus masculino inferior habetur, ob temperamentum humidum & frigidum: & sic locum in muliere hæc virtus non habet, utpote quæ respicit ingenium acre, excellens, igneum: Vel Extraordinarie, quatenus nimirum Deus sexum hunc masculis interdum virtutibus exornat, aut ex foeminis viros facit, si non corpore saltem animo. Plura vide apud Picolh. gradu 6. cap. 10. sub finem.
units.tr: As to the second part of the question, although some deny that this virtue is found in women, experience teaches the contrary. For if nature has made a woman clever, if study has made her learned, if education has made her pious, if experience has made her wise, why should she not also be granted heroic virtue? Semiramis, Zenobia and others from antiquity can be cited as women of plainly heroic virtue. And, lest we go too far afield (since experience supplies many examples from every age and time), let us bring forward in the midst of them that Queen Elizabeth of England, whose keenness of mind, together with her ready greatness of spirit, people marvel at even to the point of astonishment, or at least ought to marvel at. Yet women seem to be deprived of this praise by Aristotle, who in Politics 1, ch. 4, says that in no way is it the virtue of women as it is of men. But the whole matter is settled by a distinction. For the nature of women is considered in two ways: either ordinarily, insofar as this sex is regarded as inferior to the male because of its moist and cold temperament; and in this sense this virtue has no place in a woman, since it concerns a keen, excellent and fiery intellect. Or extraordinarily, insofar as God sometimes adorns this sex with manly virtues, or makes women into men, if not in body at least in mind. See more in Piccolomini, Grade 6, ch. 10, near the end.

units.la: V. An Heroes recte aequiparentur Deo? Resp.
