Id plerumque fieri, si non ab Historicis, à Poëtis tamen veteribus, idque propter singulares & divinas virtutes, quas in quibusdam supra vulgus, imo supra excellentissimos quosque reperierunt hominum. Nam Homerus Hectoris enarraturus laudes, Priamum talia fantem introducit:
units.tr: V. Are heroes rightly equated with God? Answer: This is commonly done, if not by historians then at least by the ancient poets, and this on account of the singular and divine virtues which they found in some men above the common crowd, indeed above all the most excellent men. For Homer, about to recount the praises of Hector, introduces Priam speaking thus:

units.la: ᾿Αδρὸς γε ἀνὴρ θνητῶν ... θεοῖς.
units.tr: Truly he was a man ... like the gods. [᾿Αδρὸς γε ἀνὴρ θνητῶν ... θεοῖς.]

units.la: Et plurimos Ethnicarum gentium Heroas Deorum cum hominibus concubitu oriundos credula vetustas credidit, nimirum quia hac virtute praediti magis ad Dei, quam hominis similitudinem accedere videbantur: Et recte quidem. Etenim plerique mortalium mediocres tantum impetus habent & assuefacti sunt, ut actiones virtuti consentaneas mediocres edant, ut in Agamemnone videre licet, qui prudentia militari prae caeteris Graecis excellere videbatur, item in Themistocle Athenien- sium duce celebri. Justitia etiam singularis erat in Aristide & in Catone apud Romanos. Paucissimi reperti sunt, qui ultra hos virtutum gradus niterentur: proinde ob raritatem Heroes illi & Diis geniti, & Diis similiores, quam hominibus vulgo finguntur. Picol. gradu 6. cap. 15. Occasione hujus quaestionis facile cognoscitur, cur novem vulgo statuantur κατ' ἐξοχὴν Heroes apud Judaeos tres Josua, David & Judas Macha chabæus: apud Ethnicos item tres Hector, Alexander Magnus, & Julius Cæsar; apud Christianos itidem tres, Arthurus Britanniæ Rex, Carolus Magnus & Godefredus Bilioneus, in quibus omnia Heroicæ virtutis requisita illuxisse videntur, ut apud Historicos facile depi ehendere licet.
units.tr: And the credulous antiquity believed that many heroes of the heathen nations were born of the union of gods with men, namely because those endowed with this virtue seemed to draw closer to the likeness of God than to that of man. And rightly so. For most mortals have only moderate impulses and are so accustomed that they produce moderate actions consonant with virtue, as one may see in Agamemnone, who seemed to excel the other Greeks in military prudence, and likewise in Themistocles, the famous leader of the Athenians. Among the Romans, Aristides and Cato were also distinguished for singular justice. Very few have been found who strive beyond these grades of virtue; therefore, because of their rarity, those heroes are feigned to be born of gods and to be more like gods than like men, as is commonly imagined. Piccolomini, Grade 6, ch. 15. From the occasion of this question one readily understands why it is commonly stated that nine heroes are preeminent (κατ' ἐξοχὴν): among the Jews, three: Joshua, David and Judas Maccabeus; among the heathen likewise three: Hector, Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar; among Christians again three: Arthur, King of Britain, Charlemagne and Godfrey of Bouillon. In these men all the requisites of heroic virtue seem to have shone forth, as may readily be discovered in the historians.

units.la: VI. Cur filii Heroum noxæ dicantur, & cur multi ex parentibus virtute clarii orti degenerent? Resp. Quod ad priorem partem quæstionis attinet, putant plerique id contingere, quia nutritio liberorum eadem ubique non reperitur: Et quod temperamentum liberis non idem cum parentibus nascatur. 2. Quia magnis negotiis occupati Heroes domesticæ educationis, quam debebant, curam gerere nō possunt. Unde indulgentiore ista & dissolutiore disciplina filii corrupti à virtute patrum degenerant. 3. Vel quia hoc fine Deus talia exempla vult exstare, ut agnoscamus virtutem excellentem non esse rem hæreditariam, sed donum cœleste, quod à Deo sit inprimis petendum atque exspectandum. Pro secunda parte hujus quæstionis eadem penè causæ sunt. Nam non solan tura bonos homines effici omnium scriptorum consensu constat, habilem natura facit, non non dat habitum, inclinat, non cogit, & nisi doctrina & præcepta Philosophiæ & bonorum morum præstò sint, quid mirum, si plerunq; præceps ad malum agatur? 7. Polit. cap. 15. 2. Quia ut Plutarchus ex Xenophonte, inquit: Homines, qui alioqui sunt nobiles & virtuosi, aliquando vel opum ac divitiarum vel pulchritudinis gratia ignobilem & nō bene moratam uxorem sibi adjungunt, quæ cum sit conjun- Kkk &issictissimum quoddam in generatione filiorum principium, ita validissimū esse potest ad naturā eorundem depravandam, si sit mala. 3. Quia non parum momenti ad prolis naturam adfert, quo loco & qua ætate maritalis conjunctio nobilium fiat. Nam non omnis ætas generationi apta reperitur saltem perfectæ, adolescentium fœtus immaturi ut corpore, ita etiam mente esse solent. Extrema quoque senectus ad procreationem minus habetur idonea, sed illaætas, in qua corpus & mens maxime vigent, habetur accommodatissima. 4. Observarunt etiam Medici in ipso generationis actu interdum peccari. Nam sunt, qui languidè & ofc tanter, sunt, qui ebrii, sunt, qui non adeo intenta in rem ipsam mente actum hunc exercet, quorum fœtus à natura & indole parentum degenerare solet, ut experientia docet. 5. Et hoc simul considerandum, quod sicut omnium rerum, ita quoque e Prosapiarum vicissitudo sit in hoc mundo, nec velit Deus, ut semper una vel altera familia emineat, reliquæ pulvere quasi obsitæ in obscuro semper latitent: ideo familiæ alicujus splendorem obliteraturus Deus, & eam ad viliorem conditionem redacturus, Heroicos illos spiritus ipsi admit, unde paulatim ipsam inclinare & in pejus ruere necesse erit: aliam contra nova aliqua luce irradiaturus, novis simul dotibus ornat, ut præclaras concipiat virtutum flammas, quibus ad magnos honores posteritati ejus aditus paratur. Exemplum singulare videre licet in familia Turcarū Hottomannica, quā intra paucos annos ex pastoribus & latronib. ad eam dignitatem Deus evexit, ut non modo Europæ topæ, sed Asiæ & Africæ etiam summo terrori & horrori sit, & Monarchicum trium orbis terrarum partium sceptrum gerat.
units.tr: VI. Why are the sons of heroes said to be worthless, and why do many born of parents distinguished by virtue turn out degenerate? Answer. As regards the first part of the question, most think this happens because the upbringing of children is not the same everywhere, and because children are not born with the same temperament as their parents. 2. Because heroes, occupied with great affairs, cannot give the care to domestic education that they ought. Hence sons, corrupted by this more indulgent and loose discipline, degenerate from the virtue of their fathers. 3. Or because God wishes such examples to exist for this purpose: that we may recognise that excellent virtue is not an inherited thing but a heavenly gift, which must be sought and awaited from God above all. For the second part of the question the causes are almost the same. For it is agreed by the consensus of all writers that good men are not made by nature alone. Nature makes a person apt; it does not give the habit; it inclines, it does not compel. Unless the teaching and precepts of philosophy and of good morals are at hand, what wonder if a person is often driven headlong to evil? 7. Politics, ch. 15. 2. Because, as Plutarch says after Xenophon: men who are otherwise noble and virtuous sometimes take to themselves, for the sake of wealth or riches or beauty, a wife who is of humble birth and not well brought up. Since marriage is a most powerful principle in the begetting of children, it can be so strong in depraving their nature, if she is bad. 3. Because the place and the age at which a noble marriage takes place contribute no small weight to the nature of the offspring. For not every age is found fit for generation, at least not a perfect one: the offspring of adolescents are usually immature in body and likewise in mind. Extreme old age too is held less suitable for procreation, but that age in which body and mind are at their strongest is held most suitable. 4. Physicians have also observed that sin is sometimes committed in the very act of generation. For some perform it languidly and carelessly, some when drunk, some whose mind is not intent on the act itself; and their offspring tend to degenerate from the nature and disposition of the parents, as experience teaches. 5. And this must be considered at the same time: as with all things, so too in this world there is a succession of lineages, and God does not wish one family or another always to stand out while the rest lie hidden in obscurity, as if covered with dust. So God, about to obliterate the splendour of some family and reduce it to a humbler condition, withdraws from it those heroic spirits, whence it must gradually decline and fall into worse. On the other hand, about to irradiate another family with some new light, he adorns it at the same time with new gifts, so that it conceives brilliant flames of virtue, by which access to great honours is prepared for its posterity. A singular example may be seen in the Ottoman family of the Turks, which within a few years God raised from shepherds and robbers to such dignity that it is the object of the greatest terror and horror not only to the parts of Europe but also to Asia and Africa, and holds the monarchical sceptre of the three parts of the world.

units.la: VII. An Heroum exitus raro sint felices, & cur? Resp.
units.tr: VII. Whether the ends of heroes are rarely happy, and why? Answer.

units.la: Plena sunt historiarum volumina de infelici & tristi Heroum exitu, ut in Alexandro, Julio Cæsare & Cyro videre est, cujus causas investiganti variæ occurrunt: 1. Quia Heroes igneæ sunt naturæ, & ob spirituum copiam varios sentiunt impetus, quorum vehementia abripiuntur, & à vera rationis norma deflectentes in miseriarum abyssum præcipitantur. 2. Quia magnitudine invidiæ tanquam mole quadam premuntur, siquidem idem est invidiæ, qui virtutis gradus, & ab invidis in magnas calamitates conjiciuntur, quod exemplum Scipionis & aliorum testatur. 3. Quia multis periculis & insidiis scilicet obnoxii quibus non raro solent opprimi. Tantò igitur ardentius orare debent Heroes, ut à Deo regantur & dirigantur, ne in miseros & infelices hujusmodi exitus incidant.
units.tr: Histories are full of the unhappy and sad ends of heroes, as can be seen in Alexander, Julius Caesar and Cyrus. Investigating their causes, various ones present themselves: 1. Because heroes are of a fiery nature and, on account of their abundance of spirits, feel various impulses, by whose vehemence they are swept away, and, deviating from the true norm of reason, are plunged into the abyss of miseries. 2. Because they are weighed down by the greatness of envy as by a certain mass, since the degree of envy is the same as the degree of virtue, and they are cast by the envious into great calamities, as the example of Scipio and others attests. 3. Because they are liable to many dangers and plots, by which they are often overwhelmed. Therefore heroes ought all the more fervently to pray that they be ruled and directed by God, lest they fall into such wretched and unhappy ends.

units.la: VIII. An Heroibus omnia sint faciliora & proclíviora quam aliis? Et affirmatur propter istas rationes: 1. Quia non tantum peculiari naturæ instinctu & impetu feruntur ad agendum, sed etiam singulari Dei afflatu & ductu. 2. Quia vehementissimo ardent amore & desiderio virtutis & honestatis, quo excitantur ad agendum. 3. Quia opportunitates & occasiones rerum gerendarum majores habent, quam alii homines. 4. Quia felicitatem & successum majorem quam alii in agendo à Deo consequuntur, ita ut felicissimè illis succedant omnia, quæ aliis hominibus nunquam succederie voluerunt. 5. Quia nullis voluptatum illecebris à proposito & conatu abstrahuntur, nullis molestiis & difficultatibus retardantur, sed omne, quod ipsis obiistit, strenuè perun̄punt. 6. Quia adversissima quæque & quibus alii homines succumbunt miserrimè, cum admiratione perferunt, atq; ita humanam conditionē vincunt, ut et in summis miseriis decus tū personæ tū virtutis suæ tueantur. Hinc etiam fit ut cum Deus aliquid singulare & admirandum in Ecclesia, Scholis & Rebuipublicis vult efficere, tum excitat Heroica ingenia, quorum opera præter omnium spem & expectationem celeriter & felicitèr id perficiat.
units.tr: VIII. Whether all things are easier and more inclined for heroes than for others? It is affirmed for these reasons: 1. Because they are carried to act not only by a peculiar instinct and impulse of nature but also by a singular inspiration and guidance of God. 2. Because they burn with the most vehement love and desire for virtue and honour, by which they are roused to act. 3. Because they have greater opportunities and occasions for accomplishing things than other men. 4. Because in acting they obtain from God greater felicity and success than others, so that all things succeed for them most happily, things which never succeeded for other men, however much they wished. 5. Because they are not drawn away from their purpose and endeavour by any allurements of pleasure, nor delayed by any troubles or difficulties, but strenuously break through whatever stands in their way. 6. Because they bear the most adverse things, by which other men are most wretchedly overcome, with admiration, and so conquer the human condition that even in the greatest miseries they preserve the honour both of their person and of their virtue. Hence it also happens that when God wishes to bring about something singular and admirable in the Church, in schools and in commonwealths, he then rouses heroic talents, through whose work he accomplishes it quickly and happily, beyond all hope and expectation.

units.la: IX. An feritas sit deterior vitio communi? Statuitur thesis affirmativa propter has rationes:
units.tr: IX. Is savagery worse than common vice? The affirmative is maintained for these reasons:

units.la: 1. Quia id est deterius, quod præstantiori opponitur. Feritas autem opponitur virtuti Heroicæ, quæ præstantior est virtute communi innuente Philosopho 7. Nicom. cap. 1. 2. Quia feritas hominem omni recta ratione usu privat, eumq; infra humanam conditionē depressum belua in summo gradu assimilat. Vitium autem commune hoc non facit. 3. Quia feritas tantum cadit in homines insigni scelerum turpitudine notatos, vitium autem commune non item. Sed contra objicitur: Si homo vitiosus, qua vitiosus, deterior sit quavis bestia, teste Aristotele cap. 6 lib. 7. Nicomach. Sequitur vicium commune deterius esse feritate? Resp. Feritatem esse triplicem, ut jam diximus, aliam naturalem, aliam morbosam, aliam moralem. Vitium quidem commune esse deterius feritate naturali & morbosa, non autem est deterius feritate morali, siquidem hæc sua pravitate superet non modo vicium commune, sed omne id, quod ab hominibus in communi forte collocatis, excogitari possit. Plura qui legere volet de virtute Heroica, Picolhomineum consulat toto gradu sexto.
units.tr: (1) That which is opposed to something more excellent is worse. Savagery, however, is opposed to heroic virtue, which is more excellent than common virtue, as the Philosopher indicates in Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 1. (2) Savagery deprives a man of all right reason and its use, and, sinking him below the human condition, makes him resemble a beast at its highest degree. Common vice does not do this. (3) Savagery befalls only those marked by notorious baseness of crimes, whereas common vice does not. But it is objected: if a vicious man, insofar as he is vicious, is worse than any beast, as Aristotle testifies in Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 6, does it follow that common vice is worse than savagery? Answer: savagery is threefold, as we have already said: one natural, another morbid, another moral. Common vice is indeed worse than natural and morbid savagery, but it is not worse than moral savagery, since this surpasses in its depravity not only common vice but everything that men placed in the common lot could devise. Whoever wishes to read more on heroic virtue should consult Piccolomini, the whole of grade six.

units.la: De Amicitia.
units.tr: On Friendship.

units.la: HUcusq; de virtutibus moralibus seorsim & per se: Nunc de earum unione & conspiratione quadam tractandum videtur, quæ unio vulgo Amicitia dicitur, de qua agit Philosophus lib. 8. & 9. Nos breviter tantum ad mentem Philosophi, hoc ordine eam persequemur, ut 1. De nominis origine agamus, & quot modis hoc nomen sumatur. 2. Quæ sint veræ ipsius causæ. 3. Quomodo generaliter definiri debeat. 4. De speciebus amicitiæ, quas singillatim cum suis definitionibus & proprietatibus explicabimus. 5. Quæ sit dia & officia amicus amico præstare debeat, ad colendam & conservandam amicitiam, inprimis vero honestam. 6. Variæ pro natura amicitiæ illustranda discuriendæ veniunt quæstiones. Quod ad primum, dicitur Amicitia ab amore, ut aliquot in locis docet Cicero, nempe in Dialogo de Amicitia: 1. de natura Deorum, & 2. de finibus. Sumitur vero nomen Amicitiæ duobus modis, late sive impropriè, & stricte sive proprie. Impropriè seu late. 1. Pro συμπαθεία quadam naturali sive illa sit inter res inanimatas ut inter metalla amicitia quædam reperitur, ut inter plumbum & stannum, sive inter res animatas ratione carentes, ut inter herbas & plantas & varia animalia, de quorum συμπαθεία gunt Physici, & egregie Erasmus in Dialogo de amicitia. 2. Amicitia late sumitur pro cognatione naturali, cujusmodi est inter parentes & liberos, inter fratres & sorores, aliósve consanguineos. 2. Pro conjunctione voluntaria vel coniugium, ut inter maritum & uxorem, vel affinium, vel civium, vel contribulium, &c. quo seníu Philosophus 8. Nicomach. cap. 9. dicit in omni societate esse aliquod jus & aliquam amicitiam: Imò tantum esse amicitiæ quantum juris: Idcirco eodem cap. aliquot argumentis confirmat Amicitiam nihil aliud esse quam societatem & communionem hominum inter se.
units.tr: Hitherto we have treated the moral virtues separately and in themselves. Now it seems right to treat of a certain union and conspiring of them, which union is commonly called friendship, and of which the Philosopher treats in Books 8 and 9. We shall pursue it briefly, following the mind of the Philosopher, in this order: 1. We shall discuss the origin of the name and the ways in which the name is used. 2. What its true causes are. 3. How it ought to be defined in general. 4. The kinds of friendship, which we shall explain one by one with their definitions and properties. 5. What duties and services a friend ought to render to a friend in order to cultivate and preserve friendship, especially honourable friendship. 6. Various questions arise which must be discussed to illustrate the nature of friendship. As to the first, friendship is said to derive from love (amor), as Cicero teaches in several places, namely in his dialogue On Friendship, and in On the Nature of the Gods, book 1, and On Ends, book 2. The name friendship is taken in two ways: broadly or improperly, and strictly or properly. Improperly or broadly: 1. For a certain natural sympathy (συμπάθεια), whether it is found among inanimate things, as a certain friendship is found between metals, for example between lead and tin, or among living things lacking reason, such as herbs and plants and various animals, about whose sympathy the natural philosophers write, and Erasmus admirably in his dialogue On Friendship. 2. Friendship is taken broadly for natural kinship, such as exists between parents and children, between brothers and sisters, or other blood relations. 2. For voluntary union or association, such as between husband and wife, between relations by marriage, fellow citizens, fellow tribesmen, and so on. In this sense the Philosopher, in Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 9, says that in every society there is some right and some friendship; indeed, there is as much friendship as there is right. Hence in the same chapter he confirms by several arguments that friendship is nothing other than the society and communion of men with one another.

units.la: Proprie vero seu strictè sumitur Amicitia pro relatione sive habitudine unius amici ad alium, dum unus cum alio in consensu voluntatis & actionum conspirat, & hoc sensu de eo hîcagitur.
units.tr: Properly or strictly, however, friendship is taken for the relation or disposition of one friend toward another, when one agrees with the other in the consent of the will and in actions. It is in this sense that we are concerned here.

units.la: Causæ verò amicitiæ sunt maximè duplices: Efficiens & Finis. (Nam de formali & materiali in qua, sive subjecto, ubi de Definitione agendum fuerit.) Quod ad efficientę, etsi omnes eam dari affirmant, tamen quanquam illa sit, nô satis inter Philos. convenit. Alii enim statuunt oriri ex indigentia, ut Plato in Lysíde sub finem illius Dialogi, & adfert rationes duas: 1. Quia nemo amicitiam cum alio contrahit, nisi aliquod in eo bonum appetat. Omnis autem appetitio præsupponit indigentiam ejus, quod appetitur. Unde Socrates apud Platonem in Convivio fingit ποῖον, id est, paupertatem seu indigentiam, esse matrem amoris. 2. Quia sine amicitia nemo potest bene beateq; vivere, propterea quod illa explcat indigentiam boni ad bene beateque vivendum necessarii. Vide Picolhom. cap. 5 grad. 7. Alii ex similitudine vitæ & morum oriri contendunt, propter pter has causas: 1. Quia simile amat simile, & ut Cicero ait in Dial. de amicit. nihil amabilius, nihil copulatius quam morum similitudo bonorum. Unde etiam ab eodem ea dicitur amicitia jucundissima, quæ similitudo morum conjugavit. 2. Qua dissimilitudo vitæ & morum est causa corrumpens amicitiæ. Ergo similitudo est ejusdem causa procreas. Alii ex boni in aliis cogniti approbatione & appetitione, five illud bonum fit verum bonum, five apparens, & rursus five honestum five utile five jucundum. Et pro hac opinione sunt rationes etiam duæ: 1. Quia nulla est vera amicitia absque amore. Amor autem oritur ex boni in alio cogniti approbatione & appetitione. 2. Quia immediatè oritur ex mali in alio cogniti aversatione & fuga. Ita tamen in causis procedendum videtur, ut procreantes amicitiæ causæ statuantur, aut per fe & primaria aut per accidens & secundaria. Primaria sunt ipsa natura: unde ἀνθρωπῷ φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον dicitur 1. Nicom. cap. 7. 1. Polit. cap. 2. Natura ipsa dux est ad benevolentiam præcedes judicium, & amicitiæ seminarium inserit, sicut præclarè docet Plutar. Φιλαδελφίας. 3. Ætqualitas & similitudo ætatis, ingenii studiorum & inprimis morum & virtutis. Nam idem velle atq; idem nolle, ea demum firma amicitia est, ut inquit Comicus. 3. Conversatio, convictus & consuetudo, cujus ea vis est, ut non corporis modo, sed & animi habitum immutet ad rei amatæ formam. Unde sæpius fit, ut homines diverfiffimis ingeniis non raro firmissimas inter fe colant amicitias. 4. Propinquitas & cognatio. Nam, ut inquit Cicero, pro Rofcio Comado, multum
units.tr: The causes of friendship are chiefly twofold: efficient and final. (The formal and material cause, that is, the subject in which friendship inheres, we shall take up when we come to the definition.) As to the efficient cause, although all affirm that there is one, the philosophers do not agree sufficiently on what it is. Some hold that it arises from need, as Plato does at the end of his dialogue Lysis, and he gives two reasons: 1. No one enters into friendship with another unless he desires some good in him. Every appetite, however, presupposes a lack of what is desired. Hence Socrates in Plato's Symposium pretends that Poros [πόρος], that is, poverty or need, is the mother of love. 2. Without friendship no one can live well and happily, since friendship supplies the lack of the good necessary for living well and happily. See Piccolomini, ch. 5, grade 7. Others maintain that friendship arises from similarity of life and character, for these reasons: 1. Like loves like, and, as Cicero says in the dialogue On Friendship, nothing is more lovable or more binding than the similarity of good characters. Hence the same author calls that friendship most delightful which the similarity of characters has joined. 2. Dissimilarity of life and character is a cause that corrupts friendship; therefore similarity is the cause that produces it. Others hold that it arises from the approval and desire of a good known in another, whether that good is a true good or an apparent one, and again whether it is honourable, useful or pleasant. For this opinion there are also two reasons: 1. There is no true friendship without love, and love arises from the approval and desire of a good known in another. 2. It arises immediately from the aversion and flight from an evil known in another. Yet it seems that in causes one must proceed so that the causes producing friendship are set down either as per se and primary, or as per accidens and secondary. The primary cause is nature itself; hence man is called by nature a political animal [ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον], Nicomachean Ethics 1, ch. 7, and Politics 1, ch. 2. Nature itself is the guide to benevolence, preceding judgement, and plants the seed of friendship, as Plutarch teaches admirably in his work On Brotherly Love. 3. Equality and similarity of age, of talents, of studies, and above all of character and virtue. For "to will the same things and to refuse the same things, that is at last a firm friendship," as the comic poet says. 3. Conversation, living together and custom, whose force is such that it changes not only the body but also the habit of the mind, to the form of the beloved thing. Hence it often happens that men of very different talents not rarely cultivate most firm friendships with one another. 4. Nearness and kinship. For, as Cicero says in Pro Roscio Comoedo, the bond of blood counts for much, and we all experience this through a certain instinct of nature. Secondary causes, however, can be various, above all utility. For, as Cicero says in Laelius, most people love their friends chiefly as cattle, from whom they hope to gain the greatest profit. 2. Need, of which we spoke above in discussing Plato's opinion. 3. Pleasure: for scarcely any other cause instils in the minds of young people a desire for company and familiarity than mutual delight. 4. Abundance of goods: as flies fly to the smell of the kitchen, so not a few friends flock to the smoking fragrance of fortune. 5. Shared fellowship in honours, in circumstances as prosperous as adverse: thus those who have together suffered shipwreck or endured the same chains readily love one another. 6. Praise: whence Isocrates' precept to Demonicus, that one should praise the man whose friendship one seeks, because praise is the beginning of friendship, as blame is of enmity. See Piccolomini, grade 7, ch. 2.

units.la: 1. Quia ... (marginal numerals 1–4 are printed in the text itself as section markers and are copied above as they stand.) tum valet sanguinis cognatio: Et hoc in stinctu quodam naturae experimur omnes. Secundaria autem causae possunt esse variae, inprimis utilitas. Nam, ut inquit Cicero, in Lelio, plerique amicos tanquam pecudes pottissimum diligunt, ex quibus speranr se maximum fructum esse capturos. 2/ Indigentia, de qua supra egimus, ubi de Platonis opinione. 3. Voluptas: neque enim causa fere alia conversationis & familiaritatis juvenum animis instillat desiderium, quam mutua oblectatio. 4./Bonorum affluentia. Ut enim muscae ad culinae nidorem advolant. Ita amici haud pauci ad fortunae odorem fumigantem. 5/ Societas in honoribus, in rebus tam secundis quam adversis. Sic qui simul fecere naufragium vel unam pertulerunt vincula facile amant se invicem. 6. Laus: unde illud Isocratis ad Demonicum praeceptum: Ut cujus amicitiam ambit, illum laudet, propterea quod laus sit amicitiae initium, sicut vituperatio simultatum. Vide Picolhom. gradu 7. cap. 2.
units.tr: 1. Because ... the bond of blood counts for much, and we all experience this through a certain instinct of nature. Secondary causes, however, may be various, above all utility. For, as Cicero says in Laelius, most people love friends chiefly as cattle, from whom they hope to reap the greatest profit. 2. Need, of which we spoke above, in discussing Plato's opinion. 3. Pleasure: for scarcely any other cause instils in the minds of young people a desire for company and familiarity than mutual delight. 4. Abundance of goods: as flies fly to the smell of the kitchen, so many friends fly to the smoking scent of fortune. 5. Shared fellowship in honours, in prosperous as well as adverse circumstances: those who have together suffered shipwreck or endured the same chains readily love one another. 6. Praise: whence Isocrates' precept to Demonicus, that one should praise the man whose friendship one seeks, because praise is the beginning of friendship, as blame is of enmity. See Piccolomini, grade 7, ch. 2.

units.la: Ut de efficiente sic de finali causa inter Philosophos non satis convenit. Nam quidam finem contendunt esse voluptatem, quae ex mutua animorum connexione percipitur: quidam dicunt amantem optare, ut cum amet vice versa ametur. Plato in convivio una cum Diotima ait, amantem optare ex pulchro aliquid procreare pro sui aeternitate. Sed cum Aristophane, inquit, amantem expetere unionem aut unitionem cum amato. Peripatetici dicunt amanti optare id bonum, quod ex unione in nos redundat. Picolh. cap. 4. gradu 7. Alii vero vitae honestae bonarumque conjunctionem, ut idem testatur cap. 3. Alii vero boni in alio cogniti approbati & cupiti adeptionem & fruitionem, quarum opinionum haec ultima videtur maxime vera esse. Nulla enim amicitia vel conservatur, nisi eo fine, ut amici bonum in aliis amicis cognitum approbatum & desideratum adipiscantur, eq; cum voluptate quadā fruantur.
units.tr: As with the efficient cause, so with the final cause the philosophers do not agree sufficiently. For some contend that the end is the pleasure perceived from the mutual connection of souls; others say that the lover desires that, loving in return, he may be loved in turn. Plato, in the Symposium, together with Diotima, says that the lover desires to beget something beautiful for the sake of his own immortality. But, he says, with Aristophanes, the lover seeks union or fusion with the beloved. The Peripatetics say that the lover desires that good which flows back to us from the union. See Piccolomini, ch. 4, grade 7. Others say it is the conjunction of an honourable life and goods, as the same author testifies in ch. 3. Others say it is the attainment and enjoyment of a good known, approved and desired in another, and of these opinions this last seems most true. For no friendship is preserved unless for this end: that friends obtain the good known, approved and desired in one another, and enjoy it with a certain pleasure.

units.la: Haecde causis: Tertiò consideranda venit Definitio: Et varie à variis definitur. Plato in Lysíde definit amicitiam, quod sit ex indigentia consurgens appetitio illius, quod proprium ac cognatum est. Sed haec definitio late patet: Nam & omni amori competit. Cicero lib. de amicit. dixit primò amicitiam esse voluntatem studiorum sententiarumq; summam consensionem. 2 Eam esse omnium divinarum humanarumque rerum cum benevolentia & charitate summam connexionem. Ubi Cicero potius amicitiae fructum, quam essentiā & principia eam constituentia explicat. Praeterea minus recte cum amicitia humana permisceat divinam. D. Augustinus in lib. de amicit. (si modo ille illius sit) inquit: Ego amicitiam nihil aliud esse credo, quam inter duos tantam voluntatum societatem, ut nihil velit unus, quod alter nolit, & ea sit inter utrosq; in bonis malisque consensio, ut nos spes, non sensus, non honor, non quicquam, quod alterius sit, alteri denegetur ad utendum, ut unusquisque, sicut erga se, ita afficiatur erga proximum: in omni officio & obsequio, quod rependant invicem: quae verba quandam amicitiae potius descriptionem, quam veram definitionem continent. Aristoteles 8. Nicom. cap. 2. sic describit: quod sit benevolentia mutua & mi-
units.tr: So much concerning causes. Third, we come to the definition, and it is defined in various ways by various writers. Plato, in the Lysis, defines friendship as an appetite arising from need for that which is one's own and kindred. But this definition is too broad, for it also applies to every love. Cicero, in his book On Friendship, first says that friendship is a goodwill toward pursuits and opinions, and the highest agreement of minds. Second, he says it is the closest bond between all divine and human things, joined with goodwill and affection. Here Cicero explains the fruit of friendship rather than its essence and the principles that constitute it. Moreover, he wrongly mingles human friendship with divine. Saint Augustine, in his book On Friendship (if indeed it is his), says: "I believe friendship is nothing other than such a sharing of wills between two people that neither wills anything the other does not will, and such agreement between them in good and evil that neither hope, nor feeling, nor honour, nor anything that belongs to one is denied to the other for their use, so that each is disposed toward the neighbour as toward himself, in every duty and service that they render to one another." These words contain a description of a kind of friendship rather than a true definition. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 2, describes it thus: that it is a mutual goodwill and affection, begun for the sake of virtue, pleasure, or utility.

units.la: Kkk 5 seita festa vel virtutis vel voluptatis vel utilitatis causa cœcepta: cum qua definitione sensu pene congruit illa Keckermanni: quod sit unio duorum vel plurium in aliquo bono morali nempe honesto, jucundo & utili, lib.3. fyst. Eth. c. penult. Hæc definitio causam formalem includit nempe unionem, & subjectum nempe duos vel plures honestatis studiosos, & finem etiam nempe conspirationem in bono morali: peccat in hoc tantum, quod in definitione includat divisionem; quem errorem taxat Arist. 4. Top. cap. 2.
units.tr: This definition agrees almost exactly in sense with that of Keckermann: that it is a union of two or more persons in some moral good, namely the honourable, the pleasant and the useful. Keckermann, Systema ethicae, book 3, near the end of the chapter. This definition includes the formal cause, namely the union; the subject, namely two or more who pursue honour; and the end, namely a shared pursuit of moral good. It errs only in this, that it includes division within the definition, which error Aristotle censures in Topics 4, ch. 2.

units.la: Species amicitiæ sunt perfecta & imperfecta. In perfecta hæc perpendenda sunt: 1. Definitio. 2. Proprietates quæ illi competunt. Philosophus 8. Nicom. cap. 4. Definitur perfecta unio duorum sibi mutuo notorum, orta ex mutua & efficaci benevolentia, quam peperit consensus in vera virtute morali, ad exercitia virtutis facilius & rectius obeunda: vel ut Picolhomineus definit cap. 3 gradu 7. Est proborum hominum mutuus, conspicuus confirmatusque amor ex probitatis cognitione cosurgens ad vitæ honestæ conjunctionem. Dicitur hæc amicitia perfecta, quia versatur inter vere bonos, & tendit ad bonum perfectius, nempe ad honestatem, quam sic includit, ut jucunditatem & utilitatem non excludat. Amicitia completitur in se omnia φιλητά, nempe honestum, jucundum & utile, Aristoteles lib. 8. Nic. cap. 3. subjiem fere. Perfectæ hujus amicitiæ proprietates sunt variæ: 1. Quod sit bonorum tantum. Nam fundamentum in sola virtute habet, & quod sit virtute tantum similium. Philosophus 4. cap. 8. Nicom. Cicero 1. officior. Et per proprietatem hanc perfectam ab imimperfecta distinguit Philosophus loco cit. quod scilicet imperfecta inter virtute dissimiles, & malos interdum esse possit: perfecta non possit. II. Quod sit admodum rara, cujus rationes lib. 8. cap. 3. duas adfert Philosophus: 1. Quia tantum est inter bonos; bonorum autem virorum magna est raritas & exiguus numerus juxta illud Poëtæ:
units.tr: There are two species of friendship, perfect and imperfect. In perfect friendship the following must be weighed: 1. the definition; 2. the properties that belong to it. The Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 4, defines it as the perfect union of two people who are known to each other, arising from mutual and effective goodwill, which consent in true moral virtue has produced, so that the exercises of virtue may be performed more easily and rightly. Or, as Piccolomini defines it, ch. 3, grade 7: it is the mutual, conspicuous and strengthened love of upright men, arising from the knowledge of uprightness, which leads to the partnership of an honourable life. This friendship is called perfect because it exists between truly good people and tends toward a more perfect good, namely honour, which it so includes that it does not exclude pleasure and utility. Friendship in itself comprises all the lovable things [φιλητά], namely the honourable, the pleasant and the useful, as Aristotle says in Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 3, near the middle. The properties of this perfect friendship are various. 1. It is only of good people. For it has its foundation in virtue alone, and only between those alike in virtue. The Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 4, ch. 8; Cicero, On Duties 1. And by this property the Philosopher, in the passage cited, distinguishes perfect from imperfect friendship: imperfect friendship can exist between people unlike in virtue, and even with bad people, while perfect friendship cannot. II. It is very rare. The Philosopher, in book 8, ch. 3, gives two reasons for this: 1. Because it exists only among good people, and good men are very rare and few in number, according to the poet's line:

units.la: Rari quippe boni numero sunt vix totidem, quot Thebarum portæ, vel divitis oflia Nili.
units.tr: For good men are rare indeed; there are scarcely as many as the gates of Thebes, or the mouths of rich Nile.

units.la: 2. Quia ratio quis tam diu vivit, ut eum possimus exacte explorare. Hinc Cicero: Ex omnibus seculis vix tria aut quatuor paria amicorum reperta fuerunt, hæc tamen paria amicorum vulgò à veteribus numerantur: 1. Theseus & Perithous. 2. Achilles & Patroclus. 3. Orestes & Pilades. 4. Damon & Pythias. 5. Æneas & Achates. 6. Nisus & Euryalus. 7. Lælius & Scipio. 8. Cicero & Atticus. In sacris literis est celebre par Jonathan & David 1.Reg. 18. Et inter Christianos Gregorius & Basilius Nanzian.
units.tr: 2. Because it requires that one live so long that we can examine him exactly. Hence Cicero: "Among all the ages, scarcely three or four pairs of friends have been found." Yet these pairs are commonly reckoned by the ancients as: 1. Theseus and Perithous; 2. Achilles and Patroclus; 3. Orestes and Pylades; 4. Damon and Phintias; 5. Aeneas and Achates; 6. Nisus and Euryalus; 7. Laelius and Scipio; 8. Cicero and Atticus. In Holy Scripture a famous pair is Jonathan and David, 1 Reg. 18. And among Christians, Gregory and Basil of Nazianzus.

units.la: III. In amicitia perfecta non recipiuntur, nisi quorum virtus longo tempore est explorata, ut hoc modo scilicet omnis dubitandi ansa abscindatur. Nam experientia filia temporis res certissimè explorare solet. Aristoteles loco cit. Cicero in Læl. Seneca epist. 3.
units.tr: III. Only those whose virtue has been tested over a long time are admitted into perfect friendship, so that by this means every occasion for doubt is cut away. For experience, the daughter of time, is wont to test things most certainly. Aristotle, in the passage cited; Cicero, On Friendship; Seneca, Letter 3.

units.la: IV. Quod quamvis sit firma & stabilis, difficulter tamen possit, si vel alter amicorum deserta virtute perversè improbus evaserit, vel virtute rebus gestis aut aliis bonis itaque alterum superavevit, ut propter mutatum viræ institutum una vivere commodè, mutuaque officia exercere non possint. V. In hac nullius solet esse locus querelis, calumniis, suspicionibus, aut injuriis, cujus rationes Philosophus 8. Nicom. cap. 4. reddit has: 1. Quia non facile quicquam alicui de eo creditur, quem ipse diu probaris aut spectaris. 2. Quia amicus verus vero amico maxime credit. 3. Quia ab utroq; summa diligentia adhibetur, ne alter ab altero injuria afficiatur. Conglutinat enim amicitia amicorum officia, ut certent inter se officiis, offensiones autem abominentur. Et cap 13. ejusdem lib. probat, quod in hac amicitia nullae oriantur querelae, quia amicus amico servat aequalitatem, & potius amicum sibi quam se amico praeferre conatur.
units.tr: IV. Although it is firm and stable, it can with difficulty continue if either friend abandons virtue and turns wickedly bad, or if one surpasses the other in achievements or other goods, so that because of a changed way of life they cannot live together comfortably and perform mutual duties. V. In this friendship there is usually no place for complaints, slanders, suspicions or injuries. The Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 4, gives these reasons: 1. Because one does not easily believe anything against a person whom one has long tested and observed. 2. Because a true friend believes a true friend most fully. 3. Because each takes the greatest care that the other is not wronged. For friendship binds the duties of friends together, so that they vie with one another in duties, and they shrink from offences. And in ch. 13 of the same book he shows that in this friendship no quarrels arise, because a friend keeps equality with a friend and strives to prefer his friend to himself rather than himself to his friend.

units.la: Altera amicitiae species est imperfecta amicitia, quae per similitudinem amicitiae perfectae constituitur & denominatur. Nam constat solam amicitiam eam, quae ex honestate provenit aut honestatem pro fine habet, perfectam amicitiam esse dicendam, ut docet Aristoteles 8. Nicom. cap. 4. D efferunt autem istae duae species praecipue obiecto, cum prior fit circa bonum honestum, altera circa bonum jucundum tantum & utile. In hac amicitiae specie consideranda veniunt: 1. Definitio. 2. Proprietates in genere. 3. Ejusdem species cum suis quoque definitionibus & proprietatibus. Definitur vero, qua plures utilitatis vel jucunditatis gratia inter se conjunguntur, ut non pro fine habeant honestatem praecipue, sed aut utilitatem privatam aut jucunditatem quae ipsi referuntur. Proprietates sunt tres inprimis: 1. Quod aliquo modo stabilis sit, duobus nempe causis & temporibus, primo, quando utrinque fit par officium compensatio in eodem genere. Secundo si diuturna consuetudo accedat: Tunc enim tales incipiunt, piunt, se magis ac magis mutuò ampleƈti non tan-tum propter voluptatem & utilitatem, sed etiam propter virtutem. Et hinc fit, ut Philosophus 8.lib. cap.4.doceat,ex amicitia imperfecta sæpe gigni per-sectam propter diuturnam temporis contuetudi-nem:cujus rei manifestum deprehenditur indicium in amicitia contracta in Scholis, quæ initio colitur propter jucunditatem, postea temporis progressu co-mutatur in amicitiā perfectā, sicut Quintilianus in-quit: Nullas amicitias firmiores esse quam quæ in Scholis cœperunt. Secunda proprietas: quod querelis, calumniis, injuriis, suspicionibus scaret & patet, contra quod fit in amicitia perfecta. Quæ proprie-tas, ut docet Philosophus cap.13 lib.8. non tam amici-tiæ jucundæ, quam utili competit. Nam in jucunda delectatio & voluptas plerunque quæritur: in utili vero, propterea quod utrque amicus laboret ταλε-ξιας, & plus appetat, quam alter possit aut velit præ-stare: Hinc mutuis querelis laborare solet. Tertia proprietas, quod hanc ut plurimum cum hominib. inferioris sortis colunt Magnates & Principes viri. Nam ejusmodi amicis delectantur Magnates, quia non possunt omnia per semetipsos agere, idcirco amicis tanquam samulis utuntur, qua de re Æneas Sylvius lib.2.de rebus gestis Alphonsi, multa disserit. Tyranni vero utuntur ad tempus familiaritate subditorum, ut cum divites illi facti sint, eorum spoliisditescant. Idcirco interrogatus Diogenes, quomodo amicis uteretur Dionysius Syracusarum Tyrannus; Ut vasculis, inquit: Nam cum plena sunt, evacuat & vasa abjicit. Species imperfectæ amicitiæ sunt pro-duplic duplici fine, quem respicit: Jucunda & utilis. Jucunda dicitur, quâ, propter jucunditatem & voluptatem, plures inter se amore & benevolentia conjunguntur, hujus duæ sunt proprietates: Prior quod majorem habeat affinitatem cum amicitia perfecta quam amicitia utilis. 8. Nicom. cap. 6. Rationes sunt duæ: 1. Quia amicitia jucunda magis solet esse ingenua & liberalibus ingeniis digna. Utilem enim amicitiam plerumq; sectantur homines sordidi & avari, qui quæstum ex amicitia faciunt. 2. Quia etiam beati & felices homines magis expetunt amicos jucundos propter conversationem: Utiles autem non curant, quia iis non egent. Secunda, quod ad hanc juvenes, ut sunt aptiores, ita e m libentius colant, cujus rationem reddit Philosophus cap. 3. 8. Nicom. Quia magis secundum affectus vivunt & actiones suas jucunditate metiuntur, itaq; appetunt mutuam conversationem, qua se invicem oblectant. Idem repetit cap. 5. ejusdem lib. Utilis amicitia dicitur, quâ, propter quæstum & commodum plures inter se amore conjunguntur. Proprietates sunt vulgò quatuor: 1. Quod maxime in senibus cernatur, & in iis etiam cujuscunq; sunt ætatis, qui emolumento ducuntur. Idcirco cap. 3. lib. 8. ad hanc amicitiam refert Philosophus φιλίαν ξενικὴν qualem caupones & hospites mercenarii gerunt erga eos, qui ad eos divertunt. 2. Quod conversationem mutuam non admodum admittat aut requirat, nempe propter ἀηδονεξίαν & suspicionem. 3. quod omnium maxime obnoxia soleat esse querelis, ut jam dictum fuit, & idcirco et omnium maxime instabilis. Aristote-les les hb.cit. c.13. 4. Quod tum maximè oriantur querelæ, quando is, qui beneficium accepit, non tantum retribuit, quantum sperabat se recepturum, is, qui beneficium dabat. Amicitia utilis subdividitur in duas species moralem, quâ beneficia retribuuntur, non ex aliquo pacto, sed benevolentia & libero utriusque arbitrio: Et in galeam, in qua beneficia communicantur expresso quodam facto & conditione remunerationis, atque ita evidenter determinatur, quid & quantum alteri alter debeat retribuere. Et hæc legalis duplex statuitur: Latior seu liberalior, in qua retributio & compensatio etiam expresse postulatur, tamen permittitur fidei & integritati accipientis, vel alioquin prorogatur in aliud tempus, neque amoris & benevolentiæ cujusdam causa, sed quoniam videmus eum, qui beneficium accipit, non statim habere unde possit compensare. Et hæc amicitia plerumque solet esse inter principem & subditum, dominum & famulum. Alia est strictior & vulgo dicitur mercatoria, in qua statim fit compensatio de manu in manum vel ex pacto vel quasi ex pacto. Et de hac amicitia legali hoc notandum, quod in ea non facile oriantur querelæ, quia nempe clarè definitur quid, quantum & quando fit retribuendum: Et nisi alteruter retribuat poterit cogi jure, ut stet promissis, quod in morali amicitia præsertim ea quæ honestatem respicit, fieri non solet. Porro amicitia imperfecta alia dicitur Homogenea, in qua se amici amant, propter unam eandemque rem nempe aut tantum propter utilitatem aut tantum propter voluptatem: alia Heterogenea in qua se amici amant propter res diversas, exempli gratia: unus alter amat alterum propter jucunditatem, alter vero amat eum propter utilitatem. Sumitur haec divisio ex 1. c. lib. 9. ubi hanc posteriorem speciem, nempe Heterogeneam lepidissimo declarat exemplo. Erat, inquit, quidam, qui amicitiam contraxit cum Citharaedo, ut disceret ab eo fidibus canere, ac promiserat quanto melius caneret, tanto se plura daturum. Citharaedus sperabat mercedem, alter vero cum bene didicisset canere, dixit se redditurum voluptatem pro voluptate. Tale quid contigit non itaque in Gallia, cum fidicen quidam oblectaret sua Musica, quendam magni nominis nobilem, et magna inde mercedem sperasset, nobilis exprompsit aliquot aureos, quos cum sonum quendam in mensa edidisset, quaesivit a fidicine, quomodo illi hic sonitus placeret: Perioptime, inquit fidicen: Tibi igitur satisfactum est, inquit nobilis, cum pro sonitu tuarum fidium sonitum meorum aureorum reddiderim.
units.tr: Another species of friendship is imperfect friendship, which is constituted and named by way of resemblance to perfect friendship. For it is agreed that only that friendship which arises from virtue, or has virtue as its end, is to be called perfect friendship, as Aristotle teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 8, cap. 4. These two species differ chiefly in their object: the former concerns the honourable good, the latter only the pleasant and the useful. In treating this species of friendship three things are to be considered: 1. its definition; 2. its properties in general; 3. its species, together with their own definitions and properties. It is defined as the bond by which several people unite with one another for the sake of usefulness or pleasure, so that they do not principally make honour their end, but either private advantage or the pleasure that is referred to themselves. Its properties are three in the first place: 1. that it is in some measure stable, namely for two reasons and at two times: first, when there is an equal exchange of services of the same kind on both sides; second, when long-standing familiarity is added. For then such people begin to embrace one another more and more, not only for pleasure and advantage but also for virtue. Hence the Philosopher, in book 8, chapter 4, teaches that from imperfect friendship perfect friendship is often born through long habit over time. A clear sign of this is found in the friendship formed in the schools, which at first is cultivated for pleasure and afterwards, as time goes on, is changed into perfect friendship; as Quintilian says: "No friendships are firmer than those that began in the schools." Second property: it abounds in complaints, slanders, injuries and suspicions, the opposite of what happens in perfect friendship. This property, as the Philosopher teaches in book 8, chapter 13, belongs not so much to pleasant friendship as to useful friendship. For in pleasant friendship it is mostly delight and pleasure that is sought; in useful friendship, however, because each friend labours for greed [πλεονεξίας] and wants more than the other can or is willing to give, it is usually troubled by mutual complaints. Third property: that this friendship is for the most part cultivated with men of inferior rank by magnates and princes. For magnates take delight in such friends, because they cannot do everything by themselves, and so they use their friends as servants; on this matter Aeneas Sylvius, in book 2 of his Deeds of Alfonso, discusses much. Tyrants, however, use the familiarity of their subjects for a time, so that when those subjects have become rich, the tyrants may grow rich from their spoils. Hence when Diogenes was asked how Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, used his friends, he answered: "As vessels. For when they are full, he empties them and throws them away." Species of imperfect friendship are two, according to the double end it regards: pleasant and useful. It is called pleasant when, on account of pleasure and delight, several people are joined to one another by love and goodwill. Of this there are two properties. The first is that it has greater affinity with perfect friendship than useful friendship has. Nicomachean Ethics 8, cap. 6. There are two reasons: 1. because pleasant friendship is usually more gentlemanly and worthy of liberal minds; for it is mostly sordid and greedy men who pursue useful friendship, making gain out of friendship. 2. because also blessed and happy men seek pleasant friends more for their company, but do not care for useful ones, since they have no need of them. Second, that young people, being more suited to it, cultivate it more willingly; the Philosopher gives the reason for this in cap. 3, book 8 of the Nicomachean Ethics: because they live more by their feelings and measure their actions by pleasure, and so they seek mutual company by which they delight one another. He repeats the same in cap. 5 of the same book. Useful friendship is that by which several people are joined to one another in love for the sake of gain and advantage. Its properties are commonly four: 1. that it is seen most of all in old people, and also in those of any age who are led by profit. For this reason, in cap. 3, book 8, the Philosopher refers to this friendship the kind of friendship [ξενικὴν] that innkeepers and hired hosts bear towards those who lodge with them. 2. that it does not greatly admit or require mutual company, namely because of unpleasantness [ἀηδονεξίαν] and suspicion. 3. that it is usually most liable to complaints of all, as has already been said, and therefore is also the most unstable of all; Aristotle, in the book cited, cap. 13. 4. that complaints arise most of all when he who has received a benefit does not return as much as he who gave it hoped to receive. Useful friendship is subdivided into two species: the moral, in which benefits are repaid not by any agreement but by goodwill and the free choice of both parties; and the legal, in which benefits are exchanged with a certain expressed act and a condition of reward, so that it is clearly determined what and how much each owes the other to repay. This legal friendship is established in a twofold form: the broader or more liberal, in which repayment and compensation are also expressly demanded, yet it is left to the good faith and integrity of the recipient, or else it is deferred to another time, not for the sake of any love or goodwill, but because we see that the one who receives the benefit does not at once have the means to repay. This friendship is usually found between prince and subject, lord and servant. The other is stricter and is commonly called mercantile, in which compensation is made at once, hand to hand, either by agreement or as if by agreement. And concerning this legal friendship, it is to be noted that complaints do not easily arise in it, because it is clearly defined what, how much and when is to be repaid; and if either party does not repay, he can be compelled by law to keep his promises, which is not usually done in moral friendship, especially that which regards honour. Further, of imperfect friendship, one kind is called homogeneous, in which friends love one another for one and the same thing, namely either only for usefulness or only for pleasure; another is heterogeneous, in which friends love one another for different things: for example, one loves the other for pleasure, while the other loves him for usefulness. This division is taken from Nicomachean Ethics 9, cap. 1, where the Philosopher explains this latter species, the heterogeneous, by a most charming example. "There was," he says, "a certain man who entered into friendship with a harpist, so that he might learn from him to play the lyre, and had promised that the better he played, the more he would give. The harpist hoped for a reward, but the other, when he had learned to play well, said that he would repay pleasure with pleasure." Something similar happened not long ago in France: when a certain lyre player was delighting people with his music and had hoped for a great reward from it, a nobleman of great name took out a few gold coins, and when he had made a certain sound on the table with them, he asked the lyre player how that sound pleased him. "Most excellently," said the lyre player. "Then you are satisfied," said the nobleman, "since I have paid you the sound of my gold coins for the sound of your strings."

units.la: Nunc consideranda veniunt, quae studia et officia amicus amico praestare debeat ad colendam et confervandam amicitiam praesertim honestam. Et his quinque comprehensa videntur: 1. Debet amicus ad praestandum mutuum amorem bene velle suo amico. 2. Ei benefacere. 3. Idem cum ipso in rebus honestis sentire. 4. Congaudere cum ipso in rebus secundis, et condolere in rebus adversis. 5. Ejus convictum, hoc est, consuetudine et conversatione delectari. Illorum autem officiorum mensura et regula debet esse verus et incorruptus amor sui. Quae enim unus quis sibi ipse cupit et tribuit aut ab amico tribui vult, ille etiam amico, qui nihil aliud est, quam alter idem, velle & tribuere debet. Haec hucusque de doctrina Amicitiae
units.tr: Now we come to consider what duties and services a friend ought to render to a friend in order to cultivate and preserve friendship, especially honourable friendship. These seem to be comprised under five heads: 1. In order to show mutual love, a friend ought to wish well to his friend. 2. to do him good. 3. to agree with him in honourable matters. 4. to rejoice with him in prosperity and to grieve with him in adversity. 5. to take delight in his company, that is, in habitual dealings and conversation. The measure and rule of these duties ought to be true and uncorrupted self-love. For whatever one wishes for himself and bestows upon himself, or wishes to be bestowed upon him by a friend, he ought also to wish and bestow upon his friend, who is nothing other than another self. So far, concerning the doctrine of friendship.

units.la: Nunc quaestiones quasdam ex 9. Nicom. pro scopo Philosophi subjiciamus, ut hic de amicitia tractatus sit illustrior & omni hominum generi utilior. Prima quaestio sit: An amicitia sit ita simpliciter necessaria, ut sine ea ne vivere quidem possimus? Resp. Per distinctionem inter amicitiam latius acceptam sive potius amorem ipsum, & amicitiam proprie sic dictam.
units.tr: Now let us put some questions from the ninth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, in keeping with the Philosopher's purpose, so that this treatment of friendship may be clearer and more useful to every kind of person. The first question is: is friendship so simply necessary that we cannot even live without it? Answer: this is settled by distinguishing friendship in the broader sense, or rather love itself, from friendship properly so called.

units.la: 2. Inter vivere simpliciter & bene vivere. Amicitia latius accepta non tantum ad bene vivendum, sed etiam ad vivendum necessaria videtur, & in omni aetate & in omni fortuna. In omni aetate 1. quia infantibus & pueris necessaria est ad nutritionem & educationem. Nisi enim amarentur a suis, hunc quae nutrirentur & educarentur. 2. adolescentibus ad promotionem rerum praeclare gerendarum. 3. senibus ad sublevandam eorum imbecillitatem. In omni fortuna, & quidem 1. divitibus, ut opes suas possint recte possidere isque frui: pauperibus ad subsidium & solatium adversus egestatem & miseriam: Amicitia enim, ut inquit Cicero, secundas res splendidiores facit, & adversas communione temperat, & leviores reddit. Amicitia vero proprie sic dicta, etsi non sit necessaria ad simpliciter vivendum, necessaria tamen est ad bene vivendum, hoc est, ad consequendam felicitatem civilem, eamque tutam fovendam tum ornandam, idque docet Philosophus 8. Nicom. cap. 1. idque docere possunt variae rationes: 1. Quia non aqua, igne & aere pluribus locis utimur quam amicitia. 2. Quia qui amicitiam è vita tollunt, Solem è mundo tollere videntur. Cicero in Lælio. 3. Quia vita sine amicis insidiarum & metus est plena, ut præclare docet Cicero 1. de finib. 4. Quia amicitia est pietatis custos & æqualitatis magnitudo, ut docet Ambrosius lib. 3. officior. sub finem. 5. Quia nulla domus tam stabilis nulla tam firma civitas reperitur, quæ non odiis & dissidiis funditus everti possit: Unde Agrigentinum Gæcum dixisse ferunt, quæ in rerum natura toroque mundo consistarent, quæq; moverentur, ea contrahere amicitiam, dissipare discordiam, juxta illud: Concordia res parvæ crescunt, discordia maximæ dilabuntur.
units.tr: 2. Between simply living and living well. Friendship in the broader sense seems necessary not only for living well but also for living at all, and at every age and in every condition. At every age: (1) it is necessary for infants and children for their nourishment and upbringing, for unless they were loved by their own people they would not be nourished or brought up; (2) for young people, to advance them in performing noble deeds; (3) for the old, to support their weakness. In every condition: (1) for the rich, so that they may rightly possess their wealth and enjoy it; for the poor, as help and comfort against want and misery. For friendship, as Cicero says, makes prosperity more splendid, tempers adversity by sharing it, and makes burdens lighter. Friendship properly so called, although it is not necessary merely for living, is nevertheless necessary for living well, that is, for attaining civil happiness and for keeping it safe and adorned. The Philosopher teaches this in the eighth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 1, and various reasons can show it: (1) because we use water, fire and air in no more places than we use friendship; (2) because those who remove friendship from life seem to remove the sun from the world, as Cicero says in the Laelius; (3) because life without friends is full of snares and fear, as Cicero teaches admirably in the first book of the De finibus; (4) because friendship is the guardian of piety and the greatness of equality, as Ambrose teaches in the third book of the De officiis, near the end; (5) because no house is so stable and no state so firm that it cannot be utterly overthrown by hatreds and dissensions. Hence they say that Gaecus of Agrigentum said that the things which exist in the nature of things and in the whole world, and which are moved, bring about friendship and scatter discord, in accordance with that saying: "By concord small things grow, by discord the greatest things fall to pieces."

units.la: II. An amicitia sit anima civitatis, eiq; plus prasidii infit quam vel ipsi justitia? Resp.
units.tr: II. Is friendship the soul of the state, and does it bring more protection than justice itself? Answer:

units.la: Id præter concursum prudentum confirmari quotidiana experientia, quod comprobavit Menenius Agrippa eleganti Apologo de membrorum adversus ventriculum conspirantium dissolutione. Sicut enim ubi membrum alterius ministerio se subtrahit toti corpori imminet interitus: ita nulla civitas tam firma esse poterit, quæ non odiis & dissidiis tandem funditus evertatur. Proinde qui saluti Reipubl. consulere voluerunt, majorem semper amicitiæ, quam justitiæ rationem habuerunt eò quod nullum concordiæ contra dissensiones magis sit auxilium, quam quod in amicitia cernitur. Aristoteles 8. Nicom. cap. 1.
units.tr: Apart from the agreement of the wise, daily experience confirms this, as Menenius Agrippa demonstrated with his elegant fable of the limbs that conspired against the belly and so fell apart. For just as, when one limb withdraws its service from the rest of the body, ruin threatens the whole body, so no state can be so firm that it will not in the end be utterly overthrown by hatreds and dissensions. Therefore those who have wished to look after the safety of the commonwealth have always paid greater regard to friendship than to justice, because there is no greater help against dissensions than what is seen in friendship. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book 8, chapter 1.

units.la: III. An amicitia nobis fato competat, an verò prudentia? Resp.
units.tr: III. Does friendship come to us by fate, or rather by prudence? Answer:

units.la: Quosdam esse, qui affirmant primum, propterea quod Plato dicat in Lyside fato amorem & benevolentiam conciliari Platoni adstipulatur Cic. Secundo etiā quia ex instinctu naturæ amor excitari solet, fato quodam hominibus competere putant. Nam quæ instinctu naturæ fiunt, & fato dicuntur fieri ex Stoicorum sententia. Verum hanc opinionem esse falsam, inde evincitur, quia sic amor & amicitia omnibus æqualiter convenient: Contrarium cuius experientia docet. 2) Quia si συμπτώσει hæc amoris a fato perveniret, tunc dissolvi amicitia aut amor inter homines non posset, cum quæ fato fiunt, necessario dicantur fieri. A prædestinatione vero provenire Amicitiam hinc constat, quia omnis virtus hinc provenit. Ergo & amicitia, cum sit conspiratio plurium virtutum. 3) Quia nemo amicitiam cum alio colit, nisi ex prælectione quadam consideret in alio aut virtutū aut morū similitudinē quandā, aut boni alicujus, quod ipsi arridet approbatione aut inexistentiam. Vide Picolh. grad.7. c.6.
units.tr: Some affirm the first, because Plato says in the Lysis that love and goodwill are brought together by fate, and Cicero agrees with Plato. Secondly, they think that friendship falls to people by a kind of fate, because love is usually aroused by an impulse of nature; for things done by an impulse of nature are said, in the opinion of the Stoics, to be done by fate. But that this opinion is false is proved from this: thus love and friendship would come equally to all, the contrary of which experience teaches. (2) For if this love came about by chance [συμπτώσει], then friendship or love could not be dissolved among people, since things that happen by fate are said to happen necessarily. That friendship arises from predestination is clear from this: every virtue arises from it, so friendship too, since it is a union of several virtues. (3) Because no one cultivates friendship with another unless, after some prior consideration, he notices in the other some likeness of virtues or of morals, or some good which pleases him by its approval or its presence. See Piccolomini, Grades, book 7, chapter 6.

units.la: IV. An πάντα φίλων κοινά?
units.tr: IV. Are all things common among friends?

units.la: Resp. Concedi posse sano sensu. Nam quia amicitia sine communione esse & conservari nequit, ideo cōmunio quædā inter amicos esse debet. Sed illa intelligitur partim de conversatione mutua, partim de mutua officiorum honestorum præstatione, partim de communi & licito bonorū fortunæ usu. Non enim simpliciter omnia inter amicos sunt communia, sed tantum ea, quæ salva honestate & pietate salvâque interdum rerum proprietate, ut uxorum, liberorum, &c. amicus unus alteri communicare potest.
units.tr: Answer: this may be granted in a sound sense. For since friendship cannot exist or be preserved without sharing, there ought to be a certain communion between friends. But this is understood partly of mutual conversation, partly of the mutual performance of honourable duties, and partly of the common and lawful use of the goods of fortune. For not all things are simply common among friends, but only those which a friend can share with another without harm to honesty and piety, and sometimes without harm to the ownership of property, such as wives, children, and so on.

units.la: V. An omnia in gratiam amicorum sint facienda & patienda?
units.tr: V. Must everything be done and endured for the sake of friends?

units.la: Resp. Cum amicus, ut paulo ante dictum fuit, sit alter idem, & quasi una anima in duobus corporibus. poribus, videtur inde concludendum hoc ipsum: Verum hæc sententia simpliciter admitti nō debet, nisi restringatur ad omnia, quæ cum honestate & pietate non pugnant. Nihil enim in ullius gratiam amici debet fieri, quod honestati aut pietati adversatur. Idcirco recte Pericles dixit: Gratificandum esse amicis, sed usque ad aras. Et Cicero lib. 1. offic. cum in amicitia, quæ honesta non sunt, postulantur, religio & fides anteponenda est amicitiæ: qua de re vide Danæum cap. 7. de amicit. Et Gellium lib. 1. cap. 3. Et præclarè Philosophus 9. Nicom. cap. 1. Cum amicitia nō, nisi ex virtute nascatur, intra virtutis cancellos te continere debet. Ac licet amicorum nævi præsertim non admodum deformes sint, tolerandi ac dissimulandi, scelera tamen & flagitia minimè sunt toleranda, sed propter illa amicitiæ renunciandum, ne infamiæ nota contrahatur cum plerumque tales habeamur, quales sunt ii, cum quibus conversamur. Præclarè Plinius lib. 12. cap. 1. Torpedo piscis, inquit, haud nocet, nisi contactu, & virus suum etiam ab aere per linum & arundinis internodia ad piscatoris manum mirè transmittit: Sic improbi & pestilentes, nisi cum iis habeas commercium, & quocunque consuetudinis contactu morum venena affiant. Secundum quid igitur, non simpliciter quæstio hæc intelligi debet.
units.tr: Answer: Since a friend, as was said a little earlier, is another self and, as it were, one soul in two bodies, it seems to follow that this very thing should be granted without qualification. But this opinion should not be admitted without qualification, unless it is restricted to all those things that are not incompatible with honesty and piety. For nothing ought to be done for a friend's sake that is opposed to honesty or piety. So Pericles rightly said: One must gratify friends, but only up to the altars. And Cicero, in the first book of the De officiis, says that when things that are not honourable are demanded in friendship, conscience and good faith must be put before friendship; on this matter see Danaeus, chapter 7, On friendship. Also Gellius, book 1, chapter 3. And the Philosopher admirably, in the ninth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 1: since friendship arises only from virtue, you must keep yourself within the bounds of virtue. And although the minor blemishes of friends, especially those that are not very ugly, must be tolerated and overlooked, crimes and disgraceful deeds must by no means be tolerated; rather, friendship must be renounced because of them, lest the mark of infamy be contracted, since we are usually taken to be such as those are with whom we associate. Plinius, book 12, chapter 1, puts it admirably: the torpedo fish, he says, does harm only by touch, and it wonderfully transmits its poison even through the air, along the line and the joints of the reed, to the fisherman's hand. So it is with wicked and pestilential men: unless you have dealings with them, and the poisons of their morals breathe upon you by any contact of habit. The question, therefore, must be understood in a qualified sense, not absolutely.

units.la: VI. An in amicitia requiratur convictus & conversatio crebra? Et statuitur thesis affirmativa propter has rationes: 1. Quia non potest esse mutua officiorum communicatio sine conversatione. 2. Quia inter quos vel nulla vel rarior est conversatio & collocutio, in eorum amicitia facile erunt pritur suspicio, diffidentia & tandem plenaria oblivio & dissolutio amicitiae. Unde etiam inter amicos absentes crebrò requiritur per nuncios aut literas commercium. 3. Quia amici conversatio necessaria est in utraque fortuna, in secunda quidem ad jucunditatem, in adversa verò ad auxilium & solatium. Nam vita solitaria in utraque fortuna solet esse permolesta. 4. Quia videmus juvenes propterea ad conciliandam amicitiam esse aptos, quod sint in conversando amabiles: Contra senes non esse aptos ad concilandam amicitiam, quia sunt morosi & solitarii. 5. Quia amici conspectus amico solet esse valde jucundus. Nam dum sui quasi imaginem in altero videt, vehementer gaudet, dum scilicet habet, qui cum tanquam cum seipso colloqui possit. 6. Quia omnis societas requiritur conversationem. Ergo & amicitia. 7. Quia ex conversatione amicus cognoscit amicum suum esse incolumem, quo nihil ei contingere debet gratius. 8. Quia possunt inter se amici per conversationem exercere studia virtutis, & alter per alterum fieri melior. 9. Quia ad contrahendam amicitiam necessaria est conversatio, quatenus ex eapaulatim nascitur morum & studiorum similitudo, qua efficacissime gignit virtutem. Unde Plutarchus de φιλοφιλία. Amicitia, inquit, requirit tria; virtutem tanquam honestum, consuetudinem, tanquam dulce, mutuam operam tanquam necessarium. Vide Philosophum 8. Nicomach. cap. 5 & lib. 9. cap. 12. Ubi tamen contra hanc sententiam hoc objicit: Si in amicitia requiritur convictus & conversatio crebra, sequitur amicitiam non posse esse inter absentes, praesertim magno locorum intervallo distinctos? Resp. Philosophus, amicitiam considerari posse duobus modis: vel secundum habitum & propositum mentis, vel secundum actam. Priori modo posse et esse inter absentes, pofteriori autem modo tantum inter præsentes. Deinde etiam non tantum h bitualis, sed etiam actualis amicitia poterit esse inter absentes, si modo literas frequentes inter se commutent. Illud enim literarium colloquium analogia respondet colloquio & conversationi, quæ est inter præsentes.
units.tr: VI. Is close living together and frequent association required in friendship? The affirmative thesis is upheld for these reasons: 1. Because there cannot be a mutual sharing of duties without association. 2. Because between those who have little or no association and conversation, suspicion, distrust and at last complete forgetting and dissolution of friendship will easily arise. Hence even between absent friends frequent intercourse is sought through messengers or letters. 3. Because the company of a friend is necessary in either fortune: in prosperity for pleasure, but in adversity for help and comfort. For a solitary life is usually very wearisome in either fortune. 4. Because we see that young men are fit to win friendship for the reason that they are pleasant in conversation; whereas old men are not fit to win friendship, because they are peevish and solitary. 5. Because the sight of a friend is usually very pleasant to a friend. For while he sees, as it were, an image of himself in the other, he rejoices greatly, since he has someone with whom he can converse as with himself. 6. Because every society requires association. Therefore friendship does too. 7. Because through association a friend knows his friend to be safe, and nothing could happen to him that ought to be more welcome. 8. Because friends can, through association, practise the pursuits of virtue together, and one can become better through the other. 9. Because association is necessary for forming friendship, inasmuch as from it a likeness of manners and pursuits gradually arises, which most effectively begets virtue. Hence Plutarch, in his treatise on love of friends [φιλοφιλία]: friendship, he says, requires three things: virtue as the honourable, companionship as the pleasant, and mutual service as the necessary. See the Philosopher, Nicomachean Ethics 8, chapter 5, and book 9, chapter 12. There, however, he raises this objection against this opinion: if close living together and frequent association are required in friendship, it follows that friendship cannot exist between absent persons, especially those separated by a great distance of places? Answer: the Philosopher says that friendship can be considered in two ways: either according to the habit and disposition of the mind, or according to its activity. In the former way it can and does exist between absent persons; in the latter way only between those who are present. Moreover, not only habitual but also actual friendship can exist between absent persons, provided they exchange frequent letters. For that literary conversation corresponds, by analogy, to the conversation and association that exist between those who are present.

units.la: VII. An pugnent inter se amicitia & charitas lex?
units.tr: VII. Do friendship and the law of charity fight against each other?

units.la: Resp. Pro affirmativa quæstionis hæc duo militant fundamenta, 1. Generale Dei præceptum, quo omnes alios homines mutuo diligere jubemur, sicut nos ipsos, Rom.13.verf.8. Ergo fi arctam illam amicitiam inter aliquos contrahere liceat, jam haud leviter recedi-tur ab hac generali de omnibus æquè amandis regula. 2. Quia secundum illud Matth.5.verf.34. Tanta nostra esse debent erga omnes homines etiam inimicos officia ut majora & alia etiam amicis præstare non possimus. Ergo vel hac etiam ratione tollitur arctior ista amicitia, quæ reddit nos ad alios homines præter amicos coledos negligentiores, quia contenti amicis subvenisse, alios laborantes fere prætermitimus. Pro negativa sunt argumenta longè majoris momenti: 1. Scripturæ auctoritas, quæ eos colendos docet, quos in amicitiam recepimus: Itaque ipse Dei Spiritus execratur & damnat eos, qui interiorem illam amicitiam & animorum conjunctionem violant, Psal.40. verf.10. Psal.55. verf.21. Esa.3.verf.5. Mich.7.verf.5. & 6. &c. 2. Exemplum pio-rum, qui arctam inter se contraxerunt amicitiam, ut fecerunt Jonathan & David. 3. Natura ipsa & communis omnium gentium vox, quæ amicitiæ jus concelebrat, & introduxit. Itaque ab iis hanc sententiam expressit, Non pluribus locis aqua & igne utimur, quam amicitia. Proinde ad argumenta contrariae sententiae facile responderi poterit. Neque enim invicem haec pugnant: Amor sive dilectio proximi & amicitia. Secundo etiam locus ille Matthaei potius animum vincendi cupidum respicit, quam ut prohibeat singularem inter duos aut plures amorem. Imo Deus ipse facit gradus quosdam charitatis, dum monet, non eodem modo diligendam esse uxorem, quo parentes, sed majori diligendam esse uxore amore. Matth. 18. Sic plus debemus liberos diligere, quam extraneos, plus fide domesticos, quam infideles, Coloss. 3. & Galat. 6. Deinde etiam ipse Christus, cujus omnis actio nostra debet esse institutio, magis Johannem, quam caeteros suos discipulos dicitur dilexisse Joh. 13. verf. 23. & cap. 21. verf. 20.
units.tr: Answer: For the affirmative side of the question two grounds stand: 1. The general command of God, by which we are ordered to love all other men mutually, as ourselves, Romans 13:8. Therefore, if it were lawful to form such a close friendship with some, we would already be departing, not lightly, from this general rule of loving all equally. 2. Because according to Matthew 5:34, our duties towards all men, even enemies, ought to be so great that we cannot render greater ones, or other ones, even to friends. Therefore, on this ground too, that closer friendship is removed, which makes us more negligent in cultivating other men besides friends; for, content to have helped friends, we pass over almost everyone else who is in need. On the negative side there are arguments of far greater weight: 1. The authority of Scripture, which teaches that we should cherish those whom we have received into friendship. Thus the Spirit of God himself curses and condemns those who violate that inner friendship and union of souls: Psalm 40:10; Psalm 55:21; Isaiah 3:5; Micah 7:5 and 6, etc. 2. The example of pious men who formed a close friendship between themselves, as Jonathan and David did. 3. Nature itself and the common voice of all nations, which celebrates and has introduced the right of friendship. Hence the saying that expresses this opinion: We use water and fire in no more places than we use friendship. Accordingly, the arguments for the contrary opinion can easily be answered. For these things do not fight against each other: love or affection for one's neighbour and friendship. Secondly, that passage of Matthew looks rather to the spirit of one eager to conquer, than forbids a special love between two or more persons. Indeed God himself makes certain degrees of charity, when he warns that a wife is not to be loved in the same way as parents, but that a wife is to be loved with greater love: Matthew 18. So we ought to love our children more than strangers, and our household more than unbelievers: Colossians 3 and Galatians 6. Moreover, Christ himself, whose every action ought to be our instruction, is said to have loved John more than his other disciples: John 13:23 and chapter 21:20.

units.la: VIII. An amicitia facile & cito cum aliqua fit contrahenda?
units.tr: VIII. Can friendship easily and quickly be contracted with anyone?

units.la: Et statuitur thesis negativa propter quatuor rationes: 1.
