Quia ad amicitiam contrahendam opus est tempore & consuetudine vitae longiori, juxta proverbium: Multi salis modii una edendi, ut homines inter se veram amicitiam contrahant. 2. Quia cum in animis hominum multae sint latebrae, multi recessus, prius explorari oportet, an alter alterius amore dignus sit, & num alter alteri tuto fidere possit, quae amicitia confirmetur. 3. Quia sicut in aliis rebus quod cito fit, cito perit, ita amicitia etiam, quae cito suscipitur, cito definit, ut videre licet in amicitia ista, quae contrahitur inter juvenes, qui propter mobilitatem quandam ingenii, subinde animum mutant. 4. Denique quia argumentum magnae habetur temeritatis cito alicui fieri amicum priusquam illum recte nosse didiceris.
units.tr: The negative thesis is affirmed for four reasons: (1) Friendship requires a long passage of time and a longer shared life, according to the proverb: men must eat many measures of salt together before they form true friendship. (2) Since the hearts of men contain many hiding places and many recesses, one must first test whether the other is worthy of love and whether he can be trusted, for friendship is strengthened by such trust. (3) As in other things, what is quickly done is quickly undone; so friendship too, if it is entered into quickly, ends quickly. This can be seen in the friendships formed among young men, who, because of a certain fickleness of mind, change their feelings from time to time. (4) Finally, it is regarded as a great rashness to make someone your friend quickly, before you have learned to know him properly.

units.la: IX. An amicitia cum multis contrahenda? Resp. Negative propter has causas:
units.tr: IX. Should friendship be contracted with many? Answer: No, for these reasons:

units.la: 1. Quia vera amicitia in summo gradu amoris consistit, qui ad unum potius quam ad multos extendi potest. 2. Quia in vera amicitia alter debet valde placere alteri amico. Unus autem simul pluribus valde placere non potest, cum sint diversis plerumque ingeniis, & hoc huic, illud illi placeat. Imo, qui studet omnibus placere, tandem nemini placet. 3. Quia ad amicitiam contrahendam requiritur diuturna exploratio eorum, qui amici sunt futuri. Plures autem difficulter recte explorare & probare possumus. 4. Quia nemo potest multis simul gratificari & inservire, quod eleganti similitudine declarat Plutarchus in περὶ φιλίας. Ut fluvius, inquit, in multos diductus rivos, fluit tenuior ac languidior; sic benevolentia in multos distracta languescit. 5. Quia multitudo amicorum homini plus taedii & molestiae, quam voluptatis adfert, non secus ac copia condimentorum non reddit cibos suaviores, sed nauseam saepe creat. 6. Quia cum amicus teneatur ad amici fortunam conformari, si plures haberet amicos, cogeretur ad variam eorum fortunam simul laetari & tristari multisque affectibus contrariis duci. 7. Quia περὶ φιλίας prohibet Pythagoras in Symbolo suo: Ne multis manum injicias: Et Aristoteles virum bonum neque vult esse φίλον neque πολύφιλον. Nam quemadmodum Briareo giganti manuum, & Argo oculorum multitudo nihil felicitatis attulit, sic neque amicorum plurimorum copia propter rationes jam dictas 8. Nicom. cap. 5.
units.tr: (1) True friendship consists in the highest degree of love, and this can be extended to one person rather than to many. (2) In true friendship, each friend must greatly please the other. But one person cannot greatly please many at the same time, since they are usually of different dispositions, and this one pleases one man and that one another. Indeed, whoever tries to please everyone ends by pleasing no one. (3) To contract friendship one needs a lengthy testing of those who are to become friends, but we can test and prove only a few with difficulty. (4) No one can serve and oblige many at once, as Plutarch declares with an elegant comparison in his essay On Friendship [περὶ φιλίας]: as a river, divided into many channels, flows thinner and weaker, so goodwill, spread among many, grows faint. (5) The multitude of friends brings a man more weariness and trouble than pleasure, just as a abundance of seasonings does not make food tastier but often produces nausea. (6) Since a friend is bound to share his friend's fortune, if he had many friends he would be compelled to rejoice and grieve at their varied fortunes at the same time, and be pulled by many contrary emotions. (7) Pythagoras, in his symbol about friendship, forbids us to lay hands on many: "do not lay your hand on many." Aristotle also holds that the good man wants to be neither a friend [φίλον] nor a man of many friends [πολύφιλον]. For just as the multitude of hands of the giant Briareus and of eyes of Argus brought no happiness, so neither does the abundance of very many friends, for the reasons already given. See Nicomachean Ethics 8, ch. 5.

units.la: X. An quilibet sibi maximè debeat esse amicus? Et respondetur ex Philosopho lib. 9. cap. 8. per distinctionem: φιλαυτίαν esse vel proborum vel improborum. Illa sic dicitur, quando nempe ratio sensibus mancipatur, & quisque sibi soli placet, reliqua despectui habens. Hæc, quando rationi sensus obediunt; & summa laude digna æstimatur. Deinde diligere sese dupliciter sumitur, vel ut objectum dilectionis, vel ut subjectum: Diligere ut objectum, non se, sed Deum tenetur homo, & tanti facere, quanti sua natura, si fieri possit, exi stit. Diligere ut subjectum, in bono honesto seipsum maximè debet. Nam tales erga alios, qualis quisque in seipso deprehenditur; Et nemo non sui perfectionem inprimis quærere debet. Plura de hac quæstione vide apud Picolhom. gradu 7. cap. 17. per totum.
units.tr: X. Ought each man above all to be his own friend? The answer, from the Philosopher, book 9, ch. 8, is given by a distinction: self-love [φιλαυτία] is of two kinds, that of the good and that of the wicked. The latter is when reason is enslaved to the senses, and each man pleases himself alone, holding all others in contempt. The former is when the senses obey reason, and it is judged worthy of the highest praise. Further, to love oneself is taken in two ways, either as the object of love or as its subject. As object, man is bound to love not himself but God, and to value himself as highly as his nature, if it were possible, permits. As subject, he ought above all to love himself in the honest good, for men are found to be towards others as they are found to be in themselves; and no one should fail to seek above all his own perfection. More on this question may be found in Piccolomini, grade 7, ch. 17, throughout.

units.la: XI. An amicitia contrahenda cum illis, qui fortunæ dignitate nos excedunt?
units.tr: XI. Should friendship be contracted with those who surpass us in fortune or dignity?

units.la: Resp. Per negationem propter has rationes: 1. Quia amicitia cōstari debet inter eos qui ejusdem naturæ & conditionis sunt, quique solius honestatis desiderio feruntur. Dispares enim mores disparia studia sequuntur, & studiorum dissimilitudo dissociat amicitias. 2. Quia in amicitia dispari infinita rixarum & suspicionum sparguntur semina, quibus amicitiæ pestis capitalior nulla exstit. 3. Quia qui potentia cæteris præstant, imperfectâ ratum colunt amicitiam, ut supra dictum. Neque enim quærunt jucundas cum virtute, neque ullas cum honestate, sed quoad jucunditatem quærunt eos, qui sunt faceti, quoad utilitatem, qui sunt laboriosi & folertes ad efficienda ea, quae imperantur. Vide c.13. Ecclesiastici, ubi egregie de hac quaestione disseritur.
units.tr: The answer is no, for these reasons: (1) Friendship ought to be formed between those who are of the same nature and condition, and who are drawn by the desire for honesty alone. For unlike characters follow unlike pursuits, and difference in pursuits dissolves friendships. (2) In an unequal friendship countless seeds of quarrels and suspicions are sown, and no pestilence is more deadly to friendship. (3) Those who excel others in power cultivate an imperfect friendship, as said above. For they seek neither pleasant companions for virtue's sake, nor any for the sake of honesty; with regard to pleasure they seek those who are witty, and with regard to usefulness those who are industrious and skilful in carrying out what they command. See Ecclesiasticus, ch. 13, where this question is treated excellently.

units.la: XII. Huic quaestioni recte haec propter affinitatem subjicitur: An scilicet inter diversa religionis homines amicitia colipossit & subsistere?
units.tr: XII. Closely related to this question, and rightly added on account of its affinity, is this: can friendship both be cultivated and endure between men of different religions?

units.la: Resp. Etsi sunt, qui negent propter has rationes: 1. Quod ut amicitiae sedes est in corde, ita etiam religionis: Ideo si dissentiant, uno in loco simul consistere non possunt. 2. Quia Hieronymus in Epistola ad Paulinam plane hoc negat: Tamen per distinctionem concedi potest. Nam amicitia consideratur, vel civiliter vel Theologice & spiritualiter. Nam sicut virtus est vel spiritualis vel moralis, ita & unio virtutis seu amicitia talis est, quarum una non tollit alteram, sicut honestas non tollit pietatem: Et possum alicui amicus esse moraliter, cui non sum amicus spiritualiter, id est, possum cum aliquo conspirare in exercitiis honestatis, cum quo non plane consentio in exercitiis pietatis. Exemplum evidens videre licet in regibus & magnatibus, qui quanquam religione plerumque differentiant, fraternitatem tamen & amicitiam Politicam inter se colunt; quod per foedera, auxilia, in pecunia & militibus ultro citroque; transmissa & per affinitatem saepenumero declarant.
units.tr: Although some deny it, for these reasons: (1) Just as the seat of friendship is in the heart, so too is the seat of religion; therefore, if they disagree, they cannot dwell together in one place. (2) Jerome in his Letter to Paulina denies this plainly. Nevertheless it can be conceded by a distinction. For friendship is considered either civilly or theologically and spiritually. Just as virtue is either spiritual or moral, so too the union of virtue, or friendship, is of such a kind that one does not abolish the other, just as honesty does not abolish piety. I can be a friend to someone morally, to whom I am not a friend spiritually; that is, I can join with someone in the practice of honesty, with whom I do not wholly agree in the practice of piety. A clear example can be seen in kings and magnates, who, although they usually differ in religion, nevertheless cultivate brotherhood and political friendship among themselves, which they often declare by treaties, mutual aid, money and soldiers sent back and forth, and by intermarriage.

units.la: XIII. Ad quam amicitiae speciem referenda sit illorum amicitia, qui in eodem periculo sunt constituti, itemque amicitia peregrinantium?
units.tr: XIII. To which kind of friendship should the friendship of those who are placed in the same danger be referred, and likewise the friendship of travellers?

units.la: Resp. Amicitiam periculorum referri posse ad amicitiam jucundam: quia gratum est hominibus, habere socios malorum, sicut milites se mutuo amant processuri in aciem, cum jucun-dum sit ipsis, quod habeant periculi cofortes. Pere-grinantium vero amicitia etiam ad jucundam referri potest, quanquam peregrinantes præter jucundu, honestum etiam respiciant, si nempe alter alterius opera possit à prædonibus aut latronibus liberari.
units.tr: Answer: The friendship of those in danger can be referred to pleasant friendship, because it pleases men to have companions in evils. Soldiers love one another as they go forward into battle, since it is pleasant for them to have comrades in danger. The friendship of travellers can also be referred to pleasant friendship, although travellers, besides what is pleasant, also look to what is honourable, namely if one can free the other from robbers or brigands by his help.

units.la: XIV. Num continuò dissolvenda amicitia, si vel cum improbo contracta fit, vel post contractam improbus evadat? Resp. Per distinction em, Nam malum hoc, quod lædere potest amicitiam vel majus est, vel minus. Si mjus, nempe si alter ex amicis in virtute non permaneat, vel ex fideli fiat infidelis, vel ex Christiano Turca aut Paganus, & in errore suo permaneat, tunc dissolvi poterit amicitia. Si vero minus sit malum, & non plane discedat ab omni virtute, sed ad tempus exorbitet, ita ut in viam revocari possit, & spes emendationis supersit, tunc amicitia dissolvi non debet, quam diu spes aliqua superest, fore, ut aliquando ad se amicus redeat.
units.tr: XIV. Must a friendship be dissolved at once if it was formed with a wicked man, or if a friend becomes wicked after it was formed? Answer: This requires a distinction. The evil that can harm a friendship is either greater or lesser. If it is greater, namely if one of the friends does not remain in virtue, or changes from faithful to faithless, or from Christian to Turk or pagan and remains in his error, then the friendship can be dissolved. But if the evil is lesser, and he does not wholly abandon all virtue but strays for a time, so that he can be brought back to the right path and hope of amendment remains, then the friendship ought not to be dissolved as long as some hope remains that the friend will one day come back to himself.

units.la: XV. Quo loco habendum illud: Ama, ut aliquando osurus? Resp. Etli à quibusdam hoc probetur, indignam tamen esse amicitia hanc sententiam propter has causas: 1. Quia amicitæ veræ repugnat, quæ nullũ suspicionibus aut calumniis locũ relinquit. 2. Quia sic nulla amicitia firma & stabilis inter homines esset, propterea quovis vero circumferretur, cũ ista amicitia ex præcedente aut odio aut semine odii facilime mutari possit: Proinde magis placet illud Isocratis: Neminem citò in amicitiam recipe: Quem vero recepe-ris, da operam, ut eum perpetuò ames. Cui adstipulatur & Solon: Amicum ne temere asciveris, ascitum ne leviter re-jeceris.
units.tr: XV. In what sense is that saying to be understood: "Love as one who will someday hate"? Answer: Although some approve this saying, it is nevertheless unworthy of friendship, for these reasons: (1) it is contrary to true friendship, which leaves no room for suspicions or calumnies; (2) if it were accepted, no friendship among men would be firm and stable, since it would be tossed about by every turn of fortune, for such a friendship could very easily be changed by a preceding hatred or by the seed of hatred. Therefore the saying of Isocrates pleases more: "Admit no one into friendship quickly; but whom you have admitted, take care to love perpetually." Solon agrees: "Do not take a friend rashly, and do not lightly reject one you have taken."

units.la: XVI. An amico reconciliato fidendum?
units.tr: XVI. Can a reconciled friend be trusted?

units.la: Resp. Siracidem cap.12. verf.10. hoc dissuadere, ne quis inimico in aeternum fidat. Et Cicero reconciliationem ejusmodi suspectissimam habet. Hinc Antigonus Syriae Rex nimium fidens sodalibus ab illis occisus est. Et idem de Dione refert Plutarchus in vita ipsius: Et Curtius 4. de gestis Alexandri Magni dicit, Philippum in acie tutiorem fuisse, quam in theatro, ubi inter amicos conciliatos sedebat. Nam plerique ex malitia ingenii injuriarum memores esse solent, beneficiorum vero raro aut nunquam, quae ipsorum solet esse ingratitudo. Pro determinatione quaestionis sciendum reconciliationem firmam vix esse posse: 1. Ubi ob scelera & flagitia alterutrius amicitia erat soluta. 2. Nisi plane & plene conspiciatur omnes etiam reliquias odii esse evulsas. Nam quod dicit Poeta: Manet alta mente repositum Judicium Paridis spreta, injuria forma.
units.tr: Answer: Ecclesiasticus, chapter 12, verse 10, advises that no one should trust an enemy forever. Cicero also regards such a reconciliation as most suspect. Hence Antigonus, king of Syria, who trusted his companions too much, was killed by them. Plutarch reports the same of Dion in his life. And Curtius, book 4, on the deeds of Alexander the Great, says that Philip was safer in battle than in the theatre, where he sat among his reconciled friends. For most men, from the malice of their nature, are wont to remember injuries, but benefits rarely or never; this is the ingratitude of such people. To settle the question, it should be known that a firm reconciliation can hardly be made: (1) where the friendship was dissolved on account of the crimes and disgraces of one of the parties; (2) unless it is plainly and fully seen that every remnant of hatred has been plucked out. For what the poet says is true: "The judgement of Paris and the spurned beauty, the injury, remain stored deep in the mind."

units.la: Nam nisi melior sit ingenii indoles, & major in homine pietas, vix unquam reconciliatio solet esse firma, ut exempla veterum & recentiorum ubique demonstrant.
units.tr: For unless the disposition of the mind is better and the piety in the man greater, a reconciliation is hardly ever firm, as the examples of ancients and moderns show everywhere.

units.la: XVII. Uno ex amicis defuncto, quid cum illius filius superstes amicus agere pro jure sua in patrem amicitia debeat, & utrum eadem amicitia ad filios defunctorum continuetur?
units.tr: XVII. When one of the friends has died, what ought the surviving son of his friend to do, by right of the friendship his father had with him, and does the same friendship continue to the children of the deceased?

units.la: Resp. Hic cum Isocrate ad Demonicum: τηρεῖτε τὰς παῖδας ὥσπερ τῆς πάτρας, ὅτω ἡ τῆς φιλίας παρὰ τῆς πατρικῆς κληρονομίας. Ratio fit: 1. Quia inter maxima bona amicitia paterna cesetur, longeque pulchrior saepe omni paterna haereditate ac utilior. 2. Quia voto parenparentum ita amicitia contrahitur, ut initiæ à sese amicitiæ fructus ad posteros etiam & liberos pervehiat, quia non sibi tantum sed & suis quisq; pius & fidelis maxime prospicit. 2. idipsum probatur exemplo Jonathæ & Davidis. Nam David amicitiam, quam cum patre contraxerat, ad filium Jonathæ extendit. 1. Samuel. 9. Verumtamen hæc amicitia cum parentibus contracta non tam fervens & feria esse solet erga liberos, nisi ingenii, morum & virtutis similitudo ad id alliciat. Ideo interdum pius affectus, inter dum reliquiæ amoris erga parentes benevolentiam liberis conciliant, non vero & arctam illam amicitiam, quæ prius inter vivum & defunctum exercebatur, nisi eadem causæ in liberis insint.
units.tr: Answer: Here, with Isocrates to Demonicus: "Keep the friendships of your fathers as you keep their inheritance" [τηρεῖτε τὰς παῖδας ὥσπερ τῆς πάτρας, ὅτω ἡ τῆς φιλίας παρὰ τῆς πατρικῆς κληρονομίας]. The reason is: (1) because paternal friendship is counted among the greatest goods, and is often far more beautiful than any paternal inheritance and more useful. (2) Because, by the vow of parents, a friendship is so contracted that the fruit of the friendship begun by them is carried on to posterity and to their children, since every pious and faithful man provides chiefly not only for himself but also for his own. The same is proved by the example of Jonathan and David: for David extended to Jonathan's son the friendship he had contracted with the father. 1 Samuel 9. Yet a friendship contracted with parents is not usually as fervent and constant towards their children, unless a similarity of disposition, manners and virtue draws them to it. Therefore sometimes a pious affection, and sometimes the remnants of love for the parents, win goodwill for the children, but not that close friendship which was practised between the living and the dead, unless the same causes are present in the children.

units.la: XVIII. An in adversa vel secunda fortuna magis amicis indigeamus?
units.tr: XVIII. Do we need friends more in adversity or in prosperity?

units.la: Resp. Per distinctionem ex Philosopho 9. Nicomach. cap. 11. Quod quidem amici magis necessarii sunt in adversis, at pulchriores in secundis. Huic suaviter accinit Cicero: Et secundas res splendidiores facit amicitia, & adversas partiens communicans; leviores. Ad splendorem amicitiæ faciunt, quia eo melius amicitiæ munera obire valemus, auxilio operâ nostrâ indigentibus beneficia exhibere. Verum si ulterius progrediamur, tam læto, quam tristi fortunæ statu amicis egemus. Nam prout cuique homini res accidunt, ita firmi amici sunt, si labant res lapsæ, itidem & amici collabascunt. Idcirco ingeniis ægro animo solamen est, unum aliquem in conspectu habere, cujus fide & virtute fretus forti perferre animo asperà quæas. Taceo, quod tum vires amicitiæ maximè illucescant, ut pulchrè Ovidius Scilicet ut fulvum spectatur in ignibus aurum, Tempore sic duro est experiunda fides.
units.tr: Answer: By a distinction, following the Philosopher in Nicomachean Ethics 9, chapter 11: friends are indeed more necessary in adversity, but more beautiful in prosperity. Cicero sings sweetly in harmony with this: "Friendship makes prosperity more brilliant and, by sharing and dividing adversity, makes it lighter." Friendship adds to its own brilliance because we are better able to perform the duties of friendship and to give help and service to those in need. But if we go further, we need friends in a happy state of fortune as much as in a sad one. For whatever happens to a person, so are his friends firm: if his affairs totter and fall, his friends too collapse with them. Therefore it is a comfort to a troubled mind to have someone in sight whose faithfulness and virtue give it the confidence to bear with a brave spirit the hardships it must suffer. I say nothing of the fact that the strength of friendship then shines most clearly, as Ovid nicely puts it: "Just as gold is tested in the fire, so loyalty must be tested in a hard time."

units.la: Er praeclarè Comicus: Is amicus est, qui in re dubia tum juvat, cum opus est. Rursus re um omnium copia fruc-tes, ne in magnum incidant periculum, si vel elati nimium efferantur, vel ex divitiarum affluentia sui obliviscantur, tum quoq; opem amicorum implorare decet, quorum consilio regantur, ne aliquid praeter rectum & aequum faciant. Hinc concludi-tur amicis in adversa fortuna opus esse, ut solamen & auxilium praestent: res etiam secundas effl gita-re amicos, ut consilio, ne devient, dirigantur. Vide Picolh.cap. 23.gradu 7.
units.tr: And the comic poet says well: "He is a friend who helps in a doubtful matter when help is needed." Again, those who enjoy an abundance of all things ought, so that they do not fall into great danger if they become too elated, or forget themselves through the flood of riches, also to seek the help of friends, by whose counsel they may be guided and not do anything contrary to what is right and fair. Hence it is concluded that friends are needed in adversity, to offer comfort and help; and also that in prosperity friends are needed to direct us by their counsel, so that we do not go astray. See Piccolomini, chapter 23, grade 7.

units.la: XIX. An amicitia praestet affinitate?
units.tr: XIX. Does friendship surpass kinship by marriage?

units.la: Resp. Diver-sae esse hominum hac de re opiniones. Nam Cice-ro acerrimus amicitiae defensor amicitiam praefe-rendam censet: Namque hoc praestat amicitia assi-nitati, inquit, quod ex propinquitate benevolentia tolli, ut experientia docet, ex amicitia non potest. Sublata enim: benevolentia amicitiae nomen tolli-tur, propinquitate manet. Econtra sunt, qui na-turae ductum sequi suadent sanguinisque conjun-ctionem velut causam amoris principalem eligi. Hinc Plutarchus lib. de fraterno amore, ex sententia Hesiodi, inquit,
units.tr: Answer: On this matter the opinions of men differ. For Cicero, the keenest defender of friendship, judges that friendship is to be preferred: "For friendship has this advantage over kinship by marriage," he says, "that goodwill, as experience teaches, can be removed by a near relationship but cannot be removed from friendship. For when goodwill is taken away, the name of friendship is lost, but kinship remains." On the other side, there are those who urge us to follow the guidance of nature and to choose the bond of blood as the chief cause of love. Hence Plutarch, in his book on brotherly love, following the opinion of Hesiod, says:

units.la: Æqualem fratri caveas fecisse sodalem.
units.tr: "Beware of making a companion equal to your brother."

units.la: Natura enim nos cum affinibus & sanguine junctis ligat, cujus instinctum ac ductum excutere non possumus. Nam utut incidant offensiones, injuriae, & caetera, quae vinculum amoris disrumpere possint, natura tamen semper nos memores reddit illius pro-pinpinquitatis, quam ipsa conciliavit: E contra præferendam amicitiam suadet hæc ratio: Quia amici virtute animique effectu ligantur & jucundiorem cum ve o amico ducimus vitam quam cum affinibus aut cognatis: Et experientia docet amico nos sæpius credere quam cognatis: Res tota distinctione expediri poterit. Nam amicitia consideratur vel absolute in se vel comparatè, quatenus nimirum ad conjunctionem sanguinis accedit. Amicitia in se considerata longè præcellit dignitati affinitatis tanquam dilectæ virtutis filiola. Posteriori modo accepta palmam lubens concedit affinitati tam ex naturæ quàm virtutis generè oriundæ Picolhom cap. 16.
units.tr: For nature binds us to our relatives and blood-kin, and we cannot shake off its impulse and guidance. For although offences, injuries and other things may arise which could break the bond of love, nature nevertheless always keeps us mindful of that kinship which it itself has established. On the other hand, the following reasoning urges that friendship be preferred: because friends are bound together by virtue and by the disposition of their minds, and we find life more pleasant with a true friend than with relatives or kinsmen; and experience teaches that we trust a friend more often than kinsmen. The whole matter can be settled by a distinction. For friendship is considered either absolutely, in itself, or comparatively, insofar as it is joined to the bond of blood. Considered in itself, friendship far excels the dignity of kinship by marriage, as a beloved daughter of virtue. Taken in the second way, friendship willingly yields the palm to kinship, which arises both from nature and from the kind of virtue it involves. See Piccolomini, chapter 16.

units.la: XX. Huic etiam propter summam conjunctionem addi potest hæc, An inter fratres reperiatur vera amicitia?
units.tr: XX. To this, on account of the closest connection, may be added this question: Is true friendship found among brothers?

units.la: Resp. Interdum reperiri, interdum non. Quæ concludant amicitiam inter fratres sunt hæc: 1. Naturæ instinctus. 2. Conjunctio sanguinis. 3. Cohabitatio. Nam plerumque ad annos maturitatis fratres cohabitare solent. 4. Familiaritas contracta ab incunabulis, quæ præcipuum amicitiæ ligamentum esse solet. Interdum tamen non reperitur. Nam historiæ testantur fratres odio plusquam Vatiniano inter se conflagrasse. Vide Senecam in Thebaide de Etheocle & Polynice, quorum tanta fuerunt odia, ut cum mutuis se vulneribus interemissent, & cadavera rogis esset supremis impositæ, flamma se dissecuit & in diversum abiit, ita ut non tantum in vita, sed & in morte odiū illud permaneret. Hinc Aristoteles 7. Polit. cap. 5. docet fratrum odia deterrima ac perniciosissima esse. Hujus causæ hæc esse possunt: 1. Quia amor naturalis, ubi se lætum cernit, à summo gradu benevolentiæ in summum odii gradum se convertere solet. 2. Ira major reperitur in his odiis quam in aliis. Nam fratres propter conjunctionem sanguinis à se invicem læsi debere minime putant. Quod si contingat præter meritum, tunc omnem iram, invidiam, odii molem evomere solent, & in vindictam parato nimis in malum pectore incumbere: Picolhom. gradu 7. cap. 16.
units.tr: Answer: Sometimes it is found, sometimes not. The following arguments conclude that there is friendship among brothers: (1) the instinct of nature; (2) the bond of blood; (3) living together, for brothers usually live together until they reach maturity; (4) familiarity formed from the cradle, which is usually the chief bond of friendship. Yet sometimes it is not found. For histories bear witness that brothers have blazed with hatred for one another beyond even that of Vatinius. See Seneca in the Thebaid, concerning Eteocles and Polynices, whose hatreds were so great that, when they had killed each other with mutual wounds and their bodies were placed on the funeral pyre, the flame divided itself and turned in opposite directions, so that this hatred remained not only in life but even in death. Hence Aristotle, Politics 7, chapter 5, teaches that hatreds between brothers are the most wicked and the most destructive. The causes of this may be these: (1) because natural love, when it sees itself wronged, is accustomed to turn from the highest degree of goodwill to the highest degree of hatred; (2) a greater anger is found in these hatreds than in others, for brothers, because of their blood-kinship, think that they ought least of all to be harmed by one another; and if it happens beyond what is deserved, then they are accustomed to pour out all their anger, envy and mass of hatred, and to fall upon the one who is prepared for vengeance with a heart too inclined to evil. See Piccolomini, grade 7, chapter 16.

units.la: XXI. An amicitia publica præstet privata? Et respondetur breviter, præstare propter has causas: 1.
units.tr: XXI. Is public friendship better than private friendship? The answer briefly is that it is better, for these reasons: 1.

units.la: Quia bonum, quo communius, eo melius. Ergo & amicitia publica præstantior erit privata. 2. Quia sicut medicina, quæ toti confert corpori, præfertur illi, quæ uni aut altero membro prodest, ita de amicitia publica censendum. 3. Quia amicitia publica salutem Reipup. in primis spectat, & utilitatem, privata unius aut alterius tantum respicit commodum. Verum hic distinctione opus erit. Si amicitia late sumatur, tunc publica præferenda venit privatæ. At si stricte & proprie, quatenus scilicet consideratur ut conspiratio duorum aut plurium in aliquo bono honesto, hic proprie amicitia in Repub. locum non habet, sed potius dicitur amor civium mutuus, aut συμπάθεια quædam, quâ omnia Reipublicæ membra se mutuo prosequuntur tanquam unius corporis membra. Picel.c.15. hac utitur distinctione scilicet amicitia publica extensione quâ ad plures extenditur, sit præferenda privatæ. Non autem intensione, quâ primariò dirigitur in privatum duorum aut plurium commodum, secundariò tantum in finem aut salutem Reipub. Verùm hæc distinctio non magni esse momenti videtur.
units.tr: Because the good that is more common is the better. Therefore public friendship will also be superior to private friendship. 2. Because just as a medicine that benefits the whole body is preferred to one that helps only one or another member, so public friendship should be judged. 3. Because public friendship primarily regards the safety and advantage of the commonwealth, while private friendship looks only to the advantage of one or another person. But a distinction is needed here. If friendship is taken broadly, then public friendship is to be preferred to private. But if it is taken strictly and properly, insofar as it is understood as the agreement of two or more in some honourable good, then properly speaking friendship has no place in the commonwealth. Rather, it is called the mutual love of the citizens, or a certain sympathy [συμπάθεια], by which all the members of the commonwealth care for one another as the members of one body. Picolhomini uses this distinction: public friendship, by its extension, in that it reaches to more people, is to be preferred to private friendship; but not by its intension, by which it is directed primarily to the private advantage of two or more, and only secondarily to the end or safety of the commonwealth. Yet this distinction does not seem to be of great importance.

units.la: XXII. An felix egeat amicis? Resp. Si felicitas in felici consideretur secundum essentiam & naturam suam internam, tunc amicis egere non videtur, cum nullis externis indigeat bonis. Nam ut dicitur cap. 8. lib. 1. Nicom. felicitas in se est αὐτάρκης sibi omnia sufficiens.
units.tr: XXII. Does the happy man need friends? Answer: If happiness is considered according to its essence and inner nature, then it does not seem to need friends, since it lacks no external goods. For, as is said in cap. 8. lib. 1. Nicom., happiness is in itself self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης], sufficing for itself in all things.

units.la: At verò si consideretur felicitas secundum existentiam in hoc vel illo subjecto, tunc felix omnino amicis egere videtur. Nam cum in usu virtutis sit posita felicitas, qui suo usu frui poterit? si amicis destituatur, cum amicitia sit usus & fructus virtutis. Propterea inter maximas Tyranni calamitates hæc numeratur, quod amicis careat. Et Alexander Magnus, qui proximum tenuisse gradum ad felicitatem putatur interroganti cuidam, ubi thesauros haberet, amicos ostendit, innuens se nulla felicitate frui posse absque amicorum opera.
units.tr: But if happiness is considered according to its existence in this or that subject, then the happy man seems altogether to need friends. For since happiness lies in the use of virtue, who will be able to enjoy its use if he is deprived of friends, since friendship is the use and fruit of virtue? For this reason, lacking friends is counted among the greatest calamities of a tyrant. And Alexander the Great, who is thought to have held the next place to happiness, when someone asked him where he kept his treasures, showed him his friends, implying that he could enjoy no happiness without the help of friends.

units.la: XXIII. Hinc breviter quæritur: Num homo secundam fortunam & dignitatis gradum magis pro se quam pro amico optare debeat? Resp. Amici considerandi sunt in pari fortunæ gradu vel in impari. In pari nihil sibi optare debet, quod non amico, propterea quod amicus sit alter idem: Et ut ait Comicus; Idem velle, idemq; nolle firmam facit amicitiam. In impari gradu, si nos superamus amicum divitiis aut dignitate, tunc optare debemus, ut communi nobiscum utatur fortuna, si ille nos superet, optare debemus, absque illius detrimento tamen & damno ut illi æquiparari possimus, quo scilicet mutua benevolentia & amoris officia invicem fovere & confirmare. xe magis magisque possimus. Picolhom. capite 24.
units.tr: XXIII. Here the question is briefly asked: Ought a man to wish a second fortune and a higher rank of dignity more for himself than for his friend? Answer: Friends must be considered either in equal or in unequal rank of fortune. In equal rank a man ought not to wish for himself anything that he does not wish for his friend, since the friend is another self. And as the Comic poet says, "to want the same things and to refuse the same things makes a firm friendship." In unequal rank: if we surpass our friend in riches or dignity, then we ought to wish that he share our fortune in common; if he surpasses us, we ought to wish, without any loss or damage to him, that we might be made equal to him, so that by mutual goodwill and the offices of love we may cherish and strengthen one another more and more. Picolhomini, chapter 24.

units.la: XXIV. An quod dicitur a Comico, & vulgo creditur: Amantium irae amoris redintegratio fit? Resp. Si intelligas de ira ex levi causa orta, aut de amore lascivo, qui voluptatem pro fine habet, & in quo suspiciones, irae, injuriae oriri solent, esse veram sententiam quia cum ea voluptate privamur, quam summopere optamus, evenit ut mox ob indigentiam vehementius in eam feramur, dulciusque, si potiri possimus, illa fruamur, non secus ac dum aliquandiu detinemur, ne aeque inspiremus, mox vehementius illum ducimus acanhelamus. At si de amicitia vera sumatur raro contingere solet, ut amor jam longo tempore confirmatus & ex injuriis utrinque aut alteruta saltem ex parte illatis laesus in integrum restituatur. Vide quaest. 16. Picolh. cap. 21. XXV. Qui fit, quod benefactores ardentius ament eos, quibus benefaciunt, quam contra clientes illos, a quibus beneficia accipiunt? Resp. Ejus rei causas aliquot acute investigasse Aristotelem lib. 8. sub finem & lib. 9 sub initium, e quibus prima est, quia is, qui beneficium accepit, est quasi opus & factura benefactoris. Omnis autem opifex magis suum opus amat, quam opus opificem. 2. Quia honestum magis est amabile, quam utile. Dare autem est honestatis, accipere utilitatis. 3. Quia quod magis est durabile, magis est amabile. Honestas autem est magis durabilis. Idcirco beneficiens semper habet in memoria honestatem benefacti sui. Is autem, qui beneficium accepit, utilitatem tantum censet: utilitas autem cito perit, ideo minus amat. 4. Quia benefacere magis accedit ad amoamorem actívum, qui est præstantior: beneficia accipere pertinet ad passionem, quæ est minus præstans. s. Quia difficilius & laboriosius est beneficia dare quam accipere. Ergo ex ea quoque magis oritur amor. 6. Denique quia dare majorem parit homini felicitatem quam accipere, juxta illud Act. 20. & 2s.beatius est dare quam accipere.
units.tr: XXIV. Is what the Comic poet says, and what is commonly believed, true: that lovers' quarrels bring about the renewal of love? Answer: If you understand it of anger arising from a slight cause, or of wanton love, which has pleasure for its end, and in which suspicions, quarrels and injuries are wont to arise, then the saying is true. For when we are deprived of the pleasure we most desire, it comes about that, through want, we are carried more vehemently toward it, and enjoy it more sweetly if we can gain possession of it; just as when we are held back for some time from breathing, we then gasp for breath more violently. But if it is taken of true friendship, it rarely happens that a love already long confirmed, and wounded by injuries inflicted on both sides or at least on one, is restored entire. See question 16; Picolhomini, chapter 21. XXV. Why do benefactors love more ardently those to whom they do good than the clients from whom they receive benefits love them in return? Answer: Aristotle, in book 8 near the end and book 9 near the beginning, has acutely investigated several causes of this, of which the first is that the one who has received a benefit is, as it were, the work and product of the benefactor. But every craftsman loves his work more than the work loves the craftsman. 2. Because the honourable is more lovable than the useful. To give belongs to honour, to receive to utility. 3. Because what is more lasting is more lovable. But honour is more lasting. Hence the benefactor always keeps in memory the honour of his good deed. But the one who has received a benefit regards only the utility, and utility perishes quickly; therefore he loves less. 4. Because to do good comes closer to active love, which is the more excellent; to receive benefits pertains to passion, which is less excellent. 5. Because it is more difficult and laborious to give benefits than to receive them; therefore love arises more from this as well. 6. Finally, because giving brings a man greater happiness than receiving, according to that saying in Act. 20.: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."

units.la: Ultimò & hoc quæritur; An pro amico mortis adeundum sit periculum? Resp. Esse rationes pro & contra. Nam pro affirmativa faciunt hæ: 1. Quia Pythagoræ hoc erat dogma, ut amicus pro amico mortem subiret, si modo à periculo amicum liberare posset: Cujus rei exemplum illustre fuit in Damone & Pythia Pythagoricæ sectæ Philosophis. 2. Quia idem amico optandum, quod quis sibi optari velit, ut ex quæst. 23. patet. At unusquisque ex instinctu naturæ sibi longam & prosperam optat viam. Ergo & amico id optare debet: Et per consequens omni modo amicum mortis periculo eripere tenetur. 3. Quia sic sibi famam comparat immortalem & omnium admirationem, ut videre licet in Alcesta, quæ pro conjuge mortem subiit, & in Codro Atheniensium rege, qui pro salute patriæ voluntariæ se morti devovit. 4. Quia sic summum amorem, quo major exprimi nequit erga amicum exprimit, Johan. 15. vers. 13. At pro contraria sententia sunt: 1. Quia cum lege naturæ pugnat, ut quis se vita privet, ad quam naturæ instinctu conservandam tenetur. At nulla virtus moralis naturæ contraria esse debet, sed potius naturam in actionibus hominum perficere. 2. Quia qui hoc facit, contra justitiam peccat, justi- iustitia vero exigit, ut suum cuique tribuatur, sive illud sit debitum naturæ, quod in morte naturali peditur, sive juris & facti, quod in violenta morte exigitur. 3. Quia nihil tale in Scripturis præcipitur, immo directè legi divinæ repugnat: Non occides. 4. Demum quia nemo sibi morte cōscifcere debet, quia sic Deo naturæ & legibus humanis repugnat, & Reipubl. uno sui membro privat. Vide cap. 9. lib. 3. Nicomach. Quod tamen fit cum se morti, quis pro amico devovet: Proinde etsi summus in amicitia amor maximumque benevolentiæ & conjunctionis vinculum esse debeat, nemo mortem pro amico subire tenetur, neque in morte naturali cum sic amicum liberare non possit, neque in violenta. Nam ea vel infligitur propter causam honestā, verbi gratia: propter religionem aut patriam, & sic invidus esset, quia amicum hoc honore privaret: neque propter causam inhonestam. In hac enim amico favere non debet, cum contra amicitiæ finem pugnet, nempe honestatem. Hoc tamen concedi posset, quod si quis amicum suum morte liberare ullo modo queat, in hoc incumbendum esse, ita tamen ut nunquam contra jus nec divinum nec humanum agat. Nam ut supra diximus amico gratificandum, sed usque ad aras. Atque hæc hucusque de doctrina Amicitiæ, quæ explicatur totus liber VIII. & IX. Aristotelis. Plura qui legere volet de Amicitia, Ciceronem legat in Lælio, & Picolhomineum gradu 7. per totum, &c.
units.tr: Finally, this too is asked: Must one undergo the danger of death for a friend? Answer: There are reasons both for and against. For the affirmative these count: 1. Because it was a doctrine of Pythagoras that a friend should undergo death for a friend, provided he could free him from danger; a famous example of this was in Damon and Phintias, philosophers of the Pythagorean sect. 2. Because one ought to wish for a friend what one would wish to be wished for oneself, as is clear from question 23. But everyone by the instinct of nature wishes for himself a long and prosperous life. Therefore he ought to wish this for his friend too, and consequently he is bound in every way to snatch his friend from the danger of death. 3. Because in this way he wins for himself immortal fame and the admiration of all, as may be seen in Alcestis, who underwent death for her husband, and in Codrus, king of the Athenians, who voluntarily devoted himself to death for the safety of his country. 4. Because in this way he shows the highest love, than which no greater can be shown toward a friend: John 15, vers. 13. On the contrary side are these: 1. Because it is contrary to the law of nature for someone to deprive himself of the life which, by the instinct of nature, he is bound to preserve. But no moral virtue ought to be contrary to nature; rather, it ought to perfect nature in human actions. 2. Because he who does this sins against justice. Justice requires that each be given his due, whether it is the debt of nature, which is exacted in natural death, or the debt of right and fact, which is exacted in violent death. 3. Because nothing of the kind is enjoined in Scripture; indeed it is directly opposed to the divine law: "Thou shalt not kill." 4. Lastly, because no one ought to bring about his own death, since in this way he goes against God, nature and human laws, and deprives the commonwealth of one of its members. See book 3, chapter 9 of the Nicomachean Ethics. Yet this happens when someone devotes himself to death for a friend. Therefore, although the highest love in friendship, and the greatest bond of goodwill and union, ought to exist, no one is bound to undergo death for a friend, neither natural death, since in that way he cannot free his friend, nor violent death. For violent death is inflicted either for an honourable cause, for example for religion or country, and then he would be envious, since he would deprive his friend of this honour; or for a dishonourable cause, in which case he ought not to favour his friend, since this is against the end of friendship, namely honour. This, however, could be conceded: that if someone can in any way free his friend from death, he should apply himself to this, yet in such a way that he never acts against either divine or human law. For, as we said above, one should gratify a friend, but only up to the altars. And so far on the doctrine of friendship, which is explained in the whole of Aristotle's books 8 and 9. Whoever wishes to read more about friendship, let him read Cicero's Laelius, and Picolhomini, degree 7, throughout, etc.

units.la: SUMMA LIBRI X.
units.tr: SUMMARY OF BOOK X.

units.la: Philosophus in 10. lib. de voluptate & felicitate agit, at de felicitate copiose satis toto lib. 1. (ubi felicitatis naturae proprietates, ac varias quaestiones ultro citroq; disceptatas fusius explicavimus) egisse videmur: restat, ut de ea voluptate, quae ipsa felicitatem veluti umbra corpus, aut ut regnum corona insequitur, breviter agatur.
units.tr: The Philosopher treats of pleasure in Book 10 and of happiness, and we seem to have dealt with happiness fully enough throughout Book 1, where we explained at length the natural properties of happiness and the various questions debated on both sides. What remains is to treat briefly of that pleasure which follows happiness itself, as a shadow follows a body or a crown follows a kingdom.

units.la: DE VOLVPTATE EFFECTV Summi Boni.
units.tr: On the Effect of the Highest Good: Pleasure

units.la: OSTQVAM de Felicitate tanquam summo hominis bono, & de mediis ad ipsam ducentibus tam moralibus quam intellectualibus scilicet virtutibus, ex mente Aristotelis hucusq; egimus: Ratio instituti postulat, quo melius & plenius de bene beateq; vivendi modo doctrina tradatur, ut de effectu summi boni, nempe de voluptate paucis agatur, propterea quod Aristoteles lib. 17. Nic. à cap. 11. usque ad finem lib. & lib. 10. ab initio usque ad cap. 6. de ea ex professo agat, & ideo quidé de ea agat, quia nihil aliud est, quam tranquillitas quaedam animi ex gaudio & laetitia rerum bene gestarum perfecta, quae ipsum virtutis exercitium statim sequitur, & propterea à Philosopho cap. 4. lib. 10. vocatur perfectae
units.tr: Having so far treated of happiness as the highest good of man, and of the means leading to it, both the moral and the intellectual virtues, according to the mind of Aristotle, the plan of this work requires that, so that the teaching on living well and happily may be delivered more fully and completely, we should say a few words about the effect of the highest good, namely pleasure. Aristotle treats of it expressly in book 7 of the Nicomachean Ethics, from ch. 11 to the end of the book, and in book 10 from the beginning to ch. 6. He treats of it because it is nothing other than a certain tranquillity of mind, complete with joy and gladness over things well done, which immediately follows the very exercise of virtue. For this reason the Philosopher, in ch. 4 of book 10, calls it the end that supervenes upon a perfect operation.

units.la: operationis finis superadveniens, non quod ultimi- rerum humanarum finis aliquis sit adhuc ulterior finis, sed quia homo, qui perfecte secundum omnes virtutes operatur, tum demum ex ista operationis perfectione summam sentit voluptatem & lætitiam animi, quâ tanquam signo certo se ad finem & perfectionem virtutum omnium pervenisse novit. Et cum voluptas ipsam insequatur perfectam omnium virtutum operationem, non secus ac lumen sequitur lucem, hæc causa impulit Epicurum & ejus sectatores ut in voluptate situm esse summum bonum asseruerint. Non male tamen, si credimus Aristotelilib.7.Pol.cap.4. propterea quod summum bonum necessario sequatur, sed in hoc erraverunt, quod felicitatem a suo consequente ut causam ab effectu, non distinxerint. De voluptate ista quatuor breviter quæremus: 1. Quid sit: Nam dubitare an sit, est sensibus ipsis tam externis quam internis repugnare, cum nihil sit vita saltem sensitiva præditum, quod non aliquam naturæ instinctu insitam habeat voluptatem. 2. Quotuplex sit, seu quam varias habeat species. 3. Ut natura ipsius melius innotescat, quas habeat proprietates & accidentia. 4. Nonnullas de voluptate tam in genere quam in specie quæstiones subjiciemus. Quod ad primam, nempe quid sit? Ex definitione cognoscitur. Definitur vero voluptas, cap.4.10.Nicom. perfectio operationum bene ab animalibus administratarum, vi quadam jucunda pollens: seu, quod eodem recidit, perfectio operationum in animalibus, cum desiderio jucundi & amabilis conjuncta. Hæc definitio ut melius intelligatur tur tria hæc observanda veniunt: 1. Forma 2. causa efficiens voluptatis 3. subjectum, in quo reperitur. Forma generis ambitu continetur. Est enim voluptas secundum naturam & essentiā suam, perfectio operationū in suo subjecto, adeò ubi res aut operatio ad finē suam pervenit & delectatio simul ad finem accessit, ibi voluptatem cum perfectionis operatione conjunctam adesse constat, adeo ut vera forma voluptatis in perfectione operationis non immeritò cōsistere dicatur. 2. Causa efficiēs in brutis quidem est sensus externus. A sensibus siquidem externis, cum ratione & judicio intus destituantur, voluptates suas plerumque hauriunt, in hominibus verò est tam sensus externus, quam internus & intellectus etiam in suum objectum agens. Nam ut ibi perfectissima dicitur operatio, ubi & sensus & intellectus salvo & in columni modo se habent, & in objectum suum præsens accommodatum & in suo genere optimum sine impedimento agunt, ibi perfectissima etiam generatur voluptas. Aristoteles 10. Nicom.cap. 4. 3. Subjectum voluptatis duplex statuitur. Unum propinquius, alterum remotius subjectum remotius sunt animalia, ut in definitione exprimitur, eaque tam ratione carentia quam prædita ratione. Et rationem hanc addit Philosophus loco citato, cur omnibus animalibus voluptas tribuatur, quia omnia vitam amant, & idcirco voluptate quoque capiunt ex amore vitæ suæ. Nam voluptas & dicitur vitā perficere & in longius protrahere. Propinquius subjectum voluptatis sunt sensus & intellectus. Nam voluptates & intrinsecus ex interna animi commotione jucunda, & extrinsecus ex operatione externa percipiuntur: Aristoteles loco citato, Quod ad secundam quæstionem quotuplex sit, seu quâ varias habeat divisiones? docet Philosophus variis in locis, ut capp. 10. & 11. lib. 3. Nicom. & cap. 11. lib. 7. cap. 5. lib. 10. Hic nonnullas tantum pro ratione instituti subjiciemus.
units.tr: Not because there is some further end beyond the final end of human affairs, but because a man who acts perfectly according to all the virtues then feels from that perfection of his action the highest pleasure and gladness of mind, by which, as by a sure sign, he knows that he has reached the end and perfection of all the virtues. And since pleasure follows the perfect performance of all the virtues just as light follows the light of a lamp, this circumstance led Epicurus and his followers to assert that the highest good lies in pleasure. They were not wrong, if we believe Aristotle in Politics 7, ch. 4, since the highest good necessarily follows; but they erred in this, that they did not distinguish happiness from its consequence, taking the effect for the cause. We will briefly inquire into this pleasure under four heads: 1. What it is. For to doubt whether it exists is to contradict the senses themselves, both external and internal, since nothing endowed with even a sensitive life lacks a pleasure implanted by an instinct of nature. 2. How many kinds there are, or what various species it has. 3. What properties and accidents it has, so that its nature may be better known. 4. We shall add some questions concerning pleasure, both in general and in particular. As to the first, namely what it is, this is known from the definition. Pleasure is defined in ch. 4 of book 10 of the Nicomachean Ethics as the perfection of operations well carried out by living beings, possessing a certain pleasant power; or, which comes to the same thing, the perfection of operations in living beings joined with a desire for what is pleasant and lovable. So that this definition may be better understood, three things are to be observed: 1. the form; 2. the efficient cause of pleasure; 3. the subject in which it is found. The form is contained within the scope of the genus. For pleasure, according to its nature and essence, is the perfection of an operation in its subject. Hence, where a thing or an operation has reached its end, and delight has arrived at the same end, there pleasure joined with the perfection of the operation is plainly present, so that the true form of pleasure may not unreasonably be said to consist in the perfection of the operation. 2. The efficient cause in brutes is indeed the external sense. For since they lack reason and judgement within, they mostly draw their pleasures from the external senses; but in humans there is both the external sense and the internal sense, and the intellect also acting upon its object. For as the operation is called most perfect where both the sense and the intellect are in their proper and sound condition, and act without hindrance upon a fitting object that is present and in its own kind the best, there most perfect pleasure is also produced (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 4). 3. The subject of pleasure is set down as twofold: one nearer, the other more remote. The more remote subjects are living beings, as the definition expresses, and these include both those without reason and those endowed with reason. The Philosopher adds this reason, in the passage cited, why pleasure is attributed to all living beings: because all things love life, and therefore they also take pleasure from the love of their own life. For pleasure is said both to perfect life and to prolong it. The nearer subjects of pleasure are the senses and the intellect. For pleasures are perceived both within, from an inward pleasant stirring of the mind, and without, from external operation (Aristotle, in the passage cited). As to the second question, how many kinds there are, or by what various divisions, the Philosopher teaches this in various places, as in chs. 10 and 11 of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, ch. 11 of book 7, and ch. 5 of book 10. Here we shall set down only a few, as the purpose of this work requires.

units.la: Prima divisio sumitur à subjecto in quo inest voluptas. Nam alia est voluptas corporis, alia animi (desumitur hæc divisio ex cap. 10. lib. 3. Nicom. ubi objectum Temperantiæ exquirit Philosophus.) Voluptas animi est commotio quædam, quæ animum jucunditate quadam afficit. Aristoteles ibid. Percipitur verò hæc voluptas ex variis rebus & potissimū ex hisce quatuor: 1. Ex cognitione & contemplatione rerum. 2. Ex actionibus seu operationibus virtutum. 3. Ex colloquio & consortio amicorum & eorum omnium, quorum societate aut sodalitate delectamur. 4. Ex adeptione earum rerum, quas studiosè appetimus, cujusmodi sunt opes, divitiæ, dignitates, honores, uxor, liberi, quæ in bonorum numero habentur, & quæ ab hominibus cum desiderio habendi expetuntur. Voluptas corporis est ea, quæ ex rationis rectæ præscripto, naturali necessitati satisfaciens, corpus & sensus ipsos externos jucunda aliqua commotione & naturæ amica afficit, pro ratione scilicet sensuum. Alia enim ex visu, alia ex auditu, alia ex odoratu, alia ex gustu, alia ex tactu percipitur voluptas, de quibus vide Aristotelem cap. 10. 3. Nicomach. Neque enim hic quamlibet voluptatem corporis intelligimus, (nihil enim nobis comcommercii est cum ea, de qua Cicero lib.2.de leg. ait, quod sit imitatrix tantum boni, malorum omnium mater, cujus blanditiis corrumpuntur ea, quæ sua natura bona sunt,) sed veram hic corporis voluptatem exprimimus, quæ duobus hisce limitib. circumscribitur, ut per ea naturali necessitati satis fiat, idq; vel in conservatione individui, ut in cibo, potu, alimento, vel in conservatione speciei, ut in Venere aliisque necessitatibus, quibus rerum species natura conservari & propagari voluit, & de hac voluptate eleganter Virgilius in quodam Epigrammate:
units.tr: The first division is taken from the subject in which pleasure inheres. For one pleasure belongs to the body, another to the mind (this division is drawn from ch. 10 of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics, where the Philosopher inquires into the object of temperance). Pleasure of the mind is a certain stirring which affects the mind with a kind of delight (Aristotle, ibid.). This pleasure is perceived from various things, and chiefly from these four: (1) from the knowledge and contemplation of things; (2) from the actions or operations of the virtues; (3) from the conversation and company of friends, and of all those with whose fellowship or companionship we take delight; (4) from the attainment of those things which we eagerly desire, such as wealth, riches, dignities, honours, a wife, children, which are counted among goods and which men seek with a desire to possess them. Pleasure of the body is that which, following the prescription of right reason and satisfying natural need, affects the body and the external senses themselves with some pleasant stirring friendly to nature, according to the nature of each sense. For one pleasure is perceived through sight, another through hearing, another through smell, another through taste, another through touch; on these see Aristotle, ch. 10 of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics. For here we do not mean any pleasure of the body whatever (we have nothing in common with that pleasure of which Cicero, in De legibus book 2, says that it is only an imitator of good and the mother of all evils, whose flatteries corrupt things that are good by their own nature). Rather, we express here the true pleasure of the body, which is bounded by two limits, so that by them natural need is satisfied, either in the preservation of the individual, as in food, drink and nourishment, or in the preservation of the species, as in sexual union and the other necessities by which nature willed that the kinds of things be preserved and propagated. Of this pleasure Virgil speaks elegantly in a certain epigram:

units.la: Vina sitim sedent, natis Venus alma creandisServiat, hos fines transfilisse nocet.
units.tr: Wine allays thirst, and kindly Venus serves the begetting of children; to overstep these bounds is harmful.

units.la: 2. Ut ratio huic necessitati modum præscribat, ne scilicet homines voluptati amplius indulgeant, quam naturæ necessitas, exigit. Quantum vero exigit natura necessitas ipsa docet ratio, quia, ut præclare canit Claudianus in 4. Consulatu Honorii:
units.tr: 2. Reason must prescribe the measure for this need, so that men do not indulge in pleasure more than natural necessity requires. How much natural necessity requires, reason itself teaches, since, as Claudian sings well in the Fourth Consulship of Honorius:

units.la: Hanc alta capitis fundavit in arceMandatricem operum prospecturamque laboriIpse Deus:
units.tr: This God himself established in the high citadel of the head, as the director of works and the overseer of labour.

units.la: Secunda divisio sumitur a quibusdam proprietatibus. Nam voluptatum quædam sunt honestæ, perinde ut ipsæ actiones, quæ scilicet operationes secundum virtutem sequuntur: quædam sunt inhonestæ seu turpes, quæ fœdas vitiorum insequuntur actiones: quædam sunt inter medias seu indifferentes, quæ operationes per se nec bonas nec malas, (quales sunt plerumque naturales functiones, quæ tum demum bonæ & malæ dicuntur, quando bono vel malo fini adhibentur, sponte suceptas & non
units.tr: The second division is taken from certain properties. For some pleasures are honourable, just as the actions themselves are, namely those which follow activities according to virtue; some are dishonourable or base, which follow the foul actions of vices; some are between, or indifferent, which follow activities that are neither good nor bad in themselves (such as, for the most part, the natural functions, which are called good or bad only when they are applied to a good or bad end, and which follow when undertaken voluntarily and not hindered

units.la: Mmm f impeimpeditas insequuntur. Ariftoteles 10. Nicom. cap. 5. Notandum tamen, hanc divisionem vix cadere in omnes voluptates in genere, sed plerumque in voluptates corporis,quæ vel pro bona vel mala dispositione animi, aliam atque aliam induunt naturam.
units.tr: Mmm f impeimpeditas insequuntur. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 5. It should be noted, however, that this division hardly applies to all pleasures in general, but mostly to bodily pleasures, which take on a different nature depending on whether the disposition of the mind is good or bad.

units.la: Tertia: Quædam voluptates sunt puræ & sinceræ, utpote quæ nihil turpitudinis & molestiæ habent admixtum, cujusmodi sunt omnes fere voluptates animi bene difpoliti, & rationem bene audientis: quædam sunt impuræ & mixtæ: cujusmodi sunt voluptates corporis & sensuum exteriorum & præsertim illæ voluptates, quæ ex gustu & tactu percipiuntur, quia in horum sensuum voluptatibus, quam reliquorum omnium moderandis, major reperitur difficultas. Ariftoteles loco cit. & Ludovicus Vives de anima pag. 108. Et ratio hujus divisionis hæc esse poterit, quia quemadmodum operationes metis sunt puriores & sincériores corporis operationibus, utpote quæ ab omni materiæ contagione, à qua infici possunt, procul sunt remotæ, ita etiam sensuum voluptates aliæ aliis sunt puriores vel impuriores secundum sensuum ipsorum puritatem vel impuritatem. Major enim plerumque reperitur impuritas in gustu & tactu, quam in reliquis sensibus. Siceria voluptates quæ istis operationibus sunt cognatæ, & ipsas immediate consequuntur, sunt puriores vel impuriores aliæ aliis pro ratione ipsorum principiorum unde manant.
units.tr: Third: Some pleasures are pure and unmixed, since they have no admixture of baseness or distress. Of this kind are almost all the pleasures of a well-ordered mind that listens to reason. Others are impure and mixed, such as the pleasures of the body and of the outer senses, and especially those perceived through taste and touch, because it is harder to govern the pleasures of these senses than those of all the others. Aristotle, loc. cit., and Ludovicus Vives, De anima, p. 108. The reason for this division may be as follows. Just as the operations of the mind are purer and more sincere than the operations of the body, being far removed from all contagion of matter by which they could be infected, so too the pleasures of the senses are purer or less pure according to the purity or impurity of the senses themselves. For impurity is usually greater in taste and touch than in the other senses. Moreover, the pleasures that are akin to these operations and immediately follow them are purer or less pure, one than another, according to the nature of the principles from which they flow.

units.la: Quarta: Voluptates quædam sunt necessariæ, utpote sine quibus homo, neque esse neque vivere potest, & vel spectant ad conservationem individui, ut eæ voluptates quæ ex cibo & potu percipiuntur, dum scilicet per alimentum naturæ imbecillitas sustentatur & fovetur, vel ad propagationem speciei, ut voluptas ex Venere. 2. aliæ voluptates sunt non necessariæ, utpote sine quibus homo & esse & vivere potest, quæ tamen appetitui sunt gratæ & animum ipsum jucunda commotione afficiunt, ut sunt eæ voluptates, quæ ex honoribus, divitiis, dignitatib. & cæteris fortunæ bonis hauriuntur, & quia neq; ad constitutionem animi requiruntur aut corporis, & multos vixisse homines absque iis constat, ideo dicuntur voluptates non necessariæ homini. Aristoteles lib.7.cap.11. Nicom.
units.tr: Fourth: Some pleasures are necessary, in that without them a human being can neither exist nor live. They concern either the preservation of the individual, as the pleasures received from food and drink, by which the weakness of nature is sustained and cherished, or the propagation of the species, as the pleasure of sex. Other pleasures are not necessary, in that a human being can both exist and live without them. Yet these are agreeable to appetite and move the mind itself with a pleasant stirring, as are the pleasures drawn from honours, riches, dignities and the other goods of fortune. Because they are not required either for the constitution of the mind or of the body, and it is evident that many people have lived without them, they are called pleasures not necessary to man. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 11.

units.la: Quinta: Voluptates quædam sunt naturales, quæ alias humanæ dicuntur. (Nam in homine & hominis potissimum respectu hæc voluptatum spectatur divisio,) utpote quæ homini jure divino & naturali sunt concessæ & licitæ, cujusmodi sunt voluptates, quæ ex præscripto rectæ rationis, dictamine Dei & naturæ audièrs fiunt: Quædam voluptates sunt non naturales seu inhumanæ, utpote quæ communiter hominum naturæ adversantur: aliquos tamen pro tempore juvant, qui beluinam aut monstrosam induisse videntur naturam, verbi gratia: Si quis cædibus aut crudelitate delectetur aut esu carnium humanarum aut concubitu Sodomitico & nefariis ejusmodi facinoribus. Aristoteles cap.15. lib.7. Nic.
units.tr: Fifth: Some pleasures are natural, which are otherwise called human. (For this division is considered chiefly in man and with respect to man.) They are granted to man and are lawful by divine and natural right, as are those pleasures that arise in accordance with the prescription of right reason, under the dictate of God and of nature as heard. Some pleasures are not natural or are inhuman, since they commonly oppose the nature of man, although they please for a time certain people who seem to have put on a beastly or monstrous nature. For example: if someone takes delight in slaughter or cruelty, or in eating human flesh, or in Sodomitic intercourse and such heinous crimes. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7, ch. 15.

units.la: Sexta: Voluptates aliæ sunt communes, quæ non tantum hominibus sed & brutis competunt, ut sunt illæ quæ ex gustu & tactu percipiuntur: aliæ sunt propriæ, quæ uni alicui vel generi hominum aut animinimalium aut genti aut aetati, sunt peculiares, pro variarum diversitate naturarum aut constitutionum, de quibus Virgil. 2. Eclog. Trahit sua quemque voluptas.
units.tr: Sixth: Some pleasures are common, belonging not only to men but also to beasts, such as those perceived through taste and touch. Others are proper, peculiar to one person or to a kind of men, or to an animal species, a nation or an age, varying according to the diversity of natures or constitutions. Of these Virgil says, in the second Eclogue: "Each is drawn by his own pleasure."

units.la: Aristoteles cap. 5. lib. 10. Nicom.
units.tr: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 5.

units.la: Septima: Animalium specie distinctorum voluptates, quemadmodum & eorundem actiones recte specie distinguuntur. Operationibus enim variantibus & voluptates etiam, utpote quae sunt illarum consecutiones & perfectiones, specie variare necesse est. Semper enim: se referunt ad naturam suorum principiorum, unde emanant, verbi gratia: alia est voluptas equi, alia asini, alia hominis & caeterorum etiam animalium, quae specie inter se distinguuntur. Et ratio hujus rei haec est, quia species diversae habent formas diversas. Formae diversae diversas etiam edunt operationes, ex diversis operationibus diversae exurgunt voluptates. Unde si principia, unde fluunt voluptates, sunt specie distincta, & ipse voluptates erunt specie distinctae. Aristoteles cap. 5. 10. Nicom.
units.tr: Seventh: The pleasures of animals distinct in species are, just as their actions are, rightly distinguished by species. For since the operations differ, the pleasures too, being their consequences and perfections, must necessarily differ in species. For they always refer to the nature of the principles from which they flow. For example, the pleasure of a horse is one thing, that of an ass another, and that of a man and of the other animals, which are distinct from one another in species. The reason for this is that different species have different forms; different forms produce different operations; and from different operations different pleasures arise. Hence, if the principles from which pleasures flow are distinct in species, the pleasures themselves will also be distinct in species. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 5.

units.la: Tertio loco succedunt proprietates, quae variae sunt, ex quibus natura voluptatis facilius innotescit. Prima est, quod nulla voluptas sit perpetua, cum nulla potentia sensus & intellectus valeat continuo operari. Cessante autem intellectus & sensus functione cessat etiam voluptas, quae ex ista functione sequitur. Et ratio haec esse potest, quia homo propter potentiam finitam in operatione defatigatur. Unde cessat tandem actio. Cessante vero operatione seu actione, voluptas etiam fructus & consequens actioactionis cessat, & finem suum habet. Caeterum hic regeri potest, hoc verum esse de operationibus iis, quae ab organo corporeo aut sensitivo proficiscuntur, non autem de iis, quae ab intellectu promanant, propterea quod intellectus ad actiones suas obeundas nulla corporea instrumenta adhibeat, & idem propter essentiam suam & naturam nobiliorem non defatigetur? Resp. Etsi intellectus per se & in se consideratus in operatione non defatigetur, propterea quod instrumentis corporeis in operando non utatur, per aliud tamen defatigari poterit, propterea quod utatur iis, quae absque corporeis & sensitivis organis esse nequeunt. Nam ut dicitur, 3. de anima cap. 7. Intelligens anima, absque phantasia esse nequit. Haec autem absque organis corporeis non consistit, cum ab iis subinde sustentetur, & ab iis mutuetur rerum imagines, in quas operatur, & quas postea intellectui ipsi repraesentat. Cessantibus itaque corporis & sensuum exteriorum operationibus, cessat etiam operatio intellectus, si non immediate, mediate tamen, propterea quod Phantasia & memoria ad suas actiones obeundas plerumque utatur. Aristoteles 10. Nicomach. cap. 4. & Donatus ibid. Secunda proprietas est, quod voluptas iisdem actionibus converseetur, ex quibus oritur. Nam cum ex actionibus bonis & naturae amicis sua trahat originem, iisdem etiam actu persistentibus conservatur. Et ratio pendet ex illo axiomate: Actu manente causa, manet etiam effectus, ut contra evanescente causa, evanescit quoad actum effectus. Tertia: Nova initia plerumque delectant, & magis quidem delectant, quam vulgaria, trita aut quotidiana, propter duas potissimas potissimum causas: 1. Quia in res novas magis intentus est animus. Nam illa propter novitatis suae naturam magis arridենt, & quia antea neque intellectui ipsi sunt obiectae, magis alliciunt, unde animum acrius ad operandum commovent. Quo autem perfectior est operatio (quod experientia in novis magis quam veteribus docere solet) eo major est voluptas. 2. Quia potentia operandi in novis adhuc est integra, quae postea paulatim in veteribus defatigatur & fit remissior. Aristoteles 10. Nicom. cap. 5. Quarta: Voluptates quaeque rariissimae, quae non saepe occurrunt, sunt omnium gratissimae. Sed si in infinitum, quae modum excedat, fiunt ingratae, & ut ait Epictetus: Si quis crebro nimium res usurpet exquisitissimas, tunc gratissima quaeque fiunt molestissima. Unde illud Mimographi: Nulla est voluptas, quae non assiduitate sui fastidium pariat. Quinta: Animalia bruta ratione carentia specie eadem, eadem etiam specie & communes invicem habent voluptates, verbi gratia: Voluptas hujus equi a reliquorum ejusdem speciei individuorum voluptate non est specie diversa. Et ratio haec esse poterit, quia bruta cum ratione destituantur, actiones suas plerumque edunt ex naturae quodam instinctu, qui instinctus pro diversis formis diversimode se habet. Sed in una eadeque forma uniformiter, nisi impediatur, operari solet. Et hinc fit, ut in animalibus ejusdem speciei voluptates sunt quoque ejusdem speciei Arist. 10. Nic. c. f. VI. Individuorum humanorum voluptates, licet individua sint ejusdem speciei, sunt inter se plurimum diversae & specie distinctae, adeo ut quae uni grata & jucunda sint, alteri aceracerba & molesta admodum sint: Et vice versa. Et id accidit vel propter diversum temperamentu, ꝯ in diversis reperitur individuis hominib. vel propter diversum vitæ statum & conditionem, vel propter diversas animi & corporis proprietates. Nam licet Individua forma & essentia specifica inter se conveniant, proprietatib. tamen individuantibus plurimum inter se discrepant, verbi gratia: non eadem delectant senem, quam puerum aut adolescentem: non eadem virum delectant quæ mulierem, non eadem Theologum, quæ mercatorem aut militem: Non eadem sunt grata docto & sapienti, quæ indocto & insipienti: non deniq; eadem delectant virum probum & virtute præditum, quæ improbum & vitiis dedicatum. At licet non easdem, quoad speciem expetant voluptates; quoad genus tamen easdem expetunt, propterea quod in natura animalis eadem ratio locum habeat in iis, quæ in animalibus ratione destitutis, ut supra ex proprietate quinta patet. Septima : Humanarum voluptatum, illæ sunt reliquis potiores & insigniores, imo proprie & per se voluptates tantum sunt dicendæ, quæ viri boni & virtutum functiones comitantur. Nam virtus in viro bono & omnium actionum ipsius & omnium voluptatum, quæ sequuntur actiones, est & omnino esse debet, mensura & regula. In unoquoque autem genere mensura reliquorum est optimum quid, propria, quod non tantum ad finem dirigat, sed viam & rationem demonstret, qua facilius omnia finem suum assequantur. Improborum autem voluptates, cum ex pravis & vitiosis resultent actionibus, appaapparenter& secundum quid tantũ voluptates sunt dicendæ,& aliquibus tantum, nempe iis, qui corrupto & vitiato sunt rationis iudicio, & qui pestifero animi morbo laborant, nempe cum affectus, qui sunt communes hominibus cum brutis, dominantur; Ratio ipsa per quam à brutis homo distinguitur, ancillatur.
units.tr: In the third place come the properties, which are various, and from which the nature of pleasure is more easily known. The first is that no pleasure is perpetual, since no power of sense or intellect can operate continuously. When the function of intellect and sense ceases, the pleasure that follows from that function also ceases. The reason may be this: man, because of his finite power, becomes wearied in operation, and so the action eventually ceases. When the operation or action ceases, the pleasure, which is the fruit and consequence of the action, also ceases and comes to its end. But here it may be objected: is this true only of those operations that proceed from a bodily or sensitive organ, and not of those that issue from the intellect, since the intellect uses no bodily instruments for performing its acts and, because of its nobler essence and nature, is not wearied? Answer: although the intellect, considered in itself and by itself, is not wearied in operation, because it does not use bodily instruments in operating, it may nevertheless be wearied through something else, because it uses those things which cannot exist without bodily and sensitive organs. For, as is said in 3. De anima, ch. 7, the understanding soul cannot exist without phantasy. But phantasy does not subsist without bodily organs, since it is continually sustained by them and borrows from them the images of things upon which it operates and which it afterwards presents to the intellect itself. Therefore, when the operations of the body and of the outer senses cease, the operation of the intellect also ceases, if not immediately, yet mediately, because phantasy and memory are generally used in performing their actions. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 4., and Donatus, ibid. The second property is that pleasure is conserved by the same actions from which it arises. For since it draws its origin from good actions that are friendly to nature, it is also preserved while those same actions persist. The reason depends on this axiom: when the cause remains in act, the effect also remains; conversely, when the cause vanishes, the effect vanishes as far as its act is concerned. The third: new beginnings generally delight, and delight more than common, worn-out or everyday things, for two chief reasons. (1) Because the mind is more intent upon new things. For these, by reason of the nature of novelty, please more, and because they have not been previously presented to the intellect, they attract more, and so move the mind more keenly to act. The more perfect the operation (which experience usually teaches more in new things than in old), the greater the pleasure. (2) Because the power of acting is still whole in new things, whereas afterwards it gradually wearies in old things and becomes more slack. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 5. The fourth: the rarest pleasures, which do not occur often, are the most welcome of all. But if they are repeated without limit, beyond measure, they become unwelcome. As Epictetus says: If someone often uses the most exquisite things to excess, then every most welcome thing becomes most troublesome. Hence that line of the mime-writer: No pleasure is there which by its constant repetition does not beget weariness. The fifth: brute animals lacking reason that are of the same species also have the same, and mutually common, pleasures. For example, the pleasure of this horse does not differ in species from the pleasure of the other individuals of the same species. The reason for this may be that, since brutes are destitute of reason, they usually perform their actions from a certain instinct of nature, and this instinct stands differently according to different forms. But in one and the same form they generally operate uniformly, unless they are hindered. Hence it comes about that in animals of the same species the pleasures are also of the same species. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10, ch. 5. The pleasures of individual human beings, although the individuals are of the same species, are very diverse among themselves and distinct in species, so that what is pleasant and agreeable to one is very bitter and distasteful to another, and vice versa. This happens either on account of the diverse temperament found in different individuals, or on account of the diverse state and condition of life, or on account of diverse properties of mind and body. For although individuals agree with one another in specific form and essence, they differ greatly in the individuating properties. For example: what delights an old man is not what delights a boy or a young man; what delights a man is not what delights a woman; what delights a theologian is not what delights a merchant or a soldier; what is agreeable to the learned and wise is not what is agreeable to the unlearned and foolish; and finally, what delights a upright man endowed with virtue is not what delights a wicked man given over to vices. Yet although they do not seek the same pleasures in respect of species, they do seek the same in respect of genus, because in the nature of an animal the same reason holds in these as in animals destitute of reason, as above, as is clear from the fifth property. Seventh: Of human pleasures, those are superior and more distinguished than the rest, and indeed only those should properly and in themselves be called pleasures, which accompany the good man and the functions of virtue.
