For virtue in the good man is, and altogether ought to be, the measure and rule of all his actions and of all the pleasures that follow actions. In every genus, the measure of the rest is something best and proper, which not only directs to the end but also shows the way and method by which all things more easily attain their end. But the pleasures of the wicked, since they result from depraved and vicious actions, are to be called pleasures only apparently and in a certain respect, and only for some people, namely those whose judgment of reason is corrupted and vitiated, and who suffer from the pestilent disease of the mind, that is, when the affections, which are common to men and beasts, hold sway, while reason itself, by which man is distinguished from the brutes, serves as a handmaid.

units.la: Restant iam paucæ de voluptate quæstiones discutiendæ, quarum prima sit. Quid statuendum sit de illa controversia, qua voluptatem modo omnem, modo quàdam, modo nullam esse bonam, sed nusquam cum summo bono coniunctam probabiliter veteres dixerunt. Et quandoquidem tres istas de voluptate opiniones fovebant veteres, sicut ex 7.&10. Nicom. tunc etiam ex Picolhomineigrad.9.cap.17.&18. liquet, operæ pretium erit tres istas opiniones una cum suis rationibus breviter examinare. Prima: opinio fuit eorum, qui statuebant nullam voluptatem esse bonum quid, neque per se neque per accidens. Et pro hac opinione tuenda quinque afferebant rationes, quarum 1. est, quia omne bonum obtinet rationem finis 1. Nicom. cap.1. Finis enim & bonum convertuntur. At nulla voluptas obtinet rationem finis: id quod patet ex definitione, quæ vulgò traditur, nempe quod voluptas nihil sit aliud quam generatio lætitiæ & progressus sive motus ad finem. At vero nulla generatio poterit dici finis, nõ magis, quam ædificatio domus, poterit dici finis domus. 2. Ratio, quia vir prudens & virtute præditus fugit omnes voluptates. 3. Nicom. c.11. Quodvero vir prudens fugit, id bonum esse nequit. Virtus enim & quivis virtute præditus tus, non nisi malum vitare solet: Cum vero Philosophi ipsius judicio, attestante etiam experientia, vir prudens & temperans fugere debeat voluptates sequitur nullam voluptatem esse bonam. 3. Ratio, quia voluptas prudentiam obscurat, & rationi iniqua est & mentis oculos perstringit, ne possit mens ipsa verum a falso discernere, neve etiam ea, quae sui sunt officii, exequi. Quod autem prudentiam impugnat & obscurat & rationi ipsi adversatur, id in bonis non est habendum aut saltem prudentia ipsa & ratio in bonis haberi no debent, quod est absurdum.
units.tr: There remain a few questions about pleasure to be discussed, the first of which is: What is to be decided about that controversy, in which the ancients, it is likely, said that pleasure is sometimes wholly good, sometimes good in some respects, sometimes not good at all, but never joined with the highest good? And since the ancients held these three opinions about pleasure, as is clear from Nicomachean Ethics 7 and 10 and also from Piccolomini, book 9, chapters 17 and 18, it will be worthwhile to examine these three opinions briefly, together with their reasons. The first is the opinion of those who held that no pleasure is a good, either in itself or incidentally. To defend this opinion they advanced five reasons. (1) Every good has the character of an end (Nic. 1, ch. 1), for end and good are convertible. But no pleasure has the character of an end. This is evident from the definition commonly given, namely that pleasure is nothing other than the generation of joy and a progress or motion towards an end. But no generation can be called an end, any more than the building of a house can be called the end of the house. (2) A prudent man endowed with virtue flees all pleasures (Nic. 3, ch. 11). But what a prudent man flees cannot be good, for virtue, and anyone endowed with virtue, is accustomed to avoid only evil. Since, then, by the judgment of the Philosopher himself, which experience also attests, the prudent and temperate man ought to flee pleasures, it follows that no pleasure is good. (3) Pleasure obscures prudence, is hostile to reason, and dazzles the eyes of the mind, so that the mind can no longer distinguish truth from falsehood, nor carry out the tasks that belong to it. But whatever attacks and obscures prudence and opposes reason itself must not be counted among goods; or at least prudence and reason themselves must not be counted among goods, which is absurd.

units.la: 4. Quia voluptas nullius artis opus est, siquidem nulla ars eam efficere possit, licet variae artes media ad voluptatem comparandam tradant. At vero nullum est bonum humanum, quod no ab arte aliqua proficiscitur. Id quod hinc patet, quia artes Dei indulgentia hominibus ideo sunt concessae, ut varia media ad vitam ducendam necessaria per eas homines acquirere possint. Proinde cum media omnia, quae vitae necessariae sunt, ab arte aliqua proveniant, necesse est, & ipsum finem provenire, quia media sunt causa finis. 5. Quia voluptates non tantum a pueris sed a brutis expetuntur. At vero pueri & bruta a solo sensu & appetitu excitantur ad aliquid appetendum, & id, quod appetunt, non a judicio sed a sensu & appetitu aestimant. Verum summum bonum non solo sensu & appetitu, sed ipsa ratione est aestimandum, in mentis actio secundum virtutem. 1. Nicom. 6. Neque solum summum bonum hoc modo aestimari debet, sed etiam quicquid cum summo bono conjungitur. Unde sequitur, nullam voluptatem tem esse bonum quid, neq; etiam cum summo homi-nis bono conjungi. Econtra aliquas voluptates esse bonas ex Aristotelis lib.7.de moribus ad Nicom. patet ex variis locis & quidem ex capp.12.13.& 14. 1.ratio est haec: Quicquid opponitur malo, illud est bonum: Contrariorum enim contraria est consequentia 3.Top. cap.4. At voluptas opponitur malo. Nam opponitur dolori. Dolor vero est malum quid, quia impedit actiones, quo minus procedant in suo tenore. Nam saepenumero accidit, ut dolore ab honestis actionibus abstrahantur homines, 2.Nicom. cap.3. quia honestae actiones difficultatem plerumque habent adjunctam. Difficultas parit molestiam & dolorem. Unde ad dolorem vitandum, cum sit naturae inimicus, solent homines honestis actionibus saepenumero se subducere. Unde quaedam voluptas erit bona, aut saltem dolor non erit malus, sicut jam probatum fuit. 2. Si omnis voluptas est mala, etiam voluptas viri boni, quam ille ex honestis virtutum actionibus percipit, non erit bona sed mala & fugiends. Et sic tales actiones non essent revera jucundae, neque vita viri boni magis esset expetenda, quam alterius cujusquam vita, cum nihilo plus utilitatis aut commodi afferat, neque etiam felix, quia jam summam afflecutus esset bonitatis perfectionem, majori frueretur voluptate, quam infelix, quae omnia sunt absurda & contradictionem implicant. 7. Nicom. capp.12.& 13. -3. Idipsum ex natura & distributione bonorum demonstratur. Quemadmodum enim aliud est simpliciter bonum & revera tale, aliud alicui tantum & secundum quid tantum bonum: Ita & natura & habitus, unde voluptates proficiscuntur, bifariam se habent: Et sicut se habent natura & habitus, ita etiam operationes ex iis promanantes. (Effecta enim sequuntur naturam causarum suarum:) At omnis voluptas est operatio quaedam aut naturae aut habitus, quod sic demonstratur: quia proficiscitur vel a primaria dispositione animi aut corporis & sicad naturam refert ginem, vel a crebris & continuatis animi aut corporis actionibus: Et sic profluit ab habitu. Unde tam sequitur quandam voluptatem esse per se bonam, quandam alicui & per accidens tantum. Aristoteles 7. Nicomach. cap. 13. & 1. magn. moral. cap. 7.
units.tr: (4) Pleasure is the work of no art, since no art can produce it, although various arts teach means of procuring pleasure. But there is no human good that does not proceed from some art. This is clear, because God in his indulgence gave arts to men so that through them they might acquire the various means necessary for leading life. Therefore, since all the means necessary for life come from some art, it is necessary that the end itself should come from art too, because means are the cause of the end. (5) Pleasures are sought not only by children but by brutes. But children and brutes are moved to desire something by sense and appetite alone, and they judge what they desire not by reason but by sense and appetite. The highest good, however, must be judged not by sense and appetite alone but by reason itself, in the activity of the mind according to virtue (Nic. 1, ch. 6). Nor should the highest good alone be judged in this way, but also whatever is joined with it. Whence it follows that no pleasure is a good, nor is it joined with the highest good of man. On the contrary, that some pleasures are good is clear from Aristotle, Ethics book 7, in various passages, and indeed in chapters 12, 13 and 14. First, the argument runs thus: whatever is opposed to evil is good, for the consequence of contraries is contrary (Top. 3, ch. 4). But pleasure is opposed to evil, for it is opposed to pain, and pain is an evil, because it impedes actions from proceeding in their course. For it often happens that men are drawn away from honourable actions by pain (Nic. 2, ch. 3), because honourable actions usually carry difficulty with them, and difficulty brings annoyance and pain. Hence, in order to avoid pain, which is nature's enemy, men often withdraw themselves from honourable actions. So some pleasure will be good, or at least pain will not be bad, as has already been proved. Second, if every pleasure is bad, then even the pleasure of a good man, which he derives from honourable actions of virtue, will not be good but bad and to be fled. Then such actions would not truly be pleasant, nor would the life of a good man be more desirable than anyone else's life, since it brings no greater usefulness or advantage; nor would he be happy, since, having already attained the highest perfection of goodness, he would enjoy a greater pleasure than the unhappy man. All of which are absurd and involve a contradiction (Nic. 7, chs. 12 and 13). Third, the same follows from the nature and distribution of goods. For just as one thing is good simply and truly, while another is good only for someone and in a qualified sense, so too the natures and habits from which pleasures arise are of two kinds; and just as nature and habit are, so too are the operations that proceed from them, for effects follow the nature of their causes. But every pleasure is some operation either of nature or of habit. This is shown thus: it proceeds either from a primary disposition of mind or body, and so belongs to nature, or from frequent and continued actions of mind or body, and so flows from habit. Hence it follows that some pleasure is good in itself, and some is good only for someone and incidentally. Aristotle, Nic. 7, ch. 13, and Magna Moralia 1, ch. 7.

units.la: 4. Idem etiam colligitur ex alia bonorum distributione. Nam si omne bonum sive habitus vel operatio ab habitu profecta, ideo quidam habitus erit bonus, quaedam etiam operatio bona. Et si quaedam operatio sit bona, jucunda & cum voluptate conjuncta, etiam & quaedam voluptas quae istam insequitur operationem, erit bona. Quae ratio, ut melius intelligatur, sciendum est duplices esse operationes: 1. Quaedam proficiscuntur ab ipso habitu, seu a natura integra, quae ad statum & quasi perfectionem suam est perducta, ita ut nulla laboret indigentia. Et tales operationes sunt simpliciter jucundae. Quaedam spectant ad naturae defectum supplendum & restituendum: Et tales operationes non sunt per se & simpliciter, sed per accidens tantum jucundae, quatenus nimirum per eas dolor restinguitur, qui ex defectu naturae laborantis sentitur, ac per repletionem hujus defectus seu per reparationem naturæin integrum, quam comiratur voluptas, tollitur, Aristoteles loco cit. Proinde veterum rationes, qui statuebant omnem voluptatem per se malam esse, necullam esse bonam, neque per se neque per accidens, facilè fuerit diluere. Nam, quod ad primam, qua dicitur voluptatem esse generationem, id falsum esse evincunt duæ rationes: 1. Quia omnis generatio est substantiarum proprie. Aristoteles f. Phyf. ἀxpoατ.cap 1. text. 8. & 9. & 1. de generat. & corrupt. cap. 3. text. 18. Nam generatio proprie est motus à non esse ad esse per quem ex corruptione unius substantiæ alia generatur, ut verbi gratia: quando ex semine fit equus, corrumpitur & destruitur forma seminis, ant qua n fit equus. At per voluptatem nulla substantia generatur, cum voluptas sit accidens tantum, & accidentia non generent substantiam: 2. Quia nulla generatio est perfecta operatio sed medium tantum, tendens ad perfectionem, cum sit motus tendens à non esse ad aliquod esse. At quædam voluptas est perfecta operatio, nimirum ea quæ ex perfecto habitu aut natura integra proficiscitur, verbi gratia: quæ proficiscitur ex perfecta sanitate, ex virtutibus & ex fine omnium virtutum, nempe ex ipsa felicitate. Et ejusmodi actus per se nō propter aliud expetitur. Quod verò ad reliquas voluptates, quæ ex desiderio naturæ re aliqua indigentis proficiscuntur, quales sunt voluptates ex cibo aut potu, eas quidem largimur, non esse perfectiones aut finem rei sed motum quendam & progressum ad finem. Ideo in prima ratione committitur, fallacia à dicto secundum quod ad dictum simpliciter, cum quod de voluptatibus in genere probandum fuit, de quibusdam tantum probatur. Ad secundam rationem per distinctionem voluptatis respondetur. Nam quædam voluptates sunt simpliciter veræ & bonæ, quædam per accidens tantum: quædam sunt honestæ, quædam turpes, & inhonestæ, ut ex tertia divisione voluptatis patet, Temperans verò cum dicitur fugere voluptates, non fugit omnes in genere sed turpes tantum & vitiosas, quæ aut in defectu aut in excessu peccant. Voluptates bonas experit, quia ejusmodi voluptates pro objecto habet. Quod si omnes in genere fugeret voluptates, non esset temperans aut virtute præditus sed peccaret in defectu & fieret insensilis aut stupidus. Aristoteles 3. Nicom. cap. 12. Ad tertiam etiam per distinctionem responderi poterit. Nam voluptates sunt vel propriæ cujusque actionis, quæ ipsam actionem comitantur, vel alienæ, quæ ad ipsam actionem non spectant. Prioris generis voluptates actionem nullo modo impediunt aut prudentiæ adversantur, sed potius juvant & promovent, quia agentem in agendo alacriorem reddunt, quod manifestum evadit in iis, qui cum alacritate quadam & lætitia animi aliquid agunt. Alienæ verò voluptates, quæ neque ad actionem pertinent, neque etiam juvant, sed importune adhibentur tantum, illæ quidem prudentiam & consilium impediunt. Et sicut ait Cicero in in Catone majore, virtutem omnem quasi excludunt. Proinde fallum illud, veram & propriam voluptatem prudentiæ adversari aut rationi iniquam esse. Aristoteles 7. Nicom. cap. 12. Ad quartam per negatiotionem respondetur, propter duas rationes: 1. Quia falsum, nullum esse bonum humanum, quod non ab arte aliqua proficiscatur, cum multa sint bona quæ dicuntur humana, & tamen vere sint naturalia & à natura ipsa proveniunt primum, non ab arte, ut sanitas, bona dispositio animi & corporis & alia ejusmodi. 2. Falsum etiam illud, voluptatem nullius artis esse opus, cum multæ sint artes ad voluptatem excitandam tantum inventæ, unguentaria, culinaria, Musica, ars pingendi & cæteræ ejusmodi artes à diversis hominum ingeniis, affectibus suis inventæ & excultæ placandis. Et tantum de prima opinione.
units.tr: Four. The same is also gathered from another distribution of goods. For if every good, whether a habit or an operation proceeding from a habit, is good because of the habit, then some habit will be good, and also some operation. And if some operation is good, pleasant and joined with pleasure, then also some pleasure that follows that operation will be good. To understand this reasoning better, it must be known that there are two kinds of operations. (1) Some proceed from the habit itself, or from a nature that is whole, brought to its state and, as it were, its perfection, so that it lacks nothing. Such operations are simply pleasant. Others concern supplying and restoring a defect in nature; such operations are not pleasant in themselves and simply, but only incidentally, inasmuch as through them the pain is relieved which is felt from the defect of a suffering nature, and that pain is removed by the filling up of this defect, or by the restoration of nature to wholeness, which pleasure accompanies (Aristotle, loc. cit.). Therefore the arguments of the ancients, who held that every pleasure is evil in itself and that none is good, neither in itself nor incidentally, are easily refuted. As for the first, which says that pleasure is a generation, two arguments prove this to be false. (1) Because every generation is of substances, properly speaking. For generation properly is a motion from non-being to being, by which one substance is generated from the corruption of another; for example, when a horse is generated from seed, the form of the seed is corrupted and destroyed, or what was not a horse becomes one. But through pleasure no substance is generated, since pleasure is only an accident, and accidents do not generate substance. (2) Because no generation is a perfect operation but only a middle stage tending towards perfection. But some pleasure is a perfect operation, namely that which proceeds from a perfect habit or a whole nature; for example, that which proceeds from perfect health, from the virtues, and from the end of all the virtues, namely happiness itself. Such an act is desired for its own sake and not for the sake of something else. As for the remaining pleasures, which arise from the desire of a nature in need of something, such as pleasures from food or drink, we grant that these are not perfections or the end of a thing, but a certain motion and progress towards the end. Therefore the first argument commits the fallacy of moving from what is said in a qualified sense to what is said absolutely, since what was to be proved of pleasures in general is proved only of some. To the second argument we reply by a distinction of pleasure. Some pleasures are truly and simply good, and some only incidentally; some are honourable, and some base and dishonourable. When the temperate man is said to flee pleasures, he does not flee all pleasures in general but only the base and vicious ones, which sin either by defect or by excess. He experiences good pleasures, because such pleasures are his proper object. If he fled all pleasures in general, he would not be temperate or endowed with virtue, but would sin by defect and become insensible or stupid (Aristotle, Nicom. 3, cap. 12). To the third argument too a reply can be made by distinction. For pleasures are either those proper to each action, which accompany the action itself, or those foreign to it, which do not pertain to the action itself. Pleasures of the first kind in no way impede the action or oppose prudence, but rather help and promote it, because they make the agent more eager in acting. Foreign pleasures, however, which neither pertain to the action nor help it, but are brought in unseasonably, do indeed impede prudence and counsel; and, as Cicero says in the Cato Maior, they all but shut out every virtue. Therefore the assertion that true and proper pleasure opposes prudence or is hostile to reason is false (Aristotle, Nicom. 7, cap. 12). The fourth argument is answered by denial, for two reasons. (1) It is false that no human good exists which does not proceed from some art, since many things called human goods are truly natural and come from nature itself first, not from art, such as health, a good disposition of mind and body, and other things of this kind. (2) It is also false that pleasure is the work of no art, since many arts have been invented only to arouse pleasure: perfumery, cookery, music, the art of painting, and other such arts, invented and cultivated by different human talents to satisfy their own affections.

units.la: Secunda opinio circa voluptatem erat eorum, qui statuebant quasdam voluptates quidem bonas sed admodum paucas, plerasque autem malas esse. Rationes erant duæ: 1. Quia voluptates plerumque sunt turpes, ut communi constat Praxi & quamplurimæ nobis probro dari solent, quicquid autem turpe est & probrosum, non potest dici bonum. 2. Quia ut plurimum hominibus sunt noxiæ, morbos concilient, & secum in exitium trahunt, & famam insuper lædunt, adeo ut vix ulla unquam reperiatur voluptas, quæ non cum uno aut altero vitio sit conjuncta. Vel enim habet contemtum aliorum, vel sui oblivionem, vel naturæ ipsi aliquid infensum. Sed & hic respondemus cum Philosopho 1. distinguendum esse inter voluptates honestas & turpes, 2. voluptates per se non esse noxias, sed tantum per accidens, quatenus scilicet utentium vitio fiunt vel turpes vel immoderatæ, 3. non omne noxium, esse mamalum. Etenim diligens in literis studium nocet interdum valetudini, non est tamen propterea per se & sua natura quid malum. Vinum nocet f. bricitanibus, non tamen ideo in se est malum: Cibi delicatiores nocent iei familiari, propterea quod maiori quam viliores precio comparentur, sed tamen per se non sunt mali.
units.tr: The second opinion about pleasure was held by those who maintained that some pleasures are indeed good but very few, while most are bad. There were two reasons: (1) Most pleasures are shameful, as common practice makes plain and as very many people are in the habit of reproaching them; but whatever is shameful and disgraceful cannot be called good. (2) For the most part they are harmful to human beings: they bring on illness, drag people down to ruin, and moreover damage reputation, so that hardly any pleasure is found that is not joined with one vice or another. For either it involves contempt of others, or forgetfulness of oneself, or some hostility to nature itself. But here too we answer, with the Philosopher, that (1) a distinction must be made between honourable and shameful pleasures; (2) pleasures are not harmful in themselves but only incidentally, insofar as they become shameful or excessive through the fault of those who use them; (3) not everything harmful is evil. For diligent study of letters sometimes harms health, yet it is not therefore evil in itself or by its nature. Wine harms the feverish, yet it is not for that reason evil in itself. More refined foods harm the ordinary household, because they are bought at a higher price than cheaper ones, yet they are not evil in themselves.

units.la: Tertia opinio circa voluptatem fuit eorum, qui concesserunt voluptates quidem inter bona numerandas esse, sed ita tamen ut nulla illarum cum summo bono possit esse conjuncta. Ratio, quia summum bonum est ultimus finis seu perfectio hominis, sed voluptas non est finis, ut ex sententia veterum docet Philosophus 3. cap. 1. Nicom. Et definitur vulgo ab illis, generatio sensibilis ad naturae restaurationem: proin ad media felicitatis potius secundaria quam ad primaria referri debet, & per consequens felicitatis ipsius comes esse nullo modo potest, cum media finis tui, utpote perfectionis respectu, principia quaedam videantur. Respondemus hic voluptatem quidem non esse summum bonum, nec sententiam aut partem ipsius reipsa constituere, interim tamen poterit esse effectio ipsum summum bonum insequens, & ab eo inseparabilis, idque cum Philosopho quatuor hisce rationibus astruimus: 1. Omnis perfecta operatio habitus secundum naturam non impedita illa est aut summum bonum aut saltem semper illi conjuncta, ut ex definitione summi boni 6. cap. 1. Nicom. tradita constat. Unde cum quaedam voluptas sit operatio habitus secundum naturam non impedita, fit ut aut summum bonum aut illi saltem connexa videatur. 2. A communi Philosophorum opinione idipsum probatur, quia plæriq; Philosophi vitam beatam etiam jucūdam esse censent atque ita voluptatem, tanquam individuū comitem cum beatitudine connectunt, necabsq; ratione quidem. Nulla enim operatio perfecta, qua talis, poterit esse impedita, ideoque beatitudo cum sit operatio perfecta, à qua omne removetur impedimentum, conjunctam habeat summam voluptatem, necesse erit. 3. Si in summo bono nulla voluptas esset, felix sine voluptate viveret, eademque de causa in dolore & molestia viveret, nec denique viri boni vita jucūdior esset, quam cujusvis flagitiosi hominis, quæ cum ipsa refellat experientia, sequitur summum bonum cum voluptate conjunctum esse, ac proinde bonum jucundissimū esse appellandum 4. Ratio, à naturali appetitu omnium brutorum & hominū ducitur, quia nō solū homines, sed etiā bruta animalia voluptatem tanquam naturæ suæ aliquid amicum expetunt, & hoc communi appetitu naturaliter ipsis quasi tacitè indicare videntur, eam qua fruuntur voluptatem rationem habere summi boni etiamsi veram voluptatem nec intelligant nec expetant, sed eam tantum quæ sensibus ipsorum videtur esse grata & jucunda. Plura de hac quæstione videre licet apud Picolh. grad. 9. ubi de summo bono capp. 17. 18. & 19.
units.tr: The third opinion about pleasure was held by those who conceded that pleasures are indeed to be counted among the goods, but in such a way that none of them can be joined with the highest good. The reason is that the highest good is the ultimate end or perfection of a human being, but pleasure is not an end, as the Philosopher teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 3.1, according to the view of the ancients. And commonly they define it as a sensible process towards the restoration of nature; therefore it ought to be referred to the secondary means to happiness rather than to the primary ones, and consequently it can in no way be a companion of happiness itself, since means seem to be certain principles of the end, as it were with respect to perfection. We answer here that pleasure is indeed not the highest good, nor does it actually constitute that good or any part of it; nevertheless, it can be an effect that follows the highest good itself and is inseparable from it. And we establish this with the Philosopher by four arguments: (1) Every perfect activity of a habit in accordance with nature, when unimpeded, is either the highest good or at least always joined to it, as is clear from the definition of the highest good given in Nicomachean Ethics 6.1. Hence, since some pleasure is an activity of a habit in accordance with nature, unimpeded, it follows that it appears either to be the highest good or at least connected with it. (2) The same is proved from the common opinion of the philosophers, since most philosophers judge that the blessed life is also pleasant, and so they connect pleasure with blessedness as its inseparable companion, and indeed not without reason. For no perfect activity, as such, can be impeded; therefore, since blessedness is a perfect activity from which every hindrance is removed, it must necessarily have the highest pleasure joined to it. (3) If there were no pleasure in the highest good, the happy man would live without pleasure, and for the same reason would live in pain and discomfort; nor, finally, would the life of a good man be more pleasant than the life of any wicked man. Since experience itself refutes this, it follows that the highest good is joined with pleasure, and therefore it must be called the most pleasant good. (4) The argument is drawn from the natural appetite of all brute animals and human beings. For not only human beings but also brute animals seek pleasure as something friendly to their nature, and by this common appetite they seem to indicate to us, as it were tacitly, that the pleasure they enjoy has the character of the highest good, even though they neither understand nor seek true pleasure, but only that which seems pleasing and agreeable to their senses. More on this question may be seen in Picolh., Grade 9, where he treats of the highest good in chapters 17, 18 and 19.

units.la: Secunda quæstio, quæ de voluptate movetur est, An corporis voluptates sint simpliciter mala, ut quibusdam placet?
units.tr: The second question concerning pleasure is: Are bodily pleasures simply evil, as some hold?

units.la: Et statuitur Thesis negativa cum Philosopho 7. Ethicorum cap. 12. propter hanc rationem ab absurdo do petitam. Si corporis voluptates sint simpliciter malæ, sequitur corporis dolores esse simpliciter bonos. Contrariorum enim contraria est natura & qualitas. Sed consequens hoc est absurdum, cum universali repugnet experientiæ. Omnes enim in genere judicant dolores corporis sive magni illi sint sive parvi, malos esse & fugiendos, nō propter excessum quemadmodum voluptas, sed simpliciter, quia naturæ ipsi adversantur. Nam animum turbant, corpus consumunt, utrique hostes sunt: Ideoque dolor nō proprie propter excessum voluptati est contrarius, sed simpliciter ei opponitur, ut bono opponitur malum. Notandum vero voluptates corporis dici bonas duplici ratione. 1. Propter negationem mali, quia non sunt in se malæ, si legitimè adhibeantur: quicquid autem malum non est, illud aliqua ratione poterit dici bonum. 2. Cum limitatione, quatenus intra terminos suos se continent, neque modum excedunt, quem recta præscribit ratio & naturæ postulat necessitas. Hunc enim modū quatenus excedunt, desinunt esse bonæ, cum ad excessum tendant & finem proprium non colliment. Aristoteles 7. Nicom. cap. 14.
units.tr: And the negative thesis is affirmed, with the Philosopher in Nicomachean Ethics 7.12, on the basis of this argument from absurdity. If bodily pleasures were simply evil, it would follow that bodily pains are simply good, for contraries have contrary nature and quality. But this consequence is absurd, since it contradicts universal experience. For all people in general judge bodily pains, whether great or small, to be evil and to be avoided, not because of excess, as with pleasure, but simply, because they are opposed to nature. For they disturb the mind and waste the body; they are enemies of both. Hence pain is not properly opposed to pleasure because of excess, but is simply set against it, just as evil is set against good. It must be noted, however, that bodily pleasures are called good in a twofold way. (1) On account of the absence of evil: they are not evil in themselves if they are rightly employed; and whatever is not evil can in some sense be called good. (2) With a limitation: insofar as they keep within their proper bounds and do not exceed the measure which right reason prescribes and the necessity of nature requires. For insofar as they exceed this measure, they cease to be good, since they tend towards excess and do not attain their proper end. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7.14.

units.la: Tertia quæstio sit: An præstantiores sint animi quam corporis voluptates, & num illa magis quam hæ oblectent?
units.tr: The third question: Are the pleasures of the soul more excellent than those of the body, and does the one delight more than the other?

units.la: Respondetur per affirmationem utriusque. Nam præstantiores sunt propter tres rationes: 1. Quia illarum non poterit esse excessus vitiosus cum proficiscatur exactionibus virtutum & nulla virtus nimia esse possit, sicut cap. 12. lib. 3. Nicom. dictum fuit. Harum vero, id est, corporis voluptatum sunt excessus varii & insolentes, ut experientia docet. 2. Quia voluptates animi percipiuntur ex rebus sua natura jucundis & proveniunt ab operatione perfectæ naturæ: Hæ vero (corporis voluptates) prodeunt ex rebus solum per accidens jucundis, quatenus nimirum naturæ imperfectioris & indigentiæ medicina quædam sunt. Jam vero ea, quæ ex causa per se existunt, præstatiora sunt iis, quæ ex causa per accidens. 3. Ratio quia illæ nunquam habent adjunctum dolorem, propterea quod tendât semper ad bonum. Hæ vero sæpius propter vitiofitatem adjunctam & pœnitentiam, quam hominum animis imprimunt. Magis vero oblectant animi, quam corporis voluptates, quod secundo statutum fuit, propter duas rationes: 1. Quia corporis voluptates in sensu tantum sunt, animi voluptates in intellectu Ideo subjecti respectu præstant istæ illi. Nam quanto intellectus sensu st præstantior, tanto etiam magis afficiunt & delectant animi voluptates. 2. Animi voluptates diuturniores sunt: magis igitur oblectant. Citò enim sabit, quod ex gustu vel tactu percipitur jucundum & quamvis vel gravis collum alicui contingeret, quod sibi optavit Philoxenus diuturnioris voluptatis gratia, percipiendæ, momentanea tamen illa foret voluptas, cum tantum præsente objecto & in actu vigeat, absente deficiat. At diutissimè oblectant, quæ ex scientia & virtute percipiuntur voluptates. Magis, n. & fortius uniuntur intellectui objecta intelligibilia, q corporis voluptates jungûtur sensui, nempe nullâ aliam ob causam q quia intellectus est immaterialis, sensus vero mate-
units.tr: The answer is yes to both. The pleasures of the soul are more excellent, for three reasons: (1) Their excess cannot be vicious, since they arise from the exercise of the virtues, and no virtue can be excessive, as was said in chapter 12 of book 3 of the Nicomachean Ethics. The pleasures of the body, by contrast, have various and unusual excesses, as experience teaches. (2) The pleasures of the soul are received from things that are pleasant by their own nature, and they arise from the activity of a perfect nature. The pleasures of the body arise only from things that are pleasant by accident, insofar as they are a kind of remedy for an imperfect nature and its needs. Now things that exist through a cause in themselves are more excellent than those that exist through a cause by accident. (3) The pleasures of the soul never have pain attached to them, because they always tend towards the good. The pleasures of the body, however, are often followed by vice and by the regret which they impress on human minds. The pleasures of the soul delight more than those of the body, which was the second point proposed, for two reasons: (1) The pleasures of the body are only in the senses, while those of the soul are in the intellect. Therefore, with respect to their subject, the former are surpassed by the latter; for the more excellent the intellect is than the sense, the more the pleasures of the soul move and delight us. (2) The pleasures of the soul last longer, and so they delight more. For what is perceived as pleasant through taste or touch soon passes; and even if one were to enjoy a long neck, such as Philoxenus wished for the sake of a longer-lasting pleasure, that pleasure would still be momentary, since it flourishes only while the object is present and in act, and fails when it is absent. But the pleasures that come from knowledge and virtue delight most lastingly. For intelligible objects are joined to the intellect more closely and more strongly than bodily pleasures are joined to the senses, and for no other reason than that the intellect is immaterial while the senses are material; and so the intellect is not wearied by understanding in the way the senses are weakened by sensing.

units.la: riaº rialis, atq; idcirco non ita intelligendo defatigatur intellectus, sicut sentiendo sensus debilitatur.
units.tr: Hence the intellect is not tired in this way by understanding, as the senses are weakened by perceiving.

units.la: Quarta quaestio: Hinc quaeri poterit, cum animi voluptates longe sint praestantiores & nobiliores, quam corporis, qui fit ergo quod homo ita rerum suarum extreme prodigus, & qui humi defixus, hasce potius quam illas expetat? Hujus rei ex Philosopho duas damus rationes: 1. Quia homines existimant voluptates corporis esse medicinas quasdam adversus dolores, qui naturae molesti sunt, quosque omnes, ut naturae hostes aversantur, & a nobis totis viribus repellere studemus. Quemadmodum enim contra oes alios morbos, qui naturali laedunt, sic etiam contra dolores expetunt homines remedia. Cum vero dolori voluptas sit contraria, idcirco per voluptatem existimant homines se posse corporis dolores aut expellere aut lenire, ne prorsus saeviant aut suo impetu tantum efficiant. Contraria enim contrariorum sunt remedia, & contria contrariis curantur. 2. Quia voluptates corporis magis afficiunt sensus quam animi quae animum duntaxat aliqua delectatione perfundunt. Atqui maxima pars hominum ea tantum quaerit, quae sunt sensibus grata & jucunda, quaeque oblectare & recreare possunt, ut patet in iis qui, ut suavius edant ac bibant, condimentis quibusdam aut aliis rationibus fame & sitim accerunt & provocant: Arist. 7. Nic. cap. 14. Et Casus in spec. moral. quaest. lib. 7. c. 14.
units.tr: Fourth question: From this one may ask: since the pleasures of the soul are far more excellent and noble than those of the body, why is it that man, so extremely prodigal of his own goods, and fixed to the ground, seeks these rather than those? On this matter we give two reasons, drawn from the Philosopher: (1) Men think that the pleasures of the body are a kind of medicine against pains, which are troublesome to nature. All of these pains, as enemies of nature, they turn away from and strive with all their strength to drive from us. For just as men seek remedies against all other diseases that harm the natural state, so they seek them against pains as well. But since pleasure is contrary to pain, men therefore think that by pleasure they can either expel or soften the pains of the body, lest they rage utterly or do more harm by their force. For contraries are remedies of contraries, and contraries are cured by contraries. (2) The pleasures of the body affect the senses more than the pleasures of the soul, which only bathe the soul in some delight. Yet the greater part of mankind seeks only those things which are pleasing and agreeable to the senses and which can delight and refresh them, as is plain in those who, in order to eat and drink more pleasantly, provoke and increase hunger and thirst by certain seasonings or other means: Aristotle, Nic. 7, chapter 14. And Caesar Casus, in Speculum moralium quaestionum, book 7, chapter 14.

units.la: Quinta quaestio. Moveri potest, Cur non idem hominibus semper sit gratum; aut cur id, quod aliquando parit voluptatem, non semper pariat? Respondetur tres hujus rei esse rationes: 1, Quia corpore & anima constat homo, quae duo, ut sunt diversissima (aliud enim est immortale, aliud mortale, aliud simplex, aliud compositum, aliud corporeū, aliud incorporeum) ita eidem homini secundum duas iStas partes, non possunt esse eadem grata & jucunda, sed aliud animo aliud corpori gratum & molestum esse solet.
units.tr: Fifth question. It may be asked: Why is the same thing not always pleasing to men, or why does what sometimes produces pleasure not always produce it? The answer is that there are three reasons for this: (1) Because man consists of body and soul, which two, being so very different (for the one is immortal, the other mortal; the one simple, the other compound; the one corporeal, the other incorporeal), cannot for the same man be pleasing and agreeable in the same way according to these two parts. Rather, what is pleasing and unpleasant to the soul is usually not so to the body.

units.la: 2. Corpus nostrum, cum ex quatuor constet Elementis, & hæc qualitates habeant contrarias, idcirco etiam fit, ut variis imo sæpè contrariis rebus homo afficiatur & delectetur Aristot. 2. de ortu cap. 3.
units.tr: (2) Our body, since it consists of the four elements, which have contrary qualities, is also affected and delighted by various and often contrary things. Aristotle, De generatione, chapter 3.

units.la: 3. Ratio est, quia natura hominis est prava & perversa bonum enim est semper sibi simile & uno eodemque modo se habet. Imò quo magis aliquid est bonum, eo magis est simplex & un forme: Malum autem multiplex & varium est, ut recte docet Philosophus 2. Nicom. cap. 6. Ergo & vicissitudo & varietas rerum naturæ hominum propter pravitatem suā jucunda esse videtur, proinde ut homo malus atque imprŏbus mutabilitatem atque inconstantiam tanquam suis affectibus, quid gratum, amat. 7. Nicom. cap. 14.
units.tr: (3) The reason is that the nature of man is depraved and perverse. For the good is always like itself and remains in one and the same way; indeed, the more a thing is good, the more simple and uniform it is. But evil is manifold and various, as the Philosopher rightly teaches in Nicomachean Ethics 2, chapter 6. Therefore change and variety in the things of nature seem pleasant to men because of their own depravity; so the bad and wicked man loves changeability and inconstancy as something agreeable to his affections. Nic. 7, chapter 14.

units.la: Sexto breviter & hoc quæritur; An homines vitam expetant propter voluptatem, an verò econtra voluptatem propter vitam? Et posterius affirmatur propter duas rationes: 1. Quia voluptas oritur ex eo, quod actio cum natura congruat, & id sentiamus atque cognoscamus, unde lætitia & jucunditate afficimur: Quareid ante omnia expetendum est, ut acto habeatur perfectissimá. 2. Nec ignorat quisquam perfectionem institutam esse propter id, quod perficit, verbi gratia: Omnes vident cibum esse præstabiliorem aut saltem esse debere suo condimento, cum condimentum cibi tantum gratia, non econtra quæratur. Petrus Martyr 2. Classe Loc. Commun. pag. 333.
units.tr: Sixthly, this too is briefly asked: Do men desire life for the sake of pleasure, or on the contrary pleasure for the sake of life? The latter is affirmed, for two reasons: (1) Because pleasure arises when an action agrees with nature, and we feel and recognize this, whence we are moved by joy and delight. Therefore that is to be desired above all, so that the activity may be had in its most perfect form. (2) No one is unaware that a thing made for the sake of what it perfects is more excellent than it, for example: everyone sees that food is more valuable than its seasoning, or at least ought to be, since seasoning is sought for the sake of food and not the other way round. Peter Martyr, Loci communes, Class 2, p. 333.

units.la: Ultimò & hoc quæritur: Cur voluptates à Deo hominibus sint datæ? Resp. Tres hujus rei dari possunt causæ: 1. Quia vita per illas ducitur commodius & opera vitæ necessaria ad conservationem nostram libentius obimus, medicamurque promtius quotidianis nostris defectibus. 2. Quia juvenes honestis & moderatis voluptatibus ad honesta officia & præclaras actiones invitantur, doloribus autem à vitiis & sceleribus abterrentur. 3. Addit Augustinus has infimas voluptates Dei quædam esse veluti vestigia & summi boni tenuem quasi umbram, quâ possimus incitari ad vehementis illius desiderium. Itaque valent voluptates ad nos expergefaciendos, ne vitiis inhæreamus, sed ad aliquid magnum & excellens insurgamus. Verum in voluptatibus hisce non insistendum, sed ad meliora semper assurgendum, utque in his non maneamus, Deus ex sua bonitate amara multa dulcibus hisce voluptatum illecebris aspersit. Petrus Martyr in lib. 1. Nicom. cap. 8. Verum hic finis fit, & quod Diogenes quondam dixit, cum lectis de immortalitate animæ Platonis libris, reperisset variis indiciis & variis rationibus à Platone scriptum, futuram vitam hac lógé esse meliorem, cum ibi Deo ipso veluti summo bono & summa voluptate homines fruantur: Esto, inquit, mihi Deus summum bonum & summa voluptas. Et cum sit ultimus ille finis propter quem creatus erat homo, ideo etiam Christiani omnes hoc in votis una cum DioDiogen- habere debent, quod dicitur Apocal. 22. verf. 20. Nai ἔρχῃ κύριε Ἰησοῦ, ὅπ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἡ ἀὶ αὐτῆς ἡ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν.
units.tr: Finally this too is asked: Why have pleasures been given to men by God? Answer: three causes can be given for this: (1) Because life is led more agreeably through them, and we more willingly undertake the works of life necessary for our preservation, and more promptly heal our daily defects. (2) Because young people are invited by honest and moderate pleasures to honourable duties and excellent actions, and are turned away from vices and crimes by pains. (3) Augustine adds that these lowest pleasures are, as it were, certain traces of God and a faint shadow of the highest good, by which we may be stirred to desire that vehement good. So pleasures serve to awaken us, so that we do not cling to vices, but rise up to something great and excellent. Yet we must not rest in these pleasures, but always strive upwards to better things; and so that we may not remain in them, God in his goodness has mingled bitter things with these sweet allurements of pleasures. Peter Martyr, on Nicomachean Ethics 1, chapter 8. But here an end is made, and with it what Diogenes once said, when, having read the books of Plato on the immortality of the soul, he found that Plato had written in various ways and for various reasons that the future life is better than this one, since there men enjoy God himself as the supreme good and supreme pleasure: "So be it," he said, "God to me the supreme good and supreme pleasure." And since that is the ultimate end for which man was created, all Christians ought likewise to have this in their prayers, which is stated in Apocalypse 22, verse 20: [Ναί, ἔρχου κύριε Ἰησοῦ] "Yes, come, Lord Jesus."

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END.
